# [The Complete Works of Hugh of Saint-Victor]

## Preliminary Matter

[Col. IX]

# Essay on the Foundation of the School of Saint-Victor in Paris

By Abbé Hugonin, Licentiate in Letters of the Faculty of Paris, former pupil of the Carmelite ecclesiastical school.

To His Grace M. D. A. Sibour, Archbishop of Paris: the homage of profound veneration.

Flavien Hugonin.

## Introduction

[Col. XIII]

The sciences, letters, and arts seem to be reborn in the twelfth century. Monasteries multiply; rival schools arise on every side; illustrious professors appear and gather numerous disciples around themselves. Men do not fear to leave their native land, nor do they dread privations, provided that at this price they may hear the lectures of a skilled master. Supreme pontiffs and princes foster and sustain this movement by their privileges and their examples. While troubadours and trouvères, in poetry too often licentious, cultivate the vernacular language, the scholastics cultivate thought and labor to organize knowledge.

Among the celebrated schools of this period, that of Paris holds first place. None gave more comprehensive instruction; none counted so many students and more distinguished masters; none enjoyed greater privileges. The Trivium and Quadrivium were taught there in their full extent; medicine had its doctors there; canon law and theology their public chairs. Its reputation was so great that people flocked thither from every quarter to receive its learned instruction. At that period we find there Italians, Germans, Englishmen, Swedes, and Danes; even Slavs were not unknown there.

Accordingly, nothing equals the splendid titles given to it by contemporary authors. Paris is the tree of life planted in the earthly paradise, the source of all wisdom, the lamp of the house of the Lord, the ark of the covenant, the queen of nations, the treasure of princes. Before it Athens and Alexandria grow pale. There, it was said, harvests and rich vintages grow; there David strikes the ten-stringed instrument and sings his hymns to a mystical melody; there Isaiah is commented upon and his prophecies interpreted; there all the prophets unite their harmonies in a harmonious concert; there a word ever wise awaits strangers in order to instruct them; there is a carnation ever ready to open.

It was not solely the masters’ reputation that drew this crowd of foreigners to Paris. It was also the beauty of its situation, the honors rendered to the clergy, conveniences of every kind, and abundance of every good. The episcopal school was no longer the only one enjoying renown; others arose beside it and shared its glory. Together, during the course of this century, they formed the most brilliant academy, which later gave birth to the University. Our purpose is not to embrace them all in a single picture. We have chosen one alone: the school of Saint-Victor. The reputation it enjoyed in that age, the influence it exercised upon later centuries, the originality of its Platonic doctrines, and the illustrious men it produced seemed to us to merit special attention. We shall confine ourselves to studying its foundation. Three men seem to us to have contributed particularly to it: William of Champeaux, who gathered its first elements; Gilduin, who was its legislator; and Hugh, the first doctor whose doctrine and method we positively know.

Here are the principal manuscripts which we consulted for the history of this abbey; they are located in the Imperial Library:

1. *Liber ordinis*, Library of Saint-Victor, no. 987.  
2. *Antiquitates ejusdem abbatiae* [Antiquities of the same abbey], by J. Thoulouse, no. 1038.  
3. *Annales Ecclesiae S. Vict. Par.* [Annals of the Church of Saint-Victor in Paris], J. Thoulouse, no. 432.  
4. *The Lives and Holy Maxims of the Illustrious Men Who Flourished in the Abbey of Saint-Victor*, by Simon Gourdan, no. 1040.  
5. *Epitoma in philosophiam de Grammatica* [An Epitome of Philosophy concerning Grammar], by Hugh, no. 1058.

We examined several others, which for the most part are only partial reproductions of the preceding ones. See nos. 664, 670, and 15 of the Saint-Victor collection in the Imperial Library.

# Essay on the Foundation of the School of Saint-Victor in Paris

[Col. XIII]

## Chapter One. Foundation under William and Gilduin

[Col. XIIIA]

The origins of Saint-Victor in Paris have greatly exercised the sagacity of critics. The manuscript annals of this abbey mention a chapel preceding the twelfth century. Lobineau, in his *History of the City of Paris*, Hélyot, Sauval, and Duboulay, on the authority of Alberic’s *Chronicle*, suppose the existence of a priory of black monks, or Benedictines, from Marseilles. They cite the *Chronicle of Jumièges* [Note: [Col. XVD] *History of Paris*, vol. I, p. 145.—*Universal History of Paris*, vol. II, pp. 24 and 39.] in which regular canons are mentioned as established outside Paris, near a chapel dedicated to Saint Victor. Finally, in a charter of Philip I, dated 1085, Anselm, abbot of Saint-Victor, appears among the signatories.

These testimonies did not appear decisive either to Leboeuf [Note: [Col. XVD] He even denies the existence of the charter, vol. II, p. 542.], Jaillot [Note: [Col. XVD] *Critical, Historical, and Topographical Researches on the City of Paris*, district of Place Maubert, p. 151.], or Saint-Victor. Indeed, if one examines them carefully, they offer more than one ground for suspecting their accuracy.

In the same passage in which it speaks of the black monks of Marseilles, Alberic’s *Chronicle* attributes to Hugh the establishment at Saint-Victor of the regular canons of Saint-Ruf from the city of Valence. This is an evident error. In the charter of Louis VI, which we possess in its entirety, [Col. XVB] there is no mention of monks, but of canons; and we know, from unimpeachable witnesses, that Hugh was received at Saint-Victor by Abbot Gilduin, a canon of Saint Augustine. It is true that Duboulay, to resolve this difficulty, distinguishes two Victorines bearing the name Hugh: one a prior, and the other the man who later became celebrated for his learning and piety [Note: [Col. XVID] *Universal History of Paris*, vol. II, p. 24.]. But this distinction is wholly gratuitous. For why is no mention made anywhere of Prior Hugh, and why is Duboulay the first to note his existence? How did the canons of Saint-Victor, who so religiously preserved the names of all their priors, forget that of their founder? How can one explain the fact that the author of the *History of the Illustrious Men* [Col. XVC] of this abbey, who so carefully gathers ancient traditions, preserves an absolute silence on this matter?

The name of Abbot Anselm, recorded in the charter of Philip I dated 1085, has given rise to another mistake: a simple copy has been confused with the original document. The words concluding it leave no doubt as to the value of the signatures: “I, Brother Andrew, humble abbot of Saint-Magloire in Paris, attest that I have seen the privilege of the most illustrious King Philip and have read it word for word, as it is contained in the present writing.” There follow, in the same formula, the signatures of Brother Anselm, humble abbot of Saint-Victor [Col. XVD] in Paris, and Brother Theobald, humble abbot of Sainte-Geneviève. Now in 1085 the abbot of Saint-Magloire was Haimon, and the abbot of Sainte-Geneviève was Higolte. Andrew was abbot of Saint-Magloire in 1248, and Thibaud or Theobald was abbot of Sainte-Geneviève at the same period. The abbot of Saint-Victor, their contemporary, was Ascelin, whom the copyist made into Anselm.

Finally, if the regular canons of Saint Augustine [Col. XVIA] had succeeded the Benedictines of Saint-Victor of Marseilles, why do the foundation deed, the charter of Louis VI, Simon Gourdan, the annalists of Saint-Victor, Abelard, Hildebert of Le Mans, and all the biographers of William of Champeaux make no mention of it? Thus the opinion of Lobineau and Duboulay rests only upon simple conjectures, which perhaps have no other origin than a similarity of name.

Nevertheless, the existence of a small chapel prior to William of Champeaux is incontestable. If Simon Gourdan is to be believed [Note: [Col. XVID] *History of the Illustrious Men of Saint-Victor*, by Simon Gourdan, manuscript, vol. I, p. 126.], it served some devout solitaries who came, far from the tumult of the city, to devote themselves to prayer and meditation on Christian truths. This practice [Col. XVIB] was not new. In the first centuries of the Church, and before the foundation of monasteries, great cities had their hermitages. Antioch in the East, Rome and Milan in the West, furnish more than one example. These hermits were not subject to a common rule. Their lives were divided among prayer, meditation, and manual labor. It is not implausible that Paris produced similar solitaries in the twelfth century. The place where the abbey of Saint-Victor later arose was suited to this kind of life. It was wild, distant from the city, and surrounded by woods; it formed a kind of new Thebaid, in which imitators of Antony and Pachomius could peacefully devote themselves [Col. XVIC] to religious exercises [Note: [Col. XVID] *History of the Illustrious Men of Saint-Victor*, manuscript, vol. I, p. 127.]. Besides, whatever opinion one adopts, it is certain that the school of Saint-Victor which we propose to make known goes back only to William of Champeaux.

William of Champeaux, so called from his birthplace, was archdeacon and scholasticus of the church of Notre-Dame in Paris. He had studied theology under Anselm of Laon. The lessons of so good a master were like a fruitful seed deposited in fertile ground. Anselm’s disciple was one of the learned professors who brought distinction to the school of Paris. He gave it, over its rivals, a superiority which it had not possessed before him and which it always knew how to preserve.

[Col. XVID] Young men from the most distant provinces, and even from foreign countries, flocked there, eager to hear the celebrated professor whose name everywhere inspired respect and admiration. After visiting the most renowned schools, Abelard settled in Paris because nowhere had he encountered a master more learned and more capable. Beneath the cloisters of Notre-Dame, William taught rhetoric, dialectic, and theology simultaneously, surrounded [Col. XVIIA] by the esteem of Galon, his bishop, the love and respect of his disciples, and the regard of the clergy. He received an honorable testimony of this in 1107, when he was summoned to the numerous Council of Troyes, convened and presided over by Pope Paschal II.

If he allowed himself to be seduced by the splendor of so much glory, as the letter of Hildebert of Le Mans seems to imply, the seduction was not long-lasting. In 1108 he abandoned his chair and his archdeaconry to withdraw to Saint-Victor, where he took the habit of a regular canon of Saint Augustine. Gilduin, Godfrey, Robert, Gontier, Thomas, and several other disciples followed him into retirement [Note: [Col. XVIID] *History of Illustrious Men*, Introduction.]. If Abelard is to be believed, ambition [Col. XVIIB] led William to Saint-Victor. By this hypocritical step he sought to rise more securely to the episcopate [Note: [Col. XVIID] *History of Calamities*, p. 5.]. But William’s illustrious rival yields too readily to the promptings of self-love and jealousy; the suspicions he maliciously seeks to insinuate have no plausibility and are even contrary to contemporary testimony. In the twelfth century especially, William needed only to continue in the career he had embraced and retain the offices with which he was invested in order to attain the episcopate: he was archdeacon and scholasticus of one of the foremost churches of the kingdom. Each of these functions, taken separately, naturally led him to the highest dignities of the Church, particularly considering the reputation [Col. XVIIC] he had acquired in them. Pontiffs were then more rarely chosen from among religious than from among distinguished professors. Most of the great bishops of that period owed their elevation to the brilliance of their teaching. Ivo, bishop of Chartres; Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans and later archbishop of Tours; Baudry, bishop of Rennes; Alberic, archbishop of Bourges; Goscelin or Joscelin, bishop of Chartres; Gilbert de la Porée, bishop of Poitiers; Ulger, bishop of Angers; and Gautier of Mortagne, bishop of Laon, had been scholastici of some cathedral. We also know how much influence the archdeacon had in the nomination of a bishop, when every church had the right to present its candidate for the king’s approval. Besides, we find this malicious insinuation against William only in Abelard. The *Chronicle of Morigny* represents him not only as very learned in the Holy Scriptures, but as full of zeal, piety, and religion [Note: [Col. XVIID] Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. V, p. 879.]. It is indeed difficult to believe that the intimate friend of Saint Bernard, Hildebert of Le Mans, Anselm of Laon, Galon of Paris, and of all whom the twelfth century had most distinguished for learning and virtue was at heart merely a hypocrite and an intriguer, veiling beneath [Col. XVIIIA] the appearance of affected piety a miserable ambition.

In withdrawing to Saint-Victor, William had renounced teaching and the applause of the school: he wished to live alone with God in meditation upon eternal truths. But his former pupils could not consent to his silence. They urged him to continue his lessons in the retreat he had chosen, and the bishop of Le Mans thought he ought to add his entreaties to those of so many friends; he wrote the new solitary a letter which we possess entire. “Your manner of life and your conversion,” he told him, “have filled my soul with joy and made it leap for gladness.” He then congratulates him for having embraced true philosophy; [Col. XVIIIB] he recalls with praise the example of Diogenes; he exhorts him to devote himself wholly to God and to withhold nothing from his holocaust. Then he adds: “But what use is wisdom kept hidden and treasure buried? Gold shines more brightly in open daylight than when shut up in darkness; pearls differ in no way from worthless tufa if they are not displayed to view. Thus knowledge that is communicated increases; it despises a miserly possessor, and, if not revealed, slips away. Therefore do not close the streams of your teaching; rather, according to Solomon’s counsel, let your fountains flow abroad and let your waters be divided in the public squares” [Note: [Col. XVIID] *Universal History of Paris*, vol. II, p. 25.].

[Col. XVIIIC] William could not resist requests so gracious and pressing: he resumed his lessons, and this was the origin of the celebrated school of Saint-Victor in Paris. His disputes with Abelard are well known, as is the affected moderation with which the latter recounts his victories. Yet they were not as disastrous for William as Abelard seems to suggest. We do not see that the influence and reputation of the learned professor suffered greatly from them. It was even at this time, when his rival portrays him as humiliated and abandoned by all [Note: [Col. XVIIID] *History of Calamities*, p. 6.], that he was raised to the episcopal see of Châlons. From that point his life became highly active. He showed himself great in the episcopate, as he had shown himself learned and capable in public teaching. He was the animating spirit of all [Col. XVIIID] the councils, so numerous at that time in Gaul. In 1114, two years after his elevation, he attended the Council of Beauvais, where he was the firmest support of Conon, legate of the Holy See, who worked with such zeal and firmness for reform of morals and restoration of discipline. In 1115 [Note: [Col. XVIIID] *Universal History of Paris*, vol. II, p. 44.], he took part in that of Reims, where, according to a contemporary author, he appeared as the pillar of the doctors [Note: [Col. XVIIID] Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, vol. XIV, p. 285.]. The same year, in the octave of the feast of the Apostles, he sat at that of Châlons, and in 1120 at that of Beauvais, from which there remains to us only the canonization of Saint Arnould. In 1119 he had been sent by Calixtus II, together with Pons, abbot of Cluny, to Emperor Henry to prepare the peace that was to be negotiated at the Council of Reims between Church and Empire [Note: [Col. XIXD] Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, book XIV, pp. 252, 263.]. It was he who spoke and persuaded the emperor to renounce investitures; it was he who translated into French, at the council, the address of the bishop of Ostia; it was he who, sent again to the German prince, did not fear vigorously to remind him of the promises he refused to fulfill. Saint Bernard chose him to receive the abbatial blessing from his hands. His episcopate was too brief for the good and glory of the Church. He died on 18 January 1121, after governing the diocese of Châlons for seven years and six [Col. XIXB] months. There survive from him a small treatise on the soul, a work on the Eucharist published by Mabillon, and a collection of sentences contained in an unpublished manuscript located in the Imperial Library, under no. 220 of the Notre-Dame collection. These writings are insufficient to make William’s doctrine known to us. After reading them, one is still obliged to rely upon Abelard’s incomplete and obscure testimony.

Before leaving his retreat, he had entrusted the community of Saint-Victor to Gilduin, the dearest of his disciples. Gilduin was a native of Paris; he enjoyed a well-founded esteem, acquired more by his wisdom and virtue than by his learning. Louis VI chose him as his confessor [Col. XIXC] and always treated him with filial respect. Under his administration, the community of Saint-Victor became a rich and powerful abbey. Louis VI endowed it with truly royal munificence. He granted it letters which are, as it were, its charter of foundation.

In them he declares that, after consulting the bishops and lords of his court, he established in the church of Saint-Victor regular canons occupied in praying to God for him and for his kingdom; that he endowed and enriched them through his generosity so that they might not be diverted from this holy exercise by the concern of providing for the necessities of life. There follows an enumeration of the estates of which he [Col. XIXD] puts them in possession. They were a farm at Puteaux with all its rights; Orgenois in the territory of Melun; twenty arpents of meadow near Corbeil; a farm in the territory of Buci; a property at Fontenay near Paris; and several others mentioned in the same letter. He leaves the canons complete freedom in choosing their abbot. They are not obliged to wait for the consent of the king or of any other persons; but, after electing him themselves from the members of their community or another house of their order, they are to present him to the bishop of Paris to receive the abbatial blessing [Col. XXA]. He did not wish to withdraw them from the jurisdiction of the archbishop of Sens and the bishop of Paris, as his predecessors had done with respect to several religious houses; but he granted them the privilege of freeing the male and female serfs of their church without any further permission from himself or his successors. No mention is made in this charter of the Rule of Saint Augustine [Note: [Col. XIXD] *Antiquities of the Royal Abbey of Saint-Victor*, Paris, shelf 2a.].

The signatories are Daimbert, archbishop of Sens; Radulf, archbishop of Reims; Louis, king; Lisiard, bishop of Soissons; Ivo of Chartres; Manasses of Meaux; Hubert of Senlis; Galon of Paris; John of Orléans; Geoffrey of Amiens; Humbald of Auxerre; Philip of Troyes; and the great officers of [Col. XXB] the crown. William of Champeaux, who obtained these letters, did not subscribe them: he had probably not yet received episcopal consecration. The date of this important document is the fifth year of Louis’s reign and the 1113th year of Jesus Christ; it agrees with that which was read at Saint-Victor upon the tomb of the same king. Pope Paschal II confirmed the new foundation in the following year.

Louis VI soon added other gifts to these first acts of generosity: with the consent [Col. XXC] of the abbots and canons of all these churches, and with permission from the archbishop of Sens and the other diocesan bishops, he granted the canons of Saint-Victor the royal right of presentation in several churches in the collegiate churches of Château-Landon, Melun, Étampes, Dreux, Mantes, Poissy, Pontoise, Montlhéry, and Corbeil [Note: [Col. XXD] *Antiquities of the Royal Abbey of Saint-Victor*, shelf 2a.].

Later, in 1146, Henry, his son, a canon of the Church of Paris, gave them a prebend in the church of the Holy Spirit—Saint-Spire of Corbeil—of which he was abbot [Note: [Col. XXD] *Universal History of Paris*, vol. II, p. 228.].

The canons of Saint-Victor wished to preserve in their annals the memory of these benefits and to transmit to their successors a testimony of their gratitude. One reads in their necrology: “On the calends of the month of August, the anniversary of Louis, king of France, who, bearing a singular affection for our church, endowed and enriched it by [Col. XXD] his benefactions, as is contained in our privileges” [Note: [Col. XXD] *Annals of Saint-Victor*, fol. 12.]. The enumeration of the donations follows. Then they add: “We moreover hold ourselves obliged to declare to later ages that, for the glory and adornment of our church, he made it a gift of his chapel, containing many holy and most precious relics. Therefore we hold ourselves deeply indebted to so great and illustrious a benefactor.”

Every day a Mass was said for the repose of his soul, and a poor person was fed in his name. Each year the anniversary of his death was celebrated. [Col. XXIA] On the day of this anniversary a poor person was completely clothed, and one hundred others were fed with bread, wine, and meat [Note: [Col. XXID] *Annals of Saint-Victor*, fol. 12.].

The bishops of Paris imitated Louis VI’s generosity toward the canons of Saint-Victor. Galon and Gilbert ceded to them part of their rights over the waters of the Seine, both with regard to mills and fishing, as is stated in Gilbert’s letters dated 1122 [Note: [Col. XXID] *Antiquities of the Royal Abbey of Saint-Victor*, shelf 2a, fol. 10.]. In 1124 or 1125, Stephen gave them the vacant prebends of his cathedral, of Saint-Marcel, Saint-Germain-l’Auxerrois, Saint-Cloud, and Saint-Martin of Champeaux in Brie. The king permitted them to enjoy these during the first year of their vacancy, as is shown by Bishop Stephen’s letters and by the [Col. XXIB] charter of Louis VI, subscribed by him, Queen Adelaide, their son Philip, the bishops and abbots concerned, and the five great officers of the crown.

Later, at the request of Pope Innocent II and with the consent of the dean and chapter, Stephen granted them a full prebend in his cathedral, and likewise in the other collegiate churches of Saint-Marcel, Saint-Germain-l’Auxerrois, Saint-Cloud, and Saint-Martin of Champeaux. This donation was confirmed in the year 1135 by the king, who added to these prebends another in the church of Sainte-Geneviève, with the consent of the dean and chapter [Note: [Col. XXID] *Ibid.*, shelf 4a.]. Finally, Stephen bequeathed them at his death his library, which contained precious works. [Col. XXIC] The dean and canons of the cathedral of Paris also wished to contribute to the establishment of Saint-Victor; they gave the canons a farm with 120 arpents of land in the vicinity of Chevilly and Orly, together with tithes, *champarts*—customary shares of agricultural produce—and all other appurtenances [Note: [Col. XXID] *Ibid.*, shelf 3a.].

Most of these donations are recorded in their necrology. Each year they celebrated the anniversary of their benefactors with numerous alms.

The growth of their revenues enabled them to multiply. At his death Louis VI bequeathed 2,000 livres to twenty abbeys of their order [Note: [Col. XXIID] *Liber ordinis* [Book of the Order], fol. 1.]. By 1138 they already formed a considerable congregation. In that year the regular canons of Saint-Vincent of Senlis undertook to attend the general chapter of the order. At the death of Gilduin, first abbot of Saint-Victor, it contained forty-four houses [Note: [Col. XXIID] *Ibid.*].

Moreover, the canons made good use of their wealth: they devoted it to the relief of the poor, and especially of young students whom love of learning drew to Paris. We have proofs of this in several documents of the period. Guérin, prior of Saint Alban’s in England, [Col. XXIIA] writes to Richard, prior of Saint-Victor, to thank him for the assistance he had supplied to his brother Matthew. “To his venerable and justly honoured friend Richard, prior of Saint-Victor: greeting and the sentiments of a rightful friendship from Guérin, prior of the church of Saint Alban. I give thanks to your charity for the singular favour and special generosity with which you have honoured my brother Matthew, who has gone into exile among you for love of learning. Nothing could express the charity and devotion which your kindnesses inspire in me. Would that I could give you, by my actions as well as my words, proofs of the affection I bear you! How could I have expected the goodwill which you have shown [Col. XXIIB] towards my brother Matthew, since I had by no means deserved it? I now see how deeply your prudence has engraved in his memory this saying of Cato: ‘If you wish to be loved, love.’ It remains, therefore, for you to continue what you have so generously begun and to provide him with a cassock. As for me, though unable to repay your kindnesses, I shall not be unable to love you [Note: [Col. XXIID] *Hist. Univers. Paris*, vol. II, p. 304.].”

This letter, written in a somewhat affected style but full of the tenderest and most delicate sentiments, shows us that at this period a literary intercourse had been established between the abbey of Saint-Victor and that of Saint Alban. After commending his brother to Prior Richard, Guérin [Col. XXIIC] mentions a small gift which he is sending him—not, he says, as the price of benefits received, but as a token of friendship. In return, he asks for the names of the writers of Saint-Victor, so that, if he does not possess their works, he may procure them and enrich England with the treasure of learning. Nothing, moreover, was more natural than these friendly relations. At Saint-Victor we find canons, priors, and even an abbot who were English by birth.

But it was not only toward Englishmen that they exercised this generous hospitality. Gratian of Pierre de Léon, consul of the Romans, thanks them in a letter for the hospitality they had granted [Col. XXIID] to his brother Hugh. They treated several other French or foreign students with the same kindness, including Peter Lombard, at the request of Saint Bernard, the most devoted friend of the canons of Saint-Victor.

Charitable and beneficent toward those who sought their aid, the canons of Saint-Victor also showed themselves respectful and devoted toward the bishops of Paris. They were their wisest counsellors, the firmest supports of an authority which they often shared, and the most zealous [Col. XXIIIA] defenders of their rights. Thomas, prior of Saint-Victor and Hugh’s master, died a victim of this devotion: he was murdered by the nephew of the archdeacon whose claims concerning episcopal jurisdiction he opposed.

By such conduct they gained the esteem and confidence of all. Contemporary authors accordingly vie in celebrating their piety and learning. Innocent II, in a letter addressed to Stephen, bishop of Paris, praises their religious spirit, their regular observance, and their faithful keeping of the canonical rules and the discipline of the Church. He says that their conduct brings glory to God and that their example edifies the people.

James of Vitry, in his *Western History*, extols their humility, holiness, and learning. [Col. XXIIIB] “This congregation,” he says, “is like the lamp of the Lord set upon the lampstand. It enlightens not only the city but distant regions; it teaches peoples to know God and moves them to love Him.” He also compares it to the Pool of Bethesda and to the bronze vessel placed in the Temple of God. “It supplies the students of Paris, and the multitude who flock there from every quarter, with the waters of purification. This holy and venerable congregation, in the camp of the soldiers of the Lord, is the refuge of the poor, the consolation of those who weep, the support of the weak; it restores the strength of the weary, raises those who fall, offers all students a secure harbour, and opens a merciful bosom to those who wish [Col. XXIIIC] to escape the shipwreck of this world. It receives them kindly, maintains them, and feeds them. From its origin it has been adorned and embellished by Parisian doctors, learned and upright men, who shone in its midst like glittering stars or precious stones [Note: [Col. XXIIID] *Hist. occid.*, p. 28.].”

In this passage the cardinal alludes to one of the offices exercised by the canons of Saint-Victor. It was from among them that the bishop chose a grand penitentiary, who was principally to exercise his ministry toward the students. He had authority to absolve reserved cases and even, in the bishop’s absence, to reconcile the excommunicated [Note: [Col. XXIIID] Among the unpublished manuscripts of Saint-Victor there are two collections of cases of conscience.].

[Col. XXIIID] Several dioceses wished to obtain religious whose reputation was so great and whose lives were so exemplary. Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, asks Stephen, bishop of Paris, to send him a canon of Saint-Victor to govern the abbey of Les Vertus. “The brethren of that community,” he says, “have unanimously requested a Victorine as pastor, and the abbot has laid down his authority into my hands in order to place himself under his guidance [Note: [Col. XXIIID] *Hist. Univers. Paris*, vol. II, p. 121.].” John of Naples requested the same favour; the bishop of Halberstadt established them in his diocese; and when [Col. XXIVA] the king of France and Pope Eugenius wished to reform Sainte-Geneviève, they introduced canons of Saint-Victor there [Note: [Col. XXIVD] *Ibid.*, p. 217.].

The great men formed in their midst justified this reputation. The abbey of Saint-Victor gave the Church seven cardinals, two archbishops, six bishops, fifty-four abbots established in various places, and men who acquired a well-deserved reputation in every branch of learning cultivated at that period [Note: [Col. XXIVD] *Maxims and Illustrious Men of Saint-Victor*, vol. I, introduction.].

## CHAPTER II. RULE OF THE CANONS OF SAINT-VICTOR

The designs of Louis VI had been fulfilled. Enriched by the liberality of their powerful and generous protectors, the canons of Saint-Victor [Col. XXIVB] could peacefully devote themselves to study and to the exercises of religious life. Yet these very riches would soon have produced dissipation and disorder among them, had they not been subject to a wise discipline and had a strong constitution not maintained perfect regularity in the monastery. This was Gilduin’s work. This constitution and these rules have been carefully preserved for us; through them we may enter the cloisters of Saint-Victor and, as it were, attend the canons’ daily occupations, labours, and every exercise.

This study has seemed to us both interesting and useful, whether from the historical or the [Col. XXIVC] philosophical point of view. For there is a necessary connection between a person’s thoughts, character, genius, and habits. Knowledge of one’s inner life facilitates knowledge of one’s doctrines. A friend understands a friend at half a word, and people who associate closely can read one another; they judge and assess each other’s opinions and conduct with greater certainty.

The abbot was the superior of the canons and was to stand to them in a father’s place. His election took place with great solemnity. At his death, the brethren fasted and kept silence until his funeral.

After the funeral ceremony, the prior rang the bell and all went to chapter. Prostrate upon their stalls, they prayed and sang [Col. XXIVD] psalms, after which each took his seat. The prior then spoke to the brethren concerning the election. Seven of the most distinguished were chosen to form a council. They were to deliberate among themselves and elect the religious whom they judged best able to govern the community; the others prayed in silence. The canons were forbidden to meet or discuss the forthcoming election among themselves. If the electors could not agree, their number was increased. If the prior was absent but still within the province and could return within three days, they waited for him; otherwise they proceeded. No one had a deliberative vote, much less could anyone be elected, unless he was at least a subdeacon and was neither excommunicated nor under interdict. Nor could anyone be elected before the age of twenty-five or unless he had spent three or four years in the abbey.

When the council’s choice had settled upon one of the canons, the chapter was assembled, and the senior member announced the election in these words: “I elect such-and-such a one prelate of this house.” The elect was immediately led to the abbot’s seat, where he received the homage of all the brethren. The ceremony ended with the singing of psalms suited to the occasion.

On the following day, all who belonged to [Col. XXVB] his obedience came to chapter and, prostrate before the new abbot, laid their keys at his feet. He ordered them to rise and take them back. The abbot addressed this question to them: “Do you promise me the obedience which you owe me, according to the rules of Saint Augustine and according to the promises you made on the day of your profession?” They answered: “I promise it.”

At the general chapter immediately following the election, the abbot himself made this promise: “I, N., humble abbot of N., saving the liberty, privileges, and other rights of our church, promise obedience to the general chapter and fidelity on behalf of myself and our house.” When a reasonable cause prevented him from attending the chapter, [Col. XXVC] he sent his signed profession, which did not excuse him from making it orally at the next meeting.

Once the election was completed, the prior and subprior, accompanied by some of the senior brethren, went to the bishop. They made known to him the abbot whom they had elected and arranged with him the day on which he should come to receive the abbatial blessing from his hands.

On the appointed day, all the religious went to the choir and waited in silence for the abbot’s return. He entered through the door of the great church, passed through the middle of the choir, and all bowed as he passed. Those accompanying him went at once [Col. XXVD] to their stalls, except the prior and subprior, who alone conducted him from the entrance of the choir to the steps of the sanctuary. The abbot prostrated himself upon a carpet, and the canons sang psalms, gradual chants, and prayers [Note: [Col. XXVD] *Liber ordinis*, fol. 1 and following.].

These impressive ceremonies were naturally suited to impress the imagination and awaken the faith of these simple men. In the person of the abbot they saw God’s representative. The respect with which they surrounded him made obedience more certain and easier.

This respect was to be shown outwardly. No one [Col. XXVIA] passed before the abbot without saluting him. Everywhere except in the cloister, people rose when he entered and did not sit until he himself sat down or commanded them to do so. In the cloister and choir, they merely bowed as he passed, unless he introduced a stranger; then all rose out of respect for the guest who honoured them by his presence.

One is struck by the courtesy which thoughts of faith inspired in these good religious, who lived amid a society scarcely emerged from barbarism and not yet stripped of the violence of its character and the coarseness of its manners. Such examples were not without value even for the progress of civilization.

[Col. XXVIB] The abbot’s authority was gentle and sovereign, but neither arbitrary nor uncontrolled. It was to be exercised according to the laws of the order and under the supervision of the general chapter and the bishop. Although his office was for life, he could be deprived of it and even expelled from the community if he abused his power. The history of Saint-Victor offers an example as early as the eleventh century. Ervise, a worldly and dissipated abbot, was compelled, despite his intrigues and the moderation of Richard, his prior, to resign his dignity and leave his abbey.

The abbot was assisted in the general government of the community by officers all of whom [Col. XXVIC] were subordinate to him.

The prior replaced or assisted him in exercising his office. He was chosen by the abbot, who in this circumstance was to take the counsel of the elders. After the election, the abbot presented him to the chapter, and the elect went to kneel at his feet. The abbot then addressed to him these words of the Psalmist: “May the Lord preserve your going in”; the brethren answered: “And your coming out.” His place was on the left, opposite the abbot. He gave the signal for the exercises by ringing the bell, corrected the reader in choir and chapter, and had special charge of discipline. He also supervised all subordinate employees, but had authority neither to dismiss nor appoint them. In his absence, [Col. XXVID] his functions were fulfilled by the subprior.

The chamberlain was the monastery’s steward. He took care of all its property; but he was only an administrator and could alienate nothing. Every week he was required to render the abbot an account of his administration.

The cellarer was responsible for preparing and distributing food. There was to be only one kitchen and one cellarer. He could, however, light several fires and take assistants from among the lay brethren. He was especially charged [Col. XXVIIA] with care of the sick and of the strangers to whom hospitality was given.

The refectorian was responsible for the refectory. He prepared everything necessary for the meal: bread, wine, water, and linen. He changed the tablecloths every eight days and the napkins every three days, keeping everything very clean.

The sick were entrusted to an infirmarian and the poor to an almoner. The almoner did not merely supply their needs during life: after their death, he procured suitable burial for them and had prayers offered for the repose of their souls. Such touching and delicate solicitude was inspired by genuine charity.

[Col. XXVIIB] This virtue was likewise to belong to the porter. He was instructed to be courteous and full of kindness toward everyone. When a religious appeared at the gate, he greeted him with a bow. If it was a layperson, he first admitted him, then gently and humbly asked what he desired. If the stranger requested hospitality, he asked him to wait until he had notified the abbot and the guest-master [Note: [Col. XXVIID] *Liber ordinis*, fols. 8, 9 [lacuna].].

The guest-master received strangers and discharged toward them every duty of the most affectionate hospitality. When the porter had notified him, he went without delay to his guest, even during the chanting of the office. He came to greet [Col. XXVIIC] him and led him in silence, unless questioned. When he had brought him into the oratory, he presented holy water to the abbot, who sprinkled him; in the abbot’s absence, he did so himself. He led strangers to choir and refectory at the appointed hours, but never to chapter. Finally, he supplied them with all things they needed.

All the monastery’s books were entrusted to the cantor’s custody, and he at the same time fulfilled the office of librarian. He possessed their catalogue and made an inventory of them two or three times a year, carefully examining whether they had suffered any damage in order to repair it. He [Col. XXVIID] lent a book only against an equivalent pledge. In a register he entered the book’s title, the name of the person to whom he handed it over, and the pledge received for it. Valuable books could not be lent without the abbot’s permission. He also cared for all charters and other writings concerning the monastery. He supplied copyists with what they needed. He saw that they lacked nothing and copied only works assigned them by the abbot. All who knew how to write were required to place themselves at his disposal when he demanded it. He was responsible for correcting manuscripts. All [Col. XXVIIIA] books used in the office were to be properly punctuated, so that the brethren would not be perplexed and their chant might be perfectly regular [Note: [Col. XXVIID] *Liber ordinis*, fols. 11, 12.].

Thus every officer had his determined function, and all their labours combined to establish perfect order in the monastery. When respected, this order was the principle and guardian of peace and tranquillity of soul, as necessary for the speculations of learning as for progress in Christian piety. Was not the life of these men—so orderly and calm amid the violent manners of that age, inspired by religion with benevolence toward all and especially with that respect which distinguishes civilized from barbarous peoples even more than politeness and elegance of manner—a fine spectacle? The barbarian fears, admires, and loves; only the civilized person respects. Yet respect is at once the manifestation and the safeguard of human dignity. Thus monastic rules, which so deeply impressed this respect upon souls, had a greater part in the civilization of the world than is ordinarily attributed to them.

This regularity would have been neither lasting nor useful had the canons given themselves over to idleness. Every hour of their day was regulated, and none was not devoted to a specified occupation. They rose in the middle of the night to offer God a sacrifice of praise; and during [Col. XXVIIIC] nature’s repose their voices and hearts rose to celebrate His greatness and implore His goodness. They left the dormitory all together, preceded by a torch, and went to choir to sing the major office.

Simon Gourdan reports a singular custom observed at Saint-Victor. To stimulate piety further and prevent drowsiness during the long night watches, a religious carrying a book walked on each side of the choir. The others were to salute him as he passed. If he noticed that one of them was not singing, he placed the book before him and, after making a prostration or a profound bow before the sanctuary [Col. XXVIIID] and in the choir, returned to his place. The canon who had received the book kissed the ground and in turn walked about. The abbot and the infirmarian alone were excused from this ceremony [Note: [Col. XXVIIID] *History of Illustrious Men*, vol. I, fol. 424.].

The major office was followed by that of the Blessed Virgin. The whole lasted about three hours. The canons then withdrew to the dormitory in order and silence.

After several hours’ rest, at the abbot’s signal they came to wash their hands in summer. From there they went to church, where they recited the *Pater*, the *Ave*, and the *Credo*, and afterwards to the cloister, after which they devoted themselves [Col. XXIXA] to prayer, holy reading, and study until the second signal for Prime. This was followed by a first high Mass and the Prime of the Blessed Virgin. In winter they came from the dormitory to the church to sing Prime, and from the church went to the washing-place.

When the office had ended, the community went to the cloister. Some prayed, others read and studied, others confessed or celebrated the holy sacrifice; others, prostrate at the foot of the altars, meditated upon the great truths of faith.

At the bell’s signal, all entered chapter. The martyrology was read; and after a prayer and a reading from the Gospel or from some chapter of the Rule of Saint Augustine or Saint [Col. XXIXB] Benedict, the anniversaries were announced. The abbot, or the person he had appointed, then spoke and delivered a kind of conference or lesson. Some subject of dogma or morals, some point of Christian piety, was treated, or passages of Holy Scripture were expounded. Several of Hugh’s works seem to be the results of these conferences. The cantor then announced the order of the office and designated those who were to perform some function in it.

Then took place the confession of faults (*coulpe*). Each humbly acknowledged his faults and received a salutary penance from the abbot. No one was exempt from this exercise, neither officers nor the infirm. The abbot gave such admonitions as he considered necessary and consulted the [Col. XXIXC] religious concerning the affairs of the monastery.

It was also there that kings, bishops, and abbots who requested it were associated with the prayers of the community, something very customary according to Simon Gourdan. They were brought into chapter and made to touch the book of the Rule while kneeling.

The gathering ended with the recitation of several psalms, and everyone withdrew to the cloister.

These exercises of piety and study were succeeded by manual labour. At the prior’s signal, the canons went in procession up to the dormitory, tucked up their robes and rochets, girded them, put on a tunic of coarse linen falling to mid-leg, and took a small hood or *camail*. They came down in order, preceded by the prior in the abbot’s absence and followed by the subprior, singing psalms. Thus they went to the garden, to the enclosure where the tools and the task each was to perform [Col. XXIXD] were distributed. They worked in strict silence. The infirm remained in the cloister, recited psalms, served, or celebrated the holy sacrifice of the Mass. In rainy weather and during the severity of winter, they undertook another kind of occupation. Whatever its nature [Col. XXXA] might be, no one could excuse himself from it. It was forbidden to rest or abandon it for any necessity whatever without express permission [Note: [Col. XXIXD] *History of the Illustrious Men of Saint-Victor*, vol. I, fols. 156, 157.].

Copyists alone were exempt from manual labour. Ordinarily, the clerics or best-educated monks were assigned to this noble task. “Let him,” says the Rule of Saint-Ferréol, “exercise his fingers upon vellum who does not furrow the earth with the plough.” No occupation was more honourable or more coveted. In the tenth century Cassiodorus gives the most splendid praise of scribes or copyists. God, it was said, blessed the work of their hands and taught them, as a special grace, the right discernment between sound readings and [Col. XXXB] erroneous readings. Among copyists were counted saints and illustrious doctors: Saint Fulgentius, Saint Dunstan, Saint Anselm, Alcuin, Lanfranc, and several others. Ancient hagiographers took care not to omit this circumstance in the lives of the most renowned persons: they say that such persons employed their leisure in copying books and collating texts. This was to say how distinguished they were by learning. A historian even thinks it necessary to relate, to Charlemagne’s glory, that he wrote with his own hand a copy of the Holy Gospel.

Love of letters was not always the source of such fine zeal. Literary feeling was very weak in that age; this should not [Col. XXXC] surprise us. The taste for, and the need which it creates to study, the masterpieces of art and genius belong only to the maturity of societies as of individuals. Happily Christian faith supplied what was lacking. In his Capitularies, Charlemagne exhorts the scholars of his age to correct manuscripts and reform language, giving as his reason that it is shameful for a person, in prayers, in the praises addressed to God, and in converse with Him, to violate grammatical rules and speak to Him in a barbarous tongue. Thoughts of faith and the desire to preserve intact and multiply copies of the holy books and works of the Fathers were the principal motive of the multitude of [Col. XXXD] copyists. Some exceptional men, such as Cassiodorus, Alcuin, and others—whether because they understood, more or less vaguely, that Christianity, being connected with the history of the whole human race, can regard no monument of past ages as indifferent, or because of a sincere love of learning and letters—extended their care to sacred and profane authors alike and imparted a beneficial impulse which was sometimes followed without being understood. It would be unjust to impute to Christianity what was lacking in men whose education it had scarcely begun, and to deny its salutary influence.

[Col. XXXIA] The canons of Saint-Victor did not neglect so useful a work. An unpublished customary of that abbey supplies us with curious information concerning the choice of the place assigned to copyists and the discipline to which they were subject.

This place was to be outside the conventual buildings, but within the cloister enclosure, “so that,” it is said, “they might in that place apply themselves more peacefully to their work, without disturbance or noise.” As soon as they were seated and at work, they were to maintain the strictest silence among themselves. No one was to waste time wandering here and there. No one was to enter this reserved place except the abbot, the prior, the subprior, and the librarian. If anyone wished to communicate privately with one of the copyists [Col. XXXIB] and could neither speak with him there nor postpone the matter until the hour for conversation, the librarian was permitted to lead him to the monastery’s parlour, ordering him to exchange a few words quickly and briefly. Such was the discipline of Saint-Victor.

Elsewhere the rule was even more severe. Thus, in the abbeys of Cîteaux, the copyists’ room, commonly called the *scriptorium*, was divided by partitions into a great number of cells, each person having his own. All conversation was impossible, and the most absolute recollection was not merely a duty but a necessity. Distraction would indeed have caused many inaccuracies which, multiplied, would have disfigured [Col. XXXIC] the most precious manuscripts. Accordingly, scrupulous vigilance was always recommended to copyists. We read in Alcuin’s verses on a scriptorium: “Come, come here and take your places, you whose office it is to transcribe the divine law and the sacred monuments of the wisdom of the Fathers. Take care not to mingle frivolous talk with these wise discourses. Watch that your heedless hand commits no error. Carefully seek out pure texts, so that your pen, in its rapid flight, may travel along the straight path. It is a great honour to copy holy books, and this labour finds its reward.”

In a great many monasteries, scribes [Col. XXXID] were divided into two sections: some copied; others, more learned, revised and corrected the copies. Traces of these corrections are found in many manuscripts.

The highly honourable office of copyist was not entrusted to chance. The customary of Saint-Victor tells us that the abbot himself designated those who were to fulfil it. Great familiarity with reading ancient texts and proven skill in the art of writing conferred the much-coveted right to occupy a seat in the scriptorium. Once one had obtained this office, one went to the librarian responsible for distributing the work among copyists. He supplied the new occupant of the scriptorium with [Col. XXXIIA] skins, pens, ink, a penknife, a scraper, and scissors. He further directed him to copy a particular chapter or book, to begin at a particular page and finish at another. By an express provision of the abbatial decree, he was forbidden to make any other transcription for his own use. If a religious who knew how to write was not a member of the college of copyists, he could make no copy without the abbot’s permission, who decided whether it was expedient to grant or refuse it.

To these rigorous ordinances, scrupulously observed, we owe the fine manuscripts of the Middle Ages. Thus were formed the rich libraries of Saint Gall, [Col. XXXIIB] Bec, York, Saint-Martin of Tournai, Fulda, and particularly that of Saint-Victor.

When the hours devoted to these various labours had passed, the community went back up to the dormitory to resume the regular habit. It then descended to the cloister.

Each sat there, neither back to back nor facing another, but in a straight line, always with a book before him. This was Holy Scripture, the works of the Fathers, the Acts of the Martyrs, the Lives of the Saints, or the Homilies of the holy doctors. Slightly apart, and in the cantor’s presence, they rehearsed what was to be read or sung in church. There also some studied chant; others learned the psalter and hymns by heart; others performed [Col. XXXIIC] what the abbot had prescribed for them. Great silence and singular modesty were observed. No one made the slightest sign, crossed his legs, stretched out his feet, leaned upon the desk, watched his neighbour, or gave himself to idleness.

At the abbot’s first signal, they recollected themselves; at the second, they entered the chapel to sing Terce, high Mass, and Sext.

The meal ordinarily followed the office, except on fast days. All the religious were required to attend; they first formed ranks in the cloister. At the first stroke of the bell, they washed their hands; at the second and third, they went to the refectory. The priest serving for the week blessed the table, and the abbot [Col. XXXIID] blessed the reader. No one was permitted to unfold his napkin until several verses of Holy Scripture had been heard. Very strict silence and exact discipline were observed. The two dishes customarily served consisted only of vegetables. It was not permitted to ask for fish; it was given only rarely, and to the most infirm with the abbot’s permission. Meat never entered the refectory.

At the end of the meal, the abbot gave a signal and folded his napkin; all did likewise with him. The leftovers were collected in a basket. When the reader had ceased reading and pronounced the formula, “But thou, O Lord, have mercy upon me,” the thanksgiving was sung [Col. XXXIIIA], continuing as they went to the church. The almoner and the reader stopped at the entrance and went back: the former to take his meal, the latter to distribute alms to the poor.

Except on feasts with nine lessons, the four feasts of Easter and Pentecost, and three days in each week of Lent, it was permitted to speak only once, in a place of the cloister appointed for that purpose. Everyone took part in this recreation. It was presided over by the abbot, the prior, or some other religious appointed by him. This relaxation was undertaken simply and charitably. It was then that one might make known one’s needs; the abbot or his officers hastened to provide for them. It was then also that attention was given to regulating the chant [Col. XXXIIIB] or the ceremonies of the Church, which were to be observed with the most scrupulous exactness.

The remaining time until Vespers was spent in study, reading holy books, or manual labour. After Vespers they remained in the cloister until the collation, or reading, held in the chapter house. This reading was drawn from Cassian’s *Conferences*, the *Life of the Desert Fathers*, Saint Gregory’s *Dialogues*, Hugh of Saint-Victor’s *Explanation of the Rule of Saint Augustine*, his treatises on the *Pledge of the Soul*, and Saint Bernard’s sermons on the Gospel *Missus est*.

All attended this reading and listened to it reverently and in profound silence until the signal given by the abbot. They then went to the refectory, [Col. XXXIIIC] preceded by a torch in winter, and thence to the church to sing Compline. The weekly minister went out first and sprinkled the community, which withdrew to the dormitory. The religious arranged themselves in order; the abbot said the prayer, and, after each had saluted him, they went peacefully to take their rest. [Note: [Col. XXXIIID] *History of Illustrious Men*, vol. I, fol. 163 ff.]

This life, as austere as that of monks and regular to the point of monotony, could suit only souls of a particular temper. If the Church has always taught that religious life is good in itself, and even necessary in God’s designs—so that evangelical counsels as well as precepts might always be practised, and so that the example of humility, poverty, and chastity might remain among peoples as [Col. XXXIIID] a voice eternally raised against pride, selfishness, excessive attachment to finite goods, and that frightful corruption of morals which has at all times devoured societies—she has never imposed it or claimed that this life should be the universal law. She rejects the utopias of certain modern philosophers, just as she rejected the contrary opinions of Luther and Calvin. Not only does she compel no one to enter this path; she permits no one to undertake it except after long and serious trials. Such too was the practice of Saint-Victor.

[Col. XXXIVA] Those who requested admission to the community were tested for a long time, and their reception as novices was attended by a solemnity capable of making a deep and lasting impression upon them. No one was to be admitted to put on the canon’s habit unless he had been fully instructed concerning the step he was about to take.

On the appointed day, the master of novices led the postulant to the chapter house. The latter prostrated himself full length at the abbot’s feet, and the abbot questioned him as follows: “What do you ask?” The postulant replied: “I ask for God’s mercy and the clothing of your congregation.” The abbot said: “May the Lord grant you a share in the fellowship of his elect.” The assembly added: “Amen.”

[Col. XXXIVB] The postulant then rose and remained kneeling before the abbot. The latter recalled to him the harshest and most difficult points of the rule, the scrupulous exactness with which a canon was bound to fulfil it in its entirety, and the severity with which the cowardly and rebellious were judged. He asked the postulant whether he was resolved to observe it. Upon his affirmative answer, he further inquired whether he was professed in any church, had left any congregation, was married, had pledged his faith, had any mutilated or broken limb, any deformity or infirmity, had been born of lawful marriage, was bound by any vow, was free or enslaved, could read and sing, and was sufficiently learned to enter [Col. XXXIVC] holy orders. After this examination, the postulant was clothed in a sleeveless woollen tunic, to distinguish him from the professed. This ceremony took place in the chapter house or in the church upon the steps of the altar. During the clothing, the *Veni Creator* was sung or chanted. [Note: [Col. XXXIVD] *Liber ordinis*, fol. 15.]

Hugh of Saint-Victor’s *Institutions for Novices* teaches us with what care they were prepared later to fulfil the functions of canons. This work is worthy of the piety and learning of our Victorine; from the outset it traces for the novice the path upon which he must enter and shows him its end from afar. “This path,” he says, “is knowledge, discipline, and goodness. Knowledge leads to discipline, discipline to goodness, and [Col. XXXIVD] goodness to blessedness.” Thus they sought to cultivate his intellect through meditation and study, and his heart through the practice of Christian virtues. We shall not conceal that this latter point was always regarded as the more important. Not all religious in monasteries, any more than all secular persons in the world, are destined for learning; but all can and must attain virtue.

Nothing could be wiser than the principles that guided them in this difficult work. For them human perfection did not consist in [Col. XXXVA] performing extraordinary actions, but in performing the most ordinary actions well; works, indeed, do not make perfection, but manifest it. A person is not charitable because he gives alms; rather, he gives alms because he is charitable. In a word, a virtuous person is himself—his soul’s disposition, the order reigning among his faculties, the triumph of reason’s and faith’s noble and generous instincts over base and coarse instincts; his will captive to truth and duty; a lyre all of whose strings yield only perfectly true notes; a gentle and melodious harmony. If such is real and solid virtue, it must show itself everywhere and in everything: in small matters as in great, in ordinary circumstances as in extraordinary ones, whether the salvation of a people or the most trifling interest is at stake.

Such was the point of departure. For this reason they laboured to perfect the novice in his slightest actions. No means seemed more effective to them than forming him in an intelligent and scrupulous observance of the rule. Hence those details which appear minute and sometimes even childish, and which are so interesting to us because they acquaint us with the manners of the age and with the superiority of religious over worldly persons, even in matters relating to courtesy and elegance of conduct. We shall cite a few [Col. XXXVC] examples.

Hugh prescribes to novices how they should behave at table, and with a subtlety worthy of La Bruyère describes the faults they often brought from society into the cloister:

“There are some,” he says, “who, when taking their places at table, display through anxious agitation and the disorderly movements of their bodies the intemperance of their minds. They shake their heads, uncover their arms, and stretch out their hands. To see their laborious efforts and indecent gestures, you would say that they are about to swallow at once all the dishes set before them. They catch their breath and sigh heavily; from their places, with eyes and hands, they range over the foods [Col. XXXVD] near and far from them. They hasten to break the bread, to pour wine into the chalices and cups, and to turn the dishes about. Like a king beneath the walls of a besieged city, on the point of ordering an assault, they hesitate on which side to begin the attack; they would like to break in on every side.”

He then adds, as though fearing that he had pursued such details too far: “Perhaps I have said more than I ought; perhaps I have passed the bounds of moderation. But shamelessness does not know how to blush: its disgrace must be made evident if it is to take notice of it.” [Note: [Col. XXXVD] *Institut. novitiorum*, vol. II, col. 949.]

[Col. XXXVIA] Elsewhere he attacks, with the same zeal and acerbity, faults no less gross:

“There are some,” he says, “whose throats are afflicted with a rather ridiculous disease: they can swallow only rich and delicate dishes. If they are sometimes served plain or scanty food, they complain of indigestion, dryness of the stomach, dizziness, or other similar ailments.

“Others despise the delicacy and luxury of food with great courage, but reject with equal petulance the use of ordinary fare. They must have unusual dishes; so that, for a single man’s stomach, a troop of servants must scour the district, seek out some unknown root in deserts or mountains, or little fishes in deep chasms, or out-of-season fruits on withered shrubs, in order to satisfy his appetite.

“Others demand minute care in preparing their food; they require innumerable preparations and seasonings. At one time they need food soft, at another hard; at one time cold, at another hot; at one time boiled in water, at another roasted; at one time seasoned with salt, at another with pepper, at another with cumin. They should not merely be reproved, but made ridiculous.” [Note: [Col. XXXVID] *Ibid.*, col. 950.]

He also recommends simplicity in [Col. XXXVIC] clothing: garments ought neither to be too costly, too fine, or too delicate; nor of a colour too brilliant, wholly unsuitable to a religious; nor excessively large and trailing, too long, too narrow, or cut according to the vanity of the age. One must be modest even in the way one arranges them.

“There are fools,” he says, “who desire to please fools. They arrange their garments with a certain art: some cast them back in a ridiculous way; others, to give themselves an air of dignity, spread and extend them as far as they can; others fold them and gather them into a single bundle; others divide and bind them so tightly that they take on all the forms [Col. XXXVID] of the body and offend the eye; others shake them about, and, giving their undulating folds to the winds, indicate by the mobility of their clothing the levity of their minds; others, as they walk, trace furrows in the sand with their winding tails. These tails and trailing fringes, like a fox’s tail, erase behind them the traces of their steps—and rightly so, assuredly—that after they have passed, their memory may perish and they may no longer live in the remembrance of the living. By this they show that they belong to the number of those of whom the Psalmist says: ‘Not so are the wicked, not so; they are like dust [Col. XXXVIIA] which the wind carries away from the face of the earth.’” [Note: [Col. XXXVIID] *Institut. novitiorum*, vol. II, col. 936.]

The novice must watch over his bearing. The movements of the body reveal the movements of the soul; both must be regulated. Slowness in bodily movement is a sign of sloth; softness, of disorder; and petulance, of pride; rapidity, of inconstancy; and disarray, of anger. Hugh compares the body to a republic:

“When everyone in a state performs the function proper to him, within the bounds fixed by duty and propriety, order reigns, and the society is vigorous and beautiful. There are persons,” he says, “who do not know how to keep their bodies in due harmony. There are [Col. XXXVIIB] some who listen only with open mouths; others put out their tongues like thirsty dogs; others, in every action, move it round their lips like a millstone; others, when speaking, stretch out their fingers, knit their brows, roll their eyes in their sockets, or fix them like one sunk in deep meditation; others raise their heads, toss their hair, drape themselves in their garments, lean sideways, put one foot forward, and strike a singular pose; others imitate I know not what kind of figure: they close one eye and open the other; some speak with their mouths half open, in a very ridiculous manner. A thousand other singularities disfigure the face, which is the mirror in which [Col. XXXVIIC] good discipline is reflected. Its movements must be regulated with all the greater care because the slightest defects are noticed. It must express a gentle austerity and an austere graciousness.”

“There are some,” he says elsewhere, [Note: [Col. XXXVIID] *Institut. novit.*, vol. II, col. 942.] “who sail with their arms: they walk upon the earth with their feet while flying through the air with their hands. What a monster is one who represents at the same time the gait of a man, the motion of a ship’s oars, and the flight of a bird. I would gladly apply to him these words of Horace:

> If a painter wished to join a horse’s neck to a human head . . .”

[Col. XXXVIID] This part of the novice’s education was called discipline. But while correcting his faults and refining his manners, care was not neglected to enlighten his mind by sacred and secular learning, especially in those who showed happier aptitudes.

When the trial of the novitiate was judged sufficient, the novice was admitted to profession. The abbot notified him in the chapter house, and he prepared to receive the sacraments of penance and the Eucharist. The master of novices had him write out his profession. On the appointed day, he prostrated himself in the chapter house. The abbot [Col. XXXVIIIA] put this question to him: “What do you ask?” He replied: “God’s mercy.” Then, rising at the abbot’s command, he approached him, bent the knee, and placed his joined hands in the abbot’s. The abbot then said to him: “My brother, do you give yourself to God, to serve him in the fellowship and obedience of this congregation, to embrace the life of a canon according to the rule of Saint Augustine and the customs of this place, which have been established, or shall hereafter be established, by God’s will?” The novice replied: “I give myself.” The abbot said: “May the Lord God grant you to fulfil by your works what you have begun by your desires.” The assembly answered: Amen.

The librarian [Col. XXXVIIIB] was to have prepared a copy of the rule, and the refectorian a loaf of bread. The abbot presented both to the novice, saying: “We grant you a share and fellowship in our brotherhood in spiritual and temporal things . . .” He gave the book to the librarian and the bread to the almoner, and the solemn Mass was sung. All the religious were required to attend it. The abbot celebrated it, and relics were placed upon the altar.

At the offertory, the master of novices led the newly professed man to the foot of the altar steps, where, kneeling, he received the abbot’s blessing. Afterwards he was clothed in the canon’s habit. He held his profession of faith in his hand. At the master of novices’ signal, he read it aloud on the right-hand side [Col. XXXVIIIC] of the altar. It ran as follows: “I, N., promise, with God’s help, perpetual chastity, renunciation of all private property, and obedience to you, Father Abbot, and to all your canonically instituted successors, according to the rule of Saint Augustine.” He then offered this profession upon the altar; bowing, he kissed it, saluted again, and returned to his place. There, standing, he said three times aloud: “Receive me, O Lord, according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my hope.”

If several were being professed, they performed the same ceremonies in turn. Afterwards, they all prostrated themselves upon the steps of the altar. The abbot intoned [Col. XXXVIIID] the antiphon and chanted psalms, prayers, and collects. At the end the assembly said: Amen. The new canons then went to kiss the abbot, whom they saluted before and after; then the deacon, subdeacon, prior, and successively all the canons. [Note: [Col. XXXVIIID] *Liber ordinis*, fol. 16.]

In the rule we have just reviewed, no mention is made of the school of Saint-Victor. We see only that certain hours were devoted to reading or study. But, apart from the conference, which ordinarily concerned matters of piety or asceticism, and the public reading called the conference (*collation*), we do not find [Col. XXXIXA] regular lessons established in this abbey. One ought not to infer from this that the school did not exist; that would contradict contemporary authors who speak of it with praise and would make inexplicable the production of so many works of philosophy, theology, grammar, history, and even literature, which won for the Victorines so great a reputation for wisdom and learning. The only conclusion that can strictly be drawn from this silence is that the author of the *Liber ordinis* and Simon Gourdan, in his *History of Illustrious Men*, reported only the general rules of the monastery. There must have been particular regulations for those engaged in study. This is not mere conjecture. Thoulouse, in his *Antiquities of the [Col. XXXIXB] Royal Abbey of Saint-Victor*, explicitly attests the existence of this school and of certain rules imposed upon the students.

It is certain, first, that William of Champeaux, at the request of his friends, and especially of Hildebert of Le Mans, resumed in his retirement his lessons in dialectic, rhetoric, and philosophy; Abelard attests this. Abelard himself, on returning from Brittany, came to place himself once more under the discipline of his former master. Now this teaching was not interrupted. Thoulouse reports that, in an old chronicle of the Abbey of Saint-Victor extending from Trajan’s reign to that of Frederick II, the holiness of the canons and the number of their students were celebrated. [Col. XXXIXC] “In the same house of Saint-Victor,” he adds, “there were courses in letters. They were taught to young canons and even to those of more advanced age. This practice dates from William of Champeaux.” He then names William’s successors in the chair of Saint-Victor: Blessed Thomas, a martyr to his devotion to the bishop of Paris; and the latter’s grand penitentiary, Hugh; Nantère, Richard, Walter, Geoffrey, Anselm, Richard, Jacob, a Roman by origin, John of Reims, and Theobald, a contemporary of Saint Bonaventure and Saint Thomas. From this time onward, there is no longer any doubt: we find readers in theology and the same public exercises as at the University of Paris.

[Col. XXXIXD] The same author has preserved regulations applying only to the scholastics. On double feasts they were obliged to attend all the canonical hours, Mass, and chapter. But it is added that in the morning they may go to the professors’ lectures, *ad sermonem* (“to the lecture/discourse”). Other details of the same kind follow, determining when they were to submit to the common rule and what dispensations were granted to facilitate their studies. [Note: [Col. XXXIXD] *Antiq. reg. S.-Vict.*, stella 7, fol. 240 ff.]

Nevertheless, the historians of Saint-Victor, and even the manuscripts we have consulted, tell us [Col. XLA] little about the instruction given there. To supply this deficiency, we have selected from among the teachers of this school Hugh, the first whose works we possess. They will furnish us with interesting information on this subject.

## CHAPTER III. LIFE OF HUGH.

Hugh’s name and native land have provoked learned disputes. Vinnigenstadius, a Saxon writer cited by Derling, calls him Herman. Leibniz maintains that the name Hugh was unknown, or at least very rare, in Germany; that our Victorine was called Heymon; and that it was through ignorance that the French gave him the name by which he is [Col. XLB] known among us.

It is far more difficult, and at the same time more interesting, to determine his birthplace. The first editor of his works, Thomas Garzon, a regular canon of Saint John Lateran, appears to believe that Rome was his native city and makes him a canon of his own order. A German author, Hartmann Schedel, makes him born in France. Neither of these opinions is serious.

The author of his *Life*, the historian of Saint-Victor, all without exception the writers of that abbey, the second editor of his works, the epitaph on his tomb, Trithemius, Alberic of Trois-Fontaines, Bellarmine, Paul Lange, Engelhusius, in the chronicle published at Halberstadt at the beginning of the [Col. XLC] fifteenth century, a fourteenth-century manuscript, the younger Meibomius, who summarizes in a learned dissertation all the preceding testimonies, and in general all historians and critics down to Mabillon, give him Saxony as his native land. [Note: [Col. XXXIXD] Dom Ceillier, vol. XXII, p. 200.]

The learned Benedictine broke this unbroken chain. [Note: [Col. XLD] In Mabillon, *Analectis*, vol. I, p. 263; folio edition, p. 133.] According to this learned critic, Hugh was Flemish, and Ypres was his birthplace. The authors of the *Literary History of France*, Dom Ceillier, Fleury, Father Longueval, Rohrbacher, and most subsequent writers adopted his opinion. Let us examine their reasons.

Against all the traditions of Saint-Victor and the most indisputable monuments [Col. XLD] preserved in that abbey, Mabillon sets only two testimonies: one from a manuscript in the library of Anchin, the other from Robert of Torigny, abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel.

The manuscript bears this inscription: “In the year 1142 from the Incarnation of the Lord, Lord Hugh of Saint-Victor died, on the third day of the Ides of February. He was born in the district of Ypres, whence he went into exile in his childhood.” Whether these lines were written by a man fully informed about what he reports, or by one who could easily have been mistaken about the fact he records, is unknown.

Robert of Torigny relates with what eagerness young men of noble family flocked to Saint-Victor; then he adds: Among them was Master Hugh, a Lorrainer, who became illustrious by his learning and religion. Now, according to Mabillon’s argument, part of Flanders was then included in Lorraine. These two testimonies therefore confirm one another.

However weighty these authorities may be, they cannot be compared with those establishing the contrary view without serious doubts arising in the mind; the light is not complete, nor the conviction unshakable; the question is not settled, and one may pursue further research without rashness.

This is what Christian Gottfried Derling did in [Col. XLIB] a dissertation defended on 21 December 1745 and dedicated to the Count of Blankenburg. [Note: [Col. XLID] *Dissert. de Hugone a Sancto Victore*, Helmstedt, 1745, quarto.] The author had in his hands ancient Halberstadt manuscripts unknown before him, or at least whose testimony had not yet been produced. We should wish for more modesty and moderation in his criticism. We condemn his outbursts against a man as worthy of respect as Dom Mabillon. Above all, we protest against the epithets “proud” and “ignorant,” which in no way suit that learned and pious Benedictine. But, apart from these faults, which nothing can excuse, the young doctor’s proofs seemed solid to us, and the details he reports concerning Hugh’s family and early years worthy of interest. We shall follow him in his [Col. XLIC] narrative and argument.

Hartingam was one of the most celebrated regions of Saxony. There flourished, in the twelfth century, the family of the Counts of Blankenburg, powerful through its rich estates and influence. Its origin is obscure. It is known, however, that at the end of the eleventh century one of its members died, leaving two sons, Hugh and Poppo. Hugh embraced the ecclesiastical state, and Poppo inherited his fathers’ title and estates. His administration was prosperous; he governed the paternal inheritance until the beginning of the twelfth century. Three sons survived him: Reinhard, Conrad, and Sigfrid. The first was raised to the episcopal see of Halberstadt; the second succeeded his father [Col. XLID] in governing his county. By a wife whom the chroniclers do not name, but whose character and virtues they praise, he had two children: Hugh, who was our Victorine, and Burchard.

Reinhard distinguished himself in the cultivation of letters. His relatives sent him early to Paris to pursue his course of studies. William of Champeaux had just withdrawn to Saint-Victor; Reinhard followed him there and became one of his most illustrious disciples. Having formed himself in that school through study and the practice of Christian virtues, he returned to his homeland. It was then that he was raised to the see of Halberstadt. He always retained so [Col. XLIIA] great an esteem for the canons of Saint-Victor that he brought some of them to Saxony to kindle in the monasteries he had founded or restored in his diocese the love of study and to establish perfect discipline there. Later he urged his nephew Hugh to come and draw from this abbey, whose renown grew daily, lessons in learning and wisdom. His personal merits, learning, and piety would have led him to the most honourable offices, had he not preferred religion and justice to the splendour of a brilliant position.
