His devotion to the Roman pontiffs, in the disputes that so long divided priesthood and empire, incurred the emperor’s resentment and kept him from the dignities that prince bestowed upon his favourites.

[Col. XLIIB] Hugh, his uncle, had earned through the purity of his morals and the innocence of his life the archdeaconry of Halberstadt. At a very advanced age, he yielded to the entreaties of his grandnephew; he accompanied him on his journeys and withdrew with him to the Abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris, where he peacefully ended his career. He was Saint-Victor’s benefactor, as his nephew was its light. The great church was constructed almost entirely at his expense. One reads in the Necrology of Saint-Victor: “On the third day of the Nones of May, the solemn anniversary of the priest Hugh, of blessed memory, archdeacon of the Church of Halberstadt, who came to us from Saxony with his nephew, Master Hugh, canon of our church.”

[Col. XLIIC] Such were the relatives of our Victorine, illustrious through birth, learning, and piety. These details, drawn from manuscripts of the Church of Halberstadt, conform perfectly to the account of his biographers and to the tradition of Saint-Victor. This body of authorities would at least form a strong presumption against Dom Mabillon’s opinion; but we have still more positive authorities, confirming the former and giving them full evidence.

It is reported in the great Saxon chronicle, written before the fourteenth century in the language of Lower Germany: “Berthold, a monk of Hamersleben, read diligently the works of Hugh [Col. XLIID] of Saint-Victor, and by this reading acquired great learning and great influence. Hugh was lord of Blankenburg; scorning dignities and yielding to the counsels of his kinsman Bishop Reinhard, he went into exile from his homeland; and after traversing Saxony and Flanders, he was received at Paris with great distinction.”

This passage contains a double testimony. The chronicler positively affirms that Hugh belonged to the noble family of the Counts of Blankenburg; he adds that he was related to Reinhard, bishop of Halberstadt. Now we know independently that Reinhard belonged to the same family.

[Col. XLIIIA] A thirteenth-century manuscript, written in Latin and preserved in the library of Halberstadt, contains these words: “At that time flourished Hugh of Saint-Victor, of the Saxon family of Blankenburg.”

A passage from an undated manuscript, but one which, so far as can be conjectured from the handwriting, goes back to the fourteenth century, reads: “Hugh, son of Lord Conrad, an illustrious doctor, trained in the Abbey of Saint-Victor . . .” The remainder has been erased.

We read in the *Life of Reinhard*: “While Reinhard occupied the episcopal see of Halberstadt, that illustrious author, Hugh of Saint-Victor, also called Herman, lived in the monastery of Hamersleben. He had already applied himself to writing. He belonged to the dynasty of Blankenburg. He was entrusted by his relatives [Col. XLIIIB] to the religious of Hamersleben to study letters there. The love of learning with which he burned subsequently kept him there, despite his relatives, until war broke out throughout Saxony under the reign of Henry, and he thought of taking flight. Therefore Bishop Reinhard sent him to Paris. He entered the monastery of Saint-Victor and established his residence there because of the great multitude of learned persons who lived in it.”

Finally, a handwritten Halberstadt chronicle, in Latin, by a religious of that monastery, written approximately around the time of the Thirty Years’ War, furnishes us with a further document in the life of Reinhard: “Then flourished at Paris the celebrated Hugh of Saint-Victor, a regular canon of the Order [Col. XLIIIC] of Saint Augustine, Saxon by origin and of the family of Blankenburg, a man very learned in the divine Scriptures and without equal in secular philosophy. Reinhard sent him at his own expense to study at Paris, because of his talents and the disturbances in Saxony.”

Thus the traditions of the Church of Halberstadt, the monastery of Hamersleben, and the Abbey of Saint-Victor confirm one another. They form an imposing testimony that leaves no doubt as to Hugh’s true homeland.

They may even be reconciled with Robert of Torigny’s account, cited by Dom Mabillon. This chronicler tells us, indeed, that Hugh was a Lorrainer. [Col. XLIIID] But we know that historians of this period included under that name Flanders and part of Lower Saxony. This is proved by a passage from the monk of Jumièges, reported by Garzon; it uses nearly the same words as the abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel:

“Among those flocking to Saint-Victor was Hugh, a Lorrainer, so called because Lorraine and Saxony are neighbouring regions.”

As for the manuscript in the library of Anchin, which makes Hugh a native of Ypres in Flanders, one may presume, without excessive rashness, that the historian was misled and assigned him this origin because he passed through the schools of Flanders as he had passed through those of Saxony. Besides, [Col. XLIVA] what weight can this isolated testimony carry against the traditions, so universal and so constant, which we have reported?

Hugh of Saint-Victor was therefore born at Hartingam in Saxony, of Conrad, Count of Blankenburg, in the year 1096, and not in 1098, as Ellies Dupin states. For Osbert, likewise a canon of Saint-Victor and his contemporary, who has left us so moving an account of his death, reports that he died in the year 1140 at the age of forty-four.

From childhood he displayed the happy dispositions with which nature had endowed him. His parents conceived the finest hopes for him, and resolved to entrust his education only to skilled hands. Rheinard, his great-uncle, bishop [Col. XLIVB] of Halberstadt, was consulted concerning the selection of the masters who were to form him alike in literary cultivation and in the practice of virtue.

At that time monasteries were, in Germany, the only schools for youth.

The first seeds of learning had been sown amid this still barbarous society by a poor missionary. Germany’s soil was not barren. Before long illustrious men appeared and seemed to prepare for their country an age of civilization and glory: Rabanus Maurus, Alcuin’s disciple and superior to his master in learning; the learned Hatto, fellow pupil of Rabanus Maurus at the school of Tours and his successor at the abbey of Fulda; Walafrid Strabo; Einhard of Odenwald, who [Col. XLIVC] strove to reproduce the precision of Suetonius, whom he had chosen as his model; Gottschalk, a prolific but rash writer; Regino, a skilful casuist; Otfrid, who successfully softened the roughness of his native tongue—all flourished in the abbeys founded by Saint Boniface.

But the invasions driven back or held in check by Charlemagne’s powerful arm began again. They destroyed monasteries, scattered scholars, burned libraries, and brought back barbarism, which once more weighed upon German soil until the accession of the Saxon princes.

With them the monasteries rose from their ruins, no longer, as formerly, in the mysterious [Col. XLIVD] obscurity of the forest of Fulda. The barbarian had not spared the fine trees that sheltered the convent; their cloisters rose in the great cities and near the palaces inhabited by the prelates and magnates of the realm: at Brandenburg, Havelberg, Naumburg, Ripen, and Magdeburg. Schools arose on every side. Adelbold founded one at Utrecht, where the son of Henry I came to study the ancient languages, dialectic, and poetry. Liège possessed gymnasia entrusted to monks, which every cleric was required to attend. Bremen had Danish princes and sons of noble families among its pupils. In the convent of Saint Michael there was a school of grammar whose statutes the bishop had drawn up. At Paderborn Bishop Meinwerk had summoned [Col. XLVA] philosophers, rhetoricians, geometers, musicians, and poets. The University of Cologne was known throughout Germany; its protector was Bruno, brother of Emperor Otto, one of the most learned men of his age. In these various schools the study of pagan authors was joined to that of Holy Scripture and the Fathers.

The monks multiplied copies of them, which were deposited in the libraries that every bishop established in his diocese. Nor did they confine themselves merely to studying and imitating the ancients: gratitude inspired poets who sang of the noble deeds of the Saxon princes, conquerors of barbarians and protectors of learning. [Note: [Col. XLVD] Documentary materials for the *Life of Luther*, by M. Aduin, vol. I, p. 320.]

The most celebrated schools of Saxony were [Col. XLVB] that of the monastery of Hirsau, restored by Adalbert of Calw and made illustrious by its abbot William—a profound philosopher, skilful dialectician, excellent musician, astronomer, and the most learned man of his century; that of the monastery of Erfurt; and that of the monastery of Ilsenburg, founded by its abbot Hercaud and distinguished by the scholars whom it gathered within its walls. [Note: [Col. XLVD] Hurter, *Life of Gregory VII*, vol. I, pp. [Col. XLVID] 204–205.]

Bishop Reinard chose for his nephew Hugh the monastery of Saint Pancras at Hamersleben. It was one of the foundations with which he had enriched his diocese. He had summoned there the canons of Saint-Victor, whose piety and abilities he knew. His confidence was not disappointed: the Victorines brought religious virtues and love [Col. XLVC] of study to Hamersleben. The monastery of Saint Pancras became for the whole of Saxony a school of wisdom and learning. The foundation charters of the bishop of Halberstadt inform us that it was attended by a large number of young people.

It was amid this literary and scientific movement, soon to be checked by civil war, that Hugh entered the monastery of Hamersleben to begin his studies. There he found a residence suited to his talents and tastes. While still very young, he displayed his ardour for learning. “I venture to affirm,” he says in his *Didascalicon*, “that I neglected nothing which might instruct me. I learned many things which might appear trivial or [Col. XLVD] even ridiculous to some persons. I remember that, while I was still a pupil, I tried to retain the names of all the objects that fell beneath my gaze or served my use. I believed this knowledge necessary for studying their nature. Every day I reread portions of the arguments that I had briefly set down in writing, so as to engrave in my memory the thoughts, questions, objections, and solutions that I had learned. I often argued a case and arranged a controversy; I carefully distinguished the office of [Col. XLVIA] the orator from that of the rhetorician or the sophist. I calculated; with black charcoal I drew figures upon the pavement. I clearly demonstrated the properties of the obtuse, acute, and right angle. I learned to measure the area and solid content of figures. I often spent nights contemplating the stars; often, tuning my *magadam* [uncertain instrument-name], I studied the difference of sounds and delighted my mind with the sweetness of harmony.” [Note: [Col. XLVID] *Didascalicon*, book VI, ch. 3, vol. II, col. 799.]

This peaceful and laborious life had so many charms for him that he resolved to devote himself to it irrevocably. He embraced the Rule of Saint Augustine, despite the advice of his parents, who dreamed for him of a distinction other than that of letters. Yielding to what he believed to be the voice of Providence, he [Col. XLVIB] laboured, without knowing it, more surely for his glory. As Count of Blankenburg, he might have won renown through valour on a battlefield or through wisdom in governing his county; but his fame, like a voice repeated by mountain echoes, would have grown ever fainter and perhaps would never have reached us. Now his name is inseparably united with things that shall not perish: with theological learning, of which he was the restorer; with the immortal names of Peter Lombard and Saint Thomas, who always regarded him as their master.

Yet the political and religious wars that arose under Henry IV disturbed him in his retreat and compelled him to leave his homeland. [Col. XLVIC] Reinhard, his uncle, advised him to seek in Paris the learning and peace that he could no longer find in Saxony. Hugh therefore departed, like Abraham of old, say his ancient biographers. His uncle Hugh consented to follow him into exile. Together they travelled through Saxony, Flanders, and Lorraine. Everywhere they were received eagerly and honourably because of the nobility of their birth. They then went to Saint-Victor at Marseilles, and afterwards to Saint-Victor at Paris, where Hugh was in some measure to find again his former masters and the former rivals of his labours.

It was under Gilduin’s highly prosperous government that Hugh of Blankenburg came to seek [Col. XLVID] refuge in the abbey of Saint-Victor with his uncle, venerable for his age and virtues. The name of his family was not unknown there. The memory of Reinhard was still alive and ever dear to the canons. His youth, the precocious maturity of his mind, the learning he already possessed, the gentleness of character and refinement of manners breathed forth in his writings, the fatigue of a long and arduous journey, and the sorrows of exile—all must have interested them in his favour and won every heart for him. He was received with joy, and the canons were proud to possess among them a young [Col. XLVIIA] man of such noble and illustrious family who, through the qualities of mind and heart, inspired the finest hopes.

We know nothing of Hugh’s life at Saint-Victor except that he continued his studies under Prior Thomas, successor of William of Champeaux; that he himself succeeded his master in the honourable office of scholasticus; and that he discharged it gloriously until his death.

Osbert, a canon of Saint-Victor who performed the duties of infirmarian, has left us a moving account of Hugh’s final moments in a letter to another canon, named John. We translate it as we read it in Dom Martène.

“To John, his beloved brother in Christ: Brother Osbert, [Col. XLVIIB] greeting in the Lord.

Your piety, dearest brother, has inspired in you the desire to learn from me some particulars concerning the death of your dear master Hugh, so that you may know in truth how he conducted himself in his last illness.

Receive, then, what you have desired in a holy, just, and devout manner in every respect. Perhaps you would wish for a long account; you would like to know every circumstance of his death. I cannot tell you everything. Yet I shall relate what I saw; for, unless I am mistaken, you ask me only for what I myself saw and heard.

I shall not speak of the sincere, complete, [Col. XLVIIC] and perfect confession which he made to the lord abbot and myself with considerable care; nor of the abundant tears he shed; nor of the great contrition of his heart; nor of the frequent thanksgivings he offered to the Lord Jesus Christ for his present illness, often allowing this cry of praise to escape from his heart: ‘Blessed are you, Lord my God, for eternity.’ I shall immediately recount what he said and did in the last moments of his life. That shall be the subject of my account to you.

On the eve of the day on which he left this life, I came to him in the morning and asked how he was. ‘Well,’ he said to me, ‘in soul and body.’ He added, ‘Are we alone?’ I [Col. XLVIID] replied, ‘Yes.’ ‘Have you celebrated the holy Mass?’ ‘Yes.’ ‘Come near and breathe upon my face in the form of a cross, that I may receive the Holy Spirit.’ I did as he wished. Immediately, gladdened and strengthened, I believe, by the Holy Spirit, he exclaimed: ‘Now I am in peace; now I walk in truth and purity; now I am established upon the rock, and nothing can henceforth shake me. Now let the whole world come with its pleasures: it shall not have my esteem, even if it were itself my entire reward; for it I shall do nothing against God. Now I recognize God’s mercy toward me. Of all the graces [Col. XLVIIIA] which God has bestowed on me throughout the whole course of my life up to this day, none can be sweeter, gentler, or more pleasing to me than that which he deigns to grant me at this moment. Blessed be the Lord, my God, for eternity.’

After these words, he humbly sought absolution for all the faults he might have committed against God. I gave it to him and left him to rest as he wished. I moved away from his bed.

The following night, about cockcrow, his condition became more grave and his strength declined. I hurried to him; his first word concerned the salvation of his soul. When the brothers present had given him absolution, I suggested that he receive holy anointing, and he requested it [Col. XLVIIIB] joyfully. He himself ordered everything necessary to be prepared without delay. When all was ready, day was beginning to dawn; the brothers assembled and came to him, as was customary, reciting psalms and prayers. I then asked whether he wished to receive the anointing from my hands or preferred to wait for the lord abbot. The latter was then absent, but had been summoned and was expected to come promptly to the sick man. He replied: ‘Do what you must do, since you are gathered here.’ A great number of religious, monks, regular canons, priests, and other clerics had hurried there; several laymen also were present.

“After administering extreme unction to him, [Col. XLVIIIC] I asked whether he wished to receive the body of Our Lord. It had not been brought to him because he had communicated the day before yesterday. ‘My God!’ he exclaimed with a kind of indignation, ‘you ask me whether I wish to receive my Lord! Run to the church and bring me quickly the body of my Master.’ When I had carried out his orders, I approached his bed and, holding the sacred bread of eternal life in my hands, said to him: ‘Adore and acknowledge the body of your Lord.’ Then, raising himself as far as he could and stretching both hands toward the Blessed Sacrament, he said: ‘In your presence I adore my Lord, and I receive him as my [Col. XLVIIID] salvation.’ After consuming the sacred host, he asked for a cross which was beside him; taking it into his hands, he traced upon himself the sign of salvation, and, having devoutly embraced it, he placed the feet of the crucifix upon his lips and held it thus for a long time, as though he were gathering in his mouth the blood which had flowed from the Saviour’s wounds. He clung to it like a child at its mother’s breast and sucked it, pouring forth torrents of tears.

There was a moment of silence, after which I recalled to him this verse of Holy Scripture: ‘I commit my spirit into your hands.’ He thought I was questioning him and asking him for its explanation; he replied: ‘The Lord Jesus, when about to [Col. XLIXA] leave this world, said to his Father: “I commit my spirit into your hands,” and his Father received it.’ ‘And you,’ I replied, ‘who are likewise about to leave this world, must pray that God may receive your soul.’ At these words he gathered his strength for a moment; then, uttering sighs heard by all, he said: ‘Lord, into your hands and your power I commit this spirit which you have given me and which I received from you.’ He spoke and fell silent. As his last hour drew near and he could no longer utter a word, he collected himself once more; then, recovering his senses, he began to speak, but his nearly extinguished voice could not be heard. I asked what he was saying; in a clear voice he replied: ‘I have obtained it.’ [Col. XLIXB] I said, ‘What have you obtained?’ He was no more. This was on the eleventh day of February in the year 1138. He was buried in the cloister, near the church door. [Note: [Col. XLIXD] *Life of Hugh*, in vol. I of his works.]”

Subsequently his remains were transferred into a chapel within the church itself. There a painting was displayed containing a list of his works, with this epitaph:

> Here in this tomb lies Hugh, a most celebrated doctor,  
> Whom a small urn contains—an outstanding man.  
> Foremost in doctrine and second to none in love,  
> He shone in intellect, conduct, speech, and style.

A singular anecdote reported by Thomas of Cantimpré, a faithful echo of popular traditions, informs us that he had a [Col. XLIXC] weak and delicate constitution. One of his fellow canons, he says, implored him while he was still alive to appear to him after his death. “Gladly,” Hugh replied, “if this power is granted me through the life and death of the Saviour.” In the meantime he died. Shortly afterward he appeared to his friend, who was awaiting him. “Here I am,” he said; “ask what you wish; I cannot stay.” The canon, trembling but nevertheless full of joy, said to him: “How are you, dear friend?” Hugh replied: “Very well now; but because during my life I refused to receive the discipline, perhaps there is not a demon of hell who did not strike me violently as I passed through purgatory.” The narrator adds that he had [Col. XLIXD] not been subjected to this penitential exercise because he had very tender flesh and a delicate nature. [Note: [Col. XLIXD] *Universal History of Paris*, vol. II.]

His memory remained dear for a long time to the canons of Saint-Victor. His name is often mentioned in their annals with reverence and affection. Yet his glory extended far beyond the cloisters of his abbey. He was certainly one of the most illustrious men of his age through virtue and learning. James of Vitry, in his *Western History*, after a lofty eulogy of the community of Saint-Victor and of the great men it [Col. LA] produced, adds: “The most celebrated and renowned of all was Hugh: harp of the Lord, organ of the Holy Spirit, joining pomegranates, symbols of virtues, to little bells, symbols of preaching. By his example and devout manner of life, he led a great number of Christians to the practice of good; by teaching sweeter than honey, he gave them knowledge. Through the books that he composed, as subtle as they were gracious, on faith and morals, he dug a great number of wells of living water. He uncovered the secrets of divine learning. His memory has remained among us like a delightful perfume, like fragrant honey, like music at a feast, like a ship carrying abundant fruits [Col. LB] to posterity.” [Note: [Col. LD] *Historia occidentalis*, ch. 28.]

Trithemius depicts him as a man profoundly versed in the Holy Scriptures, without equal among the ancients in philosophy, another Augustine, the most celebrated doctor of his age, of penetrating genius, elegant in style, and as venerable for his conduct as for his learning. [Note: [Col. LD] *Universal History of Paris*, vol. II, p. 748.] Miracles were even attributed to him. It is certain that he was as much venerated for his holiness as he was honoured for his learning. Posterity, which knows him only through his works, has not contradicted the universal testimony of his contemporaries.

## CHAPTER IV. HUGH’S PHILOSOPHY. THE RELATIONSHIP OF PHILOSOPHY AND THEOLOGY.

[Col. LC]

Aristotle did not reign alone in the Middle Ages; Plato had his disciples; and since Boethius, who seems to have wished to reconcile the two rival schools, the chain of Platonic philosophers was never entirely broken. Alongside scholasticism mysticism arose and developed. Hugh of Saint-Victor was one link in this chain and one of the most illustrious mystics of the twelfth century. He professed Plato’s doctrine, not as that philosopher had taught it, but as Saint Augustine had corrected, purified, and completed it through Catholic dogma.

It is not, however, in the purely [Col. LD] philosophical works of our Victorine that one must seek Platonism. In his time philosophy was little cultivated for its own sake. Sacred learning was almost the sole field upon which intellectual activity was exercised; or at least all the other sciences served only as preparation for the study of theology.

Fortunately, theology is not philosophy’s enemy. These two sciences are not opposed. If they were, one would necessarily have to choose: adopt one and reject the other. For if one were good, the other would be bad; if one were useful, the other harmful; if [Col. LIA] one contributed to the development of the human mind, the other would lead societies toward decline. But this hostility does not exist. Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Saint Augustine, Saint Anselm, Saint Thomas, and so many others who have known so well how to reconcile them bear witness to this. They are two lights kindled at the same hearth and illuminating the same path; they are two sisters who join hands, and offer their hands to humanity to lead it toward the same end.

The mere exposition of Hugh’s doctrine will furnish fresh testimony in favour of this truth which so many enlightened men are striving today to establish.

The starting-point is evidently the very notion [Col. LIB] of knowledge.

“Knowledge, according to Hugh, is the natural result of exercising the faculties of the soul; it is divided into two principal branches: theology properly so called, and philosophy, which comprises all the arts.” [Note: [Col. LIC] *Didascalicon*, book I, ch. 1, vol. II, col. 741.]

These two parts of knowledge are distinguished from one another by their object. “God,” he says, “has made two works which encompass the whole universe of beings: creation and restoration. Through creation things which were not came into being; through restoration things that existed became better. Creation, therefore, is the production of the world and all its elements. Restoration is the Incarnation of the Word, and all the sacraments—those which [Col. LIC] preceded it from the beginning of the world, and those which followed it and will yet follow it until the consummation of the ages . . . For the incarnate Word is our king; he came into this world to fight the devil. All the saints who existed before his coming are like soldiers marching before his face; and those who came after him and are yet to come are soldiers following him. He himself is in the midst of his army, marching at the centre of his battalion; and although in so great a multitude the weapons—that is, [Col. LIIA] the sacraments and religious observances—are different, those who precede and those who follow, all arrayed around the same king, fight beneath the same standard, pursue the same enemy, and gain the same victory. The science of creation is philosophy; the science of restoration is theology.” [Note: [Col. LIC] *De sacramentis*, prologue, book I, ch. 2, vol. II, col. 183: “There are two works in which are contained all things that have been made. The first is the work of creation; the second is the work of restoration. The work of creation is that by which things that did not exist were made to exist. The work of restoration is that by which things that had perished were made to exist in a better condition. Therefore, the work of creation is the creation of the world with all its elements; the work of restoration is the incarnation of the Word with all its sacraments, whether those which preceded from the beginning of the age, or those which follow until the end of the world . . . For the incarnate Word is our king, who came into this world to fight against the devil; and all the saints who were before his coming are, as it were, soldiers advancing before the face of the king, and those who afterwards came and shall come until the end of the world are soldiers following their king. The king himself is in the midst of his army, proceeding protected on either side and surrounded by his troops. And although, in this great multitude, the types of weapons differ in the sacraments and observances [Col. LIIC] of the peoples preceding and following, nevertheless all are shown to serve one king, follow one standard, pursue one enemy, and be crowned with one [Col. LIID] victory. In all these things are considered the works of restoration, in which the entire purpose of the divine Scriptures is engaged. Worldly or secular writings have as their subject the works of creation. Divine Scripture has as its subject the work of restoration.”]

If philosophy and theology have as their object, respectively, scientific knowledge of the natural world and scientific knowledge of the supernatural world, they find in this object both what distinguishes and what unites them. They are distinct because these two worlds are distinct; they are united because these two worlds are manifestations of the same Word of God.

[Col. LIIB] Hugh develops this truth, which reveals to us the secret bond that connects and subordinates to one another these two branches of universal knowledge, and which shows us their excellence.

Philosophy, he says, is love of wisdom: of that wisdom which needs nothing, which is a living mind, the sole and first principle of all things. It is the illumination of an intelligent mind by this wisdom which draws and calls it. It is a kind of friendship between a pure mind and the Divinity. [Note: [Col. LIID] *Didascalicon*, book I, ch. 3, vol. II, col. 743: “Philosophy is love, pursuit, and in a certain sense friendship with wisdom . . . This love of wisdom is the illumination of an intelligent mind by that pure wisdom, and in a certain sense its drawing back and calling to itself, so that the pursuit of wisdom appears to be friendship of the Divinity and of that pure mind.”]

Elsewhere he explains every term in his definition.

Philosophy is the love of wisdom which needs nothing. By these words one must understand [Col. LIIC] divine wisdom, which can experience no need because it loses nothing of what it contains, and contemplates all things—the present, past, and future—in one and the same glance.

It is called a living mind because nothing erases what is impressed upon the divine reason; it is subject to no forgetfulness.

It is the first principle of all things because all things were formed in its likeness. [Note: [Col. LIID] Same work, same place, book II, ch. 1, vol. II, col. 751: “Philosophy is the love of wisdom, which, needing nothing, is a living mind and the sole primordial principle of things . . . By the addition ‘which needs nothing, a living mind, and the sole primordial principle of things,’ divine wisdom is signified. It is said to need nothing because it contains nothing less, but beholds past, present, and future things all at once and together. It is called a living mind because whatever once exists in the divine reason is never erased by any forgetfulness. It is the primordial principle of things because all things were formed in its likeness.”]

According to Hugh, then, philosophy is the knowledge [Col. LIIIA] and love of God’s reason or wisdom manifested through creation. This wisdom is not distinct from God: it is his intelligence, his Word, his Son eternally begotten in the bosom of his Father.

In his *Commentary on the Gospel of Saint John*, he explains this passage: “All things were made through the Word, and nothing which has been made was made without him; life was in him.” After giving the two versions of this text, he adopts Saint Augustine’s and says: “All things were made through him; nothing was made without him; what was made was life in him.” He then adds: [Note: [Col. LIIIC] *Explanatory Notes on the Gospel of John*, ch. 2, vol. I, [Col. LIIID] col. 834: “Lest anyone view God according to created things, and suppose that, just as mutability is in them, so it is in the Creator, he shows that God created all mutable things without change. For it is said of him: ‘remaining himself unmoved . . .’ For just as, when an artisan conceives something in his mind, the likeness remains and is not changed when the work is moved, so God, Creator of all things, from eternity comprehends in his wisdom all things that he was going to make, but immutably. Hence there is not complete similarity between the mind of the artisan and the divine mind, because there is motion in the artisan’s conception: there is before and after, and therefore change. But in divine comprehension there is no motion and no change, since God himself is that very comprehension. Hence it is said that he has ordered all things sweetly—that is, without motion or labour. For this sweetness it is said there that what was made is life; for the Father has life in himself. Therefore the life which is in him differs from the life of a human being, which is the soul, and from the life of the soul, although the soul’s [Col. LIVC] life is the soul itself; for it has in itself the motion of living and does not derive it from another creature. Yet the soul itself is inferior in three respects to the life which is God: it is mutable, it has a beginning, and it can have an end. But God’s life is unchangeable and has neither beginning nor end. Hence it alone is true life. As the Evangelist says, ‘what was made in him [Col. LIVD] was life’: that is, God, from whom are all things, fulfilled in time without change what he had foreseen from eternity. For through wisdom, which he himself is, God disposed all things from eternity and fulfilled in time what he had disposed. Thus all things have both life and being from God’s wisdom; and consequently they are rightly called life there, because they derive life from it. Or, they were life in him because every thing that was made was made according to the wisdom of God, which is the life of all things. For this was God’s exemplar, after the likeness of which this whole sensible world was made. Nor should one say that certain principles exist in the divine mind, standing beneath the Creator and above creatures. For there is nothing in God which is not God, nor can there be a diversity of properties where there is nothing but being. For in God, being and living are the same. Therefore he is a simple essence, lacking parts and properties.”]

“Lest anyone should assimilate God to creatures and suppose that mutability is in him as [Col. LIIIB] it is in them, the Evangelist first shows that he created all changeable things without losing his immutability. For it is said of him:

> Remaining unmoved, you yourself grant motion.”

Just as a workman conceives in his mind a model which remains and does not change along with the work that outwardly manifests it, so God, the creator of all things, comprehends from all eternity, in his wisdom, all the things that he was to make; and this wisdom is unchangeable. The likeness between the workman’s understanding and the divine reason is therefore not complete. In the workman’s conception there is movement, because there is succession and variation. In God’s reason there is neither movement nor variation, God himself being [Col. LIIIC] his own reason. Therefore it is said that he orders all things sweetly, that is, without movement and without toil. This sweetness leads the Evangelist to say that what was made is life in him; for the Father has life in himself. Hence the life which is in him differs from the life of man, which is the soul, and even from the life of the soul itself, although the life [Col. LIVA] of the soul is the soul itself; for it has within itself the movement of life and does not receive it from another creature. Yet the human soul is inferior to the life which is God in three respects: because it is mutable, has a beginning, and can have an end. The life of God is immutable; it has neither beginning nor end. Therefore it alone is true life.

This is what causes the Evangelist to say that what was made is life in him: that is, God foresaw all things in eternity and made them mutable in time. For God, through the wisdom which is in him, ordered all things from eternity; and what he ordered from eternity, he accomplished in time. Thus all things received both life and existence from [Col. LIVB] the wisdom of God. It is therefore right to say that they were life there whence they drew life; or again, that there was life there, because everything that was made was made according to the wisdom of God, which is the life of all things. This was God’s exemplar, and the whole world was made in the image of this exemplar. It is the archetypal world, after whose image the sensible world was made.

For one must not say that there are ideas in the divine intelligence situated beneath the Creator and above the creature; there is nothing in God which is not God. There can be no diversity of properties where nothing exists but being. In God, to be and to live are one and the same thing. Therefore he is a pure essence, without [Col. LIVC] parts and without properties.

In this Commentary one recognizes the disciple of Saint Augustine much more than the disciple of Plato. But he is an intelligent disciple, not merely the echo of his master’s teaching: he has meditated upon it, understood it, savored it. He does not reproduce it as a servile compiler, laboriously and heavily, but with freedom, ease, and an originality proper to himself.

[Col. LVA] Saint Augustine developed the same doctrine in commenting upon the same passage; and he did so in circumstances showing how important it was in his eyes. For it was not in some learned commentary, in a dogmatic treatise, or before select men trained in the meditations of learning; it was in a popular discourse, in familiar instruction, and among ordinary believers. He therefore did not regard it as one of those idle speculations, those arbitrary theories permitted in schools but banished from Christian pulpits. Nor was it thus received by the crowd pressing around him. One does not know what one should admire more: the flexibility of the holy doctor’s genius, striving to make these sublime truths perceptible in order to instill them into simple and sometimes uncultivated minds; or the eagerness of his hearers, who never tired of hearing him and, in their enthusiasm, interrupted him with frequent applause.

We place this passage beside that of Hugh; it will show us how the disciple knew how to appropriate the master’s lessons.

> [Note: [Col. LVC] *Tractates on the Gospel of John*, 1: “Therefore, brothers, all things absolutely were made through him, and without him nothing was made. But how were all things made through him? ‘What was made in him is life.’ For it can be said thus: ‘What was made in him is life.’ Therefore everything is life, if we pronounce it in that way. For what was not made in him? … If therefore all things are in him, most beloved brothers, and what was made in him is life, then the earth too is life, then wood too is life … It is improper to understand it this way, lest the same most filthy sect of the Manichaeans again creep in upon us and say that a stone has life, that a wall has a soul, and that a little cord, wool, and clothing have souls. For such are the ravings they are accustomed to utter; and when they have been checked and refuted, they bring forward Scripture, as though from the Scriptures, saying: Why was it said, ‘What was made in him is life’? …
>
> “What does this mean? The earth was made, but the earth itself which was made is not life. Yet in Wisdom itself there is spiritually a certain rational principle by which the earth was made; this is life. How can I explain it to your charity? A craftsman makes a chest. First he possesses the chest in his art; [Col. LVIC] for unless he possessed it in his art, whence could he bring it forth by making it? But the chest is in the art in such a way that it is not itself the chest seen by the eyes. Invisibly it is in the art; [Col. LVID] visibly it will be in the work. Behold, it has been made in the work: has it ceased to be in the art? Both that chest was made in the work, and that which is in the art remains; for that chest can decay, and another can again be made from that which is in the art. Consider, therefore, the chest in the art and the chest in the work. The chest in the work is not life; the chest in the art is life, because the soul of the craftsman lives, wherein all things are before they are brought forth.
>
> “Thus, therefore, most beloved brothers, since the wisdom of God, through which all things were made, contains all things according to art before it makes all things: the things made through that art are not at once life; but whatever was made is life in him. You see earth: earth is in the art. You see heaven: heaven is in the art. You see sun and moon: these too are in the art. But outwardly they are bodies; in the art they are life. See whether you can understand this in some measure; for a great thing has been said.”]

“All things were made through the Word, and without him nothing was made. But how were all things made through him? What was made was life in him. If everything that was made is life in him, are we not saying that everything is life? For what thing was not [Col. LVC] made through him? Not only was everything made through him; everything was made in him. But if everything made was made in him, and everything made in him is life, then the earth is life, wood is life … This cannot be said, lest the coarse sect of the Manichaeans present itself to us and tell us that a stone has life, a wall is animated, and a small cord, wool, and clothes have a soul. This is indeed what they teach in their madness; and when one refutes and confounds them, they appeal to the Holy Scriptures and produce [Col. LVIA] as proof of their opinion this saying of the Gospel according to Saint John: ‘What was made in him was life.’ Saint Augustine rejects this reading and insists that one should read, not ‘What was made in him was life,’ but ‘What was made was life in him.’

“What does this mean?” he adds. “The earth was made, and it is not life. In Wisdom itself there is a certain spiritual idea through which the earth was made, and this idea is life. I shall explain my thought as best I can. A craftsman makes a piece of furniture: first he has that piece in his art; he conceives in his mind the idea of an object, for if he did not possess this idea, how could he execute it? He would make it without knowing what he was doing, without [Col. LVIB] understanding and without wisdom.

“But this idea in his mind is not the object that strikes our gaze. It is invisible in the art; it will be visible in the work. Once it has passed into the work, does it cease to be in the workman’s mind which conceived it?

“It has been expressed in the work, and it has remained in the art. For this object, the workman’s outward work, may decay, and the workman may make a new one according to the same model. Distinguish carefully, then, the object in the art from the object in the work. The material, physical object is not life, although it is quite real; but the object in the art is life, because the soul of the craftsman—in which all things exist before they [Col. LVIC] are manifested—is life.

“In the same way,” the holy doctor continues, “in the same way, most beloved brothers, the wisdom of God, through whom everything was made, contained all things according to art before making them. Consequently, everything made by this art is not life in itself; but everything that was made is life in the Word. You see the earth: this earth is in the art. You see the heaven: heaven is in the art. You see the sun and moon: they are in the art. Outwardly they are bodies; in the art they are life. Understand, if you can,” [Col. LVIIA] Saint Augustine adds, “for I have told you a great truth.” [Note: [Col. LVIIC] Augustine, *On John*.]

Indeed, he has just laid the foundation of a great and beautiful philosophy. Hugh, like his master, is convinced of the importance of this doctrine. He reproduces it in every form in several of his works.

In his *Treatise on the Sacraments*, he says: “Every creature has a cause and an image in the reason of God and in his eternal providence; and by means of this cause and according to the model of this image it was created in its substance. But there is a great difference and a great distance between having a likeness and an image in God, and having God himself as likeness and image. Although nothing in [Col. LVIIB] God is less than God, different from him, or other than him, it is one thing to be made in the likeness of that which is in God, in his reason and in his providence, and another to be made in the likeness of God and to be like God. For all things were in God before they were in themselves. They were in him according to the reason, cause, and providence from which they were to pass into existence.”

> [Note: [Col. LVIID] *De Sacramentis*, book I, part V, chapter 3, vol. II, col. 247: “Although every creature had its cause and likeness in the divine reason and in his eternal providence, from which and according to which it was perfected in its own substance, yet there is a great difference and a great distance between having a likeness in God and having God himself as one’s likeness. For although in God nothing can exist as if less than, different from, or other than God, nevertheless it is far otherwise for something to have been made according to the likeness of that which is in God, in his reason and in his providence, and to have been made according to the likeness of God and to be like God. For indeed all things were in God before they existed in themselves, according to the reason, cause, and providence from which they were to come to be.”]

Meditating on this magnificent doctrine, his heart grows warm and his mind is exalted; he does not know how to express the feelings of admiration and love crowding into his soul.

“The good Word and wise Life which made the world,” he says, “is manifested in the contemplation of creation. The Word itself was invisible, and it made itself visible and was seen through its works.” [Note: [Col. LVIID] *Didascalicon*, book VII, chapter 1, vol. II, col. 811.]

[Col. LVIIC] “Oh, if only I could comprehend in their particulars, and express worthily, the beauty of the creatures which I ardently love … It is sweet and pleasant to me; it is an ineffable happiness to treat these subjects often. This study enlightens my reason, delights my soul, and stirs my heart, so that, carried away in admiration, I cry out with the Prophet: ‘How beautiful are your works, O Lord! You have made all things in your wisdom … You have made me glad in your works; I shall triumph in the works of your hands! How beautiful are your works, O Lord! How deep are your thoughts! The foolish man does not know these things; he does not understand [Col. LVIIIA] them.’” [Note: [Col. LVIID] *Didascalicon*, book VII, chapter 4, vol. II, col. 814.]

“… For the world is a book written by the very finger of God. Every creature is like a sign, not invented by man but established by the divine will. An illiterate person sees an open book: he perceives the marks, but knows neither the letters nor the thought they express. Likewise the foolish person, the animal man who does not perceive the things of God, sees the outward appearance of visible creatures but does not understand the thoughts which they manifest. The spiritual man, on the contrary, beneath this outward and sensible appearance contemplates and admires the wisdom of the Creator; just as, in one and the same writing, one person praises the color or shape of the letters, while another praises the thought which they express. Thus it is good to contemplate [Col. LVIIIB] and admire God’s works continually, but only for one who knows how to turn the beauty of bodily things to spiritual use.”

> [Note: [Col. LVIIIC] Same work, same place: “Just as, if an illiterate person [Col. LVIIID] sees an open book, he looks at the figures but does not recognize the letters, so the foolish and animal man, who does not perceive the things of God, outwardly sees the appearance in these visible creatures, but inwardly does not understand their rationale. But the spiritual person, who can judge all things, while outwardly considering the beauty of the work, inwardly grasps how marvelous is the Creator’s knowledge. Thus there is no one for whom the works of God are not wonderful; but the foolish man marvels in them only at their appearance, whereas the wise person, through what he sees outwardly, investigates the profound thought of divine wisdom. It is as if, in one and the same writing, one praised the color or formation of the figures, while another praised its meaning and signification. It is therefore good to contemplate and admire divine works, but for one who knows how to turn the beauty of bodily things to spiritual use.”]

Creation, therefore, is the manifestation of God’s thought and wisdom, just as speech manifests man’s thought and wisdom, or as a work manifests the thought and wisdom of the artist. The world is a great book; it is a discourse revealing God’s glory and power. Therefore man must read this book; he must listen to this discourse and so rise to the knowledge of the Creator—not only by inference, as one rises from effect to cause, but by contemplation, as one rises from sign to the thing signified, from [Col. LVIIIC] word to thought.

Such was the original order. But human intelligence, weakened by sin, languishing and sick, almost always stops at the sensible and gross element, at the outward and material sign. Creation has become dark to it; it is a veil which has ceased to be transparent for it. It lives more by sensations than by truths; it is more in the contingent and mutable than in the necessary and immutable. The animal part dominates and holds the intelligent part captive. Therefore God willed, through the incarnation, to make a new manifestation of his Word, which would be at once a [Col. LIXA] restoration and a continuation of creation.

We read in the *Commentary on the Divine Hierarchy*: “Two images were set before man by which he might see invisible things: one of nature and one of grace. The image of nature was the appearance of this world; the image of grace was the humanity of the Word. In both God was shown, but in neither was he understood. Nature, indeed, displayed the Maker through its beauty, but could not illumine the eyes of the one contemplating it. But the humanity of the Savior was a remedy, so that the blind might receive light, and also instruction, so that when seeing they might recognize the truth. He made mud from spittle and anointed the blind man’s eyes; he washed and saw. And what afterward? Then he said to one who saw and yet did not know: ‘I am he; and he who speaks with you is the Son of God’ (John 9).”

> [Note: [Col. LIXC] *In Explanatione coelestis hierarchiae magni Dionysii*, chapter 1: “Two images were set before [Col. LIXD] man, in which he could see invisible things: one of nature and one of grace. The image of nature was the appearance of this world; the image of grace was the humanity of the Word. In both God was shown, but in neither was he understood, because nature by its appearance displayed its maker but could not illumine the eyes of the contemplator. But the humanity of the Savior was both a remedy, that the blind might receive light, and instruction, that when seeing they might recognize the truth. He made mud from spittle and anointed the blind man’s eyes; he washed and saw. And what then? Afterwards he said to the one seeing but not yet knowing: ‘I am he, and he who speaks with you is the Son of God’ (John IX).”]

Elsewhere he says: “Man possesses a twofold sense: one operates through the organs of the body; by it we are related to outward and sensible things. The other is reason; it relates us to spiritual and invisible things.” Angels have only the second; brute animals only the first; and human beings both.

The angels, whose sense was inward, contemplated the things which were inward and, through them, the things which were outward. Brute animals, whose sense was outward, apprehended only the visible things outside, but not the invisible [Col. LIXC] things within. For those who see invisible things see visible things in them, because visible things are known through invisible things. But those who see visible things do not thereby see invisible things, because the sense by which invisible things are perceived comprehends lower things in higher ones, whereas the sense by which we apprehend visible things does not comprehend higher things in lower ones. Thus there was one creature whose sense was wholly inward, and another whose [Col. LXA] sense was wholly outward. Man was placed between them, and possessed an inward and an outward sense: an inward sense for invisible things and an outward sense for visible things; inwardly, the sense of reason; outwardly, the sense of the flesh. Thus he could enter and contemplate, go out and contemplate again: inwardly, wisdom; outwardly, the works of wisdom; and he could be refreshed by this twofold contemplation—seeing, rejoicing, loving, and praising. Wisdom was inward pasture; the work of wisdom was outward pasture. Man’s sense was admitted to range through both, and to find nourishment in both. It traversed them through knowledge and was nourished by love. Wisdom was a book written within; the works of wisdom were a book written without.

> [Note: [Col. LIXD] *De Sacramentis*, book I, part VI, chapter 5, vol. II, col. 266: “The angels, whose sense was inward, contemplated the things which were within, and through them the things which were without. Brute animals, whose sense was outward, came into contact with the visible things which were without, but not likewise through them with the invisible things which were within. For those who see invisible things see visible things in them, because visible things are known through [Col. LXC] invisible things; but those who see visible things do not equally see invisible things in them, because the sense by which visible things are apprehended does not grasp the higher things in the lower. Thus one creature existed whose sense was wholly within, and another whose sense was wholly without. And man was placed in the middle so that he might have sense within and without: within for invisible things, without for visible things; within through the sense of reason, without through the sense of flesh; that he might enter and contemplate and go out and contemplate: wisdom within, the works of wisdom without; that he might contemplate both and be refreshed from each, see and rejoice and love and praise. Wisdom was pasture within; the work of wisdom was pasture without. And man’s sense was admitted to go to both and find refreshment in both: to go through knowledge and be refreshed through love. Wisdom was a book written within; the work of wisdom was a book written without.”]

The two senses of which Hugh speaks are plainly sensation and the subjective idea, or apprehension of truth. Sensation corresponds to the physical world, and the idea to the spiritual world, which is none other than the very Word of God, of which the physical world is merely the manifestation. Sensation reaches the sign; the idea reaches the thing signified. The sound of speech strikes the ear and produces a sensation in the soul, while light illumines the understanding. This clear and profound distinction between sensation, idea, and the proper nature of each establishes a fine harmony between the metaphysics and psychology of our Victorine, and [Col. LXC] reveals to us God’s plan in the creation of the world.

For in man’s present state, as a consequence of a law which itself results from the union of soul and body, sensation and idea are inseparable. Sensation, blind in itself, is always accompanied by the idea; and it is by the idea that we know all things—that is, through the Word of God, who is the light enlightening every person coming into this world. Thus sensation binds to the soul the body, of which the physical world is merely the extension, just as the idea binds the soul to God. Through sensation the body shares in [Col. LXIA] the intellectual life of the soul; through the idea the soul participates in God’s intellectual life, since the same truth which is the principle of God’s life is the principle of the soul’s life. We grasp the bond joining all creatures to one another and creatures to God, and we glimpse the sublime hierarchy of beings.

Hugh develops this thought in language allegorical in a manner most familiar to him: “Moses,” he says, “went up the mountain, and God came down upon the mountain. Had Moses not gone up, and God not come down, they would not have met.” There are great mysteries in all this. The body goes up and the spirit comes down; the spirit goes up and God comes down. In ascending, the body rises above itself; in [Col. LXIB] descending, the spirit lowers itself beneath itself; then it rises above itself, and God lowers himself beneath himself in descending. The body rises through sense; the spirit descends through sensibility; it rises through contemplation; and God lowers himself through revelation. There is theophany in revelation, understanding in contemplation, imagination in sensibility—in sense, the instrument of sensibility and the source of imagination. See,” he adds, “Jacob’s ladder: it rested upon the earth and its summit touched heaven. Earth is the body; heaven is God. Minds ascend through contemplation from lower things to higher things, from corporeal beings to spiritual beings, by means of the senses and sensibility; to God, by means of contemplation and revelation. God rests upon the summit of the ladder in order to incline higher things toward lower things.”

> [Note: [Col. LXIC] *De unione corporis et spiritus*, vol. III, col. 285: “Moses went up the mountain and God came down upon the mountain. Therefore, unless Moses had gone up and God had come down, they would not have met as one. There are great mysteries in all these things. The body goes up and the spirit comes down. The spirit goes up and God comes down. That to which the body rises is higher than the body; that to which the spirit descends is lower than the spirit. Again, that to which the spirit rises is higher than the spirit, and that to which God descends is lower than God. The body rises through sense; the spirit descends through sensibility. Likewise, the spirit rises through contemplation; God descends through revelation. Theophany is in revelation; understanding in contemplation; imagination in sensibility; in sense, the instrument of sensibility and the origin of imagination. See Jacob’s ladder: it stood upon the earth and its summit touched heaven. Earth: the body; heaven: God. Minds ascend by contemplation from lower things to higher, from body to spirit, through the mediation of contemplation and revelation. But the Lord rests upon the ladder so that higher things may incline toward lower things.”]

Such, according to Hugh, is God’s plan in the first manifestation of his wisdom through the natural world: the first book in which he wrote his name, so that every intelligence might read it, and in reading know him, and in knowing glorify him.

Hugh adds: “Wisdom afterwards willed that it [Col. LXIIA] should be written in another manner, still outwardly, so that it might be seen more plainly and known more perfectly; so that the eye of man might be illumined by the second writing, since it had grown dark in relation to the first. Therefore he made a second work after the first, and it was clearer because it not only showed but also enlightened. He assumed flesh without losing divinity, and he was set forth as a book written within and without: outwardly in humanity, inwardly in divinity; so that outwardly he might be read through imitation, inwardly through contemplation; outwardly for healing, inwardly for blessedness; outwardly for merit, inwardly for joy. Inwardly, ‘In the beginning was the Word’; outwardly, ‘the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.’ Thus the book was one: written once within and twice without—first without through the creation of visible things, and a second time without through the assumption of flesh; first for delight, second for healing; first for nature, second against sin; first that nature might be sustained, second that life might be healed and nature made blessed.”

> [Note: [Col. LXIIC] *De Sacramentis*, book I, part VI, chapter 5, vol. II, col. 266, bottom: “But afterwards Wisdom willed that it should still be written outwardly in another manner, so that it might be seen more plainly and known more perfectly; so that the eye of man might be illumined by the second writing, because it had become dim toward the first. Therefore he made a second work after the first, and it was more evident because it not only showed but also enlightened. He assumed flesh without losing divinity, and was set forth as a book written within and without: outwardly in humanity, inwardly in divinity; so that it might be read outwardly through imitation, inwardly through contemplation; outwardly for healing, inwardly for blessedness; outwardly for the mind, inwardly for joy. Inwardly, ‘In the beginning was the Word’; outwardly, ‘the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.’ Therefore the book was one, written once within and twice without: first outwardly through the creation of visible things, second outwardly through the assumption of flesh; first for delight, second for healing; first for nature, second against sin; first that nature might be sustained, second that life might be healed and nature made blessed.”]

Creation and incarnation are thus God’s two great works. Both are manifestations of his intelligence and his Word. But in the first we know him through his [Col. LXIIC] works, as we know the thought of an artist through the products of his art; in the second he comes to us in person. The first is a book written by his hand; the second is rather a word proceeding from his mouth.

God wished to associate man with the accomplishment of his works, as he had associated him with his own life by communicating his truth. Through man, he continues to write in this great book and to trace new words in it. What is the institution of the woman, if not the association of man with God’s action in perpetuating and preserving the human race? What is [Col. LXIIIA] art? What is the artist? What are his works, if not words revealing an idea? The artist takes raw matter—marble, stone—works it, shapes it, gives it a face. But there is an inward model on which he fixes the gaze of his intelligence, and which guides his hand and his art. This model is reproduced; it has passed into matter, is its form, and gives it unity and beauty. Matter expresses it and reveals it; and if I know how to read this writing, if there is something of the artist in me, then in contemplating his work I contemplate his idea and share in his delight.

But is this model itself something real? Is it pure imagination, a mere modification of my soul? No: art is more than [Col. LXIIIB] the echo of a blind sensation, and the sense of beauty belongs to a higher order than material pleasures. It has its seat in the higher part of the soul; an unintelligent being has never known or experienced it. If this model has objective reality, did intelligence create it? But how could man, who cannot produce unformed matter and has only the power to modify it—and even that within certain limits—create this idea, more excellent than matter, since it is the idea that gives matter its unity and beauty? It remains, therefore, to recognize that the artist merely contemplates it. But it does not exist because he sees it; he sees it because it exists. It existed before he [Col. LXIIIC] discovered it; it existed eternally in the divine intelligence.

We now understand the sublimity of the arts and the dignity of the artist: they appear to us as continuing the work of creation. God finds and contemplates within himself these eternal models of beings; man must seek them in God. God possesses them as his own natural good; man possesses them as an alien good communicated to him. God creates the matter which must express his thought; man receives it as he receives the idea. He creates nothing; he merely joins the one to the other. Inspired by religion, the arts accomplish a similar work in the supernatural order.

Here is another remarkable passage, taken [Col. LXIIID] from the treatise *On the Wisdom of Christ, and on Christ the Wisdom*: “The Word was wisdom … [lacuna] This wisdom is the light which, according to Scripture, enlightens every person coming into this world. But, you will say to me, does it also enlighten the wicked? Yes, because it is also written that the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. For just as there is only one sun by which all things are illumined, although it is not perceived by every eye [Col. LXIVA] which sees by its means, so the true light of which Scripture speaks is poured out upon all people, shines for all, and enlightens all. But some see only with its aid; others see it itself. The wicked are enlightened in order to see everything except him who makes them see; others, on the contrary, are enlightened in order to see him who serves as their light. Thus, referring the various objects of their knowledge to him, they love only in him everything that they see, and love him himself above everything that they see. All people, therefore, participate in this light, but those do so in a more excellent way who have the happiness of knowing it itself.”

We can only indicate these ideas, which arise naturally from Hugh’s doctrine and complete it. [Col. LXIVB] They suffice to show us how he conceived God’s general plan in all his works, and, within that plan, the distinction and union of the natural and supernatural worlds, and consequently of philosophy and theology. They are distinguished and united in their object, which is truth; they are distinguished because God has given a twofold manifestation of that truth in creation and in the Incarnation; they are united because there is but one eternal, indivisible, infinite truth, one light that enlightens every person coming into this world, one wisdom and one Word of God. It is the unity, identity, and unalterable [Col. LXIVC] purity of truth that unites all intelligences with one another, binds them to God, and establishes, in the intellectual world, a holy and living harmony.

To these two revelations correspond two kinds of knowledge, related to one another as their objects are: one natural, the other supernatural; distinct, yet united—distinct as the revelations themselves are, united because it is the same faculty that receives them both. Hugh acknowledges them. He affirms the existence of reason together with the existence of faith, communicated to reason in order to heal and perfect it. … “There are,” he says, “two modes, two ways, two manifestations through which, from the beginning, God, hidden, has disclosed himself to the [Col. LXIVD] human heart: human reason and divine revelation. Reason discovers God by a twofold inquiry: it discovers him within itself and in things outside itself. Likewise, divine revelation makes known by a twofold intimation the God who was unknown, or in whom there was only doubtful belief. It indicates what was not known; it confirms faith in what was already known.”

> [Note: [Col. LXIIID] *De sacramentis*, bk. I, pt. III, ch. 3, vol. II, col. 217: “There are two modes, two ways, and two manifestations by which, from the beginning, God—hidden—has been disclosed and proclaimed, though concealed, to the human heart: partly by human reason, partly by divine revelation. Human reason, indeed, apprehends God [Col. LXIVD] by a twofold inquiry: namely, partly within itself, partly in those things which were outside itself. Similarly, divine revelation, by a twofold intimation, both indicated him who was unknown or doubtfully believed, and confirmed what was partly believed and not known.”]

The Apostle sets forth these two [Col. LXVA] modes of divine manifestation by which God is known by human beings through human reason and through divine revelation. “What is known of God,” he says, “was manifest in them.” — The Apostle is speaking of pagan philosophers. — “God revealed it to them.” He adds: “For the invisible things of God, understood through the creation of the world by means of the things that have been made, are seen.” When the Apostle says, “What was known of God,” that is, what was intelligible concerning God, he shows that not everything was hidden, just as not everything was known. When he says that what was intelligible concerning God was manifested *in* them, and not *to* them, he clearly shows that this manifestation was made to them not only through divine revelation, but also through the human [Col. LXVB] reason that was in them.

> [Note: [Col. LXVD] *De sacramentis*, bk. I, pt. III, ch. 3: “The Apostle explains both modes of divine manifestation, by which God has either been known by man through human reason or made manifest to man by divine revelation, saying: ‘What was known of God was manifest in them, for God revealed it to them.’ And then he adds: ‘For his invisible things, understood from the creation of the world through the things that have been made, are seen.’ … For when he says, ‘What was known of God,’ that is, what was knowable concerning God, he shows that neither was everything hidden nor everything manifest. But when he says, ‘It was manifest in them,’ and does not say, ‘It was manifest to them,’ he plainly shows that it was made known to them not only by the divine revelation made to them, but also by the human reason that was in them.”]

Whether Hugh rightly or wrongly understands the Apostle’s thought matters little; we shall examine only his personal doctrine. Now it is evident that he recognizes the value of natural reason and presents divine revelation merely as assistance given to it—assistance which, far from destroying it, perfects it.

In chapter 5 he says again: “We must consider how the human mind, which is so far from God, could comprehend so much concerning him, whether directed by its own reason or aided by divine revelation.”

> [Note: [Col. LXVD] *De sacramentis*, bk. I, pt. III, ch. 5, col. [Col. LXVID] 218: “Now we must … consider how the human mind, which is so far from God, could comprehend so much concerning God, either directed by its own reason or aided by divine revelation.”]

A few lines below: “Human reason, directed by its own light and instructed by the [Col. LXVC] natural and visible creatures placed outside itself, has risen toward knowledge of the true.”

> [Note: [Col. LXVID] *Id.*, ibid.]

In chapter 6: “Let us first consider what was in reason itself, since this too was for it the first and principal mirror in which truth is contemplated. In it the invisible God could first and most especially be seen, so far as manifestation is concerned, because it was made nearest and most akin to his image and likeness. This, moreover, was reason itself and the mind using reason, made according to the primary likeness of God, so that it could find by itself him by whom it was made.”

> [Note: [Col. LXVID] *De sacramentis*, bk. I, pt. III, ch. 6, col. 219: “And let us first consider what was in it [reason], since this too was its first and principal mirror for contemplating truth. In it, therefore, the invisible God could first and most especially be seen, so far as manifestation is concerned, because it had been made nearest and most akin to his image and likeness. This, moreover, was reason itself and the mind using reason, made according to the primary likeness of God, so that it could find by itself him by whom it was made.”]

These two distinct revelations provide the distinct principles of two sciences which are harmonized as they are, yet are never confused. The human intellect does not possess in itself either existence or truth. God communicates both to it. On receiving truth it adheres to it, [Col. LXVD] and by adhering to it [Col. LXVIA] enters into possession of natural or supernatural life, according as the truth communicated to it belongs to one or the other of these orders. But its activity does not stop at this first act: it studies the truth it possesses; it contemplates, analyzes, and penetrates it more deeply; it makes it more its own; it is illuminated, warmed, and quickened by its rays; and it is, in a sense, transformed into truth itself. Thus pure crystal is illumined by the sun’s rays, diffuses light and warmth around it, and, without losing its own nature, becomes like another sun. This labor is the work of science. Therefore every science resting upon other foundations is false; every philosopher or theologian who gives it as a basis a principle contrary to these primary truths, or who, in the chain of deductions, reaches consequences contradictory to them, builds an edifice on sand or pulls down with one hand what he builds with the other. If, in the supernatural order, these first principles are called principles of faith, the authority that preserves them, without preventing their development, does not make science impossible; on the contrary, it protects science by keeping it within its proper limits.

Thus we return to our Victorine’s starting-point: science is the result of the exercise of our faculties; it is essentially the work of man, just as intellect and faith are essentially the work of God. The first [Col. LXVIC] principles of reason and the principles of faith are immutable, but science is mobile: it can progress or decline. At the same time we reach this conclusion: philosophy and theology are united and distinct, like their object and their principles. They must proceed together, without fighting one another and without being confused with one another; they have the same origin and lead to the same end.

# CHAPTER V. HUGH’S METHOD. HIS MYSTICISM

Hugh’s method is naturally connected with the general principles of his doctrine. For if all beings are revelatory words, if all [Col. LXVID] God’s outward works form a great book expressing his wisdom and truth, we must [Col. LXVIIA] attain knowledge of them as one reaches knowledge of thought through speech, and knowledge of an idea through a sign: that is, by meditation and contemplation. Hugh therefore takes pleasure in setting out their rules. They recur in a thousand places in his writings. He himself collected and summarized them in a short treatise, *On the Art of Meditating and Speaking*, preserved for us by Dom Martène.

Three things are necessary for the true student to make progress in science: certain dispositions of the will, certain qualities of the intellect, and wise cultivation.

The first disposition is a high esteem for truth, leading us to neglect no kind of knowledge; [Col. LXVIIB] the second is not to be ashamed to learn, even from those beneath us; the third is to practise humility when one possesses knowledge.

The qualities of the intellect are a happy natural endowment, quick to grasp truth, and a faithful memory that retains it. Memory is cultivated by repeated exercises. To lighten its burden and make it more powerful, what is entrusted to it must be summarized; details weary and exhaust it.

Genius is developed by reading and meditation, the two great means through which truth is communicated to the intellect.

Meditation begins with reading, but it is not bound by reading’s rules. The intellect [Col. LXVIIC] delights in giving itself free scope wherever it can rest its gaze upon the contemplation of truth. It takes pleasure in seeking the causes now of one thing, now of another; in penetrating the deepest truths; and in dispelling every obscurity and uncertainty.

Reading is the beginning of science, and meditation is its crown. Whoever loves meditation and makes it familiar by frequent practice gains a pleasant life and prepares for himself great consolation in tribulation. Above all, meditation drives from the soul the tumultuous noise of earthly things and makes it taste, even in this life, as it were the first fruits of [Col. LXVIID] eternal rest. In meditation, it learns to [Col. LXVIIIA] know through creatures him who made them. For this reason it enlightens the soul through knowledge and fills it with joy.

Hugh distinguishes three degrees in meditation: thought, meditation properly so called, and contemplation. At the first degree the intellect stops at the general notion of the things it perceives; at the second it fixes its gaze upon truth itself, studies and considers it attentively, strives to free it from the shadows surrounding it, and to penetrate what is most secret in it. Contemplation is the clear and free vision of the mind, perceiving without clouds truths hitherto obscure.

He establishes this distinction between meditation and contemplation: meditation has as its object a truth still obscure, contemplation an evident truth. In meditation the mind seeks to tear away the veil; in contemplation it enjoys the truth it possesses. Contemplation begins with creatures, rises to the Creator, and rests in him.

In the same work he establishes three other degrees in meditation: meditation properly so called, speculation, and contemplation.

In meditation, because the disturbance of the senses and the images arising from the lower part of the soul obscure the intellect, there is a struggle between spirit and flesh.

In speculation the intellect has conquered and rules the senses. But its first sight of [Col. LXVIIIC] pure truth dazzles it. Carried away in admiration, it is agitated and, as it were, outside itself.

In contemplation it is calm; it tastes delights in the full possession of truth and is intoxicated with happiness.

In his *Commentaries on Ecclesiastes*, Hugh makes his thought tangible through a beautiful comparison:

> [Note: [Col. LXVIID] *In Ecclesiast.* homily 1, vol. I, col. 117 middle: “In meditation there is, as it were, a certain struggle of ignorance with knowledge, and the light of truth somehow gleams amid the darkness of error. It is like fire in green wood: at first it catches only with difficulty; but when it has been stirred by a stronger breath and begins to burn more fiercely in the material placed beneath it, we see great masses of smoky darkness rise up and envelop the still modest flame of its sparks, until at last, as the fire gradually grows, all vapor is consumed and the darkness cast down, and a serene brightness appears. Then the victorious flame, running through the whole pile of crackling fuel, reigns freely; circling about the material subjected to it, it touches it with a gentle drawing motion, consumes and penetrates it by licking, and does not rest until, penetrating and entering its innermost parts, it has in some manner drawn into itself all that it finds [Col. LXVIIID] outside itself. But after the fire has burned what was to be consumed, and what has been consumed has wholly passed from its own nature into the likeness and property of fire, every crash falls silent and every noise is hushed; the darts of flame that stood out in the midst are removed, and that fierce and devouring fire, having made all things subject to itself and, by a kind of friendly likeness, embodied with them, settles into deep peace and silence, because it now finds neither anything unlike itself outside itself nor anything opposed to it against itself. Thus fire first appears with flame and smoke; then fire with flame but without smoke; finally, pure fire without flame and smoke.
>
> “So indeed, when our carnal heart, like green wood, has not yet been dried out from the moisture of carnal desire, and receives some spark of divine fear or love, the [Col. LXIXD] smoke of disturbances and passions struggling through wicked desires first arises.
