Then, when the mind is strengthened and begins to burn more powerfully and shine more brightly with the flame of love, all the darkness of disturbances immediately vanishes, and the mind, now pure, opens itself to the contemplation of truth. Finally, after the heart has been pierced by continual contemplation of truth and has entered to the very marrow, with the entire affection of the soul, into the fountain of supreme truth itself, then, wholly kindled, as it were, into that same sweetness and transformed into the fire of love, it rests in complete peace from every noise and disturbance [Col. LXXD].
>
> “First, therefore, because counsel is sought amid the dangers of temptations, meditation is like smoke with flame. Second, because with a pure mind the heart opens itself to the contemplation of truth, the beginning of contemplation is like flame without smoke. Third, because truth has now been found and charity perfected, nothing further is sought beyond the one thing; in the fire of love alone it gently rests in supreme tranquillity and happiness.”]

“The fire,” he says, “takes hold of green wood only with difficulty. But if stirred by a breath, it catches and fastens upon the material given over to it. Then black whirlwinds of smoke rise, and amid them are a few faint sparks. Little by little the blaze increases, the vapor is absorbed, the smoke disperses, and a pure, brilliant radiance appears. [Col. LXVIIID] The victorious, crackling flame runs through the pyre. [Col. LXIXA] Free, it flits about the wood over which it rules; it grazes, penetrates, and crowns it, and does not rest until, insinuating itself into its innermost parts, it has changed into itself all that it found outside itself. But when everything is consumed and has taken on the likeness and property of fire, the noise ceases, the crackling is quieted, the blazing brands are removed, and this fierce and devouring fire, after subjecting all things to itself and, in some sense, transubstantiating all things through a friendly likeness, remains in profound peace and deep silence, because it finds nothing different from itself, no enemy to oppose it. Thus one first sees fire, flame, and smoke; then fire and flame [Col. LXIXB] without smoke; finally fire without either flame or smoke.

“Likewise, our carnal heart is like green wood: it is still penetrated by the moisture of concupiscence. If it receives some spark of divine fear or love, passions rise up: this is the smoke swirling about. Then the mind is strengthened; the flame of love increases and shines with greater force and brilliance. Soon the smoke of passions vanishes. The mind, now pure, rises to the contemplation of truth. Finally, when the heart has been penetrated by truth through this continual contemplation, when it has been kindled by it, when it has been transformed, as it were, into the fire of love, every noise ceases, every agitation is calmed, and it rests in peace. Thus, when amid [Col. LXIXC] trials the soul seeks enlightenment in meditation, there is first flame and smoke. When it has reached the contemplation of truth, in that first instant in which it takes full possession, there is flame without smoke. Finally, when possession of truth is made perfect through charity, there is nothing more to seek: it rests sweetly in the fire of love, in tranquillity and happiness.”

Thus it is through meditation and contemplation that the mystic attains knowledge. The outward and sensible sign, which veils the idea from his intellect, stimulates his activity and awakens, by its presence, his sleeping soul. Having emerged from this kind [Col. LXIXD] of sleep in which it was plunged, the soul fixes its gaze upon the transparent veil illuminated by truth and tries to lift it, so as to contemplate truth more freely in its beauty and splendor.

It is not curiosity alone that impels the [Col. LXXA] mystic to seek truth; it is the desire for perfection. For the end of knowledge, in his view, is the complete development of one’s faculties. Knowledge puts the intellect in possession of truth, which is the principle of life, and gives love its proper object. Intellect goes before, but love always follows, because man is a loving being just as he is an intelligent being. Intellect goes forth to conquer truth; love rests in its enjoyment: it is triumph after battle, peace after war. Intellect begins the work; love crowns it. Science should never separate these two great faculties; it must develop and perfect both, otherwise it would cultivate only one part of man and would be [Col. LXXB] incomplete.

Scholasticism does indeed follow another path. It proceeds through reasoning: it defines and divides; it relates facts to principles and draws consequences from them; it employs analysis and synthesis in turn. While the mystic rushes forward impetuously, his eyes fixed upon the end he seeks to attain, the scholastic advances slowly and cautiously; he surveys the ground and gently removes obstacles. His pace is not swift, but it is sure. Plato’s idealism is the foundation of mysticism, and Aristotle’s dialectic the necessary instrument of scholasticism.

These two methods, apparently opposed, [Col. LXXC] are nevertheless only two different paths tending to the same end: the perfection of man in intellect and will through a fuller possession and purer enjoyment of truth. They therefore do not exclude one another. They answer to two distinct faculties: meditation and reasoning. The former is better suited to discovering truth; the latter to demonstrating or expounding it. The one is more analytic, the other more synthetic. Neither should be condemned in favor of the other. Most great medieval writers knew how to reconcile them and employed them in turn. St Thomas and St Bonaventure were both mystics and scholastics. [Col. LXXD] Hugh of St Victor himself, though inclined toward mysticism by character and genius, left us several scholastic works. Still less should they be confused with the abuse made of them by superficial and frivolous minds. There is a true and a false scholasticism, a true and a false [Col. LXXIA] mysticism. In his sometimes reckless eagerness to reach the goal, the mystic may leave the path leading to it or shatter himself against an unforeseen obstacle. Through excessive caution, the scholastic may forget the end he has proposed to himself and vainly weaken his strength. When he ceases to regard dialectic as merely the instrument of science and makes it his object, he exhausts himself without result. The more numerous his efforts and ingenious his devices, the more childish and sometimes ridiculous they become. They are no more than children’s games, tolerated and even applauded at that age when the intellect needs to acquire suppleness and strength—but only on condition that they remain simple exercises preparing it for the [Col. LXXIB] conquest of truth. The false scholastic resembles men of extraordinary strength who, instead of applying it to useful and honorable labor, display it in the public square to amuse idlers and the curious.

The false mystic is a weak intellect whose gaze cannot rest upon any serious object. Imagination then takes its place; and, instead of the truth it cannot attain, it creates a thousand phantoms and toys with them at will. I would compare it to a man whose diseased eyes could not endure the light or distinguish the objects it illuminates and who, thus deprived of the sight of the world, constructed an imaginary world whose existence and nature were subject to the caprices of his imagination. [Col. LXXIC] His sensibility evaporates, his faculties become excited, but they lack their proper nourishment: they do not possess truth. Excessive hunger often produces delirium.

False scholasticism is ordinarily merely childish or ridiculous; false mysticism can become dangerous when it abandons the fundamental principle that ought to be its point of departure. It appears at almost every period in the history of the Church: at times timid and reserved, veiling its errors beneath the appearance of false piety; at times resolute and dogmatic, rigorously formulating its doctrine. Then it condemns reason as wholly corrupted and completely powerless; [Col. LXXID] it rejects every outward sign, every intermediary between God and the human intellect. God communicates himself directly to the soul; he does everything in it—thinking and willing, knowing and loving. There is no longer, as in true mysticism, a perfection and development of man’s intellectual and moral life through participation in God’s life, but an absorption of the former into the latter. Thus the false mystic’s great work is to destroy his personal activity by gradually diminishing and, if possible, annihilating every act of his faculties: it is contemplation in repose. Perfection, for him, is a state of passivity in which the soul receives the lights of truth without reacting upon it. Having reached that state, he [Col. LXXIIA] participates in God’s very prerogatives: he is immutable like God, sinless like him. For him there is neither outward authority, nor positive or natural law, nor distinction between good and evil. The most shameful passions may stir; their impure waves never reach the higher part of the soul to defile it. It is henceforth in a region pure and inaccessible to the slightest breath of tempest; or rather its life is extinguished, and nothing remains in it but God’s incorruptible life.

Such in particular was the mysticism whose principles the authors of the Reformation renewed by denying human freedom and intellectual activity, and by teaching God’s direct and sole action in producing within us good and evil, faith [Col. LXXIIB] and unbelief, sin and justification. The numerous sects of Anabaptists and illuminists who followed them merely developed their doctrines and drew out their consequences. Yet such men have been celebrated as emancipators of humankind, as heroes of liberty. They overthrew authority, indeed, but replaced it with fanaticism.

Such is not the doctrine of these medieval mystics—Hugh of St Victor, St Bonaventure, and St Thomas. Their mysticism is not a pious daydream, nor the aberrations of a delirious imagination; it is not the denial of reason and the destruction of science; it is not an absorption of the soul into God which makes human [Col. LXXIIC] personality disappear; it is not a vaporous pantheism; it does not identify all things with God. It does not deny creation; on the contrary, the idea of creation is its starting-point. It forms part of an elevated and generous philosophy; it rests upon serious principles, which at least deserve to be studied before being condemned. We may summarize them in a few words:

1. All God’s outward works manifest his thought and Word, as speech manifests human thought. We are associated with this great revelation, and that is the purpose of the law of labor imposed upon all.

[Col. LXXIID] 2. This manifestation has occurred through creation: this is the natural world; and through the Incarnation: this is the supernatural world.

3. To attain true knowledge of God through his works, one must have a pure heart, because true knowledge unites the soul to God and sin obstructs that union. Meditation is the path leading to it.

4. Since the end of science is the perfection of man—that is, the full development of his activity and life—it must exercise intellect and love, furnishing these two faculties with the nourishment necessary to them.

5. Science is always imperfect on earth. Only at the end of our pilgrimage shall we find, [Col. LXXIIIA] in our final end, that full and peaceful possession of truth by intellect and love.

# CHAPTER VI. STUDIES IN THE TWELFTH CENTURY.—HUGH INTRODUCES NOTHING NEW.—HE OPPOSES THE COMIFICIANS.—THE PURPOSE AND DIVISION OF SCIENCE

Hugh did not merely occupy a chair at St Victor; he directed studies, determined the subject-matter of instruction, and marked out the path to be followed by masters and pupils alike. We know the plan he adopted; and if we compare it with that which governed the schools of his time, we shall find that Hugh did not depart from old traditions. He even respected [Col. LXXIIIB] and defended them against the attacks of rash innovators.

The curriculum of studies was not organized in the twelfth century as it is today. Literature did not have the importance it has rightly acquired in modern times. Yet it was not fear of pagan authors that held people back from this study, nor fear of becoming pagan by reading Cicero, Virgil, and Horace. Indeed, what is surprising in reading the writings of that period—when literary cultivation was only a preparation for the other sciences and extended very little beyond grammar—is not ignorance of pagan antiquity, but the numerous citations and evident allusions to passages of writers from Augustan Rome, in treatises seemingly least likely to call forth such recollections. We do not speak of Bernard of Chartres, William of Conches, and John of Salisbury, who for a time rekindled the torch of letters; of Guibert of Nogent, who nearly lost himself through his passionate cultivation of Ovid’s poems; or of the many versifiers of that century, such as John, monk of Saint-Evroul, Baudri of Bourgueil, Hildebert of Le Mans, and so many others, who sometimes tried to introduce into their usually prosaic style a few poetic expressions drawn from Virgil, Horace, or Lucan. The theologians themselves were not strangers [Col. LXXIIID] to these readings. More than one trace of them is found in St Bernard, despite the austerity and busyness of his life. Geoffrey of Vendôme, author of many interesting letters and several theological and ascetical treatises, cites Terence, Juvenal, Lucan, and Horace. The same writers seem familiar to Hugh of St Victor, who moreover knew Seneca and Cicero and copied entire pages from them.

Our surprise disappears if we study this period more closely. Positive testimony tells us that the works of pagan authors were in students’ hands. We read [Col. LXXIVA] in Peter of Blois: “Besides the classical books, I read with profit Trogus Pompeius, Josephus, Suetonius, Hegesippus, Quintus Curtius, Tacitus, and Livy, whose histories are altogether useful for the formation of character and the advancement of learning.” He speaks only of historians; they were not the only authors he used. Thus he adds: “I read many others who do not treat history. Their number is incalculable. They are all like gardens from which modern writers may gather aromatic flowers and, through the elegant sweetness of their style, learn to write as they did.”

> [Note: [Col. LXXIIID] Epistle 101.]

Nevertheless, these testimonies should not lead us to conclude that letters were flourishing. [Col. LXXIVB] A few outstanding men undoubtedly raised them to a degree of perfection not attained since the barbarian invasions. Abelard’s style is pure and often elegant. Hildebert of Le Mans’s poems lamenting the persecutions he suffered at the hands of Rotrou, count of Maine, are not without delicacy and grace; and John of Salisbury’s verses singing the vices of the court are sometimes worthy of Ovid. But these examples are rare. Even the most accomplished writers are uneven. The great models were indeed studied, but generally not seriously. Most readers sought in Horace or Virgil less the talent for expressing their thought with delicacy and purity, [Col. LXXIVC] nobility and simplicity, than vain and pretentious erudition. All intellectual activity was directed toward the liberal arts, in which literature occupied only a very narrow place.

The elementary education preparing students for theology was in fact confined to the trivium and quadrivium. All the monuments of the period attest this.

We read in Orderic Vitalis and in an old supplement to the letters of Peter of Blois that, after the death of Ingulf—secretary to William the Conqueror and abbot of the monastery of Crowland—Geoffrey succeeded him in office. He was French and a native of Orléans. From his [Col. LXXIVD] earliest youth he had followed instruction in the liberal arts and was sufficiently versed in literature. Disgusted with the world and filled with longing for heavenly goods, he embraced religious life in the monastery of Saint-Evroul, founded in the time of Childebert, king of the Franks.

Appointed abbot of Croyland, he took with him the monks Gislebert, Odo, Terric, and William, men, Vital tells us, highly skilled in philosophical theorems and the other foundational sciences. Every day they went to Cambridge, where they had rented a barn, and taught publicly. In a short time they gathered a great number of pupils. In the second year after their arrival, their [Col. LXXVA] hearers multiplied to such an extent that no barn, house, or even church could contain them. They therefore established different schools on the model of that at Orléans.

Very early in the morning, Odo, a distinguished grammarian and satirist, taught the children entrusted to him grammar according to the teaching of Priscian, along with Remigius’s commentaries on that same author. At the hour of Prime, Terric, a subtle sophist, expounded Aristotle’s logic to adolescents, following the commentaries of Porphyry and Averroes. At the hour of Terce, Brother William commented upon the rhetoric of Tully and Quintilian. Master Gislebert preached the word of God to the people in several [Col. LXXVB] churches every Sunday and feast day. He knew little English, but was highly skilled in Latin and French. He inveighed especially against Jewish practices. On ferial days, before the hour of Sext, he commented upon some pages of Holy Scripture before priests and men of letters, who chiefly made up his audience [Note: [Col. LXXVD] *Hist. univers. Paris*, vol. II, p. 28.].

This arrangement interests us in more than one respect. According to Vital, the school of Cambridge had been formed on the model of that of Orléans. The latter was too close to that of Paris not to undergo its influence and to reproduce, approximately, its teaching and practices. John of Salisbury confirms this conjecture in the account he has left us of [Col. LXXVC] his studies.

“While still young,” he says, “I crossed into France to devote myself to study. It was the second year after the death of Henry, that lion of justice. I first attended the lectures of the Peripatetic Palatinus, an illustrious and admirable master, who presided over the schools on Mount Sainte-Geneviève. At his feet I learned the first rudiments of his art, and received, with all the eagerness of my soul and according to the measure of my little understanding, the words that fell from his mouth. After his death, which seemed to me too untimely, I attached myself to Alberic, the most illustrious and highly esteemed of dialecticians and the most vigorous defender of the sect of the Nominalists. [Col. LXXVD] Thus I spent almost two years on the Mount, studying dialectic under Alberic and Robert of Melun. The former, excessively scrupulous, found some difficulty everywhere; in open country he encountered obstacles, and, as the proverb says, every reed seemed knotty to him. The latter was always ready to answer, seeking no evasion and shirking no problem: the one subtle in his numerous questions, the other brief and easy in his answers. Whoever had united the qualities of these two men would have been without equal in disputation. Both had penetrating minds and great persistence in work. They would [Col. LXXVIA] have shone brilliantly in the physical sciences had they cultivated letters more fully and followed the tracks of their forebears rather than applauded their own discoveries . . . . . I became familiar with them with the laws of dialectic and the rudiments of the sciences taught to children, in which these masters were highly skilled and practiced. Thus I thought that I knew all these things as well as my nails and fingers. I possessed this learning very thoroughly, and my youthful levity made me value my knowledge more highly than it deserved. I thought myself a little scholar because I could repeat everything I had heard” [Note: [Col. LXXVID] *Metalogicon*, book II, ch. 10.].

He further tells us that he studied grammar [Col. LXXVIB] under William of Conches, and rhetoric under Bishop Richard, “a man,” he says, “versed in every discipline, who had more heart than speech, more learning than eloquence, more truth than vanity, more virtue than display. With him I reviewed what the others had taught me and acquired further knowledge belonging to the quadrivium.”

In this faithful and lively picture of the Paris schools, we find the same instruction that the monks of Croyland gave at Cambridge: grammar, rhetoric, dialectic, logic—in a word, the trivium and quadrivium. Dialectic seems the most important part. John devotes almost two years to it exclusively. The [Col. LXXVIC] teachers of it are skilled in disputation but poorly versed in letters, though their renown is great. Literature was wholly included within grammar, at least for the greater number of pupils; and grammar extended little beyond the most common rules of language. The works of Priscian, which supplied the text for instruction, include in a first volume called the *Minor* the alphabet and the first rudiments of the language. The second, or *Major*, includes declensions, conjugations, syntax, and prosody. We possess an unpublished treatise by Hugh of Saint-Victor that gives us no better idea of the teaching [Col. LXXVID] of grammar. Its subjects are: letters, syllables, diction, discourse, orthography, analogy, etymology, gloss, accent, barbarism, solecism, tropes, fable, history, and so forth. It was rare to encounter a grammarian such as Bernard of Chartres, who explained good authors in his lectures and, while explaining them, accustomed his pupils to apply principles to the text; who did not confine himself to giving elementary rules of speech, but made them observe rhetorical turns and the devices of persuasion, noted the properties of terms and [Col. LXXVIIA] metaphorical expressions, and the merit of order and arrangement of subject matter—in a word, who was not content to teach correct writing and speaking, but also a certain elegance.

The school of Saint-Victor differed little from that of Sainte-Geneviève, if it is the former that Hugh intended to depict in his treatise *On the Vanity of the World*. It is a dialogue between master and disciple:

“The Master: Turn yourself once more in another direction and look.

“The Disciple: I have turned and I see.

“The Master: What do you see?

“The Disciple: I see an assembly of students. Their multitude is great; I behold persons of every [Col. LXXVIIB] age—children, adolescents, young men, and old men. Their studies too are diverse. Some are training their still uncultivated tongues to form unfamiliar letters and utter sounds unusual to them. Others first learn, by listening, the inflections, compounds, and derivations of words; then they repeat them among themselves and, by repeated rehearsal, strive to commit them to memory. Others furrow wax tablets with a stylus. Others, guided by the pen in a learned hand, trace various figures in different ways and colors upon parchment. Others, with more ardent zeal, appear occupied with more serious studies: they engage in disputations with one another and strive, by a thousand entanglements and riddles, [Col. LXXVIIC] to deceive one another in turn. I also see some there calculating. Others, striking a stretched string mounted on wood, produce melodies of diverse sounds. Others explain certain descriptions and figures of measurements. Others clearly represent by instruments the courses and positions of the stars and the revolution of heaven. Others discuss the nature of plants, the constitutions of human beings, and the qualities and powers of all things” [Note: [Col. LXXVIID] *De vanitate mundi*, book I, vol. II, col. 709. “M[aster]. Turn yourself once more in another direction and look.—R[esponse]. I have turned and I see.—M. What do you see?—R. I see schools of learners. The multitude is great; I behold there every age of humankind: boys, adolescents, young men, old men. Their pursuits too are diverse. Some are learning to bend their still uncultivated tongue to form unfamiliar letters and utter unusual sounds. Others strive first to learn by hearing the inflections, compounds, and derivations of words; then, discussing them with one another and repeating them over and over, to commit them to memory. Others engrave wax with a stylus. Others, with the pen guided by a skilled hand, draw figures in various fashions and diverse colors upon parchment. Others, however, with a keener and more fervent [Col. LXXVIIID] application, seem to engage in debates among themselves about weighty matters and strive to deceive one another in turn by certain entanglements and riddles. I also see some calculating there. Others, striking a string stretched upon wood, produce melodies of diverse sounds. Others explain certain descriptions and figures of measurements. Others plainly describe by instruments the courses and positions of the stars and the revolution of the heaven. Others discuss the nature of plants, the constitutions of human beings, and the quality and powers of all things.”].

This curious picture agrees with the details drawn from the accounts of Orderic Vital and John of Salisbury: everywhere we find the same object of instruction and approximately the [Col. LXXVIID] same division of the sciences. Hugh therefore introduced no innovation in this matter. But he endeavored to connect these different studies with a philosophical idea [Col. LXXVIIIA] that is the very end one should propose in cultivating them. That end is the perfection of the human being.

“Human beings,” he says, “had received three gifts from God, constituting their dignity and greatness: they were his image and likeness, and their body was immortal. Sin, corrupting these gifts, produced ignorance, concupiscence, infirmity, and bodily mortality. Learning offers three remedies for these three maladies: the illumination of the understanding, which disperses ignorance; virtue, which combats concupiscence; and the mechanical arts, which provide for the needs of life. Hence the three great divisions of knowledge: theoretical knowledge, which includes theology or theodicy, physics, [Col. LXXVIIIB] and mathematics; practical knowledge, divided into ethics, economics, and politics, regulating the life of the individual, the household, and society. Logic is added as an appendix: it teaches how to treat properly every part of knowledge; it includes reading, writing, orthography, the art of composition, and eloquence” [Note: [Col. LXXVIIID] *Didascalicon*, book VI, ch. 14, vol. II, col. 809.].

Hugh indicates the subject of each division of knowledge. “Theology,” he says, “treats the invisible causes of visible phenomena; mathematics, the visible forms of visible beings; arithmetic treats numbers, music harmony, geometry space, and astronomy the motion of the stars” [Note: [Col. LXXVIIID] Same work, same place.].

He distinguishes three kinds of music: cosmic [Col. LXXVIIIC] music, the harmony of the heavens, stars, and elements; human music, the harmony among the limbs and organs of the body, and among the faculties and passions of the soul. The friendship uniting human beings is a music.

We would not wish to justify in every detail this classification or the notions Hugh gives of each science in particular. Yet it is impossible not to acknowledge the truth of the principle from which he starts. Thus, the direct end of knowledge is not the increase of public wealth and of physical enjoyments. The human body is worth more than the material world, and the soul is worth more than its [Col. LXXVIIID] body. Now in every work the end is superior to the means, because means exist for the end, not the end for the means. It is therefore to reverse [Col. LXXIXA] this order to place the soul in the service of the body and the body in the service of matter. This must often be repeated to a materialistic age: the first end of knowledge is human perfection; only on this condition are its advances, and those of the arts, advances of humanity.

Hugh held a profound esteem for knowledge not only because of its end, which he defined with such precision, but also because of its object, which he always contemplated in God.

“Human beings,” he says, “are accustomed to love their knowledge because of its works. Agriculture is loved because of the fruits it yields. The same is true of painting and all other arts, in which skill is too often accounted nothing [Col. LXXIXB] if it produces no useful result. If this principle is applied to God, one must say that his work is more excellent than his wisdom, and prefer the creature to the Creator—which would be blasphemy. It must therefore be acknowledged that knowledge is preferable to its works, and that it should be loved for its own sake. If, by chance, work is preferred to wisdom, that judgment proceeds not from truth but from error; for wisdom is life, and the love of wisdom is the blessedness of life. Therefore, when it is said that the Father of wisdom delights in her, far be it from us to think that he loves his wisdom because of the works he produces through her; rather, he loves his works because of [Col. LXXIXC] wisdom. Hence he says: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I have placed all my delight.’ He does not say: I have placed my delight in the earth or in heaven, in the sun or moon, in the stars, or even in the angels, who are the most excellent creatures; for if these creatures have pleased him, they could please him only in his Son and through his Son” [Note: [Col. LXXIXD] *De Trinitatis summa per visibilia cognitione*, ch. 22, vol. II, col. 832. “For human beings often customarily love their knowledge for the sake of its work, not the work for the sake of knowledge . . . . But if this is said of the wisdom of God, then indeed the work is preferred to its maker. Therefore it must be said that wisdom is always more precious [Col. LXXXD] than its work and that wisdom must always be loved for its own sake. But if at any time its work is perhaps preferred to wisdom, this comes not from the judgment of truth but from human error.”].

But in what order should the various branches of knowledge be studied? Hugh remains faithful to the old method: he wishes the successive parts of the trivium and quadrivium to be traversed. He traces this classification back to Pythagoras. He complains that the schoolmen of his day depart from this beaten path and study [Col. LXXIXD] without order and without profit.

“It is reported,” he says, “that some men were so zealous in studying the seven liberal arts that they had perfectly impressed them upon their memory, so that if any writing came into their hands, or if any question arose to be solved or proposition to be proved, they possessed the rules and principles necessary to clarify what was obscure or establish what was [Col. LXXXA] disputed. They had no need to consult books: they possessed everything in memory. Hence one sees in that age learned men who wrote more than we could read. Now our schoolmen do not follow, or do not wish to follow, a method in study. Hence many study and few attain knowledge. For my part, it seems to me that frivolous reading should be avoided no less carefully than idleness. In a good and useful undertaking, it is bad to do good negligently; it is still worse to expend much labor entirely in vain” [Note: [Col. LXXXD] *Didascalicon*, book III, ch. 3, vol. II, col. 768.].

However just this criticism may be, one should not infer from it that the twelfth century was an age of [Col. LXXXB] decline in the sciences and letters. Sound minds are always few in number, even in the happiest times. Abuses before one’s eyes strike more forcibly than abuses no longer present. Hence the habit, even among wise and moderate people, of praising the past and blaming the present.

Thus the schoolman must learn the seven liberal arts contained in the trivium and quadrivium. If he has any leisure left, he will study what Hugh calls the appendages of the arts: the various genres of poetry—comedy, satire, heroic, lyric, didactic, and iambic poems—fables, and history. But he adds: “The [Col. LXXXC] arts rise as far above these ancillary studies as the pale olive rises above the pliant willow, and the rosebush with crimson flowers above humble lavender:

> As far as the pliant willow yields to the pale olive,  
> as far as lowly lavender to crimson rosebushes.

The many quotations of this kind found in his writings prove that he had leisure to acquire this learning, which he regards merely as the ornaments of knowledge. Verses of Virgil, Horace, and Terence come naturally beneath his pen. Hence this purer and more delicate taste, this severe criticism of the obscure and diffuse style of unlettered writers. He attacks their indigestible compilations. He sharply condemns [Col. LXXXD] the foolish pride of certain teachers: “They speak of everything,” he says, “on every occasion. They do not teach; they parade their knowledge. They speak of declension in connection with dialectic and of dialectic in connection with grammar. Would to God that everyone judged them as I myself judge them” [Note: [Col. LXXXD] *Didascalicon*, book III, ch. 3, vol. II, col. 768.].

By these words Hugh plainly alludes to the sect of the Cornificians, if that name may be given to men without principles or doctrine. They despised literature and eloquence and disdainfully rejected the seven liberal arts. Nature alone was their guide, and dialectic the sole object of their studies. “The Greeks, Hebrews, and Latins,” they said, “learned to speak their language from their nurse before teachers of grammar had arisen among them. If you possess natural genius, labor develops it little; if you do not possess it, labor is useless.” John of Salisbury refutes them indignantly in his *Metalogicon* and exposes them to ridicule. Not without cause, if they are judged from the crude trivialities of their dialectic, of which he quotes several examples. They seriously debated [Col. LXXXIB] such questions as: Is a pig being led to market held by the rope or by the man who leads it? . . . . When one buys a whole cape, does one also buy its hood? These problems were regarded as insoluble [Note: [Col. LXXXID] *Metalogicon*, book I, ch. 3.].

Since two negations make an affirmation, they multiplied negations in a sentence to such a degree that beans had to be used to count them and to determine from their number whether the proposition was affirmative or negative. Poets and historians were branded with infamy; whoever studied them was *asello Arcadio tardior*—“slower-witted than an Arcadian donkey”; his mind was blunter than lead and stone. Everyone laughed at his expense [Note: [Col. LXXXID] Same work, same place.].

“They remained in the rank of pupil,” John of Salisbury adds [Col. LXXXIC], “only for as long as a bird needs to clothe itself in feathers; and immediately they take flight: they have become masters.”

The same author tells us what became of these false doctors. They failed in their mad undertaking. Some took up medicine, which they treated much as they had treated the trivium and quadrivium. If their patients died, they gloried in it: they had been the first to predict their death. If they recovered, the cure was due to their skill and experience. Others went to hide their shame in cloisters; still others sought their fortune among the [Col. LXXXID] great [Note: [Col. LXXXIID] *Metalogicon*, book I, ch. 3.]. William of Conches, Bernard of Chartres, and John of Salisbury were their most severe opponents. Hugh joined his efforts to those of these able masters. Like them, he defended the rights of learning; he caused it to flourish at Saint-Victor throughout the time during which he directed the school of that illustrious abbey.

He did not content himself with determining the order to be followed in teaching the different branches of knowledge; he investigated the historical origin of each. The chapter devoted to this inquiry gives us an idea of his learning and of that of the writers of his age.

[Col. LXXXIIA] Among theologians he counts, among the Greeks, Linus; among the Latins, Varro; among the French, Scotus Eriugena. Among physicists, among the Greeks, Thales; among the Latins, Pliny. Among arithmeticians, among the Greeks, Pythagoras and Nicomachus; among the Latins, Apuleius and Boethius. Tubal was the inventor of music. Pythagoras—or, according to others, Mercury, who first made the tetrachord—made it known to the Greeks; or, according to still others, Linus, Zethus, and Amphion did so. Egypt saw the birth of geometry. The most illustrious geometer among the Greeks was Euclid, and among the Latins Boethius. Eratosthenes was also very skilled in this art. He attributes the invention of astronomy to Ham, son of Noah. The Chaldeans were the first to cultivate astrology, [Col. LXXXIIB] and Abraham, according to Josephus, was the first to teach it to the Egyptians.

We shall not continue to recount this long catalogue, in which Socrates, Plato, Cicero, Fronto, Hesiod, the Carthaginian Mago—author, according to Hugh, of a work on agriculture—Cato, Marcus Terentius Varro, Cornelius, Julius Atticus, Aemilianus, Columella, Palladius, and Vitruvius appear in turn. Beside these historical names he cites the fabulous names of Minerva, Isis, and Osiris, and those of Daedalus, Prometheus, Apollo, and Asclepius. Nor does he forget the first author of culinary art, whom he calls Apitius. “He was a Roman,” he says. “After consuming his property in practicing this art, he perished by voluntary death.” [Col. LXXXIIC] He also indicates the origin of games at Rome. “They were first celebrated,” he says, “among the Lydians. These later passed from Asia into Etruria under a Tuscan leader. Among the ceremonies of their superstitious worship, they established spectacles. The Romans imitated them. They brought in Lydian actors, who gave their name to these games” [Note: [Col. LXXXIID] *Didascalicon*, book III, ch. 2, vol. II, col. 767.].

It is probable that Hugh drew this information from the *Etymologies* of Isidore of Seville, whom in the same chapter he cites together with Origen, Plato, Saint Denis, Saint Augustine, Saint Jerome, and Saint Ambrose; or from similar works, so frequent in preceding centuries. Nevertheless, these details attest his extensive reading [Col. LXXXIID] and uncommon learning. One might regard this little treatise as an unformed seed of literary history and place it beside John of Salisbury’s criticisms, so judicious and at times so sharp and subtle.

## CHAPTER VII. HUGH’S WORKS.—HIS COMMENTARIES.—HIS ASCETICAL BOOKS.—HIS THEOLOGICAL TREATISES.—HIS CONTROVERSY.

We have set forth the fundamental principles of Hugh’s doctrine; it remains to complete this study with a few details, which [Col. LXXXIIIA] we shall give in a rapid survey of his writings.

Hugh had practiced from his earliest youth the laborious art of composition. According to the testimony of the author of the *Life of Reinhard*, his uncle, he wrote in the monastery of Halberstadt. But these early attempts were probably only drafts that have not come down to us. It was at Saint-Victor in Paris that he composed the works we possess. They are numerous and varied, and attest a lofty mind, a loving heart, a great habit of meditation, extensive learning, gentle and sensitive piety, and literary cultivation—imperfect, certainly, but remarkable for its age. It has even been thought that he knew Hebrew and Greek. In his [Col. LXXXIIIB] commentaries he compared the Vulgate text with the original text of the sacred books, probably following the writings of Saint Jerome or some other commentator [Note: [Col. LXXXIIID] We shall cite several examples in chapter 7. In the *Notes on Genesis* (vol. I, beginning), at the words *et factus est homo in animam viventem*—“and man became a living soul”—he adds *vel mutabilem, ut est in Hebraeo*: “or mutable, as it is in the Hebrew.” In Jacob’s prophecy on his deathbed, the patriarch says of Judah: *Pulchriores sunt oculi ejus vino*—“His eyes are more beautiful than wine.” Hugh adds: *in Hebraeo habetur rubicundus*: “in the Hebrew, ‘ruddy’ is found.” A little later: *Nephthalim cervus emissus*—“Naphtali, a released stag”; *in Hebraeo habetur, cerva emissa*: “in the Hebrew, ‘a released hind’ is found.” It would be easy to multiply such examples.]. Not only does he give Greek etymologies for a great many words, following the custom of his contemporaries, who found ready-made learning in glossaries; but in a passage of his commentary on the *Hierarchy*, he corrects Scotus Eriugena’s Latin translation [Note: [Col. LXXXIIID] Here is the obscure text of the translation: “*interpretatio igitur hierarchiae est ad Deum quantum possibile similitudo et unitas*”: “therefore the interpretation of hierarchy is likeness and unity toward God, insofar as possible.” Hugh observes that the translation is not exact: “*quod in Graeco dicitur σκοπός et quod translator interpretationem vocat, magis proprie intentio vel directio nominatur*”: “what is called *skopos* (σκοπός, ‘aim’ or ‘target’) in Greek, and what the translator calls ‘interpretation,’ is more properly termed ‘intention’ or ‘direction.’”—Vol. I, col. 994.].

Hugh’s works may be regarded as summaries of his lectures. Indeed, he was above all a teacher, as were all the notable men of that period. At times he taught grammar and philosophy; more often [Col. LXXXIIIC] theology. At times he gave the evening conference to the canons of Saint-Victor; at times, in diocesan synods, he was charged by his bishop to address the clergy of Paris. Hence these works on philosophy, grammar, and theology; these ascetical treatises; these pious explanations of Holy Scripture. “I have abridged,” he says in the preface to his commentaries on Ecclesiastes, “what I recently taught you orally concerning this book of Solomon” [Note: [Col. LXXXIVD] Vol. I, col. 113.]. And in the preface to his treatise *On the Sacraments*: “This book will contain the same truths I have already set forth, with the advantage that they will be treated with greater care and precision than in my [Col. LXXXIIID] earlier works, where I merely touched upon them in order to give my pupils a first acquaintance with them” [Note: [Col. LXXXIVD] *De sacramentis*, vol. II, col. 183.]. These testimonies may be applied to most of his works. From this point of view they have a particular interest: besides [Col. LXXXIVA] their intrinsic merit, they possess historical value.

The principal works may be divided into three classes: commentaries, ascetical books, and theological treatises.

Commentaries were common in the twelfth century. Teaching ordinarily preceded writing, and teaching was almost always the explanation or development of a text. To teach, in the established expression, was to “read.” This method produced happy results and often contributed to the progress of learning. Was it not itself a genuine advance beyond the compilations of preceding centuries—useful, certainly, but always indigestible—which merely preserved from oblivion the names and notions of the sciences and arts? The commentator cultivated this arid ground and made it fruitful through labor; at the same time he developed the powers of his mind, increased his knowledge, and thus prepared himself for more useful and serious productions.

But it was especially upon Holy Scripture that the most illustrious teachers loved to exercise the subtlety of their minds. Abelard, at the height of his glory, commented upon Ezekiel; and, if we believe his own testimony, this new instruction was received so favorably by his disciples that it gained him a reputation equal to [Col. LXXXIVC] that which he had acquired through teaching philosophy [Note: [Col. LXXXIVD] Letter I to Heloise.].

Hugh’s commentaries contain in germ all his other writings. At times they are merely small notes or explanatory notes [Note: [Col. LXXXIVD] *Adnotationes elucidatoriae*—“elucidatory annotations”; *adnotatiunculae*—“little annotations”; *notulae*—“brief notes.”], disconnected and unsystematic, on isolated verses. They clarify an obscure passage, solve an objection, or, more often, offer a pious and mystical reflection. Sometimes they are homilies; elsewhere he proceeds according to the scholastic method, through questions and answers, divisions and subdivisions. By turns he is theologian, ascetic, mystic, historian, philosopher, and controversialist; he is an orator in his homilies on Ecclesiastes, a historian in his notes on Genesis, [Col. LXXXIVD] a philosopher in that same commentary when he refutes Plato on the origin of things or explains his physics in connection with the account of creation; he is a theologian when he combats the opinions of certain contemporaries concerning the origin [Col. LXXXVA] of evil, the existence of two souls within us, or optimism; he is a mystic in his allegorical or anagogical interpretations of the sacred text. We shall cite a few examples of this latter kind, which will make the genius of our Victorine better known.

Explaining the passage in the Second Book of Kings in which David, as a very wise prince among his counselors, is compared to the worm that gnaws wood, he says: “The tender worm pierces the hardness of wood: nothing is softer when it is touched, nothing harder when it itself touches. It is the image of humility and gentleness united with strength” [Note: [Col. LXXXVD] *Notes on II Kings*, vol. I, col. 105.].

Here is how he explains the first verse of [Col. LXXXVB] the first Psalm: “Blessed is the one who has not gone to the assembly of the wicked, has not planted his foot in their ways, and has not sat in their poisoned chair.” “The soul that clings to God remains in its homeland; when it turns its thought toward earthly and passing things, it leaves its homeland and takes the road of exile. It goes by vanity, halts through delight, sits through consent, and through despair establishes its dwelling irrevocably in the foreign land” [Note: [Col. LXXXVD] *Notes on the Psalms*, ch. 2, vol. III, *Miscellanies*, book II, at the beginning.].

On the following verse, “His will is in the law of the Lord, and he meditates on it day and night,” he says: “Those have the law in their heart who know truth; but those who love it have their heart [Col. LXXXVC] in the law. Those who have the law in their heart but not their heart in the law bear it and are not borne by it. For them it is a burden, not a support, because knowledge without charity is a weight, not a prop” [Note: [Col. LXXXVD] Same work, same place.]. Saint Bernard expressed the same thought in more graceful language when he compared the law, known and loved, to the bird’s wings: it is a burden, yet by it the bird rises toward heaven [Note: [Col. LXXXVID] St Bernard, Letter 72.].

In medieval works, charity sometimes lends delicacy to feeling, inspires the imagination, even makes up for a real lack of literary cultivation, and spontaneously produces, without artifice, the charms of language. But taste is as imperfect as the language. There is not that reflective awareness of literary beauty which, though insufficient to produce it, avoids gross defects. Hence those inequalities which surprise and astonish at first sight: childish and trivial pages beside the most delicate passages.

Hugh did not always preserve himself from these faults. We find an example in two dialogues, one between Justice and Mercy, [Col. LXXXVIA] and the other between God and the devil. He introduces the second on the occasion of this verse of Psalm XV: “The portion of my inheritance which has fallen to me is fair.” “Everything,” he says, “belonged to God, and everything was his. But everything was possessed by the devil, because sin had made him master of the world.” A dispute arises between the two. At last they come to an agreement. God gives his enemy everything that he will see. The latter raises his eyes: he sees only the heights, and thinks he has seen everything. But he has not discovered the valleys, plains, and mountains, because pride blinds him. Then God exclaims: “The portion of my inheritance which has fallen to me is fair.” [Note: [Col. LXXXVID] *Adnot. in Ps.*, cap. 12, tom. III, in *Miscell.* lib. II.]

[Col. LXXXVIB] We must nevertheless add that such lapses are very rare in the writings of our Victorine. These dialogues and his allegorical personifications were, moreover, in the taste of the age, and that taste endured until the dawn of the century of Louis XIV. Some are not without interest even for us, because of the great truths they express in a popular form. Dramas of this kind made those truths more perceptible to these childlike peoples. They captivated their imagination, which predominates at that stage in nations as in individuals. They more readily impressed upon their minds the sublime teachings of faith.

It has been observed before us that religious men, working chiefly to reform the corrupted nature of [Col. LXXXVIC] man, often possessed an uncommon knowledge of his passions and vices, and that medieval psychology is almost entirely contained in ascetic books. Hugh was no stranger to this study and knowledge. In his *Septenary*, he analyzes the principal passions of the human heart. This little treatise is not without merit. At times, it is true, its author is merely ingenious; but more often his penetrating gaze accurately grasps the nature of the vices he studies, the relations that unite them, and the remedies suitable to them. He describes their character with originality and precision. If it were permissible to compare him with an ancient philosopher of wider genius and [Col. LXXXVID] more extensive learning—the tutor of Alexander—we should say that the latter established with greater exactness and rigor the outward effects of the passions, while the former understood their disorder better. The first recounts what he experiences and what he sees in others; the second, keeping his eyes fixed always upon the divine order and upon humankind’s relation to God, shows in every vice a violation of that order and of those relations.

“The first corruption of love,” he says, “is pride, which perverts it by turning it away from the whole [Col. LXXXVIIA] and directing it toward that which is only a part. For every good derives from the supreme Good, and there is less good in it than in him from whom it comes. Whoever delights in any good apart from the supreme Good loses the whole by wickedly choosing a part. Pride, by in some sense separating the part from the whole, takes beauty away from the rational soul. It is the principle of all disorder in the moral world; it destroys its unity and overturns its laws. Therefore all other vices derive from it as from a common source. They are its bitter fruits and its punishment.” [Note: [Col. LXXXVIID] *Alleg. in Matth.*, cap. 4, tom. I, col. 775.]

“Jealousy is born from pride, for it is hatred of another’s happiness. Whoever loves himself more than, or as much as, the supreme Good cannot love others; [Col. LXXXVIIB] even their happiness wounds him. In pride there is disordered love of what one is; in jealousy, unjust sorrow that others are. The wound of pride is all the more fatal because its malice is less felt. The more gently it introduces itself, the more deeply it penetrates. By contrast, the wound of envy is painful. Therefore it sometimes appears evil; it is not merely a vice, but a bitter vice.” [Note: [Col. LXXXVIID] *Id. ibid.*]

“Anger is the irrational disturbance of the soul. These three vices are opposed to God: pride denies him, envy accuses him, and anger drives him away. Whoever seeks his glory in himself alone denies every superior; whoever envies the good of others accuses their benefactor; whoever admits disturbance into his soul puts [Col. LXXXVIIC] the lover of peace to flight. These three vices blaspheme God. Pride says: ‘God is not’; envy and anger say: ‘God acts wrongly.’” [Note: [Col. LXXXVIID] *Id. ibid.*]

“The other capital vices are the punishments of the first three. The soul, having separated itself from God and lost the supreme Good, becomes, solitary and desolate, bitter and painful to itself. Deprived of inward goods, it is driven by avarice toward outward goods. Sadness produces pain, and avarice produces toil.” [Note: [Col. LXXXVIID] *Id. ibid.*]

The commentaries we have just reviewed sometimes deal with the literal sense, sometimes with the allegorical sense; occasionally Hugh combines them. He recognizes, in fact, with Saint Augustine and the whole [Col. LXXXVIID] Christian tradition, different interpretations of sacred text. His entire doctrine on this subject still rests on symbolism: it is a new application of it. The Old Law is the figure of the New Law; the New Law is itself the figure of glory. Everything Jesus Christ did in the New Law, everything that was prefigured of him in the Old Law, is the rule of what we must do; for he is the head, model, universal type whom each person must reproduce. The Old Law, considered [Col. LXXXVIIIA] as figurative of the New Law, yields the allegorical sense; the New Law, considered as a figure of glory, yields the anagogical sense; what was prefigured of Jesus Christ or accomplished by him yields the moral or tropological sense. Hugh cites the history of Job as an example. The literal sense is that which follows from the natural meaning of words. But the events recounted in this story are like new words forming a new language, and that language itself has a double significance. Job in abundance, honored by wise and powerful men, presiding over their counsels, protecting and relieving the weak and unfortunate; Job in misery, drenched with bitterness, sitting upon his dung heap among friends who slander [Col. LXXXVIIIB] his innocence; Job restored to the splendor of his first prosperity: this is the figure of the Son of God in his three states—of glory in the bosom of his Father, of humiliation upon earth and especially during his Passion, and of triumph after his Resurrection and on the day of his Ascension. Such is the allegorical sense. The same patriarch is the figure of the innocent and happy man, the sinful and unhappy man, and the restored and glorious man. Such is the anagogical sense. “All must be studied,” says Hugh, “for the fruit of Holy Scripture is the knowledge given us by the first two, and the virtue taught us by the third.” [Note: [Col. LXXXVIID] *De Scripturis et scrip. sac.*, cap. 3, tom. I, [Col. LXXXVIIID] initio.—*De sacrament.*, t. II, cap. 4, 5.—St Thomas, *Summa theol.*, I, q. 1, art. 3.]

But the mystical sense rests upon the literal sense; therefore the latter must first command our attention. [Col. LXXXVIIIC] Hugh composed a special chapter on its importance and necessity. He rises against the false mystics of his time, who neglected the historical study of the holy books and found it easier to indulge their imagination than patiently to seek the truth God had hidden beneath the shell of events. He cites a curious example of these childish and ridiculous explanations. People asked why the lion sleeps with its eyes open; they answered that it was a figure of Jesus Christ in death: his humanity slept, but his divinity watched. [Note: [Col. LXXXVIIID] *De Scripturis et scriptoribus sacris*, cap. 5, t. I, col. 13 med.]

Hugh’s symbolic interpretation thus differs essentially from mythical interpretation. [Col. LXXXVIIID] The mythic interpreters reject facts and destroy historical truth; they put ideas in place of persons and philosophy in place of history.

The literal explanation of the first verses of Genesis gives us an idea of our Victorine’s physical knowledge.

“God,” he says, “first created prime matter, and with it time, which he defines as the succession of mutability. This matter occupied the same space [Col. LXXXIXA] that it occupies now. It was formless—not because it had no form, but because it had no beauty. The heavens, air, and fire surrounded the earth and formed dense darkness around it. On the first day God separated fire from the other elements. Thus he produced light, which traveled the same course that the sun was later to travel. Bede had believed that the firmament was formed of condensed and hardened waters; Hugh rejects this opinion. He thinks that they remain suspended like vapors and clouds. He teaches that the sun alone is composed of fire and is merely a more perfect form of light, just as the New Testament is only the Old Testament perfected. The other stars are not luminous [Col. LXXXIXB] in themselves: they shine by reflection, *relucent, non lucent*—they reflect light, they do not emit it.” [Note: [Col. LXXXIXD] *Adnot. in Pent.*, cap. 6, tom. I, col. 35 med.: “One inwardly springing fountain of love pours forth two streams. One is love of the world, covetousness; the other is love of God, charity. The human heart is, indeed, the middle point from which the fountain of love bursts forth. Love is the affection of a heart for something because of something: in seeking it, desire; and in enjoying it, joy. It runs through desire and rests through joy. Here is your good, and here is your evil, O human heart, because you are good, if you are good, from no other source, and evil, if you are evil, from no other source, than that you love well or ill what is good. For everything that exists is good; but when what is good is loved wrongly, that thing is good, but this is evil. Therefore neither the one who loves is evil, nor what he loves is evil, nor the love by which he loves is evil; rather, to love wrongly is the whole of evil . . . . .”]

Asceticism and mysticism have sometimes been confused; wrongly so. The ascetic aims at human perfection by the exercise of Christian virtues; he is above all practical. The mystic tends toward the same goal, but through knowledge and love of truth, through meditation and contemplation: he is above all speculative. The Rules of Saint Benedict, Saint Augustine, and Chrodegang, and Cassian’s *Institutes*, are ascetic treatises; the *Hierarchy* of Saint Dionysius and Saint Bernard’s commentary on the Song of Songs are mystical treatises.

Hugh clearly states the principles of his asceticism in the *Institutions for Novices*: they are knowledge, discipline, and goodness. Knowledge enlightens [Col. LXXXIXC] the understanding; discipline regulates conduct; goodness is the fruit of both, and itself leads to blessedness. For him, the principle and end of perfection is intelligent love. He refers all things to it as to a common center. It is the virtue he meditates upon most fondly and recalls most often. He does not seek merely to inspire it by cold exclamations; he probes its nature in order to show its excellence. “Love,” he says, “is a single fountain that flows and divides into two streams: love of God is charity, and love of the world is covetousness. Between God and the world is placed the human heart, from which the fountain of love escapes . . . . . [Col. XCA] Thus love is the affection of a heart for an object on account of a motive; it seeks that object—this is desire; it enjoys it—this is joy. By desire it hastens onward; by joy it rests. There lies your good or your evil, O human heart! For you are good, if you are good, and evil, if you are evil, only because you love well or ill what is good. For everything that exists is good. But when what is good is loved wrongly, the object of love is good, but to love it wrongly is evil. Therefore neither that which loves nor that which is loved is evil, nor the love by which one loves; but loving wrongly is all evil . . . . .

“In order that the rational spirit might be capable of enjoying so great a blessedness—that is, God—he gave it love as a spiritual palate [Col. XCB] for tasting inward sweetness. By that love it must taste the delights of its felicity and cling to them with tireless desire. Thus by love God joins the rational creature to himself, so that, always cleaving to him, it might in some manner suck through affection the good by which it was to be blessed, drink it through desire, and possess it through joy. Suck, little bee, suck; suck and drink the ineffable sweetness of your sweetness. Immerse yourself in its delights and fill your heart; they will never fail, unless you are the first to grow weary of them. Cleave, then, and cling; take and enjoy. If your taste is eternal, your blessedness too will be eternal like it.” [Note: [Col. XCD] *De substantia charitatis*, t. II, col. 16: “That the spirit might be fit to enjoy so great a blessedness, he made within it love, a spiritual palate, in some manner signifying the tasting of inward sweetness; so that through that very love it might taste the delight of its happiness and cling to it with tireless desire. Therefore through love God joined the rational creature to himself, so that, always adhering to him, it might in some manner suck through affection that good by which it was to be made blessed, drink from it through desire, and possess it in joy. Suck, O little bee, suck. Suck and drink the ineffable sweetness of your sweetness. Immerse yourself and be filled, for he does not know how to fail unless you begin to grow weary. Therefore cleave and cling, take and enjoy. If the taste is everlasting, blessedness also will be everlasting.”]

[Col. XCC] Hugh has left us a great number of theological works which attest the profound study he had made of our dogmas. The theologians of that time were divided into two classes. The first confined themselves to establishing Catholic doctrine by Holy Scripture and tradition: they established the faith of the Church and called rash anyone who carried his gaze and ambition beyond it. Their method was called positive. The others, driven by the need felt by every elevated intellect to search out truth, to be illuminated by its light, and to account for its faith, began where the former stopped. Dogmas were for them merely the principles of a new science, which was to be the work of the free [Col. XCIA] exercise of intellectual activity. They alone deserve the name theologians; their method was generally called scholastic, although mysticism belongs to this class. Unfortunately there were among them minds more ardent than sound, more curious than profound, consumed by restless activity, seeking only to satisfy it by exercising it, and to excite applause by the subtlety and novelty of their reasoning. Instead of patiently studying Catholic dogma, deducing its consequences, penetrating its mysterious depths, and discovering its harmony, they distorted it. It was to overturn the foundations in order to raise the building; to set it upon shifting sand; to replace [Col. XCIB] immutable truth with imaginary conceptions. These rash dialecticians nearly ruined theology. Cries were raised not only against them, but against true scholasticism; and then, as today, men more zealous than enlightened condemned learning instead of restraining its abuses. But the movement had begun. Scholasticism triumphed through the genius of Albert the Great, Saint Thomas, and Saint Bonaventure. The theological science was definitively constituted.

Hugh was the predecessor of these great men. Hildebert of Le Mans had, indeed, composed before him a theological Summa; but it was only a simple exposition of Christian truths [Col. XCIC] according to the positive method. Hugh, in his own, adds speculation, and that is probably why Duboulay and Mosheim regard him as the first author of this kind of writing, later to become so common. [Note: [Col. XCID] “Hugh published a book which he called the *Summa of Sentences*. Hence books of theological *summae* and *summaries* began to be called and designated thus; and the theologians called *summists* owe to him their origin and designation.” Duboulay, *Hist. univ. par.* I, II, p. 64.—Mosheim likewise says: “In this age Hugh of Saint Victor is reported to have been the first to set forth in this manner—the manner of writers of sentences—the precepts of religion [Col. XCIID] arranged in a suitable rational order; many others followed him.” *Instit. histor. eccles.*, p. 413.]

Yet, like all those who first enter a new career, he was surpassed by those who followed in his footsteps. His Summa, very remarkable for its period, is imperfect; its classification is not always natural or consonant with the real and ontological order.

His *Treatise on the Sacraments* is superior. The whole is more complete and better ordered, although still not without defects. Yet was it not already a great thought and a noble undertaking [Col. XCID] to classify in a scientific order all the data of Christian faith?

We are pleased to be able to confirm our personal convictions by the testimony of a modern theologian, as worthy of respect for his virtue as distinguished for his learning.

“Hugh’s work,” says M. Laforêt, “exercised the greatest influence upon all the theological summae [Col. XCIIA] which the Middle Ages saw arise, among which those of Peter Lombard and Saint Thomas hold first rank. It was Hugh who inspired the celebrated Lombard, and the latter in turn became the master of all theologians.” [Note: [Col. XCIID] *Coup d’oeil sur l’hist. de la théol. dogm.*, by M. Laforêt, p. 59, Louvain, 1851.] “In his speculations, always sound and often very profound, he ordinarily relies upon the works of Saint Augustine. That incomparable doctor is his guide; it is in his school that he formed himself. He had so nourished himself upon the ideas of the bishop of Hippo that, in reading his principal dogmatic writings, we were surprised to encounter, on almost every page, thoughts visibly borrowed from this Father, although Hugh does not always give notice of them.” [Note: [Col. XCIID] *Id. ibid.*]

[Col. XCIIB] “In our view Hugh remains a theologian of the first rank. Above all, his *Treatise on the Sacraments* is a very rich mine for theological learning; it contains a multitude of very profound insights on a great number of dogmas. It would be desirable for this work to be less forgotten by those who make a special study of dogmatic theology. Hugh’s diction is clear, easy, flowing; and one does not find in him that apparatus of divisions, subdivisions, objections, and replies which undoubtedly have their usefulness when used with moderation, but which too often, in the writings of the scholastics, encumber the reader instead of assisting him.” [Note: [Col. XCIID] *Id.*, p. 62.]

While fully subscribing to this judgment, we [Col. XCIIC] would add, however, that our Victorine manifests in his minor treatises a special fondness for contrasts and antitheses. In this too he was an imitator of Saint Augustine. But these antitheses do not weary as they do in Seneca. The reader perceives that they are not merely conceits, but arise naturally from the need to express precisely a thought often difficult to grasp. Besides, this form is not peculiar to him. Antithetical style is one of the characteristic features of medieval writers. Hugh knows when to break its monotony and vary his language. His fertile imagination supplies him with elegant metaphors and felicitous comparisons, [Col. XCIID] even in the most abstract matters. Does he wish to prove that creation does not destroy God’s immutability? He says: the sun shines; a cloud forms; it is illumined; yet the ray is not elsewhere than before. The cloud is where it was not, but the ray has not begun to be where the cloud began to be illuminated. The same is true of God: he shone everywhere [Col. XCIIIA] before the creature existed, and he remained always the same where the creature was made. The creature therefore brought no change in him. [Note: [Col. XCIIID] *Summa*, tract. I, cap. 4, tom. II, col. 47: “Just as, if a cloud is set against a ray of the sun, the ray is nevertheless not elsewhere than before. The cloud indeed is where it was not, but the ray [is unchanged; the printed Latin is defective]; it did not begin to be where the cloud began to be. So God, since before that creature [Col. XCIVD] existed he was everywhere, was in that same place where it was made. Therefore he is not now elsewhere than before.”]

The nature of these works enables us to understand still better the character of his genius and that of the school he directed. Let us return, indeed, to the twelfth century, when the human mind seems to awaken from a long slumber; when the desire for learning and the passion for study kindle in every heart; when teaching leads to glory almost as much as arms; when numerous schools arise and fight among themselves. In this first awakening, true learning is difficult to attain and minds are impatient. Thus controversy is the easiest and shortest path to [Col. XCIIIB] celebrity. There especially one displays the resources of one’s mind and proudly deploys a subtle and ingenious dialectic. What glory when one reduces an illustrious adversary to silence! The scholastics clap their hands and gather in greater numbers and with greater ardor around the victor’s chair. The schools were like tournaments in which less account was taken of the combatants’ personal strength than of their skill and success in the contest. Hugh tells us that he himself hesitated whether he should sacrifice theology to dialectic and the labor of composition to that of public controversies. [Note: [Col. XCIVD] Tom. III, col. 335, prologue to *Speculum de mysteriis Ecclesiae*.] Fortunately, love of true learning prevailed.

He took no part in the disputes of his contemporaries; [Col. XCIIIC] his character, his tastes, his very method, and the principles of his philosophy kept him from them. By more serious and patient labor, he exercised a more useful influence upon his century. In this respect he was the opposite of Abelard. The latter provoked applause and ran after celebrity; the former sought truth. One was agitated in the schools; but the flexibility of his mind and the brilliance of his speech only imperfectly compensated for the imperfection of his learning. More subtle than profound, more erudite than learned, he sometimes rashly shakes the very principles of sound philosophy. The other, amid solitude, determines with a sure gaze the limits and object of [Col. XCIIID] learning: now he rises to God, attends, as it were, his counsels, and clearly expounds the general plan that God realizes in all his works; now he penetrates into the human heart and reveals its miseries and its greatness. He is rather a philosopher and theologian than a controversialist.

Yet he sometimes enters the lists. But when he fights, he is less an athlete than a soldier; he does not seek to display his skill or strength, but to defend truth. There is perhaps [Col. XCIVA] no error of the twelfth century that he did not at least point out in his writings. He refutes the heresies of Eutyches and Pelagius, renewed by Abelard, and that of Jovinian, reproduced by an unknown author. He rises against those who taught that there are two souls in us, one heavenly and one earthly, or who maintained that human souls generate one another. With remarkable precision he resolves objections drawn from the existence of moral evil; he vindicates the freedom of God and of humankind against the optimists, and God’s spirituality against those who localized the divine essence. He writes against Archbishop John of Seville, who claimed that a Christian may outwardly apostatize from faith while retaining it in the heart.

[Col. XCIVB] A few examples will give us an idea of the vigor of his argumentation.

God is infinite; therefore he is present everywhere. Theodoric, Abelard’s disciple, and, if their contemporaries are to be believed, Abelard himself, were troubled by this consequence. They did not hold sufficiently pure ideas of divine life and its spirituality; they could not conceive immensity without extension, and thought it contrary to simplicity. God is everywhere; otherwise his being would be limited. God is not substantially everywhere; otherwise he would be divisible like the space containing him. To escape this difficulty, they imagined God’s substance as an indivisible point occupying an indivisible part of space, and exercising [Col. XCIVC] from that secluded place its power beyond all created worlds. The divine nature was like a luminous hearth projecting its rays afar.

This new and strange opinion provoked serious controversies. William of Mortagne, one of the period’s most celebrated theologians, wrote against these rash dialecticians who limited and localized the very essence of God. Yet he relies more upon Holy Scripture than upon philosophical reasoning. Hugh penetrates further into the question. “God,” he says, “cannot be present in his creatures in such a way that one says he is in a place: he is in his creatures not by a local presence, but through himself, [Col. XCIVD] governing and preserving them without intermediary, just as the soul is wholly in every part of the body. If the soul withdraws from the body, it dies and falls into dust; hence it is evident that the soul is the life of the body. Thus God is, by his whole essence, in every creature, giving it being. If he withdrew, the creature would return into nothingness, just as a body without a soul is reduced to dust. How does God govern and preserve the creature? How does the soul govern [Col. XCVA] and preserve the body? I do not know; I know only that God is essentially present in all creatures.” [Note: [Col. XCVD] *Notulae sup. Joan.*, cap. 2, tom. I, col. 827.—*Sum. theol.*, pars I, cap. 4, tom. II, col. 47.—*De sacram.*, lib. I, pars III, cap. 17, tom. II, col. 223.]

The reconciliation of God’s freedom in the creation of the world with his wisdom, immutability, and foreknowledge is one of the most serious problems ancient and modern philosophy has attempted to resolve. God is an infinite substance and an activity without limit. He is not merely intelligent and loving: he is intelligence and love. He possesses the perfection of these faculties and the fullness of their exercise. Nothing develops in him; there is no seed that has not reached its complete flowering. He is, in the sublime expression of the scholastics, pure act. This full and perfect life which he enjoys, he [Col. XCVB] manifests outwardly by creation; but that manifestation adds nothing to his nature—not one degree of activity, not the least perfection. A learned person is learned when silent and when speaking. His knowledge is not his speech. It is in him; it is himself: his speech merely reveals it. The same is true of the life of God: creation neither increases nor perfects it; it makes it known. The act constituting God as living is essentially other than that by which he manifests his life outwardly. The first is intelligent, spontaneous, but necessary. The second is intelligent, spontaneous, but free. We thus have two different terms corresponding to two notions engraved in indelible [Col. XCVC] characters upon our intelligence: the necessary and the contingent. God wills the necessary as necessary and the contingent as contingent.

Descending into our own consciousness, we find an image of what we discover in God. We will our blessedness; this will is intelligent, spontaneous, but necessary. To attain it, we perform this or that act, and these acts are intelligent and spontaneous, but free. Not only can I choose between good and evil—which is not the essence of freedom—but I can choose between one good act and another; while performing one, I am conscious that I can perform the other.

But if God’s freedom in creating the [Col. XCVD] world is of this kind, how are we to understand his foreknowledge and wisdom? How was God free to create what he foresaw from eternity that he would create? How is this creation free, if the laws of his wisdom impose it upon him? And how is it wise, if his wisdom did not impose it upon him?

Hugh sets forth very concisely the argument of the optimists of his time. It appears to belong to Abelard and his school.

“God cannot do anything other than what he has done, and he cannot do better. For if God can [Col. XCVIA] do anything other than what he has done, he can do what he did not foresee; and if he can do what he did not foresee, he can act without foreknowledge. For he has done everything that he foresaw he would do, and he has done nothing that he did not foresee. Therefore, if his power cannot change and do what he did not foresee; if it cannot be futile and fail to do what he foresaw, it necessarily follows that he has done everything that he foresaw and cannot do anything that he did not foresee. Now it is certain that he foresaw everything he has done, and did everything that he foresaw. Therefore, if he can do nothing without providence or foreknowledge, he can absolutely do nothing other than what he has done.”

“Secondly, God cannot do anything better [Col. XCVIB] than what he has done; for to do, and not to do, the best is to do badly . . .” [Note: [Col. XCVID] *De sacr.*, lib. I, pars II, cap. 22, tom. II, col. 214.]

Hugh has not weakened his opponents’ proofs. He first refutes them by a general argument: “Everything made is finite. Therefore, to confine God’s power to what has been made is to limit that power itself.”

But can he do anything other than what he has done without injuring his providence? Hugh lays down the principle that resolves the difficulty: foreknowledge is not the cause of creation. The world does not exist because God foresaw it; he foresaw it because it was to exist.

Could God have made something better than what he has made? Hugh answers by this dilemma: the totality of creatures [Col. XCVIC] cannot be better, either because it is the highest good, or because it cannot receive a degree of goodness beyond those which it possesses. If it is the highest good, in the sense that it is absolute goodness and lacks nothing, it is equal to God. Then either the goodness of the creature is exaggerated at the Creator’s expense, or the goodness of the Creator is depreciated in favor of the creature. If, on the contrary, it cannot be more perfect because it is incapable of receiving one further degree of perfection, that incapacity is itself a defect, and one can conceive a world which does not possess it. [Note: [Col. XCVID] Id. ibid.]

These extracts, which we do not wish to multiply further, suffice to make us understand [Col. XCVID] that Hugh could, like many others, have distinguished himself amid the controversies agitating the schools by the subtlety and penetration of his mind, and even by the artifices of his dialectic. We ought to be grateful to him for having devoted himself to a more serious study and for having renounced some applause in order to attain results more useful to learning.

The prince of ancient philosophers, Plato, had established the most brilliant school of philosophy of which Greece could boast; but his disciples continued [Col. XCVIIA] his teaching poorly. Aristotle, the most illustrious of them, became his adversary and did not blush to become his detractor. Speusippus, who remained faithful to him, followed in his master’s footsteps only timidly and uncertainly. More than once he distorted his doctrine while seeking to defend it. Hugh was more fortunate: among the scholastics of Saint-Victor he found a disciple worthy of him.
