Like him, he was foreign to France; Scotland was his native country; like him, a mystical and dogmatic theologian; like him, a disciple of Saint Augustine and Plato; like him, using knowledge in order to arrive at love, which is the perfection of life; like him, accepting the principles of faith as the foundation of theological science, but not believing that it condemned [Col. XCVIIB] reason to immobility or forbade it all speculation. [Note: [Col. XCVIIC] *On the Trinity*, book I, chapter 1. Richard comments, in the sense of the ancients, on the prophet Isaiah’s text that had become so famous: *Nisi credideritis, non intelligetis*—“Unless you believe, you will not understand.”

“Faith is the door of the sanctuary; through it one enters. But once the door has been opened, one must not remain on the threshold of this temple, so rich in wonders of every kind; one must continually advance, striving to understand more and more the truths received by faith.”

Elsewhere he says: “If the beginning of every good resides in faith, its completion and perfection are found in knowledge. Let us therefore labor to attain this perfection; let everything serve us as a step by which to pass from faith to knowledge; let us employ all our efforts to understand what we believe . . . . . But what wonder if our soul is troubled and darkened in the presence of the mysteries of the Godhead, when it is [Col. XCVIID] almost at every moment defiled by the dust of earthly thoughts! ‘Come forth from the dust, O virgin, daughter of Zion!’ If we are true sons of Zion, let us set up this sublime ladder of contemplation; and, taking flight like eagles, let us escape the earth in order to soar in the height of heaven.” —Ibid., chapter 3.]

Together with Hugh, he was the principal representative of Platonic philosophy in the twelfth century, the glory of the school of Saint-Victor and the light of his contemporaries. Their names are as inseparable as their writings. We must return to them in order to find the first link in that chain of illustrious theologians who established theological learning upon foundations so broad and solid, and who raised that magnificent edifice—sometimes enveloped in whirls of dust, or even covered with mud, but always unshaken amid the greatest storms. This is what gives that school a truly historical importance. The twelfth century prepares the thirteenth. The school of [Col. XCVIIC] Saint-Victor dominates the twelfth, not through the brilliance of its controversies, but through patient labor, begun [Col. XCVIIIA] and pursued in the heart of the deepest solitude.

Yet this was not its only claim upon the memory and gratitude of future generations. Hugh and Richard were its most illustrious doctors in the twelfth century, but they were not the only ones. Besides Peter Lombard, who was received at Saint-Victor at Saint Bernard’s request, Simon Gourdan cites Stephen of Tournai, a distinguished canonist; Obizon, an illustrious physician [Note: [Col. XCVIID] *Life and Maxims of the Illustrious Men of Saint-Victor of Paris*. Manuscript, introduction, p. 1.]; Abbot Achard [Note: [Col. XCVIID] John of Salisbury, *Metalogicon*, book III, chapter 3; id., book IV, chapter 3; *Life and Maxims of the Illustrious Men of Saint-Victor*. Manuscript. There was another Victorine of the same name who composed rhymed proses.], English by birth, philosopher, man of letters, and theologian alike; Adam [Note: [Col. XCVIIID] He composed a book on the Temptation of Jesus Christ, a Treatise on the Trinity, Homilies, and the Life of the monk Gazelinus; *Universal History of Paris*, vol. II, under the year 1161, and *Catalogue*, p. 715. Simon Gourdan, manuscript.], also English, a celebrated grammarian, skillful rhetorician, and subtle philosopher, a disciple of Abelard; Arnulf, brother of [Col. XCVIIIB] John, bishop of Séez, who practiced poetry [Note: [Col. XCVIIIC] We shall quote some of his verses, in which he speaks with little modesty of his own fame; he addresses them to a certain Nepos.

> Once all Normandy called me a celebrated poet,  
> And scarcely did all Gaul grant me an equal;  
> One believed me among the foremost, the other the foremost;  
> Nor did the former call me her own, but the latter did.
>
> Yet everywhere I was celebrated as great with varied honor,  
> Illustrious abroad, and with especial distinction at home.  
> Now perhaps a new age, powerful in producing novelty, has brought you forth—  
> A model for the untrained, an object of envy to the good;
>
> [Col. XCVIIID] Learning has fashioned you, an old poet, from a boy  
> And has given your age words not its own.  
> Your words savor of old age and profess Virgil himself;  
> A page blossoms, beardless, with hoary maturity.
>
> My Muse herself, astonished at your days and your words of days,  
> Grew pale before your days and words.  
> And when, as usual, I had taken up my tablets,  
> She deprived my tongue of speech and my hand of the stylus.
>
> Therefore I yield to you the Muses and sacred Helicon,  
> And abandon the sweet waters of the sacred spring.  
> Cultivate those things which you know; the favor you understand how to retain  
> You can preserve only through diligent assiduity.]; Walter, of whom we still possess two manuscripts, a vehement adversary of all the heretics of his time; and, finally, a great number of others whom it would take too long to enumerate.

We shall not pursue further the history of this school, whose last distinction was the poet Santeuil. We have reached the limit we had set ourselves, and we believe that from what precedes we may draw the following conclusions:

1. At the beginning of the twelfth century a school was established at Saint-Victor in Paris.

2. At that period this school represented, in its doctrines, Platonic philosophy; it was [Col. XCVIIIC] at once mystical and dogmatic.

3. It was in this school that the first [Col. XCIXA] attempts at the theological syncretism which we see attaining its highest degree of perfection [Col. CA] in the works of Albert the Great, Saint Thomas, and Saint Bonaventure were made.

Seen and read at Paris, at the Sorbonne, 6 May 1854, by the dean of the Faculty of Letters of Paris. J.-VICT. LE CLERC.

Seen by the rector of the Academy of the Seine. CAYX.

Paris, 24 May 1854.

[Col. XCIX]

# CRITICAL STUDY OF THE WORKS OF HUGH OF SAINT-VICTOR, BY ABBÉ HUGONIN, Licentiate in Letters of the Faculty of Paris, former student of the Carmelite ecclesiastical school.

[Col. XCIXB] We shall summarize the critical work that has been done on this subject and add our own observations. We do not, however, claim to clarify every doubt, resolve every problem presented by this study, or furnish definitive results. Hugh’s editors have heaped together indiscriminately, without discernment or selection, the works of the Victorine and a multitude of apocryphal pieces. The ancient catalogues and even the manuscripts themselves are not always trustworthy guides; thus the critic finds himself at every step confronted with insurmountable difficulties and reduced to his own conjectures. Those who preceded us have made ample use of this privilege, and their contradictory opinions have multiplied the obscurities and [Col. XCIXC] doubts. We thought it would be of little use to add new ones; when we cannot attain certainty, we shall content ourselves with faithfully setting forth the opinions of the different critics who preceded us.

In this study we shall review the treatises attributed to Hugh of Saint-Victor. We shall follow the same order as the Rouen editors.

[Note: [Col. XCIXD] The references in parentheses indicate the place of each work according to the new order followed in our edition, in which the authentic works have been gathered under the headings *Exegetica*, *Dogmatica* [Col. CD] and *Mystica*, while doubtful writings or writings foreign to Hugh of Saint-Victor have been placed in appendices. EDITOR.]

The work which begins the first volume is entitled *On Sacred Scriptures and Sacred Writers* (*De Scripturis et Scriptoribus sacris*) (vol. I, beginning). It may be regarded as an introduction to the study of Holy Scripture, and consequently of theology as a whole.

Hugh treats of the nature of the sacred books and of the characteristics distinguishing them from profane works, [Col. XCIXD] of their division, the canonical books, the authors [Col. CB] who composed them, and the fruits that may be drawn from reading them.

The divine Scriptures are inspired by God. They make human beings divine; they teach them to reform themselves in the image of their Creator, by knowing him and knowing themselves; for God is truth without error, goodness without malice, and blessedness without misery.

Hugh already establishes the clear and profound distinction that we shall so often find in his writings between the natural world and the supernatural world, creation and incarnation.

He divides the Holy Scriptures into two parts, the Old and New Testaments. The Old Testament comprises the Law, or Pentateuch; the Prophets; [Col. CC] and the Hagiographa, or historical books.

The New consists of the Gospels, the writings of the apostles, and the writings of the Fathers; Hugh does not consider the latter inspired. He names each book and cites the Hebrew names, which he interprets. He does not place among the canonical books the Book of Wisdom, Ecclesiasticus, Judith, Tobit, or the Maccabees; he puts them on the same level as the writings of Saint Jerome, Saint Augustine, Saint Gregory, Isidore of Seville, Origen, the Venerable Bede, and the other doctors. One may be surprised that our Victorine, who so often relies on the testimony of Saint Jerome and Saint Augustine, who cites [Col. CD] and comments upon them, should have had so imperfect a knowledge of the canons of Holy Scripture.

[Col. CIA] Along with the Catholic doctors, he recognizes that Holy Scripture contains a literal, an allegorical, and an anagogical sense. Nevertheless, he teaches that not all our sacred books ought to receive this triple interpretation. He attacks the false mystics who give themselves over to imagination instead of patiently seeking the truth which God has hidden beneath the husk of facts, and who neglect the literal sense. But at the same time he recognizes the importance of the allegorical sense; he enters into rather minute detail on this subject and gives the rules that must be followed in discovering it. One must observe, he says, circumstances, places, times, and numbers, for all these things may be symbolic. He proves this by examples; [Col. CIB] we shall cite only one. A circumstance of place: Judaea lies between Egypt and Babylon; the Jews are in turn subdued, first by the Egyptians and then by the Assyrians. The Egyptians signify our evil desires; the Assyrians signify the demons who tempt us. The conflict within us always begins with the former, and only through it can the latter overcome and enslave us.

Following Saint Augustine and several other Christian philosophers, he gives his mystical theory of numbers. He attributes the last books of Kings to David, Job to Moses or to some prophet, and Esther to Ezra. He does not know the author of Judith, Tobit, the Maccabees, or the [Col. CIC] Book of Wisdom; he merely reports the view of those who thought the latter work to be by Philo the Jew.

He recounts the wonderful history of the translation of the Septuagint, but with Saint Jerome’s corrections, Jerome having regarded it as fabulous. He then enumerates Aquila’s version, that of Symmachus, that of Theodotion, the Vulgate translation—whose author he did not know—the two versions of Origen, and that of Saint Jerome.

In the *Explanatory Notes on the Pentateuch* (vol. I, col. 29), after commenting on Saint Jerome’s prologue, he himself gives a short introduction. He explains the Greek and Hebrew title of this [Col. CID] work and indicates its author’s purpose. The Pentateuch is historical and prophetic; Moses is both historian and prophet. He is a historian because he recounts the origin of the world, societies, empires, and especially of the Jewish people, whose legislation he proposes to make known. He is a prophet not only because of the prophecies contained in his book, but because the facts he recounts are themselves prophetic and figurative of future events.

If we compare this passage with Hugh’s teaching on the allegorical interpretation of Holy Scripture, we have difficulty understanding why the Benedictines found it obscure and incomplete. “Hugh,” they say, “shows, but imperfectly, [Col. CIIA] that Moses acts the part of a prophet; as a historiographer he succeeds better in developing this writer’s purpose by treating of the origin of the world.” Yet he scarcely develops this purpose; he merely indicates it. Moses proposed, he says, to make known God’s power in creating the world and his wisdom in adorning it.

Hugh then rapidly surveys the chapters of Genesis and explains their principal verses. At verse 14 of chapter I (vol. I, col. 36, lower column), where Moses recounts the creation of the heavenly bodies, the Victorine gives, as an opinion held in his time by certain holy persons, that Hercules or Prometheus were the inventors of astrology. He condemns that science. He recognizes, indeed, that the stars [Col. CIIB] exercise an influence on bodies, but denies that this influence binds freedom.

The notes on Exodus (vol. I, col. 61) are shorter than the preceding. Though quite judicious, they contain nothing especially interesting. This is the Benedictines’ judgment, and we readily subscribe to it.

Hugh develops his treatment more fully in the book of Leviticus (vol. I, col. 74). In Dom Brial’s judgment, this is the part of the Pentateuch he treated best.

His explanations of Numbers and Deuteronomy scarcely fill a page (vol. I, cols. 84–86) and do not deserve the name of commentary. They are notes gathered here and there and united by an unskilled hand. They contain such gross [Col. CIIC] blunders that the Benedictines suspected interpolation.

Hugh’s *Annotations* on Judges (col. 87) and Kings (col. 93) are of the same kind. The analysis he gives of the former is merely a short indication of its subject matter. It is followed by several literal explanations of verses chosen here and there, without connection or method. He explains more fully Deborah’s song (vol. I, col. 89) and the history of Samson (vol. I, col. 94). We have noted objections presented forcefully and clearly, and sensible solutions which presuppose a great knowledge of the sacred text.

Hugh had especially undertaken to explain the [Col. CIID] literal sense of the Pentateuch, and he generally remains quite faithful to his purpose. Yet he sometimes returns to the moral and allegorical sense. They are like little digressions in which he gives his faith and piety nourishment that seems necessary to him. He does so without effort. Perhaps it was for him a means of raising his pupils’ minds to God and teaching them to sanctify their studies by pious reflections. I know that this gentle and unctuous piety was not always a characteristic of schools in the Middle Ages; the students had not yet entirely stripped themselves of the roughness of the age. They were violent in their passions, in their disputes, and even in the manifestation of their faith. But [Col. CIIIA] in this respect Hugh was not of his century; and probably he communicated to his disciples his gentleness and piety, his feelings and his tastes.

This is a point upon which critics have not dwelt enough: they have considered too much in themselves the small commentaries we have just studied. To judge them fairly, one had to take circumstances into account. Any attentive reader will readily recognize that these commentaries are not regular compositions; they are simple collections of notes, and these notes themselves are often only summaries of the lectures which our Victorine gave to his disciples. But these disciples consisted in large part of the canons of Saint-Victor, whose discipline and fervor were [Col. CIIIB] celebrated throughout the world, according to contemporary testimony. Should one be surprised that he spoke to them in the language of mystical piety, the ordinary language of the Church in most of its offices? This was indeed what had to please his hearers and hold them all the more strongly, just as the subtleties of scholasticism charmed and transported with admiration the numerous youth who crowded around Abelard’s chair.

The Benedictines judge our Victorine’s notes on the Book of Psalms (vol. III, col. 589) severely. “Rarely,” they say, “does he successfully explain the letter; his moralizations and allegories would be more estimable if they were less frequent and did not so often lack [Col. CIIIC] accuracy.”

In these notes Hugh seems to us to adhere preferentially to the moral instruction that can be drawn from reading the Psalms. They appear principally intended to help the canons of Saint-Victor, or certain other religious, recite the canonical hours devoutly. Hugh addresses them to a religious whose name he does not give. “It is for you, my dear brother,” he writes at the beginning of this little commentary, “that I have lightly explained some verses of the Psalmist. I have drawn a small drop from a bottomless abyss.”

The titles of the works we have just reviewed give us a fairly exact idea of them. They are not treatises or commentaries, but explanatory notes, little notes; their style is clear and simple, without art or ornament. They attest in our Victorine sound judgment, a cultivated mind, and erudition uncommon in the age in which he lived. Most of the literal explanations he gives of the sacred text may be read in modern commentaries.

The explanation of Ecclesiastes (vol. I, col. 113) bears different titles. With M. Hauréau, we believe that they indicate only one work. In the preamble Hugh tells his disciples that he has put in writing certain of the most important points which he had developed before them. This work is therefore truly a summary of his lessons. It [Col. CIVA] is not merely a simple collection of notes like the preceding works, but a genuine commentary divided into homilies. Only the first nineteen remain to us. They comprise the explanation of the first four chapters.

Hugh again attacks both those who abuse mystical interpretations and those who reject them. “There are many,” he says, “who do not understand the power of the sacred Scriptures, who veil their splendor and disfigure their beauty by extraneous explanations; instead of revealing hidden mysteries, they obscure evident truths. For my part, I think equally blameworthy those who obstinately deny that one should seek in Holy Scripture a [Col. CIVB] mystical sense hidden beneath the veil of allegory, and those who superstitiously seek one where none exists.”

Now, according to Hugh, Solomon in Ecclesiastes proposed much more to inspire contempt for human things than to expound mysteries. Consequently, in interpreting it one should adhere rather to the literal than to the figurative sense. This is the rule he imposes on himself, and he remains fairly faithful to it.

This commentary appeared to the Benedictines dry, diffuse, and burdened with useless discussions in which philosophy, history, and morality are mingled. They admit, however, that several passages are developed with clarity and precision; we would add, with warmth. They cite, among others, the paraphrase of these words [Col. CIVC] from the second chapter: *Tradidit mundum disputationibus eorum*—“He gave the world over to their disputations.” We shall further recall the passage we cited elsewhere on meditation and contemplation.

In the *Commentary on the First Three Chapters of Jeremiah’s Lamentations* (vol. I, col. 255), Hugh announces from the outset that he will expound the literal, allegorical, and anagogical senses; but he often forgets the first and attaches himself almost exclusively to the other two.

The explanation of the prophet Joel (vol. I, col. 321) is more literal. Hugh summarizes this work in three words: “The prophet terrifies, consoles, instructs.” He terrifies by predicting the scourges about to fall upon Jerusalem; he consoles by announcing their [Col. CIVD] end; he instructs by showing, in a more distant future, the incarnation of the Word. The Benedictines observe that he draws upon Jewish traditions and cites Hegesippus, Boethius, and Avicenna. We must add that he cites them without naming them: he speaks explicitly only of Hebrew tradition.

The Benedictines, so severe in their criticism of our Victorine’s works, find that his remarks on Obadiah (vol. I, col. 371) are not without merit. Obadiah had prophesied against Idumaea. For Hugh, this province is a figure of the world according to the allegorical sense, and of the flesh according to the anagogical sense. He confuses Obadiah the prophet with the other Obadiah who, under Ahab’s reign, had [Col. CVA] hidden and fed a hundred prophets in caves. He invokes the testimony of Herodotus (vol. I, col. 390, line 1) and of other Greek and Latin historians whose names he does not cite.

These last three commentaries are neither simple collections of notes like the first works we discussed nor a continuous discourse like the explanation of Ecclesiastes. Scholastic form predominates in them, and the interpreter often proceeds by divisions and subdivisions.

The opuscules we have just reviewed certainly belong to our Victorine; no critic disputes this.

The latest editors of his works had printed after them the *Allegories on the Old and New [Col. CVB] Testament*. This is not their proper place. [Note: [Col. CVD] In our edition, the first part of the *Allegorical Extracts* is placed in the Appendix to the dogmatic works (vol. III, col. 191); the second in the Appendix to the commentaries on Scripture [Col. CVID] (vol. I, col. 633); the third in the Appendix to the mystical works (vol. III, col. 899).] Indeed, in a first preamble we read: “Receive then, my dear brother, this second part of our extracts, which you requested as nourishment suited to your soul.” In a second preamble we read: “After setting forth the origin and distinction of the arts, we have recounted the birth, progress, and fall of all kingdoms down to our own time. Now we shall explain, according to the order of history, the obscure depths of the allegories of the Old and New Testament.” The manuscript confirms these testimonies. There can consequently be no doubt that these allegories form the second part of the extracts of which we shall speak in their proper place. It is probably [Col. CVC] for this reason that we find no work under this title in the catalogues published by M. Hauréau.

The same editors had added to the allegorical interpretation of Saint Matthew two opuscules that do not at all form part of that commentary. The first is an explanation of the Lord’s Prayer (vol. I, col. 779); the second bears the title *Septenarium*, or *On the Seven Septenaries* (*De septem septenariis*) (col. 405). Both are listed in the two catalogues published by M. Hauréau. I am surprised that Dom Ceillier did not notice them: he affirms that they have not yet been printed. In the first, Hugh opposes the seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer to the seven capital sins. In the second, he adds to the seven petitions and the seven capital sins the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, the seven cardinal virtues, and even the beatitudes, which he likewise reduces to seven.

Besides the authority of the manuscripts, which attribute all these writings to Hugh, one observes in them several passages borrowed from his explanation of Obadiah and repeated almost word for word in his *Sum of Sentences* and his treatise *On the Sacraments*.

We find another septenary at the end of the notes on Obadiah. It is almost similar to that [Col. CVIA] which precedes, but it does not form a separate work: it is part of the commentary.

In the Rouen edition, the nineteenth chapter of the *Allegories on the New Testament* contains a short treatise on the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit, mentioned in several catalogues of our Victorine’s works. [Note: [Col. CVID] See vol. I, col. 410.] It is an explanation of these words of Saint Luke the Evangelist: *Si enim vos cum sitis mali, nostis bona dare filiis vestris, quanto magis Pater vester coelestis dabit Spiritum bonum petentibus se*—“For if you, though you are evil, know how to give good things to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him.” This treatise is not part of the commentary. Hugh first opposes the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit to the seven capital sins, as in the preceding *Septenaries*. He then abandons this comparison and undertakes to show generally [Col. CVIB] what effects the Holy Spirit produces in souls.

The explanation of the *Magnificat* (vol. I, col. 413), mentioned by several catalogues, is another small opusculum wrongly interpolated until now into the *Allegorical Notes on the Gospel of Saint Luke*. The author does not concern himself at all with the allegorical sense: it is a literal interpretation intermingled with digressions on controversial matters. Here Hugh refutes two opinions taught in his time: the existence of two souls in a human being, one sensitive and the other rational; and a sort of optimism that placed limits on God’s freedom. We shall find the refutation of the same error in his book of *Sentences*. What he says concerning the four [Col. CVIC] fears is found word for word in that same work. The resemblance of doctrine and even of expressions, joined to the authority of the manuscripts, proves that this opusculum belongs to our Victorine and not to Saint Augustine, to whom it was long attributed.

M. Hauréau, in the catalogues he has published of the works of Hugh of Saint-Victor, appends to this title, *Notulae super Joannem* (*Notes on John*) (vol. I, col. 827), the following note: “The Benedictines do not wish this commentary to be by the Victorine. It must belong, they say, to some teacher of sophistical theology. Whoever this alleged logician may be, he had very pronounced tendencies toward mysticism, since he worshipped the true God under the form [Col. CVID] of an essence wholly present within all creatures: *Deus tota essentia sua in omni creatura est*—‘God is, by the whole of his essence, in every creature.’ What, then, is this doctrine—or rather this strange language (for one must not here give the words the meaning they appear to have)—if not the language of the theologians and philosophers of Saint-Victor?”

Thus M. Hauréau claims this commentary for our Victorine because he finds in it a strange language which can only be that of the theologians and philosophers of Saint-Victor. Doubtless, when he wrote these lines, the learned [Col. CVIIA] critic had forgotten the texts he had studied so patiently. He knows well that in the twelfth century the expression “God is essentially in his creatures” is not strange; that it belongs to a great theological controversy; that it is found in William of Mortagne combating the errors of Abelard and his disciples; and that Saint Thomas and his school in the following century did not fear to employ it. Besides, the words accompanying those cited by M. Hauréau sufficiently explain the author’s thought and completely justify it. “God,” he says, “is in his creatures in three ways; he is there by his power and by his essence, for these two attributes are one and the same thing . . . God cannot be [Col. CVIIB] in his creatures in such a way that one says he is in a place. He is in his creatures, not by a local presence, but by himself, governing and preserving them without intermediary, just as the soul is wholly in every part of the body. If the soul withdraws from the body, it dies and falls into dust. It is therefore evident that the soul is the life of the body. Thus God is, by his whole essence, in every creature, giving them being. If he withdrew, the creature would return to nothing, as the body without the soul is reduced to dust. How God governs and preserves the creature, and the soul the body, I do not know; but I know only that God is essentially in his creatures.”

The whole passage therefore amounts to saying that God [Col. CVIIC] is present to creatures as the soul is present to the body: not by a local presence, but nevertheless essentially. There are not in God parts corresponding to the parts of creatures; nor is God merely at one point in space, from which he exercises his power at a distance where he is not, as the disciples of Abelard maintained. We cannot, consequently, accept M. Hauréau’s conclusion as legitimately deduced from his premises. Other evidence must be sought elsewhere in order to establish with certainty whether or not this work belongs to our Victorine.

The manuscripts and catalogues already cited attribute it to him. In it we recognize [Col. CVIID] the stamp of Hugh’s genius, despite its scholastic form: it is his style, his philosophy, and his theology. The author of this work is plainly a disciple of Saint Augustine. He has read and meditated upon him; he probably had before his eyes this Father’s treatises on the Gospel of Saint John. He borrows Augustine’s explanations and adopts his opinions. In this commentary we find several rather striking resemblances to the *Questions on Saint Paul*, of which we shall shortly speak. Thus, in both works he teaches the rather singular opinion that the philosophers of antiquity knew the Trinity but did not love it. He explains the origin of evil in the former much as in the latter; in both [Col. CVIIIA], and in nearly the same terms, he sets the Manichaeans against the Pelagians. Nevertheless, the authors of the *Literary History of France* and Dom Ceillier hold that this work is not by Hugh; the latter gives no reason for his opinion, while the former supports it with the following arguments.

The author of the commentary, explaining the words *in principio erat Verbum* (“In the beginning was the Word”), says that the sacred writer rightly employed *erat* (“was”) and not *fuit* (“was”). The Word was through his generation, but he has not ceased to be because he has not ceased to be begotten. He observes with Saint Augustine that, when Holy Scripture uses the perfect in such a case, it adds *hodie* (“today”): *hodie genui te* (“today I have begotten you”). Now Hugh would teach the contrary in his *Summa* (vol. II, col. 54, middle). [Col. CVIIIB] Yet it is enough to compare the two indicated passages to be convinced that the contradiction is far from evident.

The second proof adduced by the Benedictines in support of their opinion is more serious. The commentator on Saint John seems to condemn those who distinguish quality and quantity in divine knowledge, and who maintain that in Christ’s soul there is knowledge equal to that possessed by the Divinity—not in quality, but in quantity—the soul receiving, and the Divinity possessing by nature, infinite knowledge. Now we know that this is Hugh’s opinion. In several of his works he teaches the equality of divine and human knowledge in Jesus Christ. His treatise *De anima Christi* has no other [Col. CVIIIC] purpose than to develop this thesis.

In the face of these difficulties, we cannot conclude anything with certainty. Nevertheless, it seems to us more probable that this commentary is truly the work of Hugh of Saint-Victor.

Critics do not agree concerning the author of the explanatory notes on Saint Paul’s Epistle to the Romans (vol. I, col. 879) and the two Epistles to the Corinthians (vol. I, col. 903). The same controversy exists concerning the commentary entitled *Questions and Decisions on All the Epistles of the Same Apostle* (vol. I, col. 431). Neither work is mentioned in M. Hauréau’s catalogues. Oudin and Dom Ceillier do not acknowledge them as [Col. CVIIID] Hugh’s work. “It is not,” says Dom Ceillier, “either the method or the style of the Victorine. It is the work of some scholastic of the thirteenth century, when the common practice was to elucidate difficulties only by questions and answers.” The authors of the *Literary History* adopted the contrary opinion. They reply to Oudin and Dom Ceillier that a similar method occurs among twelfth-century writers: such is Abelard’s commentary on Saint Paul, as are also some works of Honorius of Autun, especially his treatise *De affectibus* (“On the Affections”). Moreover, in these commentaries attributed to Hugh, we find the view he professes concerning the equality of divine and human knowledge in Jesus Christ. There also occur [Col. CIXA] formulas peculiar to him. Thus, when he ventures certain conjectures, he adds: *salva reverentia secretorum* (“with due reverence for the mysteries”); or again: *absque praejudicio melioris sententiae* (“without prejudice to a better opinion”). At page 383 (vol. I, cols. 439–40), the author sets forth the theory of God’s twofold manifestation through the natural world and the supernatural world, and in nearly the same terms as in several works unquestionably belonging to our Victorine. Elsewhere, he gives an enumeration of the various vanities that recalls a similar passage in the *Commentary on Ecclesiastes*. Finally, in the explanation of the First Epistle to the Corinthians (vol. I, col. 524, line 55), the author refers to his treatise *On the Sacraments* and to his book of *Sentences*, concerning doctrines which we find exactly [Col. CIXB] developed in works bearing these names, which no one disputes belong to our author.

There can consequently be no doubt that this work ought to be restored to him.

The catalogues published by M. Hauréau mention two commentaries by Hugh on the works of Saint Denis: one *On the Angelic, or Celestial, Hierarchy*, and the other *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. The Benedictines add a third, on the letters of the same saint. According to these critics, the latter two, which are unpublished, are found in manuscript no. 1619 of the Imperial Library. M. Hauréau indicates a similar manuscript in the library of Saint-Martin of Tournai, where it is said that the translation of Saint Denis’s text is by Hugh [Col. CIXC] of Saint-Victor. (SANDERUS, *Bibliotheca manuscripta Belgica*, vol. I, p. 112.)

In the works of our Victorine (vol. I, col. 923), we read the first of these commentaries, which no critic disputes belongs to him. But is he the author of the translation which he comments upon? We have seen that the manuscript in the library at Tournai affirms this. The authors of the *Literary History* do not affirm it as positively as M. Hauréau seems to say. They merely state, in a footnote, that this translation was corrected by Hugh of Saint-Victor. Perhaps they allude to this passage: *Interpretatio igitur hierarchiae est ad Deum quantum possibile similitudo et unitas*—“The interpretation, therefore, of hierarchy is likeness and unity toward God insofar as possible.” Hugh observes that the translation is not exact: “What [Col. CIXD] in Greek is called σκοπός (*skopos*, ‘aim’), and what the translator calls *interpretationem* (‘interpretation’), is more properly termed *intentio et directio* (‘intention and direction’).”

This passage proves that the translation is not Hugh’s. Moreover, one may ascertain that it does not differ from Scotus’s translation. Hugh’s own editors were not mistaken on this point, as may be seen from the title they placed at the head of this commentary.

Did Hugh comment upon the two *Hierarchies* and the Letters of Saint Denis? In the manuscript indicated by the Benedictines, several glosses were placed in the margin of the *Celestial Hierarchy*: that of Maximus, that of John Scotus, that of John of Scythopolis, [Col. CXA] surnamed the Saracen, and that of Hugh, as printed in his works. But in the margin of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* there is only one gloss, that of Maximus. It is true that the catalogues of the Imperial Library give this gloss to the Victorine, but a great number of manuscripts attribute it to Maximus. As for the Tournai manuscript, no commentary is mentioned, but a translation. If, then, as M. Hauréau’s catalogues state, Hugh commented upon the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, that commentary remains to be found.

The one which we possess (vol. I, col. 923) is dedicated to Louis the Younger. This prince had caused the church of Saint-Victor to be built. By dedicating this commentary to him, Hugh wished to offer testimony of his [Col. CXB] gratitude.

Dom Brial finds it lengthy and diffuse. Nevertheless, it contains fine doctrines. It is not always useless even for understanding the text of Erigena’s translation, which is very obscure. It is the first commentary known to us on the works attributed to Saint Denis.

We believe that the first chapter is the opusculum listed in certain catalogues under the title: *De differentia divinae ac mundanae theologiae* (“On the Difference between Divine and Worldly Theology”).

The opusculum which begins the second volume bears the title *Institutiones in Decalogum* (“Instructions on the Decalogue”; vol. II, col. 9). It is not mentioned in M. Hauréau’s catalogues, but its attribution to Hugh is not contested. His style and clear traces of his doctrine are found in it.

[Col. CXC] The fourth chapter of the preceding opusculum forms a small independent treatise, under the title *De substantia charitatis* (“On the Substance of Charity”). It was long attributed to Saint Augustine and is not unworthy of him. The latest editors of this Father’s works printed it anonymously in the appendix to the sixth volume of his works, where it is much more complete. It has rightly been restored to our Victorine. It bears his name in a Vatican manuscript. (MONTFAUCON, vol. I, *Bibliotheca manuscript[a]*, p. 66.) Trithemius and M. Hauréau’s catalogues confirm this testimony. Such is the opinion of Dom Brial and Dom Ceillier.

Dom Brial highly praises the *Explanation of the Rule of Saint Augustine* (vol. II, col. 881). [Col. CXD] “It is,” he says, “a work equally worthy of Hugh’s piety and learning. Everywhere one sees a master thoroughly penetrated by the truths he teaches. His reasonings are sound, solid, and based upon the great principles of religion.” Yet in the fifteenth century an anonymous writer undertook to show that this work contained fourteen errors. The very brief censure he composed is found in a manuscript of the Imperial Library containing only writings concerning the usages and government of the Dominicans, which suggests that this anonymous author belonged to that order.

The great value of this censure is that it proves the work belongs to Hugh of Saint-Victor. This testimony is confirmed by Alberic of [Col. CXIA] Trois-Fontaines (*ALBÉRIC*, *Chronicle*, p. 260) and by the annals of Saint-Victor. These manuscript annals inform us that it was read at the *collation*. Yet it is not listed in M. Hauréau’s catalogues.

Several manuscripts, the oldest of which dates from the twelfth century, together with the testimony of Henry of Ghent (*De script. eccles.*, chap. 7, in appendix) and Trithemius (p. 363), leave no doubt that the *Instruction of Novices* (vol. II, col. 925) belongs to our Victorine. This work is divided into twenty-one chapters preceded by a prologue in which, assuming the purity of the motives that led the novice to embrace religious life, he sets out the plan of his treatise thus:

> “The way you must follow is knowledge, discipline, and goodness. Knowledge leads to discipline, discipline to goodness, and goodness to blessedness. This is the subject on which, with the Lord’s grace, I propose to speak to you, so that you may walk without fear of going astray on the way that leads to him.”

[Col. CXIB] He concludes the treatise thus:

> “This is what I had to say to you, my dearest brothers, concerning knowledge and discipline. As for you, ask God for goodness.”

The Benedictines regret that he did not treat this last point. As it stands, they esteem it a work complete in its kind, a useful manual not only for persons consecrated to God but also for all who live [Col. CXIC] in society.

It is of interest because of the rule it prescribes concerning modesty and neatness in clothing, decency of bearing, reserve in conversation, temperance at meals, mutual tokens of esteem and friendship in social intercourse, zeal for observances—in a word, all the social virtues that serve to cement peace and concord. Irony naturally finds its place in the descriptions he gives of certain faults related to his subject. We have cited elsewhere several examples.

M. Hauréau’s catalogues mention two other analogous treatises, the first entitled *On the [Col. CXID] Profession of Monks*, and the second *On the Discipline of Monks*. Must we suppose that the author of these catalogues was mistaken and attributed to Hugh a treatise bearing the same title in the works of Saint Bernard? Must it be identified with the *Instruction of Novices*, and said to be the same work under two different titles; or is it one of Hugh’s works, distinct from the first but hitherto unknown? We have insufficient grounds for adopting an opinion. As to the treatise *On the Discipline of Monks*, the Benedictines knew it; they say that it forms part of Saint-Victor manuscript 199, now 137. It is found joined to the *Instruction of Novices* in a great number of manuscripts. It does indeed form, in the [Col. CXIIA] works of Hugh, chapters 10–21 of the same treatise.

It has sometimes been doubted whether the four books *On the Cloister of the Soul* (vol. II, col. 1017) were the work of a monk or of a regular canon (*NANGIUS*, *Chronicle*, under the year 1140). The author himself settled the question by declaring who he is: “A humble canon,” he says, “I speak of monks”; in his introduction he recommends that his name not be disclosed. The recommendation of the humble writer was followed only too faithfully; hence the uncertainties of criticism.

In a manuscript from the monastery of Châminot, in the diocese of Châlons-sur-Marne, one reads: “Beginning of the prologue of an anonymous author, followed [Col. CXIIB] by the treatise *On the Cloister of the Soul*. It is nevertheless said that the author is Hugh of Corbie, canon of Saint-Laurent.”

Casimir Oudin asserts that he saw several similar manuscripts, of equally early date, in different libraries of the Cistercian order, whereas he encountered only recent and few manuscripts bearing the name of Hugh of Saint-Victor (vol. II, col. 1108).

Several manuscripts of the Imperial Library attribute it to Hugh Foliet, or de Foulloi, prior of the canons of Saint-Laurent.

Finally, it is mentioned once in the first catalogue of M. Hauréau, and twice in the second, [Col. CXIIC] as belonging to Hugh of Saint-Victor.

Three persons therefore contend for this work: Hugh Foliet, or de Foulois, or de Foulloi, monk of Corbie; Hugh, canon of Saint-Laurent; and Hugh of Saint-Victor. Dom Brial (*Literary History of France*, vol. XIII, p. 492) establishes that Hugh of Foulloi was never a monk of Corbie, but a canon of Saint-Laurent of Heilli, a priory of the Order of Saint Augustine which was temporally dependent upon the Order of Corbie. Thus the monk and the canon are one and the same person, leaving only two claimants: Hugh of Foulois and Hugh of Saint-Victor. Now, if one observes that all manuscripts earlier than the thirteenth or fourteenth century bear the name Hugh of Foulois, [Col. CXIID] and combines this proof with the testimonies cited above, one cannot doubt that the canon of Saint-Laurent is the true author of the *Cloister of the Soul*. M. Hauréau observed that the catalogues and manuscripts crediting Hugh of Saint-Victor with it are only a protest by the Victorines against universal opinion. Thus, in a Saint-Victor manuscript (no. 808), the hand of a religious erased the name of Hugh of Foulois, which had been placed at the head of the work by the hand of a twelfth- or thirteenth-century copyist. Some manuscript copies were also composed from fragments of the original work and other fragments borrowed from the works of the canon of Saint-Victor. No. 577 of the Saint-Victor collection [Col. CXIIIA] offers us a curious example of this substitution.

The second book of the *Cloister of the Soul* contains interesting details concerning the organization of a monastery and the life of religious at that period.

The four books *On the Soul* (vol. III, col. 165) are found separately in manuscripts; it is probable that they belong to different authors. The first, initially attributed to Saint Bernard, was printed among the apocrypha in the new edition of his works under the title *Meditation on the Inner Man*. The same is true of the third, which seems merely a continuation of the first and bears, among Saint Bernard’s works, the title *The Inner House*, or *The Edification [Col. CXIIIB] of Conscience*. If the author of these two works is the same, he is certainly not Hugh of Saint-Victor, since he himself tells us:

> [Note: [Col. CXIIID] Book III: “I stand, as it were, a kind of monster among the sons of God, having the habit of a monk but not the manner of life, in a great throng.” [Col. CXIVD]]

that he is a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict. Dom Brial maintains that no manuscript bears Hugh’s name. M. Hauréau cites several in which it occurs, including no. 364 A of the Sorbonne and 678 of Saint-Victor. The first appears to date from the end of the thirteenth century.

The second book was printed in the appendix to the sixth volume of Saint Augustine’s works. The editors of this Father rightly observe that it is only a compilation composed of passages taken from Gennadius, Boethius, Cassiodorus, Isidore of Seville, Alcuin, Hugh of Saint-Victor, and [Col. CXIIIC] several others. [Note: [Col. CXIVD] Appendix, vol. VI.] It is therefore not by Saint Augustine. Nor can it be by Hugh of Saint-Victor, for it cites fragments of a letter of Isaac, abbot of l’Étoile, who is later than he. It is ordinarily attributed to Olcher, a friend of that abbot.

The fourth book forms a separate work; it too is only a compilation, whose author is unknown. The first eleven chapters are taken from the *Manual* printed in the appendix to volume IV of Saint Augustine’s Works; the twelfth is read word for word in the anonymous treatise *On Charity*; the following five seem to break away from those preceding: they are a dialogue among several allegorical personages.

[Col. CXIIID] Two titles which we read in M. Hauréau’s catalogue must be connected with this treatise *On the Soul*. The first is *De conscientia* (“On Conscience”), which is the third book of this treatise; the second is *Confessio ejusdem ad abbatem* (“Confession of the Same to the Abbot”). This opusculum appeared unpublished to the Benedictines, but it forms the final chapters of the third book *De anima*. It is unfortunate that the interlocutors were suppressed in the edition of Hugh’s works. This suppression makes the discourse obscure.

Most critics, on the faith of the manuscripts, attribute the treatise *De medicina animae* (“On the Medicine of the Soul”; vol. II, col. 1183) to Hugh of Foulois. It bears his name in a manuscript from the abbey of Alne cited by Dom Mabillon, [Col. CXIVA] and in manuscript 2896 of the Imperial Library. In some others (1009, 2494) it accompanies other writings regarded as belonging to Hugh of Foulois. Furthermore, there are rather perceptible connections between this work and the *Cloister of the Soul*: not only the same taste for allegories, but the same style, several similar expressions, and the same way of citing Scripture and the Fathers. Nevertheless, in several manuscripts of Saint-Victor and the Sorbonne, it appears among the works of our Victorine.

The author of the *Cloister of the Soul* had found in material cloisters the characteristics of the spiritual cloister. In the *Medicine of the Soul*, he claims to find in the structure of the human body all the affections [Col. CXIVB] of the soul. He attempts to show that there is a perfect analogy between bodily diseases and spiritual diseases, between the remedies for the former and the remedies for the latter. This design, as is evident, presupposes some knowledge of medicine. The author seems to have acquired some; he cites Hippocrates and employs the principles of the art current in his time. This opusculum consists of twenty-four chapters, but the editors suppose it incomplete.

The circumstances that gave rise to this work explain the originality of its form. It had been composed for a physician named John; then it was lost. The author wrote it again, but with much less care, for another [Col. CXIVC] friend who requested it.

It was in the abbey of Hamersleven, as we have seen in its history, that Hugh received his first education. There he was early formed in learning and virtue. To testify to his gratitude toward his former masters, he addressed to them the opusculum entitled *De arrha animae* (“On the Earnest of the Soul”; vol. II, col. 951), a soliloquy on the soul’s pledge. In the prologue he says that he sends them this writing so that they may learn where true love must be sought. “My purpose,” he says, “is not to charm you by the graces of style, but only to attest to you, through edifying instruction, the constancy of my attachment.”

[Col. CXIVD] This soliloquy is a conversation of the soul with God, without noise and without witnesses. “In such circumstances,” says the man, “I shall not be ashamed to ask my soul what is most secret in it, and I may hope that it will tell me the truth without shame.” Accordingly, he questions his soul about what it loves above all things and proves to it that it ought to fix all its thoughts and affections upon God. This is the summary of that dialogue, whose style is not elegant.

The opusculum bearing the title *De laude charitatis* (“In Praise of Charity”; vol. II, col. 969) corresponds much better to Hugh of Saint-Victor’s learning and piety. Its style [Col. CXVA] is entirely fitting: lively, flowing, full of illumination and unction. In it one sees a writer aflame with the fire inspired by the object of his study. Charity itself speaks of charity and praises itself. Among the praises he gives it, we shall cite the following passage:

> “God,” he says, “is charity. The other virtues are not so named. Certainly, patience, humility, and temperance are called gifts of God; but it is not permitted to say that they are God himself. The reason for this difference is evident when the effects of these virtues are compared with those of charity. For whereas the former may be common to the good and the wicked, the latter belongs only to the good and the elect, so that no one can be evil while possessing it.”

The prologue is addressed to a man named Peter. Our author tells him that he set his hand to this writing only out of regard for him and in order to renew himself in charity.

*De modo orandi* (“On the Manner of Praying”; vol. II, col. 977). This opusculum is dedicated to an unnamed friend. It is a sketch rather than a complete treatise. Trithemius and the manuscripts assign it to Hugh, as they do the preceding work. The editors acknowledge that the manuscripts they consulted attribute it to him, but add that neither his genius nor his manner of writing is recognizable in it. It is mentioned in the catalogues published by M. Hauréau under the false title *De virtute ordinis*. This is an evident error by the copyist, [Col. CXVC] who should have read, as the manuscripts indeed read, *De virtute orandi* or *orationis* (“On the efficacy of praying” or “of prayer”). It seems unwise to determine on the basis of style the author of a work probably written in haste, without labour or care. We prefer to rely upon the manuscripts.

The Benedictines rightly reject as unworthy of Hugh of Saint-Victor the treatise *De amore sponsi* (“On the Love of the Bridegroom”; vol. II, col. 987). It is an allegorical commentary on the fourth chapter of the *Song of Songs*; its style is low and grovelling, its reflections childish, its allegories unsuitable. Everything indicates an author without judgment and little skilled in the art of writing. Moreover, contrary to Hugh’s practice, he cites Holy Scripture according to another version [Col. CXVD] than the Vulgate. Nevertheless, M. Hauréau’s catalogue mentions it, and Dom Ceillier attributes it to our Victorine.

Hugh’s editors do not recognize his style in the opusculum entitled *De fructibus carnis et spiritus* (“On the Fruits of Flesh and Spirit”; vol. II, col. 997). The definitions of pride and anger differ from those in the *Septenary*. But in chapter XIX we find a short passage on charity reproduced from the little treatise *De substantia charitatis*. We do not believe that dryness of style is a sufficient reason for removing it from the works of Hugh of Saint-Victor; it is a natural consequence of the author’s purpose, which was to set out precisely the genealogy of vices and [Col. CXVIA] virtues. Genealogical trees were made which later became very fashionable in the schools. The custom was to draw them on skins and attach them to the walls of each classroom for the convenience of teachers and students. The work of which we speak contains one of this kind, and it is not useless if the reader is to follow the author’s thought.

The two treatises printed under the titles *De nuptiis carnalibus* and *De nuptiis spiritalibus* (“On Carnal Marriages” and “On Spiritual Marriages”; vol. II, col. 1202) are among those falsely attributed to Hugh of Saint-Victor. Dom Brial restores them to Hugh of Foulois. It is surprising that this monk, so humble, withdrawn, and exclusively occupied with spiritual things, ostentatiously displays wholly secular learning: he proves the disadvantages of marriage by Theophrastus, Cicero, Cato, Socrates, Philip king of Macedon, Euripides—whose tragedies, he says, are all full of curses against women—Plato, Seneca, and Xenophon.

The opusculum *De arte meditandi* (“On the Art of Meditation”; vol. II, col. 993) is not disputed as Hugh of Saint-Victor’s. Together with Dom Brial, we bring under one examination three writings disputed in Hugh’s case. They are a *Moral Description of Noah’s Ark* (vol. II, col. 617), a *Mystical Description* of the same ark (vol. II, col. 681), and a treatise *On the Vanity of the World* (vol. II, col. 703). The first is recalled in the second, [Col. CXVIC] and the second in the third; they therefore belong to the same author. To the various means Oudin employs to strip Hugh of Saint-Victor of them and transfer them to Hugh of Foulois, we have but one answer: at one point the author refers to his treatise *De tribus diebus* (“On the Three Days”), which no one, by Oudin’s own admission, disputes belongs to our Victorine. We find it difficult to understand how Dom Brial’s continuators, while refuting their colleague’s opinion in the article on Hugh of Foulois, go so far as to deny the existence of Hugh of Saint-Victor’s treatise *De tribus diebus*.

The *Moral Ark* is mentioned in M. Hauréau’s catalogue. The manuscript reproduced by the Victorines in the edition of 1648 is incorrect and incomplete. [Col. CXVID] They would have found a better reading in a very fine twelfth-century manuscript of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, no. 856.

The treatise *De vanitate mundi*, also mentioned in M. Hauréau’s catalogue, is a dialogue whose interlocutors are two persons designated by the letters D and I. According to the Victorines and the Benedictines, these letters mean *docens* (“the teacher”) and *interrogator* (“the questioner”). But a Sorbonne manuscript, no. 304, gives us another key to the puzzle by replacing D with Dindimus. It remains only to translate I as Indaletus. Indaletus and Dindimus are two characters whom our Victorine introduces in his *Epitome in Philosophiam*. This is a further [Col. CXVIIA] proof that the treatise *De vanitate mundi* is not the work of the canon of Saint-Laurent.

The approximate period in which the *Mystical Ark* was composed is known from the author’s enumeration of popes, which ends with Honorius II. In order to be understood, it presupposes a diagram of the allegorized object; without this, it would be wholly unintelligible. Such a diagram is indeed found at the head of several manuscripts.

On the occasion of the respective location of the land of Babylon and Egypt, Hugh promises to show, in a description of the world map, that the former lies north and the latter south of Jerusalem. This world map was undoubtedly a geographical map; two manuscripts prove [Col. CXVIIB] that this map existed in the fourteenth century. Neither the Benedictines nor M. Hauréau found it again. The latter only timidly advances the hypothesis that an opusculum entitled *De locis circa Jerusalem* (“On the Places around Jerusalem”), found in a Saint-Victor manuscript no. 567, formerly 801, together with other works of the same doctor, might be regarded as a fragment of that description.

The *Extracts* form a work divided into three parts which have nothing in common except the title and prologue. The editors therefore, in conformity with most manuscripts, did not hesitate to separate them. But the order in which they arranged them is not the true one. They placed second that which ought to have been first.

> [Note: [Col. CXVIID] This transposition had to be retained in our edition, owing to the division of the *Works* [Col. CXVIIID] of Hugh of Saint-Victor into *Exegetica*, *Dogmatica*, and *Mystica*. EDITOR.]

[Col. CXVIIC] The first part (vol. III, col. 191) contains: 1. a division of all the arts, with the history of their origin and their definition, copied almost word for word from the *Didascalicon*; 2. a compendium of geography drawn from the ancients, as though the world had not changed in the course of centuries; 3. a summary of history ending, for the East, with the Empress Irene and, for the West, with King Philip Augustus. This proves that it is not by Hugh, since Hugh had died by that time.

The second part (vol. I, col. 633) contains an allegorical explanation in thirteen books of the most noteworthy passages of Holy Scripture.

The third contains (vol. III, col. 899) one hundred sermons. In the fourth of these sermons the treatise *On Consideration* by Saint Bernard is cited. It was composed only after the elevation of Pope Eugenius III, and therefore after the death of our author: further proof for supposing that this extract is not by Hugh.

But to whom should this compilation, estimable in certain respects, be attributed? The manuscripts differ on this point. Besides a fairly large number assigning it to Hugh of Saint-Victor, some credit Richard, others Hugh of Foulois; several, finally, give no author’s name. One of the reasons proving against Hugh proves against Richard as well, who died in 1173: he did not see the reign of [Col. CXVIIIA] Philip Augustus. As for Hugh of Foulois, although the date of his death is uncertain, it is nevertheless beyond doubt that he did not outlive Richard.

In all likelihood, it is a collection made by one of the disciples of Hugh and Richard, who gathered here and there, but especially from Victorine writings, whatever seemed most suitable for his purpose. One might then suppose that among the hundred sermons just mentioned are, in part, those composed by Hugh and Richard. But how are they to be distinguished?

The treatise *De bestiariis* (“On Beasts”; vol. III, beginning) comprises four books. The first treats birds; the second, wild beasts; the third is a compilation [Col. CXVIIIB] of the first two; and the fourth is a kind of dictionary in which the properties of animals, plants, and minerals are explained alphabetically. The author of this compilation is uncertain. The Benedictines attribute the first book to Hugh of Foulois, the second to Henry of Ghent, and the third and fourth to William Perrault. These attributions may not be beyond dispute.

The *Didascalicon* (vol. II, col. 739) consists of seven books. The author announces his purpose at the outset in these terms: “Two things are essential for learning the sciences: reading and meditation. Three things must be observed in reading: first, to know what one ought to read; second, [Col. CXVIIIC] to know the order that ought to be followed in reading; third, to be instructed in the true method of reading. We shall develop these three rules in this treatise, whose purpose is to initiate the reader into the knowledge of letters, both secular and divine.” He divides his work into two parts. In the first he treats of the arts—their origin, number, and divisions; he enumerates their inventors; he indicates those to which one ought preferably to attach oneself; finally, he crowns this first part with a rule of life which he sets out for his readers. In the second he treats of the sacred books, determines their number, the rank they hold among themselves, the names of their authors, and the meaning of those [Col. CXVIIID] names. Finally, he teaches how they should be read in order to derive genuine profit from them. (This fourth book and part of the fifth of this collection form, with slight differences and very minor additions, the opusculum published in the first volume under the title *On Sacred Scriptures and Their Writers*.) In every edition, the first book ends at chapter 13, which contains a recapitulation of the preceding twelve. Dom Mabillon is responsible for discovering and publishing (*Analecta*, folio edition, p. 132) a new chapter, which he maintains should constitute the fourteenth. This passage, however, appears to us extraneous in the place where that critic wishes to put it. Perhaps [Col. CXIXA] it is better joined to chapter 8 of book III; its title is *On the Spirit*. The third book is of interest for the historical details it supplies concerning teaching in the twelfth century. The teachers are sharply criticized there. Hugh does not spare the pupils in the fourth book. The seventh seems to be an independent work which the author, according to all the manuscripts, had entitled *On the Three Days*. Its purpose is to raise the human being to the knowledge of God through the sight of created things; it contains magnificent passages.

The treatise *On Power and Will*, vol. II, col. 839, recalls the theological debates of the twelfth century. It discusses the question then agitating the schools: “Which is greater: the will [Col. CXIXB] or the power of God?” Critics are divided over the author of this book. Oudin and Dom Ceillier remove it from the catalogue of Hugh of Saint-Victor’s works. Their reasons are that it is merely a succession of scholastic arguments, indicating a later author, and that it contains barbarous expressions not used in the writings of our Victorine. Dom Brial replies that this scholastic form was not foreign to the twelfth century; that such barbarous expressions as *amplius* in place of *insuper* or *praeterea* (“moreover” or “further”) occur in Hugh’s most securely authenticated works; and that, besides, the substance of the discussion belongs to controversies to which Hugh most often returns. It is optimism that is there refuted as an opinion. Now we know that Abelard [Col. CXIXC] and his disciples taught it at that time. Several arguments are found which he had already employed in his explanation of the *Magnificat* and which we also read in his *Summa*. Dom Brial’s opinion seems to us the more probable.

We join the two treatises entitled *On the Soul*, or *On the Knowledge of Christ* (vol. II, col. 841), and *On the Four Wills in Christ*, because in the author’s thought they follow one another.

There can be no doubt concerning the author of the opusculum *On Christ’s Knowledge and on Knowledge in Christ* (col. 845). Hugh names himself in the prologue; and even had he not named himself, many circumstances would identify him. Moreover, it is known that Hugh and Walter of Mortagne, [Col. CXIXD] bound together by the closest friendship, had had some oral disputes over this question: in Jesus Christ, is the knowledge of the man equal to the knowledge of God—finite or infinite, perfect or imperfect? Hugh maintained that it was equal. Arnulf, archdeacon of Séez and later bishop of Lisieux, having heard from his mouth what he thought on this matter, was surprised and asked Walter to write to him, urging him to retract. Walter carried out the commission and wrote a letter equally praiseworthy for its moderation and learning (*ibid.*). Hugh’s reply is the opusculum in question. He first declares that he ventures only reluctantly, and out of deference to his friend, to treat in writing [Col. CXXA] so thorny a subject; that he would wish people to refrain from publicly discussing such matters; and that, in the necessity imposed upon him, he will avoid appearing rash by reporting only what he has received from learned persons who had treated the matter before him. Coming then to the point, he first sets forth what led Walter to deny the equality of the knowledge of Christ’s soul with that of his divinity: namely, that to posit equal knowledge in both would be to make the creature equal to the Creator. “Not at all,” Hugh replies, “because it is one thing to be wise, another to be Wisdom itself.” Walter was among those whom Hugh’s answer did not persuade; but it must have made him admire how much [Col. CXXB] plausibility a bad cause assumed in Hugh’s hands. There are fine things in this treatise. By comparing this writing with *The Four Wills in Jesus Christ*, one sees that the latter is the continuation of the former and that both belong to the same author. In the first book we read: *Quaeris de anima Christi utrum aequalem cum divinitate scientiam habuerit*—“You ask whether the soul of Christ possessed knowledge equal to that of the divinity”; in the second: *Quaeris de voluntate Dei et de voluntate hominis similiter*—“You ask similarly concerning the will of God and the will of man.” Do not these latter words indicate the continuation of the discussion which Hugh had begun concerning the wisdom proper to Jesus Christ? Indeed, at the end of his letter Walter had concluded that, if equality of knowledge in the two natures were admitted, it would [Col. CXXC] likewise be necessary to recognize in them equality of power and will. Thus, in order to complete his answer to his opponent, Hugh undertook to treat of the different wills of Jesus Christ. One may say that, as much as Hugh seemed inclined to merge the divine and human knowledge in the Savior, so careful was he to distinguish the wills. He recognizes in him a divine will and a human will; and he subdivides the latter into a will of reason, of piety, and according to the flesh. The two fragments, one entitled *On the Union of Body and Spirit*, and the other *On the Unity of the Word of God*, are taken from the first book of the *Miscellanies*, of which we shall speak below.

Scholastic subtlety had given rise to [Col. CXXD] an error which could be pernicious: nihilism. It consisted in maintaining that Jesus Christ, insofar as he is man, was not something, without nevertheless denying that human nature was hypostatically and without mixture united to the Word. The Word, in becoming incarnate, the nihilists said, clothed himself in our nature in the manner of a man putting on a garment. This is the comparison employed by the Fathers and drawn from Saint Paul. Now, a man who possesses a garment is not something more than he would be if he did not possess one; indeed, he is something less if that garment lowers his dignity. Humanity, therefore, having this twofold relation to the Word, in no way authorizes one to say that he is something insofar as he is man. Thus [Col. CXXIA] Hugh sets forth this opinion in his *Questions on Saint Paul*.

The *Apology of the Incarnate Word* (vol. III, col. 295), intended to combat it, is a fabric of nineteen questions and answers. The *Exposition* and the *Gloss* are cited there several times. It maintains the equality of human and divine knowledge in Jesus Christ, which strongly characterizes our author. In a manuscript of Saint-Victor that appears to us to belong to the twelfth century, this work bears the title: *Objections against Those Who Say That Jesus Christ, insofar as He Is Man, Is Not Something*.

Under the title *Conferences on the Incarnate Word* (vol. III, col. 315), three writings have been brought together which are [Col. CXXIB] found scattered in the manuscripts, where each has its own particular heading. The first, entitled *On the Threefold Silence*, is copied almost word for word from the *Questions on the Epistle to the Galatians*. In both works the author distinguishes three kinds of silence: the silence in which man did not know his sickness, that which preceded the Law; the silence in which he despaired of his healing, namely his state under the Law; and finally the silence in which he recovered health, namely that in which he has found himself since the coming of the Messiah. The second writing aims to prove that the Word, in becoming incarnate, took only human nature and not a person; it closely resembles what is said on the same subject in the *Questions [Col. CXXIC] on the Epistle to the Romans*. As for the third, it is manifestly falsely attributed to our author. This is Dom Brial’s opinion. Most critics attribute to Hugh of Saint-Victor the opusculum entitled *On the Perpetual Virginity of Mary* (vol. II, col. 837). Dom Brial denies it to him for a reason that has weight. The aim of this treatise is to establish that Mary had made a vow of virginity before her marriage, and that in marrying Saint Joseph she did not change her resolution. Hugh of Saint-Victor, on the contrary, teaches in his *Summa of Sentences*, treatise VII, chapter 10, that Mary had not made a vow of continence before her marriage. These two works, therefore, are not by the same author. Now, the *Sentences* is unquestionably Hugh’s; consequently *On the Perpetual [Col. CXXID] Virginity of Mary* does not belong to him. This opinion nonetheless presents certain difficulties. The dedication of the work begins with these words: *Sancto pontifici G. Hugo beatitudinis tuae servus*—“To the holy bishop G., Hugh, servant of your blessedness.” It is therefore by a doctor named Hugh. This doctor wrote in the twelfth century, since manuscripts survive from that period. It is true that masters named Hugh are not lacking; but tradition identifies none of them as the author of this work except Hugh of Saint-Victor. In addition to the testimony of the two catalogues which he publishes, M. Hauréau cites: (1) the positive testimony of Henry of Ghent, who says, concerning our Victorine, in his book *On Illustrious Writers of the Church*: *Respondit cuidam [Col. CXXIIA] beatae Virginis Mariae cum derogatione obloquenti et calumnianti quod Virgo virginum diceretur*—“He replied to a certain person who, derogatorily speaking against and maligning the Blessed Virgin Mary, objected that she was called ‘Virgin of virgins’”; (2) a manuscript in the library of Laon, containing several works of the canon of Saint-Victor, copied and collected in the twelfth century. The treatise *On the Perpetual Virginity of Mary* is among these works. (*Catalogue of the Manuscripts of the Departmental Libraries*, Library of Laon, no. 463.)

The large work entitled *Miscellanies* (vol. III, col. 469) is, like the *Allegorical Extracts*, a collection of fragments drawn from various writings, whose compiler is unknown. These *Miscellanies* are ordinarily divided in the manuscripts into two quires. The first contains two books: one book of elucidations upon various texts of Holy [Col. CXXIIB] Scripture and various points of morals, under two hundred titles or chapters; another, a kind of abridged commentary on the Psalms, which we reviewed above. The second quire consists of four books containing sermons or portions of sermons, letters, remarks on Scripture, extracts from moral treatises—all under different titles and with no connection among them. Title 53 of book II, *On the Breasts Attributed to the Bride*, is an abridgment of Saint Bernard’s tenth sermon on the *Song of Songs* (Saint BERNARD, vol. I, 1287); title 107, *On the Three Kisses*, is drawn from the same Father’s eighty-seventh sermon *On Various Subjects* (*ID.*, *ibid.*, 1239). The end of title 132, *On the Threefold Oil*, was likewise drawn from that Father’s fifteenth sermon. In title 58 of the third book one sees part of a sermon by Geoffrey, fourth abbot of Clairvaux, found among the falsely attributed works of Saint Bernard, vol. II, p. 1309. From this we infer that this compilation was made at about the same time as that of the *Extracts*, and that, being rather similar in taste, they have the same author. Although we have detached from this collection those pieces which appeared to us unquestionably to belong to Hugh, we are inclined to believe that it contains many others which he might claim; but by what means may they be distinguished? We must, however, remove from it, with Dom Brial, three letters that cannot [Col. CXXIID] be denied to Hugh of Saint-Victor (vol. II, col. 1011). The first two are written to one Ranulf of Mauriac, whom he calls his brother. One is a complimentary letter in which he assures Ranulf of his friendship and asks for the continuance of the latter’s. The other contains answers to four questions on as many passages of Holy Scripture. The third is more important. Around the year 1136, the Arabs established in Spain inflicted a violent persecution upon the Christians of the city and district of Seville under their rule. John, archbishop of Seville, instead of encouraging the people by his example and words, raised the banner of apostasy and doctrinally taught the weak to imitate him without remorse. His doctrine consisted [Col. CXXIIIA] in saying that one may outwardly abandon the Christian faith, provided one preserves it in the depths of one’s heart. Hugh, considering the disastrous consequences of such detestable error taught by an archbishop, could not restrain his zeal. He wrote this prelate a learned and moving letter in which he shows into what abyss he and his flock are casting themselves. Baronius thought so highly of this letter that he cited it in full in his *Annals*.

Finally, the Benedictines also attribute to Hugh the opusculum *On the Food of Emmanuel*, found under title 2 of the first book of the same *Miscellanies* (vol. III, col. 477), as well as that entitled *On the Threefold Vice, the Threefold Sin, and the Threefold Remedy*, read under title 33 of the fourth book.

[Col. CXXIIIB] Critics do not agree on the author of the treatise *On Jephthah’s Daughter* (vol. III, col. 323), nor on that of the *Mirror on the Mysteries of the Church* (vol. III, col. 335), both twice mentioned under different titles in M. Hauréau’s catalogues.

The three books *On Ceremonies and Sacraments, Ecclesiastical Offices and Rites* (vol. III, col. 381) were first published without an author’s name. They subsequently took a place in the Paris edition of the *Library of the Fathers* under the name of Hugh of Saint-Victor; the Victorines who edited them ranked them among his works. The Benedictines attribute them to Robert Paululus.

According to the printed editions, three writers dispute the work entitled *Canon of the Mystical Offering, on the Seven Orders [Col. CXXIIIC] of the Mass* (vol. III, col. 455). It is found in the edition of our Victorine among the works of Saint Thomas Aquinas; finally, Dom Tissier mixed it among the works of William of Saint-Thierry in the *Library of Cîteaux*. Dom Brial, on the evidence of English manuscripts, attributes it to John of Cornwall. But it must be acknowledged with all critics that Hugh is the author of the treatise entitled *Dialogue on the Sacraments of the Law of Nature and of the Written Law* (vol. II, col. 17). It is a dialogue between master and disciple. One puts forward the questions, the other resolves them. This work may be regarded as an introduction to the *Summa of Sentences*.

[Col. CXXIIID] The two principal theological productions of our Victorine are the *Summa of Sentences* (vol. II, col. 41) and the great treatise *On the Sacraments* (vol. II, col. 173). The *Summa* is a true compendium of the whole of theology. It is divided into seven treatises. The first deals with faith, hope, and charity; with the distinction and equality of the three divine persons; with predestination, the will of God, his foreknowledge, his omnipotence, and the mystery of the Incarnation. The second concerns the creation and state of angelic nature; the third, the creation and state of human nature; the fourth, sacraments in general and the commandments of God; the fifth, baptism; the sixth, the sacraments of confirmation, the Eucharist, penance, [Col. CXXIVA] and extreme unction; the seventh, the sacrament of marriage. This classification is far from perfect: it is neither natural nor in harmony with the real and ontological order. The *Summa* opens with the theological virtues. Yet, especially in theology, it is not logical to begin with man. Theology is the study of God in himself—God as principle, God as the end of creatures. Hugh treats the mystery of the Incarnation before speaking of the creation and condition of man, which is a manifest inversion of the real order. Besides this defect in the ordering and arrangement of the dogmas, Hugh’s *Summa* contains gaps: it does not embrace every article of the Christian creed or every law of morals. But we must [Col. CXXIVB] observe that no medieval writer presents to us a genuinely consecutive division of the various branches of theological science; and, regarding *summae* in particular, everyone knows that they are true theological encyclopedias in which morality, canon law, and liturgy proceed side by side with dogmatics.

The treatise *On the Sacraments* is more perfect. It is indeed the most substantial theological work of the learned Victorine. Under this title Hugh includes all the mysteries, or in general all the articles, of the Christian faith. He begins with Holy Scripture and first remarks, very correctly, that its proper object is humanity’s restoration. [Col. CXXIVC] But in order fully to set forth what concerns humanity’s restoration, Scripture also had to speak, at least briefly, of what relates to the creation both of humankind and of the world made for humankind. It had to indicate humanity’s primitive condition and how humanity fell, the better to make restoration understood. Guided by this principle, Hugh divides his work into two books. The first explains what pertains to religion from the creation of the world until the Incarnation of the Word; the second continues from the Incarnation to the consummation of all things. Here is a summary outline of the work. The first book comprises twelve parts: [Col. CXXIVD] it treats (1) the creation of the visible world; (2) the cause of creation and the primordial causes of all things; (3) after establishing that the cause of creation is in God, in the divine perfections, the author approaches the study of God’s nature and the mystery of the Trinity; (4) the will of God in particular; (5) the angels; (6) the creation of man and his state before sin; (7) the fall of man and its consequences; (8) restoration; (9) the institution of the sacraments; (10) faith; (11) the sacraments of the natural law; and (12) the sacraments of the written law.
