The second book treats: (1) the Incarnation of the Word; (2) the unity of the Church, which is the body [Col. CXXVA] of Jesus Christ; (3) ecclesiastical orders; (4) sacred vestments; (5) the dedication of churches; (6) baptism; (7) confirmation; (8) the Holy Eucharist; (9) the lesser sacraments, *de minoribus sacramentis*, or pious ceremonies established by the Church; (10) simony; (11) marriage; (12) vows; (13) virtues and vices; (14) the sacrament of penance; [Col. CXXVIA] (15) extreme unction; (16) the end of man; (17) the end of the world; and (18) the state of the world to come. This outline shows that the general plan of this work constitutes a more complete and better ordered whole than that of the *Summa*; nevertheless, it is not without defects. These two works are too much neglected; they contain deep and sound views on theology.

[Col. CXXV]

## NOTICE ON HUGH OF SAINT-VICTOR BY BENEDICTINE RELIGIOUS OF THE CONGREGATION OF SAINT-MAUR

(*Literary History of France*, vol. XII, p. 1.) [Note: [Col. CXXVD] We give from this notice only the historical and bibliographical portion. The critical portion is supplied by the study given above, in which the author has made use of the work of the Benedictines and more recent publications. EDITOR.]

### § I.—History of His Life

[Col. CXXVA]

[Col. CXXVB] History has occupied itself more with generally praising the merit of Hugh of Saint-Victor than with recounting in detail the events of his life. Opinions are divided concerning the country in which he was born. We say the country, for the precise place is entirely unknown. Robert of Mont [Note: [Col. CXXVD] *De abb.*, ch. 5.], writing about fifty years after his death, assures us that he was Lorrainer: *Magister Hugo Lothariensis*—“Master Hugh of Lorraine.” An ancient manuscript from the abbey of Anchin, whose testimony Father Mabillon accepts [Note: [Col. CXXVD] Mabillon, *Annals*, vol. I, p. 327.], places his native country in the territory of Ypres. According to the learned Benedictine, these two authorities are easy to reconcile: since Flanders bordered what was formerly called Lorraine, someone born on the borders of these two provinces could indifferently be called by the name of either. But those who make Hugh a Saxon likewise rely upon Robert’s passage to establish their view. Indeed, ancient Saxony touched Lorraine at another extremity; and the anonymous writer of Jumièges [Note: [Col. CXXVD] Anonymous of Jumièges, p. 301.] expressly says that Hugh, though in fact Saxon, was regarded as Lorrainer because of the proximity of the two regions: *Hugo Lothariensis dictus a confinio Saxoniae*—“Hugh was called Lorrainer because of the border of Saxony.” Alberic of Trois-Fontaines [Note: [Col. CXXVD] *Chronicle*, under the year 1130, p. 264.] and John of Saint-Victor, writers respectively of the twelfth and fourteenth centuries, support this explanation; and their votes have carried those of almost all critics down to the present day. Nevertheless, Dom Mabillon’s view seems to us the better founded, especially since Dom Martène and Dom Durand discovered a new manuscript at the abbey of Marchiennes [Note: [Col. CXXVD] *Literary Journey*, p. 92.]. This document, equal to that of Anchin in antiquity, states not only that Hugh was born near Ypres but also that in childhood he was transferred out of his homeland [Note: [Col. CXXVID] *Works: On Didactic Learning*, book III, ch. 20, vol. II.]: a circumstance—the latter one, we mean—all the more remarkable because it is attested by Hugh himself and helps explain why he was considered Saxon. “I,” he says, “have lived in exile since childhood”: *Ego a puero exsulavi* [Note: [Col. CXXVID] *German Affairs*, vol. III, p. 432.]. Saxony, where he spent the first years of his youth, was therefore not his native country. What he adds in the same place also deserves to be reported, to destroy the prejudice [Col. CXXVIB] of certain writers concerning the alleged nobility of his origin: *Et scio … quo maerore animus pauperis tugurii fundum deserat*—“And I know with what sorrow the soul leaves the ground of a poor hut.” In speaking thus, did Hugh mean to represent himself as a nobleman—and, if one believes the younger Meibom, a nobleman [Note: [Col. CXXVID] “In the year of the Incarnation of the Lord 1141 died Lord Hugh, canon of Saint-Victor, on the third day before the Ides of February [11 February], who, born in the territory of Ypres, was exiled from childhood.” This is what is read at the end of this manuscript, which contains several works of Hugh.] descended from the illustrious house of the counts of Blakemberg?

Providence took care of the young Hugh in his exile and placed him among the regular canons of Hamersleben, in Saxony, to receive his education. The eminent virtue that shone throughout his life bears witness to the rich foundation of piety he acquired in that school. He himself took the trouble to tell us of the progress he made there in letters [Note: [Col. CXXVID] *Life of Hugh*, works, vol. I; vol. II, *On Didactic Learning*, book VI, ch. 3.]. “I do not hesitate to affirm,” he says, “that, far from ever having neglected anything in order to perfect myself in the sciences, I learned many things which others treat as trifles, even as extravagances. I remember that, while still a child, I carefully applied myself to learning the names of everything [Col. CXXVIC] that falls under the senses, especially of things used in life, being persuaded that it is impossible to attain knowledge of things without first knowing what they are called. Taking care to put into writing the most important opinions and questions, objections and solutions, I reviewed them all in my memory; I discussed and compared them with one another by reasoning. On every subject I distinguished the different ways of treating it—as grammarian, rhetorician, and philosopher. I studied combinations of numbers, drew figures on the ground, and clearly demonstrated the properties characterizing each kind of angle: obtuse, right, and acute. I even learned to measure the area and solid content of figures. The visible heavens too were an object of my curiosity. How often I passed the long winter nights in contemplating the stars! Finally, I exercised myself in instrumental music, both to know the difference of sounds and to enjoy, in hours of relaxation, the pleasing charms of harmony. All this, I confess, was only youthful amusement; nevertheless, I drew profit from it.”

[Col. CXXVIIA] Once his studies were completed, he resolved to renounce the world. Hugh, his uncle and archdeacon of Halberstadt, when consulted concerning this plan, did not confine himself to approving it; he also wished to adopt it for himself and to carry it out with his nephew. After having thoroughly tested themselves, they set out together around the year 1118 for the abbey of Saint-Victor at Marseilles, but it was not there that God called them. During their brief stay, report informed them of the remarkable growth of the nascent abbey of Saint-Victor in Paris. At this news they recognized the refuge they had come to seek in France and hastened to arrive there. Abbot Gilduin, then governing the house, received them with joy upon the proofs they gave him of the sincerity of their vocation. Young Hugh, full of fervor, applied himself wholly to imitating the models of learning and virtue before his eyes, and soon equaled them.

Content to instruct and edify himself, he [Col. CXXVIIB] thought only of living in silence and obscurity; but his merit betrayed him. Thomas, prior of Saint-Victor, was then directing the school of that abbey. After the catastrophe of which he was the victim in 1133 [Note: [Col. CXXVIID] Dom Rivet places Thomas’s death in 1130, but it is certain that it occurred in 1133. See Mabillon, notes on Bernard’s epistle 158.], Hugh replaced him in directing that school, after having for some time been his colleague. The manner in which he taught theology, to which he principally devoted himself, gained him a great reputation. An enemy by temperament of disputes, and by religious conviction of profane novelties, he studied scrupulously to follow the paths trodden by the ancients, without falling into the deviations of certain doctors of his day or taking part in their vain controversies. Hence the praises lavished upon him from all sides, whose unanimity was so perfect that no malicious tongue dared disturb it. Even the cornificians [Note: [Col. CXXVIID] John of Salisbury, *Metalogicon*.], a sect devoted to calumny because unable to do good, were compelled to respect his merit. [Col. CXXVIIC] In a word, the bias of his century in his favor was such that people did not hesitate to call him the second Augustine. Posterity, though it has not confirmed this title for him, has shown scarcely less veneration for his authority. Saint Thomas—to say all—regarded him as his master; and theologians still today take pride in following his doctrine in nearly every point.

Wholly given over to study and the exercises of religion, say the latest editors of his works, he never held any dignity in his cloister, not even that of prior. Yet Walter of Mortagne calls him such in the letter he wrote to him, as do the Anonymous of Jumièges, Sixtus of Siena, Garzonius, and several modern writers. Trithemius [Note: [Col. CXXVIIID] *Ecclesiastical Writers*, ch. 363.] even gives him the title of abbot. But the records of Saint-Victor that mention Hugh apply neither designation to him. Moreover, the latter title is explicitly [Col. CXXVIID] contradicted by the very complete catalogue of the abbots of Saint-Victor, in which our author’s name does not occur.

As a consequence of the rule of life he had prescribed for himself, he was not seen, like several learned men of his century, taking a role in the affairs of Church and State. History speaks of only one occasion when he left his cloister. It was when King Louis the Younger [Note: [Col. CXXVIIID] *Maurin Chronicle*, p. 385.] deputed him in 1139, jointly with Alvise, bishop of Arras, and Natalis, abbot of Rebais, to appoint a successor to Thomas, abbot of Morigny, who had resigned.

His career was far less long than the multitude of his writings might suggest. [Col. CXXVIIIA] Excessive labor doubtless helped shorten it. Full of merit and of learning which he had devoted to the glory of religion and the spread of knowledge, he died at only forty-four years of age. Osbert, his fellow religious and friend, left us a short but highly edifying account of his death. He himself attended him in his final illness [Note: [Col. CXXVIIID] *Life of Hugh*, beginning, *Works*]. “After administering extreme unction to him,” he says, “I asked whether he did not still wish to receive the body of Our Lord. ‘Alas,’ he replied, ‘you ask me whether I wish to receive my God. Run as quickly as possible to the church and bring me the body of the Lord.’ Having done this, I said to him before giving him this sacrament: ‘Adore the body of your Master.’ To which he replied, rising: ‘I adore the body of my Lord, and I receive it as my salvation.’” This account praises Hugh’s piety and attests, independently of his writings, the purity of his belief concerning the mystery of the Eucharist.

[Col. CXXVIIIB] Critics do not agree on the year of his death. Some place it in 1140, others in 1141, several in 1142, and finally a small number put it as late as 1143. But Osbert, in his account, settles our doubts on this point by saying that Hugh died on Tuesday, 11 February—which coincides with the year 1141, according to our present manner of beginning the year.

His body was buried at the entrance of the cloister, with this epitaph, which has since disappeared. It was composed by his fellow religious, Simon Chèvre-d’Or:

> Beneath this tomb lies Hugh, a most celebrated doctor.  
> How brief an urn contains so eminent a man!  
> Preeminent in doctrine, second to none in the world,  
> He shone in intellect, morals, speech, and writing.

From the cloister he was transferred in the year 1335, through the care of Aubert de Mailli, abbot of Saint-Victor, and with the permission of Pope Benedict XII, into the great church, and placed in the choir (now the chapel of Saint-Denis [Col. CXXVIIIC]), beneath a plain tomb without inscription.

At present the following verses are read at the site of his first burial:

> Under this stone lay Hugh, a man Saxon by origin,  
> Two hundred years, but with three years subtracted therefrom.  
> At first he caused himself to be laid in the lowest part of the cloister,  
> To be trodden underfoot, unwilling to be adorned by the world.  
> On the eleventh day of February his bones are raised from the earth  
> And transferred to the left side of the choir,  
> In the year of Christ one thousand three hundred and thirty-five;  
> The choir of brethren stands on either side.

Leaving aside the error that makes Hugh a Saxon, there is another error in this monument which proves that its author understood calculation no better than versification. It is the word *tribus*, placed after *ducentis* in the second verse. The authors of the new *Gallia Christiana* say that *quinque* should stand there; in our view it should be *sex*, because we place Hugh’s death one year later than is done in that work.

Hugh the Elder survived his nephew; for it is the former who is mentioned in a letter of Pope Eugenius to Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, in which he asks him to provide Hugh of Saint-Victor with money and a mount for his journey to Rome. This same Hugh subsequently obtained the bishopric of Tusculum, with the title of cardinal.

## § II.—Editions of his works

I. The complete collection of the works of Hugh of Saint-Victor has been printed as many as six times. It first appeared in one folio volume, printed at Paris in the year [Col. CXXIXA] 1518 by André Boucard for J. Petit, with this title-page: *The complete works of Master Hugh of Saint-Victor, together with his Life, never before published anywhere* [Note: [Col. CXXIXD] *Bibl. Carthus. Lig.*]. This edition contains no writings of our author other than those already published separately.

The second edition consists of three folio volumes, published in the same city through the care of the canons of Saint-Victor [Note: [Col. CXXIXD] *Bibl. S. Vict.*], in 1526, by Bade Ascensius and J. Petit. At its head is a dedicatory epistle by Jean Bordier, abbot of Saint-Victor, to Jean Boudet, bishop of Langres. Thomas Garzoni, a regular canon of the Congregation of Saint John Lateran, oversaw the third edition, which appeared at Venice in 1588 from Jean Somasque, in the same format and the same number of volumes as the preceding one. This editor is rightly blamed because, prompted by an ill-considered zeal for the honour of his order, he calls our Victorine, without regard for plausibility, a regular canon of Lateran.

The fourth and fifth editions were both issued [Col. CXXIXB] in 1617, after the Venetian edition: one at Mainz, by Antoine Hiérat, and the other at Cologne [Note: [Col. CXXIXD] Fabr., *Bibl. Lat.*, bk. VIII, p. 882.]. Finally, in 1648, the religious of Saint-Victor reproduced at Rouen, through Berthelin, the collection of our author’s writings, in the same order followed by the preceding editors.

If one seeks learning and criticism in an edition, it is in none of these that one should look for them. Hugh’s genuine and supposed works are confused together and thrown in almost at random. There are neither variants nor notes on obscure passages of the text, save for a few remarks by Garzoni which ordinarily bear little on the difficulty requiring elucidation. What is strangest is that the last edition, which ought to have been the most carefully prepared, at least typographically, proves to be the most negligent in that respect.

II. Besides these general editions, various treatises of [Col. CXXIXC] our author have been printed separately on several occasions. His *Didascalicon* was first made public in 1483 together with the Vocabulary of Wenceslas Brak [Note: [Col. CXXIXD] Simler, *Bibl.*, p. 307.].

III. Gessner [Note: [Col. CXXIXD] *Bibl.*, fol. 340v.] speaks of an edition which he does not characterize in any way, in which he had seen the book on the Trinity—this is the last book of the *Didascalicon*—the *Allegories on the Old and New Testament*, and the books of the *Cloister of the Soul*.

IV. Henri Estienne published in 1506 at Paris, in one quarto volume, under the editorial care of Pierre La Porte—and not Josse Clictou, as Simler says—“with Pierre La Porte himself as its diligent reviser” (*Petro Porta ipsius recognitore sedulo*), several short works attributed in manuscripts [Note: [Col. CXXIXD] *Bibl. Reg.*] to Hugh of Saint-Victor: namely, the book on the Trinity; the treatise on the religious state, or *On the Instruction of Novices*; the four books of the *Cloister of the Soul*; the fragment in praise of charity; the *Soliloquy on the Pledge of the Soul*; the short work on the manner of praying; [Col. CXXIXD] the various expositions of the Lord’s Prayer; the explanation of the five septenaries; and the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

This is not the place to point out to the reader what this collection contains that is foreign to our author, as is true also of all the collections reviewed in this paragraph. The preceding paragraph has made known Hugh’s genuine writings that have appeared in print; the final one will indicate in detail those falsely attributed to him.

[Col. CXXXA] V. The same Henri Estienne, assisted on this occasion by Clictou, published in 1517, in one quarto volume, the second part of the *Allegories*.

VI. The *Questions on Saint Paul* [Note: [Col. CXXIXD] *Bibl. Victor.*] came from the presses of Thierry Martin of Aalst at Louvain in 1517, through the care of Nicolas de Boisleduc, in a quarto volume that also contains the works of Saint Pacian.

VII. The exposition of the Rule of Saint Augustine is the work of Hugh that has received the greatest number of editions. It was brought to light in 1513 [Note: [Col. CXXIXD] *Bibl. S. Vinc. Cenom.*], and published with a commentary by Humbert, general of the Dominicans [Note: [Col. CXXIXD] *Bibl. Mazar.*]. In 1561 a new edition appeared at Venice in one quarto volume [Note: [Col. CXXXD] *Bibl. Victor.*]. A third was issued at Dillingen, by Meyer, in octavo, in 1581 [Note: [Col. CXXXD] Fabr., *Bibl. Lat.*, bk. VIII, p. 884.]. At Como in Milanese territory [Note: [Col. CXXXD] *Ibid.*], the work reappeared in 1605, in the same format, through Jerome Frouam. A fifth edition was produced at Rome in 1625 [Note: [Col. CXXXD] *Bibl. Mazar.*].

Finally, there are three other editions without date, city, [Col. CXXXB] or printer’s name: one in octavo and the other two in duodecimo. In the first, the work stands alone under this title: *Exposition on the Rule of Saint Augustine concerning love of God and neighbour.* In the second, it follows the Constitutions of the Brothers of Charity. In the last, which is in Gothic type, it is preceded by Trithemius’s treatise *On the Property of Monks*. This exposition was also honoured by being translated into French; that translation, made by Brother Charles de la Grange, appeared at Paris in 1691, through Guillaume Després, in one duodecimo volume.

VIII. We know of only one separate edition of the *Instruction of Novices* [Note: [Col. CXXXD] *Bibl. Mazar.*]. It was prepared by Dom Guillaume Rapaille de Forès, a religious of the abbey of Saint-Vincent at Le Mans, who had this work printed at Paris in 1515 by Bade Ascensius under the title *Mirror of Monastic Life*. The same volume contains the commentary of [Col. CXXXC] Fernand, likewise a religious of Saint-Vincent, on the Rule of Saint Benedict.

IX. The treatise on the manner of praying [Note: [Col. CXXXD] *Bibl. Mazar.*] was issued in 1521 by the same printer in an octavo volume. At its head stand the Rule of Saint Benedict, revised by Saint Dunstan, and the work attributed to Saint Bernard, *On the Solitary Life*. At the abbey of La Couture at Le Mans there is a copy of these three works wholly conforming to the preceding one, bearing the date 1519. Is it a different edition or not?

X. The short work *On Three Vices, Three Sins, and Three Remedies* [Note: [Col. CXXXD] *Bibl. San-Genov.*], which is title 33 of Book IV of the *Miscellanies*, was inserted in 1648 at the end of the collection in three quarto volumes printed by Bernardin Masius at Louvain, under the title: *A Selection of the More Notable Short Works of Saint Augustine and His Ancient Disciples against the Pelagians and Their Remnants*.

[Col. CXXXD] XI. The book *The Pledge of the Soul* was translated into French by an anonymous author [Note: [Col. CXXXD] *Bibl. Font. Ebr.*] and published at Paris by Simon Vostre in an octavo collection in 1507 under the title: *The Book of the Bride’s Pledge, compiled by Master Hugh of Saint-Victor*.

XII. The *Mirror of the Church* [Note: [Col. CXXXD] Fabr., *Bibl. Lat.*, bk. VIII, p. 887.] appeared at Rome in 1591 with two other writings falsely attributed to our author: namely, the three books *On the Sacraments and Ecclesiastical Offices*, and the *Canon of the Mystical Offering*, [Col. CXXXIA] in one folio volume entitled: *Writers on the Divine Offices of the Catholic Church*. Melchior Hittorpius additionally inserted this work in his *Auctarium*, or Supplement to the *Library of the Fathers*, printed at Paris in 1610.

XIII. Fabricius maintains that the two books *On the Sacraments* form part of a folio collection published at Strasbourg in 1465, without indicating the title of that collection.

XIV. At the Charterhouse of Le Liget in Touraine, there is preserved a copy of a quarto edition of several writings of Hugh, dated Cologne, Gymnicus, 1621; but we have been unable to discover in detail what it contains.

XV. Father Vignier, of the Oratory, published in the second part of his Supplement to the Works of Saint Augustine (p. 215) a treatise *On the Seven Vices and the Seven Gifts of the Holy Spirit*, already inserted [Col. CXXXIB] in 1634 under the name of Saint Augustine by Guillaume Camerarius in a *Collection of Monuments of the Holy Fathers*. But this treatise is none other than that on the Seven Petitions of the Lord’s Prayer, found in chapters 3 and 19 of the second book of the *Allegories*, and separated by us from it in order to assign it to Hugh of Saint-Victor. The most recent editors of Saint Augustine had already made this criticism before us; persuaded that this short work belonged to Hugh, they had contented themselves with placing its beginning in the appendix to their sixth volume, with corrections supplied by the manuscripts.

XVI. In the same appendix is found our author’s short work *On the Substance of Love*, preceded by an editorial notice that deserves to be read.

## § III.—His unpublished works

[Col. CXXXIC] In the obscurity of several libraries there still remains a fairly large number of manuscript works bearing the name of Hugh of Saint-Victor, awaiting a favourable hand to bring them to light. We can promise only a simple list of most of these, since we have not always been in a position to examine them continuously.

I. In manuscript no. 227 of the library of Saint-Victor, fol. 41, there is a treatise on practical geometry, in which the author says at the beginning:

> “I have been compelled to set forth practical geometry for our people, not as though coining a new work, but as gathering together ancient things scattered abroad.”

II. This work, which occupies only ten folios, is followed by an abridgement of Dindimus’s philosophy: *Epitome of Dindimus on Philosophy*. It is addressed to a friend or fellow brother named Indalet, and begins with these words:

> “Often, Brother Indalet, this Dindimus of ours used to furnish us encouragements in the best studies; but now, behold, it is the third day since he has declined to be present with us as usual.”

III. Three folios later comes a treatise on grammar in the form of a dialogue between the master, who takes the name Sosthenes, and the disciple. It begins thus:

> **SOSTHENES.** What is grammar?  
> **DISCIPLE.** Grammar is the knowledge of speaking correctly according to the precepts of liberal letters; having been discovered among the disciplines after the common letters, it has become the rule and origin of the others.

[Col. CXXXIIA] IV. In manuscript 688, fol. 15, of the same library, is a short work entitled: *On the Seven Steps by Which One Comes to Wisdom*. The opening sentence demonstrates that it is only a fragment of a larger work:

> “Before all else, then, one must be converted through fear of God to the knowledge of his will.”

V. Manuscript 724 of the same library contains: first, a short work attributed to Hugh of Saint-Victor, under the title *On the Salvation of the Soul*, whose opening words are: “Since we are set amid sorrows,” etc.; second, a writing entitled *Hugh, On Hearing Confessions*, at whose head one reads:

> “When you demand from your neighbour some thing which he owes you, you shall not enter his house to take a pledge, but shall stand outside; and he shall bring out and give you what he has” (Deut. 24). From this authority a certain great man draws and preaches that a confessor ought not to search the breast of the penitent.

[Col. CXXXIIB] VI. Manuscript 816, again from Saint-Victor, states at its head, though in a recent hand, that the works it contains belong to our author. Among those not printed is found, at fol. 83, an address to the clergy, whose text is: “Judas, do you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?” Another sermon (fol. 87) is entitled *A Useful Sermon*. It concerns these words of Scripture according to the Old Latin version: “When you sit at the table of a rich man, put a knife to your throat” (Prov. 23).

Then, after a fragment of the work of the *Allegories*, occurs, at fol. 90, a chapter entitled *On the Anointing of the Kings of France*. It says, [Note: [Col. CXXXID] “The same ampulla is larger than a small nut and is still in the monastery of Blessed Remigius outside the walls of the city; it is always full and is never emptied. When the kings of the Franks are first crowned, they are anointed with that oil. Nevertheless, they remain in the city of Reims for a week in the same garments. The monks of Saint-Remigius carry the ampulla with a great procession to the archiepiscopal seat, accompanied by an armed multitude; and when the anointing has been performed, they return immediately with it. The kings of the Franks possess this privilege, because they alone are anointed with heavenly oil. On that day the archbishop bears all the king’s expenses, and sometimes spends seven hundred or eight hundred marks, or more. Afterwards he may be crowned wherever he wishes, customarily at Saint-Denis, or elsewhere, as circumstances require.”], after recounting the miracle of the Holy Ampulla brought to Saint Remigius for the anointing of King Clovis, that this same vessel, as large as a medium-sized walnut, is preserved in the abbey of Saint-Remigius outside the walls of Reims; that it always remains full and is never emptied; that the liquid it contains serves to anoint [Col. CXXXIIC] the kings of France when they are crowned for the first time; that after this ceremony the new monarch remains for a whole week at Reims in the same vestments used for his consecration; that the monks of Saint-Remigius bring the Holy Ampulla in procession to the cathedral, accompanied by a multitude of armed men, and take it back as soon as the anointing is completed; that our kings are regarded as privileged because they alone are anointed with heavenly oil; that the archbishop of Reims is obliged to defray the king’s expenses on the day of his consecration, sometimes spending seven hundred, sometimes eight hundred marks or more; and that after this the king may be crowned wherever he wishes, whether at Saint-Denis, as is customary, or elsewhere, if circumstances demand it.

One sees from this final detail that consecration was then distinguished from coronation. At fol. 91 there is another short work entitled *Certain Questions and Expositions*. Its opening words are: “Through the things we take, let us take the things that are more excellent.” A small treatise on the Incarnation occupies the last place in this manuscript. It begins:

> “Since we are about to treat of the Incarnation of the Word, let us first see why the Son alone was incarnate.”

VII. Manuscripts 801 and 814 present, under our author’s name, a universal chronicle with this title: *A Device of Memory Concerning the Three Greatest Circumstances of Events, namely Persons, Places, and Times*. The work is more complete in the [Col. CXXXIIIA] first of these two copies. This universal chronicle is divided, as it were, into three parts and preceded by a prologue (fol. 1) beginning:

> “Son, wisdom is a treasure, and your heart is a chest.”

The first part begins with the creation of the world and ends with the death of the Emperor Augustus. Properly speaking, it is only a chronology of the patriarchs, judges, and kings of Israel and Judah down to King Agrippa, joined to an account of the establishment of several empires and the names of their rulers. The author first follows the computation of the Hebrew text in the chronological list of the patriarchs, and then gives it according to the computation of the Septuagint. After this, he describes (fol. 9) the genealogies of these same patriarchs and their descendants, followed by a list of the prophets of the Old and New Testaments. This list, which fills only two and a half pages, is succeeded by that of the cities belonging to each of the ten tribes. Next comes the [Col. CXXXIIIB] division of the world into Europe, Asia, and Africa; then the subdivision of the provinces composing each of these parts, and the names of their chief cities.

A chronological succession of popes from Saint Peter to Honorius II, with the length of each pontificate carefully marked, makes up the second part of the work. It is connected with the preceding section by these words:

> “Next I shall endeavour to set forth, in a like order, the succession and names of kingdoms and kings, as they have run from the Incarnation of the Word down to our own times.”

It reviews all emperors from Julius Caesar to Michael Curopalates, and from the latter to John Porphyrogenitus, who was called Calo-John. Between these two periods is placed an abridged chronicle of the kings of the Franks from Priam to Louis the Fat; of the kings of the Vandals from Genseric to Gelimer; of the dukes of Normandy from Rollo to Henry I; and of the [Col. CXXXIIIC] Lombard kings from Agelmund to the son of Desiderius. This section ends with an unsystematic catalogue of several ancient historians, the first of whom is Pompeius Trogus and the last Victor, historian of Africa.

The third part contains the chronology of the western emperors down to Henry V, combined with the succession of popes, which ends with Honorius II. The indictions and years of Jesus Christ are carefully marked, the last being the year 1135.

Although it is certain from the testimony of Alberic of Trois-Fontaines, and from that of Hugh himself, as we have reported above, that he composed a universal chronicle for the use of his pupils, we nevertheless do not hesitate to maintain that this is not his work. What persuades us of this is that none of the passages from our author’s *Chronicle* cited by Alberic is found in it.

VII. The same must be said of an abridged chronicle, [Col. CXXXIIID] *Abridged Chronicle*, which fills the space from folio forty-two to folio seventy-eight in the same manuscript. The date at which it ends, 1190, reveals the ignorance of the copyist who attributed this piece to Hugh of Saint-Victor. It is nevertheless appropriate to give notice of it here. The name “abridged” suits it very well, since it is contained in thirty-six quarto folios; among these are first eleven, from the fifty-third to the sixty-fourth, which make a digression on the principal feasts of the year, and then another digression at folio seventy-four on the cardinals, *On the Cardinals of Rome*.

Yet, in its brevity, it contains matters worthy of notice. The following details will demonstrate this.

[Col. CXXXIVA] Under the year 713, speaking of Austregisilus, it says:

> “Austregisilus, patriarch and primate of Aquitaine, flourishes.”

Here is proof of the antiquity of the claim of the archbishops of Bourges. Another proof from the same period has been seen above in the article on Gerard of Angoulême (vol. XI, p. 605).

Under the year 912, it names the successors of King Charles the Simple as follows:

> “After Charles, who was surnamed the Simple, Robert the outsider and Rudolph the outsider reigned in Francia.”

This term *alienus* can mean nothing other than that Robert and Rudolph were strangers to the house of Charlemagne. The author does not include King Odo among the kings of France.

These words under the year 988 deserve attention:

> “After him [Louis], Hugh usurps the kingdom; he was the nephew of the first Emperor Otto, who was the son of Henry, king of Germany; and Henry was the son of Otto, duke of the Saxons. We have written this for those who are accustomed to disparage the modern kings of the Franks, as though they were not born of royal stock; whereas this Hugh, of whom we have made mention above, and from whom they descend, proved to be closely related to the imperial line.”

One sees from this passage that in the twelfth century the system had not yet been imagined that makes our kings of the third race spring from the stem of Charlemagne, since the chronicler, here defending them, traces their origin only through the mothers by whom they descended from Otto I. Had he believed that he could praise them equally on the paternal side, he would not have omitted it.

Since these two chronicles are foreign to our author, shall we say that the one he composed no longer survives? Not at all; but we shall content ourselves with saying that we have sought it in vain in the most celebrated libraries of France. It is not in the King’s library, for the work announced in the catalogue of that library under the title *Chronicle of Hugh of Saint-Victor*, [Col. CXXXIVC] no. 4842, is only a fragment of the first chronicle, reduced to eight folios, lacking beginning and end. Neither will it be found at Saint-Germain-des-Prés; but there one will see the first part of the one just cited, bearing this inscription: *Treatise on the Names of Lands*, and in the margin, in a recent hand: “Hugh of Saint-Victor.” Perhaps it might be found in the Vatican Library among the manuscripts of Alexandre Petau, where indeed there is a work entered as: *Chronicle of Hugh of Saint-Victor* [Note: [Col. CXXXIIID] Montf., *Bib. ms.*, p. 73 A.].

VIII. A treatise *On the Discipline of Monks* forms part of manuscript 199, whose writing appears to belong to the twelfth century. The name of Hugh with which it is adorned seems to have been added subsequently. The work begins:

> “Discipline is good and honourable conduct, for which it is too little merely not to do evil; rather, it strives also to appear blameless in the things it does well.”

This is what we have discovered at Saint-Victor.

[Col. CXXXIVD] The King’s library also contains several unpublished writings of our author, different from those just named.

IX. Under no. 2525 are found three commentaries of Hugh of Saint-Victor on as many books of Holy Scripture. The first, on the Song of Songs, begins:

> “God shall be known in its steps. Thus says the other version, where ours has: God shall be known in its dwellings.”

The second, also found under no. 2524, concerns Ecclesiasticus. These are the first words of its prologue:

> “The palace of the supreme king is completed in four things: that is, in foundation, walls, roof, and ornament.”

The third concerns the Book of Wisdom and opens:

> “Son, desiring wisdom, preserve justice.”

[Col. CXXXVA] These three commentaries, whose principal basis is allegory, are exceedingly diffuse. At intervals there are some quite fine moral passages and some literal explanations that are not to be despised.

X. Manuscript 3007 contains three writings of Hugh, the first two of which have already been published. The title of the first is: *Book of Four Questions by Hugh of Saint-Victor*. These four questions concern the consequences of the fall of the first man, and constitute the same work entitled in a manuscript of the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés (no. 1206): *Letter of Hugh of Saint-Victor on Adam’s Transgression*. It is dedicated to an unnamed abbot, who may very well be Saint Bernard, as a recent hand has written in the margin in the second of the two copies cited.

Whatever the case, the following words, which form the opening, present this abbot as a man of rare merit:

> “I know, lord, that it was not so much necessity as charity, the queen of your mind, that compelled you to seek a response from our littleness concerning the question of our first transgression.”

Entering upon his subject, the author distinguishes three states of man. He calls the first, which is ours, the *state of transgression* (*status praevaricatorius*); the second, which was man’s state before sin, the *state of being able to go either way* (*status utrobitorius*); and the third, the state of the saints in heaven, the *state of confirmation* (*status confirmatorius*). As he then says, this distinction corresponds to that given by Saint Augustine for the same states: “not able not to sin,” “able to sin,” and “not able to sin.”

His principal purpose is to justify Providence in relation to predestination. He assumes as a certain principle that God predestined among human beings only the number necessary to fill the number of angels who fell. Starting from this hypothesis, he asks and examines why God multiplied the human race beyond that number. He gives various philosophical reasons for it, [Col. CXXXVC] which would take too long to report. The work is full of very subtle logic, but logic nevertheless incapable of lifting the veil from a question impenetrable to the human mind.

XI. Manuscript 2049 contains a writing entitled: *Hugh, On Offering Sacrifice*. Its opening words are:

> “What shall I render to the Lord for all that he has rendered to me? I will show you, O man, what is good, and what the Lord requires of you.”

XII. *Hugh’s Opinion on the Body and Blood of the Lord*: this is the title of a writing found under no. 2531. The author begins:

> “Since the whole of human nature was corrupted in soul and body, it was fitting that Christ, who had come to set both free, should be united to both, so that soul might fittingly be freed through soul, and body through body.”

XIII. A letter answering a friend concerning the solitary life, bearing our author’s name and surname, forms part of manuscript 6785. It begins:

> “You, a learned man, challenge one who is foolish. You ask what is to be done because, though placed in the religious habit, you do not possess works worthy of your profession.”

XIV. Toward the end of the same copy are six philosophical books of Hugh of Saint-Victor. At the head of the prologue one reads:

> “Of all things to be desired, wisdom is first, for in it lies the source of perfect good.”

The first chapter—or, if one wishes, the second, since it seems to presuppose a preceding one—begins:

> “Pythagoras was the first of all to call the study of wisdom philosophy, and preferred that men be called philosophers rather than, as before, sages.”

The author divides all the primary sciences into four: theoretical, practical or moral, mechanical, and logical.

[Col. CXXXVIA] XV. Manuscript 3307 contains a short work entitled *On Discipline by Hugh of Saint-Victor*, whose first words are:

> “There is a certain good end, and there is a certain evil end.”

XVI. *Hugh’s Confession to an Abbot* forms part of manuscript 2922 and begins:

> “Alone I shall enter into the solitude of my heart, and shall converse for a little while with my heart.”

XVII. Besides Hugh’s printed commentary on the *Celestial Hierarchy* attributed to Saint Denis, manuscript no. 1619 of the same library—the King’s Library—contains two other commentaries of our author not yet published: one on that saint’s *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, and the other on his *Letters*. This copy is not unique. A similar one is found in the library of Saint-Martin of Tournai [Note: [Col. CXXXVD] Sander, *Bibl. mss. Belg.*, part I, p. 112.]; and at its head it is said that Hugh of Saint-Victor made the translation of Saint Denis’s text. This is [Col. CXXXVIB] the best thing about it; for the glosses are of no great use.

XVIII. In the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés we found under no. 131: *Hexaemeron of Hugh of Saint-Victor*. It is a philosophical and theological treatise in which the most important questions concerning the work of the six days are resolved in a highly subtle and no less sound manner.

XIX. Under no. 1206 of the same repository, the treatise *On Adam’s Transgression* is followed by a short work *On Obedience*, likewise attributed to our author.

XX. The library of Saint-Martin of Tournai preserves works of Hugh of Saint-Victor [Note: [Col. CXXXVD] Sander, *Bibl. mss. Belg.*, part I, p. 112.], besides writings already mentioned, including a short work that begins with this Scriptural sentence:

> “Though man was in honour, he did not understand.”

XXI. In the monastery of the Dunes and in that of Liessies there is a *Book on Music by Hugh of Saint-Victor* [Note: [Col. CXXXVD] *Ibid.*, p. 26.].

[Col. CXXXVIC] XXII. In the library of the regular canons of Corsendonk in Flanders are seen: first, *Know Thyself* (*Gnothosolitos*) of Master Hugh of Saint-Victor, beginning with the words “You know, most dearly beloved”; second, another work by the same author, whose opening words are: “By the inspiration of his grace” [Note: [Col. CXXXVID] *Ibid.*, part II, p. 66.].

We shall end this list here. It would be easy to extend it further if we wished to copy the catalogues of the various libraries of Europe. But we believe our readers will excuse us this labour, which could offer them nothing certain, since Hugh’s same writings often bear different titles in different manuscripts.

We should very much have wished to find in our researches our author’s great letter to Saint Bernard on baptism, to which that saint made the reply included among his works. Hugh’s opinion—or rather, that of the person for [Col. CXXXVID] whom he consulted the saint—was that the desire for baptism, taking Christ’s words literally, was not sufficient for salvation. In Saint Bernard one may see the illuminating solution he gives to this difficulty [Note: [Col. CXXXVID] Bernard, *Works*, p. 625.].

## § V.—His genius, learning, and manner of writing

The twelfth century produced scarcely any scholars who united, to a more eminent degree than Hugh of Saint-Victor, variety of knowledge, subtlety of mind, soundness of judgment, ease of writing, and a good use of all these qualities.

1. One cannot read his writings without recognizing in them evident traces of almost every kind of literature held in honour in his age. He knew of geography what a man of letters could then know: that is, what the ancients had said about it, since no modern had yet laboured to perfect this science and enrich it with new discoveries. Arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy had, as he himself relates, been the amusements of his youth. He took care to cultivate the first three at a more advanced age, and one sees in him knowledge fairly extensive for the period, whether in his manuscript treatises on practical geometry and music or in his other writings.

He had studied ecclesiastical and secular history, though less in original authors than in chroniclers who copied and often distorted them. If the treatise he composed on grammar does not prove that he excelled in the theory of that art, it at least attests that he understood its mechanism very well.

[Col. CXXXVIIB] With regard to the learned languages, there is no doubt that he had a sound smattering of Greek, as is shown by his translation of the works of Saint Denis. [Note: [Col. CXXXVIID] These works had already been translated in the ninth century by John Scotus, called Eriugena. Hugh seems [Col. CXXXVIIID] to have made considerable use of this translation; but he did not copy it slavishly.] The case is less certain with Hebrew. What is scattered through some of his writings may well have been borrowed from interpreters and commentators on Holy Scripture, especially Saint Jerome. In an age when knowledge of natural things was so ill-formed, it would be an exaggeration to bestow upon him the name of physicist. Yet what he says incidentally concerning the order of nature, the elements, and the properties of bodies shows that in this respect he was not below his contemporaries.

2. But of all the human sciences which he cultivated, dialectic was that in which he bore away the prize. This art, so well suited to refine even the coarsest minds, made marvellous progress in that of Hugh, naturally lively, receptive, and subtle. The extracts which we have given from his polemical writings show the degree to which he carried [Col. CXXXVIIC] acuteness in the most abstract and tangled matters, the precision and soundness of the solutions which he knew how to give to the greatest difficulties, and the skill with which he disentangled himself from the most captious sophisms. Even in questions where he departs from the truth, the subtlety of his mind still compels admiration. Could one, for example, defend more plausibly than he did the equality of divine knowledge and human knowledge in Jesus Christ?

3. With talents so marked for disputation, it would have been easy for him, had he wished, to extend the licence of nascent scholasticism and to subject the most sublime dogmas of religion to reasoned systems. But sound judgment, assisted by the lights of grace, made him understand the danger of going beyond the bounds set by antiquity. Convinced that reason ought to come only second in the study of religion, he made it his chief concern [Col. CXXXVIID] to draw this knowledge from its two essential sources, Scripture and tradition. Hence the contempt which he displays for the frivolous and often rash questions which the idleness of the schools brought forth [Col. CXXXVIIIA] daily before his eyes, which contentious quibbling sustained, and which the lack of authorities rendered interminable. We have seen his complaints about this disorder and this enormous abuse of reason.

4. One may judge how full he was of reading the Fathers from that body of theology which he was the first to undertake, and whose several parts he was able to furnish with a great number of their texts, generally chosen well enough. Saint Augustine was the one whom he had read most assiduously and from whom he drew the greatest assistance. His attachment to the teaching of that Father gained him among his contemporaries, as has been said, the magnificent epithet of “a second Augustine.” Some even called him “the soul of Saint Augustine.” Since then, the latter title has been found ridiculous and the former exaggerated. Indeed, however much esteem our Victorine deserves, and however carefully he followed in the footsteps of the great bishop of Hippo, there will always be a very great distance between his [Col. CXXXVIIIB] intellectual powers and those of that incomparable doctor. Moreover, what a disproportion lies between the methods followed by the two! Nothing is more orderly or more noble than the course of the holy doctor. Filled with his subject and master of his material, he proceeds straight to the goal, without digression, diversion, or retracing of his steps. He says nothing superfluous; he says everything in its proper place, and leaves nothing to be desired. Is it so with our Victorine? Let us take in hand his two most considerable writings, those which have brought him the greatest honour with posterity: his *Summa* and his *Sacraments*. It cannot be denied that they contain excellent things, and in great number. But after all, these treatises are memoranda, not finished works. All the pieces of which they are composed form only a crude and ill-conceived whole. Frequent repetitions, irrelevant discussions, palpable inequality in the treatment of subjects of approximately equal importance, [Col. CXXXVIIIC] essential omissions—all natural consequences of a poorly conceived plan and hasty execution: such, in our view, are the blemishes which disfigure these two great productions.

5. As for his diction, it is a vivid image of the ease of his genius, the clarity of his ideas, and the simplicity of his character. In him one finds neither bold tropes, inflated expressions, nor convoluted sentences—faults fairly common among writers of his century. Common terms and natural turns of phrase make up all the ornament of his style. In short, his manner of writing would almost be a model in the didactic genre if it were more sustained, ordinarily less dry, and more free from the idioms of the age.

Let us not forget, moreover, that Hugh’s career ended at the age when many celebrated authors have scarcely begun to give the public the first fruits of their studies. Within so narrow a span of years, [Col. CXXXVIIID] industrious as he was, had he written less, he would doubtless have written better. But what might he not have promised, if age had matured the marvellous disposition for letters which he possessed!

[Col. CXXXVII]

## FABRICIUS’S NOTICE

(*Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. III, p. 300.)

[Col. CXXXVIID] Hugh of Saint-Victor, born of an illustrious family among the Saxons, as Henry [Col. CXXXVIIID] Meibom, in his dissertation on the native country of Hugh the Victorine, vol. III of *Writers of German Affairs*, p. 429 ff., G. G. Leibniz in the preface to the second volume of *Historical Accessions* and in a note inserted in the *Acts of the Learned* for 1698, p. 354, and likewise Polycarp Leyser in his dissertation *On the First Three Doctors of Sacred Theology from the Saxon Nation*, Helmstedt, 1720, quarto, have demonstrated by evidence that cannot be denied—against the opinion of learned men who make him a Lorrainer [Note: [Col. CXXXVIID] What if he was called Lorrainer from Royal Lutter in the territory of Brunswick?] or a Fleming from Ypres. Others call Hugh Parisian or French, because he was an Augustinian regular canon in the monastery of Saint-Victor outside the walls of Paris. Because of the soundness and abundance of his learning, and the didactic books which he published, he was also called “the Teacher” (*Didascalus*); [Note: [Col. CXXXIXD] Labbe, vol. I, *De Scriptoribus Ecclesiasticis*, p. 480.] by others also “the tongue of Augustine” or “another Augustine.” He died in the year 1140 or 1142, [Note: [Col. CXXXIXD] Pagi, under the year 1140, no. IX; Mabillon, vol. I, *Analecta*, p. 263.] scarcely forty-four years old. After certain separate editions of individual works, listed by Gesner in his *Bibliotheca*, his writings appeared together at Paris in 1526; then, under the care of Thomas Garzoni of Bagnacavallo, a Lateran regular canon, at Venice in 1588; afterwards at Mainz and Cologne in 1617; and finally, revised by the Regular Canons of Saint-Victor at Paris, preserving the order of the earlier editions, at Rouen in 1548, folio, in three volumes.

The contents of the first volume [Note: [Col. CXXXIXD] We add the volume and column according to the order of our new edition. Patristic Edition.] are as follows:

*Preliminary Notices concerning Sacred Scriptures and Sacred Writers*, p. 1 (col. 9).
