Two books *On the Sacraments of the Christian Faith*, from the Strasbourg edition of 1465, folio, pp. 487–712 (vol. II, col. 173).

Concerning the *Chronicle*, which has not yet seen the light, Alberic writes under the year 1130: “Up to this point Master Hugh of Saint-[Col. CXLIIA]Victor arranged his chronicle concerning Roman pontiffs and emperors. Hence it is evident that he flourished at this time. This man wrote many praiseworthy works, which are kept in book-chests, among which are these: Hugh *On the Sacraments*; Hugh *On the Hierarchy of Dionysius*; Hugh’s *Didascalicon*; Hugh *On the Three Virtues*, Faith, Hope, and Charity. He also expounds in eloquent language the Rule of our blessed father Augustine, and is said to have written many other things. He also writes a rather long letter to Blessed Bernard. They say that he was born in Saxony. But the Hugh who wrote morally and allegorically on the nature of birds, and on the cloister of the soul, and on the medicine of the soul, was, as is said, a canon of the Premonstratensian order. The third Hugh, who wrote the *Lesser Ecclesiastical History* for Adela, countess of Champagne, mother of Count Theobald, was a Black monk of Fleury—that is, of Saint Benedict on the Loire, in the diocese of Orléans.” From this passage of Alberic it is evident that Oudin is mistaken in denying, vol. II, p. 159, that Hugh the Victorine was the author of the *Chronicle*, and in maintaining that it should be attributed to the monk of Fleury.

[Col. CXLI]

## TWO ANCIENT CATALOGUES OF THE WORKS OF HUGH OF SAINT-VICTOR

(The first was published and annotated by D. Hauréau, *Bulletin des comités historiques*, July 1851, p. 177.)

“We borrow these documents,” says M. Hauréau, “from a manuscript of the Abbey of Saint-Victor which successively bore the numbers 122 and 668, and which now appears under number 473 among the volumes of that abbey that entered the National Library. It is a collection written in the fourteenth century and composed of various fragments relating to the history of Saint-Victor, followed by several theological opuscula. It was doubtless from this source that Martène took the notice on Adam of Saint-Victor which he inserted in volume VI of his *Amplissima Collectio*; but he neglected other notices, no less interesting, which concern Hugh and Richard. We shall publish them successively.

“Today we shall give an encomium of Hugh of Saint-Victor and two catalogues of his works, to which it will be necessary to add some notes.”

### I

[Col. CXLIC] It should be noted that about the year of the Lord 1038, the canonical order of Saint-Victor at Paris enjoyed celebrated renown throughout the world, especially because of certain famous and distinguished persons, adorned with virtue and learning, whom it sent out into churches in various and diverse parts of the world, like a fruitful vine putting forth shoots to be transplanted. For at this time professed canons from there had been received as prelates in the Roman Church: two cardinals, Master Ivo the cardinal and Lord Hugh, bishop of Tusculum; Master Achard, bishop of Avranches; likewise nine abbots: Abbot Ralph of Saint-Geneviève at Paris; Abbot Odo of Saint-Euverte at Orléans; Abbot Roger of Saint Mary [Col. CXLID] of Auges; another, of Saint Bartholomew at Noyon; Garnerius of Saint Vincent at Senlis; Baldwin of Saint Mary of Hautecroix; Guibert of Saint Augustine [Col. CXLIIC] of the Wood in England; Richard of Saint James of Guiguemora in La Marche; Master Andrew; and Masters Hugh, Richard, Adam, and Thomas, then prior of Saint-Victor and the one who guided Stephen, bishop of Paris, in the cautious and subtle governance of his episcopate. Thus, as appears in Stephen’s own letter to Pope Innocent, Stephen himself did nothing in this business, but the said Prior Thomas did everything. For this reason he was killed and made a martyr by the nephews of Naucherius, archdeacon of Paris, a noble but dissolute man. When this man was rebuked and reproached by the said Prior Thomas, he rose against him, began to persecute him, and at last had him cruelly killed by his nephews. Therefore, so that his death might be avenged, Saint Bernard the abbot and the aforesaid Bishop Stephen reported to Pope Innocent how this had happened. Consequently, at their urgent command, the pope caused him to be removed from the cloister and honourably buried within the church, namely in the Chapel of the Holy Cross, on the seventh day before the Ides of March [9 March].

Around this time Master Hugh of Saint-Victor died, on 10 February, pre-eminent in the philosophical disciplines and theology, as is evident from his books and treatises. For he composed two books *On the Sacraments*, containing several parts; *On the Cloister of the Soul*, entitled under the name of Hugh of Fouilloy, monk of Corbie; *On Noah’s Ark*; *On the Bride’s Pledge*; *On the Soul of Christ*; five books of the *Didascalicon*; one book *On the Perpetual Virginity of Saint Mary*; one book *On the Angelic and Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*; and many treatises concerning theology, such as *On the Power of the Order*; *On Praise*; *On the Five Sevens*; *On the Instruction of Novices*; one book on the *Magnificat*; one book on the *Lamentations of Jeremiah*; one book on Ecclesiastes; a *Map of the World*; *Selections by the Same Author*; books on Grammar; an *Epitome of Philosophy*; an *Exposition on Ezekiel*; and many other subtle works.

[Note: [Col. CXLIIIA] *Works*, vol. II, col. 173.]

[Col. CXLIVA]

*On the Cloister of the Soul*, entitled under the name of Hugh of Fouilloy, monk of Corbie.

[Note: [Col. CXLIIIA] The work entitled *On the Cloister of the Soul* has been printed several times. The manuscripts attribute it to Hugh of Saint-Victor, to Hugh of Fouilloy or Foulois, a monk of Corbie, and to Hugh, canon of Saint-Laurent. The *Literary History* (vol. XIII, p. 492 and following) establishes that Hugh of Fouilloy was never a religious of Corbie, but a canon of Saint-Laurent of Heilly, a priory of the Order of Saint Augustine which, in temporal matters, depended on the abbey of Corbie. Thus the canon of Saint-Laurent and the supposed monk are one and the same person. It remains to investigate whether this Hugh of Fouilloy is designated as the author of the *Cloister of the Soul* with better grounds than our Victorine. Since both were mystics, at approximately the same degree, the author cannot be recognized by studying the doctrine of the work. But it should be observed that, whereas manuscripts of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries name Hugh of Saint-Victor, the earlier manuscripts are all in the name of Hugh of Fouilloy. To this already very strong evidence are added the most explicit testimonies of William of Nangis and Alberic of Trois-Fontaines. Casimir Oudin and the authors of the *Literary History* therefore do not hesitate to place the *Cloister of the Soul* among the works of Hugh of Fouilloy. The school of Saint-Victor long protested against [Col. CXLIIIC] this attribution. The catalogues reproduced here indicate this sufficiently. In a Saint-Victor manuscript numbered 808, a religious erased the name of Hugh of Fouilloy, “of Fulleio,” which had been placed by a twelfth- or thirteenth-century copyist at the head of the work claimed by the Victorines for their glorious colleague. Finally, some manuscript copies of the *Cloister of the Soul* were composed from fragments of the original work and other fragments borrowed from the works of the religious of Saint-Victor. No. 577 of the Saint-Victor collection offers a curious example of these substitutions. The fourth book of this copy contains none of the profane or mystical allegories that offended the taste of the Benedictines (*Literary History*, vol. XIII, p. 497); it contains a treatise on the modes of contemplation.]

*On Noah’s Ark.*

[Note: [Col. CXLIIIC] This is probably the work designated by our second catalogue under the title *Four Books on Noah’s Ark*. This descriptive paraphrase in four books was published in the second volume of Hugh of Saint-Victor’s *Works* (col. 617). It must be distinguished from another treatise entitled *Description of Noah’s Mystical Ark*. We should observe that the editors of the 1648 edition neglected to seek the best texts of *On Noah’s Ark*: the text they brought to light is often incorrect and, moreover, incomplete. Various manuscripts would have supplied them with several chapters to add to the fourth book. Among others, we should mention no. 856 of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, a very fine twelfth-century manuscript.]

*On the Bride’s Pledge.*

[Note: [Col. CXLIIID] The title is inaccurate. It should read *On the Soul’s Pledge*, or, better, *Soliloquy on the Soul’s Pledge* (vol. II, col. 951).]

*On the Soul of Christ.*

[Note: [Col. CXLIIID] *Decision of the Question Concerning the Soul of Christ*, vol. II, col. 841.]

*Didascalicon*, five books.

[Note: [Col. CXLIIID] *Works*, vol. II, col. 739, under the title *Books of the Didascalicon*. The editors of 1648 did not notice that book IV and part of book V of this collection, with very slight differences and a few additions, constitute the short work published in vol. I of the *Works*, p. 1, under the title *Preliminary Notes on Sacred Scriptures and Sacred Writers*. The *Six Philosophical Books*, which the *Literary History* says conclude manuscript 6785 of the former Latin collection of the National Library (*Literary History*, vol. XII, p. 60), are not found in that volume but in no. 2532. This is not an unpublished work, as the Benedictines claim, but a copy of the *Didascalicon*, beginning in the second chapter with the words: “Of all things sought, wisdom is the first.” Our catalogue assigns only five books to the *Didascalicon*. Seven are counted in the 1648 edition.]

*On the Perpetual Virginity of Saint Mary*, one book.

[Note: [Col. CXLIVB] *Works*, vol. II, col. 837. The Benedictines deny this work to the canon of Saint-Victor and attribute it to Hugh of Fouilloy; but they give no reason in support of their opinion (*Literary History*, vol. XII, p. 68). In his notice on Hugh of Fouilloy (*Literary History*, vol. XII, p. 502), Dom Brial observes that the doctrine of this short work scarcely agrees with that of a chapter in the *Summa* published under the name of Hugh of Saint-Victor. No one disputes the *Summa* to the Victorine; therefore, according to Dom Brial, the treatise *On the Perpetual Virginity of Mary* must be removed from the catalogue of his works. There is some difficulty in this. The dedication of the work begins with the words: “To the holy Bishop, G., Hugh, servant of your blessedness.” It is therefore by a doctor named Hugh. There was no shortage of such men in the Middle Ages; but since there are manuscripts of this treatise dating from the twelfth century, its author must necessarily be sought among masters named Hugh who taught before the thirteenth century. Tradition, however, designates none of them as having discussed the question of perpetual virginity except Hugh of Saint-Victor. In addition to the testimony of our two catalogues, there is the following evidence. First, that of Henry of Ghent, who, in his book *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*, says of our Victorine: “He replied to a certain blessed Virgin Mary who spoke insultingly and calumniously, objecting that she was called the virgin of virgins.” This contradicts Dom Brial. Moreover, a manuscript in the library of Laon contains several works of the canon of Saint-Victor, copied and assembled in the twelfth century; the treatise *On the Perpetual Virginity* is among them (Catalogue of the Manuscripts of the Departmental Libraries, Laon Library, no. 463). This proves that even in the twelfth century he was regarded as its author. It is also found in Sorbonne no. 304 and Saint-Victor no. 137, other collections of the Victorine’s works formed in the thirteenth century. These are arguments against Dom Brial. We shall refrain from pressing them and shall avoid reaching a conclusion.]

*On the Angelic and Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, one book.

[Note: [Col. CXLIVD] *Ten Books in Explanation of the Celestial Hierarchy of the Great Dionysius the Areopagite*; *Works*, vol. I, col. 923. Only this commentary on the *Celestial Hierarchy* has been printed. Our catalogue also mentions a commentary on the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*. The Benedictines say the following about it: “Besides Hugh’s printed commentary on the *Celestial Hierarchy*, the manuscript of the King’s Library numbered 1619 contains two other commentaries by our author that have not yet appeared: one on this saint’s *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, and the other on his Letters. This copy is not unique. A similar one is found in the library of Saint-Martin of Tournai; at its head it says that the translation of Saint Dionysius’s text is by Hugh of Saint-Victor (Sanderus, *Belgian Manuscript Libraries*, part I, p. 112). This is the better part, for the glosses are not of great use.” There are several errors in these lines. Sanderus, and the Benedictines after him, give the Greek text’s translation a singular origin. This translation, they say, would be the work of Hugh of Saint-Victor. But no: this hypothesis must be rejected at the outset. Hugh of Saint-Victor, who did not know Greek, could not have translated a Greek book. We have before us a volume of the National Library to which the Benedictines refer. It indeed contains several works of the false Dionysius, translated into Latin and accompanied by various glosses; but the text of these works is John Scotus Eriugena’s Latin version, exactly as it is found in the oldest manuscripts. As for the glosses, there is another error. Several glosses have been placed in the margin of the treatise on the [Col. CXLVC] *Celestial Hierarchy*: that of Maximus, that of John Scotus, that of John of Sythopolis, surnamed the Saracen, and that of Hugh of Saint-Victor, as we find it in the first volume of his *Works*. But in the margin of the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* there is only one gloss, that of Maximus, according to John Scotus Eriugena’s version. If the catalogue of the National Library assigns this gloss to the Victorine, it is mistaken. The Benedictines could easily have corrected this error from a large number of other manuscripts. As for the Tournai manuscript, here is Sanderus’s note: “Likewise, eight books of Dionysius translated by the same Hugh from Greek into Latin.” It is probable that the work divided by Sanderus into eight books is the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, which consists of seven chapters, and not the *Celestial Hierarchy*, which has fifteen; but, let it be noted, the reference here is to a text, and Sanderus does not say that any gloss is joined to that text. The Tournai volume therefore presents no analogy in this respect with no. 1619 of the King’s collection; it contains only a Latin version wrongly attributed to the canon of Saint-Victor. If, therefore, as one of our catalogues declares, Hugh of Saint-Victor commented on the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, that commentary remains to be found.]

And many treatises pertaining to theology, [Col. CXLVA] such as *On the Power of the Order*;

[Note: [Col. CXLVD] This is doubtless the treatise entitled in almost all manuscripts *On the Power of Praying* or *On the Power of Prayer*. It is printed in vol. II of the *Works*, col. 977, under the title *Book on the Manner of Praying*.]

*On Praise*;

[Note: [Col. CXLVD] The title is incomplete; it should read *On the Praise of Charity*; *Works*, vol. II, col. 969.]

*On the Five Sevens*;

[Note: [Col. CXLVD] *Works*, vol. I, col. 405.]

*On the Instruction of Novices*;

[Note: [Col. CXLVD] *Works*, vol. II, col. 9.]

one book on the *Magnificat*;

[Note: [Col. CXLVD] *Works*, vol. I, col. 413.]

one book on the *Lamentations of Jeremiah*;

[Note: [Col. CXLVD] *Works*, vol. I, col. 255, under the title *Explanatory Notes on the Lamentations of the Prophet Jeremiah*.]

one book on Ecclesiastes;

[Note: [Col. CXLVIA] This is doubtless the same work designated in the second catalogue under the title *Fifteen Homilies on Ecclesiastes*, vol. I, col. 113. In the printed work there are nineteen homilies, and, as the *Literary History* observes, they do not go beyond the fourth chapter of Ecclesiastes. There is therefore reason to believe that we do not possess this commentary in its entirety.]

a *Map of the World*;

[Note: [Col. CXLVIB] In one of the chapters of the *Mystical Ark*, Hugh of Saint-Victor undertakes to explain more fully elsewhere the respective positions of Egypt and Palestine, and he makes this undertaking in the following terms: “How this agrees with the situation of the places will later become clear in the description of the Map of the World, since Babylon lies north of Jerusalem and Egypt to the south.” The authors of the *Literary History* say in this connection: “If this latter work exists, it has escaped our searches; but there can be no doubt that the world map which was its subject was a geographical map.” Our two catalogues prove that this *Map of the World*, or this *Description of a World Map*, by Hugh of Saint-Victor existed in the fourteenth century; but has it not since been lost? Perhaps a short work entitled *On the Places around Jerusalem*, found in a Saint-Victor manuscript (no. 567, formerly 801), together with other works by the same doctor, should be regarded as a fragment of this description. But this is a hypothesis which we advance with the greatest hesitation.]

*Selections by the Same Author*;

[Note: [Col. CXLVIC] This title occurs again in the second catalogue. We do not know to what work it should be applied, unless to certain extracts from Hugh’s works that were held at the abbey of Saint-Victor.]

books on Grammar;

[Note: [Col. CXLVIC] Unpublished works. Our manuscripts offer only one treatise by Hugh of Saint-Victor on Grammar, and even that is a modern copy found in Saint-Victor no. 1058. The authors of the *Literary History* inform us that this abbey possessed an older manuscript of the same treatise, in a volume formerly numbered 227; but it does not appear that this volume entered the National Library.]

an *Epitome of Philosophy*;

[Note: [Col. CXLVID] Unpublished. We know two manuscripts, one in Saint-Victor no. 1038 and another, older, in Sorbonne no. 364 A. In the latter volume, which appears to be from the thirteenth century, it bears the following title: “Hugh’s *Epitome of Philosophy*, and it should immediately precede the *Didascalicon*.” It is a dialogue among various interlocutors—Sosthenes, Indaletius, and Dindimus—whose subject is the definition of the various parts of philosophy. It begins with the words: “Often, Indaletius, brother Dindimus …” Platonic theses will be found in it. From the beginning of scholastic teaching, rationalist theologians studied Aristotle, while the mystics preferred Plato.]

an *Exposition* [Col. CXLVIA] on Ezekiel;

[Note: [Col. CXLVID] Unpublished. The second catalogue gives the title *Literal Exposition of Ezekiel’s Vision*. We know no manuscript of this literal commentary on Ezekiel.]

and many other works, both numerous and subtle.

It is also reported of him that, when he was already almost at the point of death, so afflicted that he could retain no food because of his extreme weakness, he was divinely inspired and distinguished an unconsecrated host from a consecrated one. The brothers had brought him the former lest he be distressed, and he said: “May God have mercy on you, brothers; why did you wish to deceive me? This is not my God whom you have brought.” [Col. CXLVIIA] Immediately, astonished, they brought the Body of the Lord; but, unable to receive it, he raised his hands toward heaven and said: “Let the Son return to the Father, and the spirit to Him who made it.” As he said this, the Lord’s Body vanished between his hands together with his soul; and he was buried in the cloister beside the entrance of the church of Saint-Victor of Paris.

He was Saxon by race and birth, from a powerful family. He brought his maternal uncle to Saint-Victor, at whose expense almost the whole church of Saint-Victor and all its workshops were built.

## II

[Col. CXLVII]

On folio 5 of our manuscript there is an epitaph of Hugh of Saint-Victor, entirely devoid of interest. We omit it in order to give the second catalogue of Hugh’s works, for which this emphatic prose serves as a preface.

[Col. CXLVIIB]

Two books *On the Sacraments*. The first contains twelve parts, while the second contains sixteen.

[Note: [Col. CXLVIIB] *Works*, vol. II, col. 173. In these editions the second book of the *Treatise on the Sacraments* consists of eighteen chapters.]

*On the Medicine of the Soul*.

[Note: [Col. CXLVIIB] *Works*, vol. II, col. 1183. The authors of the *Literary History* do not hesitate to count this work among those that should be restored to Hugh of Fouilloy. The reason given by Dom Brial is that it contains a great number of allegories, and that this abuse of mystical tropes can be observed in Hugh of Fouilloy’s other writings. We grant this; but is the taste of the canon of Saint-Victor therefore purer than that of the canon of Saint-Laurent? Dom Brial adds that four manuscripts of the National Library attribute *On the Medicine of the Soul* to Hugh of Fouilloy. We examined these manuscripts, and the name of Hugh of Fouilloy is found only in no. 2896. It is true that elsewhere this little work accompanies others regarded as belonging to Hugh of Fouilloy; but in several manuscripts of Saint-Victor, the Sorbonne, and elsewhere, it appears among the works of the Victorine. We shall therefore likewise refrain from either disputing or confirming the attribution preferred by the authors of the *Literary History*.]

*On Meditation*.

[Note: [Col. CXLVIID] *Works*, vol. II, col. 993, under the title *On the Art of Meditation*.]

*On the Incarnation of the Word*.

[Note: [Col. CXLVIID] The first chapter of the second book of *On the Sacraments* bears the title *On the Incarnation of the Word*. We nevertheless believe that the work designated here is the one entitled *Apology Concerning the Incarnate Word*.—*Works*, vol. III, col. 295.]

*On the Three Wills in Christ*.

[Note: [Col. CXLVIID] *Works*, vol. II, col. 841. Casimir Oudin had thought it necessary to dispute this short work and the following one to the canon of Saint-Victor. The Benedictines claimed them for him (*Literary History*, vol. XII, p. 21).]

*On the Power and Will of God*.

[Note: [Col. CXLVIID] *Works*, vol. II, col. 839.]

*On the Wisdom of Christ*.

[Note: [Col. CXLVIID] *Works*, vol. II, col. 841.]

*On the Substance of Love*.

[Note: [Col. CXLVIID] *Works*, vol. II, col. 15, under the title *On the Substance of Charity*. This work was attributed to Saint Augustine before the manuscripts were examined more carefully.]

*On the Works of the Three Days*.

[Note: [Col. CXLVIID] *Works*, vol. II, col. 811. This is the seventh book of the *Didascalicon*. In most manuscripts it is separated from the others and forms a distinct treatise.]

[Col. CXLVIIIB]

Books *On the Soul*.

[Note: [Col. CXLVIIIB] *Works*, vol. II, col. 165. There is scarcely any connection among these four books. Accordingly, they have often been dispersed: the first and third were placed among the works of Saint Bernard, and the second among those of Saint Augustine. Ellies Dupin wishes to attribute all four to Hugh of Fouilloy, but nothing authorizes him to do so. Without claiming them for the Victorine, we shall observe, against the testimony of the authors of the *Literary History*, that several manuscripts of these four books *On the Soul* bear the name of Hugh of Saint-Victor. It is enough to designate Sorbonne no. 364 A and Saint-Victor no. 678. Both begin: “Here begins the book of Master Hugh of Saint-Victor *On the Soul*, containing four separate books.” Sorbonne no. 364 A appears to date from the end of the thirteenth century.]

Four books *On the Cloister of the Soul*.

*A Little Book to a Companion Wishing to Marry*.

[Note: [Col. CXLVIIIC] *Works*, vol. II, col. 1202. As the authors of the *Literary History* observed, most manuscripts attribute this work to Hugh of Fouilloy (*Literary History*, vol. XIII, p. 500).]

*Exposition of the Lord’s Prayer*.

[Note: [Col. CXLVIIIC] Our catalogue places two expositions of the Lord’s Prayer among the works of Hugh of Saint-Victor. Both have been printed. The first is chapter 2 of book II of the *Allegories on Saint Matthew*, *Works*, vol. I, col. 779; the second begins at chapter 3 and ends at chapter 14 of the same *Allegories*. The authors of the *Literary History* declare that they do not accept these two short works as being by the Victorine; but they give no justification for this declaration, which may be rash, since it is contradicted by a great many manuscripts.]

Four books *On Noah’s Ark*.

The *Didascalicon*, *On the Study of Reading*, five books.

*On the Power of Prayer.*

*On the Instruction of Novices Entrusted to Religious Life.*

*On the Discipline of Monks*.

[Note: [Col. CXLVIIID] The authors of the *Literary History* place a treatise *On the Discipline of Monks* among Hugh of Saint-Victor’s unpublished works and mention it in these terms: “A treatise *On the Discipline of Monks* forms part of manuscript 199 of Saint-Victor, whose script seems to belong to the twelfth century. The name of Hugh with which it is adorned appears to have been added afterward. The work begins as follows: ‘Discipline is good and honorable conduct, for which it is too little merely not to do evil.’” We shall correct only the principal errors of this notice. In fact, this supposed treatise *On the Discipline of Monks* is found as a separate work in Saint-Victor manuscript 199, now 137; but it is joined to the treatise *On the Instruction of Novices* in a very large number of other manuscripts. How did the Benedictines fail to know that it had been published? It forms part of the *Works*, vol. II, col. 925, where it constitutes chapters 10–21 of the treatise *On the Instruction of Novices*; and that is its proper place, since it is not a treatise but a fragment.]

[Col. CXLIXA]

*On the Soul’s Pledge.*

*On the Canticle of Blessed Mary*.

[Note: [Col. CXLIXB] *Works*, vol. I, col. 413.]

Four books *On the Vanity of the World*.

[Note: [Col. CXLIXB] *Works*, vol. II, col. 703. Oudin had attributed this book to Hugh of Fouilloy. His reasons did not seem convincing to the authors of the *Literary History*. As Oudin observed, *On the Vanity of the World* is by the same author as the short works on Noah’s Ark; but there is no reason to dispute these short works with Hugh of Saint-Victor. We add that *On the Vanity of the World* is a dialogue, and that its interlocutors are designated in the printed text by the letters D and I. According to the editors of the *Works* and the Benedictines, these letters presumably mean *Docens* (“Teacher”) and *Interrogator* (“Questioner”); but a Sorbonne manuscript, no. 304, gives us another key to the riddle by replacing D with *Dindimus*. We would then have only to render I as *Indaletus*. Indaletus and Dindimus are two figures whom our Victorine had already introduced in his *Epitome of Philosophy*, and this is further evidence that *On the Vanity of the World* is not the work of the canon of Saint-Laurent.]

*On the Praise of Charity.*

Likewise another treatise on the Lord’s Prayer.

*On the Seven Gifts*.

[Note: [Col. CXLIXC] This is another title for the treatise *On the Sevens*.]

*On the Bridegroom’s Love for the Bride*.

[Note: [Col. CXLIXC] *Works*, vol. II, col. 987. The Benedictines judge this work unworthy of Hugh of Saint-Victor (*Literary History*, vol. XII, p. 70).]

*A Treatise on Beauties*.

[Note: [Col. CXLIXC] A mystical title for some fragment incorporated into the *Miscellanies*.]

*On Sacred Scripture and Its Writers*.

[Note: [Col. CXLIXD] *Works*, vol. I, col. 9.]

*Epitome of Philosophy.*
