[Note: [Col. CXLIXD] *Works*, vol. I, col. 29 and following.]

*A Mirror by the Same Author on the Mysteries of the Church.*

[Note: [Col. CXLIXD] *Works*, vol. III, col. 325. It is probable that the author of the catalogue designates the same work later under the title *Mystery of the Church*.]

*On the Profession of Monks.*

[Note: [Col. CXLIXD] We do not know this treatise, if it is to be distinguished from the one entitled *On the Instruction of Novices and the Discipline of Monks*. There is a treatise by Saint Bernard which, in the manuscripts, bears the title *On the Profession of Monks*.]

[Col. CLA]

*Distinctions of Words.*

[Note: [Col. CXLIXD] It is unknown to what work this title refers. It may be the treatise *On the Properties and Epithets of Things*, which in the *Works*, vol. III, at the beginning, forms the fourth book of the *Bestiary*. We cannot too often point out that the editors of the *Works* constructed works in several books from short works which the manuscripts offer separately.]

*On Conscience.*

[Note: [Col. CLB] It is found under this title in Sorbonne no. 723, formerly 675. It begins: “This house in which we dwell threatens us with ruin on every side.” But it is the third book of the treatise *On the Soul*.—*Works*, vol. III, col. 165.]

*The Same Author’s Confession to an Abbot.*

[Note: [Col. CLB] This short work appeared unpublished to the authors of the *Literary History*, who noted it in a royal manuscript, no. 2922. It is also found in Sorbonne no. 723, where it begins: “Alone I shall enter the solitude of my heart.” But it is not unpublished. In the edition of the *Works*, it occupies the final chapters of the third book of the treatise *On the Soul*; it begins at chapter 32 of that third book. It is a dialogue between a monk and his abbot. It should be observed that in the edition of the *Works* it is continuous discourse. The suppression of the interlocutors certainly does not help to make the work intelligible. But the Victorine editors did not look so closely. Chapter 21 of book III of the treatise *On the Soul* also bears, in the printed text, the title *Confession to an Abbot*.]

*On the Difference between Divine and Worldly Theology.*

[Note: [Col. CLC] In the printed text this is the first book of the *Commentary on the Celestial Hierarchy*.]

Fifteen chapters on the *Celestial Hierarchy*.

*Benjamin by the Same Author.*

[Note: [Col. CLC] Erroneous attribution. It is a work by Richard of Saint-Victor.]

*Mystery of the Church.*

*Literal Exposition of Ezekiel’s Vision.*

*Exposition on the Canticles.*

[Note: [Col. CLC] Unpublished. The authors of the *Literary History* mention a manuscript copy in the National Library, no. 2525 of the former collection. We may perhaps have encountered another. Laon Library no. 471 contains a large number of short works by the Victorine, among which, between the *Sentences* and the *Didascalicon*, is a commentary on the *Song of Songs*. Since this manuscript is from the twelfth century, one may suppose that it contains the work designated by our catalogue.]

*The Same Author’s Bestiary.*

[Note: [Col. CLD] *Works*, vol. III, at the beginning. This *Bestiary* consists of four books, the first of which Dom Brial attributes to Hugh of Fouilloy, the second to Alain of Lille, and the third and fourth to William Peraut (*Literary History*, vol. XIII, p. 498). All these attributions seem to us approximately equally open to question.]

Fifteen homilies on Ecclesiastes.

A book on Grammar.

*The Same Author’s Sentences.*

[Note: [Col. CLD] *Works*, vol. II, col. 41. This is one of Hugh of Saint-Victor’s most substantial and highly esteemed works. It is therefore inexplicable that the canons of Saint-Victor published this work of their illustrious colleague from a text incomplete and defective in every respect when they had much better texts at their disposal. Saint-Victor no. 796, formerly 1085, a twelfth-century manuscript, contains several rare and valuable treatises of that period, including a copy of Hugh’s *Sentences* that ends with several unpublished chapters. [Col. CLIA] The printed text stops in the middle of an argument concerning second marriages; the manuscript completes that argument, and other chapters complete the work. Another volume from the same [Col. CLIB] period, no. 457 in the Latin collection of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, offers further differences: eleven unpublished chapters precede the chapter that comes first in the edition of the *Works*.]

[Col. CLIA]

*A Most Beautiful Exposition of the Rule of Blessed Augustine.*

[Note: [Col. CLIB] *Works*, vol. II, col. 881.]

*The Same Author’s Histories.*

[Note: [Col. CLIB] Several manuscripts exist under the titles *Histories*, *Chronicles*, and *On the Three Greatest Circumstances*; but, according to the Benedictines, these titles were given to various compilations that do not appear legitimately attributable to Hugh of Saint-Victor. Thus, they say, we do not possess his *Chronicle*. This is the conclusion of the *Literary History*, but that conclusion seems to us poorly justified. The Benedictines identify two *Chronicles* attributed, they say, to Hugh of Saint-Victor. We know four. The first is in Sorbonne manuscript no. 304. It is an imperfect work that appears to be wrongly placed among the Victorine’s works. The second, whose trace we had little difficulty recovering, is printed in vol. III, cols. 215–283, of Hugh of Saint-Victor’s *Works*. How did the Benedictines fail to know of its existence? The third, contained in the Saint-Victor manuscripts identified by the Benedictines—that is, manuscripts 567, formerly 801, and 577, formerly 814—is composed almost entirely of fragments borrowed from the printed text. If it does not contain various passages cited by Alberic of Trois-Fontaines, there is no reason for surprise, since this third *Chronicle* is an abridgement of the second. As for the fourth, it is indeed found in [Col. CLIIB] the manuscript identified by the Benedictines, under the title they report. But who, before them, attributed it to the canon of Saint-Victor? Not the copyist, whom they accuse of ignorance. They attribute this error to him, but he did not commit it. To establish, moreover, that this fourth chronicle does not belong to Hugh of Saint-Victor, it is enough to observe that he himself is designated in it in these terms: “Second to none in the world in knowledge of the Scriptures.” We regard the printed text as the authentic work of our Victorine.]

One book on the *Lamentations of Jeremiah*.

One book on the angelic *Hierarchy of Dionysius*.

Notes on certain verses of the Psalms.

[Note: [Col. CLIIB] *Works*, vol. III, col. 589.]

*On the Perpetual Virginity of Blessed Mary.*

A book *On the Cloister of the Soul*, entitled under the name of Hugh of Fouilloy, monk of Corbie.

Notes on John.

[Note: [Col. CLIIB] *Works*, vol. I, col. 827. The Benedictines do not wish this commentary to be by the Victorine. It should belong, they say, to some professor of sophistical theology. Whoever this supposed logician was, he had very pronounced tendencies toward mysticism, since he worshiped the true God under the form of an essence that resides wholly within all his creatures: “God is, with his whole essence, in every creature.” What doctrine, then, is this? Or rather, what is this strange language?—for the words must not here be given the meaning that seems to belong to them—if not the language of the theologians and philosophers of Saint-Victor?]

[Col. CLIIA]

*A Mirror by the Same Author.*

[Note: [Col. CLIIC] A work unknown to us, unless it is the *Mirror on the Mysteries of the Church*, which has already been designated twice in this catalogue.]

*On the Food of Emmanuel.*

[Note: [Col. CLIIC] *Works*, vol. III, col. 477.]

*Map of the World.*

*Selections by the Same Author.*

He also composed many other short works, known to Him through whose gift and grace he compiled so many and such subtle volumes. These have been briefly set down here so that the devout observer of this tomb and the pious reader of this little document may offer the most abundant thanks to God, through whose gift and grace these things have been obtained.

[Col. CLI]

# PREFACES TO THE EDITION OF THE YEAR 1525

[Col. CLID]

To the most reverend Father in Christ and most worthy Peer of France, Lord Michael Boudet, most prudent Bishop of Langres: Brother John Borderius, humble abbot of Saint-Victor, greetings.

Solomon, most eminent, as everyone knows, for the torrent of his wisdom, most reverend bishop, says not only, “Drink water from your own cistern and streams from your own well” (Prov. 5), but also, “Let your springs flow abroad, and distribute your waters in the streets” (ibid.). Having searched these words thoroughly, even to their inmost marrow, he seems to have intended, among certain other meanings of the divine mysteries, this very point: namely, that we should not shut up within domestic walls the literary memorials of men—especially of writers who benefit the commonwealth—nor merely delight the private studies of a few, allowing them to remain only between their breasts, though these otherwise swell with the milk of charity.

For, by the authority of Him who is Truth itself, neither a city set upon a mountain ought to be hidden [Col. CLIID], nor a lamp placed under a bushel-measure, but raised upon a lampstand. Hence we read this aptly written: “Hidden wisdom and an unseen treasure—what benefit is there in either?” (Ecclus. 20.) To consider all these things more carefully, and to carry out what has been considered more diligently, we are spurred no little by this our grievously unhappy age, which has produced monstrous heretics who bewitch even the devout minds of the pious; has heaped up teachers with itching ears; has introduced deceitful doctrines; and has brought forth crafty destroyers of orthodox teaching. No person of sound mind will deny that antidotes must be prepared against their poisons, arrows sent out to scatter them, and thunderbolts multiplied to confound them.

Accordingly, both lest, by attending to private benefit, we should appear to set aside—or rather to make light of—the public good; and lest, when we are able to do something, we should be said to be unwilling to provide any assistance against these scoffers at truth [Col. CLIIIA], we have taken care to gather the wheaten sheaves of our Hugh, called of Saint-Victor, which stood scattered through our literary threshing-floor, called a library, and in certain other places belonging to others; to bind them into three volumes or bundles; and to send them into the public granaries for public use. Thus, perhaps, we may make the bundles made from the tares of those enchanters and enemies of brotherly honour crawl as it were upon the ground, while we cause men, clothed in this many-coloured tunic, to adore the bundles of his resplendent and perfect righteousness; or, rather, we may cause their cauterized teaching and snares—especially under the feet of the foolish—to yield before this undefiled doctrine.

How devout, how holy, and how fully conscious of truth in every respect are the teachings of this our Hugh, ought to be judged not by us, as members of his own household, but by the judgment of any others whatsoever. Yet we hope that all will say—even those whose dimmed eyes find light hateful, and who are accustomed to raise laughter over the writings of others with hooked noses or wrinkled brows—that they are such as may deservedly be embraced by every sincere worshipper of Christianity. For, to express something briefly of their merits: what is holier than these writings? What more religious? What more remote from every leaven of error? Above all, they are remote from that most impious error which some of the aforementioned investigators of truth most wickedly clamour into the most sacred sacrament of the altar.

Indeed, how much faith and reverence this our Hugh bestowed upon this supremely blessed sacrament of the altar is especially evident from the fact that, at the end of his life, he most wisely refused to use a host which he had perceived, by an inward apprehension of the spirit, not to have been consecrated. “This,” he said, “is not my God.” But when a consecrated host was offered him, he did not receive it because of the imminent danger of repeated vomiting caused by an injured stomach; and he said, “Let the Son return to the Father, and the spirit to God who made him.” We believe that this occurred on the strength not so much of internal as of external testimony.

Therefore, most worthy bishop, we could not—and ought not—not dedicate to your most celebrated name these such holy wheaten sheaves [Col. CLIIIC] of so holy a man: that is, these most holy works of our Hugh, overflowing with pure wheat and breathing forth the pure and sincere doctrine of that grain of wheat, Jesus Christ. We do so both because you are an outstanding cultivator and lover of holy works, and because you can employ these works, as you employ others, to uproot the plantation of these new doctrines, which the heavenly Father has not planted. For you are no lukewarm persecutor of them, in deed as well as word. Finally, you are a sincere lover and constant champion of this our Victorine monastery, of which that Hugh was both a blessed pupil and a father to be revered.

You will therefore receive, most reverend Father, these works which we judged should be dedicated to you; and, from the inborn and native kindness that is yours, you will defend them against the malicious teeth of malicious men. Farewell; always mindful and loving of your happy Victorines. From this same our Victorine monastery, on the Nones of October, in this year of human salvation 1526.

### A Little Elegy by Brother Robert Battheus, a Victorine monk, to the Same Most Reverend Bishop of Langres

Great is your praiseworthy integrity of life,  
And your virtue, O bishop beloved of noble leaders.

The native Gallic world, with truth-speaking voice,  
Sings that you are always a safe refuge of the people.

But this our house beholds you as lofty in character  
And renowned as a Father in holy religion.

With a sincere mind you recall the ancient fathers,  
The established lights of the Victorine Fathers;

Whence, among all men, by night and day, like a bright lamp,  
Our greatest Hugh is given to you.

Receive him, we pray, with gentle hands and a friendly spirit:  
It will be a welcome gift, as I know.

### Poem to the Same Most Reverend Father in Christ, Lord Michael Boudet, Most Deserving Bishop of Langres, and Father and Leader of the Gauls

[Col. CLIVA]

Bright lamp of the Franks, their peers, and their leaders,  
Bishop of Langres, in no way unworthy of this summit  
Of honour: you are such as the Apostle prescribes—  
Or nowhere in the whole world is any bishop to be found.

For you do not swell with display or proud arrogance;  
You are not wrathful, nor abandoned to luxury;  
You are no mad lover of wealth or pursuer of empty acclaim,  
Nor, like the great multitude, do you make your belly a tomb.

Rather, you are simple, humble in mind, and gentle in heart;  
Sober, with your loins girded, chastising  
Your own body by a strict rule, yet generous toward all;  
A protector and guardian of what belongs to others,  
Lavish with your own money, and ever the sincere lover  
Of the Victorine brothers. Since the holy house owes you much  
And has nothing with which it can repay you worthily,

[Col. CLIVB]

It dedicates to you its own Hugh. Receive the gift  
Than which it can offer nothing greater; nor, though you have given  
Very much, should you seek in return more or greater things.

### Sapphic Poem by Brother Robert Battheus to the Venerable Father, Brother John Simon, Prior of Saint-Victor, a Man of Exceptional Prudence

The supreme Ruler alike of heaven and earth,  
For the blessed gifts of your mind,  
Has adorned you through many sacred years  
With the office of the cloister.

Many of us are bound to render fitting gratitude  
To the very name that is yours,  
And to bring forth praise  
For labour meritoriously undertaken.

Foremost among all these, I come to be remembered,  
One of your servants,  
Holding the due rank  
Of our company of young men.

For you have been given us as a sound and truthful teacher,  
By the will of the Father,  
Whom the beautiful elm in its famous arms  
Represents.

Thus, for many years I have served the Lord  
Of princes and likewise of kings,  
In lowly station, sustained  
By a fatherly providence.

In this distinguished house of blessed Victor,  
I peacefully sucked the breasts  
Of the venerable consecrated mother,  
Full of bright nourishment.

And then, as sweet and solid food,  
You first gave us, while still untrained,  
The little book of Father Hugh,  
With serene mind.

This book has always been accustomed to be offered  
Into the ready hands of devout young men,  
And thus to be presented as a book  
On the state of beginners.

Indeed, I carried it everywhere, richly filled  
With the varied flower of virtue;  
I went on my way pleasantly and elegantly,  
Nor was I ashamed of it at any time.

For from tender years it imbued all its fellow brothers,  
Turning them in mind toward its counsels  
And in spirit toward the mother  
Religion.

Thus it leads us, followers of the strict life,  
To the havens of eternal rest,  
Keeping the mean throughout  
With blessed steps.

And since once, when I was a novice,  
You gave me a little light from Hugh,  
If it pleases your mind,  
Receive him now gathered complete.

### Twelve-Line Poem of the Same Author to the Reader

[Col. CLVA]

Receive with a cheerful countenance, candid reader,  
The great work of the illustrious master Hugh.

It recalls the erring, governs the tractable, incites the lofty,  
Instructs the attentive, and ennobles the devout.

It does not permit the illustrious race of men to go into outer darkness  
By a deceitful path.

Indeed, whoever accompanies the journey once begun  
Receives solid fruit enduring through all time.

What more splendid gifts, I ask, of the divine will  
Could the mind of one who contemplates desire?

Therefore receive the ordered volumes of the eloquent Father:  
They bring Virtue and a safeguard.

### Poem by Brother Francis Grin, Whose Verse Was “Thunderbolts,” etc., to the Volume and Its Author

Monuments long awaited by ancestors now buried,  
What, I entreat, held you hidden from the sun  
For so long after the generations had passed? What night  
Or darkness concealed your faces?

[Col. CLVB]

Were you weary, perhaps,  
And forgetful of your foreign dwelling-place?  
O sole hope and delight of scholars,  
Kind Hugh, now flourishing in the paradisal seats,  
May I at last be permitted to walk in your gardens.

Under your auspices may I touch the leaping streams  
Of the sealed fountain, and pluck the flowers of spring.  
Yet let first thanks be rendered to Christ the head,  
From whom is every good, and by whose breath  
The lamp of such great radiance, once shining only for itself,  
Will henceforth shine throughout the whole world.

### Ascensius to Hugh Concerning His Works

Hugh, foster-child of the celebrated house of holy Victor,  
Interpreter of wisdom and approved leader in sacred matters,

You pour out into the deepest hearts of Christ’s worshipping choir  
The divine streams drawn from Christ’s breast.

As you look straight at the rays of Hyperion,  
You are known to be Jupiter’s bird.

[Col. CLVC]

Therefore Christ’s bird nourished you in its own nest,  
That you might cut off the mysteries of the lofty Beginning.

Moreover, expounding the divine volumes of great Moses,  
You pursue them with a double interpretation.

You likewise explain the sacred deeds of Judges and Kings,  
And the tripods of the prophets and the melody of the Psalmist.

You do not pass over the Lamentations, nor the closed riddles  
Of the peaceful king whose book is called Ecclesiastes.

Likewise, resolving the enigmas of the Gospel and of Paul,  
You complete a volume in the Dionysian citadel.

A second volume soon contains morals, cloisters, prayers, souls,  
arks, living creatures, deeds, and discourses.

The rites of temples, the opinions of doctors, sacred things  
Together with sacraments, belong to the third sequence:

All things which the bishop, leader, and peer of Langres  
Has at heart and will not allow to perish by any hostile tooth.

### Poem in Praise of the Author by Brother Jacques Gault, Victorine Monk of the Order of Saint Augustine

[Col. CLVD]

Whoever wishes to overcome the dreadful dangers of a declining life,  
Or joyfully enter upon the straight way;

And whoever seeks to climb the star-bearing dwelling  
Of the highest heaven, the shining halls of the lofty sky:

Let him hasten here, putting aside sluggish steps;  
Let his pursuit fly through this holy work.

Whatever the divine volumes of the sacred law contain,  
This work recounts in wonderful measures.

This work is brilliant, pleasing, praiseworthy, and polished;  
Every vice flees far from the reader.

The golden path of tranquil life is shown;  
By so bright a light the way is made safe for you.

It teaches the sacred laws of righteousness by which men go upward;  
By its own art it teaches them to climb into Christ’s kingdom.

That Hugh was surely no son of a mortal man,  
But born from divine seed.

His speech was ready, more torrent-like than all waters;  
His faith unerring, and likewise his love of religion.

[Col. CLVIA]

A grammarian, rhetorician, geometer, painter, trainer,  
Augur, philosopher, and one himself acquainted with the stars:

Among those whom fame has carried far through the world,  
He bears away the foremost prizes of the victorious ivy.

Though common people continually celebrate him in the common tongue,  
His fame can never perish.

Thus he has obtained immense praise for eternal years,  
Which no age can remove through the centuries.

Rather, let Hugh be inscribed among the bright stars,  
And may this celebrated name shine before God.

Though at last he has departed from our region,  
Yet now he flourishes on high before God.

The upright life of Father Hugh is deservedly praised,  
For great grace descended upon him from the heavenly places.

Whoever is able to drink in the thought of this approved author  
Should not be sluggish in seeking out his genius.

It is filled with fruits and fragrant flowers,  
And it possesses also the fruits of outstanding Pallas.

Holy Victor sends you out into countless lands,

[Col. CLVIB]

So that everyone may enjoy this excellent gift.  
Go, O glory of kings, traverse the vast world;  
Teach the mystical temples of your Lord.

### Poem by Brother Mathurin Lorrin of Paris, Humble Monk of the Same House, to the Very Reverend Father and Lord, John Bordier, Most Watchful Shepherd of Saint-Victor beside the Walls of Paris

The nourishing breath of the sacred south wind filled  
Your breast, and here it left flowers, fruits, and fragrance:

You summit of pure religion, foster-child of virtue;  
The fair Victorine company applauds you.

All the Parisian people sing of you as the polished mirror of the populace  
And the perpetual light of the temple.

The powerful venerate you with the honour due to a superior,  
And the poor rejoice to have you as a humble Father.

You go before the flock that is to follow you; you duly pursue  
The path which ripe old age has given.

[Col. CLVIC]

Behold Hugh’s work, which, brighter than stone in doctrine,  
Was built to wear down stony hearts with strength.

The land of Saxony produced this stone;  
The Victorine house, by its skill, raised the man on high.

O hard rock! a seat hateful to ships  
Which savage Boreas drives in a swelling storm.

Take hold of the prow, and may the highest heaven direct  
Your course and govern your sails with full favour.

Thus entrust yourself safely to the seas: if the waters swell in fury,  
Sure salvation awaits you beneath the rock’s shelter.

It will drive away the winds and will not allow their force to prevail.  
You will strike the rock, and it will yield sacred streams.

The waters will become sweet; you will drink and give drink to the flock.  
Thus it will receive weary bodies in its peaceful bosom.

### Epigram on the Great, Manifold Greatness and Excellence of Master Hugh of Saint-Victor, Canon and Theologian, by the Most Learned Brother John Conrad, Monk of the Same Profession and Fellowship

[Col. CLVID]

Great indeed is Victor’s house; but Hugh, greater than all,  
Gave it a greater name throughout the world.

Great in ancestry, great in deeds, and great in name;  
Great in intellect, and no less great in piety.

Great in the eyes of the world, but greatest because he despised it;  
And therefore his whole life was most great.

Great miracles proved his great death,  
And great ash was taken from his holy tomb.

He was once great, but now he himself will become  
Greater through the great memorials of his hand.

He will always be greater, the more he is read;  
And, the more he is read, the more he will yet be reread.

Would you have me repeat it? Hugh was great in birth, life,  
Name, monastery, religion, and books.

Indeed, perhaps these things should not even be judged great,  
Unless he himself were greatest before God.

### Another Short Poem by the Same John Conrad, in Which the Enemy of Human Salvation Complains of the Losses Inflicted Both by the Whole Victorine Monastery and by Hugh

[Col. CLVIIA]

That rival dragon, exiled from the heavenly seats,  
Who presses upon land and sea with his dominion,

When he read the author and the title of this volume, said:  
“I see wars against me; wars are being prepared.”

Then he growled to himself with immense fury  
And uttered these words with a dreadful roar:

“Formerly the world subject to our laws  
Readily yielded to my rule and commands.

Behold, a small people arising from a humble place,  
Indeed despised by the world, has destroyed my entire kingdom.

Here it has built cells for itself by the Seine;  
It lies hidden here, yet oppresses me throughout the whole world.

You will think me wholly unarmed if you see  
That it makes war with a naked body;

Yet it courageously repels all my weapons.

[Col. CLVIIB]

Its naked flesh is harder than marble.  
Neither frost by chance can penetrate it, nor flame melt it;  
No thirst breaks it, nor dreadful hunger.

Indeed—who would believe it?—it places such trust in these arms,  
And harms us from the very source from which I might do harm.

Besides its leader, there is another leader: king and priest;  
I myself do not sufficiently know which of them offends me more.

That one, displaying his wounds—he whose name is Victor—  
Thereby rouses his men and makes them great-hearted.

This one is Augustine, bishop of African Carthage:  
Truly African, knowing a thousand advantages of war;

Truly African, who craftily uncovers every one of my frauds  
And reveals to his people all my counsel.

Now with these voices, now with those, he continually thunders;  
Everywhere his wondrous speech sounds out whatever is needed.

He rebukes some, moves others, flatters and attracts still others,  
And moves them by promising greater benefit.

[Col. CLVIIC]

At times he raises threats and displays dangers.  
In short, he knows how to vary a thousand tones in manifold ways.

Wretched me! Nor was it enough that I should be so afflicted by these two:  
From them has sprung a new offspring.

Alas, grief! It imitates its fathers and, with equal zeal,  
Daily wages war against us.

Of all this offspring I most detest three—Richard,  
Adam, and Hugh, greatest of the three.

This is another Augustine in eloquent speech,  
Matching him in intellect.

For many envious ages our guile held this man  
In the maternal embrace of a library.

But now, unless it be some unknown man, the Abbot Bordier—  
May he never fare well!—has ordered him to go forth.

He will go, and will range triumphantly through the whole world;  
Everywhere he will plant the banners of his genius.

What then can I strive against? We yield—alas!  
You have conquered, Victor, you and your race.”

### Exhortation by the Same Brother John Conrad to Master Hugh to Go Forth at Last into Public

[Col. CLVIID]

Go out into the open field, foster-child of Victor,  
And wage Christ’s battles as a good soldier.

That your conqueror once bore splendid trophies  
When he conquered the world, the devil, and the flesh.

You also conquered these; but herein is greater glory for you:  
Your writings teach us also to conquer.

For he is judged greater in heaven who teaches and does  
What is right, than one who only teaches.

Therefore go on: you who have long triumphed in victorious warfare,  
Make us too conquer now by your counsels.

Be present as our leader in war; unfurl the banners  
Of your divine intellect. The world will rejoice to follow them.

### Jodocus Badius Ascensius to Lord John Bordier, Most Worthy Superior of the Canons of Saint Augustine’s House of Saint-Victor, and Most Prudent Restorer of the Whole Order in France: Greeting

Most certainly, most wise abbot, you have acted with excellent judgment, as in all things, in taking pains in these days to have the highly finished literary monuments of the most learned theologian Master Hugh, surnamed of Saint-Victor, published and dedicated to Michael Boudet, the admirably praised and ever-praiseworthy Bishop of Langres, Duke and Peer of France [Col. CLVIIIA]. They ought indeed to be published, since they contain the most ready antidotes against every poison of heresy that has long been raging. For Hugh wrote, so graphically, accurately, and learnedly concerning the sacraments—especially the Eucharist—vows, free will, and every truly Christian devotion and holy conviction, that no one before him did so.

They ought, moreover, to be dedicated to so great a protector, since—far be envy from the saying—among the bishops of France there is none other than he who is more inclined in spirit to defend true piety and sound doctrine; greater in authority; more favoured by magnates and nobles; more prudent in his own counsel; or, what I think you considered first, a more honoured cultivator [Col. CLVIIIB] or more constant patron of your monastery, once an academy of the greatest men. Finally—and this commends no less the wisdom of your decision—one could scarcely find anyone more devoted to this same study of Hugh’s writings.

You therefore did a remarkable service to his studies in dedicating to his most auspicious name the most excellent works of your Hugh, divided into three almost equal volumes. In the first of those volumes Hugh expounds most of the sacred books with a twofold gloss, literal and allegorical; and he does so in such a way that, while he surpasses almost all others, he easily surpasses even himself—that is, all the powers of human intellect—in his interpretation of Ecclesiastes, Jeremiah’s Lamentations, and the Gospel of Saint John; in his ingenious resolution of questions on the Catholic Epistles; and finally in his explanation of the Celestial Hierarchies of the divine Dionysius.

The second volume contains very many works of his, altogether golden, which are especially useful for monastic formation and instruction. In the third, however, he discusses theological matters more profoundly and centrally, as speakers are accustomed to do in their perorations: namely, the incarnation of the Word [Col. CLVIIIC], Christ’s wills, the perpetual glorious virginity of Christ’s mother, and the sacraments of the human condition and restoration.

Since all this is so, most eminent Father, I could not conceal, even in this somewhat rough little letter, the joy that I conceived at your undertaking and deed—especially since they pleased me in very many respects. First, because you dedicated the aforementioned works to that hero, as I had most earnestly desired; then because I hope that no small advantage will accrue to our humble household through his protection and favour. For I do not think that what has pleased so great a Plato could be mocked or displeasing to any Momus or misanthrope. Then I greatly congratulate Hugh himself on being defended by so great a protector from the bites of envious persons. And finally, to say nothing of much else, I seem to have rendered some service to that most beautiful whole order of canons, since I do not grind down with a Theonian tooth your honourable zeal on behalf of your own; rather, with Pyladean praise, I proclaim it in this register [Col. CLVIIID], and disclose with what zeal and at what expense you caused these works of Hugh to be copied, reviewed, and printed.

If we too contributed anything toward this undertaking, we refer it all to you, so that you may more freely bestow it also upon that very man to whom we too owe everything. Farewell, Father most worthy of esteem; receive our efforts favourably. From our little printing-house, on the Ides of October 1526.

### Poem by Brother Robert Barthei to His Reverend Father, John Bordier, Abbot of Saint-Victor

You who are called everywhere a pious and wise Father,  
Shining with outstanding beauty of character,

Not without cause did the sacred waters of the font  
Give you the worthy name of John with magnificent praise.

For the grace gained by your exceptional gifts  
Is known to be of no slight weight.

[Col. CLIXA]

You utter no biting speech with a viper’s mouth,  
Nor harbour the bitter draughts of cruel gall.

Neither vain love, jealousy, guile, murmuring,  
Nor rage, impiety, or ambition possesses you.

Rather, in word, example, lineage, and life,  
You go before each man as a light of the Victorines.

Those who know you may behold your calm and gentle face,  
O beloved shepherd, once the storm has been removed.

It is now evident that you follow, chastely and wholly,  
The sound footsteps of our master Hugh.

His brilliant work, the consoling divinity of study,  
Is brought into the light by the skill of a learned man.

Trampling down the aberrant notions of impious thought,  
It rejects every harmful poison of heresy,

And scatters the devout seeds of ripened grain,  
Casting away darnel and evil seeds.

[Col. CLXA]

By it may the renowned, living assembly of your people be fed  
And sing a melody with uplifted voice.

### Brother Francis Grivus to His Reverend Father in Christ, John Bordier, Abbot of the Victorines

Bordier, greatest glory of the cloistered life:  
Under your leadership Hugh, once mourned, has happily revived.

Without doubt the whole world owes you poems,  
And every generation of descendants the praise of future ages.

But who, alas, could render fitting thanks  
For so great a gift, or poems worthy  
Of your services, since you seek the benefit of the people,  
Not your own advantage?

For the rewards of virtues cannot be contained  
In mortal songs, because they are known to Him alone  
Who will be your worthy reward after death.

[Col. CLIX]

## Prefaces to the Edition of 1648. The Life of Hugh the Victorine, in Which Is Inserted Osbert’s Letter on Hugh’s Illness and Death.

[Col. CLIXB] Hugh of Saint-Victor, born of distinguished Saxon lineage, made the end of the tenth century—in which he received the use of light—more illustrious. When he had completed his tender boyhood, he was entrusted, in the diocese of Halberstadt, to the monastery of Saint Pancras, to be instructed by its Canons Regular. That he made no slight progress in literary studies is shown both by the well-known truth of the matter itself and by Hugh himself, *Didascalicon*, book III, chapter 3. If anyone requires the words, they are these:

“I venture to affirm that I have never despised anything whatsoever that pertained to learning, but have often learned many things which might seem a joke or madness to others. I remember, while I was still a student, taking pains to know the names of all things set before the eyes or brought into use, judging freely that a man cannot pursue the nature of things when he still does not know their names. I often kept watch as a nocturnal watcher through the winter vigils.”

But when he reached his eighteenth year, he began to contemplate flight from the world. [Col. CLIXC] He communicated this to his uncle Hugh, archdeacon of the Church of Halberstadt, who immediately joined in this plan. Thus the two, alike in spirit, left their homeland. They set out for Marseilles, to the monastery of Saint Victor; and there, after pouring out prayers to God and receiving as a gift relics of the most glorious martyr, they flew to Paris, drawn by the fame of the newly founded Victorine house, which at that time was being spread far and wide throughout the world.

These sacred relics were one tooth and certain portions of the head and shoulder, which they offered to Gilduin, the first abbot of Saint Victor. Into his hands they made their vows and professed the Rule of Saint Augustine. It was about the year of the Lord 1115, and the seventeenth day of June, when these things were done, not without the inspiration of divine providence.

After some time, when his profession had been confirmed, Hugh was placed first over the philosophical schools and then over the theological schools of the monastery. The abundant fruits of these schools were soon attested by the approving praise of all who had heard this master. For from the instruction of so eminent a man there proceeded countless renowned philosophers and theologians, who poured out everywhere among the nations the learning they had drawn from him and advanced without stumbling even to the highest ranks of ecclesiastical dignity.

Why should I mention abbots, bishops, cardinals, and others whose names alone a page would not suffice to record? Each has his own deeds; each, his own life. Hugh lived his own life, not that of his disciples. Here his own ornaments are sought, not those of others. Therefore Master Hugh devoted all the remaining time of his life—twenty-five years—to this kind of scholastic exercise and likewise to other pursuits belonging to piety and to the pure observance of religious life. Accordingly, he wrote certain books that explain the sense of Scripture and the divine rites of the sacraments; others that set forth how the religious life is to be ordered piously and commendably; and finally others that embrace varied and manifold learning. All these undoubtedly caused Hugh to be called both a bright light of his own age [Col. CLXB] and a second Augustine.

Hence Saint Thomas, Bonaventure, Scotus, and other doctors of the schools frequently praise our Hugh as a supporter of their opinions and follow him as their patron. The matter is too well known to need proof from the examples occurring everywhere in their commentaries. Wholly devoted, therefore, to letters and monastic instruction, he held no office in the monastery, not even that of prior—far less was he abbot, contrary to what certain later writers, Trithemius, Sixtus of Siena, Garzonius, canon of the Lateran, and others, have reported from uncertain rumor.

He died on the third day before the Ides of February, in the forty-fourth year of his age, in 1140. That Gilduin, the first abbot, was still alive then and continued to live afterward is shown by letters addressed to him by Celestine [II] (A.D. 1143), Eugenius III (A.D. 1147), Anastasius IV (A.D. 1153), and Hadrian IV (A.D. 1154), preserved in the monastery archive.

Vincent of Beauvais [Note: [Col. CLIXC] *Speculum historiale*, book XXVII, chapter 18.], Durandus of Mende [Note: [Col. CLXC] In the *Rationale divinorum officiorum*, book IV, chapter 41.], and John of Paris [Col. CLXIA] [Note: [Col. CLXID] In his *Memorial of Histories*, under the year 1139.] report that Hugh, when he lay near death upon his bed, refused an unconsecrated host which was offered as viaticum. But what James of Vitry and Caesarius—contemporary witnesses—and a certain manuscript poem report about Maurice, bishop of Paris, they wrongly transfer to our Hugh.

To these is added an unpublished letter concerning Hugh’s illness and death, written by Brother Osbert, superintendent of the infirmary, to his familiar friend Brother John. It runs as follows:

“To his beloved brother in Christ, Brother John: Brother Osbert wishes continual well-being in the Lord.

You ask, dearest brother, with a devout desire, that I should write something to you concerning the passing of your beloved Master Hugh, so that you may know according to the truth how he was in that final illness. Receive, then, what you desire—holy, devout, and just in every respect. Yet perhaps you do not wish me to speak so briefly, but desire to hear more fully about his end. I cannot recount everything; nevertheless, receive these few things which I saw while present. For this, unless I am mistaken, was your request: that I should write nothing to you except what had been seen or heard by me.

[Col. CLXIB] I say nothing of the pure, full, and perfect confession which he made to the lord abbot and to me, quite diligently, with tears poured out beyond human measure and with great contrition of heart. Nor do I pursue the frequent thanksgiving which, in my hearing, he gave to our Lord Jesus Christ for his present illness, often uttering from the exultation of his heart that psalm: ‘Blessed be the Lord my God for ever.’ I do not dwell upon these things. I shall come to what he said or did near the end of his life; and these shall be the subject of the following account.

On the day before he passed from this life, I came to him in the morning and asked how he was. When he answered that he was well in both soul and body, he said to me: ‘Is anyone besides the two of us here?’ And I said: ‘No.’ Then he said: ‘Have you celebrated Mass today?’ When I replied that I had done so: ‘Come,’ he said, ‘and breathe upon my face in the form of the holy cross, that I may receive the Holy Spirit.’

[Col. CLXIC] When I had done as he commanded, he himself added those words of David: ‘I opened my mouth and drew in the spirit’ (Psalm 118 [119]). Faithfully understanding and believing that the apostles received the Holy Spirit from the breathing of the Lord Jesus, he opened his mouth and, as it were, drew spirit from spirit. And because he knew, according to the Lord’s saying, that all things are possible to one who believes, he believed that he could receive from a human being what did not come from a human being.

O man Catholic in every respect! Even when placed at the point of death, he faithfully believed that the Holy Spirit could be given to him by a priest because of the mystery and communion of the Lord’s body and blood, and he sought it with such devotion. Then, immediately made joyful and, I believe, strengthened by the Spirit of God, he burst out rejoicing into these words:

‘Now,’ he said, ‘I am secure; now I walk in truth and purity; now I am founded upon the firm rock and can no longer be moved. Now, even if the whole world with all its pleasures came before me, I would count it as nothing, nor would I do anything against God for the sake of all of it. Now especially I know God’s mercy toward me, so that of all that God has done for me throughout my whole life until this day, nothing can be as pleasing, as sweet, or as acceptable to me as this which God has deigned now to do with me. Blessed be the Lord my God for ever.’

Having said this, he humbly asked me to absolve him from all that he had done against God. I then left him to rest, after first granting the absolution as he requested, and so withdrew from his bed.

But in the following night, near cockcrow, he began to grow seriously ill, and more ill than usual. When I came to him, as soon as he began to speak he spoke to me about the salvation of his soul. Then, when he was being absolved by the brothers present, I suggested to him that he receive holy anointing. He received the suggestion with joy and commanded us not to delay in preparing what was necessary.

[Col. CLXIIA] When all had been completed, daylight had already dawned, and the brothers gathered around him and performed, according to custom, the visitation with psalms and prayers. When this was finished, I asked whether he wished to wait until the lord abbot arrived; for he was not then present, though word had been sent that he should come quickly. He replied: ‘Do,’ he said, ‘what you are going to do, since God has gathered you together.’

For many venerable religious were assembled around him—monks, Canons Regular, priests, and other clerics; nor was there any lack of laypeople. After the anointing had been celebrated, I asked whether he wished to receive the body of the Lord. It was not then prepared, because he had communicated three days previously. But he answered me with great rebuke: ‘My God! Do you ask whether I wish to receive my God? Run quickly to the church and quickly bring the body of my Lord.’

When I had done as he commanded, I came before his bed holding in my hands the holy bread of eternal life. ‘Adore,’ I said, ‘and recognize the body of our Lord.’ Raising himself as much as he could and lifting both hands toward those holy things, he said: ‘I adore before all of you my Lord, and I receive him as my salvation.’

[Col. CLXIIB] Then, after receiving the body of Jesus, he asked that the cross which was present there be given to him. When he had received it in his hands, he signed himself with that cross; and after kissing it very devoutly, he took the feet of the Crucified into his mouth. Holding the feet in his mouth for a long time, he sucked, with tears springing up, the blood which seemed to flow from the feet through the painter’s art, like an infant at its mother’s breast.

It is credible that, just as before us who stood by he had eaten the flesh of the Son of Man, so that wise man then wished somehow visibly to drink his blood as well. A little while after this, when I suggested that he should say that verse, ‘Into thy hands, O Lord, I commend my spirit’ (Psalm 30 [31]), he replied: ‘I think you suppose that I raise a question about that verse.’ And he said that he wished to hear its solution from me.

[Col. CLXIIC] ‘The Lord Jesus Christ,’ he said, ‘when he was about to leave this world, said: “Father, into thy hands I commend the spirit which thou gavest me and which I received from thee.” Having said this, he was silent; and when the hour of death rushed upon him and he was for a little while unable to speak, the Father himself received him.’

To him I said: ‘And you, who are about to leave this world, ought to say this, so that God may receive your spirit.’ Accordingly, after considering for a little while and drawing deep sighs, he finally burst out, while we all heard, into these words: ‘Into thy hand,’ he said, ‘and into thy strength I commend, O Lord, the spirit which thou gavest me and which I received from thee.’

Having said this, he fell silent; and when the hour of death rushed upon him and he was for a little while unable to speak, he returned again, and, recovering his breath, began, I know not what, to say to himself. When I asked what he was saying, he replied in an audible voice: ‘I have attained it.’ And I said: ‘What have you attained?’ But because of his exceeding distress he could not utter complete words; and when he was asked again, as far as we who stood about him could understand, he answered: ‘He will receive my spirit.’

[Col. CLXIID] Then, striking his breast with his own hand, he invoked the blessed Mother of God, saying: ‘Holy Mary, pray for me.’ Recovering his breath: ‘Saint Peter,’ he said, ‘pray for me.’ Shortly afterward he said to me: ‘Which saint shall I invoke further?’ When I named Saint Victor, he said: ‘Saint Victor, pray for me.’

He said these things and fell silent. The mouth of the righteous man, accustomed to bring forth wisdom, was closed; and the tongue of the wise man, which he had adorned best according to knowledge, clung to his palate. After this he survived for about one hour. Thus, while the brothers stood by and prayed, he rendered up his spirit into the hands of him to whom, as we believe, he had long before entrusted it, and in whose strength he had commended that same spirit.

The venerable and most learned doctor Hugh passed from this world [Col. CLXIIIA] in the confession of the supreme Trinity, on the third day before the Ides of February, Tuesday, at the third hour of that day: good, humble, gentle, and devout.”

Among the events that followed Hugh’s death, the following is certainly worthy of record, which John Aquila, cleric of Charles of Valois, affirmed in this public instrument:

“To all Christ’s faithful, John Aquila, humble servant of Christ, eternal salvation in the Lord.

The benefits of almighty God clearly bestowed upon his faithful and prudent servants ought not to be hidden or placed beneath the bushel of forgetfulness, but upon the candlestick of unceasing remembrance, so that they may shine before all who are established in God’s house and may furnish an example to posterity of how each person should endeavor to return to the Lord the talent entrusted to him multiplied.

Now among God’s other benefits divinely granted to me, John Aquila, priest though unworthy, almighty God, through his ineffable clemency, deigned to grant me one benefit—not through my merits, but by the sole graciousness of his mercy—through the merits and intercession of the renowned and holy memory of the reverend Master Hugh of Saint-Victor, formerly a canon and distinguished master of sacred theology in the monastery of Saint Victor at Paris.

[Col. CLXIIIB] Although he has not been entered by our most holy mother Church in the catalogue of saints, and therefore I do not dare presumptuously, through my own rashness, to call or name him a saint, yet, on account of his authoritative writings, praiseworthy deeds, holy works in which he flourished and bore saving fruit during his life, and his other merits, I devoutly believe that he is of great merit before God among the other blessed.

And lest, through silence or ingratitude concerning the benefit miraculously bestowed on me by God through the merits, as I devoutly believe, of the said venerable Master Hugh, I should incur God’s displeasure and his own—which may it never be!—I have considered it right, by the tenor of the present document, to publish for those now living and for posterity a certain miracle as it actually occurred.

In the year of the Lord 1325, in July, about the feast of blessed Mary Magdalene, a grave illness attacked my lord, Charles, Count of Valois, in whose service I was engaged. Since physicians despaired of his life or recovery from this illness, I judged it salutary to have recourse to the mercy of almighty God and the aid of the saints. Going about Paris among religious houses and collegiate churches, I humbly requested that Masses of the Holy Spirit and other prayers of intercession be celebrated for the same count.

[Col. CLXIIIC] While I was pursuing this purpose, it happened that I came in person to the monastery of Saint Victor at Paris. Entering its cloister, I called to mind the authoritative writings, praiseworthy deeds, and other holy and fruitful works of the aforesaid venerable master of holy memory. A canon of that house led me to his tomb, showing me a small and humble stone sepulchre at the entrance through which one goes from the said cloister to the church of that place.

There I devoutly vowed to God and the Blessed Virgin that, if through the merits and intercession of the aforesaid venerable master it should please God to prolong my aforesaid lord’s life, I would devoutly render my offering to God, blessed Mary, and the said master. With all the affection of which I was capable I humbly implored God’s grace and mercy, and that of the Blessed Virgin his Mother, and the merits and intercession of the said venerable master.

[Col. CLXIVA] As I devoutly believe, at the very hour, or almost the hour, when the vow was made, my aforesaid lord, through God’s grace, *craticavit* [reading and meaning uncertain] and recovered so completely from his illness that he lived for some time afterward. And I fulfilled the promise of my vow according to my means, recounting and disclosing to one of the brothers of that monastery what had then miraculously occurred in the person of my said lord, to the praise and glory of God and through the merits of the aforesaid venerable Master Hugh of Saint-Victor, of holy memory.

I further make this same fact known to all of us Christ’s faithful through this present writing, with my customary sign, which I have hitherto used as a public notary by apostolic authority, so that we may always endeavor together, with God’s help, to advance from virtue to virtue and from good to better. These things were done at Paris in the aforesaid year and month.

I, John Aquila, cleric of Saintes, public notary by apostolic authority, have affixed to this present writing with my own hand my customary sign in testimony of the foregoing.”

This miracle, by which God wished Hugh’s holiness to be most fully attested, caused his body afterward to be transferred from the cloister to a place behind the high altar, where it is still visited, deposited in an elevated tomb, with an epitaph composed by Abbot William of Saint-Lô. From that time this tomb began to be held in somewhat greater veneration. For on certain feasts, the deacon who serves at high Mass goes to incense the altar of Blessed Dionysius and the tombs of Reginald, bishop of Paris, and of our Hugh. [Col. CLXIVC]

Moreover, the famous name of so great a doctor perhaps caused the Canons Regular of Saint John Lateran to claim Hugh as their own. But this was attempted so unskilfully by Garzonius, canon of the Lateran, that the falsehood of the matter collapses of itself. For in Hugh’s works, which Garzonius arranged to have printed at Venice in 1588, he prefixed to every treatise and book the title: “Of Master Hugh of Saint-Victor, Canon Regular of the Lateran”—than which nothing is more false or more foreign to ancient tradition.

The Paris edition of 1526 is very different. In it, as also in the manuscript copies from which it issued, the name “Lateran” is neither read nor ought to be read. The necrologies of Saint Victor and many ancient writers confirm this: they call Hugh not a Lateran canon, but a Parisian canon of Saint-Victor.

[Col. CLXIII]

## Testimonies of Certain Ancient Writers Concerning Hugh Victorinus

[Col. CLXIIID]

**Necrology of Saint Victor at Paris, third day before the Ides of February**

The anniversary of the devoutly remembered Master Hugh, who from the earliest flower of his youth gave himself in this our house to the service of God, and received so excellently the gift of heavenly wisdom bestowed upon him from above that in the whole Latin Church no one could be found comparable to him in wisdom. This is wonderfully attested by the books which he composed here among us, radiant in eloquence, subtlety, and sublimity of thought.

[Col. CLXIVD] We also wish especially to commit this to memory: after seeking with much labor and obtaining with much difficulty the relics of blessed Victor, he brought them here to us from the city of Marseilles and enriched our Church with so desirable and incomparable a treasure. Therefore may the memory of this most illustrious master be observed every year.

**Robert of Torigni, in the appendix to Sigebert’s chronography, under the year 1140**

Hugh, canon of Saint Victor at Paris, distinguished for religious devotion and learning, and second to none in skill in the seven liberal arts, died. Among the many useful works he wrote, he also produced a very necessary book *On the Sacraments*, comprised in two volumes. In the second volume of this book he inserted a remarkable account concerning a certain pilgrim whom the devil, appearing in the form of Saint James, deceived into killing himself with his own hand. When the devil was dragging him away, Saint James came upon them, snatched him from the devil’s hand, showed him many things, brought him before God’s judgment, and obtained that he should be restored again to life.

[Col. CLXVA] At the request of King Louis, he also explained the *Hierarchy* of Saint Dionysius the Martyr, a work full of obscurities.

**Saint Bernard, Letter 77, to Master Hugh of Saint-Victor**

If I seem to you to have replied rather slowly, know that I also received late that to which I was to reply. For what you had sent did not reach me immediately, but was long held back at Pontigny. Once I received it, however, I made no delay in replying. Yet I did so more briefly than perhaps your purpose demanded, though not entirely beyond what my occupations allowed. Still, I took care that you should not be in any way unaware of what I thought concerning the questions asked, leaving it to your leisure and ability to establish these same judgments of mine more fully, should you see that this is necessary. Nor do I doubt that you have ready at hand sound arguments and fitting authorities by which you can easily do this.

**An anonymous monk of Jumièges, etc.**

At the time when, that is, the Cistercian and Carthusian orders were founded, Master William of Champeaux, formerly archdeacon of Paris, a most learned and devout man, assumed the habit of a Canon Regular with certain disciples outside the city of Paris, at a place where there was a certain chapel of Saint Victor the Martyr, and began to build a monastery for clerics. When he was made bishop of Châlons, the venerable Gilduin, his disciple, became the first abbot there.

[Col. CLXVC] Under his governance many noble clerics, educated in secular and sacred letters, came together to dwell in that place. Among them Master Hugh, called Lotharingian because of the borderland of Saxony, flourished most greatly in learning and in humble religious devotion. He issued many books, which need not be enumerated because they are commonly available.

**A manuscript abridged chronicle in the library of Saint Victor**

[Col. CLXVD] Master Hugh of Saint-Victor was second to none in the world in literary learning.

Does curiosity, or assiduity in study, urge you to beg for the tasteless herbs and bark of a most worthless man, when you sit at the tables of wealthy Augustine, gracious Gregory, rich Jerome, glorious Ambrose, Bede rich in coin of every currency, Hilary as deep as the great sea, Origen of most delightful speech, and countless others—of whose crumbs beneath the table I am not worthy even to gather? If new things please you, behold the writings of Master Hugh; behold those of Saint Bernard, in which neither roses nor lilies are lacking.

**James of Vitry, cardinal, book II of the *Western History*, chapter 24**

Among the Canons of Saint Victor there was a most famous and eminent minstrel of the Lord, an organ of the Holy Spirit, called Master Hugh of Saint-Victor. Joining pomegranates to bells, he encouraged many to uprightness by the example of his holy conduct and instructed them in knowledge by his honeyed teaching. Digging many wells of living waters in his books, in which he discoursed as subtly as sweetly on faith and morals, he opened to many the uncertain and hidden things of divine wisdom, leaving to posterity his immortal glory like a composition of fragrance and the work of a perfumer—sweetened like honey in everyone’s mouth, like music at a wine banquet, and like ships bearing fruit.

[Col. CLXVIA]

He also wrote a book which he called *The Sum of His Sentences*. He wrote two codices, each with many divisions and chapters, *On the Sacraments of the Old and New Law*. He wrote other books *On the Spiritual Building*, *On Knowledge*, *On Vanity*, and *The Ark of Noah*. He expounded Jeremiah’s Lamentations in three ways; he expounded the Canticle of the Blessed Virgin. He also wrote another book which he called the *Didascalicon*.

# The Works of Hugh of Saint-Victor, Canon Regular of Saint Victor at Paris. Part One — Exegetical Works

## I. On Sacred Scripture

[Col. 0009]

# Preliminary Notices on the Sacred Scriptures and Their Writers

## The Chapters Are These

**Chapter I.** Which writings ought uniquely to be called by the name of divinity.  
**Chapter II.** That divine Scripture is distinguished from other writings in its subject matter and manner of treatment.  
**Chapter III.** On the threefold meaning of sacred Scripture.  
**Chapter IV.** That not everything found in divine discourse, but only certain matters, is to be brought under this threefold interpretation.  
**Chapter V.** That literal and historical interpretation is necessary.  
**Chapter VI.** On the order, number, and authority of the books of sacred Scripture.  
**Chapter VII.** On the writers of the sacred books.  
**Chapter VIII.** On the restoration of the library of the Old Testament.  
**Chapter IX.** On the different translations of sacred Scripture.  
**Chapter X.** On the writers of the New Testament.  
**Chapter XI.** On the apocryphal Scriptures.  
**Chapter XII.** On the interpretation of “Bible” and the various names of books.  
**Chapter XIII.** On the fruit of divine reading.  
**Chapter XIV.** What benefit sacred Scripture receives from other learning; what it gives to other learning; and the six circumstances by which things signified are mystically discerned; first, the three which are thing, person, and number.  
**Chapter XV.** On numbers in sacred Scripture, signifying in nine ways.  
**Chapter XVI.** On the three other circumstances, namely places, times, and deeds, in sacred Scripture.  
**Chapter XVII.** On the subject matter of sacred Scripture.  
**Chapter XVIII.** On the difficulties of sacred Scripture, especially in its histories.

**Chapter I. — Which Scriptures, etc., as was set forth above.**

[Col. 0009A]

The reader of the divine Scriptures must first be instructed to know which writings are uniquely worthy to be honored with the name of divinity. For some have spoken through the spirit of this world and have written many things. We read the poems of poets, in which there is, together with pleasure, some usefulness also; as someone says:

> Poets wish either to profit or to delight.  
> —HORACE, *Art of Poetry*, 333.

Logic, mathematics, and physics teach a certain truth, but they do not attain that truth in which the soul’s salvation lies, without which whatever exists is futile. The philosophers of the Gentiles also wrote ethics, in which they depicted, as it were, certain limbs of the virtues, severed from the body of goodness; but the limbs of the virtues cannot be alive without the body of the love of God. All virtues make one body, whose head is love. Nor can the body’s limbs live unless they receive sensation from the head. Therefore those writings in which truth is not apprehended without the contagion of error, and by which the soul is not restored to the true knowledge or love of God, are by no means worthy to be reckoned under the name of divinity. Only that Scripture is rightly called divine which, breathed forth by the Spirit of God and set forth through those who spoke by the Spirit of God, makes a human being divine, refashioning him in the likeness of God by instructing him toward knowledge and exhorting him toward the love of Him. In it, whatever is taught is truth; whatever is commanded is goodness; whatever is promised is happiness. For God is truth without deception, goodness without malice, happiness without misery. If, therefore, you wish by sound judgment to distinguish divine Scripture from other writings which do not deserve this name, consider carefully the very subject-matter about which and in which its treatment is occupied, since knowledge of things contributes to the opening up of words. For you will understand more easily what is said if you know well what is being spoken of.

> [Note: Col. 0011D. See further Driedo, book I, chapter 1, *On Ecclesiastical Writings and Doctrines*; and *The Economy of the Bible*, book I, table 5.]

## CHAPTER II.—That divine Scripture is distinguished from other writings by its subject-matter and manner of treatment.

There are two works of God by which all created things are brought to completion. The first is the work of creation, by which things that did not exist were made; the second is the work of restoration, by which things that had perished were repaired. The work of creation is the creation of the world with all its elements. The work of restoration is the incarnation of the Word with all its sacraments: both those which preceded the incarnation from the beginning of the world, and those which follow after it until the end of the world. The first works, therefore, were made for service, that they might be subject to humankind standing in righteousness. The second, however, were made for salvation, that they might raise up humankind fallen through sin; and for this reason they are greater. Thus the former, as though some small and slight indication of divine power, were completed in a short time—namely, in only six days. The latter, however, as surpassing the former by comparison and possessing a greater effect of power, cannot be completed except in six ages.

Consider, then, in these matters the subject-matter of the divine Scriptures, so that you may be able to distinguish them from other writings both by that of which they treat and by the manner in which they treat it—that is, by subject-matter and method. For the subject-matter of all other writings consists in the works of creation; the subject-matter of the divine Scriptures consists in the works of restoration. This, then, is the first distinction, in what they treat. Again, if other writings teach any truth, it is not without the contagion of error; if they seem to commend any goodness, it is either mixed with malice, so that it is not pure, or it is without the knowledge and love of God, so that it is not perfect. Therefore, just as that which is thought divine in them casts the reader’s mind down toward earthly things through accompanying falsehood, so also that which seems earthly in sacred Scripture raises it, through the true knowledge of the Creator—which is commended in all these things—to think upon and love divine and heavenly things.

> [Note: Col. 0011D. Georg Eder, in his *Economies of the Bible*, book I, tables 12, 13, 14, and 15 [Col. 0012D], records several noteworthy distinctions between sacred Scripture and other writings.]

## CHAPTER III.—On the threefold understanding of sacred Scripture.

Sacred discourse is expounded according to a threefold understanding. The first exposition is historical, in which the primary meaning of the words is considered in relation to the things themselves of which the text treats. For sacred discourse possesses a characteristic differing from other writings: in it, first, through the words that are recited, certain things are treated; and those things in turn are set forth in place of words to signify other things.

History is called from the Greek word ἰςορέω, *historeō*, meaning “I see and narrate.” This is because among the ancients no one was permitted to write accounts of deeds unless he had seen them himself, lest falsehood be mingled with truth through the writer’s fault in saying more, less, or otherwise than was right. In this sense “history” is properly and strictly used; but it is commonly taken more broadly, so that “history” denotes the sense obtained in the first instance from the signification of words in relation to things.

The second exposition is allegorical. Allegory occurs when, through that which is set forth as signified by the letter, some other thing—done in the past, present, or future—is signified. It is called allegory, as it were, “other-speaking” (*alieniloquium*), because one thing is said and another is signified. It is subdivided into simple allegory and anagogy. Simple allegory occurs when one invisible event is signified through a visible event. Anagogy—that is, “an upward leading”—occurs when an invisible event is disclosed through a visible one.

Let one example of this threefold understanding be offered. There was a man in the land of Uz, named Job, who, formerly rich, came to such misery that, sitting upon a dung-heap, he scraped the discharge from his body with a potsherd. The historical sense is plain. Let us come to allegory, so that we may consider other things to be signified through things signified by words, and one event through another event. Job, therefore, whose name is interpreted “suffering,” signifies Christ, who, formerly equal to the Father in the riches of glory, stooped down to our misery and sat humbled upon the dung-heap of this world, sharing all our defects except sin.

Let us also inquire what deed to be done—that is, what deed worthy of being done—is signified through this event. Job can signify any righteous person, or a penitent soul, which gathers together in its memory a dung-heap from all the sins it has committed and does not cease to weep, sitting and meditating upon it not for an hour only but perseveringly. These deeds, literal in themselves, which represent such spiritual matters, are called sacraments.

> [Note: Col. 0012D. On the kinds of exposition of divine Scripture, see what F. Sixtus collects more fully and abundantly in his *Bible*, book III, part I, near the beginning; and Georg Eder, *Economies of the Bible*, book I, tables 65, 66, 67, 68, 69, 70, and 71.]

## CHAPTER IV.—Not everything found in divine discourse, but only certain things, must be forced into the aforesaid threefold interpretation.

[Col. 0012D]

Certainly, not everything found in divine discourse must be forced into this threefold interpretation, as though each item were to be believed to contain history, allegory, and tropology together. Even if these can suitably be assigned in many cases, it is nevertheless either difficult or impossible to maintain this everywhere. For just as in a lyre and similar musical instruments, not everything that is touched gives forth some musical sound, but only the strings, while the other parts of the whole body of the lyre are made so that there may be something to which the strings are fastened and toward which they are stretched by the craftsman who is to produce the sweetness of melody; so in divine discourses some things are set down which require only spiritual understanding; some serve the seriousness of moral conduct; some are spoken according to the simple historical sense; and some can suitably be expounded according to history, allegory, and tropology.

> [Note: Col. 0013D. Almost the same point is noted by Dr. Georg Eder in his *Economies of the Bible*, book I, table 72.]

## CHAPTER V.—That literal and historical interpretation is necessary.

> [Note: Col. 0013D. See the *Sacred Library*, book III, part I [Col. 0014D], title: “On the use and usefulness of historical and mystical exposition.”]

Since mystical understanding is gathered only from those things which the letter first sets forth, I wonder with what face certain people boast that they are teachers of allegories when they still do not know the primary signification of the letter itself. “We,” they say, “read Scripture, but we do not read the letter. We do not concern ourselves with the letter; rather, we teach allegory.” How then do you read Scripture and not read the letter? For if the letter is taken away, what is Scripture?

“We read the letter,” they say, “but not according to the letter. For we read allegory and expound the letter not according to the letter but according to allegory.” What, then, is it to expound the letter except to show what the letter signifies? “But,” they say, “the letter signifies one thing according to history and another according to allegory. Thus a lion according to history signifies a beast; according to allegory it signifies Christ. Therefore the word ‘lion’ signifies Christ.”

I ask you who maintain this: why does the lion signify Christ? Perhaps you answer as people commonly answer in such cases, by reference to a fitting likeness offered for the proposed signification: “Because a lion sleeps with its eyes open,” or something of that sort. Therefore the lion signifies Christ because it sleeps with its eyes open. You have thus said that the word “lion” signifies Christ because it sleeps with its eyes open. Either, then, withdraw the proposition you set forth, or change the reason you added. Either the proposition is false in which you said that this word, “lion,” signifies Christ, or the reason you added is unsuitable—namely, that the lion signifies Christ because it sleeps with its eyes open. For it is not the word that sleeps with its eyes open, but the animal itself which the word signifies.

Understand, therefore, that when the lion is said to signify Christ, it is not the name of the animal but the animal itself that signifies Him. For the animal is said to sleep with its eyes open and, by a certain likeness, thereby figures Him who slept in the sleep of death in the humanity He assumed, but kept His eyes open, vigilant in His divinity. Therefore do not boast of understanding the Scriptures while you remain ignorant of the letter. To be ignorant of the letter is to be ignorant both of what the letter signifies and of what is signified by the letter. For what is signified by the first signifies a third thing.

Since, therefore, those things which the letter signifies are signs of spiritual understanding, how can they be signs to you when they have not yet been signified to you? Do not, then, make a leap lest you fall headlong into a precipice. He proceeds most rightly who proceeds in order. First, therefore, strive by reading to acquire knowledge, for mystical signification, of those things which sacred discourse sets before you, so that after you have known them in their outward form, you may afterward gather by meditation what you may apply, through likeness, either to the edification of faith or to instruction in good morals.

“But not everything,” they say, “can be read according to the letter or suitably understood in that way. For when the prophet says that he saw a fiery river proceeding from beneath God’s throne, and testifies that certain winged and eyed creatures were flying and crying around it (Dan. VII; Ezek. I), as well as many similar things, there is no doubt that, of the things sacred discourse narrates, some are suitably received according to the letter and others are understood as spoken only figuratively.”

They speak thus as though we supposed that everything said through the letter must be received in precisely that way and that nothing else is to be understood from what is said. Yet this other thing is not said by the letter, but is signified through what the letter says. Even in what is received as figurative speech, the letter is not denied to have its own signification. For when we assert that what is said is not to be understood just as it is said, we affirm that this very thing has in some manner been said. Thus something is said and signified by the letter even when what is said is not understood as it is said, but rather another thing is understood which is signified through that which is said.

Thus, then, something is altogether said and signified by the letter; and first that which is signified by the letter must be understood, so that afterward what is signified through it may be understood. We wish the reader to be warned in this manner, lest perhaps he despise these first rudiments of instruction. Let him not think contemptible the knowledge of those things which sacred Scripture sets before us through the primary signification of the letter, because these are the very images by which the Holy Spirit has portrayed mystical meanings for bodily senses, capable of grasping invisible things only through visible things; and through proposed likenesses He has fashioned a clear demonstration of what must be understood spiritually.

If, as these people say, one were to leap immediately from the letter to what must be understood spiritually, then the Holy Spirit would in vain have introduced into sacred discourse figures and likenesses of things by which the mind might be instructed toward spiritual realities. For, as the Apostle testifies, what is carnal comes first, and afterward what is spiritual (1 Cor. XV). Even the Wisdom of God itself, unless it had first been known bodily, could never have illuminated the sight of the weak-sighted mind for spiritual contemplation of it.

Do not, therefore, despise the lowliness in the word of God, because through lowliness you are illumined toward divinity. Perhaps all that the word of God possesses outwardly appears to you like mud, and therefore you trample it underfoot because it is mud, and despise what the letter narrates as having been done bodily and visibly. But listen: by this mud which is trampled beneath your feet, the eye of the blind is illumined for seeing (John IX). Read Scripture, then, and first learn carefully what it narrates bodily. For if you diligently impress upon your mind the form of these things according to the sequence of the narrative presented, afterward, by meditation, you will draw forth the sweetness of spiritual understanding as though from a honeycomb.

## CHAPTER VI.—On the order, number, and authority of the books of sacred Scripture.

All divine Scripture is contained in two Testaments:

> [Note: Col. 0015D. On these matters you have fuller treatment in F. Sixtus, *Library*, book XI, part I, almost throughout; in Georg Eder, *Economies of the Bible*, book I, tables 17 through 47; in Dr. Michael de Medina, in his *Commentaries*; and likewise in Peter Aureolus, in his *Compendium* [Col. 0016D].]

the Old and the New. Each Testament is distinguished into three orders. The Old Testament contains the Law, the Prophets, and the Hagiographa; the New contains the Gospel, the Apostles, and the Fathers.

The first order of the Old Testament—that is, the Law, which the Hebrews call *Thorath*—has the *Pentateuchon*, that is, the five books of Moses. In this order the first is *Beresith*, which is Genesis; the second, *Hellesmoth*, which is Exodus; the third, *Vagethra*, which is Leviticus; the fourth, *Vagedaber*, which is Numbers; the fifth, *Elleaddaberim*, which is Deuteronomy.

The second order is that of the Prophets, and it contains eight volumes. The first is *Bennum*, that is, “son of Nun,” also called Joshua, Jesus, and Jesus Nave. The second is *Sothim*, the Book of Judges. The third is Samuel, which is First and Second Kings. The fourth is *Malachim*, which is Third and Fourth Kings. The fifth is Isaiah; the sixth, Jeremiah; the seventh, Ezekiel; the eighth, *Thereasra*, which is the Twelve Prophets.

Then the third order has nine books. The first is Job; the second, David; the third, *Masloth*, which in Greek means *Parables* and in Latin *Proverbs*, namely those of Solomon; the fourth, *Coeleth*, which is Ecclesiastes; the fifth, *Sirasirim*, that is, the Song of Songs; the sixth, Daniel; the seventh, *Dabreiamin*, which is Paralipomenon; the eighth, Ezra; the ninth, Esther. Thus they amount altogether to twenty-two.

There are besides certain other books—such as the Wisdom of Solomon, the Book of Jesus son of Sirach, Judith, Tobit, and the Books of Maccabees—which are indeed read but are not written in the canon. To these twenty-two books of the Old Testament are joined eight books of the New Testament. In the first order of the New Testament are the four Gospels: those of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John.
