In the second, likewise, there are four: namely, the Acts of the Apostles; the fourteen Epistles of Paul woven together into one volume; the Catholic Epistles; and the Apocalypse. In the third order, decretals, which we call canonical—that is, regular—hold the first place. Then come the writings of the holy Fathers: Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, Gregory, Isidore, Origen, Bede, and other doctors, which are innumerable.

Yet these writings of the Fathers are not counted in the text of divine Scriptures, just as in the Old Testament, as we have said, there are certain books not written in the canon but nevertheless read, such as the Wisdom of Solomon and the rest. The text of divine Scriptures, therefore, as a whole body, is principally contained in thirty books: twenty-two in the Old Testament and eight in the New, as was shown above. The other writings are attached, as it were, and flow from these preceding books.

In these orders, especially those of the two Testaments, a correspondence is evident: for just as the Prophets followed the Law and the Hagiographa followed the Prophets, so the Apostles followed the Gospel and the Doctors followed the Apostles in sequence. And by a wonderful ordinance of divine providence it has been arranged that, although complete and perfect truth is present in each Scripture, none is superfluous.

> [Note: Col. 0015D. On these matters you have fuller treatment in F. Sixtus, *Library*, book XI, part I, almost throughout; in Georg Eder, *Economies of the Bible*, book I, tables 17 through 47; in Dr. Michael de Medina, in his *Commentaries*; and likewise in Peter Aureolus, in his *Compendium* [Col. 0016D].]

## CHAPTER VII.—On the authors of the sacred books.

> [Note: Col. 0016D. On this subject in particular see F. Sixtus, in his *Library*, book XI, part I, who seems to discuss the authors of the sacred books with great learning.]

Moses wrote the five books of the Law. Joshua, after whom the Book of Joshua is named, is believed to have been its author. The Book of Judges is believed to have been published by Samuel. Samuel himself wrote the first part of the Book of Samuel; David wrote the remainder to the end. Jeremiah first collected *Malachim* into one volume, for previously it had been scattered among the histories of individual kings. Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel each composed the books inscribed with their names.

The book of the Twelve Prophets is likewise designated by the names of its authors: Hosea, Joel, Amos, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. They are called Minor Prophets because their discourses are brief, and therefore are contained in one volume. Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, however, are the four Major Prophets, each distinguished in its own volume.

Some believe the Book of Job to have been written by Moses, others by one of the prophets, and still others by Job himself. David produced the Book of Psalms. Ezra afterward arranged the Psalms as they now stand and added the titles. Solomon composed the Parables, Ecclesiastes, and the Song of Songs. Daniel was the author of his own book. The Book of Ezra bears its author’s name as its title; in its text are contained together the discourses of Ezra himself and Nehemiah. Ezra is believed to have written the Book of Esther.

The Book of Wisdom is nowhere found among the Hebrews; hence even its title has more the flavor of Greek eloquence. Some Jews maintain that it is by Philo. The son of Sirach, a Jerusalemite and grandson of Jesus the high priest, whom Zechariah mentions, most certainly composed the Book of Ecclesiasticus. This book is found among the Hebrews, but is reckoned among the apocrypha. As for Judith, Tobit, and the Books of Maccabees—of which, as Jerome testifies, the second is shown to be more Greek—it is entirely unknown by what authors they were written.

## CHAPTER VIII.—On the restoration of the library of the Old Testament.

Ezra the scribe, after the Law had been burned by the Chaldeans, restored the library of the Old Testament when the Jews entered Jerusalem, inspired by the divine Spirit.

> [Note: Col. 0017D. The *Sacred Library*, book XI, part I, title “The Two Books of Ezra,” mentions this.]

He corrected all the volumes of the Law and the Prophets which had been corrupted by the Gentiles, and arranged the whole Old Testament into twenty-two books, so that there might be as many books in the Law as there were letters.

## CHAPTER IX.—On the different translations of sacred Scripture.

[Col. 0017B]

It is established that the Scripture of the Old Testament was first published in the Hebrew language.

> [Note: Col. 0017D. F. Sixtus gathers much concerning this matter in part II of his *Library*, book VIII, where he discusses translations of sacred Scripture.]

Later Ptolemy, surnamed Philadelphus, who held the kingdom of Egypt second after Alexander the Great, had the library of the Old Testament translated from Hebrew into Greek by seventy interpreters whom he had received from Eleazar the high priest. Some say that, so that he might not be deceived by falsity in their translation, he separated them, placing each one in a separate cell. They, however, translated everything through the Holy Spirit in such a way that nothing was found in the manuscript of one which was not likewise found in that of another. For this reason their translation is one. But Jerome says that this account should not be believed.

> [Note: Jerome, *Prologue to the Bible*.]

After the Lord’s ascension, when the apostles preached the Gospel, this same translation was found among the Gentiles, and according to it the churches of Christ first began to read sacred Scriptures. Later, because certain things were found lacking in that translation which the authority both of Christ himself and of the preaching apostles had declared to be contained in the Hebrew truth, others also attempted to translate sacred Scripture from Hebrew into Greek. Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion thus made the second, third, and fourth translations. The first of these, Aquila, was a Jew; Symmachus and Theodotion were Ebionite heretics. Nevertheless, it became the practice that, after the Seventy Interpreters, the Greek churches received and read their copies.

After these came the fifth translation, called the Common Version, which was found at some time in Jericho; but who its author was remains unknown to this day. Origen made the sixth and seventh, and Eusebius and Pamphilus published copies of them. Jerome came eighth, translating no longer from Hebrew into Greek as the earlier translators had done, but from Hebrew into Latin. Because his translation was found to accord more closely with the Hebrew truth, the Church of Christ throughout the Latin world decreed that this translation alone should be read and held authoritative in preference to all other translations, which faulty translation had corrupted—whether the first, made from Hebrew into Greek, or the second, from Greek into Latin.

But when corrupt custom—often preferring what is customary to what is true—gained strength, and different persons followed different translations, all things eventually became so confused that now one scarcely knows to which translation each reading should be attributed.

## CHAPTER X.—On the writers of the New Testament.

Several persons wrote Gospels, but some, lacking the Holy Spirit, attempted rather to arrange a narrative than to weave together historical truth. Therefore the holy Fathers, instructed by the Holy Spirit, received only four Gospels as authoritative: those of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, in likeness of the four rivers of Paradise, the four poles of the Ark, and the four living creatures in Ezekiel (Ezek. I).

Matthew first wrote his Gospel in Hebrew. Mark, second, wrote in Greek. Luke, third, the most learned in Greek speech among all the Evangelists, wrote his Gospel for Archbishop Theophilus, to whom he also wrote the Acts of the Apostles. John, fourth and last, wrote his Gospel. Paul wrote fourteen Epistles. There are seven Catholic Epistles: one of James, two of Peter, three of John, and one of Jude. John the Apostle wrote the Apocalypse on the island of Patmos.

> [Note: Col. 0017D. F. Sixtus discusses this very extensively in his *Library*, book XI, part I, title “On the Scriptures and Writers of the New Testament” [Col. 0018D].]

## CHAPTER XI.—On apocryphal writings.

These are the writers of the sacred books, who, speaking through the Holy Spirit, wrote precepts and a rule of life for our instruction. Besides these, other volumes are called apocryphal. They are called apocryphal—that is, hidden and secret—because they are doubtful. Their origin is hidden, and it is not apparent to the holy Fathers by whom they were published. Although some truth may be found in them, nevertheless, because of their many falsehoods, they have no canonical authority; for they are rightly judged not to be the works of those to whom they are ascribed. Many writings under the names of prophets, and more recent writings under the names of apostles, are put forth by heretics. All of these have, upon examination, been removed from divine authority under the name of apocrypha.

> [Note: Col. 0018D. On apocryphal writings see what the same F. Sixtus collects in detail in his *Library*, book XI, part I, title “On Apocryphal Scriptures”; and Dr. Georg Eder, *Economies of the Bible*, book I, table 44.]

## CHAPTER XII.—On the meaning of “library” and the various names of books.

> [Note: Col. 0018D. On these matters see Isidore of Spain, *Etymologies*, book VI.]

“Library” (*bibliotheca*) takes its name from Greek because books are stored there. For *biblion* means “of books,” and *theca*, “a repository.” A codex is a collection of many books; a book (*liber*) is one volume. *Codex* is so called metaphorically from the trunks of trees or vines, as though it were a trunk (*caudex*) containing in itself a multitude of books like branches. A volume (*volumen*) is so called from rolling. A *liber* is the inner bark of a tree, on which the ancients used to write before the use of parchment; whence copyists were called *librarii*, and from this the written volume was called a *liber*. A treatise is a manifold exposition of one subject.

Sacred Scripture is called a testament by analogy with human custom. In ancient times those who lacked children adopted sons; and when they appointed them heirs, they called witnesses and wrote a deed. Yet it was not so binding that it could not be changed before the testator’s death. In like manner, God, having one only Son by nature, wished to adopt many by grace. At first He chose Abraham alone, commanded him to leave his kindred, and promised him the land of Palestine; yet Abraham himself is not read to have possessed anything of it. Thereafter, when the children of Israel had been led out of Egypt, He promised the same land of Palestine again; and, lest they should doubt, He made a testament as assurance of the promised inheritance—namely, the Law given through Moses.

But because God could not die, and a testament had to be confirmed by the death of the testator, a mystical lamb was slain in His place; with its blood the book and the whole people were sprinkled, in confirmation of the promised inheritance. In the same way, the Lord Jesus Christ, calling not one person only but all nations to an eternal inheritance, made a testament, namely the Gospel. For its confirmation, that ancient lamb is not slain; rather, He himself—because He was human and could die—underwent death. And as God had summoned witnesses for giving the Old Testament, namely Aaron, his sister Miriam, and Hur, so Christ, who promised greater things, summoned more witnesses: the Apostles and the martyrs.

The first is called the Old Testament either because it was given earlier or because it was instituted concerning things that grow old. The second is called the New Testament because it speaks of things immutable and ever new.

A prophet is so called in three ways: by office, by grace, and by mission. By office, as when someone was chosen who, at the approach of war, would consult the Lord concerning doubtful matters, whether through an assumed ephod or in some other manner. By grace, as one to whom the Lord through inward inspiration gave knowledge of matters which he could possess neither by nature nor by instruction, but by grace alone, as David, Daniel, and Job. By mission, as one whom the Lord sent to preach what He had inspired in him, such as Jonah.

Yet just as in these days no one is called a bishop unless he possesses the dignity and authority of the office, even though some have the merit and virtue of that title more abundantly than those who are bishops, so neither were persons called prophets unless they were prophets by office or by mission. Therefore David, Job, and Daniel, although they contain prophecies in their books, are nevertheless placed among the Hagiographa; whereas, conversely, Joshua, the Book of Judges, and the Books of Samuel and Kings, which weave—or seem to weave—history alone, are counted among the Prophets.

It is also asked why only nine are called Hagiographa—that is, holy writers—when this name is suitable to all authors of sacred Scripture. The answer is that whatever has no special characteristic by which it may be distinguished from the rest receives the common name as though it were a proper name, not by prerogative, but rather as though from a certain lowliness in comparison with the others. Thus, among the nine orders of angels, the lowest simply receives the common name; when one asks who it is, the answer is, “It is an angel,” although principalities and powers are angels as well.

An apocryphal book—that is, a doubtful and hidden book—is so called in two ways: either because its author is uncertain, or because it has not been received and confirmed by the common agreement of the faithful synagogue or Church, even though nothing unsound is found in it. Thus the Book of Job is apocryphal because its author is uncertain; nevertheless, it has been confirmed in the canon by the authority of the faithful synagogue. Likewise Ecclesiasticus, the Book of the Wisdom of Solomon, the two Books of Maccabees, Tobit, Judith, and the Book of Jesus son of Sirach are apocryphal; yet they are read and belong to the Old Testament, but are not confirmed in the canon.

## CHAPTER XIII.—On the fruit of divine reading.

Whoever approaches divine reading should first recognize what its fruit is. Nothing should be sought without a reason; nor does desire draw one toward what promises no benefit. The fruit of divine reading is twofold: it either instructs the mind by knowledge or adorns it with morals. It teaches both what is delightful to know and what is beneficial to imitate. Of these, the former—knowledge—has more to do with history and allegory; the latter—instruction in morals—has more to do with tropology. All divine Scripture is directed toward this end.

> [Note: Col. 0019. For a fuller explanation of the fruit of divine reading, see Georg Eder, *Economies of the Library*, table 84.]

The seven liberal arts serve this knowledge. The *trivium* concerns the signification of words; the *quadrivium* concerns the signification of things. Grammar teaches one to speak correctly and pronounce words properly. Dialectic is useful for distinguishing their meanings and for seeking truth through disputation. Rhetoric concerns both. Physics teaches the inner natures of things; mathematics, their outward figures and numbers.

## CHAPTER XIV.—What fruit sacred Scripture receives from other disciplines, and what it contributes to them; and on the seven circumstances by which signified things are distinguished.

A careful investigator of sacred discourse must by no means neglect the significations of things. For just as knowledge of primary things is acquired through words, so through the signification of those same things there is apprehended and made manifest an understanding of realities perceived by spiritual recognition. In other writings the philosopher knows only the signification of words; but in the sacred page the signification of things is far more excellent than that of words: for human convention instituted the former, while nature dictated the latter. [Col. 0021A] The one is the voice of human beings; the other, God’s voice to human beings. The signification of words rests on human agreement; the signification of things is natural and derives from the operation of the Creator, who wills certain things to be signified by others.

Moreover, the signification of things is far more manifold than that of words. For few words have more than two or three meanings; but any thing can be as manifold in signifying other things as it has visible or invisible properties in common with other things. These primary things, signified by words and themselves signifying secondary things, are considered as distinguished by six circumstances: namely, thing, person, number, place, time, and action. For in these the signification of primary things with respect to secondary things is considered.

[Col. 0021B]

By “thing” [*res*], however, in this place we understand any material or inanimate substance, whether heavenly or earthly: such as stones, wood, plants, and other things of this kind, which exist in the elements or from the elements. Every thing proposed for signification in sacred Scripture signifies either according to its external form or according to its internal nature. Yet here we use “thing” broadly, as containing the six aforesaid circumstances, under which “thing” also falls—that is, the material object proposed in the first circumstance. Therefore every thing signifies either according to its internal nature or according to its external form.

Under external form are included the shapes and colours of things, [Col. 0021C] which we perceive by sight. To internal nature belong the other properties of things, which we apprehend through the remaining senses: sweetness in taste, perceived by the palate; fragrance in odour, perceived by smell; melody in sound, which we perceive by hearing; smoothness or roughness in a body; and the like, which we perceive by touch. That first circumstance, namely “thing,” taken strictly in this place, signifies in two ways. For example, snow, by its internal nature—that is, its coldness—denotes the extinction of the heat of lusts; and by its external form—that is, its whiteness—it denotes purity of works.

A person is an individual essence of rational substance. Persons are those mentioned in sacred Scripture in whom the signification of mystical realities is prepared according to events, works, [Col. 0021D] or any other mode. Thus a person in sacred discourse signifies: Jacob, who received his father’s inheritance, designates Christ or the Gentile people; Isaac, who blessed his son, figures God the Father. Number likewise signifies: for example, the number six signifies perfection. Hence blessed Augustine says: “It is not because God created all his works in six days that the number six is perfect; rather, because it is perfect, God chose that number beforehand for his work.” But because number is known to have manifold signification, it must be treated somewhat more fully.

## CHAPTER XV.—On the mystical numbers of sacred Scripture

[Note: [Col. 0021] On the mystical numbers of sacred Scripture see Rabanus, Jodocus Clichtoveus, and, among more recent writers, Petrus Bongus of Bergamo.]

[Col. 0022A]

They signify in these nine ways:

|  |  |
|---|---:|
| According to the order of position | 1 |
| According to the quality of composition | 2 |
| According to the mode of extension | 3 |
| According to the form of arrangement | 4 |
| According to calculation | 5 |
| According to multiplication | 6 |
| According to the aggregation of parts | 7 |
| According to multitude | 8 |
| According to intensification | 9 |

Numbers, therefore, signify in divine discourse in nine ways: according to the order of position, according to the quality of composition, according to the mode of extension, according to the form of arrangement, according to calculation, according to multiplication, according to [Col. 0022B] the aggregation of parts, according to multitude, and according to intensification.

According to the order of position: unity, because it is first among numbers, signifies the beginning of all things. Two, because it is second and is the first to depart from unity, signifies sin, by which there has been a deviation from the first good. Numbers signify according to the quality of composition: thus two, because it admits division and can be divided into two, signifies corruptible and transitory things. But three, because, with unity intervening as the middle term, it does not admit division into two equal parts, designates things indissoluble and incorruptible.

Numbers signify according to the mode of extension: [Col. 0022C] seven, as exceeding six, signifies rest after work; eight, as exceeding seven, eternity after mutability; nine, as falling short of ten, deficiency within perfection; eleven, as exceeding ten, transgression beyond measure.

According to the form of arrangement, ten, extending lengthwise, signifies the uprightness of faith. One hundred, because it expands in breadth, signifies the breadth of charity. One thousand, because it rises in height, designates the height of hope: uprightness toward oneself, breadth toward one’s neighbour, height toward God. Therefore, among these three members, ten is nearest in positional order to the first and principal unity; one thousand is nearest in form of arrangement. The former is nearer in place; the latter more similar in perfection.

[Col. 0022D] According to numerical calculation, ten signifies perfection because the extension of counting ends with it.

Numbers signify according to multiplication: twelve is a sign of universality because it is completed by the reciprocal multiplication of three and four; for four is the form of bodily things, and three of spiritual things.

Numbers signify according to the aggregation of parts: six is a form of perfection because its parts—three, two, and one—when added together complete the whole; they neither exceed it [Col. 0023A] nor fall short of it, as is fitting for perfection, in which there ought to be neither more nor less than is right.

Numbers signify according to the multitude of their parts: two, because of its two units, signifies love of God and neighbour; three, because of its three, the Trinity; four, because of the four seasons, temporal things, since the year and the world are divided into four parts; five, the five senses; seven, the present age, which revolves through seven days.

Numbers signify according to intensification when the matter requires something to be made more weighty, and when what has been said before must be answered with a certain emphasis. Such is the passage in Leviticus: “I will add sevenfold chastisements for your sins” (Lev. XXVI), where nothing other than the multiplicity of punishment is signified, expressed [Col. 0023B] by the number seven. From a few examples the wise reader should learn to weigh many.

## CHAPTER XVI.—On the mystical places, times, and actions of sacred Scripture

We have treated these matters concerning numbers somewhat more extensively because of their manifold signification. Let us now turn our discourse to the fourth circumstance, namely place. Places signify; hence the Lord willed particular acts to be performed in fixed and determinate places for the sake of signification. For example, the children of Israel, descending into Egypt under the compulsion of famine, were oppressed by grievous slavery; but, led out from there by the Lord, they journeyed through the desert for forty years and came into the land of promise, which lies between [Col. 0023C] Babylon and Egypt. Both nations—that is, the Egyptians and Assyrians—took them captive, but the Egyptians first. All these things are fitting for signification.

Egypt, a land abounding in pleasure and delights, signifies the world—not this created structure, but the pleasures of the world and secular desires. The desert signifies the religious life, through which, as though returning to our homeland, we fast from the vices and desires of this age. Babylon lies to the north, where there are perpetual cold and darkness, since that region is never touched by the sun. Therefore, by the Assyrians—that is, the Babylonians—demons are suitably designated, since they chose the north as their dwelling, benumbed by the cold of unbelief and deprived of the light of truth. The Egyptians oppress Israel first; [Col. 0023D] then the Assyrians. For the devil can do nothing in us unless we are first drawn away by our own desires. Hence: “Do not deliver me, Lord, to the sinner according to my desire,” that is, to the devil (Ps. CXXXIX).

Times signify. For example, Jesus was in Solomon’s porch, and it was winter. Winter is mentioned so that, through the character of the season, the character of minds might be designated: namely, the torpor and unbelief of the Jews.

An action signifies, as is clear in the Gospel. Jesus came to Bethany and raised Lazarus; then he came by the Mount of Olives into the valley of Jehoshaphat and sent his disciples into the city for the she-ass, and so forth. Bethany means “house of obedience.” Christ comes only to one who is obedient [Col. 0024A] in order to raise Lazarus—that is, the soul formerly dead in sins. Since, therefore, there are six circumstances said to signify, whichever of them signifies either signifies a deed by a deed, and this is allegory; or signifies a deed to be done, and this is morality. In these two we are instructed toward knowledge of truth—that is, the soundness of faith—and toward love of goodness—that is, the perfection of good works. For these two reasons sacred Scripture ought to be read: namely, that we may believe sincerely and act rightly.

## CHAPTER XVII.—On the subject matter of sacred Scripture

The subject matter of divine Scripture is the incarnate Word together with all his mysteries, both those preceding from the beginning of the world and those to come until the end of the age. [Col. 0024B] It must be understood that this entire course and extension of time is to be divided into two states, old and new; into three times, of natural law, written law, and grace; and into six ages.

The first age is from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to David; the fourth, from David to the Babylonian deportation; the fifth, from the Babylonian deportation to Christ’s coming. Again, the five preceding ages—that is, from Adam to Christ—are distinguished into four successions. The first, that of the patriarchs, was from Adam to Moses. The second, from Moses to David, is that of the judges. The third, that of the kings, was from David to the Babylonian deportation. The fourth was from the Babylonian deportation to Christ; and this was the succession of priests.

[Col. 0024C] They are called states because they concern the condition of humanity. The state is called old because humanity remained in guilt and punishment until Christ’s resurrection. It is called new because of the renewal of human life effected through Christ’s grace until the end of the age. Again, the time of natural law is so called because man was left to his own natural judgment without a common commandment. The time of written law is so called because at that time the written law gave the people of God commands for living. The time of grace is so called because Christ freely granted the power to fulfil what the law commanded.

They are called six ages after the likeness of human ages. For the world has been an infant, a child, and so forth. It should be noted that these ages are not distinguished according to equal spans of time, [Col. 0024D] but according to common renewals of events: such as the Flood, the choosing of Abraham, the establishment of kings, the deportation to Babylon, and Christ’s coming.

It is called the succession of patriarchs because in that time fathers alone ruled over their sons. This lasted until Moses, who, being the first to hold authority among God’s people, was appointed judge not merely over his own sons but over the whole people of Israel, although there had already been many kings among the Gentiles. Or the succession is called that of patriarchs because in that time those primordial fathers succeeded one another, from whom the human race was dispersed, families derived, and countries named: thus the Edomites from Edom, the Levites from Levi, and the Jews from Judah.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—On the difficulties of sacred Scripture

[Note: [Col. 0025] The teaching of Melchior Cano, in book XI of his *Loci Theologici*, contributes much to this entire chapter.]

[Col. 0025A]

Many things occur in sacred Scripture that create difficulties of understanding for those ignorant of the sequence of events. For example, what is read in the book of Judith: that Arphaxad, king of the Jews, had subjected many nations to his rule and fought against Nebuchadnezzar, king of the Assyrians; and that, having prevailed in war by right, he gave that king of the Assyrians hope and confidence of subduing all kingdoms to his dominion. Thereupon Nebuchadnezzar sent Holofernes, commander of his army, to subdue the nations. After conquering the rest, Holofernes besieged the Jews when they attempted rebellion at Bethulia; and, Achior, leader of the sons of Ammon, relating the matter, he learned that this was the people who, recently returned from captivity, possessed the same highlands.

If, therefore, we ask [Col. 0025B] at what time these events occurred, or who this Nebuchadnezzar was who reigned at Nineveh—when Nebuchadnezzar is reported to have reigned not at Nineveh but at Babylon, and is read to have been king not of the Assyrians but of the Chaldeans, and when there can be no doubt that he was already dead at the people’s return from Babylonian captivity—no small uncertainty arises for those who carefully consider these matters.

Accordingly, they say that this Nebuchadnezzar should be understood as Cambyses, son of Cyrus. The Hebrews called him a second Nebuchadnezzar because, as was believed, he imitated the deeds of that Nebuchadnezzar and exercised great cruelty against the children of Israel. The remaining details might perhaps have fitted, were it not that the book of Judith says that the word came in the house of Nebuchadnezzar in the twelfth year [Col. 0025C] of his reign, whereas Cambyses, son of Cyrus, is reported to have reigned for only eight years. Yet we discover that many scribal errors occur in the numbers of books. Nevertheless, the diligent reader ought not to be disturbed in matters of this kind, because it is something to have approached the truth even where one does not succeed in grasping it wholly.

Certain things are also said in the books of Maccabees and in Daniel that you cannot easily understand unless you first know those who succeeded Alexander the Great in the kingdoms of Syria and Egypt. In Daniel, indeed, you frequently hear the king of the north mentioned; there, by the south one must understand literally nothing other than the kingdom of Egypt, and by the north nothing other than the kingdom of the kings of Syria. Their kings are recorded as having relations with one another at different times, now in peace and now in war. Unless you first know their deeds, you will not easily discern these changes.

Likewise, what we read in the book of Maccabees—that Antiochus and Demetrius and their successors fought one another in opposition for the kingdom of Syria, each party claiming the kingdom as though by paternal right—you will not be able to understand why it happened unless you learn how Seleucus, son of Antiochus the Great and king of Syria, when dying, left his brother Antiochus Epiphanes as successor. When he died, Demetrius, son of Seleucus, left the city of Rome and came into Syria, [Col. 0026A] namely into his father’s kingdom. When his arrival became known, the army that had belonged to Antiochus Epiphanes killed that Antiochus’s son, Antiochus Eupator. Thus Demetrius obtained the kingdom.

But Alexander, son of Antiochus Eupator, when he had grown up, gathered an army and, after overthrowing Demetrius, recovered the kingdom. Afterwards Demetrius, son of Demetrius, expelled Alexander and recovered power for himself. Then a certain Tryphon killed Alexander’s son, whom he had undertaken to rear. But when he was eventually overthrown, the kingdom remained in the family of Seleucus. We have set out these matters briefly for the clarity of reading, so that what has been written may either not be read or be understood.

These were the times notable for the Maccabees. The first of them, Judas, inflamed with zeal for the divine law, vigorously repelled the attacks of the Greeks. When he died, his brother Jonathan succeeded him. At last John Hyrcanus, son of Simon, succeeded his dead brother, alike in blood and courage; after John came his son Aristobulus, and after Aristobulus his son Alexander. After him his wife Alexandra held the rule of the family, but bestowed the pontifical dignity on her son Hyrcanus.

[Col. 0026B] In the time of this Hyrcanus, certain bandits who had gone out from Jerusalem carried off plunder near Ascalon. Among the other captives there was brought captive to Jerusalem a young man named Antipater, son of a certain Herod, an Idumaean by descent, who had been priest of Apollo’s temple at Ascalon. This Antipater served for several years in Hyrcanus’s household; conspicuous for ability and integrity, he became favoured by his lord Hyrcanus, to such a degree that Hyrcanus entrusted his whole household to him.

About this time it happened that Antigonus, the younger brother of Hyrcanus the high priest, drove Hyrcanus from the high priesthood and seized the dignity of the priesthood. When Pompey, consul of the Romans, was then leading his army through Syria, the aforesaid Antipater, sent by his master Hyrcanus, came to Pompey and obtained that he should march with an army upon Jerusalem, overthrow Antigonus, and restore the priestly dignity to Hyrcanus. Pompey therefore restored Hyrcanus, imposed a tribute to be paid from the land, and, as he departed, appointed this Antipater over the entire region.

Antipater, however, mindful of the former favour, behaved kindly toward Hyrcanus, [Col. 0026D] and discharged his entrusted office with such moderation that he pleased both Jews and Romans. He had a son named Herod. After his father’s death, both by the merit of his own ability and by the favour arising from his father’s devotion, he received a crown from the Romans and became king. This is the Herod in the thirty-first year of whose reign Christ was born. Since he, being a foreigner, was the first to receive the kingdom of Judaea, he was alarmed when he heard from the Magi of the birth of the king of the Jews. Lest he should perhaps lose the kingdom he had usurped, he attempted to destroy the one whom he feared as successor. He therefore killed the innocents so that, with all dying, the one whom alone he pursued [Col. 0027A] might not escape.

This Herod also, after the other wives whom he had previously taken, when he had become king married a certain Mariamne, niece of Hyrcanus the high priest. By her he had two sons, Alexander and Aristobulus. But when she later became haughty both on account of her beauty and the dignity of her family, she grievously embittered his mind against herself. This trouble was increased because other concubines accused her of adultery, so much so that she was even said to have sent a painted portrait of herself to Antony, the Roman consul then active in the eastern regions, to stir his heart to love her.

Broken by this suspicion, Herod disclosed the secret to his brother-in-law, with whom he was accustomed to share his plans, and ordered her to be killed. The latter, considering the force of love and knowing that repentance would follow commands issued in rage, secretly reproved Mariamne and showed her what danger threatened unless she humbled herself before her husband. Fear made the defiant woman gentle; and so, after a brief change of conduct, she restored Herod’s affection for herself.

Meanwhile, when one day he was alone with her and playfully caressed her, boasting of his love, she said: “But how do you love one whom you would rather have dead than alive? For you ordered me to be killed.” Recognizing that he had been betrayed, he rose in fury. Since he had already heard certain unfavourable words concerning an affair between her and his brother-in-law, he now believed the rumour as though proved and ordered them both killed. Afterwards, however, moved by remorse, he exchanged rage for rage, and at every moment, calling for Mariamne, said that he could not live without her.

[Col. 0027C] Then came the pernicious accusation of the concubines, alleging that her sons were being armed against their father to avenge her blood. He therefore sent letters to Rome and obtained from the Senate permission to kill the parricides and plotters against his life. Thus, after the mother and her sons had been slaughtered, he too subsequently wasted away through prolonged sufferings and ended his life by a miserable death.

He left as successors his sons: Archelaus, king in Judaea; Herod, tetrarch in Galilee; Philip, tetrarch in the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis; and Lysanias in Abilene. Archelaus, after reigning for nine years after his father, was accused before the Romans by the Jews of arrogance; he was deprived of his kingdom and sent into exile at Lugdunum, where he also died. The Romans then placed governors over Judaea.

Herod, tetrarch of Galilee, took from his brother Philip his wife, named Herodias, daughter of Aretas, king of the Arabs, and joined her to himself in marriage contrary to custom. For this [Col. 0028A] crime, when he was rebuked by John the Baptist, he beheaded John at Herodias’s instigation. This is Herod the tetrarch, son of Herod the Great, who is recorded as having gone up to Jerusalem at the Lord’s Passion; and who, when Jesus was sent to him by Pilate the governor, mocked him after clothing him in a white garment and sent him back to Pilate to be judged.

Now Aristobulus, son of Herod the Great and brother of this Herod, born of his mother Mariamne—whom, as stated above, Herod his father had killed on suspicion of parricide—had a son named Agrippa. When he came of age and saw himself deprived and disinherited, he gathered whatever money he could and went to Rome. There he became a close associate of a certain Gaius Caligula, nephew of Tiberius Caesar. When this Gaius assumed the empire after Tiberius’s death, [Col. 0028B] he made Agrippa king in Phoenicia because of the merit of his former devotion.

When Herodias heard this, she began to reproach Herod for cowardice: he was richer and more powerful, yet had not obtained this dignity for himself from the Roman prince. Provoked by this reproach, Herod set out for Rome with Herodias, taking much money with him. When he complained before Gaius that this honour had not rather been conferred on him, Gaius, angered at one seeking what had not been granted, decided that even what had been granted should be taken away. Thus Herod and Herodias together were sent into exile in Spain. Such was Herod’s end.

But Agrippa, surnamed Herod, is the one who killed James, brother of John, with the sword and delivered Peter, sent to prison, to four squads [*quaternionibus*] of soldiers to be guarded. One day, when he had come forth to plead a cause with the Tyrians and Sidonians and was acclaimed, because of the splendour of his gilded garments shining in the sun’s ray, as “a god and not a man,” he was puffed up with pride and suddenly struck by an angel. After some days, while his illness persisted, he died.

His son Agrippa succeeded him. In the Acts of the Apostles (Acts XXV) he is recorded as having come down with Bernice, [Note: [Col. 0027D] In other copies she is called Beroronice.] his mother, to visit and greet Festus the governor; and he is remembered as having conversed pleasantly on certain matters with Paul when Paul was presented to that governor (Acts XXVI). In his time the kingdom of the Jews was overthrown by Titus and Vespasian.

Therefore the first Herod was the one under whom Christ was born and who massacred the little children. The second was his son, under whom Christ suffered and who beheaded John the Baptist. The third was Herod Agrippa, whose grandfather was the first Herod; the second was his uncle, who killed James.

[Col. 0029]

# EXPLANATORY ANNOTATIONS ON THE PENTATEUCH,

## WHOSE CHAPTERS ARE AS FOLLOWS:

On the prologue of Saint Jerome to the Pentateuch. Chapter I. On the name of the first book of the Pentateuch. Chapter II. That in writing Genesis Moses was both historian and prophet, and that two things must be considered in it: the truth of events and the form of the words. Chapter III. What Moses’s intention is in Genesis, and whether all things were created at once. Chapter IV. On prime matter: when, where, and of what sort it was created. Chapter V. On the distinct works of the six days. Chapter VI. Explanations of both the words and the meanings of Genesis, through nearly every chapter, as we shall note them. Chapter VII. Explanatory annotations on Exodus, which comprise the following. Chapter VIII. The annotations on Leviticus contain these chapters: On the name of Leviticus, and on the five matters distinctly treated in it—sacrifices, persons, times, places, and causes—Chapter I, which is noted in the Pentateuch. Chapter VIII. On sacrifices, offering, and libation. Chapter II and book X in its entirety. On the persons by whom the aforesaid things are performed. Chapter III and book XI in its entirety. On the times and causes for offering in them. Chapter IV and XII. On places, causes, and the literal exposition of Leviticus. Chapter V and XIII. A few annotations on Numbers. Chapter XIV. Also a few annotations on Deuteronomy. Chapter XV.

## CHAPTER I.—Explanatory annotations on the prologue of Saint Jerome to the Pentateuch

[Col. 0029A]

*Desiderius* is a proper name; hence “my Desiderius,” with “friend” understood: “I have received your desired letters.” He shares a name with Daniel, since Daniel himself was called by the angel “a man of desires,” just as this man is now called Desiderius. The name is said to have been imposed by a certain presage of future things, so that in his being called Desiderius it might be signified that he would become desirable or would request desirable things.

*Pentateuchon* is a Greek name, which when translated into Latin means “of five volumes.” For Greek πέντε (*pente*) means “five” in Latin; τεῦχος (*teuchos*), “a volume.” Hence the *Pentateuchon* is a work of five volumes [Col. 0029B] or books. It signifies the five books of the Law published by Moses.

Some interpret *suggillationem* as detraction or oppression, as though *subgulationem*, from *sub* and *gula*, just as *suffocatio* is said to be, as it were, *subfaucatio*, from *sub* and *faux* (“throat”). Thus they test talent as though it were wine: when new wine arrives, the old turns sour. Yet the comparison is not exact, because by the judgment formed from present things the wisdom of the ancients appears sweeter in a paltry portion.

In my judgment, whatever I can do in the house of the Lord is small and contemptible. To the old edition—that is, the translation of the Seventy, which is older than the others—he added the translation of Theodotion, [Col. 0030A] supplementing it from Theodotion’s translation because it had formerly contained less. Then, having added two signs, namely the asterisk and the obelus, he marked out the entire work—that is, the whole sequence—of that old edition. For he placed the asterisk, which means “little star,” in places where, having made an addition, he clarified it by supplying what had previously been lacking. But he attached the obelus, called “a dart,” because it signifies that the things to which it is affixed are, as it were, to be pierced and destroyed, to passages in which that same old edition contained superfluities.

[Note: [Col. 0029] On these signs see a fuller treatment in F. Sixtus, in his *Bibliotheca*, book III, part I, and in my book, *Discourses of the Kabbalists*.]

That the aforesaid edition of the Seventy lacks many things found in the Hebrew truth is shown by the authorities promulgated by the Evangelists and Apostles. In them we read many things from the Old Testament which are not found in our codices according to the seventy interpreters: such as, “Out of Egypt I called my son,” and the other things following in the text. All these require their own *syntagma*, that is, their own composition. Lest anyone say that this is contained in the Hebrew truth in sense but not word for word, he therefore says that they “require their own syntagma,” so that they may be expressed in the form and composition of their own words. Since, therefore, they are not found in the Seventy, let us turn to the Hebrew truth, where they are found.

Many people, not knowing [Col. 0031A] that such a deficiency now exists in the translation of the Seventy, follow the ravings of apocryphal books, in which there is neither authority nor truth. They prefer “Iberian trifles”—that is, the sayings of those same books, comparable to Spanish fables—to authentic books, that is, Hebrew books, in which authority and truth are primary.

But if it is asked why the Seventy erred in this way, he says: “It is not mine to set forth the causes of their error.” Yet the Jews say in their defence that they deliberately did this: they either omitted altogether or translated differently certain things that were in the Hebrew truth, especially where sacred Scripture testifies to something about the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, because of Ptolemy. He knew the unity of the Godhead as a worshipper of one God, but was unable to comprehend the mystery of the Trinity, especially lest it should seem more Platonic than divine. Plato had propounded certain traces of the Trinity ἐν τῷ περὶ τοῦ ἀγγαθοῦ καὶ νοῦ, that is, “in the book *On the Good and the Intellect*,” [Col. 0031B] or “in *Agathon and Intellect*,” and concerning the soul of the world.

But even if this excuse for the error of the seventy interpreters is perhaps accepted, it is in no way to be approved that some people falsely claim that they were divided one by one into separate cells and wrote precisely the same thing. For if this had been true, Aristarchus, the *hyperaspistes*—that is, defender and champion—of that Ptolemy, who faithfully defended Ptolemy’s deeds, and Josephus, who wrote of them much later, would not have been silent. If, divided in this manner and without mutual comparison, they had said exactly and indiscriminately the same things, they ought to be called seers and prophets rather than translators—which it is not fitting to say.

For it is one thing to be a seer and another to be an interpreter. Unless perhaps some foolish person should wish to maintain that seer and interpreter are the same thing. If that were granted, the following absurdity would result: Cicero, who translated certain books of orators from Greek into Latin, would be said to have translated them under the inspiration of a rhetorical spirit. This is what he says: unless perhaps Cicero must be thought to have translated under the inspiration of a rhetorical spirit Xenophon’s *Oeconomicus*, Plato’s *Pythagoras* [Note: [Col. 0031D] Rather, *Protagoras*.], and Demosthenes’ speech “For Ctesiphon”—that is, those books of which the first is entitled Xenophon’s *Oeconomicus*, the second Plato’s *Pythagoras*. Just as we read of the work entitled Plato’s *Timaeus*, a book that Plato himself composed and entitled with the name of his disciple Timaeus, [Col. 0031D] perhaps Plato similarly composed this book and wished it to be called Plato’s *Pythagoras*: either because Pythagoras speaks in it, or because what is written there is said about him.

Likewise, Xenophon’s book, to which the title *Oeconomicus*—that is, “the household manager”—is prefixed, is called Xenophon’s *Oeconomicus*. The third book, whose title is “Demosthenes for Ctesiphon,” belongs to Demosthenes himself and was composed for Ctesiphon’s case, just as Cicero’s book in which the case of King Deiotarus is argued is called Cicero’s *For Deiotarus*. Therefore, if we call the seventy interpreters seers because they were interpreters, we shall also call Cicero, who was an interpreter, a seer.

Or another absurdity follows: if we assert that they spoke by the Holy Spirit, we find that the same Holy Spirit spoke differently through them and differently through the Apostles, and that the Holy Spirit contradicts himself: through the former he falsely testified that something was written which the latter altogether passed over in silence. From all these things it is clear that the seventy interpreters spoke by a human, not a divine, spirit; and therefore, if they erred as human beings, there is no absurdity in it.

Therefore, O jealous defender who so vigorously uphold the seventy interpreters, why are you tormented by envy when you hear them criticized? If anywhere I seem to you to err in translation, ask the Hebrews whether our translation or theirs is truer. They will tell you that what they have concerning Christ, your codices written according to the seventy interpreters do not contain. If you should say that the Hebrews have testimonies falsely appropriated by the Apostles, because they are not found in the translation of the Seventy, and that they subsequently produced them and added them to their books, that is another kind of defence; yet it has no plausibility, since they would willingly wish to deny not only false things but even true things, if they could.

Finally, if you say that the translation of the Seventy ought therefore to be preferred to the Hebrew truth because Greek manuscripts are truer than Hebrew ones, and Latin ones truer than Greek, you achieve nothing. For, conversely, Greek is truer than Latin, and Hebrew than Greek.

## CHAPTER II.—On the name of the first book of the Pentateuch

[Col. 0032C]

This book, which is the first of the divine volumes, is called in Hebrew *Beresith*, which has the same force as if one said “In the beginning.” Some Hebrews have the custom of giving their books names from the beginning of the book, that is, from its first word; just as we call one Psalm “Have mercy on me, O God,” and another, “Blessed are the undefiled.” In Greek, however, it is called *Genesis*, both because of the generation of heaven and earth, which it treats first, and because of the creation of humankind or the propagation of the human race over the whole face of the earth. In these three developments this book properly comes to rest and ends.

## CHAPTER III.—That in writing Genesis Moses was historian and prophet, and that two things must be considered in it: the truth of the events and the form of the words

[Col. 0032D]

Moses should be understood, in this book, as a historiographer, weaving a history from the beginning of the world down to the death of Jacob. And just as he prophetically recounts certain things that occurred before the creation of humankind, so too, in the blessings of Jacob which he introduces there, he foretells certain future events after Jacob’s death. Thus the manifestation of future things is evidence for faith in past things; just as, conversely, according to Gregory, who says somewhere that the manifestation of past things is faith in future things. In this book, however, two things especially are to be observed [Col. 0033A]: namely, the truth of the events performed and the form of the words. For just as through the truth of the words we know the truth of the events, so conversely, once the truth of the events is known, we more readily know the truth of the words; for through this historical narration we are led onward to an understanding of higher realities.

## CHAPTER IV.—What Moses’ purpose is in Genesis, and whether all things were created simultaneously.

His purpose in this book is chiefly to show three things. First, God the Creator, created matter and its formation; and all this to the praise of God and the benefit of humankind, for whom it is beneficial to admire and venerate God. In that he created—that is, made the world from nothing—we admire his power. In that he adorned it—that is, made the world beautiful—we admire his wisdom. For in this our authors differ from the philosophers: the philosophers posit God merely as craftsman and set down three principles—God, matter, and archetypal ideas—whereas our authors posit one principle only, namely God alone.

And although all interpreters of the divine word agree on this point, namely that there is but one principle, there is nevertheless a great question concerning the manner of creation. Some say that God made all things simultaneously; others distinguish the work across six days [Note: [Col. 0033D] On the question at issue, whether God created all things simultaneously, see what F. Sixtus notes in his *Bible*, book V, part II, annotation 24. See immediately below, on Genesis II.], and say that this distinction is figurative and solely for the sake of mystery, and did not occur literally in that way. They seek to prove this by the authority: “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. 18). They also draw another passage from the same book, where, after the works of the six days, it recapitulates: “These,” it says, “are the generations of heaven and earth, when they were created, in the day in which God made heaven and earth and every shrub of the field” (Gen. 2).

They also give this reason: that it does not suit God to make anything imperfect, disordered, or misshapen after the manner of a human being. Yet these authorities are easily resolved. Against this argument, too, we may say that God, who could make all things in a moment, distinguished his works through six days, not because of any incapacity on his part—for there is none—but for the instruction and example of rational creatures. For just as he first gave things existence and afterwards gave them beauty, so also to angel and human being, to whom he had given rational existence, if they had persevered, he would have given blessed existence also; and this would have been their beauty.

Because the angel neglected this example, looking to his own existence, which was rational, and presuming too greatly upon himself, he fell irrecoverably, just as others were immovably confirmed. But for the restoration of humankind, God chose to distinguish his work through six days, so that in this human beings might have their minds occupied with their own instruction. That God is said to have created anything imperfect or formless is neither harmful nor inappropriate, since this can be said by comparison with the greater perfection or beauty which he himself afterwards added in due time. Thus every day he makes children imperfect in relation to the growth that follows, though perfect in the number of their parts—hands, feet, and the other limbs. This opinion seems the more probable.

## CHAPTER V.—On prime matter: when, where, and of what sort it was created.

[Note: [Col. 0033D] On this subject see the notes of F. Sixtus [Col. 0034D] in his *Bible*, book V, part II, on the opening words of Genesis.]

It is also asked when, where, and of what sort the matter of things was created. But it is agreed that it was created at the beginning of time, before every day: that is, such that time and matter began simultaneously, and the angel in that same time. Concerning this it has been said: “Wisdom was created first of all things,” but not before the establishment of the world, as certain Greeks supposed. Alluding to this opinion, Jerome says: “Who knows for how many years or lustrums angels praised their Creator before the world?” [Col. 0034B] And Solomon says something similar in one place: “Who knows whether the spirit of beasts is borne downward, and that of human beings upward?” (Eccles. 1 [3:21]). Yet neither puts forward as an assertion what he proposes as a question.

Therefore we say that time and matter were created simultaneously, because time is nothing other than the succession of mutability, which began to exist with mutable matter. Moreover, where matter now exists in formed fashion, there it is believed first to have been created, then filling the same local capacity that it now fills. It was created formless, not wholly devoid of form; but it may be called formless in comparison with the beauty and order that followed.

The earth was in the middle, having within itself channels and veins—that is, receptacles of waters flowing both over the earth and within it. The other three elements, however, mingled together into one like a dense cloud, were borne above the earth on every side and over its whole surface, up to the highest empyrean. For this reason they are called by the name of “earth,” where it says: “God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1).

## CHAPTER VI.—On the works of the six distinct days.

[Note: [Col. 0034D] On this whole subject read the annotations of F. Sixtus, *Bible*, book V, part II.]

On the first day God separated fire from the other elements; and this is what he himself says: “Let there be light,” that is, let fire be distinguished from the other elements. For in this place “to be made” is understood as “to be distinguished.” God made all things both by creating and by distinguishing, not by laborious action but by his will alone, which was eternal.

The separated fire gave some sort of light to the lower world [Col. 0034D] and had circular motion; like a luminous cloud it was carried round, as the sun now is. By its rising and setting he made the first three days and nights. What its shape was—whether round or elongated—is unknown. This light is believed to have been created in the place where the sun rises. Thus the beginning of that first day was not preceded by dawn or morning, that is, light heralding the sunrise. Scripture carefully intimates this when it defines the natural day by its two extreme points: “And evening came,” it says, which is the end of the artificial day; “and morning came,” which is the end of the night [Col. 0035A]. For the day begins with the rising of the sun and ends at its setting. This can be demonstrated by the equality of day and night at the equinox. And that entire interval is one natural day.

On the second day the firmament was made, to divide the waters from the waters. Bede says that the firmament consists of waters solidified like crystalline stone; this seems likely, since its colour indicates it to our sight. Others say that it is of a fiery nature. That waters are above the firmament is found both in Genesis and in the Prophet, where it is said: “Waters that are above the heavens, praise the name of the Lord” (Ps. 148). What sort of waters these are is not certain to us. Some interpreters say that they are solidified there as ice; but it seems more likely to me that they remain there suspended in vapour, like vapour, smoke, or mist [Col. 0035B].

On the third day the waters were gathered into one place: that is, into their proper channel and into the abyss, the womb of waters; or into the place of the great sea and of all the other seas; or into a subterranean hollow. Hence rivers were led away through *tracones*, that is, underground conduits, beneath the earth and over the earth. The dry land appeared and received the power of producing vegetation.

On the fourth day, from the aforesaid light or fire, improved in form and brightness, he made the sun. We infer that the sun was made from the fire mentioned above from the fact that, in a certain manner, the Gospel was made from the Law, and at the wedding wine from water. For as through signs we sometimes comprehend the truth of the things signified, so conversely, through the things signified, both here and often elsewhere, we may infer the truth of the signs. The sun alone has light proper to itself, and it alone was made of fire. All the stars, however, like the moon, were made of airy matter, and they shine by reflection rather than emit light [Col. 0035C].

On the fifth day fish and birds were made from the waters; whence the verse: “Some you send back to the deep, / Some you raise into the air.” [Note: [Col. 0035D] From an ancient hymn.] On the sixth day the earth brought forth animals of different kinds; and on the same day humankind was made in the image and likeness of God. And rightly was humankind made after all things, since it was to be set above all things.

These are the works of the six days. During the first three days God created and ordered all things in matter [Col. 0035D]; during the following three days he adorned them. But now let us come to the literal sense.

## CHAPTER VII.—Explanatory notes on both the words and the meanings of Genesis, almost chapter by chapter, as we shall annotate them.

[Note: [Col. 0035D] It will not be unhelpful for readers to attend to the annotations of F. Sixtus [Col. 0036D] in his *Bible*, book V, part II, at the beginning.]

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” He calls the three higher elements “heaven.” “But the earth was empty and void.” Empty of seeds; void of shoots; or empty because of its hollowness, void because in so great a hollow of the earth there was nothing but air and mist. “And darkness was upon the face of the abyss.” By “darkness” we may mean that mist, namely the mixture of the three elements—fire, air, and water—and by “abyss,” the hollow. Or otherwise: he calls the mist “abyss,” and darkness “the absence of light.” “And the Spirit of God was borne over the waters.” He calls God’s intention his Spirit, as though an artisan presiding over the work to be fashioned. He calls that mist “waters” because of its mobility. Thus he calls the same thing at one time “abyss” because of its depth, at another “darkness” because of the absence of light, and at another “waters” because of its mobility.

Observe that earth and air did not change their former places, as fire and water did, because human nature requires earth and air everywhere: earth, for support; air, in order to draw and release the breath by which life subsists. But it does not always need the heat of fire and the moisture of water [Col. 0036B].

“Let lights be made in the firmament of heaven.” Here he begins to speak of the adornment of the three following days after the distinction made in the three preceding days; and first he speaks of the adornment of the upper regions. Just as the sun begins and ends the day by rising and setting, divides it into fixed portions by its course, and distinguishes it from night by the splendour of its light, so the moon and stars divide the night.

Time is distinguished by the sun, and this is now necessary for the restoration of humankind. For since time is the succession of mutability, it must now exist, so that humanity may pass from this state of imperfection to immutability and perfection. Once that has been attained, change will not be necessary; rather, it then becomes evil, for change falls back from perfection into imperfection [Col. 0036C].

“And let them be for signs and seasons,” namely for some of our activities, such as sowing, harvesting, crossing the sea, and the like. For they do not impose any necessity upon our minds, depriving them of free choice by inclining them toward whatever actions, as astrologers falsely maintain. Yet it is true that they in some manner govern bodies. For God made three things in creatures of remarkable power and efficacy: herbs, stones, and stars. Herbs cool and heat, and alter the whole condition of the body; they received that power from the Lord in creation. Stones likewise alter bodily conditions in diverse ways. All stars indeed, and especially the planets, have their effects upon subject bodies, altering them through the medium of the air [Col. 0036D].

When bodies are altered, the souls joined to them are also altered, because of their affinity with them; they receive joy, sorrow, and like affections from external things. Yet these affections do not rule human souls so completely that our actions follow them rather than the discernment of the mind and free choice. This opinion, as some holy persons say, arose from Hercules, Atlas, and Prometheus, who are believed to have been incarnate demons. They handed down astrology—a false doctrine—but supported it with certain plausible arguments in order more easily to deceive people and instil this anxiety in them [Col. 0037A].

“A living and moving, or mutable, soul”—as it stands in Hebrew. For God made everything made for human beings subject to change and death; but humanity alone for immortality. “Which the waters had brought forth,” that is, “brought forth,” or “after God had created [them].” “Increase,” that is, “multiply”: so that one expression is a gloss upon the other.

He sets down three classes: cattle, creeping things, and beasts. Cattle are all animals that become tame. There are three kinds of creeping things: dragging creatures, serpentine creatures, and crawling creatures. Dragging creatures are worms, which first fix their mouths in the earth and then draw themselves along. Serpentine creatures are snakes, which have no feet outside their skin but have ribs within, on which they lean as they move all together. Crawling creatures have feet outside the skin, such as frogs, lizards, and newts. “Beasts” are called wild creatures that wound by claw, tooth, or the brutish stupidity of their disposition, as does the wolf [Col. 0037B].

“Let us make humankind in our image and likeness.” First he said: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” Then he said: “Let there be light.” Here he adds a third utterance: “Let us make humankind,” and so forth. In this three stages may be identified: first, the work; next, the informing word; third, deliberation, in that he adds here: “Let us make humankind,” and so forth.

He does not introduce deliberation because he is not equally able to make great and small things; rather, he does so in order to show the dignity of the human creature and to make us careful not to disdain taking counsel from equals or inferiors, since he speaks thus to the angels, by whose ministry perhaps the human body was formed. Or, better, let us understand this as the counsel of the Trinity: the plural word denotes the distinction of persons; the subsequent singular phrase, “in our image and likeness,” the unity of essence.

Let us see what he calls “image” and what “likeness.” An image consists in similar features; likeness in participation in some identical property. We may call the image of God in humanity the recognition of truth, and likeness the love of unity—both of which are found in God and in human beings. Humankind was made in God’s image according to the soul. For just as the image of a thing is seen in a mirror, so the soul can know God in its reason. It is “in the image,” because it is not altogether like him. The Son is the image of the Father, not “in the image,” because the Son has by nature everything that the Father has [Col. 0037D]. But humanity is God’s image in such a way that it is “in the image,” because it possesses what belongs to God not by nature but by participation or imitation.

Or “in the image of God” means in the image that is in God, just as all creatures are in his mind; “in likeness” means that the human being is like God himself, in that as all things come from one God, so all human beings come from one human being. Or image means that the human being is rational; likeness, that as God rules human beings, so the human being rules animals.

“Let him rule over the fish of the sea,” and so forth. Humanity ought to have ruled all things, but through sin lost dominion both over the greatest and the least. Yet it retained dominion over intermediate things as a consolation. It lost dominion over the greatest, such as lions [Col. 0038A], so that it might recognize that it had lost its proper dignity. It lost it over the least, such as fleas and flies, in order to recognize its own lowliness. Thus the Lord sent an army of wasps in vengeance against Egypt, so that their lowliness might be marked.

“He created him in the image of God.” This is repeated for emphasis, so that, in what God marks, the human being may be found like God—that is, in simplicity of substance and multiplicity of knowledge—and this according to the soul. “And they were very good.” Observe three grades: simply good, each individual creature; very good, all things taken together; supremely good, God alone.

“(Gen. II.) These are the generations of heaven and earth.” This recapitulation seems contrary to the above exposition of the six days [Note: [Col. 0037D] F. Sixtus makes many notes relevant to this point in his *Bible*, book V, part II, on chapter 2 of Genesis.]. There he seemed [Col. 0038B] to say that all things were created in six days; here, however, in one day. But if “day” is understood broadly as “time,” the solution will be both plausible and easy, and the phrase will then be understood to refer to the period of the six days.

“Generations” can be understood either actively or passively. Passively: these are the heavens and earth generated, that is, such as they are. Or actively: God worked upon them. “Before it sprang up,” and so forth. That is, God worked thus before trees and herbs grew successively, as they now do by the operation of an artisan imitating and assisting nature: namely, in a moment he produced a perfect tree, bearing fruit; and likewise, and so forth.

“Before it germinated”: because everything came forth together into a perfected state. “For God had not caused it to rain,” and so forth. He explains why growths of things would then arise neither by the work of nature, as now, nor by the work of an artisan, saying: “For it had not rained,” so that the earth, made fertile by the heat subsequently coming upon it, might sprout forth—which is the work of nature. “Nor was there yet a human being,” that is, an artisan, “to cultivate the earth.” “But a fountain rose,” and so forth. It is as if he said: it had not rained, but a fountain rose. This is to say: although the created trees and herbs did not have the assistance of rain for their growth, they nevertheless had in the fountain a means of preservation from drying out.

This fountain may be understood as the abyss, namely the womb of all waters from which all springs and rivers of water issue; or read the singular for the plural, so that “fountain” means “fountains.” It rose, watering the entire surface: not causing a flood, but supplying moisture as nourishment for the earth, as it does now [Col. 0038D]. For not only the land near riverbanks is moistened and irrigated by the water of the nearby river; rather, it is believed to be infused through *tracones* in every direction for as much as twelve or sixteen stadia.

“Therefore the Lord God formed the human being,” and so forth. Since there was no human being to cultivate the earth, therefore he formed one, and so forth. Here for the first time he calls God “Lord,” because only then was he truly Lord, when he had a servant—namely, a human being. He makes no mention of the angel; but, as a historiographer concerned with visible things, he says that the human being—that is, the body—was formed from mud, which is clinging earth, thereby indicating that the human being was made mortal, that is, able to die; or he admonishes the human being thereby to consider his own lowliness, that he may pursue humility [Col. 0039A].

“And he breathed”—namely into the prepared body—“a soul,” especially into its face, because there the soul’s operations are vigorous in the bodily senses, and there it is more easily discerned than in other parts whether a person lives or not.

“But the Lord God had planted a paradise of delight from the beginning.” Not before he created heaven and earth, as Jerome seems to mean, but from the time of the founding, which was on the third day. “Into which he placed the human being.” God chose to make him outside paradise, so that he might understand that he was placed in paradise by grace, not by nature.

“The tree of life.” These two trees—the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil—are said to have been in the middle because of the greater sacraments which they signify; and they have these names for different reasons. The tree of life was so called because it possessed a nature capable of prolonging human life, if eaten in due measure. For the human being was made both mortal and immortal: immortal in the sense that he could avoid death through the sustenance of food, which he required; mortal because he could perish through external violence. But God had so fortified him inwardly by the tree of life taken as food and outwardly by divine power that he could avoid death. Inwardly, he barred the gate of negligence through human reason; outwardly, he barred the gate of violence through divine protection. Unless the human being, misusing reason, opened the gate of negligence, nothing harmful could ever enter through the gate of violence. But because he would not guard himself by preserving the gate entrusted to him, God deservedly withdrew [Col. 0039C] his protection.

The tree of knowledge was so named not because of a nature which it possessed in itself, but because through it it became known whether the human being was good or evil—that is, obedient or disobedient. Or it was so called because by obedience to it humanity would have the good things to which it was to pass, whereas through disobedience it would receive the evils with which God had threatened it. Or because through it humanity learned both by experience.

What, then, are the chief sacraments for the sake of which these trees were placed in the middle of paradise? Understand them thus. The tree of life was given to humanity for the support of temporal life; but by obeying with regard to the tree of knowledge, humanity was to receive eternal life.

“And a river went out.” This is the fountain mentioned above, or a river rising from that fountain [Col. 0039D], at first one and later divided into four, from a certain place of delight—that is, paradise. It did not rise there only to go immediately forth to other places; rather, it went out in order to water paradise. “Which from there is divided”: either in paradise itself, after it had flowed as one for some time, or after it had gone forth from paradise.

It is asked how these rivers arise in paradise and yet have known sources in our land, as Bede says. Hence some affirm that the whole earth would have been paradise if humanity had not sinned, but was made wholly an exile through sin. We, however, though this may plausibly be said, assert only what the saints commonly assert: namely, that paradise is a defined place in some part of the earth; that those rivers have their source in paradise; and likewise that, having there been swallowed by the earth, they arise again outside paradise [Col. 0040A], and that these second sources are known to us.

“God commanded him concerning every tree of paradise,” and so forth. See: he gives the commandment by which, if the human being kept it, he would preserve paradise. There is only this commandment: “Do not eat of the tree of knowledge.” What precedes—“Eat of every tree of paradise”—is permission. First he gently persuades by permitting, then he will speak more harshly in prohibiting.

But it is asked why God did not give humanity the good he intended to give without any commandment at all. Why, too, did he permit so many things and prohibit one alone? Why, furthermore, did he not command what he prohibited to be eaten—that which would have been easier for humanity, while obedience would have been equivalent in merit? The commandment was given so that through the merit of obedience humanity might obtain the good more gloriously. Many things were granted so that provision might be made for human frailty and that disobedience might have no excuse [Col. 0040B]. He did not command the eating of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, so that obedience might be pure. For the devil could have alleged that the human being ate from that tree not so much on account of the commandment as for his own advantage.

“Let us make for him a helper like himself.” Since he already had many aids, but all were unlike him. “He brought them to Adam,” and so forth. This occurred either on the sixth day, as the order of the narrative seems to indicate, or after a long time, when perhaps he saw various animals in various places. The reason they were brought to him is this: he was to be lord over all of them, and therefore it was fitting that he give them names according to his own judgment.

“Therefore he cast Adam into a deep sleep.” This was done so that, if he had removed the rib while Adam was awake, God might seem to have harmed him; but he took it so gently that he did not even wake him while sleeping [Col. 0040C]. The question some ask—whether Adam had more ribs beforehand on the side from which the rib was taken, because if so Adam had a superfluous rib; or, if he had no more than on the other side, he was afterwards diminished—is frivolous. For neither are children’s teeth, which later change, called superfluous; nor are the children themselves judged diminished, though they do not yet possess their full natural growth.

Rather, one should observe that the matter from which woman was made was taken neither from the man’s head nor from his feet, lest she be thought mistress if from the head, or slave if from the feet. It was fitting, therefore, that it be taken from the middle—that is, from the rib—so that she might be understood as a companion.

It is also asked whether woman was made from that rib with the addition of matter taken from outside, or from the rib alone. Some say that something was added. But if God took material from outside to complete the woman’s body from that rib, since what was added was greater than the rib itself, Scripture ought rather to say that woman was made from that material, from which she received the greater part of her substance. It remains, therefore, to say that the rib was multiplied within itself and that the woman was formed from it, with no external addition taken [Col. 0040D]. For it was a greater thing to make all things from nothing than to multiply a small quantity of substance into itself. We say the same of the five loaves in the Gospel.

“And he filled up flesh in its place.” This was so that there should not be an ugly hollow if it were entirely empty; or, if bone were regenerated for bone [Col. 0041A], no sign would remain of the removed rib, through which it is established that the whole human race has only one origin. Therefore the sign was retained, like Christ’s scars as a triumph.

“Wherefore a man shall leave,” and so forth. Only these two relationships are excluded in paradise: namely, lest a father have intercourse with his daughter, or a son with his mother.
