The Law, however, excludes ten persons; the Gospel, all persons up to seven generations. What does it mean when it says “he shall leave”? Does it mean that he must first do so and then depart? No. Rather, “he shall leave” means that he will never cling carnally to them. Nor should it be said that he leaves them in residence or entirely in affection, but in the privilege of affection which he ought to transfer to his wife. He also leaves paternal subjection and guardianship, from which he has been emancipated [Col. 0041B], once he becomes head of a household, so that he may devote care to his own family.

“And the two shall be in one flesh”: that is, there will be such love between man and woman that the spirit of either will make no distinction between the flesh animated by itself and the beloved flesh of the other; and, if they could, they would gladly dwell in one and the same flesh. Since they cannot effect this unity in reality, they effect the union that they can through love; or they will be “in one flesh,” namely by cooperating in the generation of one flesh—that is, offspring.

(GEN. III.) But the serpent, etc. [Note: [Col. 0041] The annotations of the aforesaid F. Sixtus in Book V, Part II of his Bible, where he undertakes to annotate the third chapter of Genesis, will be useful for this chapter.] Man was permitted to be tempted, because otherwise it would not have been glorious to stand firm. But note that he was not tempted through some ordinary beast, such as a dove or lamb, lest he be able to excuse the transgression by saying, “Who would suppose [Col. 0041C] that deceit was present in such an appearance or form?” Why did God command you? He cautiously pretends to doubt the prohibitory command, so as both to make the woman doubt and to show that God, who prohibited the fruit of so good a tree, did not love them as much as he ought. Lest perhaps we die. Note: the Lord affirmed it, saying, “You shall die by death.” The woman doubted, saying, “Lest perhaps we die.” Therefore the devil, hoping by this to achieve what he wanted, openly as an adversary denied it, saying, “You shall by no means die.” Your eyes will be opened. He promises her divine knowledge, by which God perfectly comprehends the natures of all things in a single glance: “And you shall be like gods, knowing good and evil.” He promises two things—dignity and abundance of possessions—in order to persuade [Col. 0041D] one thing, namely the eating of the fruit. Through the two things which he promises, he leads her into pride and avarice. Hence the woman herself, wavering in doubt and weighing the devil’s promises and God’s prohibition, looked at the tree; and thus gluttony so captured her that, even without the devil’s promises, she was justly persuaded by sight alone to eat from the tree, so that “the one who is filthy may become filthier still.”

The eating of the fruit is nevertheless called the first sin; but this must be understood as the first actual sin, since pride and avarice preceded it. The eyes of both were opened—not because they saw things they had not seen before, but because through sight they perceived and thought something such as they had not thought before. And when they realized that they were [Col. 0042A] naked—that is, that nakedness was unfitting because of the unlawful movement—they wished to cover those parts in which they felt the unlawful movement, since they could not remove it. This penalty was justly inflicted upon man by the Lord: because reason would not obey its superior, namely God, its inferior, namely the flesh, would not obey it. Yet through God’s mercy, and so that man might survive, it came about that the other parts of the body stand still or move at reason’s command. One part, however, does not obey reason, as a sign of transgression—namely, the sexual organs. This is clearly because the entire propagation of the human race was to pass through that part. Upon it, as upon a gate, is inscribed the sign of the parents’ disobedience: the imposed disobedience of the limbs.

Fig leaves. From this some suppose that the fig tree [Col. 0042B] was the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. And because the Lord said to Nathanael in the Gospel, “Before Philip called you, when you were under the fig tree, I saw you” (John 1). The voice of the Lord walking. See how great God’s mercy is: he does not wish immediately to confront them concerning their fault, lest, having lost their shame, they become shameless and obstinate. Instead, he gives them room for repentance and deliberation; thus he walks, so that they may hear and thereby remember God himself. Adam, where are you? A question either of rebuke or of compassion. Because I was naked. Note that he acts foolishly, offering in his own excuse what rather turns into his accusation; for by this he is more convincingly shown to have sinned in the fruit than excused. For who told you? As if he said: “You wished to excuse yourself by nakedness, but it instead accuses you, because [Col. 0042C] it signifies that wickedness and sin preceded within you. And it truly does signify this; for who but your wickedness told you that you were naked?” The woman whom you gave me, etc. Convicted of the deed, he shifts the blame onto the woman, and the woman likewise onto the serpent; thus each turns the fault back upon God the author.

Because you have done this, you are cursed. He did not immediately pronounce sentence upon sinful man; rather, having asked a question, he gave him time to reflect upon his case and repent. But upon the devil he immediately lays sentence, because he had previously sinned in himself and had now driven man to sin. Thus, rendered more guilty, he deserved to be allowed to tempt all others who would come after. And all this is to his own detriment. And [Col. 0042D] just as one exalted Lucifer fell, and all who assented to him fell with him, so here this one alone, in the serpent, deceived the woman; and because all the others assented to him, all received the curse with him. For it is not the serpent but the devil hidden in the serpent who is cursed. Yet he is called by the serpent’s name because he had put it on as though it were a garment—mockingly, just as if a thief put on a monk’s clothes in order to steal more secretly among monks and, when caught in theft, were mockingly called a monk because of the clothes he had assumed. In calling him so, it attributes to him things belonging to the serpent; the narrative is metaphorical.

I will put enmities between you, etc. [Col. 0043A] Here it is suggested that Eve, coming to her senses, did penance; hence the devil grieved. As though he said: “You were rejoicing just now because you had cast her down; but in vain, because you have been defeated by a woman.” Your seed, etc. He calls the other demons the seed of the devil. The woman’s seed is other human beings, some of whom were [variant: are] to be saints; and these will crush the head, that is, the devil’s pride concerning fallen man. And you will lie in wait for his heel—that is, you will always pursue him in order to deceive him. I will multiply your miseries, in comparison with the man’s miseries. And your conceptions. This does not seem to be a curse but rather a blessing, for under the Law a barren woman was cursed. But in saying this he looks either to the pain of giving birth, or to the futility of conceiving: because she will not give birth as often; or because they were to die even after birth; or because not all [Col. 0043B] were predestined to eternal life, as would have been the case had she not sinned. In pain you shall give birth, etc. This pain surpasses all pains. And you shall be under your husband’s power—not merely under governance, as before, but under violent domination, so that he may afflict you with wounds.

The ground shall be cursed, etc. It will not of itself willingly bear fruit for you to live on, or it will sometimes not answer to your labor. You shall eat the herbs of the earth. Earlier he had said, “Behold, I have given you every green herb and every fruit-bearing tree for food.” But there he gave them herbs for the use of animals, while for themselves he gave fruit-bearing trees for food; here, however, in cursing, he gives humans herbs for food—the food, namely, of beasts. She was to be the mother, that is, the future mother, of all living. He made for them tunics of skin, either from the elements through [Col. 0043C] the agency of angels, or he taught them to make them by stripping skins from animals. Behold, Adam has become like one of us. This is mockery, referring to his foolish credulity regarding the serpent’s words: “You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil.” And although Eve alone, not Adam, believed this, it is nevertheless imputed to him as the superior and teacher. Such mockery is sometimes deserved and just, as here; sometimes it arises from the wickedness of the mocker and is the figure called sarcasm.

Now therefore, lest perhaps he put forth his hand, etc. Here it is suggested that even after sin, if man ate of the tree of life, he would become immortal. [Note: [Col. 0043D] Guglielmus Boriglion observes that *in aeternum* does not have a strict but a broad sense here, that is, “for an age.”] The sentence is incomplete. What is omitted, the historian makes clear by adding, “He sent him out,” etc.; this indicates what had been left unfinished above. “Let us send him out of paradise,” and then [Col. 0043D] there would follow, “He sent him out,” etc.

The cherubim and the flaming, turning sword. Since both man and the devil had sinned in paradise, both were expelled. And lest either of them be allowed to enter again, a guard and impediment were set against both: the cherub to repel the devil, fire for man. It should be noted that God makes, or has made, an appearance of fire—as is read in the Life of Saint Nicholas—whose nature is said to be such that if anyone puts his hand into it, he feels heat but suffers no burning. That fire is of such a nature that it burns a spirit and needs no matter to consume, just as neither does that which is in the [Col. 0044A] sphere of the sun. Our fire, however, both needs matter and burns only a body.

(GEN. IV.) Abel was a shepherd, etc. [Note: [Col. 0044D] See the annotations of F. Sixtus on Genesis 4, in Book V of the Holy Bible.] He passes briefly over matters which need not be narrated. Cain offered from the fruits of the earth. We believe that God taught Adam divine worship, by which he might recover God’s favor, which he had lost through the sin of transgression; and Adam himself taught his sons to give tithes and firstfruits. The Lord looked upon Abel, etc. God is believed to have had this custom toward those earliest fathers when they sacrificed: he sent fire from heaven to consume the sacrifices of those pleasing to him. That gifts pleased him not in themselves but by the merit of the offerer is suggested by the fact that he is said to have looked first upon Abel offering, before looking upon the gift [Col. 0044B].

Sin will be present at the doors. Something is said to be at the doors for two reasons: either that it may enter or that it may go out. The same may be understood here of sin. Sin is at the door in order to enter after an evil thought: the ready occasion for sinning, which a person deserves because of an evil will, and which God in just judgment sets before him. A human being’s acting well or badly is therefore called willing good or evil, because the human will is free for either the one or the other without external assistance. Sin at the door in order to go out is a perverse will, which cannot be hidden but must sometime emerge and appear through some sign. Its desire will be under you. That is, it will be in your power to guard yourself either against the inner perverse will or against the external occasion of sin.

Where is Abel, your brother? The Lord everywhere requires confession, lest the will be able to excuse itself. The voice of blood, etc. Because it demands vengeance, it cries out. A wanderer, namely by changing dwellings; a fugitive, through fear. My iniquity is greater. See how sin always increases: first he committed fratricide; then, wishing to conceal the deed by a lie, he denied it; now, convicted of the crime, he despairs. From the face of the earth and from your face. He thinks every human consolation is being taken from him—namely, human kindness and divine converse. Whoever kills Cain. To his own harm, because I will him to be punished sevenfold: that is, punishment will be inflicted upon you temporally, or Cain’s killer will be punished in many ways—indeed, more than Cain, because of God’s prohibition of homicide, which had not been given to Cain. In [Col. 0044D] Cain, a sign: that is, a trembling of the limbs, like that of one *fanaticus*, that is, frenzied [spastic, i.e. shaken and unable to stand], whereby he appeared worthy of mercy, because he had been struck by God’s wrath and excommunicated.

Cain knew his wife, who conceived and bore a child. After sin, men are said to know their wives and wives to conceive and bear; this indicates both that children were born sinners and that all these descendants of Cain are marked as having been sinners by their own deeds. I killed a man for my wound. An ancient tradition of the Hebrews holds that Lamech was blind, yet devoted himself to hunting by means of a certain device [Col. 0045A]—namely, a bow that does not miss: whatever animal touches its taut string draws the bow and is wounded. If it is asked why he hunted when eating meat was not permitted before the flood, we answer: for the skins of animals, from which they made shoes and leather garments. Therefore, when on one occasion Lamech and the boy guiding him were hunting, and Cain, like a madman, ran through that place, Lamech killed him by following his guide’s direction. Then, angered by this, he killed the boy who had been guiding him. Therefore he laments both killings to his wives in this manner: “I killed a man,” etc. Sevenfold vengeance, etc. As though he said: “Cain was greatly punished, but Lamech will be punished much more greatly.”

There is also another opinion concerning Lamech’s lament. [Col. 0045B] [Note: [Col. 0045D] Petrus Bongus also touches upon other interpretations not to be despised in his work *On the Mystical Numbers of Sacred Scripture*, under the numbers 7 and 77.] Some say that Lamech’s two wives continually mistreated him without cause. Thus, angry on one occasion, he met them and addressed them in these words: “Hear, wives of Lamech,” etc. “Have I killed a man, or committed some other crime for which I ought to be treated in this way? Certainly sevenfold vengeance will be taken upon Cain”—that is, Cain’s killer will suffer a great penalty—“but a much greater penalty will be inflicted upon you on my account.” He began to call upon the name of the Lord. Either by inventing a new form of worship or new prayers for calling specially upon God, or images for representing God and loving him more.

(GEN. V.) This is the book of the generation, etc. [Note: [Col. 0045D] Please see the annotations of F. Sixtus on this chapter, [Col. 0046D] in Book V, Part II of his Bible.] He recapitulates in order that, Cain’s offspring having been rejected, the propagation of the human race through Seth may be shown. And he called [Col. 0045C] their name Adam. At first Adam was their common name; afterward the man alone retained it as his proper name. He begot in his image: a mortal begot a mortal; or body begot body, not soul soul. This one will console us from the works and labors of our hands, etc. This is a prophecy: by “works” sins are signified, and by “labors” the penalty of sin. Or, “he will console us”—namely, after the human race has been destroyed by the flood, it will at least be restored through this man; the flood will be inflicted by divine vengeance because of the works of our hands and our labors. In the ground which the Lord cursed when speaking to Adam: “Cursed is the ground in your work.” When Noah was five hundred years old, he begot—that is, he began to beget—not that he fathered the three at once, but in succession.

[Col. 0045D] (GEN. VI.) When the sons of God saw, etc. [Note: [Col. 0046D] The aforesaid F. Sixtus makes very fine annotations on this chapter in Book V of his Bible.] In Hebrew it is, “sons of angels,” whether good or apostate angels, whom some think to have had intercourse with women and to have begotten the strongest and largest men. My spirit will not remain—that is, the spirit which I gave man for life, namely the soul. Because he is flesh: that is, the whole human being depresses the whole human being and reduces the spirit to animality, whereas the spirit should instead have raised flesh to spirituality. One hundred and twenty years, etc. Just as he threatens Hezekiah with imminent death and, because he relents, postpones death, so he had granted these people a period of one hundred and twenty years for repentance; and because they became worse through patience, the granted period is shortened (Isa. 28). Nor does God’s counsel change in any of these cases, but only the sentence. Likewise, his general statement, “My spirit will not remain in man,” does not conflict with the fact that Noah, the eighth, is preserved by his mercy: he threatens universally, yet as one benign he punishes only in part. Giants were on the earth, so that their enormous bodies might signify the pride of their minds. Mighty ones from of old: that is, mighty in worldly matters; or, such mighty ones as had not been seen from the beginning of the world.

But God saw that great was their wickedness, etc. He repeatedly mentions and emphasizes their wickedness in order to show that God’s patience could not lightly have been moved to so great a destruction of the human race without a most just cause. He repented that he had made man. For he repented by changing what he appeared to have begun in paradise, where he spoke thus to human beings: “Increase and multiply, and fill the earth.” Foreseeing for the future. Not that he now came, through imprudence, to something he had not expected—for nothing is hidden from him—but he who prevents a thing from happening foresees it no less than the person to whom it is forbidden diligently avoids it. Touched with pain of heart. Note: pain arises only from the loss of something loved. Hence, when we lose a thing about which we do not care, we say, “It does not touch our heart.” Therefore, the deeper the love, the more deeply the pain touches. Here, however, the destruction of a beloved thing is at issue, and therefore great pain is rightly said [Col. 0046C] to be present. From man to animals. He displays the greatest wrath of God, passing from the greatest to the least, and then from the lowest to the highest.

These are the generations of Noah—namely, the sons already mentioned; and he repeats them again in order to add: “The earth was corrupt before the Lord,” etc. He repeats and emphasizes all this to display the increase of wickedness and the just wrath of the avenger. When he says “before the Lord,” note the role of the judge: God is said to know as judge, who is said not to know a thing unless it has been proven before him; although he knows it in himself, he does not know it for vengeance. This crime, however, was so manifest that it needed no proof; or “before the Lord” means before the Lord who observed their sin. For they sinned so heedlessly that they did not even consider it sin. The end of all flesh, etc. According to the universal desert of sinners, a universal punishment of all would follow; but through mercy it is moderated in part.

Three hundred cubits. A cubit properly measures a foot and a half; but Moses here speaks of the geometric cubit, which he knew in Egypt and which contains nine complete cubits. Hence it is clear that the ark was of such size as to suffice for receiving all the animals that came to it. There are differing opinions as to the ark’s construction: whether it was broad below and, rising to the top, became narrower and narrower, or whether its walls rose equally, or even stood farther apart above than below, and only the roof was peaked [Col. 0047A]. Upper chambers, that is, terraces, from *coena*, “meal.” *Tristega*, that is, three-storied divisions according to the length of the compartments, said from *tris*, “three,” and *stega*, a place where one stands in a ship. You shall bring two into the ark. Here he notes the pairing of male and female.

(GEN. VII.) You shall take seven each. [Note: [Col. 0047D] Do not hesitate to consult the annotations of the aforesaid Holy Bible, Book V, Part II, on this chapter of Genesis.] Here he notes the number: seven in every kind, not fourteen; likewise two from each unclean kind, not four. All the fountains of the great deep were broken open, etc. It is asked whether the flood was produced solely from the waters then existing, or whether the air and other elements were changed [Col. 0047B] into waters, both rainwater and flowing water, by which the flood was made. This is indeed doubtful, as is also the question whether, when waters are raised upward in vapor to moderate the upper heat, water below is diminished or the same quantity remains there. The floodgates of heaven were opened. Some hold that the firmament was opened and the waters above the heavens descended through rains; this too is doubtful.

(GEN. VIII.) But God remembered Noah [Note: [Col. 0047D] See F. Sixtus’s annotations on Genesis 8 in Book V, [Col. 0048D] Part II, of his Bible], namely according to effect, not affection. He seemed to have forgotten because he had left him in danger for so long; now he is said to remember because he delivers him. After one hundred and fifty days. Namely, from Noah’s entry into the ark, that is, from the first day of the sixth month of the inundation. [Col. 0047C] For one hundred and fifty days make five full months, and this day is the eighteenth day of the seventh month of the year. The ark rested in the seventh month, on the twenty-seventh day. This is the twentieth day of the ninth month, namely of the year not of the inundation. For in the tenth month, namely of the inundation, on the first day of the month—which is the eighteenth of the ninth month—the mountain peaks appeared. And when forty days had passed, that is, after the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month, he sent out the raven, etc. He also sent out the dove, etc., seven days after sending out the raven. From this it is inferred that in the second sending of the dove he says, “having waited another seven days,” namely after the first sending. But she came to him in the evening, on the nineteenth day [Col. 0047D] of the first month of the six hundred and first year; but from the inundation it was the second day of the twelfth month, that is, forty days less. And he nevertheless waited another seven days, so that nine days of the twelfth month from the inundation might be completed; but it was the twenty-fifth day of the six hundred and first year.

Therefore, in the six hundred and first year, etc. Note that what follows in the coherence of the narrative cannot follow in the order of events. Rather, let us understand it as said by recapitulation, what the narrator had earlier omitted. But if anyone objects that in the [Col. 0048A] six hundred and first year, on the first day, Noah saw the surface of the earth dried, while we have already said that on the nineteenth day of that same month the dove brought a branch, though eight days earlier—that is, on the twelfth day of that same month—when sent out, it had found no place for its foot to rest, let him know that it is the dove’s nature that its foot cannot rest in mud. Nor is the earth called dried in this place because water was wholly absent, but because the force of the waters had withdrawn and no water remained except muddy water. Hence in the second month he says that the earth was dry, which is more.

(GEN. IX.) Your terror and dread shall be upon every living creature. [Note: [Col. 0048D] See the annotations of the aforesaid F. Sixtus in his Bible, Book V, Part II, on this Genesis chapter.] For even a lion is not so violent, unless provoked, that it does not fear a human being. It shall be food for you. Here it appears that human beings were not destroyed in the flood because of eating meat; therefore it is not food but its intemperate use that is condemned. You shall not eat flesh with its blood. He forbids this as a sign, so that they may understand that they ought to refrain from shedding the blood of human flesh, which it is not lawful to eat, when they are so strictly forbidden the eating of the blood of lawful flesh. And that this is to be understood as prohibited, he himself shows by adding, “For your lifeblood,” etc. Here properly is the prohibition of homicide through the penalty that he threatens; the preceding prohibition is a certain suitable preparation for making this one. For if beasts deserve penalty and retribution when they shed human blood—not through malice but through their beastliness and irrationality—how much more should a human being, who uses reason, suffer punishment if he sheds human blood? I will require it from the hand of beasts, so that at the resurrection the entire substance of a person may be restored to him, even though it had first passed into the substance of the beast eating the person. And from the hand of man, in two ways: either by restoring the substance or by inflicting vengeance.

I will remember my covenant—that is, I will cause you to remember, so that you may trust and not fear perishing again by a flood. Now Ham himself is the father of Canaan. This was stated beforehand because Noah was immediately to curse his grandson Canaan for the sin of Ham, Canaan’s father. The father’s shameful parts were uncovered. From this it appears that people in ancient times did not use breeches. He told his two brothers. [Col. 0048D] Ham’s great wickedness is shown: it did not suffice him that he alone had seen it, unless he also made others participants in his impiety. Cursed is Canaan. As if he said: “Just as I have no joy in you, my son, so may you be unable to rejoice in your own son.” He introduces the curse where joy is usually greatest, for parents especially rejoice in their children. And blessed be the Lord God of Shem. He blesses not Shem but his God, so that we may understand that every good thing is to be ascribed not to ourselves but to God.

(GEN. X.) These are the generations of Noah—those, namely, [Col. 0049A] that follow, divided into seventy-two patriarchs, peoples, and diverse languages: fourteen sons of Japheth, twenty-seven sons of Shem, and thirty-one sons of Ham, all seventy-two in number, whether counted as sons or peoples. From these the islands were divided. After the division of tongues, the earth was divided in this way: Japheth’s sons occupied the northern part of Asia and all Europe; Ham’s sons, the southern part of Asia and all Africa; while Shem’s sons possessed the middle of Asia, which is greater than Europe and Africa.

He began to be mighty in the earth. This Nimrod, surpassing other men in bodily size and strength, began by violence to exercise dominion over the rest. He led them into idolatry, so that they worshiped fire as a god, because he saw that the greatest benefits on earth came through the favor of the sun, which is fiery. The Chaldeans later followed this error. He committed manifold injury against both God and humanity: God alone ought to rule over humanity, but Nimrod took this away by interposing himself and reducing humanity to ignorance, depriving it of due worship; he injured humanity because he oppressed it under unjust dominion and led it into error by deception.

(GEN. XI.) The tower was made by his counsel and command. The wicked consented willingly; the better people, however, including Shem, Eber, and the other good men, consented under compulsion. The book says that the reason for making this tower was that, before they were divided into different lands, they might make something glorious for the remembrance of posterity. [Col. 0049C] Others say that they made it to guard themselves against a similar flood, so that God might not be able to harm them if he should again punish human beings through a flood. It may also be said that Nimrod built it through desire for kingship. Thus, once the languages were divided, he remained there with his household while the others departed, and Asshur was expelled, though that dwelling belonged to him by paternal right because he was descended from Shem, the elder son.

Asshur, departing for the land afterward named Assyria from him, multiplied until King Ninus, who sprang from his offspring. He founded a city and conquered Ham in war, who had lived until that time. Ham became king of Bactria, Ninus’s neighbor, and was called Zoroaster, inventor and author of the evil art of mathematics. Foreseeing the benefit of posterity against both floods, he also wrote the seven liberal arts [Col. 0049D] upon fourteen columns—seven of bronze and seven of brick. Ninus, having gained victory, burned his mathematical books. After this, made bolder, he attacked Nimrod, that is, the Chaldeans, and acquired Babylon, transferring there the seat of his empire. Hence the following text says: “Asshur went out from that land,” etc.

That he was called a hunter seems to mean that he tightly enclosed human beings just as a hunter does beasts. Thus, the proverb in common speech was formed in this manner: “You are cruel like mighty Nimrod,” etc. This is the great city—namely, Nineveh. From whom came the Philistines and the Caphtorim. These are peoples that proceeded from them, yet not after the division of tongues but before it, so that peoples might depart in their own languages; otherwise seventy-two languages would not be found. Nor can we say that these names were proper names of persons, because the book does not state whose sons they were. And the borders of Canaan came to be, etc. Moses, speaking to his own people, describes the borders of the land of Canaan because they were to possess it by God’s promise.

But Arphaxad begot Shelah. Note that according to Luke he had a son named Cainan, whom Luke placed in Christ’s genealogy [Col. 0050B] before Shelah. Therefore, unless we include this Cainan in the number of the others, the seventy-two will not be complete. These are the families of Noah. He repeats this generally concerning Noah’s generations in order to come to the division of languages through the pride of the tower. Note that all the preceding patriarchs, who descended from Noah’s three sons and begot the persons named above, had, besides those whom the book names, certain other unnamed sons who remained in their fathers’ own households. But the sons who are named established separate households from those of their fathers.

Aram died before Terah. [Note: [Col. 0049D] F. Sixtus has a fine annotation in his Bible, Book V, part, on this chapter.] Either he was put to death in the sight of his father by being cast into the fire which he refused to worship, or he died before his father died.

(GEN. XII.) Say, I pray you, that you are my sister. [Col. 0050C] It is asked why so just a man should have wished, by lying, to preserve the life of his body at the cost of the death of his soul; or to provide for his own life while neglecting his wife’s chastity—as though God could not equally preserve his life and the woman’s chastity. [Note: [Col. 0050D] F. Sixtus fully answers this question in his Bible, Book V, Part II, annotations on Genesis 22.] But it is certain that he did not lie, because she was his sister. Again, if one utters a word or gives a sign to signify what is not so, not for deception but for usefulness, correction, or rebuke, it is not called a lie. Thus the Lord himself pretended to be going farther with Cleophas and the other disciple (Luke, final chapter); yet he did not wish to leave, but to be detained, in order to rebuke and strengthen them. Likewise Elisha, when bound, said to those seeking him that he was not the one whom they sought and promised to lead [Col. 0050D] them to him; he led them into the midst of their enemies, as they had deserved before God. He was a messenger of the divine will, not his own, and is not accused of lying, just as one who reports another’s words is not. Or let us grant that Abraham lied: as a human being, this is not surprising, for he did not always speak truth. Did not blessed Peter lie through fear of death during the Lord’s Passion? But it must be known that the falls of holy men, when they occur by God’s permission, are set before us as a hope of rising again.

The Lord struck Pharaoh, namely with sterility. For during that period the Lord closed all Pharaoh’s wives and those of his household, so that they could not conceive. Pharaoh gave orders concerning Abraham to his men, namely that they should provide him a safe escort to take out all that he possessed, so that no one might harm him.

(GEN. XIII.) And there he called upon the name of the Lord. This can be understood in two ways: either that he called upon the Lord then, when he had made the altar, or now. If you go to the left. By granting Lot the power of choice, he removes from Lot’s mind the thought that Abraham wishes to leave him in order to choose and keep for himself the better part of the land. To you will I give it, and to your seed—that is, to you in your seed, not in your own person. Forever: not because they possessed it continually from that time onward, but because no limit is set for losing it [Col. 0051B] or having it taken away. Thus Melchizedek is said to have neither father nor mother solely because Scripture did not name them.

(GEN. XIV.) Chedorlaomer. [Note: [Col. 0051D] Consult F. Sixtus’s annotations on this chapter in his Bible, Book V, Part II.] He gathered all those who were distant to aid him against the five kings of Sodom who had rebelled against him. King of nations. It does not say of which nations, because he ruled over several. And against King Bela. This one is not named because he had sinned less than those named. But Melchizedek, bringing forth bread and wine. Among gentiles this is a sign of peace, as the olive branch also used to be. Note the order: bringing these forth, he blessed—namely, in relation to God Most High, to whom this belonged. For he was priest of God Most High. Or understand it thus: bringing forth bread and wine, which were not mere food [Col. 0051C] but a sacrifice; for he was a priest, etc. I lift up my hand. He was not greedy for earthly things. To the Lord God, who can give better things. From a thread of the weft. By this he denotes inward things. Even to a sandal strap. By this he signifies outward things, and jointly excludes everything.

(GEN. XV.) Lord God, what will you give me? He says this not from distrust but from a desire to know what ought to be given. And the son—that is, of the steward. This Damascus, etc. As though angry, he speaks elliptically.

(GEN. XVII.) That soul shall be cut off from the people. [Note: [Col. 0051D] See F. Sixtus’s annotations on that chapter in his [Col. 0052D] Bible, Book V, Part II.] If, upon reaching the age of discretion, he neglects to receive it, he will either be put to death or expelled from the people.

[Col. 0051D] (GEN. XVIII.) And when he had lifted up his eyes. [Note: [Col. 0052D] Likewise see the annotations of the same author on this chapter, Book V, Part II, of the Holy Bible.] He did not see them coming from afar; rather, they appeared suddenly, which is a sign of power. With life as companion. This is a manner of speaking: either, “with life accompanying you, because you will live,” and then it is also a promise. Why did your wife laugh? He rebukes the husband because it is his task to correct his wife. I will go down. God goes down when he involves himself in lower things. Will you destroy the just with the wicked? Cautiously, by this argument, he wishes to arrive at sparing even the unjust for the sake of the just; yet he asks whether God wishes to kill the just because of the unjust—which ought not to be.

[Col. 0052A] (GEN. XIX.) “Certainly not.” They do not refuse to enter the city; rather, by a rhetorical manner of speaking they imply that the citizens are unworthy hosts with whom they should lodge. “I shall not be able to do anything.” This is an expression of ordinary human usage, as though he said: “Since I have resolved to act thus, I cannot act otherwise.” “The Lord rained.” “From the Lord.” The Lord present upon earth rained from the Lord present in heaven: the Lord judging, from the Lord commanding. “Abraham rose early in the morning.” Note the holy man’s concern: he rises early in order to see whether the Lord had spared those for whom he had prayed. “He remembered Abraham.” Yet not in order to save the unjust for the sake of the just, but lest he destroy the just man for the unjust, as he had first promised Abraham. “But he did not perceive either when she lay down,” [Col. 0052B] etc. It seems remarkable that he lay with his daughter and did not perceive that he was committing such an act; but we may suppose that Lot had been accustomed to have his wife with him, and, having become drunk, thought that she was present. Thus, because of his drunkenness, he neither perceived nor considered that it was his daughter. Nevertheless both father and daughter sinned, although neither had a malicious intention. Moab, which is interpreted “from the father,” received this name because she had conceived him by her father. The other called her son Ammon, which is interpreted “son of my people”; and she did not disclose her crime so plainly, but merely indicated that she had conceived by someone of her own people.

(GEN. XX.) “Abraham departed from there into the southern country,” etc. “He sojourned in Gerar.” This seems [Col. 0052C] to have been said by recapitulation, because it says that Sarah pleased Abimelech on account of her exceptional beauty; and this does not seem true, since it was already stated above that she was old, spent, and that her womanly functions had ceased because of old age. It may also be said that, although she had advanced greatly in years, she had nevertheless not lost the great beauty which she possessed naturally. “But God came to Abimelech in a dream.” We must understand that the same happened with Pharaoh, although it is silent about it there. “The daughter of my father,” that is, the daughter of Terah. For some say that, after Abraham’s mother had died, Terah, Abraham’s father, took another wife and begot Sarah by her; and thus she was not the daughter of Aram. Or [Col. 0052D] it may be said that she was the daughter of Abraham’s father, that is, Terah, because she was his granddaughter. Or otherwise, “the daughter of my father,” that is, of him who is my brother. “This shall be to you as a covering of the eyes,” that is, for purchasing veils or head-coverings, so that you may no longer uncover your face and be loved by someone and taken, as has now happened. Or otherwise, “as a covering of the eyes,” that is, as a reproach and shame; for those who are ashamed of some deed are accustomed to cover their eyes, and it means that henceforth you should beware of an occurrence of this kind. Remember that you were found out in this, namely, when you said that your husband was your brother. “But when Abraham prayed, God healed Abimelech and his wife,” etc. What [Col. 0053A] is here added concerning Abimelech—that God healed him, his wife, and the maidservants whose wombs he had closed so that they might not bear children—must be understood as having happened in the same way to Pharaoh, although it is not stated there. Thus it is here disclosed by what scourge Pharaoh was scourged, namely sterility, and that he too was healed through Abraham’s prayer in the same manner as Abimelech.

(GEN. XXI.) “God opened her eyes, and she saw a well.” The well was not suddenly made; rather, one that had previously existed was suddenly seen by her.

(GEN. XXII.) “Take your only-begotten son, whom you love,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0053D] Consult Fr. Sixtus’s Notes on this chapter in his Bible, book V, part II.] By all these words he intends to inflame more and more the father’s natural love for his son, so that afterwards he may prefer love of God to his carnal love; and, once he has overcome it, the victory may be more glorious. [Col. 0053B] “On the third day, lifting up his eyes.” Since there are not three days’ journeys from Beersheba to Jerusalem, some say that the mountain upon which Abraham sacrificed was not the same as that upon which Christ was crucified. But those who say this are mistaken, as we believe. For Abraham could have made short stages, as a man who was deeply anxious both about the death of his son and about the Lord’s command, and therefore thought less about hastening his journey. “Your only-begotten son,” in relation to the free woman. “Your seed shall possess the gates of its enemies,” that is, they shall be strong and warlike, and thus shall take the cities of their enemies by force; or, because judgment is customarily rendered at the gates, it signifies that they shall be judges of their enemies.

(GEN. XXIII.) “But what is this?” As though he said: [Col. 0053C] “It would be a great thing for you, and I would burden you. Rather, do what you wish and give me nothing.” Or otherwise: “What is this?” As though he said: “Why, is this amount small in my view? I shall never be a seller for so small a price; rather, take it without payment.” “The double cave.” It was a kind of underground house in which there was an upper chamber; many could be buried in it in separate graves, both below and above. Ephron, who sold it, did not sin; nor did Abraham, who bought it. Nor would anyone sin even today if he bought a plain field in order to make a cemetery there; but one who sells a cemetery commits a grave sin.

(GEN. XXIV.) “O Lord, God of my lord.” [Note: [Col. 0053D] Consult the aforesaid Notes on this chapter in his Bible, book V, part II.] He speaks according to the opinions of the nations, each of which had [Col. 0053D] its own gods. “Therefore the girl to whom I shall say,” etc. This is divination; yet he does not sin, since he did it at the prompting of the Holy Spirit. “She set down the pitcher upon her arm”: she lowered it from her shoulder down over her forearm, so that he might drink more conveniently. “To wash the camels’ feet,” that is, to wash them, lest dirt harm them. “Bread before him.” This notes that in the Old Testament food is scarcely ever said to be set out except as “bread”—not because they lived on bread alone, but because bread is the principal item at table, and especially because it signifies the principal and spiritual bread. “He answered [Col. 0054A] him,” namely Bethuel, the girl’s father. “And the Lord has blessed my master.” Throughout this whole speech he seeks to persuade the parents to be willing to give their daughter to Abraham’s son, because he is loved by God, rich, young, heir-to-be of all his father’s inheritance, and finally because he had come by divine guidance and, perhaps, by chance. From all this God’s will had been proved, and it ought not to be opposed. “And if they do not give her to you.” See how he almost places the burden of refusal upon them if they do not assent to what Abraham not only desires, but to which the Lord also directs. “If you show truth and mercy.” He often joins these two: truth is where a thing is equitable; mercy, where it may be refused and there is no one to compel it. “The matter is from the Lord.” He responds to that argument [Col. 0054B] which is the strongest. “For Rebekah as a gift,” as it were, as earnest money. “Let us ask her own will.” From this arose the custom of seeking consent in betrothals. He loved her so much as to temper grief, though not wholly remove it; nor was this said for the sake of lust, but of consolation.

(GEN. XXV.) “All that they possessed.” He gave Isaac the chief capital—such as houses and buildings. “Sell me your birthright.” Either the firstborn animals, which fell to the elder beyond his allotted share, or the priestly dignity was called the birthright. For we cannot understand this of the paternal blessing. In what follows Esau will say: “Behold, a second time he has supplanted me: he has taken away my birthright; now likewise he has stolen my blessing.” “Behold, I am dying,” as though he said: “I shall not [Col. 0054C] live forever, but shall die, and I do not know when; what then will the birthright profit me?” “Swear to me, therefore.” He does not trust him to keep the agreement without an oath. “And with a dish of lentils.” Here he shows what the aforesaid stew was.

(GEN. XXVI.) “He dug wells by the torrent of Gerar.” [Note: [Col. 0054D] See Fr. Sixtus’s Notes on this chapter in his Bible, book II, part II.] For there is no water in a torrent except briefly after rain, and it immediately fails. “Now the Lord has made room for me.” It is clear that they regarded a well in a dry foreign land as a great blessing.

(GEN. XXVII.) “So, blessing him, he said to him: ‘You are,’” etc. [Note: [Col. 0054D] See the same author’s Notes on Genesis XXVII, in the same place.] He does not yet give the blessing; rather, it is a preparation for the blessing that he asks: “Are you my son Esau?” and the other things which follow. *Fragrance* is said from *fragrant*, and that from *breaking* [Col. 0054D], for fragrant things emit a stronger smell when broken. “Like the scent of a field full,” namely, of fragrant flowers. “Which the Lord has blessed,” by conferring a great abundance of such flowers. “May God give you of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth.” Here is contained a blessing of temporal things, which principally consists in these two joined together, namely the dew of heaven and the fatness of the earth. For if it rains but the ground is not fertile, or if it is fertile but it does not rain, there is no complete abundance. And it should be noted that [Col. 0055A] this blessing took effect not according to the intention, indeed, but rather according to the words. Thus, if a bishop, thinking he was ordaining one of the clerics of his own church, ordained a cleric of another church who resembled him, then the one who fraudulently presented himself would truly be ordained, not the one whom the bishop thought he was ordaining. It is also asked whether, if by some deceit a woman is substituted for a man to marry, while he thinks that he is marrying another woman, the marriage should be valid. But it must be known that it should not be held valid, because in marriage whatever must be binding is made ratified by the consent of both alone. If, however, both afterward wish to consent, there will be a marriage, and it is considered valid. It must also be known that among the ancient patriarchs this grace was granted them by the Lord, [Col. 0055B] that whichever son they blessed would increase even in temporal things above his brothers. “I have made him your lord.” Here it appears that he cannot alter the blessing once given. “In the fatness of the earth and the dew of heaven shall your blessing be.” As though he said: “You shall receive a share, not an imperfect portion.” “If Jacob takes a wife,” etc. He does not wish to reveal Esau’s hatred to him, lest the father should hate his son Jacob.

(GEN. XXVIII.) “He took of the stones that lay there,” etc. [Note: [Col. 0055D] See the same author’s Notes on Genesis XXVIII, in the same place.] It is likely that Jacob was not traveling there alone, because he slept outside the city which had formerly been called Luz and was later called Bethel by him, on account of the vision he saw while sleeping near the city with a stone placed beneath his head. “How terrible [Col. 0055C] is this place!” Worthy of reverence, namely with fear because of the majesty seen there. “He set it up as a pillar,” namely, as a sign and memorial of his vision. “And this stone which I have set up,” etc. He calls both the city and the stone itself “the house of God,” that is, Bethel.

(GEN. XXIX.) “He removed the stone with which the well was closed.” From this too it is clear that Jacob was not alone, but had brought companions from his father’s household with him. “He wept aloud.” This is a sign of affection. “Having heard the reasons for the journey”: not that he had gone into exile out of fear of his brother, but that he had come to take a wife from his own kindred. “My mouth and my flesh.” These are words of affection, as though he said: “Whatever reason has brought you here, it is right that I receive you.” “You wished to do this.” Why have you inclined yourself to this intention, [Col. 0055D] as though he said: “What have I done to deserve this from you?”

(GEN. XXX.) “Am I in God’s place?” [Note: [Col. 0055D] See Fr. Sixtus’s Notes on the chapter in his Bible, [Col. 0056D] book VII.] That is, in God’s place, so that I may restore what he has taken away? “He slept with her, and God heard.” In this it appears that he purchased intercourse not from lust, but solely for the sake of offspring. For God would not hear dishonorable vows. “I want nothing,” namely, to receive now from what is yours. Or: no fixed reward, but what God may give me according to a definite agreement. “And all that shall not be spotted,” etc. It is understood: “if I take them.” “You will accuse me of wrongdoing.” “Jacob separated the flock,” [Col. 0056A] namely, separating the rams from the ewes until the time of watering, so that the rams mounted the ewes only when both saw the rods in the troughs.

(GEN. XXXI.) “For I have seen all that Laban has done to you.” See how, by a divine response, it appears that he did not sin by any fraud, because it was just that he should receive a different payment than the wives whom Laban ought to have given him freely.

(GEN. XXXIII.) “As though I had seen the face of God.” He flatters him lest he die. “So Esau returned that same day by the route by which he had come, to Seir.” It does not seem true that with so great a company he returned all the way to Seir in one day; rather, he set out for it that day, but did not arrive there on the same day.

[Col. 0056B] (GEN. XXXIV.) “When the pain of wounds is most severe.” Perhaps he touches upon the physical explanation that on the third day the pain of wounds is more severe.

(GEN. XXXV.) “Cast away the foreign gods,” etc. Perhaps some persons among Jacob’s company worshipped foreign gods. Or otherwise: it was customary among those ancients, although they believed in one God alone, nevertheless to possess certain images which they revered—not believing them to be gods, as idolaters do, but in order to remember through them the supreme God. Yet Jacob now forbids these images, lest they turn to something worse and his household possess them. “And pouring out oil.” On this second occasion he now pours out oil.

(GEN. XXXVI.) “But he took his wives and sons,” etc. Why does it say that after the death of his father Isaac [Col. 0056C] Esau took all the possessions he had in the land of Canaan to Mount Seir and thereafter remained there, when it had already been said that Esau was living on Mount Seir? He had even departed from there to meet his brother Jacob; and again, leaving his brother, he returned there to dwell. We may answer that he came with his wealth to celebrate his father’s funeral; or, rejoicing at his brother’s arrival and wishing to dwell with his brother, he came into the land of Canaan and remained there until his father’s death. Afterwards he withdrew to Mount Seir, which is what is now said. “Now these are the kings who reigned in the land of Edom.” It is likely that, after the Law had been burned by the Babylonians, this section was added to the Law at its restoration [Col. 0056D] by Ezra, who could know which kings had preceded Saul, king of Israel, among the people of Esau. For it seems frivolous to say that Moses related this through the spirit of prophecy. “And these are his generations.” He returns to the generations of Jacob previously introduced, in order to pursue them.

(GEN. XXXVII.) “A tunic woven in many colors with varied threads and strands.” [Note: [Col. 0055D] Consult the aforesaid Fr. Sixtus’s Notes on this chapter in his Bible, book VII.] From this and many other concurrent causes, envy was formed and increased; for the Lord provides occasions for sinning to those who have deserved them. Hence above: “If [Col. 0057A] you do evil, sin will at once be at the door.” “I saw as it were the sun and the moon.” The dream alludes to this: if his mother were alive, she, like his father and brothers, would adore him. “Shall I and your mother?” His father says this in order to show that the dream is without an interpretation, because it cannot apply to his mother that she should adore him; and by this he intends to soften the brothers’ envy. “And sitting down to eat.” Reuben was absent. Without his knowledge, a new plan was devised to sell him; Reuben, however, had intended secretly to draw him out from the cistern and restore him to his father. Hence he grieved deeply after he did not find him there. “Resin and stacte.” Resin is called whatever remains from a tree, whether liquid or hardened like gum. Stacte is the flower of myrrh; it is also called *gutta* (“drop”) and aloe. “Midianites and Ishmaelites”: the same people; [Col. 0057B] or, if distinct, merchants from both peoples were present, who sold Joseph.

(GEN. XXXVIII.) “At the same time Judah went down.” [Note: [Col. 0057D] Consult Fr. Sixtus’s Notes on this chapter in his Bible, book V, part II.] He returns to relate matters concerning the other sons of Israel. “An Adullamite man.” This man was Judah’s shepherd, and yet he took the man’s daughter for his wife. “Go in to your brother’s wife.” Note that they observed many practices before the Law which were afterwards written into the Law: for example, the command that a son should go in to his brother’s wife, and the command in what follows that Tamar be burned as though caught in adultery. A *theristrum* is a garment so fine that a woman can see others through it, though her face cannot openly be seen. The woman conceived from one act of intercourse. Judah cannot be excused from having sought intercourse from lust alone, [Col. 0057C] because he thought her a prostitute; Tamar, however, is excused because she so greatly desired offspring.

(GEN. XXXIX.) “Nor did he know anything else except the bread which he ate,” that is, the Egyptian had no concern for any of his possessions. Rather, he had entrusted everything to Joseph, being ignorant—that is, taking no concern—of anything else apart from the bread he ate. Or it may be said that, although Joseph served in this way, he derived no profit from his service except his food.

(GEN. XL.) “For otherwise they were in charge of the cupbearers,” etc. As though he said: “It is no wonder that he was angry with these men, because in the royal household they were in charge of such duties as could easily give him offence.” This is the interpretation of the dream. Today we are not permitted [Col. 0057D] to interpret any dream; rather, it is forbidden.

(GEN. XLI.) “No one shall move hand or foot,” etc. This is hyperbolic speech, signifying the greatness of his authority. Or we may say that “to move hand or foot” here means to undertake major affairs, such as building a tower or changing one’s dwelling, whether by leaving or entering Egypt. When he says, “I am Pharaoh,” he confirms what follows as though swearing by his own name. “He clothed him in a linen robe.” A *stola* is so called from the Greek *stolon*, “long”; it is a long garment covering the whole body down to the ankles, also called a *talaris* or *poderis*. The garment now used by priests is called an *orarium*, from praying, because no public prayer is made without it, such as exorcisms, absolutions, the blessing of water, and other things of this kind. [Col. 0058A]

(GEN. XLII.) “You are spies,” etc. Some matters are omitted here which will be stated later as though by recapitulation: namely, that Joseph first asked them whether they had a father, whether they had another brother, and their whole lineage in order. Once he knew these things, he wished to charge them with a crime, not maliciously, but in order that they might bring to him their brother Benjamin by the same mother. Even if he lied, it need not concern us, because he did not act maliciously. “And when one sack was opened in order to give,” etc. The same must be understood of the others, [Col. 0058B] as will be made clear later.

(GEN. XLIII.) “The man questioned us in order about our family.” It should not be believed that they lied to their father in order to defend themselves; rather, what had been stated above is now added here. “Until Joseph came in at midday,” etc. Here the frugality of the ancients is noted: they were not so gluttonous as to eat before noon, like those of whom it is said: “Woe to the land whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning!”

(GEN. XLIV.) “And in which he is accustomed to divine.” He pretends this in order to aggravate the charge of their wrongdoing, not because Joseph had truly involved himself in such wrongdoing. “Let it be according to your judgment.” Their judgment is that one should become a slave, because this is contained [Col. 0058C] in their proposal, although they had also proposed more. “Do you not know that there is none like me in knowledge of divination?” This is mockery. “You previously asked your servants,” etc. From this it is clear that they had not lied to their father when they said, “The man questioned us in order about our family,” because now, placed in such danger, they could not lie to him about a known matter.

(GEN. XLV.) “My glory.” He does not say this proudly, but for his father’s consolation and joy. “His spirit revived,” through consoling joy coming after desolation. “It is enough for me.” As though he said: “I care little about the glory of his ‘punishment’ (?), provided only that he lives.”

(GEN. XLVI.) “The Egyptians detest all shepherds [Col. 0058D] of sheep,” because they do not eat sheep, but rather worship them as a god, namely Ammon.

(GEN. XLVIII.) “God Almighty appeared to me at Luz.” He repeats this in order to show, through the blessing received from God, that he has authority to establish Ephraim and Manasseh as heads of families and to adopt them. “Rachel died.” He mentions this misfortune—that she died before her time—so that the increase of Rachel’s sons, whom he names here, may be a consolation for their mother’s misfortune. Or he excuses himself for not having buried Rachel, once dead, where he now wished to be buried. “And when Joseph had taken them from his lap,” that is, from their father’s embrace, Jacob bowed in worship, that is, humbled himself before God, prostrating himself [Col. 0059A] on the ground. “He placed Ephraim,” etc. Or we may say that Joseph humbled himself to receive the blessing for his sons. “And he blessed Joseph,” namely in his sons; hence the entire blessing is subsequently ascribed to the sons.

(GEN. XLIX.) “You are my strength.” You ought to have been my strength, and yet you have been poured out like water, that is, made as worthless as water poured from some vessel. “Do not increase,” that is, do not rise to the dignity of rule over the others which you ought by the law of birth to have obtained, had you not sinned. “Instruments of iniquity,” because, holding within themselves the perverse purpose of wrongdoing, they concealed and plotted like vessels. “Resting, you have lain down as a lion and as a lioness.” Metaphorically he indicates that he will be a strong warrior whom [Col. 0059B] no one will dare disturb. “The sceptre shall not be taken away,” that is, a certain dominion, such as that he was first to enter the Red Sea, or first to offer an offering in the desert when the tabernacle was built, and other slight precedence of this sort. “Until he comes who is to be sent.” In Hebrew it is: “Until Shiloh comes,” where Saul was anointed king by Samuel. The sense is: up to Saul, and after him Judah shall have the leadership, because he rescued Joseph from the hands of his brothers. What follows, “And he shall be the expectation of the nations,” the Hebrews refer wholly to Judah himself, concerning whom the Lord answered: “Judah shall go up for you into battle.” He calls the various tribes “nations.” “Binding his colt to the vine.” As though he said: there shall be such fertility in his vineyard that one ass will be able to be laden from one vine, [Col. 0059C] and will be tied to it until it is loaded. What follows, “And to the vine,” etc., is a repetition; and in Hebrew it reads, “and to the vine, the foal of an ass,” not “O my son.” “He shall wash in wine,” etc. This too is an exaggeration of fertility; “and in the blood of the grape” is likewise a repetition. Calling both cloak and robe by the name of any garment. “His eyes are more beautiful than wine.” In Hebrew it is “redder,” and according to the Hebrews it indicates the abundance of wine, which appears in the eyes of drinkers. “His teeth whiter than milk.” This too, according to them, indicates an abundance of sheep and milk, evident in teeth that have eaten it. “Zebulun on the shore of the sea,” etc. Here the place of his dwelling in the promised land is indicated. “Issachar, a strong ass.” This predicts that he will remain [Col. 0059D] on the borders of different regions and become a merchant, gaining much profit thereby; this is indicated when it says, “And he became subject to tribute,” not that he would become anyone’s slave. “He saw rest.” He calls “rest” the fertile land which he possessed, as he also implies by saying, “And the land, that it was very good.” “Dan shall judge,” etc. Lest this one too be deemed inferior to the others because he was the son of a handmaid, he says that he shall judge like the rest. He says this on account of Samson, whom he metaphorically calls both serpent and horned serpent, because, humble and walking upon the ground rather than mounted, he struck down many Philistine horsemen. The phrase “biting the horse’s hoofs” is a metaphorical allusion. “I shall wait for your salvation, O Lord.” As though he said: “Although he will be so great and of such character, he should nevertheless not [Col. 0060A] be thought the Messiah, that is, Christ; rather, I shall await another Savior.” “Gad, girded,” etc. This notes that Reuben, Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh crossed the Jordan before the others in order to acquire the promised land for their brothers; afterwards they returned again to their own land on this side of the Jordan, which they had requested because it was fit for pasture. Some nevertheless say that before all three returned together, after the promised land had been conquered, Gad alone returned to rescue his children and wives whom enemies had attacked while they were on campaign beyond the Jordan. They wish this to be understood from the words, “He shall be girded behind.” “Asher, rich in fatness,” etc. According to the Hebrews, this merely indicates the future abundance and luxuries. “Naphtali, a stag let loose.” A stag let loose is so called [Col. 0060B] because the land he received bore ripe grain earlier than the others. Hence at Passover the first sacrifice was offered and praise to God, which he calls “words of beauty.” “Joseph, a growing son.” This indicates the double portion which his sons received, and also the portion which Joseph himself separately obtained. “Beautiful in appearance.” It hints at his beauty, because of which Egyptian women loved him; this is explained where it says, “The daughters ran along the wall,” namely to see him. But for the same reason men hated him, as is said there: “But they embittered him,” etc. Or this may be referred to his brothers, who envied him even though he would become so great. But from these evils the Mighty One of his father [Col. 0060C] Jacob—that is, God—delivered him. For his bow, namely Joseph’s, rested in the strong one, namely God; and the bonds, the hindrances, of his arms, and thence of all his works, were loosed by the hands of the Mighty One—that is, through divine operation. “They were loosed from there,” that is, by the Mighty One of Jacob’s father. He became in Egypt the shepherd of his entire household. And through this shepherd—though from God—Israel became a stone, that is, firm. Or, as it is in Hebrew: “From there he shepherded the stone of Israel.” “With blessings of heaven and of the deep.” In these two—that is, the upper good of heaven and the lower good of earth—he indicates complete abundance of temporal goods. “Of breasts and womb”: the order is reversed, and it indicates the blessing of conception and of nourishment; for one does not avail without the other. “The blessings have been strengthened”: [Col. 0060D] may your father’s blessings, beyond the blessings of those who preceded, namely Abraham and Isaac, who blessed their sons, be heaped upon Joseph through the blessing of his father Jacob. “Until the desire of the everlasting hills should come,” that is, until he comes who is desired by all nations, who is Christ. Or: “until the everlasting hills are joined to heaven,” which is what is found in Hebrew; that is, may Joseph be blessed everywhere, as one is accustomed to say, “So long as heaven and earth hold together,” that is, throughout the whole world. “On the crown of the Nazarite,” that is, of the one sanctified and held worthier among his brothers. “Benjamin, a ravening wolf,” etc. Because this tribe was very warlike; and, as is the custom of plunderers, what they acquired they immediately gave away lavishly, for one to whom wealth comes easily spends it easily. “With their own blessings,” [Col. 0061A] either for the greater part, according to Scripture’s custom, or because he gave each one, according to his merit, a blessing or a curse—yet rather by prophecy than by imprecation.

(GEN. L.) “They were born upon Joseph’s knees,” that is, Joseph held them upon his knees when they were born.

Repetition of certain passages that read differently in Hebrew.

“He drew his feet up upon the bed.” In Hebrew it is: “He bowed toward the head of the bed.” “His eyes more beautiful than wine,” that is, redder from wine or because of wine. “And his teeth whiter than milk,” that is, from milk or because of milk drunk. “Dan shall judge his people, as another tribe in Israel.” He says this because Dan was born of a handmaid, lest he be thought liable to rejection like Ishmael. Afterwards he does not repeat this concerning the other sons of handmaids, because he had said it first concerning this one, so that it may be understood similarly of the others. [Col. 0061B] “Naphtali, a hind let loose.” In Hebrew it reads “a hind let loose,” on account of Deborah, who ran impetuously to battle. “And giving words of beauty,” on account of her song, which she composed after the victory. “From there the shepherd, the stone of Israel, went forth.” In Hebrew it reads: “From there, shepherd, stone of Israel.” “Until the desire of the everlasting hills should come.” In Hebrew it is: “Unto the desire of the height of the age,” that is, unto that which can be desired more highly and greatly than anything else in this age.

End of the Explanatory Little Notes on Genesis.

CHAPTER VIII. The same author’s explanatory Little Notes on Exodus follow.

[Col. 0061C]

(EXOD. I.) “They built store-cities for Pharaoh, Pithom and Rameses.” In Hebrew, where we have “store-cities,” there is a word which, by shifting a point now to the right and now to the left, is pronounced either *miscenoth* and means “of the poor,” or *miscenoth* and means “of storehouses.” According to the implication of the first pronunciation, the sense is that cities of the poor were built: cities formerly weak and dwelling-places of poor people were made stronger through the labor of the Hebrews. But according to the sense in which *miscenoth* means “storehouses,” the meaning is that cities were constructed so strong that the king’s treasures could be stored there for safekeeping because of the site’s strength—whether there had previously been cities there or not. “To the Hebrew midwives.” Some say that these two, Shiphrah and Puah, were Hebrews; hence they preferred to preserve the children rather than [those who were] Egyptian women. Their piety was therefore more commendable. But it is asked how only two midwives could have sufficed for the entire kingdom. The answer is that these two were leaders and had many subordinate midwives under them. They did indeed lie, but their lie was venial because of their piety. They showed mercy to the infants, but because of the lie their merit was diminished and converted into a temporal reward. Thus each in some sense lessened the other and reduced it to a middle condition: the fault of lying diminished the merit of piety, just as piety diminished the condemnation due to the lie. “He built houses for them”: [Col. 0062A] by granting abundance or children. Otherwise: “He built houses for them,” namely, Pharaoh built houses for the Hebrews, because he wished those who had been gathered in Goshen to dwell scattered throughout Egypt, so that male children born might more easily be oppressed by the Egyptians.

(EXOD. II.) “The bank”: the hollow of the riverbank. “Moses arose and defended the girls.” It is clear from this undertaking, which could not have been carried out by one person, that Moses was not alone but had brought companions with him. “He swore,” that is, he entered into an agreement after many words had been exchanged between them concerning other matters before they reached the agreement, words which are nevertheless omitted.

(EXOD. III.) “The place on which you stand is holy ground.” For no other reason than the divine presence. “You shall have a sign when you have brought them out.” How could something future and remote be a sign for something he was about to do shortly? [Col. 0062B] We say, therefore, that “you shall have a sign” means this, namely, that I have sent—that is, am sending—you, shall be a sign to you that you will bring the children of Israel out of Egypt; so that “when you have brought them out” begins another narrative. “I am who I am.” As though he said: “I shall not tell them my name—those, namely, who ought to know my name”; and this is said ironically, as though he said, “Is my name unknown?” Or thus: Do not distrust what you are to speak or say to him, because I am he who is with you, that is, by whose help you shall perform those miracles. Or otherwise: “I am he who is immutably”; whose proper name is *Being* (*ENS*). “He shall ask for vessels of silver.” The Hebrews relate that the children of Israel enjoyed such favor from the Lord among the Egyptians that they asked for their vessels as gifts, and the Egyptians gave them. Our interpreters, however, say it is more likely that they received them on loan. [Col. 0062C]

(EXOD. IV.) “I am not eloquent from yesterday and the day before yesterday.” Note that God spoke to Moses at intervals of time. Hence he says, “From yesterday and the day before yesterday I am not eloquent,” in comparison with God. Some say that Moses was not eloquent because he had long remained in the land of Midian, and had therefore somewhat forgotten the Egyptian language. Aaron, however, always remained in Egypt; thus he is given as Moses’ interpreter before Pharaoh. “Who made the mouth of man?” As though he said: “He who gives a mouth can give words.” “Who made the mute and the deaf, the seeing [Col. 0062D] and the blind?” To one I gave the instrument; to another, the instrument and, along with the instrument, the function. Therefore, he who gave sight to the eye can give speech to the mouth: go on, then. “In which he shall perform signs”: not only those which he performed for Israel, but also those which he performed before Pharaoh. He seems here to have distinguished all these, but Scripture passes over them here lest it tell them twice. “Those who sought your life.” The Pharaoh then reigning was not the one from whom Moses fled when he went into Midian. “And you shall say to him: Thus says the Lord God: I said to you,” etc. These are the words which Moses spoke to Pharaoh in the final plague. Hence he places here words in the past tense, by which it is signified that other threats had preceded them, such as: “I said to you, and you refused.” With these words, in the final plague he reproaches Pharaoh for contempt of God in the preceding [Col. 0063A] warnings. “She circumcised the foreskin of her son.” Why does it not say “of her sons”? Because perhaps the mother had retained for herself, as her own, one son—the elder—uncircumcised. Moses, however, had circumcised the other, as though his own; this is also suggested by the interpretations of their names. Or perhaps they were taking only the elder son with them and had left the younger with his grandfather.

(EXODUS V.) And those who were set over them were scourged. Note that there were different kinds of overseers: some were Hebrews, who were beaten; others were Egyptians, who beat them and violently exacted labor from the Hebrew overseers themselves.

(EXODUS VI.) “And I did not make known to them my name Adonai.” As though he said: Although I, who am almighty, [Col. 0063B] appeared to them, I did not make known to them my strength and power, to which my name *Adonai* belongs; rather, I made known mercy or wisdom, to which *El* and *Elohim* belong. Or thus: I did not make known to him the name *Adonai*, which I shall now make known by giving the land of promise to the children of Israel. Therefore, although until now I called myself Almighty, I had not yet shown myself to be Lord, as I shall now do, so that they may know that they rightfully possess what they receive through my gift.

“Over which I raised my hand.” It is the custom of one swearing to raise a hand toward sacred things, in order to confirm by them what he swears; thus God too is said to have raised his hand concerning that land, in order to confirm it as Abraham’s inheritance.

“These are the heads of the houses by their families.” Note that he does not set forth here all twelve tribes, but [Col. 0063C] only three, so that he may come to Levi, who was the third, and show that Moses and Aaron—of whom the present discussion is concerned—descended from him. This is why he says all this.

“This is Moses and Aaron on the day when,” etc. Lest, because these names are shared, they be understood to mean different persons, he identifies those meant: those who were present on that day when the Lord spoke to them about leading the people out of Egypt.

(EXODUS VII.) Pharaoh called the wise men and sorcerers. In this and the following miracles Pharaoh always has recourse to his magicians, testing whether they can do the same things that Moses did. For he did not think these things were done by divine power and will, but by Moses’ skill and sorcery; and thus, if they did the same things, he thought that for this reason he ought not to let [Col. 0063D] the people go.

“Each cast down his rod, and they were turned,” etc. All this was done by demons, either truly changing the forms of things, as they seemed to do, or rather deceiving human sight and thereby serving those men all the more, while deceitfully pretending that they were compelled by their incantations. But concerning the serpent which Moses made, there is no doubt that it was real and that it incorporated into itself the others which it devoured.

“He shall go out to the waters”: for the purpose of walking, upon the bank of the river, namely the Nile.

“And they did likewise”: in other waters.

(EXODUS VIII.) “This is the finger of God.” In this he sinned most grievously, because he did so knowingly.

“So that there may not be flies there.” The same must be understood of the other plagues.

(EXODUS X.) “I shall not see your face again.” Supply: unless you summon me first; for afterward he did see him when Pharaoh summoned him. [Col. 0064A]

(EXODUS XI.) “Therefore speak to all the people.” By recapitulation this must be understood as having been said, and as having already been announced by Moses to all the Hebrews: that on such a day, during the final plague, they should do this.

“And the Lord will give favor.” From this it is implied that it is true that they asked, not as a loan, but as a gift.

(EXODUS XII.) “This month shall be for you the beginning of months,” etc. What is said—that the Lord spoke—is all to be understood by recapitulation: namely, that long before, the Lord gave Moses the commands, and through him informed the others concerning taking a lamb or kid on the tenth day, keeping it until the fourteenth day of the first month, and then sacrificing it; concerning smearing the lintel [Col. 0064B] and doorposts with the lamb’s blood against the destroying angel, who was to pass through Egypt and kill Egypt’s firstborn on that same fourteenth night; and concerning many matters connected with these. They necessarily had to know these things beforehand, in order to be ready to depart on that night.

“A male of one year.” It should be written in two words: that is, one year old.

“He shall take a neighbor”: yet in such a way that the person taken in does not therefore cease to sacrifice his own animal.

“You shall take also a kid.” Whoever does not have a lamb should at least sacrifice a kid according to the rite of the lamb.

“The whole multitude shall sacrifice it”: not that all should sacrifice one animal, but that no household should lack its own.

“For it is the Passover,” not because the children of Israel were passing over, but because the Lord was passing over in the destroying angel; [Col. 0064C] as the following text indicates, namely: “And I shall pass through.”

The addition, “on that night,” rather than “on this night,” is a sign that everything previously said here concerning the paschal lamb and the connected matters is said by recapitulation.

“You shall have this day as a memorial.” Here he gives the command concerning the future celebration of Passover in remembrance of this event. All this, like the preceding material, is here spoken by recapitulation, as is noted there: “For on this same day I shall bring out the host,” etc.

“None of you shall go out,” etc. From this it is evident that they received permission only during the night; they departed on the fifteenth day.

“And, bowing down, the people worshiped,” etc.: namely, when they heard these commands of the Lord through Moses. And after departing from the assembly which Moses had held, they did as [Col. 0064D] he had commanded when the appointed time arrived—namely, in the middle of the night, etc. As though he said: the Lord fulfilled what he had previously promised through Moses.

“There was no house in which there did not lie a dead person.” It is remarkable if every house had someone firstborn. But there could have been one among the herds or flocks even if none was present among humans; or the statement may be qualified: there was no house in which there was a firstborn that lacked a dead person. Or perhaps the Lord then arranged matters so that in every house there was some firstborn.
