“So the people took the kneaded flour.” This was not done by God’s command, nor because of the urgency of the time, as some mistakenly think, since the Hebrews had learned long beforehand that they would leave Egypt on that day. Rather, it followed the custom of that land, where dough is usually kneaded and stored so that as much bread as is needed may be baked every day. [Col. 0065A]

“In one house”: that is, one lamb in one house, so that none of the meat is taken outside.

(EXODUS XIII.) “Consecrate to me every firstborn”: in exchange for the slain firstborn of the Egyptians. They were consecrated for the service of the Levites, so that they might redeem themselves through the Levites, who served the Lord in their stead, on behalf of all Israel.

“In a pillar of cloud and fire.” It was one and the same pillar: providing shade against heat and light against darkness, so that it might be a guide at both times.

(EXODUS XIV.) “Opposite Baal-zephon, before it.” That “it” may refer to Baal-zephon, and then the wording is straightforward; or it may refer to Pharaoh, so that the relative pronoun “it” is inserted before the thing to which it refers, contrary to ordinary usage, as in: “Its foundations are in the holy mountains” (Ps. LXVIII), etc. [Col. 0065B]

“And the angel of the Lord moved away.” At one time the action is attributed to the Lord, at another to the angel, because in truth the angel of the Lord was present as minister, while the Lord worked in him and through him.

“He went behind them,” to defend them through the cloud: by the same thing at once giving light to his own and darkness to the others.

“The Egyptians entered after them.” It is asked: if they did not see those going ahead because the intervening cloud blocked them, how could they follow? Or if they saw the miracle of the sea, how dared they pursue them? The answer is that they could not see them distinctly, but, because they perceived that they were leaving, they followed them little by little by another route, not knowing that they—or the Israelites—were entering the sea. [Col. 0065C]

“And behold, looking down upon the camp through the pillar.” What does it mean that God is said to look down upon the camp through the cloud, except that the cloud which had formerly caused darkness for the Egyptians gave them light? Yet all this was done for their confusion: namely, so that they might see themselves trapped.

“He destroyed the army,” etc. He briefly comprehends the whole affair and then repeats the same thing more fully, namely at: “And the Egyptians said,” etc.

“And when the Egyptians fled,” etc. First the Egyptians were routed and struck down by the Lord; finally they were overwhelmed by the waters.

(EXODUS XV.) “The depths covered them.” From excessive joy the same thing is often repeated in different ways.

“The depths gathered together”: that is, the profound masses of waves and waters.

“You blew with your spirit, and they were covered.” This indicates the ease of divine power. As though he said: as easily as someone scatters dust by blowing, so easily did you destroy them.

“The earth swallowed them.” Under one common name he calls the two lower elements, as also there: “When, therefore, all animals had been formed from the ground”; and elsewhere: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth,” etc. [Col. 0065D]

“The peoples rose up and were angry,” etc. Thus far the song concerns a past event. From this point onward, whatever follows is prophecy concerning the future. For from the great joy which they had in the present, the Holy Spirit entered their hearts, and all prophesied the same things.

“For ever and beyond”: that is, throughout the whole present age and also the future one. Or, throughout the whole span which began with the world and will end with the world; and “beyond,” not in respect of duration, but in respect of dignity—namely, above all and over all. [Col. 0066A]

“So Miriam took,” etc. This happened after the men had sung, so that the women also might sing what the men had sung.

(EXODUS XVI.) “In the evening you shall eat flesh, and in the morning you shall be filled with bread.” In the evening, when complete satiation is more suitable; in the morning, content with ordinary bread.

“Like something pounded with a pestle”: namely, like coarse meal crushed in a mortar, that is, with a pestle.

“But some of them left it until morning.” They distrusted that manna would be found on the following day.

“On the sixth day they gathered double food.” It seems that they gathered it through a miracle, because although God gave this command to Moses, Moses is not yet found to have commanded the people; rather, he replied to the leaders as though astonished. “This is the word which he commanded,” etc. Or we may understand that Moses did give this command, although Scripture has not yet said so. [Col. 0066B]

“Tomorrow, whatever must be done, do today; and whatever must be baked”—that is, whatever it would have been necessary to prepare or bake if it were not the Sabbath—do or bake today, because tomorrow is the Sabbath rest.

“How long will you refuse to believe my commandments and my law?” The Law had not yet been given, but he calls any commandment a law, as in the observance of the Sabbath and the measure of the homer.

“Like fine flour with honey”: that is, honeyed fine flour. Others, however, say that it tasted to each person like whatever he most desired.

“Fill a homer from it, and let it be kept.” This is said by anticipation.

(EXODUS XVII.) “Why do you test the Lord?” To test God is to ask something of him in order to discover, from a certain distrust, whether God loves a human being.

“Moses’ hands were heavy,” because he had stood all day with his hands raised. He was weary and could no longer lift his hands, nor even stand; therefore Aaron and Hur made him sit and raised his hands.

“At the edge of the sword”: in the force of the sword.

“Write this memorial in a book,” lest it be consigned to forgetfulness in the future. [Col. 0066C]

(EXODUS XVIII.) “When he had entered the tabernacle.” Some understand this to mean the tabernacle of the Lord, and say that it is said by anticipation. But this is unnecessary, for he never sacrificed in the Lord’s tabernacle, nor even entered it, because he was a Gentile.

[Col. 0066D]

(EXODUS XIX.) “On this day”: that is, on the third day, just as “in the third month.”

“I shall now come to you”: that is, on the third day from this one, when the Law was to be given.

“So Moses reported the words of the people to the Lord.” By brevity he omits the fact that Moses first brought God’s words to the people, and that the people agreed to do everything; but he immediately says that this agreement was reported to God by Moses. Or we may say that everything from the place, “And when Moses had reported,” etc., to this point is an interpolation, so that this verse should be connected in the order of the narrative with what precedes; and then the whole interpolation should follow in this way: “The whole people answered that they would do it; Moses reported this to the Lord. When he had reported,” etc. The Lord said to him: “I shall now,” etc.

“He shall be pierced with arrows.” Perhaps he would have said more explicitly, “with projectiles,” so that it may be understood that he is to be killed by blows of stones divinely flying against him. Moreover, he first stated: “No hand”—namely, no human hand—“shall touch him.”

“Do not go up onto the mountain; when the trumpet begins to sound, then they shall go up”: that is, they shall not go up until the trumpet sounds. Some maintain that it was a human trumpet established for the purpose of giving the people this signal of duty; but to me it seems more likely to have been divine.

What follows, “Then they shall go up the mountain,” is remarkable, since touching the mountain had previously been forbidden. They say, indeed, that touching was forbidden while the Lord was present, but that ascending was permitted, though not commanded, when he was absent or had withdrawn. According to this opinion, this is implied here, as also is the time when they were not to touch it. When ascending was allowed, it was indicated by a different sound of the trumpet. [Col. 0067B] [Col. 0067A]

But it seems more probable to me that here he says that they must by command go up the mountain as far as its foot, not to its summit. Hence, in what follows Moses is commanded to take care that the people do not cross the established boundaries—that is, that they do not ascend to the hill or to the summit—which was forbidden under penalty of death.

“And when they had washed their garments.” It seems strange to say that, after garments were washed, they would be ready on the third day from the washing, and then to command the washing afterward. But perhaps the order of sanctification was this: that they washed their garments immediately on the first day, then, abstaining from impurities and fasting, prepared themselves for the third day. This is what he wished to indicate.

“Moses spoke, and the Lord answered him.” Note the sequence. A little earlier he was leading the people out of the camp; here he is said to speak with the Lord, and immediately it adds: “The Lord descended and called Moses to the summit of the mountain.” Was Moses speaking with the Lord while he was below with the people? This should not be believed. Rather, the order of the narrative is somewhat confused, and it is as follows: while Moses was below, leading the people out, the Lord descended upon the mountain and called Moses to its summit; and thus they conversed. In this conversation Moses is commanded to descend to the people and warn them not to cross the appointed boundaries out of desire to see God, lest they die. [Col. 0067C]

Against this command Moses said to the Lord: “The multitude cannot go up,” etc.—as though he said, “They may not go up and hear you. Who, then, will hear you?” The Lord answers: “Go and descend; and you and Aaron shall again come up to me”—as though he said, “So that I may speak with you the things which the people cannot hear from me.”

Thus two utterances of God are noted: the first, which occurred in the Ten Commandments, addressed publicly to the whole people; the second, private, to Moses on the mountain’s summit. [Col. 0067D]

(EXODUS XX.) “I am the Lord.” He spoke this while all heard. Everything that follows as far as “You shall not take the name of your God in vain” belongs to the first commandment; from there to “Remember the Sabbath day,” etc., to the third.

“Visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation.” It is evident that this is properly said of those children whom fathers begot after committing their crimes. They are deservedly punished for their parents, like one of their members, because in those wrongdoers they were in some sense present seminally and sinned; hence the lame and blind are born because of their parents’ crime. [Col. 0068A]

The phrase “to the third and fourth generation” is used because parents commonly live that long and can see their descendants condemned because of their own sin. Or we may say that a definite number is used for an indefinite one, as likewise on the other side he shows mercy “unto thousands” to those who love him, etc. And there is no doubt that, because of the goodness of their fathers, the Lord acts more favorably toward their children.

“You shall sanctify the Sabbath day.” Four Sabbaths are mentioned in Holy Scripture: first, God’s Sabbath, in which he is said to have rested after completing his works; second, that which the people of Israel are commanded to observe; third, that which the people of God are commanded to keep spiritually; fourth, that which in the promise God pledges to his lovers: Sabbath for Sabbath. [Col. 0068B]

The first, God’s Sabbath, was only a sacrament of the second, that is, of the legal Sabbath; that Sabbath in turn was a sacrament of our Sabbath, in which we must cease from every evil work. But our Sabbath too is a sacrament and the merit of that future sabbatism, where Sabbath will be received for Sabbath. Therefore there are two outward Sabbaths, one God’s and one human; and two inward Sabbaths, one God’s and one human. The first and last are the Lord’s; the two middle ones are human.

“You shall not covet the house,” etc. If anyone wishes to make two commandments out of the first commandment, he will make this one commandment; but if he leaves the first undivided, he must divide this one into two, place the command concerning another man’s wife before that concerning another man’s possession, and not insert one within the other. [Col. 0068C]

“Moreover, the Lord said to Moses: ‘You shall say these things,’” etc. From this point the Lord speaks commands and judgments to Moses alone; all these are, as it were, an explanation of the ten commandments previously given.

“You shall make for me an altar of earth.” Yet in what follows it was made of bronze. But that altar too was filled only with earth when sacrifices were offered; and this is the Jewish interpretation of the altar.

[Col. 0068D]

(EXODUS XXI.) “And if anyone strikes a woman,” wishing to help another man against whom he is fighting.

“A son or a daughter”: not of the man whose ox it is, but of another person; this is evident from what he adds concerning the slave.

(EXODUS XXII.) “Especially if it had come as hired for the wage of its work.” As though he said: a person does not repay a thing received on loan when he loses it in the owner’s presence; and, above all, he does not repay a thing which he has hired and likewise loses in the owner’s presence. The text says that it “had come,” that is, had been sold—not indeed finally, but for the wage of its work: that is, the payment which its work, namely its use, demanded, so that “its” refers to the hired thing.

“It is the only thing with which he is covered.” He speaks here of the very poor person [Col. 0069A] who has only one garment and could not live if it were not returned to him. But lest the rich person lose his money, he may bring witnesses and return the garment to the other before them; afterward, if he wishes, he may seek payment.

(EXODUS XXIII.) “Nor shall you join your hand.” It denotes the custom of confirmation.

“You shall not decline in the judgment of the poor.” In this command he forbids contempt, lest someone abandon a legal case because the matter is insignificant.

“You know the souls of strangers”: that is, their feelings, how easily they are saddened.

“My name is in him.” I shall make my glory and power manifest through him.

(EXODUS XXIV.) “And he said also to Moses: ‘Go up to the Lord, you and Aaron,’” etc. Here is a confusion of order: for how is Moses commanded here to go up the mountain when, according to the proper sequence of the narrative, he is already on the mountain and alone hears the judgments which he is to proclaim to the people? But one must know that, according to the order of events, the entire following chapter from the words “So Moses came and told the people” through “Moses and Aaron went up,” etc., must be inserted here. Then this chapter agrees suitably, since Moses is commanded to ascend with those with whom he did ascend; and the second chapter, “So Moses came,” etc., agrees with the preceding narrative in which Moses sets out the things the Lord had commanded him. [Col. 0069B]

“Moses and Aaron went up,” etc. Here Moses went up for the third time. His first ascent was on the day when they came to Mount Sinai, whether in the first or third month, when they were instructed concerning purification in order to receive the Law on the third day. His second ascent was after the Ten Commandments had been heard from the Lord, in order to hear the judgments narrated thus far. Now he ascends for the third time, taking with him Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders of Israel, that they might be witnesses for him. Therefore all of them went up with him toward the middle of the mountain until they saw God, and immediately all except Joshua were ordered to return. Yet it is not wholly certain whether Joshua remained with Moses on the mountain during those forty days. [Col. 0069C]

What immediately follows—“The Lord said to Moses: ‘Come up to me on the mountain’”—must be understood thus: from the hill where he was, he was to proceed to the higher parts of the mountain. Yet he is not called to the actual summit even then, but in what follows, where it says, “On the seventh day,” etc.

“Wait here.” I do not think that he commanded them to wait upon the hill, but on the plain with the people, as the following text requires.

“If any questions should arise,” etc.

“And when Moses had gone up”: leaving Aaron and the elders, he advanced a little toward the summit, but did not approach it before the seventh day, when he would be called again. [Col. 0069D]

(EXODUS XXV.) “That they may take for me firstfruits.” By “firstfruits” he means not the first produce of crops, as the proper sense of the word would require, but a certain separated portion of each person’s money, set aside for divine work in building the tabernacle, just as firstfruits are usually set apart for God. It is as much as each is willing to give, not a fixed portion [Col. 0070A] such as a tithe; and this is indicated by the following text: “Whoever offers willingly.” For he does not wish them to be compelled, but that each should offer as much as he wishes.

“You shall make above it a golden crown all around.” This is improperly called a crown, for it is not round; rather, according to the form and dimensions of the ark, a certain surrounding rim—also called a border—was made around its upper part.

“You shall make for it a golden lip.” This lip was a certain descending rim, just as the aforesaid crown was an upright rim.

“A chased crown.” We say the same concerning this crown as concerning the above-mentioned one: namely, that it was a certain border attached to the table and sculpted from the table itself according to its dimensions. “Chased” must be understood to mean that it was artistically carved in the manner of a ring turned on a lathe. [Col. 0070B]

“And above it another small golden crown.” This indicates that it was made with plain workmanship, yet of gold, smaller than the lower one, and likewise continuously attached to it, almost as though it were the same thing.

Again, “a chased crown four fingers high”: that is, the circuit of the lip, which is called a crown not because it is round but because it surrounds.

But the words which follow, “and above it another small golden crown,” that is, golden, do not seem to be found in the Hebrew text.

“Below the golden crown shall be rings.” He has now called the two crowns, as it were, one crown, and shows the rings which were at the feet of the ark for carrying it, immediately beside the table, not down at the bottom toward the ground.

(EXODUS XXVI.) “With embroidered work.” AUGUSTINE: “Embroidery is a needle by which, after the cloth has already been made, gold or silver threads are inserted, so that gold embroidery [*auriphrygium*] or different figures may be produced in the cloth itself.” [Col. 0070C]

“And what remains over in the coverings,” etc. The construction is awkward, but the meaning is this: the surplus of the coverings beyond the curtains is one covering according to the length of the tabernacle; from one half of it one front of the tabernacle is made, and from the other half the remaining front, together with two cubits in the length of all the coverings, fully covering the sides of the tabernacle down to the ground.

“And one joint shall hold them all together”: that is, the same similar joining shall bind them all.

“You shall make five bars of shittim wood.” It cannot be maintained that the bars of the side and of the front were of the same length: the former were six cubits, whereas the latter were two.

“From top to top”: that is, in the middle between the two extremities. [Col. 0070D]

(EXODUS XXVII.) “You shall make for its uses”—that is, for the altar—pots to receive ashes, tongs, forks, and fire-pans. In the Hebrew it reads thus: “You shall make its pots, to receive its ashes, and its shovels, and its basins, and its hooks, and its fire-pans.” The shovels, namely, were for removing ashes; the pots for receiving them; the basins for pouring blood; the hooks for removing meat from cauldrons; and the fire-pans for carrying coals.

It follows: “And a grate.” Supply, “you shall make for it”: a bronze work in the form of a net, at whose four corners shall be four bronze rings. You shall place these beneath the rim of the altar; and the grate shall reach to the middle of the altar.

There is great uncertainty about this grate both among the Hebrews and among our own authorities, especially because the Hebrew text seems to differ somewhat from our translation. For it reads thus: “You shall make *nuchhar*, a work of bronze netting; and upon the net you shall make four bronze rings at its four ends or horns; and you shall give it, namely the *nuchhar*, or place it, namely the net, beneath the base of the altar from below, and the net shall extend to the middle of the altar.” [Col. 0071A]

Accordingly, under this reading *nuchhar* does not seem to mean a grate upon which meat was to be roasted. Rather, it is a square, perforated work, made on every side for lightness in the likeness of a vessel, in which the altar appears, as it were, to sit. The wall surrounding the altar rose to the middle of the altar’s height, and from its four upper corners [Col. 0071B] hung four rings; with poles inserted through them, the altar resting upon it was carried. For the altar is not said to have had other rings by which it was carried, apart from the rings of the net.

But whether this net was divided from and detachable from the altar, independently containing the lower part of the altar in its own base and enclosing the altar’s walls by surrounding them with its own walls; or whether it was joined by cast work below to the lower edge of the walls and, with its base at some distance in breadth from the walls all around, then raised its own walls to the middle of the altar—this is not sufficiently clear. The following arrangement, however, seems more suitable.

Some say that this altar had neither a covering above nor a base beneath, but only walls, which were filled with earth, in accordance with the words: “You shall make for me an altar of earth” (above, chapter XX). In its upper enclosure fire was built, on which the burnt offerings placed there were consumed. [Col. 0071C]

There were also those who maintained that a grate was placed between the altar’s walls, rising to the middle of its height; that beneath this grate a small inner hearth was formed; that fire was built there through an opening facing the eastern wall of the altar; and that meat placed upon the grate was thus roasted within, the smoke going out through the altar’s open upper mouth. To prevent any suspicion that the adjacent fire might burn the wooden inner walls of the altar, they assert that the same wood was fireproof.

But if those timbers must be thought to have been such that they could not be damaged at all either by water or by fire, it does not appear why they needed to be covered externally with bronze plates. Nor is it sufficiently clear how the grate itself could suitably have been placed inside with its poles, how the altar could have been carried with poles inserted through its rings, or how the grate’s rings could have been positioned beneath that inner hearth. [Col. 0071D]

(EXODUS XXVIII.) “You shall make in the breastpiece chains joined one to another.” “Joined one to another” should not be understood as though one chain were joined to another, but as describing the construction of a chain, in which rings are joined with rings or threads twisted with threads. Thus, where we say “joined,” the Hebrew has more expressly: “braided with braided and dense work.”

According to the Chaldee, it means “at the ends”: that is, placed at the outer or marginal corners, as it were at the boundary—that is, the end—of the breastpiece.

“You shall place in the breastpiece of judgment doctrine and truth.” For “doctrine and truth,” the Hebrew has *urim tumim*. *Urim* is interpreted “doctrine” or “judgment”; *tumim*, “truth.” Hence the lots formerly used to ascertain the truth were called *urim tumim*. Characters were inscribed in different letters; when these were cast, the combination of the letters appearing on top showed, by a true indication, what should be done or avoided: “You shall place in the breastpiece of judgment doctrine and truth,” namely, these names in its weaving. [Col. 0072A]

“Always before the Lord”: at the customary times when ministry was performed before the Lord.

“You shall make also a plate of purest gold, on which you shall engrave with the work of an engraver, ‘Holy to the Lord’”: namely, these two words. Where we have “Holy to the Lord,” the Hebrew has *anoth adonay*. But this name, namely *adonay*, is written with four letters—*he, ioth, beth, vau*—which is interpreted “this beginning of the passion of life,” and is called ineffable.

“Always upon his forehead”: namely, at the appropriate time.

“You shall bind the tunic made of fine linen”: that is, arrange or fit it.

“From the loins to the femora,” that is, the thighs: the flesh of shame extends only so far, although the breeches extend farther. [Col. 0072B]

(EXODUS XXIX.) “You shall sanctify the consecrated breast and shoulder.” Thus far what is said concerns the present consecration of Aaron and his sons; what follows concerns future, continuing custom: namely, because the priests offered the breast and shoulder from their peace offerings at their consecration, they should receive these same portions from the children of Israel from their peace offerings by a perpetual law.

“You shall sanctify”: that is, confirm. Note that the first ram was offered as a burnt offering; the second as a peace offering. Therefore the Lord had his portion, the shoulder and the fat; Moses, who offered it, had the breast; Aaron, whose offering it was, had the remaining flesh, which he took and ate with his sons in the court of the tabernacle, as the children of Israel would afterward do.

“And it shall be Holy of Holies”: that is, holy for offering holy victims in sacrifice. [Col. 0072C]

(EXODUS XXX.) “Of another composition”: other than the one of which I am about to speak.

“When you take the sum of the children of Israel”: that is, when you number them, which will occur in the book of Numbers.

“And he specifies the measure of cassia, myrrh, and oil of calamus”: that is, of each kind.

“You shall make no other”: namely, for common use. [Col. 0072D]

(EXODUS XXXI.) “Behold, I have called by name Bezalel,” etc. From this an insoluble question arises for me. [Note: [Col. 0071D] The solution is found in Nicholas of Lyra’s exposition of this chapter.] For it is read in the book of Chronicles that Caleb was the father of Hur, and that Caleb was not more than forty years old at the Exodus from Egypt; therefore Bezalel can now be no more than two years old.

(EXODUS XXXII.) “But Joshua, hearing the tumult of the people,” etc. In both the ascent and the descent Joshua is said to have been with Moses, but he is not said to have remained with him on the mountain. Hence a question has arisen: whether he fasted there with Moses for so long, or not. [Col. 0073A]

“He broke them,” etc. Whether he did this from human emotion or by divine inspiration is not clear.

“You know that the people are prone to evil.” What he could not prevent, he allowed with grief; yet he stripped them of the precious ornaments which they loved most, so that at least by this means he might restrain them from that foolish desire. Yet even so he could not.

“This calf came out”: namely, by human work, not by miracle.

“And naked among enemies”: stripped of the wealth represented by the aforementioned ornaments; by “enemies” he means the neighboring peoples.

“Whoever is for the Lord, join himself to me”: that is, whoever has zeal for God, let him take vengeance with me upon the sinning people. [Col. 0073B]

“Blot me out of your book.” He says this not from reason, but from an outburst of human feeling and great trust in God.

To be written in the book of life or blotted out of it is understood in two ways: either according to God’s foreknowledge, or according to one’s present state. According to the latter, it sometimes happens that, if a person remained as he is, he would be saved; but because he abandons the righteousness which he presently has, he is said to be blotted from the book of life, in which God wrote him when he gave him that righteousness. But one who is written according to foreknowledge will never be blotted out according to that same foreknowledge.

“Therefore the Lord struck the people”: namely, with the aforementioned slaughter carried out by the Levites. From this it is also evident [Col. 0073C] that it was done by God’s prompting, not through Moses’ ill will.

(EXODUS XXXIII.) “Lest I destroy you.” I might become angry at your folly if I were continually among you. “Once I go up into your midst, I shall destroy you.” This is a threat; and note that He says, “I shall go up.” For ascent is either from lower things to higher, or from hidden things to manifest, as here. He promises that He will reveal Himself to them in their evil. “Put off your adornment,” that is, the first tabernacle in which the Lord was consulted before that great one was made, concerning which the Lord instructed Moses on the mountain; or “put off” means, set it up outside the camp. “That I may know what I shall do”: He speaks in human fashion. “Their adornment at Mount Horeb.” The tabernacle was near [Col. 0073D] the mountain as long as Moses remained on the mountain; and there Aaron and the seventy elders dealt with doubtful matters brought to them from the camp. But after the people sinned and Moses came down, the Lord commanded that the tabernacle be moved away from Mount Horeb toward the people. Moses then placed it outside the camp, not within it.

“He called the name.” Not only then, but previously as well, so that we should take the perfect for a pluperfect. “I have known you by name.” It is a great sign of affection when a king, not neglecting his servant, knows his servant’s own name and calls him to himself by it. Thus here concerning God and Moses it should be understood that God had given him a special grace beyond others, just as a proper name signifies a special property. “Show [Col. 0074A] me your face,” that is, your presence. “I shall give you rest,” by leading you into the land of promise. “I shall show you all good”: this will be in the future, in which the vision of God will be eternal life. And in the present: “I shall be called in the name of the Lord,” that is, I shall cause myself to be called the God who leads you, by the miracles that I shall perform. And if anyone asks why I do this, there is no other reason than that I will it; and this is: “I shall have mercy on whom I shall will,” etc.

And this is all on Exodus; for in the remaining chapters I have so far found nothing written by our Hugh.

THERE FOLLOW THE NOTES OF THE SAME AUTHOR ON LEVITICUS, WHOSE CHAPTERS ARE THESE:

On the name of Leviticus and the five matters distinctly treated in it: sacrifices, persons, times, places, and causes. Chapter I, which is chapter [Col. 0074B] IX in the Pentateuch. On sacrifices, offerings, and libations. Chapters II and X. On the persons by whom the aforesaid things are performed. Chapters III and XI. On the times of offering. Chapters IV and XII. On places, causes, and the literal exposition. Chapters V and XIII.

## CHAPTERS I AND IX.—On the Name of Leviticus and the Other Matters Already Mentioned

The book of Leviticus is called in Hebrew *Vagethra*, which sounds as though one said, “he called.” For it received its name from its beginning, according to the custom of Hebrew books, which are usually named from their openings. It is called Leviticus among us, from the Levites, because it treats more fully of the ministry of the Levites. For there are five things: the sacrifices offered to God; the persons [Col. 0074C] by whom they are offered; the times when they are offered; the places where they are offered; and the causes for which they are offered. These are distinctly treated in this book. We must therefore give some preliminary account of each, as the plan of the introduction requires.

## CHAPTERS II AND X.—On Sacrifices, Offering, and Libation

First, then, a threefold distinction presents itself among things duly offered. An offering was made either from animals, and was called a sacrifice; or from dry material, such as bread or flour, or things made from these, which was properly called an offering; or from liquids, such as wine and similar things, which Scripture specifically calls a libation. Although Scripture sometimes customarily calls sacrifice an offering [Col. 0074D] and conversely an offering a sacrifice, we nevertheless think that, more properly, sacrifices should be understood as animal offerings, offerings as dry offerings, and libations as liquid offerings.

Moreover, some sacrifices were called whole burnt offerings because they were wholly burned; others were sacrifices in which one part was burned and another reserved. Again, among those in which one part was burned and another reserved, some were offered for sin or guilt. In these, apart from what was burned as the Lord’s whole burnt offering, all the rest went for the priests’ consumption. Others were called peace offerings, offered either in thanksgiving, in fulfillment of a vow, or from voluntary devotion. Of these, one part was burned in the altar fire; another, namely the breast and the right shoulder, belonged to [Col. 0075A] the priests; and the rest was received by those offering them.

In a whole burnt offering, the priest who offered it received only the skin. In sacrifices, apart from the fat, kidneys, covering of the liver, and other things consumed by the fire, all the remainder belonged to the priests. Likewise in peace offerings, the altar fire consumed the fat; all inner fat; the two kidneys with the fat covering the loins; the covering of the liver with the kidneys; and, where appropriate, the tail also with the kidneys and all the entrails. The priest received the breast and right shoulder, while all the remainder belonged to those who had offered the peace offering.

Again, when the whole burnt offering was made from cattle or sheep, only males were commanded to be offered. But in sacrifices for sin [Col. 0075B] and guilt, as also in peace offerings, either females or males could be sacrificed, in the order in which the Law commanded them to be sacrificed. Thus, in a sin offering, when someone of the people sinned through ignorance, he was commanded to offer a she-goat; but in peace offerings the offerer could offer a male or female for a vow, because the offering was voluntary.

Peace offerings were so called either because they were not offered for any guilt, or because they made peace on every side by giving each person what was his own: for in them a part was burned among the Lord’s sacrifices, a part went to the priests, and the rest belonged to the offerers. Peace offerings were made either in thanksgiving, when someone delivered from danger offered a gift to the Lord in gratitude; or in fulfillment of a vow, discharging what had been promised; or from voluntary inclination.

When an offering was made, it had to be either of fine flour, that is, very finely ground flour; or of loaves baked in an oven; or on a griddle without frying; or in a pan with frying. Oil was poured over the fine flour and frankincense placed upon it; oil was poured over the other offerings without frankincense. But honey and leaven were universally excluded from the Lord’s offerings. For even when firstfruits of these, like those of other things, were offered, they were nevertheless not placed upon the altar, nor was any part of them burned in the altar fire; they were only elevated before the Lord, and afterwards received by the priests. Salt, however, was commanded to be mixed with all sacrifices, that is, offerings. [Col. 0075D]

We understand libation to concern liquids, such as oil and wine.

## CHAPTERS III AND XI.—On the Persons by Whom the Aforesaid Things Are Performed

Now, since we have shown the differences among things offered, it follows that we should also distinguish the persons by whom they are offered: namely, those who give the gifts and those who, in their ministry, offer sacrifices. For both are said to offer: those who give, and those through whom they give. It belongs to priests to offer sacrifices, not especially to one alone, lest, if the necessity of sacrificing were imposed daily upon one man, he should seem forbidden marital intercourse, according to the statement that a man from whom the semen of intercourse proceeds [Col. 0076A] is forbidden to enter or touch holy things and is decreed unclean until evening. Daily sacrifices and offerings, however, could be performed in turn by all the priests, except for that sacrifice in which the high priest alone was commanded once a year to enter the Holy of Holies with blood. Yet whoever offered the sacrifice, there was an equal portion for all priests, distributed alike among each.

## CHAPTERS IV AND XII.—On the Times and Causes of Offering at Them

The times for offering were diverse. There was a sacrifice called daily because it had to be offered every day. For God commanded two lambs to be sacrificed as a whole burnt offering each day, one in the morning and the other in the evening; and this was called the daily, continual, and perpetual sacrifice. On every Sabbath it had been ordained that two further lambs be added as a whole burnt offering, besides the daily whole burnt offering, making four together.

Moreover, on the Kalends, that is, at the beginnings of individual months, there were added to the daily sacrifice as a whole burnt offering two bulls, one ram, seven lambs, and a goat for sin. In the first month, that is, the month of Passover, called the month of new things, besides the paschal lamb sacrificed on the fourteenth day at evening, on the following—that is, the fifteenth—day there were added to the daily sacrifice as a whole burnt offering two bulls, one ram, seven lambs, and a goat for sin. The same was done on each of the seven days of unleavened bread. [Col. 0076C]

At the feast of firstfruits also, held seven weeks after Passover had passed, that is, on the fiftieth day—when they first began to offer loaves from the new crops to the Lord, just as at the feast of the new grain they put the sickle to the harvest and made an offering from crushed grain—two bulls, one ram, and seven lambs were added to the daily sacrifice. I think that this fiftieth day should be calculated from the sixteenth day of the first month, immediately following the fifteenth, not from the fifteenth, as some think. They hold that this sixteenth day was the day on which the sickle was first put to the harvest and the sheaf of firstfruits was elevated before the Lord.

Then, on the first day of the seventh month, that is, at the feast of trumpets, there were added to the daily sacrifice as a whole burnt offering one bull, one ram, seven lambs, and a goat for sin, besides the whole burnt offering of the Kalends. Some believe that this feast was called the feast of trumpets because then, according to the cycle of the year, after the prescribed sequence of Scripture had been completed, they began again from the beginning to read and recite the same Scriptures. [Col. 0076D]

Next follows, on the tenth day of the same month, the feast of expiation, when the children of Israel are commanded to afflict their souls. Some suppose this was on account of the sin of the calf which they made while Moses delayed on the mountain, and that Moses obtained from God forgiveness of its guilt at this very time. For ancient tradition reports that the Law was given in the Ten Commandments on the fiftieth day after the fifteenth day of the first month, which according to the Hebrews is the sixth day of the third month. After that day Moses went up to God on the mountain; when the fast of forty days was completed, he received two stone tablets inscribed with those commandments. Coming down to the foot of the mountain and seeing the calf, he broke them. Then, after another forty days, he went up again with other tablets, which, by the Lord’s command, he had made like the former ones, and received the same commandments. Finally, ascending for a third forty-day period, he obtained forgiveness for the offense.

If after this number one adds two days—the first believed to have been between the first and second ascents, the second between the second and third—the tenth day of the seventh month results. It was fittingly commanded that this day be celebrated yearly and called the day of expiation, because on it, as they afflicted their souls for the sin committed, they expiated their guilt by repentance. [Col. 0077B]

Last follows the feast of *scenopegiae*, that is, of tabernacles, held in remembrance of the wandering, because the children of Israel, leaving Egypt, lived in tents through the wilderness. This feast was transferred from the first month, when they left Egypt, to the seventh, because it was not suitable for two feasts to be celebrated at once; and because, after the feast of firstfruits, it was not easy for the entire people to assemble in one place before the harvests had been gathered. Some suppose that this feast was instituted in the seventh month because of the seven clouds by which, according to ancient tradition, the people departing Egypt were overshadowed.

They hold that the eighth day, which seems to have been added for celebration contrary to the custom of the Old Testament, does not belong to this feast but is a separate feast to be celebrated at another time, except that by dispensation it was joined to this feast lest the people suffer inconvenience both from repeated assemblies and from the approaching winter. They prove this from the authority of Deuteronomy, where only seven days are mentioned when the feast of tabernacles is prescribed. [Col. 0077C]

## CHAPTERS V AND XIII.—On the Places, Causes, and Literal Exposition of Leviticus

(LEVITICUS I.) Having briefly set forth these matters, we shall come to the literal sense. [Note: [Col. 0077D] See the Annals of F. Sixtus on this chapter, in his *Bibliotheca*, book V, part II.]

“At the entrance of the tabernacle of testimony.” In one and the same place the victims, whether for whole burnt offerings, peace offerings, sin offerings, or guilt offerings, were slaughtered—that is, cut up—by the priests and offered by the people. This place is designated by different names. There were fifty cubits from the eastern entrance of the court to the entrance of the court, namely that of the tabernacle of testimony. There were two porticoes, one for Israelite men and the other for women. Between these and the entrance of the tabernacle stood the altar of whole burnt offerings, not in the entrance itself but farther up toward the south. The victims were offered and slaughtered beside the altar, on the northern side, more nearly at the entrance of the tabernacle.

“The head, namely, and everything adhering to [Col. 0078A] the liver.” He named the head rather than the breast or shoulder because the head was not offered separately by one of the priests or Levites, as the other members were; rather, what adhered to the liver, together with the feet and the entrails washed with water, was joined with it. One priest elevated these four things and placed them upon the altar. Eight other priests offered the remaining members. Thus nine priests offered all the members of the whole burnt offering, thoroughly washed in water. Two more offered the blood, so that there were twelve together. It was fitting that the things sacrificed in God’s worship should also be offered by several priests.

(LEVITICUS II.) “He shall take a handful full of fine flour and oil, and all the frankincense.” He might have said more expressly, “all the frankincense together with the incense,” since, with the incense joined, it includes all. “But if the sacrifice is from the griddle, the fine flour shall likewise be mixed with oil.” In Hebrew, for “griddle” stands *marhesit*, which properly means a frying-pan, in which frying takes place; and this seems to be suggested by the very sound of its name. For *marhesit* is interpreted “counsellor,” because of the crackling of frying and the whispering or murmur by which it seems to imitate one deliberating. But where Leviticus has “an offering from a frying-pan,” the Hebrew has *mahhebat*. Thus one may distinguish: *michar*, that is, a sieve or net; *mahhebat*, that is, a pan, where cooking is done in liquid; and *marhesit*, that is, a frying-pan, where frying is done. [Col. 0078B]

“No leaven or honey shall be burned in the sacrifice of the Lord. You shall offer only their firstfruits and gifts.” For in what follows it says that two leavened loaves were offered with the thanksgiving offering. Of these, one was offered to the Lord as firstfruits and became the priest’s. Thus it should be understood that when leaven and honey were offered as firstfruits, none of them was burned upon the altar, as with other firstfruits; rather, after first being elevated before the Lord, they went to the priest’s use.

“But if you offer to the Lord a gift of the firstfruits of your crops.” Here he intends to speak of the Passover offering. “You shall offer your firstfruits to the Lord, pouring oil upon them and placing frankincense upon them.” The frankincense is included because it is an offering to the Lord. Of this the priest burned, as the memorial of the gift, a portion of the crushed grain and a portion of the oil; but you shall burn all the frankincense, so that no part of it remains, as a part remains of the grain and oil, but all is burned. This, then, was not done with firstfruits of leaven and honey. [Col. 0078D]

(LEVITICUS III.) “If his offering is a sacrifice of peace offerings,” etc. Peace offerings were sacrifices offered by those who, not because of a preceding offense but as persons at peace, offered to God; or they were called peace offerings because they made peace, distributing to all each person’s own share. For everyone shares in them and nothing falls to one person alone. A portion of them was burned as God’s sacrifice; a portion went to the priests’ use, namely the breast and right shoulder; and the rest belonged to the offerers.

For there was one kind of sacrifice in which God alone had a share: the whole burnt offering, the sin offering for the priest, and the sin offering for the whole people. Of these, the first was wholly burned in the altar fire, while the other two were burned partly on the altar and partly outside the camp. There was another sacrifice in which part went to God and part to the priests, as in the sin offering for a ruler and for individual persons among the people. There was another in which a part was burned before the Lord, a part came for the priests’ consumption, and the remainder belonged to the offerers, as in peace offerings. In these, the fat with certain other parts belonged to God; the breast and right shoulder to the priest; and the rest to the offerers, as we have already said above. [Col. 0079A]

But of the other flour offerings, apart from the handful burned as a memorial before the Lord together with all the frankincense—of which none was reserved—all that remained went to Aaron and his sons. Likewise, of that baked in an oven, on a frying-pan, or on a griddle, part was burned before the Lord as a memorial, and what remained belonged to Aaron and his sons. So too with the firstfruits, except for leaven and honey, of which nothing was burned.

(LEVITICUS IV.) “If a soul sins through ignorance and does anything from among all the commandments of the Lord which He commanded should not be done”: the sentence hangs thus far, and is afterwards distinguished by subdivision. If indeed the one who did this is the anointed priest, he shall offer, etc. But if the whole congregation of Israel, etc. But if a ruler sins, etc. All these subordinate clauses correspond to the first proposition, where it is said: “If a soul sins.”

But when it says, “If he does anything from among all the commandments of the Lord which He commanded should not be done,” it may be understood either that God commanded certain things to be observed only as figures, and that after the truth has been recognized it is sinful to retain them; or that “commandment” is used broadly for command and prohibition, as if it said: “If he does anything among those things contained in the Lord’s commands, concerning which it is commanded that they not be done.” [Col. 0079C]

“If indeed the one who did this is the anointed priest, sinning in this way and causing the people to offend, he shall offer,” etc. When it says, “he sins, causing the people to offend,” this should be understood either of every sin of a priest, which is always more serious because he provides others an example of wrongdoing; or of his sinning in such a way as to make the people sin, by suggesting or recommending something in word or example by which others are provoked to sin. This is more serious than if he sinned alone. Certainly, as it is expressed more clearly in Hebrew: “If the anointed priest sins to the guilt of the people,” that is, in the likeness of some very guilty member of the people, so that one who ought to be an example to others in righteousness becomes like the others in guilt.

Where it is so often said, “before the Lord,” “before the tabernacle,” “before the altar,” it must be understood to mean where God’s presence was through sacred things. And where it is often said, “The priest shall pray for him,” it can be understood in another sense: namely, he shall pardon or effect remission for him, so as to show that forgiveness of the offense comes about through the priest’s prayers. [Col. 0079D]

[Col. 0080A] (LEVITICUS V.) “If a soul sins and hears the voice of one swearing, and is a witness, because he either saw it himself or knows of it, unless he reports it, he shall bear his iniquity.” Some think this chapter should be understood as follows. If someone sins by hearing before him the voice of one swearing to speak the truth, and is a witness—that is, knows of it—and knows the truth because he saw the matter concerning which testimony is requested, or knows of it in another way, then, unless he reports it as he knows the truth, he shall bear his iniquity, that is, he shall be guilty.

Or, if a soul sins when it hears someone swearing falsely and, being—or being able to be—a witness of that falsehood because it saw it or knows of it, fails to report that he is swearing falsely, it sins. Yet one must observe this measure: that one reveal his sin for correction, not for that person’s injury. Or one sins in this way: if, having heard someone swear falsely, one testifies against him, saying that one has seen that he swears falsely or knows this in some other way, when this is not so; unless afterwards one reports either the truth itself as one knows it, or at least to the priest one’s own guilt for having borne false witness, one shall bear one’s iniquity.

“A soul that touches anything unclean,” etc. In this chapter he censures forgetfulness of contact with an unclean thing; in the following one, the act itself. Whoever touches an unclean thing becomes unclean, and sins if through carelessness, forgetting his uncleanness, he does not observe the rite of cleansing. Again, if after forgetfulness he remembers his uncleanness, he will be liable for guilt because he did not observe cleansing, [Col. 0080C] and needs to be purified by sacrifice.

“A soul that swears and utters with its lips that it will do either something very evil or something good, and confirms this by oath and word; and, forgetting its oath and neglecting its word, afterwards recognizes its offense”—namely, that it did not fulfill what it swore, or perhaps that it swore evil—“let it do penance for its sin.” Some hold that the fault here lies not in making an oath, but in the oath’s being false, though ignorantly so; when this is afterwards recognized, amendment is commanded, although one cannot properly be said to have forgotten what one did not know.

What follows—“He shall offer from the flock a lamb or a goat”—is not to be understood as expiation for this offense alone, but also for the preceding three. “He who first offers for sin.” Where we have “for sin,” the Hebrew has “for expiation.” For the word *hatrat* means “for expiation.”

“If a soul, transgressing rites through error, sins in things consecrated to the Lord, it shall offer for its guilt an unblemished ram.” Here he intends sin to mean when someone appropriates for personal use things consecrated to the Lord, or eats of victims from which priests alone were permitted to eat. In this case he is commanded both to restore the damage he caused and add a fifth part; and, for his guilt, to offer an unblemished ram bought for five shekels.

“If a soul sins through ignorance and does one of the things forbidden by the Law of the Lord, and recognizes that it is liable for sin in its iniquity, it shall offer to the priest an unblemished ram from the flock, according to the measure and valuation of the sin.” This command seems to differ from what he said above, that a soul of the people of the land sinning through ignorance must offer a she-goat for its expiation, in that there the transgressor is said to have offended against the Lord’s commandments, whereas here he is described as having sinned not only against the Lord’s commandments but also against the Lord Himself. Hence it is fittingly understood that here “guilt” signifies a sin in which one sins against the Lord—that is, against things consecrated to the Lord—and differs from the preceding case only in this: there damage is caused and sin committed; therefore the damage is commanded to be restored with an added fifth, and the sin expiated by sacrificing a ram. Here, however, because no damage has been caused, the sin alone is cleansed by sacrificing a ram. [Col. 0081B]

This ram is commanded to be offered according to the measure and valuation of the preceding sin, because the sin is the same here, although the damage is not similar. In both cases one sins within the same category, although in different ways: for example, there by unlawfully taking and appropriating sacred things, here by unlawfully touching them. Hence it follows: “He”—namely, the priest—“shall pray for him, because he did it unknowingly, and it shall be forgiven him, because through error he sinned against the Lord.” In Hebrew it is thus: “The priest shall effect remission over him for the error in which he erred and did not know; and that guilt shall be forgiven him, in which, sinning, he sinned against God.” Likewise in the following chapter.

[Col. 0081C] (LEVITICUS VI.) “A soul that sins and, despising the Lord, denies to its neighbor a deposit,” etc.—that is, one who, despising the Lord, knows the secret and denies the deposit, and the other following offenses—shall be expiated by sacrificing a ram, because it is reckoned in the same valuation as the aforesaid cases. “It shall burn on the altar all night until morning.” He is speaking of the daily whole burnt offering; nor need one ask why here he omits the evening sacrifice, since earlier in Exodus he had first mentioned the morning sacrifice.

(LEVITICUS VII.) “Whatever is prepared on a griddle or in a frying-pan shall belong to the priest by whom it is offered.” Here distinguish so as to infer: another offering, whether mixed with oil or dry, shall all be divided in equal measure among Aaron’s sons individually. Or, “it shall belong to the priest,” because it does not come into lay use, as in peace offerings, but is divided equally among Aaron’s sons.

“Of these one is offered to the Lord as firstfruits.” In the peace offering, loaves of four kinds were offered; and one from each kind was offered to the priest as his own, like firstfruits. The remaining loaves belonged to the Israelite who offered them, and he ate them in the court.

“The flesh that touches anything unclean shall not be eaten, but shall be burned with fire. Whoever is unclean shall eat of it.” In Hebrew it is thus: “The flesh that touches every polluted thing shall not be eaten, but shall be burned with fire; and flesh: every unclean person shall eat flesh.” This can be understood thus: whoever does not eat that polluted flesh is clean.

“A polluted soul which eats from the flesh of the peace-offering victim,” etc. By “a polluted soul” here, and then by the added words, “a soul that touches a human uncleanness,” he means one defiled by its own uncleanness and by another’s. “This is Aaron’s anointing.” In Hebrew: “Increase,” namely, that which was given to him by the Lord through a perpetual law from sacrifices offered by the people of Israel, is here called his anointing. [Col. 0082A]

(LEVITICUS VIII.) “But the fat and the tail.” During the seven days in which Aaron was consecrated and instructed for the priesthood, Moses acted as high priest. He received from Aaron and his sons those things which Aaron would later receive from the rest of the offering people, and each day sacrificed them on the altar of whole burnt offering, which he anointed on the first of those seven days. These days were at the end of the first year, so that the eighth day, on which Aaron began to sacrifice, was the first day of the second year; and on that day fire came forth from the Lord and consumed Aaron’s whole burnt offering. For Moses had sacrificed during the preceding seven days with earthly fire. On the same eighth day Nadab and Abihu were consumed by avenging fire because, after the heavenly fire had been sent by the Lord, they brought in strange fire.

“Cook the flesh before the doors of the tabernacle.” As laypeople did with the flesh of peace offerings which they made, so Aaron and his sons had to do in this offering of theirs. Moses received from it only as much as Aaron would afterwards receive from others. “As has been done at present.” It is as if He said: As Aaron is now instituted and consecrated, so his successors will be instituted.

[Col. 0082C] (LEVITICUS IX.) “And he said to Aaron: Take from the herd a calf for sin.” Its flesh, because it was offered for the priest’s sin, was burned outside the camp with its skin; likewise, the ram offered as a whole burnt offering was wholly burned. But for the people’s sin he slaughtered a goat, a calf, and a lamb; for a whole burnt offering, an ox and a ram; and peace-offering victims. It is not contrary that above He commanded a calf to be sacrificed for the sin of the whole multitude, while here a goat is prescribed: there it was for a definite offense committed, here for a general one; and there separately for the multitude and separately for rulers, while here for rulers and the people together. Therefore the goat and calf are fitting. But, after the goat, when he adds the calf, it is uncertain whether it is for sin or a whole burnt offering.

“Besides the ceremonies of the morning whole burnt offering,” that is, the lamb which was offered daily both morning and evening. Thus, when the sin offerings, whole burnt offerings, and peace offerings had been completed, he came down. He did not descend from steps, since it was prohibited to ascend the altar by steps; rather, he came down perhaps from some higher position where he stood at the edge in order to minister suitably, lest the altar’s height be an impediment. [Col. 0082D]

(LEVITICUS XI.) “Everything that walks on four feet but has longer hind legs.” Because of those four feet, you ought—that is, are able—to eat them; and birds are being discussed here. “Every gathering of waters shall be clean”: whatever falls into it, it cannot itself become unclean, just as a spring cannot.

[Col. 0083A] (LEVITICUS XIV.) “Two living sparrows for himself,” such as it is lawful to eat. He does not say this to distinguish them from other sparrows, but from other birds which are not lawful to eat. “The purified person shall enter the camp,” yet not on the same day as his shaving and purification; but after that day he shall still wait seven days outside the camp, outside his own tent, namely before he is allowed to enter his own house; or, if they are on campaign—as now in the wilderness—before he enters his own tent. Yet in the meantime he is not thereby allowed to enter the tents of others.

(LEVITICUS XV.) “Everyone whom such a person touches,” that is, one made unclean by contact with an unclean thing; “touches,” I say, without having first washed his hands, that is, before washing his hands. “By the contact of uncleanness, if indeed that vessel is earthenware,” etc. When he inserts, “He shall wash his garments,” he shows how the person is to be cleansed, and then returns to the subject he proposed: “an earthen vessel,” etc. [Col. 0083B]

(LEVITICUS XVI.) “He shall gird himself with a linen belt; he shall place a linen *cydaris* [turban] on his head,” etc. On every day on which the high priest sacrificed, he wore golden garments; but when he entered the Holy of Holies, he retained only the linen garments. “According to this rite he shall do for the tabernacle,” that is, he shall do the same for the tabernacle of testimony, likewise making expiation for it.

(LEVITICUS XVII.) “Any man of the house of Israel, if he kills an ox, sheep, or goat in the camp or outside the camp, and does not bring the offering to the entrance of the tabernacle for the Lord, shall be guilty of blood.” This must be understood only of the period when they were dwelling in the wilderness and had the Lord’s tabernacle near them. For in the land of promise, those far from the place of sacrifice were permitted to slaughter livestock for food and eat the meat, even if they did not sacrifice them. [Col. 0083C]

(LEVITICUS XVIII.) “What is born at home or abroad,” that is, from lawful intercourse or from concubinage.

(LEVITICUS XIX.) “The fruits that germinate shall be unclean for you”: this is not in the Hebrew. “In the fourth year it shall be sanctified,” that is, given to the Lord, and yet it may be redeemed with another price.

(LEVITICUS XX.) “Of your seed,” that is, of your children, “you shall not give,” that is, sacrifice to the idol Moloch, according to the custom of the nations.

[Col. 0083D] (LEVITICUS XXII.) “Unclean through a dead body,” that is, the uncleanness arising from a corpse.

(LEVITICUS XXIII.) “On the day after the Sabbath, and he shall sanctify it,” that is, the sixteenth day of the moon. On that day it was consecrated and first elevated before the Lord, then roasted by fire, ground into flour, and made into a sacrifice. From that day seven weeks were counted; the first day after them was Pentecost, which is always the sixth day of the third month, as also happened at the giving of the Law.

It should be known that this sheaf and all the festival sacrifices, like the daily whole burnt offering, were received jointly from all Israel; and the rich person contributed no more than the poor person to the collection, which was kept at the high priest’s discretion. “In the seventh month, on the first day of the month.” On this day Moses came down from the mountain after completing three forty-day periods, during which he also fasted. For, when the first was completed, Moses came down because the people had sinned with the molten calf; and, after vengeance had been done and the tablets broken, on the next day he went up the mountain and fasted another forty days in order to obtain forgiveness. When these were completed, the Lord told him to descend and cut other tablets, upon which the Lord Himself promises in Deuteronomy that He will again write the Ten Commandments. [Col. 0084A]

When Moses had done this and again went up on the day after his descent, he fasted a third time; and on the final day of the third forty-day period, when Moses was to descend, the Lord appointed for him the feast of expiation as a sign and memorial of the forgiveness of sins which the Lord then granted the people through Moses’ prayers.

This feast had to be held from the fifteenth day, after the whole gathering of fruits, because offerings had to be made to the Lord from every kind of fruit. Why, then, is it held on the fifteenth day of the month? Because on the fifteenth day of the month—though not of this month, but of the first—the children of Israel began to dwell in booths of cloud. Seven clouds surrounded the tabernacle and indeed the whole people on every side. “A staff,” that is, rather, “strength.”

(LEV. XXVI; LEV. XXVII.) “An unclean animal, which cannot be offered to the Lord,” etc. Here he speaks of an animal which could be offered to the Lord if it lacked blemish. “But if he wishes to give it,” etc. “Everything that is consecrated to the Lord, whether man or animal.” This consecration is called in Hebrew *ḥerem*, “anathematization,” because such things were withdrawn from ordinary human use. Whatever was thus consecrated to the Lord could by no redemption return to a human being; even if a father had consecrated his daughter, she would die before she could be redeemed; and this is what “shall surely die” means. The Lord killed only the males among the firstborn of Egypt; therefore he commanded that only males, both among humans and among other animals, be redeemed. Even if a female were born first, whenever sons were born after her, they were not required to be redeemed.

## Chapter XIV.—Explanatory Notes on Numbers

(NUM. XIV.) “For the Amalekites and the Canaanite dwell in the valleys”: since no safe passage lies through them, therefore tomorrow move camp and return.

(NUM. XVIII.) “Of the sceptre,” that is, the household, “of your brother [father],” that is, of Moses: this means, “Take the Levites with you.” “Sceptre” is used for kindred, because it is a person’s honour and exaltation. Or “sceptre” stands for the divine office and ministry, to serve which is to reign. “Take the sceptre of your brother,” who is a Levite—that is, those who perform his office, that they may minister to you.

(NUM. XXI.) “Therefore it is said in the book of the wars of the Lord”: this same writing is to be understood, in which the wars of the Lord are recounted—the wars which he fought for his people. In it is also said what Israel, about to fight King Sihon at the torrents of Arnon, said: “As the Lord acted for us at the Red Sea, drowning the Egyptians, so he will act at the torrents of Arnon, overthrowing the Amorites.” It is also said in this book that the crags of the torrents bent down, intending to provide shade so that the children of Israel might rest at Arnon. “The crags of the torrents bent down”: mute elements hasten to obedience; and what can mortal man do? It is a figure of speech using hyperbole. Or, “the crags of the torrents bent down,” that is, the proud and impetuous were humbled, being unable to resist.

From the place where, that is, where they had pitched camp in the wilderness, there appeared a well made by divine power. Before it appeared, the Lord said to Moses concerning it: “Gather the people, and I will give them water.” Then, that is, after the promise had been made, Israel, exulting in hope, sang this song:

> “Rise up, O well, overflowing abundantly to the very top.”

The children of Israel sang this in refrain. “The well which the princes dug, and the leaders of the multitude prepared.” How did they prepare it? “By the lawgiver, and with their staffs.” For men could dig the ground, but they could not obtain water unless God gave it. By such a digger and such a giver water was given to the people in the wilderness.

Leaving that wilderness, they came to Mattanah; from Mattanah to Nahaliel; from Nahaliel to Bamoth; from Bamoth to the valley—which valley is in the region of Moab, on the summit of Pisgah; that is, in the region where the summit of Pisgah stands and looks toward the wilderness. Then Israel sent messengers to Sihon as far as Jesboth [Jabbok] and the children of Ammon, but no farther, because the borders of the Ammonites were held by a strong defence.

[Col. 0085C] Heshbon was the city of Sihon, king of the Amorites, who fought, etc. Therefore he who devastated the Moabites is spoken of in a proverb made concerning this matter:

> “Come to Heshbon: let Heshbon itself, the city of King Sihon, be built and established.”

For the city of a victorious king ought to be built up and exalted, because from that Heshbon fire went out, and likewise a flame went out from it, which is the stronghold of King Sihon. That flame devoured Arnon, namely the city of the Moabites, and the inhabitants of the heights of Arnon, because they lived in its high places and towers, or in places where idols were worshipped. Hence it is rightly said:

> “Woe to you, Moab!”

Why? Because you have perished, O people of Chemosh [Cathmos], that is, worshippers of the idol Chemosh. Abandoning them justly—or because Chemosh was unable to defend them—he gave the sons of that people to flight and the daughters to captivity, to Sihon king of the Amorites. “The yoke,” that is, their power, of the Moabites perished from Heshbon to Dibon; and the Moabites themselves, fleeing and weary [fallen], reached Jophah [Nophah], even to Medeba.

(NUM. XXIV.) “He shall destroy the remnants of the city,” namely Seir. He also saw the Kenite, and, taking up his oracle, said:

> “Your dwelling indeed is strong; but though you set your nest in the rock, and are chosen from the stock of Cain [Ken], how long can you remain?”

In this place Cain does not mean the son of Adam who killed his brother Abel, but Cain from whom the people called Kenites derive their name: after *c* in the first syllable *ae* follows; but in the final syllable *i* both precedes and follows. [Col. 0086A] Or, according to others, Ham, son of Noah. But in the Hebrew original, where it says, “though you are chosen from the stock of Cain, how long can you remain?” it seems to mean only this, as though it said: “The Kenite shall be destroyed.” Thus it should be read: “Though you set your nest in the rock, the Kenite shall be destroyed”—that is, you, though you appear so secure and fortified, will nevertheless be destroyed. For Assyria shall carry you away.

And these are the notes on Numbers. We lack the remainder.

## Chapter XV. Notes on Deuteronomy, likewise defective and, in some manner, interrupted

(DEUT. III.) “I also gave Gilead to Machir.” By anticipation he calls the land Gilead, a name later bestowed from Gilead, who descended from Machir. “And to the tribes of Reuben and Gad I gave from the land of Gilead as far as the torrent Arnon.”

(DEUT. XXII.) “You shall not sow your vineyard with another seed,” besides the vine; for if you do this, it is unlawful, and they shall be sanctified—that is, they shall not pass to your use. Yet this results from prohibition alone, not from nature. “You shall make cords in the fringes at the four corners of your cloak.” They used square cloaks, on which they are commanded to make phylacteries.

(DEUT. XXVII.) “You shall set up great stones and smooth them with lime, so that you may write upon them all the words of this law.” Therefore, in commanding the erection of great stones, he indicates a great structure; and thus the question is resolved: namely, how Joshua could write the Deuteronomy of the Law upon the altar which he erected, especially since the structure was large and only the commandments, rather than everything contained in this book, ought to have been written.

(DEUT. XXIX.) “He blesses himself in his heart, saying: ‘Peace shall be mine, and I shall walk in the hardness of my heart’; and the drunken shall take up the thirsty.” That is, the soul already intoxicated by the practice of sin, which neither feels nor fears wrongdoing, shall take up—or draw into fellowship in sin—the thirsty one: another soul, thirsty through concupiscence while in the heat of temptation, but not yet daring to drink the draught of a wicked deed. Therefore, lest this happen, he adds: “And the Lord shall not forgive him,” that is, the sinner and the one who causes another to sin. Care must be taken lest there be among you “a root producing gall”: that is, such a person from whom malice proceeds to others and corrupts many.

“Things hidden by the Lord our God; things made manifest belong to us and to our children for ever, that we may do all the things of this law.” This must be referred to what precedes, because he had said: “Because they forsook the covenant of the Lord which he made with their fathers,” that they should keep his commandments and the secrets which he had revealed to them, things which had been hidden by the Lord our God. “He has not done so for every nation, nor has he made his judgments known to them” (Ps. CXLVII). And therefore, because they have been revealed to us and to our children yet to be born after us for ever—or that we may do them for ever—if we do not keep them, all these evils shall come upon us.

[Col. 0087]

## EXPLANATORY NOTES ON THE BOOK OF JUDGES, first setting forth the name and miscellaneous contents of the book, then the literal sense, with one added note on the book of Ruth. (G)*

[Col. 0087A] The Book of Judges, called *Sophtim* in Hebrew, is ordered seventh after the five books of Moses and the Book of Joshua. It describes the times of the judges who judged the people of Israel after Joshua until Eli the priest. On the surface of the letter it appears clearer than the other books.

(JUD. I.) “Judah shall go up.” By Judah here we must understand not an individual but the people, namely the tribe of Judah, just as by Simeon we understand the tribe of Simeon, which the tribe of Judah calls to its aid in fighting the Canaanites. “They seized him and cut off the extremities of his hands and feet.” Some, following the Hebrew truth, have thought the more exact translation to be: “having cut off his thumbs,” because once a thumb is cut off, a person is thereafter unfit to bear arms.

“They brought him to Jerusalem.” Since the Jebusites are recorded to have held Jerusalem until David’s time, how are the children of Israel said to have brought Adoni-bezek to Jerusalem as though to their own city? But what follows resolves the question: “Therefore the children of Judah attacked Jerusalem, captured it, and struck it with the edge of the sword.” It must be understood thus: first they took the city, and then they brought the captured king to the city which had been captured and made subject to their rule.

“Caleb gave her the upper watering-place and the lower watering-place.” By upper and lower we understand upland and lowland regions. “The children of the Kenite, Moses’ kinsman, went up from the city of palms with the children of Judah into the wilderness of his allotment, which is south of Arad, and dwelt with him.” This Kenite is Jethro, or Reuel, father of Zipporah, Moses’ wife, from whom the Kenites take their name. They are said here to have gone up to the children of Judah and to have lived with them.

“But the children of Benjamin did not destroy the Jebusite inhabitant of Jerusalem; and the Jebusite dwelt with the children of Benjamin in Jerusalem unto this present day.” Since above the children of Judah are recorded to have attacked and captured Jerusalem and given the whole city to fire, how is it said here that the children of Benjamin did not destroy the Jebusite inhabitant of Jerusalem, but rather that the Jebusite himself dwelt with the children of Benjamin in Jerusalem unto this present day? It is therefore understood that, after the children of Judah had captured and devastated the city, the children of Benjamin—whose possession lay wholly beside the tribe of Judah and reached Jerusalem—began to live there. They allowed the Jebusite inhabitant of the place, subdued by the children of Judah, to dwell with them. Thus Jerusalem was inhabited jointly by Jebusites and children of Israel [Col. 0088A] until David’s time, until at last David entirely expelled the Jebusite, Jerusalem was assigned to the lot of the children of Judah, and it was called the city of David.

(JUD. II.) “The angel of the Lord went up from Gilgal to the place of weeping.” By anticipation it is now called “the place of weeping,” for the name was given later. “Joshua therefore dismissed the people.” How, when he has already said that Joshua was dead, and that after his death Judah went up to battle before the children of Israel, together with all the things said thus far—how does he now subsequently recount that Joshua dismissed the people? The narrative returns to what preceded, as though saying: in the fact that, after Joshua’s death, the children of Israel preserved those nations whom the Lord had commanded to be destroyed, it is evident how, after Joshua dismissed them, left to themselves they despised the commandments of God. For after Joshua dismissed the people and died, and the other elders who knew the law of God had departed, the following generation, abandoning the worship of God, began to serve idols and by wicked deeds to provoke God’s wrath against itself. Thus “Joshua therefore dismissed the people” must be referred back to the preceding narrative.

(JUD. III.) “He raised up for them a saviour, Ehud, son of Gera, son of Jemini.” Jemini is Benjamin himself. For Benjamin is interpreted “son of the right hand.” Therefore, remove *ben*, which means “son,” and what remains, *jamini*, makes *jeminus*, that is, “right-handed,” “of the right side,” or “right”; it is called from the right hand in whatever manner it may be formed. Hence it should not be written *geminus* with *g*, as though it meant “double,” but *jeminus* with *j* and *e*, so that *jeminus* is derived from *jemin* or *jamin*, just as *dexter* is derived from *dextera*, “right hand.” Thus the children of Jemini are called children of Benjamin.

(JUD. IV.) “He himself dwelt in Harosheth of the nations.” This region is called “of the nations” because it was inhabited not by one people alone but by many nations. “She sent and called Barak son of Abinoam.” This Barak is thought to be the same man as Lapidoth. We believe this opinion arose because both names are found to have one meaning: Barak or Lapidoth means “lightning” and “flash.” Therefore Barak himself is Lapidoth, her husband, whom the woman, about to go to war, summons as a man.

“Heber the Kenite had formerly separated from the other Kenites, his brothers, the children of Hobab, Moses’ kinsman.” We read in Exodus how Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, came to him in the wilderness, bringing Zipporah his wife and his sons; then, when Jethro himself was returning to his own land, Moses retained with him Hobab, Jethro’s son and his own kinsman, namely the brother of his wife, so that he might proceed with the children of Israel to the land of promise. From the descendants of this Hobab, Heber descended.
