He separated from his other brothers, the children of Hobab, who dwelt among the children of Israel—as we read above in this Book of Judges, that the children of the Kenite went up from the city of palms with the children of Judah into the wilderness of the allotment and dwelt with them. Departing for another place in that same region, namely the valley of Sennim, he dwelt there; and his wife killed Sisera.

(JUD. V.) “Deborah and Barak son of Abinoam sang on that day, saying: ‘You who freely offered your lives from Israel to danger, bless the Lord.’” Deborah and Barak sang this song after their victory in praise of God.

> “Lord, when you went out from Seir and passed through the regions of Edom, the earth moved, and the heavens and clouds dropped water. The mountains flowed away before the Lord, and Sinai before the Lord, the God of Israel.”

He recalls God’s past wonders in order to magnify the present ones. He means that formerly, when God went before his people, leading them out of Egypt through the wilderness joined to the land of Edom and Seir, even mute elements felt the Creator’s presence and, as though alarmed and shaken by neighbouring majesty, by their movement itself rendered acknowledgement to the present divine power.

“The earth moved.” Behold the sign of the Deity’s presence: he who alone established it could move it. In Exodus we read (ch. XIX) how, when the Lord descended upon Mount Sinai, the whole mountain smoked; the whole mountain was terrible, smoke rose from it as from a furnace, and a very thick cloud covered it. There, therefore, the earth moved and smoked because of the Creator’s presence; there the heavens, dripping water in the thickest cloud, testified by a kind of sweat to their fear and reverence; and the mountains, covered by the shadows of the clouds, flowed in the shifting of the flying clouds and the descent of water.

“Sinai before the God of Israel.” In this one clause he comprehends all that preceded: Sinai was moved before the Lord; Sinai dripped water; Sinai flowed away before the Lord. For what he had first set forth almost generally because of the greatness of the miracle—“the earth moved, the heavens and clouds dripped water, the mountains flowed”—he then specifies where all this was fulfilled, saying, “Sinai before the Lord.” But “the mountains flowed” may be understood as hyperbole, as though they melted from excessive terror. Moreover, “the earth moved” may aptly refer to the disturbance of the people dwelling on the earth, who, having heard of such great wonders, were moved and troubled.

It follows: “In the days of Shamgar son of Anath, in the days of Jael, the paths ceased; and those who travelled upon them went by devious tracks.” Having recalled ancient wonders, he proceeds to recount new miracles. He means that before her time the children of Israel were so constrained on every side by fear of their enemies [Col. 0090A] that the paths lay unused, no one walking upon them; and if anyone was compelled to proceed upon them, he avoided enemy attacks by travelling secretly not on the public road but by winding byways. This also occurred in the days of Shamgar, who, though of such strength that he slew six hundred with one ploughshare, nevertheless could not establish in the land such a great and enduring peace as God has now given his people through this victory.

This is what follows: “The strong men of Israel ceased and rested,” namely, because they were unable to resist their enemies, “until Deborah arose—arose, I say, a mother in Israel.” Therefore the Lord chose new wars, destroying the strong by the weak and casting down proud enemies through a woman. And, to make God’s miracle greater, this was accomplished not only under a woman commander, but also by a small force in battle. For it follows: “Was shield or spear seen among forty thousand in Israel?” Among so many thousands there was none to raise shield or spear against the enemies, except a few, namely ten thousand, who gave themselves to peril for the salvation of their people. Of them he adds: “My heart loves the leaders of Israel”; and again to them: “You who freely offered yourselves to danger, bless the Lord.”

“You who ride upon shining asses, sit in judgment, and walk upon the road.” You who now, with enemies overthrown by God’s help, possess glory, authority, and peace, do not forget the works of the Lord by which these things were bestowed upon us. “Speak where the chariots were shattered and the army of the enemy was strangled.” By shining asses he means glory; by sitting in judgment, authority; by walking on the road, peace. Therefore there let the just deeds of the Lord be told, regarding the destruction of the enemies; and his mercy toward Israel’s strong ones, regarding the liberation of his own. Then the people of the Lord went down to the gates: those who previously did not dare to go out for fear of their enemies, after the enemies’ defeat not only went out but also held dominion.

Hence follows joy and thanksgiving: “Awake, awake, Deborah. The Lord fought among the mighty: from Ephraim,” or “in Ephraim,” “he destroyed them in Amalek, and after him”; or, as some think more correctly translated from Hebrew: “and after you, in Benjamin, against your peoples, O Amalek.” The meaning is that, to increase present joy, he adds God’s past and future wonders to those now occurring. The Lord fought among the mighty from Ephraim. The Lord fought among those strong men from Ephraim, and through them destroyed those who were in Amalek. Or he fought among the strong who were in Ephraim and through them destroyed those in Amalek, so that the sense is: “I destroyed those who were in Amalek,” as above. He notes how, in Moses’ time, Joshua—who was from Ephraim—overcame Amalek, the Lord fighting through him and in him; this concerns the past.

Then he adds concerning the future, indicating that the Lord will still destroy Amalek through Saul, who is to be born from Benjamin. This is what follows: “And after him,” that is, Ephraim—or “after you, O Ephraim”—the Lord fought among the mighty in Benjamin, that is, through the strong men who will be in Benjamin, namely through Saul, who will be born from Benjamin. He will fight, I say, “against your peoples,” that is, against your peoples, O Amalek.

It follows: “Leaders came down from Machir, and from Zebulun those who led the army into battle.” This concerns the present history. For he praises those from Machir, Zebulun, and Issachar who did not hesitate to undergo the danger of war for their people. On the contrary, he rebukes those who withdrew themselves—Reuben and Gad, or Gilead, Dan, and Asher—and marks them as deserving ridicule for their neglect. This is what follows: “Reuben, divided against himself, was found to have the contention of great-souled men.”

In Hebrew it is written: *Biflagoth Ruben gotholib helchiche lem*, that is, “the divisions of Reuben, great cunning of heart.” They think this should be understood thus: by great cunning of heart Reuben separated himself from the others and set his borders far from the press of warfare, in such a division on both sides that, wherever wars might arise, from one side or the other, there would come to him, resting safely, not the weight of battle but only the light whistle of report. Hence he adds: “Why do you live, O Reuben, between two boundaries?” That is, so that you may attach yourself to neither side. You do this in order to hear whistles, that is, only a faint report safely from afar—the whistles, I say, of flocks, that is, camps and armies—so that you may hear and do nothing. Hence, in mockery, he again repeats: “The divisions of Reuben, great cunning of heart.”

But if it is read thus, “Reuben’s division against himself was found to be the contention of great-souled men,” it may be understood in this way. When Reuben was divided against himself—that is, when he doubted, fluctuated within himself with varied thoughts and contrary desires, and disputed with himself whether he should go to war or not, and delayed in this uncertainty—the great-souled men of Zebulun and Naphtali were found ready for contest and conflict. Or: Reuben, divided from the others and withdrawing lest he go to battle—which was nevertheless against himself, that is, against his own honour—showed that the contention of the great-souled men was found.

Then he turns mockery also upon the others: Gilead, Dan, and Asher were inactive, but Zebulun and Naphtali offered their lives to death in the region of Rome [Merom]. He identifies the place where battle was fought. In Hebrew it is written: *Romae Zachae*, which is interpreted “upon the height of the plain.” It means that in the plain where they fought, they became superior to their enemies by giving themselves to danger. Thus *Romae* should not be understood as a place-name but signifies “height”; the translation erred in this.

“The stars, remaining in their order and course, fought against Sisera.” Scripture does not affirm, as astrologers suppose, that Sisera was conquered through the fate of a constellation; rather, figuratively it says that the heavenly things themselves seemed to have directed their efforts toward his overthrow, because the Lord of heaven, by his providence, ordained that he should be conquered. Thus, just as mountains, valleys, or any other earthly things are rebuked or praised when something blameworthy or praiseworthy is done by people dwelling in them and ruling over them, and those places themselves are said to have done what was done by people in them, so stars are said to have done from heaven what God, ruling over them in heaven, did.

“The stars, remaining in their order, fought.” He shows their intention and reason in saying, “remaining in their order.” For they remain where they linger and direct their effort intensely; and they remain in order where, in what they do, they do not abandon reason.

“Curse the land of Meroz [Meros or Merotz],” said the angel of the Lord. Either a messenger of God who came to me said this, or I myself, being an angel of God, say to you on his behalf that you should curse the land of Meroz. It is the name of a region or of the man who owned it, from whom the land of Meroz took its name. “Curse its inhabitants.” He gives the reason: “because they did not come to the help of the Lord,” that is, to assist the mighty ones.

(JUD. VI.) “Joash, father of the family of Ezri [Ozri].” Here “father” means the greater, older, more honourable person among the others of that family, from which he himself also came.

(JUD. IX.) “From the temple of Baal-berith.” *Berith* means “conspiracy”; hence Baal-berith is the idol of conspiracy. “He killed his brothers, the sons of Jerubbaal, seventy men.” If he killed all seventy, how did one of them remain? But it is said thus: he killed seventy and one remained—as though it were said: he killed seventy besides the one who remained. “My wine, which gladdens God when it is sacrificed, and men when it is drunk.” “What is this Abimelech?” That is, he is a person of no value. And another point: he appointed his servant Zebul, some low and contemptible man, ruler over noble men.

(JUD. XI.) “Jephthah spoke all his words before the Lord in Mizpah.” By “words” he means the things that had taken place between him and the princes of Gilead concerning his leadership. He spoke them before the Lord to confirm the covenant between them. “Unless you are better than Balak son of Zippor”: that is, you repeat what seemed more properly to belong to him, because this land was his, and we took it from them with the consent of our God. Yet he is known never to have reclaimed what was taken away. Unless, perhaps, you can teach and show that he ever contended to recover this land from Israel or fought against it—namely, throughout all the time, now three hundred years, that Israel has dwelt in Heshbon and its territories, etc.

“If you deliver the children of Ammon into my hands, whoever first comes out I will offer as a burnt offering to the Lord.” Following the custom of the Gentiles, he vowed human blood, just as we later read that the king of Moab offered his son upon the walls. This was therefore contrary to the law, unless perhaps he is excused by a hidden divine prompting, so that he was rightly numbered by the Apostle among the saints (Heb. XI).

(JUD. XII.) “The men of Gilead struck Ephraim, because he had said: ‘Gilead is a fugitive of Ephraim, and dwells in the midst of Ephraim and Manasseh.’” In Hebrew it is written *Atem Galaad*, interpreted “you, Gilead,” spoken with indignation. It is as though one said: “Who are you?” or “What sort of people are you who dwell among us? You, Gilead, between Ephraim and Manasseh.”

(JUD. XIII.) “And the Spirit of the Lord began to be with him in the camps of Dan.” Or this phrase, “in the camps of Dan,” may be understood as meaning “in the army or companies of Dan.” Or “the camps of Dan” identifies the place where Samson first lived. Perhaps it is said by anticipation, because later we read that the place where six hundred men of the tribe of Dan lived at Kiriath-jearim of Judah received the name “the camps of Dan” from them. Unless, perhaps, we cannot suitably understand that place here because that place is called Kiriath-jearim of Judah, whereas this one is named between Zorah and Eshtaol.

(JUD. XIV.) “For three days they could not solve the riddle.” [Col. 0093B] “And when the seventh day came, they said to Samson’s wife: ‘Entice your husband.’” She poured out tears before Samson, and during the seven days of the feast she wept with him. This is the sequence of the narrative. But a difficulty seems to arise from it. For if the limit fixed for solving the riddle was the seventh day, and they, having accepted the riddle, worked for three days to solve it without success, then at last, as is read, when the seventh day came, spoke to Samson’s wife; and she, moved both by their entreaties and threats, only then wrung from Samson by tears the solution of the riddle for herself: how can it stand that she wept with him throughout the seven days of the feast? How could she, seeking the solution, have wept through all seven days of the feast, when she first began to ask on the seventh day?

But if, after the three days in which they had laboured unsuccessfully to solve the problem, they spoke to Samson’s wife on the fourth day, even then it cannot stand that she is said to have wept seven days for the solution. Therefore, if, as written, after accepting the riddle they tried for three days to solve it, and then on the fourth day spoke to her, how is it true that it was said, “when the seventh day came they spoke to Samson’s wife” that she might discover its solution, and that she, making herself importunate to her husband during the four remaining days, finally on the seventh day wrung out the solution and reported it to her fellow-citizens?

It is therefore true that it is said that “for three days they could not solve the riddle”; but what follows, “And when the seventh day came,” must be read and punctuated separately, so that it is not joined to the next clause thus: “For three days they could not solve the riddle. And when the seventh day came …” Pause here, so that it is understood: “then they solved it.” He then explains how they found its solution: because they spoke to Samson’s wife—after the third day, namely, when they had failed. And she, accepting their requests, wept with her husband during the seven days of the feast—not, however, all seven days, but during the four days remaining of the seven after the three days. Thus she wept “seven days,” that is, during those seven days she wept. “She wept seven days,” that is, she wept until the completion of seven days.

(JUD. XV.) “Samson, son-in-law of Thanmatha.” Thanmatha is a place from which comes *Thanmathaeus*, a gentilicial name, not a proper name. “Though you have done this”: although you have inflicted this vengeance upon my father-in-law in revenge for my injury, you have not yet appeased me so that I shall not still demand vengeance from you. “And he struck them with a great slaughter, so that in astonishment they laid shin upon thigh.” Scripture wished to portray astonishment by the shin laid upon the thigh. For persons who are astonished and weary are accustomed at times to place a bent lower leg upon the other thigh, and to sit with the calf—that is, the lower part of the leg—resting upon the thigh, as though lacking counsel and not knowing where they can move themselves.

In Hebrew it is written: *Sogal ghereth*, “shin upon thigh,” so that it may be said, “He struck them with a great slaughter, shin upon thigh.” Yet this may be referred to the same meaning. Another meaning is: “He struck them with a great slaughter,” namely, in such a way that he struck shin upon thigh—that is, having struck the thigh, he struck the shin also. Since persons standing or walking rest upon their shins, but those sitting upon their thighs, we may not inappropriately understand foot-soldiers by “shin” and horsemen by “thigh.” What then is it to strike shin upon thigh except to destroy the lesser men as well as the greater?

“In the place afterwards called Lehi,” that is, “jawbone,” where their army was scattered—that is, dispersed or poured out or spread abroad, covering the ground in a great multitude. “As flax is consumed at the smell [heat] of fire.” *Lina*, “flax,” is written without *g*, whence *linea*, “linen garment”; it is not *ligna*, “wood,” with *g*, whence *lignea*, “wooden house.” By “smell,” moreover, understand the first warming of the fire, since light material is burned by an easily kindled flame.

“With the jawbone of an ass, *homor hemor*; with the jawbone of an ass I struck a thousand men.” In Hebrew it is written: “With the jawbone of an ass, *homor hemor*; with the jawbone of an ass I struck a thousand men.” *Homor hemor* is interpreted “heap upon heaps,” as though he said: that is, a heap from the dead bodies which I laid low with the jawbone of an ass. When he says “heap upon heaps,” it should be understood thus: he had struck them down in different places and made many heaps; but from all of them there was formed, as it were, one pile and a great heap.

Therefore the name of that place was called “the Spring of the Caller from the Jawbone.” Lest it should seem contradictory that above this place is said to be called Lehi, “jawbone,” while here it is said to be called not simply “jawbone” but “the Spring of the Caller from the Jawbone.” For just as in Genesis Abraham is recorded to have called a place “The Lord sees,” and Scripture immediately adds, “To this day it is said: ‘On the mountain the Lord will see’” (Gen. XXII), so here the place is called Lehi, “jawbone,” and yet later the name of that place is said to be not “jawbone” but “the Spring of the Caller from the Jawbone.”

“The name of that place was called Jawbone.” It was also called “the Spring of the Caller from the Jawbone,” so that, because of different events, there should be one name for the place—that is, the field—because of the killing of men, and another for the spring because of the issuing of water. The spring is therefore called “the spring from the jawbone,” namely produced from it; and that same spring is called “of the caller,” namely Samson, who called upon God and brought it forth from the jawbone.

But the Hebrew interpreter says that “of the caller” should be referred not to prayer but to the naming of the place, so that the sense is: the name of the place is “the spring of the caller from the jawbone,” that is, he who wishes to name or call the place by its name says that the spring from the jawbone should be called Lehi, “jawbone.” If, therefore, the name of the place is “of the caller” or “of the one naming the spring from the jawbone,” the name belongs both to the caller and to the place: to the caller because he says it, and to the place because he says it about the place. He says it because he wishes to name that place or spring, declaring that that place or spring is to be called “from the jawbone,” and “jawbone.” For, naming from the cast-off jawbone, he calls the place or spring Lehi, that is, “jawbone.”

(JUD. XVI.) “With ambushes hidden with her.” It should not seem surprising that the Philistines, seeking to kill Samson, did not dare to attack him either asleep or bound until they had obtained a true test of his strength. For they were filled with such terror that they did not even dare to approach him, lest, if they suddenly rushed upon him asleep or bound, before they could kill him he might awake, burst his bonds, and slaughter them all—as when someone is afraid even of a sleeping lion and does not dare to approach and touch it, lest it suddenly awaken and rush upon the author of its wound, raging more cruelly the more enraged it is.

[Col. 0096A] (JUDGES XVII.) “And he filled the hand of one of his sons, and he became his priest.” The phrase “he filled the hand of one of his sons” should be referred to the gifts with which he hired him, as seems to be stated more explicitly from the Hebrew: “He invested the hand of one of his sons,” giving him the means to exercise the priesthood. There was also at that time another young man from Bethlehem of Judah, from his own kindred—that is, Judah’s. He was a Levite both by office and by lineage: through his father from one tribe, through his mother from another; and he lived there, that is, in Bethlehem. “He had a boy with him.” He calls him a boy either in respect of age, because he was young, or in respect of service, because he was a servant.

(JUDGES XVIII.) “And they used his lodging.” By “lodging” he means a private conversation or a chamber in which he stayed apart.

(JUDGES XIX.) “They were sons of Jemini,” that is, sons of Benjamin. “Now we are going to the house of God.” He calls the tabernacle at Shiloh the house of God, or alternatively the shrine which Micah had built, with the carved image which he had made.

(JUDGES XX.) “Wishing to kill me and tormenting my wife with an incredible frenzy of lust.” Modestly he passes over what they wished to do to himself, mentioning something else in its place.

[Col. 0087]

## A Short Note on the Book of Ruth. (G)*

(RUTH IV.) “The man took off his sandal.” The man who yielded his legal right to his neighbour took off his sandal and gave it to the neighbour to whom he yielded. [Col. 0096C] Therefore Boaz, who was the kinsman, said to the other man, who yielded to him: “Take off your sandal,” etc.

[Col. 0095]

## Explanatory Notes on the Books of Kings: first on the number of the books, then on their interpretation

[Col. 0095D] The Book of Kings is divided among us into four sections. The first two are called by the Hebrews the Book of Samuel; the following two, *Malachim Ramatham*, as in Hebrew—or, as some have it, *Arimathaim*, whence Arimathea in the Gospel.

## Short Notes on First Kings

(I KINGS II.) “Until the barren woman bore many,” that is, seven. For after Samuel she had three sons and three daughters [the letter has two]; thus, seven. They add a seventh, born as one of the sons; he too is hers, so that there may be seven. “You shall see your rival in the temple amid all the prosperity of Israel.” You shall see it in your sons; for they themselves will see it after you.

(I KINGS III.) “Eli was lying on his bed, and his eyes had grown dim, and he could not see”: make the division here. There follows, “And the lamp of God was not yet extinguished. [Col. 0096D] But Samuel slept in the temple of the Lord, where the ark of God was; and the Lord called Samuel.” This—that Samuel slept in the temple of the Lord—was before the lamp of God was extinguished. The statement that Samuel was called by the Lord before the lamp was extinguished may be understood as though it said that he was called at night; or because Samuel himself, who was not yet accustomed to converse with God, while the lamp was lit could see that no one other than Eli was in the temple. Having learned that Eli himself had not spoken, he would not doubt that this was the voice of God.

(I KINGS VI.) “From the fortified city even to the unwalled village.” When it says that the five cities gave five mice and five golden anuses, and then adds, “from the fortified city even to the unwalled village,” this must be understood to mean that the five provinces gave five mice, and that each gave one of the five anuses. Although, by reason of their rank, the cities—as the capitals of the provinces—are said specially to have given them, the money was collected not only from those in the cities but also from the unwalled villages; that is, from the least as well as the greatest, so that, as the danger was shared by all, the offering might be that of all. Thus everyone gave throughout the whole land from end to end. This is what follows: “And as far as great Abel.” He means the stone of which he had spoken above: “There was there a great stone, and they split the wood of the cart and laid the cows upon it.” This stone, then, was, as it were, the boundary of the Philistine land and Israel, as far as which the Philistines followed the ark of the Lord; there [Col. 0097B] the men of Beth-shemesh, having received the ark, offered burnt offerings. Up to this stone, therefore, all the unwalled villages and fortified cities of the Philistine land contributed money and expenditure for rendering the due offering to the Lord. This is what is meant by “as far as great Abel,” “as far as the great stone.” For the name itself also signifies “stone.” In Hebrew *Abel* means “stone,” so that it should be understood as a proper name derived from a common noun.

Upon this stone they placed the ark of the Lord, as was said above. “And the ark remained until that day”—namely, the day on which the Lord struck the men of Beth-shemesh in the field of Joshua. Their fault may also be noted in this: they did not bring it into a house but left it outside, where it could be viewed irreverently by everyone. [Col. 0097C] For the men of Kiriath-jearim did not do this later, and therefore they were not struck.

“And he struck of the people seventy men and fifty thousand of the common people.” Some think that by the seventy men the elders and leaders of the people are to be understood, so that the following words, “fifty thousand of the common people,” mean that in the death of these men a loss was suffered as great as if fifty thousand common people had been slain. But in the Hebrew “of the common people” is not found. They therefore think the preceding statement should be understood thus: “He struck of the people seventy men and fifty thousand,” as though it said, “He struck fifty thousand and seventy of the people.” Nor were these only men of Beth-shemesh, lest he seem to have struck down not merely persons from among the people, but the people itself; rather, they were from the whole province and region surrounding the city of Beth-shemesh.

It gives the reason why they were struck, saying: “Because they had looked upon the ark of the Lord”—not reverently, nor with the fear fitting for so great a thing, but boldly rushing in and gazing upon the ark of the Lord. It was proper that, since they had heard that the Philistines—who were unworthy to retain the ark of God—had been struck for their presumption and rashness, they themselves too, mindful of their weakness, should approach to look upon it with great reverence and fear. Since, therefore, they were struck for their presumption, the text indicates this by naming those struck. Hence, in what follows, Uzzah, when he stretched out his hand to support the same ark, was struck and died, because, when the vehicle tilted and threatened to fall, he did not consider the majesty of Him who presided. [Col. 0098A]

(I KINGS VII.) “And it came to pass, from the day on which the ark of the Lord remained in Kiriath-jearim, that the days were multiplied—for it was now the twentieth year.” That is, from the time when it entered Kiriath-jearim until this time, when Samuel says to all the house of Israel what follows: “He called its name, the stone of help.” Therefore the earlier statement that Israel pitched camp beside the stone of help is said by anticipation: that is, in the place where this stone was later set up and so named.

(I KINGS IX.) “That he might not go up to the high place.” After Shiloh, before the building of the Temple, high places—that is, elevated places where sacrifice was offered to God—were not condemned. Later, once the place of sacrifice had been fixed, they became unlawful.

(I KINGS XII.) “The army of Hazor,” that is, the army of King Jabin, who lived in Hazor, mentioned above as “Hazoreth of the nations.”

(I KINGS XIII.) “Saul was a son of one year when he began to reign, and he reigned two years over Israel. And Saul chose for himself three thousand from Israel.” Some explain it thus: Saul himself, when he began to reign, was “a son of one year”; or Saul himself was a son of one year, that is, innocent and simple like a child one year old. And for two years he reigned in that simplicity; afterwards he changed for the worse. The Hebrews say that Saul reigned only two years, while Samuel judged Israel for twenty years.

According to this view, [Col. 0098C] “Saul reigned two years over Israel” is understood thus: when he began to reign and was “a son of one year”—that is, had already completed one year in the kingship—he did what follows: “He chose for himself three thousand from Israel.” For David too is later said, in the same manner of speech, to be “a son of thirty years,” that is, to have been thirty years old when he began to reign. This idiom is frequent and customary in Hebrew: “son of iniquity,” “son of peace,” “son of one year,” “son of thirty years.”

“Jonathan struck the Philistine garrison which was in Gibeah,” that is, their army which was staying in that place. “When the Philistines heard this, Saul sounded the trumpet.” When Saul learned that the Philistines had heard that Jonathan his son had struck their garrison, knowing that they would come to avenge those who had been struck, [Col. 0098D] he sounded the trumpet throughout the land, saying, “Let the Hebrews hear.” He sounded the trumpet so that the Hebrews might hear that the Philistines had been struck and might be encouraged for battle. And this happened. For all Israel heard the report, namely, that Saul had struck the Philistine garrison—the report attributing to the king what his son had done. Thus Israel, taking courage, rose against the Philistines. Therefore the people of Israel, running after Saul, cried out for battle at Gilgal.

“But the Hebrews crossed the Jordan.” Here he calls Hebrews the portion of the people living beyond the Jordan, namely the tribes of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh; the rest he calls Israel. Hence Saul sounded the trumpet so that those far away might hear the report of victory. Scripture distinguishes them by the name Hebrews, playing on the term, because they frequently had to cross the Jordan in coming to assist the rest of Israel; for “Hebrew” means “one who crosses.”

(I KINGS XV.) “Moreover, the triumphant one in Israel will not spare, nor will he be moved by repentance.” The Hebrew has it thus: *Vagham, Neza Izrahelloe Zachir*, that is: “Moreover, the strength of Israel will not lie.” This means that God, who is the triumphant one in Israel—for through him Israel triumphs and conquers—the strength of Israel, that is, he who gives Israel strength and fortitude, will not lie by changing his word, as you have just tried to nullify his word by not doing what he commanded. Rather, he will not lie, [Col. 0099B] but will bring his word to effect; or he will not spare, as though changed by some compassion so as not to fulfil what he had determined, as you previously wished to seem merciful by sparing men deserving death and thus making God a liar. Nor will he be turned by repentance, so as to repent of what he proposed and thereby change and not do what he had intended. For he is not a man, that he should repent. A human being, who can will evil and can change, can repent.

(I KINGS XVI.) “For is his anointed before the Lord?” That is: is this man now presented and brought before you one whom you have provided to be your anointed? Jesse therefore brings his seven sons before Samuel, and Samuel says to Jesse: “The Lord has chosen none of these.” How can it be true that Jesse brought his seven sons to Samuel, and that Samuel testifies that none of those brought was chosen, when David, one of the seven, had not yet been brought and was chosen? It must therefore be understood that he brought six, excepting the one whom he said remained, and it is true that the Lord chose none of the others.

(I KINGS XVII.) “David brought the Philistine’s head to Jerusalem.” From this it appears that even at that time both the children of Israel and the Jebusites had a common habitation in Jerusalem. David brought the Philistine’s head there, as to a more eminent city, for the glory of his triumph. “From what stock is this young man descended? And Abner answered,” etc. How does Saul here fail to know David [Col. 0099D] and inquire about his descent, when above he is said to have sent to Jesse, his father, saying, “Send me David your son, who is among the pastures”? David is also stated to have come to Saul, stood before him, been loved by him, and been made his armour-bearer. But it should be noted that powerful men, placed amid the daily throng of people, cannot recognize all those about them, especially those whom neither personal rank commends nor long association makes familiar. Since David, still a boy and insignificant, had stayed with Saul for only a short time and was not worthy of royal intimacy, it is not surprising that Saul now, seeing him step forth for so outstanding a deed, did not recognize him distinctly. The fact that he previously calls him by name when sending him to Jesse his father is by no means to be ascribed to personal acquaintance: he called him by that name because he had learned it from the report of those informing him, not because he recognized him through an earlier familiar acquaintance.

(I KINGS XVIII.) “And Saul placed him over the men of war.” This must be understood to have been done not from love but from hatred, so that David, exposing himself to battles through a desire for praise, might perish. For Saul had already heard the women singing: “Saul has struck down thousands, and David tens of thousands.” Provoked to anger by this praise of David, he began to devise his death. Therefore it adds: “Now when David returned after striking the Philistine,” etc. This had already happened, but is narrated out of sequence. “You shall become my son-in-law in two matters”: first, concerning Merab, who was promised, and then Michal, who was given.

[Col. 0100B] (I KINGS XXI.) “The vessels of the young men were holy. Now the way is polluted, but even today it shall be sanctified in the vessels.” He speaks according to the rite of the Law, by which it was unlawful for consecrated bread later to be put into vessels in which common food had previously been placed. Therefore he says that the vessels of the young men—that is, of his companions—were holy, because they contained nothing common that would prevent their receiving consecrated food. “Now this way,” he says, “is polluted”; that is, we are polluted on the journey, perhaps by seeing or touching something, and consequently, according to the custom of the Law, we ought rightly to be forbidden to touch sacred things. “But even today it shall be sanctified in the vessels”; that is, we shall be excused concerning any unclean things that we may have touched. We shall be excused, I say, because of the clean vessels which we carry.

[Col. 0100C] (I KINGS XXVI.) “If the Lord incites you against me, may he smell the sacrifice.” God is appeased, if this comes from his wrath; I have no other counsel regarding this matter. “But if the children of men do this, they are cursed in the sight of the Lord,” because those who drove me out act unjustly, etc.

(I KINGS XXIV.) “He has been with me for many days or years.” Above it was said that he had been in the land of the Philistines only four months; yet here Achish says that he has remained with him for many days or years. Perhaps this is said so that they might draw a stronger proof of David’s loyalty from the length of time; and for this reason he added “years.”

## Short Notes on Second Kings

[Col. 0100D] (II KINGS I.) “David composed this lament over Saul and over Jonathan his son; and he commanded that the children of Judah should be taught the bow,” that is, the art of archery, because Saul and Jonathan his son had died by Philistine arrows, so that, should war arise anew, they might be able to defend themselves against their adversaries. “As it is written in the Book of the Just.” Some think that the Book of the Just is this same book, on account of Samuel and David, of whom it chiefly treats. Others interpret the Book of the Just as the Law of Moses, in which the pattern of righteousness is set before human beings. From it they suppose that in certain passages the art of archery is shown to be useful, as perhaps in the saying in Genesis where Jacob says that he took a portion from the hand of the Amorite by sword and bow. Others interpret “Book of the Just” not as a book of persons [Col. 0101A] but of judgments or commandments—as though it said “in the book of law.” The sense would then be: he commanded the children of Judah to be taught the bow, so that this should be held as though it were a law and be observed inviolably, in accordance with what is written in the book of law and set forth by the precept of the Law.

“The shield of the mighty”: it must be pronounced in the plural, though he explains it in the singular by adding, “the shield of Saul.” This is a manner of speaking in which something is proposed generally, to which a singular application is joined. It occurs in rhetorical amplification, when something is narrated with intense force: “The shield of the mighty has been cast away—the shield of Saul—as though he had not been anointed with oil,” as though he were a base man, a man without divine consecration.

Then follows: “From the blood of the slain, from the fat of the mighty, Jonathan’s arrow never turned back.” It is as though he said: Jonathan’s arrow did not turn back in battle so that, once shot, it should ever recoil ineffectually from the blood of the mighty and the fat of the vigorous; rather, it penetrated forcefully, shedding blood and cutting through the fat of the mighty whom it slew. “Jonathan has been slain in your high places, O Israel. I grieve for you, my brother Jonathan.”

(II KINGS V.) The saying came to David from them, that is, from the Jebusites: “You shall not enter here unless you remove the blind and the lame.” They placed blind and lame men on their walls, so as to say to the approaching David: “You shall not enter here”—in contempt of him, of course, as though such persons sufficed to repel his force. Therefore they said: “You shall not enter here unless you remove these blind and lame persons who have been set before you to resist you.”

[Col. 0101C] For David had proposed on that day a reward to the man who should strike a Jebusite and reach the pipes of the roofs—that is, the channels of the drains projecting from the roofs of the houses at the top of the wall, to carry off rainwater. David offered a reward to the one who, first climbing as far as the channels projecting above, should enter the city. He does not specify the reward here, but explains it in the Book of Paralipomenon: he would make him commander of the army. Thus Joab, ascending first, became chief of the military force.

“From Mello, and inward.” Mello was a place in the city; beginning from it, he built around and inward.

[Col. 0101D] (II KINGS VII.) “Before your people you did terrible things,” that is, for your people. For you took from them the reason for acting. “Whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt.” Stop here; then join, “a nation and its God,” supplying: where shall we find such a nation and such a God of it as your people Israel and you, their God?

(II KINGS XI.) “She was purified from her uncleanness”: that is, she washed herself after intercourse, or her menstrual flow ceased because of conception.

(II KINGS XIV.) “Upon me, my lord the king, be the iniquity, and upon my father’s house; but let the king and his throne be innocent.” It is as though she said: Take care that your promise not prove empty; for it does not befit you, who are king and lord, that iniquity should be found in you, as it may be in [Col. 0102A] me and my father’s house—that is, people like me. The greater you are, the more shameful is your iniquity. “Let the king remember the Lord his God,” that is, let him fear the Lord his God. “That they may not be multiplied”: that is, that he may not permit the blood-avengers—the kinsmen of the slain—to multiply and rise up repeatedly for vengeance; then they will not kill my son.

“Let your handmaid speak,” etc. Having received assurance concerning the case which she had invented as her own, she now introduces the point by which she compels the king, through his own judgment, to spare, saying: “Why have you devised such a thing?”—that is, why have you banished your son for the killing of his brother? This was against the people of God, because this example may later harm the people of God if the people imitate it and act likewise. Therefore come now, because it is good to spare and have mercy. For this reason I have come, to speak to you, O king my lord, this word which I made concerning my son.

What follows, “in the presence of the people,” is expressed more plainly in Hebrew: *chi, chire*, that is, “for they terrified me.” It is as though she said: because those who wished to kill my son terrified me, I came to obtain pardon. Yet it can appropriately be understood also in the preceding words, so that the sense is: I came to speak this word, pressed upon and urgently compelled by the people, who demand my son’s death. “And your handmaid said: Let me speak to the king, if perhaps the king may do the word of his handmaid”—that is, perhaps he may hear me pleading for my son. And the king heard.

[Col. 0102C] Therefore let your handmaid say: “May the word of my lord the king be fulfilled,” so that you may preserve in your own case the judgment which you made concerning mine; for you, like an angel of God, ought to be moved from truth neither by anger which you may have against anyone nor by favour. “By the life of your soul, my lord the king, there is neither to the right nor to the left”: that is, nothing at all deviates from anything that you have said, but it is as you say—namely, that the hand of Joab is with me. “You are wise in all these things, to understand everything”: that is, what ought expediently to be done in all matters to be carried out upon earth. It is flattery, intended to make him consider what ought to be done as a wise man.

(II KINGS XV.) “They carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord, and they set down the ark of God.” Some think that the ark of the Lord was set down so that David might consult the Lord. [Col. 0102D] But because the Lord was unwilling then to answer him, David said to Zadok: “Carry the ark of God back into the city,” namely Jerusalem. Others think that it was set down to await the people who were crossing. Hence what follows: “Abiathar went up,” that is, he stood apart in a higher place, waiting until all the people had gathered.

(II KINGS XVII.) “He went in to Abigail, the daughter of Nahash.” Nahash is Jesse, David’s father.

(II KINGS XXI.) “From the beginning of the harvest until water dripped upon them.” Note that in those regions, in summer—especially at harvest-time—neither thunder sounds nor rain falls until about the Kalends of September.

“And war again arose between the Philistines and Israel; and David went down,” etc. The woman whom Scripture here calls Arepham [Arafam] is believed to have been Orpah the Moabitess, Naomi’s daughter-in-law, Ruth’s companion. From her lineage these four giants were born, who are here said to have fallen by the hand of David and his servants. Scripture repeats from earlier events in recounting these wars, perhaps in an order different from that in which they occurred.

In the first, Abishai son of Zeruiah killed Jesbidenob; in the second, Sibbecai killed Sephi [Zap]; in the third, David—who here is called *Adeodatus*, because he was given by God for Israel’s deliverance, “son of the forest,” because he was taken from pastures and woodland, *polymitarius*, because he adorned the worship of God with manifold beauty in psalms and songs, and “the Bethlehemite,” on account of his homeland—[Col. 0103A] namely David himself, killed Goliath the Gittite. This battle seems to have been the first, although it is mentioned here as the third. In the fourth, Jonathan killed the man who had six fingers on each hand and foot, who likewise was of the stock of Arepha [Arafa].

(II KINGS XXIII.) “These are the last words which David spoke.” Namely, those stated above, or those which follow: “David son of Jesse said.” In the manner of Scripture, he speaks of himself as though of another: “The man said, to whom it was appointed to be the Anointed of the God of Jacob”—that is, to whom grace or the office was granted concerning the Anointed of the God of Jacob, namely that he should be the Anointed of the God of Jacob. In Hebrew it is: “The man said, raised up above the Anointed of the God of Jacob,” that is, the man who is the Anointed of the God of Jacob, whom the God of Jacob himself raised up—that is, exalted—so that he should be above all.

“The excellent singer, or psalmist, in Israel.” What did he say? Namely this: “The Spirit of the Lord spoke through me, and his word was upon my tongue. The God of Israel spoke to me, and the Mighty One of Israel spoke to me.” What did he say to me? Namely, that he who is just ought to rule human beings. Yet he must rule in the fear of God, so that he governs those beneath him by justice while always subjecting himself, through fear, to the God above him. Or he said to me that the just ruler of human beings, ruling in the fear of God, shines and grows. He said this to me so that I might know how I should preside and how I should be subject; and through this I have become splendid—like the light of dawn, shining brightly in a cloudless morning when the sun rises—and I have become fruitful, as grass springs from the earth through rains, [Col. 0103D] that is, through the watering of rain.

Yet this has not come about through my merits. For before God, whose is the whole world, my whole house—that is, my family and offspring—is not such that he should enter into an everlasting covenant with me, firm in all respects and secure, unless his grace had done this. From this grace comes all my salvation and all my desire: that is, whatever I will and desire is given and fulfilled through it; and nothing concerning me or belonging to me fails to grow and prosper.

“But transgressors,” such as Saul was, “shall all be plucked out like thorns,” because they are unworthy to remain in the field of God. Thorns are not gathered by hand, because they are unmanageable and prick those who touch them through rebellion. And if anyone wishes to touch them—that is, to rebuke and correct them—[Col. 0104A] he will arm himself with iron and a spear-shaft. The spear is wood; the lance-head is iron. It is as though he said: whoever wishes to rage against them will use not words alone, by which they may be instructed, but vengeance, by which they may be uprooted, so that, uprooted, they may be burned with unquenchable fire and consumed utterly. Note that striking is done with wood and cutting with iron. Thus the spear-shaft is vengeance that not only torments but exterminates.

“These are the names of David’s mighty men.” Here he enumerates those who excelled in courage in David’s army, among whom he includes David himself, because a king’s glory would not be complete in having brave soldiers unless he too were brave. For this reason he puts David before all the rest, as stronger than the strong, so that their commendation too might redound to his glory. He first counts three separately, as surpassing all: first and chief among them he places David; second, Eleazar; third, Semmaa. These are the first three. Then he names three others and sets forth their deed of valour: breaking through the hostile camp, they brought water from the cistern at Bethlehem. Yet although they shone gloriously among the other thirty distinguished men, he testifies that they were by no means equal to the first three. Then he adds the rest: thirty-six in all, and with Uriah thirty-seven. These are they.

Joab is not counted, either because he was leader of the others and well known, or because of the deaths of Abner and Amasa.

“David sitting in the seat.” Behold his teaching office, deservedly, because he was most wise. “He is like the very tender wood-worm.” The wood-worm, tender and soft in itself, pierces hard wood. When it is touched, nothing is softer; when it touches, nothing is harder. Therefore, in being called “very tender,” his humility and gentleness are indicated; in being called a “wood-worm,” his strength is signified. When David was injured, nothing was gentler; when he wished to injure, nothing was fiercer.

There are three principal virtues: wisdom, humility, and strength. No one else could possess all of these except the one alone in whom the Spirit of God was directed. Three further qualities follow as images of these: discipline, corresponding to wisdom; gentleness, to humility; constancy, to strength. These latter three are perversely imitated by the three that follow: hypocrisy imitates discipline; sloth, gentleness; obstinacy, constancy.

“David sitting in the seat, who killed eight hundred in one assault.” We do not read where this was done, except insofar as it is mentioned here. In Hebrew it is: “Eight hundred at one time.” This can be understood as though it said: David is compared to a wood-worm because of his strength, by which he penetrates all things and nothing can resist him—so much so that [Col. 0105C] he can rush upon eight hundred at one time and conquer.

“After him, Eleazar,” namely second in courage after David, among the three mighty men who were with David when the Philistines reproached Israel—namely, for cowardice and inability to resist them—and the Philistines gathered there, where David was, for battle. The Jews say that this happened at the same place where Goliath reproached the armies of Israel. We read nothing else except what is stated here.

“And after him, Semmaa son of Aggae of Arari. And the Philistines gathered in a station.” The connection does not seem coherent; but it should be read thus: “After him, Semmaa.” He too likewise struck the Philistines; and it adds, “because the Philistines gathered in a station,” that is, in a place where they stood and remained after pitching camp. When the people of Israel fled before the Philistines, he stood in the midst of the field—that is, in the open ground from which the people had fled—and protected it, that is, defended the field, so that he might hold it after the enemies had fled or been overthrown.

“And also before this,” namely in another battle which had taken place before this, three mighty men went down, who were chiefs among the thirty [Uriah not included], that is, more distinguished than the other thirty. They came at harvest-time to David in the cave of Adullam. Of all these things we can have no knowledge other than what we infer from what is stated in this place.

“He struck the two lions of Moab.” In Hebrew it is read more plainly: “the two leaders of Moab.” “And he went down and struck a lion in the midst of a cistern.” It was great boldness to descend alone against so fierce a creature. Yet he had not attained to the three first named, so as to be their equal. “And David made him his confidential adviser,” that is, counsellor, privy to secrets; either this should be taken as one expression, or “from secrecy,” that is, concerning secrets—as though it said that he made him his counsellor concerning, or in, secret matters.

(II KINGS XXIV.) “And the anger of the Lord was added.” He added this to the punishments stated above, that is, this wrath. “And the Lord himself moved David against them,” that is, to do what would be against them—David, I say, saying to Joab, “Go, number Israel.” This is what follows: “The king said to Joab.” “But David’s heart struck him,” that is, his conscience reproached him for what he had done.

## Short Notes on Third Kings
(III KINGS VI.) “And he made in the temple slanting windows,” that is, arched at the top, or slanting throughout—that is, wider on the inside for the sake of light. “Against the walls,” that is, externally along the walls, he made chambers, as it were terraces, all around in three stories: the lowest narrower, the middle broader, the highest broadest, so that the columns by which the upper parts were supported would not touch the lower chambers, but each would rise externally from the ground. These chambers were like rooms attached outside to the wall. The beams by which the chambers themselves were supported he placed around the house [Col. 0106C], that is, he joined them to the house—yet around it externally, so that they did not adhere to the walls of the temple, that is, were not fixed into the walls, because a certain projection made in the wall all around received and supported them at the end touching the wall, while at the other end they rested upon columns. Or this may be understood of beams inside the house, arranged in the same manner. “He also covered the house with cedar ceilings.” He made the roof of the house flat, according to the custom of the region, as were the external chambers. Therefore he placed cedar ceilings in the roof of the house, and covered the house with timber and the floor with fir boards. “And he built cedar chambers of twenty cubits”: he separated twenty cubits of the sixty which were the length of the house, in the rear part of the house [Col. 0106D], that is, the western part, since the entrance was on the east. And in that part likewise, building cedar chambers from the floor upward, he made from that portion of the house the house of the oracle, the Holy of Holies—that is, so that it itself should be the Holy of Holies; I mean the inner part, because entrance into it was not open except through the other parts. But the temple itself before the doors of the oracle was forty cubits long. For from the doors of the oracle to the eastern gate there were forty cubits; all of which was called the Holy Place. “And its joints”: he calls joints the places where the chambers were joined. But he had made the oracle in the middle of the house, that is, within the house, in the inner part, that is, farther from the entrance. The oracle itself was twenty cubits long, twenty cubits wide, and twenty cubits high [Col. 0107A]. From this it is clear that the oracle was twenty cubits lower than the rest of the house. “And he covered the altar with cedar.” This is the altar of incense, which stood before the oracle, that is, the Holy of Holies. “And he covered the whole altar of the oracle with gold.” This is the same altar which above he says was covered with cedar; now with gold, standing before the oracle. “One wing of a cherub was five cubits,” namely, wide, and the other five, so that from the tip, that is, the extremity, of one to the tip of the other, across, there were ten cubits, its breadth being equal to its height. For the body of the cherub was held between the spread wings. “And he placed the cherubim in the middle of the inner temple,” that is, of the oracle, their faces turned eastward toward the mercy-seat placed before them. Thus one wing of one [Col. 0107B] touched the southern wall, and one wing of the other the northern wall, while the remaining two joined one another in the middle of the oracle: such was the spread of the wings as was the width of the oracle. “And he made in them,” namely in the walls, cherubim: he carved other forms of cherubim in various places on the walls, and palms of hands, and other varied figures. At the entrance of the oracle he made two small doors, as he specifies afterwards. Two doors of fir wood, one on this side and the other on that. Each door was double, that is, had two leaves, and held together, because the joined leaves opened upon the post set in the middle. “And he built the inner court,” which was enclosed by the outer one, arranging three courses in the wall: three of polished stones and one of cedar timbers.

[Col. 0107C]

(III KINGS VII.) “He also built the house of the forest of Lebanon.” Because of the vastness and multitude of its workmanship, the house is compared to a forest; or because its material was taken from Lebanon. He made four walks between cedar columns, and lined the entire roof-chamber with cedar planks, which was supported by forty-five columns. One row had fifteen columns. According to this arrangement there were three rows of columns within and four walks, that is, intervals: one interval from the wall to the first row of columns; another from the first to the second; another from the second to the third; and again another from the third to the wall. In the Hebrew it reads: “Cedar planking above the rows [Col. 0107D] of forty-five columns; fifteen in each row.” This can be understood thus: we should say not that there were forty-five columns, but forty-five planks—that is, boards—of which the ceiling was constructed; and that there were three rows in the ceiling, each containing fifteen boards. This is what it says: “its covering had three rows,” understood, “looking one toward another three times.” In these rows, each board of one row faced a corresponding board in the other row, so that one was joined to another three times; that is, three boards in each row were joined to three opposite boards of the other row, their ends being inserted one into another. “And above the columns were square beams, all alike.” In the Hebrew this is given thus: “And all the doors and posts were square, one opposite another.” But when it says here “square doors,” that is, not rounded at the top, this was perhaps said by comparison with those at the entrance of the oracle, which were so formed. “And he made a portico of columns,” that is, a portico in which he likewise placed columns. This portico was fifty cubits long, according to the width of the house; and another portico before the larger portico, that is, in front of the greater portico. He also made “the portico of the throne,” in which he made a tribunal. The throne belongs to one reigning, the tribunal to one judging; and it is a small room in which one sits to judge, either privately to dictate judgment or publicly to pronounce it. “Hewn and polished both within and without,” that is, cut and smoothed on both surfaces [Col. 0108B] of the wall. “And externally, extending with such workmanship to the greater court.” The greater court was outside, the lesser court inside. Likewise, in the inner court of the house of the Lord and in the portico of the house of the Lord, such workmanship was done. That in building the walls he placed in alternating rows now square or polished stones, now cedars, that is, incorruptible timbers, was done so that the variety of the structure itself might be more pleasing and more fitting. But the courts of the house of the Lord were distinct from those of the king’s house, both outer and inner.

“And he cast,” that is, artistically composed or fashioned, two bronze columns, that is, cast from bronze. These columns were made not to support the structure but for ornament, and were erected in the portico of the temple [Col. 0108C]. They were eighteen cubits high; twelve cubits in circumference—that is, a line of twelve cubits went around each column. This was the measure of its roundness. If a line of twelve cubits were drawn around it, it would encircle it and embrace its whole circumference. Or the circumference of the column, measured by the course of a line, was twelve cubits; or a line, cast in the work and carried around it, encircled it for twelve cubits. The capitals placed upon the tops of the columns were large, each five cubits high; their workmanship and construction are described as follows. Each capital was cast, like a network and chains wonderfully interwoven with one another. As appears from this description, the capitals themselves were cast not solid but pierced through everywhere, so that their connections within and without represented the form of a net. These interlacings and intricacies were varied in seven ways from bottom to top around the circumference of the capital, which seven patterns are indicated by seven lines. Then two rows of pomegranates surrounded the capital, so that the pomegranates hanging outside seemed, as it were, to cover the little nets of the capitals—that is, the capitals themselves, which were upon the tops of the columns [Col. 0108D]. These capitals upon the tops of the columns were fashioned in something like the work of a lily; that is, upon these same capitals, with the pomegranates, there was above a likeness of lily leaves. What follows—“in the portico, four cubits”—is obscure. Perhaps it may be understood thus: the capitals themselves were not round above, like the columns upon which they were placed, but square, having four cubits on each side. Therefore the words “in the portico, four cubits” should not be read as saying that the portico itself was four cubits; rather, that the capitals, four cubits in extent, were fashioned in the portico. “And again other capitals upon the tops of the columns above, according to the measure of the column, opposite the nets.” Whether these second capitals were placed above the former or beside them, the text does not sufficiently make clear.

“He also made the molten sea.” It signifies a large round bronze basin, cast in bronze, thirty cubits around and ten across. When it says that a cord of thirty cubits encircled the basin [Col. 0109B], this must either be understood simply as indicating the extent of its circumference, which could be encircled with a rope of that length; or understand the rope to be a bronze twisted band, cast as part of the work in the likeness of a rope and encircling the sea itself. “A carving beneath the rim went around it for ten cubits.” How could it go around for ten cubits, when the circumference itself was said to be thirty cubits? Did it not go all around, but only ten cubits of its circumference were carved? Or did the circumference narrow downward below the rim, so that it could be encircled below the rim by ten cubits, where the carving went around in two rows near the lower part of the basin, where it touched the twelve cast bronze oxen upon which it stood? For this seems to mean that the base of the basin was square, ten cubits on each side, in which there were two rows of carved ornament, with twelve oxen placed beneath it; upon this the sea itself was founded [Col. 0109C]. The thickness of the basin, that is, its solidity, was three inches. The basin held two thousand baths and three thousand measures. The quantity is equal despite the differing number. For they are equivalent; or, if the same measure is meant, two thousand baths when heaped up for dry goods are as much as three thousand when levelled for liquids. For a heaped measure contains a level measure and one-half of it. “And he made ten bronze bases.” These bases were prepared not for the sea but for other basins, each of which was set upon one of them. “The work of the bases was carved openwork,” that is, the bases were made with openwork carving. And there were carvings between the joints, and between the crowns and braids: lions, oxen, and cherubim; and likewise between the joints, and beneath the lions and oxen, as it were straps hanging down in bronze. The description is obscure, and it is not easy to determine what should be understood. It seems, however, to mean that upon the bases themselves, on each side, there were different rows of carvings; and where these rows or lines met, various carvings were carried along in a line, making a division between line and line. The lines themselves, like little panels lying open between one line and another, had circles carved in them like crowns and braids, some containing lions, others oxen, others cherubim. “And likewise above between [Col. 0110A] the joints”: above where? Perhaps this means that carvings of this kind were not made over the entire surface, but formed, above and below, upon the sides of the bases, as it were borders and ornaments. “And beneath the lions and oxen, as it were bronze straps hanging down.” And there were four wheels on each base, and bronze axles, and supports raised at the four sides, as though to hold the bases set upon wheels and the basin placed upon the bases. “The mouth of the basin also was inward.” This seems to say that from the bottom of the basin a sort of round pipe rose within to a height of one and a half cubits, of which one cubit projected above the basin, while half a cubit was within the depth of the basin. At the top of this pipe was the mouth of the basin itself, through which the waters flowed out. But at the corners of the columns, that is, of the bases, there were various carvings; and the middle intercolumnar spaces—that is, those between the corners—were square, not round. These are the flat sides of the bases, which he calls square intercolumnar spaces because they appeared above the four small supports raised at the four corners. But at the top of the base, that is, the base itself at its summit, it was one cubit and a half [Col. 0110B], so that it might suitably carry the basin placed upon it. He also carved upon those panels which were of bronze, and upon the corners; perhaps he means the supports which were at the corners of the columns, upon which likewise carvings were made.

“But he placed the sea on the right side of the temple, opposite the east, toward the south,” that is, at the angle where the eastern and southern walls of the house met. “The two columns, and the two cords of the capitals upon the capitals of the columns.” In the Hebrew it is thus: “The two columns and the crowns upon the tops of the columns, and the two networks.” By the crowns upon the tops of the columns someone might perhaps understand nothing other than the round capitals placed upon the columns. But because he has named cords, he seems to have intended something else, which nevertheless is not sufficiently clear unless we say that in the capitals themselves a carving was made in the form of a crown or of a cord drawn around and encircling them.

(III KINGS VIII.) “The cherubim spread their wings over the place of the ark, and covered the ark and its poles above.” And when the poles projected and their ends appeared [Col. 0110D] outside the sanctuary before the oracle, they did not appear farther outside. That is, they were extended forward only far enough that, reaching to the veil, they touched and pressed slightly against it, so that their ends could be noticed through the veil by those standing outside; yet they did not pierce the veil or project outside beyond it. “If a man sins against his neighbour,” namely in this way: if he is bound by some oath—that is, if he is bound to his neighbour by an oath and does not keep what he swore; and, compelled by the person to whom he swore, comes before your altar in your house in order to clear himself by testimony in the presence of the Godhead—if he denies before you the oath which he secretly made to his neighbour concerning any matter [Col. 0111A], and does not reverence your presence enough to refrain from lying: “You will hear in heaven,” that is, you will know and understand the deceit of the one who acts fraudulently, and you will do this—namely, judge your servants, not according to the lie which he tells human beings, but according to what you know, from whom the truth cannot be hidden: condemning the wicked and justifying the just.

(III KINGS IX.) “He called them the land of Cabul,” that is, muddy or marshy land, because of the worthlessness of the gift.

(III KINGS X.) “In the house of the forest of Lebanon,” because perhaps its material was taken from Lebanon.

(III KINGS XI.) “He built Millo and levelled the hollow of the city of David his father,” building Millo [Col. 0111B]; that is, he levelled that place, namely the lower part of the city, which previously was a hollow and, as it were, the sewer of the city of David his father, so that it might be level with the higher part of the city—thereby seeming to do injury to his father by making what was meanest and most despised equal to his greatest works. In the Hebrew it reads: “He built Millo and closed the opening of the city of David his father.” This can be understood to mean that he built Millo and raised it high, and by this closed the exit which had formerly been in the city of David his father, constructing this building opposite the gate of the city. The book of the words of Solomon is not found here among us, just as neither is the book of the words of the kings of Israel or Judah.

[Col. 0111C]

(III KINGS XII.) “He went up upon the altar.” This is said as though he went up to the altar. He went up in order to place incense upon the altar, or something of that kind.

(III KINGS XIV.) “You have cast me behind your body,” that is, you have despised me.

(III KINGS XVIII.) “He repaired the altar of the Lord which had been destroyed, and built an altar of stones in the name of the Lord.” It is as though he said: he cleared the place where an altar had formerly been destroyed and built another, new one.

(III KINGS XIX.) “Every mouth which has not worshipped him by kissing his hand,” namely Baal’s hand. In the Hebrew it reads: “Every mouth which has not kissed him.” It indicates the manner of reverence in bending the knees and kissing with the mouth.

[Col. 0111D]

(III KINGS XX.) “All the things for which you first sent your servant to me I will do; but I cannot do this thing.” This is as though he said: in the beginning of your demand, I will comply concerning the giving of silver and gold; but I cannot do this thing, namely, give up wives and children as well. “Who will begin the battle?” And he says: “You,” lest there seem to be a contradiction with what he had previously said—that victory was to be won through the foot-soldiers of the princes of the provinces. But now I want the king himself to begin the battle. Thus it is said that he should not wait for the enemies’ assault, but that he himself—that is, his forces—should begin the battle; or he himself will begin by bringing out the whole army, and afterwards the foot-soldiers of the princes of the provinces will win the victory. This is what follows: “But the young men went out in the first line.” Therefore, when the king began the battle with all his forces, these men, going before, gained the victory.

(III KINGS XXI.) “Proclaim a fast and make Naboth sit,” etc. He wishes the work of wickedness to be begun religiously, so that the cruelty of murder may be concealed beneath the devotion of a fast. “Naboth blessed God and the king.” This is irony, as though he had cursed the king and thereby God, whose minister he is. “You have killed and moreover taken possession. And after these things you will add.” In the Hebrew it is: “Have you killed, and after this will you inherit?”—as a question, as though he says: Is it not enough for you to have killed a man, unless you also possess his inheritance? “In this place,” etc. How was it said to Ahab: “In this place where dogs licked Naboth’s blood, they shall lick your blood also” [Col. 0112B], when Naboth’s blood was shed in Jezreel, while dogs licked Ahab’s blood by the pool of Samaria? But “in this place” means in such a place—that is, shed as vilely as you shed Naboth’s blood.

NOTES ON FOURTH KINGS.

(IV KINGS III.) “Make the bed of this torrent ditches and ditches.” Or, as others think it should be said, “many ditches”: that is, dig the dry bed of this torrent, now dried up, more deeply or more profoundly and in many places, so that it may receive the waters coming upon it in abundance.

(IV KINGS V.) And Naaman said, “As you wish.” Let your will be done. Behold, I no longer ask you to accept what is mine; but I entreat you nevertheless to grant what is yours. Grant to your servant that from this holy land, in which the true God is worshipped, I may take and carry with me the load of two mules. Why he wished to carry earth he adds below: “For your servant will no longer offer burnt offering or sacrifice to foreign gods, but to the Lord.” He still wished therefore to carry earth, in order to make from it in his own land an altar to the Lord upon which he might sacrifice. “So he departed from him after a certain stretch of land.” He seems to have been misled by the ambiguity of the expression into understanding both a space of land and a time. For in the Hebrew it is expressed more clearly: “So he departed from him for, as it were, some space of land”; and thus the following is appropriately joined: “And Gehazi, the servant [Col. 0112C] of the man of God, said.” It is similar to what is read in Genesis: “And it was springtime, and I was entering Ephrath” (Gen. XLVIII). In the Hebrew it is expressed more clearly: “And there was still a space of land,” understood, “remaining; and I was entering Ephrath.”

(IV KINGS VI.) “A fourth part of a cab [Note: [Col. 0111D] Some read ‘cabi.’] of doves’ dung.” A cab is a measure. They suppose that doves’ dung was seized by those suffering hunger because grains brought from afar by doves might perhaps have been mixed with the dung and picked out, providing some refreshment for the starving.

(IV KINGS VIII.) “And when the next day came, he took a coverlet and poured water upon it,” or, “water drenched him,” that is, he soaked it. This means that he took a cloth, moistened it in water, and spread it over his face. Hazael himself took the cloth and, once moistened, spread it over [Col. 0113A] his master’s face, namely to cool his face because he was burning with fever. In the Hebrew it is expressed more clearly: “He spread it over his own face,” so that one understands not Hazael but Ben-hadad himself to have moistened the cloth and spread it over his own face for relief. Yet it could be of no use, because he died. When he was dead, Hazael reigned in his place.

(IV KINGS XIII.) “But Joahaz entreated the face of the Lord, and he heard him, and the Lord gave Israel a saviour”: namely, his son Joash, because he later delivered Israel from the hand of the king of Syria.

(IV KINGS XVI.) “Also the Musach of the Sabbath.” It signifies a roof or covering where the king was accustomed to sit on the Sabbath beside the temple. Therefore he altered this Musach and the king’s entrance—that is, the externally situated portico through which he entered—into the temple of the Lord, because of fear of the king of the Assyrians [Col. 0113B].

(IV KINGS XIX.) “Have you not heard what I did from the beginning?” That is, how formerly I drowned Pharaoh and the Egyptians when they pursued my people? “From ancient days I formed it,” that is, in ancient days I worked it, namely that vengeance. “And now I have brought it,” that is, now again I wish to recall it as an example, so that I may exercise the like upon you. “But this shall be the sign to you, Hezekiah”: namely, that I shall overthrow and drive back your enemy. This shall be the sign of the ensuing favour: that, after his departure, I shall cause the land devastated by him to sprout abundantly, so that my afflicted people may be relieved by abundance. “Therefore in this year eat what you find.” That is, be content with what you can have, so that, if anything is lacking, you may endure it patiently. And if you have nothing to sow, do not fear. In the second year, the shoots growing of themselves will multiply so greatly that the abundance of crops will suffice both for present sustenance and future sowing [Col. 0114B]. Therefore, “in the third year sow.” Moreover, you will be able to know that this will happen from the fact that I shall now repel and destroy the king of the Assyrians who threatens you.

[Col. 0113]

NINETEEN HOMILIES ON SOLOMON’S ECCLESIASTES,

WHOSE SUBJECTS ARE THESE:

In Homily XIX on Ecclesiastes: on the varied exposition of Sacred Scripture and Solomon’s purpose. Preface. On the title of the work, Solomon’s names and books, the opening of this book, and the explanation of vanities. Homily I. On proving the vanity of all things under heaven: through the corruption of the elements, the generation of things, and the forgetfulness of things that have been. Homily II. How Ecclesiastes proves through his own works that all human works are vain, with an epilogue of what has preceded. Homily III. On the threefold vanity of things and humanity’s most wretched occupation. Homily IV. On the literal and moral exposition of the words of Ecclesiastes. Homily V. What it is to be stretched out in a most wretched occupation. Homily VI. That the perverse are difficult to correct, etc. Homily VII. That a human being flees from truth, as Adam fled and hid himself in Paradise. Homily VIII. On the various vain attempts of Ecclesiastes. Homily IX. On the remainder down to the passage: “The fool walks in darkness.” Homily X. How wisdom reaches mightily from end to end, etc. Homily XI. On the words, according to another translation, “The eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth,” where our text has “The fool walks in darkness,” and on the remainder of the second chapter. Homily XII. How all things have their time. Homily XIII. An explanation of the remaining things that have their time, and a repetition of what has been said. Homily XIV. On time and things subject to time, according to another interpretation. Homily XV. On the spiritual understanding of what has been said about time. Homily XVI. On the confusion of minds caused by the passage of time. Homily XVII. On the perverse morals of human beings, and what Ecclesiastes judged concerning them. Homily XVIII. On the oppression and abandonment of the innocent, and the vain and foolish judgment of the ungodly about this life. Homily XIX.

PREFACE. On the varied exposition of Sacred Scripture and Solomon’s purpose.

[Col. 0113C]

What I recently discussed before you concerning Solomon’s book called Ecclesiastes [Col. 0114C], I now briefly set down in writing, because certain matters there seemed worthy of remembrance. Every Scripture, when expounded according to its proper interpretation, shines forth more clearly and opens an easier way for readers to understand it [Col. 0115A]. Many people, failing to understand the power of the Scriptures, obscure their grace and beauty with alien expositions; and though they ought to disclose what is hidden, they even obscure what is plain. Yet those seem to me liable to a similar fault who either stubbornly deny that mystical understanding and the depth of allegory in Sacred Scripture should be sought where it exists, or superstitiously insist that it must be imposed where it does not exist.
