Therefore, in this work I do not think much effort should be spent in pursuing throughout the whole course of its narrative tropological meanings or mystical allegorical senses—especially since the author here aims not so much to instruct conduct or recount mysteries as to move the human heart, by the manifest truth of his arguments and evident exhortation, to contempt for worldly things [Col. 0115B]. Yet I do not deny that this narrative contains many obscure mystical points requiring their own explanation, especially in what follows: for as the narrative proceeds, according to the advance of contemplation it touches more and more upon spiritual things and is raised from visible things. But it is one thing to attend to that toward which the entire intention of the writer and the whole course of the narrative are directed; another to think that certain things said incidentally in a mystical sense, and to be understood spiritually, should not be carelessly passed over.

We therefore undertake to explain the surface of the narrative, which possesses so great a charm of expression and thought, so that, through this modest little night-work providing a path to understanding, you may henceforth rejoice that what you now read as written has been understood by you [Col. 0115C].

HOMILY I. On the title of the work, Solomon’s names and books, the opening of this work, and the explanation of vanities.

(ECCLESIASTES I.) “The words of Ecclesiastes, son of David, king of Jerusalem.” This is the title of the book. In it are briefly expressed both the character of the work which follows and, at the same time, the person of the author is commended. For in the word “words” a manifold discussion is indicated, brought to various conclusions. Since in this book the morals, pursuits, and works of many people are described [Col. 0115D], the speaker must necessarily take up the voices of many and express many opinions in his discourse, in order that he may present in his own person the roles of many, although he alone is the one speaking. Near the end of the book he testifies that he has spoken with many and that many were in him, saying: “Let us all hear together the end of the discourse: Fear God and keep his commandments; this is the whole human being.” This is also why he wished to call himself Ecclesiastes in this work: because his discourse here is directed not particularly to any one individual but to the whole Church, that is, to the assembly or multitude of the people; and in this book his discourse serves at once to depict and to instruct the morals of many. We read indeed that Solomon was called by three names: Jedidiah, which means “beloved”; Qoheleth, which in Greek is Ecclesiastes and in Latin is called a preacher; and Solomon, which means “peaceful” [Col. 0116A]. Now he may be called Ecclesiastes, or preacher, because he instructs the Church or assembly—that is, the multitude of the people—as he is clearly shown to have done in this book. But history plainly shows that Solomon was beloved by the Lord and enjoyed great peace in his kingdom until the last period of his life, when he violated the Lord’s covenant and law. Therefore, in accordance with these three names he composed three books. The first is entitled Parables, or Proverbs of Solomon; the second, which we now have in hand, is called Ecclesiastes; and the third is called the Song of Songs [Col. 0116B]. In the first, as from a fatherly affection, he addresses a beloved son and exhorts him by frequent admonition to turn away from vices and pursue virtues. In the second, he warns a man advanced in mature age not to suppose that anything in worldly things is permanent. Finally, when he is now perfected and freed from the world beneath his feet, he joins him to the embraces of the bridegroom in the Song of Songs. Nor were the Gentile philosophers accustomed to instruct their hearers very differently, setting before those to be instructed first ethics, then physics, and finally theology.

Having set these matters before us in order to open the meaning of what is to be said, let us now approach the course of the book itself. Solomon’s subject in this work is all things subject to vanity, that is, perishable and transitory things [Col. 0116C]. His intention is to persuade us to contempt for the world. His method of treatment is as follows. He shows, according to a threefold vanity, that all things are subject to vanity—that is, are perishable and transitory: both the things made for human beings, the things made by human beings, and the things existing in human beings. In the things made for human beings, vanity is that of changeability. In the things made by human beings, vanity is that of curiosity. In the things existing in human beings, vanity is that of mortality; and all is vanity. We shall discuss these matters more fully later, if first we treat what must be said concerning the kind of contemplation itself, in which the mind of the contemplator, lifted up, could either see or set forth such new and wonderful things concerning the condition of human existence [Col. 0116D]. Let us therefore see what he says:

“Vanity of vanities,” said the Ecclesiast, etc. But where, do you suppose, was this man’s mind when he said these things? He was a man, but he was above man. For unless he had transcended man, he could not have seen that every man is a liar. Therefore we must first consider this consideration of his, and distinguish the kinds of spiritual speculation.

There are three modes of vision in the rational soul: thought, meditation, and contemplation. Thought is when the mind is fleetingly touched by an awareness of things, when the thing itself is suddenly made present to the soul through its image, either entering through sense or arising from memory. Meditation is the sustained and shrewd reconsideration of a thought, striving either to unfold something involved or to penetrate by searching what is hidden. Contemplation is the penetrating and free gaze of the soul, diffused everywhere over the objects to be perceived.

This seems to be the difference between meditation and contemplation: meditation is always concerned with things hidden from our understanding, whereas contemplation concerns things manifest either according to their own nature or according to our capacity. Meditation is always occupied in investigating one matter; contemplation is extended to comprehend many matters, or even all things. Meditation, therefore, is a certain inquisitive and shrewd power of the mind, striving to investigate obscurities and unravel complexities. Contemplation is that liveliness of understanding which, having all things openly before it, comprehends them in manifest vision. Thus, in a certain sense, contemplation possesses what meditation seeks. [Col. 0117A]

There are two kinds of contemplation. One is prior and belongs to beginners: the consideration of creatures. The other is later and belongs to the perfect: the contemplation of the Creator. In Proverbs Solomon proceeded as though meditating. In Ecclesiastes he ascended to the first degree of contemplation. In the Song of Songs he raised himself to its highest degree.

In meditation there is, as it were, a struggle between ignorance and knowledge; and the light of truth somehow gleams amid the darkness of error. It is like fire in green wood: at first it catches only with difficulty; but when it has been stirred by a stronger blast and begins to burn more fiercely in the material laid beneath it, then we see great clouds of smoky darkness rise and envelop the flame itself, which still glimmers only faintly at intervals, until at last, as the blaze gradually increases, all vapour is consumed and the darkness dispersed, a clear brightness appears. Then the victorious flame, running through the whole mass of the crackling pyre, reigns freely; flying about the material beneath it and touching it lightly, it burns it up and penetrates it by licking it. Nor does it rest until, advancing inward as it penetrates, it has in some sense drawn into itself all that it finds outside itself. [Col. 0117B–C]

But after the fire has consumed what was to be burned, and that material has, as it were, wholly passed from its own nature into the likeness and property of fire, then every crash falls away and every noise is stilled; the darts of flame rising from the midst are removed, and that fierce and devouring fire, with all things subject to it incorporated into it by a kind of friendly likeness, settles into a deep peace and silence, because it now finds nothing unlike itself outside itself, nor anything opposed against itself. First, therefore, fire was seen with flame and smoke; next, fire with flame but without smoke; lastly, pure fire without flame or smoke. [Col. 0117D]

So indeed the carnal heart, like green wood not yet dried of the moisture of carnal desire, when it conceives some spark of divine fear or love, first produces, through the resistance of evil desires, the smoke of passions and disturbances. Then, when the mind has been strengthened and begins, together with the flame of love, to burn more powerfully and shine more clearly, all the darkness of disturbances immediately vanishes; and now, with a pure mind, the soul is expanded toward the contemplation of truth. Finally, after the heart has been penetrated by continual contemplation of truth and has entered, from its inmost depths and with the whole affection of the soul, into the very fountain of supreme truth, it rests in that very sweetness, as though wholly kindled and changed into the fire of love, most peacefully free from every noise and disturbance.

First, then, because counsel is sought amid the dangers of temptations, meditation is like smoke with flame. Second, because with a pure mind the heart is expanded toward the contemplation of truth, the beginning of contemplation is like flame without smoke. Third, because truth has now been found and charity perfected, nothing beyond that one thing is sought; in the fire of love alone it is sweetly refreshed with the highest tranquillity and happiness. [Col. 0118A–B] Then, when the whole heart has been transformed into the fire of love, God is truly felt to be all in all, when He is received with such inward love that nothing remains in the heart, even concerning itself, apart from Him.

Therefore, to distinguish these three by their proper names: the first is meditation; the second, speculation; the third, contemplation. In meditation, the disturbance of carnal passions, rising importunately, clouds the mind kindled by devout affection. In speculation, the novelty of an unusual vision raises the mind into wonder. In contemplation, the taste of wondrous sweetness transforms the whole soul into joy and delight. Thus, in meditation there is anxiety; in speculation, amazement; in contemplation, sweetness. [Col. 0118B–C]

Yet spiritual speculation itself often refreshes the mind with great delight when, after the struggle of temptations and the darkness of error, it suddenly settles it in unexpected peace and bathes it in unfamiliar brightness. Thus this man, caught up in mind above all perishable and transient things, saw that among all things there was nothing that remained; and, as if terrified by the astonishment of this new and unfamiliar vision, he cried out: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.”

For he beheld the universe and saw it wholly subject to vanity; and he called its vanity “the vanity of vanities”—that is, the vanity containing every vanity—as though it were the genus of all genera, because it contains within itself every genus of things. For all things are vanity; and from all things comes the universe; and the whole universe is vanity.

But now, since we have said enough for the present concerning the kind of contemplation by which this human mind could perceive these things concerning man or human affairs, let us return to our purpose. We shall consequently distinguish the kinds of all vanities which, enlightened by this contemplation, it discovered to inhere in perishable things. For in striving first clearly to explain the whole subject-matter of the work, we also open its text more plainly to its readers. For its entire discourse is woven from the vanity of temporal things. [Col. 0118C–D]

There are, therefore, three kinds of vanities which this book particularly treats, in which it comprises every vanity; and it declares that all things done under the sun are subject to these. The first is the vanity of mutability, which belongs by condition to all perishable things. The second is the vanity of curiosity or covetousness, which belongs to human minds through their disordered love of transient and vain things. The third is the vanity of mortality, which belongs to human bodies through punishment.

The first vanity, then, is natural and fitting or appropriate. The second is blameworthy, because perverse. The third is penal and wretched. We call natural vanity—that is, fitting mutability—appropriate because the ordered alternation of transient things establishes a greater beauty of the universe, and its instability is arranged for its greater advantage. For by the variety of things, weariness is removed from human minds, and, as was said, the beauty of the universe is increased. [Col. 0119A–B]

For bodily nature, whose beauty is perfected through diverse species and forms, is adorned with greater beauty by its very mutability. Through intervals of time and the alteration of things passing away in time and succeeding in time, it receives what it could not receive all at once, because its forms come to it successively, though they could not belong to it simultaneously.

But that vanity which rules wicked minds is so much uglier than all the rest because mutability was foreign to spiritual substance not only through grace but even through nature. Therefore this vanity alone is reproved among all others, and alone among all others is shown to be unjust and perverse.

The penal vanity which belongs to human bodies through mortality is called wretched for this reason: man now has, as the punishment of sin, that he is subject to the condition of things which pass away in time, whereas at his creation he had received the privilege of standing above the condition of all visible things. For the condition of transient things is that all which arise should set, and all which grow should grow old. But human nature, though taken from corruptible matter, had been raised above corruption by grace and strengthened against corruption. It had received this gift: that it should indeed have a beginning with the other creatures, but should not have an ending; and that it should receive increase through the stages of age among those who are born, but not among those who die, and should not suffer decline. [Col. 0119C]

Man lost this dignity through the sin of transgression, when, stripped of the robe of immortality and fallen back into the condition of his origin, he heard from the Creator’s judgment: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. III). Therefore this vanity—to which the other creatures are born subject—is assigned to man alone as punishment, because man alone had received by grace the privilege of standing above it.

Since, then, we have distinguished three vanities, the first, the vanity of mutability, is the cause of sin; the second, the vanity of covetousness, is sin; and the third, the vanity of mortality, is the punishment of sin. The vanity of covetousness is reproved in the vanity of mutability; it is punished in the vanity of mortality. For, as the Psalmist says: “Man, when he was in honour, did not understand; but he was compared with the senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. XLVIII). For unless he had first inclined himself through the disordered desire of the flesh toward what belongs to beasts, he would never have been made like beasts through the mortality of the flesh. But now, because through the desire of his mind he began to lean upon mutable things, he too could not remain stable in that in which he had been stable. [Col. 0119D–0120A]

We may distinguish these vanities by another division also, so that what is explained in more ways may be recognized more plainly. One vanity is in created things; another in human works; another in bodies; another in minds. The first is mutability; the second, curiosity; the third, mortality; the fourth, iniquity.

The vanity of mutability is considered in things in two ways: either because they are empty or because they are transient. In the former they are vain because they display what they do not possess; in the latter they are vain because they do not remain in what they possess. There they are vain because they have form alone and do not have essence. Here they are vain because, although they have some essence, they possess no abiding substance. There they are vain because they present an appearance without truth. Here they are vain because they pretend stability and yet pass away. Thus all perishable and transient things are false and deceptive; those who love vain things and trust in vanity fail, and through vanity become not merely vain but vanity itself. [Col. 0120A–B]

The vanity of covetousness consists in three things: namely, the lust of the eyes, the lust of the flesh, and the pride of life. In all these there is vanity. For all things pertaining to the flesh, whether they appear good or bad, are neither truly bad nor truly good; nor can they always remain, whether good or bad, what they are. Therefore it is as vain to place hope in things that appear good as to fear things thought evil.

For what does the lust of the eyes do? See what it does, and you will find how great a vanity lies hidden, cloaked beneath this veil. It seeks the deceptive colours of things and slippery spectacles. Forgetful of itself, it pours itself outward; giving itself wholly to curiosity, it goes around everything and surveys the whole world, to see whether perhaps something new, unusual, or wonderful may appear—what this thing or that may mean, what appearance each has, or what significance it claims. With every movement of things it is ever distracted, ever headlong, rash, brazen, unstable, wanton, impatient, and slippery; often exulting in vain hope, often trembling in empty fear; having no inward root, but always suspended in anxious expectation of outward changes. [Col. 0120C–D]

Before danger it wavers; before a crisis it trembles. Whatever may happen either way, whether good or evil, it both fears and desires; in vain it turns aside toward either merely on suspicion. It burns in the manner of one unable to endure suspense, waiting to see what will happen; it is dissolved by present things, dulled by settled things, and altered by the inconstant fluctuation of its mind at every change of events, whether sorrowful or joyous.

Consider, then, how vain this is. Certainly every creature is to a man what he himself is to it: outward things cannot injure a good mind or benefit a bad one. Thus none of these things can be either evil to the good or good to the bad, except insofar as the soul itself progresses by despising them, or declines by loving them perversely or fearing them vainly. How great, then, is the vanity of attending to these things with such anxiety and curiosity as though they mattered for granting or taking away salvation, while either failing to attend to or disregarding the inward goods in which true salvation consists! [Col. 0121A]

What shall I say about the lust of the flesh? How vain it is, since the pleasure of the flesh, however great it may be, can neither help when past nor remain when present. What benefit is there in striving so hard to defend flesh that must die against corruption by luxury of delights and abundance of pleasures, when no one can preserve it from corruption? And what can be more vain than the pride of life, whether it wishes to glory in riches or in dignities?

For who does not vainly glory in being burdened more heavily than others? This, assuredly, is all that riches and dignities confer upon their possessors: what they seem to receive in them beyond others, by that very thing they are found more burdened than others. In acquiring or preserving those same things, they are always worn down more by labour or afflicted more by care. But in all these things there is great vanity and superfluous care. [Col. 0121B]

The vanity of mortality consists in two things: the punishment which wears us down and the punishment which dissolves us. The punishment which wears us down first makes us grow old through the failing of life. The punishment which dissolves us afterwards compels us to go into decay and to return through the corruption of the flesh to the dust from which we were taken in the flesh.

From this, therefore, let man consider in what vanity every human being lives: he suffers unwillingly the corruption of the flesh because he voluntarily works the corruption of the mind. Therefore he is wholly subject to vanity who flows away in body through mortality and in mind through iniquity. But one of these is his from himself, the other is his against himself, and the whole is in himself. [Col. 0121B–C]

At the very beginning of his book the author distinguishes these three kinds of vanity. Afterwards, by pursuing each separately throughout the whole course of his work, he discusses and expands them copiously, everywhere reproving among these three that fourth kind of vanity which we said belonged to wicked minds, and showing that this alone is liable to blame and deserves punishment.

First he sets forth the vanity which belongs to created things through mutability: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.” Then, in second place, he adds the vanity which is in human works: “What profit has a man from all his labour which he labours under the sun?” In third place he adds that vanity which belongs to human bodies through mortality, saying: “A generation passes away, and a generation comes.”

According to these three distinctions, he also divides the whole sequence of the work that follows into three parts, assigning a portion to each. In the first part, which begins, “The sun rises and sets,” he discusses the vanity of mutability. In the second part, which begins, “I, Ecclesiastes, was king of Israel in Jerusalem,” he treats at greatest length the vanity of human covetousness. In the third part, which is placed as a conclusion in the final position of the discussion and begins, “Remember your Creator in the days of your youth,” he recalls the vanity of mortality, so that the human mind may hear at the end what it most needs to grasp by attentive consideration and recall more frequently to memory. [Col. 0121C–0122A]

We have prepared these remarks, according to the measure of our understanding, for those entering upon the reading of Ecclesiastes, the second of Solomon’s books. But we confess that to explain fittingly its entire breadth exceeds our powers. In matters of this kind, veiled in deep profundity, we seek rather to hear a teacher than to assume the role of teacher. For, as Plato says, it is better modestly to learn another’s teachings than shamelessly to thrust forward one’s own. If we should be able to say anything fitting on this subject, it will be beyond hope and expectation; if anything useful, it will not be beyond intention.

He first places before his book a kind of prologue, in which he distinguishes the threefold subject-matter of the following work that we have mentioned and which he afterwards discusses more fully. The prologue, therefore, extends from “Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity,” to “The sun rises and sets.” From there the first part of the book begins, and the remainder is as we have said. Let us now consider the words of the text itself, to see whether we can grasp in them anything from what has been said above. [Col. 0122A–B]

“Vanity of vanities,” said the Ecclesiast, “vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.” The phrase “said the Ecclesiast,” in which he speaks of himself as though of another, must be pronounced with emphasis. For since he put forward his own person by way of authority, he fittingly spoke of himself not as himself but as another, so that, because he had to say something great concerning himself as the matter required, he might say it more becomingly and soberly of himself in another person than in his own.

Thus Balaam, speaking of himself, says: “The hearer of the words of God has spoken; he who has beheld the visions of the Almighty, who falls and has his eyes open” (Num. XXIV). So too John, in his Gospel, speaks of himself as though of another: “This is that disciple whom Jesus loved, who bears witness concerning these things; and we know that his witness is true” (John XXI). And Paul, speaking of himself to the Corinthians as though of another, says: “I know a man in Christ—whether in the body or outside the body I do not know, God knows—such a one caught up to the third heaven, and such a one caught up into paradise, and hearing secret words which it is not lawful for a man to speak” (II Cor. XII). [Col. 0122B–D]

But whenever this manner of speaking is adopted in Scripture, it is done either for humility’s sake or for wonder: that is, when we wish to say great things, we ascribe them, as it were, to others, lest it seem proud or excessive if we attribute them to ourselves. For we ought to remove great things from ourselves because of humility and display marvelous things from afar, as it were, because of wonder. Things are less wonderful when they come closer to knowledge.

Therefore, so that the minds of all may be raised to the statement that follows and awakened, as it were, by the miracle of novelty, it is rightly said: “The Ecclesiast said.” As though it were said: What so great and such a man said could not be vain, even though he spoke about vanity. The Ecclesiast himself, the common teacher and instructor of all, said it. What did he say? Hear what he said, and attend. For the words spoken are no small thing: “Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.” [Col. 0122D–0123A]

If all is vanity, then he himself who said this is vanity. How then will it be established that what vanity said about vanity is not vain? But if it is true that what he said is vain because he is vain, it should not be heard but rejected. What then shall we say? Either not all is vanity, as he said, and he spoke falsely; or all is vanity, as he said, and he himself, being vanity, spoke vainly.

But surely, as he himself said, all is vanity, and he who said it is vanity—not only vanity, but universal vanity—and nevertheless what he said is not vanity but truth. For in what he said he was not vanity, because he said against vanity what he said concerning vanity; and it is evident that he could not be opposed to vanity in that in which he was vanity. There was therefore something in him which was not vanity, and it could speak against vanity not vainly. But what was this, or where was it? [Col. 0123A–B]

Certainly, if we say that it was this body, or something in the body, which spoke without vanity about vanity, then could a body which corrupts, which is subject to vanity and born for vanity, ever be without vanity—though it lives wholly in vanity? We remember the Psalmist’s saying: “Every living man is wholly vanity” (Ps. XXXVIII). For that which dies is the very thing which lives; it is born in order to live and lives in order to die. But what is it that dies, except that which is deprived of life? Therefore that in man which is extinguished from life is what dies. And what is this except body and bodily sense? For it does not remain after the living creature, by which that creature itself is animate; and when it ceases to be sentient, sensation ceases to be.

Therefore what dies in man is what lives in man, and it is subject to vanity because it is liable to mortality. Bodily sense, then, could not reprove vanity, since in it nothing can be found free and pure from vanity. What, then, must we say that it was? Was it the soul? Have we not shown above that it too is subject to vanity? For in it we placed the vanity of iniquity, which is more deformed than all other things because the other vanities have from it alone either their harmfulness or even their very existence. Without this vanity, neither would the vanity of mortality exist nor would the vanity of mutability be harmful. [Col. 0123B–D]

How then can the soul, subject to such great vanity, reprove vanity truthfully? Or is something found surviving in it, free from vanity? And was it without cause that it was said: “Every living man is wholly vanity”? For man is universal vanity because he is subject to vanity both in body and mind. What man? Every living man. Not every man who is life, but every living man. For man is both life and living. Where is “life,” and where is “living”? Life is in that which gives life; living is in that which is given life.

Moreover, both the flesh lives from the soul and the soul from the flesh; and each lives. But does the flesh have from the soul all that it lives? The soul, in the flesh, does not have all that it lives. For it also lives in God—and would that it might live! What lives in the flesh is vain; what lives in God is not vain but true, because it is from truth. Therefore, in that part in which it lives from truth, it truly reproves vanity; and we discover how vanity reproves vanity, not through vanity but through truth. [Col. 0123D–0124A]

Thus the Ecclesiast, whose mind had been raised above every vanity and had reached truth itself, saw sublimely in that very truth what he truthfully said in reproving vanity: “Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.” The repetition of the words signifies both the greatness of the matter and the startling novelty of the speaker’s amazement. The saying is expressed with intensification.

For there are certain degrees, and, as it were, advances for one proceeding both toward better and toward worse. Thus we say “Song of Songs” and “age of ages,” just as it is here said, “Vanity of vanities.” By a corresponding interval and similar difference, the Song of Songs is understood to surpass a song by as much as a song surpasses a word, and then a word silence. Likewise, the age of ages surpasses an age by as much as an age alone surpasses a moment, and again a moment nothing. [Col. 0124A–B]

Here, by a contrary progression, vanity of vanities is worse than simple vanity by as much as simple vanity is removed from solid and abiding essence. The sentence may thus be read by means of its repetition: “Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity,” so that complete vanity may be expressed in all things and some highest totality may be understood to be composed from all things, containing every vanity. Thus each individual thing is vanity by itself, while the whole universe, gathered from all things, is vanity of vanities.

So in the creation of things, when God completed His works, each work separately is called good (Gen. I), and finally, when all things were perfected, the universe is called very good. For if what is good in part is found better in the whole, then what is evil in part must also be worse in the whole. Therefore universal vanity is vanity of vanities and the vanity of all vanities; all things are the universe of vanity.

Or that vanity of human minds is here reproved by comparison with other vanities. Since it arises, as it were, from other vanities and surpasses every vanity by its comparison with vanity, it is deservedly called vanity of vanities. [Col. 0124B–D]

This threefold repetition of vanity may also fittingly be referred to the three kinds of vanity mentioned above: one vanity, as it were, is human work; another is mortal nature; the third is this whole mutable world with its universe. For this man considered the works of mortals and saw that each comes to completion through labour and pain. What has been made endures only a short time; and transient things leave no fruit behind them.

He saw with what great distress and misery human life is worn down daily without cease, even in those things it does for its consolation; and how it almost always suffers more loss in seeking a remedy than it receives consolation in receiving relief. Wondering and astonished at how vainly every living man is troubled in all these things, he said: “Vanity of vanities.”

Then, considering the very condition of mortals and finding in it a greater and more miserable vanity, he saw that, if it is thought a great vanity when what man makes passes away, then it is altogether a lamentable and wretched vanity when what man is cannot remain. Therefore, doubling his cry again, he said: “Vanity of vanities.” Finally, beholding the inconstancy and fluctuation of all mutable things hurrying toward their setting, he added, as though bringing all to a final conclusion: “All is vanity.” [Col. 0124D–0125A]

“What profit has a man from all his labour which he labours under the sun?” “What profit has he beyond,” is understood—beyond what was said of all things: “Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.” It is as though he said: If all things are subject to vanity, how can human works be exempt from vanity? If, in some respect, what God created is vain, how much more vain is what man makes? If what the Eternal made is temporal, what is that which the temporal being makes?

Therefore, what profit has a man from all his labour which he labours under the sun? He labours under the sun, namely, either acting or suffering. Distinguish these two: one who acts and one who suffers labours under the sun. Both labour: the one who acts labours, and the one who suffers labours. But the difference is that one labours unwillingly, as it were, and the other willingly. For one who acts labours and himself causes that from which he labours. But one who suffers labours and does not himself cause it, but endures that from which he labours. [Col. 0125A–B]

These are the two kinds of persons living in this world: those who labour and act, and those who labour and suffer. Who are those who labour and act? Hear the Psalmist: “Surely every living man is wholly vanity. Surely man passes in an image; yet he is troubled in vain. He heaps up treasure and does not know for whom he will gather it” (Ps. XXXVIII).

Who are those who labour and suffer? Hear the Apostle Paul: “The creation,” he says, “was made subject to vanity unwillingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope” (Rom. VIII). Therefore both labour: those for whom this life is sweet, and those for whom this life is bitter. The former labour to enjoy its pleasures; the latter labour to be freed from its misery. The former labour, fearing that they may leave here soon; the latter labour, fearing that they may remain here long. The labour of the former is reproved for vain anxiety; the labour of the latter is crowned for patience. [Col. 0125B–D]

To the former it is said: “Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matt. VI); and, “Do not be anxious, saying: What shall we eat, or what shall we drink, or with what shall we be clothed?” (ibid.). To the latter it is said: “Be patient; strengthen your hearts” (Jas. V); and, “If we suffer with him, we shall reign with him. If we die with him, we believe that we shall also live together with him” (II Tim. II).

To the former it is said: “Children of men, how long will you be heavy of heart? Why do you love vanity and seek falsehood?” (Ps. IV). To the latter it is said: “Blessed are all who fear the Lord, who walk in his ways. Because you shall eat the labours of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall be well with you” (Ps. CXXVII).

Therefore the labour of the former has punishment in its work and punishment in its recompense. But the labour of the latter indeed has punishment in its work, but reward in its recompense. In the labour of the former there is true misery; in the fruit of their labour, false and vain consolation. In the labour of the latter there is temporal and transient affliction; in the fruit of their labour, eternal blessedness. [Col. 0125D–0126A]

Therefore the labour of the former is empty in its fruit and real in its misery; the labour of the latter is transient in its punishment and eternal in its fruit. There, the evil in which some good seems to be present is vain; the evil of the latter, which appears, is as it were vain because it is transient; but the good which does not appear is everlasting.

It should not, therefore, seem surprising that we call the wicked, in this life, those who labour and act, but the good only those who labour and suffer. For, if we look more closely at the truth, we shall find that the wicked always labour by acting, and the good always by suffering. For just as lack of self-control agitates the wicked even when they appear at rest, so patience preserves the good tranquil even when they are placed amid labours.

Hence, in a certain wonderful way, whenever any good and righteous people wear themselves down for God by voluntary affliction, they labour even while suffering. For, setting themselves against themselves, they impose upon themselves outwardly harsh disciplines; yet inwardly they remain quiet and undisturbed, bearing them in patience. [Col. 0126A–B]

But all perverse people and lovers of the carnal life, even when they endure evils externally inflicted by another’s violence, themselves cause that from which they labour, because inwardly they disturb themselves with the goads of anger and impatience. Therefore the good labour in this life, but the wicked labour even for this life. For the temporal labours to which all wicked and perverse people submit themselves to attain temporal sweetness are patiently endured by the good for eternal consolation.

But because this mortal life, in which and for which men labour, moves daily through the span of living toward life’s end, every human labour is rightly counted among the vanities, when it is said: “What profit has a man from all his labour which he labours under the sun?”—that is, apart from vanity. [Col. 0126B–C]

It should be noted, however, that he does not say, “What more is human labor?” but: “What, he says, does a man have in addition from all his labor at which he toils under the sun?” Hence it is plain that the subject here is not so much human labor as the fruit and profit of human labor; for the question is not what a man’s labor is or what kind it is, [Col. 0126D] but what fruit a man obtains from all his labor at which he toils under the sun. And this whole fruit is declared to be nothing other than vanity, when it is said, “What has he in addition?” As though it were said: A man has nothing in addition from his labor except vanity. Therefore vanity is the entire fruit of human labor, and every man labors in vain, receiving nothing from all his labor except vanity.

Was, then, the labor of the saints who served God faithfully, and for love of him endured so many punishments and kinds of torment, vain? Who would dare say this? For how was the labor of those vain who, though afflicted for a little while, reached enduring joys through passing pains, and through temporal death obtained everlasting life? [Col. 0127A] Or is that labor to be called vain because what they suffered passed away, though in another respect it is not vain, because what they received remains? For the Psalmist seems to imply that even the labor of the righteous is vain, insofar, that is, as it concerns transitory punishment and this, as it were, imaginary appearance of misery, when he says: “You who fashion trouble in the commandment” (Ps. XCIII [94]). For God, as it were, fashions labor for his chosen ones when outwardly, seeming angry, he imposes punishment upon them through temporal judgment, while inwardly, through the providence of his mercy, he preserves for them the rewards of eternal blessedness. Therefore, because the Psalmist calls fictitious the labor of the righteous and this imaginary pain—which has the appearance of misery but not true misery—he plainly shows that the same thing may not improperly be called vain in a certain respect. Behold, then, the labor of the work passes away. What was vain passes away; what was transitory has passed away: the labor has passed away, the pain has passed away. Has the fruit of the work, or the reward of the labor, passed away? Therefore it is permissible to say: behold, according to one manner of speaking, labor itself and temporal pain are not improperly called vain. Yet can the reward of that labor ever rightly be called vanity? Far be it! How, then, shall what was said stand: “What does a man have in addition from all his labor?” This was said concerning the reward of labor, not labor itself; concerning its benefit, not the work: “What does a man have in addition from all his labor?” Behold, a man has something in addition—indeed, much in addition—[Col. 0127C] and you say, “What does he have in addition?” Therefore he added and said: “At which he toils under the sun.” Behold, we have resolved the difficulty of this question. For here he plainly shows which labors he charges with vanity: those which, he says, are done under the sun.

What does “done under the sun” mean? Perhaps what he says, “under the sun,” should be understood simply: men dwelling in this lower region of the world receive the light of the sun from above, and are illuminated in order that they may see to perform works necessary for human use. For this reason the times of human life have by divine providence been distributed in alternating succession: so that the change of alternating seasons itself might restore feeble bodies wearied by excessive exertion in their activities. Thus night and day endlessly succeed one another in equal alternation, so that by day the sun, passing above from rising to setting in its course, diffuses its light everywhere below; and, illuminating human eyes by its presence and stirring other earthly living creatures to the exercise of action, it at once supplies the opportunity for work. But at night, withdrawing itself from human sight and, as if with certain swaddling-cloths of infancy, covering the lights of mortals with the veil of darkness, it cherishes wearied limbs in rest and sleep, so that, restored, it may return them more eagerly to labor and daytime exercise. Beholding this wonderful order of divine dispensation, when the Psalmist praised God’s works, he mentions this among the rest as something outstanding and worthy of no slight praise, saying: “He made the moon for the seasons; the sun knew its setting. You appointed darkness, and night came to be; in it all the beasts of the forest will pass through. The young lions roar that they may seize prey and seek their food from God. The sun arose and they were gathered together, and they shall be laid in their dens. Man shall go out to his work and to his labor until evening” (Ps. CIII [104]). [Col. 0128A]

This is also why God, when Noah came out of the ark after the flood, promises as though it were some great sign of his mercy and gift of bounty, saying: “All the days of seedtime and harvest, cold and heat, summer and winter, night and day, shall not cease” (Gen. VIII). Therefore he aptly described men, stretched out below in this ark of the world through the various courses of mortal-life occupations, as laboring under the sun; so that this too pertains to the vanity of human work: the light from above, passing by and to be ended in darkness, illuminates a man for work. For he considered how abject and miserable is the condition of mortals, who creep over the surface of the earth like worms, some crawling in empty curiosity; suddenly, when light is poured down from above, they are aroused as though for mockery to grasp what they vainly desire, and shortly afterward, when that light is withdrawn, they are again wrapped in sudden blindness and cannot at all proceed further to fulfillment. Therefore the very light by which they are illuminated is shown from above, at a distance and far off, and inaccessible to man, so that it may be proved not to stand at all in human power; and so that a man may receive from it only as much as the grace of God, who bestows and orders all things, permits—not as much as the perverse will of a man serving desire craves. [Col. 0128C]

Great, therefore, is the vanity of laboring under the sun, and slight the confidence of laboring under the sun. Although its light is pleasant to the sight and delightful to behold, it cannot always be present to human eyes or be of benefit. But if one wishes to carry reflection still higher and examine the matter more subtly, we may understand time to be signified by the name “sun,” so that “under the sun” is the same as saying “under time.” For because the course of times is especially distinguished through the sun, and the nature of temporal things is varied, time itself is fittingly expressed by “sun,” when “under the sun” is said; it is the same as saying “under time.”

But did he also intend to suggest something by saying not “in time” or “with time,” [Col. 0128D] but “under time”? Must we distinguish in order to understand that some things were made, as it were, with time, while others are made either in time or under time? Let us distinguish, then, if we can, perhaps so that we may discover why he said that the vain works of men are done rather under time than either with time or in time. Everything made was made either with time or in time. Those things were made with time whose origin time did not precede: such as angelic nature, and that unformed matter of visible things which God created in the beginning. Those things were made in time whose origin time preceded, such as the works of the six days in which God perfected and completed [Col. 0129A] the fabric of this sensible world; and also all things which afterward were made formally or essentially were made in time.

Again, among things done in time, some are done both in time and under time; others are done in time only, not under time. Those things are done in time but not under time which indeed begin in time but do not end in time. Those things are done in time and under time which both begin in time and end in time. Again, among things done under time, some are done for time, others for eternity. Therefore those done for time are vain both in act and in fruit. But those done for eternity are vain in act indeed, yet are not vain in fruit, because, although they pass away in their performance, they remain in recompense.

For a good work [Col. 0129B] is not merely that which appears outwardly transitory, since it consists both in visible action and invisible devotion. For just as a human being consists of a living being and life—and the living being dies, but life does not die—so surely a good work has in itself visible action and invisible devotion. Visible action is, as it were, the body; inward devotion is, as it were, the spirit. Action lives through devotion, just as the body lives through the soul. But devotion gives life to action, just as the soul gives life to the body. For every action without devotion is dead. Therefore visible action itself, as it were, lives; invisible devotion is life itself. But what lives dies; what is life itself does not die. For transitory action, just as it has its beginning from time, so it ends in time. Therefore what dies, what ends, what passes away, what is given over to mutability, is itself subject to vanity. But what is life, what remains, what does not admit an end or corruption, does not admit vanity.

Let it therefore be said: “What does a man have in addition from all his labor at which he toils under the sun?”—understood, “except vanity.” Nothing in addition, because all things done under the sun are vain. And what would he have from vain things except vanity? What then? Will good works done under the sun contribute nothing in addition to their workers except vanity? And how did we say above that this question was resolved by the phrase “under the sun”? Behold, the same question arises again for us, no less difficult than above, because we cannot deny that good works too are done under the sun—that is, under time, according to the explanation given above—[Col. 0129D] and yet we do not dare say that nothing except vanity is attained from them. And behold, the book plainly says: “What does a man have in addition from all his labor at which he toils under the sun?”

But if we wish to consider the words themselves more carefully, it is plainly shown which works are charged with being vain. For he did not say: “What does a man have in addition from all his labor which is done, or which was done, under the sun?” Rather, he says: “which the man himself toils at under the sun.” Therefore he charges not so much the labor as the laborer with being under the sun. Thus, because the man himself, placed under the sun, toils, what he toils at is vain. But who is the one who toils under the sun? He who, oppressed by love of temporal and passing things, labors either to obtain them if he does not have them or to preserve them if he has them. This man toils under the sun, and this man toils in vain. But he who practices good works in hope and desire of eternal things does not toil under the sun, even though the labor in which he toils is under the sun; for though the work he performs is temporal, he nevertheless transcends in mind and devotion all temporal and perishable things. Therefore this man does not toil in vain, even though that in which he toils is vain, because that for which he toils is not vain. And when that which is vain, in which he toils, has passed away, he has ready that for which he toils, which is not vanity. Therefore such a person does not belong to this saying: “What does a man have in addition from all his labor at which he toils under the sun?” For he does not [Col. 0130B] toil under the sun, but above the sun, who does not establish the reward of his labor in unstable things that pass away with time.

“A generation passes away, and a generation comes.” Behold vanity. “A generation passes away, and a generation comes.” Human nature, corrupted in the first root of its race, conceived this, and it sprang up, sown with this same condition, throughout every offspring of posterity. For when the first parent of the human race heard, “You are earth and to earth you shall go,” he became mortal; because he fell from the state of incorruption, he began, as it were, through mortality to pass from life to death. All men after him, who descend from him through bodily birth, travel this same way. This is that vanity of which the Psalmist spoke, saying: “Truly every living man is altogether vanity. Truly man passes away in an image” (Ps. XXXVIII [39]). [Col. 0130C]

Therefore he added this vanity, as though greater than the rest and more terrible to human minds because of the dreadful necessity of death, in the final place, so that a man might hear at the end that in which he more evidently recognizes the misery of his condition. For the first vanity is not even in a name, nor is it referred to man. The second vanity is not in man, though it is referred to man. The third vanity is both in man and referred to man. Accordingly, advancing as it were by stages ever upward, he first set forth that vanity which is neither a punishment of man nor a fault. Then he added that vanity which is not man’s punishment but is his fault. Finally, he added that which is not a fault but a punishment—[Col. 0130D] though such a fault can never be without punishment, nor can such a punishment, at least in those to whom the sacrament of salvation does not bring help, be wholly free from fault. But I called the former a man’s fault, not a punishment, and the latter a punishment, not a fault, because in the former a man’s desert is seen, while in the latter judgment is found. Therefore he placed this punishment last as though it were more grievous and more dreadful than the others. Although it is not a worse fault, it is nevertheless more troublesome to the flesh and more effective in rousing fleshly minds.

Let him say, then: “A generation passes away, and a generation comes.” As though he said: If you think that everything you do, being vain, is to be disregarded, is even this to be disregarded—that you yourselves are vanity? “A generation passes away, and a generation comes.” If those who are dying depart and those who are destined to die succeed them, what joy is there? Indeed, the grief of the living seems to receive consolation in those being born; yet that by which it is thought to be ended and cease is precisely what makes it always continue. For it is grief that the dying depart. What consolation follows from the arrival of those who are to die? A consolation that ends in mourning. And what could be more vain in either case? “A generation passes away, and a generation comes.” If this lamentable calamity engulfed only a few, or at least not all, it would seem bearable; but now a savage plague draws all with it into destruction. “A generation passes away, and a generation comes.” If it passes away, where does it go? If it comes, from where does it come? Alas, dreadful lot! How can you be secure, O man, wrapped in such great darkness? Behold, you know that by living you are moving toward death. But can you know [Col. 0131B] what you will be like or where you will be after death? Consider, then, in how great a vanity you live: every day you see pass away what you are, yet by no means can you know what you will be. “A generation passes away, and a generation comes.”

“But the earth stands forever.” Listen, man, and blush. “The earth stands forever.” Why does the earth stand while you cannot stand, you for whose sake the earth was made? Perhaps you will say that it stands for your consolation. It stands in order to send forth those who arrive, bear those who pass through, and receive those who depart. For those born come from the earth through bodily origin; while living, they pass over the earth through bodily changeability; and, dying, they return to the earth through bodily corruption. Therefore it stands for your consolation; indeed, it stands for your confusion. How? See how it stands, what sort it is that bears, whom it bears, and what sort of earth it is from which it bears them.

What sort of earth does it bear? Hear what sort: “Cursed is the earth in your work; it shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you” (Gen. III). But whom does it bear? Hear again: “Cursed are you above the earth” (Gen. IV). And of what sort of earth does it bear them? “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread; and you shall eat the herbs of the earth” (Gen. III). [Col. 0131C] Therefore the cursed bears the cursed. Yet it bears them. But in bearing them it has something for your consolation and something for your punishment. What is for your consolation comes with your labor; what is for your punishment comes through your labor. It has bread; it has also thorns. Bread with your labor, for your consolation; thorns through your labor, for your punishment. “In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread”: this is for your consolation with your labor. “When you have worked, the earth shall not give you its fruit, but shall bring forth thorns and thistles for you”: this is for your punishment through your labor. Therefore it stands not only for your consolation, but much more for your confusion. It stands not only to relieve your misery, but as testimony and punishment for your fault.

The earth stands, and you stand upon the earth. That which bears you is stable, and you who are borne fall. Why is this? Are you not also earth? What, then, was said to you: “You are earth, and to earth you shall go”? Therefore you are earth, you are upon earth, and you are from earth. Why, then, do you not stand forever? Have you become weaker than that earth from which you were taken? What, then, did the craftsman’s hand accomplish if it did not advance [Col. 0132A] its work into something better? Was there, then, no knowledge in him, or was he found weak, so that in his hands that good material became worse? Far be it! Indeed, he made you far better than that from which he made you; for he made the earth stable, but made you immortal from the earth. Therefore he made you better than that from which he made you. Your corruption, therefore, did not proceed from the maker who made you with such power and such goodness that he could make nothing less perfect than the perfect, and would will nothing worse than the best. Thus the best craftsman made a good creature; his eternal incorruption and immortal goodness neither produces defect nor receives defect.

But perhaps the material is to be blamed, since it was such that nothing else could be made from it. For the material was earth, and a clay vessel came forth. What? Is this remarkable? [Col. 0132B] Then, in saying this, you ought to have considered that, if you are a clay vessel, you have been hardened from soft mud into pottery; and though your clod had no nature of firmness, it nevertheless had a nature capable of being made firm. If it did not have it by nature that it should be this, it nevertheless had by nature the capacity to become this by grace. Therefore your material did you no harm: it preserves whole both what nature bestowed and what grace gave, and does not diminish either. For the earth stands forever. What does “stands” mean? It perseveres in what it was made; it preserves its nature; it does not abandon its condition; it retains uncorrupted what it received. The earth was made, and remains earth; it is never anything other than what it is. And when it is something else, it is something else not through the failing of corruption, but through the advance of elevation.

Likewise in you it has become something else, and will become something else, than it was when born; yet through elevation, not corruption. And when in certain earthly things it seems to change from one thing into another, it is nevertheless never other than what it is: for it is earth and always earth; that which changes is earth, and that into which it changes is earth. And when this changes into that, or that into this, what is earth does not change, since it is the same in both. Therefore the earth has movement within the bosom of its nature, and has activity producing, from what it is, that which it is; it does not have passage beyond the bounds of its nature from what it is into what it is not. And therefore the earth stands forever in what it is. [Col. 0132C]

Why, then, did you not stand in that in which you were made upon the earth, just as the earth stands in that in which it was made? Why did you degenerate, so that you do not at least imitate your material, which preserves what it is so fully that, although you were made earth, you cannot be anything other than what earth is? You flow down to it through your fault; you are not permitted to proceed beyond it by its nature. Behold how greatly it preserves what it is: when it receives you, though flowing and unstable, it does not allow you to pass further into something other than itself. Whence, then, comes your flowing away? Seek carefully and consider. Neither your maker nor your material caused this in you; for the latter, standing forever, preserves in you too what it itself is, while the former, by making you for eternity, gave you more than it itself is. Whence, then, comes this to you, except from your own fault? From that fault now comes your punishment: that you return to that over which it had been given you by grace always to stand. [Col. 0133A] Therefore you pass away, while the earth stands as testimony against you, so that, accusing you as mortal and receiving you when you die, it convicts you before it punishes you. Therefore the earth stands forever. “A generation passes away, and a generation comes; but the earth stands forever.”

These things we have said, according to the smallness and scantiness of our understanding, as an introduction to the book of Solomon called *Ecclesiastes*, by no means presuming that we have said what ought chiefly to have been said. For it is already a great thing for us only not to have said what ought not to have been said. Moreover, it must be understood that this book requires a certain new manner of exposition. Since it is wholly directed toward moving the affections of the human heart, one must often shape the discourse in it as though conversing rather than expounding. Hence it is necessary sometimes to linger longer over words even in matters that seem plain and clear, so that the very repetition of the expression may touch and penetrate the hearer’s heart more forcefully and effectively. Whoever wishes to treat this Scripture differently, even if he suitably serves his hearers’ understanding, may perhaps make less progress toward edification because he does not retain its force and distinctive character. [Col. 0133B]

## HOMILY II. On the demonstration of the vanity of everything under heaven: through the corruption of the elements, the generation and succession of things, and the oblivion of things that have been.

The words of Ecclesiastes, which testify that all things under the sun are vain, have somehow, as they were read just now, become sweet in our ears. And behold, we have begun gladly to hear of our evils, and although we do not love them, we nevertheless love to hear them. For we do not love our evils, but we love to hear of our evils, because by hearing of evils we do not love, we remember the good things we do love. And this very remembrance of good things, even amid evils, is sweet to the soul; and indeed it is sweeter by as much as the evils themselves are more bitter, which by hearing or feeling we recognize to be far from those good things for which, if only through remembrance, we long. This was all that we now marvel to have tasted so greatly in this discourse, in which the hardship of our exile is described for us and our misery and calamity—what they are and how great—is declared.

For our mind, awakened in hearing of its evils as though from some sleep of its former condition, suddenly recognized where it was; and, amazed and wondering at so great an abyss of ruin, it began at the same time to consider from what height it had fallen into this very depth of misery. Since it could not yet attain that height in reality, it sighed for it with a certain marvelous longing of inward ardor. This, therefore, was what drew our affection in those words that recounted our misery. This makes us always willing to hear our evils in this way, and prevents anything from being bitter when it is received together with that which is so sweet. This daily makes lamentations themselves sweet to the wretched, and delightfully nourishes the afflicted with tears amid sighs and groans, because amid adversities remembrance of the things loved is sweeter; the soul itself burns more intensely in desire for what is absent, is more sweetly touched by the memory of what is past, [Col. 0134A] and is more powerfully inflamed by the delay of what is to come.

Our Ecclesiastes knew this very well. Throughout his whole discourse he so carefully pursues the vanity of passing things that, through consideration of it, he admonishes the human heart to meditate upon heavenly things and awaken in the desire for eternal things. For he knew that the more clearly the vanity of things that pass away in time is recognized, the more sublimely the inward eye of the mind is opened toward the state of eternity. Therefore, beginning in this first part of his work, he shows that all things under the sun are vain; that is, that whatever is visible is subject to corruption or liable to mutability. For he shows that neither in heaven, nor under heaven, nor upon earth, nor in the earth, is there anything perpetual that does not undergo change or pass into alteration. Thus none of all things that are ceaselessly drawn into what they are not, and cannot preserve stably or incorruptibly what they are, truly exists.

“The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place; and there, rising anew, it circles through the south and bends toward the north.” This must be punctuated separately. Then follows:

“The spirit goes on, surveying all things in a circuit, and returns to its circuits.” This too must stand separately. Afterward follows:

“All rivers enter the sea, and the sea does not overflow; the rivers return to the place from which they flow, that they may flow again.” And this must be joined together.

Therefore he appears to set forth three things as evidence for the mutability of all things: the sun, the spirit, and rivers—that is, fire, air, and moisture—so that the whole may be understood as signified through a part: fire through the sun, air through spirit, and moisture through rivers. Above, indeed, he had established the earth in the middle as an immovable foundation. Now he arranges the other three elements—fire, air, and water—wavering around it in unstable movement, in order to show that in producing mutable things the power of acting, and in a certain manner the function of a craftsman, has been granted to these three elements. But the earth lies beneath, immovable, as a kind of material for all things to be produced: powerless indeed to act, but merely suited to be shaped by the work of the others into the things that are to be created. [Col. 0134D]

Therefore through these three elements nature exercises its power in that fourth element. Moving around and within it according to a marvelous law, and tempering one another, they produce from it as many innumerable forms and species of things as are shown by the continual, unceasing alternations of their approach and withdrawal in the annual, monthly, and daily changes of times. Therefore, since all growing things that arise from the earth and receive from the earth both substance and nourishment obtain the nature of vital movement from these three elements, he rightly placed in them both the origin of mutability and the nature and characteristic of all mutable things. Thus in them we may see both why whatever arises under time cannot stand, and by what course that which is not comes to be, or that which is returns to non-being.

“The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place; and there, rising anew, it circles through the south and bends toward the north.” In few words he comprehends a great matter. We should say something concerning these words as occasion requires, yet not hold the hearer’s attention too long in such matters, lest, contrary to our purpose, we seem to abandon sacred exposition and descend into describing the courses of the stars. All these things were said only so that the human mind might be more suitably stirred by an account of things it knows, and through them awakened to think about what it does not know. Therefore it ought not to seem tedious or unworthy to us to attend carefully to those matters which divine discourse has taken care to recount carefully.

He shows, then, by what course this great luminary, which illuminates all things by its presence, is carried in unceasing motion around the globe of this sensible world and effects various changes in things by its approach and withdrawal. “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place.” First he shows that it has a circular motion and always returns to that from which it proceeds, so that, because no end can be found in a circle, its course may be shown perpetual. “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place.” Then he describes the bends of its progress, saying, “It circles through the south and bends toward the north,” so that this too contributes to the great change of things: it does not always direct its course in the same manner or proceed straight ahead.

“The sun rises and sets.” It rises daily when, emerging, it is presented to human sight. It sets when, descending to the lower regions according to the curvature of its revolution, it withdraws itself from our eyes. It returns to its place because the force of its rotation drives it again beneath us toward its rising. But after rising, as it tends toward setting, it first bends toward the south, because, especially when it remains in the summer signs, it ascends from the east toward the meridian line by an oblique course. Then, descending toward setting, it again inclines northward by an oblique progression.

A further quite suitable interpretation of these words may be offered: namely, that they refer not to the sun’s daily but to its annual course. The sun rises for us when, entering through the vernal equinox, it ascends toward our pole. It sets when, departing through the autumnal equinox, it descends to the lower regions. It circles through the south when it remains in the winter signs. It bends toward the north when it is carried through the summer signs, which are nearer the northern pole. Therefore the sun rises, and with its rising all things rise together which are revived by its heat. It sets, and immediately, when the vital fire is withdrawn, all things perish which flourished through its presence. It circles through the south so that winter cold may temper the summer heats. It bends toward the north so that those things which the frost of winter and icy numbness had bound may be warmed again by summer heats and restored to life. You see, then, how many changes in things a single body brings with it.

[Col. 0136A] “The spirit goes on, surveying all things in a circuit, and returns to its circuits.” If by “spirit” we understand air, then, in a fitting order, after describing the instability of the heavenly element, he shows that the lower things too suffer the same law, saying: “The spirit goes on, surveying all things in a circuit.” As though he said: If the force of nature does not permit even the things in heaven to stand, it is necessary that the same condition of mutability govern also the things beneath heaven. Certainly, just as he attributed circular motion to the sun, so he attributes it to the air, so that its agitation may be shown perpetual.

But in adding in the plural, “It returns to its circuits,” he may signify that the movement of the air is not everywhere always the same. Rather, since it is stirred more violently in one place and more moderately in another, its very fluctuation, poured back into itself in reciprocal turns, moves diversely and does not rest uniformly. Thus we need not suppose a movement once begun to be extended to the uttermost limit, but rather that individual motions and impulses are, as it were, made within themselves and gradually come to rest as their motion weakens over distance. Moreover, the word “surveying” is fittingly attributed to this element, because by its mobility it cleanses and disperses all impurities scattered or gathered anywhere; or because, by its subtlety, it penetrates all things and diffuses itself everywhere.

Or this word may be joined to the preceding sense as follows: “The sun rises and sets, and returns to its place; and there, rising anew, it circles through the south and bends toward the north, surveying all things in a circuit.” Then, after making the division here, the following sentence is introduced: “The spirit goes on,” etc. For the sun surveys all things in a circuit through its course, because in rising or setting through the various signs it reaches every region of the world. Rising and setting in Cancer, it touches the north; in Capricorn, the south; in Libra and Aries, it passes through the middle by east and west.

It follows: “The spirit goes on, and returns to its circuits.” According to the preceding exposition, we may now understand “spirit,” not improperly, as the fiery power proceeding from the sun, which diffuses itself through all things and, invisibly penetrating all things, gives them life and motion. Hence the ancients also said that nature was an artificer-fire proceeding to produce sensible things. For in all growing things the source of vital motion and sensible life is fiery power: it gives growth to all things and, nourishing and cherishing them with invisible sustenance, finally brings them forth into invisible substance. [Col. 0136D] The poet too called this hidden power of nature, which moves and nourishes all things, “spirit”; and his words are well known:

> In the beginning, a spirit within sustains heaven and earth,  
> the flowing plains, the shining globe of the moon,  
> and the Titanian stars; and, infused through all the limbs—
“Mind moves the mass and mingles with the great body.” (Aeneid VI.688.) Although in these words he seems rather to approve the error of one who asserts that this sensible world is, as it were, an animal consisting of soul and body, and that its soul is the spirit which moves all things. But [Col. 0137A], however the opinion of those in error may be expounded, we may with sound understanding take the spirit which goes forth into all things and returns into its circuits to be the hidden power of nature, which invisibly nourishes and quickens all things and brings each to its appointed and lawful end. This spirit, then—that is, the hidden power of nature—pervades all things, because, invisibly diffusing itself through every part of things, it assigns to each its proper quality according to the capacity of its nature. It goes forth and returns, because it first advances all things that arise in time through growth, and then by old age brings them back to their origin. For it goes forth because in things being born it comes out; in things growing it proceeds up to a fixed measure. It returns because in things growing old and, through the failing [Col. 0137B] of their nature, slipping backwards, it is recalled as far as the beginning of its origin. Thus we rightly understand the courses and progressions of individual things as certain circuits and orbits returning into themselves, because all things that arise in time finally return through their setting to that from which they came forth through the beginning of birth. And each thing is shown to have, according to its own measure and the duration for which it subsists, a course distinct from another—that is, greater or less. Yet all are known to have one origin and likewise one end, because all return at their setting to the earth from which they came forth at the beginning of their rising. Therefore, just as the sun rises and sets and returns to its place, so the spirit goes forth and returns into its circuits. For [Col. 0137C], just as in the body of the sun fire moving locally is brought back to the beginning of its rising, so likewise, naturally, in all things being born, it brings back to its origin through their decline and setting the motion which it raised through the growth of things.

There follows the third clause, [Col. 0137D] in which the element of water is treated, which in the order of things is placed third after fire and is joined with it in generation. For as regards the arrangement and order of things, fire occupies the first and highest place; air is second, nearest to fire. Then water claims the third place; earth rests in the last and lowest place. Of these four, fire and water, though by nature most opposed, are nevertheless, in friendly and balanced union, the source of all things that are born. Therefore, if we attend to place or nature, we see these two as disparate from each other. If we look to their efficacy, we find both close to and friendly with one another. Therefore the element of water, which together with fire supplies the other life-giving nurture to things being born, was not to be passed over, as third after fire and air, or second together with fire among the natures of mutable things. And accordingly he describes its circuit and its course for the generation of sensible things, saying: “All rivers enter into the sea, and the sea does not overflow.” And he immediately adds the reason why the sea does not overflow after receiving all rivers into itself: namely, because they return again to the place from which the rivers come forth, that they may flow again. For channels of water, within and without, draw moisture through the whole [Col. 0138A] body of the earth in the manner of veins, so that irrigation may be distributed evenly to every part. In order that this infusion may be continual and perpetual, the course of waters has therefore been arranged in a circle; and in that unceasing circulation, so that what is poured in from above may never fail, as much as flows downward in one part is brought back to its source through hidden passages in another.

So too the food of the body is carried in a certain circuit: first descending from the palate into the stomach, then passing into evacuation; and in this very passage, by a kind of infusion of nature, nourishment is supplied to what is failing. When this has evaporated and been emptied out, it is necessary again to resort to the aid of eating in order to restore the members as they waste away. Thus, as it were, a circle [Col. 0138B] of ever-renewing need is drawn, returning to its own origin; because, while what has been taken in passes away without cessation, it is always necessary to take again what can supply substance to make up the deficiency. Therefore, whatever nourishment the substance of food supplies to the body by continual repetition in order to sustain it, precisely such nourishment the reflux of the elements pours into the body of the earth for producing offspring and quickening seeds. Fire, water, and air do not cease, by their unending approach and withdrawal, to do this: always to fill what is added and empty what recedes, so that, because the strength of the earlier infusion cannot remain, irrigation must of necessity be repeated anew to restore fullness. What assurance of perpetual continuance, then, can the nourishments of things provide, [Col. 0138C] when in all things both the repairing elements continually pass away without cessation and what has been repaired fails? Although repeated infusion seems to offer some sort of consolation for this failing, it is nevertheless a great misery always to receive in need and never to be able to be without the need of receiving. Hence it is evident that all transitory and perishable things are vain, for they are continually emptied of the solidity of their condition either by passing away or by failing.

A great spectacle, therefore, is here set before holy minds, which know how to draw knowledge of invisible things from visible ones; which know how to say to their Creator: “You have made all things in wisdom, O Lord” (Ps. 103). “You have gladdened me, O Lord, in your work, and I shall rejoice in the works of your hands. How magnified are your works, O Lord; your thoughts have become exceedingly deep” (Ps. 91) [Col. 0138D].

For behold how all transitory things, subject to vanity, are borne in a circuit. And we know that a circle has no end. Therefore things which run in a circuit do indeed run, but never arrive at an end. What rest, then, can be hoped for where no standing still can be? For where there is perpetual motion, there is no stability. But where the circuit is the path, there is no point at which the course can certainly have an end. Therefore the things which run in a circuit always run and never attain stability. They always pass away and never remain. They always come to an end and cannot find an end.
