When they have passed, they are to come; when they have come, [Col. 0139A] they do not remain.

This is the way of all mutable things, and the way of all who love mutable things and follow mutability. For of the wicked it is said: “The wicked walk in a circuit” (Ps. 11). And again: “The head of their circuit” (Ps. 139), and “Set them like a wheel, O Lord” (Ps. 82). The head also of all the wicked himself testifies concerning himself, saying: “I went around the earth and walked through it” (Job 1). And the Apostle says of him: “He goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Pet. 5). You see, therefore, how the perverse always love the circuit and do not depart from it. Accordingly, the things perversely loved by the perverse themselves all run in a circuit, as testimony against them that they too follow the circuit.

By contrast, the lover of eternal things says: “My foot stood in uprightness” [Col. 0139B] (Ps. 27). And again: “Direct me in the path of your commandments, for I have desired it” (Ps. 118). And again: “The path of the righteous is straight” (Isa. 26). And elsewhere again: “Their paths,” he says, “shall go straight, and the Lord our God shall bring them to a definite place” (Wis. 5). O straight way, where do you lead? O circuit, where do you lead? You lead and bring through. But you lead and lead astray, because those whom you lead, you destroy rather than bring through. O circuit, how you entangle, how you embrace your followers! To those running through you, you grant neither an exit from yourself nor an arrival within yourself. Therefore all transitory and perishable things are rolled through circuits while they pass away, so that we may not seek in them the good of eternity, since we see that they always both come in such a way as to pass away and pass away in such a way as not to remain.

Let us therefore still consider these circuits [Col. 0139C] of vanity. For, as has already been said, God’s wisdom wonderfully provided that the movement of all things should be carried on in a circle, so that corporeal nature, which by flowing away might at some point have felt failure, might, by always returning to its own origin, while it receives without interruption what it has poured out, pour out without deficiency what it receives, and there might be failure without failure; nor might that which can fail ever be lacking, so that it may always fail. Hence in one and the same thing both what exists is pitiable and what has been made is wonderful, because in the same work both the material is found to be frail and the craftsman’s design admirable. Corruptible nature urges contempt for the world, but the mind yields in admiration while contemplating the design.

Therefore, after setting forth the course of mutable things, [Col. 0139D] our Ecclesiastes turns to contemplate this design, in order to exercise the mind’s sight upon it through contemplation; because knowledge is not able sufficiently to comprehend it, he endeavors to venerate it with worthy admiration. For, having explained the mutability of all things according to the motion that moves them in three kinds of things—fire, air, and water—he next shows how inexplicable that same mutability is according to the motion that is moved through every individual thing rising and setting in the universe.

“All things are difficult; man cannot explain them in speech. The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing.” When any thing is seen upon its surface, neither its hidden cause nor [Col. 0140A] its nature has yet been penetrated. For what is, is seen; but what that which is seen is like, what quality it retains in secret—where bodily sense cannot gain access—why it is as it appears, whence it is so, and for what it is: what human being, not to say in all things, but even in any one thing, can fully comprehend these matters? In what great darkness, then, is a human being enveloped; by what blindness of ignorance is one constrained, whose sense can scarcely touch even a few things merely on their surface? Even if one saw all things according to their outward appearance, one would still not penetrate the hidden force of things and their invisible nature.

Therefore the universe of things is incomprehensible to human beings in both ways: [Col. 0140B] both according to outward appearance and according to inward quality. But among individual things, some come partly to the senses outwardly by their appearance; others are altogether hidden, either because they are locally remote or because, though present in place, by their subtlety they exceed the slowness of human sense. Human sense can scarcely succeed in touching anything among things; yet it comprehends nothing in the universe perfectly as it is. Therefore all things are difficult: difficult with respect to the whole, since they cannot be reached; and difficult with respect to each individual thing, since they cannot be fully comprehended by any sense or understanding. If they cannot be perfectly investigated by reason, much less can they be explained in speech.

For this itself is most ineffable in all things: [Col. 0140C] that amid such confusion of mutability no evident and manifest design is ever lacking to one who considers well; that even what is not good in things is so well ordered that, in some manner, the corruption of individual things becomes the beauty of the universe. Therefore human sense, yielding under consideration of these things, is sweetly refreshed by its own deficiency; because that which displeases according to corruption is beautiful and pleasing even in the most orderly beauty of the universe. Thus, in a wonderful and ineffable way, the Creator in his creation both punishes wickedness through the corruption of things and delights nature through beauty, so that a human being may recognize in punishment what has been deserved through sin, and in delight what has been lost. For how great an abundance of sweetness must we believe exists in the Creator of things, [Col. 0140D] if we find such marvelous delight in the beauty of creatures? Therefore, having spoken of the deficiency of human understanding amid so manifold, intricate, and varied a depth of things, he immediately adds the delightfulness of nature in their beauty.

“The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing.” Since all bodily senses find in created things their own delights, as it were their particular pleasures prepared for each: sight, visual appearance; hearing, the sweetness of melody; smell, fragrance; taste, flavor; touch, softness. All the others indeed serve bodily necessity or even pleasure. But these two senses, sight and hearing, draw their nourishment more toward spiritual delight. Hence their refreshment has no sediment [Col. 0141A], because together with the perception of sweetness they draw in no mass of corruption. For this reason their refreshment does not reach satiety of sweetness, because neither a difficulty encountered delays their desire from perceiving sweetness, nor does any succeeding annoyance restrain it.

Therefore this pure and unalloyed nourishment, without any bodily weight, passes wholly into the refreshment of the soul. Though it flows from bodily appearance and passes through bodily sense, it cannot be retained by the body, because it possesses nothing bodily and conveys nothing corporeal. Thus sight and hearing, as superior to the others and possessing no oppressive weight, have been allotted a higher seat in the body, that they may freely and without hindrance flow out toward their delights or, as those delights flow in, receive them into themselves without difficulty.

Now there are two things which enter the mind through sight from the appearance of things, [Col. 0141B] and likewise two things which enter through hearing from the perception of sounds. Through sight, the substance and form of things come to the mind’s knowledge. Through hearing, from sounds come meaning and melody. And substance from things accomplishes in the mind through sight the same thing as meaning from sounds through hearing. Likewise, form from things accomplishes in the mind through sight the same thing as melody from sounds through hearing. For there are two things by which the entire nature of the rational soul is ordered: knowledge and affection—that is, wisdom and love. If the soul perfectly possesses and rightly orders these two, it is blessed. But if it fails either to attain them to the degree required by nature [Col. 0141C], or, having attained them, perverts them against nature, it necessarily becomes miserable in that part in which it suffers either their deficiency or their disorder.

Thus the whole substance of the soul is governed by these two, knowledge and affection: through wisdom it finds truth, and through love it embraces virtue. Therefore, in order that even outward things might serve the rational soul for blessedness, these two instruments of sense were placed in the human body, so that through them notions of visible things might enter the soul and either produce wisdom or virtue in it if it had none at all, or increase them if they were deficient. Therefore the essence of things entering the soul through sight, and the meaning of sounds through hearing, produce knowledge. But the form of things entering through sight [Col. 0141D] and the melody of sounds through hearing kindle the mind toward delight. For whenever sight is affected outwardly by the appearance of things or hearing is soothed by the sweetness of sounds, the mind within awakens with wondrous affections, responding to that by which it feels itself touched outwardly. And it sometimes happens that, through the sweetness which it draws through bodily sense, it returns to the remembrance of invisible goods and, as though reminded by a likeness, begins to desire with inexpressible longing that of which it feels itself to have perceived, in bodily affection, a kind of shadow and image.

Therefore let Ecclesiastes say: “The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing.” For through these senses the beauty of visible things, while it affects the mind with delight in contemplating itself, [Col. 0142A] kindles within it an inexpressible desire for invisible goods. This desire, thirsting for ineffable sweetness, may indeed be stimulated rather than filled by whatever delight bodily sight or hearing, through which it is awakened, can bring. And however abundant or eloquent human speech may be, that desire, though it is scarcely expressed even faintly, is never perfectly explained. For from the appearance of visible things the rational soul conceives only certain seeds of joys; but as desire soon grows boundlessly, the soul itself labors in birth and cannot contain itself amid such great delight.

Therefore let no one think the sight of visible things harmful to chaste minds. For if it were altogether harmful to see the works of God, the faculty of sight would never have [Col. 0142B] been created by him. For the work of God is, as it were, his word, through which he speaks to us; and the eyes themselves are, as it were, instruments by which through contemplation the words of God are perceived. Therefore, just as the ear is an instrument for perceiving the word of a human being, so the eye is an instrument for perceiving the word of the Creator. Accordingly, in the human body the eyes are fittingly placed in front and the ears at the sides, as though this signified to us that our attention ought to be directed secondarily toward our neighbor and principally toward God.

Therefore, to show how desire for eternal things arises in the mind from the consideration of visible things, eyes and ears alone are mentioned. For through these alone, almost uniquely, a way to wisdom [Col. 0142C] and virtue lies open to the mind, because, while they perceive the unalloyed beauty of visible things more than the other senses, they alone kindle more sincerely within the love of invisible goods. “All things are difficult; man cannot explain them in speech.”

“The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing.” It is wonderful: the human heart is not sufficient for the whole world, and the whole world is not sufficient for the human heart. Why is the human heart not sufficient for the whole world? Because all things are difficult, and a human being cannot explain them in speech. Why is the whole world not sufficient for the human heart? Because the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing. Therefore knowledge yields, but affection transcends. Knowledge stretches itself as far as it can, yet cannot contain the whole; but love drinks in the whole [Col. 0142D] and still cannot be satisfied. Why is this? Because charity surpasses knowledge; and the human heart does not say “It is enough” until it comes to and finds him by whom it was made to exist and for whom it was made to be blessed in him.

Every delight, every sweetness, every beauty of created things can affect the human heart; it cannot satisfy it, except that one sweetness for which it was made. For the appearances of visible things are merely certain veins through which invisible beauty, revealing itself, flows forth even to us. Therefore, when these naturally draw our sense and affection toward themselves, they do not fill desire; rather, they stir us to seek the form of the Creator and [Col. 0143A] to desire his beauty. Thus all these things which are seen outwardly were made to stimulate human affection, not to satisfy it, so that, awakened by them, it may rise and, strengthened by them, transcend them. Therefore the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing. For what we see made beautiful delights us, but it is not enough unless we find him who made it.

Or what he says may be understood in this way: “The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing.” Since he had stated that all things are difficult and that a human being cannot explain them in speech, lest anyone perhaps suppose that they could nevertheless be comprehended by knowledge, he added: “The eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing.” As though he said: It is not surprising if a human being cannot explain in speech the difficulty [Col. 0143B] of things, since one cannot even grasp or investigate their depth by sense. Whether one seeks to discover them by oneself or hears them already discovered by another, everything one can grasp falls short of the satiety of fullness. For if one begins to contemplate by oneself, the eye is not satisfied with seeing. If one seeks to be instructed by another, the ear is not filled with hearing. The narrowness of bodily instruments, if they pour themselves outward, is not sufficient for explaining the depth or immensity of things. But if they pour themselves inward, they cannot fill the capacity of the human heart.

For because the heart of man, blinded by the darkness of sin, has no inward eye by which it fully sees the light of truth, nor ear by which it perceives the word of God sounding inwardly, [Col. 0143C] it is compelled to open bodily eyes and ears to irrigate the dryness of its ignorance, so that outwardly, at least in the appearance of things, it may draw some drop of truth, by which its thirst, though it cannot be wholly quenched, may be somewhat relieved. This is what the Lord reproaches his people through the prophet, saying: “My people have committed two sins: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living water, and have dug for themselves broken cisterns that cannot hold water” (Jer. 2).

For we know that a cistern is dug in order that water collected from outside may flow into it and may then be drawn from it again for human use. But because it has no living vein, however great it may seem and however overflowing with gathered waters, it can at some time be exhausted [Col. 0143D] and dry up; because, when what is poured into it from elsewhere has been taken away and consumed, nothing of its own remains by which it may be replenished. But a spring which has a living vein, even though small, cannot fail altogether, nor does it ever feel a deficiency in its outpouring, since an increase from its own source always comes to it without deficiency.

Therefore bodily eyes and ears, although they are chief instruments by which the way of learning is opened to the mind, nevertheless do not bring notions of visible things to the human heart from the inward fountain of truth. Rather, they lead them through the narrow channels of their capacity, like waters gathered here and there into a cistern. And because in the things they perceive they are unable either to comprehend the whole or to penetrate what is inward, it is rightly said now: “The eye is not satisfied [Col. 0144A] with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing.” For although the human mind, whether by seeing or hearing, perceives something, however little, of truth, the condition of its weakness nevertheless drives it far from truth’s fullness. It is therefore no wonder if the barrenness of human speech is insufficient to explain the difficulty of things, since even human sense yields under their consideration. Therefore all things are difficult, and a human being cannot explain them in speech: the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing.

“What is that which has been? The very thing which shall be. What is that which has been done? The very thing which is to be done. There is nothing new under the sun; nor can anyone say: ‘Behold, this is recent.’ For it has already gone before in the ages which were before us.”

Perhaps someone may suppose that the error [Col. 0144B] is here confirmed by which pagan philosophers, with astonishing madness, attempted to establish the eternity of time through the revolution of ages and the recurrence of all things to the same state. For they said that the sequence of mutable things had run from eternity in the same order in which it is now seen, and would run without end under the same law, the world in its entirety having neither beginning nor end, through certain ages succeeding one another. They said that the great age consists of fifteen thousand years—an age which they call a “year”—and that, when it has been completed, all stars having been recalled to the places from which each had gone forth at the beginning of the age, and having again begun the movement at the beginning of another age in like manner and mode, and having moved dependent nature in a like manner, [Col. 0144C] exactly all the same things would again arise in the same order in which they had occurred in previous ages, with the same essence, the same form, altogether the same places and times; and would perform a course and destiny similar to and identical with the former one, undergo the same law and experience the same fortune. Thus it would happen that the same persons would be born, would likewise beget the same children, would live with the same fortune, and would die by the same lot; there would be the same outcome of things, precisely the same quality, and the same condition and course of all things that had occupied the past times of the former age.

They asserted that such a revolution and repetition of all things, [Col. 0144D] returning always to the same state, had always existed and would always exist without end; so that, just as through the return of one star all these things are renewed each year to their former state, so through the return of all the stars and of all nature to its source, in each age and great year, all things are restored to their first condition.

How great this error is, clear reason readily proves. For that times cannot be eternal is most evidently demonstrated by this: every time had a beginning; and it is beyond dispute that everything which had a beginning at some time did not exist. Further, every past time was at some point present. But every time which was at some point present, before it was present, did not yet exist. Otherwise, if it had always been present, it would no longer have been time but eternity. Therefore, if every past time at some point did not exist [Col. 0145A], there was a time when no time existed. Thus times could not be eternal; rather, before times there was eternity without time, which times neither increased when they began nor will consume when they end.

It is clear, therefore, that the assertion of those who proclaimed the eternity of ages and declared that the beginning of mutability was without beginning is false. But lest an error of this sort appear to be confirmed in this place when it is said: “There is nothing new under the sun, nor can anyone say, ‘Behold, this is recent.’ For it has already gone before in the ages which were before us,” the following words immediately show in what sense this is to be understood:

“There is no memory of former things; nor indeed shall there be remembrance among those who shall be last of those who are to come afterward” [Col. 0145B].

For if former and last things were altogether identical with present things, [Col. 0145C] he would by no means call present people different from former people and from those who will be last in the future; nor would he say, “among those who shall be after us in the last times,” but “among us, who shall be in the last times.” Unless perhaps someone says that the first and last are to be referred to the beginning and end of the same age; otherwise there can be neither first nor last among things which were without beginning and will be without end. But his statement, “It has already gone before in the ages which were before us,” prevents first and last from being referred to the beginning and end of the same age. For in speaking of some ages as preceding and others as following, he plainly shows that he did not mean the first and last parts of the same age.

Therefore, since this opinion departs not only from Catholic truth but also from reason, let us refer this saying to the similarity of things, which were so established in their kinds from the beginning that each extends its offspring according to the likeness and form of its first origin, and nothing exists that exceeds in its kind the limit of the first ordering. Thus in the elements of the world themselves, and in all things generated or to be generated from them, nature preserves the first ordering, so that under the sun nothing can be found other than the first—that is, different or dissimilar from it. For example: from the beginning heaven has been above and earth below. From the beginning there have been lights in heaven—sun, moon, and stars—birds in the air, fish in the water, beasts on earth. From the beginning birds have flight, fish swimming [Col. 0145D], human beings walking, certain beasts creeping, and serpents crawling and dragging themselves. And all these things are as they were, remain as they are, and continue so.

And if at some time, through some miracle occurring beyond the customary course of nature, they become other than they always are, still they do not wholly become otherwise, nor always become otherwise, so that the first institution, though it may at times seem interrupted, never seems dissolved. Therefore God’s wisdom governs even this apparent confusion. What is confused to us is not confused to him. And therefore there is nothing new under the sun, because what passes temporally has been ordered from eternity by him who is above the sun. Consequently, individual things, because they cannot stand in themselves through immutability, nevertheless preserve stability in their kind [Col. 0146A] through similarity. Thus, although individual things cannot always be what they are, the whole is never found to be other than what the individual things are.

Therefore there is nothing new under the sun. How much more is this true above the sun? For there is nothing new under the sun because above the sun there is eternity. Under sun and moon there is nothing new, yet there is nothing eternal. For nothing under the sun is eternal, because everything under the sun passes away in itself; yet it is not new, because it subsists in the likeness of its kind. Therefore under the sun there is nothing new and nothing eternal. Because it has gone before in the ages which were before us, it is not new; and because there is no memory of things past, it is not eternal. Therefore, because everything that comes passes away and does not remain, and nothing under the sun abides [Col. 0146B], the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor is the ear filled with hearing. For everything that enters slips away and flees while it is thought to be held; and the verdict is fulfilled: “Vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.”

What then? Because under the sun the eye is not satisfied with seeing nor the ear filled with hearing, let it go above the sun, where not only is nothing new but nothing transitory; where there is both memory of former things and presence of future things—indeed, where all past and future things are present, because there is neither past nor future there, where everything that is is present and everything that is, is there. There, then, the eye can be satisfied with seeing and the ear filled with hearing, where consummate and full perfection is perceived, and eternity is not emptied by the fullness which has been perceived.

Thus this whole saying, by which nothing is said to be either new [Col. 0146C] or eternal under the sun, appears directed to this end: that a human being may recognize what ought to be avoided and what pursued. For in the fact that nothing under the sun is new, eternal ordering is shown. But in the fact that nothing under the sun can remain, eternity is signified in the things under the sun, though not shown to exist in them. Therefore in the very things under the sun we recognize together: in that nothing is eternal, that what they are ought to be fled; in that nothing is new, that what they are not ought to be pursued.

Accordingly, let him return to the chief judgment: that in the things under the sun eyes cannot be satisfied and ears cannot be filled, whether by knowledge, because they do not comprehend the whole of what is, or by desire, because even if they comprehend it, the whole of what is does not suffice, nor does what is present remain [Col. 0146D] for as long as it can. Let them know that everything under the sun is vanity, and that a human being can have no further gain from all one’s labor by which one labors under the sun.

Therefore let him say: “All things are difficult” to be comprehended by human sense, since they can neither be numbered in their multitude, nor comprehended in their magnitude, nor investigated in their depth. And therefore it is no wonder if speech fails where understanding yields; and for this reason a human being cannot explain them in speech, so as to give an account of individual things, because one does not know all things. For the eye is not satisfied with seeing when it considers by itself, nor is the ear filled with hearing when it is taught by another, so that either the attention going outward to investigate things may comprehend all that is outside, or the knowledge entering inward may fill all that is within [Col. 0147A]. Therefore eye and ear are not sufficient either for the whole world, so as to grasp it all, or for the whole mind, so as to fill it all.

Yet through what is outward they are admonished to go where life is, where they may find all and grasp all, because “all things were life in him, and the life was the light of human beings” (John 1). Therefore let them go there, where they may at once find all, grasp all, and possess all: where the things that shall be in time have already been made in eternal disposition. For “what is that which has been?” The very same thing, and not another, will be in time which was before times in the eternal disposition of God. Nor is anything mutable unfolded afterward in the order of things other than what was always fixed and permanent [Col. 0147B] in that settled and unchangeable divine disposition.

And so that it may clearly appear that the ensuing effect of things agrees with providence, even in the sequence of things themselves the future does not differ from the past. For “what is that which has been done? The very thing which is to be done.” Therefore, what has always been in providence will at some time be future in actuality; and what has already been done in actuality is still to be done according to likeness. But it seems to me not to be passed over that he did not say, “What is that which shall be?” and then add, “The very thing which has been,” although past things are more certain than future ones, and because, even if they are no longer, they nevertheless at one time were and were seen. Future things, however, have never been.

And therefore it would seem more fitting to put in the question that which is less certain, and in the answer that which is known to be more certain. But it should be noted that, in the order of causation, the effects of things are later than providence; in our knowledge, they are earlier. For until we behold a thing in its actual occurrence, we are wholly ignorant what has been ordained concerning it in eternal providence. Therefore, when he asks, saying, “What is that which has been?”—since providence itself is hidden in itself—he immediately sends his hearers to the actual occurrence of things in order that they may understand it, saying: “The same thing is that which shall be”; because we cannot know what precedes in foreknowledge until we see what follows in the effect of things.

And even in things themselves, we shall infer the character of past events which we have not seen from comparison with future events when they come to pass. Let him therefore say: “What is that which has been? The same thing is that which shall be.” For, as has been said, that which precedes in providence is the very same thing, and not another, which follows in the effect of things. And next: “What is that which has been done? The same thing is that which shall be done.” For the same nature of things, in each kind, has displayed in actuality among past things the same likeness that it will produce among future things when they arrive.

And therefore there is nothing new among the kinds of things under the sun whose likeness has not preceded it. Nor can anyone say, “This is new,” with respect to the likeness of its kind. For it has already preceded in its kind in the ages that were before us, to which it belongs. Yet all things flow onward, and nothing remains under the sun. Things which are fixed in the ordering disposition pass away from both our presence and our memory as they pass away in themselves. For first they are withdrawn from our presence, so that they no longer subsist in appearance; then they are also erased from memory by forgetfulness, so that they do not subsist even in recollection.

And lest perhaps the passing away of former things should not suffice to draw hard human hearts into contempt for visible things, if, once those former things had been removed, those now present could have confidence in their own stability, he therefore, after mentioning the passage of the former things by saying, “There is no remembrance of former things,” immediately shows also the destruction of these present things, saying: “Nor shall there be remembrance of those who shall come after us.” For if others are to come after us, it is certainly evident that we who now subsist, when those who are to come after us have come, shall also perhaps have been removed in the same way, and shall not then come even into the remembrance of the living.

What advantage, then, is it to us that we have succeeded in this life those removed by death, since we too, when our own time comes and we descend, shall leave others as successors? If, then, we wish to know what we shall be like in the eyes of those who are to come after us, let us consider what those long ago removed from this life before us are like now in our eyes. And, that every hope based on present things may be taken away from wicked minds, even those who are to come after us are said not to remain, nor to come into remembrance among their own descendants, lest this too should come as a consolation to perverse minds: that one who cannot endure in himself might at least subsist in his heir or successor.

Therefore he shows one and the same destruction for all things past, present, and future: “There is no remembrance of former things; nor shall there be remembrance of those who shall come after us among those who shall be in the last days”—that he may subject all things to vanity and turn the human mind from love of those things seen under the sun to desire for eternal things.

But if anyone is unwilling to be content with a simple exposition, he has another interpretation which he may fittingly, and perhaps more clearly, understand in these words already expounded. For, having said that neither the eye is satisfied with seeing nor the ear filled with hearing, he immediately adds the reason why sight cannot fill the eye nor hearing the ear: namely, because the appearances of transitory things, arriving through the senses, stir up desire, but swiftly fleeing in their passage defraud desire.

For he adds a statement about this passing away, saying: “What is that which has been?” It is no longer; for it has passed away and now is no more. The same will be true of that which is to come: for it too, when it has come, will pass away; and when it has passed away, it will no longer be. “What is that which has been done?” It too has already passed away and is no longer itself. Therefore the same will be true of that which is to be done; for when it has been done, it too will pass away and will no longer be.

But one may ask why he has mentioned only things past and future, when he intends rather to persuade us to contempt for present things. Yet this very point belongs greatly to contempt for visible things: he chose to number among things only those which the present perception of the flesh alone comprehends, as though he saw that only those things which alone appear to exist are not, so that he cannot even say, “That which is.” What is, while it is, is almost nothing; for the moments of present things flee with such hasty course and swift slipping away that they cannot even wait for the words of those speaking about them.

For though sometimes it may correctly be said, in a qualified sense, by one who asks, “It is,” yet by one who answers it is always more truly said, “It has been, and is no more.” Thus the question itself seeks an answer which is not yet; but the answer, when it comes, does not find the question, which is already no more. In true consideration, therefore, he saw as almost non-existent that alone which appears to exist. For while it begins to be out of that which is not yet, and ceases to be into that which already is not, that which is is almost nothing.

And therefore do not ask, “What is that which is?” For even that which is, by the time of the answerer, however near at hand, has already been and is no more. Rightly, then, it is said: “What is that which has been? The same thing is that which shall be. What is that which has been done? The same thing is that which shall be done.” As though he were saying: From consideration of past things weigh what you ought to expect concerning things that are to come; for both are the same. That which has been and that which shall be; that which has been done and that which shall be done: they are the same, not in essence, but in a similar nature. For that which has been, with respect to things, and that which has been done, with respect to actions, have both passed away. And that which has been done is no more.

Likewise, that which shall be among things and that which shall be done among actions will wholly pass away; and there will be nothing perpetual under the sun. Why is this so? Because the condition and nature of past things and of things to come are the same. For there is nothing new under the sun, nor can anyone say, “Behold, this is new.” For it has already preceded in the ages that were before us. And because their condition is alike, therefore future things are as past things.

And what, do you suppose, are those past things like? Hear what they are like: “There is no remembrance of former things,” he says. Therefore not only has their presence been removed by destruction, but their memory also has been erased by forgetfulness. A great ruin. Such also are the things to come. For “there shall be no remembrance of those who shall come after us among those who shall be in the last days.” And the saying is true: “Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.”

## HOMILY III. How Ecclesiastes proves, by his own works, that all human works are vain, with a recapitulation of what has preceded.

“I, Ecclesiastes, was king over Israel in Jerusalem; and I set my heart to seek and wisely investigate all things that are done under the sun.”

Who is capable of searching out the sayings of the wise and their riddles, drawing forth to taste the sweetness of wisdom hidden within and bringing its beauty into the light? If there should come to us a scribe instructed in the kingdom of heaven, who brings forth from his treasure things new and old (Matt. 13), behold, he is the one to whom God gave wisdom and understanding to open and reveal it, so that men may know that life is in it.

But what are we? Darkness, attempting to comprehend the light; attempting to think upon that which God has hidden from the eyes of men, while revealing the secret of his wisdom to his friends. What are we doing? Shall we then not meditate upon his commandments or investigate his paths? Can our heart rest until it finds wisdom? Let us at least pursue it through these very words; and if perhaps its discovery is delayed, let the inquiry itself meanwhile nourish us above all else. If we cannot teach it as found, let us nevertheless teach it as sought.

Behold, our Ecclesiastes, disputing thus far concerning the vanity of mutable things, has included so much in a brief discourse that in these words of his there appears to us this marvel: how all, from all, has been said in such a way that, for brevity, nothing seems lacking, while for clarity nothing more seems needing to be said. But wisdom accomplished this—wisdom which is wholly in the whole and wholly in each individual thing. It is not contracted by being whole in each thing, nor enlarged by being whole in all; but it is as great in each as in all, and in all such as it is wholly in each, because unity cannot be less than itself, nor infinity greater.

Therefore wisdom itself expressed in this brief body of discourse an image of the whole universe, so that we might see greatness in smallness through the small; for in itself we cannot see the whole. And there we saw the whole world and recognized that truly nothing of all things remains, but that all things under the sun flow and pass away, and that the judgment is true that all is vanity.

Now, therefore, after showing us what the things made with us are like, he proceeds to teach us what we ought to think or expect concerning the things done by us. For if even that which God has made is subject to vanity, there can be no doubt that that which man—who is vanity—does is wholly vain, and much more vain. This, then, he now begins to demonstrate: namely, that all human works done under the sun are vain, and that man has nothing more from all his labor with which he labors under the sun.

And in order to establish his assertion, he puts himself forward as an example of all that he will say, declaring that he has learned and proved by experience the truth of everything he relates. For this reason he presents his own person in such a way that it may not seem incredible that he could have had experience of all these things. Therefore he displays his power and dignity: king over Israel in Jerusalem. He also shows his wisdom: “And I surpassed in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem.” He enumerates riches: houses, vineyards, gardens, orchards, pools, male slaves, female slaves, herds, flocks, gold, and silver. Finally, lest anything be thought lacking, he adds luxury and pleasure: male singers, female singers, and the delights of the children of men. “And,” he says, “whatever my eyes desired I did not deny them, nor did I forbid my heart to enjoy every pleasure in the things I had prepared.”

And he testifies that he ran through every kind of experience of things, and found nothing in all that is done under the sun except vanity, affliction of spirit, and superfluous care. What those things are which are done under the sun has already been said above. But, that the discourse may pass more suitably to what must now be said, we shall briefly and summarily recall what has been said.

For by “sun” we showed that time is signified, because especially by the sun every change and succession of times is distinguished; so that “under the sun” means the same as “under time.” Again, in order that it might appear more clearly what things the author of vanity censured as made under time, we distinguished between things made with time and things made in time. Of the things made in time, again, some are made in time but not under time; others are made in time and under time.

Those made under time are more subject to time and liable to change, because they began in time and will likewise end in time; and therefore they are, as it were, enclosed within time so that they cannot extend in any way toward eternity, because their time both preceded their beginning and follows their end. Yet, lest vanity altogether dominate in these things and truth find no place under the sun where it may lay its head (Matt. 8), we excepted certain things from those made under time. Although we do not remove vanity from them altogether, we nevertheless forbid them to serve vanity.

For among the things done under time, some are done for time and others for eternity. Those done under time for time are vain both in act and in fruit. But those done under time for eternity are in some sense vain in act, yet not in fruit; for although they pass away in the work, they remain in recompense. Accordingly, although things of this kind have not wholly escaped vanity, they nevertheless serve not vanity but truth; nor is what they are altogether vain, because that for which they are is not vanity.

But those things done under time and for time are wholly subject to vanity, because both what is in them is vain and what comes from them is likewise vanity. These are the things presently under discussion, in which, under the sun, those who love transitory things find nothing except vanity and affliction of spirit, whether while they are being done or after they have been done.

## HOMILY IV. On the vanity of things and the worst occupation of human beings.

[Col. 0151D]

Yet even in these things vanity itself rises, as it were, by certain steps toward increase; and corruption, growing from something small, gradually increases and always advances toward worse. For among them the first origin of vanity is curiosity; then comes covetousness; and finally pleasure. Of these, the first belongs to the lust of the eyes; the second to worldly ambition; the third to the lust of the flesh.

Through these vanities the human mind, flowing away from the highest truth, is cast down so far that, at last oppressed by carnal desires and wholly bound by the enticements of pleasures, it is unable not only to remember its origin by itself but, even when admonished, is unable to will either that what is wrongly so should not be, or that what is wrongly not so should be. For what is, is wrongly so; and what ought to be is wrongly not so. And what it wills—either that what is should not be, or that what is not should be—is worse in both respects.

Our Ecclesiastes, then, begins here to demonstrate by his own example how the human mind falls from the highest truth into vanity through these stages of error, and how, driven onward by its own fault, it always proceeds toward worse. For its true good ought to have been to cling to truth and to love truth itself for its own sake. Therefore, when it abandons truth and turns away from it in the aversion of its mind, it first suffers this punishment for its rejection: that it begins to seek for vanity the truth which it refused to love in itself and for itself.

And because it has ceased to contemplate that one thing in which it saw all things, now desiring novelty rather than truth, it longs to know many things. Since it has lost that inward contemplation in which lies the true refreshment of the mind, it hungrily seeks, as though for food of understanding, knowledge of things outside itself. But because complete knowledge of truth can in no way be found in all the things that outwardly appear, the wretched sufferer begins, sick with the misery of his deficiency, as though from a certain weariness, always to run from one thing to another in desire. Rejecting former things as empty and barren, he hopes that he may attain the fulfillment of his desire in those that remain.

He is so foolish and blind that, although he sees himself always frustrated in these things and never reaching the end of his desire, he nevertheless never ceases to pursue them as vain and unfruitful. Yet a just punishment follows this shameless desire and foolish curiosity, by which he vainly stretches himself out in the knowledge of visible things while either neglecting knowledge of his Creator—in which alone true blessedness consists—though he possesses it, or pretending not to seek it though he does not possess it. For in the very place where he perversely seeks delight, he finds nothing but pain and affliction of spirit.

For finding in such great occupation a difficulty exceeding his strength, he is oppressed, as it were, by the weight of his own anxiety. While desire drives him to seek a wisdom of this kind where it cannot be found, he is at once scattered by its multitude and beaten back by its depth. This, then, is the labor and affliction of spirit by which the foolish and shameless mind is deservedly worn down for its presumption, while, forgetting not only its Creator but also neglecting itself, it is occupied in investigating lowly things that do not pertain to salvation.

Yet knowledge sought through such vanity and discovered, however slightly, by such great toil sometimes inflates the mind through pride and hurls it headlong from curiosity into self-exaltation, as from vanity into vanity. This self-exaltation, bringing in worldly ambition, makes it desirous of praise and inflames the mind with love of display and glory in riches, so that, as it slips from glory in an inward good to the pursuit of outward glory, it is always cast down into a worse vanity.

Nor can the corruption once begun stop even here. For the goods of the flesh, just as formerly, while they are not possessed, flatter desire by their appearance in order that they may be sought, so afterward, when possessed, they entice the weakened, enervated, and softened person by their use into pleasure. Thus the wretched mind, after love of vain praise and after the ardor of still vainer covetousness, is inflamed toward the final desire for pleasure, so that it begins even to sow vanity in the flesh and, after becoming flesh from the flesh, reaps the fruit of vanity in corruption.

For this is the fruit of vanity: that the wretched mind, at last overwhelmed by carnal desires and lulled by the pleasure of carnal desires, falls so deeply asleep that it now seeks wisdom not only without truth but not even in appearance. The more eagerly it pours out its whole self into experiencing the wrongly sweet pleasure of the flesh, the more it has been inwardly wearied and repelled from the effort of its inquiry, and therefore despairs of finding truth.

And because, in stretching above itself by inquiry, it sees that it has succumbed to excessive labor and difficulty, it abandons itself with all eagerness to another consolation, one which can be had without labor. Yet, finding vanity there also, it is not allowed to rest; for in the pleasure of the flesh it can neither retain delight while it is present and fleeting, nor call it back after it has passed away.

Thus, wearied and scattered on every side, it is shaken by the storm of its own vanity, so that through the very thing by which it went astray in wrongful delight it may at last, salutarily afflicted, be compelled to return. And there is often a grievous struggle in the mind: while it sees itself both delighting in low things and suffering through them, it longs greatly, from love of freedom, to abandon even what it loves, if that can be done.

Ecclesiastes will therefore set forth in the following words this struggle and tumult of the human mind through the various pursuits of mortal life, taking upon himself in a single judgment the case of all. He will show how it falls from the vanity of curiosity to the vanity of display and ambition, and then to the vanity of pleasure, as is demonstrated in the sequence and order of the book. But since we have completed what was to be said in the preface, let us now return to explaining the words of his discourse.

## HOMILY V. A literal and moral exposition of the words spoken by Ecclesiastes.

[Col. 0153D]

“I, Ecclesiastes, was king over Israel in Jerusalem.”

First, it seems to me by no means to be passed over that some believe Solomon wrote this book in repentance, and that for this reason he so earnestly censures in it the vanity of worldly things, and especially of carnal pleasure: because he himself learned all these things by experience, corrupted by luxurious indulgence and led astray by the blandishments of women. And they say that this is why he did not wish to say, “I am king over Israel in Jerusalem”: because, having laid aside the purple of kingship, he had now descended from his throne and, despising the power which he had held wrongly, was lamenting his guilt in the garb of penitence; and therefore he said that he “was” king in Jerusalem.

Would that this could be established as true, and that we had testimony concerning his repentance as certain as the evidence of his guilt is undoubted! But now, because we cannot affirm doubtful things as certain, let us pursue those matters which are not doubtful.

“I, Ecclesiastes.” As we have said, he presents himself as an example of all that he will say, so that hearers may more readily trust his words because they understand that he learned by experience, not merely by hearing, what he teaches. As though he said: “I who teach you have experienced all that I say.” For who could have known better what vanity there is at the summit of earthly power? “For I was king over Israel in Jerusalem.” It is great eminence indeed to reign over so great a people and in so noble and famous a city, to see oneself on a royal throne, set above all in power as lord and in honor.

And to what end is this? “I was,” he says—as though saying: “I am no longer,” because even if I am, I now recognize that this very thing which I am is nothing. And he next explains how he came to recognize himself as nothing, saying:

“I set my heart to seek and wisely investigate all things that are done under the sun.”

As though he said: “Outwardly swollen with power and inwardly puffed up with knowledge, I attempted to seek things higher than myself. But where I vainly swelled in presumption above myself, there by failing I truly recognized my own proper direction.”

“I set my heart to seek and wisely investigate all things that are done under the sun.” A great purpose, if it could have come to fulfillment; but how could the human mind suffice for such things? It is therefore great pride for a mortal human being to presume concerning so many things, and again great curiosity to desire so many things.

“I set,” he says. See how everything sounds of self-exaltation. He does not say, “I thought,” but “I set,” as though the thought would at least have been pardonable, and the human temptation, if a swollen thought had touched his soul suddenly and fleetingly, as sometimes happens, had not nevertheless been received or approved by consent. But now the mind, not only exalted but also blind, fell into so deep an abyss of error that it not only thought of doing what was disordered, but presumed itself capable of accomplishing what was impossible.

“I set my heart.” An immense undertaking. And what was it? “To seek and investigate”: to seek unknown things and investigate profound things. How? “Wisely.” O foolish heart! Therefore you do not seek wisdom, but only profess that you seek through wisdom. For this is what you said: “I set my heart to seek and wisely investigate all things that are done under the sun.” If, therefore, you seek wisely, you seek through wisdom. And you say: “Certainly so: I shall seek through wisdom. For I would seek badly if I did not seek through wisdom. If I sought without wisdom, even if I sought wisdom, I would seek foolishly. But to seek wisdom foolishly would no longer itself be wisdom, but folly. Therefore I shall seek wisely, and I shall seek through wisdom, and I shall seek wisdom.”

Tell me then: where will you seek the wisdom through which you will seek? And through what wisdom will you seek wisdom? “Through that by which you seek?” “I already have,” he says, “the wisdom through which I shall seek; and therefore I shall seek through the wisdom which I have. I shall not seek the wisdom through which I shall seek.”

What will you seek? “Concerning all things that are done under the sun.” What does “concerning all things” mean? Why did you not say, “All things done under the sun”? “Because,” he says, “I have set before myself something greater—much greater. For all things done under the sun are visible; and therefore, although it is great, it is not the greatest thing to seek and investigate things that can be apprehended by the eye. Therefore I shall not seek those things, but I shall seek concerning them: to seek and investigate concerning all things done under the sun. Not the things which are seen, but from the things that are seen, the things which are not seen. Not the things done under the sun which are visible, but, from the things done under the sun, their reasons and causes, which are invisible.”

“This, therefore, I set before myself: to seek and wisely investigate concerning all things done under the sun.” You certainly possess great wisdom. Who gave you such great wisdom? You are a human being, and you will wisely seek concerning all things done under the sun? Where did you get such wisdom? “God gave it,” you say. Let us now see. For you shall not pass by without examination. We first wish to know whether you can give an account even of yourself, you who have come with so great a purpose that you believe you can investigate the reason of all things done under the sun.

Speak, then: in that wisdom through which you propose to investigate the reason of all things, could you at least recognize your own capability? “Unless I hoped that I could bring the matter itself to completion,” he says, “I would by no means set myself to do what I believed entirely impossible, even if I thought about doing it.” O foolish heart! This is what I said: because you did not know yourself, you presumed to desire what was above you—blind in one respect, swollen in another, foolish in both.

You, then, will wisely investigate all things done under the sun. Investigate now; exert yourself; apply effort. Seek, and you shall find. What shall you find? You shall find wisdom. What wisdom? That you may know your own folly. For you will seek and not find what you seek; you will labor and not advance; and affliction alone will give understanding to the ear.

“For God has given the children of men this worst occupation, that they may be stretched out [or: occupied] in it.” Rightly and justly: because they refused to stand in truth, they may be divided through multiplicity, stretched out, and occupied in vanity. Therefore, he says, “I saw all things that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit.” Thanks be to God! Now you have begun for the first time to be wise. Now I see that you have wisdom through which you can seek and wisely investigate all things done under the sun. For you have found wisely and understood wisely that all is vanity and affliction of spirit.

Yet I would like to know whence came this repentance so sudden. We expected something great; and that grand purpose had made us all attentive and expectant. For who could have thought that something slight could issue from so great a promise: “To seek and wisely investigate all things done under the sun”? And afterward: “God has given the children of men this worst occupation, that they may be stretched out in it.”

What occupation do you mean? “This,” you say: “that they set their heart to seek and wisely investigate all things done under the sun.” Why then do you call this a worst occupation—to seek and wisely investigate all things done under the sun? Remove, he says, the word “wisely.” For it would not be a worst occupation wisely to seek and investigate concerning all things done under the sun. But who can do this? To investigate the causes of all things and comprehend the account of everything done under the sun exceeds human understanding.

Therefore one may propose to seek and investigate wisely concerning all things done under the sun, but one cannot accomplish it. For many things lie hidden; very many are concealed; and all things are reserved for the future. What is not permitted to be accomplished ought not to be investigated. Therefore what cannot wisely be done cannot wisely be proposed, even if it is proposed to be done wisely.

“I therefore foolishly proposed what I could not wisely do: to seek and investigate concerning all things done under the sun. Foolish in both ways: both when I proposed what I could not do, and when I did what I ought not to have done; and a third folly was added, that I was ignorant of both. Yet I sought and investigated what I had proposed to seek and investigate. I sought, and did not find what I sought. But I found something: namely, that I could not do what I believed I could; and there I recognized that God gave the children of men this worst occupation, that they might be stretched out in it.”

Thus it was useful that I had been foolish; yet folly was not wisdom. Folly was nevertheless given in order to instruct the children of men unto wisdom. They were left to themselves so that they might know themselves; and, knowing themselves, condemn and flee what they have made themselves to be.

“For God has given the children of men this worst occupation, that they may be stretched out in it.” Since the human mind refused to stand in that one good in which it could rest happily and, without distraction or occupation, possess the fullness of highest truth, it is cast out from itself and scattered into the multiplicity of visible things. The truth which, blinded within, it cannot draw from the fountain, it at least attempts to pursue, as though through certain channels of visible things, with a heart growing dry.

But the more it pours itself outward by attention to visible things, the more it is inwardly darkened from knowledge of invisible things; for the more it is scattered among outward things, the more, turned away from inward things, it is blinded. Hence Cain, when he saw his crime discovered and, reprobate through a greater crime, despaired of forgiveness for his sin, is rightly read to have said to the Lord: “Behold, you shall cast me out this day from the face of the earth, and I shall be hidden from your face; and I shall be a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth” (Gen. 4).

For the reprobate mind, cast out from the face of the Lord, is hidden when, scattering itself among outward things, it is covered all the more from the sight of inward light as it remains continually occupied in thinking upon things outside. Hence it is rightly said there: “A wanderer and fugitive.” It is a wanderer through disordered desire, and a fugitive through a sinful conscience: while it divides itself in desire through thought and turns away in conscience through despair, it, a sinner, hides from itself the light of truth so that it cannot return to itself.

Therefore God has given the children of men this worst occupation, that they may be stretched out in it. Why did he give it, that they might be stretched out in it? That they may extend and be stretched out, labor and fail, return, and that he may heal them. For if they were not stretched out or did not labor in their occupation, the occupation itself would become too sweet, and they would not wish to abandon it or return any longer; they would desire the place where truth is.

Therefore God gave them the worst occupation, that they might be stretched out in it. Let us give thanks to his mercy because he made us labor in our evil, in our turning away; because he hedged our way with thorns, so that we may return and turn back to himself, the husband, bridegroom, and friend of our soul; because it was better for us then than it is now. But we did not understand this and thought that we were well when we were badly.

Therefore he sprinkled bitterness, wormwood, and gall into the cup offered to our wrongly sweet, death-flattering turning away and worst occupation. And he gave this worst occupation to the children of men, that they might be stretched out in it. For occupation is the distraction and binding of minds which turns away, scatters, and ensnares souls so that they cannot prevail to think upon things pertaining to salvation; and therefore it is occupation.

Why is it “worst”? Because there is another evil occupation, but not the worst: namely, that which concerns the necessities of mortal life and is anxious about many things. That too is an evil occupation; indeed, to say something further, it is itself “evil,” so that the saying may rightly be understood of it: “Sufficient for the day is its own evil” (Matt. 6). This occupation is necessary to the misery of mortal life and is afterward to be swallowed up by the glory of immortal life. Therefore it is evil with respect to misery, but not evil with respect to guilt; for although it has a punishment alien from blessedness, it does not possess guilt contrary to justice and truth.

But the occupation of curiosity, by which the mind extends itself toward forbidden things and presses on to scrutinize and investigate what either does not befit it to know or is harmful for it to know—this is the worst occupation. For while the mind stretches itself beyond measure, it either gains its object and inflates the soul through empty knowledge, or, if it cannot grasp it, wears the soul out through delay and despair.

## HOMILY VI. What it is to be stretched out in the worst occupation.

[Col. 0157D] Therefore God gave this most grievous preoccupation to the children of men, that they might be stretched out in it. What does “that they might be stretched out” mean? That outwardly they may swell, inwardly become empty. For what is stretched appears indeed larger externally; but precisely from that from which it is seen to have received external increase, it is truly proved to have lost internal solidity. For while it strives to extend beyond itself into that which it is not, it begins to fail within itself and to be emptied of that which it is. Thus indeed, while the human mind is stretched by curiosity toward investigating things outside itself, it is hindered by the very preoccupation of its inquiry from being able to consider itself.

Therefore God gave this most grievous preoccupation to the children of men, that they might be stretched out in it. O most grievous [Col. 0158A] preoccupation! O destructive stretching-out! Where do you draw the mind? How much do you promise, and how much do you take away? You promise a person all that he is not, and take away all that he is. What if you gave all that you promise and took all that you take away? For what does it profit a person if he gains the whole world but suffers loss to his soul? (Matt. VI.) How much more so now, since you deceitfully promise everything and truly take everything away? You are most grievous, stretching and scattering, afflicting and tormenting minds: ever suggesting to those whom you rule objects which they must desire, though their investigation is either harmful or vain, and their discovery much more either useless or destructive.

If, then, you were sweet and could possess minds without effort, who would ever detect your evil? But now [Col. 0158B] the very toil and affliction which you inflict upon minds make you hateful; and what you promise is more readily recognized as vain while what you bring is felt to be harsh. Thus you instruct many unto wisdom, who only then fully perceive how great a vanity follows after you, when through experience they begin to feel how much difficulty lies hidden in you for those who labour.

Therefore he added and said: “I saw all things that are done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit” (Eccles. I). “I saw,” he says—but where did you see? Who taught you? “By doing,” he says, “I saw; by experience I knew.” What did you do? “I set,” he says, “in my mind to seek and investigate wisely concerning all things that are done under the sun” (ibid.). And behold, I had begun to seek and investigate, and I supposed that in such laborious study I would find some conclusion. Therefore I stretched [Col. 0158C] my mind as far as I could; I spread my thought abroad to survey all things. I took sleep from my eyes and gave no rest to my heart by night or day, until I found what my soul sought: until I found an explanation for all things done under the sun.

But what end could there have been in such great efforts? I acted and failed; I strove and was driven back, until my soul wasted away and my faculties were darkened. For amid such a multitude of things and such depth of hidden truth, while my understanding began both to scatter and to be beaten back, I could no longer sustain the burden of toil and the straitness of an inextricable struggle. Then, returning into myself and as though repulsed by that dense and immeasurable, trackless region of hidden nature against which I had tried to struggle, I began to think it foolish [Col. 0158D] and vain for a mortal man to seek with such persistent effort knowledge of those things which not only lie outside his nature, but can add nothing to his salvation if known, nor take anything away from it if unknown.

There, therefore, I saw that God gave this most grievous preoccupation to the children of men, that they might be stretched out in it; because all things done under the sun are altogether vanity and affliction of spirit. For since they bear no fruit, they are vain; and since they afflict, they are harmful. They do not help those who possess them, but they afflict those who seek them. For they cannot be sought without toil, yet they can be possessed without benefit. As soon as the mind is occupied by care and desire for seeking and finding such things, and has spread itself abroad in them through the pursuit of curiosity [Col. 0159A] and the anxiety of desire, it is rightly afflicted as the penalty of its rashness: it is scattered by multiplicity and beaten back by difficulty.

“I saw, therefore, all things done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit.” I saw also that this very purpose which I had set in my mind—to seek and investigate wisely concerning all things done under the sun—was vain. I saw that it is vain for the children of men to be occupied with the most grievous preoccupation, that they may be stretched out in it. And I saw all this when I had experienced it: I saw how great was the toil and affliction of spirit in that purpose which I had set in my mind, to seek and investigate wisely concerning all things done under the sun. And I saw that all things done under the sun are vanity and affliction of spirit. These things, then, I saw.

But why do not all the children of men likewise [Col. 0159B] see the most grievous preoccupation which God gave them, that they might be stretched out in it, so as to understand and see vanity and affliction of spirit in all things done under the sun? Why do they labour without perceiving it, are afflicted and scattered, are stretched out in the most grievous preoccupation, and do not understand their vanity and affliction of spirit in all things done under the sun? “Because,” he says, “the perverse are corrected with difficulty.” Let us speak of this more fully.

## HOMILY VII. That the Perverse Are Corrected with Difficulty, etc.

“The perverse are corrected with difficulty.” Therefore they cannot understand, because they are perverse; and so they labour without perceiving, delight in their own affliction (Job [Col. 0159C] XXX), and think themselves well when they are ill. For they are so perverse that the judgment of truth is not in them: they think evil good and call good evil; they make darkness light and light darkness; they judge bitter to be sweet and sweet bitter (Isa. V). They reckon that delights consist in sensual experience; and therefore they love their pains, willingly cast themselves into the most grievous preoccupation, and are stretched out in it. For while with blinded mind they seek what falsely seems delightful, they do not heed what truly torments and afflicts them.

Therefore they do not see their vanity and affliction of spirit in all things done under the sun, because they are perverse and are corrected with difficulty. “And the number of fools is infinite.” For they are not only turned away, but [Col. 0159D] also perverse: turned away from God, perverse within themselves. And those turned away are not easily converted, because the perverse are corrected with difficulty. For if they were corrected within themselves, they would be converted through themselves. If they first received within themselves the judgment of truth, they would afterward see by their own judgment that vanity must be fled and truth followed. But now, being turned away, they neither see the light of truth; nor, being perverse, do they see by the light of truth. Therefore they are corrected with difficulty, because they know neither how to seek rectitude and truth when absent nor to approve them when present.

Thus the perverse are corrected with difficulty, and the number of fools is infinite. For there would not be so many if they could easily be corrected. And in this the difficulty of correcting the perverse is plainly shown: that [Col. 0160A] the multitude of fools is infinite. Thus the perverse and foolish are as difficult to correct through perversity as they are bold against truth through their multitude; and therefore the perverse are corrected with difficulty, and the number of fools is infinite.

“Do you wish,” he says, “to know how difficult it is to correct the perverse? Take me as your example. Today I shall become an example to you all. For I too was once perverse and did not myself understand my perversity; yet I thought myself upright and acting rightly when I set in my mind to seek and investigate wisely concerning all things done under the sun. At that time there was no consideration of truth in me to correct and restrain me, lest I should attempt to exceed my measure or presume to seek and investigate things not given to men to know.

“Therefore I descended into the [Col. 0160B] most grievous preoccupation which God gave the children of men, that they might be stretched out in it. I scattered my mind into everything and began in thought to range through all things, seeking and investigating concerning all things done under the sun; but I could not prevail. I began to labour and be grievously afflicted with weariness; and I saw that wherever my mind turned, it was filled with pain, bitterness, and anxiety. The toil of seeking was boundless, and the fruit of discovery slight. Thus it happened that at last the punishment itself and great affliction made me prudent. And I saw all things done under the sun, and behold, all is vanity and affliction of spirit. Therefore I knew truth and rejected vanity, because I felt affliction.

“And I seemed now to be wholly corrected from my perversity; but there was still another entanglement [Col. 0160C], and I did not know that the perverse are corrected with difficulty. I was then corrected enough to recognize truth concerning vanity, but not yet corrected so as not to be proud of my knowledge of truth. One chaff of error had already been shaken off, but another, more tenacious and clinging chaff of self-exaltation remained. For the perverse are corrected with such difficulty that they either do not admit correction and cleansing at all, or do not receive them perfectly. Therefore I had begun to be corrected, but was not yet perfectly corrected; and so I knew the toil of my presumption, but did not know the proper use of my discovery. I knew that it was a vain affliction, unprofitable for salvation, to seek; but I did not yet know that it was vain self-exaltation [Col. 0160D] to be proud of discoveries.

“Therefore I spoke in my heart, saying: ‘Behold, I have become great.’ For I did not know that I had swelled with pride, and therefore I seemed great to myself and said in my heart: ‘Behold, I have become great.’ I spoke in my heart: for I swelled from my heart, and therefore spoke in my heart, because in my heart I saw that from which I had swelled, so that self-exaltation might be there where the cause of self-exaltation was. I spoke in my heart: ‘Behold, I have become great.’ How great?

“I have surpassed,” he says, “in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem.” One proceeds gradually into corruption, and the perverse mind, as its swelling grows, is always hurled toward worse things. First it judged of itself more highly than it ought; then it came even to contempt for others [Col. 0161A]. “I have surpassed in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem.”

Therefore you swelled and were puffed up because you had surpassed in wisdom all who were before you in Jerusalem. And how great a matter was this, that you should raise your neck because you had surpassed in wisdom all who were before you in Jerusalem? “Do not wonder,” he says. “Pride often delights more in being singular than in comparison. For self-exaltation does not always care to consider what sort of people those are whom it surpasses by comparison; because sometimes this alone is sufficient for its exaltation—that among all who were before it in Jerusalem, it recognizes none as its equal.

“For this reason, therefore, when I saw that I had surpassed in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem [Col. 0161B], although I saw that only a few wise men had preceded me in Jerusalem, I nevertheless gloried greatly, considering myself their superior in wisdom. For although those whom I surpassed by comparison were neither very numerous nor great, I yet saw that many wise men could come after me in Jerusalem, among whom I might stand as the foremost example of wisdom. Thus, when I preferred myself in wisdom by comparison with my predecessors, this too was involved: I gloried that I would be established as a pre-eminent example for the authority of those to come, so that I might be found the highest among those before me and the first teacher of wisdom among those after me. Therefore I spoke in my heart, saying: ‘Behold, I have become great and have surpassed in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem.’

“And my mind considered many things wisely [Col. 0161C] and learned.” Therefore you were now corrected somewhat, because you did not say, “My mind considered all things wisely,” as you had earlier proposed to seek and investigate wisely concerning all things done under the sun; but you introduced a more moderate statement, saying, “My mind considered many things wisely,” to show that you had been instructed by the most grievous preoccupation and had seen vanity and affliction of spirit, so that you would no longer presume concerning everything—though you were not yet fully corrected, so as not to be proud concerning very many things.

Thus, in seeking everything, you found very many things, not all things; and in failing with regard to everything, you understood that a person ought not to presume concerning everything. But in discovering very many things, you did not consider that a person ought not even to be proud concerning very many things. Therefore you were corrected in one respect and uncorrected in another when you said, “My mind considered many things wisely and learned.” For although they were many in relation to few, those many were nevertheless few in relation to all things. It would have been more fitting for humility that you, who had already experienced your failure concerning everything, should call your numerous discoveries not “many” in comparison with another person’s many discoveries, but rather “few” in relation to all that you could not attain.

But because the rashness of curiosity had already been repressed by its failure and affliction in investigating everything, while the swelling of self-exaltation had grown in considering very many things, you still swelled and said: “Behold, I have become great; I have surpassed in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem; and my mind considered many things wisely [Col. 0162A] and learned.” But I ask you: if you surpassed in wisdom all who were before you in Jerusalem, from whom did you learn, that you should say, “My mind considered many things wisely and learned”? If you were wiser than all, from whom could you learn what you yourself did not know?

Or were you also wiser than all because you learned from all, and all their wisdom was gathered into you alone, so that you surpassed each of them in wisdom concerning all things, since you had every one of them as teachers by learning from each individually? Or perhaps you did not learn from human beings, but the experiences of things taught you what your mind wisely considered, so that your contemplation of wisdom might become more certain in reasoning because the actual result of things clearly confirmed it to one who had experienced it. For it does not seem to suit your character [Col. 0162B] that you should learn from human beings, you who had raised yourself so far above human beings in your own estimation that you supposed you could seek and investigate not merely many things wisely, but all things done under the sun.

Therefore you contemplated and learned because you reflected and tested, in order to display the greater force and power of your intelligence by bringing every argument of your reason more clearly to the visible tests of things. And perhaps this man voluntarily became foolish in his wisdom in order to teach wisdom to fools. For he would not explain to us the paths of his error so carefully unless, even in that error, he had our instruction in mind. Therefore he still repeats and commends that bad diligence of his, and adds how he acquired the wisdom in which he swelled, saying:
