[Col. 0162C] “I gave my heart to know prudence and instruction, errors and folly.” These words can be connected in two ways with the preceding statements, under the same meaning. For, because he had begun thus in order first to reveal this self-exaltation—“I spoke in my heart”—and then added what he had spoken—“Behold, I have become great, and have surpassed in wisdom all who were before me in Jerusalem; and my mind considered many things wisely and learned”—he afterward introduced what we have now set forth: “I gave my heart to know prudence and instruction, errors and folly.”

The whole sequence may be understood as one continuation: that he said all this in his heart—namely, that he had become great; that [Col. 0162D] he had surpassed in wisdom all who had been before him in Jerusalem; that his mind had considered many things wisely and had learned many things; and that he had given his heart to know prudence and instruction, errors and folly. And after all these things, when he had thus spoken in his heart and exalted himself over the investigation and consideration of such great matters, he at last came to his senses, recognized that this boasting too was vain, and therefore added:

“And I recognized that in these things also there was vanity and affliction of spirit, because in much wisdom there is much vexation; and he who adds knowledge adds toil.”

But if someone wishes to divide the sentence, and separate the last statement we have introduced from the foregoing, [Col. 0163A] he may connect it with the preceding words as follows: as though he had spoken in his heart all the things stated above—namely, that he had become great, that he had surpassed in wisdom all who had been before him in Jerusalem, and that his mind had considered many things wisely and learned. Having said all these things in his heart, he then testifies that still higher matters remained to be investigated, as though saying: “I spoke in my heart all the things said above; and when I had spoken all these things in my heart, then at last, drawing confidence from my prior contemplation, I gave my heart to seek still higher things and investigate deeper things: namely, to know prudence and instruction, errors and folly.”

When he says that he gave his heart, this should be understood to mean that he made it free and unencumbered [Col. 0163B], so that it would not be divided by this thing or that, but would devote itself wholly to the proposed consideration. In this phrase he also expresses the pattern of pride and swelling of self-exaltation: he says that he gave his heart to the contemplation of wisdom, as though the ability to discover truth were immediately available to him if only the will to seek were not lacking.

He explains what he gave his heart for, saying: “To know prudence and instruction, errors and folly.” Above he testified that his mind had wisely contemplated and learned many things; now, after all these things, he determines to investigate so that he may know prudence and instruction, errors and folly. Hence it is clear that the earlier matters are to be referred to the nature of things, while those he now adds concern human conduct. He followed an inverted order: for one’s own life ought first to have been corrected through watchfulness regarding conduct; only afterward ought study to have been applied to other things lying outside one’s own nature, so that first the inner eyes of the heart might be cleansed from vices, and then opened for the contemplation of truth.

But self-exaltation, desiring to appear great outwardly, first sought external things [Col. 0163C], so that it might first open a way for boasting through external knowledge, and afterward cast its own interior things outward for display by searching them also. Hence, when he had rightly said that he sought prudence, he joined instruction with it; because a mind desirous of glory and display did not desire prudence of watchfulness in order to live well, but in order to teach. Therefore it judged knowledge of prudence without knowledge of instruction to be useless and fruitless [Col. 0163D] for itself.

And when he confesses that he wished to know errors and folly also, he did not wish to know evils in order to avoid them once known; rather, he sought both to exalt himself through knowledge of evils and to condemn others for their conduct. Error occurs when evil is committed through ignorance; folly, when known evil is not avoided. Thus he wished to know both good and evil alike, and with knowledge of both he simultaneously desired instruction, so that everything which the mind grasped through knowledge it might be able to make manifest for display through teaching.

But the perverse mind, finding everywhere the punishment of its own wickedness, flees everything which it disorderly sought through self-exaltation, because of toil and affliction of spirit. [Col. 0164A] For since curiosity drove him toward inquiry and pride alike toward display, it was fitting that toil should oppress the swollen man and preoccupation scatter the curious man, so that at least through punishment he might recognize his vice; and, if not love of virtue, then the pain of affliction might restrain him within measure.

Therefore above the curious man found preoccupation; here the proud man finds toil and affliction. For while he seeks to know evil and good not for edification but for self-exaltation, knowledge itself becomes testimony to his perversity, so that it may accuse through conscience the very unjust person who sought it proudly for display. For from that source through which he strives to become great in the eyes of others [Col. 0164B], he is compelled to despise himself; because while he seeks to know more in order to impart something of truth to others, he sees more in himself of perversity to condemn.

Thus the mind is angry with itself and enters into a kind of quarrel and conflict against itself, because perversity defends the foulness of vices which pride despises. In such conflict there arises great toil and vexation of pride: for while it disdains to lie subject to vices and strives to drive them away from itself, it is overcome by its perverse desires and cannot accomplish what it wills. From this point it begins even to abhor knowledge of truth itself, so that, since through weakness it cannot remove what it hates in itself, it may at least avoid seeing it through ignorance.

Therefore, after saying that he had found toil and affliction in his knowledge, and explaining whence that affliction and toil arose—“because [Col. 0164C] in much wisdom there is much vexation, and he who adds knowledge adds toil”—he immediately adds how, worn down and wearied by the same affliction of spirit, toil, and vexation, he abandoned knowledge itself and turned his mind from inquiry into wisdom, where he was afflicted, toward pleasures and delight:

## HOMILY VIII. That Man Flees from Truth: as Adam Fled in Paradise and Hid Himself.

(ECCLES. II.) “I said in my heart: I will go and abound in delights and enjoy good things.” Behold how a despairing mind throws itself wholly into pleasure, and now calls the blandishments of the flesh alone “good things,” because it finds no toil and affliction in them—as though it judged evil the inquiry into truth in which it had first laboured by stretching itself beyond measure through curiosity.

But this judgment in turn, as though it judged [Col. 0164D] evil the inquiry into truth in which it had first laboured by stretching itself beyond measure through curiosity, because it presents manifest folly, is more quickly detected; for the pleasure of the flesh, which seemed sweet to the one desiring it, is immediately rejected by the one who has experienced it. Hence he immediately adds:

“And I saw that this also was vanity. I judged laughter to be error, and I said to joy: ‘Why are you deceived in vain?’” I remember having said above how great vanity lies in the delights of the flesh. Therefore the remaining words that follow must be considered, because, though they appear plain in themselves, they may nevertheless contain something which careful investigation can add.

He says, then: “I judged laughter to be error, and I said to joy: ‘Why are you deceived in vain?’” [Col. 0165A] It is clear to everyone that, through laughter, inwardly conceived joy is in some manner drawn forth; and what lay hidden within in joy is disclosed, as though the barriers of modesty had been broken, by a certain frivolity and incontinence of the unstable mind. Therefore laughter is rightly called error: when the mind pours its joy outward through foolish merriment, it leaves the straight path by which it ought to proceed, rejoicing in God, as though going to the left.

But it must be known that spiritual joy does not dissolve the mind into laughter. Rather, only the joy conceived from the blandishment of the flesh is readily expressed through bodily movement. For since, first entering the mind, disordered joy broke the barriers of self-restraint, it afterward easily bursts forth without modesty by the same way it entered, when it has begun to grow within. The unstable mind pours forth, as though giving birth without chastity, the perverse seed which it first conceived without modesty; nor can it restrain itself from expelling the joy growing within, when the barriers of its integrity were broken at the time it conceived it.

Therefore it is first deceived when it receives inwardly, unto joy, the enticements of the flattering world; afterward it errs when it pours outward through laughter, unto the world’s wantonness, the joy conceived within. Observe that joy alone is reproved, but laughter is utterly rejected. For laughter is wholly evil; joy is not always evil, except when it is of evil. Therefore he rejects the latter and corrects the former, so that what is altogether evil may be avoided, and what can be good may be corrected. [Col. 0165C] Thus, he says: “I judged laughter to be error, and I said to joy: ‘Why are you deceived in vain?’”

Joy is deceived, then, when it delights in harmful things and thinks itself well when it is ill. It is also deceived when it is entangled in the preoccupation of present pleasures and thereby hindered from being able to consider future evils.

But why “in vain”? It is deceived in vain because worldly pleasures can indeed turn the heart away from considering future evils, but cannot free it from the pressure of evils that come upon it. It is also deceived in vain because the joys of deceptive good in which it exults are mingled with such great bitterness that they ought rightly to displease, even if they were to endure. Thus it is deceived in vain in both respects: both when it does not see the evil it suffers, and when it does not foresee the evil [Col. 0165D] it will suffer. For both manifest reason is present, capable of judging the former for one who considers it well, and present experience, capable of showing the latter to one who suffers it. Therefore he adds and says:

I therefore considered in my heart how to withdraw my flesh from wine, so that I might turn my mind toward wisdom and avoid folly, until I should see what is useful for the children of men—what ought to be done under the sun during the number of the days of their life.

O human heart, where are you? How have you come to this, that you do not know what is useful for the children of men—what ought to be done under the sun during the number of the days of their life? Where are you, that you are ignorant of this? Where are you, Adam—where are you? “I heard thy voice,” he says, “and I hid myself” (Gen. III). O hidden one, from whom did you hide yourself? O [Col. 0166A] hidden one, where are you? How far away you are, and how near! How far you are from him, and how near you are to him! Therefore: where are you? Behold, your God seeks you and cries: “Where are you?” You turn aside in order to hide; you close your eyes lest you see. But he sees you when you do not see, and indeed sees you as not seeing, because you do not wish to be seen. On account of your disposition, not any deficiency in himself, he cries and says: “Adam, where are you?”

He seeks you so that you may find yourself; and he seeks you so that you too may seek yourself and say: “Lord, where are you?” But what are you doing? For if he has lost, yet he seeks; if he has lost, he has not lost everything, because he sees what he has lost. And therefore he seeks what he has lost, because he sees what he has lost. For he would not seek unless he saw. But what of you? Adam, where are you? You have lost everything. You have lost it, because you have both lost it [Col. 0166B] so as not to possess it, and ceased to see so as not to seek it. For if you see that you do not possess something, you understand what you should seek. But now you are far away and exiled from truth, so that you cannot see whence you came or whither you must return. Therefore you ask what you ought to seek, because you do not know what you have lost. You ask what is useful for the children of men—what ought to be done under the sun during the number of the days of their life!

Oh, how you ought to have known this! But now you are hidden from truth, lurking beneath the shadow of your ignorance; because you withdrew far away and refused to be with that without which you cannot exist. For because you cannot exist without it, you seek; and because you have turned away and are hidden, you do not know what you ought to seek—although you could not altogether be hidden from it in this respect, that you do understand that you must seek something [Col. 0166C] when you see that what you seek is lacking to you. Understand, therefore, that even in this you are by no means wholly hidden; for truth follows one who flees and presents itself to one who turns away, and teaches that it must be sought by the person to whom it does not offer itself to be seen.

Yet you do not see outside truth itself that what you see must be sought by you, and that it is lacking to you, though you do not see what it is. Therefore, in truth you see that you must seek what you do not see to be truth. Why is this? Because you are hidden. For if you were not hidden, you would see that nothing but truth must be sought; and you would not seek truth itself, but possess it. Now you are hidden and do not see; nevertheless, you are not abandoned, because you are admonished to seek what you do not see. Therefore it is said to you: “Adam, where are you?”—that you may return to truth and find truth.

[Col. 0166D] You refused to stand in truth; now return to truth, because you cannot stand outside truth. You shall be a wanderer, fugitive, and unstable throughout all the days in which you are not with truth and in truth; nor will your heart find a place of rest if it refuses to stand in truth. For it can neither stand outside truth so as to seek, nor find rest apart from truth. Upward, downward, far and near, wherever it goes, it will find no rest until it finds truth. Why do you rage, unhappy one? You laugh, you weep, you are caressed, you are afflicted: what has this to do with wisdom? Since you were foolish in wantonness and pleasure, you will be miserable in affliction. What more can these things give you? “Vanity of vanities: vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccl. I).

[Col. 0167A] But you had not yet learned these things. Therefore, puffed up rather than made firm by your own understanding and wisdom—which is folly in the presence of truth—you tried to resist, and thought that you would accomplish something when you were nothing. You tried everything, and everywhere failed. Soft and hard, smooth and rough, prosperity and adversity: outside truth they can corrupt, but cannot correct. Therefore you are tossed and hurled about; you fall, collapse, and are driven onward; you desire and do not attain. Feeling your way without seeing, you advance vainly in the opposite direction, seeking truth where it is not.

And where are you? Truth is within, and you are outside; and therefore it cries to you and says: “Adam, where are you?” It asks in order to expose your ignorance; it walks in order to display your instability. “When the Lord was walking in paradise at the hour after midday, he called and said: Adam, [Col. 0167B] where are you?” (Gen. III). He did not merely walk; he walked to and fro. What is “walked to and fro”? Moving here and there, as if wandering and unsettled, not proceeding straight ahead, but going wherever—this is what it means that he walked to and fro. And why did he choose to walk thus? That outwardly he might show himself such as inwardly he had begun to be. For truth had now been set in motion and was wavering, as though to withdraw from the sinner’s heart. Or rather, truth stood firm, while the sinful conscience wavered; and therefore truth walked to and fro outwardly, because inwardly the sinner was wavering away from truth.

Yet it walked to and fro and did not depart. It did not go straight away, withdrawing as though irrevocable and never to return; but circling nearby and walking close at hand, it went and did not go, now advancing and now returning, heaving with a kind of great uncertainty—as though unwilling to leave its dwelling, yet unable to endure a polluted habitation.

[Col. 0167C] What are you doing, Adam? Why are you silent? Call back the one departing; follow the one fleeing. For it is still near and waits, perhaps it may be recalled; therefore it delays and gently threatens departure, grieving that it has been wounded and violently cast out, and showing that it wishes to return if perchance it is invited to come. Therefore it has not departed quickly, but still waits—yet it will go; and now, because there is no one to call it back, it will go. Behold, it walks in order to depart, because there is no one mindful of love, remembering charity, whose heart cares for the affection of fellowship.

O unhappy Adam, where is your remembrance? Where have you fixed your soul, that you can endure these things? Hard, hardened, and made obdurate: could not such kindness, such flame, such immense ardour of love soften you, that you might melt and run after it? But what do you do? “I heard thy voice,” he says, “and hid myself.” Why? “Because I was naked” (ibid.). [Col. 0167D] Therefore you flee truth because you love perversity.

And what does truth do? It follows the fugitive whom it has left as he departs. It has turned away from the worker of iniquity, yet recalls the one persisting in iniquity. “Adam, where are you?” “I,” it says, “know where you are; you do not know.” Therefore: where are you? Attend to where you are, so that you may correct what you have become and return to him by whom you were made.

“Adam, where are you?” “I heard, Lord, thy voice, and hid myself.” O hidden and not hidden, seeing nothing and seen: from whom did you hide yourself? You heard the voice and did not see the face. Why? Because you were hidden. This is the profit you gained by hiding yourself: that you should not see him by whom you were seen. [Col. 0168A] You could flee him, indeed, but you could not escape him, because even hidden you did not remain concealed from him. Therefore, sought, you were found, because lurking you are not concealed. But in your malice you flee again, and flee again; you are found and flee; you always flee and do not escape. Possessed, you flee; sought, you flee; sought again, you deny. Therefore, sought, you are found; denying, you are convicted; convicted, you are condemned.

Let us now see whether perhaps we have made so long a digression without cause. Let us consider our Adam—the ancient one, yet still new in reiterated wickedness. Let us consider him renewing his old pursuits and, a deserter from truth, seeking the shadow, hiding-places, and covering of leaves, everywhere convicted but never willing to be reproved; unable to remain hidden and always fleeing. Let us see, then, what he does.

[Col. 0168B] What does he do? He saw the food and contemplated it, because it was pleasant to the sight and sweet for eating (ibid.); and he opened his jaws and said: “I will go and abound in delights, and enjoy good things.” And behold, behind his back wisdom and truth cried out and said: “Adam, where are you?” But he, hearing its voice and convicted by truth crying within, could not deny truth, and said: “I heard, Lord, thy voice; and I truly saw that this was vanity; therefore I reckoned laughter an error, and said to joy: ‘Why are you vainly deceived?’”

Behold a man hearing truth and confessing truth. Who do you think he is? He seems wholly great, and near to truth, who thus professes truth. Truly great—if he is not hidden. For he hears but does not see truth, because through desire [Col. 0168C] he is outside, while truth through wisdom is within. Truth wishes to gain him and recalls him to itself; and so, again and again, it cries from within and says: “Adam, where are you?”

But he, sensing that he has been exposed and convicted, when one entrance has been blocked, seeks other hiding-places for flight; restrained from pleasure, he pours himself out into avarice. For previously he sought fruit for food; now he seeks leaves for shade. And he hides himself from the light of truth all the more deeply as he covers the vice of ambition more wickedly beneath a pretence of frugality. Therefore he continues and says: “I considered in my heart how to withdraw my flesh from wine.” Why? “That I might turn my mind,” he says, “toward wisdom and avoid folly.”

You have done this well. “For no one can serve two masters” (Matt. VI). You did well, therefore, in resolving to cut away [Col. 0168D] from yourself the clouded and darkening delight of the flesh, so that you might find the luminous delight of truth, containing no impurity. You did well in proposing to withdraw your flesh from wine, so that you might better intoxicate your soul with wisdom and gather it inwardly to itself: where wisdom shines, truth is known, and prudence is found. For this too was to avoid folly: not to pour oneself out toward the pursuit of empty and vain things, but, by restraining the whole intention of the mind and all the efforts of the heart under the governance of reason, to conform oneself to truth. You have done this well. But for how long? “Until,” he says, “I should see what is useful for the children of men—what ought to be done under the sun during the number of the days of their life.”

[Col. 0169A] See, therefore, that you persevere: that you seek in truth and seek perseveringly. For truth is found only by those who seek it in truth. Who are those who seek it in truth? Those who approach it with their whole heart; who do not come in part and withdraw in part, but come wholly and from the whole self. These seek truth in truth. But those who gather their heart in one place and scatter it in another do not approach wholly or from the whole self, and therefore do not find truth; because what they seemed to gain from truth in one place, they lose in another. They “gather wages and put them into a bag with holes” (Hag. I).

If frugality gathers and avarice scatters, what is the benefit? What does it avail if, restraining gluttony by abstinence, you have gathered up pleasure [Col. 0169B], but, opening your eyes through ambition, have dispersed it? You attend to the fact that you entered, but do not attend to the fact that you went out. If you enter and go out, you are outside; just as, if you go out and enter, you are inside. But if you are outside, wherever you may be, you are not with truth, because truth is within. And what difference does it make where you are, if you are not where truth is? From wherever you come and wherever you enter, if you are within, you are well, because you are with truth. But wherever you go and wherever you depart, if you are outside, you are ill, because you are not with truth.

Therefore, if you seek in truth, seek wholly; approach wholly; enter wholly; for truth is within. Why do you seek so long and fail to find what you seek? Because you seek badly: you seek where what you seek is not. For you seek outside, and what you seek is within. Therefore you seek badly, and therefore you cannot find what you seek; and for that reason you cannot find rest where you are, because truth is not where you are.

[Col. 0169C] Where are you? Under a shadow, under leaves; because you have lost the fruit, and therefore appearance deceives you and truth is not in you. Wherever you go, you will be defrauded: everything that you see is shadow, and truth lies hidden. What is shadow? The appearance of visible things is a shadow, and you have poured out your soul upon them and hidden yourself beneath leaves in order to lurk there. How do you seek light by entering darkness? In the fruit you perceived vanity, yet in the leaves you suppose truth to be present? If all earthly things are vain for enjoyment, how are they not much more vain merely to behold? For if they give no true good to those who enjoy them, what can they give to those who possess them without enjoying them?

[Col. 0169D] Why, then, after the good resolution of continence and the pursuit of wisdom to be sought, do you so quickly turn again to vain occupation? Why, unless because your mind has been cast outside and made wandering and fugitive over the earth? Therefore it cannot stand, because it is not fixed in truth. “For this reason,” you say, “I made my works great,” etc.

## HOMILY IX. On the Ecclesiast’s Various Vain Endeavours

“I made my works great.” What works? “I built myself houses, planted vineyards, made gardens and orchards, planted them with trees of every kind, and constructed pools of water, that I might irrigate a wood of growing trees.” This is what I said: you seek outside what you lost within. You make your works great because you have become diminished within yourself. You build houses because you have been cast out from the dwelling-place of your conscience. You plant vineyards and make gardens because the shoots of wisdom have dried up in your heart. You construct pools because you do not possess the fountain of life springing up within. You irrigate a wood of growing trees because, having lost the light of truth, you seek shadow.

[Col. 0170A] What have you to do with these pleasures, unhappy one, forgetful of your goods? Where now is what you recently resolved—to withdraw your flesh from wine—you who now intoxicate your soul with every wantonness and vanity? Is this how wisdom is sought? You seemed to have gone out from there; how have you returned so quickly? How, unless you walked in a circuit, your path became entangled, and frugality brought you back to where gluttony [Col. 0170B] had cast you down? Behold, you have again fallen into pleasure and become captive to vanity. How did you come here, unless because you heard its voice and hid yourself? For this is the shadow of vanity beneath which you hide, lest you see truth.

How, then, did you come here? Ought you not to have sought wisdom? But your mind, exiled far from truth and ignorant of the way of truth, having restrained itself from the single vice of pleasure through abstinence from gluttony, poured itself out all the more freely into every wantonness and superstition through the desire of the eyes. Thus it is now corrupted more wickedly in its entirety precisely because it seemed to have been corrected, however slightly, in one part. Previously you were being corrupted and humbled, because you saw and understood what you suffered; now, under an appearance of virtues, you have become the prey of vices.

[Col. 0170C] Avarice enters under the guise of frugality; and while it persuades the mind not to abandon moderation in the things it possesses, it causes it to preserve what brings no benefit. Then pride follows upon multiplied riches, while what was sought through ambition is possessed for exaltation. From this arose all these monstrosities of vanity: the foolish mind imagines that true good is to be found outside in the experience of things—not as though by means of external things true good were to be sought within, but as though it consisted in those things themselves. Therefore, without moderation, it spreads itself boldly through everything; and, having found affliction in abstaining from the flesh, it finds another entrance through the desire of the eyes and feeds the carnal inclination more abundantly.

[Col. 0170D] Nor is it enough for the wanton man to delight in things made for human service and enjoyment, unless pride too, transgressing the equality of the shared human condition, rules over other people. This is what, after and among his other superstitions, he adds when he says:

“I possessed male and female slaves, and had a large household.” He became lord of human beings who was a slave of vices. How much better it would be for you to have the Lord as master, and men here as companions! For there, to rule would be the virtue of one who reigns. But here, to rule is not the virtue of one who does not resist, but the injustice of one who oppresses and the advantage of one who endures. Yet the creature of glory attends to external appearance and does not attend to inward disease. It thinks that what is swollen is great, and therefore rejoices to seem great outwardly.

[Col. 0171A] But it does not fear to be empty and void within. “I possessed,” he says, “male and female slaves, and had a large household.” What could a great household do without great possessions, much money, and abundant expenditure? Therefore he adds and says:

“Also herds of cattle and great flocks of sheep beyond all who were before me in Jerusalem.” Behold abundance. Where is glory? “I heaped up for myself silver and gold, and the wealth of kings and provinces.” What glory! And what follows, except that an arrogant mind soon grows soft and enervated through wantonness, becoming prone to boasting, and says:

“I made for myself male singers and female singers, and the delights of the children of men: cups and pitchers [or: jugs] [Col. 0171B] for service in pouring wine; and I surpassed in riches all who were before me in Jerusalem. Wisdom also remained with me.”

Great confidence! Therefore you sinned without fear. Therefore you confidently poured out your heart into the delights of pleasure and upon the allurements of beauty and the enjoyments of vanity. Why? Because wisdom remained with you. For why would you seek wisdom placed within, if it had not left you wandering outside? Yet what kind of wisdom is this, which so loves roaming about and disdains seclusion? Take care lest resemblance deceive you, and what appears to be wisdom is not wisdom. Take care lest you be deceived in the shadow of leaves, where your father lay hidden, unable to see truth. For shadow makes things dark; and though it seems to provide rest, it has no light.

[Col. 0171C] Take care, therefore, lest while you seek rest beneath the shadow of leaves, you begin to suffer darkness. Nor can you, situated in shadow, discern clearly; for the image that appears in shadow is merely an image, not truth. Therefore regard this shadow of leaves with suspicion, lest you be deceived.

What are the leaves? The appearances of visible things are leaves: now they appear beautiful and green, but they will suddenly fall when the storm comes forth. What are the leaves? Houses, vineyards, gardens, pools, a wood of growing trees, households, possessions, gold, silver, the wealth of kings and provinces; lyres, citharas, pipes, organs, cups and pitchers, precious vessels, riches, pomp, and glory—all these are leaves. Why leaves? Because they are vain, perishable, transient: therefore they are leaves. They are green indeed for a brief time, but quickly dry up and fall.

[Col. 0171D] Yet while they stand they make shade and possess their own refreshment; but it is a dark shadow, hostile to light. It seems indeed to afford the flesh temporary refreshment, but it makes the eyes dim. Therefore we must regard shadow with suspicion and not readily trust things seen in shadow. Images deceive the eyes, because shadow itself is an image, not truth. This is why I said that you should regard the shadow with suspicion—you who confess that you are placed beneath leaves. You are beneath leaves, you are in shadow, and you see wisdom beside you. Look carefully lest it perhaps is not wisdom, but something else hidden beneath its appearance.

For what wisdom is there in the shadow of leaves? The shadow of leaves is delight and pleasure in the appearance and beauty of transient things. And this shadow has its own wisdom. For men call “wisdom” the cunning and shrewd pursuit and prudent preservation of this repose and tranquillity of the flesh. This is the wisdom by which “the children of this age and the children of darkness are more prudent than the children of light in their generation” (Luke XVI). It remains with those who lie in the shadow of leaves, and they cannot see the light of true wisdom—a wisdom in comparison with which this wisdom is folly.

[Col. 0172A] Since they look only to the advantages of the flesh, they do not attend to the losses of the soul; and because they wish to be cautious where there is no need for fear, they become foolish and imprudent in your eyes where there is grave danger and intolerable loss. For what wisdom is it to cherish the flesh and neglect the soul? What wisdom is it to flee with all one’s effort that which troubles the flesh [Col. 0172B] for a brief time, and not guard against that which is known to be eternally ruinous to the soul? This is the wisdom in which this man glories as he lies beneath the shadow of leaves.

O leaves, O shadow—what kind of fruit is yours? See, Adam, what your leaves are like and what your fruit is like. You hid yourself, and your leaves furnished a covering of shade so that, concealed, you would not see truth. You ate, and your fruit furnished food so that, corrupted by the meal, you might lose immortality. Recognize, wretched man; recognize your evil; recognize your misery; recognize where you are and what you have become. Turn from shadow to the brightness of light, so that you may not only hear words but also see the face of truth.

## HOMILY X. On the Remaining Vanities, as Far as the Passage: “The Fool Walks in Darkness”

[Col. 0172C]

“And when I turned myself to all the works which my hands had made, and to the labours in which I had sweated in vain, I saw [Col. 0172D] vanity and affliction of spirit in all things, and that nothing endures under the sun.”

Above we heard with what zeal this man laboured in gathering riches and increasing his possessions; and then, as he himself testified, we learned how he poured out his soul in wantonness and in testing pleasure amid the abundance of things which he had prepared. Let us now hear what he adds after all this. “When,” he says, “I turned myself to all the works which my hands had made, and to the labours in which I had sweated in vain, I saw vanity and affliction of spirit in all things, and that nothing endures under the sun.”

This first raises for us a question: how can he now say for the first time that he turned to look upon his works, when until now he seems to have done nothing but direct his attention and effort to these matters? When he made his works great, built houses, planted vineyards, made gardens and orchards, constructed pools, possessed male and female slaves, herds and flocks, silver and gold, the wealth of kings and provinces, and the delights of the children of men; when, finally, he had immersed himself not only in action but also in mind so deeply in the love and enjoyment of his possessions that he regarded this as his own proper part, and in some manner believed that he had been made for no other reason than to delight himself in all that he had prepared—did he not see what he was doing?

[Col. 0173A] But he saw the appearance; he did not foresee the corruption. He saw what the things that stood seemed to be, but did not attend to what the things that had perished had become. For love of present things, while it turned the whole intention of the mind upon itself and occupied even the eyes of the heart by entering through the bodily sight of things that appeared with deceptive appearance, at once removed the memory of the past and concealed foresight of the future. Thus it came about that, while he looked only upon things that appeared, he was unable to recognize truth even in them; and, in his own works, turned toward them, he saw the appearance to be desired, but, turned away, did not recognize the vanity to be avoided.

[Col. 0173B] It sometimes happens that temporal goods are discovered more quickly to be vain when they begin to abound more greatly—goods which, when absent, are often imagined to have been beneficial if only they had been present. But when possessed, they cannot banish the poverty of the mind even amid their abundance; then they first make plain to the one who experiences them how scant a fruit they yield to those who labour for them. Accordingly, after such abundance of every kind of possession and the enjoyment of pleasures, he fittingly says that he turned himself in order to understand his vanity. For when he began to experience that possessions could not make him happy, then he recognized that, sought through empty labour, they had made him much more miserable.

“When,” he says, “I turned myself to all the works which my hands had made”—namely, considering what fruit might follow such great labours—“then,” he says, “I found that the fruit of my labours did not recompense me with an equal balance; and therefore, looking upon the labours in which I had sweated in vain, I judged that I had laboured in vain.”

[Col. 0173C] “In all things there is vanity and affliction of spirit.” Affliction first, vanity afterwards; yet affliction also after vanity; affliction before vanity; affliction in vanity; and all is vanity, all is affliction. For all things are vain which, both while they are present, do not give their lovers what they promise, and, when they are thought to be held, pass away. But perhaps it might have seemed tolerable if there were vanity alone and no affliction. Now, however, there is affliction before vanity, affliction in vanity, and affliction after vanity: because things possessed with love can neither be acquired without labour, preserved without anxiety, [Col. 0173D] nor lost without pain. Thus all is vanity and all is affliction, because there is vanity in affliction and affliction in vanity.

For this reason he rightly says, having turned: “I saw vanity and affliction of spirit in all things, and that nothing endures under the sun.” Instructed by his own affairs, he began also to judge those of others; and what he had learned in part he declared truthfully concerning the whole, saying: “Nothing endures under the sun.”

From this it may be inferred how much, in other matters, whether tending to good or evil, it matters for a person to know what sort of person that person has been to himself. For in some respect all things begin to be to you what you yourself have been to yourself. If you do not see yourself, you see nothing rightly. If you are not deceived in judging yourself, you are easily directed in judging another.

[Col. 0174A] Thus this man too, having turned and been set straight, after adding concerning his own works, “He saw vanity and affliction of spirit in all things,” immediately, as one instructed by his own affairs, begins to judge what belongs to others and, from his judgment of his own works, forms a verdict upon all things, saying: “And nothing endures under the sun.” But since, for perfection, it is not enough to reject evils unless one also knows how to choose goods, he added and said:

“I passed over to contemplate wisdom.” *Hebrew* is interpreted as “one who passes over.” Therefore this man became a Hebrew in order to contemplate wisdom. He had indeed previously been a Hebrew according to the flesh, but he was not a Hebrew according to truth until he began to pass over to contemplate wisdom. Just as one person is called a Jew according to the flesh and another a Jew [Col. 0174B] according to truth, so one Hebrew is according to the flesh and another Hebrew according to truth. But the one who is manifestly a Jew according to the flesh, and the one who is manifestly a Hebrew according to the flesh, is neither truly a Jew nor truly a Hebrew. Rather, the one who is a Jew inwardly according to the Spirit, and a Hebrew according to the Spirit, is truly a Jew and truly a Hebrew.

For many pass over according to the flesh but do not pass over according to truth, because they do not pass over so as to arrive at truth. They cross seas and traverse remote lands more readily than they attain truth—though truth itself is near. “The word,” Scripture says, “is near you, in your mouth” (Rom. X); and the truth of the Word is in the heart; and the Word itself is truth, because truth is the Word. [Col. 0174C] Yet although truth itself is so near, nothing is farther from those who love folly. For what is more foolish than always looking downward and keeping one’s face bent toward the earth? This has been granted to beasts, to whom no desire beyond such things has been permitted. Wisdom, however, dwells on high; and those who have been likened to beasts and look upon the earth refuse to rise toward her.

This is the very folly from which this man passed over to contemplate wisdom, when he despised the false goods he had loved on earth and raised himself to contemplate and love the true goods that are above, because he saw vanity in all things below the sun. Therefore, when he had seen vanity and affliction of spirit in all things, and that nothing remains beneath [Col. 0174D] the sun, he passed over to contemplate wisdom above the sun. Oh, how difficult a passage, and how long a road for feet made weak! I do not know whether the whole life of a human being can suffice to complete this journey. For who, while dwelling in this mortal life, can fully grasp wisdom? Wisdom is drawn from hidden things and found in hidden things; wisdom always loves secrecy and does not offer herself for contemplation except to those who enter in to her.

But it is very burdensome to weak souls to leave what they have cherished and forsake what they have loved; to pass over to desire things they do not know, unless they are instructed through their sufferings; to find becoming bitter what was formerly sweet; and thus in some manner many are drawn back and compelled to enter and to pass over to contemplate [Col. 0175A] wisdom. For when they begin to taste and understand the sweetness and delight of wisdom, they no longer need to be compelled, but follow willingly. They gladly despise all things and leave everything behind, in order to pass over to contemplate wisdom. Then they arrive quickly, because they run swiftly and seek ardently; and wisdom begins to be near to them, because they themselves draw near to her and do not draw away from her toward alien desires.

Thus Moses, while he was in the wilderness shepherding animals and had an Ethiopian woman as his wife, knew as yet only a consuming fire. Therefore he wondered that the bush burned and was not consumed (Exod. III). For as long as the soul feeds its desires upon low pleasures and, bound by carnal desire, has not yet attained the embraces of [Col. 0175B] wisdom, it is in a consuming and devouring fire, even unto destruction. The flame of lust and the love of the flesh consume those whom they kindle. But love of wisdom has light without consumption; and if it kindles the cold, it does not burn up those made ardent. Therefore Moses wondered how the bush burned yet was not consumed.

For he too burned, because he had an Ethiopian wife; nor was this a miracle to him. Rather, to burn and not be consumed: what he had not experienced, that was miraculous to him. The miracle itself drew and urged him to pass over and see the greatest vision—how the bush burned and was not consumed. He began to run toward a sweeter desire and to forget the old desires in which he burned and was consumed, [Col. 0175C] and to loathe love for the Ethiopian wife, because she was black and not beautiful, unlike that Shunammite who warms old men and does not burn young men.

For that fire by which the bush burned and was not consumed signified the love of this Shunammite—that is, wisdom. Therefore Moses, after he had passed over to see the vision and had begun to perceive how sweetly her flame burned, could no longer be held by love for the Ethiopian wife. His heart kindled by a better fire, he reached even to converse with the Most High and was sent for the salvation of the people. For God spoke to him in the fire, was heard from the fire, and was understood through the fire. Within him was a flame that had kindled his heart, by which, like the bush, he burned and was not consumed. The mind itself had conceived God in the fire [Col. 0175D] and knew God through the fire. Had he not burned, he would neither have seen nor known; for the fire itself is love, and love itself is knowledge.

Thus he knew and loved; he saw and burned; he tasted and loved. Fire conquered fire; love overcame pleasure. The ugly and black Ethiopian woman was despised, blackened by her own flame, while her own love made her unlovely. She was despised in comparison with one more beautiful; and he who recognized that with her he would always remain a slave no longer wished to serve for her sake. For carnal life and the desire of the flesh are not from God the Father but from the devil as father; and they devote their lovers to the slavery of their father and subject them to his dominion.

Moses serves, then, and feeds [Col. 0176A] flocks; he purchases love for his ugly wife by shameful servitude and cannot be free until God comes in fire and appears in love. For then he easily despises what he had loved wrongly, when he begins to taste what he may desire more sweetly. Moses now considers himself unworthy to serve for the Ethiopian woman. Even if he does not afterward reject her when she follows him, he nevertheless does not receive her into love. For, having become a lover of wisdom, he ought to admit concern for the flesh in such a way that he does not submit himself through affection to its insolent wantonness, yet yields to it through compassion when it is weak and compliant.

For it is one thing to love for joy, another to endure for use; one thing to receive into the fellowship of love, another to endure in the share of compassion. The life of the flesh must be borne out of necessity; wisdom must be joined in love. The latter is to be desired for its own sake; the former is to be fled for its own sake, yet endured for our sake. Therefore, after the vision, Moses no longer serves the Ethiopian woman’s father in Midian, nor does she bear children any longer, as though driven from the marriage-bed, where love and affection have their place. Another, fairer and more lovable, was received, through companionship with whom Moses’ face would become not dark but radiant. Her love was shown in that fire when the bush burned and was not consumed.

Moses ran in order to pass over and contemplate the vision because he had not yet conceived wisdom’s fire or felt its sweetness. Therefore he wondered, and wonder itself drew him, so that by approaching he might grow warm and burn. The fire which illumined him while distant kindled him when he drew near. Therefore, as he approached, [Col. 0176C] he removed his sandal, now willingly renouncing carnal desires after tasting the sweetness and recognizing the delightfulness of that love. For what could the desire of the flesh be in comparison with love of wisdom? Thus Moses hastened to run and see the vision, and to pass over to contemplate wisdom.

And it was made clear how he passed over and how he arrived at contemplation of wisdom: how much he saw in her, how much he learned from her, and how he became wisdom’s friend, penetrating into her depths and becoming privy to her secrets. And how many from the beginning have wished in this way to pass over to contemplate wisdom! First, Abraham, that great father, went out from the fire of the Chaldeans and passed over to contemplate [Col. 0176D] wisdom. He came into the land of vision shown to him by God, saw wisdom’s brightness, and rejoiced. Isaac also had gone out to meditate and passed over to contemplate wisdom; and God spoke with him. Jacob likewise, journeying to contemplate wisdom, passed over as he came from Mesopotamia, saw the Lord face to face, and his soul was preserved (Gen. XXXII).

After these, all the patriarchs and all the prophets passed over, and all wished to contemplate wisdom. Finally wisdom herself came, and passed over, and her friends contemplated her, for she had come in order to be seen—lest she be sought in vain if she were never seen. She said to those who had passed over, that they might contemplate [Col. 0177A] her: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see. Many kings and many prophets wished to see what you see, and did not see it; and to hear what you hear, and did not hear it” (Matt. XIII). She said this and passed over, so that those who desired to contemplate her might pass over after her, lest perhaps she no longer be sought if she were always seen.

Many others followed after her, and very many passed through; and wisdom became manifold. Many wished to pass over but could not arrive, because they did not keep to the way. Some passed over and arrived. Others wished to pass over but could not pass through, because they thought they could go by themselves. [Col. 0177B] Even the philosophers of the nations wished to pass over to contemplate wisdom, but they erred and came to nothing because they thought they could lead themselves. Yet they had begun to pass over and had reached a certain point; they had approached the way but did not enter it because they did not believe in Christ.

Do you wish to know how far they had come? Bodily they were on earth, but in mind they ascended and passed beyond all earthly things by investigating the heavens. By their own ingenuity and understanding they ascended as far as the moon, the sun, and the stars of heaven—indeed, as far as heaven itself and the firmament. What remained beyond, to which they could have gone? Yet wisdom is above all things and cannot be found among all things, though through wisdom all things were made. None of these things is that from which all that exists has its being. But where could they have found it? It was not seen, and yet it was sought; nor could it remain hidden without speaking, nor be investigated so as to be found.

Wisdom was within, while they were outside. They entered inwardly in mind after her, in order to pass over to contemplate wisdom. They investigated and searched wisely; they comprehended nature’s secrets and found many hidden things. But none of these was wisdom, because all this was made through wisdom. They ascended above all things and entered within all things, and nothing remained beyond in which they could seek wisdom. They fell and failed while searching out their investigations. It seemed to them that there was something divine above all things; yet they neither knew nor understood it. Seeing further, they grew dark, because with weak eyes they struck against dazzling light. They began to think many false things about the true and to fashion God in their perverse heart, not as he was, but as he seemed to them, who could not see what he was.

They thought themselves to see well, but they became futile in their thoughts; they were more grievously blinded and found to be wandering more deeply in error precisely as they investigated more subtly. Others thought that wisdom must be sought more subtly through morals; many of them became despisers of their own possessions, but not correctors of their own vices. They too reached a certain point, because they had the appearance of truth but did not hold the truth. They cast away money but retained malice. They cleansed what was outside but kept what was inside polluted. This was not wisdom, because it was not truth, but only a false image. [Col. 0178A]

They thought they were proceeding by the road of virtues, but did not know whither they were tending, because they did not know their direction or their end. There were still others who possessed certain virtues and were borne toward them by natural inclination. They passed over and reached a certain point, and through that part of nature which had not wholly come under corruption they saw and desired the good. They were granted much capacity for the pursuit of virtues and a worthy inclination toward goodness. Who does not know what great men of virtue they too possessed, and what remarkable and worthy deeds of imitation they performed—pursuing justice, cultivating piety, preserving chastity, strengthened by patience, steadfast in fidelity, prudent in foresight? And what more shall we say? Were not all these things [Col. 0178B] good? They certainly were, but goods of nature, not of grace; of creation, not of restoration: goods which nature had preserved lest it be wholly corrupted, not goods which grace had bestowed to free nature from corruption; goods which the grace of nature, first created, had given and afterward had left to nature when corrupted, but had not added for the cleansing of corruption; goods by which the beauty of well-created nature might be demonstrated, not goods by which the exaltation of nature to be glorified might be gained.

Thus all these things were goods in their own measure, but not true goods, because they did not direct the mind through intention to the highest good. Wisdom was not found in any of these, because it was not sought in truth. Nor did wisdom draw near either to the former, to illuminate their eyes toward truth, or [Col. 0178C] to the latter, to direct their steps toward virtue. Therefore neither could the blind find her nor the lame arrive at her.

But let this our Hebrew say what he did and how much he advanced by his passage, since he too testifies that he passed over with the rest to contemplate wisdom, saying: “I passed over to contemplate wisdom.” This, therefore, is what you should consider. Whoever passes over to wisdom leaves folly behind. And what follows?

“Errors also, and folly.” If the person who passes over to contemplate wisdom passes over to wisdom, how does he withdraw from folly or leave error behind when he passes over to contemplate errors and folly? But wisdom is light, while error and folly are darkness. One who is in darkness sees neither darkness [Col. 0178D] nor light. But one who is in the light sees both darkness and light, because all things that are reproved are reproved by the light. Therefore, since he cannot see his own darkness while he himself is still in darkness, he comes from darkness to light so that by light he may see both darkness and light—not darkness through darkness and light through light, but both darkness and light through light alone.

No one goes to darkness in order to see darkness; rather, one comes to the light, so as to see by light not only light but also darkness. Whoever wishes to see his own darkness withdraws from it, lest he himself be in darkness and see nothing; he passes over to light, so that through light he may see darkness and light together. Rightly, then, when Ecclesiastes passes over to contemplate wisdom, he comes to wisdom itself as to light in order to contemplate errors also and folly, so that in wisdom he may see both darkness and light. [Col. 0179A] That is, so that in wisdom he may see what wisdom itself is, and through wisdom see errors and folly as what wisdom is not.

For whoever sees wisdom sees what wisdom itself is; and whoever sees errors and folly sees what wisdom itself is not. Yet one can see wisdom, errors, and folly only through wisdom herself. Thus wisdom is itself wisdom. Therefore, whoever passes over to contemplate errors and folly passes over to wisdom, just as whoever passes over to contemplate wisdom passes over to wisdom. Yet he contemplates the former—errors and folly—in order to flee them; while he approaches the latter, wisdom, [Col. 0179B] in order to contemplate her. Neither of the two is wisdom, but it is wisdom to contemplate both; and whoever passes over to contemplate both passes over to nothing other than wisdom, and leaves behind nothing other than errors and folly.

Therefore let him say: “I passed over to contemplate wisdom, errors, and folly.” What is error? Not knowing what is right. What is folly? Knowing and not following. What is wisdom? Knowing and loving the good. But to know and hate evil is also wisdom—and the first wisdom, because to hate evil is to have loved the good, and to have known evil is to have understood what is right. Accordingly, to know and love the good is wisdom; and this itself is to hate and know evil. All this is known in wisdom [Col. 0179C] when wisdom is seen both in what she herself is, so that she may be loved, and in what she is not, which is made manifest through her so that it may be hated.

Oh, what a good passage this is, and how happily one migrates who migrates to contemplate wisdom! What wonder if the God of the Hebrews is Lord and God, since he makes such passers-over and makes them pass over to such things? Wisdom says: “Pass over to me, all who desire me, and be filled from my generations.” For my spirit is sweeter than honey, and my inheritance sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Those who eat me shall hunger still; those who drink me shall thirst still; those who make me clear shall have eternal life” (Eccli. XXIV). [Col. 0179D] “For I illuminate all with doctrine, as though with a light before dawn, and I shall illuminate all who hope in the Lord.”

Do you wish to know how wisdom illumines those who have passed over to contemplate her? Ask this very man who passed over to contemplate wisdom, and consider how he was illumined once he began to see her. For before he passed over to contemplate her, you heard sufficiently above how blind he was: he thought he could go where there was no way for a human being; he sought and investigated all things under the sun; and he believed that it was some great achievement to investigate the nature of things that stand outside human nature—things which, even if known as far as they can be known in themselves, can neither confer salvation nor remove it if they are unknown. There he was blind, because he neither saw nor knew in himself what he could do, nor desired for himself what he ought. But [Col. 0180A] now, enlightened by wisdom, attend to what he says.

“What is man, I ask? What is he?” I do not ask what he is by wondering at his dignity, but by recognizing his weakness. What is man? Man is nothing. He is not anything such as can be found sufficient for this. Sufficient for what?

“That he may be able to follow the king who made him.” If he cannot attain the thing made, much less can he follow its maker. If he cannot investigate what has been made, how can he comprehend the one who made it? What is man, that he may be able to follow the king who made him—his king and his maker? The one who is king is himself also maker: maker because he created; king because he governs what he created and directs it [Col. 0180B] to the end for which he created it. For he created it in a great good and directs it toward the highest good.

Who follows his maker? The one who lives as he was made. Who walks according to the order in which he was established? The one who preserves unimpaired the good received at creation and guards what nature bestowed. Such a one follows his maker. And who follows his king? The one who tends toward the end to which he is directed; who hastens to arrive where he is invited; who obeys the laws of his good ruler; who freely inclines himself in all things to the command of the one who commands. Such a one follows his king.

But what man can answer God? Who will be found sufficient to render to God a return? If he goes before and you follow, then one thing belongs to him and another to you. [Col. 0180C] Indeed, if he begins the good and you complete it, what is lesser belongs to him and what is greater to you. If God goes before by beginning the good and you follow by bringing it to perfection, you will be found not only equal to God but greater. Or perhaps he goes before by showing, so that you may follow by imitation. But then where is the saying, “His mercy shall go before me and shall follow me” (Psal. LVIII.)? Where is, “From him, and through him, and in him are all things” (Rom. XI)? Where is, “What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?” (II Cor. IV)?

For if showing belongs to him but following to you, then you have something you did not receive; and not all things are from him, through him, and in him. Rather, some things belong to man and are not from him, if a human being can do something by himself that is not through him. But wisdom does not enlighten a human being so that he may think this—or say that a person can have anything as from himself when he could not even have from himself the fact that he is human. What, then, does he mean when he says: “What is man, that he may be able to follow the king who made him?”

How far, O human being, do you think man is from God, that he might attain where he is? For what is it to attain where he is, except to be what he is? And what is God? And what is man? See how far apart they are. God is just and blessed; man unjust and miserable. See how far apart are the just and the unjust, the miserable and the blessed. Misery cannot coexist with blessedness, nor can injustice attain blessedness. Justice is the way; blessedness is the homeland. But a slave of sin cannot be just unless freed from sin. [Col. 0181A]

See, therefore, that a human being cannot follow the king who made him unless first visited by his king and maker. A human being cannot go to him; but he can, if he wills, come to the human being. Therefore the king and maker of humankind came to humankind. He came to what man was and himself became what he was not. He became man for man, assuming our misery while retaining his own justice. Thus there appeared between God and human beings the mediator of God and human beings, the God-man: as God drawing near to human beings through misery, yet as man not withdrawing from God through justice.

Thus God descended to one thing and man ascended to one thing; and in one person two things were found, one from ours and one from his. For there were, as it were, three things: God, just and blessed; and man, miserable and unjust. Since these could not meet, the God-man [Col. 0181B] placed himself in the middle, joining the miserable and the just, in order through justice to conquer misery and restore justice to blessedness.

Therefore, since Emmanuel was with us through the justice he brought to us and through the misery he assumed from us, he began to return whence he had come: in the human being, through justice, conquering misery; and, through misery, recalling the human being with justice to blessedness. He held fast to justice and endured misery until he conquered misery and crowned justice. He ran and went before us, “suffering for us and leaving us an example, that we should follow his footsteps” (I Pet. II). He freed us from slavery to sin, so that we too might possess justice amid misery [Col. 0181C] and pass through misery with justice to blessedness. He promises us what he received, if we suffer what he endured, so that we may reign with him if we suffer for him.

Thus the incarnate Word, our maker and king, because we could not follow him in his majesty, went before us in our humility and established from what is ours a way by which we might arrive at what is his. Yet even so, man could not follow him unless helped by him; for a just person could not run through death to life unless he who gave justice to the sinner also gave steadfastness to the sufferer. Rightly, then, he who had contemplated wisdom and learned how entirely powerless man is in himself said: “What is man, that he may follow the king who made him?” Truly he had passed over to contemplate wisdom [Col. 0181D] and had truly been enlightened by wisdom: now far more wisely recognizing in truth human weakness than before vainly extending himself beyond human possibility.

There he was exalted in order to fail; here he was humbled in order to advance. There, by pride, he swelled beyond himself so that he might be emptied within himself; here, through humility, he gathered himself back to himself so that he might be given to the One alone. Wisdom accomplished all this after he had contemplated her, first showing him his darkness in her light, then her own light, and everything in her light and through her light. Darkness was not light, nor was darkness in the light; but darkness was seen through the light and separated from the light. And he says:

“And I saw that wisdom surpassed folly as greatly as light differs from darkness.” How was this seen? [Col. 0182A] Because wisdom illumines and folly blinds. And how can it be demonstrated that wisdom illumines and folly blinds? Attend:

“The eyes of the wise man are in his head; the fool walks in darkness.” Now it has been proved that wisdom illumines and folly blinds. In what has it been proved? Because the wise person has enlightened eyes, while the fool sees nothing. If the wise person has enlightened eyes, therefore wisdom illumines. If the fool sees nothing, therefore folly blinds. For wisdom is light and gives illumination. If you have eyes where wisdom reaches, then you see; but if you have eyes where there is no light, you have eyes yet see nothing. And what good is that? Let your eyes, then, be where the light is, lest you become like one without eyes because you do not have light.

But where is light? Light is above, where wisdom is. [Col. 0182B] Wisdom is above; light is above; and every light comes from above. As below there is darkness without light, so above there is light without darkness. In the middle, however, darkness follows light and light follows darkness. Therefore there are days of heaven which darkness does not divide and no obscurity interrupts; and there are days of earth to which darkness succeeds. For where wisdom is always, there is always light; where wisdom is not always, there is light only to the degree wisdom is present; and where wisdom is never present, there is never light.

Therefore there is light where wisdom reaches, and where wisdom does not reach there is no light. But if wisdom reaches from end to end, where is there that wisdom cannot reach—she who penetrates all and embraces all? “I alone have gone round the circuit of heaven, penetrated the depth of the abyss, and walked upon the waves of the sea” (Eccli. XXIV); “reaching mightily from one end to the other and ordering all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII). Thus it is a great question what that may be to which wisdom does not reach: where the eyes of fools are, who walk in darkness and do not see.

Let us therefore ask another Scripture where the eyes of fools are, who walk in darkness and do not see. It says: “The eyes of the wise are in his head, but the eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth.” Therefore darkness is at the ends of the earth; and fools who walk in darkness do not see because their eyes are at the ends of the earth. For if light were where their eyes are, fools would not walk in darkness; [Col. 0182D] their eyes would be illuminated and they would see. But if the fool walks in darkness and the eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth, then without doubt darkness is there, where the eyes cannot see. And where is this? At the ends of the earth.

Therefore darkness is far away, while light is near. Why, then, do we find darkness more easily than light? Perhaps because we are not far from the ends of the earth and live beside the people of darkness; we have not yet journeyed from the ends of the earth to hear the wisdom of Solomon (III Reg. X), where light is. Thus we stumble into darkness and grow dim from the light. Yet light itself is near and presses upon us; but diseased eyes love dimness and turn the light into darkness. Therefore light is near, but we are far away; darkness is far away, but we draw near to it.

## HOMILY XI. On the ends of the earth in which the eyes of fools are found; and on how wisdom reaches mightily from end to end, etc.

[Col. 0183A]

Where, however, is darkness, and where is light? What is “the end,” and the end to which wisdom reaches? What are the ends of the earth, where the eyes of fools are, who walk in darkness and do not see? And what is the head of the wise person, where his eyes are—he who does not walk in darkness like the fool but has enlightened eyes? Therefore, lest we too remain in darkness, let us seek the light of wisdom, that we may understand where wisdom herself dwells and the division of light and darkness: where light and darkness end, the boundary of each, how far wisdom herself extends, what she herself is, what is outside her, and what exists without her. [Col. 0183B]

First, we have heard of two ends: one from which and one to which Wisdom extends herself, “reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly” (Sap. VIII). Yet we do not know who these two ends are, where they are, whether these ends themselves have an end, or whether something lies beyond them which wisdom does not reach. If there is such a thing, how can they be ends if they do not arrive at an end? But if there is not, how can the ends of the earth, where darkness exists, be contained within these ends—and how can darkness exist within light, since Wisdom reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly?

First, then, there are two ends of all things. One is the end above which there is nothing; the other, the end below which there is nothing. The end above which there is nothing is the highest of all things; the end below which there is nothing is the lowest. [Col. 0183C] Thus the two ends of all things are the highest and the lowest. Whatever exists in the universe apart from highest and lowest is intermediate between highest and lowest. The more anything withdraws from one, the more it approaches the other, whether from highest to lowest or from lowest to highest.

Do you wish to know whether Scripture perhaps mentions these ends more plainly elsewhere? “If I ascend,” says the Psalmist, “into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present” (Psal. CXXXVIII). Thus he establishes heaven and hell as the two ends of his course. Nothing is higher than heaven and nothing deeper than hell. Heaven, therefore, is the highest of all things; hell the lowest, [Col. 0183D] above which there is nothing and below which there is nothing. Wisdom reaches from end to end, fills everything, and penetrates all things. “If I ascend into heaven,” he says, “you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present.”

He did not say, “You are present in heaven,” nor, “You are there in hell”; but, “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present.” Therefore, in heaven he is; in hell he is present: remaining in heaven, coming into hell; in heaven awaiting those who come, in hell following those who flee. Those ascending into heaven find him there; those descending into hell do not escape him there. “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present.” Yet you are in both places: both where you are and where you are present, reaching from end to end—from the end where you are to the end where you are present—mightily, and ordering all things sweetly.

See, now [Col. 0184A] we have distinguished the two ends to which wisdom reaches: highest and lowest. One is, as it were, wisdom’s place, where she abides; the other is a kind of course or, so to speak, the goal of her extension. The end from which wisdom goes forth is the head, before which there is nothing. But the end into which she runs is the end beyond which there is nothing. The former end is both head and end. It is head because from it, and not from above it; it is end because up to it, and not beyond it. The other end is not head, because nothing comes from it; nevertheless it is an end, because all things go as far as it and not beyond it.

That end which is above is, as it were, the principle and origin, above which there is nothing. The end which is below is, as it were, the goal and limit beyond which there is nothing. [Col. 0184B] For the origin and principle of all things is from above, while their boundary and end are below. Therefore the lower end is an end, and only an end. The upper end, however, is not only an end, but also head and end. If, therefore, heaven is above and hell below, and nothing higher than heaven or deeper than hell can be found, heaven is the beginning and hell the end. Oh, what a good beginning, and what an evil end.

Perhaps the wise man’s eyes are in his head because, being placed in the middle, he looks back to his origin, so that he may make his end where he received his beginning. For it is not good to be brought to an end in another end, where the end is one of consumption, not consummation. Therefore man, who was created for eternity, alone among all living creatures has an upright face, that he may contemplate heaven; [Col. 0184C] and tend toward the end of completion. Nor should he suppose that this visible heaven alone is to be looked up to with bodily eyes; rather, lifting the inner eyes with a clearer and more penetrating gaze of mind and vision of heart above heaven, even to the invisible things of heaven and the spiritual realities of virtues, he should ascend by contemplation, in the light of eternity, to the end that has no end.

That is the true heaven above every heaven: not merely the heaven of heaven, but the heaven of heavens. It is not second after the first, but third after the first and second. For this reason Paul boasts that he was caught up to the third heaven (2 Cor. 12), because in mind he had reached the highest of all things; and he had passed not only beyond the visible heaven, which even human thought [Col. 0184D] can surpass, but had also crossed all those things which, though invisible, were created above this whole visible realm, and had been raised to behold the first principle and the head of eternity.

This is the third heaven. For the first heaven is the visible heaven. The second heaven is the invisible heaven of the visible heaven. The third heaven is the invisible heaven of the visible heaven and of the invisible heaven. The first heaven is simply heaven, and the heaven of earth. The second heaven is the heaven of heaven. The third heaven is the heaven of heavens. And this heaven has no heaven above itself.

The first heaven is the highest state of created being. The second heaven is progress in virtue above created being. The third heaven is the height of contemplation. The first hell is the lowest state of created being. The second hell is, beneath created being, the deficiency of wickedness. [Col. 0185A] The third hell is the depth of damnation. The first heaven and the first hell are an end and an end. The second heaven and the second hell are an end and an end. The third heaven and the third hell are an end and an end.

And Wisdom is everywhere: “She reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8:1). From the first heaven to the first hell is Wisdom’s first course. For, beginning from the highest and descending downward, coming from the summit even to the bottom of things, she accompanies and sustains all that she has made, so that the things made and created by her may not subsist without her. Yet among all things that subsist, from the highest to the lowest, each thing, insofar as it degenerates more from the perfect beauty and consummate loveliness of the highest things, [Col. 0185B] seems in a manner to flee from Wisdom and to withdraw farther from her.

But Wisdom herself follows the flight of things from end to end, because, abandoning nothing whatsoever among the things she has made, she orders each thing from the highest to the lowest with the beauty proper and fitting to its kind, and thus testifies that she is present even in these things. For she who arranged the most excellent of creatures in supreme and surpassing beauty likewise fits together the lower things in due sequence and follows them with her ordering, leaving nothing disordered even to the bottom of things.

Thus Wisdom reaches to the end, even to those things which are lowest in all things, because even in them something of her is found, although through the weakness of their created condition and the deficiency of their nature they have departed far from the highest things. Yet [Col. 0185C] Wisdom herself remains, as it were, abiding in the highest things; she reaches the lowest things, as it were, by making an excursion. For the former, subsisting immutably in their perfect beauty, nowhere fall away from her likeness. The latter, fleeing through deficiency, nevertheless show that Wisdom is also present to them by that very fact that they retain some beauty in their own kind.

Therefore Wisdom reaches everywhere, because in everything that exists there is something beautiful, and everything beautiful is the work of Wisdom. But whatever in that which exists is not beautiful is not the work of Wisdom. For she made what is beautiful in everything that exists; but what is not beautiful she did not make, though she permitted it in that which she made beautiful. Why, then, did she not make wholly beautiful that which she made? And why did she not make it so that what is not beautiful [Col. 0185D] should nowhere be in that which she made?

Perhaps she was wearied in making those earlier things in which she had produced a certain supreme and perfect beauty. Therefore afterward she continued with the rest as she could: indeed, making all that she made in them beautiful, but not making it the case that what she had not made but had permitted should not be beautiful in them, because she could not make it not exist altogether. Then, descending from one thing to another and making one thing after another, she always bestowed less beauty and loveliness upon the later works, because, in making the earlier things, she had more greatly exhausted both the strength of her power—by which she might have done more—and the force and ingenuity of her wisdom—by which she knew how to do more. Therefore the order of things, [Col. 0186A] descending downward, degenerated toward the lowest things. And unless Wisdom had provided for herself by finally setting a limit to her making in these things, perhaps there would have been no further beauty that she could have bestowed upon things yet to be made.

What are we saying? Then was the wisdom of God diminished in making? And did she, grown weak, carry her work through to its end? Where, then, is she who “reaches mightily from end to end”? If Wisdom reaches mightily from end to end, then the differing beauty of created things does not arise from a deficiency in the Maker. Why, then, are not all things equally beautiful, unless it is that all things together may be more beautiful?
