For if individual things were not differently beautiful, the universe would not be incomparably beautiful; because, if supreme beauty were in each individual thing—whichever of them were that excellent thing, [Col. 0186B] superior to all the rest—then every beauty would not be in the universe.

Therefore Wisdom reaches mightily from end to end, because she pursues her works even to the bottom of things in such a way that she also regulates the deficiency of the lower things toward the beauty of the whole universe. Thus the whole is more beautiful because, within the whole, certain things suffer deficiency in comparison with and relation to others. For this very thing that seems not beautiful in some of her beautiful works is nevertheless not ugly where it is; rather, it possesses less beauty in the part because it is beautiful with reference to that for which it exists in the whole. Therefore there is ugliness in no part; nevertheless, in some parts there is greater and in others lesser beauty, because the whole possesses the greatest beauty of parts precisely because beauty in the parts is differentiated, variously diversified, and distinguished in every way.

Then it follows and says: “Ordering all things sweetly.” For she orders all things sweetly because, in so many and such diverse kinds of things, leading each thing onward to its own end, she permits nothing to disturb the harmony and peace of the universe. Rather, she assigns to each what belongs to it in such a way that things running in unlike directions conduce toward one end, and that the operation, force, and effect of one does not impede another.

O Wisdom, how widely you are diffused, and yet are not dispersed! How far you stretch yourself, and yet suffer no deficiency! How great is your course, from the highest to the lowest! As far as heaven is distant from earth, and hell [Col. 0186D] beneath the earth—where the end of earth is, and beyond which there is no earth—as far as the highest is distant from the lowest, Wisdom penetrates the whole. Yet this way of Wisdom is short, this extension is direct; and she considers all that exists a small thing for herself to traverse, grasp, and penetrate. Nothing stretched out in space is far away, if it is near by goodness.

But wickedness is much more distant from justice, and farther by far than heaven is from earth and hell beneath the earth. For justice is higher than heaven, and not only than heaven, but even than those who are in heaven. The angels are in heaven, and have been in heaven from the beginning; and from there, by justice, they ascended above that which they had been created. Justice is higher than heaven; wickedness is deeper than hell. For it is deeper than everything that is lowest in creation, because what has fallen through wickedness [Col. 0187A] is beneath every creature; nor can anything be deeper than that than which nothing is worse.

Therefore, as much as one who ascends into heaven ascends, so much does one who advances toward justice ascend. And as much as one who descends into hell descends, so much does one who falls into wickedness descend. But as much as one who ascends from hell to heaven ascends, so much does one who returns from wickedness to justice ascend. And as much as one who descends from heaven to hell descends, so much does one who rushes from justice into wickedness descend.

“And in all these things they go up to the heavens and go down to the abysses, and their soul wastes away in evils” (Ps. 106 [107]). Therefore heaven belongs to justice, and hell to wickedness. The movements of souls are violently driven, by alternating fluctuation, as if by contrary winds, continually ascending and descending; and there arise exaltations, depressions, and great disturbances in that invisible sea of surging desires. A good spirit comes and impels upward. An evil spirit comes and impels downward; and they rise to the heavens and descend to the abysses, while their soul wastes away amid the uncertainty of their evils.

And what does he say? “If I ascend into heaven, you are there; if I descend into hell, you are present.” For if you ascend to the heaven of justice, you have Wisdom there with you, holding you lest you fall. But if you descend to the hell of guilt, Wisdom is there, seizing you lest you escape. Above, she has the right hand; below, [Col. 0187C] the left: reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly. Above she is strong; below she is strong; everywhere invincible. Above she is strong, so that she may preserve from evil those who trust in her, and cast down into evil, by abandoning them, those who presume upon themselves. Below she is strong, so that she may condemn those who despise her on account of evil and justify from evil those who repent.

See how many she has preserved on high, how many she has cast down from on high, how many she has raised from the depths, how many she has abandoned in the depths. Her judgments are manifest; and one who knows himself knows how Wisdom daily works all these things in the secret place of the human heart, ever presiding in judgment. By hidden recompense and invisible dispensation, examining merits, she now receives by grace, now abandons by justice; now spares by gentleness, now punishes by severity. And when she has abandoned, she receives again; and when she has received, she abandons again, so that man may not know his end and may walk anxiously throughout every time of his life: so that those who lie fallen may not despair, and those who stand may not presume.

If they are in the heaven of justice, let them fear a fall. If they are in the hell of guilt, let them seek mercy. Therefore justice itself first descended into hell, and afterward ascended into heaven: descending, that it might give hope to those to be freed; ascending, that it might show the way to those to be glorified. Thus Wisdom reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly. For she comprehends the end of each: namely, both of the good that is in her and likewise of the evil that is not in her. Yet what is from her falls away from her in that in which it is, but nevertheless not altogether without [Col. 0188A] her; because what nature does not produce from its own self, she restrains by power within what is her own.

For evil has no proper dwelling-place. It dwells as a stranger, alien by nature from its own proper place, in another’s possession; and thus it is evident that it does not exist in what is its own. For if there were no good things in which evil existed, evil would not exist at all. Since evil is nothing other than the corruption of good, and everything corrupted is good, one thing is that from which it falls away and another that in which it subsists. That in which it subsists is good; but its falling away from the good from which it falls away is evil. A falling away from good cannot exist anywhere at all except in that which subsists in some good.

Therefore, if there were no good, there would be no evil at all, because there would be nowhere in which wickedness could exist, if Wisdom—which did not make it—did not endure it within what is her own. For Wisdom [Col. 0188B] did not make wickedness; but she permitted wickedness to exist in that which she made, so that Wisdom, set in comparison with wickedness, might overcome it and appear more beautiful by comparison. For in her works Wisdom sets herself against and measures herself against wickedness, and overcomes it in both directions, so that she may reach from end to end. Wickedness, running toward deficiency, does not escape Wisdom; but Wisdom, rising toward progress, transcends wickedness.

Wickedness running toward deficiency does not escape Wisdom because wickedness itself cannot find anything to corrupt except in those things which Wisdom created. Wisdom, on the other hand, rising toward progress, transcends wickedness because wickedness cannot corrupt the whole of what Wisdom was able to create. Therefore, that wickedness may be compared with Wisdom, nothing can be brought to non-being by wickedness which did not receive being from Wisdom; but that wickedness may be overcome, wickedness does not corrupt the whole of what was made by Wisdom.

Therefore Wisdom runs, that she may reach from end to end: transcending wickedness in incorruptible goods, to which wickedness does not approach; and following wickedness in those things that are corrupted, where wickedness does not precede her. For wickedness cannot precede Wisdom, so that it may be found earlier than Wisdom’s arising; nor can it be found later, after Wisdom’s failure—because before corruption there is found that which at some time admitted corruption; and after corruption there is found that which could not be wholly corrupted; and above corruption there is found that to which corruption did not come.

And therefore Wisdom conquers wickedness and precedes folly, because she reaches from end to [Col. 0188D] end: that is, from the arising of all good, so as to transcend wickedness, even beyond the deficiency of a certain good, so as to enclose wickedness. In that in which every good at some time existed without corruption, Wisdom is recognized as prior. But in that good which is corrupted, because after corruption some good remains which cannot be wholly corrupted, Wisdom is found afterward.

Therefore Wisdom conquers wickedness because she reaches from the end in which every good received its beginning to the end in which even corrupted good, after the loss of good, subsists in some good. She reaches mightily from end to end in order to restrain wickedness itself by power within measure and confine it by reason within order, lest corruption should extend itself to the end, destroying everything, or confusion spread itself to the utmost limits, deforming everything.

Therefore she reaches strongly everywhere, subjecting wickedness to her dominion; and whatever corruption wickedness introduces toward confusion, Wisdom converts by a marvellous and hidden law of ordering toward the beauty of her works. From what is not beautiful she brings it about that what is beautiful becomes most beautiful, and that what is good in itself may, from that which is not good, rise to the perfection of goodness.

Therefore she reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly. Nothing is excepted from her sweetness. She orders all things sweetly. What things? Crooked and straight, good and evil, subject and adverse: she orders all things sweetly—not only good things, but evil things also; not only straight things, but crooked things also; not only subject things, but adverse things also. [Col. 0189B] She orders all things sweetly.

How sweetly? Do you wish to know how sweetly she orders all things? Without violence she subjects adversities; without disturbance she directs crooked things; and in her most peaceful kingdom, which justice holds within, she causes even evils and the motions of hostile vices to serve, without compulsion, by a hidden order and most wise ordering.

For she orders all things, even unsweet things, so sweetly that all things which rise up against her will she neither powerfully extinguishes so that they are nothing, nor violently compels so that they can do nothing. Rather, permitting them to exist and allowing them power, she openly permits things running against her will, and secretly guides them to fulfill her will. When evil persons will things against her, they will them without her; but when they can do what they will, they can do so from her. And when they do [Col. 0189C] what they can, they indeed suppose and will that they themselves do what she does not will; and yet they neither do, nor can do, anything other than what she wills.

For they are openly permitted and secretly guided, that they may be ordered sweetly. Wisdom reaches them mightily in order to confine them to her ordering, and orders them sweetly lest she compel them against their will. But even if she sometimes applies outward force by punishing or restraining wicked wills, she never abandons the sweetness of her ordering. For, remaining tranquil in herself, from that very source from which she disturbs the ill-ordered peace of those who oppose her, she establishes more firmly in peace the kingdom of her justice. Therefore she reaches mightily from end to [Col. 0189D] end and orders all things sweetly.

There remains now that greatest and highest course of Wisdom, from end to end: the ends that have no end. Above is the height of contemplation; below is the depth of damnation. These ends have no further ends by which they themselves may be ended; but all things made run as far as them, and beyond them there is nothing. Beginning from the middle, Wisdom orders and directs the course of all things toward these two ends, either by advancing or abandoning: laying justice as a road for those ascending upward, leaving wickedness as a road for those descending downward, so that by justice one may go to blessedness, but by wickedness and injustice one may come to damnation.

When this has been reached, she will set all things in their own ends; and the ends themselves will never have an end. Then Wisdom herself also will reach mightily from end to end, so that she may never again fail in the recompense of the righteous or cease from the punishment of the wicked, ordering all things sweetly: here toward joy, there toward eternal punishment.

But, I ask, what sweetness will there be in hell? What sweetness can there be in eternal torments, that it may be said, “ordering all things sweetly”? Is it sweetly for this reason: that she herself who orders remains sweet, although those whom she orders are not sweet, nor is that sweet in which she orders them? Yet how does she order sweetly? Is it because the ordering itself is sweet, even though the things she orders are not sweet? And just as she orders evils not evilly but well, so she orders unsweet and bitter things sweetly?

[Col. 0190B] For evils exist, and the good Almighty has permitted evils to be evil, not so that evil things may become gifts, but so that good may come from evils and that good things themselves may shine forth more beautifully in comparison with evils. This is not because good things are increased by evils added to them, but because they are commended by comparison with them. But who is wise enough to understand these things—what evils do in the kingdom of the Good? Yet, if they did nothing in the kingdom of Wisdom, evils would not exist at all.

Therefore evils do something for the sake of which they have been permitted to exist; and both evils themselves do good, and they themselves do not make good, but he makes good from those evils—he who knows how to use both good things and evil things for good. This is Wisdom, which reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly.

## Homily XII. On the passage, according to another translation: “The eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth,” where our text has: “The fool walks in darkness”; and on the remainder of chapter two.

[Col. 0190C]

Perhaps we have lingered longer in examining these matters than the brevity of a discourse demanded, though certainly not as long as the difficulty of the matter required. Since, then, we have found the end—and the ends—of which Scripture spoke when it said that Wisdom reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly; and since it was our purpose to seek these ends because of the ends of the earth, where are the eyes of fools who walk in darkness, lest perhaps Wisdom reaches the ends [Col. 0190D] of the earth—she who reaches from end to end—and light shines in darkness at the ends of the earth, if Wisdom reaches the ends of the earth, she who reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly: since, therefore, we have found these ends, provided that what we have said concerning them can fittingly apply its truth to the interpretation of Scripture, and that there is no other, higher interpretation to which this one ought rightly to yield, it remains to inquire who these ends of the earth are that have been mentioned, where they are, what this earth itself is, and where it is, at whose ends are the eyes of fools who do not look toward their head so that they may see and not walk in darkness.

Let us first inquire what this earth is and where it is. We know that in this world there are earth and heaven, [Col. 0191A] and that between earth and heaven is everything that is in this world. For in the body of this world heaven is highest and earth lowest; and just as above heaven there is nothing of this kind which is not in heaven itself, so beneath earth there is nothing, except perhaps what is in earth.

If we say of this earth that the eyes of fools are at its ends, how can this stand? For we would be declaring those eyes more sharp-sighted than blind whose sight, we affirm, is extended even to the ends of the earth. Which of the righteous could do this: survey the circuit of the earth with his eyes and traverse in one view such distant spaces as could scarcely be covered by the labor of many years? It is ridiculous even to think that Scripture said, concerning visible earth, “The eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth,” with reference to bodily sight.

Unless perhaps someone believes that these words signify that all fools and lovers of the carnal life, who always pursue earthly goods with the whole attention of their minds, range even to foreign nations, and often to the furthest ends of the lands, to acquire and seek them. For this reason they are said to have their eyes there: because in thought and desire they are always directed there. But the wise man, who lifts up his mind and directs his intention to the things above, has his eyes in his head because he directs himself toward attaining that which is highest and principal of all.

This interpretation could be introduced quite suitably, insofar as the truth of interpretation is concerned, if Wisdom did not call us to consider a higher understanding, another earth, other ends, and other eyes. For if the head of the wise man is rightly understood spiritually, it is necessary that we interpret earth also, and its ends on account of the eyes of fools, mystically and not bodily.

Therefore, just as this visible world has its own earth and heaven, so man has his own earth and heaven. For man himself is a world, and man has been called a lesser world. His earth is his flesh, and his heaven is his soul. But in this greater world the earth is within heaven; in the lesser world, however, heaven is within earth. Yet the heaven of the lesser world is greater than the heaven of the greater world. And what is its earth in comparison with that earth? How small it is! Yet its heaven is in its earth. What is heaven in earth? The soul in the body. The soul is heaven; the body is earth. The soul in the body: heaven in earth.

Yet heaven is always above and earth below. For just as this heaven is higher than earth by its place, so that heaven is more exalted than its earth by its nature. Therefore, in the greater world, the things that are in earth are beneath earth, and the things outside earth are above earth. In the lesser world, the things within are above, and those outside are below. What are the things within, and what the things outside? Invisible things are within; visible things are outside. Therefore invisible things are above, visible things below; invisible things are above our heaven, visible things below our earth. All earthly things are beneath our earth because they were made for its service and ordered for its ministry. Therefore our earth is above earth.

And what shall I say? [Col. 0192A] Is not our earth even above heaven? Did not he who took it from us for our sake carry it there and place it there? Therefore our earth is above heaven. Our earth was first, by nature, above earth; afterward, through guilt, our earth went into earth and beneath earth; but now, through grace, our earth has been raised above heaven. Therefore all earthly things are beneath our earth.

Nevertheless, this earth itself is joined and united by a kind of friendship with earthly things, just as heaven is joined and allied with heavenly things; earth extends as far as earthly things, and heaven as far as heavenly things. Therefore earthly things are the ends of earth, and heavenly things the ends of heaven; because earth extends to earthly things and no further, and heaven to heavenly things and no further. Earth stretches itself by desire toward earthly things, and heaven stretches itself by wisdom toward heavenly things. For, as the Apostle says, “the flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. 5). The spirit desires upward and the flesh desires downward; and therefore each stretches itself contrary to the other. When each has reached the point toward which it tends, there it makes its end and stretches itself no further.

Therefore the ends of earth are earthly things, toward which the earth of the flesh is drawn by carnal desire. Our earth indeed has another end, that of judgment, but it has no other end of desire. So far is it drawn by desire, but by judgment it is led farther. By desire, concupiscence stretches toward earthly things; but by judgment, after earthly things, it is led into earth, and after earth to Gehenna. By concupiscence to pleasure; after [Col. 0192C] pleasure to wickedness; after wickedness to death; after death to damnation. “Each person,” Scripture says, “is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire. Then desire, when it has conceived, gives birth to sin; and sin, when it has been completed, produces death” (Jas. 1). “He conceived pain and gave birth to wickedness. His pain shall return upon his own head, and his wickedness shall descend upon his crown” (Ps. 7).

Thus the delights of carnal pleasures are the ends of earth, and the delights of the flesh are followed by the death of the flesh. The death of the flesh, in turn, is followed by the punishment of damnation. Therefore the ends of earth have one end, death, by which they are received and consumed; but death has damnation as its end, by which it is received and consummated. For carnal delights are consumed by death, so that they are no longer; but the death of the flesh is consummated by damnation, so that it always is.

Fools who have their eyes at the ends of earth refuse to consider these ends. For they look only upon the first ends of earth, about earth itself, where earth itself ends, and do not look beyond to another end, where these ends themselves end. They direct their attention to the ends of their desire, not to the ends of their judgment. They open their eyes to the delight of their flesh and to the enticements of their pleasures, and do not consider what will follow afterward: the damnation of delight.

Therefore they are fools who make an end in the middle of the road, where there is no end, and do not foresee the end where there is an end. “The heart of fools is where there is joy, and the heart of the wise is where there is sorrow” (Eccl. [Col. 0193A] 7). And another Scripture says: “In all your works, throughout all the days of your life, remember your last things, and you will never sin” (Ecclus. 7). Therefore fools do not fear to sin because they look only to the delight of sin and do not look to what follows afterward, the damnation of that delight.

“The eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth; the eyes of the wise man are in his head.” What is the head of the wise man? Whatever is highest for each person is that person’s head. For the head is the highest part of a human being. Therefore the head of the wise man is that which is highest for the wise man. But what is highest for the wise man except that which is highest of all? For he would not be wise if he held as highest that which was not highest. Therefore the highest of all is the head of the wise man; and perhaps Wisdom itself is this head, which the wise man places before all things that seem to offer anything desirable and in comparison with which he despises everything.

And rightly so, because Wisdom is highest of all. It is itself the wise man’s head, because the very fact that he is wise comes from Wisdom, and all that he desires to be is in Wisdom. Therefore the wise man’s head is most rightly understood as Wisdom itself, because from it comes the origin of goodness and in it consists the consummation of every good.

Thus the highest of all is the head of the wise man, and this head is none other than Wisdom itself, because Wisdom is highest of all. Therefore the supreme good is the head, and the supreme evil is the end. For there are two realities: the supreme good and the supreme evil, [Col. 0193C] set opposite one another at either extreme; and from the middle all goods and evils run toward these two ends. Every good runs toward the supreme good, and every evil toward the supreme evil. For no good is truly good unless it leads to the supreme good, nor is any evil truly evil unless it runs toward the supreme evil.

Therefore every evil similarly tends toward the supreme evil, just as every good tends toward the supreme good. But not every evil comes from the supreme evil in the way that every good comes from the supreme good. For “every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights” (Jas. 1). But what of evils? “These,” he says, “are the beginnings of sorrows” (Matt. 24). Therefore every good is from the supreme good, and every good tends toward the supreme good. Likewise, every evil tends toward the supreme evil, but not every evil comes from the supreme evil.

Thus the supreme good of all goods is both head and end. The supreme evil of all evils is not a head but only an end. Therefore every good other than the supreme good is good only insofar as it leads to the supreme good; and every evil other than the supreme evil is evil only insofar as it leads to the supreme evil. For many have possessed these intermediate goods, and they were not true goods for them because through them they did not attain the supreme good. And many have endured grave intermediate evils, and they were not evils for them because through them they did not descend to the supreme evil. The former, lifted up by false goods, fell into the supreme evil; the latter, [Col. 0194A] exercised and humbled by false evils, advanced to the supreme good.

Therefore the wise man lifts his eyes to his head, and nothing below suffices for him until he comes to that which is highest. Some have had their eyes upward but have not raised them as far as their head; rather, they remained in the middle of the body. But what could the limbs do without the head? Could limbs severed from the head live? Thus every good without the supreme good is not true good.

You have seen a man abstaining from things forbidden by the law: committing no murder, adultery, theft, or false testimony; not coveting his neighbor’s property. And you have called him a good man, of good life and good conduct, worthy of praise and worthy of reward. [Col. 0194B] Yet how many have done these things and have not pleased God, because they did not do what they did for God’s sake; and therefore they did not do well, because they did not act for the sake of the supreme good.

You have seen another ascending still higher and doing greater good: not merely refraining from evil but exercising himself in good, fasting, praying, giving many alms, showing compassion to the wretched, helping those in distress and tribulation. And you have proclaimed him great and worthy of imitation, as if near to God and chosen by him. Yet many have done all these things and made no progress because they did not make God their purpose. They did not have their eyes in their head like the wise man; rather, bending them downward toward their own temptation, wishing to please either themselves or others, and glorying in their own good without God, [Col. 0194C] they lost their good and did not attain the supreme good.

For good reason they could not keep living limbs when they had severed the head from the body. Therefore the wise man’s eyes are in his head, so that he may first go before, by the intention and desire of his mind, toward the supreme good; then follow it by diligence and action; and finally attain it by recompense. Let him go before by intention, so that he may do everything he does in order to attain it; let him follow by diligence, so that he may persevere in it; let him attain it by recompense, so that he may receive it as his reward. In this manner, therefore, the eyes of the wise man are in his head.

Therefore, since our head was below, lest perhaps our own intention too should remain below [Col. 0194D] with us, the head ascended upward to the Head, that it might draw us after itself; and behold, above there are not two heads, but one Head. For Christ as man was a head below in the world, and God the Father was a Head above in heaven. Do you wish to know that Christ is the head? “The head of the woman is the man; the head of the man is Christ” (1 Cor. 11). And Christ has been appointed by God head of the whole Church. And what does the Church itself—Christ’s bride and Christ’s body—say concerning her bridegroom Christ and her head Christ? For it is this bride who, commending her beloved in the Song of Songs, after many such things and many others, adds this in his praise, saying: “His head is the finest gold” (Song 5). Therefore Christ is a head, and Christ has a Head. And what is Christ’s Head? Hear the Apostle: “The head of the woman is the man; the head [Col. 0195A] of the man is Christ; the Head of Christ is God” (1 Cor. 11). Thus God is Christ’s Head; and Christ himself, about to ascend into heaven, said: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20). Therefore, if he ascends to God, he ascends to his Head, because God is Christ’s Head. And this Head is that finest gold which no rust consumes and no age wears away, because immortal divinity admits no corruption.

Behold, then, our Head above is Christ, and our Head above is God; and Christ and God are our one Head, because Christ too is God, and Christ is the one God; and God is Christ’s Head, and Christ is one Head, and God is Christ’s Head—as Christ is one Beginning, and God is Christ’s Head: “I,” he says, “am the Beginning, I who also speak to you” (John 8) [Col. 0195B]. For this Beginning itself is our Head, to which the wise man raised his eyes: now fixing them upon him through faith, so that afterward he may be able to have his eyes upon him by beholding him face to face. Scripture exhorts us to raise our eyes to this Beginning and Head, saying: “If you have risen with Christ, set your minds on the things above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; seek the things above, not those upon the earth. For you have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3).

For where we have died, there we ought not to set our minds; but we ought to set our minds where we have life. If we are dead upon the earth, how do we set our minds upon the earth? For what dead person has perception? Therefore we ought to perceive where we have life; to be wise where our life is hidden with Christ in God, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God [Col. 0195C]. What is it to be wise? To love him is to be wise. For love itself is savor, and affection itself is wisdom. Therefore to love the things above is to be wise concerning the things above, because love itself draws one to the place where what is loved is; and meanwhile it has its own savor by which it is refreshed, until it reaches what it loves. Therefore, because that which is loved through wisdom is above, Wisdom itself draws upward. And because that which is loved through desire must necessarily draw downward, desire itself also draws downward.

Between that to which Wisdom draws upward and that to which desire draws downward there is, as it were, a division of darkness from light. Hearts that descend below fail from the light; but those that ascend are in the light [Col. 0195D]. For those who descend to vanity fail from truth, and those who fail from truth fail from light, because truth is light. The light itself does not fail; rather, they fail from the light when they become darkness, because darkness is not light and is not illuminated by light so as to shine. Yet the light itself shines even in darkness, but the darkness did not comprehend it (John 1), so as to receive it into themselves and become partakers of it, because darkness cannot share in the light.

These, therefore, are the darknesses in which fools walk: those who set their minds on earthly things and, not understanding their honor, “are compared with the senseless beasts and are made like them” (Ps. 48). For because, after the manner of beasts, they desire earthly things alone and seek heavenly things with no affection of mind, at length they are so blinded by the pleasure of the flesh and lulled by the allurements of delights that they cannot even consider from what goods they have fallen, nor foresee to what evils they are about to come [Col. 0196A]. What, then, are these persons doing except walking in darkness, since they are so blinded by perverse delight that they can neither know true goods nor foresee true evils? What darkness they suffer within, who do not see the present light and cannot recognize that good whose presence they cannot escape by any turning away! Why is this so, except because folly has blinded their eyes—eyes which they have fixed upon the ends of the earth, resolving within themselves to turn their eyes down toward the earth?

[Col. 0196B] But perhaps someone may think there is a contradiction between the statement here that the fool walks in darkness and the statement, as mentioned above, that the eyes of fools are said to be at the ends of the earth. For both seem to be asserted: that they see and that they do not see; although both can at the same time be true, that they see and do not see. For he who said, “The fool walks in darkness,” seems plainly to have said that the fool does not see. And again, he who said, “The eyes of fools are at the ends of the earth,” seems to have said that they see something, namely the things that are at the ends of the earth. How, then, do they walk in darkness if they see? And how do they not see if they see the things that are at the ends of the earth?

But it must be understood that fools are not said to walk in darkness because they see nothing. They do see the things that are at the ends of the earth [Col. 0196C]; rather, they are so called because, whether in the things which they see or in those which they do not see, they do not see truth. For they see visible things by intention and desire, but they do not see invisible things. And in the things which they see, they suppose a good to be present which is not present; while in the things which they do not see, they do not know that the good which truly exists is there. Thus they see truth nowhere, and therefore walk in darkness even amid the things which they see.

For the delight of the flesh and the enticement of pleasure have blinded their hearts so that they do not see truth. Since the mind, intoxicated by false sweetness, thinks only of what appears sweet and pleasant in the present, it can neither remember how great is the sweetness of those goods from which it has fallen by its own turning away, nor foresee how great is the bitterness of the evils to come, toward which the downfall of its headlong course is always rushing [Col. 0196D].

And observe how the sequence of this true statement follows. Above, this man, having considered the vanity of worldly things and despised them all, transferred himself to the contemplation of wisdom, saying: “I passed over to contemplate wisdom, errors, and folly.” Then, considering that a human being’s true wisdom is nothing other than to seek true goods and to love the things above, where our King is—who went before us by ascending there, in order to show us where we should follow—he also observed how difficult it is to raise to the desires of eternal things a mind accustomed to earthly delights. He added and said: “What is man, that he should be able to follow his King and Maker?” You see, however [Col. 0197A], that he gave, as it were, a definitive judgment concerning good and evil: hearts which immerse themselves in carnal delights are darkened from the light of truth. He said: “I saw that wisdom so far surpasses folly as light differs from darkness.” Then, commending the pursuit of the one over the other, he finally added: “The wise man’s eyes are in his head, but the fool walks in darkness.”

Therefore let the concluding statement return and say: It is indeed difficult for a mortal human being to raise to contemplation of heavenly Wisdom a heart oppressed by earthly desires. Yet because wisdom is light, and all who fail from its contemplation are in darkness, it is necessary that even mortal man, insofar as ability allows, apply himself to the pursuit and investigation of Wisdom. For this is human wisdom in this life: to seek and investigate Wisdom [Col. 0197B]. To find Wisdom and perfectly grasp truth, however, has not been granted to this life but is reserved for the life to come.

Nevertheless, this inquiry into Wisdom now has its own light, by which it distinguishes those who love and seek Wisdom from those who love folly and walk in darkness. But the carnal mind, loving the pleasantness of visible light, judges the labor of seeking inward light to be vain, because it either doubts or altogether does not know that its brightness remains unquenchable in holy minds after this light has been taken away. For because it sees wise and foolish alike, by equal lot and similar condition, deprived of this visible light after the death of the flesh, it becomes doubtful even about the light of Wisdom [Col. 0197C], whether it can itself be preserved unquenchably in holy minds after the death of the flesh. Therefore, although it recognizes the pursuit of Wisdom as good and praiseworthy, it nevertheless doubts whether it ought to be purchased at so great a labor, since as yet no unquestionable reasoning has shown it whether its fruit can be everlasting.

This man therefore, seeing this wavering of the human heart within himself by contemplation of truth and feeling it through the affection of common weakness, also adopts it as a statement, showing how reflection upon mortal life itself recalled him from the pursuit of wisdom which he had sought and seen; and why he had judged the advancement of others in wisdom to be wholly vain: because, in paying the debt of death, he recognized himself to be equal to the rest. This is what he says, suddenly turning after his praise of Wisdom and commendation of its pursuit to consideration of common weakness:

“I learned that the same end is for both.” For, seeing that both the wise and the foolish are removed from this life by one and the same destruction of death, he began also to doubt whether, after this life, differing rewards according to the differing conduct of this life ought to be found. And if this is established as true, why do those who will not attain one reward after this life depart from this life by one road? But if, just as there is one passage for all, there is likewise one arrival for all, why should they run with unequal labors before death [Col. 0198A], when, departing by a like death, they would not arrive at unlike reward after death?

This is what follows: “And I said in my heart: If the same downfall shall befall both the fool and me, what does it profit me that I have given greater effort to wisdom?” For among those who believe that this life alone exists, the pursuit of Wisdom is judged wholly vain, because its labor belongs to the present life, while the reward and fruit of its labor belong to the future. Therefore, because they see the labor, they quickly grow weary of that labor and readily turn to those things which, though wisdom teaches are by no means to be sought, they judge more advantageous because their fruit is present.

But because Wisdom does not permit its labor to be wholly fruitless even in this life, and refreshes those who follow it with great inward consolation and, through the illumination of truth, persuades them amid this misery of mortality to have confidence in the reward of eternity, this man, immediately after beginning to doubt the fruit of everlasting life because of the failure of carnal life, accuses himself out of his deepest reflection for that same doubt, saying:

“And, speaking with my mind, I perceived that this too was vanity.” And immediately, adding the reason why he declares the doubt mentioned above to be vain, he introduces the vanity itself in relation to the truth by which it could have entered into doubt, saying:

“For there shall not be an eternal remembrance of the wise man in the same manner as of the fool.” For Wisdom, which does not take away mortality from the present life, grants eternity to the life to come [Col. 0198C]. And although the wise and the fool are in like condition at the departure from this life, their remembrance will not be alike in the life to come. As their differing manner of life separates them here, so there also, when they are recalled in order to be brought to judgment, a recompense differing according to their merits will divide them. Future times will not cover all things with oblivion; rather, at their time all deeds shall come into remembrance, so that every work, whether good or evil, may be summoned to judgment. Therefore the wise man’s remembrance will not forever be like that of the fool, and future times will not cover all things with oblivion, because, when the time comes, the one will receive glory for the merit of his virtue, and the other punishment for the transgression of his folly [Col. 0198D].

This, then, is why it is not vain to avoid folly and give greater effort to wisdom: when the reward of recompense is received, the greatness of the fruit of righteous labor becomes manifest. Yet this very consideration of our mortality has a certain just weariness, because it is fitting that a person should despise what he sees to be transitory even before it ends, and should not afflict himself with vain labor to acquire that which cannot endure long. For this reason he repeats his statement concerning the same equal condition of mortality, saying:

“The learned man dies in the same way as the unlearned; and therefore my life wearied me.” Such a life rightly becomes wearisome, because, being wholly subject to disorder, it does not distinguish the good from the evil or the worthy from the unworthy, either in its goods while it seems to endure or in its evils when it ends [Col. 0199A]. Its goods come without distinction to the unworthy as well as to the worthy, and its evils afflict good and evil alike by equal lot and the same outcome.

Hence even the goods of this life rightly become objects of contempt to the righteous: they afflict with varied pains those who labor for them, and, though often sought with great toil, pass without benefit to their possessors from good persons to evil and from their own owners to strangers. Considering this, he places in one category and judges with the same assessment not only those things of this life that appear evil, but also those which wear the appearance of good though they are in fact evil, and he gives one verdict on them all, saying:

“Seeing all things under the sun to be evil, and all things vanity and affliction of spirit [Col. 0199B], I again detested all my industry.” And lest you suppose that he here detests that industry by which he gave greater effort to Wisdom, rather than that by which he was occupied with those things under the sun which are vain, he immediately explains what industry he judges detestable, saying: “And that at which I labored most earnestly under the sun.” “I detested” is understood. He then immediately discloses why he detests both this industry and their industry alike, adding:

“Because I shall have an heir after me, whom I do not know whether he will be wise or foolish; and he shall rule over my labors, in which I have sweated and taken anxious care.” Finally, affirming his judgment concerning this, he adds:

[Col. 0199C] “And is anything so vain?” As though he said: I judge nothing so vain as this: one person, gathering greedily, is worn out by fruitless labor, while another, living idly and luxuriously, rules over the labors of another. For vanity is manifold where one person is afflicted without cause and another takes unlawful pleasure. The first vanity is to desire what will not profit; the second, to gather what passes away; the third, to leave to others—and especially to persons whose future character we do not know—the possession of things acquired by our labor. For if all these things would be vain even when sought and retained for our own use, what will they be when transferred to the pleasure of fools? Thus he says:

“I ceased, and my heart renounced further labor under the sun.” Repeating the reason why he ceased from labor, he adds:

“For when one man labors in wisdom, teaching, and anxious care, he leaves what he has acquired to an idle man.” This happened to Solomon himself, who labored in wisdom, teaching, and anxious care, gathered riches and amassed wealth, and at last left everything for a foolish heir to possess. For he left behind as heir to his folly his son Rehoboam, who, succeeding to his father’s wealth, squandered everything and left his father’s kingdom—which he had received amply great and splendid—divided and troubled through deficiency of judgment and satiety of heart [Col. 0200A].

But many also labor in wisdom, teaching, and anxious care, investigating with great toil and application the secrets of nature and the hidden things of truth, and transmitting their discoveries by speech and writing to the memory of posterity, so as to commend their studies. Yet they often leave what they have sought to idle persons, because subsequent negligence sometimes refuses to take up for use what the shrewd diligence of earlier persons acquired only with great labor and care.

“This, therefore, is vanity, a great evil.” It is vain to labor in the knowledge of truth in order that we may come to the notice of those who neither wish to receive truth for its own sake nor know how to approve it in others. Such labor is not followed by fruit, because the laborer gathers neither what will profit himself nor persons who, when the things gathered are left to them, are incited by any emulation of virtue to the pursuit of good. For if there is labor for the seeker and no benefit for the recipient, what profit is such labor? [Col. 0200B] And it is a great evil that one person is worn down by labor while another idly and unlawfully abuses that for which he labored. It is a great evil because the former gathers to his own harm and the latter receives to his own harm. Therefore this is vanity and a great evil.

“For what profit does a man have from all his labor and affliction of spirit by which he has been tormented under the sun?” If it profits for nothing else, it profits nothing; indeed, if it profits for nothing else, it does much harm, because the search brings great punishment, but discovery brings no fruit. For what punishment is there in never being without punishment?

“All his days are full of pains and miseries, nor does his mind rest even by night.” Very miserable is the person who cannot have quiet even during the time naturally allotted to rest. By day he is worn down by labor; by night he is tormented by concern and anxiety about his labor [Col. 0200C]. The strain and restlessness of labor harass him while awake, and burden him while asleep in his mind by images and phantasms of dreams. Thus no time is left for repose: the whole is occupied by pain and labor, and nothing is gained for usefulness or salvation.

“And is not this vanity?” Truly it is vanity, and indeed great vanity. But what then? If this is vanity, what ought to be done?

“Is it not better,” he says, “to eat and drink and show his soul good things from his labors?” If the labors that confer no benefit upon those who labor are vain [Col. 0200D], then it is better to labor and receive the fruit of one’s labors. The argument seems plain, but it admits many objections. It would be much better if it had been said differently and were everywhere found to be true: If labors from which no fruit comes to the laborers are vain, then labors of that kind ought wholly to be set aside, and one should labor rather at things in which a sure and true fruit comes to the laborer.

But now, by this reasoning, vanity has been changed, not abandoned; one vanity has succeeded another, but not all vanity has departed. Vain anxiety is rebuked so that the mind, made wrongly secure, may relax into shamefulness through sloth, idleness, and lack of self-control. For if the person who exhausts himself in superfluous labor is rightly considered blameworthy, why is the person who abandons himself to pleasure and intemperance thought pleasing on that account? But the carnal mind finds the mean of truth with difficulty; and therefore it sometimes willingly agrees to abandon one vice because it sees that through it a path is opened to another vice that pleases it more [Col. 0201A]. And it pours itself all the more boldly, with its entire intention, into the opposite course in proportion as it holds more certainly that the evil it abandons is evil.

Now it judges itself not merely deserving of no blame in its own evil, but even praiseworthy; and, while it manifestly commits evil, it wishes to appear not to do evil but rather to avoid evil. For it does not consider that, in avoiding one vice, it has fallen into another; and therefore it does not think that what it does ought to be marked unfavorably as evil, because in it it is striving, as it were, not so much to do evil as to avoid evil.

Thus here also, when he saw that those who greedily gather with labor and anxiety riches which will not profit them, and neither use what they possess nor leave it after themselves for others to possess and enjoy, are miserable and blameworthy, he freely throws himself into the contrary judgment in order to avoid their folly, saying: “Is it not better to eat and drink and show his soul good things from his labors?” There is one judgment shared by all who are inclined toward vice: they always condemn the opposite faults in order to commend their own. “Let the greedy perish,” says the glutton and spendthrift; then he devours, becomes drunk, expands and fills himself even to suffocation. “Let the greedy perish” is always his proverb. And he thinks himself commended because he is not such a person, lest he be blameworthy for being the sort of person he is [Col. 0201B].

Indeed, for this very reason he wants to appear the sort of person he is, lest perhaps he be the sort whose character he accuses others of having and does not wish himself to have—as though there were no middle course in which both might be possible: both not to be the kind of person whose character he accuses others of having and not, nevertheless, to be the kind of person he exults, with shameless boasting, to be.

“Better to eat and drink and show his soul good things from his labors.” How attractive are the words “to eat” and “to drink”! Who recoils when he hears “to eat and drink,” or thinks that anything contrary to moderation or chastity is being said here? Yet shameless disgrace lies hidden, covered by a veil of chastity. Let him say openly, then: “It is better to devour, become drunk, and serve the desires of one’s lust with unbridled freedom.” If he had said it thus, what sort of statement would it be? And yet he said precisely this, because that is what he intended to signify by saying: “It is better to eat and drink and show his soul good things from his labors” [Col. 0201C].

“And this is from the hand of God.” This is what certain persons say—the kind of people who are accustomed to say: “Let us devour, become drunk, and do good to ourselves from what God has given us, because this is from the hand of God; for these things too were given to us so that we might do good to ourselves. Why were all these things made except for human use, so that people might use them and fare well in the things God has given them?” In saying these things they become blind and are carried away without measure, abandoning chastity to their pleasures so that they may applaud themselves because God made all these things to be used. Yet they neither know nor consider that, although God made all good things for use [Col. 0202A], he made nothing for depraved and disordered uses.

“Who will devour and abound in delights as I do?” This is evil boasting. Yet there are those who glory in such things, and Wisdom ought not to have passed them by in the catalogue of vanities. Elsewhere the prophet rebukes such persons, saying: “Woe to you who are mighty at drinking wine, and strong men at mixing drunkenness” (Isa. 5). “Who will devour and abound in delights as I do?” What sort of lover of wisdom is this? How far has this mind turned backward—indeed, how far turned away and perverted from the one who shortly before saw the light of wisdom and, by so subtle a reflection, distinguished it from the darkness of folly, saying: “I saw that wisdom surpasses folly as light differs from darkness.”

Whence do you suppose this understanding was so quickly cast down [pessimatus; variant pessundatus, “sunk”] [Col. 0202B]? Or did he not say on his own account what he said about himself, namely that he was a lover of wisdom—and was this not what he said, but rather did he intend to signify certain persons like this, saying about himself what he said on their account? Or was all this in some respect truly also his own experience, and yet did he not cease to be a lover of wisdom for that reason: because in one person at the same time the sense of the flesh, in accordance with inborn corruption and the sin dwelling within him, urged wickedness, while the spirit, according to its affection for virtue and its judgment of uprightness, loved wisdom?

But see nevertheless what man is, whether in the person who said this and was such a person, or in those for whose sake he said about himself what he said, intending to indicate that they were such persons. See, indeed, what man is. “Who will devour and abound in delights as I do [Col. 0202C]?” “Why do you glory in malice, you who are mighty in iniquity?” (Ps. 51). If no one can do what you can do, it is a great thing if he can do good. But if you are more able in evil, why do you glory? For ability to do evil is not power but weakness.

“Who will devour and abound in delights as I do?” “For who,” he says, “can contradict, when God commands this? For God created gladness and wished that those who please him should rejoice in it.”

“But to the sinner he gave affliction and superfluous care, that he may labor, exhaust himself, and gather, not to possess, but to hand over to him who pleases God.” Thus, good things to the good and evil things to the evil. Consider how great this perversity is. “Iniquity lied to itself” (Ps. 26) [Col. 0202D]. Iniquity lied about itself and lied about God; yet it lied only to itself. Iniquity said: “Good things to the good and evil things to the evil” (Ecclus. 39). And where is: “Mercy and truth have met together” (Ps. 84)? Where is: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 118)? Where is: “You will save men and beasts, O Lord; how you have multiplied your mercy, O God!” (Ps. 35)? Finally, where is what Truth itself and Mercy say: “Be merciful, as your Father is merciful, who makes his sun rise upon good and evil, and rains upon the just and unjust” (Matt. 5)?

If good things alone are given to the good, what does Scripture say concerning the good: “The furnace tests the vessels of the potter, and the furnace of tribulation tests righteous men” (Ecclus. 27)? [Col. 0203A] And: “All who desire to live godly lives in Christ must suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3). “They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, naked, distressed, afflicted, of whom the world was not worthy” (Heb. 11). “In hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness” (2 Cor. 11).

Thus iniquity lied about God when it said that God gives good things only to the good and evil things only to the evil. For he gives good things to the good and evil things to the evil; he also gives evil things to the good and good things to the evil. He gives good things to the good that they may be sustained, and evil things that they may be tested; he gives evil things to the evil that they may be corrected, and good things that they may be invited. Thus iniquity lied about God when it said: God gives good things to the good and evil things to the evil. But it would have spoken truly if it had spoken of true goods and true evils: that true goods are good only to the good, and true evils evil only to the evil [Col. 0203B]. Therefore iniquity lied about God.

But iniquity also lied about itself. When did iniquity lie about itself? When it called itself goodness; then iniquity lied about itself, because iniquity is not goodness. And where did iniquity call itself goodness? When it said: “Who will devour and abound in delights as I do?” Then it called itself goodness. For this is what iniquity said, because this is the speech of iniquity and impurity, opposed to goodness and honesty. Therefore iniquity said this, and in saying it called itself goodness, because it said that the act it declared it would perform belonged to goodness alone, presuming itself to be goodness. For it said:

“God gave to the good man, in his sight, wisdom and knowledge and gladness.” First he gave wisdom and knowledge so that he might understand and know how to seek gladness in his sight [Col. 0203C], because God made it so that those who please him might rejoice in it. As though it were not wisdom—and far greater wisdom—to seek and embrace the sorrow that is according to God rather than foolish gladness, when Scripture says to the contrary: “The heart of fools is where gladness is, and the heart of the wise is where sorrow is” (Eccles. 7).

It is indeed true that God prepared gladness in his sight for his chosen ones and placed wisdom and knowledge in their hearts, so that they might know and understand how to seek it where it is. But this is not the gladness in which those who do evil rejoice, “who exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2). For that gladness is not in his sight, because Scripture says concerning those who embrace it: “You shall set them below; in your remnants you shall prepare their face” (Ps. 20). Therefore God gave gladness to the good man, but the gladness which is in his sight. Of this it is written: “Let the righteous feast and exult in the sight of God; let them delight in gladness” (Ps. 67) [Col. 0203D]. And again: “Visit us with your salvation, to see the goodness of your chosen ones, to rejoice in the gladness of your people, that you may be praised with your inheritance” (Ps. 105). And again he says: “You will fill me with gladness with your countenance; delights are at your right hand unto the end” (Ps. 15). God therefore gave this gladness to the good man in his sight.

“But to the sinner he gave affliction and superfluous care,” not by inflicting wickedness, but by descending into wickedness in a most evil occupation.

[Col. 0204A] “That he may add and gather and hand it over to him who pleased God.” Yet it is so because the one gathered riches through avarice, while the other dispersed what he received for the use of mercy. Otherwise neither is the one who gathered rightly blamed nor the one who possesses commended. But now all things are said perversely when it is said that the person who devours and abounds in delights is good, and that God gave him wisdom, knowledge, and gladness in his sight, though it was said above that fools are those whose eyes are at the ends of the earth, looking toward earthly pleasures and serving the pleasure of the flesh.

Thus iniquity lied when it said that pleasure is the reward of righteousness and that the fruit of wisdom consists in it, and when it thought bodily delights to contain the summit of happiness. But false judgment cannot stand long in glory [Col. 0204B]. Truth comes forth and prostrates falsehood. For he says:

“But this too is vanity and empty anxiety of mind.” What is this? Not only that the sinner should add and gather and not possess is vanity and empty anxiety; but it is also vanity and empty anxiety for the righteous person to seek and desire the sinner’s riches or, if he receives them, to set his heart upon them. Therefore it is altogether vanity and empty anxiety, because nothing beneath the sun can remain for the person who uses or seeks riches, pleasures, joy, and gladness. For all things pass and flow away, and nothing beneath the sun endures, so that the sentence may be fulfilled: “Vanity of vanities, vanity of vanities, and all is vanity” (Eccles. 1).

For vanity is also fulfilled in this: the human heart itself does not remain in the same condition [Col. 0204C], but always carries itself away from itself into what is other than itself, hostile to itself and alien, always drawing away from what is into what is not; and it passes and is swept along in the greatest vanity, whether from vain things to true things or from true things to vain things—vain and unstable everywhere, now desiring the highest things, now plunging itself into the lowest. There it approves truth; here it prefers vanity.

And now, contemplating the whole human race in one person, we see this greatest fluctuation of the human mind and wonder how the understanding of mortals is so swiftly submerged, and, after so sublime a contemplation of truth, allows itself to go into the alien shamefulness of disgrace. From this, indeed, no other understanding is given except that we should recognize our miserable vanity; and that in the fact that we attain high things and approve better things, we should consider what man has been made by nature, while in the fact that we desire things so miserable and abject, we should understand what man has become through his fault. Thus we may at least begin to be partakers of truth in this: that we truly recognize our own vanity [Col. 0204D].

## HOMILY XIII. How all things have their own time.

Many are the utterances of a human being, because the human heart is not one. For unless the mind first scattered itself inwardly from the fountain of truth among many desires, speech would never flow outward in so many assertions. But now, because the governing soul is divided [Col. 0205A] from the love of virtue through diverse desires into a craving for vanity, the tongue outwardly serves that same vanity by variable and inconstant judgment expressed in words. Therefore Solomon, while disputing concerning vanity, changes his opinion so often in his discourse, plainly in order to show a mind altered in thought through love of vanity. For the human heart which is not fixed in the desire of eternity can never be stable, because it is shaken from its steadiness as often as it is moved, by the heat of carnal desires, from those things to which it had clung in love toward desiring others.

For because it seeks the fruit of eternity in the use of transient things, and thinks that it finds the joy of happiness [Col. 0205B] in things made only for consolation in time, whenever experience teaches it that in things already possessed it has found either false pleasure or real misery, it immediately turns itself to seek other things, as though better, by which it may either lessen its pain or fill up its pleasure. Hence it always desires what is future and disdains what is present. Thus, in a certain remarkable way, one who is always deceived in the desire for the future is scarcely ever wholly deceived in the experience of present things. A human being is witness against himself that these very things which he loves are not true goods; for while he always longs in mind for future things and never recognizes himself as truly happy in what he enjoys, he thereby clearly proves that all these things, though fools may seek them as supreme happiness when they do not possess them, can never, when possessed, be held as supreme happiness.

[Col. 0205C] Yet the carnal mind, blinded by the darkness of its own desire, cannot clearly see what it cannot altogether fail to know: although it always perceives vanity in the experience of present things, it nevertheless never restrains itself from craving future things. It condemns what it has experienced and praises what remains to be experienced; and the more immoderately it pours itself out through desire toward things which it does not yet possess, the more heavily it is afflicted, through the loss of things it already has. Ecclesiastes has thus far expressed this fluctuation of the human mind in himself, changing his judgment so often in approving things, whether through disgust with present things or desire for future ones, as his mind changed.

For he thought [Col. 0205D] that among things revolving under time he would find something stable in which his mind could rest; and so, testing one thing after another, as it were, and condemning everything he had tested, he finally recognized that among all things there is nothing which can either remain perpetually for those who enjoy it or, while present, yield the full fruit of delight. Therefore, now reproving his own ignorance because he had believed that he could possess lasting joy in mutable things, he shows that, just as all things—not only prosperity but adversity also—are good in their proper time to one who uses them well, so even prosperity itself cannot confer true happiness upon those who perversely love temporal things as eternal and hope to become happy in them.

He therefore acted wrongly when he chose certain things among them [Col. 0206A] as though preferable to all others for delight. For the strong-minded person, hastening through temporal things toward the state of eternity, not only seeks the prosperity of this world meanwhile for consolation, but also willingly takes adversity into use, when the time requires it, for the exercise of virtue. And therefore, having tested all things by experience, he finally recognizes the condition of mutable things and confesses that nothing among all things which pass away can remain forever, saying:

> **(ECCLES. V.) “Everything has its time, and all things under heaven pass through their allotted intervals.”**

Why, then, do you either fear this world’s evils or desire its goods, when all things under heaven pass away? Rather, let this accord with truth: that in none of these things, whether good or bad, should you regard anything as supreme, because all things pass away [Col. 0206B]. Nor should you judge anything to be rejected in its proper time, because all things are justly ordered. For everything has its time, and all things under heaven pass through their allotted intervals.

Everything has its time, so that nothing may be found perpetual and always enduring. Rather, everything which exists either follows something else, so that it does not come from the beginning, or something else precedes it, so that it does not extend itself to the end. All things also have a fixed and determined time: when they begin and when they end; likewise, how long they endure, and when each thing endures, so that nothing may be without reason. And the prudent mind should endeavor to accommodate itself both to times and to temporal things, so that it may neither place its confidence in things that pass away as though they were permanent, nor presume to murmur against the Creator’s ordering in things that are well ordered [Col. 0206C].

In every event, conforming itself to true and enduring goods, it should so despise the variety of mutable things that, although it uses each thing for a time while it is present, it nevertheless never permits its mind to decline from its own steadfastness when that thing passes away. For that person is most prudent who knows how to turn passing things to use, yet does not know how to bend his mind from its stability when they fail. For all things are good in their proper time to one who uses them well; and yet all things subject to change, though they may provide some consolation in misery, cannot confer ease.

Therefore nothing is to be rejected in its proper time, and nothing chosen outside its proper time; but the mind should be prepared for the use of time in such a way that it is not changed by time’s mutability. Everything has its time, and all things under heaven pass through their allotted intervals. Why, then, should one thing be chosen for every time, when all things have their time? If one thing among all things had every time, then not all things would have their time. For if, among two contrary and mutually opposed things, it were time for one always to exist, it would be time for the other never to exist. Thus that other would have no time, since that with which it could not share the same time would have every time.

Now, therefore, because all things have their time, no single thing among them has every time; but each has its own time: a time when it is good that it should be, and a time when it is good that it should not be. [Col. 0207A] When it has time, it is good that it should be, even if the thing which it is good should be is not itself good; and when it has no time to be, it is good that it should not be, even if that which it is good should not be is good.

Job understood this. He received good things, praising God for His gifts; and the enemy supposed that the holy conscience was subject to time. He took away his riches and resources; he killed his children; he struck his flesh; he provoked him with reproaches and injuries, seeking to break by adversity one whom he could not soften by prosperity. But Job, knowing that everything has its time, restrained himself in good things through self-control, and likewise endured adversity courageously in evil things through patience.

His wife, however, being foolish and not understanding that everything has its time, thought that the rewards of merits should be measured by moments of time. Seeing him stricken and believing him abandoned, she reproached him for having worshiped God in vain and mocked him as though he had deserved scourges in return for his blessing, saying: “Now bless God, and die” (Job 2). He answered her: “You have spoken as one of the foolish women. If we receive good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not receive evil things?” (ibid.).

For everything has its time, and all things under heaven pass through their allotted intervals. If there is a time in which the weak are cherished by prosperity, there is also a time in which the perfect are exercised by adversity. If there is a time in which good things come to the good and evil things to the evil for the sake of truth, there is also a time in which evil things come to the good and good things to the evil for testing. Everything has its time, and all things under heaven pass through their allotted intervals.

[Col. 0207C] Why do you complain, being under time, about all the laws of time? It belongs to time to be subject to mutability and to suffer alternation. For if all these things do not happen in time, when are they to happen? Beyond times will be eternity, and there will be no mutability; there, then, it will not be said, “Everything has its time,” but whatever exists will exist in such a way that it cannot be one thing at one time and another at another time: what exists will always exist.

Therefore, as long as you live under time, endure the laws of time. Endure willingly, lest perhaps, even if unwilling, you nevertheless endure them. Endure the laws of time so that you may pass through time to the state of eternity. For one cannot find eternity in time, because eternity comes only after times. Those find eternity after times who, in the flow of alternating times, remain unchangeable in mind, fixed in the desire of eternity [Col. 0207D].

Everything has its time, and all things under heaven pass through their allotted intervals. For heaven itself measures the intervals of all times; all things under heaven pass through time; yet heaven itself, from which time comes, does not pass away. It is as though time comes from heaven, while in heaven there is no time; and although all things under heaven receive time from heaven, eternity nevertheless abides in heaven itself. A visible image of wisdom is a great spectacle, so that by contemplating visible things we may be stirred to emulate invisible things.

Look at heaven. It seems to move, yet it does not seem to change. But the things under heaven change; and there is the source of all motion where there is no mutability [Col. 0208A]. Thus all things pass away under heaven because all things stand firm in heaven. Even things that pass away measure their being from those things which endure, because the passing things would not have a stable continuance unless the state of enduring things were perpetual.

For those things which truly are always are, and are always what they are. There are other things which truly are not, and yet in some manner imitate those things which truly are, in order to be something in what they are. When they begin to be what they are, they pass into what they are not. They are not truly what they are, because they cease to be this; and they are not yet truly what they begin to be, because they only begin to be it and are not yet so. Thus these things wander in true being; and, in the very passing through which they run, they seem to participate in a being which they do not grasp or comprehend, though they seem to touch it, lest they be altogether nothing.

For they appear there, and when sought, they are not there, because they have gone back into the nothingness from which they came and were not from that in which they had been [Col. 0208B]. That in which they were alone truly was; and all that it was, it was of itself, nor had it received from elsewhere what it was. In it all these things were admitted, so that, from the fact that it truly was, these also might be something. Therefore, to the degree that all these things which do not possess true being in themselves participate in true being, to that degree they are; for their whole being consists in their being that which possesses true being.

And though in itself it is one, yet in them, according to the capacity of the participants, it appears to be something different, since they themselves are different in that in which there is no difference. Thus each thing has, according to participation in that which always is, greater or lesser intervals of subsistence, according as they are in that which is neither greater nor lesser, but is always itself the same [Col. 0208C]. Thus there is assigned and measured out to each its own interval and its own time: to one brief, to another long. There are days, months, years, lustra, ages, short hours, moments, and instants. All these are time in things that pass away and truly are not; but in that from which they have what they are, they are one, and there they are found not as time but as eternity.

Everything has its time, and all things under heaven pass through their allotted intervals. For among all things under heaven nothing is eternal; rather, all things are subject to time and mutability. All things at some time had a beginning and at some time will have an end. Between beginning and end lies the interval of time: it is time for that which has a beginning and an end, but eternity for that which has neither beginning nor end.

For that which began was not before it began; and when it ceased to be, it was no longer. Then it was nothing, because it was nothing. Yet even then, that which always was existed; and that same thing afterward existed when this thing existed. What began began in it; what existed existed in it as long as it existed. When this, which did not always exist, existed, that which always existed also existed, because this existed in it. For this, there was time, because it did not always exist; for that, there was eternity, because it always existed. Thus all things derive time from eternity, and all things under heaven pass through their allotted intervals [Col. 0209A].

They have time when they begin and time when they end. They have intervals during which they are to endure: this interval is the delay of subsistence between beginning and end. The intervals of many are alike and of many unlike; yet all are balanced by equal judgment. When delay occurs for those who live in joy and gladness and spend their days in prosperity, it appears to be great happiness. When long intervals stretch out for those in distress and worn down by adversities, it is judged to be great misery and great unhappiness. Yet a human being does not know his own lot and cannot search out God’s judgment concerning himself.

For even these long times have an end; and when they have come to an end, those things that seemed good no longer exist. Likewise, those things thought evil no longer exist [Col. 0209B]. Often, enduring evils succeed passing goods; and after passing evils have ended, goods without end succeed. Then former goods can be of no help amid a multitude of evils, and former evils can do no harm to those happily brought to completion amid an abundance of goods.

Therefore let no one glory beforehand in his allotted time, nor let one who is in tribulation be broken by adverse times. For all things pass away until the time comes when, in eternity, there is recompense for everything prolonged through the intervals of times, whether greater or lesser. Then the long intervals of time will not please the ungodly, when their temporal happiness has passed and they see eternal punishments for temporal deeds, while the sins which they contracted through time remain. But then even the long times of the righteous will seem brief, when they see temporal merits recompensed with eternal rewards.

Before that time, whatever is done in time remains hidden, whether it is long or short. Therefore a human being should not dare to search out God’s judgment, but should be ready for every time, whether good or evil, so that, tested through good and evil, he may pass to the good in which he shall be glorified. And if the intervals of time are meanwhile long, let him not presume in good things or collapse in evil things, because all things under heaven pass away through their allotted intervals, so that, when time under heaven has passed, the eternity which is in heaven may succeed.

“**A time to be born, and a time to die.**” Now [Col. 0209D] he develops through the succeeding examples what he had stated generally: “Everything has its time.” He enumerates both good and evil; after good, evil; and again after evil, good—nowhere evil alone or good alone. For in the time of this life it is impossible to possess good without evil, or evil without good, because all things are mixed as long as it is time for all things to have their time.
