“A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to uproot; a time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to destroy, and a time to build.” First, good and evil: a time to be born and a time to die. Then evil and good: a time to kill and a time to heal. Not good alone, nor evil alone, but both good and evil. Nor only does evil follow good, but good also follows evil; yet evil first follows good, and then good follows evil.

For there are two lives: one according to the flesh, the other according to the spirit. And we know, as the Apostle testifies, that “the spiritual is not first, but the carnal is first” (1 Cor. 15). Therefore there are two lives: the first carnal, the second spiritual. Each life has its own goods and its own evils, because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24); because He saves “humans and beasts” (Ps. 35); because He “opens His hand and fills every living thing with blessing” (Ps. 144).

For He has set before every human being both good and evil: good, by which He cherishes through mercy; evil, by which He assigns guilt through justice when examining sins. Every life has its goods and evils, so that all things may have their time and all things under heaven may pass through their allotted intervals. Both are given and both set before us: one from justice, the other from mercy. “All the ways of the Lord are mercy [and] truth.” “Mercy and truth have met together; righteousness and peace have kissed” (Ps. 84). If there were evil alone, there would be no mercy; if good alone, there would be no justice.

Therefore God sets forth both good and evil, and leaves to the human being the power of choice as to which he will receive first. For one must taste both, but which first lies within oneself. The carnal person, as though hastening toward an inheritance and avoiding judgment so as to lack blessing at the end, chooses good things first. God gives him temporal goods that have an end, so that enduring evils without end may succeed them [Col. 0210C]. But the spiritual person is first tested by adversities in order to be led to prosperity, and likewise has his own evils and goods—but evils in time and goods in eternity.

Thus every life proceeds by alternating lot toward consummation: one from goods to evils, the other from evils to goods. All things have time to be, and pass away so as not to be, running through their intervals toward the end for as long as they are. Goods pass away into evils and evils into goods; while they pass away, they sometimes endure for a time, and each has its own interval according to its ordering, until it comes to an end.

Therefore he enumerates certain alternations in the world, in order to show the fluctuation of all mutable things. First he sets forth good and evil as though describing the condition of carnal life; then evil and good, expressing the condition of spiritual life [Col. 0210D]. Thereafter he alternates and changes good and evil, and evil and good, in order to show another kind of confusion: neither do good things remain to the end for the wicked, nor evil things for the good. Even before the end, sometimes good and evil, and sometimes evil and good, follow one another.

Nevertheless, the beginning of all this variation of distribution is from good to evil, when it is said, “A time to be born, and a time to die”; and its end is from evil to good, when it is said, “A time of war, and a time of peace.” For the first life has good first and evil last. The second life has evil first and good last, with the middle of each fluctuating under the uncertain lot of evils and goods.

Among all these things enumerated as examples of the whole, some are taken from human life itself and some from things pertaining to human life, so that everything belonging to the human being may be shown mutable—a human being who perhaps would not wholly go into corruption if only he could in some measure stand firm either in himself or in what belongs to him [Col. 0211A]. “A time to be born, and a time to die” concerns human life; “a time to plant, and a time to uproot what has been planted” concerns things pertaining to human life.

For the work of a human being will perish together with the human being. As that which is born in a human being is born in order to die, so that which is planted by a human being is planted in order to be uprooted. The time of every thing under heaven lies not in human will, but in the judgment of the Creator. For there is a time for every thing under heaven when God wills it, even if a human being, when it is time, does not will what God wills.

Therefore what God does, He always does when it is time; but what a human being does, he does not always do when it is time, either because through ignorance he does not know what is right, or because through a perverse will he seeks what is disordered. Thus the time of every thing is subject to the Creator’s will: when it is time for something to occur which is to be done in time, and for everything which occurs in time. If it does not accord with His will, there was time when it occurred, but it was not time when it ought to have occurred. Therefore human works alone do not keep their times, even when they happen in time, because only in that regard does a human being fail to follow the appointed time: abusing freedom of choice, he does not govern himself under the Creator’s will.

[Col. 0211C] Therefore one thing is the time assigned to each thing by the Creator’s ordering; another is that which human presumption usurps against the Creator’s ordering. In the former time, a human being suffers the law along with the rest; in the latter, alone above the rest, he violates the law. Hence in the former case things are rightly done to him, even when he himself does not wish it; but in the latter he often acts contrary to right, doing only what he himself wishes.

“A time to be born, and a time to die.” No one is born when he wills, even if someone dies when he wills. Yet many, when they die, do not die by their will, when it is their time; and many who are born by necessity are born when it is their time. Even those born before their expected time are born when it is time, and those born after their expected time are born when it is time; because necessity confers the time of birth, while a perverse will sometimes chooses the time of death.

Therefore no one sins against time when born, but many sin against time when dying. For even if nature sometimes passes away, the will does not sin, because what is governed in one who suffers by a just ordering from above—not by his own will concerning himself—is not imputed to him as guilt. Therefore it is the time for every thing when it is just that what is to be done should be done, whatever it may be: whether by God without a human being, or by a human being with God. For there is no time in which something may be done by a human being without God, just as nothing can be justly done by a human being without God.

“A time to be born, and a time to die; a time to plant, and a time to uproot” [Col. 0212A]. Here we may discern a certain comprehensive and universal account of the mutability of all things. As we distinguished at the beginning concerning the entire sequence of the work, so here too he first expresses that mutability to which all things are subject, and then, treating more broadly the mutability in which human actions fluctuate, shows it to be more monstrous and more to be feared than all others.

For these first four items seem particularly to concern that mutability inherent in all things which have arising and passing away; all the rest properly concern that which is active in human actions. The statement, “a time to be born, and a time to die,” is said concerning things that live and feel, because all things born perish and all things grown old. “A time to plant, and a time to uproot” is said concerning things that live but do not feel. Or, speaking of things having natural origin, he first set down “a time to be born, and a time to die,” and then, for those things which are fitted for life through care and labor, he added “a time to plant, and a time to uproot” [Col. 0212B].

This, then, is that great vanity, “vanity of vanities”: it is too little that all things are mutable unless, while all things pass away, they are also swept further into their opposites. For how great is it to be removed and exiled from one’s own being and to go and proceed into contrary being, where you cannot at all begin to be what you are unless you have altogether ceased to be what you are? There is a harsh transition where that which follows cannot endure on any account unless that which precedes is first wholly destroyed.

And what do you suppose it is like when one goes from good to evil, when good things are changed into their contrary evils—especially where there is no return and no restoration can be hoped for? For evils are sometimes changed into goods and again goods into evils, and it often happens that both succeed one another alternately. This is not wholly grievous, because they are mutually tempered: evils are not great when goods follow them, nor are goods the highest good when they are terminated by succeeding evils. All this can be endured, and whatever happens admits of comparison, lest it be regarded as excessive. There is one thing which, when it happens, who can endure?

“A time to keep silence, and a time to speak; a time to gather, and a time to scatter; a time to mourn, and a time to laugh.” [Col. 0212D] All these are bearable. When any one of them happens to a human being, it passes and another comes; this too, after standing during its time, passes, and the other which had passed returns. This happens again and again for as long as one lives; and nothing remains so that it alone may always be.

“A time to be born, and a time to die.” These are not like those things, nor do they have a recurrence once they have happened. For there is one death and one birth; and as after one birth there is one death, so before one death there is only one birth. No one dies who has not first been born, nor, once having died, can anyone afterward be born. Birth is the beginning of life; death is the end. One goes from birth to death, but after death the way back to birth is not open [Col. 0213A].

For a human being’s time begins at birth and ends in death. Thus these have time unlike all the others: one, so that there may first be a time in it, and then it may no longer exist; the other, so that there may thereafter be no time in it, while that former reality remains forever. Therefore this is more grievous than all things: it has time in such a way that it is itself without time, because after its time there will be no time in which what its time has taken and consumed can be restored anew.

Therefore the time of birth appears better than the time of death, because at the time of birth life is given, whereas at the time of death life is taken away. Yet those who are born die, and those who die are born: for those born for death begin to die from the moment they begin to live under mortal decay; and those who die for life begin to live truly from the moment that, after death, they have ceased to be mortal. Therefore a good death is more to be desired than an evil life, because by a good death one proceeds to a good life, while an evil life reaches an evil death.

Therefore everything has its time, and nothing is to be rejected in its time. There is a time of birth, so that the first life may begin, which is exercised through justice in time; and a time of death, so that the second life may succeed, enjoying in eternity the reward of justice. He then adds what follows:

“A time to plant, and a time to uproot what has been planted.” This second item concerns the work of an artisan together with nature. The first work, however, was of nature alone, and was transient. Now the work of an artisan together with nature is added, and this too is shown to be transient, so that nothing may remain under the sun and joy arising from birth or planting may be tempered by the remembrance of death and uprooting [Col. 0213C].

Then follow works of the artisan alone, without the work of nature; very many are enumerated, and all are shown to be transient, so that vanity may increase by its stages. Yet all these, although vain through mutability, occur appropriately in time, so that in all of them a human being, even if unable to retain the state of eternity, may nevertheless endeavor to preserve the order of reason.

“A time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to destroy, and a time to build; a time to weep, and a time to laugh; a time to mourn, and a time to dance.” [Col. 0213D] And many other things are enumerated, and many others cannot be enumerated. In all these, human life undergoes alternation and is subject to mutability. For all these things pass over it, and one after another come upon it in turn. Things which preceded follow, and those which followed again precede; and this occurs without interruption in the waves of great fluctuation.

Laughter comes after weeping, and weeping succeeds laughter; when joy has succeeded sorrow, joys are again changed into sorrow. All these things have their time when the human will, through justice, either willingly conforms itself for the time to the divine will in doing them, or submits itself in enduring them. For all things have their time when a human being either does them according to God or suffers them for God; because all things, in their proper time, either cherish one walking according to God when prosperity occurs or exercise him when adversity happens.

Therefore all things which a human being can do justly or suffer justly have their time. But what cannot happen without injustice never has a time in which it ought to happen, because a human being has received no time for doing evil. His allotted time has been given only so that he may either correct the evils he has done or supply the goods he has not yet done [Col. 0214A].

Therefore sins have no time; and yet sins are permitted to occur in time. They are not done justly when they occur, but are justly permitted when they occur; once done, they are justly ordered. Thus there is a time for them to be permitted, but not a time for them to be done: they are not done well, but they are well permitted, so that they may be justly ordered.

“A time to plant, a time to mourn, a time to dance, a time to acquire.” Where is the time to indulge in luxury, and the time to become drunk? But the former may be done well in their proper time; therefore they have their time. The latter have no time, because they are never to be done well. Perhaps, however, the contrary may seem to follow from the statement: “a time to kill,” “a time of war,” “a time of hatred.” But all these can be done well, and therefore they have their time, when they are to be done justly.

For there is also a sword of justice, by which kings and rulers punish criminals out of zeal for equity and put to death persons condemned for their crimes, serving God in this very matter by authority received according to the precepts of divine law [Col. 0214C]. They also wage wars for the defense of their country and the peace of the churches, and overthrow the enemies of peace so that they may not oppress the innocent. There is also a holy hatred by which crimes—not human beings—are hated. It sometimes imposes outwardly a strict severity, for salutary fear and for the correction of vices, while inwardly preserving inviolate the sweetness of love by which it thirsts for human salvation.

Therefore there is a time for hatred and a time for war; and all things have their time when they are to be done justly. I may confess, as at the beginning, that I am too limited in understanding for these lofty and sublime matters to explain what ought to be explained, because it is enough, if granted, to have avoided what ought not and does not fit. For many secrets lie hidden in the depths of wisdom, and a human being cannot search out its mysteries. The words of wisdom, surpassing every understanding, scatter a certain light upon hidden things, yet that light itself is small in relation to the whole.

Therefore a human being labors when he sees that light and judges that he is entering in order to contemplate it; yet he cannot do so unless wisdom is with him and inwardly reveals to him the secrets of her ways, in that measure in which he has been made acceptable to her [Col. 0214D]. And when he has drawn much from it, that is much for him, yet it is itself little in relation to the overflowing fullness.

Therefore we have said much concerning the waves of things and the contrary agitation of what is under heaven; yet all this is still little in relation to the whole. Perhaps there will be some who think us too expansive in speaking, because they do not attend to the multitude of things that must be said and to the depth of what has been said. We have spoken this briefly, so that we may once more carry a fresh expression back to the beginning of the discourse to come and have minds more eager.

## HOMILY XIV. An explanation of the remaining matters which have their own time, and a recapitulation of what has been said.

All things have their season, and all things under heaven pass through their appointed spans. Above, Ecclesiastes had sought some one thing in the world in which his mind might rest; but he did not find it among all things, whether because each was imperfect, or because all were transient. Therefore he began to be weary of and to reject everything; yet he did not cease continually to seek in them a fullness of joy, and he could not find it. At last, then, recognizing the condition of mutable things, he saw that he had erred in both respects: both by judging evil those things which were good in their own kind, and by thinking that things which were transient could stand forever. Now therefore, correcting himself for his former judgment, he declares that all things beneath heaven are at once transient in time and good in their own time.

That the mutability and fluctuation of all these things may be understood more clearly, he shows that all things not only pass in time, but also pass in time into their opposites, saying: “All things have their season, and all things under heaven pass through their appointed spans.” And then he enumerates all things, distinguishing them according to their kinds: “A time to be born and a time to die.” First he describes the course of mutable things according to beginning and end, so that afterward he may pursue more carefully the mutability and alternation of those things which lie between.

Now there are four operations by which all temporal things, and all things which pass in time, are explained. The first is the work of God; the second, the work of nature; the third, the work of the craftsman together with nature; the fourth, the work of the craftsman alone, without nature. The work of God is to create the essence of things from nothing, to dispose the matter of things into form, and to regulate the motion of things under a fixed order. Therefore these three belong to the work of God: the essence of things, their form, and their order. But these three, as the author himself later attests concerning God’s works, are stable and do not undergo the mutability of time. For the essences of things never cease to be what they are; the forms of things preserve, according to the first institution of their Creator, a perpetual sameness in their kinds; and the motions of things never transgress the law of the first order.

For neither could the essences of things become nothing, nor the forms of things become otherwise, nor could the order and arrangement of things be otherwise than they were from the beginning. Rather, all preserve the rule of the first law and the covenant of the ancient institution; all things still keep their course without ever running otherwise. Therefore the works of God remain, because in all things what God has made is stable, so that it may remain always. Thus the work of God is to create, to form, and to order all things.

The work of nature is to bring forth the seeds of things from their hidden bosom through growth, and again, when they wither and fall through decay, to recall them to the hidden bosom from which they came. The work of the craftsman together with nature is to assist, by care and industry, those things which spring from the earth. The work of the craftsman alone is to work upon the material of things set before him, either by joining what is separate or separating what is joined; so that he can neither create with God, so that something may be which was not, nor grant growth with nature to the offspring of things, so that what was less may become greater.

There are therefore three workers in this world: God, nature, and the craftsman who imitates nature. But these three produce what they bring to effect by powers very unequal. For God, in His work, needs neither the works of nature nor the craftsman who imitates nature. For God sometimes works without nature, sometimes in nature, and sometimes above nature. Without nature He first made nature itself. For when He made nature, He did not have cooperating nature. That which did not yet exist could not work itself together with Him who alone existed. Thus He first made nature without nature, so that afterward He might make some things in nature with nature, and other things above nature.

He works with nature when He brings forth from nature, according to nature, those things which arise from it. He works above nature when, in nature, beyond nature’s customary course and original capacity, He produces something by an added and greater power. Therefore, when God works nature, and when nature works above nature, nature does not cooperate with God; for in the former case nature receives only what it did not possess, in order that it may exist, while in the latter it receives what it could not derive from that which it had received, in order that it may be able. Thus God can work without nature; nature cannot work without God, because what nature does, it does from what God does and with what God does. For God first made nature’s capacity, and, that it may come forth into effect, He again acts with that very nature which He makes. Therefore everything which nature does, God does; but nature does not also do everything which God does—He who makes nature without nature.

In the third place follow the works of the craftsman who imitates nature. He too sometimes works with God without nature, sometimes with nature without God, sometimes with God and nature together, and sometimes without God and without nature alike. He works with God when he performs works of justice, because God cooperates with a will that is upright and ordered according to justice. He works without God when he performs works of wickedness, because sins are not from God, nor can that which is done against His will be done through His cooperation. The craftsman works with nature when he adds outward care and industry to the seeds and propagating offspring of things, to which nature supplies growth. He works without nature when, apart from those matters which concern the propagation of seeds and the cultivation of things being born, and of those having the power of growth and sensation, he employs his skill upon material set before him, to bring some object whatever to completion. In such work nature only undergoes; it does not act, because it furnishes material to the worker but does not exercise the effect of working.

Such are all human works performed upon the earth. Mortal life compels many of them; desire urges many; vanity produces many. And in all these, because nothing stable is found and all things done beneath the sun pass away—whether nature produces them or the craftsman who imitates nature fashions them—the contemplator of wisdom subjects all to vanity, proving that the works of God alone endure. For no created essence is ever consumed, nor is the rationale of the arrangement or order of things changed. Therefore he first shows the works of nature to be subject to vanity: both in those things which nature alone performs, because what arises dies, and in those which the craftsman does together with nature, because what has increased grows old. Afterward he enumerates many and diverse works of the craftsman who imitates nature: some belonging to necessity, some to desire, some to vanity; and he subjects them all to vanity because he shows them liable to change.

The work of nature alone is described when it is said: “A time to be born and a time to die.”

Then the work of the craftsman cooperating with nature is added when it is said: “A time to plant and a time to uproot.” Finally, the work of man without the work of nature is joined when it is added: “A time to kill and a time to heal; a time to destroy and a time to build.” This is afterward explained more fully by the enumeration of many things, in order that it may plainly be shown how greatly and widely the vanity of the human heart is entangled and dispersed. For this especially belonged to the subject: that he should expose with more care in his discourse, and set foremost by comparison, the vanity of human minds that follows the uncertainty of mortal life, since he had undertaken to condemn it. Thus all the other matters seem to be mentioned only for this purpose: that by comparison with them, the greatness of this vanity may be recognized.

“A time to be born and a time to die.” The time to be born is when a human being must be brought into this life. The time to die is when he must be summoned away from this life. Meanwhile, after birth and before death, while he lives this mortal life, he needs support and is nourished with food so that he may subsist. There is “a time to plant and a time to uproot,” so that a human being may cultivate the earth from which he was taken, and sow, reap, plant, and gather.

These two following clauses may also be matched by distinction with the two preceding, in this way: “A time to be born and a time to plant; a time to die and a time to uproot.” For when a human being is born, it is time to plant, so that earthly life may be nourished by earthly fruits. But when a human being dies, it is time to uproot, because when mortal life is destroyed, those things too which had been established for the sake of mortal life are taken away.

But because, in addition to the fruits of the earth, the use of flesh is also permitted to human weakness, “a time to kill” is fittingly added after “a time to plant and a time to uproot.” In this consumption a necessary measure is required, lest the flesh take for an incitement to vices what it received for the support of weakness. Therefore immediately after “a time to kill” he adds “a time to heal,” namely so that we may diligently nourish and preserve at other times the life of those animals which we have received to kill at a fitting time—that is, when necessity requires it—for the support of our weakness. For this is, as it were, to heal what is infirm: to assist creatures where they are insufficient for themselves, and to restore what is failing.

Hence perhaps, fittingly, when he had said, “A time to kill,” he did not add, “a time to heal what has been killed,” as earlier, after saying “a time to plant,” he immediately added, “and a time to uproot what has been planted.” For what is planted can be uprooted, but what is killed cannot be healed. Thus perhaps, if we follow the sense of the letter, we do no injury to spiritual understanding, which must afterward be sought.

“A time to destroy and a time to build.” Let no one suppose that it is by no means necessary to inquire when a human being ought to destroy and when to build, thinking that here it is shown merely that, if a person is perhaps subject to various events of time, he undergoes these differing things even unwillingly. But, applying what has been said to a more accessible understanding, we may say that the time to kill is when God, desiring to punish human sins, brings in the sword of slaughter for correction; and the time to heal is when He refreshes the afflicted and those wounded by the blows of tribulations, restoring them by His customary compassion.

Indeed, it seems far more consistent with truth that here we should understand times of events, not times that serve human will, but those which obey divine ordering. For the time for anything is not when a human being wills it and God does not will it. A human being often wills when it is not the time; when God wills, it is always the time. Therefore all times are referred to divine ordering, and then every thing is said to have its time when it is justly ordered by God, whether for the chastisement and correction of sin or for the consolation of weakness.

“A time to kill and a time to heal; a time to destroy and a time to build.

“A time to weep and a time to laugh; a time to mourn and a time to dance.” Evils are everywhere enumerated first; goods are added afterward. For we are first justly afflicted for our sins, then graciously refreshed by God’s compassion. And it is clear how human life daily undergoes the alternation of all these things, whenever, by hidden providence, God either instructs us by scourges or consoles us by gifts. Then follows:

“A time to scatter stones and a time to gather them.” What this means according to the letter is rightly asked, since such an activity, if thought to have a time among human actions, seems altogether idle and unsuitable. Unless perhaps it should be understood thus: because he is going to say in what follows, “A time of war and a time of peace,” he fittingly places here beforehand a time to scatter stones and a time to gather them, so that when war is impending stones may be gathered for building fortifications and wall-ramparts against sieges; but in time of peace, because no dangers of war threaten, the banks of fortifications may be dispersed, so that access may lie open to all without hindrance.

Nor should it seem superfluous that, because above he had said, “A time to destroy and a time to build,” the same thing appears to be repeated a second time. For that earlier statement is more suitably understood of the buildings of houses and human dwellings; this one refers more properly to the defenses of walls.

Yet perhaps another and more fitting meaning may be understood in these words. For since above he had set forth, “A time to kill and a time to heal,” lest anyone should think that only the wicked, those who ought to be punished for their sins, are exposed to slaughter, he now shows that even the righteous are sometimes, by God’s permission, subjected along with the ungodly and sinful to deaths, exiles, and proscriptions, as an example to the wicked and for correction. Thus it is said through Peter: “It is time for judgment to begin from the house of God” [1 Peter 4]. That the righteous are signified by the name “stones” is clearly shown through Jeremiah when he says: “The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” [Lamentations 4]. And Isaiah again: “I will make all your walls of carved stones; all your children taught by the Lord” [Isaiah 54].

Therefore there is a time to scatter stones, so that the righteous may understand, from the very labor of their scattering and shaking, that true rest is not in this life. And again there is a time to gather stones, so that after the wearing down of bodily exile, lest they fail in spirit, being restored again by the temporal benefit of peace they may gain strength for eternal things. Thus what is hidden can scarcely be judged in one definite direction, because divine speech conceals itself from us in some places in order to show itself worthy of investigation even there where it seemed manifest.

## HOMILY XV. On time and things subject to time, according to another interpretation

Let us not then be weary of again attempting the difficulty of these parables, until perhaps, by the usage of discourse wearing away the bark of its words, their inner things may be laid open. For we are in times, and our discourse rolls on with us until we are established in that which is not changed by time. This is chiefly to contemplate human actions, because in them lies all that makes us groan: vanity in its entirety.

“A time to kill and a time to heal.” What have been the times to kill and the times to heal? A miserable beginning of human actions: beginning with killing and slaughter. Thus the work of a life devoted to death ought to have begun, so that it might follow the sentence of its Author: “Cursed, raging to his own death” [reading uncertain]. Let us run through past times in thought and see the wars and slaughters that have taken place from the beginning until now, of nation against nation and of innumerable peoples.

And God endured the human race to rage against its own vitals; and in all these things He worked His judgments, turning human furies toward the vindication of His justice, so that some might justly suffer what others had unjustly willed. Some rose up, and many were killed and condemned; many were killed and saved; others were delivered from a death of slaughter and reserved for condemnation; and others were delivered lest they be condemned if they were killed. In all these things He fulfilled just judgment upon them: chastising and sparing according to the measure of equity by which God orders all things.

Therefore there is a time to kill and a time to heal: some do what He wills, others suffer what they do not will, and the just Judge sits above, doing what He wills and ordering all things so that He may be feared.

“A time to kill and a time to heal; a time to destroy and a time to build.” How much have lovers of this age built from the beginning, calling their name upon their land so that they might have glorious fame among posterity! For they labored heavily in their works so that monuments of their boasting might stand after them. They prevailed to some extent, leaving great monuments of their industry to posterity; and certain traces of ruins from the ages past still appear in them. We marvel at those whom we do not see, because they could accomplish such things; yet we groan more deeply over them, because, though they were human beings made for eternity, they loved vain things, and vanished because they became vain in them.

For they themselves perished, and after them their works fell. Others succeeded, and these too made great works, and afterward departed into nothingness; and everything they had made was destroyed together with them. Again others arose and built, and did not understand where the former generation and its works were, so that they might see the vanity which is beneath the sun. And God permitted them to labor in vain, building things that would perish, so that a human being might understand his vanity: that what was built may be destroyed, and what was destroyed may again be built, and that no human work upon earth may be stable. Therefore all things have their time, so that a human being may be instructed concerning his vanity and the uncertainty of the mortal life through which he walks.

“A time to weep and a time to laugh; a time to mourn and a time to dance.” Weeping and laughter belong to the mind. Mourning—or, more properly, lamentation—and dancing belong to the body. Thus by weeping and laughter the sorrow and joy of the mind are expressed; but lamentation and dancing signify the same things when they are displayed through bodily movement.

“A time to weep and a time to laugh; a time to lament and a time to dance.” All these things have their own time among human beings while this mortal life runs its course. According to the height of His judgments and the depth of His counsel, by which He orders us, God permits them to come and vary over us by differing lot and unequal event, alternating prosperity with adversity and exchanging adversity for prosperity in their time.

Joyful times come; people laugh and dance and think themselves well off. They often forget their Creator and do not consider that they are going to die. For they look only at present things and rejoice in them as though they were to remain forever. They do not heed their condition and the uncertainty of mortal life, nor do they reflect upon dangers yet to come. Therefore they sin securely, pour themselves out into harmful pleasures, and walk after the desires of their heart and in the sight of their eyes, doing what they ought not and multiplying wrath and indignation.

God sees this and sows pains and bitterness upon the wantonness of wrongly sweet pleasures. He calls back and restrains those who are running loose, lest they proceed into every kind of alienation. Then comes the time to weep and the time to lament. People grieve and often complain against God when He deals well with them. Yet He overlooks their perversity; and after a time He again mingles prosperity with adversity, lest they fail, and again, when it is time, adversity with prosperity, lest they presume. He frequently does this, nourishing and exercising, chastising and refreshing the human being, so that he may learn to be reverent and may know that with the Lord is the power of life and death.

Therefore there is a time to weep and a time to laugh, a time to lament and a time to dance. After these comes “a time to scatter stones and a time to gather them.” This time is enumerated after the others but is ordered among them, because at one and the same time there are often causes which contribute to a single temporal arrangement.

“A time to scatter stones and a time to gather them.” The whole world is an exile for those whose homeland ought to have been heaven. Yet the minds of mortals become attached through habit, and people begin to love their own places and lands in which they were born or raised. A great forgetfulness of eternal things follows upon attachment to temporal things; and unless God wiped away these ingrained sweetnesses of the passions, there would be no way for His desire to enter us.

Therefore He gives His judgments: commotions and upheavals of nations come, and migrations of peoples. Some arise to seize what is not theirs; others are plundered and scattered. Again stronger persons, to whom power has been given, arrive and drive out those who had violently seized what belonged to others, and they possess what is not theirs. The world fluctuates within itself, so that a human being may see that there is no stable dwelling here and may gradually learn to draw the mind away and free it from the bonds of earthly pleasures.

Therefore a time to scatter stones comes, so that there may be no stable dwelling upon earth, and the human being may be compelled in exile to sigh for the homeland where joys remain unshaken and the security of peace is troubled by no coming attack. This, then, is what the scattering of stones accomplishes in its time.

But because human weakness quickly falls and cannot stand safely for long amid adversities, after the time of scattering comes the time of gathering, so that, strengthened by the quiet of time, it may learn wisdom from this very admonition and experience how great will be the joys of the coming rest. Thus it may hasten to that place where there is no fear of scattering or dread of the misery of exile for those to whom the eternity of life in their homeland has been given.

“A time to scatter stones and a time to gather them.” Then after this time another time follows, and other things are named which also often have one and the same time along with those things mentioned in these times, but often have another time separately outside these times.

“A time to embrace and a time to refrain from embraces.” Time has been granted for chaste embraces, so that flesh may be sown for propagation and the harvest of the human race—which death reaps daily throughout the whole world—may be restored through the work of generation. For the covenant of the first institution, by which flesh was to be taken from flesh without the contagion of flesh, after the sin of the first transgression is confirmed, in sinful flesh, by concession. It is so confirmed not only for fulfilling the duty, but also for providing a remedy: lest the movement of the flesh, now boiling up too immoderately, flow more shamefully into every kind of transgression if it could nowhere be lawfully relaxed.

Therefore a limit is prescribed to which the affection of the flesh may extend without injury to chastity, so that what is done by concession in the chastity of marriage, though it belongs to weakness, may nevertheless not be counted as shamefulness. But lest the allurements of pleasure again turn the mind aside into forgetfulness of the Creator, by a wholesome dispensation a person is sometimes also withheld from permitted things, lest, if he craves too immoderately those things which now seem sweet, he fail to hasten toward those which are eternal.

Therefore a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embraces have been given. The time to embrace has been given so that mortality may be renewed and the weakness of mortals sustained; the time to refrain from embraces has been given so that, while flesh is withdrawn from fleshly delight, the mind may be nourished toward spiritual delight.

“A time to embrace and a time to refrain from embraces.” For when stones are gathered, it is a time to embrace; but when they are scattered, it is a time to refrain from embraces, since times of distress have been given for this reason: that flesh, afflicted, may restrain itself from its pleasures, and then, in the time of joy and consolation, may discipline itself with fear and reverence against excess.

There are also the embraces of loved ones and the companionship of friendly society, in which, apart from carnal experience, sweet fellowship is joined by a most pleasing harmony. These too are dissolved in their time, lest the human heart rest in a human being, until that covenant of eternal love comes which is not dissolved. For all these reasons there is a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embraces: so that in time a person may not seek what is eternal, and that one who loves the fellowship of a living human being may always reflect upon separation through death.

“A time to acquire and a time to lose.” What are the goods that are first acquired and afterward lost? For certain goods had been lost and afterward acquired, so that they could not thereafter be lost. Again there were other goods unlike the former, which nevertheless seemed good. There was indeed something good in them, but not as in the first goods, which were true. These goods were not a human being’s goods unto the true good. After he had lost the true goods, he acquired false goods, thinking himself happy in them.

For he wished to console himself and to possess in time what eternity bestows. He gathered perishable things, which he could not retain. God allowed this so that he might recognize the distinction between goods and be instructed by his vanity, to turn himself toward the things which are true. Therefore God let his heart gather things that cannot stand, and in their time He now grants them to be acquired and now withdraws them when acquired, testing the human being in all his works and showing that all things beneath heaven are vain.

For this reason there is given “a time to acquire and a time to lose”: so that when a human being has attained what he desired, he may learn by experience what such joys can confer upon those who highly esteem perishable things; but when he loses what he possessed, he may recognize that all things which could be taken from him against his will were alien even while he possessed them.

“A time to keep and a time to cast away.” Temporal goods are to be kept in their time, as much as the necessity of temporal life requires. But because in the death of the flesh everything pertaining to the enjoyment of bodily life is necessarily lost, it is fitting that even before death it should be willingly cast away from the love of the heart.

“A time to tear and a time to sew.” He who tears divides things united; he who sews joins things divided and separated. The author had perceived that all these things are done without cessation in the life of human beings as long as it remains subject to change. In this life, fellowship in human interaction is sometimes to be sought, because it seems to bring some benefit; but sometimes it must be avoided, because it often brings harm.

Thus social agreement has its sewing in its proper time; and the zeal of righteous opposition has its tearing in its proper time, so that we may be united in agreement and action with those who will well and do good, but separated in mind and action from those who love wickedness and do iniquity.

But lest this meaning seem identical with the earlier statement, “a time to embrace and a time to refrain from embraces,” since there also we asserted that the joining and separation of social affection was treated: what was said there may suitably be understood to signify only love and affection; what is mentioned here may be referred to the representation of any fellowship or compact whatever, in which there is a shared agreement and a settled concord.

Thus the likenesses of things lend themselves to the understanding of wisdom, and wisdom itself uses its works in order to reveal itself in us. Many things are spoken in parables and deserve deep investigation; but not all of them wish to come forth, so that they may always be sought within.

“A time to keep silence and a time to speak.” First comes the time to keep silence, then the time to speak. For wisdom comes forth from the heart, and the tongue has nowhere else from which it can rightly utter anything unless understanding first forms the word. Therefore first comes the time to be silent, and afterward the time to speak, so that discerning thought may first gather wisdom into itself in silence before the tongue afterward sends it forth through speech for the hearing of others.

For this reason too there is a time to keep silence and a time to speak, because hearers of the word sometimes receive it with desire and love, but at other times reject it contemptuously and without reverence. Therefore the time to be silent is when we see hearers wholly impatient of admonition; but the time to speak is when we see that they either desire the word or at least wish to endure it.

There is also a time to keep silence because we ought not presume regarding matters which we cannot investigate; and likewise a time to speak, because it is necessary, for the instruction of our neighbors, not to conceal other things which we can comprehend. Hence not only human actions, but even words follow the uncertainty of fleeting life, so that vanity occupies everything and nothing stable or constant remains. For we cannot always say what we know, nor always retain what we have learned. At one time it harms us to have been silent about things that ought to have been said; at another, it is a fault to have said things which ought to have been kept silent.

Again, we often cannot when we wish; we do not wish to be wise when we can; and more often we ought not do either when we do them. In this lies great uncertainty and the deep darkness of ignorance: a human being is tossed from time to time and does not understand his own time in all his work.

“A time of love and a time of hatred.” Many things are loved in this world, and likewise very many are hated. Yet among all the things which are loved, few love truth; and among those which are hated, few hate iniquity. For this reason people love and often think that they love well, yet love badly: because in the things which they love they do not love truth, nor do they love them for truth’s sake.

Likewise, very many practice hatreds and boast of their zeal for justice and equity; yet inwardly strife lies hidden in the heart, and fierce rage feeds itself upon wicked hatred. Therefore love and hatred cannot first discern their own time, because they do not follow the judgment of justice and truth, but are carried by their own impulse into perverse desires, to do what they wish.

They love and hate, cherish and are jealous of things which they often ought not, and often at times when they ought not. A great confusion of love and hatred arises, and the heart is scattered into every vanity, desiring both what is right and what is wicked. Therefore a time of love and hatred has been set before the human being, so that he may understand and discern when, among those things which may be good or evil for a time, he ought either to seek or avoid something.

For outside time there are certain things which are not changed by time so as to become otherwise; and among these are goods and evils. Those things which are good are eternal, so that they may always be good; and those things which are evil are likewise eternal, so that they may always be evil. It is not concerning these that it is said to you: “A time of love and a time of hatred.” For there is eternal love for the former and eternal hatred for the latter, because what ought to be loved must always be loved there, and what ought to be hated must always be hated.

But meanwhile, now in time, while all things are uncertain, those things which meet us as we pass change according to time. What turns to evil for one person has proved favorable to another; what this person has sorrowfully endured as adversity, another knows to have happened happily for himself. Therefore in all things which pass in time there is a time of love and a time of hatred, so that a person may not fix his heart upon them either in love or in hatred. For things once hated may again justly be loved, and things once loved may again justly be hated.

“A time of war and a time of peace.” Because of the time to kill, the time of war is appointed; because of the time to heal, the time of peace follows. The former was mentioned first, but the latter last, so that the beginning and the end may be enclosed with all the labors and dangers between them, and thus human life—passing on to its end—may never be secure.

For a human being went forth in order to depart and not to stand with God. He made a covenant of love with the pleasure of this world so that he might rest in it. God did not will that this covenant should endure, by which he remained in alienation. He stirred up against him those things which he had loved perversely, so that they might oppose and afflict him. Thus war arose for the human being with all things in the world, so that he might find pain and affliction in them until he returned to peace with God.

Then all things will compose themselves toward His peace, so that those things which had been hostile to the proud may be subjected to the humble. For at first all things had been peaceful, just as in the end all things will be made peaceful. In between, they run their course under uncertain fortune, until they come either to the point where, falling under judgment, all things are eternally hostile, or to the happy consummation where all things are subjected.

Where eternal hatred will be, there also will be perpetual war; and where eternal love will be, there everlasting peace will stand. There it will not be said, “a time of peace and a time of war,” just as it will not be said, “a time of love and a time of hatred.” Rather, there will be war and peace: war without end, and peace without end.

Therefore let a human being not think war greatly to be feared, since peace may follow it; nor let him regard as true that peace which a succeeding war may disturb. For all things which pass away must be judged vain precisely because they cannot remain forever, alike in good and in evil.

“What has a human being more from his labor?” Therefore the labor of a human being runs in uncertainty, because he can have nothing further from his labor. Let no one be content with the things which depend upon his own labor, because all things are vain, pass in time, and are to end in time.

## HOMILY XVI. On the spiritual understanding of those things which have been said concerning time
But now it is time, after our survey of the times according to those things that roll onward outwardly in time, to recall also their spiritual meaning. Little by little [Col. 0226A] the discourse of wisdom advances toward touching spiritual things, so as to draw the disciplined mind inward. Above we distinguished two lives: one according to the flesh, the other according to the spirit. The carnal life is prior in time, because every person is first born in the flesh before being reborn in the spirit. Everyone who lives in the flesh either walks according to the flesh and has not yet attained the spiritual life, or walks according to the spirit and has renounced the carnal life. Hence every spiritual person has become spiritual out of being carnal; but not every carnal person has become carnal out of being spiritual. For the carnal life is always either the only life or the first: either every person holds it alone, never beginning the spiritual life; or, having first possessed it, he changes it through the subsequent pursuit of spiritual life. Each of these lives has its followers: the carnal life has those who love the pleasures of the present life, while the spiritual life has those who seek the delight of the life to come. The former nourish the flesh with the blandishments of earthly pleasures; the latter exercise the spirit through the pursuit of virtues, in hope and longing for future things.

With these two peoples the world runs through the changefulness of times toward its end, until the appointed covenant of justice brings judgment upon both. For it pleased God to display the riches of coming glory upon vessels of mercy, while also sustaining vessels of wrath through temporal mercy; and likewise, for the fulfilment of justice and truth, to exercise even the vessels of mercy meanwhile through the troubles of temptations. Thus [Col. 0226C] every life has both something to receive freely from mercy, lest goodness remain unknown, and something strict to experience from justice, so that truth may be made manifest. Therefore God set before every person both good and evil, in order to demonstrate both mercy and truth: the one, by which he freely bestows a benefit without merit; the other, by which he repays deserved punishment for evil merit. Therefore he ordained that a person should receive both, and left it in human power which he should wish to receive first. Yet he attached a condition to each choice, lest wrongful desire perhaps be excusable: if a person chose temporal goods in this life for pleasure, he would be unable to attain eternal goods; but if here he willingly submitted himself to the scourge of correction under the judgment of truth, he would not experience the torments of condemnation in [Col. 0226D] the future life.

The reprobate, who love temporal life and prefer its pleasure to the joys of everlasting life, embrace present goods with their whole desire and establish all their happiness in them. The elect, however, patiently endure temporal pains, that they may attain the promised joys of eternity; and in comparison with these, whatever is transitory, if it seems bitter, they do not fear, and if sweet, they do not desire. Hence the lovers of carnal life first possess goods and then receive evils, while spiritual persons are first exercised by adversities and then attain goods. For the former, good things come first and evil things last; for the latter, evil things first and good things last.

But because [Col. 0227A] again all things that pass in time are confused and mingled, so that they do not preserve their order, whether from good to evil or from evil to good, therefore meanwhile, between beginning and end, manifold alternation occurs: now evils happen after goods, now goods after evils, and both evils and goods befall people by an uncertain lot. While Ecclesiastes was setting forth a certain distinction concerning the revolving course of times and the alternation of those things which vary in time, he carefully set out all these matters as an example of the whole, in order to show together the lot of both good and evil people, and their progress running toward opposites. For after saying that all things under heaven are changed by the turning of time and carried toward opposites, he added examples and enumerated many things from every sphere, so that [Col. 0227B] the nature of all might be made evident.

Among the things he enumerated are some in which goods and then evils are mentioned, and others in which evils and then goods are mentioned, so that the condition and state of both carnal and spiritual persons may alike be recognized. There are seven in which goods are mentioned first and evils afterward, and again seven in which evils are stated first and goods afterward, so that the whole course may run in each direction to its end. For this entire present life is expressed by the number seven, since it rolls on through the course of seven days to its end. Thus the wicked have their sevenfold course, and the good likewise have theirs; because the whole life of the wicked proceeds from good to evil, and the whole life of the good from evil to good. The beginning [Col. 0227C] of the former life is in good and its end in evil; but the beginning of the latter is in evil and its end in good, while the middle stages fluctuate alternately.

For the middle stages are uncertain; and for this reason the middle item is also pronounced ambiguously, whether as from good to evil or from evil to good. The middle item was “a time to scatter stones and a time to gather”; and it has itself received an ambiguous interpretation, signifying either war or peace, so that the middle stages may remain uncertain. For if that which is stated first is evil and what follows is good, then there will be eight instances in which evils are named first and goods afterward, and six in which goods are mentioned first and evils afterward; because the life of the good rightly advances to the number of blessedness, whereas both the purpose and life of the wicked do not exceed the toil of temporality. Thus there is one truth, whichever way you bend the sense through interpretation. Many other things might perhaps fittingly have been said in this enumeration or distinction. But, avoiding weariness as far as possible, let us come to expound spiritually the things that have been said.

“Everything has its time, and all things under heaven pass according to their appointed spans.” If a human being had remained obedient to the command, he would not have belonged to the number of those things that have a time under heaven and pass away. For if his mind had not flowed away through iniquity, he would have remained stable in body also through immortality. Nor would he then have been under heaven, to revolve with those things which pass in time; rather, cleaving to the highest and true good, he would not have been subject to [Col. 0228A] the moments of time, fixed by contemplation in the solidity of eternal things. Eternity itself was the heaven in which, fixed in mind, he could not be changed by time; for, raised above times, he looked down upon all things slipping beneath him.

But after he inclined his heart so as to subject it through desire to mutable things, he began, as though fallen from heaven, to flow downward with those things to which he clung; and, carried along by the revolutions of his mutability, to feel the moments of time. Thus the human mind was made subject to times, so that evils now take their turn in it with goods, whereas before it possessed goods alone in an untroubled and unshaken state, without alternation. Therefore everything has its time, and all things under heaven pass according to their spans, so that even the person who subjected himself through love to mutable things, tossed by the waves of his own mutability under the law governing other things, cannot remain at rest.

Thus times came into the human heart when many desires entered it and mutability began to rule there. Some came and others departed, and there arose great fluctuation and instability. For now the invisible world revolved together with the visible world; moments of time began to run in it, and there came to be years and months, days and nights, sowings and harvests, rains and droughts, fruitfulness and barrenness. All these things, brought into the nature of spiritual realities by an analogy with corruptible things, are effected through the injury of sin, so that a nature made for eternity, wrongly associated with that which passes temporally, likewise fails into change.

For the shoots [Col. 0228C] of virtues rise from the first root, go on growing, and come to the effect of completion. But against them come the growths of vices and the tares sown over them; they raise themselves up in order to choke what is upright, lest it prosper. Thus great expectation arises, and hope is mingled with grave danger and fear. For if God pours out into the thirsty soul the rain of grace and the drops of his truth, a harvest of virtues springs up in manifold increase; years of fruitfulness come, and serene seasons dawn when the cloud of ignorance has been driven away. But if, angered, he withdraws his benefits and withholds his blessing in order to exercise his judgments, then sorrowful seasons follow; good produce withers in drought, and the thorns and briars of vices multiply for the toil and pain of sinful humanity.

In all these things the sinful soul undergoes its own times, looking upward toward the heaven which it has lost, immovable in eternity, while it itself rolls below in time; and within it all things that cannot stand pass through their allotted spaces and measures. Therefore everything has its time, and all things under heaven pass according to their spans.

“A time to be born and a time to die.” This is the lot of sinners in time: if perhaps some good things are born in them, they afterward die and do not endure to the end. For even among the wicked some good things are at times born; they begin, as it were, to arise and put forth a shoot. But, once born, they promptly wither because they lack moisture. They believe for a time and withdraw in the time [Col. 0229A] of temptation, so that they have time but do not attain eternity.

“A time to be born and a time to die.” For the wicked, the time to be born in good occurs when, through a sudden fervour of mind, they begin certain right actions; but immediately the time to die follows them, because, having no perseverance in good, they abandon the good they began, under the pressure of approaching trial, with the same lightness of mind with which they began it.

“A time to plant and a time to uproot.” Good things are planted in the wicked when they sometimes receive good things through right exhortation or admonition; but afterward they are uprooted when, shaken by perverse suggestion, they lose the good they had begun. Thus they are born through their own will and planted through another’s admonition; they die when their own desires [Col. 0229B] grow cold toward good, and they are uprooted when they collapse through another supplanting influence. In all these matters the wicked have their times, in which they are disposed by a just judgment toward one outcome or the other; and everywhere goods come first, while evils follow, foreseen for evil. Then follows the life of the good, in which evils precede so that goods may follow; and the very evils which run ahead cooperate for good.

“A time to kill and a time to heal.” In the elect, the old person and the carnal life that lives according to fleshly affection are first put to death; then the new person who is according to the spirit is healed, so that he may live for God.

“A time to destroy and a time to build.” Every person first constructs an evil building when [Col. 0229C] he acts in the flesh and daily adds evil to evils, so that a perverse structure rises. This must be destroyed and overthrown in those who are saved, so that justice may be built up in them.

“A time to weep and a time to laugh.” A person ought first to weep for the wrongs he himself has committed, so that afterward he may safely laugh over the good things he has received from God. For unless preceding weeping washes the conscience in contrition, laughter over outwardly cheerful things exults vainly, without inward joy.

“A time to mourn, or to lament, and a time to dance.” First the flesh ought in repentance to be afflicted with torments for wrongful pleasure; afterward it ought to be exercised in good works through the pursuit of virtues. Thus indeed the life of the righteous is trained by pains and prepared by punishments for joys, so that [Col. 0229D] it may come purified to its fruit. Its evils always precede it so that they may pass away, while its goods are deferred to the end so that they may remain without end.

In this sequence we may also consider a certain order in the correction and amendment of the soul that is to be justified. First of all, the wrongful will in the person being corrected must be put to death; then what is good must be revived, whether weak or dead. What lives badly is rightly killed, and what is badly weak is rightly healed. After the will has been changed, the mass of perverse deeds, wrongly built up, is destroyed, and the pursuits of good works, dissipated by long neglect, are rebuilt. Then weeping follows for past guilt; when it has cleansed the conscience with the fountain of tears, it is at last changed into the laughter and joy of consolation. Lamentation or mourning also follows in repentance, when the sorrow of the mind is extended even to the affliction of the flesh, so that afterward the flesh itself, worn down, may also be gladdened by its own consolation along with the exultation of the mind.

“A time to scatter stones and a time to gather stones.” If by stones we understand the strong works of virtues, what else should we understand by the scattering of stones except the multiplication of good works? To scatter stones is to offer the examples of strong deeds far and wide to the knowledge of many. To gather stones is, after the pursuit of labour, to receive the fruit of good works. Thus there is a time to scatter stones and again a time to gather stones, because a person must first exercise himself in good works through the pursuits of the active life, so that afterward he may receive the fruit of his work in the savour of contemplation. Since this savour is most delightful to those who enjoy it and full of supreme delight, seeming aptly to surpass all things that can be loved, it is immediately added:

“A time to embrace.” For there are certain embraces of wisdom and delightful bonds of inward love. When the mind, admitted within, grasps the joy of its beloved, and clasping it with certain arms of its desires, makes a covenant and asks for a compact of perpetual abiding. But because mortal life is quickly driven away from the sight of inward light by the darkness of its own obscurity, and is separated by the mutability of its condition from fellowship with eternal stability, it is fittingly added:

“A time to be far from embraces.” For after the time of embracing follows the time of being far from embraces, because the human mind, though at times raised through grace and admitted to the touch of inward sweetness, is nevertheless soon weighed down by the burden of its weakness and falls back again to earthly and customary thoughts. Although this statement seems specially to concern the wicked, because it records as it were prosperity and good at its beginning but adversities at its end, it is enough that we have observed this distinction in the preceding six items which we expounded; let us apply what follows rather to a general meaning. For one thing is indicated by arrangement, and another expressed by signification: arrangement of order suggests, as it were, a distinction of persons, while signification shows by its sense only the truth of things.

Therefore what is narrated concerning the wicked alone, by the order of an altered sequence, may without impropriety be understood alike of good and evil persons, so that sometimes what, as regards the narrative order, displays the life of the reprobate may, according to its signification, belong more especially to the good. Yet we may also understand this very statement without impropriety of certain reprobate persons. Even if at times they seem to approach the love of good, through some affection bearing the appearance of virtue, as though approaching the embrace of wisdom, yet because they do not separate their mind from carnal desires [Col. 0231A] and earthly covetousness, they quickly fall back into their accustomed state and, in the very thing in which they seemed to have drawn near, become far away.

Accordingly, just as the elect are temporarily held back from the embrace of highest truth, that they may burn more ardently in longing through this very delay and at length more fully attain that for which they have longed, so the reprobate too are temporarily permitted, in a certain manner, to approach some knowledge of it, so that they may see what will bring them shame and their wickedness may not be excused. But this is the difference: all the righteous and elect, after tasting the sweetness of inward good, are temporarily driven back in order to burn more ardently in longing; but the reprobate, after recognizing truth, are cast away, so that from this very knowledge they may take testimony against themselves for their own condemnation. The former are admitted [Col. 0231B] and repelled in order to be spurred on; the latter are admitted and cast away in order to be put to shame.

Thus most pagan philosophers were admitted; but they did not touch wisdom closely, nor did they draw it to themselves in order to enjoy its sweetness. They saw and recognized it, and thought that they loved it; but theirs was a distant and alien love, commending its appearance without drinking in its sweetness. As though with arms stretched out and hands extended from afar, they wished to make an embrace; but the beloved was not between their breasts, to be clasped firmly, to linger, and to remain. Therefore it quickly and swiftly fled from them and could not be retained by an alien love.

Thus the beloved flees. Yet the beloved does not flee in order to escape, but only hides and conceals himself in order to provoke love, so that he may be sought in longing and not found until he is loved most ardently. Often he returns again as though about to remain and offers himself to be experienced; then after a little while he slips away again, reserving the fruit for the future. In all these things there is a time to embrace and a time to be far from embraces.

“A time to acquire and a time to lose.” When is there a time to acquire, except when there is a time to embrace? And again, when is there a time to lose, except when there is a time to be far from embraces? For when the beloved is present, the success of every virtue is multiplied, and the inward house is filled with abundance and richness. Then barren things bear fruit, what had withered is enriched with fertility, and the soul itself marvels at the riches it possesses. Holy affections burn, chaste desires blaze, and hostile impulses are lulled; whatever was accustomed to resist or offer troublesome opposition goes far away, so that all things are peaceful and calm. The capacity for acting well is supplied according to one’s wish, and the abundance of a rich will overflows even into the multiplication of holy works.

This, therefore, is the time to acquire, when holy merits are accumulated and the reward of good works is multiplied in the treasuries of eternal riches. But lest unbroken success perhaps cast down the human heart through pride, the time to lose follows, so that when the success of virtues is temporarily taken away through a health-giving dispensation, the heart may be more firmly established in virtue [Col. 0232A] through humility. Thus the holy mind, resting inwardly in the embrace of wisdom, is increased with the riches of virtues; but scattered outwardly through occupations, it is constrained by need and diminished by want. Conversely, carnal people gather perishable wealth by labour and, once they begin to devote themselves to the embraces of pleasures, promptly consume it in idle and luxurious living.

We may also fittingly understand the times to acquire and the times to lose in another sense. There are two lives: the active and the contemplative. One of them, the active life, gathers gains of holy merits through laborious exercise in the pursuit of good works; the other, the contemplative life, rests in the knowledge of truth with perfected love. These lives, indeed, we rightly understand to be signified by Jacob’s two wives, Leah and Rachel. Leah is said to have had weak eyes but to have been fruitful; Rachel, on the other hand, to have had beautiful eyes but to have been barren. The active life is fruitful in the offspring of good work, but the contemplative life is clear-sighted in the knowledge of truth.

Since the virtue of holy persons is exercised in turn in each life and is transformed, as it were, through alternating change—so that now their patience is tested in the labour of work, and now their desire is refreshed by the sweetness of contemplation—it is rightly said: “A time to acquire and a time to lose.” For it is a time to acquire when the devout mind multiplies the gains of merits in the pursuit of good work; and then, as it were, the time to lose follows [Col. 0232C] when, for love of inward repose, it willingly bears the losses of action. It voluntarily sets aside, as it were, the riches of good work, in order that it may rest, even with little, in the sweetness of contemplation. Yet none of its merits is thereby diminished, since through that very longing and love of the highest good it earns more than by the pursuit of works.

“A time to acquire and a time to lose.” It is certain concerning the perverse that, if at any time they acquire something good by acting rightly, they quickly lose it because they have no perseverance in the good they began. The time to acquire could certainly profit them nothing, because the time to lose what they had acquired followed it. Often a greater loss follows them in this very respect: they become puffed up over what they acquire, but are not humbled over what they lose.

[Col. 0232D] “A time to keep and a time to cast away.” There is a time when God guards his elect from temptation, because perhaps they might have been broken by adversities; and again there is a time to cast away, when, as they must be exercised by troubles, he healthfully exposes them for a time to temptation, as though angered. God also often keeps the wicked in this life safe and tranquil from threatening troubles, in order afterward to cast them away all the more severely in judgment, the more patiently he has borne them here even while protecting his adversaries.

A person himself also ought to keep many things for a time which afterward he should cast away in their proper time: things which, kept at their proper time, can bring assistance to the one who keeps them, but which, unless cast away in their proper time, become an impediment. Earthly possessions ought rightly to be kept for a time for the support of the flesh; yet, when it is known that danger to the soul lies in them, they ought without hesitation to be cast away at the proper time. There are also many things in spiritual discipline and in the pursuit of virtues which ought at one time to be kept and at another cast away, lest perhaps a work of virtue done without discernment become blameworthy when it could have been reckoned as meritorious. For everything changes with time, and there is nothing that always remains the same. Therefore one who lives under time must weigh the causes and outcomes of all things in accordance with their times.

“A time to tear and a time to sew.” Everyone who lives in the flesh according to the flesh is, through fleshly affection, as it were one with those things which the flesh desires. It is therefore necessary that a person who turns from carnal things to spiritual things should first be torn away in mind from those things to which he had clung by affection. Then indeed he freely binds himself to spiritual things by love, once nothing remains of earthly affections to turn his mind toward alien desires. Thus there is a time to tear, so that a person may first tear his mind away from earthly desires; afterward there is a time to sew, so that by spiritual love he may begin to cling in mind to eternal and abiding goods.

Nor does it seem to be passed over that the things which are torn are substantially one, whereas the things which are sewn are essentially different but become one, as it were accidentally, through the intervening bond of thread. Thus every human being is united by nature to corruptible and perishing things, but becomes a participant in eternal things by grace. Human and divine things are sewn into one in such a way that what were two by nature become one by grace. Compunction is the needle itself, and love the thread; the needle makes a path and pierces both, so that the thread may hold both together. For sewing could not otherwise take place unless both were pierced and both held together, since one would depart from the other and easily separate itself from unity if both were not held by the bond.

For this reason the needle of compunction pierces both, and the thread of love binds both together, so that they may stand together and not depart from one another. The needle of compunction pierces human things when it pursues guilt; it pierces divine things when it searches out the hidden things of eternity. Thus compunction is twofold, and there is “the upper spring and the lower spring” (*irrigum superius* and *irrigum inferius*; Joshua 15). By the upper spring divine things are pierced, and by the lower spring human things are pierced. Through the compunction that arises from guilt, the sinful conscience is transfixed; through the compunction that arises from longing for eternal things, hidden things are penetrated. The former subtly penetrates the conscience in order to drive out harmful things; the latter searches invisible things by deep reflection in order to grasp what is loved. Thus both are pierced and both transfixed: the one by pain, through which guilt is drawn out; the other by longing, through which desired things are sought.

After this follows the thread of love, [Col. 0234A] through which a bond of unity is effected on both sides, so that, now joined together, they may not be separated from one another. For love rises on both sides, and the bond of affection meets in one: the human mind, looking back, sees how much has been entrusted to it there through mercy; contemplating divine things, it sees how much has been promised to it there for glory. It loves both, and a knot of charity is made in both, because mercy is sweet unto glory and glory delightful unto mercy. The love of these cannot be separated, because the sewing has been done and the bonds of eternal charity stand firm. Therefore then was the time to tear, but now is the time to sew.
