“A time to keep silence and a time to speak.” “Let the one who hears,” says Scripture, “say: Come” (Revelation 22). For the one who first opens the ear of the heart through obedience to the word of God afterward rightly loosens his tongue to speak to his neighbour. Whoever has not first learned, through obedience, to keep silence in another’s word of edification is shown to be liable to harm if he presumes to teach others himself. Therefore there is first a time to keep silence, so that a person may learn what he is to teach; and afterward a time to speak, so that one who has now recognized the truth may not be ashamed to speak it at its proper time. For both are faults: both when a person rashly presumes what he ought not, and when through negligence he is sluggish concerning what he ought to do. Therefore one must first take care not to commit unlawful acts, and afterward strive not to neglect duties.

“A time to keep silence and a time to speak.” Times succeed one another, and one time comes after another.

[Col. 0234C] “A time to love and a time to hate.” If someone should say that in the time of love there is a time to speak, and in the time of hate a time to keep silence, so that what is holy may not be given to dogs nor pearls cast before swine (Matthew 7), but that the righteous person should put a finger upon his mouth when the days are evil and be silent when the sinner stands against him—was justice not therefore brought into the world so that sinners might be reproved and the wicked converted, lest they perish? Therefore the times are ambiguous, because they run their course uncertainly. Yet nothing is without its time, whether it be love or hate. Love has its time, and hate has its time. To the person who is commanded to love his neighbour as himself, it is likewise said that he should hate himself. From this it is clear that one who loves God as himself, while he loves his neighbour in God, does not know how to love himself in opposition to God.

Therefore there is a time to love and a time to hate: we who strive, for God’s sake, to love our enemies should not presume, when God’s cause is injured, to love even friends against him. There is also another love and another hate: each person should love his flesh in those things necessary to sustain its weakness, and hate it in those things demanded by wrongful desires. Thus there is a time to love and a time to hate, because, so long as we live under the frailty of this mortality and bear the contradiction of sin in our flesh, we must with great discernment weigh when we ought compassionately to nourish failing nature, lest it collapse, and when again we ought to press down by affliction the movement of vices rising in the flesh, lest it grow strong.

For it is written: “No one has hated his own flesh” (Ephesians 5). And again it is said: “Make no provision for the flesh in its desires” (Romans 13). Hence it is plainly shown that the flesh must be loved insofar as compassion for nature is concerned, and hated insofar as the chastisement of guilt is concerned. Because this requires great moderation of discernment, a time is prescribed for love and hate, so that, walking in the middle path, we may neither suffocate nature while pursuing guilt nor nourish guilt while sustaining nature.

But because this cannot be accomplished without great labour and severe struggle, it follows: “A time of war and a time of peace,” so that a person may at once recognize both that no one comes to victory without conflict and that one who contends lawfully rests in peace after victory has been gained. Thus the time of peace is placed after the time of war, so that one who might have been broken by the burden of conflict may be comforted by the gift of peace.

“A time of war and a time of peace.” There are three who wage war against us: namely, the devil, the world, and our flesh. Paul recognized that he had all these as enemies, declaring that he had undertaken battle against all of them. He testified that his struggle against demons was unceasing, together with all the faithful, when he said: “For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against powers and principalities, against the rulers of this darkness, against spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 6). Again, he declared that he had a struggle against the world—that is, against perverse people who love the world—when he related that at Ephesus he had fought against beasts (1 Corinthians 15). Likewise, he testifies that he had an unceasing struggle against his own flesh, saying: “Thus I fight, not as one beating the air; but I chastise my body and reduce it to servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be found reprobate” (1 Corinthians 9).

There are, therefore, three tyrants who lead their armies out against us into battle, and each has battle-lines drawn up to wage war upon the soul. The devil marshals troops of suggestions against the faithful soul; the world brings forward prosperity and adversity to overcome us; the flesh, stirring up crowds of carnal desires, rises against us for battle. But against all these the faithful soul must fight bravely and, fortified by God’s protection, employ the missiles of virtues to overthrow the powers of the hostile force. We conquer the devil if, with perseverance, we refuse to receive his suggestions. We conquer the world if we steadfastly despise its prosperity and patiently endure its adversity. We conquer the flesh if we do not consent to its wrongful desires.

But enemies once defeated do not immediately cease, so that peace may at once exist. Rather, they try again and again, make fresh attempts, and do what they can. Often, though timid, they themselves make an attack as if daring, and do so with terror in order to test what courage is in us. Often they lay snares, advance secretly to reconnoitre, hide themselves, and wish to remain concealed until they come upon us unexpectedly. In all these things many dangers arise, with daily watchfulness and fear on every side; and there comes to be a great war and a long contest, until our side is strengthened in every way and they utterly cease in despair, withdrawing from their hope, so that they are either deterred from us or subjected to our dominion.

For this too will undoubtedly come to pass, if we do not fail in our hope and good patience: at last full and undivided peace will be restored after the labour of the contest has been completed. Then the devil will be driven from us by divine power, so that he will not dare presume against us; terrified, he will flee and withdraw in shame. The world too, which was accustomed to rage in its agitations, will be pacified, and the desires of the flesh will be lulled by a strengthened spirit. Then, in the time of our peace, we shall remember the former times when there was war; and we shall not then repent, but rejoice and exult for the days in which we saw evils, and peace will be sweet in the glad remembrance of past labours. For this reason there is a time of war and a time of peace.

“What has a person more from his labour?” What more does he have than war and peace, love and hate, and all the other things which the wheel of temporal outcomes brings forth in its revolving course? Therefore he has no more from his labour than war and peace, because by this labour he cannot possess peace alone. Thus neither does he possess peace by his labour, just as he does not possess war by his own will. For all things follow the decree of the higher dispensation; the moments of time are not subject to human choice, so that this or that may happen. Rather, in all things a person undergoes the law—whether willingly, unto merit, or unwillingly, unto punishment.

Therefore a person ought not to trust in his labour or place hope in his actions, as though he could either bring about what has not been ordained from above or prevent what has been ordained. For human labour can add nothing to the whole so as to make something greater; because the just governance of the Creator has so disposed all things in equity that whatever strives without his cooperation, abandoning the order of the universe, is moved rather toward non-being.

## HOMILY XVII. On the confusion of minds arising from the passage of time.

[Col. 0236D]

We have just passed from the times, but would that we had reached eternity! For many things still remain, and very many continue to revolve around us; and the times once more repeat their cycle on every side, so that there is no end until all things have been completed. After the mutability of things there follows, indeed, a grave confusion of minds: for hearts move along with the revolutions and passages of time, so that they do not stand in truth but flow away with the things that go in order to pass away. Therefore he withdraws from all things which waver and fluctuate outwardly, as though all these were trifling and did not work greatly toward peril; and he turns inward, and there doubles his complaint concerning the hidden vanity [Col. 0237A], examining it with a graver lament than the alien vanity which appears outside.

For the mutability of things would not have harmed us, if there had not been mutability of minds. For it was itself good that transitory things should change their appearance in due season; but it was not good that the judgments of human minds should forsake truth. We do not therefore complain that times are various, for this is good; rather, we complain that human judgments are various, for this is not good. Truth cannot be other than itself: for what is good in truth is not evil, and what is not good in truth is evil. Why, then, is it judged that this is good and that evil; and judged that this is evil and that good, when in truth [Col. 0237B], if it is evil, it is not good, and if it is good, it is not evil? One says, “It is good,” and another says, “It is evil”; he who says, “This is good,” says, “That is evil”; and he who says, “This is evil,” says, “That is good.” Yet all speak wrongly, because the whole is good. This alone is not good: that they speak wrongly concerning that which is good. Therefore all things are good; and only those are evil who ought, beyond all others, to have been good. For all other things are what they ought to be, while they alone are not what they ought to be: because they are not truthful and are not in truth. Thus all things are good in that which they are; but they are not good in that which they are, because they are not what they ought to have been. This, therefore, among other vanities, is itself reckoned a great vanity [Col. 0237C], and in comparison is set above all vanities. And he says:

> I saw the affliction which God gave to the children of men, that they might be stretched out in it.

What, then, is that affliction?

> He made all things good in their time, and delivered the world over to their disputation, so that man may not find the work which God has wrought from beginning to end.

Therefore it is not the mutability of things that afflicts man, but his own disputation afflicts him. And rightly so: for *disputatio* always signifies unrest and contention. Thus the mutability of things is not man’s labor; rather, that he has himself become restless is his labor. This restlessness itself is the great disputation [Col. 0237D] which man has in his instability, so that he does not perceive the same thing: because he is divided and made other, so that he is not wholly one.

Consider now the great disputation which man conducts upon earth. For it is extensive, prolonged, and exceedingly entangled, so that it cannot easily have an end until man himself receives his end. And now, that you may believe, see how many opinions, from the beginning, the inquisitive wise have fashioned concerning the works of God; and to this day no one has been able to impose an end upon so great a matter. They still quarrel daily and fight by contentious disputations. One says, “It is this”; another says, “It is not, but something else.” Many things are said, and falsehoods of opinions concerning the judgment of things are fabricated as though skillfully made. Very many assert [Col. 0238A] that nothing exists except that which is seen; and others come forward and maintain that nothing truly exists except that which is not seen. In all these matters they heap up and multiply their arguments, weave reasonings—and quasi-reasonings; each person’s opinion is, to him, a reasoning.

For God set his work before the eyes of men, so that he might question their hearts concerning it; while he himself lies hidden behind it, until they undergo our exercise in it. They draw upon sensation, judge with the heart, and bring forth very many things from the treasury of their judgments and from the deep abyss of their imaginings, false opinions, and empty thoughts. Some say that nature alone exists and there is nothing else; that God is nothing, but empty fear invented all things; that what exists has always been so [Col. 0238B], from the beginning and before the beginning, without beginning. The ages revolve, nature works upon itself and renews itself, and it cannot be other than it always was.

Others, on the contrary, cry out and contend on behalf of the Creator’s wrong, thinking that they defend the one whom they themselves assail with their falsehoods. They say that there is a maker who fashioned all things out of matter coeternal with himself, in order to give them a better form. These do not know the Creator’s power, but deny that anything was made from nothing; and they deny that any of the things which exist can relapse into nothing, maintaining that the Creator’s operation consists only in the alterations of things.

After them come others who contend and dispute, promising to remove error and reveal truth. They too confess that all things were made from nothing, yet deny that he through whom all things were made was made; and they say that there was once a time when nothing created existed, while he who always was existed then. Their doctrines have, as it were, a good beginning, but an evil end follows. For those who think, as it were, truly concerning the creation of things utter many falsehoods concerning their subsistence; and there is no end to human disputations and inventions. They devise essences, forms, atoms, ideas of primary constitutions, many elements, infinite origins, invisible motions, and generative agencies. In all these things semblances of reason multiply, very many disputations arise, and truth is in none of them. For he who affirms speaks falsely, and he who contradicts [Col. 0238D] speaks falsely, because, by disputing and lying, all alike have departed from truth in one vanity.

For man will not be able to find the work which God has wrought from beginning to end. Of all things made from the beginning and to be made until the end, man cannot find a single thing so as to comprehend it and know all that it is. For even if some appear to have discovered many things, all were set before them; and those things which were hidden could in no way be discovered. God delivered the world over to their disputation and set his works before them, that they might see and judge them. In them he disclosed many things which he wished to be known; but those things which he wished to remain hidden could not be found. Therefore God disclosed in them all things which became known; and man did not find them by his own understanding [Col. 0239A] until they were revealed to him insofar as God willed. Some things were set forth outwardly, and some were revealed inwardly; and man found no means by his own understanding to reach hidden things until they were manifested in himself.

And if he should contend that he himself has found some things, could he nevertheless find all that God has wrought from beginning to end? Even in the things he found, could he find all that was there, without some remainder continuing hidden and concealed, to which his understanding was not admitted, so as to find the whole? For if man had found the whole, there would be no disputation, nor would opinions run in contrary directions concerning all things in the world. We all see this world alike: it is set before our eyes [Col. 0239B], delivered to our disputation; we see this whole before us, and do not know whence it came here. For he who made it lies hidden, and he puts his work before himself so that in it he may be both hidden and manifested.

The created image, confronting human contemplation at close range, causes it neither to see its Creator as plainly manifest nor wholly to be ignorant of him. Therefore man’s understanding, stirred by the appearance of things, rises from that which offers itself to manifestation, according to an emulation of truth, and tries to search inward things. It has in the works of God the beginning of its first contemplation, but does not reach the end of God’s works so as to grasp all that is hidden. For if it could reach the end, it would certainly find God, because all things have their end and completion in him from whom they are [Col. 0239C]. Therefore it does not reach the end, because it could not find God until he himself manifested himself in us; and “those who search searches were confounded, because they failed” (Ps. LXIII), and were unable to comprehend or to put an end to their disputations.

Therefore God made the wisdom of the world foolish (I Cor. V), because he placed the world in their disputation, himself remaining hidden until those disputing and seeking vain things should fail. And man will not find every work which God has wrought from beginning to end. Afterwards God revealed himself and came forth to be found, when man could no longer boast as though he had known God by his own understanding and wisdom—he who had failed while searching into God’s work [Col. 0239D].

To this end, therefore, it served that the world was in time delivered to their disputation: that man might not find every work which God has wrought from beginning to end. These are the disputations of men, vainly and inquisitively seeking the hidden things of God’s works; they multiply them for themselves by fabricating lies about what they do not know and fortify their errors with contentious arguments. There are also other disputations, exceedingly numerous and varied, in men’s desires; from them arise pursuits of many vanities. Every person prefers what he himself loves, and all hearts are drawn into infinite divisions, so that they never agree in one thing.

Some follow wantonness, luxury, and pleasure: drunkenness, games, laughter, and dancing; and they judge this to be human happiness and the sweetest delight. Others seek honors, offices, and great renown among the peoples, commend their pursuits, and contend with grave rivalry that this is the better portion in human life. Others heap up money and pile together wealth, thinking to purchase security and great confidence against approaching want in a time of distress. These praise foresight and call carefulness better, although they themselves wish to be secure. Thus each is separately borne toward his own appetites, approving contrary things; and they dispute by wrangling and by yielding to unruly desires. The world is delivered to their disputation, so that in its abundance each may test and prove his own pleasures, see them, and consume in arguments against one another the abundance of that which each has chosen to approve in his desires [Col. 0240B]. With great obstinacy each seizes what he has himself chosen; each praises his own part; and a great disputation and contention of wills arises amid the various judgments produced by many desires.

In all these things man does not find the work which God has wrought from beginning to end. For the beginning of God’s works is the use of temporal things, but their end and completion is the fruit of eternal things. Therefore he who establishes his disputation in worldly things and seeks confirmation of his desires cannot find, in the works which God has wrought, anything from beginning to end. Although he is permitted to experience how great a delight may be in the good things of this age, he does not attain in the contemplation of God that ineffable joy which confers consummate blessedness [Col. 0240C]. For this reason the world has been delivered to lovers of the world, to whom it is not granted to deserve to find God’s works from beginning to end. Since the sweetness of eternal goods is withheld from them, carnal delights are given them, and worldly joys are exposed to the dissipation of their evil desires.

We find still other grave and manifold disputations in human judgments, stirring up dreadful quarrels, so that they even grow into blasphemy against the Creator and say what ought not to be said. For men violently seize God’s place, appoint themselves judges of the world, and dispute about the world, God’s works, his providence, and the judgments by which he orders the whole world. Some say, “God did this well”; others murmur and say, “That was not done well.” Such are the complaints and presumptions of men by which they provoke God’s wrath: because they refuse to submit to his laws, dispute about his works, and censure his judgments.

Someone perishes by a cruel death or grievous loss and is crushed by a pitiable misfortune. His enemy comes and says, “God has done well; he has judged an ungodly and sinful man according to his wickedness.” But his friend murmurs and brings a complaint against God, asking why he permitted an innocent man to perish and did not preserve the just. The one is condemned [Col. 0241A] for his wickedness, and the other is judged for his rashness. Yet men do not cease disputing about God’s works and weighing his judgments according to their own opinion; and God is reproached by the thoughts of malicious men.

Men say that God ought not to have created harmful things, nor placed in his works things that are hostile and injurious; they curse God’s good creatures and blaspheme their Creator. Why did God make frogs, flies, serpents, all poisonous things, and all hostile and pestilential things? He would have done better, they say, if he had made everything good. For there are very many evils, and all evils are not good. Yet he himself made all things good in their time; only man is evil, not understanding goodness nor retaining the judgment of truth. By an evil will he departs from goodness; and when what he wrongly does not wish comes to pass, he says that it is wrongly done, though it is done well and he himself wills evil [Col. 0241B].

Therefore evil wills and wicked desires blind human hearts, so that they do not understand what is right, because they neither love nor will what is good. They censure God because he made harmful things; yet no one censures him when his enemy is harmed, though they all are enemies of God and adversaries of truth. For this reason man does not understand the work which God has wrought from beginning to end. For the carnal man does not perceive the things of God (1 Cor. 2). He follows his own desire and praises the delight of his longings; when he is given what he loves, he thinks that matters go well with him—although this is rather done to his harm. When his desires are resisted, he murmurs and makes complaint, alleging that something is wrongly done when it is justly ordered; and he does not understand the works which God performs from beginning to end.

From the time man is brought forth from the earth until he is called back into earth, he does not understand the works which God has wrought from beginning to end. God performs many things concerning man from his beginning to his end, and man does not find the end for which all these things are done until he himself receives his end. Then he will understand; then he will find what God wrought in him from his beginning to his end, whether in mercy or in judgment, in order to bring him to such an end as his deeds from beginning to end proved that he would reach [Col. 0241D]. Meanwhile, until the end comes, all things lie hidden from beginning to end, so that man does not find the work which God has wrought from beginning to end.

Therefore man can dispute concerning the works of God which God performs from beginning to end, but cannot find the work which God has wrought from beginning to end. If man cannot find the work which God performs from his own beginning to his own end—so as even to understand what he himself has seen—how then will he find the works which God has wrought from the beginning of the world to the end of the age, which he himself could not see? Let man therefore cease disputing concerning God’s judgments by which he governs and orders the whole world from beginning to end. For man was not appointed by God as ruler [Col. 0242A] or judge of the world, but as its possessor—not to govern the elements of the world by his own strength or power, nor to dispense the developments of time according to his own judgment, but to receive the fruits of the world and the alternations of times, according to the Creator’s ordering, for the use of sustaining his own weakness. Therefore he adds and says:

> I knew that there was nothing better than to rejoice and do good in one’s life. For every man who eats and drinks and sees good from his labor—this is God’s gift.

For every man who contends and disputes concerning God’s works, finds fault with God’s judgments, and accuses his ordering in the world—this is not God’s gift, nor is it from God, but against God. He acts better who lawfully uses in this world God’s gifts, acquired by just labor [Col. 0242B], than one who quarrels against God over what occurs in this world contrary to his will or opinion. For by quarrelling and murmuring against God man cannot change his ordering. Therefore it is better to receive his judgments with fear than to murmur against him as though injured by him because of our own hurt.

God has hidden his judgments from us for this very reason: that, since we can neither penetrate them by our own understanding nor alter them according to our own will, we may fear more deeply. Therefore he continues and says:

> I learned that all the works which God made endure forever. We cannot add anything to them or take away anything which God has made, that he may be feared.

This is true not only of God’s works by which he created the essences of things and imposed form and measure upon created things according to their several kinds and species. God’s works endure forever because his ordering in them does not change, and each thing preserves its appointed nature. If things pass away, it is not from him that they do so; that they are what they are is from him, but that they cease to be is from themselves—just as their being nothing before they existed was from themselves [Col. 0242C].

This is true not only of the works of God by which he orders the world’s creation, so that they remain forever without alteration and confusion of order. It is also true of the ordering and predestination of his judgments, by which he examines human deeds: they remain forever, and he does not change the law of his providence or the decree of his purpose. As we can neither add to the kinds of things made by his works, by creating so that what was not may be, nor take away from them by destroying and annihilating them so that what was something may become absolutely nothing, so we cannot change his judgments: neither by adding, so that what he has not ordained may happen, nor by taking away, so that what he has ordained to happen may not happen.

So that he alone may be feared, and that the gaze of human conscience may always look toward him in mercy, he reserved to himself alone the power over his works and his judgments. Thus no one can change what he has established as fixed by eternal laws for fulfillment. Therefore man should not dispute over everything which happens to him, but receive God’s judgments with reverence and fear. When God grants prosperity and bestows what is pleasing, let him rejoice in God’s benefits with chaste exultation; but when adversities emerge and troubles come, let him confess his evil deserts and commend God’s justice and truth [Col. 0243A].

And if, when troubles press upon him, he sees his patience shaken, let him set against the fault of murmuring and impatience the gifts of his Creator’s bounty. Thus the mind weighed down by the burden of temptation may be softened by remembrance of God’s benefits, lest it burst forth into blasphemy. Then he will begin to do good, rejoice in his life, and see good from his labor: not only when, with thanksgiving, he enjoys the goods of this world acquired by his own effort, but also when, placed amid adversities, he rejoices through hope of future consolation for the labor of his patience. For he will eat and rejoice in God’s gifts when he exults at the gift in prosperity and is gladdened at the recompense in adversity. Thus he will at all times order himself toward peace with God, so that he may see and understand that God makes all things good in their time, and may not justly accuse him in whatever happens.

For God’s judgments are established; and nothing great or small can be changed in his laws, which stand forever. As, in all kinds of things that seem diminished or destroyed, those which pass away are restored in those which come upon them and succeed them, so that the ordering of the universe preserves its fixed and immovable order and the decree of the first ordering remains forever inviolable [Col. 0243C]—so that the determinate measure of God’s works neither passes beyond its bounds nor falls short—so also his judgments proceed according to a fixed providence, so that nothing can be added to or taken from them.

And if at any time he seems to do otherwise and judge otherwise, there is a hidden dispensation by which his purpose is not changed, though the work varies and judgment is exercised. Indeed, this itself is judgment: that judgment is sometimes deferred in order that it may be restored in its own time, so that nothing of all things made may perish, but they may remain always. For it is always the case that guilt has punishment and justice receives reward. But there is hidden punishment and manifest punishment; likewise there is hidden reward and manifest reward. God often bears with the wicked and postpones their manifest punishment [Col. 0243D], yet every wickedness has hidden punishment. God judges, but seems to defer judgment or wholly fail to notice human deeds to those who see only what is outward.

Likewise, God sometimes tests the just, exercises them through adversities and tribulations, and seems not to have a reward for justice; yet justice is never without its hidden recompense. Its manifest recompense is sometimes delayed, in order that human consciences may be tested concerning their perseverance. Because things that are outwardly manifest proceed differently, human hearts fluctuate and wonder where the judgment of truth is, when innocence is oppressed in this world and wickedness prospers. Therefore he adds and says:

## HOMILY XVIII. On the perverse morals of men, and what Ecclesiastes judged concerning them.

[Col. 0244A]

> I saw under the sun wickedness in the place of judgment, and iniquity in the place of justice. And I said in my heart: The Lord will judge the just and the wicked, and then there will be a time for every matter.

Since a grave disputation concerning God’s judgments and the contrary course of all things has arisen in human minds, and since the reasons must now be set forth why human hearts are stirred against him and rise into murmuring, we shall briefly repeat what has been said above. Thus we may state, as it were from the beginning, the point of what is to be said. Ecclesiastes had previously shown that nothing in this world can remain forever in the same condition; rather, the alternations of times, moving in contrary directions, are borne along without cessation [Col. 0244B]. Although this mutability of things is rightly ordered by the Creator of all things, the human heart is nevertheless shaken by impatience into murmuring and blasphemy against him.

Therefore, after enumerating the times of things, he added and said: “I saw the affliction which God gave to the children of men, that they might be stretched out in it. He made all things good in their time, and delivered the world over to their disputation.” This, then, is the affliction of men: their disputation against God. Since they refuse humbly to submit to God’s judgments, and obstinately censure his ordering—which is good in all things—when something occurs contrary to their perverse will, they are not merely worn down outwardly by the punishment of adversity and the distress of tribulation; much more, inwardly, they are afflicted by the fury and impatience of murmuring [Col. 0244C].

God is said to have given them this affliction, not by corrupting their minds with wickedness, but by justly withdrawing his judgments from their knowledge, so that they may thereby be proved evil. Since they cannot see with what justice that which happens around them is done, they are blinded still further from the knowledge of truth by the fault of their own impatience. Therefore he gave them affliction when he gave them disputation by concealing his judgments, so that man might not find every work which God performs from beginning to end.

For sometimes, in this world, manifest causes precede God’s judgments, when God rewards good human deeds or punishes evil ones by a consequent recompense in the present life. In these matters God’s judgments can to some degree be discerned, so that man may have some judgment concerning hidden truth and thereby revere even those things which he cannot penetrate [Col. 0244D].

But when preceding causes are hidden, or when the consequences are concealed, very many disputes and contradictions arise. Perverse human minds afflict themselves by quarrelling and murmuring against God, since they cannot penetrate his judgments or find the work which he has wrought from beginning to end. For in such great darkness they cannot penetrate to the end for which something is done, even if certain causes appear at the beginning; all things are hidden because of the end. Therefore man does not find every work of God from beginning to end; for even if he seems to see some things, he does not penetrate the whole, and the whole becomes doubtful because the whole is not manifested.

Therefore, lest man quarrel against God in doubtful matters or murmur when placed amid adversity, many prosperities and many pleasing things are granted by God’s gift, so that man may lawfully use goods acquired by just labor, rejoice, be glad, and soften his conscience toward God. Let him think well of God and neither dispute nor contend against him, as though God who has bestowed good things were hostile. This is what the following words mean: “And I knew that there was nothing better than to rejoice and do good in one’s life.” He who benefits himself in his life from the things granted to men by God’s gift for enjoyment, so that he may rejoice and be glad in his God, acts better than one who disputes and contends against God [Col. 0245B].

> For every man who eats and drinks and sees good from his labor—this is God’s gift.

Since this is God’s gift and is lawfully granted by God, it is better than disputing, contending, and murmuring, which are not God’s gift and are not granted to men by God, because they are evil and a great affliction. He is greatly afflicted who can neither love nor approve what he endures, nor change what he hates. Therefore he is greatly afflicted who disputes and quarrels against God, blaspheming his judgments and detesting his works, although man cannot in any way change the things which God performs.

Therefore what follows says:

> I learned that all the works which God made endure forever.

[Col. 0245C] As the works of creation in their kinds do not transgress the order of divine institution, so also the works of God’s judgments, by which he orders human deeds and the whole world, do not overthrow the decree of his predestination and providence, fixed forever. We can neither add anything to them, so that there may be more than has been provided, nor take away, so that the things made may be fewer, in order that God may be feared.

For this reason the ordering of visible things, in the course of passing things and the succession of alternations, does not throw order into confusion: so that man may know and understand that providence is eternal, having from the beginning ordered all things by the fixed and constant examination of its decree, according to how their outcomes should follow in their proper times [Col. 0245D]. Thus man may also learn to fear this providence in his own deeds, whose omnipotence he sees enduring in all its works, and whose firmness and unchangeableness he sees abiding in its judgments.

For the fixed ordering of God’s work and the certain measure by which he brings all things to effect in their own times plainly show that, as his wisdom is not deceived in discerning, so his counsel is not changed in judging.

> What has been done itself remains.

As in this whole body of created things, what has been done remains because the order of the dispensation is not confused, even though mutable nature undergoes variation; so also in his judgments what has been done remains, because even in what he orders differently according to the ineffable dispensation of changing times, he does not alter the decree of his providence. Therefore what has been done remains—both in the universe of things, insofar as concerns the order of the dispensation, and in the execution of his judgment, insofar as concerns the decree of predestination.

> Things that are to come have already been.

In both respects, things that are to come have already been. For in all kinds of things, what once was but now is not will again, according to the similarity and identity of nature’s course in its kind, be the same thing which is to come but is not yet. And in divine judgments we expect the same truth to be displayed in what follows as we have heard maintained in things past. For God everywhere restores what has passed away: as he repairs the loss of passing things by the multiplication in their kinds of things which succeed them [Col. 0246B], so, by judging human deeds daily, he shows that he has kept intact the ancient truth of his judgments, which he has exercised from the beginning, although it might have seemed interrupted for a time.

For with him wickedness always has punishment and virtue reward. But since some punishments are hidden and others manifest, while God endures the impious and sinful through patience and does not at once inflict manifest punishment upon them, human folly supposes that he either does not know or does not care about human deeds, or—even worse—that he approves the perversity of the wicked. Thus the human heart is shaken against God for the very reason that God is shown to be more deserving of human love and praise. Man complains that an evil man is tolerated by God, although it is clear that no man could have been good if no evil man had ever been tolerated [Col. 0246C].

Nevertheless the hearts of the weak are scandalized when they see the impious prospering and the innocent oppressed in this world, because they look only at things outwardly manifest and do not heed those things which are either hidden inwardly or reserved to be manifested in the future. The cause from which their complaint arises is made clear when the following is added:

> I saw under the sun wickedness in the place of judgment, and iniquity in the place of justice.

For he saw that in this world God permits impious persons to be judges and to obtain power, so that they may rule and oppress the innocent; and he saw unjust human deeds which ought to have been just [Col. 0246D], and in all these things a great confusion under the sun. Because God grants power in this world to the perverse, there is wickedness in the place of judgment and iniquity in the place of justice: wickedness is where judgment ought to be, and iniquity where justice ought to be.

For because the impious are set over others, those under them are iniquitous: unless the former oppressed innocence through impiety, the latter would not attack justice through iniquity. Inferiors are bold to perpetrate injustice because superiors are not dutiful in protecting innocence; for if the latter rendered judgment to those suffering wrong, the former would not have been so ready to inflict wrong. But in this too there is wickedness under the sun in the place of judgment, and iniquity in the place of justice: every man relentlessly pursues his neighbor’s evils without mercy, while each, as far as he can, tries to defend his own evils against justice. For every judge is impious in the cause of his neighbor, and unjust against his neighbor in his own cause. When his neighbor’s evils must be judged, he remembers no mercy; but when his own acts against his neighbor must be examined, he does not preserve justice. In this manner all judgments under the sun are perverse [Col. 0247A], human minds waver, and they wonder where God’s judgment is, since he tolerates these things.

Yet we can perhaps consider, in another and more fitting sense, the impiety in the place of judgment and the iniquity in the place of justice under the sun. For under the sun there is impiety in the place of judgment and iniquity in the place of justice [Col. 0247B], when in this world the righteous man suffers the punishment of the wicked, and the wicked man receives the reward of the righteous. For the good are judged in this life only so that here they may receive God’s scourges for their transgressions and pass on to their future reward more purified. But the evil, because they are reserved for future judgment, often suffer in this world not merely no adversities, but are even permitted to fulfil their desires, so that everything may succeed for them, according to their wish, for the pleasure and happiness of this present life. And the requitals seem to proceed in a contrary manner: the good receive evils and the evil goods; the judgment of the righteous appears impious, so that the innocent are oppressed and endure the punishment of the wicked, while the wicked take away the reward of the righteous. Everything appears confused and intermingled, because God does not immediately exercise judgment to deliver the innocent and the righteous from the oppression of the wicked, and to punish those who work iniquity. Hence a grievous disturbance of minds arises, and the faint-hearted are kindled with zeal, because they see only what is outward and suppose that God does not care for human affairs, but has entrusted everything to fortune and that nothing happens by judgment. And, more cruelly still, people often proceed to such perversity that God is blasphemed and said, as it were, to approve iniquity, to have impiety with him, and not to know true judgment. All this arises because under the sun there is impiety in the place of judgment and iniquity in the place of justice, and because, as though in the vanity that is under the sun, all things are confused and everything turns out differently.

Yet when a person considers the works of God and sees how he orders all things with fixed and steadfast moderation, he understands that God is the inspector and governor of all, that his judgments cannot be annulled, and that the deeds of human beings which he does not judge in this life are kept to be examined hereafter. For if, as has been proved from the ordering of his works, God is a just judge, it remains that what is not done in the present in judging human deeds must without doubt be believed to be accomplished in the future. Therefore, in order to set forth the complaint of the weak—because God, amid the changefulness and passing of this life, leaves everything as though unexamined and distributes human deeds with recompense unlike their merits—he said: “I saw under the sun impiety in the place of judgment and iniquity in the place of justice.” But immediately [Col. 0248A], considering that the just judgments of God could not possibly be annulled, he understood that judgment was only deferred, not removed, and said:

> I said in my heart: The Lord will judge the righteous and the wicked, and then there will be a time for every matter under heaven.

Then, when the Lord judges the righteous and the wicked, there will be a time for every matter under heaven, because everything done in life, whether good or evil, will then be brought to judgment. Even now indeed, in this life, the Lord judges the righteous and the wicked; but these requitals are hidden, and those which will be manifest are deferred to the future. Therefore the small-hearted murmur, complain, and suppose there is no just judgment, because they do not see the recompenses. Nevertheless, just judgment is being carried out even now, and each person [Col. 0248B] is judged according to his merits. But all this is inward, beyond the reach of the eye of flesh. Those things which are manifest are deferred until their judgment comes; then all things hidden and manifest will be made manifest, and all will be judged according to just judgment. Then the Lord will judge the righteous and the wicked, and then there will be a time for every matter under heaven.

Meanwhile all things are obscure, and they proceed together, intermingled, toward their end. The righteous are involved in one lot with the wicked while they run together on the way, so that when they have departed together they may be separated and arranged differently. Up to that point there is no distinction among all things that appear outwardly under the sun. But just as all arise together, so they live together and all pass away together. And all this happens in order that [Col. 0248C] human hearts may be tested: whether there lives in them anything of the knowledge of truth and affection for the hidden good, so that perhaps from this they may begin to draw the proof of faith that they are more than what is merely seen. For outwardly there is nothing by which this can be known; all outward proofs are removed so that what is within may begin to work and be tested for what it is worth. For if a person has recognized himself from that inward reality, he is great; and it is established according to merit that he seeks God through faith, whom he does not see by sight.

For at first he withdrew and turned himself away when he contemplated God as present; and it was a great charge and grievous fault to hate the present light. It was therefore appointed for humanity as a remedy of reconciliation: if one seeks the absent One and desires the hidden One [Col. 0248D], and knows that there is what is not seen, it may be made manifest in its own time. Therefore now all things are withdrawn, invisible things are hidden, and man is left outwardly alone with what is alien to him, seeing nothing of what is his own, so that it may be tested whether perhaps some remembrance remains in him to turn him toward seeking that One.

Therefore, considering more deeply the profundity of God’s judgments, this man sees that it is not surprising if, in the cloudiness of this life, no distinction is made between the righteous and the wicked, since our mortality is wrapped in such thick darkness that within it a human being appears even like the beasts. Therefore he adds and says:

> I said in my heart, concerning the sons of men, that God might test them and show that they are like beasts. Therefore one is the end of man and of beasts, and the condition of both is alike.

For this reason man was made mortal, and for this reason the sons of men die like beasts: that they may be tested and shown to be like beasts. For two things had been made in the human being: one according to the likeness of God, the other according to the likeness of a beast. That which was created according to the likeness of God was by nature made immortal, just as God, in whose likeness it was made, was immortal. But that which had been made according to the likeness of a beast was by nature corruptible, like those things in whose likeness it had been made. For both were taken from earth, and earth was the material of both; and that earth itself was corruptible by nature, just as those things made from earth were. Thus two things were made in man: one earthly, the other heavenly; one by nature [Col. 0249B] corruptible, the other immortal; one the likeness of a beast, the other of God.

The body was indeed earthly and corruptible by nature, made in the likeness of a beast; but the soul was heavenly and immortal by nature, created in the image of God. Body and soul, two things, were joined into one human being; and the body was granted the benefit of this fellowship, that it might share in the soul’s immortality unto incorruption. All this was done for the glory of the soul, because, standing in justice and truth, it was pleasing to God: its garment would not have been worn away if its obedience had endured. That which was the likeness of a beast in man was covered with the glory of incorruption, so that it might, as it were, be concealed; he might not see it to the shame of his love, but might behold in the whole form of his beloved that which he loved, without being separated anywhere from it.

Afterward the soul turned itself toward an alienated love, forgot what was its own better good, and looked outward upon an alien beauty. It fixed its gaze upon the adornment of its garment to delight itself there; it began to commit fornication after bodily allurements, and spiritual love was withdrawn from its eyes. God was angry; this turning away did not please him. He wished to call man back inwardly to what was true, lest his gaze should always cling to the painted images of deceptive sight. He removed the glory of his garment, so that it should go into corruption; and he commanded the soul to return, lest it give that garment life and carry it into eternity. He caused its garment to fall apart, to show man that his glory was not in that in which he saw himself like the beasts. Man fell, and [Col. 0249D] that which was earthly and corruptible was dissolved; it began to flow away, so as to return whence it had come. And this was done so that man might be tested: whether he remembered his good, and whether he knew to seek it when compelled to abandon the vain appearance and depart from that to which he had perversely clung.

Therefore God tests the sons of men and shows that they are like beasts. Hence one is the end of man and beasts, and the condition of both is alike: as man dies, so they too die. In death, then, man and beast have one condition, because as man dies, so they too die. Yet the condition of mortality comes to man by judgment, but to the beast by nature. Though they possess it alike, they do not possess it for a like cause: man came to die through fault, but the beast received death by nature. Nevertheless man is tested and shown to be like beasts, because one is the end of man and beasts and their condition is alike: man dies as they die.

> And all breathe alike.

That is, both they and he have a similar life and a similar breath of life. And in all these things:

> Man has nothing more than the beast.

For their origin is common to both, since both were made from earth; and their course is common, because together:

> All things are subject to vanity and mutability.

All things pass away; they die in the same likeness at the consummation of their end and return to the earth from which they were first taken. Thus formerly man shared with beasts one bodily origin, since the body was taken from earth, and one condition of living with beasts, in that the earthly body was nourished likewise from earth. But man did not share one end with beasts, because man was made not to die or return to the earth from which he was made. Then, through the incorruption of the body, his lowly origin was veiled; through immortality it was concealed, lest it become a reproach that man was like the beasts. Nor did God wish to show man his own ignobility, exposing him wholly in that condition. Rather, he clothed him with the beauty of immortality and set him apart from his own kind into another lot. But when man sinned against God, God deprived him of his glory and sent him back to his origin, so that by the way in which he went [Col. 0250C] he might recognize whence he had come.

Therefore one is the end of man and beasts, and the condition of both is alike: as man dies, so they too die. All breathe alike; and in all these matters man has nothing more than the beast, but all alike are subject to vanity.

> And all go to one place.

That is, to the earth, their mother and source of origin, because:

> They were made from earth and return together to earth.

And if someone wishes to say that man has more than the beast in this—that the spirit of the sons of Adam goes upward, so that, when the body dies into death, it remains alive in life; while the spirits of beasts go downward, that is, together with the death of the body [Col. 0250D] flow away into corruption—who knows this? Not because it is untrue, but because it is hidden. Therefore:

> Who knows this?

For he did not say, “This is false,” but, “Who knows this?” No one knows it. For it cannot be known by man, though it can be believed. And it is true because it is believed: what is believed is true, and faith itself is a firm, unfaltering knowledge. Yet no human being knows this in the manner in which are known things seen, heard, touched, and perceived by the other senses; or in the manner in which are known things that cannot naturally be doubted and that are demonstrated by indubitable reason even to unbelievers while they doubt. This is perceived by faith alone. Therefore those who lack faith have great doubt concerning it, because they do not know it; nor can it be demonstrated to them by those who grasp it by faith, because they themselves do not grasp faith.

Therefore they suppose that man has absolutely nothing more than the beast, because they do not know that the spirit of the sons of Adam goes upward and the spirit of beasts downward. When they are told that man has more than the beast because the human spirit goes upward to life and the spirits of beasts downward to death, they say: “Who knows this?” For they suppose that nothing can be known unless it is seen by the eye of flesh and touched by sense. Therefore they do not receive the knowledge of faith, by which alone man is restored to that in which he has more than the beast. Because they cannot see or openly touch and comprehend what it is that man has beyond the beast [Col. 0251B], they despair altogether of eternal life, disbelieve what is said, and cast themselves with all their intention into the pleasures of this present life, as though this alone were their portion and they would receive nothing further afterward.

For they do not know that this is hidden in order that it may be believed that man has more than the beast, and that man himself may be tested by God in faith through his ignorance. If it were seen, it would not be believed but known; there would be no merit, man would not be tested, the wicked would not be convicted, and the good would not be exercised. Therefore that in which man has more than the beast is hidden so that it may not be seen, that faith may have merit and unbelief a place. Many are unbelieving and say, “Who knows this?” They argue that what is certain ought not to be abandoned for the uncertain; they begin to embrace present things [Col. 0251C] and seize what is seen, so that they may hold what is certain. Yet they are deceived in the uncertain, because those things pass away and slip away while they are thought to be held; and those things which they thought uncertain come in as the certain things.

This writer displays all this and shapes his account in this direction and that, following the minds of human beings, since they themselves waver and fluctuate in the uncertainty of life’s gloomy darkness. He has stated human doubt concerning their life: they do not know whether man has more than the beast, nor do they find anyone who knows whether, after the death of the body, the human spirit remains alive in life. Now, because of this very doubt and despair concerning future life, he takes up their own voice in approval of present pleasures, saying:

> I found that there is nothing better than for a man to rejoice in his work, and that this is his portion.

Those who do not believe that there is a future life suppose that this alone is man’s portion: that he should rejoice in his work and enjoy in this life the fruit of his labour. For those who do not judge that a reward will follow after the work is completed consider that the profit of work is to be taken not after the work but in the work itself; they think only that person happy who prepares the fruit of his labour for present use, not one who reserves the reward of his work to be received later.

> For who will bring him back, that he may know what will be after him?

Once man has departed from this life, he is not brought back or recalled again into this life to experience and again feel what takes place in this age, so that he may once more enjoy its pleasures and receive the delight that will exist after him [Col. 0252A]. Therefore, while he lives, let him take as much as he can and use this world before he departs and is led out of it; for he will not return again or be brought back to know what will be after him. It may happen that another person after him will misuse things which he himself was unwilling to use, rejoicing and exulting as a stranger in his goods; and once he has been taken away, they can no longer be restored to his use.

For this reason, and for reasons of this kind, people suppose that their portion is to enjoy the world’s pleasure while they live; they believe that they were made for this alone and that they will be nothing after these things, once this life has received its end. They multiply arguments and accumulate one rationale upon another, deceiving themselves and strengthening their hearts in evil so that they may believe what is false. They build with lies a wall between themselves and truth, that they may not see it; they set forth everything and carefully seek all means by which they may plausibly demonstrate that there is no other life, that this life alone is good, that man was made only for this life, and that there will be no other after it. This entire disturbance rises from the obscurity of God’s judgments, because he placed man in doubt to test him, so that he might not see that man has more than the beast.

Yet he pursues this error again through other judgments and shows that this life, in which very many evils reign, is not good; nor can true pleasure or tranquil rest be found in it. Therefore he sows adversities over it, turns back upon it, and withdraws, so that he does not free the oppressed, that they may be greatly afflicted and that, through pain and sorrow, evil sweetness and wicked pleasure may be erased. Thus those who wish to delight in this life, make a covenant of love with the world, and perversely resolve not to seek truth, are compelled by true judgments to see the evils under the sun, lest they please themselves too much in their turning away.

Therefore, after he had said that it is good for man to rejoice in his work and that this is his portion, and had given a rule for resting in such things, this writer is moved by another consideration: this life is not such that rest can exist within it. Therefore he adds and says:

> [Col. 0252D] I turned myself to other things (Eccles. IV).

He is rightly said to have turned to other things, because he is admonished by what he is about to see to believe something other than what he had previously thought. For all these things which will then be seen teach that the true good of man is elsewhere than in this life, subject as it is to such great miseries and pains, in which innocence is oppressed and pain earns no consolation. He considered this other thing—indeed, something far other than what had previously appeared and been thought—and said:

## HOMILY XIX. On the oppression and abandonment of the innocent, and on the varying and foolish judgment of the wicked concerning this life.

> I turned myself to other things. And I saw calumnies (Eccles. IV) which are done under the sun, and the tears of the innocent [Col. 0253A], and no comforter; nor could they resist their violence, being deprived of everyone’s help.

Therefore do not think that this is your homeland. Rather, consider and recognize that you are under the sun, where all things are whirled about and everything is confused; for this has happened so that you may recognize your exile and seek another homeland. Therefore calumnies and unjust oppressions occur here: some attack others without cause, and the stronger oppress the weak without mercy. God does not bring consolation here to the innocent, because elsewhere he reserves his consolations for them; meanwhile he leaves them deprived of everyone’s help, lest they be comforted by alien help, which is not their own, and so grieve, sigh, and desire less his consolation, which they do not yet possess.

But the mind of the perverse is impatient under either form of correction: it is neither aroused by prosperity nor chastened by adversity. When they look upon the sweet things of this life, their soul clings to them and they say: “This is enough; there is no other good of man to come afterward besides this.” But when they attend to adversities, their minds grow dull, collapse, and fall into distrust; they despair of themselves because they have no other hope. They prefer not to be rather than to be in evils, because it is evil to be what they are, and they do not know that there is a good which they may desire and to which they may pass. For in the time of their pleasure they refused to learn it, so that they might rest in it in the time of evil. Therefore they do the only thing they know: when they are badly off, they wish to be nothing, because they know no other way of escaping being evil except by passing [Col. 0253C] into non-being. Therefore, upon seeing the evils under the sun, their voice is immediately introduced when it is said:

> And I praised the dead more than the living; and I judged happier than both the one not yet born, who has not seen the evils done under the sun.

This is indeed the voice of those who do not know the true good and think that everything present is the only good or evil for man. Therefore they exult beyond measure amid prosperity and despair amid evils; where their hope lies, there also their despair is established. For this reason, when they see the evils of this world, they call the dead happier than the living, and those not yet born happier than both. Since they think that only what is seen exists [Col. 0253D], when they see the misery which is in it they seek happiness no longer in another existence, because they know no existence other than this; they place it solely in non-being, because in all that they suppose alone to exist they have found unhappiness. Therefore they praise more those who were and are not than those who still are; and they proclaim happier than both those who are not yet.

For if, as it appears to them, all being is evil, not being is good, and never having been is better. For if it is evil to be evil, it is good not to be evil, and better never to have been. What is farther from evil by being in good is itself the greater good, just as what is farther from good by being in evil is itself the greater evil. If therefore being is evil, certainly not being is good, and far better than either is never to have been.

Minds under the sun thus generate from themselves such perversities that, to the confusion of all things, man himself grows dark to his own living. If man saw what man is and why man was made, he would surely recognize his good and would no longer call those who are nothing happier than those who are something. Bound by desire for so great a good, though temporal evils afflicted him and he disdained the present life, he would nevertheless love being rather than not being, because of the hope of consolation to come. But now great perversity grows in the minds of people ignorant of their own good, and vanity reaches a consummation greater than which there cannot be. For man, flowing away from true being through the vanity of his mutability, continually and without cessation ceases to be what he is and always passes into what he is not. Thus, in a manner accustomed to his own evil, he finally casts himself down into such perversity that he desires altogether to be nothing.

Many people, wishing to avoid this madness—which is, as it were, openly displayed and cannot be concealed—turn to preserve their existence. They employ great care and industry in their labours to make their lives secure from the evils under the sun. Gathering resources, multiplying riches, and diligently and anxiously seeking all other things that might console life, they do much and accomplish many deeds worthy of remembrance. Sometimes they escape another’s violence by their industry and labour, but they cannot escape another’s envy. Therefore, after the judgment of those who despair through impatience, he adds concerning them also:

> Again I considered all human labours, and I observed that their enterprises are exposed to a neighbour’s envy.

For when he considered human labours, he saw that the industrious activity of the good lay exposed to their neighbours’ envy. For just as the perverse are bound by sloth so that they do not exercise works of virtue within themselves, so they are goaded by envy to find fault with them in their neighbours.

> And this too is vanity and superfluous care.

Or this is vanity: that by envying another’s good works a person brings care upon his own soul and the anguish of malice [Col. 0254D], since by envy he harms not the person whom he envies but himself. Or this too is vanity: that a person labours excessively for these temporal goods, is anxious, and afflicts himself with superfluous care, when acquiring them more quickly incites a neighbour to envy than draws that neighbour to love. For while the industry by which a person is exercised is good, the superfluous care and anxiety by which he is afflicted are evil. At the same time vain are the confidence and hope by which true security is expected in an abundance of riches, since their acquisition rather removes security when it inflames neighbours—who perhaps might have loved us in poverty—to envy us through their rivalry. Industry, therefore, is rightly approved and vain anxiety reproved.

But then another class of people comes from the flock of vanity, seeking an occasion for its own sluggishness. These persons criticize those who work and seem, as it were, to condemn them for anxiety, in order that they themselves may be unrestrained. So vanity proceeds: it never finds the mean boundary of virtue.

> Therefore the fool folds his hands and eats his own flesh, saying: “A handful with rest is better than both hands full with labour and affliction of spirit.”

The fool folds his hands. For foolish is the person who does not know how to provide for himself in the future; foolish is the one who thinks that hands folded in idleness will be filled with riches. He folds his hands: he folds one over the other, so that they may not stretch out to work. He folds his hands as though making a pact with idleness.

> And he eats his own flesh.

He thinks that he spares his body because he does not afflict it with labours, yet his flesh is consumed by the poverty that idleness nourishes. He eats his own flesh. For he feeds himself along with his folly, and his idleness fattens him. But however much his flesh is fed in profitable leisure, so much is it wasted by the hunger that follows. Therefore he eats his own flesh, saying: “A handful with rest is better than both hands full with labour and affliction of spirit.”

It would be true that a handful is better if it did not know how to fail, and if the blessing of the widow of Zarephath had been given to everyone (III Kings XVII). But Elijah was not sent to everyone. Why then, fool, do you say that a handful with rest is better than both hands full with labour? Perhaps you consider the time when you have a handful and rest, but do not attend to the time when you will not have even that handful [Col. 0255C]: what then will you do, and what rest will you then have? Therefore you now consume the handful in rest and your idleness pleases you; meanwhile you take no care to seek with labour another handful to eat when this one fails. Therefore you now eat your own flesh, because it will suffer after this untimely idleness and will afterward repay by its wasting what thoughtless rest has spent.

Perhaps you think that every kind of vanity has now been mentioned, and that there is no other kind of vanity for the observer to find under the sun. Therefore follows:

> I considered and found another vanity under the sun. There is one, and he has not a second—neither son nor brother—and yet he does not cease to labour; nor are his eyes satisfied with riches, nor does he reflect, saying: “For whom do I labour, and why do I defraud my soul of good things?”

The one who is alone and has no other successor—neither a son whom he has begotten nor a brother with whom he himself was begotten, for he is his father’s successor—therefore has no second person to leave as heir after himself to his possessions. Yet he does not cease to gather and does not enjoy what he possesses; rather, he avariciously keeps what he greedily collected. What could be more vain? The person who labours and enjoys his labour receives some fruit. The person who labours, does not use what he obtains by his labour, yet leaves those possessions to be held by people he loves, receives some benefit from his labour: the desire and purpose of his love. But one who labours neither for himself nor for another whom he loves—why does he labour except for his own vice alone, which he serves? For he serves his vice alone, and there is no other affection which might excuse the vain anxiety and be pardoned, except that alone which vice has produced.

There are many human labours that are left to others, and those who perform them receive no fruit from them. Many also labour in wisdom, apply themselves, strive to know many things, say a great deal, and commit their thoughts to writing in order that they may be handed down to posterity; yet they receive no fruit from all this, so as to be better for it themselves, but remain empty of truth and devoid of wisdom’s sweetness. All their labour is vanity, even if it appears to approach truth. For people of this kind do not know for whom they labour and defraud their souls of good things, because they attend only to the greatness of the work, receive no fruit from it, see that no benefit comes to themselves from it, and do not know whether these very things will benefit others after them.

[Col. 0255]

## EXPLANATORY NOTES ON THE LAMENTATIONS OF JEREMIAH ACCORDING TO THE MULTIPLE SENSES, AND FIRST ACCORDING TO THE LITERAL SENSE

[Col. 0255D] **(LAM. I.) “How does the city sit solitary, full of people?”** In its literal sense, Jeremiah laments Jerusalem’s desolation, and this is the voice of one marvelling or grieving. He begins with amazement in order to display the greatness of the calamity and thereby make his hearers attentive, so that they may recognize the evils in which they are and turn to repentance.

“How does the city sit solitary, full of people?” As though he said: “City which once, in the time of David and of the other good kings pleasing to God, was full of people, consider why you now remain alone.” Why indeed, except because they offended God? He calls it solitary, that is, desolate, because the people had been carried captive into Babylon. Or, if it is referred to the same time, it is full of people and nevertheless sits alone because it does not have God propitious; for a multitude of people cannot avail where God’s help is absent [Col. 0257A]. The word “sits” pertains to abasement and humiliation.

> She has become like a widow.

That is, she has been abandoned while her husband still lives; therefore she is not a widow but like a widow, because if she repents she may still be reconciled. God is called the husband of that people because he had joined her to himself in chaste love for his worship, so that she might not commit fornication through diverse idol-worships.

> She who was mistress of the nations has become like a widow; she who was princess of the provinces has become tributary.

Formerly the foreign nations served the Jews, and the provinces of the nations were subject to them; but now they themselves, abandoned by God, have become tributary to the nations. Thus the recollection of former glory heightens present misery.

According to the allegorical sense, Jeremiah signifies within the Church any spiritual persons who, when they see a multitude of people gathered to faith and the name of Christ spread through nearly the whole world, yet find none or very few who truly follow Christ and sincerely hold his faith, grieve and lament, since all seek what is their own, saying: “How does the city sit solitary, full of people?” Why do we see so great a people in the Church, and yet see the Church solitary? Because we can scarcely find anyone who is truly with the Church.

I find something similar in the Gospel. When the Lord stood amid a crowd which surrounded and pressed upon him from every side, a woman suffering from a flow of blood came, approached from behind, and touched the fringe of his garment; and he immediately said: “Who touched me?” (Mark V). “Someone touched me.” Since he who, when the woman touched the fringe, asks “Who touched me?” as though he had experienced something new, plainly declares that he had not previously been touched, even though all were jostling and pressing him. Therefore, just as Christ remains untouched while the crowd presses upon him, so the Church, the body of Christ, sits solitary amid many: for the Catholic faith has many professors but few imitators. Likewise those then near the Lord by bodily presence could not touch him because they were far from him in faith and love [Col. 0257D].

Therefore the spiritual Jeremiah laments and says: “How does the city sit solitary, full of people?” For wherever the servants of God are without pain and lamentation, they cannot see these things.

> She who was mistress of the nations has become like a widow; she who was princess of the provinces has become tributary.

By “nations” we rightly understand all carnal persons situated within the Church; by “provinces,” all who stand outside the Church, such as pagans, Jews, and heretics. Thus the holy Church is mistress of the nations when she subjects the carnal persons within her to service through the strictness of discipline. She is princess of the provinces when, by her power, she repels unbelievers outside her, so that they cannot harm her. But if, perhaps, because sins demand it, she is abandoned by God, so that she cannot restrain those who disturb her within [Col. 0258A] or defend herself against those who attack her from without, then she who was mistress of the nations is left like a widow, and she who was princess of the provinces becomes tributary. For when she sees believers drawn into unbelief, whether deceived by heretics or broken by reward or terror from the powers of this world, what else does she do but pay tribute to foreigners?

According to the moral interpretation, the city signifies the soul, which sits solitary when it is abandoned by God, but is full of a people of virtues when it is inhabited by God. But if we find a city whose desolation is lamented, where is Jeremiah to be found? Each one of us ought to be Jeremiah, and lament his own desolation as he lamented the desolation of Jerusalem. And surely, if he so lamented [Col. 0258B] the ruin of stones, we ought far more to lament the desolation of our souls, and each say: “How does the city full of people sit solitary? How has my soul been desolated? How has it lost that good inhabitant, in whose presence it was once full of a people of virtues?” She has become like a widow, mistress of the nations. The nations are the desires of the flesh, innate in us through the corruption of our first birth, and opposed to the law of the mind; the soul rightly rules them when it is perfectly subject to God. “The princess of provinces has become tributary.” By the provinces we may understand the bodily senses, because, just as many people dwell in one province, so each of the senses has diverse movements and diverse operations, by which it is spread abroad [Col. 0258C] among visible things; and while the appetites of the individual senses are moved at the command of reason, the soul rules, as it were, over certain provinces.

Therefore, if the soul desires to rule its inferior, that is, sensuality, it must submit itself to its superior, that is, God. For it can by no means be disturbed beneath itself by its inferior so long as it has God, its ruler, above itself. But if, forgetful of the fear of the Lord, it follows its own desires, God withdraws his grace from it; and then it necessarily yields feebly to its desires—the soul which previously, being subject to God and governed by him, had powerfully restrained the appetites of its senses under the command of reason.

And note that he says “mistress,” not “ruler,” of the nations, [Col. 0258D] and “ruler,” not “mistress,” of the provinces. For vices, which are not natural, must be suppressed; but the senses, because they are natural, must not be suppressed but governed. Thus a person should be strict in uprooting the former, but discerning in moderating and guarding the latter. Yet it sometimes happens that, while a person neglects to resist the lawful desires of his flesh and to guard the movements of his senses, he is finally bound so tightly by evil habit that afterwards, even if willing, he cannot resist them. Therefore, when he is compelled to serve the vices to which he had previously consented voluntarily, what else does he do but pay tribute to evil habit?

Thus he has enumerated three goods and three evils. The goods are: a city full of people, mistress of nations, ruler of provinces; the evils: solitary, widowed, tributary. But let us see [Col. 0259A] first how she acquires the goods, and afterwards how she descends to the evils. Before the Holy Spirit comes to our heart, our soul is barren; but when he comes, he makes it fruitful, so that it bears and virtues are born within it. While these virtues are still imperfect and only beginning, and are not yet able to come forth, but are still nourished within through the grace of that same Spirit so that they may grow and become strong, what are they but certain little children being brought up in their father’s house until they reach lawful maturity? But when they have attained full growth and begin to use the solid food of wisdom, then they no longer need to be nourished as little children, but should live like a people in a city under the law of their emperor.
