But when God, presiding within, rules us, then the flesh, subject without, serves; and the more humbly we submit to him within, the more strongly we rule without. Therefore our soul, being within full of a people of virtues when it had God as king, was also without mistress of the nations—that is, of fleshly desires—and ruler of the provinces—that is, of the bodily senses. But now it is solitary because it has lost its king; a widow because it has lost its husband; tributary because, subject to vices, it serves.

“She wept, weeping in the night.” The repetition of the word indicates abundance of grief. “She wept, weeping in the night,” that is, in a time of rest, in a time of forgetfulness, when people are accustomed to forget their evils. Consider how great is the misery of one to whom [Col. 0259C] pains cannot be lacking even then, when others rest from pain.

“And her tears are upon her cheeks.” There is sometimes a grief which touches the heart in some manner, yet is not sufficient to force tears. Her grief is not such; for her tears are upon her cheeks.

“There is none to comfort her among all her beloved ones.” Either because they despise her in her tribulation, or because they cannot help in so great an evil. By the beloved ones of that people the prophet means the prophets and rulers, who had been accustomed to comfort them: the prophets by promising help from God, and the rulers by repelling enemies and defending their country. But now they did not at all comfort the people placed in tribulation, because the former proclaimed God’s wrath, while the latter were unable to resist the enemies [Col. 0259D] devastating the land and carrying the people into captivity.

Or it may be read otherwise: “She wept, weeping in the night,” that is, in secret, in concealment. This is welcome to mourners who do not wish to be comforted, but feed upon their own griefs. Or the people, placed in captivity, weep in concealment because they dare not make their sorrow known, on account of the cruel masters to whom they are subject; for they feared to provoke their anger more greatly against themselves if they appeared sad over their servitude. But such great grief cannot be concealed, because “her tears are upon her cheeks,” that is, openly and manifestly, because her face has become swollen from continual weeping. And amid such great evils, what comfort could those expect [Col. 0260A] whose very dearest ones bring them no consolation?

“All her friends have despised her.” By friends he means the neighboring nations formerly joined by treaty to the Jewish people; now, when it was under affliction, they not only despised it by refusing aid, but also became enemies by persecuting it.

According to the allegorical sense, the night is sinners, while the cheeks are preachers who, by expounding, chew up the food of God’s word and thus convey it to the weak and dull of understanding. Therefore, when the Church, in its more perfect members during this exile of the present life, weeps over the falls of the weak, it is like a people in captivity bearing tears upon its cheeks through the night. Or night can signify this present life itself, in which we live, [Col. 0260B] since we do not yet see one another’s consciences. And, as we said above, the cheeks signify those who possess knowledge of the word of God. Thus the holy Church bears tears upon her cheeks through the night when the more perfect, the more closely they behold through illumination of mind the day of eternity, the more they lament the darkness of this present life, according to Solomon’s saying: “He who increases knowledge increases sorrow [toil]” (Eccles. I).

“There is none to comfort her among all her beloved ones.” By the Church’s beloved ones we understand those same sinners whom we said above were signified by the night. While she weeps over them, she loves them; for she would never lament their destruction unless she loved their salvation and conversion. Yet she receives no consolation from them when none of them returns to repentance, since the conversion of sinners would be the consolation of those who weep. Or the Church’s beloved ones are those blessed angelic spirits, or the souls of the saints, for fellowship with whom she longs from the night of this exile; they bring her no consolation while they still allow her to remain a pilgrim apart from their society. Of her it is further said: “All her friends have despised her.” Who are called here the Church’s friends but the powerful of this world? Sometimes, while they see her raised high in temporal prosperity, they honor her and pretend affection for her; but when they see her under affliction, they persecute and despise her.

According to the moral sense, the soul has its day and its night. It has day when it is raised into the light of contemplation; [Col. 0260D] it has night when it is darkened by the gloom of temptations. Yet it laughs in the day and weeps in the night, because the mind which groans under the burden of temptations is afterwards raised up and gladdened in the joy of contemplation. Therefore the soul weeps in the night when it pierces its inwardly dark conscience with salutary grief. It bears tears upon its cheeks when it afflicts the flesh outwardly by strict chastisement. For tears are upon the cheeks when the pains of the heart proceed even to the mortification of the flesh. To heighten the grief still further, he adds:

“There is none to comfort her among all her beloved ones.” A person is abandoned by God in three ways: sometimes within but not without, sometimes without but not within, and sometimes both without and within. Job was abandoned without but not within: outwardly he endured bodily scourges, but inwardly did not lose constancy of mind. David was abandoned within but not without: inwardly his mind was subjected to lust through consent, but outwardly prophetic admonition called him back to repentance. The prodigal son in the Gospel was abandoned both within and without: by living luxuriously he inwardly dissolved into ruin, and outwardly, wasting away from hunger, found no consolation. But those whom God abandons in this way he abandons in some cases for testing, that they may be exercised through temptation; others he abandons for overthrow, that they may be cast down through temptation. Therefore the Psalmist prays: “Do not turn away in wrath from your servant” (Ps. XXVI); as though saying, [Col. 0261B] “Even if you permit me to be tempted, do not allow me to be led into temptation,” that is, to be overcome by temptation.

But because a person cannot penetrate the depth of divine judgments, anyone placed in temptation most fears that he has been abandoned when he sees himself troubled by temptations both inwardly and outwardly. Yet one more easily bears adversities outwardly whose conscience is not troubled within by delight in sin. And again, one more easily endures temptation within who has consolation without. Hence the great tribulation of this woman is shown, since she is demonstrated to have been abandoned both within and without. For the words, “She wept, weeping in the night, and her tears are upon her cheeks,” indicate that she has been abandoned within; while the words, “There is none to comfort her among all [Col. 0261C] her beloved ones,” declare that she has been desolated without.

It follows: “All her friends have despised her and have become enemies to her.” See how many are the tribulations of the righteous. Perhaps it was not enough for her, placed amid afflictions, that she received no consolation from her beloved ones, unless she also endured persecution from friends. But who are these friends who persecute us, except those of whom it will be said in the Gospel: “A man’s enemies will be those of his own household” (Matt. X)? These, then, are our enemies, our persecutors, our household, and our friends: persons related to us by ties of the flesh, who love us for the present life through fleshly affection, but oppose us as we walk in God’s way. For when we desire to withdraw from love of this world, [Col. 0261D] we immediately find those who previously seemed friends to be adversaries. At first, indeed, when we wish to turn to God, they strive under the pretext of destructive affection to call us back with flattering persuasions. But if they see us fixed and immovable in our good purpose, they at once renounce and despise us as adversaries; and sometimes, pursuing us with the fiercest hatred and afflicting us with punishments, they become true persecutors out of false friends. Let her therefore say, “There is none to comfort her among all her beloved ones,” because in tribulation she is not worthy to receive the words of the righteous as consolation; “all her friends have despised her and have become enemies to her,” because she suffers insult and contempt from the wicked.

“Judah has migrated.” It crossed over, departed, fled from its own land into Babylon, because it could not endure the heavy [Col. 0262A] servitude by which it was oppressed by the nations, supposing that it would be more tolerable to serve one nation in a foreign land than to be prey to all nations in its own land.

“She dwelt among the nations and found no rest.” It is characteristic of the afflicted always to judge the present danger more burdensome. Just as sick persons await day during the night and long for night during the day, and while they always desire their pain to pass, are always moving toward pain, so this people, while it was afflicted in its own land, sought flight; but when it was desolated in exile and, wandering as a fugitive, could find no rest, it longed to return. Here he expresses the attitude of those who fluctuate, not because they migrated voluntarily, but because, placed in distress, they changed their wishes as their minds turned in different directions.

“All her persecutors overtook her amid straits.” Hemmed in on every side, she could find no place of escape: fleeing the Chaldeans, she fell among the Egyptians; and when she fled from the Egyptians, she encountered the Assyrians.

Mystically, Judah, which means “one confessing,” signifies certain people in the Church who confess Christ’s name; yet because they are not yet firm in Christ’s love, they are ashamed to suffer adversities for Christ. Of such people it is said: “They believe for a time, and in the time of temptation fall away” (Luke VIII). Such persons, then, because of affliction and the multitude of their servitude—since, unwilling to share in the sufferings of the righteous, they become estranged from the fellowship of the righteous—have “dwelt among the nations.” [Col. 0262C] To dwell among the nations is to imitate the life and conduct of the wicked. Not to find rest is to become entangled in the affairs of this world; for, because there is no end to the affairs of this world, those who pursue them cannot have rest. Yet a person often willingly endures for love of the present life labors which he refused to bear for love of God. Thus those who depart from God are greatly reproached, and every excuse is removed from them, since it is plainly shown that they have transgressed without cause: by avoiding useful labors, they have descended into useless labors.

“All her persecutors overtook her amid straits.” So long as a person’s heart is enlarged by charity and hope of eternal goods, even if it endures tribulation outwardly, it nevertheless has no inward straitness. Therefore one can recognize from this how great a good is lost by one who loses confidence in God: the heart always suffers straitness in adversities unless it is enlarged by hope of future goods. “They overtook her amid straits,” he says. Observe what are the straits of those who depart from God: they are never secure, always tremble; in prosperity they fear, in adversity they despair.

“Judah has migrated.” There are some who, when they look upon their sins, are inflamed by a passing compunction and come as far as confession; they resolve to enter upon the paths of a better life and promise that henceforth they will not return to the vices they have committed. But because they refuse to afflict themselves with fitting satisfaction for their deeds, [Col. 0263A] and, with the Apostle, to chastise the body and reduce it to servitude (I Cor. IX), when temptation quickly comes upon them they return to the sins they had abandoned. For those who neglect to mortify the affections of vices within themselves cannot easily resist vices. Of these it is said here: “Judah has migrated because of affliction and the multitude of servitude.” For what does Judah signify except those who confess their sins? They migrate because of affliction and the multitude of servitude when, defeated, they go after their own desires because they fear to mortify those desires through affliction and the servitude of their flesh.

Against them Wisdom says: “My son, when you come to the service of God, stand in fear and prepare your heart for temptations” (Ecclus. II). For those who confess their sins and undertake to amend [Col. 0263B] their lives indeed come to the service of God. But they neglect to stand there when, defeated by adversities, they fall from their good purpose. This is what he warned: “Prepare your heart for temptations,” so that, walking in the way of God, we may be ready to endure adversities—we who, before we were in God’s way, swelled with pride because we had committed no unlawful acts.

“She dwelt among the nations and found no rest.” What is it to dwell among the nations except to comply with fleshly desires, where rest is not found: namely, the rest which the Lord promises in the Gospel to those who labor, saying, “You shall find rest for your souls” (Matt. XI); and concerning which it is said to the sinner: “You have sinned; do not add again, but rest” (Ecclus. XXI). And rightly so: those who refused to endure bodily labor come to the labor of the soul, and the madness of evil desires agitates the mind of those whose flesh is not chastised by deserved punishment. Thus Samson, with his eyes torn out, is set to the mill: for the mind, having lost the light of truth, is carried about by the appetite for earthly desires. While Samson had the hair of his head, he was invincible; but after he fell asleep in the woman’s lap and lost the hair shorn from his head, he was immediately seized and blinded by his enemies and handed over to servitude.

Samson means “their sun” and signifies the mind illuminated by divine knowledge. Samson’s head is the governing faculty of the mind. The hair of the head is the ray of contemplation. The woman’s lap is the flesh’s enticement. For as long as the mind clings to contemplation, [Col. 0263D] it cannot be overcome by temptation. But if it is relaxed into fleshly delight and falls asleep there, it immediately loses the inward light of truth; and, with the ray of contemplation cut off, it is not sufficient to resist evil movements. Finally, with its eyes torn out, it is set to the mill when, forgetful of inward sweetness, it is scattered abroad through earthly desires. For what is the mill but an unstable and restless mind which, while always striving to grasp what it desires, is, as it were, driven round by its desires and never rests? Well, then, is it said: “She dwelt among the nations and found no rest.” For the mind which follows fleshly desires is as far removed from inward rest as it is scattered outwardly among perishing things.

“All [Col. 0264A] her persecutors overtook her amid straits.” Those who fall away from the purpose of virtues are sometimes worse than those who have not yet been able to attain the purpose of virtue. For the latter hope that they can reach what they have not yet possessed; but the former are so much farther from salvation as they have more manifestly lost, in despair, the virtue they had begun. Thus these are more exposed to the snares of demons than those others: the latter are in some degree restrained by hope of future amendment, while the former are driven to ruin by their own despair. Therefore of those who, after beginning good, return to their vomit, it is said here: “All her persecutors overtook her amid straits.” For who are our persecutors except evil spirits and the desires of the flesh which wage war against us in our members? And what is straitness except the despair of a sinful conscience, which constricts the heart within? Therefore one is overtaken by all persecutors amid straits who, because he already despairs of pardon from a previous fall, does not oppose demonic promptings to sin or his own desires in guilt.

Thus Judah migrates because of affliction when one who has already begun to amend his life through confession falls from his purpose, broken by the hardship of temptations. He dwells among the nations when he fixes his mind upon the pleasure of fleshly desires. He finds no rest when concupiscence draws his heart through the precipices of vices. He is overtaken amid straits by all persecutors when, now oppressed by despair, he resists no evil promptings. [Col. 0264C]

**Epilogue of the First Alphabet**

Behold how our physician, holding the sick man in his hands, displays the skill of his art. First, by long palpation he restores senseless limbs to feeling; by gently touching painful wounds he prepares them for the incision; then he cuts, then anoints, then binds, then warms, and restores to full health. Thus this alphabet is divided into five parts. The first is lamentation; the second rebuke; the third consolation; the fourth instruction; the fifth supplication. By lamentation he touches; by rebuke he cuts; by consolation he anoints; by instruction he binds; by supplication he warms.

The lamentation extends from the beginning of the alphabet to the passage where it says: “To what shall I compare thee?” [Col. 0264D] (Lam. II), etc. There rebuke begins and continues to the passage where it says: “The Lord has done what he purposed” (ibid.), etc. There consolation begins and continues to the passage where it says: “Let tears flow down like a torrent” (ibid.). There instruction begins, in which sinners are instructed toward repentance, and continues to the passage where it says: “See, O Lord” (ibid.). From that point to the end is supplication, in which the prophet intercedes with the Lord for sinners.

Having briefly set these matters forth, let us now consider the order of the lamentation itself. First he laments them as though absent, because he ought not immediately to trouble with direct address those who were in bitterness. He also begins by lamenting first those things that are least serious, [Col. 0265A] lest the weight of sudden sorrow overwhelm the minds of mourners; and thus, gradually advancing from lesser matters to greater by enumerating them, he slowly moves the minds of his hearers to grief. First, therefore, he mourns the devastation of the region; then the destruction of public buildings; then the overthrow of sacred structures; then the defilement of holy things; then he proceeds from inanimate things to the misery of human beings, lamenting their humiliation and want, and so at last concludes his lamentation.

## (LAMENTATIONS II)

“How the Lord has covered the daughter of Zion with darkness in his fury.” This mournful beginning starts with astonishment: so suddenly has that people been cast down which formerly seemed raised to heaven. Darkness signifies the sorrow of tribulation. By “daughter of Zion” he means Zion itself—that is, the Jewish people—which he loved and guarded with fatherly affection; or the daughter of Zion itself, that is, the region of Judaea. For Scripture customarily calls metropolitan cities mothers, and the surrounding regions, as well as towns, forts, and villages, daughters. He begins, therefore, as stated above, by lamenting from afar the region itself, so that he may finally reach Jerusalem, the very head of the region. It follows:

“And he did not remember the footstool of his feet,” that is, the people humbly subject to his service.

“The Lord has cast down and has not spared.” Pause here.

“He has destroyed in his fury all the beautiful things of Jacob.” [Col. 0265C] Pause here again. Then follows:

“He has cast down to the ground the strongholds of the virgin Judah.” Pause here again. Then follows:

“He has defiled the kingdom and its princes.” What he had set forth generally in the preceding clause under the name of “the ground,” he here unfolds in parts: beautiful things, strongholds, kingdom, princes. Observe how the lament rises. First he had named merely the soil, then the land; but lest the land itself be thought barren and uncultivated, and therefore less worthy of lament, he subsequently strengthens the lament by speaking of its wealth and eminence. “He has cast down,” he says: to cast down is more than to throw down; and what is more grievous still, “he has not spared.” This was truly fulfilled in the final captivity, because they are no longer to be recalled: “he has cast down.”

What does “he has destroyed all the beautiful things of Jacob; he has cast down the strongholds of the virgin Judah” mean? By “beautiful things” understand wealth; by “strongholds,” strength and power. By Jacob and the virgin Judah the same people is signified. Jacob, however, is the general name for the twelve tribes, while Judah applies only to the two tribes. Therefore, after introducing the general name, he immediately adds the particular name, to show that he laments the captivity of the two tribes. Jacob and Judah, then, are the same people: Jacob, because robust in strength; the virgin Judah, because delicate in wealth. What, then, are “the beautiful things of Jacob” except the wealth of the strong? And what are “the strongholds of the virgin Judah” except the strength of the wealthy?

[Col. 0266A] “He has defiled the kingdom and its princes”—that is, the kingdom and princes of the virgin Judah. He says “defiled” because of the nations among whom they were dispersed, by whose association and rites those were profaned who had formerly reigned securely under God’s protection and trusted in the strength of their rulers. But now the entire kingdom, along with its princes, is defiled, because the people together with its protectors is subjugated to the nations.

“He has broken in the wrath of his fury every horn, and at the same time turned his right hand backward.” By the horn is signified the strength of its princes; by God’s right hand is understood divine protection. What, then, does it mean that God “has broken every horn of Israel” and “turned his right hand backward,” except that, in a transgressing people, he shattered every human strength and finally withdrew his protection, so that those are shown to be utterly desolate from whom, after human defenses, even divine help is taken away? “He turned back his right hand,” that is, he turned it away so as not to protect; and he stretched out his left hand to strike. Therefore it follows:

“And he kindled in Jacob, like a fire, a devouring flame round about.” Just as fire, once kindled, spreads widely and consumes all things, so the enemies of the Jews, after all strength had failed among them and divine help had been withdrawn, devastated everything with none to oppose them.

“He bent his bow like an enemy.” In the bow, a threat is understood. To bend the bow, therefore, is to intensify or defer a threat; but he who strikes after threatening has bent the bow like an enemy. Therefore it follows:

“He strengthened his right hand like a foe.” When God’s right hand is mentioned in Scripture, it sometimes signifies protection and sometimes severe striking, because the right hand is naturally readier to strike. Thus God first turned his right hand away so as not to protect; afterwards he strengthened his right hand in order to strike. The expression “he strengthened his right hand” conveys the grave indignation of one striking. Or he strengthens his right hand over those struck because he no longer intends to heal the wound which he once inflicted in anger; this properly refers to the final captivity. Hence “like a foe” is fittingly added: namely, one who strikes to destruction, not to correction. For he would not strengthen his right hand like a foe if, while that hand struck to destroy, he himself struck to correct. Therefore it must be pronounced with deep grief: “like an enemy, like a foe”—he whose wrath the guilty cannot escape, and whose mercy the enemy cannot prevent. It follows:

“And he slew everything beautiful to behold in the tents of the daughter of Zion.” Nothing is slain except what lives. Above he had said, “He destroyed all the beautiful things”; but here, wishing to say something more, he says, “He slew all things beautiful,” thereby showing that through this calamity he took away not only riches but also souls themselves. Hence it is rightly added:

“He poured out his indignation like fire.” Not like water, but like fire. For the force of waters is accustomed to cast down and scatter things, not consume them. The Lord threatens such a flood through another prophet, saying: “I will bring the waters of the flood upon the earth, to destroy all flesh in which is the breath of life” (Gen. VI). But fire does not merely destroy: it consumes. Accordingly, God’s indignation is rightly said to be poured out like fire when divine vengeance spreads even to utter consumption. Finally, the very word “pouring out” expresses the violence and, so to speak, abundance of tribulation.

“The Lord has become like an enemy; he has cast down Israel; he has cast down all its walls.” Hitherto he seems to have lamented the desolation of the daughter of Zion, that is, the region of Judaea. Now he turns to mourn Zion itself, namely [Col. 0267B] the city of Jerusalem, saying: “The Lord has become like an enemy”: a grievous sorrow. The Lord who had been accustomed to cherish and love has become like an enemy, because he no longer strikes as a father for correction, but as a foe for destruction. “He has cast down its walls,” that is, Zion’s; “he has destroyed its strongholds.” Walls are made in a city for ornament, strongholds for protection. What, then, does “he has cast down its walls; he has destroyed its strongholds” mean except that he has overthrown what was lofty and shattered what was strong?

Therefore, what he had lamented above concerning the region, he now laments as having been done also to Jerusalem: there, “the beautiful things of Jacob” signify the beauty of the region; here, “the walls of Zion,” the adornment of the city; there, “the strongholds of the virgin Judah,” the fortifications of the region; here, “the strongholds of Zion,” the fortifications of Jerusalem itself. Thus he used merely “beautiful things” there but “walls” here quite fittingly, since the adornment of a region differs from that of a city. The beauty of a region is especially observed in the abundance of crops and fruitfulness of livestock; the beauty of a city in the height of its buildings. Therefore beautiful things are said to be destroyed and walls cast down, so that you may understand everything to have been laid waste: both what adorned the city within by its beauty and what benefited the regions outside.

“And he filled in the daughter of Judah the humbled man and the humbled woman.” Having described the desolation of the region and the city, he adds, as though answering to both: “And he filled in the daughter of Judah”—that is, the Jewish people, which he had loved as a daughter with fatherly affection—“the humbled man and the humbled woman”; that is, he filled her with persons of both sexes who were humbled, so that she is full of those who have been cast down. Or by “the humbled man” we may understand the order of prelates; by “the humbled woman,” the subject people. This corresponds to what he had said above concerning the devastation of the region: “He has defiled the kingdom and its princes.” Thus we should understand by “kingdom” the same as by “the humbled woman,” and by “princes” the same as by “the humbled man.”

“And he scattered his tent like a garden.” Now he comes to lament the destruction of the sacred structures. Literally, by “tent” and “tabernacle” he signifies the Lord’s temple, which was in Jerusalem and was first destroyed by the Chaldeans and then by the Romans. He calls the temple a tent or tabernacle because in ancient times the children of Israel first in the desert, and later at Shiloh, made use of a tent and tabernacle in its place for the worship of God. Properly speaking, a tent is a place where curtains are stretched by ropes to stakes fixed in the ground. A tabernacle, however, is constructed with certain wooden panels, as is written concerning the tabernacle of the covenant, which Moses built in the wilderness: veils were spread over it outside, and curtains were extended on every side. Thus it is said of the overthrow of the temple: “He scattered his tent.”

“He demolished his tabernacle.” Literally, the language is fitting: what is spread out is scattered; what is fixed to the earth is demolished, as it were, by undermining. “Like a garden,” he says, [Col. 0268B] “he scattered his tent.” Isaiah had foretold this in these words: “The daughter of Zion shall be left like a shelter in a vineyard, and like a hut in a cucumber-field” (Isa. I). As if he said: “Just as human guardianship is removed from a garden and vineyard after their fruits have been gathered, so divine guardianship will be withdrawn from this people, because it is barren of the fruit of good work, so that it may become exposed to the scattering and plundering of its enemies.”

Or by “garden” we may understand a place of pleasure and luxury. Hence the Law forbade the planting of a grove in the courts of the Lord, because worshipers of idols too were accustomed to sacrifice beneath leafy trees and in green places, serving wantonness and pleasure. Thus he says, “He scattered his tent like a garden,” as though saying: “Because impurity and pleasure entered into the place of holiness, scattering and desolation have come.” It follows:

“The Lord has consigned feast and Sabbath in Zion to forgetfulness.” That is, he has not only rejected these things, but after rejecting them no longer seeks them. This properly refers to the final captivity, when, grace having been manifested, the observances of the former Law have been entirely overthrown and rejected. It follows:

“And [he consigned] king and priest to reproach and the indignation of his fury.” “He consigned” must be supplied. Honor is due to a king; devotion is esteemed in a priest. But now reproach is rendered to the king instead of honor, and indignation to the priest instead of devotion, so that all the excellence and religion of the Jewish people may be shown destroyed. It follows:

[Col. 0268D] “The Lord has rejected his altar.” Here he begins to treat of the defilement of holy things. “The Lord has rejected his altar”: he shows himself to be implacable when he casts away even that through which he had customarily been appeased. It follows:

“He has cursed his sanctuary.” That is, the sacrifices by which those offering them had formerly been sanctified. We now plainly see this fulfilled: legal sacrifices, which in their own time could sanctify their offerers, if they are maintained after the fulfillment of grace, henceforth provoke God to anger. It follows:

Handed over into the hand of the enemy were the walls of her towers. That is, of the sanctuary: in order to show that he no longer accepted those former sacrifices, he allowed the very place in which they had customarily been offered to be utterly overthrown, so that from this it might be plainly evident to all that, once the former place had been laid waste, the former rite ought to cease. When it says “the walls of her towers,” this should, in the literal sense, be understood as though it said, “her fortified towers,” intransitively; that is, not only the city walls outside, but also the walls of the towers within. Hence it follows:

“They raised their voice in the house of the Lord as on a solemn day.” The enemies themselves, with no one resisting them, occupied everything and rejoiced that they had prevailed.

“The Lord planned to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion.” Lest God appear to have inflicted such great evils thoughtlessly, he is said to have planned—that is, deliberated—before acting. By “the wall of the daughter of Zion” we must understand the strength and defense of the Jewish people. It follows:

“He stretched out his line.” That he might measure their merits and render to each according to his works. Or, he stretched out the line—that is, the punishment with which he would bind sinners—having prolonged his waiting through patience; but at last striking all the more severely. Therefore it follows:

“He did not turn back his hand from destruction.” That is, because he found no one free from guilt, he left no one exempt from punishment. It follows:

“The outwork mourned, and the wall was destroyed.” The word “together” is placed so ambiguously that it appears capable of referring to either: namely, either that the outwork was destroyed together with the wall, or that the wall mourned together with the outwork. Yet we may not unfittingly understand by the outwork the guardianship of human beings, and by the wall the guardianship of angels. Both were taken from the Jewish people by God’s just judgment, so that neither humans outside nor angels within could defend from approaching tribulation a people abandoned by God. On this interpretation, the distinction in which it laments that the outwork mourned and the wall was destroyed is fitting: it shows that the former—that is, good prelates—were distressed in compassion even by the overthrow of their people, while the latter—that is, the angels—were removed from their guardianship over them.

“Her gates have sunk into the ground.” That is, Zion’s. As a memorial of enduring grief, after the overthrow of all things, signs of ruin remain. For the gates remain not for defense but as signs of calamity: they are fixed in the ground so that they may lie widely open, and, their bars destroyed and broken, they have no bolts with which to provide protection. It follows:

“Her kings and her princes are among the nations.” Supply: “He destroyed and shattered [them].” This looks back to what was said, “gates and bars” (Ezek. 38): that is, kings and princes, who were the people’s defense and strength, have been cast down, rejected, and shattered. The cause of so great an evil follows, because:

“The law of the Lord is not among them.” That is, because they are transgressors of the law; and because:

“Her prophets found no vision from the Lord.” That is, because they listened to prophets who did not speak from the Spirit of the Lord.

“How he covered,” etc. Under the figure of one nation he laments the fall of the whole human race. The first human being was struck in three ways: by ignorance, concupiscence, and mortality. By mortality is meant death itself, together with all the failings and punishments that precede death itself. He therefore says: “How in his wrath the Lord covered the daughter of Zion with darkness”; because, abandoning in sin the human being whom he had created to contemplate the light of eternity, he left him in the darkness of ignorance. For Zion is interpreted “watchtower,” where an enemy’s assault is discerned from afar. To the first human being it was said: “From the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat; for on whatever day you eat from it, you shall die by death” (Gen. 2). Thus the human being is raised, as it were, upon a watchtower when he is commanded through watchfulness to avoid the danger of impending evil. What then should we understand by the daughter of Zion but the human soul, not yet strengthened by the practice of watchfulness? For just as there is “daughter of Babylon,” that is, daughter of confusion, and “daughter of Jerusalem,” that is, daughter of contemplation, so also there is “daughter of Zion,” that is, daughter of watchfulness—still tender and young in watchfulness, and not yet established in manly strength. It is as if he said: This also could have mitigated the wrath of the Judge: that the one who sinned had not yet been established, through use and experience, in obedience to the commandment.

“How he covered,” he says. What is covered is indeed hidden, not removed; because in the human being the light of reason was darkened through sin, not taken away. “How he covered”: so that he might not be able to see the things above, that is, heavenly things. It follows: “He cast down from heaven to earth the glorious Israel.” Israel is interpreted “the man seeing God.” The first human being, before he sinned, was Israel, because through the inward presence of contemplation he saw God. By “the earth of Israel,” therefore, we fittingly understand the human body. God indeed took it from earth in creation, but by immortality in some manner transferred it to heaven. Since, because of human sin, he afterwards commanded it to be dissolved in death, he cast down to earth the Israel—that is, the human body—from heaven, that is, from incorruption into corruption.

The prophet rightly, while lamenting the human fall, first mentions the darkness of the mind and then the corruption of the flesh, because that which came first in guilt ought deservedly to come first in punishment. Thus, just as the flesh would not have entered into unlawful delight unless the mind had first been corrupted, so neither would the flesh have descended into corruption unless the mind had first been blinded through ignorance. Adam himself first hid when he was sought, and then, when found, received the sentence of death. It follows:

“And he did not remember the footstool of his feet in the day of his wrath.” By the Lord’s feet are understood his commandments; by the footprints of his feet, knowledge of the commandments. By the footstool of his feet are understood those who, through obedience, are subject to God’s commandments. Thus God set his feet, as it were, upon a footstool when he imposed upon the first human being a commandment of life to be obeyed. But in the day of wrath he seemed not to remember this footstool, when he exacted with great severity the penalty of transgression from one to whom he had earlier gently given a commandment to obey.

“The Lord cast down, and did not spare.” Casting down pertains to a great and sudden ruin. See how great was the fall: from paradise into this world; from this world into hell; from immortality into death; from death into condemnation. Hence it is well added: “And did not spare.” For he would seemingly have spared the sinner if he had examined his guilt by punishment but had not compelled him, through the death of the flesh, to enter into corruption; or if, after the death of the flesh, he had at least not cast the soul also into condemnation. It follows: “In his wrath he destroyed all the beautiful things of Jacob.” Jacob is interpreted “supplanter.” In a certain sense the human being supplanted the devil, not by combat but by grace, when he received power to ascend to that place from which the devil had fallen.

This Jacob, in the first state of his creation, was beautiful within and without: his conscience flourished through innocence and his flesh through chastity. But Jacob’s beautiful things were destroyed, because concupiscence defiled the beauty of chastity and at the same time made the conscience ugly and dark through the guilt of its crime. Or, Jacob possessed beautiful things because inwardly the sight of invisible goods gladdened him, while outwardly the beauty of visible things stirred him to glorify his Creator. But Jacob’s beautiful things were destroyed, because, in punishment for the first guilt, God hid from his mind the knowledge of invisible goods and changed his sight of visible things from that spiritual delight into the concupiscence of the flesh. Hence it is fittingly added: “He cast down to the earth the strongholds of the virgin of Judah.” What do we understand by the virgin of Judah except the chaste intention of the soul? When that intention is everywhere directed according to the decision of the divine will, what else does it do but confess the Lord? The strongholds of this intention were the soul’s good desires and the body’s natural appetites. For as long as neither the flesh outwardly nor the soul inwardly desired anything disordered, the human intention was, as it were, fortified and secure in every action.

But when natural desires degenerated into alluring appetites and earthly affections, the strongholds of the virgin of Judah were cast down to earth. Thus the human intention is now not secure even in good things, since it can easily be corrupted and deceived by disordered desires close at hand. Hence it is added: “He defiled the kingdom and its princes.” The body was the kingdom of the soul as long as the soul possessed God reigning in itself through love. The princes of the kingdom were the soul’s virtues, through which the soul governed the movements and appetites of the flesh. But after the spirit swelled up against God, it immediately found the stubbornness of resistance in its own flesh. For it was arranged by God that the purity of chastity should pass into the defilement of concupiscence, so that where he had formerly gloried as humble, there he might be ashamed as proud. Therefore God defiled its kingdom—that is, the soul’s—and its princes, namely the princes of that kingdom, because through the concupiscence by which bodily integrity was violated, he also permitted the virtues of the soul to be stained.

“He broke in the wrath of his fury every horn of Israel,” etc. By the horn is signified the strength of virtue; by Israel, the human being; by God’s right hand, protection; by the enemy, the devil; by the enemy’s face, the devil’s pressure; by fire, concupiscence; and by the circuit, the body that surrounds the soul. A horn is not born together with the animal, yet the animal naturally possesses the source from which the horn arises. So the soul possesses virtues not by nature but by grace; yet grace itself works these virtues in a human being not without the natural consent of free choice. But because the human being lost freedom of choice by sinning, and God justly withdrew his grace from the sinner, “every horn of Israel” was, as it were, broken: he lost both the virtues he already possessed and the virtues that he would otherwise have deserved to obtain.

There is another point we may observe in the horn. As it grows, a horn hardens from the moisture of the flesh; and a rational creature, cooperating with grace, receives strength through the growth of virtues. Again, just as a horn protects head and feet, so virtue guards the mind inwardly and actions outwardly from injury. “He turned back,” etc. The devil followed the first human being as he walked in the way of obedience, in order to call him back; but he could not gain access to harm the human being, because God’s right hand stood between him and the human being. But when the human being voluntarily turned toward the devil’s persuasion, God immediately turned his right hand backward from the face of the enemy, so that he no longer drove away the enemy, who was pressing in to harm the human being. Thus the transgressor might feel even in punishment the guilt of his transgression. It follows: “And he kindled in Jacob like a fire,” etc.

Fire is the concupiscence of the flesh, which we contract by being born; and as long as we live in this concupiscence, we endure, as it were, while carrying a domestic enemy within ourselves. This fire is always in us, but it does not always burn or have flame. The fire is kindled into flame when the tinder of sin is stirred up into delight and consent. This flame devours in a circuit, because just as a moth consumes a garment, so corrupt delight destroys the integrity of the flesh with which the soul is clothed. It devours in a circuit because through all the bodily senses it pours out everywhere the poison of corruption in order to violate the soul’s chastity. Or we may understand by “circuit” this world. The concupiscence of the flesh devours in a circuit because, ranging through all this world’s pleasures, it labors to satisfy its evil desires.

“He stretched his bow,” etc. In the bow, a threat is understood; in the strengthened right hand, a violent blow is indicated. Thus God both stretches the bow and strengthens the right hand: he threatens the sinful human being with everlasting punishments in the future, and meanwhile also avenges his guilt by present scourges. Yet because he does this not from anger but from mercy, he is called not an enemy but “as an enemy” and “as an adversary.” This may also be read differently. God stretches the bow when he threatens sinners with punishment and yet, by waiting, postpones the sentence. But he postpones some so that, corrected, they may amend; he postpones others so that, persisting, they may be punished more severely. In those whom he awaits for amendment, he stretches the bow not as an enemy but as one favorable; but in those whom he allows to live for the increase of condemnation, he stretches the bow as an enemy. Likewise, in those whom he corrects through scourges, he strengthens the right hand, but not as an adversary; whereas in those whom he strikes to destruction, he strengthens the right hand as an adversary.

What is said, “he strengthened his right hand,” may be understood thus. God first laid on the first human being, as it were, his right hand when he inflicted upon the sinner the wound of mortality; and God still strengthens that right hand whenever he adds daily scourges to the first wound. What he said above, “He turned back his right hand,” and what he says here, “He strengthened his right hand,” are not contradictory. He turned it back so as not to protect; he turned it toward the human being so as to strike; he strengthened it so as to multiply scourges. Thus present punishment may teach those who are struck what punishment awaits in the future those who persist in evil. Hence the Psalm says: “You gave those who fear you a sign, that they might flee from the face of the bow, and your beloved might be delivered” (Ps. 59).

It follows: “And he killed everything pleasing to the sight in the tents of the daughter of Zion.” The body is the tent of the soul because the soul inhabits it by giving it sensation. The conscience also is the tent of the soul, because there each person rests with himself amid the household of his thoughts. Therefore the Lord killed everything pleasing to the sight in the tents of the daughter of Zion: outwardly, he caused all vigor and beauty of the human body to wither from its state of immortality; inwardly, he stripped the human conscience of the honorable beauty of upright thoughts. Or, by “everything pleasing” we may understand outwardly the discipline and beauty of good works and inwardly, as has been said, the purity of good thoughts.

Note that nothing is killed except what lives. Good works live when they are performed with a right intention; good thoughts live when they feel the affection of inward love. Care must be taken, when God is said to destroy and take away virtues from a human being, that he be understood to do this not by acting directly but by permitting it. For he does it because in his just judgment he permits it to happen. It follows: “And he poured out his indignation like fire.” In pouring out, abundance is signified. It is as if he said: he did not drip it out, but poured it out; like fire, not like water, but like fire. For fire consumes hard and strong things. Thus indignation is poured out like fire because, in vengeance for the sinner’s transgression, not only the flesh but the soul also is tortured.

Or, because fire hardens mud but melts or reduces hard things to ashes, indignation is poured out like fire, so that in one and the same punishment the hard and rebellious may be confounded and perish, while those who are willing humbly to acknowledge their weakness may be strengthened and saved.

“The Lord became like an enemy.” We made him an enemy, though he had not formerly been an enemy, because he hates not what he created but what we have made. It follows: “He cast down her walls; he destroyed her strongholds.” The walls of the soul are one thing; its strongholds another. Walls concern beauty; strongholds concern protection. Thus some gifts of grace adorn, such as prophecy, kinds of tongues, and interpretation of utterances; others fortify, such as faith, hope, and charity. The former, if present, furnish virtues with adornment; the latter, if absent, bring danger. The former, even if absent, do not prevent salvation; without the latter, human beings cannot attain salvation.

It is fittingly first said, “He cast down her walls,” and then added, “He destroyed her strongholds,” because, when a sinful soul is abandoned, the gifts given for manifestation are first taken from it, and afterward the foundations of faith, hope, and charity are overthrown. “He cast down,” he says, “the walls.” What is lofty is cast down; what is solid is destroyed. For, as has been said, walls pertain to glory and strongholds to protection. It follows: “And he filled in the daughter of Judah the humbled man and the humbled woman”—that is, he humbled spirit and flesh in the human being by filling them with misery and pain, so that those unwilling to be humbled through virtue might be humbled through affliction. Or, by the humbled man and the humbled woman we may understand sense and thought, so that they may be afflicted inwardly and outwardly by reproaches until, confounded, they return to repentance.

This can also be referred specifically to the Jewish people. For the prophet, considering how God, after the expulsion of the first human being, wishing to have mercy on the human race, chose this people alone in order to prepare in it the beginnings of our salvation—how he cultivated it by the commandments of the law he gave, exalted it everywhere by his protection, and after all this rejected it for sinning and transgressing—adds the second application to the first and laments, saying: “The Lord became like an enemy; he cast down her walls; he destroyed her strongholds.” For when he took away prophecy, teaching, and signs of miracles from the Jewish people, he cast down their walls, as it were. But when, through unbelief, he permitted them to be blinded and made strangers to the hope of his promise and inheritance, he destroyed their strongholds, as it were. It follows:

“And he filled in the daughter of Judah the humbled man and the humbled woman.” By the humbled man we understand the order of prelates; by the humbled woman, the subject people. Both were humbled at Christ’s coming because they denied as present the truth which they had proclaimed and believed would come. Of them he goes on to say:

“And he destroyed his tent like a garden,” etc. The tent is outside; the tabernacle is within, as also was the tabernacle of the covenant, into which Moses entered to consult the Lord. Thus the people are rightly signified by the tent and the order of prelates by the tabernacle. When God exalted that ancient people with temporal glory, he spread it out like a tent for beauty. But when, enlightening some of them with knowledge of his mysteries, he also deemed them worthy of familiar speech with him, he built, as it were, a tabernacle to dwell in. Yet because, subsequently coming in the flesh, he deprived that people—because their sins required it—of knowledge of truth, and then scattered them through the Romans among all the nations of the world, it is rightly now said: “He destroyed his tent; he demolished his tabernacle.”

It should be noted that he says the tent was not demolished but destroyed, and the tabernacle was not destroyed but demolished. What is demolished is destroyed gradually and secretly. What then does demolition express here but concealed hatred? The tabernacle, therefore, was demolished and the tent destroyed, because unless envy had driven the scribes and Pharisees, the teachers of the people, to the Savior’s death, the vengeance of captivity would not have so cruelly scattered the people itself. Observe, too, by what comparison he says the tent was destroyed: “like a garden,” he says. Just as a garden is destroyed when its fruits have been gathered, its hedge is torn down, and its guarding removed, so that people, after it ceased to bear the fruit of righteousness, immediately lost God’s guardianship and protection. This accords with Isaiah’s prophecy: “The daughter of Zion shall be left like a shelter in a vineyard and like a hut in a cucumber-field.” The Lord himself says to the Jews in the Gospel: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruit” (Matt. 21).

For the barren garden that bears no fruit—that is, the synagogue of the Jews—is destroyed; while the garden bearing fruit—that is, the Church of the Gentiles—is fortified and enclosed, as it is said in the Song of Songs: “An enclosed garden, my sister, an enclosed garden, a sealed fountain” (Song 4). He rightly calls her whom he names an enclosed garden his sister, because the Church of the Gentiles was born through faith from the synagogue, from which Christ also took flesh. Yet he destroyed that same synagogue like a barren garden because it had no fruit of righteousness. Therefore Christ’s mother—that is, the synagogue—is a destroyed garden; Christ’s sister—that is, the Church—is an enclosed garden.

It follows: “The Lord consigned festival and sabbath in Zion to oblivion.” The legal observances were certain shadows of things to come; and therefore, after Truth itself came, God no longer admits the former things to his worship. He is said, as it were, to have forgotten them because he no longer commands that they be offered to him. It follows: “The king and priest to reproach and the indignation of his fury.” Supply: “He consigned [them].” That people was governed by these two offices, namely royal and priestly. The expressions correspond: honor pertains to the king, devotion to the priest; but now reproach is set against honor and indignation against devotion. God is not appeased by their sacrifices but angered by them. As he says through Isaiah: “The blood of goats, calves, and rams I did not desire; incense is an abomination to me. When you came before my presence, who required these things from your hands?” (Isa. 1). And through the Psalmist: “I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks. Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and fulfill your vows to the Most High” (Ps. 49).

But if we turn the things said above toward the moral sense, by the tent we may not unfittingly understand good action, which is displayed outwardly for beauty. By the tabernacle, however, we understand conscience, in which each person lives with himself in a certain familiar and domestic intercourse. That the tabernacle signifies conscience is shown by the Psalmist when he says: “A voice of exultation and salvation is in the tents of the righteous” (Ps. 118). For the righteous bring forth their voice as if in tents because, from their good actions, they desire inwardly in their conscience to be known only to God.

Thus the tent is, as it were, destroyed when the radiance of a good work is driven from the state of uprightness, shaken by the wind of flattery. But the tabernacle is demolished when purity of conscience is secretly corrupted by unlawful delight. It is therefore rightly said: “He destroyed his tent like a garden.” Each person begins to be barren in this: that he seeks glory for his good work in the eyes of people. He is then undeserving of God’s protection for doing good thereafter, because he does not preserve with God the fruit of his shoot—that is, the reward of his work.

We may also note this concerning the tent: just as a tent is first stretched by ropes and then the ropes themselves are held fast by stakes fixed in the ground, so good action ought to be stretched by perseverance of intention lest it slacken; and that intention, lest it grow weak in its purpose, ought to be confirmed through hope of eternal reward, as if by certain stakes fixed into the firmness of the ground. It follows: “The Lord consigned festival and sabbath in Zion to oblivion.” What is meant by festival except inward joy, and what by sabbath except rest of mind? For he had stated two things above: “He destroyed his tent” and “he demolished his tabernacle.” He appears to answer these two points. It is as if he said: Because he destroyed his tent, he consigned festival to oblivion; but because he demolished his tabernacle, he consigned sabbath to oblivion.

For whoever seeks joy in human praise and transitory things does not remember how great is the sweetness of inward joy; and the mind by no means enjoys true peace within while it is disturbed by the enticements of vices and by attachments to fleshly desires. It follows: “The king and priest to reproach and indignation.” Our soul ought to be both king and priest: king, because it ought to rule its flesh; priest, because it ought continually to offer its devotion to God. But the king is consigned to reproach when the soul, subject to its flesh, serves shameful desires. The priest is consigned to indignation when the mind, hardened through the habit of sin, is obstinately turned away from the devotion it used to have toward God.

Therefore God is said to destroy us, demolish us, and consign us to oblivion, reproach, and indignation, because the afflicted mind complains that this is done by God when it is not prevented by him, who permits it in his judgment. For he permits us to be destroyed, so that when destroyed we forget him, and, forgetting him, come to reproach and indignation. It follows:

“The Lord rejected his altar.” Above he spoke about the blinding of the Jews; now he adds the order in which these things occurred, saying: “The Lord rejected his altar.” For what is God’s altar except Christ? Since through him as mediator God is reconciled to the human race, the sacrifice of our propitiation is, as it were, offered to God upon him. God the Father rejected this altar, as it were, when in Christ’s Passion he abandoned him, even to the gibbet of the cross, in the hands of the persecuting Jews. God the Father also cursed his sanctuary, because he first laid upon the one whom he had uniquely sanctified and sent to sanctify us the penalty of our curse to be expiated; then he made us, released from the guilt of the curse, sharers in that sanctification.

It follows: “He delivered into the hand of the enemy the walls of her towers.” The walls of the towers, which are higher in the city, signify the apostles, who at that time were more eminent in dignity and stronger in steadfastness in the holy Church. Yet they too were handed over into the enemy’s hand because, seeing Christ die, they in some sense fell through unbelief. It follows: “They raised their voice in the house of the Lord as on a solemn day.” The house of the Lord means the Church. Thus the enemies raised a voice of exultation in the house of the Lord when, with the shepherd himself dead and the sheep scattered, they gloried that they had altogether prevailed.

Or we may understand by the house of the Lord Christ himself, as the Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5). Thus the enemies raised their voice in the house of the Lord when they insulted him as he hung upon the cross, saying: “He saved others; himself he cannot save. If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we will believe him” (Matt. 27). Hence it is fittingly added, “as on a solemn day.” A solemnity is a general and common festival. Thus those raise their voice as on a solemn day who, their joy fulfilled, exult that nothing remains beyond their desires.

“The Lord rejected his altar.” God’s altar in us is our faith, upon which we offer the sacrifice of good work. This altar is rejected when our faith, stripped of good works, is reproved by God. Of this it is further said: “He cursed his sanctuary.” Our faith is sanctified when merits are added to it through the increase of virtues; the sanctuary is cursed when, after virtues have been lost, faith itself is violated by wicked actions. Hence it is further added: “He delivered into the hand of the enemy the walls of her towers.” What are the walls of the towers except the higher virtues, which are both solid through strength and raised through watchfulness? Thus the walls of the towers are handed over into the enemy’s hand when, once the soul has subjected itself to him by consent to wickedness, the adversary gains dominion even over the highest virtues. Of him it is rightly added:

“They raised their voice in the house of the Lord.” For enemies raise their voice in the house of the Lord when evil spirits, admitted within the conscience, no longer urge sin from outside against one resisting, but rule within one consenting. Therefore it is well added by way of comparison: “As on a solemn day.” The devil indeed fully exults when he finds nothing in us that resists his will.

“The Lord planned,” etc. God is said to plan an action like a human being lest he be believed to do anything rashly and without deliberation. But God’s deliberation is nothing other than his patience and justice: patience, by which he endures offenders long, that they may be corrected; justice, by which he repays those who persist according to their merits. Hence it is added: “He stretched out his line.” What is it to stretch a line over offenders except first diligently to examine the degree and measure of their offense, and then to apportion the measure of vengeance according to the measure of guilt? Therefore it adds: “And he did not turn back his hand from destruction.” It is as if he said: He exempted no one from punishment because he found no one free from guilt.

This may also be read differently. “The Lord planned,” etc. By God’s planning may be understood the hidden dispensation of his incarnation. Because, coming in the flesh, he rejected the Jews by a hidden counsel in order to gather the Gentiles to faith, he first destroyed, as it were, the wall of the daughter of Zion—that is, he withdrew his protection from the Jewish people—and afterwards stretched the line of his inheritance over the people of the Gentiles. For his line was, as it were, contracted when it was said only of the Jewish people: “Jacob, the line of his inheritance” (Deut. 32); but the line is stretched when, as has been said, the allotted inheritance is extended over all nations.

Since the blinding of the Jews preceded the enlightenment of the Gentiles, it is rightly added: “And he did not turn back his hand from destruction.” For, while stretching the line, he would have turned his hand back from destruction if, in gathering the Gentiles, he had not rejected the Jews. Thus the prophet Isaiah, foreseeing by the Spirit the faith of the Gentiles and the future blinding of the Jews, says: “You have multiplied the nation, but you have not increased the joy” (Isa. 9). For though the nation was multiplied, joy was not increased, because the fathers of old, although they rejoiced at the future salvation of the Gentiles, nevertheless also grieved at the destruction of the Jews.

Hence here too it is rightly added: “The outwork mourned, and the wall was destroyed.” What, in this passage, does the outwork signify except the fathers of old, and what does the wall signify except the Mediator of God and human beings himself? As Isaiah says: “Zion, the city of our strength; a Savior shall be placed in it as wall and outwork” (Isa. 26). For according to the form of his assumed humanity, he became, as it were, a wall for us, because he receives those who believe in him through faith and guards them by defending them against the attack of evil spirits. But since the holy fathers also continually keep spiritual watch, through preaching and example, for the protection of God’s Church, they stand outside in the city of God as an outwork.

Let it therefore be said: “The outwork mourned, and the wall was destroyed together,” because all the multitude of the fathers of old grieved because the faithless people of the Jews did not receive the Savior sent to them. But the statement “the wall was destroyed” is spoken with reference to those from whom it was taken. It was destroyed for the Jews in order that it might be built for the Gentiles, because Christ’s faith passed to the Gentiles precisely because Judaea, remaining in unbelief, rejected it. As the Psalmist says: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 118).

Through the fact that he was rejected by the faithless Jews, he was made the head of the corner, as it were, of the Gentiles and of the faithful Jews—two walls coming together from different directions into one [Col. 0279B]. The word *pariter* (“together”) may be understood in either of two ways: either that the wall mourned together with the outer wall, or that the wall was destroyed together with the outer wall. Neither interpretation departs from sound understanding. For the Gospel plainly declares that the Redeemer of the human race himself, together with the other faithful people, wept over that people’s faithlessness and destruction, where it says: “When the Lord drew near to Jerusalem, seeing the city, he wept over it and said: ‘For if you had known, you too, that days shall come upon you, and they shall surround you and hem you in on every side, and cast you to the ground’” (Luke 19).

Likewise, that the fellowship of the saints was scattered from them together with its own head is plainly shown in the Acts of the Apostles, where it is related how the Jewish nation [Col. 0279C] refused to receive faith in Christ and drove his faithful ones from its borders.

“The Lord planned,” etc. What does it mean that the Lord is said to plan before an act, except that God first bears patiently with sinners for a long time, in order afterwards to investigate their guilt more strictly through justice? Therefore it is rightly said now: “The Lord planned to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion.” For what are meant by the wall of the daughter of Zion, if not the virtues of the soul? Almighty God often adopts as sons within the bosom of his Church those whom he has already received through faith and the grace of spiritual gifts; yet afterwards, rejecting them because of wicked deeds, he deprives them even of the virtues that he had already bestowed.

But because, when we sin, he is not ordinarily angry with us so severely unless [Col. 0279D] he has first been provoked for a long time by our iniquities, it is rightly said: “The Lord planned to destroy the wall of the daughter of Zion.” As though it said: He deliberates before he strikes, and does not quickly pronounce sentence, until he has examined the fault by careful consideration. This is explained still more clearly when it says: “He stretched out his line.” For what is it to stretch out a line except to examine carefully the measure of sin?

Or, to stretch out the line is to endure those who persevere long in sin—not because he himself increases iniquity by enduring it, but because, in his just judgment, either by not correcting or by not punishing, he permits it to be prolonged in us. This iniquity is called God’s line because he finds in us that by which we are bound. Therefore we must always be watchful, lest pride elevate us through the gifts of virtues received, [Col. 0280A] or negligence dissolve us. Perhaps, while we wickedly grow secure and neglect to preserve the grace we have received, we do not know how dreadful a judgment the invisible Judge may be forming concerning us. Although he bears with us for a long time while we sin—overlooking us, indeed, but not being ignorant—we must know that where long deliberation comes first, severe punishment follows; just as we see that the more carefully someone aims a blow, the more dangerously he hurls it.

Hence it follows: “He did not turn back his hand from destruction.” This is as though it said plainly: The more he first endured by being patient, the less he now spares in striking. For it is altogether just that, if we do not withdraw our hands from unlawful work while we can, God’s hand also should not turn away from destruction in punishing [Col. 0280B] us.

It follows: “And the outer wall mourned, and the wall was destroyed together.” If, as has been said, the wall signifies the virtues of the soul, then the outer wall rightly signifies works of virtue. What does it mean, then, that when God takes vengeance on us the outer wall mourns and the wall is destroyed, except that, when his grace withdraws, both virtue is taken away and the works of virtue become foolish? Our good works mourn when, virtue having been lost, they may remain for a time but have no merit.

Some wish to understand the wall as works and the outer wall as faith. Faith is rightly said to mourn when good works are destroyed, because faith without a good work is not approved before God.

“Her gates are sunk into the earth; he has destroyed and broken her bars.” In the gates, the exalted condition of a kingdom is indicated; in the bars [Col. 0280C], strength. Therefore the gates are sunk into the earth: loftiness is humbled and cast down. The bars are destroyed and broken: strength is lost and shattered. How this came about, he adds by saying: “Her kings and her princes among the nations”—understand, “the Lord destroyed,” that is, scattered and crushed them, reducing them to nothing. He then adds the reason this befell them: “There is no law,” namely among them, because they do not keep the Lord’s law; “and her prophets have not found a vision from the Lord.”

“Her prophets” must be pronounced with bitterness. It is as though he said: He loved those more who falsely prophesied by their own spirit than those who found a vision from the Lord.

“Her gates are sunk into the earth,” etc. What should we understand by the gates [Col. 0280D] and bars of the city except the leaders of the people? For they are gates by their word, bars by their counsel, and roads by their example: bronze gates through eloquent speech; iron bars through firm counsel; smooth roads through good example. They are gates when, by the word of preaching, they bring those who stand outside into faith. They are bars when, by counsel for salvation, they strengthen and guide those established within by faith. They are roads when, for those who have just begun, they become examples of right conduct by good works.

Thus we may rightly understand the scribes and Pharisees, teachers of the Jews, by the gates of Jerusalem. Of them it is said here: “Her gates are sunk into the earth.” Gates that stand erect and have solid bars can at the proper time be shut and opened: shut, indeed, against enemies and opened to friends. But gates detached from their bars and removed neither secure the entrance nor prevent those wishing to enter. Gates sunk into the earth when their bars have been broken [Col. 0281A] do not provide security, yet they hinder those wishing to enter.

What, then, are upright gates except teachers preaching heavenly things? They hang well upon bars because the word of preaching is strengthened by the counsel of the heart. And what are destroyed and removed gates except negligent and lukewarm preachers, whom the Lord rebukes through the prophet, saying: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56); and elsewhere: “You did not go up to face the day of the Lord, so as to set yourselves as a wall for the house of the Lord” (Ezek. 13). Of these he had also said above: “Her gates are destroyed.”

But here, wishing to indicate something further, he says: “Her gates are sunk into the earth.” For to such persons the Lord says in the Gospel: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, because you have taken away the key of knowledge. You yourselves did not enter, and you prevented those wishing to enter” (Luke 11). Let it therefore be said: “Her gates are sunk into the earth.” For by earth may be understood either love of earthly things, Christ’s humanity, or the carnal observances of the law.

Thus the gates are rightly said to be sunk into the earth, because the scribes and Pharisees, teachers of the people, fixing their minds upon earthly desires, not only refused to receive Christ, but even killed Christ lest they lose that land. Or they were sunk into the earth because, attending only to Christ’s flesh, [Col. 0281C] they fell into the snare of unbelief. Or they were sunk into the earth because, spiritual understanding of the law having passed over to the Gentiles, they themselves remained in carnal observances.

Hence it is suitably added: “He destroyed and broke her bars.” For what do the bars signify except the secret and forceful counsels of the scribes and Pharisees, by which they plotted to kill Christ lest they lose their land? But he destroyed and broke the bars because he brought their counsel to nothing. The counsel was destroyed because they could not extinguish Christ by killing him. The counsel was broken because, for that very reason—that they killed Christ—they lost the land.

Therefore it follows: “Her kings and her princes among the nations”—understand, “God established them,” so that [Col. 0281D] Gentiles might reign and exercise authority over them. Thus the bars were destroyed and broken, so that they not only paid tribute to kings of the Gentiles, but also royal prefects and governors lived among them, oppressed them, and finally expelled the rebels from their land and scattered them throughout the whole world. Of them it is further said: “There is no law,” namely among them; for although they possess books of the law, since they do not believe in Christ, they do not observe the law.

But because they still promise themselves that their Christ is yet to come, a fitting answer to this is given when it says:

“Her prophets have not found a vision from the Lord.” As though it said: What they falsely flatter themselves in proclaiming concerning Christ’s coming they have found from themselves, not through the Lord’s revelation.

“Her gates are sunk into the earth” [Col. 0282A]. What should we understand by the gates of the soul except the bodily senses? We sink these gates into the earth when we incline our very senses to earthly desires. But since an outward sense never yields to shameful desires unless the inward guard of the mind has first been broken and scattered through negligence, it is rightly added: “He destroyed and broke her bars.” For he destroys the bars when, good fear having been removed, he leaves the mind wandering and undisciplined. He breaks the bars when he permits the steadfastness of the mind to be shattered and softened by vices entering in.

It follows: “Her kings and her princes are among the nations.” The nations signify vices. Therefore the kings and princes of the soul are among the nations when the vices themselves begin to rule it through consent [Col. 0282B]. Or by kings and princes we may understand the virtues of the soul itself, by which it was previously governed: kings, because they preside inwardly over the will; princes, because they move the mind outwardly to act well. This must be connected with what he had said before: “He destroyed and broke her bars”—that is, he destroyed and broke kings and princes, namely the virtues, among the nations, that is, he allowed them to be broken and oppressed through vices.

This is why he adds: “There is no law.” The mind should possess inwardly a law: namely, fear and love of God; and by the judgment of this law it should govern its outward senses. Fear, that it may not dissolve itself into wantonness with the desire of the flesh; love, that it may not become sluggish and languid in good work. But if the mind sinks its gates—that is, its senses—in earthly delights, it itself is its own judgment, since, its bars having been broken, that is, its virtues lost, it has also lost inwardly the law of life: namely, the fear and love of God [Col. 0282C]. It is fittingly still reproached:

“Her prophets have not found a vision from the Lord.” Once the mind, having lost the governing control of reason, begins to follow the judgment of its senses, it then shuns only those things which the sensuous impulse declares bad and pursues those which the fleshly impulse approves. Thus it must often be deceived: for while it considers present pleasures alone, it does not avoid future bitterness. This is why Moses so often runs to the tabernacle to consult the Lord [Col. 0282D]: for a person should neither seek nor avoid anything rashly outwardly until first, inwardly, by the judgment of the mind, he has discerned what is pleasing to God’s will.

But of the perverse soul, which everywhere follows the impulse of the flesh rather than the judgment of the mind, it is rightly said here by way of reproach: “Her prophets have not found a vision from the Lord.” For assuredly that person plunges himself into the pit of destruction who always considers what is sweet to his flesh but pays no attention to what pleases God.

“They sat upon the ground; the elders were silent,” etc. Up to this point he has described, as it were, the destruction of buildings; henceforth he laments the misery and grief of human beings. “They sat upon the ground; the elders were silent.” Sitting signifies dejection; silence, stupefaction. And fittingly [Col. 0283A] the elders, in whom the authority of counsel ought to have existed, are said to have kept silence, because the calamity was so great that it could be relieved by no counsel.

It follows:

“The virgins sprinkled ashes upon their heads.” Of their own accord they disfigure the appearance of their beauty, in order to show by their outward squalor the intensity of their inward grief. In tribulation the elders fittingly keep silent, while the virgins sprinkle ashes on their heads; for when evil presses severely, it turns mature minds to stupefaction and the wanton to impatience. Of them it is further said:

“They girded themselves with sackcloth.” This refers to the elders.

“They cast their heads down to the ground.” **ALLEGORICAL.** This refers to the virgins. Those who add voluntary afflictions even to the evils that press upon them wish to hasten death.

“They sat upon the ground; the elders were silent,” etc. The prophet’s mind, contemplating all the evils of this present life, and directing the eye of compunction from the beginning, extends its lament from the fall of the first human being to the blinding of the Jewish people, and then, descending through the evils of the present Church, to the lament at the end of time. Above, beginning as it were with lesser matters, he described ruined buildings and destroyed walls; now, proceeding as it were to greater matters, he laments human misery and grief. Thus what follows may not inappropriately be referred to the present Church.

“They sat upon the ground; the elders of the daughter of Zion were silent.” What is meant by the daughter of Zion except the present Church, which was born from the Synagogue through faith? The elders of the daughter of Zion, then, are called the prelates of the Church [Col. 0283C], whose old age is sought not in number of years but in progress in wisdom and maturity of character.
