And rightly “elders,” because they are not, like little children under the law, placed as it were under a guardian. For the ancient people were like little children, since they were nourished by the rod of the law and earthly promises until they rose to mature understanding, so as to serve God not for earthly but for heavenly things.

These elders of the daughter of Zion, therefore, ought not to sit upon the earth—that is, seek earthly and transient things—but ought by their way of life and desire to dwell in heaven, so that they may show in their conduct what they preach in word. But because the prophet foresaw that many would arise in the holy Church who, occupying a place of preeminence, would stain the dignity of their office by perverse conduct, he burst forth in a voice of grief and said: “The elders of the daughter of Zion sat upon the ground” [Col. 0283D]. For what is sitting upon the earth except ceasing from good work by giving oneself to earthly delights? But because those who act perversely by ceasing from good are ashamed to speak the word of truth, lest they become witnesses against their own perversity, he rightly added: “They were silent.” For indeed, where the guilt of crime gnaws at conscience, fear of shame binds the tongue from preaching.

It follows:

“The virgins of Jerusalem sprinkled ashes on their heads.” What are meant by the virgins of Jerusalem except the good subjects in the Church, who, preserving the integrity of faith through purity of conduct, hasten to the vision of supreme peace? And what is meant by the head except spiritual action? What is meant by ashes, left by fire, except earthly thoughts? For ashes arise, as it were, from fire when remnants of vain thoughts are generated by carnal desire.

Therefore, after the elders sit upon the earth and are silent, the virgins rightly sprinkle ashes upon their heads, because when the simple members of the Church see their prelates, setting aside the work of preaching, occupied with earthly delights, they themselves begin to take carnal delight even in the good things they do. He aptly called them the elders of the daughter of Zion and the virgins of Jerusalem, because prelates in the holy Church ought to be exalted through the foresight of vigilance. Subjects, however, in the good works they humbly perform, ought always through the intention of their minds to look toward the vision of eternal peace, so that [Col. 0284B] the former, established on high through virtue, may guard what is beneath them, and the latter, placed low through humility, may always strive upward in intention.

The prophet therefore laments that those who ought to stand upright are sitting, and that those accustomed to contemplate heavenly things cast ashes upon themselves lest they be able to raise their sight to what is above. Note also that even the perfect are said to have dust upon their feet; but those who sprinkle dust on their heads are now counted among those to be lamented. For good people sometimes contract slight stains in earthly actions through weakness; evil people, however, are defiled by the intention of praise even in matters which they seem to undertake vigorously.

It follows:

“They girded themselves with sackcloth.” What is signified by sackcloth except concern for earthly things, which pricks the conscience with the continual thorns of occupations? Thus the elders are first described as sitting upon the ground and afterwards as girded with sackcloth, because when the mind has first become lax through love of carnal delights, concern soon follows, pricking it with anxiety in fulfilling its desires [Col. 0284C]. Likewise, the virgins are said first to sprinkle ashes upon their heads, and afterward to cast their heads themselves down to the earth, because this is the order of destruction: first, each obscures the good he does by the intention of human praise; afterward he even changes those good works into wicked actions.

**MORAL.** “The elders of the daughter of Zion sat upon the ground; they were silent.” Through the different ages, sexes, and offices of persons, the inward movements of the soul are distinguished. For what offices distinguish outwardly among persons, the movements of affections perform inwardly in their several ways. What, then, should we understand by the elders of the daughter of Zion except the counsels of the faithful soul? But it must be known that the counsels of the elect are one thing, and those of the reprobate another.

The counsels of the elect are to despise this present life and its delights, preserve patience in adversity, and attain future glory through present tribulations. The counsels of the reprobate are to flee adversity, love the present life, delay amid carnal desires, and either despise or despair of the future life. Concerning the counsel of the wicked the Psalmist says: “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the wicked” (Ps. 1); and concerning the counsel of the righteous he subsequently adds in the same psalm: “Therefore the wicked shall not rise in judgment, nor sinners in the counsel of the righteous” [Col. 0285A]. If, therefore, those who turn to the counsel of the righteous rise, those who have fallen away into the counsel of the wicked are rightly said to sit, because the former tends upward and the latter downward; the former seeks heaven and the latter earth.

Thus the elders of the daughter of Zion sit upon the ground when the affections of the soul, forgetting the eternal promise, cling to earthly and transient delights. Of them it is rightly said: “They were silent.” For inward desire is like a certain cry in God’s ears. Therefore, the more the perverse mind seeks transient things outwardly, the more it falls silent inwardly from desire for eternal things.

It follows: “The virgins of Jerusalem sprinkled ashes on their heads.” By the virgins of Jerusalem we should understand the pure thoughts of the soul [Col. 0285B]. What does it mean, then, that after the elders sit upon the earth the virgins are said to sprinkle ashes upon their heads, except that when the soul’s affections are corrupted, a darkness of thoughts is immediately produced? Hence it is further added: “They girded themselves with sackcloth.” For after sitting and sprinkling ashes comes sackcloth, because from perverse delight and confusion of mind there arises, in the sinner’s conscience, a painful pricking concerning the guilt of its crime.

Finally, at the end, the climax of unhappiness is added when it says: “The virgins of Judah cast their heads down to the earth.” To cast one’s head down to the earth after girding oneself with sackcloth is, after the anguish and trembling of an evil conscience, even to despair of pardon. Therefore they are rightly also called virgins of Judah. For, to heighten the grief, their final confession is named in them, because it too, the last after all other virtues have been lost, is excluded from those who despair [Col. 0285C].

“My eyes failed through tears,” etc. **LITERAL.** The prophet, in the person of the Church lamenting her members, after enumerating the evils of those who perish, adds the compassion of the good. For the wicked are first lamented by the good rather than by themselves; and while those who are wickedly well still rejoice in their own destruction, the sighs of others show how greatly they ought to be made to weep. He therefore says:

“My eyes failed through tears; my inward parts were troubled; my liver was poured out upon the earth.” In the holy Church, the eyes are overseers; the inward parts, the merciful; the liver, those diligent and fervent in good work. For, as physicians say, the heat of digestion is in the liver. Thus, just as the liver, or *hepar*, by its heat digests raw food in the stomach and then transmits nourishing juice to all the parts of the body, so those who stir others from sluggishness to good work through the fervor of their devotion supply, as it were, nourishment to Christ’s body from their own digestion.

What, then, does it mean that, while sin ravages the faithful people, the Church’s eyes fail, its inward parts are troubled, and its liver is poured out upon the earth, except that those who truly possess Christ’s love always have compassion for the miseries of others? As the Apostle says: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (1 Cor. 40). For there is no surer indication of true charity [Col. 0286A] than the affection of brotherly compassion.

He aptly said that the eyes fail through tears, because the fault of subjects often wounds life with so violent a blow that all reason and diligence of prelates gives way, and amid such great evils there is no counsel left except to flee to tears alone and implore divine mercy. The Psalmist beautifully signifies this, saying: “They were troubled and were moved like a drunken man, and all their wisdom was swallowed up. And they cried to the Lord when they were troubled, and he delivered them from their distresses” (Ps. 106). Thus the eyes rightly fail through tears, because, when evil presses fiercely, grief makes the eye of discernment grow dim. The inward parts are troubled because the inward affection of pity is shaken. The liver is poured out upon the earth [Col. 0286B], because in the elect the cheerfulness of the mind is often bound by sorrow for another’s peril, so that they themselves are rendered more lukewarm in doing good insofar as they are afflicted more deeply by compassion for a brother’s tribulation.

Thus by the eyes, inward parts, and liver are signified those who lament, not those who are lamented. Therefore, immediately joining a judgment concerning those lamented in the following words, he explains the cause of grief, saying:

“Over the destruction of the daughter of my people.” For what is signified by the female sex except a weak people? Yet, by calling her a daughter, he shows that she has the profession of faith. By destruction, moreover, irreparable calamity is shown, just as what has been broken cannot be repaired further.

It follows:

“When the little one and the nursing child failed in the streets of the town” [Col. 0286C]. He specifies the destruction by the little one, meaning an untrained people and one simple in faith; by the nursing child, perverse teachers; by the streets of the town, the pleasures of this age. Thus the little one and the nursing child fail in the streets of the town when all who are carnal and foolish, together with perverse teachers, go by the broad road of pleasures to destruction. Note that he says, “failed.” Those who fail from goodness are more to be lamented than those who were never good.

“They failed,” etc. **ALLEGORICAL.** It is characteristic of the elect to lament the evils of others as their own. For just as, by rejoicing with the good, they become sharers in their merits, so too, by grieving compassionately with the wicked, they gain profit for themselves from the others’ destruction [Col. 0286D]. Let the sinner therefore learn how he ought to weep for his own evils when a righteous person afflicts himself with such grief for the sins of others.

“My eyes,” he says, “failed through tears.” How deeply contrite do you think this man was, who wept in this way? For he does not show merely that he shed tears once, since he says that his eyes failed through tears. But because many shed tears without being contrite in heart, he added: “My inward parts were troubled”—that is, the arrow of grief penetrated to the inmost heart; pain touched the understanding, and the affection of pity trembled.

It follows: “My liver was poured out upon the earth.” What is signified by the pouring out of the liver except bodily affliction? For because the liver receives the heat of digestion from the stomach, those who, in afflicting their body, set aside care for themselves do nothing other than pour out their liver upon the earth [Col. 0287A]. Therefore, lest his tears be thought empty, his sighs feigned, or his groans pretended, visible bodily affliction follows.

But perhaps this man grieves for parents or relatives? Hear what he says: “Over the destruction,” he says, “of the daughter of my people”—not of father, mother, brother, sister, kinsman, or relative, but, he says, “my people,” lest the impulse of the flesh, rather than the spur of charity, be thought the source of his grief. But perhaps, I suppose, he honors the famous and rich among the people with his lamentation? Notice what he says: “When the little one and the nursing child failed.” First observe his discernment: he grieves that they fail; he does not grieve that they are not rich. “The little one,” he says, “and the nursing child.” See that he has compassion upon weakness and does not revere strength or display.

But perhaps he still honors nobility of birth in the weakness of sex and age: “In the streets,” he says, “of the town” [Col. 0287B]—not in a court, not in a city, not in a town, not even in a house, but in the streets of the town. For the greater the abjection of those destroyed, the more severe—and thus the more precious—is the compassion of the mourner.

“They failed,” etc. **MORAL.** What is meant by the eyes except the brightness of contemplation; by the inward parts, the sense of inward sweetness; and by the liver, the fervor of divine love? What does it mean, then, that the prophet recounts that his eyes failed, his inward parts were troubled, and his liver poured out upon the earth over the destruction of the daughter of his people, except that the more a spiritual person pours out his mind outwardly in compassion for the tribulation of neighbors, the more he laments that those inward joys which he was accustomed to taste in tranquility are withdrawn through the disturbance of his own grief?

It follows: “Over the destruction,” etc. By the daughter of the people is meant the carnal soul; by the little one, the sense of the flesh; by the nursing child, the virtue of the mind. For the sense of the flesh, so far as it lies within itself, always desires certain childish and trivial things, unless it is restrained by discipline through the steadfastness of the mind. Thus the little one is nourished with milk because, through the virtue of the mind, it is gradually brought up to the maturity of constancy, as it were to manly strength.

It follows: “In the streets of the town.” By the town we may not inappropriately understand the body inhabited by the soul, and by the streets of the town the unstable desires of the flesh [Col. 0287D]. Why, then, are the little one and the nursing child said to fail in the streets of the town amid the destruction of the daughter of the people, except that in the carnal soul the sense is first corrupted outwardly through alluring desires, and then the virtue and steadfastness of the mind itself are softened?

“They said to their mothers,” etc. **LITERAL.** In mothers a more tender affection of love is signified; if they can, they not only listen to but anticipate their children’s desires. Why, then, do they wait for their children to ask, except because they do not possess what they can offer to the needy? And lest you suppose maternal pity to have hardened through a natural defect, hear how they formerly behaved toward their children.

They do not ask for barley and water, namely servile food, because their mothers were not accustomed to give anything of that sort; rather:

“Where,” they say, “is the wheat and the wine?” They ask for what they were accustomed to receive. Yet they do not ask so much as inquire in astonishment, because they were not accustomed to ask but to possess. But perhaps you will say that these children were wanton and delicate, seeking superfluities, which even maternal pity ought to deny them. Hear what follows.

“When they failed,” he says, “like wounded men in the streets of the city.” A double evil: poverty and disgrace. It would at least have been more bearable to fail at home and be consumed secretly by hunger than to endure, in the streets, the shame of disgrace along with wasting through hunger.

It follows:

“When they breathed out their souls in their mothers’ bosoms” [Col. 0288B]. Everything contributes to the evil. They fail in the streets; they breathe out their souls in their mothers’ bosoms, so that both their visible wasting multiplies shame and their present death multiplies grief.

“They said to their mothers,” etc. **ALLEGORICAL.** The prelates of the holy Church ought to be elders in prudence and counsel, and mothers in compassion. But because any wicked and negligent persons, when they obtain a place of preeminence, set aside care of their subjects and attend instead to their own greed or luxury, the prophet rightly says now: “They said to their mothers: ‘Where is the wheat and the wine?’” It is great grief, because what they withhold from those who ask they ought to have offered even to those who did not ask.

It must be known that the life of subjects speaks to prelates in three ways: through misery, desire, and obedience [Col. 0288C]. They ask when they are in need; they ask when they desire; they ask when they are ready to hear. They ask through misery because, when the need of the afflicted is seen, their life cries out—even if their tongue is silent—while it summons compassionate minds to help. They also ask through desire, because in some way to ask is to wish to have. Likewise they ask through obedience because, while they offer themselves ready to receive, they declare, as it were, that they are willing and desirous.

Thus the life of subjects always speaks to negligent prelates, even if not with the tongue, because the peril of the wicked and the desire and obedience of the good move them to devote themselves to preaching and to an example of good conduct. Notice that, in time of need, the children call not their fathers but their mothers. It is as though they say: If you have forgotten your obligation, at least you ought not to forget compassion.

Let dumb dogs, unable to bark, be ashamed (Isa. 56). Let those be ashamed who have become wolves from being shepherds; who feed the Lord’s flock not as shepherds but as hirelings; who are strong to tear apart and weak to protect; ready to receive and slow to give; eloquent in deceiving and unlearned in speaking well; who exact more than is due, render less than is due, or render nothing; who have transformed judgments of truth into lawsuits. Woe to them, because they do not attend to what they owe; and if they refuse to anticipate a request, let them at least listen to those who ask, because perhaps even in the request itself they may learn [Col. 0289A] what they owe.

“Where,” those people say, “is the wheat and the wine?” They do not ask for barley and water, but for wheat and wine. Let us therefore see what this wheat and wine are, and why the children do not ask for barley and water, although they are in the necessity of famine. In the Gospel we read that five thousand people were fed with five barley loaves (John 6). Afterwards four thousand are satisfied (Matt. 15), yet nothing is there said of barley loaves. Again, we read in the Gospel that six stone jars were first filled with water, and that afterwards the waters themselves were changed into wine (John 2). The Lord himself also makes mention of wheat in the Gospel, saying: “Unless a grain of wheat, falling into the earth, dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12).

What, then, is meant by wheat except Christ; by barley except the law; by water except carnal understanding; by wine except spiritual understanding? Barley and water could therefore suffice for servants who observed the law in a carnal sense. But children, who have now been adopted through grace in Christ and know how to eat Christ spiritually, desire nothing but wheat and wine. “I count all these things”—namely, legal observances—the Apostle says, “as dung, that I may gain Christ” (Phil. 3). See how he rejects the barley of the law and seeks to eat only wheat, that is, Christ. And the law is aptly understood by barley, which is rough to eat, and Christ by wheat, which is pleasant and sweet, because the law [Col. 0289C] came to punish sins, while Christ came to forgive them.

Why, then, Christ is called wheat we now learn by God’s grace both through reading and through tasting as we eat. We eat Christ in four ways. We eat Christ when, by receiving bodily the sacrament of his body and blood, we spiritually nourish our souls. We eat Christ when we love Christ by believing in him. We eat Christ when we imitate Christ. We eat Christ when, by hearing the word of God, we pass over into the manner of life of the new life. What, then, is it to seek wheat except to seek Christ, to seek the word of God, the teaching of truth, and the way of life of the new man? Therefore we seek wheat [Col. 0289D] when we desire to hear the word of life and to imitate Christ. But if we eat wheat, we ought to drink wine and not water—that is, to receive the word of God by hearing it and to water it within ourselves through spiritual understanding. For this is what is commanded us in the Law: that we should not cook the flesh of the paschal lamb in water (Exod. XII), because that which has been given for spiritual nourishment ought not to have a carnal flavour for us. Therefore let good subjects question their bad prelates and say: “Where is the wheat?” As if they said: “Where is the teaching of truth? Where are the examples of the new man?” Or, more plainly: “You neither show the truth by your speech nor present yourselves as worthy of imitation by living well. Where is the wine?” As if they said: “You, who handle even spiritual things carnally, how will you be able to call us from carnal things [Col. 0290A] to spiritual? You, who cannot forget earthly things which you seemed to have cast aside—how will you make us drunk into forgetfulness of what we possess? First eat, and afterwards refresh others; become drunk, and then make others drunk.” Shame upon us! What shall we say to these things? What wonder is it if the people love carnal things when even the clergy sell spiritual things for carnal ones? Hence it is rightly added when it is said: “When they were failing like wounded men in the streets of the city.” There are two cities, Babylon and Jerusalem. But Babylon has streets—that is, broad ways—which lead to death. Therefore, they fail in the streets of the city who, dissolving through the enticements of the flesh, grow weak in strength of mind. Or by the city we may suitably understand the Church itself; for [Col. 0290B] the holy Church has streets and also paths. For what are earthly occupations except certain streets? And what are spiritual occupations except paths? Therefore in the streets of the city are those who in the holy Church lawfully serve earthly occupations. But they fail in the streets of the city who, occupied with earthly business, do not find spiritual comforters. Certainly they would not fail if the losses which they often suffer outwardly were always repaired inwardly by the counsel and admonition of good prelates. Hence it is well said of such persons, “like wounded men.” For what are sins except wounds? Thus they fail like wounded men who tend toward destruction through negligence, just as others do through guilt. Therefore it must be pronounced with great sorrow: “like wounded men”—as if it were said: [Col. 0290C] “Why do these perish through the negligence of prelates, though they have not been wounded by crimes and disgraceful deeds?” Hence it follows: “When they breathed out their souls in the bosom of their mothers.” For what is the bosom of mothers except the soothing flattery of prelates? For mothers hold their dying children in their bosom when bad prelates do not merely fail to rouse carnal minds, dying within their own body, to good works, but even, by caressing them with flattering favour, cherish them in their destruction.

“They said to their mothers,” etc. **MORAL.** What should we understand spiritually by the children of mothers except the multitude of thoughts which, as they proceed in one mind from different affections, are like the offspring of many mothers in one house, though they do not proceed from one origin? We have said that thoughts are born from affections because, certainly, the memory of those things most frequently comes to us in thought by whose love we are affected. We readily prove this true in each vice and virtue. Hence it is said in the Gospel: “Where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Matt. VI). As if it were said: “Where your love is, there is your mind. As your affection is, so also is your thought.” But one must know that, just as affections generate thoughts from themselves, so in turn the thoughts themselves kindle still more strongly the affections from which they arise. Hence, in those who carefully guard their heart from unlawful thoughts, the roots of evil [Col. 0291A] affections finally wither away completely. On the contrary, those who neglect to exercise their mind in holy meditations gradually grow lukewarm, even if they were first warmed by some spark of divine love; so much so at last that, even if they may sometimes have thoughts arising from good affections, they nevertheless feel no inner sweetness, however slightly, distilled from them into the bosom of the mind. For this reason it is rightly said here: “They said to their mothers: ‘Where are the wheat and wine?’” For what is signified by wheat except the food of wisdom, and what by wine except inward joy? For as bodily bread restores the belly, so wisdom feeds the mind; and as wine eagerly drunk intoxicates, so inward joy alienates the mind from carnal desires. What, then, is it that hungry children seek wheat and wine from their mothers except that thoughts born from good affections, but dried up through negligence, cannot find in them the flavour of their former sweetness? Of these it is rightly added: “When they failed like wounded men in the streets of the city.” For what are the streets of the city except the wanderings of the mind? Therefore they fail in the streets of the city because, while the wandering mind does not gather them into inward rest, they do not reach the taste of the inmost flavour. To these also aptly applies what is said, “like wounded men.” For evil desires are wounds of good thoughts because, while infecting them by their admixture, they corrupt, like certain blows, the integrity of their uprightness. Therefore the barren thoughts of the soul are rightly said to fail like wounded men, [Col. 0291C] because they remain empty of the fruit of righteousness just as those thoughts which have been corrupted by unlawful desires. It follows: “When they breathed out their souls in the bosom of their mothers.” The bosom of mothers is the lukewarmness and sloth of good affections, in which little thoughts are rightly said to breathe out their souls; for when the mind grows lukewarm from the ardour of divine love, all vigour of good thoughts immediately dies.

“To whom shall I compare you?” etc. **LITERAL.** He gradually advances the lament. First he mourned the buildings, then the people, and mourned them as though absent; now at last, with hearts softened and accustomed by long weeping, he turns his words toward those present, saying: “To whom shall I compare you, and to whom shall I liken you?” As if he said: “Since your ruin is so great, to whom shall I compare you? And since you are so grievously afflicted, to whom shall I liken you?” This is plainly to say: Your evils surpass every misery both in magnitude and in manner. But because even great things can sometimes be compared with the smallest by a certain differentiated resemblance, he adds: “And make you equal,” etc. This is to say: Although other evils may be compared with you in some differentiated respect, none can be compared with you in equality. Why? It follows: “For your ruin is great as the sea.” It is remarkable that he declares her calamity incapable of being equalled with anything, and immediately makes it equal, by comparison, to the greatness of the sea. But this must be understood as though he said: Just as the sea excels all other waters both in mass and bitterness, so no calamity can be made equal to your ruin. It follows: [Col. 0292A] “Who will heal you?” As the water of the sea cannot be dried up, so your ruin cannot be measured by man; nor is there anyone in whom you may hope except God alone. “To whom shall I compare you?” Those who go back after knowing the truth are worse than those who have never known it. And the higher anyone’s rank, the more dangerous is his fall. Therefore the prophet, after above lamenting the negligence of evil prelates in the Church and the destruction of their subjects, immediately added:

“To whom shall I compare you, and to whom shall I liken you, and make you equal, O virgin daughter of Zion?” The repetition of words expresses the force of great grief. As though he spoke to the Church herself concerning her withered members and said: “Just as formerly, when you held the faith by living rightly, your glory was incomparable, so now, when you have fallen from the faith through a reprobate life, your disgrace is incomparable.” It follows:

“For your ruin is great as the sea.” **ALLEGORICAL.** What is understood by the sea except worldly life, which, while it is always drawn by unstable motion now from adversities to prosperity, now from prosperity to adversities, is tossed about as though by stormy waves? And because it never excludes fear even in prosperity or sorrow even in adversity, it is like the sea: whichever way it flows back, it does not lose its bitterness. Therefore let it be said to her who, from the sweetness of spiritual life, grows bitter through carnal desire and worldly cares—let it be said, I say: “Your ruin is great as the sea.” As if it were plainly said: You who were made sweet through contempt for the world and desire for eternal goods, apart from carnal love—how have you been turned again into bitterness? It follows:

“Who will heal you?” **MORAL.** Let the prelates of the Church hear this, those who have been appointed physicians of souls; let them hear what is said: “Who will heal you?” As if it were said: Physicians treat other sick persons, but who will treat sick physicians? If the people sin, priests pray for them. But if priests sin, who will pray for them? These things are altogether dangerous, yet true. Although we fear to hear them, we cannot deny them.

“To whom shall I compare you?” etc. The sinful soul is rebuked, whose many evils were enumerated above. By committing fornication away from the love of God, she has made her incest all the more shameful because the integrity which fell was more precious. [Col. 0292D] To her it is aptly said: “Your ruin is great as the sea.” For what is understood by the sea except a wicked conscience, which the memory of past crimes and the delight of present ones agitate, driving it here and there? For waves, as it were, coming from opposite directions collide with one another when unhappy penitence for past errors continually pulls back the miserable soul, while love of present things drives it onward. And because in so great a contradiction that poor sweetness of pleasure is always infected with mingled pain, a wicked conscience is rightly called a sea not only because of its restlessness but also because of its bitterness. It follows: “Who will heal you?” He shows that it is altogether a great and difficult matter, though not impossible for God, that such a person should return to health. Hence John says of one sinning unto death: “I do not say that anyone should pray for him” (I John V). As if he said: “Just as I do not forbid desiring his salvation, so I do not presume to command prayer for him, because the healing of so deadly a wound, though it does not exceed the power of God, nevertheless surpasses all human estimation. Therefore it is more cautiously done if, for the time being, desire alone is humbly offered to God while prayer is restrained; for perhaps, in so difficult a case, humble and fearful devotion will obtain more quickly than presumptuous petition.” He says, therefore: “Who will heal you?” As if he said: “Your wound is dangerous; it cannot be aided by human effort, and because of past guilt is not worthy to be healed by God.” [Col. 0293B]

“Your prophets,” etc. **LITERAL.** It is said reproachfully: “Your prophets.” As if it were said: “See to what misery you have been reduced by listening to false prophets, whom you loved, while refusing to hear the prophets of God speaking truth.” “They saw for you.” They saw for you because they were your prophets. Their falsehood redounded to you because their wickedness pleased you. “Your prophets saw for you.” What did they see for you? “False and foolish things.” False things, by which you were deceived; foolish things, by which you cannot be excused. If they had seen only false things in which there was at least some semblance of truth, perhaps your simplicity could have been excused through ignorance. But now, because they also saw foolish things and you nevertheless did not fear to believe, your folly is deservedly punished. But what false and foolish things did they see? False burdens—behold foolish things; false expulsions—behold false things. They promised prosperity whenever and to whomever they wished; they threatened adversity whenever and to whomever they wished. But both were false, because they promised burdens to those who were to be expelled and expulsions to those who were to be raised up. When God was angry, they announced that he would take you up for protection; when he was appeased, they threatened that he would cast you out for affliction. But the threat was false and the promise foolish. In the promise there was not only falsehood but also folly, because, although you feared terrors, it is very contrary to reason that, conscious of so great a crime, you could be deceived by empty promises. [Col. 0293D] Behold, you did not know what was going to happen; yet you did not fail to know your own evil desert, which was present. But by seeing false and foolish things they did not disclose your iniquity to you; for while they promised prosperity to the perverse in their crime and troubled the straightforward by empty terrors, they did not disclose—indeed, they veiled—your iniquity, lest you should recognize it.

Or it may be distinguished otherwise. What he said, “false and foolish,” pertains to promises; but what follows, “false burdens and false expulsions,” must both be referred to terrors. For he calls tribulation an “expulsion,” because the people were to be cast out by God; and a “burden” by analogy with a load which, when taken up, weighs down its bearer. Hence where blessed Jerome translated “the burden of Babylon,” or Tyre, or Damascus, and so forth, Symmachus and Theodotion rendered it “assumption” or “burden-bearing.” And, for the reason stated above, he fittingly calls only the terrors false, but names the promises not merely false but also foolish; for although a person cannot always know what will happen, it is very foolish not to know oneself in the present. Thus immediately after saying, “They saw for you false and foolish things,” he adds: “Nor did they disclose your iniquity to you.” For one who promises a sinner the reward of the righteous hides that person’s iniquity, as though preventing it from being seen.

“Your prophets,” etc. **ALLEGORICAL.** Just as it is a fault of evil prelates that their subjects perish through their negligence, so it is also reckoned a fault to subjects that, despising the good, they imitate the examples of bad prelates and listen to perverse teachings. Suitably, therefore, after he has reproved the perversity of prelates, he now turns words of grief in reproach also toward the subjects themselves, saying: “Your prophets saw for you false and foolish things.” The prelates of the Church are prophets when, to instruct the faith and morals of their subjects, they sometimes disclose the hidden things of the Scriptures and sometimes proclaim the future rewards of the good or the future punishments of the evil. But all perverse persons, because in speaking they seek not so much the correction of their hearers as favour, are rightly described here: “They saw for you false and foolish things.” For they see false and foolish things because they do not maintain the judgment of truth in discerning the morals of their subjects. And when, for the favour of popularity, they praise certain wicked persons in their perversities, they make foolish people still more foolish through negligent flattery. Hence it is rightly added: “Nor did they disclose your iniquity to you, that they might provoke you to repentance.” But because bad prelates sometimes persecute even innocent subjects in hatred, and, while avenging their own injuries, pretend that they are defending God’s cause, it is rightly added when it is said: “But they saw for you false burdens and expulsions.” As if it were said: “Against those with whom they themselves were angry, they announced that divine wrath and vengeance were impending, so that by calling God the avenger of their injuries they might move the minds of the people to show them reverence.”

[Col. 0294D] “Your prophets,” etc. **MORAL.** Who are the prophets of the sinful soul, who see false and foolish things for it, except the outward senses of the body and the crafty thoughts within, which the prudence of the flesh engenders? Let us consider a little more attentively how false these prophets are. Here is one of them: sight. How does it deceive by prophesying false things? If you see an object of desire, what does it foretell to you? “Love it,” it says; “follow it, seize it, enjoy it. You will be happy if you obtain such a desire.” But the unhappy soul, while wrongly credulous, follows the deceptive promise and is bound by still greater misery through the accomplishment of sin. Thus hearing, thus smell, thus taste and touch prophesy false things and ensnare those who believe them; for before desire acquires experience, they promise that all things will be prosperous and pleasant; but when miserable pleasure has been briefly tasted and has passed away, they leave behind a conscience stunned and filled with horror. Yet these prophets can be detected in their deceits all the more easily because what they promise is more clearly manifest and often lacks reason. But the craftiness of the heart is more dangerous in proportion as it is more hidden, because it not only promises deceptively, but also cunningly compels the mind to believe by a certain plausible rationale for acting. This is the prudence of the flesh which works death, possessed by the wicked children of this age, as the Lord says in the Gospel: “The children of this age are wiser in their generation than the children of light” (Luke X). This prudence produces those perverse prophets, namely, the crafty thoughts of the soul, which soothe the soul with false promises and seduce and ensnare it when it consents. One lies in wait for patience; another strives to violate chastity; one mocks contempt for the world; another teaches that one should devote oneself to hypocrisy.

Let us examine these one by one. There is one thought born from the prudence of the flesh. It says to a person: “Avenge your injury; retaliate for your wrongs. For if you endure present wrongs patiently, you will encourage others to commit future ones. Let people fear you rather than despise you. All will show you reverence if they see that you manfully avenge your injury.” See how deceitful, and how false, this most wicked prophet is. He seemed to have persuaded cunningly when he foretold that reverence would be shown to the furious man; but once he has turned him to rage, he makes him not reverend but abominable to all people. There is another false prophet, an enemy of integrity and self-restraint, who seduces a person in this manner: Often, under the pretext of health or necessity of work, he advises indulgence in more abundant and more delicate foods; but after inflaming the body through gluttony, he immediately sets before the eyes the pleasures of lust. He asserts that it is burdensome and impossible for one who is placed in flesh not to live carnally; that youthful years can easily be forgiven; that long periods still remain for repentance; that God is merciful; and that the torments of hell are either nonexistent or slight. But observe how deceitful this prophet is. He promises many pleasures enduring for a long time, but punishment small and passing quickly; whereas perhaps eternal torments follow, while that which gives pleasure cannot last even for a moment. By a certain more elaborate rationale for acting, he teaches that one should devote oneself to avarice: that such is this life that a person cannot possess honour unless he possesses means; that riches often greatly benefit not only bodies but also the salvation of souls, since the support of the poor and the building of churches proceed from them; finally, that it is better to have the means by which one may seek merit for oneself than, having nothing, to be compelled to ask others and thus become more deeply indebted. But recognize this prophet also as a liar. He declares that the merits of virtues can be increased for those possessing riches, in order to take away from lovers of riches every merit of virtue; first corrupting minds by greed to seek riches, then, after they have been acquired, by avarice to retain them. [Col. 0296A]

There is yet another of the false prophets, who advises service to hypocrisy. He declares that a good reputation is of the greatest value; that a person ought everywhere to preserve an unstained name; that, if there are sins arising from weakness rather than deliberation, they should be concealed for the sake of avoiding scandal to neighbours; that there is a double loss if, while one person is corrupted by the deed, another is corrupted by the example; that therefore a person ought always, for the instruction of others, to display a commendable bearing indicative of virtue; and that one should avoid with the utmost care lest anything unfavourable or contrary to honour should either be said or believed about oneself. He further declares that merit is greatly multiplied if a person both trains himself by the pursuit of virtue and gains others by example. O how subtle a promise! It announces that merit is to be multiplied by hypocrisy so that, after teaching a person both to conceal evils and to display good things, it may overthrow every solid foundation of good merit.

Concerning these prophets of the sinful soul, placed in tribulation, it is said reproachfully: “Your prophets saw for you false and foolish things.” As if it were said: “False was what carnal affections promised; or now, taught by punishment, recognize what you formerly refused to consider while you were being drawn into guilt. They saw false and foolish things for you.” When they persuaded you by a rationale for doing evil, they saw false things; but when they drove you, conquered by desire, even to irrational deeds, they saw not only false but also foolish things. Hence it follows: “Nor did they disclose your iniquity to you.” As if it were said: “They would disclose your iniquity to you if, before the deed, they showed what punishment would afterwards follow. But now, lest you could perceive your iniquity, a simulated rationale blinded, as it were, your right eye, and wicked pleasure your left.” Nor did they deceive merely by promising prosperity, but also by frightening through adversities. For they saw for you false burdens and expulsions: namely, burdens of evils which they said were impending, and expulsions of present goods which they announced would perish, so that, fearing to lose the goods you loved and striving to avoid the evils you feared, you might more quickly consent to commit iniquity.

“All who pass by the way clapped their hands over you; [Col. 0296D] they hissed and shook their heads over the daughter of Jerusalem.” **LITERAL.** As if he said: “Hear—and learn even from the testimony of strangers how much you are to be pitied.” Those passing by the way are understood as travellers and foreigners. For those called passers-by are shown both to come from elsewhere and to be making for another place. Insofar as they come from elsewhere, they are shown to be strangers by blood; insofar as they make for elsewhere, strangers in intention. Yet the shock of this unprecedented calamity fixes in compassion those whom both blood relationship and purpose of intention divide. “They clapped their hands over you,” he says. He aptly says “over you,” as though she had been thrown down and laid low. “They clapped their hands.” Some have thought that all these things refer rather to mockery and derision, because clapping and hissing seem to belong to those who insult. Since, however, the following clause again concerns hissing and mockery, the distinction is thought to be that these persons, like outsiders, despise her as fallen, whereas the others, like enemies and adversaries, show not merely contempt but hatred as well by hissing and exulting. This interpretation does not seem contrary to reason to us. Yet, because according to spiritual understanding these things are more suitably referred to compassion, we may fittingly say that by clapping is expressed not insult but simply the striking together of hands. The striking together of hands does not always signify the same thing; sometimes it indicates joy, sometimes grief, sometimes astonishment, sometimes compassion. Hissing likewise indicates diverse affections: sometimes contempt, sometimes despair, sometimes blandishment. Similarly, the motion of the head sometimes expresses indignation, sometimes mockery, sometimes grief, sometimes astonishment. Since these gestures correspond to diverse affections, we may understand clapping of hands as astonishment, hissing as despair, and motion of the head as compassion; or conversely, clapping as compassion and motion of the head as astonishment. For when passers-by look upon such lamentable ruins, they are stirred by a certain humanity to compassion and grieve at the present misery which they see; they despair of future restoration and wonder at former glory. Out of the grief of compassion they clap their hands; out of despair they hiss with their mouths; out of astonishment they shake their heads. This is what follows:

“Is this the city,” they say, “of perfect beauty, the joy of the whole earth?” As if it were said: “Formerly so glorious, now so miserable.” Yet, as has been said, they must be believed to have spoken this not in mockery but in compassion.

“They clapped,” etc. **ALLEGORICAL.** Let us first consider who these passers-by are, and then what the way is by which they pass. This whole present life seems to be a kind of passage, since from the moment we enter it by being born, we hasten without interruption through daily changes toward death, as is read in the Psalm: “Man—his days are like grass; like a flower of the field, so shall he flourish. For the spirit shall pass through him and he shall not remain; and he shall know his place no more” (Ps. CII). But there is another praiseworthy passage not common to everyone. For all people, as we have said, pass through by necessity of their condition; but evil people, although by their condition they cannot remain here, nevertheless fix their mind by love upon the desire for this life. Thus evil people pass through by necessity, but do not pass through in will. Good people, however, who do not love the present life but desire the future one, add their will to necessity; indeed, to say something truer, they anticipate necessity itself by their will, because they depart from here first in will [Col. 0298A] and only afterwards in death. These are the true Hebrews—that is, “passers-over”—to whom the word of Wisdom is addressed: “Pass over to me, all you who desire me” (Ecclus. XXIV). The apostle Paul also glories that he is among their number when he says: “They are Hebrews, and so am I” (II Cor. XI). In another place he shows how he is a Hebrew—that is, one who passes over: “Forgetting the things behind, I stretch myself always toward those before me” (Phil. III). And again: “I have fought the good fight, I have completed the course, I have kept the faith” (II Tim. IV). Moses also says of this passage: “I will pass over and see this great vision” (Exod. III). Therefore, because some pass through by necessity alone while others add the choice of their will also to the necessity of their condition, he rightly made clear, by a necessary addition, that when he spoke of passers-by he did not mean merely any passers-by, saying: “Those passing by the way.” For in sacred speech “way” sometimes signifies Christ, sometimes the law of God, sometimes the present life. The way signifies Christ, as he himself bears witness, saying: “I am the way” (John XIV). The way signifies the law of God, as is read in the Psalm: “Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the Lord” (Ps. CXVIII). The way signifies the present life, as is said in the Gospel: “Agree with your adversary while you are on the way” (Matt. V). For what is the divine word, except that it becomes our adversary when it opposes our wicked wills? We agree with this adversary on the way if, in this mortal life, where there is still opportunity for merit, we strive to obey the commandments of God even against our carnal wills. But in this passage the way cannot signify the present life, because, since every person travels through it by necessity of condition, the prophet would make no distinction if, while speaking of passers-by, he meant the present life by “way.” Therefore the way is Christ. And perhaps it was not without reason that, whereas the Psalmist in one place called certain persons those who “pass through” or “go beyond” the way, here he says not “those passing through the way” but “those passing through by the way.” For those pass through the way who transgress the law of God and either abandon the faith of Christ after receiving it or disdain to receive it when it is offered through the word of preaching. He therefore wished to distinguish from them those whom he calls not “those passing through the way” but “those passing through by the way.” Notice also that he did not say, [Col. 0298D] “those standing in the way,” but “those passing by the way.” For those stand in the way who keep faith idly without good works. They are indeed in the way through right faith, but do not walk by good works. But those pass by the way who, in right faith, always tend from good to better through daily progress in virtues. Therefore let it be said: “All who pass by the way clapped their hands over you.” But what is meant when the Church is told concerning her weakening members, “All who pass by the way clapped their hands over you,” except that dangers threatening neighbours move to compassion all the elect whom the pleasures of this world cannot hinder from the course of good works or from the desire for eternal things? This was beautifully signified in the Book of Kings by those two cows which bore on a new cart the ark of the Lord as it returned from the Philistines; concerning them it is written: “Taking two cows that were nursing calves, they yoked them to the cart and shut up their calves at home” (I Kings VI). And shortly afterwards: “The cows went straight by the way that leads to Beth-shemesh, going and lowing; and they did not turn aside either to the right or to the left” (ibid.). For what do the cows signify except the faithful in the Church? What the ark except the law of God? And what Beth-shemesh, which is interpreted “house of the sun,” except the heavenly homeland? Therefore the cows, as though carrying the ark laid upon them, go forward and low along the straight road to Beth-shemesh when the faithful, continually bearing in their heart meditation upon the divine law, tend by the way of good works toward the heavenly homeland and utter groans of compassion for those whom carnal affection still binds in this world. They neither turn aside from the straight path because of compassion nor cease their lowing of compassion because of their purpose in travelling. The prophet indicates the same thing in this passage, saying:

They all who pass by the way clapped their hands over you. For they clap and at the same time pass on, because they show the affection of their compassion toward the afflicted in such a way that they neither fail nor turn aside from the purpose of the straight path. The manner of this compassion is rightly added when it is said: “They clapped their hands, they hissed, they shook their head.” In sacred speech, the hands often signify action, the mouth speech, and the head the mind [Col. 0299C]. If, therefore, we say that works are signified by the hands, what should we understand by the clapping of hands except the report and reputation of good works? For the report and reputation of good works sounds in the ears of the people like a kind of clapping of hands; and often, when it has suddenly resounded, it turns everyone’s eyes toward its author, from whom it arose.

Hence it is that all the perverse, in those things which they seem to do rightly, always desire to become known: namely, so that, when they have brought their good deeds into public view, they may turn the untaught minds of the people to admiration of themselves. But the elect, in their good actions, shrink from being made known all the more as they fear more greatly that the reward of eternal recompense may be diminished for them through admiration and earthly praise. If at times they set their virtues and brave deeds before their neighbors as an example, they do this not from a desire for glory but from the love of providing help.

Thus here also, under the figure of a desolated city, it is rightly said to the multitude of sinners: “All who pass by the way clapped their hands over you.” For the elect, who pass by the way of God’s commandments from the exile of this world to the heavenly homeland, often, when they see their neighbors growing weak, set their virtues before them as an example out of charitable concern, in order to stir their minds. But those who pass by a wandering path do not mourn over those lying fallen, because they display their virtues not for their neighbors’ benefit but in order to enlarge their own glory. It follows: “They hissed,” [Col. 0300A] etc.

To form a hiss, the lips are usually drawn in from without, and the tongue is, as it were, laid beneath within, curved in the likeness of a channel, so that when breath emerges, directed and thinned through a narrow passage, it may reach the ear more softly and pleasantly, soothing it. What, then, can more fittingly be understood by the hissing of the mouth than a word of consolation? To hiss, as it were, with lips drawn together and the tongue placed beneath, is to bend every effort of speech, with softened and moderated words, to the service of consolation. Therefore those who pass by the way clap their hands over the desolate and hiss with their mouths when all spiritual persons both stir sinners to do good by examples of virtues and strengthen them in the hope of pardon by a word of consolation.

It follows: “They shook their head.” By the head we may fittingly understand the mind; by the movement of the head, compassion of mind [Col. 0300B]. Those who pass by therefore rightly shake their heads also after clapping and hissing, because they certainly cannot effectively console others’ sufferings if they have not learned truly to suffer with others’ sufferings.

See whether Paul lacked any of these things. Paul clapped with his hands when he said: “Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ” (1 Cor. 11). He hissed with his mouth when, consoling the Corinthians after repentance, he said: “I wrote to you not that you should be grieved, but that you might know the abundant love which I have for you” (2 Cor. 2). He shook his head when he said: “My little children, whom I am again bringing to birth until Christ is formed in you” (Gal. 4).

It follows in the literal sense: “Over the daughter of Jerusalem.” What does Jerusalem, interpreted “vision of peace,” signify except the heavenly homeland? It is as though sinners were told: “You cause all the elect grief over your destruction all the more grievous because it is now more certain that you ought to have belonged to the fellowship and society of the elect.” And just as your salvation would bring joy to all, so grief and sorrow of all likewise proceed from your ruin. This is what follows: “Is this the city, they say, of perfect beauty, the joy of all the earth?” The city in this place is to be understood as the catholic Church, in which the gates and walls are those who both form others by the teaching of truth and surround them with watchful care. This Church has perfect beauty when virtue adorns wisdom in its prelates, and obedience adorns the discipline of good works in those subject to them [Col. 0300C].

The beauty of this city is therefore rightly called the joy of the whole earth because its discipline has now spread through all parts of the world. Let it then be said: “Is this the city of perfect beauty, the joy of all the earth?” As if it were said: “How could that which formerly gladdened all the elect throughout the world by its beauty so quickly come into desolation?” But why, in the ruin of certain persons, is the whole Church mourned as though desolate, except because “if one member suffers, all the members suffer with it”? Therefore those who, in their own wickedness, grieve the charity of others ought greatly to fear; for surely, as the latter increase their merit by suffering with evils, so the former aggravate their guilt by grieving the good.

[Col. 0301A] “They clapped,” etc. MORAL.

One who calls a sinner to repentance by gentle exhortation does what else than feel an invalid’s wounds before cutting them? Therefore, just as a wound that cannot endure even a gentle touch of remedies is judged altogether incurable, so a sinner who rejects even mild admonition is regarded as incorrigible. This is what the prophet here reproaches the sinful soul with deep grief, saying: “They clapped over you,” etc. As though he said: “Formerly the prompting of the flesh could readily prevail upon you to persuade you into wickedness; but now every care and effort of the good has failed in correcting you. And although formerly, through contempt, you were rash in committing wickedness, now in that same wickedness you are hardened through despair: ‘All who pass by the way clapped their hands over you.’”

To show her ruin to be all the more grievous, he recalls that she had already entered upon the way of good work and had collapsed, as it were, in the middle of the journey. Therefore he calls the others “those who pass by,” in order openly to show that those who now begin deservedly to go before her through virtue were once behind her. But because charity always moves the elect to compassion at the ruin of their neighbors, they are rightly described as both passing on and clapping together: passing on by making progress, clapping by showing compassion, so that they may rejoice in their own progress without presuming to despise their fallen and weak neighbors.

“They clapped,” he says, “with their hands.” The clapping of hands signifies the example of a good work; hissing, a word of consolation; the movement of the head, the affection of compassion [Col. 0301C]. For spiritual persons, seeing people fallen through wickedness, both stir them by example, strengthen them by word, and demonstrate by the very pain of their compassion how greatly they would rejoice in their salvation.

It follows: “Is this, they say, the city of perfect beauty?” They recall what it ought to have been so that, from the memory of its former dignity, it may more readily recognize into what misery it has fallen. They call it a city, as though lofty and fortified with virtues, which formerly had God reigning in it, when it had not yet been subjected by consent to the dominion of vices.

It follows: “The joy of all the earth.” As though it were said: “The more people who ought to have rejoiced in its progress, the more are now grieved by its ruin and desolation, so that, if it is unwilling to spare itself, it may at least be ashamed to afflict others by its destruction” [Col. 0301D]. By all these means the hardened conscience is confronted, so that, with so manifold a remedy applied, it may finally be softened to repentance.

“All your enemies opened their mouth over you,” etc. LITERAL.

As if he said: “If it does not move you that you were deceived by false prophets, that, having fallen into calamity, you were made a sign and wonder to passersby, let this at least pierce your insensibility: that you have been made prey and trampling-ground, joy and mockery, to your enemies. ‘All your enemies opened their mouth over you.’” The opening of their mouth signifies cruelty and mockery [Col. 0302A]. The greedy open their mouths to devour; the proud open their mouths to mock.

“They hissed; they gnashed their teeth.” Hissing expresses contempt; gnashing, anger and indignation. “All your enemies”: the Chaldeans, the Romans. The pressure is grievous where all press upon you and all prevail.

It follows:

“And they said: ‘We will devour.’” They do not desire merely to harm a little, but to blot out completely; nor merely to blot out, but to devour, for they feed and delight themselves upon your ruin. Hence follows:

“Behold, this is the day for which we waited with longing; we found it by seeking; we saw it with exultation.” Thus, the greater the joy of those afflicting you, the more bitter and unbearable is your misery.

[Col. 0302B] “They opened,” etc. ALLEGORICAL.

The enemies of the holy Church are heretics, because they assail the steadfastness of its faith with corrupt doctrines. But they do not dare to open their mouth against it so long as they observe both wisdom and discipline flourishing in its conduct. They close their mouths before wisdom because, from those whom they see steadfast in the knowledge of truth, they conceal the teachings of their error. Likewise they close their mouths before discipline when they find nothing in the conduct of the faithful which they can blaspheme.

But if wisdom should perhaps lose discipline, they open their mouths against it in order to blaspheme; or if discipline should lack wisdom, they open their mouths against it in order to disseminate errors. But if it has neither wisdom nor discipline, they now open their mouths not merely against it but over it, in order to devour it and, as though incorporating them into themselves, to consume every remnant of truth in those whom they are able to draw into their fellowship.

It follows: “They hissed.” In the hissing we may observe the crafty and flattering persuasions by which they deceive the unwary and, like serpents, after a gentle hiss infuse the poison of death. But because the blandishments of heretics proceed not from piety but from cruelty, it is rightly added: “They gnashed their teeth.” As though it were said: “What their speech hissed was gentle, but what their intention gnashed was exceedingly cruel.”

It follows: “Behold, this is the day for which we waited, found, and saw.” They call the oppression of the good not night but day because by their unjust joy they themselves are made bright from that by which the darkness of unbelief blinds others [Col. 0302D]. “We waited,” they say, that is, with desire; “we found,” by seeking; “we saw,” with exultation. Note that what is hidden is found, whereas what is seen is open. It is as though they said: “What formerly we desired to find in secret, we now see openly.”

“They opened their mouth over you,” etc. MORAL.

Demons open their mouths against a soul when they assail, with voices of suggestion, one raised up in good desires. But they open their mouths over it when, finding it lying in wicked pleasure, they no longer urge wickedness but command it. Or they open their mouths over it when, having first drawn it to sin by flattery, they afterward cruelly demand it for punishment. Hence it is added: “They hissed; they gnashed their teeth” [Col. 0303A]. For first they hiss, and then they gnash their teeth, because, as we have said, after a flattering suggestion they cruelly demand punishment.

The punishment in question is further indicated when it is said: “And they said: ‘We will devour.’” For what else is it to devour than to swallow up into eternal condemnation one departing from the body? Yet it must be known that they can never succeed in devouring a soul departing from the body unless they have first cooked it, while it was in the body, with the fire of vices. And therefore great confidence concerning a person’s future condemnation arises in them when they rule that person through wickedness in the present life.

After saying, therefore, “They opened their mouth; they hissed,” he rightly immediately adds: “They gnashed their teeth; they said: ‘We will devour,’” because, from the moment a person is subjected through consent to sin to their suggestion [Col. 0303B], they immediately arm themselves with the fury of their coming cruelty. And because they see food already softened by long cooking, they promise themselves its near devouring. In the very name “devouring” both the vehemence of their desire is displayed and the bitterness of damnation expressed.

It follows: “Behold, this is the day for which we waited, found, and saw.” Those who say that they have found something indicate that they had sought it before finding it. Demons therefore first seek when they strive, through suggestion, to test the hidden intention of our heart. Then they wait, because, although they sometimes receive permission to tempt, they can nevertheless never compel the tempted person by force to consent. After their inquiry and waiting, they find when, after the suggestion has been introduced, they at last see manifest signs of voluntary consent emerging from the heart. Finally they see when consent to wickedness proceeds as far as the effect of action [Col. 0303C].

“The Lord has done what he planned; he has fulfilled his word,” etc. LITERAL.

Thereafter, after reproof, he adds consolation, saying: “The Lord has done what he planned,” etc. First he consoles the mourners through the justice of the Judge; then through the malice of the enemy. Through the justice of the Judge, lest they grieve over the past; through the malice of the enemy, lest they despair concerning the future. For it is great consolation to the afflicted that the punishment was inflicted by one in whom injustice cannot please. Likewise, it gives great confidence for obtaining mercy that the one opposed to us is known not to please our Judge either.

He says, therefore: “The Lord has done what he planned.” As though he said: “Our enemies exult and ascribe our ruin to their own strength; but we ought to bear their insults all the more lightly because we know more truly that our evils proceed not from their strength but from God’s just judgment. The Lord has done what he planned.” What is said to have been done with forethought is shown to have been ordered, especially since it had been predicted long beforehand, so that those who could have foreseen the danger and refused to avoid it might have no occasion for murmuring against God.

Hence follows:

“He fulfilled his word, which he had commanded from ancient days” [Col. 0304A]. He had commanded his prophets to proclaim this word, and had done so not recently but from ancient days—that is, long before it happened—so that they might repent at least after a long period of waiting. But the longer they were awaited in mercy, the more justly ought those persisting in evil to have been severely punished.

Hence follows:

“He destroyed, and did not spare.” These words properly refer to the final captivity.

“And he made your enemy rejoice over you.” The greater the joy of the oppressor, the more grievous is the misery of the oppressed. Yet the arrogance of the enemy is easily despised if his power is attributed not to himself but to God. Notice what I said: “He made your enemy rejoice over you.” For the enemy rejoices against us, but not over us, when he is permitted indeed to harm but not to overwhelm; but he rejoices over us when he not only afflicts but also overwhelms [Col. 0304B].

It follows:

“He exalted the horn of your enemies.” In the horn, strength and power are signified; by the enemies, the Chaldeans or Romans are understood.

“The Lord has done what he planned,” etc. ALLEGORICAL.

The Lord does what he planned through heretics because, while they draw some persons from the Church into their errors, others become more approved in faith and in the knowledge of truth. Hence follows: “He fulfilled his word, which he had commanded from ancient days.” For the word of God commanded from ancient days is understood as Holy Scripture, which was published to the world long ago but still remains, in great part, hidden [Col. 0304C]. It is fulfilled daily in the minds of the faithful when, tested by the questions of heretics, they grow into greater zeal for virtues and advance to a deeper understanding of the divine utterances.

Thus indeed the wicked serve the divine will even when they strive to oppose it, because through them he fulfills his purpose: he permits the reprobate to be ensnared by their errors and exercises the good. It follows: “He destroyed, and did not spare.” This happens when he permits some to be cut off from the unity of the Church through unbelief; he does not spare, because he afflicts even those who remain with the sorrows of compassion for their brothers’ ruin.

It follows: “He made your enemy rejoice over you.” The singular enemy of the Church is the devil, who persecutes the faithful with perpetual hatred, as we read in the Apocalypse concerning the dragon who pursues the woman (Rev. 12). This enemy rejoices over the holy Church when he receives from it persons through whom he afflicts it.

It follows: “He exalted the horn of your enemies.” The enemies of the Church are heretics, who daily bring forth their battle line to assault it. Their horn is said to be exalted when many abandon the faith and pass into their fellowship, so that the people of the faithful are found fewer in number [Col. 0304D].

“The Lord has done,” etc. MORAL.

It is a great mercy of God when the things a sinner perversely loves are turned to bitterness, because by this very means the sinner is compelled to return to the love of God: those things whose desire had drawn the sinner away from God’s love are seen to oppose the sinner. Hence the first consolation offered here to the sinful soul afflicted in its wickedness is that its affliction has been administered by God’s direction, so that it may fear him whose scourges it endures and at the same time trust in his mercy, since it sees itself visited even through tribulation.

“The Lord has done what he planned.” As though it were said: “Because you were unwilling to do what he commanded, he has done what he planned. And because you despised fulfilling his word, which he commanded you concerning your salvation, he has fulfilled his word, which he had threatened you concerning your tribulation.” Observe what happened in the first human being. The Lord commanded him: “Do not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil”; he threatened: “On whatever day you eat of it, you shall die.” Man refused to fulfill the command, and God fulfilled the threat.

Even now God says daily to those who long for what is unlawful and forbidden: “Do not touch; do not taste; on whatever day you eat of it, you shall die.” “I have determined; I have commanded, that every unlawful desire should be followed by its own punishment. My threat may be avoided, but my command cannot be made void. From ancient days I have commanded this; from ancient days I have shown it to be true. For this reason the first human being died; for this reason the world was destroyed by the waters of the flood. Nor can the sentence be changed in your case, for it has remained unchangeable from the beginning of the world to this time” [Col. 0305B].

Affliction is therefore rightly said to have “fulfilled the word which he had commanded from ancient days,” so that the sufferer may bear God’s justice in tribulation more patiently, seeing that from the beginning of the world it has been exercised upon sinners.

It follows: “He destroyed, and did not spare.” What is it to destroy except to scatter the things that a person had prepared for unlawful pleasure? He destroys and does not spare when he removes pleasure and at the same time punishes guilt by the tribulation that follows.

It follows: “He made your enemy rejoice over you.” Our singular enemy is the devil, who rejoices against us when power is granted to him over things outwardly attached to us. But when he is permitted to rage even against ourselves, then he rejoices over us. As we read happened to blessed Job: he first destroyed his possessions and afterward struck his flesh [Col. 0305D]. Or the enemy is said to rejoice over us when he rules us through consent to wickedness.

It follows: “He exalted the horn of your enemies.” What is more fittingly understood by the enemies of the soul than desires of the flesh, which assail it with continual temptations? We make these enemies, as it were, tributaries to us when we moderate the movement of the flesh at reason’s command. But when sinful desire begins to rule within us, and the mind follows not reason’s judgment but the appetite of the flesh, then the horn—that is, the strength—of our enemies is exalted.

God is said to do these things because, in his just judgment, he permits them to happen, so that, when the adversary is recognized to have been able to do nothing in our guilt except what was permitted, he may not be feared in punishment either [Col. 0306A]. And the more humbly should the human mind submit itself to the scourges of God’s justice, because it has learned more surely by experience that God had formerly endured its sin for a long time through patience. For in an afflicted mind the burden of tribulation is greatly lightened if it does not contradict the Judge’s equity even in its punishment.

“Their heart cried to the Lord,” etc. LITERAL.

After the justice of the Judge, he also consoles the afflicted through the malice of the enemy, because what God justly permits, the enemy wickedly carries out. For while God avenges through him his own injury against sinners, the enemy, by his wicked intention, injures God. As it is said in Isaiah: “Woe to Assyria, the rod of my fury; my indignation is in their hand” (Isa. 10); “but he does not think so.” Therefore it is rightly said here: “Their heart cried to the Lord over the wall of the daughter of Zion” [Col. 0306B].

In the cry of the heart we may understand either the cruelty or the pride of the enemies: cruelty toward those whom they oppressed; pride toward God, whom, in oppressing his people, they blasphemed and believed powerless to save. But their thought cries to God because it in a manner provokes him both to have mercy on his own people and to punish their adversaries. “It cried,” he says, “over the wall.” They were proud because they had prevailed, because they possessed the walls and fortifications of cities.

Or we may understand the wall as divine protection, over which the enemies cry because, when they are permitted to rule the people of God on account of its sins, they disparage divine power and suppose that what they do not know is happening by God’s permission and ordering cannot be prevented by him.

“It cried,” etc. ALLEGORICAL.

The wall of the daughter of Zion can signify every defender of truth, through whom the heart of the enemies cries to the Lord; for heretics then despise the author of truth more through the pride of their hearts when they convert to their errors not only simple persons in the Church but even the defenders of truth themselves [Col. 0306C].

“Their heart cried,” etc. MORAL.

If by the enemies of the soul we understand desires of the flesh, what should we understand by the heart of the enemies except the inward delight of carnal desires? And again, by the wall of the daughter of Zion, we understand the virtues. For then the delight of the flesh becomes injurious to the Creator, when evil desires rule the virtues through consent of the mind.

For it is said of God: “His place was made in peace” (Ps. 75), because God indeed rests sweetly in that mind which, gathering itself from the distractions of this world, disposes itself toward inward peace. Even if earthly desires make a clamour outside in that mind, insofar as the corruption of this life is concerned, yet if they are not admitted inwardly to consent, they do not reach as far as God’s ears.

But when delight of the flesh penetrates through consent as far as the soul’s inward places, then indeed the heart of the enemies cries to God, who sits within, so that he, stirred by the intrusive noise, rises from his repose there and says: “The cry of the Sodomites and Gomorrhites has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grave; but I will go down and see whether they have completed in deed the cry that has come to me” (Gen. 18) [Col. 0307A].

And rightly so: because wickedness is far from God, depraved desires are said to have cried not before God but to God. Praise and thanksgiving cry not only to God but also before God. Necessity and wickedness cry to God. When we praise God’s power and magnificence, or when we give him thanks for mercy bestowed upon us, then we cry before God. But when, acting wickedly, we provoke him to anger, or when placed in necessity we seek his help, then we cry to him as though from afar.

Thus wickedness cries to God; necessity cries: the former cries while provoking, the latter while supplicating; the former stirs wrath, the latter asks mercy. Of the cry of necessity it is said: “The cry of the children of Israel has come to me, and I have seen their affliction, by which they are oppressed by the Egyptians” (Exod. 3). Of the cry of wickedness it is said: “The cry of Sodom and Gomorrah has multiplied, and their sin has become exceedingly grave.” Of the cry of praise it is said: “They shall cry out; indeed, they shall sing a hymn” (Ps. 64). Of the cry of devotion it is said: “My cry entered before him into his ears” (Ps. 17).

The angels cry in heaven with the cry of praise; Moses cries in the wilderness with the cry of devotion; the children of Israel cry in Egypt with the cry of necessity; Sodom and Gomorrah cry with the cry of wickedness. But the cry of wickedness is said to reach God when malice has grown so great that it no longer deserves to be tolerated [Col. 0307C].

“Cause tears to flow like a torrent by day and night.” LITERAL.

After their minds have been raised by consolation, exhortation follows, in which sinners are invited to repentance. Nor was it without reason that, as though abruptly, he suddenly takes up another subject in the middle of the clause.
