But because, in the course of his discourse itself, an occasion for exhortation presented itself—and what is added as though inferred from what preceded usually moves minds more strongly—he says: “Cause tears to flow like a torrent.” It is as though he said: “Because your enemies provoke God to anger through pride, you, through the humility of repentance, implore his mercy.”

By the torrent, moreover, is signified the vehement movement of compunction. Its perseverance is further indicated when it is said: “By day and night.” Its urgency also is added when it follows: “Give yourself no rest.” As though it were said: “Do not interrupt or slacken the rush of your tears, but at every time and with every earnestness persist in weeping; for tears themselves also have their voice, and they will cry for you to the Lord.” This is what follows:

“Let not the pupil of your eye be silent.” This is a word of mercy. “Let the storm of tears,” he says, “darken not only the rim of the eyes but the very ray of sight itself, so that, when even what is tender is afflicted, the Judge’s compassion may be moved more quickly to mercy” [Col. 0307D].

[Col. 0308A] “Cause tears to flow like a torrent.” ALLEGORICAL.

The prophetic discourse exhorts the holy Church to offer tears to the Lord for its members who are growing weak. It compares these tears to a torrent. For a torrent is a stream collected from winter waters: it runs indeed with force, but soon dries up and passes away. What is the present life but winter, in which, before the brightness of eternal life appears, the clouds of error still envelop human hearts?

The holy Church is therefore rightly commanded to cause tears to flow like a torrent, because all the elect who long for the joys of the heavenly homeland sigh without ceasing over the misery of the present life. But this torrent of tears will undoubtedly be dried up by the heat of the coming summer when, as eternal brightness dawns, every sorrow is turned into joy, so that there can no longer be either any sorrow over those lost or any fear concerning those who may perish.

It follows: “By day and night.” By day prosperity and by night adversity are signified. Therefore, because the holy Church sees some deceived by the prosperities of this life and others crushed by adversities, it causes tears to flow, as it were, by day and night, mourning the ruin of both.

It follows: “Give yourself no rest.” When the elect mourn others, they give no rest to themselves either, because when they see the falls of others, they become more anxious for their own salvation. It follows: “Let not the pupil of your eye be silent.” The pupil of the eye, through which sight is directed, fittingly signifies all spiritual persons in the holy Church, through whose word and example the whole body of the Church is illumined [Col. 0308C]. They certainly ought not to be silent in the danger of their neighbors, but, as far as they can, to raise them both by prayers and by preaching. For because they can see their danger better than those persons themselves, they truly sin if they are not even more concerned than the latter for their salvation.

That one singular pupil through whom all are enlightened—that is, the Lord Jesus Christ—showed this well: foreseeing the ruin of the faithless city, he wept while it rejoiced; and when undergoing his passion, while praying even for his persecutors, he was concerned for their salvation. Therefore the pupil ought not to keep silent tears, because spiritual persons also ought, with an affection of compassion, to offer the word of preaching.

[Col. 0308D] “Cause tears to flow like a torrent.” MORAL.

Here a perfect form of repentance is set forth. True repentance begins from compunction, which through the water of tears washes away the stains of sins and, by watering the soul, makes it fruitful for the shoots of virtues. Hence the sinful soul is told first to cause tears to flow—that is, to lead them downward. For we lead streams of tears upward, as it were, when we sigh in longing for the heavenly homeland. But when, pierced by the remembrance of sins, we weep, we lead the streams of our tears down to lower things. Yet each person must first wash away the stains of sins in the fountain of tears and then, with conscience cleansed, direct the course of compunction toward the love of eternal things.

Moreover, in the command that the sinner lead tears downward, it is shown that humility together with compunction is necessary for the penitent, according to the saying of the Psalmist: “A contrite and humbled heart, O God, you will not despise” (Ps. 1 [as cited]).

We may observe something still more subtle in the word “leading.” What is led moves indeed by itself, yet its movement is directed by another’s judgment. There are some who, when they see others weeping, are ashamed to have dry eyes; and, forcing tears out by a kind of violence, deceive human eyes with feigned compunction. Of these we more rightly say that they extract tears than that they lead them forth. There are others who, through the impatience of their hearts and on account of an external trouble that has befallen them, shed tears; yet they by no means bring forth these tears themselves, because reason does not precede them as they flow spontaneously from an emotional movement of the heart [Col. 0309B].

But those who truly repent bring forth tears, because, though they arise of themselves from the very fountain of compunction, they direct them with reason preceding: so that they may neither burst forth through impatience nor spread themselves too freely from the secrecy of their channel into the field of human praise.

How tears are to be brought forth is beautifully suggested when it is said: “Cause tears to flow like a torrent.” A torrent runs down with great force; but the more violently it flows, the more quickly it passes away. The fervor of compunction is therefore rightly compared to a torrent, because the greater the force of sorrow in compunction, the more quickly it passes away when divine consolation intervenes.

But because beginning well profits little unless one perseveringly holds to it, he rightly adds: “By day and night.” There are some who, after tears, dissolve their minds in empty joy; and because they neglect to keep their heart perseveringly in sorrow, they lose whatever they could have obtained in the time of compunction. For the sinful conscience, just as it is often afflicted before the ardor of compunction with the grievous weariness of sorrow in remembrance of sins, is likewise sometimes dissipated after the consolation of tears by foolish joy, unless diligent restraint presses upon it [Col. 0309C].

Therefore it is most necessary that, after the grace of compunction has raised the mind from sorrow, the guard of its former sorrow should never abandon it, lest thereafter its own ease dissolve it through immoderate joy. Thus the sinner is rightly instructed to cause tears to flow by day and night. For the weariness of sorrow is like a certain night of the mind, while the day of the mind is the joy of compunction. Therefore one causes tears to flow, as it were, by night when one raises the spirit in the weariness of sorrow through compunction; one causes tears to flow by day when, after the joy of compunction, one keeps the mind in sorrow.

Let it therefore be said to the penitent: “Cause tears to flow like a torrent by day and night.” As though it were said: “You who consider that you have sinned greatly must spare yourself neither in the magnitude nor in the duration of sorrow.” But because many do not abandon the undertaking of repentance once begun, yet gradually grow lukewarm over time from the fervor with which they began, he adds, saying: “Give yourself no rest” [Col. 0310A], because devotion of humility also renders praiseworthy before God the urgency of labor.

Finally he adds and says: “Let not the pupil of your eye be silent.” What should we understand by the pupil of the eye except the humble devotion of the mind? Therefore, when no rest is given, the pupil of the eye also cries out: if, while the flesh is afflicted outwardly, the devotion of the mind prays within.

Arise, praise in the night, at the beginning of the watches.

**LITERAL.** In the literal sense, there are three watches of the night, each distinguished by a span of three hours. With a truly remarkable dispensation, the prophet, inviting sinners to repentance, does not immediately set before them the perfection of penitence itself, but advances his exhortation gradually, so that what a weak mind perhaps could not grasp all at once might more easily bear it when divided. [Col. 0310B] Above he had commanded sinners to pour out tears in repentance for their sins; here he now commands them, even in their tribulation, to praise God’s justice. There he commanded them to weep in the night; here he commands them even to rise for weeping at the beginning of the watches. Thus, to rise for weeping is more than merely to weep; and to do so at the beginning of the watches is more than merely to do so in the night. It follows:

**Pour out your heart like water.** He pours out his heart like water who brings forth tears from the deepest affection of his heart. Making this still clearer, he adds:

**Lift up your hands to him.** For the lifting up of the hands expresses the heart’s affection. Or certainly, those who raise their hands show that they are in need and desire help. Therefore the people, placed in tribulation, rightly lift their hands to him, showing that they place their hope not in their own strength but in God’s help alone. [Col. 0310C] It follows:

**For the soul—that is, for the life—of your little ones, who perish from hunger at the head of every street.** The heads of streets are places where several roads coming from different directions meet in one place. Such places are usually more frequented by people, so that the greater crowd of those wasting away there may be suggested. Observe how the matter is put in a narrow compass: it concerns obtaining life, when parents are commanded to pray for the souls of their little ones. Parents are commanded to pray for the souls of their little ones; parents ought to supplicate for their children, [Col. 0310D] because little ones bear punishment for the fault of their parents, so that the remedy may come from the source from which the danger came.

**Arise, praise in the night, etc. ALLEGORICAL.** What is signified by the night except the life of sinners? Such formerly were those to whom Paul speaks, saying: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5). Therefore the prophetic utterance admonishes holy Church to arise and praise in the night. She arises when, for the salvation of her neighbors whom she sees in danger, she raises herself from the repose of contemplation to the work of preaching. She praises in the night when, urging sinners to repentance, she discloses to them the mighty works of God. But there are many sinners who even despise to hear the word of truth; and they are the less inclined to bend the ear of their heart to the Creator’s praise in proportion as they are less awake to consider their sins. [Col. 0311A] Of them it is read in the Psalm: “In the willows in its midst we hung up our instruments” (Ps. 136). And in the Gospel: “Do not cast your pearls before swine” (Matt. 7). Therefore, when he had said, “Praise in the night,” he rightly added, “at the beginning of the watches.” As though he said: Those sinners can hear the praise of God who have begun to watch in considering their sins. It follows:

**Pour out your heart like water.** What is meant by the heart except profound understanding? And what by water except easily received teaching? Therefore he pours out his heart like water who communicates outwardly, through accessible instruction, to weak hearers what he tastes inwardly as solid food. As the Psalmist says: “Day pours forth speech to day, and night declares knowledge to night” (Ps. 18). [Col. 0311B] Whoever freely condescends to weak hearers for the love of God undoubtedly pours out his heart like water before the Lord. It follows:

**Lift up your hands to him for the soul of your little ones.** By the lifting up of hands we may understand the heart’s affection; by little ones, those weak in faith and not yet possessing mature understanding. Therefore holy Church lifts her hands to God for the soul of her little ones, because for the salvation of those still small in faith she not only devotes herself to the word of preaching, but also continually entreats divine mercy in humble devotion. Or by hands we may understand works, because he indeed lifts his hands to God for the soul of little ones who, while striving by spiritual pursuits to stir the minds of the carnal, also avoids certain lawful occupations of human life. [Col. 0311C] So did Paul, who, in order to remove from false apostles an occasion for receiving support, utterly refused to accept the maintenance due to preaching according to custom—indeed, according to divine institution—and sought his livelihood by his own hands. Concerning these little ones he further adds:

**Who fainted from hunger at the head of every street.** What are the streets except human actions? And what is the head of the streets except the concupiscence of the flesh, which is the cause and origin of all human actions? Therefore little ones faint from hunger at the head of the streets because all who are carnal, the more eagerly they thirst after earthly desires, the more they fast from the food of spiritual nourishment. [Col. 0311D]

**Arise, praise. MORAL.** Here a certain new life seems to me to arise. “Arise, praise.” What a beautiful order: first to wipe away past evils with tears; then to rise to perform good works; then to praise. For “praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15); nor can he truly do good who has not first earnestly sought effectively to amend his past evils. “Praise,” he says, “in the night, at the beginning of the watches.” A sinner under the lash offers God an acceptable sacrifice if he praises God even in his tribulation. Thus, after the prophet rightly said, “Praise in the night,” that is, in tribulation, he immediately added: “At the beginning of the watches.” For a sinner first awakens when he begins to recognize his evils. [Col. 0312A] He awakens a second time when, having recognized his evils, he corrects them through repentance. He awakens a third time when he turns himself to the doing of good. He awakens a fourth time when he preserves his good works. We must keep these four watches in the night of this present life, lest ignorance deceive us in considering our sins; lest negligence or contempt hinder us in correcting them; lest sloth make us sluggish in doing good; or presumption make us less cautious in preserving good. Therefore he praises God in the night, at the beginning of the watches, who confesses that he endures the evils he suffers by the just judgment of God because of his own iniquity. It follows:

**Pour out your heart like water before the face of the Lord.** Other liquids, when poured out, leave vessels either coated with a certain greasiness or tainted by their flavor; water alone is poured out in such a way that the cleanliness of the vessel is not stained by any residue. [Col. 0312B] Therefore those who, confessing their sins, fear to pour them out for some reason of negligence or shame retain, as it were, the remnants of thick liquid in the vessel of their heart. But those who cast out all their sins by confession yet still do not abandon the affection for sinning: although the harmful liquid has indeed been wholly cast out from them, their vessels nevertheless remain tainted by its flavor. But whoever, by pure confession and contrition of heart, reveals his secrets, retaining nothing through affection and concealing nothing through silence, pours out his heart like water before the face of the Lord.

We may still perceive something edifying in the pouring out of water: just as spilled water washes away filth, so confession, casting out sins, makes the conscience clean. [Col. 0312C] And the heart is rightly said to be poured out like water before the face of the Lord, because unless a person excludes from his heart not only wicked action but also the desire to sin, he is not fully acquitted before God, conscience bearing witness. It follows:

**Lift up your hands to him.** By hands, work is signified. Therefore the penitent lifts his hands to God when, by the performance of good works, he makes satisfaction before God for past offences. Concerning this he further adds:

**For the soul of your little ones, who fainted from hunger at the head of every street.** By little ones we rightly understand the weak thoughts of the soul; by the head of all streets, the concupiscence of the flesh, which is, as it were, the head and origin of all earthly desires and actions, like many roads. [Col. 0312D] Therefore our little ones faint from hunger at the head of the streets, because our tender thoughts, while clinging to carnal desires, lose the food of spiritual nourishment. But we lift our hands to God for the soul of our little ones when, by zeal for good works, we ask that the grace of spiritual desire may be renewed within us so as to nourish the thoughts of the soul. These our little ones faint from hunger at the head of the streets because the tender thoughts of the mind, which good desires do not nourish inwardly, are soon softened by the concupiscence of the flesh—which is the head of all evil desires—and lose all the strength of virtue. [Col. 0313A] Or concupiscence itself is hunger: in this hunger they faint, because they always hunger and cannot be filled.

**See, Lord, and consider whom you have thus harvested. LITERAL.** He does not abandon his purpose until he brings what he has begun to its end. For up to this point he dealt with sinners in order to bend them toward repentance; now, taking up the cause of the penitent, he turns his speech to God in order to pray to him for sinners. At the same time, he supplies the penitent with a form of prayer, openly showing how greatly the sinner ought to humble himself in prayer, when he himself, praying for the sins of others, prostrates himself before divine mercy with such humble devotion. Since he sees that he has undertaken a difficult cause, he does not presume to knock upon the ears of divine majesty by open petition; [Col. 0313B] but with great reverence and trembling he indicates the feeling of his petition, saying: “See, Lord, and consider whom you have thus harvested.” As though he said: Do you thus harvest, thus oppress, thus devastate your people, whom you loved so greatly and who had no protector other than you alone? Consider, I beg, the present calamity; call former love to mind, so that, if you are not moved by our prayers, you may at least be moved to compassion and mercy by your own benefits. “You have harvested,” he says. Therefore this people was not a wild wood but a vineyard, having a cultivator and bearing fruit. Yet the vine, without cultivation and fruit, is useless and more worthless than all other trees. Why then do you lay waste the one whom, by cultivating, you make precious, but by laying waste make worthless and useless? [Col. 0313C] “Whom you have thus harvested,” he says. In what manner “thus”? So horribly, so monstrously, that the vineyard itself devours its grapes and women eat their own children. Therefore he cries out and says:

**Will women then eat their own fruit?** That is, their children: little ones of the measure of a palm, that is, tender children scarcely having the measure of a palm, so that monstrous cruelty—or rather cruel necessity—may be shown. He properly says women, not mothers, because those who have not remembered maternal affection should not be called by the name of mother. “They will eat,” he says, “their own fruit.” As though he said: Other growing things bear fruit so that the nature of the kind, consumed in the parent, may be restored in the offspring of its seed; [Col. 0313D] but man, forgetful of his own nature, consumes the fruit by which he ought to have been restored. But lest, by thus intensifying the misery, he seem not to petition God but to provoke him, and almost to accuse as unjust him who has punished his people so cruelly, after recalling the punishment he also adds the fault. He uses a certain shrewd concession, so that, while he does not depart from God’s justice in confessing the fault, he may bring his petition for mercy more quickly to effect, saying:

**If priest and prophet are slain in the sanctuary of the Lord.** As though he said: Because they killed your prophets and your priests in your sanctuary—as is read concerning Zechariah, son of Jehoiada the priest, whom King Joash killed—because, I say, they killed them, women ate the fruit of their womb, as is read concerning Mary, daughter of Eleazar; and it is written in the Book of Kings (2 Chron. 26), and Josephus also testifies. [Col. 0314A] But when he says, “If [priest and prophet] are slain,” it is as though he said: Although they sinned so greatly, ought they nevertheless to have been punished by so monstrous a vengeance? Yet in this he does not rebuke God’s judgment; rather, conceding the fault and magnifying the punishment, he seeks mercy. As though he said: There is no people whom you have loved so greatly, upon whom you have bestowed such benefits; there is no people who has sinned so greatly against you; there is no people whom you have cast down, harvested, and destroyed so greatly. Therefore, I beg, see—not fleetingly, but consider carefully—our misery, [Col. 0314B] so that you may once again bestow upon us your accustomed mercy.

**See, Lord, and consider whom you have thus harvested. ALLEGORICAL.** That holy Church is called a vineyard is proved by very many testimonies of Scripture. Among them is that Gospel passage where the master of the house is said to have sent laborers into his vineyard (Matt. 20), because God the Father, when he directs preachers to instruct the Church, sends laborers, as it were, to cultivate his vineyard. For just as a vine is cultivated with great care and labor, so the life of the faithful is certainly formed unto virtue only with great care and labor. And just as a vineyard, if fertile, restores whatever labor is expended on it by the abundance of its fruits, so the life of the faithful, if it advances toward virtue through the discipline and instruction of education, [Col. 0314C] recompenses every diligence applied to it with precious fruit. Again, just as the vine without fruit is useless and more worthless than all trees, so surely those who are cultivated through the teaching of faith and nevertheless do not bear the fruit of good work are worse than those who have never come to the knowledge of truth. And it sometimes happens that God, withdrawing grace, abandons such persons all the more profoundly because he had borne with their ingratitude longer after grace had been bestowed. Yet all the perfect grieve their fall in the compassion of charity; and those who rejoiced that they were already, through faith, members of the same body with themselves cannot endure their severance without pain. [Col. 0314D] From their voice it is here said: “See, Lord, and consider whom you have thus harvested.” God is said to harvest the wicked when, having formerly cultivated them through his preachers, he leaves them barren and empty by withdrawing grace.

This harvesting may also be referred to the elect, because when some are removed from the unity of the Church by unbelief, holy Church herself seems to remain bare and, as it were, stripped. Therefore this saying must be uttered with great feeling of compassion: “See, Lord, and consider whom—your own people, your little flock—you have thus harvested.” How? He adds: “Will women then eat their own fruit, little ones of a handbreadth?” By women we rightly understand evil prelates, softened by carnal understanding and lax morals, [Col. 0315A] who eat their own fruit because they receive in the present life their reward for the labor of their ministry. On the contrary, good teachers were told: “I have appointed you that you should go and bear fruit, and that your fruit should remain” (John 15). The fruit of the elect is said to remain because in them there is preserved, for their labor, not a transient reward but an eternal recompense. Therefore women eat their own fruit because all carnal persons, receiving in this life the reward of their labor, do not preserve their fruit but consume it. What this fruit is becomes clear when it is said: “Little ones of a handbreadth.” We should understand little ones here not by age but by faith. By the palm we may fittingly understand the beginning of good work. What then does it mean that little ones are called the fruit of women, [Col. 0315B] except that the faith of believers is reckoned to teachers for reward? Carnal prelates devour them, because, while they long after earthly things, they draw those weak in faith and still beginning, through the example of evil work, to destruction—those whom they had first begotten in faith by the word of preaching. Or certainly women then eat their little ones when evil prelates in the Church, despoiling their subjects out of love for their own possessions, afflict with poverty those whom they ought to have fed with the food of heavenly nourishment. It follows:

**If priest and prophet are slain in the sanctuary of the Lord.** By priest and prophet we should here understand the same persons whom we have just understood as signified by women: namely, prelates who are prophets by their word and priests by their ministry. [Col. 0315C] By sanctuary, however, divine worship is expressed. As though it were said: If prelates perish through administering spiritual things unworthily, why then do their crimes involve innocent subjects?

**See, Lord, and consider whom you have thus harvested. MORAL.** By a fitting comparison the soul is said to be harvested by God when, because its evil merits demand it, it is stripped of the gifts of virtues by God’s just judgment. But there is one harvesting more destructive than the others. For it is less dangerous to lose a virtue than to be proud of a virtue. He who loses virtue at least recognizes his loss; but he who is proud of virtue suffers loss without knowing it. The prophet, grieving for a soul not only sinful but also vainly glorying falsely in virtue, says: “See, Lord, [Col. 0315D] and consider whom you have thus harvested.” And, as though asking, “How thus?” he adds with a cry: “Will women then eat their own fruit?” For women eat their own fruit when carnal souls feed upon works of virtue through empty glory. They eat the fruit because virtue itself is consumed by that from which the mind delights in unlawful refreshment. “Their own fruit,” he says. What kind of fruit? “Little ones of a handbreadth.” By little ones we may understand tender virtues not yet advanced to mature strength; by the palm, the beginning of good work. Therefore little ones of a handbreadth are tender virtues newly produced at the beginning of good action. What then does it mean that women are said to eat little ones of a handbreadth [Col. 0316A] except that carnal minds glory even in the beginning of good work? It follows:

**If priest and prophet are slain in the sanctuary of the Lord.** The mind of the righteous, which is God’s sanctuary, ought to possess two things within itself: prudence and devotion—prudence, by which it treads down pressing evils through foresight; devotion, by which it wipes away past evils through supplication. What then should we understand by devotion except a certain priest of the soul, continually offering before the Lord the sacrifice of expiation? And what by prudence except a prophet? Therefore priest and prophet are slain in the sanctuary of the Lord, and women eat their little ones, because the human mind would never exalt itself over its own virtue unless, through negligence, it had first grown lukewarm both in the memory of past evils and in caution regarding future ones. [Col. 0316B]

**The child and the old men [old man] lay on the ground of wrath; my virgins and my young men fell by the sword. LITERAL.** Or it should be divided thus: “The child and the old man lay on the ground; the virgins and the young men fell by the sword.” Or thus: “The child, the old man, and the virgins lay on the ground, and the young men fell by the sword.” This perhaps fits better, because virgins are not usually slain by the sword in war but carried off for plunder—unless the very savagery of the enemy is indicated by this, namely, that they spared not even virgins. He says, then, that the fighting people, together with kings and princes, fell by the sword, while the remaining multitude, of different sexes and ages, was dispersed in captivity. [Col. 0316C] “The child,” he says, “the old man, and the virgins”—weak age and weak sex—“lay on the ground,” cast down without mercy or human feeling, on the ground of wrath. Not merely on the ground, which might have sufficed as punishment for such persons, but on the ground of wrath: either in their own land, which the Lord in his wrath permitted to be devastated and laid waste, or in a foreign land, to which the Lord’s wrath drove them. It follows:

**You killed in the day of wrath; you struck, and do not have pity [did not have pity].** As though he said: We ascribe our calamity to you, Lord; with you we plead the cause of our misery. For the blow inflicted by the fury of a raging enemy was first decreed by your anger, provoked by our sins. You killed those who fell by the sword; you struck those who lay on the ground; [Col. 0316D] and you do not have pity, so that, when you see so many already perished, you may at least turn away the scourge of your indignation from those still surviving. I beg you, Lord; I beseech you, Lord: have mercy, so that, having fallen into destruction while you were angry, we may escape it when you show mercy.

**The child and the old men lay on the ground. ALLEGORICAL.** As the people, so also the priests. They lay on the ground: they rested in earthly desires. Nor did they merely rest—which was signified above when it was said, “The old men sat on the ground and were silent”—but they also slept, because they lay down so that they no longer know themselves, and, all reason being lulled, do not consider whence they came or whither they are tending. To them Paul says: “Awake, you who sleep; arise from the dead, and Christ will enlighten you” (Eph. 5). [Col. 0317A] Alas, how badly those lie who lie on the ground! How badly those sleep who sleep on the ground! They rest on the ground, and when they awaken, find none of their riches in their hands. For whatever is loved temporarily is like a dream and vanishes when a person begins to awaken in death. “They lay,” he says, “on the ground of wrath.” What should we understand by the ground of wrath except this world, in which the human race, cast out from the happiness of paradise and condemned to exile because of the punishment for the first guilt? What madness, then, for a person to seek rest in this pilgrimage, when he does not doubt that he has been cast into it by the wrath of divine vengeance? It follows:

**My virgins and my young men fell by the sword.** By the sword in this place the teaching of heretics is signified, of whom it is said in the Psalm: “Their tongue is a sharp sword” (Ps. 56), because, while they draw some from the unity of catholic faith into their errors, they cut off, as it were, members from the body. By virgins and young men, however, the faithful are signified: they are virgins because they corrupt the integrity of faith by evil works; and they are young men because, through steadfastness of mind, they do not yield when adversities press upon them. [Col. 0317B] What then does it mean that virgins are said to fall by the sword except that, as the Apostle testifies, “evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15), and the doctrines of heretics, in which they prevail in violating the chastity of faith, afterward also overthrow the integrity of good works? Young men fall by the sword when those whose constancy could not be conquered by adversities, cut down by verbal deceits, collapse into unbelief.

Or, if we follow the other division, virgins lie on the ground when those whose minds thirst after earthly desires outwardly feign chastity of intention by the performance of works. By young men we may also understand the proud, those presuming upon their own powers, because especially at that age human life flourishes in heat and strength. [Col. 0317C] Therefore young men fall by the sword because, since you, God, despise the proud, it is clear that those overthrown by the errors of heretics would by no means fall away from the knowledge of truth unless they had first held lofty opinions of themselves. It follows:

**You killed in the day of wrath; you struck, and did not have pity.** He killed those who fell through unbelief; he struck those wounded through the love of charity at the fall of the perishing. [Col. 0317D] He does not have pity because, while he does not raise up the fallen, he does not even console the sorrow of those who stand.

**The child and the old men lay on the ground of wrath. MORAL.** The ground of wrath is our mortal flesh. Before the sin of the first man it produced the shoots of virtues; afterward, under the sentence of the curse, it began to produce the thorns and briars of vices. The little child is the sense of the flesh, because, so far as it is concerned, it always desires certain childish and vain things. But just as we understand the sense of the flesh by the child, so we may fittingly understand the judgment and appetite of the mind by old men, because the mind ought to be mature in discernment and not rash in desire. [Col. 0318A] Therefore the child lies with the old men on the ground of wrath when the carnal mind subjects to its delight not only the sense but also the judgment and appetite of our corruption—that corruption which the vengeance for transgression brought—and believes that it rests where it has been cast down to be scourged. It follows:

**My virgins and my young men fell by the sword.** By virgins we may understand chaste thoughts; by young men, the strength and constancy of mind; by the sword, the adversary’s temptation. Since the age of youth flourishes in greater strength, what else are the strength for acting rightly and steadfastness in persevering than certain young men in the rational soul? For they are prompt to begin a work and persist without failing in the work begun. [Col. 0318B] Thus it is rightly said first that old men lay on the ground, and then it is recalled that virgins and young men fell by the sword. For once the judgment and appetite of the mind are corrupted by earthly delight, a temptation arriving afterward easily violates the integrity of good thoughts and weakens the strength and constancy of the mind. For, as has often been said, thoughts proceed from affections; when thoughts are corrupted from corrupt affections, they draw bitterness as branches from an infected root. And when the carnal mind desires or discerns nothing outside the flesh, all its strength and constancy are soon softened into a temptation of the flesh. Nor should this be passed over: when the old men sit on the ground, the virgins sprinkle their heads with ashes; when the old men are clothed in sackcloth, the virgins cast their heads to the ground; [Col. 0318C] when the old men lie on the ground, the virgins fall by the sword. For indeed, in proportion to the corruption of affections grows the corruption of thoughts. It follows:

**You killed in the day of wrath; you struck, and did not have pity.** God sometimes permits certain virtues in the soul to be killed by temptation and others to be wounded, so that, while the tempted person sees that he has still retained certain goods, he may not fall wholly into despair; but while he sees that he has lost some, he may not presume upon his own powers; and may recover more truly what he lost, in proportion as, taught more subtly by his own loss, he sees that what he retained does not come from himself. But because many are permitted to be tempted not for correction but for overthrow, a person who cannot always know the cause of his temptation ought always to fear danger. [Col. 0318D] Therefore it is rightly added in the voice of the trembling: “And you do not have pity.” This is surely a sentence of fear, not of assertion. Because he does not quickly deliver from temptation, the tempted person thinks that his scourge is one of wrath rather than mercy; yet this is not the thought of one despairing but of one fearing, as we have said.

**You summoned [them] as to a solemn day. LITERAL.** As though he said: Enemies are indeed always ready to harm, but unless summoned they cannot come. Therefore this speaker does not accuse but honors God, attributing nothing to the enemies’ powers but exalting divine power even in his own oppression. “You summoned,” he says. As though he said: Theirs was the willing; yours was the permitting, so that from this very fact you may recognize that delivering us is also yours. [Col. 0319A] “You summoned [them] as to a solemn day,” that is, to a day of gladness and joy—not because your goodness delighted in our misery, but because their malice exulted in it, so that this very thing may move you to mercy and make you more quickly compassionate toward us when you see them rejoicing unjustly over us.

**Those who would terrify me from every side.** Those who would hem me in on all sides, so that I could not escape the hands of persecutors; after the likeness of hunters who drive wild beasts into nets with shouting. He notes that time when, as the Jews fled, neighboring nations on every side blocked the protection afforded by flight, lest they escape the hands of enemies: when Zedekiah, fleeing with an army of warriors, was seized in the plain of Jericho, brought back to Riblah to the king of Babylon, and there, after his sons were killed before his eyes, was himself blinded and carried off to Babylon. Hence it follows: [Col. 0319B]

**And there was none in the day of the Lord’s wrath who escaped and remained.** “Remained” means, understood implicitly, alive; or remained in his own land and was not carried away captive.

**Those whom I brought up and nourished.** I brought them up for discipline and nourished them for strength—therefore all the more to be mourned.

**The enemy consumed them.** That is, he destroyed them even to annihilation.

**You summoned [them] as to a solemn day—those who would terrify me from every side. ALLEGORICAL.** The time of the final judgment may fittingly be signified in this place. That day is called solemn either because then the joys of the righteous will begin, or because then all things will be brought forth openly for examination. [Col. 0319C] Indeed, no one awaits that time without terror, just as there is no one to whom it happens to pass through the course of this present life without sin. But the elect, while they afflict themselves with lamentations over the misery of the present life, also set before the eyes of their mind the evils yet to come; and by anxiously considering future terrors, they judge themselves here so that they may escape judgment there. They consider the most savage exactors, the demons, at whose presence even the elect will be terrified. They will press in on those to be judged from every side, so that no one will have a place of escape unless the mercy of the Judge should temper the severity of vengeance. [Col. 0319D] At that time the enemy will consume and draw with himself to destruction many who, having been brought up in the discipline of the Church and nourished by the teaching of truth, seemed worthy to be counted among the children of God.

This may also be said of pagans, heretics, or any unbelievers, especially in the time of Antichrist, when the devil will be let loose on every side in his members for the persecution of the faithful. That day is called solemn because then the wicked will rejoice at the oppression of the good. There is none who escapes and remains, since they punish bodily those who persist in truth, while they kill spiritually those who agree with them. Hence it follows: “Those whom I brought up and nourished, the enemy consumed,” because then many will collapse into unbelief who were brought up in the discipline of the Church and nourished by doctrine. [Col. 0320A] “I brought up,” he says, “and nourished”—not merely “nourished”—because the enemy consumed even the strong, whom the weight of tribulation overwhelmed. The enemy can indeed afflict the good through persecution, but cannot consume them; whoever is overcome by tribulation, however, is consumed by the enemy.

You called as to a solemn day those who would terrify me on every side. Human life is like a certain circuit: after the course of temporal actions, it finally returns through death to that place from which it came forth through birth. Yet in this circuit the faithful soul celebrates a solemn day, because, while it is fixed by inward joy in the love of eternal things, it is kept free from every unlawful outward occupation. But when the mind recalls to memory its past [Col. 0320B] evils and, by considering them, is kindled more fully with compunction, it is as though persons about to celebrate a solemnity were summoned from the circuit. As the Psalmist says: “The remnants of thoughts shall keep a feast-day for you” (Ps. 75). But because, before the ardor of compunction, the recollection of past evils shakes the sinner’s mind with a certain terror of its guilt, he rightly says that these are called both from the circuit and alike to solemnity and terror.

It should nevertheless be known that one person is terrified in one way who remembers having done no good at all, and another in another way who recognizes that certain evils, for which he has reason to fear, are mingled with his good deeds. Therefore, when a person surveys his actions and finds in them some grounds for confidence but others for fear, he is indeed terrified [Col. 0320C], but not, as it were, in a circuit; for in one respect his sinful conscience is constricted by the memory of its guilt, while on the other it is enlarged by confidence in good work. But when all his deeds accuse the sinner’s mind from every direction, then he is terrified as though in a circuit; for, seeing on every side all things to be feared, he is hemmed in within himself by sheer anguish.

This may also fittingly be said in the person of the sinful soul when, departing from the body, it is troubled as the remembrance of its evils confronts it on every side. Hence it was rightly said: “You called.” For so long as a person remains in this life, he ought continually to recall his past evils to memory, that he may voluntarily terrify himself into repentance, as the Psalmist testifies concerning himself, saying: “My sin is ever before [against] me” (Ps. 50). And elsewhere he says: “I will think upon my sin” (Ps. 37). But whoever here refused to remember his evils, there God will call them before the eyes of his mind as testimony for condemnation, so that he may there be terrified by their remembrance unto punishment, since here he refused beneficially to be terrified unto repentance. Thus the divine voice speaks through the same Psalmist: “I will rebuke you, and set them before your face” (Ps. 49).

The manner of this summons is further shown when it is said: “As to a solemn day.” For a solemn day is a day of rest; it is a day of summons, when work is not permitted, but each person then begins joyfully to enjoy those things which he had previously prepared for himself with labor. What then is the day of death but [Col. 0321A] a solemn day, on which there remains no further opportunity for working, but each begins to enjoy the recompense and reward of his works, the fruit of past labors? It follows:

“And on the day of the Lord’s wrath there was none who escaped and was left behind.” The day of the Lord’s wrath is the end of each individual, when each is compelled with great strictness to render an account, though previously in his life he was graciously awaited for repentance as though on a day of mercy. Therefore it is rightly said of the day of wrath: “There was none who escaped and was left behind.” He escaped, that is, his conscience; he was left behind for repentance.

Observe what is said: “He escaped,” namely, conscience. An evil conscience is a great torment. Yet sinners can here escape [Col. 0321B] their conscience: while given over to outward pleasures, they in some manner consign for the time being to forgetfulness the evils they endure inwardly. For the thorn of conscience now pricks the heart less sharply when it is covered, so to speak, by a bandage wrapped around it of earthly pleasure. But there they will be unable to escape the torment of conscience, because when the bodily sense is shut outwardly in death, the horror of past evils is opened inwardly to the mind. Then the unhappy soul, though too late pierced with compunction, would wish by repentance to amend what it cannot escape from in its conscience. But by God’s just judgment, the one who formerly neglected the time granted for repentance is no longer left behind, because, once the irrevocable sentence has been pronounced, there is no further delay in this life for repentance. Thus it is rightly said [Col. 0322A]: “On the day of the Lord’s wrath there was none who escaped and was left behind.” For when the hour of death comes, each is compelled to return to his own conscience, and, accompanied by it, to be removed from this life without delay to receive the Judge’s sentence.

It follows: “Those whom I brought up and nourished, the enemy has consumed.” Do not suppose that only the punishment of conscience is prepared for sinners. “Those whom I brought up,” he says, “and nourished, the enemy has consumed,” because indeed the strength and beauty of mortal bodies, which are here fed by unlawful desires, will there be consumed in torments by torturing angels. They are said to be consumed, not because punishment reduces their substance to nothing, but because pain, running through the very depths of nature, leaves nothing untouched. Or, by those “brought up” [Col. 0322B] and “nourished,” we may understand the desires of the flesh themselves: they are brought up through pride and nourished through luxury; and the more we feed them by satisfying them, the more we inflame them toward appetite. The enemy consumes these brought-up and nourished desires—that is, death, of which the Apostle says: “Death, the last enemy, shall be destroyed” (1 Cor. 15)—because when our flesh is cut down in death, all its desires are likewise extinguished, as the Psalmist says: “On that day all their thoughts shall perish” (Ps. 45). Consider, too, how fittingly, at the end of the lament, the final punishment of the sinful soul is mourned, so that we may understand with what misery the evils previously mentioned are followed.

[Col. 0321]

## Explanatory Little Notes on the Prophet Joel. (G)*

[Col. 0321C] **(JOEL 1.)** “The word of the Lord which came to Joel son of Phatuel.”

**Historically.** Three things are to be considered in a word: sound, form, and meaning. The sound of persecution, the form of the voice, the meaning of the expression. A blow pertains to vengeance, a voice to joy, an expression to grace. For vengeance strikes, the voice consoles, the expression instructs. It instructs the son; it consoles the hired servant: it instructs the son eagerly thirsting for his father’s teaching; it consoles the hired servant laboring anxiously under judgment. The grace of obedience instructs the son; the reward of righteousness consoles the hired servant; the punishment of wickedness afflicts the slave. Sound pertains to punishment, voice to reward, meaning to grace.

These three, therefore, are considered in the word which came to Joel, because in the outcome of the following prophecy [Col. 0321D] there is foretold both the vengeance upon enemies, the consolation of the afflicted people, and the instruction of the elect. The sound of the utterance, therefore, is directed to the adversary; the form of the voice, to the afflicted people; the meaning of the word, to the prophetic mind and to the choir of the elect. For by that through which the adversary [Col. 0322C] is afflicted, the people are consoled; and the mind of the elect, understanding this, glories in the Lord. Therefore sound is made for the carnal, form is directed to the animate, meaning to the spiritual.

Moreover, this is the word of the Lord. In the Lord likewise three things are considered: vengeance, zeal, and recompense. Vengeance for fault, zeal for discipline, reward for obedience. “For the word of God is living and effectual, and sharper than any two-edged sword” (Heb. 4). It is penetrating because it destroys wickedness; living because it restores to grace; effectual because it brings to glory. It is penetrating in judgment, living in deed, effectual in promise. Penetrating, because its judgment is hidden; living, because its act bears fruit; effectual, because its promise is not falsified. Penetrating, because it destroys mightily; living, because it gives life powerfully [Col. 0322D]; effectual, because it renders effectively. This is the word of the Lord which came to Joel son of Phatuel.

First it must be seen that the construction has an ellipsis. For in saying, “The word of the Lord which [Col. 0323A] came to Joel son of Phatuel,” something must be understood in order to complete the sense, either thus: “This is the word which came”; or thus: “The word which came shows these following things.” It follows:

“Hear this, elders, and give ear, all inhabitants of the land: has this happened in your days, or in the days of your fathers? Tell your children of it, and let your children tell their children, and their children another generation.”

At the magnitude of the coming calamity, he is carried into astonished amazement. But lest these things seem to be despised, he summons the authority of the elders; lest they seem of slight or trifling importance, he arouses the inhabitants of the land, saying: “Hear, elders,” and so forth. The wisdom of the elders lends authority to the astonishment; the concern of the inhabitants gives credence to the amazement: namely, so that no doubt at all can be entertained concerning the coming misfortune, to which the authority of the wise and the public concern of the peoples seem certainly to bear witness. He proceeds, expressing the parts of the calamity, saying:

“What the caterpillar left, the locust ate; what the locust left, the cankerworm ate; and what the cankerworm left, the rust ate. Awake, drunkards, and weep; howl, all you who drink wine in sweetness, because it has perished from your mouth.”

Having shown the first part of the calamity, and the ensuing cry of lamentation, he undertakes to show another kind of misfortune and attempts to descend to that form of lament. For he says:

“For a nation has come up upon my land, strong and innumerable. Its teeth are like the teeth of a lion, and its molars like those of a lion’s whelp. It has made my vine a wilderness and stripped the bark from my fig tree. Stripping it bare, it despoiled it [Col. 0323C] and cast it down; its branches have become white.”

Behold the lament. Now he adds the calamity, saying:

“Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth over the husband of your youth.” And so, alternating calamity with lament, he proceeds as far as the words: “To you, O Lord, I shall cry.” There he makes a suppliant invocation to God, a pitiable description of the calamity, and a humble and heartfelt entreaty for its removal.

According to some, he indicates the dreadful approach of the Babylonians into Judaea, their hostile assault, their savage spirit—raging everywhere, laying all waste, destroying everything. Or, more truly, he indicates the pride of the Assyrians and the bold savagery of that nation, thirsty for blood, eager for glory, exposed to misfortunes, prone to victory. Under Sennacherib they devastated all Judaea and besieged Jerusalem. And because they ascribed the success of their enterprise not to divine judgment but to their own strength, when the king fled with a few men, all the rest were struck down by an angel and perished in one night.

By the caterpillar Joel denotes the Assyrians; by the locust, the Babylonians; by the cankerworm, the Persians and Medes; by the rust, the Macedonians. All these, in succession over time, laid waste the people of God; and if one left anything flourishing, green, or perhaps unconsumed, when another followed, it was trampled down and reduced to nothing. Let anyone who wishes to be assured on this matter read ancient Josephus, the traditions of the Jews, and the other histories pertinent to it.

[Col. 0324A] **Allegorically**, however, he speaks of the persecution of the universal Church, which is said to be fourfold: for it is recorded that it was first attacked by idolaters, second by heretics, third by pseudo-Christians, and fourth that it is to be attacked by Antichrist. Foreseeing this with prophetic eye, Joel, because of the magnitude of the persecution, summons the elders and inhabitants of the land into fellowship in his astonishment. It is as if he said: “I see the coming misfortunes of Christ’s bride; I behold her calamities; I discern her various labors. But I call upon the wisdom of the spiritual and the concern also of the carnal, so that what they have heard may be handed down in succession to posterity, until dawn rises from heaven, the Bride of the Lamb comes, and the Church springs up; that, fortified by our oracle, she may remain steadfast: lest, deceived, she receive a rival in place of her husband; choose a flower without [Col. 0324B] fruit, coinage without silver, a sheaf without grain, or a shadow without a body.”

By the caterpillar he denotes idolaters; by the locusts, heretics; by the cankerworms, pseudo- and carnal Christians; by rust, the malicious contrivance of Antichrist. The first, because of the filth and variety of idolatry; the second, because of the flight of knowledge, agility of intellect, and arrogance of pride; the third, because of the heat and uncleanness of carnal desire; the fourth, because of the enormity of his cruelty. For after the Church escaped the shipwreck of idolatry, she fell into the waves and storms of heretics; but when, under the blowing of the spiritual west wind, the storm was changed into a gentler breeze, she again labored long in enduring the heat of carnal people. At last, harassed in many ways, variously tortured, and most grievously distressed by the son of perdition, “who shall exalt himself above all that is called God” (2 Thess. 2) or is worshipped, she will finally, with serenity restored, return to the harbor of freedom and enter the dwelling-place of peace.

And this is what he says: “What the caterpillar left, the locust ate,” and so forth. This is the nation said to have come up upon the land—that is, upon the Church—strong and innumerable: strong in magnitude, innumerable in multitude; strong in cruelty, innumerable in persistence. The lion is the devil, or one supreme in earthly power, such as some heresiarch or Antichrist himself. The teeth are his attendants; the lion’s whelps, the nobles or subordinate kings; the molars, executioners. The one whom above he called land he now calls fig tree and vine, that is, the Church [Col. 0324D]: land because of the stability of faith; vine because of the severity of repentance; fig tree because of the sweetness of love. Or land because of the foundation of righteousness; vine because of the joy of spiritual understanding; fig tree because of the sweetness of heavenly teaching. Or land because of the fruit of spiritual exercises; vine because of the grace of heavenly gifts; fig trees because of the sweetness of eternal joys.

These things the Lamb, Christ, bestowed upon his bride, the Church: the first in the garden, the second in the wine-cellar, the third in the bedchamber. For in the garden she is exercised; in the wine-cellar she is gladdened; in the bedchamber she is made blessed—first by works of repentance, second by gifts of grace, third by the kisses of wisdom. But the aforesaid nation stripped, bared, and cast her down. The bark [Col. 0325A] is religious exercise, the leaves are words, the fruit merits: exercises of grace, words of doctrine, merits of glory. But the aforesaid nation stripped, bared, and cast her down because, as persecution grew severe, the exercises of religion grew cold, the words of preaching fell silent, and the merits of virtues were diminished in many.

**Tropologically**, however, the prophet speaks of the temptations of the soul. He shows a spiritual nation coming up against it, a troop of vices invading, trampling, and overcoming it by God’s just judgment, saying: “What the caterpillar left, the locust ate; what the locust left, the cankerworm ate; and what the cankerworm left, the rust ate.” I know that some before me have said that these four signify the four disturbances of the mind, and have referred the caterpillar to fear, the locust to hope, the cankerworm to joy, and rust to grief. Boethius says of these:

> “Put away joys; banish fear and hope;  
> Let grief be absent.  
> The mind is clouded and bound with reins  
> Wherever these hold sway.”

But we leave them their interpretation and hasten to other matters that seem more fitting. “What the caterpillar left, the locust ate,” and so forth. The caterpillar, then, is luxury; the locust, *cenodoxia*, that is, vain glory; the cankerworm, *gastrimargia*—gluttony; rust, anger or impatience. What is left by the caterpillar is chastity; what is left by the locust, humility; what is left by the cankerworm, sobriety; what is left by rust, gentleness and patience of mind. Therefore the second consumes what the first left, the third what the second left, the fourth what the third left. For it very often happens that empty glory arises from continence, drunkenness and revelry follow humility, and anger or [Col. 0325C] impatience follows sobriety.

For it sometimes happens that a mind still imperfect, imagining that it has conquered itself and reached the summit of righteousness, falls away from victory; and, when it sees itself to have overcome one enemy, thinks that it has endured the whole business of war and defeated the entire army. But while the deceived mind rejoices in its triumph over one foe, it does not see, poor thing, that another draws his sword and threatens death at close range. Hence, exulting over the death of luxury, it is presently struck by the sword of vain glory, as though secure and less watchful. If it happens to overcome this by humility of mind, gluttony immediately insinuates itself. For when the unwary mind sees chastity restraining the flesh and humility repressing the mind, it at once hastens to yield to pleasure, saying thus:

[Col. 0325D] “Since neither does the wind of vain glory stir my mind nor the enticement of carnal desire tickle my flesh, it would be a kind of cruelty if I tortured my fellow citizen with the goads of dire necessity. Peace restored to me in both matters urges and permits me to provide pleasant things.”

Thus gluttony is introduced, and the fellow citizen is killed. But if, through divine help and personal effort, it happens to overcome this also, then, thinking itself wholly escaped from shipwreck, it again falls into that misfortune. For, seeing continence rise in the flesh, humility in the mind, and abstinence in the body, the mind now presumes upon perfection and looks down upon others. If anyone resists its endeavor, opposes its assault, or crosses its inclination, it immediately [Col. 0326A] loosens the reins of anger and bursts into words of impatience, saying: “You were born wholly in sins, and do you teach us?” (John 9). The order of things requires that what is prior hold the first place, and what is inferior lie below. It is written: “The spiritual person judges all things, and is himself judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2). And in the Law the mouth of the leper is commanded to be covered (Lev. 13). Therefore first learn rightly, that you may teach soundly; first live well, that you may rebuke justly.

Hence the Lord says through Job: “Remember the battle, and add no more speech” (Job 40). It is as though he said: “The more subtle the weapons of spiritual wickedness are, the more watchful the mind must show itself against them” (Eph. 6). Nor should you become impatient over the grace of triumph, or exalted over victory over some enemies, when you lie open to the snares of many and are surrounded by many. Therefore Joel says: “What the caterpillar left, the locust ate; what the locust left, the cankerworm ate; and what the cankerworm left, the rust ate.” It follows:

**Allegorically.** “Awake, drunkards, and weep. Howl, all you who drink wine in sweetness, because it has perished from your mouth.” It is as if he said: “The day of destruction is near, and the times of temptation hasten to arrive. Awake, therefore, from the sleep of deadly negligence, from the bed of carnal desire, because you are drunk with the prosperity of transitory pleasure. Pour forth tears of compunction; utter the howling of confession, you who burn with the wine of transitory delight. For it has perished,” he says, “from your mouth.”

Hence James says: “Let the humble brother glory in his exaltation, and the rich in his humiliation, because [Col. 0326C] he shall pass away like the flower of grass. For the sun has risen with its heat and has dried up the grass; its flower has fallen and the beauty of its appearance has perished. So also shall the rich man wither in his ways” (James 1). Awake unto repentance; weep unto pardon; howl unto grace, you who drink the wine of transitory pleasure in sweetness, who are made drunk by the glory of momentary vanity; for it is written: “They slept their sleep, and all men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Ps. 75).

It follows: “Because it has perished from your mouth.” Hence James says: “Come now, rich people, weep, howling over your miseries that shall come upon you. Your riches have rotted, and your garments have been eaten by moths. Your gold and silver have rusted, and their rust shall be a testimony against [Col. 0326D] you and shall eat your flesh like fire. For you have stored up wrath for yourselves in the last days” (James 5). The wine, I say, has perished from your mouth, because it is written: “Laughter shall be mingled with grief, and mourning occupies the end of joy” (Prov. 14).

Hence it follows: “For a nation has come up upon my land, strong and innumerable. Their teeth are like the teeth of a lion, and their molars like those of a lion’s whelp. It has made my vine a wilderness and stripped the bark from my fig tree. Stripping it bare, it despoiled it and cast it down; its branches have become white.” This nation is the crowd of wickedness, the multitude of superfluity, the troop of curiosity, the cohort of pleasure, the people of vanity. This nation is strong in the assault upon virtues and innumerable in the persistence of temptations; it is strong in victory of crime [Col. 0327A] and innumerable in the urgency of suggestion.

The lion is the devil, and its teeth are the wicked movements of the mind; the molars are consent; the lion’s whelps are acts. The land is the soul; it is also the fig tree because of the sweetness of heavenly contemplation. Or it is land by the humility of repentance, vine by the subtlety of understanding, fig tree by the sweetness of eminent grace. Or it is land by the rigor of abstinence, vine by the fervor of righteousness, fig tree by the sweetness of heavenly wisdom. But the aforesaid nation stripped, bared, and cast it down: it stripped it in act, bared it in perception, cast it down in affection—of uprightness in act, honorableness in perception, goodness in affection. Or: of righteousness in act, continence in perception, mercy in affection. The branches are the soul’s desires, through which it extends as far as works; they become white when they do not lose the native color of virtue. It follows:

“Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth over the husband of your youth. Sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of the Lord. The priests, ministers of the Lord, have mourned. The region has been laid waste. The ground has mourned, because the wheat has been devastated. The wine has been confounded, and the oil has languished. The farmers have been ashamed, and the vinedressers have howled over wheat and barley, because the harvest of the field has perished. The vine has been confounded, and the fig tree has languished. Pomegranate and palm, apple tree and every tree of the field, have dried up, because joy has been confounded away from the children of men.”

**Historically.** He calls the synagogue a virgin because of the faith in the one God which it received. The Gentiles, however, were harlots and fornicators because of the varied worship of idolatry. [Col. 0327C] He summons this synagogue to lamentation and sackcloth over the husband of its youth, because, owing to the multitude of slaughter and the fury of hostile devastation, the rite of ceremonies and the worship of the Law ceased. For the worship of the Law was the synagogue’s husband. Hence the Apostle says: “A woman is bound by the law of her husband so long as her husband lives; but if he dies, she is released from the law of her husband” (1 Cor. 7). The synagogue likewise was bound to the worship of the Law by obligation until Christ. Hence Christ himself says: “The Law and the prophets were until John” (Matt. 1). But when Christ came, it hears: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5).

**Allegorically.** He calls the Church a virgin because of faith in the one God and the integrity of the sacraments. The Church is a virgin, and her husband, Christ, is a virgin. He is rightly called the husband of her youth, because it is written of him thus in Jeremiah: “The Lord creates a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31); and: “A man of sorrows, acquainted with bearing weakness” (Isa. 53). Again, in Isaiah, in the person of the Father: “I,” he says, “am the Lord, calling a bird from the east, from a far land the man of my will” (Isa. 46)—surely a man of youth. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “I am my beloved’s, and his turning is toward me” (Song 7). It is as if she said: “As I am his alone, so he is mine alone; and as I belong to him alone, so he belongs to me alone.”

This virgin is summoned to lamentation and sackcloth over the husband of her youth because, on account of the misfortunes set forth below, the Church is rightly admonished to weep. For when sins demand it [Col. 0328A], the order, condition, splendor, and worship of the Church are neglected, altered, deformed, and obscured: the order of precepts, the condition of counsels, the splendor of judgments, the worship of sacraments. Order through negligence or carelessness; condition through desire; splendor through avarice; worship through irreverence. Therefore, over contempt for her husband, the Church is most rightly stirred by Joel to lamentation: “Lament,” he says, “like a virgin girded with sackcloth over the husband of your youth, because sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of the Lord.”

Sacrifice is what is offered from something solid; libation, what is offered from something liquid. By these are signified the sacraments of the Church, which are administered partly in solid and partly in liquid form. But both perish from the house of the Lord, not in substance but in reverence, because, when the wickedness of vices prevails, scarcely anyone is found in the Church who administers or receives the sacraments worthily. Hence it follows: “The priests, ministers of the Lord, have mourned.” They are called priests because they give the sacraments; ministers because they minister the word of life. The priests mourn the contempt or disobedience of those subject to them in matters of precepts, and also the irreverence which they themselves justly deserve in matters of the sacraments.

Hence the Lord says through Malachi: “Behold, I come to you, O priests, who despise my name and offer polluted bread upon my altar, and say: ‘In what have we polluted you?’” (Matt. 1). “In that you say”—that is, cause it to be said—“The table of the Lord is polluted.” Therefore, if you are a minister and priest, rest in the Law and glory in God, know his will, approve the better things, instructed [Col. 0328C] through the Law; if you trust that you are a guide of the blind, a light to those in darkness, an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of children, possessing in the Law the form of knowledge and truth—do you then, who teach another, not teach yourself? You who say that one must not steal, do you steal? You who preach that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who abhor idols, do you commit sacrilege? You who glory in the Law, do you dishonor God through transgression of the Law? “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Rom. 2).

Hence Jeremiah says: “From the priests wickedness has gone forth” (Jer. 23). And Zephaniah: “The priests have polluted your sanctuary; they have acted unjustly against the Law” (Zeph. 3). And Malachi: “But you have departed from the way and caused many to stumble in the Law; [Col. 0328D] you have made my covenant void, says the Lord” (Mal. 2). Behold their evil merits. It follows concerning their mourning and irreverence, of which the Lord says through Malachi: “I shall send want upon you, and I shall curse your blessings, and I shall curse them, because you have not laid it upon your heart” (ibid.). Again, through the same prophet: “Behold, I shall cast your arm away and scatter upon your faces the dung of your solemnities” (ibid.). Again he says: “For this reason I have made you contemptible and low before all peoples, because you have not kept my ways and have shown partiality in the Law” (ibid.). It follows:

“The region has been laid waste; the ground has mourned, because the wheat has been devastated. The wine has been confounded, and the oil has languished. The farmers have been ashamed; the vinedressers have howled [Col. 0329A] over wheat and barley, because the harvest of the field has perished. The vine has been confounded, the fig tree has languished; pomegranate and palm, apple tree and every tree of the field, have dried up.”

The region is the breadth of the Church’s obedience; the ground, the humility of repentance; wheat, the soundness of doctrine; wine, the subtlety of spiritual understanding; farmers and vinedressers, priests and preachers. They are called farmers because they shape morals; vinedressers because they pour into the minds of hearers the joy of eternal things. They are farmers because they train people for the practice of righteousness; vinedressers because they stir the minds of hearers to love wisdom. Or they are farmers because by their teaching they uproot earthly works and desires; vinedressers because they promise spiritual gifts and bring the joy of eternal things into the minds of hearers.

Barley is simple and historical doctrine; the harvest of the fields is the fruitful simplicity of good works; the vine is the abundance of divine knowledge; the fig tree is the sweetness of contemplation and the delight of eternal things. The pomegranate is the fervor of martyrdom; the palm, contempt for the world; the simple apple tree, the work of faith; all the other trees are works of repentance or mercy. We omit fitting each individual item to its proper place, hastening to other matters; we leave this, easily and usefully, as an exercise for the reader. It follows:

“Because joy has been confounded away from the children of men.” Joy is rightly said to be confounded by the failure of the things mentioned before: for through want of them the people are endangered, the priests despised, and the Churches weakened.

[Col. 0329C] It should also be known that joy is divided fourfold. There is joy in wickedness, joy in vanity, joy in charity, and joy in blessedness. Of the first it is written: “Those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things” (Prov. 2). Of the second: “They take up tambourine and lyre, and rejoice at the sound of the organ” (Job 21). Of the third: “The saints shall exult in glory; they shall rejoice upon their couches” (Ps. 149). Of the fourth: “Blessed are those who dwell in your house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise you” (Ps. 83). Therefore the joy of charity and the reward of blessedness have been confounded away from the children of men, because when the aforementioned virtues fail—where knowledge of truth and love of virtue do not precede, and merits cease—no rewards of salvation follow, whether here or in the future [Col. 0329D].

**Tropologically**, what we have said allegorically about the Church may be interpreted of the soul’s condition. For the soul is a virgin by the condition of nature, a virgin by the privilege of grace, and also a virgin by the reward of glory. Disordered desire makes the soul a harlot; manly repentance restores chastity to it; wise innocence restores virginity. For the soul is, as it were, chaste when, through works and the desire for righteousness, it has entered upon the suffering and fear of repentance, but has not yet been raised to the summit of innocence. Therefore the soul is a harlot in the brothel; married in the courtyard; continent in the house; a virgin in the bridal chamber. In the first, desire is displayed; in the second, it performs works of repentance; in the third, weeping for her husband, it is moved by longing for righteousness; [Col. 0330A] in the fourth, it delights in virginal embraces and the kisses of wisdom.

Thus the soul is a harlot through the wickedness of desire; chaste through the humility of continence; continent through purity of righteousness; a virgin through the sublimity of contemplation. Christ, the espouser of virginity, is the husband of her youth. But because it has departed from him through the vice of perverse desire, it is admonished to return to him through mourning, works, and the habit of repentance. And this is what he says: “Lament like a virgin girded with sackcloth,” and so forth.

Sacrifice is mortification of the flesh; libation, weeping of compunction; the region, serenity of conscience; the ground, humility of self-knowledge. Wheat is love of righteousness; wine, fervor of wisdom; oil, the fragrance of mercy; the fig tree, the sweetness and delight of contemplative [Col. 0330B] joy. Barley is the lowliness of repentance. Farmers are groanings and movements of compunction. Vinedressers are the desires of compunction and sighs of contemplation. The palm is contempt for earthly things. The pomegranate is ardor and thirst for rewards. The simple apple tree is good affections. The other trees are desires of the remaining virtues, or rather their works and advances. When these are lost, joy is confounded; when they are possessed, an ordered and glorious reward is prepared. It follows:

“Gird yourselves and mourn, priests; howl, ministers of the altar. Enter; lie in sackcloth, ministers of my God, because sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of your God. Sanctify a fast; call an assembly. Gather the elders, all inhabitants of the land, into the house of your God, and cry to the Lord. Ah, ah, ah, for the day [Col. 0330C]; for the day of the Lord is near, and it shall come like devastation from the Mighty One.”

“Truly dark is the water in the clouds of the air” (Ps. 17), because knowledge is hidden in the prophets. Indeed, the Lord made darkness his hiding place because he surrounded prophetic utterance—in which hidden food lies concealed for many—with great and numerous obscurities, with the coverings of words and expressions. Behold, Joel pursues the course of calamity with marvelous skill in speaking and elegantly strives, by an urbane and ornamented style of discourse, to move the Judge. First, indeed, from the manner and order of the misfortune; then from the dignity, habit, and order of supplication, he relies upon the remedy of mercy.

The order of the calamity is this. First he shows things without sense laid waste; then things afflicted which possess sense alone [Col. 0330D]; then beings using reason carried captive: so that the order of mercy may accompany the order of calamity—first sparing nature, second sentience, third reason. The Creator belongs to nature, the Ordainer to sentience, the Savior to reason; first nature, second glory, third grace. First sparing, lest he corrupt nature; second, lest he destroy form; third, lest he withdraw grace. It is as if he said: “We rightly beseech you, Lord, for nature, because you created it; rightly for form, because you formed it with senses; rightly for grace, because you freely illumined it with reason. Preserve, therefore, Lord, in the rational creature the grace of virtue and the light of reason. Protect in the sentient creature the gift of form and the habit of its constitution. Preserve in the natural creature the work and safeguard of its condition.”

[Col. 0331A] In the manner of supplication also, he employs the dignity of virgins, the rank of priests, and the habit of penitents, so that through the humility of penitence the servant may move his Lord, through the reverence of holiness the priest may move God, and through the affection and union of marriage the virgin-bride may move her husband—to pardon, to grace, to glory. The servant pleads for pardon; the priest for grace; the bride for glory: for the pardon of sins, the grace of gifts, and the glory of rewards. This is the most perfect kind of supplication: one prays for the removal of sickness, the restoration of health, and the preservation of freedom, so that a remedy may be applied to disease, caution to a gift, and protection to a good. We have said this by way of digression; now let us return to the exposition of the text.

[Col. 0331B] HISTORICAL.

He presents the aforesaid disaster under another figurative form of words. He summons priests, elders, and inhabitants of the land to mourning, sackcloth, and fasting, in the hope that God may turn and forgive.

ALLEGORICAL.

It signifies the Church’s spiritual misfortunes and losses, showing in her a failure of religious observance, contempt for holiness, and danger to good order. Therefore it first invites the priests to repentance: for especially through their negligence the worship of righteousness, the rigor of discipline, the pattern of teaching, and the very countenance of the Church have fallen into irreverence. Hence the people too, running through the various hiding places of vices, have perished. Thus Jeremiah says: “The kings of the earth and the inhabitants of the city did not believe that enemy and foe would enter through the gates of Jerusalem, because of the sins of her prophets [Col. 0331C] and the iniquity of her priests, who shed the blood of the righteous in her midst.
