They wandered as blind men; they were defiled with blood” (Lam. 4).

“Gird yourselves,” he says, “and mourn, O priests.” Since mention has been made of girding, let us see what distinction can be made from it. For in the divine utterance we read of some who are girded, others who are belted; and among the belted, some are girded about the loins, while others have a golden belt about their breasts. Humble penitence makes men girded up; manly and steadfast obedience makes them girded; perfect patience makes them belted. Bodily continence or holiness belts them about the loins; the golden belt about the breasts is the perfect purity of the inward person, or divine knowledge.

This is the order of perfect [Col. 0331D] conversion. This is the rule of devout religious life: first, the perverse person returns through humble penitence; then, being turned from opposition, he turns toward obedience; next, once converted, he ascends to the splendor of holiness; finally, steadfast and patient, he flies by purity of mind to the summit of heavenly wisdom.

“Therefore gird yourselves and mourn, O priests; howl, ministers of the altar. Enter and lie down in sackcloth, ministers of my God, because sacrifice and libation have perished from the house of your God.” Here the order of perfect penitence is set forth, by which priests are commanded to return to the state of obedience. For three things are necessary to perfect penitence: compunction of mind, confession of mouth, and mortification of flesh—compunction for offenses, confession of sins, mortification of vices; compunction for [Col. 0332A] vanity, confession of iniquity, mortification of excess.

In the present passage the prophet indicates these things, relating weeping to compunction, howling to confession, and sackcloth to mortification. When he commands them to enter into sackcloth, he indicates that mortification of the flesh ought not to pour itself out indiscriminately, but should make our reasonable service highly profitable. Hence the Apostle says: “I beseech you, through the mercy of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy, pleasing to God—your reasonable service” (Rom. 12).

One enters into sackcloth whenever the flesh is mortified purely, devoutly, and with discernment. A person does not enter sackcloth but unsews it whenever, exceeding the measure, he torments and wears down his flesh. One does not enter into sackcloth but anoints sackcloth when he unlawfully indulges the flesh [Col. 0332B] and cultivates its desires. But whoever devoutly embraces the yoke of abstinence enters into sackcloth. Whoever delights in mortification of the flesh lies down in sackcloth. Whoever pursues abstinence under forced exaction is tortured in sackcloth.

The house of God is the Church; sacrifice and libation are twofold sacraments. Sacrifice concerns things offered from what is solid; libation, things offered from what is liquid. Solid things are those relating to offerings, both spiritual and bodily; liquid things, to baptism and anointings. Or sacrifice pertains to action, libation to contemplation. In action there are indeed affliction and anxiety; in contemplation, sweetness and delight. In the sacrifice of action a person is beneficially afflicted; in the libation of contemplation [Col. 0332C] the soul is happily soothed and gently refreshed.

It follows:

“Sanctify a fast; call an assembly. Gather the elders, all inhabitants of the land, into the house of your God; and cry to the Lord: ‘Alas, alas, alas for the day! For the day of the Lord is near, and it shall come like devastation from the Mighty One.’”

After the priests have been purified by penitence and ordered through obedience, they rightly summon an assembly to the Church and fittingly gather elders and inhabitants of the land, in order to obtain pardon, appease the wrath of the heavenly Judge, and obtain mercy. For it is written: “Whoever stops his ear from hearing the law, his prayer shall be abominable” (Prov. 28). Hence it is also said elsewhere: “Cease to do perversely; learn to do good; seek judgment; [Col. 0332D] help the oppressed; judge for the orphan; defend the widow; and come, and accuse me, says the Lord” (Isa. 1).

Observe, reader, the order by which mercy is obtained and divine clemency entreated—the manner of approaching the throne of grace. First one must sanctify the fast; then call the assembly; then gather the elders and the people; then cry to the Lord together. The Savior shows us how to sanctify a fast, saying: “But when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face” (Matt. 6). In the face is action; in washing, compunction; in anointing, compassion; in the head, devotion of mind. The sanctification of fasting requires all these things: compunction must purify abstinence, compassion must order it, devotion must sustain it, and action must shape it. Compunction [Col. 0333A] toward oneself; compassion toward one’s neighbor; devotion toward God. Action, however, relates its work to one’s fellow.

An assembly properly consists of the wise. Elders are the prudent. The inhabitants of the land are inquirers into the law. Crying to the Lord is supplication for a remedy against disaster. The prophet shows in the present passage what such supplication ought to be, saying: “Cry to the Lord: ‘Alas, alas, alas for the day! For the day of the Lord is near.’”

We ought not to suppress what we received from a certain Jew, eloquent and skilled in the fables of Gamaliel. He says that Joel, foreseeing the impending destruction of the coming captivity, strives, with the feeling of one mourning—so the text reads—to extinguish the onslaught of the heavenly Judge; recalling the past to memory, he endeavors to circumvent the Judge and hastens to bend him toward mercy, saying: “Alas, alas, alas for the day! [Col. 0333B] For the day of the Lord is near.”

He uttered “alas” three times because there were three principal calamities of the Jewish people. The first was when they were held by the Egyptians; the second, when by the Assyrians; the third, when by the Babylonians. *A* is an interjection of one mourning and wonderfully setting forth a pitiable event. He says therefore: “Alas, Israel entered Egypt; Jacob was a sojourner in the land of Ham” (Ps. 104). “Alas, as whirlwinds from the south come from the desert, they come from a dreadful land” (Isa. 21). “Alas, a great eagle with great wings, long in the extension of its limbs, full of feathers and variegation, came to Lebanon and took the marrow of the cedar” (Ezek. 17).

As though he said: Alas, we gave our hand to Egypt, and from this comes grief. Alas, to the Assyrians also, that we might be filled with bread, and from this comes sorrow. Alas, the Lord has cast off [Col. 0333C] his altar and cursed his sanctification (Ps. 76), and from this comes terror. As though he said: Alas, will God cast off forever, or will he no longer add that he may yet be favorable? Alas, how long shall my enemy be exalted over me? (Ps. 12). Alas, you, Lord, rising up, will have mercy on Zion, because it is time to pity her, because the time has come (Ps. 102).

In another sense, he uttered “alas” three times because there are likewise three evils: ignorance, concupiscence, and misery. Violation of the natural law brought ignorance. Transgression of the written law spread disordered concupiscence. Contempt for prophecy produced misery. Let it then be said: Alas, the natural law has been violated; hence grief, but this was punished in Egyptian captivity. Alas, the written law has been violated; hence sorrow, [Col. 0333D] but this was punished in Assyrian captivity. Alas, prophecy is despised; hence terror, but you also purpose to punish this by Babylonian captivity. Alas, we have fallen into the misery which you punished. Alas, we have fallen away into concupiscence, which you punished. Alas, we shall fall into dreadful misery, which you have ordained.

Alternatively, what we have said concerning the threefold captivity may be referred to the final one. For there were three most wretched disasters of the Babylonian captivity: the overthrow of the Temple, the destruction of the city, and the migration of the people. As though he said: Alas, your people shall be led away into captivity in exile; but have mercy, Lord, on your people, upon whom your name has been invoked (Ecclus. 36), and on Israel, whom you made equal to your firstborn. Alas, the city shall be destroyed; but have mercy [Col. 0334A] on the city of your sanctification, Jerusalem, the city of your rest. Alas, the Temple shall be overthrown; but hear, Lord, the hymn (3 Kings 8) and the prayer which your servants pray before you today, that your eyes may be open (ibid.) over this house by day and night.

These things have been said historically.

But they may be interpreted otherwise allegorically. For Joel, foreseeing the ruin of his people at the coming of Jesus Christ, laments in compassion; and by lamenting exhorts them to caution, saying: “Alas, alas, alas for the day! For the day of the Lord is near, and it shall come like devastation from the Mighty One.” As though he said: Alas, he shall come who will turn impiety away from Jacob and remove the yoke from Israel. Alas: “He has neither form nor beauty; we saw him, and there was no appearance” (Isa. 53). Alas: “His face was as though hidden [Col. 0334B] and despised; hence we did not esteem him. Truly he himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (ibid.). Alas: “We considered him as though leprous, struck by God, and humbled” (ibid.).

Alas, because we saw and did not recognize; alas, because we heard and despised. Alas, because we received him doing good and killed him while praying for us. We heard words, received benefits, and saw miracles. But alas, we despised the words; alas, we were ungrateful for the benefits; alas, we disparaged the miracles. We heard him teaching on the mountain, but alas, we passed these things by with a deaf ear—hence grief. We saw him feeding the crowds by the sea, but alas, we did not care—hence sorrow. We saw him hanging on the cross, [Col. 0334C] but alas, we despised him—and hence terror.

We heard his teaching, received his life, and saw his death. His teaching enlightened our blindness—alas, we did not obey it. His life gave form to ours—alas, we did not receive it. His death captured our death—alas, we despised it; indeed, we brought it about.

“The day,” etc., according to the rules of allegory, signifies the time of the Word’s incarnation; “the day of the Lord” represents the Lord himself. It is rightly called the Lord’s day, because then the judgment of the world came about, according to the Gospel: “Now is the judgment of the world; now the ruler of this world shall be cast out” (John 12).

“The day of the Lord” is understood in three ways: as the time of the incarnation, the day of a person’s death, or the day of the final judgment. [Col. 0334D] It is rightly called the day of the Lord alone, because his power alone is recognized: his wisdom in the first judgment conducts the examination, in the second distinguishes merit, and in the third apportions reward.

It follows:

“Have not provisions perished before your eyes, joy and exultation from the house of your God? The beasts have rotted in their dung. The granaries have been demolished; the storehouses have been scattered, because the wheat has been confounded. Why has the animal groaned? The herds of cattle have lowed, because they have no pasture. And the flocks of livestock [of shepherds or of swine] have perished. To you, Lord, I shall cry, because fire has consumed the beautiful things of the desert, and flame has kindled all the trees of the region. The beasts of the field also looked to you, as a threshing-floor thirsting for rain, because [Col. 0335A] all the springs of water have dried up and fire has devoured the beautiful things of the desert.”

Having set forth the manner of supplication, he adds the cause of grief, so that, when many great losses are apparent, supplication may be extended in devotion and fervor. These are the losses: the foul rotting of the beasts of burden, the distress of animals, the destruction of livestock, the demolition of granaries, the scattering of storehouses, and the barrenness of pasture. Their cause is this: the burning of beautiful things, the kindling of trees, and the drying-up of springs.

Just as bodily nourishment is evidently threefold, so too is spiritual nourishment. Some things contribute to health but not strength; some to strength but not health; and some both to health and strength. From the first arises an elegant and fitting form; from the second, manly and steadfast boldness; from the third, beauty of form and fecundity of power. But since we have touched on carnal things, let us now return to spiritual matters. [Col. 0335B] There are four: commandments, exercises, virtues, and charisms. Commandments are for health; exercises for strength; virtues for form; charisms for boldness.

Joy concerns transient things; exultation, eternal things. These provisions—exultation and joy—have perished from the house of God, that is, from the Church, because commandments are trampled down, virtues despised, exercises have disappeared, and charisms have withdrawn. Hence the Savior says: “When the Son of Man comes, do you suppose that he will find faith on earth?” (Luke 18). Again he says: “Foxes have dens and birds of heaven nests, but the Son [Col. 0335C] of Man has nowhere to lay his head” (Luke 9). And Paul says: “In the last times people shall be lovers of themselves, covetous, haughty, proud, blasphemers, disobedient to parents, ungrateful, wicked, without affection, without peace, slanderers, incontinent, cruel, without kindness, traitors, insolent, puffed up, lovers of pleasures more than of God, having indeed an appearance of piety but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3).

Beasts of burden are the lustful; herds are the curious; swine [livestock] the gluttonous; animals, the wanton and covetous. Granaries are authoritative utterances; storehouses, the volumes of interpreters; pastures, the sufferings and deeds of the saints, in which examples are found both of the form of life and of the seemliness of conduct. Wheat is spiritual doctrine; dung is vice and sin. [Col. 0335D] In my haste I leave the adaptation of each of these things to the reader’s intelligence.

It follows: “To you, Lord, I shall cry, because fire has consumed the beautiful things of the desert,” etc. The prophet makes the fire an occasion for addressing the Lord, showing the cause of all the aforesaid evils: namely, that when examples of virtue cease, when the teaching of life falls silent, when the fervor of religion grows lukewarm, and when the rigor of perfection becomes sluggish, virtue flees as vices succeed it; the light of knowledge is extinguished as darkness rises; the beauty of religion grows black through increasing negligence; and, in the mind, joy and exultation are punished by the ruin wrought by punishments, as distresses swarm.

Hence Isaiah says: “Therefore my people have been led captive because they lacked knowledge. Their nobles have perished through hunger and their multitude has dried up from thirst. [Col. 0336A] Therefore hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth without any limit; and its mighty men, its people, its high ones, and its glorious ones go down into it” (Isa. 5).

Allegorically, the field is secular life; the region, ordinary ecclesiastical life; the desert, the perfection of religious life. The beautiful things of the desert are the highly adorned hearts of monks and anchorites; the trees of the region are the companies of the Church’s prelates; the beasts are the simple and unlearned; the springs of water are teachers of peoples; the fire is covetousness; the flame, lust.

It follows:

JOEL 2. “Blow the trumpet in Zion; howl upon my holy mountain. Let all the inhabitants of the land be disturbed, for the day of the Lord is coming, for the day of darkness [Col. 0336B] and gloom is near, a day of cloud and whirlwind. Like morning spread out over the mountains, a great and mighty people,” etc.

After the invocation and the many-sided exposition of the disaster, the prophet returns to exhortation of the people, showing the greatness of the impending calamity, the approaching ruin of captivity, so that he may move the people to fear of divine judgment, beneficially stir them to the sorrow of compunction, and profitably arm them for the love of obedience. He does this from the multitude of the disaster, the character of the enemy, the kind of victory, the weight of misery, the ease of triumph, the zeal of evil, the fear of the besieged rulers, and the cowardice of the surrounded people. To fit each point to its proper place is not the purpose of one hastening to explain what follows. [Col. 0336C] Therefore we leave these matters, like the rest, to the reader’s exercise.

The prophet therefore exhorts, hyperbolically, that the trumpet be sounded in Zion, that howling be raised upon the holy mountain, and that all inhabitants of the land be struck with fear. He exhorts, I say, that all together be cast at the feet of divine judgments, if somehow God may look from his prepared dwelling upon the children of men; if he may at some time turn the storm into a breeze; if at last he may lead them back from the shipwreck of captivity to the harbor of consolation, saying: “Blow the trumpet in Zion,” etc.

By Zion understand the citadel of the Temple; by the mountain, the city; by the land, the suburbs. In Zion are the king and princes; in the Temple, prophets and priests; in the land, the people and lesser ranks. The day of the Lord is the coming of the Babylonian army. It is deservedly [Col. 0336D] called the Lord’s, because by divine will it avenges the Lord’s injury, caused by the people’s disobedience. On that day darkness and gloom, cloud and whirlwind are inflicted on the Jewish people: darkness, because they did not know his counsel; gloom, because they did not fear his judgment; cloud, because they did not deserve his aid; whirlwind, because by wickedly provoking him they fell into the shipwreck of so great a disaster.

That day comes like morning spread over the mountains, because they did not contemplate God’s counsel and wisdom, and in the time of their blindness were suddenly overtaken by the distress of necessity, justly fell, and lost foresight in their affairs.

It should be known that Joel in the present passage speaks historically of the Babylonian captivity, as is manifestly inferred from the following words. For he says:

[Col. 0337A] “Like morning spread over the mountains, a great and mighty people. None like it has been from the beginning, nor shall there be after it through the years of generation upon generation. Before its face is a devouring fire, and behind it a burning flame. Before it the land is like a garden of delight; behind it, a desolate wilderness; nor is there anyone who escapes it. Their appearance is like the appearance of horses, and they run like horsemen. They leap over the mountain-tops like the sound of chariots, like the sound of a flame of fire consuming stubble, like a mighty people prepared for battle. Before it peoples shall be tortured; all faces shall be reduced to a cooking-pot. They shall run like mighty men; like men of war they shall climb the wall. Men shall walk in their own paths and shall not turn aside from their tracks. [Col. 0337B] No one shall press his brother; each shall walk in his own path. They shall also fall through the windows and shall not be harmed; they shall enter the city, run along the wall, climb the houses, and enter through the windows like a thief.”

This cannot rightly be understood of Egyptian bondage or Assyrian captivity. In those cases the people alone are taken captive; but in this, namely the Babylonian captivity, the whole region is devastated, the land wholly laid waste, the city destroyed, the kingdom scattered, the Temple utterly overthrown, and the priesthood removed from the midst. Joel carefully describes the arrangement, manner, practice, and undertaking of the Babylonian army, commending it for its multitude, strength, savage cruelty, destructive force, proud ferocity, splendid military equipment, prudent vigilance, terror of harsh rule, subjection of enemies, fear and dread of those who collapse, ease of victory, strength of constancy, providence of concord, protection of itself, protection of its enterprise, and plundering of the enemy.

It follows:

[Col. 0337C] “Before it the earth trembled; the heavens were shaken. The sun and moon were darkened, and the stars withdrew their brightness.”

The earth is the people; the heavens, priests and righteous persons; the sun, the king; the moon, justice; the stars, prophets. “Before it,” he says, “the earth trembled,” because, when the misery of captivity came upon them, prophecy fell silent, royal majesty perished, the worship of justice vanished, and the people, oppressed by disaster, succumbed in fear.

It follows:

[Col. 0337D] “And the Lord gave his voice before his army, because his camps are exceedingly many, because they are strong and carry out his word.”

ALLEGORICAL.

The voice of the Lord is the inspiration of the people; the face of the army was its order, worship, splendor, rite, form, and manner: the order of banners, worship of gods, splendor of arms, rites of operations, form of government, manner of marching. Hence they are strong; hence they carry out his word.

We have briefly touched on these matters historically; now let us examine them allegorically. Some refer this captivity to the final judgment, interpreting the ruin as occurring then because of the aforementioned crimes. This seems to be supported by the Psalmist’s saying: “He sent among them the wrath of his indignation, indignation and wrath and tribulation, visitations through [Col. 0338A] evil angels” (Ps. 77). But I do not see how certain details accord with this interpretation. For how, in that judgment, will their appearance—that is, the appearance of demons—be like the appearance of horses? How will they run as horsemen? How will they leap over mountain-tops? How will they climb a wall like men of war, when it is written even of the good angels in relation to them, as Job says of the apostate angel: “When he is raised up, the angels shall fear and, terrified, shall be purified” (Job 41)?

We leave the obscurity of this explanation to a more penetrating intellect, perhaps framing another interpretation that is clearer and more closely obedient to the text, without prejudice to a better opinion. The prophet Joel, therefore, with the eye of prophecy foresees spiritual Babylon tyrannically laying waste the whole world and cruelly ruling humankind: “He swallows a river and is not weakened; he has confidence that the Jordan may flow into his mouth.” [Col. 0338B] He sees the gentile people devoted to idols, deprived of the grace of prophecy, and bereaved of the privilege of grace. He also contemplates Christ’s coming, the Word’s incarnation, the mission of the Paraclete, the preaching of the apostles, the corner joining the two peoples, the reception of the gentile people and of a very small part of the Jewish people, and contempt for the greater remainder.

Therefore, because of the grace of the received Jewish portion, he exhorts them to sound the trumpet in Zion; because of the wrath directed at the rejected remnant, to howl on the mountain, saying: “Blow the trumpet in Zion; howl upon my holy mountain.” Since it is written, “On that day two shall be in the field, in the bed, at the mill: one shall be taken and the other left” [Col. 0338C] (Matt. 24), he commands those who are to be taken to sound the trumpet in Zion, and those left behind to howl upon the holy mountain.

Zion is the Church, stationed as a watchtower for the coming of her bridegroom. The holy mountain is Christ, of whom the Psalmist says: “The mountain in which it pleased God to dwell” (Ps. 67). Thus some sing and some howl in this Emmanuel. Hence Simeon says: “Behold, this one is set for the fall and resurrection of many in Israel” (Luke 2). These things are said about the Jewish people.

It follows concerning the gentiles: “Let all the inhabitants of the land be disturbed,” etc. The gentiles are rightly called inhabitants of the land because they sought only earthly things and loved only earthly things. Of them the Lord says through the Psalmist: “They indeed sought my soul in vain; they shall enter into the lower parts of the earth; they shall be delivered into the hands of the sword; they shall become portions for foxes” (Ps. 62).

Moreover, at Christ’s coming some gentiles were disturbed unto salvation, while others were disturbed unto death. For there is a confusion that brings death, and a confusion that brings glory. Of those disturbed unto salvation it is read in the psalm: “Seeing thus, they were amazed; they were disturbed; they were moved; trembling seized them” (Ps. 47). Of those disturbed unto death Isaiah says: “The earth shall be shattered with breaking; the earth shall be crushed with crushing; the earth shall be shaken with shaking; the earth shall be stirred with stirring like a drunken man, and it shall be removed like the tent of one night” (Isa. 24).

The day of the Lord is the coming of Christ. This day was one of darkness for rejected gentiles, of gloom [Col. 0339A] for heretics, of whirlwind for faithless Jews, and of cloud for Catholics. Gentiles, blinded by the incarnation of the Word and unable to attain the power of the holy sacrament, said: “Mary either bore a child or did not bear one. If she bore one, she lay with a man. If she lay with a man, what was born was derived from the sinful mass. But what is born from a sinful mass falls under sin. Since this cannot happen to God, Mary’s son was not God.”

Likewise Avicenna: “Two contraries cannot exist together in the same thing. But if Mary’s son is God and man, since God is impassible while man is passible, and the passible and impassible are contraries, two contraries are found together in one.” Thus indeed, Lord, in the multitude of your power your enemies lie to you (Ps. 65). [Col. 0339B] But if Mary did not bear a child, God did not become man. If this is true, the Christian doctrine is utterly false. These are the darknesses of the gentiles, of which Isaiah says: “Behold, the spirit of Egypt shall be broken within her, and I shall overthrow her counsel” (Isa. 19).

Gloom also occupied the heretics. For one whose sight is clouded sees matter from afar but does not perceive form. So too many heretics possessed matter for belief, but lacked the form of faith. Some correctly believed the unity of person in the incarnate Word, but did not soundly believe unity of substance. Others, conversely, soundly affirmed diversity of nature in him but wrongly affirmed diversity of person. Some affirmed unity in the divinity of the Godhead, but unequal power and equal dignity. [Col. 0339C] Very many affirmed equality in all things, but denied unity of nature. Some impiously divided what is one; others madly confused what is divided. This was the gloom of the heretics, of which the Psalmist says: “And darkness was under his feet” (Ps. 17): namely, because in mercy he recalled some heretics from the shipwreck of unbelief, but by just judgment permitted most to go to destruction.

For the Jews also Christ’s incarnation was a whirlwind. Of them the Psalmist says: “According to the multitude of their impieties, cast them out, for they have provoked you, Lord” (Ps. 5). This certainly occurred when the Jewish people were partly slain by the Romans, partly bound in chains, partly relegated into exile, and partly scattered most wretchedly throughout the whole world.

[Col. 0339D] But for Catholics the incarnation of Christ was a day of cloud, which provided them with the shade of grace, the rain of doctrine, sweetness of conscience, and security of glory: shade against the heat of temptation; rain against the dryness of heretical perversity or persuasion; sweetness against the sting of inward reproach; security against the shipwreck of despair. He gave them rain on the mountain, provided shade on the cross, sweetness in the tomb, and security in the resurrection. Hence Isaiah says: “And a tabernacle for shade by day from heat, and for refuge from whirlwind and rain” (Isa. 4).

Alternatively, there are four kinds of people: first, those who never believe; second, those who believe only with difficulty and late; third, those who believe readily and early; and fourth, those who believe readily but not early. [Col. 0340A] To the first kind the incarnation of the Word was a day of darkness; to the second, a day of gloom; to the third, a day of cloud; to the fourth, a day of whirlwind.

This day was like morning spread over the mountains. The mountains are the apostles; morning is the illumination of faith; spreading is love working through faith. Thus Christ’s coming, the Word’s incarnation, was like morning spread over the mountains, because it is written: “His going forth is prepared as the dawn; and he shall come to us as the early and latter rain upon the earth” (Hos. 6).

Or the mountains may be understood as the powerful persons of this age, the philosophers of this world, whom the Word’s incarnation suddenly covered over: by it the wisdom of the age was made foolish, the prudence of the world confounded, and the power of the age trampled down. [Col. 0340B] Hence the Apostle says: “What is weak in God is stronger than all people, and what is foolish is wiser. And God chose the weak things to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1).

It follows: “A great and mighty people.” He calls the company of apostles and the Church of neophytes a people. This people was great, not in numerical quantity but in dignity of merit; mighty, not by bodily strength but by virtue of mind. Great, therefore, not in number but in merit; mighty, not by the force of flesh but by the counsel of mind. Great, because it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18). Mighty, because it is written: “The apostles went rejoicing from the presence of the council because they were judged worthy to suffer reproach for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5). [Col. 0340C] Great, and therefore impenetrable; mighty, and therefore unconquerable.

It follows, continuing its praises: “There has been none like it from the beginning, nor shall there be after it through the years of generation upon generation.” The Savior plainly says this in the Gospel: “Blessed are the eyes that see what you see; for many kings and prophets desired to see what you see and did not see it, and to hear what you hear and did not hear it” (Matt. 13). Isaiah marvels at their glorious life, saying: “Who are these who fly like clouds, and like doves to their windows?” (Isa. 60). In the dove is simplicity of understanding; in the cloud, the building-up of character: namely, the rain of saving doctrine and purity of conscience. In flight are the two wings of love and the ascent of heavenly contemplation.

[Col. 0340D] It follows: “Before its face is a devouring fire, and behind it a burning flame.” The devouring fire is fiery preaching, consuming sins and devouring vices. The burning flame is the radiance of miracles, through which a saving burning and fiery compunction arise in the hearts of the rebellious.

It follows: “Before it the land is like a garden of delight, and behind it a desolate wilderness; nor is there anyone who escapes it.” The garden of delight is the land of curiosity. The garden of delight is the mire of pleasing excess. The garden of delight is the theater of worldly pleasure. The desolate wilderness is mortification of the flesh, contempt for the world, and self-abasement. The apostles made the garden of delight a desolate wilderness, because they reduced the vanity of that wilderness to contempt for the world, curiosity to self-abasement, and excess to mortification.

[Col. 0341A] It follows: “Nor is there anyone who escapes it,” because one necessarily either earns reward by imitating apostolic life and teaching, or incurs punishment by despising it.

As the appearance of horses is their appearance, and like horsemen so they run. In the first is denoted the neighing and ardour of preaching; in the second, conflict for the faith and the toil of engagement. It follows: “Like the sound of chariots over the tops of the mountains they shall leap, like the sound of a flame of fire devouring stubble; like a strong people prepared for battle.” Here, in brief, is inserted the labour and victory of the evangelists, who by their life, miracles, and teaching shattered the pride of the proud. The chariots are the evangelists, the mountains the proud, the sound the preaching of faith, the flame [Col. 0341B] miracles, and the stubble sins.

It follows: “Before his face the peoples shall be tormented; all faces shall be gathered into a pot.” The torment of the peoples is their salutary compunction; the gathering of faces into a pot is their own true and sincere self-knowledge.

It follows: “They shall run like mighty men; like men of war they shall climb the wall.” First is denoted the success of preaching; second, victory in struggle and the obedience of mortification for the faith.

It follows: “Men shall walk in their own ways, and shall not turn aside from their paths.” First is denoted the concord of the preachers; second, perseverance in virtues and faith.

It follows: “No one shall press upon his brother; each shall walk in his own track.” The prophet still pursues the unanimity of the apostles and their most harmonious purpose: they so [Col. 0341C] sowed the Gospel in the world that none should arrogate to himself another’s seed. Hence the Apostle: “I do not dare to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me for the obedience of the nations, by word and deed, in the truth of signs and wonders, in the powers of the Holy Spirit; so that from Jerusalem and round about as far as Illyricum I have filled up the Gospel of Christ” (Rom. 15). Again, in the same place: “Thus I preached this Gospel, not where Christ had already been named, lest I should build upon another’s foundation” (ibid.).

It follows: “And they shall fall through the windows, and shall not be broken down.” The five windows are the dispensation of the Incarnation, or the five modes of divine contemplation. The first mode of contemplation is reflection upon sin and Gehenna; the second, contempt for present things and hope for things to come; the third, judgment and kingdom; the fourth, the condition of the body and its glorification—its condition insofar as it will be passible or impassible, its glorification insofar as it will possess ineffable beauty or resplendent brightness; the fifth, becoming one spirit with God, which is complete conformity in all things. Through these windows the apostles and apostolic men fall beneficially, when, through devout reflection upon these matters, they humbly cast themselves down before their Creator. By thus falling they are not broken down; rather, they are raised up and strengthened, according to the saying: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 14). Hence in the Apocalypse John says: “When those four living creatures gave glory, honour, and blessing to him who sits upon the throne, who lives for ages of ages, the twenty-four [Col. 0342A] elders fell down before him who sat upon the throne, and worshipped him who lives for ages of ages. And they cast their crowns before the throne, saying: ‘You are worthy, O Lord our God, to receive glory, honour, and power’” (Rev. 4), etc.

The five windows of the Incarnation are, namely, his birth, manner of life, teaching, resurrection, and ascension. Through them are seen those five things spoken of concerning contemplation. For through his birth sin and Gehenna were made manifest to many. His manner of life openly taught contempt for present things and the directing of hope toward eternal things. His teaching indeed treats sufficiently of judgment and kingdom. In the resurrection the condition and glorification of the body were shown, because as he himself rose in glory, so too shall we through him. In the ascension, moreover, it was made known to us in some measure how [Col. 0342B] our spirit must be united with God. For the human body could not be raised upward or conveyed without any vehicle except through the divinity united to it.

Through these windows also apostolic men fall, because by diligent meditation upon the aforesaid things they thoroughly humble themselves, crush their flesh, and mortify their members, while truly and particularly directing them toward those things. Yet they are not broken down, because neither the goodness, nor the truth, nor the justice, nor the chastity upon which they rely knows how to harm, deceive, despise, or corrupt; nor does the wisdom, power, might, or eternity to which they are joined know how to be deceived, weakened, overcome, or changed.

It follows:

“They shall enter into the city; they shall run upon the wall; they shall climb up into the houses.” The city here is an assembly of people gathered [Col. 0342C] to live in common. The wall is obstinacy of mind; the houses are the individual consciences hardened by sins. So great shall be the grace and strength of the apostles and apostolic men that they shall even overcome an assembly of malicious people, dissolve obstinacy by the spirit of fortitude, and gain the individual consciences for the spirit of grace and prayer.

It follows: “They shall enter through the windows like a thief.” The windows here are fear—namely, of eternal punishment—sorrow at present exile, hope of heavenly reward, the brevity of this life, and the mutability of fortune. The first looks westward, the second northward, the third eastward, the fourth southward; the fifth considers the centre of this world. Through these they secretly enter the individual [Col. 0342D] consciences, which they readily overcome by gathering the aforesaid things before the eyes of the mind. Fear pricks, sorrow drives out, hope draws, brevity urges, and fortune’s instability puts to flight; and thus the mind of the neophyte hastens in flight toward its homeland.

It follows: “Before his face the earth trembled, and the heavens were shaken.” The earth is sinners; the heavens are the righteous. But the earth trembled at the presence of the apostles unto repentance. All the righteous who were in the world, hearing their teaching, life, and renown, were moved, counting their own righteousness as nothing.

It follows: “The sun and moon were darkened, and the stars withdrew their brightness.” The sun is the wisdom of the age; the moon, the power of this world; the stars, the schools of philosophers; the brightness of the stars, the observance and reputation of the schools. But the sun and moon were darkened [Col. 0343A] before the apostles, because through the foolishness of God the wisdom of the age was destroyed, and through the weakness of God worldly power was trampled down. By the power of signs, the brilliance of miracles, and the bare truth of words, the artificial arrangement of rhetorical colours was abolished, the rhetorical brilliance of speech was obscured, and the observance and splendour of empty schools was voided.

Hence the Psalmist: “You broke open springs and torrents; you dried up the rivers of Ethan” (Ps. 73). By the springs, he understands philosophers; by Ethan, the devil, whose name is interpreted “strong”; his flame consists of the kinds of perverse schools.

It follows: “And the Lord gave his voice before the face of his army, because his camps are exceedingly many, because they are strong and do his word.” The voice of the Lord is divine inspiration—the heavenly voice, I mean, that anointing which teaches concerning all things. Of it the Psalmist says: “The voice of the Lord breaks cedars. The voice of the Lord prepares the deer. The voice of the Lord cuts through the flame of fire. The voice of the Lord shakes the wilderness” (Ps. 18). This voice makes camps, because it joins and orders the companies of the saints. These are indeed many, strong, and do his word: many in the dignity of their merits; strong in the power of signs and authority of miracles; doing his word through obedience to commandments, the eminence of spiritual exercises, and the excellence of counsels.

It follows: “For great is the day of the Lord, and terrible.” For Christ’s coming magnified believers and the righteous; it terrified and condemned unbelievers [Col. 0343C] and reprobates. Great indeed, because “those whom he predestined, them he also called; and those whom he called, them he also justified; and those whom he justified, them he also glorified” (Rom. 8). Terrible, because “it shall be more tolerable for the Ninevites on the day of judgment than for this most wicked generation” (Luke 11). For they believed at Jonah’s preaching; and behold, here is one greater than Jonah.

It follows: “Who shall endure it?” For who can worthily receive within himself the Creator of nature, the fountain of life, the bridegroom of grace, the coming of the Saviour? Or who can endure the weight of wrath, the burden of misery, the punishment of vengeance, “the worm that does not die, the fire that is not quenched” (Mark 9)?

It follows:

“Now therefore, says the Lord, return to me with your whole heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning; and [Col. 0343D] rend your hearts, and not your garments. And return to the Lord your God, because he is gracious and merciful, patient and of great mercy, and ready to relent from evil. Who knows whether God will turn and forgive, and leave behind him a blessing, sacrifice and libation to the Lord our God?”

**Historically.** Under the person of the Lord, the prophet exhorts his people to implore divine mercy and strike upon the ears of highest clemency with lamentations and tearful cries, saying: “Return to me with your whole heart, in fasting and weeping and mourning,” etc. As if he were plainly saying: Since the time of captivity draws near and the Babylonian presses upon you, press on therefore in supplication; devote yourselves to prayer. Return to me, that the Babylonian may turn back; return [Col. 0344A] to me, that the enemy may be turned backward. For “with the holy you will be holy, with the chosen you will be chosen, and with the perverse you will be perverse” (Ps. 17).

**Allegorically**, under the person of the Lord he admonishes every estate of the Church together to flee from the wrath to come, extinguish the flood of sins with tears of repentance, and placate the anger of the heavenly Judge by works of mercy, saying: “Now therefore says the Lord: Return to me,” etc. As if he said: Since the day of destruction is near and the times hasten to be present; since a day both very terrible and great presses upon you; since scarcely anyone will escape the wrath to come; since the strict Judge cannot be conquered, because he is power; cannot be deceived, because he is wisdom; cannot be corrupted, because he is justice; cannot be endured, because he is eternal; cannot be avoided, because he is everywhere—yet he can be entreated, because he is mercy; can be appeased, because he is goodness; can cleanse, because he is the fountain of grace; can satisfy, because he is the bread of life; can soothe, because he is anointing; can adorn, because he is fullness; can make happy and blessed, because he is blessedness. Therefore, you who have turned away, fearing his justice, turn and flee to his mercy. Flee from him to him: from the rigour of justice to the bosom of mercy.

The Lord, who is to be feared, says this; he who is truth commands what is just, useful, and honourable. “Return,” he says, “to me,” etc. There are four things: two evils and two goods; one evil and another worse, one good and another better. Turning away and overthrow: behold the two evils. Conversion and return: behold the two goods. Turning away from God comes through negligence; overthrow comes from the Devil through malice. Conversion to God comes through repentance; return to him through innocence.

Turning away occurs in three ways: through vanity, pleasure, and curiosity—through the vanity of the world, pleasure in oneself, and curiosity about one’s neighbour. Overthrow also occurs in three ways: through precipitancy, malice, and despair—through the precipitancy of sin, the malice of envy, and despair of pardon. But conversion occurs in three ways: confession, compunction, and mortification—confession of the mouth, compunction of the mind, mortification of the flesh—so that truth may be in the mouth, purity in the mind, and chaste sobriety in the flesh. Return also occurs in three ways: devotion, love, and contemplation—devotion to grace, love of justice, and contemplation [Col. 0344D] of glory.

Therefore you who have turned away from God through the vice of negligence, who have been overthrown and submerged in the flood of malice, “return,” he says, “to me with your whole heart.” There is conversion of heart and conversion of deed. Conversion of heart, moreover, is one thing when it is with the whole heart, another when it is in part. The Lord seeks that which is with the whole heart, because it suffices for salvation. He rejects the other, which is partial, because it is feigned and far from salvation. Hence it is written: “The Holy Spirit of discipline will flee from the feigned” (Wis. 1).

For there are three things in the heart: reason, will, and memory. Reason concerns future things, will present things, memory past things. Reason seeks future things, will loves present things, memory retains past things. Reason enlightens, will loves, memory preserves. Therefore, when reason [Col. 0345A] seeks and finds the highest good, will receives and loves it, and memory carefully preserves and more closely embraces it, then the soul turns itself to God with its whole heart. But when reason, lulled to sleep, ceases to seek heavenly things; or when lukewarm will does not care to love; or when sluggish memory scorns to preserve, then the soul becomes feigned—first falling into the vice of ignorance, second into the fault of negligence, third into the sin of malice. In either case the soul is manifestly feigned; otherwise ignorance could be driven away by the light of reason, negligence excluded by the zeal of the will, and malice lulled to sleep by the diligence of memory.

Reason seeking therefore gives birth to learning; will embracing, to love; memory holding fast, to edification. The first produces the light of knowledge, the second the affection of justice, the third preserves the treasury [Col. 0345B] of grace. This is the conversion of heart which God requires. This is that which altogether suffices for salvation. Conversion of deed follows: “In fasting,” he says, “and weeping and mourning.” Mourning refers to confession, weeping to compunction, fasting to mortification.

It follows:

“And rend your hearts, and not your garments.” The rending of hearts is the dispersal of evil affections. Garments are the examples of the saints. We are therefore commanded to rend our hearts but preserve those garments unharmed, because an impure will must be chastised and purified by the austerity of repentance, while the examples of the saints must be taken as instruction in justice.

Hence Job says: “You renew [Col. 0345C] your witnesses against me, and multiply your wrath against me, and punishments wage war within me” (Job 10). Again, the same: “He shall look upon men and say: ‘I have sinned and truly done wrong; and I have not received what I deserved.’ Then he shall see the face of the Lord in joy, and he shall restore to man his righteousness” (Job 33). The examples of saints are indeed of great usefulness: they instruct us unto knowledge, draw us toward pardon, kindle [the text reads *accedunt*, perhaps *accendunt*] us unto grace, form us unto justice, and advance us unto glory. Hence in the Psalmist’s words: “He made a memorial of his wonderful works” (Ps. 110), etc.

It follows: “And return to the Lord your God.” “Lord,” he says, because he is to be feared; “God,” because he is to be loved; “your,” because he is Creator. “Your,” he says, because he is the Creator of nature; “God,” because he is the giver of grace; “Lord,” [Col. 0345D] because he is the avenger of sin.

It follows: “Because he is gracious and merciful, patient, and abundant in mercy [of great mercies], ready to relent from evil.” He is gracious, enduring the sinner’s anger; merciful, enduring cruelty; patient, enduring contempt; abundant in mercy, enduring hatred; ready to relent from evil, enduring the shipwreck of despair. Gracious, I say, because he turns the anger of enemies into gentleness; merciful, because he turns cruelty into piety; patient, because he turns contempt into compunction; abundant in mercy, because he turns hatred into love; ready to relent from evil, because he raises the abyss of despair into the grace of contemplation.

These have been expounded in their natural order; now let them be expounded in an artificial order. He is therefore ready to relent from evil [Col. 0346A] when he draws despair to repentance; abundant in mercy when he draws hatred to pardon; patient when he draws contempt to grace; merciful when he draws cruelty to innocence; gracious when he draws anger and rancour to the glory of kisses.

It follows: “Who knows whether he will turn and forgive, and leave behind him a blessing?” Here “who knows” does not signify doubt but love. As if he said: Who knows whether a person will turn and God forgive? Let conversion only come first; no delay of pardon follows. But no one knows the day and hour of conversion except the Son alone, and him to whom the Son wills to reveal it. “For the Spirit breathes where he wills; and you hear his voice, but do not know whence he comes or whither he goes” (John 3).

It follows: “And leave behind him a blessing.” There are three kinds [Col. 0346B] of divine blessing: the first he gives before himself; the second he bestows beside himself; the third he leaves behind himself. There are likewise three kinds of good people. The first are the innocent; the second, those who immediately recover their senses; the third, those who finally repent. The innocent are those who always live without crime, who continually stand before God, who constantly walk in his presence. Those who immediately recover are those who fall indeed, but to whom the divine hand is soon extended and who rise again at once. Those who finally repent are those who long rest in their own dregs and finally, by divine prompting, rise to repentance.

To the innocent the Lord gives blessing before himself; to those who immediately recover, he bestows it beside himself; to those who finally repent, he leaves it behind himself. To the innocent [Col. 0346C] he gives the first fruits of blessing; to those who immediately recover, its riches; to those who finally repent, its remnants.

It follows: “Sacrifice and libation to the Lord our God.” These are the remnants of blessing: namely, works of sacrifice and libation. Sacrifice concerns the mortification of the flesh; libation, the compunction of the mind. Since we have perpetrated wicked works of the flesh and followed unlawful pleasures of the mind, let us render opposites for opposites, so that we may extinguish the works of the flesh through mortification and unlawful pleasures through compunction.

Alternatively: sacrifice can be understood as righteous action, libation as holy contemplation. In this sense libation is attributed to God, sacrifice to the Lord. For one must act rightly because the Lord is to be feared; God is tasted, and therefore is to be loved.

It follows:

“Blow the trumpet in Zion; sanctify a fast; call an assembly; gather the people; sanctify the Church; unite the elders; gather the little ones and those nursing at the breast. Let the bridegroom go forth from his chamber, and the bride from her bridal room. Between the porch and the altar the priests, ministers of the Lord, shall weep, and shall say: ‘Spare, O Lord, spare your people; and do not give your inheritance to reproach, so that the nations rule over them. Why should they say among the peoples: “Where is their God?”’”

The prophet still commands his people to persist in devout prayer and humbly apply themselves to supplication, showing that every age, rank, sex, and condition is subject to danger. Therefore he counsels that supplication be made by all together.

**Allegorically.** Having shown the Church its dangers, [Col. 0347A] he exhorts them to hasten to the harbour of repentance, lest they perhaps feel the hand of the Lord growing heavy upon them. “For it is terrible to fall into the hands of the living God” (Heb. 10). He says therefore: “Blow the trumpet in Zion,” etc. We pass over the exposition of these matters, because elsewhere we have said much about them. The elders are those perfected in virtue; the little ones are those endowed with simplicity and innocence; those nursing at the breast are unlearned persons placed under instruction. The elders are united because they use reason; the little ones and those nursing are gathered because they are placed under instruction and serve under the rod.

The bridal chamber is love; the bedchamber, contemplation. Yet the same soul becomes bridegroom and bride in different respects. It is a bride when, secretly united to the Word by love, it conceives with a certain, so to speak, ineffable sweetness which it displays as certain heavenly signs break forth outwardly. It becomes bridegroom too when, joined to wisdom and devoted to it alone, it bears offspring through spiritual union by the ministry of teaching. Thus teaching in wisdom makes the bridegroom; the prerogative of grace makes the bride.

But in a time of affliction let the bridegroom go forth from his bedchamber—that is, from the pursuit of wisdom—and let the bride leave her bridal chamber—that is, descend from the privilege of contemplative grace—and let them undergo the squalor of repentance, in pursuit of pardon. For when the heavenly Bridegroom sees his bride weeping and groaning, anxious and supplicating, bearing the burden of the day and heat with others and for others, he is immediately turned from anger, has compassion on the sufferer, and, impatient of delay, is soon appeased and grants pardon through the sweetness of the heavenly kiss; [Col. 0347C] he grants to his one beloved the favour of the people.

Hence Moses, on behalf of the people in the role of a bride, prays: “I beseech you, Lord, this people has sinned a great sin, and made for themselves gods of gold. Either forgive them this offence, or, if you will not, blot me out of your book which you have written” (Exod. 32). To him the Lord says: “I will forgive them for the present; but on the day of vengeance I shall visit them” (ibid.). Hence we frequently read in the Old Testament that, for Isaac’s sake and for Jacob’s sake, very many sins were forgiven to the transgressing people and many calamities ceased.

Alternatively: the bedchamber is carnal will; the bridal chamber is curiosity. Therefore, in a time of mourning and repentance to be performed, curiosity must be excluded and carnal will banished, so that iniquity may be expiated and the Divinity propitiated by the sacrifice of continence and mortification. Thus Isaiah says: “O Lord, in distress they sought you; in the tribulation of murmuring your instruction was with them” (Isa. 26).

It follows: “Between the porch and the altar the priests, ministers of the Lord, shall weep and say: ‘Spare, O Lord, spare your people,’” etc. The porch is fear of God; the Holy of Holies is contemplation of the Bridegroom; the altar is perfect love. The people are in the porch; the high priest is about the altar. In the middle of the temple the priests mourn and the ministers groan; all equally perform the office of reconciliation. Between the porch and the altar the priesthood makes supplication for the people, because it is both pressed by fear lest divine mercy abandon the people and governed by love, so that with humble conscience it presumes to approach the throne of grace.

Between the porch [Col. 0348A] and the altar God is appeased, because the person whom fear keeps from unlawful things and love raises to lofty things is wholly reconciled. Between the porch, I say, and the altar fruitful and humble repentance is made: fear pricks it, lest it grow sluggish; love kindles it, lest it grow lukewarm. It is useful and fruitful, I say, because fear has excluded rash presumption and love has cast off the shame of faint-heartedness.

Therefore they say: “Spare, O Lord, spare your people,” etc. There are three principal judgments of a human being: the first concerning oneself; the second concerning one’s neighbour; the third concerning oneself and one’s neighbour. In the first one ought to be strict, in the second merciful, in the third just. For each person ought strictly to accuse himself, mercifully judge his neighbour, and justly examine himself and his neighbour. Since, then, we are lenient and merciful toward ourselves but strict and severe toward our neighbour, we say: “Spare, O Lord, our own leniency; spare our strictness toward our brother; spare, I say, what we have done unjustly toward ourselves; spare what we have done wickedly toward our neighbour.”

Or, because there are two places and likewise two dangers joined to them—places, the world and hell; dangers, vanity and calamity—we say: “Spare, O Lord, from the vanity of the world; spare from the calamity of the underworld. Spare, I say, from the first lest it afflict us; spare from the second lest it swallow us up.”

Or, because the human person consists of a double nature, namely body and soul—and in each nature we have frequently sinned, for in the soul we have acted impiously and in the body wickedly—let us say: “Spare, O Lord, the impiety of the mind; spare the iniquity of the body.”

Or, because two laws have been given us, the law of nature and [Col. 0348C] the written law, and we are transgressors of both, let us say: “Spare, O Lord, the violation of the first; spare the transgression of the second.”

Or, because action is given us for the perfection of this present life, while contemplation is given as a pledge of blessedness for a foretaste of the future; and because in action we have been negligent, while from contemplation we have become proud, let us say: “Spare our negligence; spare our pride.”

“Spare your people”: people, that is, the assembly of persons gathered to you to live justly. “Your,” created by you and redeemed by you—whether either sense be intended by “your.”

It follows: “And do not give your inheritance to reproach, so that the nations rule over them.” As if he said: “Do not hand over to beasts the souls that confess you; do not forget forever the souls of your poor” (Ps. 73).

It follows: [Col. 0348D] “Why should they say among the peoples, ‘Where is their God?’” As if he said: When your people are deprived of counsel [the reading is uncertain] and, oppressed by the wicked, seem to lack help, you are judged by unbelievers to be either wicked or powerless. “But by this I have known that you desired me: because my enemy shall not rejoice over me” (Ps. 40).

It follows:

“The Lord was zealous for his land, and spared his people.” Zeal is an ardour of mind disposed toward compassion for nature, punishment of sin, and devotion to grace. Zeal therefore usefully scourges the servant, beneficially corrects the son, and carefully and faithfully preserves marriage: the servant by punishment, the son by compassion, marriage by devotion. Historically, the land is the synagogue; allegorically, the Church; morally, the faithful soul: the first because of earthly desire, the second because of [Col. 0349A] stability in faith, the third because of the virtue of humility and the dryness of abstinence.

It follows: “And the Lord answered and said to his people: ‘Behold, I shall send you grain, wine, and oil, and you shall be filled with them; and I shall no longer make you a reproach among the nations.’” And the other things that follow, up to the words: “And it shall come to pass after these things: I shall pour out my Spirit upon all flesh.”

Truly, “God does not despise a contrite and humbled heart” (Ps. 50). Truly, in due time he looks upon the quiet, humble person who trembles at his words. Truly, “the valleys abound with grain”; truly, he desires mercy more than sacrifice, and knowledge of God more than burnt offering. This the present prophetic utterance demonstrates. For above, in the course of his supplication, he lamentably described the coming and cruelty of enemies, the crushing of the land and devastation of animals, pestilence and destruction, the people’s confusion, the affliction of the elders, and the squalor of the virgins; and he prescribed the rigour of repentance, the dryness of abstinence, the depth of sobs and groans, and discipline. He acted, received, returned: he practised repentance, received mercy, returned to grace.

O fruitful and manly repentance! O woman of strength, most faithful mediatrix of sinners, to be embraced! O second plank after shipwreck! O refuge of the poor, help of the wretched, hope of exiles, support of the weak, light of the blind, consolation of the bereaved, rod of the wanton, bolt against vices, storehouse of virtues! You alone bend the Judge, arraign the Creator, and cast down the Almighty: when conquered, you conquer; when tormented, you torment; when wounding, you heal; when you beneficially succumb, you triumph gloriously. You alone, while all others are silent, boldly ascend the throne of grace. You reconcile David while leading him by the hand; restore Peter; enlighten Paul; confidently insert the publican, taken from the tax office, into the choir of apostles. You raise Mary from the brothel into heaven and unite her to Christ; you place in Paradise the thief fastened to the cross, still flourishing with blood. What more need be said? The heavenly court belongs to your jurisdiction.

This the present prophetic page clearly teaches, when by the labour and fruit of repentance the people not only escaped the shipwreck [Col. 0349D] of misfortune and returned not merely to their former state of grace, but even rejoiced in the coming of the Saviour, was enlightened by his teaching, shaped by his life, healed by his passion, strengthened by his resurrection, glorified by his ascension, endowed in the present with the same Paraclete Spirit, doubled its crown, and carried off double rewards.

Let the dog-like eloquence of worldly rhetoric be silent, which declares the divine utterances rustic and unpolished. Behold, in the present passage a coloured sentence is set forth according to the rule of antithesis, returning opposites for opposites. Against the land’s devastation he sets its abundance; against hunger, satiety; against reproach, the security of glory; against the enemies’ invasion and cruelty, their stench and destruction; against the barrenness of fruits and the dryness of trees, their shoots and abundance; against hunger for the word and thirst for teaching, he introduces the fountain of life and the teacher of righteousness; against sadness, joy; against confusion, consolation; against reproachful speech, glory; against death, life; against ashes, a crown. I leave it to the reader to match each thing with its counterpart, because I hasten to explain the winding folds of allegory.

It should be known, however, that the present passage is an evident prophecy of the coming of the Saviour, through whom the spiritual enemy is extinguished, spiritual hunger expelled, abundance restored, and grace renewed. “Behold,” he says, “I shall send you grain and wine,” etc. Grain is the teaching of life; wine, the ardour of spiritual understanding; oil, the sweetness of conscience. Or grain is the grace [Col. 0350B] of the Eucharist; wine, spiritual joy; oil, which floats above all liquids, the grace of contemplation. Or by wine are understood works of repentance; by grain, works of wisdom; by oil, because it anoints, works of mercy; because it shines, works of grace; because it nourishes, works of justice.

It follows: “And you shall be filled with it.” Truly, one whose inner being is filled with such feasts does not remain fasting. “And I shall no longer make you a reproach among the nations.” That is, no one who pursues and loves such things incurs reproach, but is crowned with glory and honour.

It follows:

“And him who is from the north I shall remove far from you, and cast him out into a land impassable and desolate; his face toward the eastern sea, and his end [Col. 0350C] toward the last sea. And his stench and rottenness shall rise, because he acted proudly.”

**Historically.** According to some, he speaks of Sennacherib and his army. He acted proudly when he blasphemed God; he was cast out into an impassable and desolate land when, fleeing through the desert in Persia, he was killed by his sons in the temple of his god Nesrac. What he says—“his face toward the eastern sea, and his end toward the last sea”—means this: his intention was to cross the Jordan and conquer Jerusalem; but the outcome was otherwise, because he fell near the Euphrates in Persia. The Hebrew language calls gatherings of waters “seas.” Thus, by the eastern sea he here means the Jordan; by the last sea, the Euphrates. His words, “His stench and rottenness rose,” refer to the destruction of his army. Of it Isaiah says: “The angel of the Lord went out and struck one hundred and eighty-five thousand in the camp of the Assyrians. They arose in the morning, and behold, all were dead bodies” (Isa. 33).

According to others, who judge more soundly, the discourse concerns Nebuchadnezzar. He was expelled into an impassable and desolate land when, made mad, he lived for a long time with brute animals. His face was toward the eastern sea and his end toward the last sea because, as the histories assert, his intention was first to conquer the eastern region and then to subject the western region to himself. The statement that [Col. 0351A] his stench and rottenness rose means this: Hebrew tradition teaches that, after Nebuchadnezzar’s death, his son Evilmerodach, fearing that his father might return to life, drew his body out of the tomb, burned it, and reduced it to ashes. He divided these into four pouches and tied them around the necks of four eagles; having stationed these in the four quarters of the world, he allowed them to fly away.

**Allegorically.** The discourse concerns the ancient enemy, the apostate angel, who through Christ’s incarnation, the word of faith, and the grace of baptism was expelled into the barrenness of the Gentile and Jewish people. The eastern sea is the elect; the last sea, the reprobate; the face, intention; the end, confinement. Or the eastern sea is the first fruits of the election of the Gentiles; the last sea, the faith of the Jews; his stench is the death of Antichrist; his rottenness, the sentence of judgment upon him.

**Morally.** The land is the reprobate soul; impassable, because it lacks the visitation of elect angels; desolate, because it lacks the fruit of virtues and seed of good conduct. The demon’s expulsion is confession of sin. The eastern sea is the mind made bitter through compunction and made eastern through the devotion of contemplation. The last sea is the mind made bitter by the stench of conscience and swallowed up by despair of pardon. His face is the crafty intention to harm; his end, the fury and madness of triumphing. His stench is hatred of sin; his rottenness, contempt for the world.

It follows:

“Do not fear, O land”—behold the consolation of the land—“exult [Col. 0351C] and rejoice, because the Lord has acted mightily.” Rejoice, Judaea, at the confusion and death of your enemy. Rejoice, Church, at the coming of your Saviour in the flesh. Rejoice, faithful soul, at the coming of your bridegroom into the mind. Rejoice in the merit of virtues; exult in the reward of heavenly things; rejoice in gifts of grace; exult in crowns of glory.

It follows:

The beasts of the field, do not fear; for the beauties of the wilderness have sprung up; for the tree has borne its fruit: the fig tree and the vine have yielded their strength.

**HISTORICALLY.** After the destruction of the enemy, after the shipwreck of captivity, Judaea recovered the tranquil countenance of her former prosperity, the promise of abundance.

**ALLEGORICALLY** [Col. 0351D], however, the tree of the Lord’s Passion bore its fruit; the fig tree, the power and sweetness of the resurrection. At the coming of the Paraclete, the vine of the apostles yielded the fruit of propagation. Hence the beauties of the wilderness sprang up, because glorious religious communities were propagated through imitation of the Passion, hope of the resurrection, and apostolic teaching and life. The beasts of the field are persons living a secular life. Let the beasts of the field therefore not fear, because the beauties of the wilderness have sprung up: for, through the teaching and holiness of religious persons, secular people are drawn to reverence for the sacraments, obedience to the commandments, innocence of conduct, the higher way of the counsels, imitation of the Lord’s Passion, hope of the heavenly resurrection [Col. 0352A], and concern for, and fruitfulness in, religious propagation. It follows:

And you, daughters of Zion, rejoice in the Lord your God; for he has given you the teacher of righteousness, and he will cause the early and the latter rain to descend upon you, as in the beginning. And the threshing-floors shall be filled with grain, and the presses shall overflow with wine and oil. And I shall restore to you the years which the locust, the bruchus, the blight, and the caterpillar consumed: my great strength, which I sent among you. And you shall eat, eating, and shall be satisfied; and you shall praise the name of the God of Israel, who has done wonderful things with you; and my people shall not be put to shame for ever. And you shall know that I am in the midst of Israel. I am the Lord your God, and there is no other; and my people shall not be put to shame for ever.

**HISTORICALLY.** [Col. 0352B] After consoling the land, its fruits, trees, and animals, he proceeds to console human beings, saying: “And you, daughters of Zion, rejoice,” etc. “For I have given you the teacher of righteousness.” The Hebrews maintain that the teacher of righteousness is Hezekiah, of whom it is written: “He destroyed the high places, broke the statues, cut down the groves, and smashed the bronze serpent which Moses had made” (4 Kings 18). Therefore after him there was none like him among all the kings of Judah, nor among those before him. And he clung to the Lord and did not depart from his footsteps, and he kept the commandments which the Lord had commanded. Other Hebrews identify him with Josiah, of whom it is written: “This man did what was right in the sight of the Lord, and walked in all the ways [Col. 0352C] of David his father; and he did not turn aside either to the right or to the left” (2 Chronicles 34).

**ALLEGORICALLY.** The teacher of righteousness is Christ: the teacher who teaches humanity knowledge; indeed, the teacher who “found every way of instruction and gave it to Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved.” He is the teacher of righteousness, of whom it is written: “Master, we know that you are true and teach the way of God in truth, and care for no one; for you do not regard the persons of men” (Matthew 22). Of righteousness indeed, because he “shook his hands free from every bribe”; truly of righteousness, because he renders to each according to his works (Matthew 16). Of righteousness, I say, because he justly blinds, justly justifies, justly reproves, justly glorifies, and justly condemns.

The early rain is knowledge of the spiritual Law; the latter rain [Col. 0352D] is the grace of the Gospel. Or the early rain is the utterances of Christ himself and of his apostles; the latter rain, the expositions, canons, and decrees of the spiritual Fathers. The threshing-floors are the minds of believers, accustomed to the yoke of discipline, worn smooth by the paths of religion, and refined by the traditions of regular discipline.

The winepresses are the hearts themselves, placed between hope and fear, having constancy below and patience above: constancy in temptation and patience in tribulation—in the temptation of vices and the tribulation of scourges. Constancy presses and holds off from above; patience lies below and bears the weight. Constancy repels vices; patience bears struggles. Between these two the holy mind, as though placed in a winepress, is pressed, cleared of sediment, and strained: it is pressed by scourges [Col. 0353A], cleared of vices, strained free from idleness. It is pressed by calamity, cleared of iniquity, strained free from vanity. Hence is drawn forth the groaning of pure confession; hence flow the anxious tears of compunction; hence pour the sighs of joyful devotion; hence melt the desires of sweetest love; hence are drawn the clearest drops of contemplation.

Grain is the perfection of righteousness; wine, the brightness of spiritual understanding; oil, the sweetness of a most pure conscience. It follows: “And I shall restore to you the years which the locust consumed,” etc. For at Christ’s coming the years which the aforesaid plague had devoured are restored to us, because in him he gave us true humility against the locust, saying: “Learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart” (Matthew 11). Against [Col. 0353B] the *bruchus*, perfect sobriety, saying: “See that your hearts are not weighed down by dissipation, drunkenness, and the cares of this life” (Luke 21). Against blight, perfect patience, saying: “If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, offer him the other also” (Matthew 5). Against the caterpillar, perfect chastity, saying: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning” (Luke 12), etc.

He exterminated the locust, therefore, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit. Blessed are those who mourn” (Matthew 5). The *bruchus*: “Blessed are the merciful” (ibid.). The blight: “Blessed are the peacemakers. Blessed are the meek” (ibid.). The caterpillar: “Blessed are the pure in heart” (ibid.). It follows: “My great strength, which I sent against you.” Christ was indeed the great strength whom the Father sent into the world, since he is “reaching mightily from end [Col. 0353C] to end and disposing all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8). He conquered the devil, despoiled hell, erased the written bond, brought back the captive, led the servant by the hand, and kept himself unharmed.

It follows: “And you shall eat, eating, and shall be satisfied,” etc. You shall eat the food of sweetness, namely the teaching of righteousness; the food of strength, namely the bread of life. It follows: “And my people shall not be put to shame for ever.” As though he said: Because they endure shame and reproach with me in the present, everlasting joy shall be upon their heads. Hence the Saviour says to the disciples: “You are those who have remained with me in my temptations; and I appoint for you, as my Father appointed for me, a kingdom” (Luke [Col. 0353D] 22), etc. It follows:

And it shall come to pass after these things that I shall pour out my Spirit upon all flesh; and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy. Your old men shall dream dreams, and your young men shall see visions. But even upon my servants and maidservants in those days I shall pour out my Spirit. And I shall give portents in heaven and on earth: blood, fire, and a vapour of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes; and it shall come to pass that whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.

Let Appella the Jew be ashamed here; let him be ashamed of his blindness and madness—he who boasts that he is a guide of the blind and possesses the lamp of the Law—so that in this passage he may detect the darkness of his error and the gloom of his ignorance. Let my ass [Col. 0354A] lay down its burdens for me; let it wait until we go up the mountain, and after we have worshipped, we shall return to it; and, seeing that rest is good and that the land is most excellent, let it put its shoulder under the burden. Let it tell me, I say, where the Lord poured out the Spirit; let it tell where sons, old men, and young men saw prophecies, dreams, and visions. But since it may somehow be able to explain these matters away, let it at least say where the Lord gave blood, fire, and vapour; where the sun was turned into darkness and the moon changed into blood. And when it cannot show this, let Christ’s wisdom reign, glorified by its children.

The present text, therefore, is properly understood of Christ’s coming; the prophecy, closed concerning the sending of the Paraclete Spirit, is plainly opened. But first we must consider what is said: “And it shall come to pass [Col. 0354B] after these things.” What does “after these things” mean? What had he said above to which what follows ought to be referred? We must therefore see how the text coheres. For above the prophet had set forth in many ways the common misfortune of humankind: he had foretold the prayers of the people, the laments of the priests, the desolation of the virgins, and the sighs of the fathers. Then he introduced Christ’s coming, the incarnation of the Word, and the dispensation of the mystery for the liberation of the people and the removal of misfortune; and afterwards he added the illumination of the Gentiles and the perfection of all things, saying: “And it shall come to pass after these things: I shall pour out my Spirit,” etc.

We read that the Lord took from the spirit of Moses and placed what had been taken upon the seventy elders. We likewise read that Elisha received a double spirit [Col. 0354C] of Elijah; but until now we have not read that Christ poured out his own Spirit. Here, however, he poured it out: he did not take it from Moses, nor seize a double portion from Elijah, but generously distributed what was his own.

We should note what is said: “I poured out.” First he poured, secondly he poured in, thirdly he poured out. He poured in Paradise, poured in in the wilderness, and poured out in the upper room. In Paradise, by giving the law of nature; in the wilderness, the precepts and ceremonies of the written Law; in the upper room, the fullness of grace. Hence of the first it is said: “The Lord breathed into Adam” (Genesis 2). And of the second: “God called Moses from the midst of the darkness” (Exodus 24), etc. Hence the *infula* is so called as though *intus fula* [“dark within”], because spiritual understanding was enclosed beneath the veil of the Law and overshadowed by the darkness of its outer bark. [Col. 0354D] But in the third instance the Holy Spirit descended in tongues of fire, because “from his fullness we have all received” (John 1). Thus he first poured by watering the threshing-floor of nature; secondly poured in the torrent of teaching; thirdly poured out the river of grace.
