These three may also fittingly be referred to the incarnation of the Word. For before the resurrection he poured, teaching openly, performing miracles, and bestowing benefits. After the resurrection he poured in, revealing himself, as it were, secretly to those whom he wished; breathing the Spirit upon the disciples seated in the closed room and saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20), etc. On the day of Pentecost he poured out the fullness of grace. He poured out, I say, not by diminishing anything of divine wisdom, but by granting more abundant gifts of grace than usual. As [Col. 0355A] though he said: At the beginning of the world I watered dry nature; amid the desolation of the wilderness, I dripped teaching into the bosom of Moses’ Law; in the fullness of time I shall pour out the abundance of grace.

This outpouring was indeed necessary and fitting in the last time. For there were three things: ignorance, concupiscence, and malice—ignorance of good, concupiscence for evil, and the malice of impenitence. Therefore the Son came, the wisdom and power of God; the Paraclete, his goodness, was sent. Wisdom poured forth removed the blemish of ignorance; power poured in cleansed the filth of concupiscence. The outpouring of the Spirit washed away the dregs of malice. Wisdom enlightened, power healed, goodness calmed. Foreseeing this, and extending the eye of prophecy into the future, the Psalmist said: “According to the multitude of your mercies blot out my iniquity [Col. 0355B]. Wash me yet more, O Lord, from my iniquity; and cleanse me from my sin” (Psalm 50). As though he said: Blot out by pouring forth, wash by pouring in, cleanse by pouring out. By pouring forth wisdom, blot ignorance from my eyes; by pouring in power, wash concupiscence from my inmost parts; by pouring out goodness, eradicate malice from my whole body.

It follows: “Upon all flesh.” “Upon all flesh” is said hyperbolically; or “upon all flesh,” that is, upon flesh of every kind. What is meant by “of every kind, universal”? Namely, every age, every condition, every profession, every order. Observe the richly ornamented abundance of divine speech, to be preferred to the flowers and colours of Quintilian and Tully. Observe, I say, these three placed in succession: prophecy, dreams, vision. [Col. 0355C] Observe then three others: sons, old men, young men. Sons prophesy, old men dream, young men see. Sons prophesied—for example, Agabus concerning Paul’s bonds; Paul also concerning the destruction of the Roman Empire and the coming of Antichrist; likewise the four daughters of Philip, etc. Old men also dreamed—for example, Paul, to whom the Lord appeared, saying: “Cross over into Macedonia and help us” (Acts 16). Young men saw—for example, Paul, who was caught up into the third heaven and then into Paradise; Peter also saw the angel of the Lord leading him out of prison; John also saw the Lord speaking with him and saying: “Come, my dear one; it is time for you to feast in my presence with my brethren.”

Mystically, humble penitence makes one a servant or maidservant; steadfast obedience makes one young; just innocence makes one old; perfect love adopts one as son or daughter. [Col. 0355D] There are also three kinds of vision. The first is material, the second spiritual, the third intellectual. The first is with matter and form; the second without matter but with form; the third without matter and without form. The first apprehends things composed of elements; the second imagined things; the third is foreign to every delimitation, in some manner apprehending God, and also virtues and vices.

There are likewise three kinds of dreams: one of the sediment-laden mind, another of the sober mind, the third of the clarified mind. The first kind serves falsehood; the second is subject either to truth or to falsehood; the third contemplates truth. And, to introduce something from the secrets of natural philosophy [Col. 0356A], the first kind occurs before the digestion of real phantasms, the second during their digestion, the third after their digestion. In the first kind the soul is overwhelmed by the mass of phantasms: hence the error of falsehood. In the second, because the soul begins to be clarified, it begins to behold some light; yet, because it remains largely sediment-laden, it quickly yields, deceived, to falsehood. In the third, the burden of sediment-laden phantasms is strained out completely: hence the splendour of truth. Thus the first kind of dream is deceptive, the second revelatory, the third contemplative.

There are also three kinds of prophecy. The first is wonderful, the second uncertain, the third humble. Prophecy is divine inspiration, pronouncing hidden events with unchanging truth. Humble prophecy, then, concerns the elements and things composed of elements; uncertain prophecy concerns human conduct and human counsels; wonderful prophecy concerns the truth of God’s judgments and his mysteries. Humble prophecy concerns what is near and known; uncertain prophecy, what is near and unknown; wonderful prophecy, what is hidden and unknown. The first and second kinds therefore belong to daughters, the third to sons. At the coming of the Paraclete, then, sons and daughters prophesy in every kind of prophecy; old men dream with the contemplative kind of dream; young men see with the intellectual and revelatory kind of vision.

Servants also receive the outpouring of the Spirit. But because there are three kinds of servants, we must see who are God’s servants receiving the outpouring of the Paraclete. The first are servants of nature, the second of sin, the third of grace. The first are servants of the world, the second [Col. 0356C] of sin, the third of Christ. Upon these last the Paraclete is poured out.

But Christ’s servitude also has three distinct degrees, corresponding to three fears. The first is fear of punishment, by which evil is avoided: this is good. The second is fear of losing one’s reward, by which one labours anxiously in the Lord’s vineyard: this is better. The third is fear of giving offence, by which a person fears all his works, knowing that God will not spare the offender (Job 9): this is best. A servant at the first degree receives a pouring; at the second, an infusion; at the third, an outpouring. It follows:

“And I shall give portents in heaven above and on earth below: blood, fire, and a vapour of smoke. The sun shall be turned into darkness,” etc. The Lord gave portents [Col. 0356D] in heaven, because in his Passion the sun hid the rays of its light. We also believe that the moon was turned to blood, although we read this in no history, because it was spoken by the prophet; and, since it was affirmed by the apostles, there can be no doubt about it. He gave portents on earth, because the earth trembled with so violent and unprecedented a movement that tombs were opened and rocks were split (Luke 21). He gave blood when Christ, before his Passion, prayed at length and, having entered into agony, drops of blood ran down to the ground. The vapours are the flow of his tears. The fire is the Holy Spirit.

**ALLEGORICALLY.** The sun is Christ; the moon, the Church. The sun turned into darkness is Christ fastened to the cross. Hence Jeremiah, speaking of the blindness of the Jews, says: “You will give them, Lord, [Col. 0357A] a shield of heart—your labour” (Lamentations 3). The moon turned into blood is the Church imitating Christ’s Passion. Blood signifies the profession of the martyrs. Fire signifies the choir of virgins burning with the ardour of love. Vapour is the frequent and devout compunction of the continent. These things indeed followed, so that the moon was turned, before the great and terrible day came. The great and terrible day is the day of the Passion and resurrection: great for believers, terrible for unbelievers; terrible for those who said, “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matthew 27); great for those who said, “Truly this man was the Son of God” (Mark 15).

Otherwise: the sun turned into darkness is Christ obscured in the hearts of the elect at the point of death. Hence in the Gospel some said of him: [Col. 0357B] “But we had hoped that he was the one who would redeem Israel” (Luke 24). Hence through Job: “My brothers have withdrawn from me, and those who knew me have departed from me as strangers” (Job 19). The moon turned into blood is the Synagogue blinded in Christ’s Passion, perpetually condemned by the blood of its testimony. Blood, fire, and vapour signify the threefold plague of the Jews: blood, the slaughter of their bodies; fire, the burning of their goods and possessions; vapour, their banishment through seas and islands. If anyone doubts these things, let him read Josephus in the *Antiquities* and Hegesippus.

This concerns Christ’s coming in the flesh; now let it speak morally of the Paraclete’s coming into the mind. For when the Paraclete deigns to visit a faithful soul, he first finds it abounding in vices [Col. 0357C], immediately pierces it through the spirit of fear unto penitence, and thus makes it his maidservant. He then allows it gradually to grow through works of penitence; afterwards, through devout obedience to the commandments, it begins to grow young; then, through innocence of conduct and the higher way of the counsels, it matures; finally, through the privilege of love, it is admitted into partnership in the inheritance.

According to the laws of tropology, vision is proper self-knowledge; dream is ecstasy of mind; prophecy is contemplation of the bridegroom; heaven is the mind; earth, the flesh; or heaven is the contemplative life, earth the active life. Vapour is compunction of mind; blood, mortification of the flesh; fire, the fervour of love. The sun turned into darkness is the mind confounded in self-knowledge; the moon turned into blood [Col. 0357D] is the flesh subjected to its own mortification.

It follows: “Before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes.” The day of the Lord is God’s illumination through ecstasy arising from the bridegroom’s love. The Lord is great because he despises all earthly things; terrible because he beholds dreadful and stupendous things. He is great because he reveals eternal things; terrible because he promises incomprehensible things. Here “terrible” is used not for the terror of confusion, but for the reverence of wonder. “Great” is said not for a defect, but for a virtue. The aforesaid four things precede this day: for while self-knowledge merits the judgment of sin, compunction of mind the gift of pardon, mortification of flesh the counsel of righteousness, and fervour of love the privilege of grace, there immediately follows the day of glory [Col. 0358A], namely ecstasy of mind and contemplation of the bridegroom.

It follows: “And whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.” Whatever we have interpreted concerning Christ’s coming in relation to the sending of the Paraclete, the Jews refer to the coming of their Messiah. At that coming, as they say, the observance of the Law will be completely restored and their former prosperity renewed. The Jewish people alone will receive the Messiah; they alone will call upon him, and he will hear them. Certain teachers, however, transfer the interpretation of the aforesaid prophecy to the Last Judgment, in which whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved, because then the elect alone shall call upon him, while the reprobate, struck dumb by the terror of the Lord’s presence, shall be silent. For to call upon him is to summon him to oneself through security of conscience and the strength of one’s merits.

But we, without prejudice to anyone’s [Col. 0358B] opinion, also refer this saying—“Everyone, whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved”—to Christ’s coming in the flesh and the Paraclete’s coming into the mind. Hence Jerome says: “What follows, ‘Everyone, whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved,’ is better understood of the day of Christ’s Passion or resurrection; but the invocation in which salvation consists is made up not only of speech, but also of heart and work. Therefore, on account of the grace of this threefold invocation, it should be believed to belong not to the foolish but to the perfect: for what the heart believes, the mouth confesses, and the hand completes in action.” Nor should this invocation be thought a matter of little importance. Although the Apostle says: “No one says, ‘Jesus is Lord,’ except in the Holy Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12), nevertheless this saying itself should be weighed not in speech alone [Col. 0358C] but also in affection. Hence we read of Samuel: “And Samuel was among those who call upon his name” (Psalm 98); and of Moses and Aaron: “They called upon the Lord, and he heard them” (ibid.). Conversely, concerning the reprobate: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 7).

**MORALLY.** After the portents given in heaven, after the light of self-knowledge, after the smoke of devout compunction, after the blood of just mortification, after the fire of perfect love, the sweetness of contemplation alone remains. He therefore says: “And it shall come to pass,” that is, then, “everyone, whoever calls upon the name of the Lord, shall be saved”; because upon the flower-strewn bed of contemplation, calling upon the Lord’s name is nothing other than the attainment of desired [Col. 0358D] salvation, the most longed-for union of bridegroom and bride.

Thus the bride had been saved; thus she had called upon the Lord’s name, when she said: “Your name is oil poured out” (Song of Songs 1). The bride had received the oil poured out of the Name: because he is light, she was illumined by his presence; because he is anointing, she was healed by his touch; because he is the bread of life, she had been satisfied by his embrace. She was illumined by knowledge of the Spirit, healed from the vanity of the world, and satisfied by the kiss of the Word. And this is invocation of the Name. This is attainment of salvation, reception of kisses, sharing of the bed, union of Word and soul. In it everyone is indeed saved, because with this light no one is blinded, with this strength no one is made weak, and with this salvation no one is endangered. It follows:

[Col. 0359A] For on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be salvation, as the Lord has said, and among the remnant whom the Lord shall call (Joel 3). For behold, in those days and at that time, when I restore the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem, I shall gather all nations and lead them down into the valley of Jehoshaphat; and there I shall contend with them concerning my people and my inheritance Israel, whom they scattered among the nations, divided my land, and cast lots over my people. They gave a boy for a prostitute and sold a girl for wine, that they might drink.

Let us first examine this chapter morally; then let us proceed with pleasure to the obscurities of allegory and tropology. The Jews promise themselves here—indeed, dream—that in the last time they shall be gathered by the Lord and brought back to Jerusalem. Not content with this prosperity [Col. 0359B], they assert that God himself will hand the sons and daughters of the Romans into their hands, so that they may sell them not to Persians, Ethiopians, and the other neighbouring nations, but to the Sabaeans, a people most remote, because the Lord has said that he will avenge the injury done to his people. So they say, as do our Judaizers, who promise themselves a thousand-year kingdom within Judaea’s borders, a golden Jerusalem, the blood of victims, sons and grandsons, incredible delights, and gates distinguished by a variety of gems.

This passage is most difficult in its anagogical sense and admits of multiple explanations. In tropology we may refer all these statements to that to which the apostles Peter and Paul referred them: namely, the time when the Lord suffered and rose again. For it cannot be that the preceding things are understood in the time of the Passion and the following matters on the day of judgment—especially since there follows: “For behold, in those days and at that time”—and this verse, connecting what follows with the preceding matters, says that all are to be accomplished in one time. Let it therefore be said: “On Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there shall be salvation, as the Lord has said,” etc. The remnant are the apostles and the other disciples. Hence Isaiah: “Unless the Lord of Sabaoth had left us a seed” (Isaiah 1), etc. “As the Lord has said.” Where, or through whom, did the Lord say this? Through Isaiah: “From Zion,” he says, “shall go forth the Law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isaiah 2). And through the Psalmist: “The Lord,” he says, “loves the gates of Zion more than all the tents of Jacob” (Psalm 86).

It follows: “For behold, in those days,” etc. For in the days [Col. 0359D] of the Passion and resurrection, when the Lord restored the captivity of Judah and Jerusalem—when, that is, by choosing some from the children of Abraham he called them to himself, and by calling justified them—he gathered and led down all nations into the valley of Jehoshaphat. For by just and gratuitous mercy he made some vessels of mercy unto glory, and others, vessels of just wrath unto destruction and dishonour (Romans 9). For he said to Moses: “I shall have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I shall grant mercy to whom I will grant mercy” (Exodus 33). Jehoshaphat is interpreted “the judgment of the Lord,” by which the condemnation of the reprobate is signified. Therefore, at the time of the elect’s conversion, the multitude of the impious is rejected, because in the moment and mystery of the Lord’s Passion lies the cause and sum of salvation and perdition. [Col. 0360A] Hence the Apostle: “As many of us as were baptized in Christ Jesus were baptized in his death” (Galatians 6). Again the same Apostle: “For I bear in my body the marks of Jesus Christ” (ibid.). Here the Lord says to Moses: “When the angel sees the blood upon the lintel and upon both doorposts, he shall pass over the door and shall not permit the destroyer to enter your houses and harm you” (Exodus 12). Hence the Lord says through Ezekiel: “Do not kill anyone upon whom you see the *Thau*” (Ezekiel 9). And the Apostle says: “Almost all things are cleansed in blood, and without the shedding of blood there is no remission” (Hebrews 9).

It follows: “And there I shall contend with them,” namely in the valley of Jehoshaphat. The Lord contends with the nations on behalf of his people and inheritance, for the reasons set forth below; because thence the nations receive the judgment of condemnation, whence they fell into the crimes that follow. This testimony concerns idolaters and heretics, who, by seducing the Lord’s people, divided that people itself and divided his land [Col. 0360B], separating it among themselves by many errors and compelling it into idolatrous worship—so that some worshipped Jupiter, others Phoebus, others Juno, others Minerva, Rust, Anubis, the crocodile and ibis, owls, hawks, and storks. Heretics likewise divided the Lord’s land, that is, the Church, and cast lots upon the people of the Church when, seducing them and leading them into heretical error, Arius made Arians, Sabellius Sabellians, Manes Manichaeans, and others made others into disciples of their own error.

It follows: “They gave a boy for a prostitute and sold a girl for wine, that they might drink.” Here he accuses each party—heretic and idolater alike—on three charges: avarice, lust, and gluttony. Of avarice, because he cast lots over the Lord’s people. Of lust, because he prostituted the boy. Of gluttony, because he sold the girl for wine.

**ALLEGORICALLY.** Each deceives the boy—the Church’s people, pure in faith, upright in hope, sincere in love—by evil persuasion and deceitful promise: the idolater places him in the brothel of idols, and the heretic confines him in the hovel of errors. “And they sold a girl for wine, that they might drink”: because the idolater, corrupting the soul still tender in faith and delicate in morals by gifts and promises, and the heretic [Col. 0360D] ensnaring it with the poisonous colouring of words and seducing it with sophistical arguments, enslaved it to heresy or idolatry, receiving from its overthrow the wine of delight.

**MORALLY.** There are two spiritual captivities: the captivity of Judah, that is, confession; and the captivity of Jerusalem, that is, contemplation. When contemplation is taken captive, the soul is immediately assaulted by cares, occupied with business, and beset by tumults and unlawful desires. But when confession goes into captivity, then the wretched soul descends into the darkness of vices and the calamity of despair. Then demons divide the Lord’s land, that is, the faithful soul, among vices; they cast the lot of sins over the people of virtues. Then they prostitute the boy, that is, purity of mind, [Col. 0361A] to unlawful desires. Then they sell the girl, that is, innocence of heart, for wine—that is, temporal joy and earthly pleasure.

But when, on the day of salvation and at the acceptable time, the Dayspring from on high deigns to visit, he pours in knowledge of truth and confession is then recalled; he grants love of virtue and contemplation is restored. Then the nations of vices are led down into the valley of judgment; and, because of the injustice they committed against the choir of virtues, they take the road to destruction. We may refer the preceding matters to the day of judgment; but because we hasten to other things, we choose to leave them to the reader’s judgment. It follows:

But what are Tyre and Sidon to me, and all the territory of the Philistines? Will you render retribution to me? And if you take vengeance against me, swiftly and quickly [Col. 0361B] I shall return your recompense upon your own head. For you have taken my silver and my gold, and brought my desirable and most beautiful things into your shrines. And you have sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem to the sons of the Greeks, to remove them far from their borders. Behold, I shall raise them from the place where you sold them, and I shall turn your recompense upon your own head. And I shall sell your sons and daughters into the hands of the sons of Judah, and they shall sell them to the Sabaeans, a distant people, because the Lord has spoken.

The Jews suppose these things are said against Tyre, Sidon, and the territory of the Philistines, because in the time of the Jewish captivity, when they were defeated by the Romans, they persecuted God’s people—indeed, in that people, God himself who presided over the people. “Therefore I,” he says, “shall repay [Col. 0361C] you for what you did to my people—indeed, to me—because you took my silver and gold, that is, the vessels of the Temple and whatever was most precious, and consecrated them to your idols.”

History, however, reports that the Chaldeans did this more particularly, for they placed the vessels of the Lord’s Temple in their own temple. Hence Belshazzar later drank from the bowls, and immediately his kingdom was transferred to the Medes and Persians. But because these events are said to occur after the great and terrible day of the Lord, which the apostles interpret as the Lord’s resurrection, while the Hebrews defer it to the future time of judgment, they should rather be understood of the Romans: namely, that Vespasian and Titus, after the Temple of Peace had been built at Rome, consecrated the Temple vessels and all the offerings in its shrine—[Col. 0361D] as Greek and Roman history relates.

Mystically, however, the subject is Christ’s coming in the flesh. By Tyre, Sidon, and the Philistines may be understood idolaters and heretics; if it concerns his coming for judgment, demons; if his coming into the mind, vices and carnal passions. Yet the Lord will swiftly and promptly render recompense to all; for of his first coming it is written: “Whoever does not believe has already been judged” (John 3). Likewise: “Now is the judgment of the world” (John 12), etc. Of the second: “Depart from me, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25). And of the third: “Poor little one, storm-tossed, without any consolation: behold, I will set your stones in order and found you upon sapphires” (Isa. 54), etc. Silver is eloquence; gold, wisdom; desirable things, things most religious; [Col. 0362A] beautiful things, things most honorable. What is honorable pertains to reputation; what is religious, to conscience. Shrines are the worship of idols, or the sects of heretics, or habits of vices. The sons of Judah are the active; the sons of Jerusalem, the contemplative. Greeks are liars—men, that is, or movements of the soul, who speak falsely. For “Greeks” is interpreted “is and is not,” by which deceit and falsehood are signified; through these things mentioned above, moreover, their assembly, or the choir of virtues, is made far from its own borders. But God, the Lord of vengeance, will swiftly render recompense: he who turns back the enemies’ requital. Hence it follows: “Behold, I will gather them,” etc. “And I will sell your sons and daughters into the hands of the sons of Judah; and they shall sell them to the Sabaeans, a distant nation.” Allegorically, the sons of those aforesaid are the disciples of Gentiles or heretics; morally, the movements of vices. [Col. 0362B] The hands of the sons of Judah are confessions and works of penitence. Thus those aforesaid are beneficially delivered into these hands: for the former return through confession of faith to the grace of baptism; and the latter, through confession of sin and works of penitence, fly toward pardon of guilt, the grace of obedience, and purity of innocence. And for this reason they sell them to the Sabaeans, a distant people: because, having purified those aforesaid in the manner stated, they apply them, through hatred of sin, to self-abasement and contempt of the world. For Saba is interpreted “captivity.” Therefore, first, iniquity is made captive by hatred of sin; second, curiosity by self-abasement; third, vanity by contempt of the world. Alternatively, those aforesaid sell the aforesaid, once trained, to the Sabaeans because, after works of penitence, after the devotion of [Col. 0362C] obedience, after fruits worthy of righteousness, they raise them up to the repose of contemplative joy. Saba is called a distant nation. Hence the contemplative household is called a remote nation, because it is set apart far from the crowds of vices, the cares of affairs, and the exercise of active works. It follows:

“Proclaim these things among the nations: sanctify war; rouse the strong. Let all men of war approach and come up; beat your ploughshares into swords and your hoes into spears. Let the weak say: ‘I am strong.’ Break forth and come, all nations round about, and gather together. There the Lord will cause your strong men to fall. Let the nations arise and come up into the valley of Jehoshaphat, for there I shall sit to judge all the nations round about. Send forth sickles, for the harvest is ripe. Come and go down, for the winepress is full. The presses overflow, because their wickedness has multiplied. Peoples, peoples in the valley of cutting-off, for the day of the Lord is near in the valley of cutting-off. The sun and moon have been darkened, and the stars have withdrawn their brightness.”

The Jews refer this passage to the exceedingly savage nations Gog and Magog (of whom we spoke above), supposing that at the end of time, when Jerusalem has been rebuilt under a thousand-year reign, they will come against God’s people and rush into the valley of Jehoshaphat, which lies to the east. They say that the time of their slaughter has arrived and that the vintage for shedding their blood is imminent. The Jews dream these things in vain. But let us disclose the truth of the matter and pursue it allegorically; then let us pass on to investigate the delightful mysteries of tropology.

If the present passage concerns the Lord’s coming in the flesh, the letter is fittingly read thus. The prophet therefore exhorts the divine seers and his fellow-prophets to proclaim day by day the salvation of the Lord, to declare his glory among the nations and his wonders among all peoples: to announce, I say, the incarnation of the Word, the passion and resurrection of Jesus Christ; the coming of the Paraclete upon the apostles, their preaching, the power of signs, the grace of miracles, conflicts of words, struggles of contests, and bodily sufferings—together with manly constancy in all things and a swift victory over the nations. This is what he says: “Proclaim these things among the nations.” As though he said: [Col. 0363B] “Do not spare; do not be silent.” Thus it will be glory for the nations to be conquered; indeed, to yield in this way is a glorious victory. “Sanctify war.” For if that whose end is good is itself good, then this war too is undoubtedly holy, since its end is holy. To sanctify this war is to endow war with holiness. Is not war sanctified where virtue triumphs and vice is slain? Is not war sanctified, I say, where victory is reckoned to the conquered, a crown to the one who yields, a reward to the fugitive, and a kingdom is attributed to the defeated? Therefore rouse the strong—namely, the apostles and apostolic men. What is it to rouse except to awaken upward? What is it to awaken upward except to announce as lifted up on high, fortified with virtues, and adorned with miracles? Therefore let men of war—that is, preachers of the word, leaders of the heavenly warfare—approach preaching and mount upon the necks of the nations. Let them ascend, I say, above the nations’ yoke of faith through the power of prodigies and the flashing brightness of miracles.

Then the prophetic speech turns to them, saying: “Beat your ploughshares into swords, and your hoes into spears.” What are ploughshares except mortified members? What is it to beat ploughshares into swords except frequently to expose mortified members to death for the care of faith and the power of the word? This was done by those of whom the Acts of the Apostles says: “The apostles went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been counted worthy to suffer disgrace for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5). Hence the Apostle: “For I think that God has displayed us apostles last of all, as men sentenced to death, because we have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men” (1 Cor. 4). Likewise the same Apostle: “To this present hour,” he says, “we hunger and thirst, are naked, are beaten with fists, are homeless, and labor, working with our own hands. When reviled, we bless; when persecuted, we endure; when slandered, we entreat. We have become like the refuse of this world, the offscouring of all things, to this day” (ibid.). Behold how the ploughshare is beaten. Now let us see how it is changed into a sword: “It is better for me to die,” he says, “than that anyone should make my glory void. For if I preach the Gospel, it is no glory to me, for necessity is laid upon me. Woe to me if I do not preach the Gospel! But if I do this willingly, I have a reward; if unwillingly, a stewardship has been entrusted to me” (1 Cor. 9).

[Col. 0364A] Hoes are the various compunctions of the mind. Spears are severe threats. What, then, is it to beat hoes into spears except, from the various compunctions of the mind, to conceive zeal for faith, power in speech, and forcefulness of expression? Hence the Bridegroom says to the bride in the Song of Songs: “Your eyes are like pools in Heshbon, which are by the gate of the daughter of the multitude” (Song 7). The bride’s eyes are the brightness of faith and understanding of divine speech. Heshbon is interpreted “girdle of sorrow”; the pools of Heshbon are various kinds of compunction. Therefore the bride’s eyes are like pools in Heshbon, because they are made all the brighter from being more frequently washed in the aforesaid pools. The sword is a manly resolve concerning the present; the spear, a saving threat concerning the future. Through contempt of themselves and mortification of the flesh, therefore, teachers receive from God confidence for fraternal correction; through the devotion of compunction, power and grace for threatening. It follows: “Let the weak say: ‘I am strong.’” For it is written: “When I am weak, then I am stronger and powerful” (2 Cor. 12). Likewise it is said: “Power is perfected in weakness” (ibid.).

The prophet, foreseeing the election of the nations, the glory of believers, their conversion to the faith, vice becoming weak in them, and virtue triumphing, says:

“Break forth from the hiding places of temples, from the corners of idols, and come by the steps of faith and fruits of penitence, out of the circuit in which you walked as impious persons, who, despising truth, long groped after falsehood. Gather together [Col. 0364C] within the nets of the divine word, within the sheepfolds of faith, within the enclosures of the Lord’s eye. There the Lord of faith will cause his strong ones to fall”—that is, through the fervor and power of divine speech, teachers will subject to himself kings, nobles, wise men, and philosophers. Hence Isaiah: “All the flocks of Kedar shall be gathered to you; the rams of Nebaioth shall minister to you” (Isa. 60). Elsewhere: “The glory of Lebanon has been given to it, the splendor of Carmel and Sharon” (Isa. 35). Likewise another prophet: “The nation and kingdom that will not serve you shall perish” (Jer. 27). But Isaiah says: “The glory of Lebanon shall come to you: fir tree, box tree, and pine together, to adorn the place of my sanctification” (Isa. 60). The same prophet says in the same place: “The sons of those who humbled you shall come to you bent low, and all who slandered you shall worship the footsteps of your feet” (ibid.).

Since it is of such importance to yield to the victor, and of such benefit for warriors to be overcome, let the nations arise and come up into the valley of Jehoshaphat—that is, into the humility of judgment. For Jehoshaphat is interpreted “judgment of the Lord,” because there, the Lord says, “I shall sit to judge all the nations round about” (Joel 9). Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “For judgment I came into this world, that those who do not see may see, and those who see may become blind” (John 9).

There follows the voice of the Savior exhorting his apostles to gather new fruits, to convert the nations, saying: “Send forth sickles, for the harvest is ripe.” See how great is the agreement of prophecy with the evangelical saying. For the Savior says thus to the apostles in the Gospel: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the workers are few” (Matt. 9). Likewise in the present prophecy: “When the harvest is ripe, send forth sickles.” There are three sickles of those who bring peoples to faith in the Trinity and send new fruits into the Lord’s granaries. The first is preaching of the word; the second, the form of catechizing; the third, the sacrament of baptism. It is as though he said: “Preach, instruct, wash. Preach the rule of faith, instruct toward penitence, wash unto pardon.”

There follows the voice of the Lord himself, exhorting his disciples in the care of faith and teaching of the word to the struggle of martyrdom: “Come,” he says, “and go down. Come by the steps of preaching; go down to the labor and humility of most fruitful suffering, because through bodily sufferings and the power of miracles many thousands of neophytes [Col. 0365B] will receive with you the most glorious rewards of a glorious contest; and those who share in sorrow will also share in joy.” This is what he says: “For the winepress is full; the presses overflow.” But when he says, “Their wickedness has multiplied,” if he speaks of neophytes, it is rightly understood thus, as though he said: “Wickedness has multiplied and been brought all the way to its end; it ought not to advance any further, for a different judgment has here set it a limit.” But if he speaks of the reprobate: “Wickedness has multiplied,” that is, it has been brought to its height and its decisive point, so that they may be cast out from the glory of the kingdom and the sheepfold of faith, while the elect—troubled by their wickedness and cruelty—may be admitted to joys and crowned with glory and honor through the merit of martyrdom.

Observe the harmony of Gospel and prophecy. The Savior says to the apostles in the Gospel: “Lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest” (John 4). He himself says through the prophet here: “Come and go down, for the winepress is full; the presses overflow,” etc. It follows: “Peoples, peoples in the valley of cutting-off.” The repetition of “peoples” is an emphatic urging of the work, a commendation of the undertaking. As though he said: “Peoples, peoples in the valley of cutting-off”—that is, in the humility of judgment and the discernment of faith—life is to be sought for the sake of salvation, the summit of righteousness. This is what follows: “For the day of the Lord is near in the valley of cutting-off.” For the prosperity of eternal recompense and the brightness of blessed contemplation follow the humility of true confession.

It follows: “The sun and moon have been darkened, [Col. 0365D] and the stars have withdrawn their brightness.” The sun is worldly philosophy; the moon, secular power; the stars, the remaining authorities. The sun and moon have been darkened in the humility of judgment, because once the wise of this world and the powerful of this age came to the brightness of faith, they immediately recognized the darkness of their own error. The stars withdrew their brightness because, when they saw Christ’s disciples embrace contempt of the world, self-abasement, and thirst for the struggle of martyrdom in the cause of faith—when they saw them shining with signs, adorned with prodigies, and glorious through miracles—they were immediately turned from pride, cast down from earthly rank, followed Christ’s humility, and bent their necks to faith. This is for the stars to withdraw their brightness: for the powerful of this age and nobles of this world, by embracing the humility [Col. 0366A] of faith, to despise utterly the flower of the world.

This concerns Christ’s coming in the flesh. But if it is read concerning the final coming, as some prefer, the interpretation will be easy in part; but the explanation of certain things will be difficult, absurd, and unsuitable. For in that strict judgment, what will be the ploughshares? What swords? What hoes? What spears, sickles, and winepresses? Yet those who maintain this resort to allegory. To accommodate them, we say that the aforesaid nations are led into the valley of judgment so that they may be killed and fall, so that they may be judged by the Lord. Neither the sun nor moon nor the other stars will be able to behold the sorrow of that day and the torments of the perishing; rather, they will withdraw their brightness and will not dare to look upon the severity of the Judge, who renders each person’s deed upon [Col. 0366B] his own head. Not because they are more merciful than God’s judgment, but because every creature, in the torments of others, fears its own judgment. It follows:

“And the Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will utter his voice; and heaven and earth will be shaken. And the Lord is the hope of his people and the strength of the children of Israel. And you shall know that I am your Lord,” etc.

Let us follow the vengeance already begun and the explanation concerning the final coming. When the brightness of the sun, moon, and all the stars has been changed into darkness, the Lord will roar like a lion from Zion, or cry out; and his voice will be so high and terrible that the hinges of heaven and the foundations of earth will be shaken. And although he will be so severe toward those who are to be punished, he will nevertheless be merciful toward his people and give strength to those called children of Israel—that is, those who see God with the mind, who have not walked by crooked ways but, proceeding on Christ’s way, have done all things rightly. Then both those punished in Gehenna and those taken up in glory will know that the Lord dwells in his watchtower, Zion, and in Christ, his holy mountain—that is, in him who had prepared himself as a dwelling worthy of God.

But if it is read of the first coming, the explanation will be easy and fitting. It is no wonder that, in the humility of judgment, through the power of the word and discernment of faith, the nations submit themselves to the Son of God, who is “the living word of God, effective and sharper than every two-edged sword” (Heb. 4). Living, because he does not change; effective, because [Col. 0366D] he does not fail; penetrating, because he is not deceived. He does not change in what he promises; he does not fail in what he does; he is not deceived in judgment. His promise does not die through forgetfulness; his work is not overcome by difficulty; his judgment is not deceived by ambiguity. He promises truthfully, acts powerfully, discerns subtly. He is living, that you may believe; effective, that you may hope; penetrating, that you may fear. He is living in commandments and prohibitions; effective in promises and threats; penetrating in judgments and condemnations. Therefore, since the word of God is living, one must believe that he promises true things; since he is effective, one must believe that he fulfills what he promises; since he is penetrating and cannot be deceived, one must grieve at having offended him and beware henceforth of offending him.

Three things must be considered in this word: sound, voice, and understanding. In sound there is noise; in voice, meaning; in understanding, perfection of intellect. Noise pertains to threatening; voice, to consolation; understanding, to the perfection of knowledge. Thus noise belongs to the torment of penitence, voice to the grace of pardon, understanding to the brightness of glory. This is what he says: “The Lord will roar from Zion,” etc. The Lord’s roar is the noise of speech. Hence these three: roar, voice, knowledge. Roaring is made by threatening, voice by consolation, knowledge by contemplation. By threatening, he draws to penitence; by consoling, he restores to grace; by contemplating, he raises to glory. Through the roar, earth is moved to penitence; through the voice, heaven is moved to grace; through understanding, “we know you, the one only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent.” [Col. 0367B] This is what is said: “And you shall know that I am the Lord your God, dwelling in my holy mountain.”

But if the present prophecy is understood concerning Christ’s coming into the mind, this is the sum of its tropology. One must go into the valley of judgment; there the cause of salvation, the form of penitence, and the rule of righteousness must be sought. There the enemy is slain, the citizen is freed, the one raised up is exalted, and the exalted one is perfected. There are three judgments: one’s own, human, and divine. One’s own judgment arises from compunction of heart and human penitence; human judgment, from public discipline; divine judgment reveals hidden and secret things. Through one’s own judgment the enemy is slain and the citizen is freed. Through human judgment, he is polished and exalted. Through divine judgment, he is perfected to the utmost.

Each of these judgments is rightly said to be situated in a valley, because each humbles and depresses the mind; each shakes the human heart with fear and torments it in diverse ways. The first humbles the mind through terror of Gehenna; the second depresses the soul by the weight of discipline; the third casts down the soul through love of righteousness. Therefore, in the first judgment there is victory over the nations and death of the strong; in the second, abundance of winepresses and grace of gifts; in the third, hope of the people and strength of the children. The day of the Lord is said to be near the valley of judgment. The day of the Lord is the day of penitence, the day of discipline, and the day of glory. Near the first valley is the day of penitence; near the second, the day of discipline; near the third, the day of glory. Hence the Psalmist: “Declare day by day his salvation” (Ps. 95)—that is, from the day of penitence, the day of discipline; from the day of discipline, the day of glory. [Col. 0367D] This is what is said: “And you shall know that I am the Lord your God, dwelling in Zion, my holy mountain.” It follows:

“And Jerusalem shall be holy, and strangers shall no longer pass through her. And it shall come to pass on that day: the mountains shall drip sweetness, and the hills shall flow with milk. Waters shall go through all the streams of Judah; and a fountain shall go forth from the house of the Lord and shall water the torrent of thorns.”

The Jews, and our own Judaizers, refer these things to the fables of a thousand years, when they suppose that Christ will dwell in Zion and that the people of the saints will be gathered in a golden, jewel-adorned Jerusalem, so that those oppressed by all nations in this age may rule over all nations in that same age. This is what the Jewish fable dreams, while truth supplies us something altogether different. Jerusalem signifies the Church of this present time; it also signifies the faithful soul; and likewise her who is above, free, our mother (Gal. 4).

The letter may be understood of the threefold coming, and what is said may fittingly be understood of each. After the sending of the Paraclete, the preaching of the apostles, and the conversion of the nations in the valley of judgment through discernment of faith, Jerusalem is made holy, and strangers no longer pass through her. Idolaters, heretics, and schismatics are called strangers. All of these came unanimously at the beginning of the primitive Church to attack her, but they did not pass through her; for although they strive to attack the chastity of her faith, [Col. 0368B] they cannot at all break her unity or violate her charity. They came indeed armed with fantastic arguments and sophistical reasoning, but they could not pass through: repelled by the truth of the word, overcome by the reasoning of judgment, cast down by the testimonies of Scripture and the heat of faith. They came prepared to contend, but did not pass through; they were compelled to retreat.

From the very name of holiness its manifold power and nature are shown. That which is called *sanctum* in Latin is called ἄγιος (*agios*, “holy”) in Greek. *Agios* is said to be a compound name from ἀ- (*a-*, “without”) and γῆ (*gē*, “earth”); for γῆ means “earth.” Hence that is called holy which is made without earth and raised above earth. Holy were those of whom it is written: “Our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3). Holy also were those of whom it is said: “Among whom you shine as lights in the world, holding fast the word of life” (Phil. 2).

Therefore Jerusalem is holy in her sacraments, commandments, judgments, counsels, and promises. Her sacraments are without dregs; her commandments, without burden; her judgments, without dispute; her counsels, without jealousy; her promises, without the paint of falsehood—without the jealousy of envy, the dispute of controversy, the burden of exaction, or the dregs of desire. Therefore she is holy whose understanding is contemplative, affection heavenly, perception spiritual, and action angelic. Hence John says in the Apocalypse: “I saw the holy city, the new Jerusalem, coming down from heaven, adorned as a bride for her husband” (Rev. 21). It follows: “And strangers shall no longer pass through [Col. 0368D] her.” Hence Nahum: “Celebrate your feasts, O Judah, and fulfill your vows; for Belial shall no longer pass through you; he has utterly perished” (Nah. 1).

It follows: “And it shall come to pass on that day: the mountains shall drip sweetness,” etc. That day is the coming of the Paraclete; the mountains are the apostles; the hills, the disciples; the streams, subject peoples; sweetness, wisdom; water, teaching. There are three kinds of teaching: contemplative, allegorical, and moral. The contemplative is pure; the allegorical, naked; the moral, alone. Moral teaching is alone from matter; allegorical teaching is naked from form; contemplative teaching is pure from every limitation. The moral kind shapes life without matter; the allegorical enlightens knowledge without form; the contemplative raises one to wisdom without imagination. Alternatively, water is the historical condition; milk, moral teaching; sweetness, spiritual edification. They shall drip from the heights, flow in the plains, and go in the valleys. God’s heights are his invisible judgments; his plains, his manifest counsels; the valleys, humble penitence, obedience to commandments, and works of mercy.

It follows: “And a fountain shall go forth from the house of the Lord and water the torrent of thorns.” The house of the Lord is the beauty of the primitive Church; the fountain, the fullness of evangelical teaching; the torrent of thorns, the violence, fury, and cruelty of the nations. The fountain going forth from the house of the Lord watered the torrent of thorns when, through the apostles and their successors, evangelical teaching initiated the Gentile people to the end, converted it to faith, and brought it to the grace of baptism. It follows:

[Col. 0369B] “Egypt shall be a desolation, and Idumea a wilderness of destruction, because they acted unjustly against the children of Judah and shed innocent blood in their land. But Judea shall be inhabited forever, and Jerusalem from generation to generation.”

Nothing happens on earth without cause. Nor is it without reason that the Lord rains upon one city and leaves another without rain. Behold: Egypt and Idumea remain desolate for the causes set forth, while Judea and Jerusalem, because they lived innocently, continually, and obediently, are inhabited forever and rejoice. Egypt is the part of the Gentile people that is rejected and blinded through ignorance. Idumea is the part of the Jewish people rejected and abandoned by God through crooked and unclean desire. Judea is the Lamb’s wife, Christ’s bride, confessing her ignorance, being pierced with compunction and crushing herself because of disordered desire; confessing to herself the darkness of ignorance, the filth of desire, and the horror of wickedness; confessing to God the grace of pardon, purity of innocence, and sublimity of glory. It follows:

“And I shall cleanse their blood, which they had not cleansed [which I had not cleansed]; and the Lord shall dwell in Zion.”

Here, through Christ’s coming, the remedy of grace against the shipwreck of original sin is covertly introduced. For this blood—that is, original sin—could by no justice or power of any person be cleansed or erased except by the blood of the immaculate Lamb, who knew no sin. Hence [Col. 0369D] the Apostle: “Without the shedding of blood there is no remission” (Heb. 9). Likewise the same Apostle: “For such a high priest was fitting for us: holy, innocent, undefiled, separated from sinners, and made higher than the heavens” (Heb. 7). This is what the Lord says through the prophet in the present passage: “I shall cleanse their blood, which they had not cleansed”—that is, which they had been unable to cleanse. And then the Lord shall dwell in Zion: then, that is, when all things have been subjected to him and he himself shall subject the kingdom to God and the Father. Then he shall dwell in the watchtower, because his vision will be given to the elect for glory. Then he shall be all things in all (1 Cor. 15): life, power, bread, drink, form, salvation, light, fountain of life, guide, law, medicine. Thus he shall be all things in all, according to the saying: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16 [17]). Hence: “This,” he says, “is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you sent” (John 17). Hence the saying of the wise man:

> To behold you is the end,
>
> the beginning, bearer, guide, path, and goal alike.

This concerns Christ’s coming in the flesh. Let us now speak of his coming for judgment.

“And Jerusalem shall be holy, and strangers shall no longer pass through her.” After the sentence of judgment has been pronounced, after the separation of the elect from the reprobate, the assembly of the saints will be joined to the angelic choirs; and then Jerusalem, the Lamb’s wife, will be raised above earthly things. Then God “will wipe away every tear from the eyes of the saints; and there shall no longer be mourning or crying or any pain, because the former things have passed away” (Rev. [Col. 0370B] 21). There will no longer, I say, be the cry of temptation’s suggestion, the pain of temptation, or the mourning of compunction, because the former things have passed away. What are the former things? The serpent’s suggestion, the woman’s delight, the man’s consent. But suggestion has passed away through granted impassibility; delight, through perfect charity; consent, through complete blessedness. Hence Isaiah: “Arise, arise; put on your strength, O Zion; put on the garments of your glory, O Jerusalem, holy city, for the uncircumcised and unclean shall no longer pass through you” (Isa. 52).

It follows: “And it shall come to pass on that day: the mountains shall drip sweetness,” etc. Through mountains, hills, and streams is shown diversity of merits; through sweetness, milk, and water, diversity of rewards. But the fountain that goes forth from the house of the Lord to water the torrent of thorns is what is said elsewhere: “Everlasting joy shall be upon their heads” (Isa. 35); and: “The Lamb who is in their midst will shepherd them and lead them to springs of the waters of life” (Rev. 7). Then Egypt and Idumea will become a wilderness of destruction, while Jerusalem with Judea will be inhabited through generations of years; for to the former it will be said: “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25); and to the latter: “Come, blessed of my Father; receive the kingdom” (ibid.).

Then the Lord will cleanse the blood of the elect, which they had not previously cleansed, because, as teachers maintain, when the elect see the apostate angel punished by an irrevocable sentence, bound with an unbreakable chain, and condemned to a dreadful punishment, they will be shaken with fear; and by that very fear they will be purified from what they had cleansed only with difficulty. According to Job’s saying concerning the apostate angel: “When he is raised up, the angels will fear, and, terrified, will be purified” (Job 41). [Col. 0370D] After these things the Lord will dwell in Zion—that is, in the watchtower of vision—because then he will gird himself, make them recline at table, and, passing among them, minister to them.

Morally, this concerns the coming of Christ the Bridegroom to his bride, to the dove, the unique, beloved, faithful soul. When the Lord, dwelling in Zion, on the holy mountain—that is, in the sublimity of contemplation—enters more closely into the union of love with the bride; when the Bridegroom offers heavenly kisses and serves her with the dishes of paradise in angelic attendance, then Jerusalem becomes holy—holy, surely, because she has been raised above earthly things: raised above iniquity, raised above curiosity, [Col. 0371A] suspended above pleasure, set apart from vanity. Then strangers no longer pass through her, because neither the evil one’s suggestion, nor the spirit’s exaltation, nor the flesh’s titillation, nor the world’s assault dare in any way provoke her: her whom the Bridegroom’s blessedness places, enclosed in the chamber of contemplation, upon the bed of union. Strangers no longer pass through her, I say, because she who is joined to the impassible one and united to the blessed one is not disturbed, even briefly, by any annoyance of things. I mean that through the Bridegroom’s grace she is made impassible, not created impassible in her substance. It follows:

“And it shall come to pass on that day”—that is, in that brightness of contemplation—“the mountains shall drip sweetness, the hills shall flow with milk, and waters shall go through all the streams of Judah.” Mountains are the heights of contemplations; hills, works of innocence; streams, exercises of penitence; sweetness, perfect love; milk, holy devotion; water, devout compunction. Therefore, on that day—that is, in that blessedness of union—the bride, through the joy of contemplation, receives the sweetness of perfect love. Descending from it and returning to herself, she overflows with the milk of devotion. Thus, tormenting herself from love of higher things, she immerses herself in the waters of compunction; emerging from them, she is exercised through harsh penitence; afterward she is drawn to works of innocence; finally she flies to contemplation, saying: “What have I in heaven? And apart from you, what have I desired upon earth?” (Ps. 72 [73]). Likewise: “My soul chose hanging” (Job 7).

Then a fountain goes forth from the house of the Lord and waters the torrent of thorns, because the abundance and privilege of spiritual [Col. 0372A] grace flow from the secret joy of a most pure conscience, blunting the stings of vices, restraining the motions of temptations, calming the breath of desires, and refining the seat of affections. Then ignorance is driven away; then carnal desire is cast down, because the mind is illumined by the brightness of contemplation and desire is healed through perfection of love. Egypt is interpreted “darkness,” through which ignorance is signified; Idumea, “earthly,” through which carnal desire is designated. But Judea and Jerusalem shall be inhabited forever. Judea means confession; Jerusalem is called “vision of peace.” For a devout and perfect mind either descends to knowledge of itself and confesses its sins to God through the humility of compunction, or ascends to knowledge of God through the grace of contemplation [Col. 0372B] and is raised to the vision of peace; and then within it “a sound of exultation and confession” is made, as of one feasting. The faithful soul never abandons Judea, because either, moved by compunction, it confesses crimes; or, devoutly, gives thanks for the gifts of grace; or, raised on high, pours forth a hymn while receiving rewards.

Then also the Bridegroom cleanses the blood that until now could not be cleansed, because through the fellowship of union the Bridegroom grants the bride the privilege of perfection, so that nature may feel contrary to nature, which nature naturally opposes. Then the Lord of nature, through the privilege of grace, dwells in Zion—that is, in the watchtower of glory. May he deign to cleanse our nature and grant us his grace unto the glory of that very sublimity—he who lives and reigns, three and one. Amen.

[Col. 0371]

## MORAL EXPOSITION ON OBADIAH. (G)*

### PREFACE

[Col. 0371C] Obadiah, fourth in the order of the prophets, is simple in speech and manifold in meaning; sparse in words, but abundant in thoughts. According to Solomon’s saying, “A wise man is known by few words” (Ecclus. 20), he directs his prophecy literally against Idumea, sharpens his pen allegorically against the world and tropologically against the flesh, and, bearing the type of the Savior, subtly introduces his coming: the coming through which the world is destroyed, the flesh crushed, and freedom [Col. 0372C] restored. Hence: “If the Son makes you free, you shall truly be free” (John 8). This is the Obadiah who, under King Ahab, fed a hundred prophets hidden in caves; while he supplied bodily nourishment, he received spiritual nourishment from God. The aforesaid man prophesied at the same time as the other prophets—namely Amos, Joel, and Hosea. He lies buried in Samaria with Elisha and John the Baptist.

## THE EXPOSITION BEGINS

[Col. 0371]

[Col. 0371D] **(OBADIAH I.) The Vision of Obadiah.** Obadiah is interpreted “servant of the Lord,” by whom the Savior is signified. Thus in Isaiah, speaking in the person of the Father to the Son, it is read: “Hear, Jacob, my servant, and Israel whom I have chosen” (Isa. XLI). Again, to the same one: “You are my servant, Israel; I have given you as a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation [Col. 0372D] unto the end of the earth” (Isa. XLIX). Hence the Savior himself, reproaching the human race, says: “You have made me serve in your sins” (Isa. XLIII).

Since there are four kinds of servitude—necessary, conditional, remunerative, and free—let us see under which kind of servitude freedom served, power was weakened, blessedness humbled itself, and Deity bowed down. For he did not serve in the first manner, who did nothing from necessity; nor in the second, who led captivity captive; nor in the third, who gave gifts to men; but in the fourth. Hence: “You did not require burnt offering and sacrifice for sin; then I said: Behold, I come” (Ps. XXXIX). Again: “At the head of the book it is written concerning me, that I should do your will; O my God, I have willed it, and your law is in the midst of my heart” (ibid.). Truly free servitude: through it neither was nature corrupted, nor condition changed, nor a bargain made; but identity of will bent itself to obedience. Hence: “You were sold for nothing, and you shall be redeemed without silver” (Isa. LII).

This concerning the name. Now let us speak of the vision. It is the prophetic manner of speech to indicate a coming consolation where a vision is mentioned. Thus Obadiah set forth at the beginning of his prophecy, under the title of a vision, the destruction of an enemy people, namely Idumaea, which brought great consolation to the Jewish people, saying: “The Vision of Obadiah.” To guard humility, the prophet speaks of himself as though of another; for one deserves to lose a privilege who abuses a granted gift or permitted authority.

The vision of Obadiah is the incarnation of the Word. Of this vision the Psalmist says: “The Lord looked down from heaven; he saw all the children of men” (Ps. XXXII). The eyes of the Word were judgment and mercy. With these eyes he beheld the pattern of our redemption, when he displayed the incarnate truth of judgment and the mercy of reward: judgment of discernment and mercy of remission. With these eyes [Col. 0373C] he looked upon Peter, when by the truth of judgment he called him to weeping, and by mercy blotted out his sin (Luke XXII). By opening the first, he washes away guilt; by the second, he restores grace.

The bride praises these eyes in the Song of Songs, saying: “Your eyes are like doves above streams of water” (Cant. V). The waters are the gifts of heavenly wisdom; the streams are the varieties of gifts; the dove is the grace of the giver. Therefore the eyes are doves above streams of water, because both by the truth of judgment he freely enlightens and by the kindness of mercy freely adorns with gifts. Therefore the vision of Obadiah is the incarnation of Wisdom, which looked upon the world with both eyes. As in the Gospel of John: “The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us, [Col. 0373D] and we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I).

It follows:

**“Thus says the Lord to Edom.”** That is, against Edom. What is it to speak except to bring forth a word? And what is it to bring forth a word except to come forth from hidden things? Therefore the Lord speaks—that is, the Father brought forth the Word—when the Son went out from the Father and came into the world. But because he came to triumph over the devil, he is “Lord”; because he came freely to liberate the human race, he is “God”; because he came to trample down the world and its pomp, he is the one who speaks against Edom: the Lord, who is to be feared; God, who is to be loved; against Edom, which is to be trampled down. Feared by the devil, loved by his people, the world is to be trampled down by him. He is Lord by the kind of victory, and God by the gifts of grace, against [Col. 0374A] Edom by healing the sickness of desire. Therefore Lord, because he manfully struck down the enemy; God, because he mercifully freed the citizen; against Edom, because he warred against the world’s desire.

Edom is Esau himself, who is also called Seir: the brother of simple Jacob. Because of desire for lentils he lost the glory of the birthright; because of envy of his brother he lost the grace of his father’s blessing. Thus, violently stirred to hatred against his brother, while he cherished poison hidden in his heart and corrupted the bonds of love, he inflamed his inmost being to his brother’s murder, seeking an opportunity and a time of misfortune. Hence he said: “The day of mourning for my father is coming, and then I will kill him” (Gen. XXVII).

By him, therefore, are signified the prudence of the flesh, the desire of the world, a most evil seed, wicked and criminal sons, enemies of God’s grace. Edom is earthly; Esau, bloody; Seir, hairy. Bloody with sins, hairy with occupations, earthly with cares. The world is bloody, indeed, among idolaters; hairy among heretics; earthly among carnal persons and pseudo-Christians. But against Edom the Lord sent the Word, which both erased the handwriting of sin, bestowed spiritual rest, and promised eternal blessedness. Pardon destroyed the handwriting; grace, occupation; glory, care: pardon for sinners, grace for the devout, glory for those who are eternal. Hence David: “He sent his word and healed them, and delivered them from their destructions” (Ps. CXVI). This Word, I say, “enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I). This Word catches the little foxes [Col. 0374C] destroying the vineyards (Cant. II); this Word makes poor and enriches, humbles and exalts (I Kings II).

It follows:

**“We have heard a report from the Lord, and he has sent an envoy to the nations.”**

**LITERAL.** What he had previously said obscurely, he now makes clearer: namely, Christ’s coming for the destruction of sin, the salvation of the world, knowledge of the truth, and love of the highest good. The envoy is he of whom Haggai says: “Behold, the Desired One of all nations comes, and his glory fills the whole earth” (Hag. II). This envoy, under the appearance of poverty, brought us the riches of immortality. Hence the Apostle: “For our sake he became poor, that we might be enriched by his poverty” (II Cor. VIII).

This envoy brought three things with him: light, ointment, [Col. 0374D] and bread—light for the blind, ointment for the sick, bread for the hungry. He set forth light on the mountain, bread in the upper room, ointment on the gibbet of the cross. He placed light in prison, bread in the desert, ointment in the theatre: in the prison of ignorance, the theatre of carnal desire, the desert of human misery. For Christ illuminated the world by expelling ignorance; he satisfied it by ordering desire; and he changed it for the better by driving out misery. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV): the way by enlightening, truth by healing, life by making blessed. First against ignorance, second against desire, third against misery.

One must ask where, or from whom, the prophet received anything concerning this embassy. Let Moses step forth into the midst and reveal what he received concerning it: “The Lord,” he says, “will raise up a prophet from among your brothers; him you shall hear as myself” (Deut. XVIII). Isaiah likewise says: “From the ends of the earth we have heard praises, the glory of the Just One” (Isa. XXIV). Consider, reader, the praises and glory of the Just One: glory in the future, praises in the present. For he merited manifold praise, because he granted health to the sick, abundance to the needy, and freedom to captives. Therefore let his praise be in my mouth, who strengthened me with health, enriched me with abundance, and granted me freedom. If, after this earnest, I receive it purely and faithfully, I do not at all doubt that I shall receive the glory of the Just One. “For we have heard a report from the Lord, and he has sent an envoy to the nations.”

The expression “we have heard a report,” though less Latin in form, is faithfully rendered from Greek. The repetition of the word indicates the force of the utterance.

Historically, however, the coming of the king of Babylon against the Idumaeans is signified. The Lord sent him insofar as, by a just judgment, he permitted him to come. For he was called “the hammer of the whole earth,” through whom the Lord deigned to execute the judgments of most righteous vengeance, and through whom, by God’s just judgment, the pride of innumerable peoples was crushed. Hence it is read in another prophecy: “Son of man, what shall be given to the king of Babylon for the labor by which he served me at Tyre? Give him the kingdom of Egypt.” Consider, reader, the pattern of divine providence, the order of vengeance, and the rule of justice. The Babylonians conquered the Assyrians; the Medes, the Babylonians; [Col. 0375C] the Macedonians, the Medes; the Romans, the Macedonians; Christ, the Romans. But the final victory was accomplished not by cruelty, but by kindness and clemency. Upon the others, however, punishment was fittingly inflicted according to the quality of their deserts. We have said these things by way of digression in accordance with the history.

Now let us examine them allegorically. “The envoy,” he says, “having been sent, came from the valley of Hebron to Shechem” (Gen. XXXVII), because Christ, strong in divinity and increasing the kingdom of eternity through the ranks of heavenly hosts, came to the labor of the Passion; but he wandered in the field, finding in the world no one free from sin. Hence, seeking his brothers, he descended into Dothan (ibid.), because, thirsting for our reconciliation, he humbled himself even to the exhaustion of death. Hebron means “strength” or “eternal increase”; Shechem, “shoulders”; Dothan, “failure” or “defect.”

Therefore “we have heard a report from the Lord, and he has sent an envoy to the nations,” because in the incarnation of the Word we have received certain news of our redemption. How promptly and devoutly he fulfilled his embassy and accomplished our redemption, he himself is about to make known.

**“Rise,” he says, “and let us rise against him in battle.”**

**LITERAL.** Great was the dignity of our creation, but greater is the reverence due to our restoration. For man is read to have been created with divine counsel; but restored with the same counsel, to which grace was added. There, it was said by counsel that man should be made; here, counsel is taken and the Son is secretly sent to redeem him. There human dignity was displayed in the manner and form of the counsel; here the privilege of grace and the excellence of nature appear in the quality of the mystery and the magnitude of the suffering. In both works we are stirred to love, but in the second we are inflamed to greater devotion.

**ALLEGORY.** Hence the Son says: “Rise, and let us rise against him in battle.” “Rise,” he says, to the angels; “let us rise,” Father, I, and the Paraclete. In saying this, I do not divide the unity of the divine essence, but faithfully distinguish the properties of the persons. “Against him”: against the devil, against the world, against sin, against the flesh. “Rise,” he says, to the angels. Hence Isaiah, under the same person: “Go, swift angels, to a nation torn and shattered, to a dreadful people, after which there is no other” [Col. 0376B] (Isa. XVIII). Hence, in the same prophet, concerning the Son: “I will send him,” he says, “to a deceitful nation, and I will command him against the people of my wrath, that he may take spoils, seize plunder, and make him a trampling-place like the mud of streets” (Isa. X). Hence the Son says to the Father through the Psalmist: “My heart is ready; my heart is ready” (Ps. CVII). Hence, concerning the Spirit, the Father says to the Son: “Behold my servant, whom I have chosen; I have put my Spirit upon him; he shall bring forth judgment to the nations” (Isa. XII). Again, the Father says concerning the Son and the Paraclete Spirit: “Cease from man, whose breath is in his nostrils, for he is accounted exalted” (Isa. II).

**MORAL.** Consider carefully how readily the angels are sent [Col. 0376C] to overthrow enemies, and how the blessed and holy Trinity works redemption. I am most certain of victory where power enters the conflict, wisdom orders the work, kindness supplies patience, and promises rewards. “Let us rise,” says the Son: the Father by powerfully driving out the adversary; I by wisely concealing the mystery—“for if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (I Cor. II); the Spirit by kindly receiving and healing the miserable person, for “the spirit of wisdom is kindly, and will not free the cursed man from his lips” (Wis. I).

Let the Father rise by powerfully casting down the enemy for the Son; I will rise by wisely teaching the ignorant. Let the Father’s power shine forth in the overthrow of enemies. Let the Father loose the bonds of human captivity; [Col. 0376D] let the Son enlighten the darkness of human blindness; let the Spirit bestow gifts and desires of charity. Let the reader beware of confusing the Trinity of persons or dividing the unity of the divine essence. For by these things which I distinguish, I show the property of the persons; I do not confuse the unity of nature. Otherwise, as the Trinity is one in nature or essence, so also its operation is wholly one. For it is written: “Whatever the Father does, the Son also does likewise” (John V); nor is the Spirit excluded from this, who is and is called and believed to be the same essence, the same power, the same wisdom, the same God, etc.

It follows:

**“Behold, I have made you small among the nations; you are greatly despised. The pride of your heart has lifted you up, you who dwell in the clefts of the rocks, who exalt your throne, who say [Col. 0377A] in your heart: Who shall bring me down to the earth?”**

**LITERAL.** Historically, the prophet, in the person of the Lord, rebukes, reproves, threatens, and commands the Idumaean: because he rose against his brother, namely the Jewish people; insulted him in the time of his calamity; and instructed, supported, and aided his enemies in attacking him. He shows both what he was by the debt of nature or the merit of his people, and what he became through his own fault. God shows him these three things: the debt of nature, the defect of guilt, and the punishment of penalty. That is, he is contemptible by nature, foul by fault, and detestable in punishment. He shows the first when he says: “Behold, I have made you small among the nations,” etc.; the second there: “Though you are exalted like an eagle,” and what follows; the third there: “They have sent you to the boundary.” When he says that the Idumaean people dwell in clefts of rock, he touches upon a custom peculiar to that people: because of the scarcity of wood and the heat of the sun, they live in caverns of rocks and earthen caves.

**ALLEGORICALLY.** The Lord inveighs against the Gentile people, which, having despised the Creator, the beauty of its own nature, the honor of divine grace, the gift of knowledge, and the worship of righteousness, turned to the filth of idolatry, the uncleanness of morals, the trifles of errors, and empty philosophy. From the very source from which it ought devoutly to have subjected itself to the Creator, it armed itself with a stiff neck and swelled up against him. Therefore he says to it: “Behold, I have made you small in understanding, Gentile in worship, contemptible in conduct”; that is, by just judgment I permitted you to become so. Small, I say, in understanding of the truth; Gentile in rite and ceremony of unbelief; contemptible in deeds of iniquity.

Moreover, to crown its wickedness, the wind of pride puffed it up; by whose deserved consequence it fell into the darkness of unbelief and the gloom of errors. Nor was it content with these things alone: by preaching errors, asserting darkness to be light and evil good, and declaring truth to be falsehood, it led others to ruin. Hence follows: “The pride of your heart has lifted you up, you who dwell in the clefts of the rock and exalt your throne, who say in your heart: Who shall bring me down to the earth?” Consider the order of misery, the course of falling, and the shapeless pattern of departure from God. The swelling of pride comes first; the darkness of ignorance follows; the unbelief of idolatry succeeds. This is followed by delight in, and consent to, uncleanness; then by the preaching of wickedness; and finally by contempt for virtue and hatred of justice.

For when it says, “Pride has lifted you up,” the swelling of pride is shown; by “rock,” the unbelief of ignorance; by “clefts,” the schisms of idolatry; by “dwelling,” consent to uncleanness; by “exalting the throne,” the preaching of wickedness. In saying in his heart, “Who shall bring me down to the earth?” it signifies contempt for virtue and hatred of justice. But “God, the Lord of vengeances, God acts freely in vengeance” (Ps. XCIII); he is exalted in judging the earth, while he repays the proud. Hence it is said:

**“Though you are exalted like an eagle, and though you set your nest among the stars, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord.”**

[Col. 0378A] **LITERAL.** Their deities seemed like stars to the Gentile people.

**ALLEGORY.** Sophists and philosophers, however, are like eagles. In a certain respect philosophers and sophists seemed eagles when they raised the eyes of their hearts to the sun of righteousness and fixed the gaze of their minds steadily upon the very ray of truth. But the eagle is immediately drawn back from there, because after receiving an innate knowledge of truth, on account of their pride philosophers and sophists return to the gloom of errors. Hence the Apostle: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give thanks, but became vain in their thoughts” (Rom. I).

The Gentile people placed their nest among the stars when they set the hope of their salvation either in angels or in human beings, whom they falsely believed to shine forth in the light of wisdom and splendor of righteousness.

It follows:

**“If thieves had entered you by night, if robbers, how would you have been silent? Would they not [nonne; nunquid] have stolen what was sufficient for themselves? If grape-gatherers had entered you, would they not at least have left you a cluster?”**

**LITERAL.** The robbers were the powerful persons of the age; the thieves, the priests and other worshippers of idols; the grape-gatherers, philosophers and sophists. For these three especially flourished in idolatry: philosophy, empty superstition, and infamous power. Worldly philosophers boasted that they possessed understanding of truth; worshippers of idols, the holiness of religion; powerful persons, dominion of freedom. But of the first it is written: “Their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deut. XXXII). Of the second: “Let all who worship graven images be confounded, and those who glory in their idols” (Ps. LXXVI).
