Of the third: “The powerful shall suffer powerful torments, and a stronger torment awaits the stronger” (Wis. VI).

As though the Lord said: See that I alone am, and there is no other God besides me. I will kill and I will make alive; I will strike, and I will heal; and there is none who can deliver from my hand. If I destroy, no one builds; if I shut up, there is no one who opens (Deut. XXXII). None is like me among the mighty, none among lawgivers; I am magnificent in holiness, terrible and praiseworthy, and performing wonders. What neither worldly power, deadly superstition, nor empty philosophy could accomplish, my power, my wisdom, and my kindness achieved. My power destroyed, my wisdom built, my kindness adorned. It destroyed the falsehood of errors; built the truth of doctrines; adorned by pouring in the abundance of charisms. Of the first it is written: “God, whose wrath no one can withstand” (Job IX). Of the second: “Wisdom has built herself a house” (Prov. IX), and the rest. Of the third: “His Spirit adorned the heavens; by his helping hand the twisting serpent was brought forth” (Job XXVI).

**ALLEGORY.** The power of the age and the superstition of the idol each stole for itself what was sufficient. But philosophy left behind some clusters, because neither the first could give freedom, nor the second security, nor the third truth for salvation, or show it. It had shadow, not body; it displayed an image, not the reality. But the incarnate Word has unfolded everything plainly; [Col. 0379A] he possesses all things completely; he searches out Esau’s hidden things. He brings everyone to his own end, when by just judgment he imposes on each person the end due to that person’s merit. Hence the Psalmist: “There is none who can hide himself from his heat” (Ps. XVIII).

God’s heat is read to be threefold. One is that of final damnation; another, of merciful vengeance; another, of gracious love. Of the first it is written: “A fire has been kindled in my wrath, and it shall burn unto the lowest depths of hell” (Deut. XXXII). Of the second: “Our God is a consuming fire” (Heb. XII). Of the third: “The Lord lives, whose fire is in Zion and whose furnace is in Jerusalem” (Isa. XXXI). Therefore none shall hide from his heat, because the impenitent shall be tormented by the fire of damnation; the penitent purified by the fire of vengeance; and the innocent made joyful by the fire of love. Hence the Savior says of himself: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Rom. XII). Again, the same: “‘As I live,’ says the Lord, ‘every knee shall bend to me, and every tongue shall confess to me’” (Rom. XIV). And this is what follows:

**“How they searched out Esau; they investigated his hidden things; they sent you forth to the boundary.”**

**LITERAL.** For Christ, his apostles, and their successors searched out Esau’s hidden things, because by life, morals, and doctrine they refuted and condemned the pomp of the world, its desire, its foolish wisdom, and its idolatry. Christ condemned the first in the manger; the second in the desert; the third on the mountain; the fourth in the Jordan: when the King of glory willed to be wrapped in swaddling-clothes; the bread of life to suffer hunger; the wisdom [Col. 0379C] of God to become foolish; and Deity to be supported by a servant. How the apostles and their successors fought against the world and the error of the Gentiles, their writings teach and the marks of Christ’s sufferings testify. Hence follows: “They sent you forth to the boundary.”

**ALLEGORY.** The aforesaid men sent the world forth to the boundary. For when they broke the jars of their bodies, sounded the trumpets of preaching, and shone with the lamp of miracles, the world was terrified, fell conquered, and offered its neck to the chains of faith. Hence the Psalmist: “They saw it and thus were amazed; they were troubled and moved; trembling seized them” (Ps. XLVII). They were amazed by preaching of unheard-of newness; they were troubled at the hearing, having suffered the ardor of charity; they were moved by miracles of brightness hitherto unseen. Thus they sent Esau forth to the boundary; that is, they led the world to the divinely appointed article of faith. Hence it follows:

**“All the men of your covenant mocked you; the men of your peace prevailed against you. Those who eat bread with you shall lay snares beneath you.”**

**LITERAL.** These men had entered into a covenant with the devil and the world through the worship of idolatry; they had made peace through the inclination of desire. They ate bread with him through preaching error and the proliferation of wickedness. But the men of the covenant mocked him, because those who had served the world too zealously and had offered more devoted worship to idolatry afterwards raised the sword of preaching against the world, set the shield of faith against idolatrous worship, and opposed the safest harbor of religion to the abyss of carnal desire.

[Col. 0380A] **ALLEGORY.** Therefore his friends mocked him by annihilating his foolish wisdom; they prevailed by destroying idolatry; they laid snares by annihilating carnal desire. They did the first by teaching the truth of faith; the second by displaying the radiance of miracles; the third by enduring bodily suffering. Hence the Lord says to Job concerning the devil: “Will you bind him for your maidservants?” (Job XIV). Although servants have a lowly condition, strength nevertheless flourishes in them; but in maidservants, strength is weakened along with the condition of their sex. Yet the Lord declares that he will bind the devil, or the world, for his maidservants, because, coming for our redemption and sending forth his preachers against the world, he chose the foolish instead of the wise, the weak instead of the strong, and the poor instead of the rich.

Therefore the Lord cast down strength and the world’s pomp by his maidservants, because, as Paul testifies: “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (I Cor. I). Hence Solomon fittingly says, among other things concerning the building of Wisdom’s house: “She sent her maidservants to summon us to the citadel and the walls of the city” (Prov. IX). That is, he chose to have weak and despised preachers who might gather faithful peoples to the lofty structures of the spiritual fatherland. Hence in the Gospel the Lord praises Nathanael, yet does not number him among the lot of preachers (John I), because those who came to preach had to be such as possessed nothing of their own light, so that what they did might be recognized as belonging wholly to truth alone, in proportion as it was plainly seen that they had not themselves been fit for this work. Therefore, so that wondrous power might shine forth through the preaching of tongues, something more wondrous was first done: the preachers themselves possessed no merit.

But since he has shown whom the Lord sends against the devil or the world, he now adds what those who are sent do. It follows in the same book of Job: “His friends shall cut him up; merchants shall divide him” (Job XL). Those whom the Lord calls maidservants, friends, and merchants through Job, Obadiah calls men of covenant, men of peace, and table-companions. Then he calls these same persons assailants, mockers, and those who lay snares.

For holy preachers were first maidservants through fear, then became friends through faith, then merchants through the work of preaching. First, I say, they were in covenant with the world or devil through the unbelief of idolatry; they became at peace with shameful desire; they were table-companions through the teaching of wickedness. Afterwards they became mockers through the grace of faith, assailants through obedience, and those who lay snares through the teaching of truth. Hence Solomon says concerning the holy woman: “She made linen cloth and sold it, and delivered a girdle to the Canaanite” (Prov. XXXI). In the linen cloth is signified the subtlety of preaching. The Church made and sold this cloth, because the faith which she had woven by believing she gave by speaking, and in the faithful received the life of right conduct. She also gave a girdle to the Canaanite, because by the vigor of manifested righteousness she bound the loose works of Gentile life, so that what is commanded may be held fast in practice.

Therefore, in seeking, the Lord finds his preachers as maidservants; in transforming, makes them friends; in enriching, renders them merchants; and leads those enriched with virtues as far as the exercise of the business of faith. Thus, by rebuking and persuading the members of the devil and the children of this age, they may cut them down the more severely, the more truly, having become friends through love of truth, they attach themselves to him; and may snatch souls of sinners away from him the more swiftly, the sooner, having become capable merchants, they display within themselves most ample storehouses of virtues.

Therefore Obadiah says in the person of the Lord: “Those who eat bread with you shall lay snares beneath you,” because those who formerly lived dissolutely, made the soul a slave to the flesh, [Col. 0381B] and shared in the table of demons by consenting to vices, discern more subtly, detect more quickly, judge more keenly, and condemn more vigorously the devil’s cunning, the world’s cares, and the flesh’s enticements. For he first gathered the unlearned and afterwards philosophers; he did not teach fishermen through orators, but educated orators through fishermen.

It follows:

**“There is no prudence in him.”**

**ALLEGORY.** Prudence unto salvation is foresight; and it was in neither the devil, the world, nor the flesh. For the devil fell through pride, the world is corrupted through vanity, and the flesh is weakened through pleasure: the devil through arrogance, the world through wantonness, the flesh through desire.

What we have interpreted concerning the devil or the world can be referred to heretics or the flesh. Heretics, spiritual robbers invading the holy land and perverting the canonical Scriptures, have brought this about: “They sharpened their tongues, they stretched their bow—a bitter thing—that they might shoot the blameless in secret” (Ps. LXIII). Against them Obadiah, in the person of the Son, directs prophetic speech, saying:

“Rise,” he says, “and let us rise against him,” that is, against the assembly of heretics, “in battle.”

**MORAL.** Because heretical perfidy advances many things contrary to the health of faith, and many things injurious to the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, the Son has resolved, with the gravity of counsel and the weight of assistance, to overthrow their madness. “Rise and let us rise,” etc. Arius asserts that the Son is less than the Father; Macedonius that the Paraclete is less than both; Sabellius identifies the Father himself with the Son; Manichaeus denies that the Word became flesh. One perversely divides what is one; another most vainly confounds what is divided.

Against the destruction of their madness, the Son, seeing the necessary power of the Father, his own wisdom, and the kindness of the Holy Spirit, says: “Rise, and let us rise.” The Father, destroying the falsehood of heretics through power; I, by teaching the truth of faith; the Holy Spirit, by pouring in charity: so that, because we are one in deity, essence, and will, by one encounter we may either bring those joined together back to unity or drive the reprobate to eternal calamity.

It follows:

[Col. 0382A] **“Behold, I have made you small among the nations; you are greatly despised.”**

**MORAL.** The assembly of heretics was small among the nations and deservedly contemptible: small in understanding, contemptible in conduct; small in knowledge of truth, contemptible in deeds of iniquity. The Lord gave them this when, by judgment, he permitted them to become such, etc.

It follows:

**“Pride drives you out, you who dwell in the clefts of the rock, who say in your heart: Who shall bring me down to the earth?”**

**MORAL.** Pride came first among heretics, and heretical error most justly followed it. For if they thought humbly concerning God and thought humbly of themselves, they would by no means abandon the way of the humble along which they were walking. Hence Truth itself: “Upon whom,” he says, “shall my Spirit rest, but upon the humble, quiet, and trembling at my words?” [Col. 0382B] (Isa. LXVI). Therefore the Spirit of truth dwells in a mind of humility, because whoever despises humility, willingly or unwillingly abandons truth. For it is written: “There fell those who work iniquity” (Ps. XXXV).

The rock is the Catholic faith or authentic Scripture. The clefts are the varieties of heresies and opinions contrary to the truth of faith. The throne is heretical teaching; the exaltation of the throne is the spread of perverse teaching.

It follows:

**“Who shall bring me down to the earth?”** To say this is blind and arrogant presumption, etc.

It follows:

**“Though you are exalted like an eagle, and though you set your nest among the stars, from there I will bring you down.”** A heretic is like an eagle when his understanding is illumined by subtle intelligence; he sets his nest among the stars when, by false innocence and feigned righteousness, he compares himself with the merits of the saints. But the Lord brings him down to earth when, by just judgment, ignorance blinds his subtle intelligence and open wickedness exposes his faithless righteousness. Hence the Psalmist: “Contempt was poured out upon princes; and he caused them to wander in a pathless place, and not in the way” (Ps. CVI), etc.

It follows:

**“If thieves had entered you, if robbers by night, how would you have been silent? Would they not have stolen what was sufficient for themselves? If grape-gatherers had entered you, would they not at least have left clusters for you?”** As if the Lord said to heretics: If anyone secretly, like a thief, or openly, like a robber, attempts to assail your madness, or to refute your propositions, by which you strive to establish your errors and, as though by gathering grapes, reduce them to wine, and presses out the wine of sound understanding for your confusion, at once they rise against him; scale is joined to scale. For those whom a like guilt joins in united obstinacy are likewise massed together in perverse defense, so that those who were grieved at one another’s reciprocal injury may defend one another’s crimes by alternating defense. But if heretics are so ready to mount a proud defense of falsehood, I shall be readier to avenge truth and attack errors.

It follows:

**“How they searched out Esau; they investigated his hidden things! They sent you forth to the boundary—all the men of your covenant; they mocked you, all the men of your peace prevailed against you. Those who eat bread with you shall lay snares beneath you.”** The prophetic Spirit covertly introduces the teaching of the apostles and the victory of orthodox Fathers over heretics: they investigate hidden sophistries, draw out poisonous meanings, and, with reason compelling them, lead them to the boundary of truth. Among their number were Augustine, Cyprian, Ambrose, Hilary, Jerome, and others of this kind. Some of them had entered into covenant and at times maintained peace with the heretics; they had even eaten bread with them. Among them was Augustine, who had been a Manichaean with the Manichaeans, but upon recovering his senses utterly destroyed their sect. Therefore the Fathers mocked the heretics by reasoning; prevailed by bringing forward testimonies; and laid snares by recalling their assemblies.

Therefore there is no prudence in him. That is, in the assembly [Col. 0383B] of heretics, where reason also convicts falsehood, divine utterance confirms truth, and the grace of conversion exposes unbelief. These things may, moreover, be applied tropologically to the flesh. For the flesh is not without reason signified by Esau: it is hairy with desires, bloody with vices, and earthly with harmful works—desires of vanity, vices of curiosity, works of iniquity. Hence the Apostle says: “I know that no good dwells in me, that is, in my flesh” (Rom. VII). Again, the same Apostle: “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God” (Rom. VIII).

One must understand, however, that when divine speech attacks the flesh, it accuses not nature but fault; not the condition of nature but the defect of righteousness; not the union of the elements but the motions of vices. For just as in man there are two natures, namely spirit and flesh [Col. 0383C], so there are two motions by which each is moved: one toward the affection of righteousness, the other departing from the affection of grace. Hence virtue and vice arise: so that the motion of the spirit is virtue, whereas the motion of the flesh is nothing other than a motion of the mind not obeying the spirit. The former is spiritual and makes men spiritual; the latter is carnal and makes men carnal. The former is called spirit; the latter is designated by the name of flesh.

But since an occasion has presented itself to speak of the origin of virtue and vice, it is pleasing to go back a little more deeply and examine more closely all the general motions of the soul. The general motion of the soul, then, is divided fivefold. At one time the human heart is moved only by the devil; at another, by man alone; sometimes only by God; sometimes by man and the devil; sometimes by man and God. The first is through the suggestion of sin; the second through simple consideration of nature; the third through a momentary inspiration of grace; the fourth through unlawful delight; the fifth through the affections of virtues and contemplation of the Bridegroom.

The first and second are harmless to man; the third glorious; the fourth penal; the fifth remunerative. The fourth is vicious and must be condemned; the fifth belongs to virtue and must be crowned; the third must be eagerly received. The second, together with the first, is indifferent. The fourth belongs to the flesh, the fifth to the spirit; the third to God; the first and second to neither. The general motion of the flesh is sevenfold. At one time it is against God, at another against one’s neighbour, sometimes against oneself, often against the world [Col. 0384A], and very often against business or work. At one time it is directed toward one’s neighbour, and at another toward oneself. Against God: pride; against one’s neighbour: envy; against oneself: anger; against the world: avarice; against work: acedia. Toward one’s neighbour: lust; toward oneself: gluttony, or *gastrimargia*.

These seven vices are that household which the Lord left in the midst of His people, in order that He might train Israel by it; and their character may also be indicated by the meaning of their names. These, then, are the names. The first is called the Perizzite; the second, the Hittite; the third, the Hivite; the fourth, the Amorite; the fifth, the Girgashite; the sixth, the Jebusite; the seventh, the Canaanite. The first is interpreted “conquering”; the second, “wasting away” or “enduring navigation”; the third, “gathering stones”; the fourth, “embittered” or “making bitter”; the fifth, “driving out the settler” [Col. 0384B]; the sixth, “trodden down” or “treading down”; the seventh, “changed” or “changing.” By the first is signified pride; by the second, envy; by the third, anger; by the fourth, acedia; by the fifth, avarice; by the sixth, lust; by the seventh, *gastrimargia*.

But since we intend to proceed to what follows, we leave the application of each to the reader’s easy exercise. It must be understood, however, that that motion is especially called carnal which serves the flesh alone and is ministered through the flesh, which in the present passage is signified by Esau. This motion lays snares for its brother Jacob, because it attacks virtue in three ways: by the incontinence of lust, by the excess of gluttony, and by the wantonness of the senses. By the first the flower of chastity is overthrown; by the second, the honour of sobriety; by the third [Col. 0384C], the beauty of moral decency.

Therefore Esau also received a threefold name, by which the aforesaid misfortune is signified. He is earthly through *gastrimargia*; bloody through lust; hairy through wantonness. Hairy through the excess of curiosity; bloody through the vicious outflow of desire; earthly through both, burdened by the appetite for feasting and drunkenness. Obadiah, therefore, attacks the flesh under the person of the Lord; indeed, the Lord through His friends undertakes to conquer it, saying to them:

“Rise up, and let us rise against him in battle.”

**MORAL.** For “those who belong to Christ have crucified their flesh with its vices and desires; but you are not in the flesh, but the Holy Spirit dwells in you” (Gal. V). “What is born of flesh is flesh, and what is born of spirit is spirit” (John III). “He who sows in the flesh shall reap corruption; but he who sows in the spirit shall reap eternal life from the spirit” (Gal. VI). “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Mark XIV).

It is read in the Psalm: “In a desert land, trackless and waterless: so I appeared before You in the sanctuary” (Ps. XIV). And through Solomon: “I resolved,” he says, “to withdraw my flesh from wine, that I might transfer it to wisdom” (Eccl. II). And the Bridegroom in the Song of Songs says: “I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of incense” (Cant. II). And through Job: “The deep says, ‘It is not in me’; and the sea says, ‘It is not with me’; nor is it found in the land of those who live pleasantly” (Job XXVIII). And in Jeremiah: “Those who feasted luxuriously perished in the streets; and those nourished in saffron embraced dung” [Col. 0385A].

Rise, therefore, my friends, for vengeance upon the enemy, for the mortification of the flesh. “And by as much as she prepared herself and lived in delights, by so much give her torment and mourning” (Lam. IV). Therefore you must not at all fear the outcome of the struggle, nor must you in the least despair of the hope of triumph. For He who helps you cannot be conquered, because He is omnipotence; He who teaches you cannot be deceived, because He is wisdom; He who promises cannot be corrupted, because He is righteousness; He cannot be resisted, because He is eternal; He cannot be avoided, because He is everywhere.

Rise, I say, friends: for the enemy is weak, the place suitable, the helper unconquered, the victory certain, the merits many, the rewards worthy. The enemy is the weak flesh; the place, the present life; the helper, highest Deity; the reward, the vision of the Trinity. Rise from the sleep of torpor [Col. 0385B], from the bed of sorrow, from the languor of desolation: first through the vigilance of discernment, second through the mortification of the flesh, third through the joy of spiritual consolation. “Let us rise against him in battle,” because the enemy is contemptible.

Hence, turning to the enemy, he says: “Behold, I have made you small among the nations; you are exceedingly contemptible.” For the motion of the flesh, among the vices mentioned above, is small because momentary; corruptible because dishonourable. It is small because, where it has poured forth pleasant honey, it flees and strikes hearts it has wounded with an excessively clinging bite. It is contemptible because pleasure, bought with pain, harms. It is small because it neglects goods; contemptible because it performs evils. It is small because it seeks transitory things; contemptible because it despises eternal things [Col. 0385C]. Small in affection, contemptible in act; small in work, contemptible in desert. It follows:

> “The pride of your heart has lifted you up, dwelling in the clefts of the rock, who say in your heart: ‘Who will bring me down to earth?’”

The rock here is understood as the soul, which is called whole when no carnal passion rules it. It is cleft when it is scattered by the assault of vices. The clefts, therefore, are carnal desires. For he exalts his throne who commends the works of the flesh in contempt of God. To say in one’s heart, “Who will bring me down to earth?” is, having despised God, to place one’s hope of salvation and eternity in worldly pleasure and in oneself.

In this three vices are noted: hatred of good, love of evil, and forgetfulness of God. Observe carefully [Col. 0385D] how swiftly the unhappy soul falls: suddenly it fails from the state of righteousness and in a moment descends into the depth of wickedness. First, inwardly, it conceives a pestilent pleasure; then it places glory in it. In this it fixes consent, and afterward applies deliberation; thereafter it produces the deed; afterward contempt of God; then the preaching of sin; thereafter hatred of good; then love of evil; finally forgetfulness of God.

This is the Decalogue of disobedience, which the Lord gave Moses on Mount Sinai, interpreted “humility.” He had fulfilled this Decalogue who said: “I do not know the Lord, and I will not let Israel go” (Exod. V). So also had others who said: “Who is the Almighty, that we should serve Him?” (Job XXI), and: “What does it profit us if we pray to Him?” (ibid.). So too had others: “Let us crown ourselves with roses before they wither. Let us leave everywhere signs of our joy. Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we shall die. For this is our lot and our inheritance” (Wis. II; Isa. XXII). It follows:

> “If you are exalted like an eagle, and if you place your nest among the stars, from there I will bring you down, says the Lord.”

The apostate angel was an eagle by condition, but through pride became Leviathan. The stars are classes of men shining in the world above others by the lamp of nobility, the brightness of learning, or the splendour of riches. The nest is the pageantry of dishonourable pleasure. Thus the Lord says to Esau—that is, to the flesh—“If you are exalted like an eagle,” and so forth. As if He said: If the wealth of Egypt should fall to your lot, if the flower of the age should smile upon you, if pageantry should answer your desire [Col. 0386B]; if you have carefully tended your skin, if you have feasted splendidly, if you have grown fat with riches, sleek with delights, enlarged by attendants—yet “the moth shall be spread beneath you, and worms shall be your covering” (Isa. XIV).

Hence the Apostle: “Food is for the belly, and the belly for foods; but God will destroy both it and them” (I Cor. VI). Hence the Lord through John in the Apocalypse: “Because you say, ‘I sit as a queen, and I am not a widow, and I shall not see mourning,’ therefore in one day your plagues shall come: death, mourning, and famine; and fire shall consume you” (Apoc. XVIII), “because mighty is the Lord who judges her.” Again, in the same book: “Render to her as she herself rendered to us; and repay her double, doubly, according to her works: in the cup which she mixed, mix for her double” (ibid.).

> “If thieves had entered in to you, and robbers, how would you have been silent? Would they not have stolen what was sufficient for themselves? If grape-gatherers had entered in to you, would they not at least have left you grapes?” [Col. 0386C]

Thieves are pretenders and the crafty, who provoke God’s wrath. Robbers are sufferings and diseases. Demons, moreover, are grape-gatherers. The first hypocritically mortify the flesh; the second torment it most grievously; the third disfigure and humble it. Yet all take what is sufficient for themselves, because neither demon, disease, nor hypocrite does anything except what divine providence permits in its ordering. Hence the Lord says through Job: “I surrounded the sea with my bounds, and set a bar and doors, and said: ‘Thus far shall you come, and no farther; and here you shall break your swelling waves’” [Col. 0386D] (Job XXXVIII).

The Lord surrounds the sea when He moderates, by the dispensation of His judgments, the assaults of those things that afflict the flesh, so that the raging swell of its heated violence may secretly be broken upon the level shore. Thus the Lord says: “If thieves had entered in to you,” and so forth. As if He said: If those who can do nothing without My judgment afflict you so severely, to your disadvantage and distress, what will My friends do, who by afflicting you will please Me while providing for your benefit? Hence it follows:

> “How they searched Esau out! They investigated his hidden things!”

The friends of Christ, disciples of truth, investigate the hidden things of Esau—that is, of the flesh—because they strive to cut away not only the manifest works of the flesh but also the superfluities of carnal thoughts. Hence Job says: “Why do I tear my flesh with my teeth and carry my soul in my hands?” (Job XIII). Again: “I made a covenant with my eyes, that I might not even think of a virgin” (Job XXXI). It follows:

> “They have driven you out unto the boundary.”

By “boundary” he means the outlet of the doorway. For Esau—that is, the flesh—has a chamber, a house, a courtyard, and a bed. The bed is iniquity; the chamber, excess; the house, curiosity; the courtyard, pleasure. Pleasure moves the affection, curiosity the sense, excess the consent, iniquity the performance of deeds. Holy men therefore drive Esau out unto the boundary, because they remove iniquity from deed, excess from consent, curiosity from sense, and pleasure from anxious affection. They drive the flesh out unto the boundary, I say, when they withdraw it to [Col. 0387B] a just and necessary measure.

This had been done by him who said: “For Your sake we are put to death all day long; we are accounted as sheep for slaughter” (Ps. XLIII). This also the Apostle did when he said: “We brought nothing into the world; doubtless neither can we take anything out of it. But having food and clothing, let us be content with these” (I Tim. VI), and so forth. It follows:

> “All the men of your covenant mocked you; all the men of your peace prevailed against you. Those who eat bread with you shall lay snares beneath you.”

“Wonderful, O Lord, has Your knowledge become from me” (Ps. CXXXVIII). Wonderful, I say, are You in Your saints: You who give strength and power to Your people; who bring forth those bound in strength; who turn the sea into dry land, that they may cross the river on foot when it is dry; who willed that children of the world, friends of the flesh, servants of vices, companions at table of demons, should become despisers of the world [Col. 0387C], tramplers of the flesh, persecutors of vices, mockers of demons; who proclaimed consummation out of execration and falsehood.

Hence it is written: “In the field of Jezreel dogs shall lick the blood of Jezebel” (III Kings XXI). In a dog, according to its negative signification, three things are considered; and according to its good signification, likewise three. According to the evil sense: rage, lust, barking. According to the good: faith, zeal, teaching. Faith for guarding; zeal for avenging; barking for teaching. Jezreel is interpreted “seed of God”; Jezebel, “vain flux.” By Jezreel is signified fear of God; by the field, exercise and labour; by Jezebel, care for and love of the flesh.

Therefore, in the field of Jezreel dogs lick the blood of Jezebel, because holy and God-fearing men, through exercise and the love of divine fear, utterly destroy the care for and love of the flesh. Hence the Psalmist says: “Pierce my flesh with Your fear, for I feared Your judgments” (Ps. CXVIII). And this is what Obadiah says: “All the men of your covenant,” and so forth. Note these three: covenant, peace, and banquet. They had entered a covenant with the flesh through affection; peace through consent; a banquet through act: through the affection of desire, the consent of wantonness, the act of wickedness.

Three other things are set against these three. Against desire: mockery; against wantonness: attack; against wickedness: snares. The snares are fasts; the attack, spiritual exercises; the mockery, virtues. For fasting weakens the strength of the flesh—that is, its wickedness [Col. 0388A]; spiritual exercise destroys the wantonness of the senses; and the choir of virtues cuts away disordered desire. It follows:

> “There is no prudence in him.”

For in Esau—that is, in the flesh—no traces of prudence appear unless the standards of the aforesaid three shine forth. The first excludes the flesh’s wickedness; the second lulls its wantonness; the third drives out its desire, and so forth. It follows:

> “Shall I not on that day, says the Lord, destroy the wise from Edom and prudence from Mount Esau? And your mighty men shall fear from the south, so that every man may perish from the house of Esau.”

According to the historical sense, the Lord threatens destruction to the people of Idumaea. According to allegory, He threatens heretics or the Gentile people. According to the tropological sense, the flesh. That day of which the Lord speaks historically signifies the coming of the Babylonians for Idumaea’s destruction; allegorically, Christ’s coming in the flesh for the calling of the Gentiles; tropologically, His coming into the mind for conversion to religion. Here “day” signifies prosperity or joy granted to neighbouring nations over Idumaea’s destruction; likewise, to those called to the faith through their conversion; likewise, to those changed to religion through their sanctification.

Wisdom in this place signifies the inclination toward wickedness; prudence, the cunning of worldly craft; might, the horn of secular power; mountain, the exaltation of pride; south, the heat of impure desire, and so forth. It follows:

> “Because of the slaughter and because of the iniquity done to your brother Jacob, shame shall cover you, and you shall perish for ever.”

Historically, the Lord shows the reason for Idumaea’s overthrow: it acted unjustly against the Israelite people, withholding counsel, withdrawing help, and killing many of them in the time of siege and calamity. Allegorically, the Lord declares that heretics perished for this reason: they acted unjustly against the Church in many ways, striving to corrupt her faith, tear the Bridegroom’s garment, and ravage the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth; persecuting, banishing, and surrounding ecclesiastical men, and corrupting many by force, fraud, and money. Tropologically, He indicates the destruction of the flesh because, at the time of temptation, it rose unjustly against the mind’s dominion and unjustly laid waste every precious thing of virtue [Col. 0388D]. It follows:

> “On the day when you stood against him, when foreigners took his army captive and strangers entered his gates, and they cast lots over Jerusalem, you also were one of them. You shall not despise your brother in the day of his exile. You shall not rejoice over the sons of Judah in the day of their destruction. You shall not open your mouth in the day of distress. Neither shall you enter the gates of My people in the day of their ruin. Neither shall you look with satisfaction upon his evils in the day of his desolation. You shall not stretch out your hand against his army in the day of his desolation; nor shall you stand at the exits to kill those who flee. Nor shall you be sent out against his army in the day of its desolation. You shall not shut up their survivors in tribulation, for near is the day of the Lord upon all nations.”

> “As you have done, so shall it be done to you; He shall turn your recompense upon your own head.”

Historically, he shows the inhumanity of the Idumaeans and their cruelty toward the Israelite people, whom they not only failed to aid in the time of distress but also joined with the enemy to attack. This is what he says from “On the day when you stood” through “You shall not despise.” Allegorically, he shows the savagery of heretics toward Christians. In the time of the primitive Church, when idolaters persecuted, afflicted, and slaughtered Christians, heretics not only afforded no defence, but were especially a scandal, snare, ruin, and captivity to them. Jerusalem is the Church; its gates are its prelates; its army is the Christian people.

Tropologically, he shows the wantonness of the flesh rising against the soul in time of temptation. The flesh not only failed, by restraining its senses and chastising its members, to offer them in service to righteousness and God for sanctification, but, making them weapons of iniquity for sin, caused them to serve impurity and iniquity for the destruction of the soul [Col. 0389B]. Jerusalem is contemplation; its gates are the eminence of purity, the hope of immortality, and the perfection of charity.

After showing the savagery of those mentioned above, he next declares their most deserved recompense, and their powerless intention to destroy the aforesaid people under God’s just judgment, saying: “You shall not despise,” and so forth. As though he said: You shall not despise, because you will drink from the same cup. Historically, the day of exile is the harshness of captivity; allegorically, the course of the present life; tropologically, the heat of manifest temptation. The sons of Judah are the sons of the Church. The day of destruction and distress is an evident fall into heresy or a sudden fall into carnal temptation. The gate of the people is soundness of faith or confession of sin. The exits of the ways are the manifold uncertainty of opinions or the many-shaped occasions of carnal temptations. Confinement is unbelief and despair. The day of the Lord is Christ’s coming, or the prosperity of vengeance, or the illumination of grace. “Upon all nations,” because God makes some vessels of mercy by grace, while by justice He leaves others as vessels of wrath fitted for destruction and dishonour, and so forth. It follows:

> “As you have done, so shall it be done to you; I will turn your recompense upon your own head.”

For there is no punishment more just than that by which retaliation is received. He who prepares a pit, it is just that he should fall into it.

> “As you drank upon My holy mountain, all nations shall drink continually; they shall drink and be swallowed up, and they shall be as though they were not.”

Historically, the prophetic speech is directed to the Idumaeans; allegorically, against idolaters and heretics; tropologically, against the flesh and its animal senses, its desire and carnal impulses. Historically, the mountain is that earthly city Jerusalem; allegorically, Christ and the Church; tropologically, holy contemplation. To drink upon the mountain is to delight and rejoice over the overthrow of the aforesaid city, the contempt of Christ, the rejection of the Church, or the fall of a soul adorned with virtues and raised to contemplation of the Bridegroom.

Let us read Herodotus and Greek and barbarian histories, and we shall see how, under the Assyrians and Babylonians, that saying was fulfilled: “Near is the day of the Lord upon all nations” [Col. 0390A] (Ps. CXXXVI). The meaning of what follows—“As you have done, so shall it be done to you; He shall render your recompense upon your head”—is that which we read in the Psalm: “Remember, O Lord, the sons of Edom in the day of Jerusalem, who say: ‘Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundations’” (ibid.).

For just as you drank with the Babylonians upon My holy mountain and rejoiced, so all the nations whom you had with you in Babylon’s garrison, turned against you, shall drink and rejoice; and they shall not merely drink, but shall swallow you up, so that the Idumaeans may be as though they were not. Or indeed, after those nations have swallowed you, they themselves shall be swallowed up by the Medes. This vengeance will proceed thus: you shall consume Jerusalem; the Babylonian shall consume you; the Mede and Persian shall consume the Babylonian.

Let us follow the order of the interpretation. Near is the day of the Lord upon all nations, O heretic: near is the time of judgment in which all nations must be judged. As you acted against churchmen, so shall it be done to you. For as you rejoiced in their slaughter, celebrated a banquet, and upon My holy mountain—that is, the Church—drank not My cup but that of the devil, concerning whom Habakkuk says: “Woe to him who gives drink to his friend and makes him drunk by mixing in his gall, that he may look upon his nakedness” (Hab. II), so all nations—or the opposing powers assigned to punishments, or hostile virtues—shall drink and swallow up your blood; and finally, when torment comes upon all [Col. 0390C], they too shall be as though they were not.

For one who perishes from Him who is—and who said to Moses, “He who is has sent me to you” (Exod. III)—is, according to the rule of Scripture, said not to be. Hence we also read in Esther: “Do not hand over, Lord, Your kingdom to those who are not” (Esth. XIV). Likewise through Isaiah: “As though they were not, so are they before Him; they are accounted by Him as nothing and emptiness” (Isa. XL).

We may interpret this passage otherwise. Because you rejoiced in the ruin of My servants, the same persecution shall come against you also; and as you rejoiced with the other nations against My people, so all nations shall come against you too, and shall devour and drink, and shall crush you with like punishment. Tropologically, it is directed against the flesh which had said: “I sit, and I shall not see mourning” [Col. 0390D] (Apoc. XVIII). Hence it is said to it: “By as much as she prepared herself and lived in delights, by so much prepare for her torments and mourning” (ibid.). Hence the Psalmist: “Wretched daughter of Babylon: blessed is he who repays you your repayment” (Ps. CXXXVI), and so forth. Hence Nahum, speaking to the spirit: “Enter into the mud and tread it down; hold the brick fast while kneading it” (Nahum III), calling the flesh a brick. It follows:

**LITERAL.** “And upon Mount Zion there shall be salvation, and it shall be holy. And the house of Jacob shall possess those who had possessed them. And the house of Jacob shall be fire, and the house of Joseph flame, and the house of Esau stubble. They shall be kindled among them and shall devour them; and there shall be no remnant of the house of Esau, because the Lord has spoken.”

Idumaea having been overthrown and devoured by the hostile nations with whom it had formerly entered into a covenant against Jacob, there shall be survivors upon Mount Zion [Col. 0391A], and there shall be salvation, and it shall be holy. That is, either the Lord Himself will return to the temple which He had abandoned because of the people’s sin; or understand “holy” absolutely, that is, the Holy of Holies. Under Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, the house of Jacob shall possess those who had possessed it as an inheritance; and the house of Jacob—that is, the house of Judah—shall be fire, and the house of Joseph, of the ten tribes, flame. But the house of Esau—that is, the Idumaeans, who had proved so fierce and cruel toward their brother—shall become stubble. And as fire and flame consume stubble, so the two kingdoms, joined in covenant by the union of a single rod, according to Ezekiel, shall lay waste Idumaea and devour it. There shall be no survivor from the people who can report the destruction to the neighbouring nations.

All that we have said and shall say, they promise themselves will occur in the future time when, in place of Christ, they shall receive Antichrist, the prophecy of the Saviour being fulfilled: “I came in the name of My Father and you did not receive Me; if another comes in his own name, him you will receive” (John V). Whatever we have interpreted against Idumaea, they imagine against the Roman Empire.

**MORAL.** Certainly, what we said was fulfilled historically under Zerubbabel, we affirm is daily accomplished prophetically and according to mystical senses in the Church, and is fulfilled in each person’s kingdom of the soul against the flesh. Mount Zion is allegorically the Church; tropologically, the soul set upon the watchtower of heavenly things and raised by the joy of contemplation. Therefore, when Christ enters Egypt upon a light cloud and descends into Dothan [Col. 0391C], while the Saviour sanctifies the Church by the washing of saving water through the word—He who is truly its sanctification, so that He may present it to Himself without spot or wrinkle—Mount Zion is said to be sanctified, because the Saviour, its sanctification, as I have said, is joined to it by grace and mystery.

Hence the Son Himself says to the Father: “Father, sanctify them in truth” (John XVII). “Your word is truth.” Again He says: “For them I sanctify Myself” (ibid.). See, reader, the new and wonderful kind of sanctification in the form of our redemption: how great was the dignity of humanity’s creation, and how much greater was the importance of its restoration. For the Father sanctifies, the Word sanctifies, and the Spirit sanctifies. What is it to sanctify except to make holy? What is it to make holy except to free from earthly appetite, earthly affection, earthly understanding, and earthly contagion? For Greek *hagios*—that is, “holy”—is said in Latin to mean “without earth.”

Certainly, in every human being there are naturally three things, oppressed by earthly contagions, stained with the filth of vices, and subjected to the proud tyranny of demons. These are the capacity, the will, and the knowledge. Human power had been weakened, the will wounded, and knowledge disturbed. The Apostle had experienced weakened power when he said: “I delight in the law of God according to the inward man; but I see another law in my members resisting the law of my mind and leading me captive under the law of sin which is in my members” (Rom. VII).

He knew the will to be wounded when he said: “For the good that I will, I do not do; but the evil that I hate, that I do” [Col. 0392A] (ibid.). He had also seen knowledge disturbed, saying: “For we know in part and prophesy in part” (I Cor. XIII). The Psalmist likewise briefly indicates this, saying: “My heart has been troubled” (Ps. XXXVII)—behold the wounded will; “and my strength has left me” (ibid.)—behold weakened power; “the light of my eyes, even that is not with me” (ibid.)—behold darkened knowledge.

But upon Mount Zion—that is, in the height of the watchtower, in the perfection of the Church—there shall be salvation: through the power of the Most High, through the incarnation of the Word, through the coming of the Paraclete. And that mountain, namely the Church, shall be holy, wholly raised from earthly things in act, understanding, and affection, receiving power in the sacraments, wisdom in the commandments, fruitfulness in gifts: power from the Father [Col. 0392B], wisdom from the Son, fruitfulness from the Spirit, through the charity poured into us by Him.

In saying this I do not divide the unity of the divine essence, nor confuse the properties of the Persons; rather, in the divine operation I rightly and faithfully show the distinction of the Persons and the unity of the essence. Mount Zion, therefore, is holy at the coming of the Saviour, because at the coming of her Bridegroom the Church received from Him the holiness of sacraments, the sanctity of commandments, and the sanctification of gifts. By Him, I say, she is sanctified—that is, raised from earthly things by faith in the sacraments; by Him she is raised through hope in the commandments; by Him she is exalted through charity in heavenly gifts.

Thus sanctified, she sanctifies and heals; illumined, she illumines; what she has received, she bestows, so that both the one sanctified and the one sanctifying may be from one. [Col. 0392C] It follows.

And the house of Jacob shall possess, etc. The house of Jacob the supplanter is the Church, the bride of the Savior, of whom the Apostle says: “Moses indeed was faithful as a servant for a testimony to those things which were to be spoken; but Christ as a son in His house; and we are that house, provided that we hold firm unto the end the beginning of our hope” (Heb. III). This Jacob—that is, the wrestler—is the Savior of humankind. Historically, we find that Jacob wrestled four times: three times with his brother and once with the angel. First in the womb; second over the dish of lentils; third over the oracle of his father’s blessing; when returning from Mesopotamia, he wrestled with his brother, as has been said above. Allegorically, our wrestler, the stronger one who came upon the strong man’s house, entered it and bound the strong man. With the angel, in the fourth place, [Col. 0392D] he plundered his goods; to him the Father gave the contest, perhaps that he might conquer, so that all might know that wisdom was stronger than all things.

Our Jacob, I say, is said already to have wrestled three times; he is certainly believed to be about to wrestle a fourth time. First, in the womb; second, on the cross; third, in the tomb; fourth, at the last judgment, against wicked servants and seed. In the womb, by freedom from sin; on the cross, by the acquisition of glory and the honor of kingship; in the tomb, by the immortality of life and the glory of triumph; at judgment, by the right of victory and the rigor of justice. First, therefore, he supplanted the devil in the womb, because “he watched, and became like a solitary sparrow upon the roof” (Ps. CI). Second, on the cross: “When I am lifted up from the earth,” he says, “I shall draw all things to myself” (John XII). [Col. 0393A] Third, the Jew, according to the saying of the Psalmist: “Through the greatness of thy power thine enemies shall lie to thee” (Ps. LXV); and in Genesis: “Judah is a lion’s whelp: thou hast gone up to the prey, my son; resting thou hast couched as a lion, and as a lioness: who shall rouse him? The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor the ruler from his thigh, until he comes who is to be sent; and he shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX). Fourth, too, he shall supplant the troop of goats, saying: “Depart, ye cursed, into everlasting fire” (Matt. XXV).

You see, then, little man; you see, dust, worm, earth, ashes; you see, I say, what the sun of righteousness endured for you, what the Lord of hosts did for you, what the King of glory suffered through you. Hence he himself says through Isaiah: “You have made me labor in your sins; you have made me serve in your iniquities” (Isa. XLIII). Likewise [Col. 0393B] the same through the same prophet: “I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was not a man with me. I looked around, and there was no helper; I sought, and there was none to assist; but my own arm shall save for me, and my indignation itself has assisted me” (Isa. LXIII). Consider how indignation assisted him. For his indignation is his incarnation itself, by which he destroyed death, overcame him who had the power of death, conquered sin, and subjected the world to himself.

He wrestled first for you, that you might conquer the arrogance of the devil and his kingdoms; second, that you might overcome the luxury and glory of the world; third, that you might expel the lust of the flesh and the wantonness of the senses. But he will undertake the final struggle so that, having despised all those things mentioned above, you may possess, as victor, the crown of glory. These are the four watches of which we read [Col. 0393C] in the Gospel: “And if he come,” he says, “in the second watch, and if he come in the third” (Matt. XIV), etc. “Blessed are those servants.” And concerning the fourth, in the same place: “In the fourth watch,” he says, “I come to them upon the sea” (ibid.). The first watch shakes the mind from the sleep of wickedness; the second, from the languor of curiosity; the third, from the torpor of unlawful pleasure; the fourth, from the negligence of vanity. The first triumphs over sin, the second over the world, the third over the flesh, the fourth over death and its sting.

He left this pattern of life, this rule of discipline, this fourfold struggle, to his bride. Hence he says also to his apostles: “I appoint unto you a kingdom, as my Father appointed unto me” (Luke XXII), etc. The Church’s first struggle was with idolaters; the second, with heretics; [Col. 0393D] the third, with the carnal; the fourth, with pseudo-Christians. First she supplanted through confession of the one God; second, through the rule of holy faith; third, through the bond of ordered love; fourth, through the thirst, zeal, ardor, and joy of blessed contemplation.

Of the first, it is said to the bride: “Who is she that comes forth like the rising dawn, fair as the moon, chosen as the sun, terrible as an army arrayed in order?” (Song VI). Likewise of the second: “How beautiful are thy steps in sandals, daughter of the prince” (Song VII). Of the third: “Who is she that comes up from the wilderness, abounding in delights, leaning upon her beloved?” (Song VIII). Of the fourth: “Who is she that comes up through the wilderness like a little column of smoke, from the spices of myrrh and frankincense?” (Song III). Hence Obadiah says: “And the house [Col. 0394A] of Jacob shall possess those who possessed it”; for the Church, by the aforesaid kind of struggles, knows how gloriously to triumph over the aforesaid enemies—either by subjecting them to herself by authority, or by devoutly converting them to her faith and discipline. It follows:

“And the house of Jacob shall be fire; and the house of Joseph a flame; and the house of Esau stubble: and they shall be kindled among them, and shall devour them; and no remnant shall remain of the house of Esau, because the Lord has spoken.” ALLEGORICALLY. By the house of Jacob and Joseph one Church is signified, possessing a twofold condition through the double gift of grace, and a twofold adornment of religion according to the double degree of discipline. For the house of Jacob is the active household; the house of Joseph, the excellence of contemplatives. Jacob, indeed, is called “wrestler,” Joseph [Col. 0394B] “increase” or “increasing.” The house of Jacob labors in the conflict with vices, sweats in the exercise of virtues, burns in the wrestling-ground of discipline, and is troubled in works of penitence. But the house of Joseph rejoices in the increase of counsels, delights in the disclosure of mysteries, exults in the variety of dishes, and dances in the sweetness of kisses.

Thus the house of Jacob sweats in the field of action; the house of Joseph rests in the bed of contemplation. Jacob flees into Mesopotamia, rising by night; Joseph feasts with his brothers and rejoices in the burning noon. The former flees vices, with penitence as guide; the latter celebrates banquets with his brothers, that is, receiving the converse of the spirits who enter. Fire is the heat of manly penitence; flame, the brightness of divine contemplation. [Col. 0394C] Fire is compunction of mind; flame is the fiery contemplation of the bridegroom. In fire two things are considered, but in flame three. In fire, heat and ardor; in flame, heat, ardor, and brightness. Fire consumes and kindles; flame devours, kindles, and enlightens. The fire of penitence consumes guilt and kindles nature; consumes vices and kindles merits; consumes iniquity and kindles toward virtue. But the flame of contemplation consumes vanity, kindles toward perfect charity, and enlightens toward the bridegroom’s brightness. It consumes whatever is shapeless, kindles toward heavenly things, and enlightens toward the invisible.

Through these things and those like them, the house of Esau becomes stubble; because iniquity is wiped out by works of penitence, perverse curiosity is exterminated by works of righteousness, [Col. 0394D] the unlawful pleasure of the flesh by works of grace, and the vanity of the whole world is driven out by works of glory. Esau is interpreted “bloody”; he is Seir, that is, “hairy”; he is also Edom, that is, “earthly”: bloody through iniquity, hairy through curiosity, earthly through pleasure. Bloody in deed, hairy in understanding, earthly in affection. This is the house of Esau: the troop of demons and ostriches, the herd of swine, the phalanx of goats, the slavery of wickedness, the cohort of uncleanness, the company of gluttony.

Certainly, one part of these is kindled by the fire of the house of Jacob—namely, the ardor of penitence and the heat of compunction; another part is devoured by the flame of the house of Joseph—namely, the warmth of divine love and the brightness of heavenly contemplation. Then they are kindled among them and devour them: [Col. 0395A] Esau, that is, because they either drive out their rebellious and savage children as those to be devoured by avenging flames and the fires of hell, or mercifully incorporate them into themselves through the grace of conversion and the force of love, and faithfully convert them to themselves.

We may interpret tropologically what has been said above allegorically. For when the bridegroom deigns to visit his bride, the bride’s chamber is immediately adorned: adorned, I say, with the gold of faith and the silver of wisdom; with gems of virtues, veils of holiness, roses of modesty, lilies of chastity, violets of purity. The bed is surrounded with the purple of mortification, the linen of devotion, and the coverlet of love; fragrant herbs of heavenly affections are scattered around it. Around the bride’s neck fragrant balsam of holy renown breathes forth; in her hands most precious ointments give off their scent. “My hands,” she says, “have distilled myrrh, and my fingers are full of the finest myrrh” (Song V). [Col. 0395B]

When Helios—that is, the sun—looks down from above upon this, he immediately leaps upon the mountains, crossing the hills and running through the garden, passing through the wine-cellar, hastening to the bridal chamber; and, rushing into the embrace of the bride, he places her upon the bed of contemplative glory, saying: “Thou art wholly fair, my beloved, and there is no spot in thee” (Song IV). Thus salvation comes about on Mount Sion, in the height of perfection, in the watchtower of contemplation. Then that aforesaid mountain becomes holy—indeed, becomes sanctification itself. For if it is true—indeed, because what is read in the Apostle is true—“He who is joined to the Lord is one spirit with him” (I Cor. VI), the spirit cleaving to truth becomes truth; cleaving to holiness, [Col. 0395C] it becomes holiness.

And then the house of Jacob shall possess those who possessed it. The house of the wrestler is the conscience of the Savior’s bride. This conscience has afflicted and supplanted Esau by a fourfold struggle. For before anyone attains perfection, before he passes to the citadel of contemplation, he is troubled and sweats in the wrestling-ground and stadium of this fourfold struggle. First, while he lies hidden in the womb—that is, while he remains in the world—hastening toward the birthright, that is, hastening toward the exercises of religion; second, by purchasing the right of the firstborn at the price of lentils, that is, by abstinence from food; third, by extorting the grace of his father’s blessing through a kind of deception; fourth, by wrestling spiritually with the angel.

First he supplanted through confession; second, through submission in profession; third, through the confession [Col. 0395D] of love; fourth, through contemplation of heavenly brightness. First he supplanted through penitence; second, through obedience; third, through innocence; fourth, through spiritual sympathy. In the first struggle iniquity is overcome; in the second, accursed curiosity; in the third, unlawful pleasure; in the fourth, seductive vanity. The iniquity is the devil’s, curiosity the neighbor’s, pleasure one’s own, vanity the world’s.

The house of Jacob becomes fire, the house of Joseph flame, and the house of Esau a brothel of every shame. In the house of Jacob burns the fire of manly penitence, and in the house of Joseph shines the flame of wisdom. In the house of Esau the stubble of every malice abounds; in Esau are truly a brothel, deceit, fraud, and dissimulation, because he is hairy; the lust of the flesh and the lust [Col. 0396A] of the eyes, because he is bloody; falsehood, cruelty, and devastation, because he is earthly. Certainly, in the supplanting conscience, which devours the stubble of vices, burns the hay of offenses, and reduces the wood of sins to ashes, there burns the healing fire of penitence, which exterminates Esau’s iniquity and overwhelms his pestilential curiosity.

Moreover, in the mind there shines the flame of heavenly wisdom, kindled by divine love, illumined by the sun of righteousness, turned toward him by the continual pursuit of love, fixing the spiritual eyes of the purest heart unceasingly upon his beauty; utterly kindled in the progress of virtues, in the contest of heavenly affections, in the desire for the heavenly embrace, in hope of the divine touch, in the fragrance of kisses, in thirst for desires above the heavens. From it proceed [Col. 0396B] the fruits of innocence, the gems of grace are born, flowers and works of glory spring up, by which Esau’s disordered pleasure is burned up and seductive vanity utterly crushed. For the flame of heavenly wisdom consumes sins, kindles merits, and illumines rewards.

“And those who are toward the south shall inherit the mountain of Esau; and those who are in the plains, the Philistines: and they shall possess the region of Ephraim and the region of Samaria; and Benjamin shall possess Gilead.” LITERALLY. When Judah has returned to his kingdom, he who dwelt in the south and possessed the whole region, according to the division of Jesus son of Nave [Joshua], which slopes toward Scorpion—that is, all of Achartumna—they who had previously been confined within narrow boundaries shall possess the mountain of Esau, namely the mountains [Col. 0396C] of Seir and the highlands which Edom had formerly possessed.

But those who live in Shephelah, that is, in the plains of Lydda and Emmaus—indicating Diospolis and Nicopolis, respectively—shall possess the Philistines, that is, the five cities of the Philistines: Gaza, Ascalon, Ashdod, Ekron, Gath; or that whole district which, according to the Acts of the Apostles, is called Salonae. The boundary of the children of Judah shall also be extended as far as Ephraim, where Neapolis now stands, and as far as the region of Samaria, where Sebaste was founded. But Benjamin, whose boundaries extend from Jerusalem toward the north, shall possess all Arabia, formerly called Gilead and now called Gerasa, according to the seventy Interpreters; and Mount Ephraim, and the plains of Samaria, and Benjamin, and Gilead, shall be possessed by those who [Col. 0396D] were in the south. Whether this happened, God knows. For it may have been fulfilled in part during the five hundred years up to Christ’s advent. And after Christ’s advent it has been more truly fulfilled through the expansion of faith—which I know with complete certainty—because it is fulfilled daily in us and confirmed in the kingdom of the Church. It follows:

“And the captivity of this host of the children of Israel shall possess all the places of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath; and the captivity of Jerusalem, which is in Bosphorus, shall possess the cities of the south. And saviors shall ascend Mount Sion to judge the mountain of Esau; and the kingdom shall be the Lord’s.”

Those who returned from Babylon to Judaea, according to the book of Ezra and Nehemiah, shall properly be called “the captivity.” That entire host of the children of Israel, toward the south, west, and north alike, shall possess the Idumaeans, the Philistines, Mount Ephraim, and Samaria. Benjamin, because it borders upon the wilderness, shall specially possess Gilead. But toward the east they shall rule over all who are in the land of the Canaanites, as far as Zarephath of the Sidonians, where formerly a widow fed Elijah. Moreover, those who have been carried away from Jerusalem itself, the metropolitan city, to Bosphorus, shall possess the cities of the south which are in the tribe of Judah. For, having returned to their own city, they shall occupy the places near the city. And when these things had been fulfilled, as is written in the book of Judges, the Lord sent saviors to save the people from captivity. Thus they shall approach and come [Col. 0397B] to Mount Sion, in order to judge and distinguish, as a mountain subject and serving them, Mount Esau—that is, the Idumaeans—and when all have been subdued, the kingdom shall be the Lord’s.

Jerome says: “We have learned from the Hebrew teacher who instructed us in the Scriptures that, according to Hebrew truth, Sapharat at present is called Bophorus [Bosphorus], not Ephrata, as seemed good to the Septuagint. And it is, as it were, a region of vision, to which Hadrian transported captives. Therefore, when our Christ shall come, that captivity too shall return to Judaea.” Yet we may understand some place whatever of the Babylonian kingdom, which I judge otherwise. For it is the prophets’ custom, when they speak against Babylon, the Ammonites, Moabites, the Philistines, and other nations, to employ many of their words [Col. 0397C] and preserve the idioms of the provinces. Since, therefore, the boundary in the Assyrian language which is called *Jebul* in Hebrew is called *sapharat*, I conjecture this to be the sense: “The captivity of Jerusalem, which is scattered through every boundary and region, shall receive the cities of the south,” that is, of its own tribe.

This is Jerome from the Hebrew—or rather, the Hebrew from Jerome. But since we have interpreted according to history as far as we were able, and have guided our little ship among craggy rocks, let us spread the sails of spiritual understanding, so that, with the Lord breathing upon us and disclosing his mysteries, we may joyfully reach port.

ALLEGORICALLY. Behold, Obadiah here describes the land historically and divides it spiritually. We read of many divisions in the divine utterance: divisions of the Red Sea, whence comes the saying, “Who divided the Red Sea into divisions” (Ps. CXXXV); and in the Apostle: “There are divisions of graces, but the same Spirit; and there are divisions of ministries, but the same Lord; and there are divisions of operations, but the same God, who works all in all” (I Cor. XII).

We also read that there have been four divisions of the land. The first was made by Joshua; the second by Ezekiel; the third by Obadiah here; the fourth, moreover, by the Savior. The first is the sacrament of the second, the second of the third, the third of the fourth. Hence the first stands in the same numerical relation to the second historically as the second does spiritually to the third, and the third to the fourth. Observe, reader, the form of the order and the splendor of the proportion. For as the first [Col. 0398A] is to the second, so the third is to the fourth; and as the first is to the third, so the second is to the fourth, and so the second is to the third. I leave the reader’s instruction concerning the judgment of proportions to arithmetic. But our purpose is to investigate the hidden recesses of allegorical obscurity and bring its darkness into the light of explanation.

The first division of the land occurs after enemies have been conquered or subjected; the second without hostile surrender or civil change; the third with the voluntary subjection of enemies; the fourth without the condition or bond of subjection, but with the glory and joy of mutual love. The first division comes about with punishment and misery; the second with punishment but without misery; the third without punishment and misery, while shame itself remains; the fourth without punishment and misery, all languor having been removed.

Struggle is the refusal to consent to sin; misery is being unwillingly vexed by an unlawful incentive; the shame of misery is being stimulated by it; removal of languor is the exclusion of temptation. There are four freedoms: freedom of choice, freedom of exercise, freedom of counsel, and freedom of joy. The first division was made with freedom of choice, but not with freedom of exercise. For the will, moved by its own choice, conquered those whom it could, but did not subject all whom it wished. Thus it possessed freedom in the capacity and motion of judgment, but not in the business of exercise; had it truly possessed that, it would have subjected all to itself at a nod.

The second had the first and second freedoms, but lacked the third; for, moving by its own will, it uses the desired capacity for exercise, yet it lacks freedom of counsel, because it has not known how to attain the limits of knowledge and order, of end and beginning. [Col. 0398C] The third possessed all these three but lacked the fourth, because it obtained will in its movement, capacity in its act, and clarity in understanding, but did not have security in affection. The fourth, however, possesses all things: free will in choosing, swift capacity in acting, sincere clarity in intention, and secure perpetuity in enjoyment.

The first freedom is therefore common to all; the second is general to converts, but particular to the imperfect; the third is general to the perfect and particular to those serving God in this world; the fourth is unique to those who contemplate the bridegroom and rejoice with him. The first belongs to servants, the second to hired laborers, the third to friends, the fourth to sons. The first division comes through the grace of compunction; the second through the discipline and resolve of conversion; the third through ecstasy of mind and the eminence of contemplation; the fourth through the assumption of glory and honor, and immediate immortality unto the vision of God.

The first occurs when we withdraw from the darkness and slavery of sin; the second, when we pursue the fleeing bridegroom to the mountain of myrrh and the hills of Lebanon; the third, when we ascend through the wilderness as an army arrayed in order; the fourth, when we enter the courts of the heavenly city with hymns. Four things are given to the elect for usefulness, salvation, and blessedness: exercises, joys, merits, and rewards—the exercises of religious life, the joys [Col. 0399A] of contemplation, the merits of perfection, the rewards of the most blessed vision; exercises of discipline, joys of spiritual union and heavenly embrace, merits of righteousness, and rewards of glory. The first division therefore pertains to exercises, the second to joys, the third to merits, the fourth to rewards.

Hence in the first division, Joshua says to the children of Israel: “These are the nations which the Lord thy God left in thy midst, that by them he might instruct Israel” (Judg. III). Again it is written: “But the children of Judah could not destroy the Jebusite, an inhabitant of Jerusalem” (Judg. I). Likewise in the same book: “The children of Manasseh could not overthrow these cities, but the Canaanite began to dwell in his land. But after the children of Israel had grown strong, they subjected the Canaanites and made them tributary to themselves, yet did not kill them” (ibid.).

[Col. 0399B] Concerning the second division, Ezekiel reads thus: “This is the land which you shall cast by lot to the tribes of Israel, and these are their portions, says the Lord” (Ezek. XLVIII). On the north side are three gates for three tribes; on the south side, as many for another three; on the east side, as many for another three; on the west side, as many for another three. From each side you shall measure five hundred cubits and four thousand. What are these four sides except the four principal kinds of compunction through which the holy mind enters and proceeds toward the temple of holy contemplation? They are: fear of punishment, sorrow for present exile, hope of the heavenly reward, and affection for the spiritual marriage. Fear is the western side; sorrow, the northern; hope, the eastern; love, [Col. 0399C] the southern.

What are the three gates situated on each side except occasions of the aforesaid compunction consecrated to the Trinity—to faith, hope, and charity? For one who rightly fears punishments flees vices by faith, tends toward merits by hope, and runs toward rewards by charity. But one who grieves over the misery of present exile tends toward obedience by faith, hastens toward righteousness by hope, and flies to glory on the wings of charity. Moreover, one who thirsts for the unfading reward flees the shipwreck of vices by faith, enters the stadium of the spiritual contest by hope, and hastens toward the reward at the urging of the pursuit of love. Certainly, one who desires the union of the heavenly One removes from himself every stain of iniquity by faith, follows everywhere and always the rule of innocence by hope, burns for the heavenly marriage with ardent desire of charity, and hastens to the spiritual nuptials with vehement [Col. 0399D] eagerness.

In all these, the vision of the Trinity, the eternity of glory, and the possession of blessedness are enclosed. The fact that it reckons five hundred cubits and four thousand from the gate to the temple signifies this: both the hundredfold and the thousandfold signify perfection. The hundredfold multiplied five times signifies the honorable and perfect continence of the senses. The thousandfold multiplied four times signifies, according to the faith and rule of the Gospel, purity of conscience, perfection of life, and innocence of conduct. Therefore, through the four thousand is designated integrity of life; through the five hundred cubits, soundness of reputation. These aforesaid measures are reckoned from the gate to the temple, because from entry into compunction to the joy of holy contemplation, honorableness of the senses, integrity of life, and purity of conscience are necessary. [Col. 0400A] Necessary, I say, are continence of the senses, righteousness of actions, and innocence of affections.

Thus one goes from the gate to the temple, because through the keeping and diligent observance of the aforesaid things one arrives at the union of spiritual marriage and the sweetness of the bridegroom. Hence it is added subsequently: “And the name of the city from that day shall be, The Lord is there” (ibid.). From that day, that brightness, that union, that joining, the city’s name is “The Lord is there,” because he guards the departure of his bride toward action and her entry into contemplation. He guards the gates of profession, watches over the streets of religious life, honors the temple of sanctification, fortifies the citadel of perfection, protects the people of spiritual exercises, and preserves the choir of heavenly morals.

[Col. 0400B] In it, moreover, the Lord is the bread of life, the wine of heavenly righteousness, the garment of righteousness, the law of mercy, the light of spiritual understanding, and the water of spiritual teaching. Why say more? Since the name of the city is “The Lord is there” (Rom. I), God becomes all things to all in it. We have said these things briefly concerning the first and second divisions.

It remains to say something concerning the third and fourth. And as the first pertains to exercises and the second to joys, so the third concerns merits and the fourth rewards. And as those two are distinguished by the number ten on account of perfection in action, so these are divided by the number seven on account of spiritual perfection and the joy of heavenly contemplation. Therefore Obadiah says:

[Col. 0400C] “And those who are toward the south shall inherit the mountain of Esau,” etc. Under this sevenfold scheme, seven divisions of land are set against the seven principal vices; seven petitions of the Lord’s Prayer, seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, seven virtues opposed to those vices, and finally seven beatitudes. In the first place are set the seven vices, against which are opposed the antidotes of all the aforesaid things.

The first of the vices is pride; the second, envy; the third, anger; the fourth, acedia or sadness; the fifth, avarice; the sixth, gluttony; the seventh, lust. Against these, in the second place, are established the seven petitions contained in the Lord’s Prayer. The first, by which one says to God, “Hallowed be thy name”; the second, “Thy kingdom come”; the third, “Thy will be done, as [Col. 0400D] in heaven, so on earth”; the fourth, “Give us this day our daily bread”; the fifth, “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors”; the sixth, “And lead us not into temptation”; the seventh, “But deliver us from evil.”

Afterward, in the third place, follow the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit. The first, the spirit of the fear of the Lord; the second, the spirit of piety; the third, the spirit of knowledge; the fourth, the spirit of fortitude; the fifth, the spirit of counsel; the sixth, the spirit of understanding; the seventh, the spirit of wisdom. Then, in the fourth place, succeed four virtues. The first, poverty of spirit, that is, humility; the second, meekness or kindness; the third, compunction or sorrow; [Col. 0401A] the fourth, hunger for righteousness or good desire; the fifth, mercy; the sixth, purity of heart; the seventh, peace. Finally, in the last place, are arranged the seven beatitudes: the first, the kingdom of heaven; the second, possession of the land of the living; the third, consolation; the fourth, satisfaction in righteousness; the fifth, mercy; the sixth, the vision of God; the seventh, sonship of God.

Pride is love of one’s own excellence. Envy is hatred of another’s happiness. Anger is unjust fury, or the unlawful madness of an agitated mind. Acedia, or sadness, is the disordered bitterness of the soul, or the perverse weariness of the mind joined with grief. Avarice, which is an immoderate desire for possessing, is signified by Mount Esau. By the Philistines, whose name is interpreted “falling through a cup,” is signified envy; for it falls as though through an alien draught, because it envies another’s happiness.

Make this first distinction in such a way that you understand the vices themselves as certain diseases of the soul, or wounds of the inner person; the person himself as sick; God as physician; the gifts of the Holy Spirit as antidote; virtues as health; and beatitudes as the joy of blessedness. Thus there are seven capital or principal vices, and from them all evils arise. These are the springs of the dark abyss from which the rivers of Babylon go forth, spreading drops of iniquity poured out over all the earth. Of these rivers the Prophet sang in the person of the faithful people: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept when we remembered thee, Sion” (Ps. CXXXVI).

Concerning these seven devastating vices, which corrupt the entire integrity of nature and at the same time produce the seeds of all evils, we think it sufficient to speak insofar as is necessary for the present exposition. There are seven, therefore: of these, three strip a person bare; the fourth scourges the stripped person; the fifth casts out the scourged person; the sixth seduces the cast-out person; the seventh subjects the seduced person to slavery. Pride takes God from a person. Envy takes away the neighbor. Anger takes away the person himself. Sadness scourges the despoiled person. Avarice casts out the scourged person. Gluttony seduces the cast-out person. Lust subjects the seduced person to slavery. Let us now return and explain each in order.
