For pride is love of one’s own excellence, when the mind loves the good it possesses in isolation—that is, apart from him from whom it received the good. [Col. 0401D] O pestilential pride, what are you doing? Why do you urge a streamlet to separate itself from its fountain? Why do you urge a ray to withdraw itself from the sun? Why, except that the former, when it ceases to be supplied, may dry up; and the latter, when it turns away from that which illumines it, may become dark? And that each, when it ceases to receive what it does not yet have, may immediately lose even what it has? Thus it comes about that it cannot usefully possess even what it has, because it does not love that good in him from whom it has it.

For whoever knows how to love no good except that which he possesses in himself must necessarily do so; and when he sees in another a good which he does not possess, his own imperfection torments him all the more bitterly, the less he loves him in whom all good consists. Therefore envy always follows pride: because one who does not fix love where all good is, the more perversely he is exalted by his own good, the more grievously he is tormented by another’s good. Thus the punishment most justly assigned to his self-exaltation is the envy that it begets from itself. Because it refused to love every good and the common good, it now rightly wastes away through resentment at another’s good. Surely the success of another’s happiness would not burn it, if it possessed through love him in whom all good exists. Now, therefore, the more it exalts itself through pride against the Creator, the more it falls beneath its neighbor through envy; and the more deceitfully it is raised up there, the more truly it is cast down here.

But the corruption once begun cannot stop at this point. As soon as envy has been born from pride, the wretched mind itself begets anger from envy. For it is angry with itself on account of its own imperfection because it does not rejoice through charity in another’s good. And therefore even what it has begins to displease it, because it recognizes in another what it cannot possess. What, then, it could have possessed wholly through charity in God, it sought through self-exaltation to possess outside God; through envy it loses its neighbor, and through anger itself. Since, therefore, having lost all things, the unhappy conscience has nothing in which to rejoice, it is battered within itself by sadness; and, because it refused devoutly to rejoice in another’s good, it is justly tormented by its own evil.

After pride, envy, and anger, which despoil a person, sadness immediately follows, which scourges the one laid bare. Avarice then succeeds, casting out the scourged person because, having lost inward joy, it compels him to seek consolation outside. Afterward comes gluttony, which seduces the cast-out person, because it first attacks the mind that longs for external things, as though from close at hand, and through natural appetite draws it into unlawful excess. Finally lust comes upon it, violently subjecting the seduced person to slavery; because, once the flesh has been swollen by overindulgence, the softened and feebly dissolved mind cannot overcome the rising heat of desire. Thus the mind, shamefully subdued, serves a most cruel dominion; and unless the implored mercy of the Savior comes to its aid, there will no longer be any means by which freedom, once lost, may be restored to the captive in bondage.

Accordingly, seven petitions follow against the seven vices. By them we pray that he may help us—the one who both taught us to pray and promised that he would give to those who pray the good gift needed to heal our wounds and loosen the yoke of our captivity. But before we proceed to explain these petitions, we first wish, by another comparison, to show how great a corruption the aforesaid vices produce in us, so that, the more dangerous the sickness is shown to be, the more necessary the remedy may be proved.

Through pride the heart is swollen; through envy it dries up; through anger it bursts; through sorrow it is worn away and, as it were, reduced to dust; through avarice it is scattered; through gluttony it is infected and, as it were, moistened; through lust [Col. 0403A] it is trampled down and reduced to mire. Thus the wretched person may now say: “I am fixed fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no firm ground. I have come into the depths of the sea, and the tempest has submerged me” (Ps. 68).

And when the mind has been fixed in this mire of the deep, wrapped in the mud of defilement and uncleanness, it cannot at all be pulled out unless it cries to him and asks his help, of whom the Psalmist speaks, saying: “I waited patiently for the Lord, and he inclined to me and heard my prayers, and brought me up from the pit of misery and from the mud of dregs” (Ps. 39). Therefore he himself taught us to pray, so that we may understand that our whole good comes from God.

The first petition, then, is against pride, in which we say to God: “Hallowed be thy name.” Here we ask him to grant us fear and reverence for his name, [Col. 0403B] so that we may be subject to him through humility, since through pride we have proved rebellious and defiant. To this petition is given the spirit of the fear of the Lord, so that, coming into the heart, it may create there the virtue of humility, which heals the sickness of pride, in order that the humble human being may reach the kingdom of heaven which the proud angel lost through self-exaltation.

The second petition is against envy, in which it is said: “Thy kingdom come.” For the kingdom of God is the salvation of human beings, because God is said to reign in human beings when they themselves are subject to him—now by cleaving to him through faith, and afterwards by cleaving to him through sight. Therefore whoever asks that God’s kingdom may come surely seeks the salvation of all; and by asking for the common salvation of all, [Col. 0403C] shows that he rejects the vice of envy. To this petition is given the spirit of piety, so that, coming into the heart, it may kindle it toward kindness, in order that the person may himself attain that same possession of the eternal inheritance to which he desires others to come.

The third petition is against anger, in which it is said: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” By this one indicates that whatever God’s will dispenses, whether in oneself or in others, according to the determination of his good pleasure, is pleasing to oneself. To this petition, therefore, is given the spirit of knowledge, so that, coming into the heart, it may instruct and beneficially pierce it, so that a person may know that the evil he suffers proceeds from his own fault; but that whatever good he possesses comes from God’s mercy; and thus may learn, whether in the evils he endures or in the goods he does not possess, [Col. 0403D] not to be angry with the Creator, but to display patience in all things.

Thus anger and indignation of mind are most fittingly softened through compunction of heart, which, through the working of the spirit of knowledge, is inwardly born from humility. Conversely, “anger kills the fool,” when, agitated and blinded by the vice of impatience, he recognizes neither that he has deserved the evil he suffers nor that he has received by grace the good he has. The reward of consolation follows this virtue—that is, compunction or sorrow—so that one who here willingly afflicts himself before God through lamentations may deserve there to find true joy and gladness.

The fourth petition is against sorrow, or acedia: “Give us this day our daily bread” [Col. 0404A]. Sorrow is weariness of mind accompanied by grief, when the mind, as it were, wastes away and is embittered by its own vice; it does not desire inward goods and, with all its strength deadened, is cheered by no desire for spiritual refreshment. Therefore, to heal this vice, we must implore the Lord’s mercy, that in his customary compassion he may offer food of inward refreshment to the soul languishing in its weariness, so that what, being absent, it does not know how to desire, once prompted by the taste of its presence it may begin to love.

Therefore the spirit of fortitude is given to this petition, that it may raise the failing soul, so that, restored by the strength of its former vigor, it may recover from attachment to its weariness to a desire for inward savor. The Spirit creates in the heart a hunger for righteousness, so that, while here it is strongly inflamed through the desire of piety, there [Col. 0404B] it may receive as its reward the full satisfaction of blessedness.

The fifth petition is against avarice: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” It is just, indeed, that one who has refused to be greedy in exacting a debt should not be anxious in repaying one. And therefore, when through God’s grace the vice of avarice is removed from us, we are granted, under the stated condition of salvation, the way in which we ought to be released from our debt. To this petition, therefore, is given the spirit of counsel, to teach us gladly in this age to extend mercy to those who sin against us, so that in the future, when we must render an account for our sins, we may deserve to find mercy.

The sixth petition is against gluttony: “And lead us not [Col. 0404C] into temptation,” that is, do not permit us to be led into temptation. This is the temptation by which the enticement of the flesh often strives, through natural appetite, to draw us into excess; and secretly introduces pleasure while openly flattering us under the pretext of necessity. We are certainly not led into this temptation when we take care to provide nature with support according to the measure of necessity, yet always remember to restrain appetite from the enticement of pleasure.

That we may be able to do this, the spirit of understanding is given to us when we ask, so that the inward refreshment of God’s word may check outward appetite, and the mind may be strengthened by spiritual food, so that bodily want cannot break it nor fleshly pleasure overcome it. For this reason the Lord himself, when his tempter, as he was hungry, made a deceitful suggestion concerning outward bread, answered: “A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4). He thus clearly showed that, when the mind is refreshed inwardly by that bread, it is not greatly troubled if outwardly it suffers bodily hunger for a time. Therefore the spirit of understanding is given against gluttony; but, coming to the heart, it cleanses and purifies it.

The seventh petition is against lust: “Deliver us from evil.” For although, as we have said elsewhere, evil is manifold—evil of the body and evil of the soul; evil which is fault and evil which is punishment; evil of this age and evil of the future—nevertheless [Col. 0405A] lust may in a certain way be considered the chief evil, since it reduces the person caught by its enticements to [Col. 0406A] slavery. Hence, through the gift of wisdom, we ask to be delivered, saying: “Deliver us from evil. Amen.”

[Col. 0405]

## A SHORT WORK ON THE FIVE SETS OF SEVEN, OR SEPTENARIES

### CHAPTER I.—What the five sets of seven contained in Sacred Scripture are

[Col. 0405B]

Brother, I have found five sets of seven in Sacred Scripture. If I can, as you ask, I wish first to distinguish them from one another by enumerating each separately; then to show what correspondence they have among themselves by comparing each item with its counterpart.

> [Note: What follows, down to “The seventh petition,” etc., may be read above at col. 400, line 37, with a few changes.]

In the first place are set the seven vices: first pride, second envy, third anger, fourth sorrow, fifth avarice, sixth gluttony, seventh lust.

Against these, in the second place, are set the seven petitions contained in the Lord’s Prayer: the first, in which one says to God, “Hallowed be thy name”; the second, “Thy kingdom come”; the third, “Thy will be done, as in heaven [Col. 0405C] so on earth”; the fourth, “Give us this day our daily bread”; the fifth, “And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”; the sixth, “And lead us not into temptation”; the seventh, “But deliver us from evil.”

Afterwards, in the third place, follow the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: first, the spirit of the fear of the Lord; second, the spirit of piety; third, the spirit of knowledge; fourth, the spirit of fortitude; fifth, the spirit of counsel; sixth, the spirit of understanding; seventh, the spirit of wisdom.

Finally, in the fourth place, follow the seven virtues: first, poverty of spirit, that is, humility; second, gentleness or kindness; third, compunction or sorrow; fourth, hunger for righteousness or good desire; [Col. 0405D] fifth, mercy; sixth, purity of heart; seventh, peace.

Last, in the fifth place, are arranged the seven beatitudes: first, the kingdom of heaven; second, possession of the land of the living; third, consolation; fourth, satisfaction of righteousness; fifth, mercy; sixth, the vision of God; seventh, being made children of God.

Make this first distinction in such a way that you understand the vices as illnesses of the soul, as it were, or wounds of the inward person; the person himself as the sick patient; God as the physician; the gifts of the Holy Spirit as the antidote; the virtues as health; and the beatitudes as the joy of blessed happiness.

### CHAPTER II.—How great a ruin the seven deadly vices bring upon a human being

There are, therefore, seven capital or principal vices, and from them all evils arise. They are the sources and dark abysses from which flow the rivers of Babylon, spreading drops of iniquity over all the earth [Col. 0406B]. Of these rivers the Psalmist sang in the person of the faithful people: “By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept while we remembered thee, O Zion. Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments” (Ps. 136).

We shall speak of these seven devastating vices, which corrupt the whole soundness of nature and at the same time produce the seeds of every evil, as much as we think sufficient for explaining the present matter. There are seven, then: three of them strip a person; the fourth scourges the stripped person; the fifth drives out the scourged person; the sixth deceives the expelled person; the seventh subjects the led-away person to slavery.

Pride takes God from a person; envy takes away the neighbor; anger takes away [Col. 0406C] the person himself; sorrow scourges the stripped person; avarice drives out the scourged person; gluttony deceives the expelled person; lust subjects the deceived person to slavery. Let us return and explain them individually in order.

We said that pride takes God from a person. Pride is love of one’s own excellence, when the mind loves the good it possesses in isolation—that is, apart from him from whom it receives the good. O deadly pride, what are you doing? Why do you urge the little stream to separate itself from its spring? Why do you urge the ray to turn away from the sun? Why, except that the former, once it ceases to be filled, may dry up, and the latter, once it turns away from what illumines it, may become dark; and that each, when it ceases to receive, may immediately lose even what it has?

This indeed is what you do when you teach people to love gifts apart from the giver: so that one who perversely claims for himself a part of the good [Col. 0406D] that was given by him may lose the whole good that is in him. Thus it comes about that he cannot usefully possess even what he has, because he does not love it in him from whom he has it. For as every good truly comes from God, so no good can be possessed usefully apart from God. Indeed, by this very fact the thing possessed is lost when it is not loved in and with him from whom it is possessed.

For if anyone knows only how to love in himself the good that he has, it necessarily follows that, when he sees in another the good he does not possess, his own imperfection torments him all the more bitterly because he does not love him in whom every good consists. Therefore envy always follows pride, because the one who does not fix love where all good is, the more perversely he exalts himself on account of his own good, the more grievously he is tormented by another’s good.

Thus a most just punishment has been assigned to his self-exaltation: the envy [Col. 0407A] it produces from itself. Because it refused to love the good common to all, it now rightly wastes away through jealous resentment of another’s good. The success of another’s happiness would surely not burn such a person if, through love, he possessed the one in whom all good exists. For he would not judge another’s good foreign to himself if he loved his own good there, where he possessed both his own and the other’s good together.

Now, therefore, to the extent that he exalts himself through pride against the Creator, he falls through envy beneath his neighbor; and to the extent that he is falsely raised up there, to that extent he is truly cast down here. Yet the corruption once begun cannot stop even here. For as soon as envy has arisen from pride, it produces anger from itself; because the miserable mind now grows angry with itself on account of its own imperfection precisely because it does not rejoice through charity in another’s good. Therefore even what it possesses begins to displease it, because it recognizes in another what it cannot possess.

Thus the person who could have possessed everything in God through charity loses, through envy and anger, even that which he sought through self-exaltation to possess apart from God. For after losing God through pride, he loses the neighbor through envy and himself through anger. Since, therefore, with all things lost, nothing remains from which the unhappy conscience may rejoice, it is dashed against itself through sorrow; and it is justly tortured by its own evil because it refused devoutly to rejoice in another’s good.

After pride, envy, and anger, which strip a person, sorrow immediately follows, scourging the naked person. Then avarice succeeds, driving out the scourged person [Col. 0407C], because, once inward joy has been lost, he is compelled to seek consolation outside. Afterwards gluttony comes, deceiving the expelled person, because this vice, first tempting from close at hand the soul that longs after outward things, entices it through natural appetite into excess. Finally lust comes upon it, violently subjecting the deceived person to slavery. For after the flesh has been inflamed through debauchery, the softened mind, weakened and slackly dissolved, cannot overcome the heat of lust that follows.

Thus the mind shamefully subjected serves a most cruel dominion; and unless the mercy of the Savior, being entreated, comes to its aid, there will no longer be any means by which lost freedom may be restored to the captive in slavery.

### CHAPTER III.—Which gifts of the Holy Spirit correspond to the first three petitions of the Lord’s Prayer, and which vices they heal

[Col. 0407D]

Accordingly, seven petitions follow against the seven vices. By them we pray that he may help us—the one who taught us to pray (Luke 11) and promised that he would give to those who pray the good Spirit to heal our wounds and loosen the yoke of our captivity. But before we proceed to explain them, we first wish by another comparison to show how great a corruption the aforesaid vices produce in us, so that, the more dangerous the sickness is shown to be, the more necessary the remedy may be proved.

Through pride the heart is swollen; through envy it dries up; through anger it bursts; through sorrow it is worn away and, as it were, reduced to dust; through avarice it is scattered; through gluttony it is infected and, as it were, moistened; through [Col. 0408A] lust it is trampled down and reduced to mire. Thus the wretched person may now say: “I am fixed fast in the mire of the deep, and there is no firm ground. I have come into the depths of the sea, and the tempest has submerged me” (Ps. 6 [an apparent citation error in the source]).

And when the mind has been fixed in this mire of the deep, wrapped in the mud of defilement and uncleanness, it cannot at all be pulled out unless it cries to him and asks his help. Of him the Psalmist speaks, saying: “I waited patiently for the Lord, and he inclined to me. And he heard my prayers, and brought me up from the pit of misery and from the mud of dregs” (Ps. 41 [an apparent citation error in the source]).

Therefore he himself taught us to pray, so that we may understand that our whole good is from him, and that both what we ask and what we receive when asking are his gift, not our merit. The first petition [Col. 0408B] against pride is the one in which we say to God: “Hallowed be thy name.” By this we ask him to grant us fear and reverence for his name, so that we may be subject to him through humility, though through pride we have proved rebellious and defiant.

To this petition is given the gift of the spirit of the fear of the Lord, so that, coming into the heart, it may create there the virtue of humility that heals the sickness of pride, in order that the humble person may reach the kingdom of heaven which the proud angel lost through choice.

The second petition is against envy: “Thy kingdom come.” For the kingdom of God is the salvation of human beings, because God is said to reign in human beings when they themselves are subject to God, now by cleaving to him through faith and afterwards by cleaving to him through sight. Therefore whoever asks that the kingdom of God may come surely seeks human salvation; and, by asking for the common salvation of all, shows that he rejects the vice of envy.

To this petition is given the spirit of piety, so that, coming into the heart, it may kindle it toward kindness, in order that the person may himself attain the same possession of the eternal inheritance to which he desires others to come.

The third petition is against anger: “Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth.” The person who says, “Thy will be done,” does not wish to contend, but indicates that whatever God’s will dispenses, whether in oneself or in others, according to the determination of his good pleasure, is pleasing to him. Therefore the spirit of knowledge is given to this petition, so that, coming into the heart, it may instruct it and beneficially pierce it, so that a person may know that the evil he suffers proceeds from his own fault; but that whatever good he has comes from God’s mercy; and thus may learn, whether in the evils he endures or in the goods he does not possess, [Col. 0408D] not to be angry with the Creator but to display patience in all things.

Anger and indignation of mind are thus most fittingly softened through compunction of heart—which, through the working of the spirit of knowledge, is inwardly born from humility—because, conversely, anger kills the fool when, agitated and blinded by the vice of impatience amid adversities, he recognizes neither that he has deserved the evil he suffers nor that he has received by grace the good he has. The reward of consolation follows this virtue, that is, compunction or sorrow, so that one who here willingly afflicts himself before God through lamentations [Col. 0409A] may deserve there to find true joy and gladness.

### CHAPTER IV.—Which gifts likewise correspond to the final four petitions, and for which evils they provide a remedy

The fourth petition is against sorrow: “Give us this day our daily bread.” For sorrow is weariness of mind with grief, when the mind, as it were, wastes away and is embittered by its own vice; it does not desire inward goods and, with all its strength deadened, is cheered by no desire for spiritual refreshment. Therefore, to heal this vice, we must implore the Lord’s mercy, that in his customary compassion he may offer food of inward refreshment to the soul languishing in its weariness, so that what, being absent, it does not know how to desire, once prompted by the taste of its presence, it may begin [Col. 0409B] to love.

Therefore the spirit of fortitude is given to this petition, that it may raise the failing soul, so that, restored by the strength of its former vigor, it may recover from the failing caused by its weariness to a desire for inward savor. The spirit of fortitude creates in the heart a hunger for righteousness, so that, while here it is strongly inflamed through the desire of piety, there it may receive as its reward the full satisfaction of blessedness.

The fifth petition is against avarice: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” It is just that one who has refused to be greedy in exacting a debt ought not to be anxious in repaying one. Therefore, when through God’s grace the vice of avarice is removed from us, we are taught, under the proposed condition of salvation, how we ought to be released from our debt.

To this petition, therefore, is given the spirit of counsel, which teaches us gladly in this age to extend mercy to those who sin against us, so that in the future, when we must render an account for our sins, we may deserve to find mercy.

The sixth petition is against gluttony: “Do not lead us,” that is, “permit us to be led,” into temptation. This is the temptation by which the enticement of the flesh often endeavors, through natural appetite, to draw us into excess, secretly introducing pleasure while openly flattering us under the pretext of necessity. We are certainly not led into this temptation when we take care to provide nature with support according to the measure of necessity, [Col. 0409D] yet always remember to restrain appetite from the enticement of pleasure.

That we may be able to do this, the spirit of understanding is given to us when we ask, so that the inward refreshment of God’s word may check outward appetite; and the mind, strengthened by spiritual food, may neither be broken by bodily want nor overcome by fleshly pleasure. For this reason, the Lord himself, when his tempter made a deceitful suggestion to him, hungry as he was, concerning refreshment by outward bread, answered: “A human being does not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4). He thereby clearly showed that, when the mind is refreshed inwardly by that bread, it is not greatly troubled if outwardly it suffers bodily hunger for a time.

Therefore the spirit of understanding is given against gluttony. Coming to the heart, it cleanses and purifies it; healing that inward eye with the knowledge of God’s word, as though with a kind of eye-salve, it makes it so luminous and clear that it becomes keen-sighted even for contemplating the brightness of divinity itself. Therefore, against the vice of gluttony the remedy of the spirit of understanding is applied. From the spirit of understanding purity of heart is born; and purity of heart merits the vision of God, as it is written: “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5).

The seventh petition is against lust: “Deliver us from evil.” Appropriately indeed, the slave asks for freedom; and therefore the spirit of wisdom is given to this petition, to restore to the captive the freedom that was lost and, aided by grace, to enable him to escape the yoke of unjust domination which by his own strength [Col. 0410B] he could not overcome.

For *sapientia* (“wisdom”) is said to derive from *sapor* (“taste”): when the mind is touched by the taste of inward sweetness, it gathers its whole self inwardly through desire and no longer visibly dissolves outwardly in fleshly pleasure, because it possesses wholly within itself that in which it delights. Thus inward sweetness is fittingly set against outward pleasure, so that the more the former begins to have savor and delight, the more freely and willingly the latter is despised. At last the mind is made peaceful within itself; since there is nothing it desires outside, it rests wholly inwardly through love.

Therefore the spirit of wisdom, touching the heart with its sweetness, both tempers the heat of concupiscence outwardly and, when concupiscence has been quieted, creates peace inwardly. Thus, while the whole mind is gathered to inward joy, the human being may be fully and perfectly re-formed in the image of God, as it is written: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God” (ibid.). Behold, brother, I have fulfilled your request, not as I ought, but as I was meanwhile able. Receive the little handbook on the five septenaries for which you asked; and when you look at it, remember me. May the grace of God be with you. Amen.

### CHAPTER V.—On the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit separately

It is written: “For if you, though you are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the good Spirit to those who ask him?” (Luke 11). Therefore the heavenly Father will give the Spirit to his children who ask him. Those who are children seek nothing else; those who seek something else are hired servants, slaves, [Col. 0410D] not children. Those who seek silver, seek gold, seek transient things, seek things that are not eternal, seek the service of slavery, not the spirit of freedom.

What is sought is given. If you seek bodily things, you receive no more than you seek. If you seek spiritual things, what you seek is given, and what you do not seek is added. Spiritual things are given; fleshly things are added: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. 6). Therefore, when you are about to ask the Father—and the Father who is in heaven—seek heavenly gifts, not earthly ones: not bodily substance, but spiritual grace.

For he will give the good Spirit to those who ask him; he will give his Spirit to heal your spirit. He will give the Holy Spirit and heal the spirit of sinners. This one is sick; that one is the medicine. Therefore, if you wish to heal this one [Col. 0411A], seek that one. If you ask for the spirit, ask for the Spirit. Do not fear to apply medicine to illness. Illness does not corrupt medicine; medicine breaks up illness. It does not infect medicine, but fails away because of it.

Therefore do not fear to invite the holy Spirit of God into your sinful spirit because you are sinful and unworthy of his fellowship. This does not happen because you are worthy, but so that you may become worthy. He comes to you in order to make his dwelling in you. He will not find it when he comes; rather, he will come in order to make it. First he will build; afterwards he will dwell. First he will heal; afterwards he will illuminate. First toward health, afterwards toward delight.

Therefore, if you are a child and ask the Father, trust; do not fear. God hears; the Father answers. As he cannot fail to hear because he is God, so he cannot fail to answer because he is loving. Therefore he will give you what you ask, if you ask rightly; and your prayer will not go in vain if it is worthy to be heard. You have asked for the healing of illness: you will receive medicine. Your vices are your illness; the Spirit of God is your health.

Against the sickness of pride, the medicine of the spirit of fear will be given you, that it may heal the corruption of self-exaltation and restore the health of humility. Individual vices have individual medicines: seven vices, seven spirits; as many illnesses, so many medicines. What are the seven spirits? They are the seven gifts of the Spirit; the gifts are the Spirit, and the Spirit is the gifts. The gift of the Spirit is Spirit: the Spirit gives himself. One Spirit grants himself sevenfold. Therefore one Spirit, seven spirits: because he is given sevenfold and breathes into us sevenfold [Col. 0411C]. Seven breathings-forth, yet one Spirit; one medicine heals seven illnesses. Therefore one, seven: one nature, seven operations; one substance, a sevenfold effect.

The first spirit is the spirit of fear; the second, the spirit of piety; the third, the spirit of knowledge; the fourth spirit, the spirit of fortitude; the fifth spirit, the spirit of counsel; the sixth spirit, the spirit of understanding; the seventh spirit, the spirit of wisdom. “One and the same Spirit works all these things” (1 Cor. 12). He himself is fear; he himself is piety; he himself is knowledge; he himself is fortitude; he himself is counsel; he himself is understanding; he himself is wisdom. He becomes all these things for you, though he is one in himself. In receiving him, who is not diverse, you are formed toward diverse things. Therefore he is multiplied in you, though in himself he is always one and the same.

For he who is your love is also your fear. Jacob swore to Laban “by the Fear of his father Isaac” (Gen. 31). He who brings to completion is also he who begins. He first comes to you in order to make you fearful; lastly, in order to make you loving. It is the same light that stings bleary eyes and gently delights clear ones: it produces different effects because it finds different conditions, though in itself it remains one. It would likewise be one in you if it found you one.

If you have a healthy eye, you receive light without pain. But if the eye is sick, its coming becomes burdensome. Yet it is beneficial that it should come even so, because unless you are pained, you are not enlightened. Medicine and illness, two contraries, struggle. Medicine is for you; illness is against you. If illness were not resisted, health would not follow [Col. 0412A]. If medicine were not resisted, pain would not be felt. The struggle of contraries is your pain. Yet do not blame the medicine but the illness: attribute the pain which the two inflict to one alone. Medicine wishes to benefit; illness intends to injure.

Therefore illness alone has peace, but not health. Medicine alone has health, but not pain. When they are together, pain is the conflict of contraries: one wishes to enter in order to confer a benefit; the other refuses to depart in order to do harm. In this pain, then, illness is to be accused, not medicine, because what causes torment comes from illness. If illness were absent, there would be health and no pain.

Thus the Spirit comes and, breathing upon you, pours himself into you. Because you bear within you what is contrary to him, you do not immediately yield to him [Col. 0412B], but oppose him, lest he enter into you peacefully. Yet he comes and enlightens you, so that you may see in yourself what you had before but did not see; and you did not see it because you did not attend to it. When he comes, you are enlightened and made alive: enlightened, so that you may see; made alive, so that you may feel. For you feel what is present and see what lies before you.

You see one thing and foresee another; you feel one thing and sense another as present. You see evil and foresee evil: you see present evil, and foresee future evil. You feel guilt; you sense punishment as present. Before the Holy Spirit came to you, blind, you neither saw, nor, being dead, felt; and therefore you did not see because you did not look, nor did you feel because you did not attend. But after the good has returned, you are awakened and enlightened by its taste so that you may recognize evil.

First, you recognize the evil that you were suffering, namely guilt; then also the evil which you were incurring from it and for it, namely punishment. The good that came taught both: so that present evil might be felt and future evil foreseen. From this arises that medicinal pain: when, made sensitive to the evil you suffer, you begin to grieve in order to correct yourself; and, enlightened concerning the evil you deserve, you begin to fear in order to guard against it. Unless you grieved, you would not correct yourself; and unless you feared, you would not guard against it.

First, therefore, you are enlightened concerning guilt, so that you may see it; then concerning punishment, so that you may fear it. Finally, made sensitive by fear, you grieve for guilt and correct it, because perhaps you would not grieve unless you feared. For unless punishment were seen and feared, no one would grieve over a guilt that pleased him. Therefore the punishment that follows guilt is shown [Col. 0412D] to you, so that the guilt which delights in experience may at least displease in tribulation; so that you may begin to observe that even what seems sweet in it is evil, since what is received from it and after it is so bitter.

Therefore you are enlightened and afflicted, because you see what terrifies and possess what pains. If you were not enlightened, you would not be tormented, because you would not see what you feared. Again, if there were not in you something due to the flames, fire would be seen without pain, and you would receive enlightenment without feeling affliction. Punishment terrifies; guilt fears. All this comes from the coming of light: by it punishment is displayed so that it may be seen, and guilt is made perceptible so that it may be recognized.

Yet one thing is that by which you see, another that which you see; one thing is that by which you are enlightened, another that toward which you are enlightened. That by which you are enlightened warms and nurtures; that toward which you are enlightened terrifies. Yet the terror is, as it were, imputed to the light, because before you were enlightened you were not terrified. Nevertheless, it is beneficial that terror should come, because unless punishment terrifies, guilt is not corrected.

Therefore the light does you good when it shows what torments you, because through it the light corrects what wickedly delights you. Thus you are enlightened in order that you may be terrified. The first light is terrible—or rather, the darkness seen through the light is terrible—because it cannot be seen without terror, nor felt without pain, especially by one who recognizes that he has deserved to feel what he sees impending and is unable to avoid.

Thus fear is born when danger is foreseen. It has punishment in the evil that torments, not in the evil that liberates—evil, I say, which is not evil. For every punishment is an evil, but not every punishment is bad. Whatever contributes and benefits toward something is good, even if it is not good in itself. Therefore a lesser punishment comes that a greater punishment may be avoided; and this is good, yet it comes from what is not good [Col. 0414A].

For through punishment we are freed from punishment; and it is beneficial to feel for a time what is burdensome, lest we must always feel what is intolerable. But he who is your true good works this good of yours out of what is not your good; later he will work another good of yours, which is not only through him but from him. First, from your punishment he works your deliverance; afterwards, from his sweetness he works your joy. Yet in both cases he is one and the same: here, the one who works; there, both the one who works and that from which he works.

[Col. 0413]

## EXPLANATION OF THE CANTICLE OF THE BLESSED MARY (Luke 1)

### PROLOGUE
[Col. 0413B] I find in the divine Scriptures this to be a very great difficulty: that whenever the surrounding subject compels us at times to seek some great and sublime meaning, there the letter seems to offer nothing beyond the ordinary and nothing difficult to express. For I do not think it so laborious for the reader’s mind to grasp matters new and wondrous that are set forth, however profound and shadowed by figures of speech they may be, as it is to raise to a sublime understanding those things which, at first approach, it finds modest and humble.

For behold, who does not know that the Song of Mary, which the holy Church throughout the world celebrates with such famous and continual—indeed daily—recitation, contains mysteries of the greatest spiritual meaning? For, to pass over what alone might have sufficed to commend its authority—namely, that not without great and very reasonable cause ecclesiastical custom has preserved this song, above all the other songs found in sacred Scripture, in such great veneration—to pass this over, who can doubt that blessed Mary, newly filled with such fullness and grace by the Holy Spirit’s coming upon her, could not have uttered in praise of her Savior something slight and not beyond the capacity of earthly minds?

It is certain, then, that, pouring forth from so great a fullness and rejoicing to her Jesus with such devotion in that new joy, unfamiliar to human minds, she proclaimed her new gladness at the new coming of the eternal Lord by a new praise and singular proclamation. Yet, as we run through the sequence and text of that very song, we find certain things proposed in the manner of a plain narrative, so that at first sight nothing further seems to be sought in them; although, even if these things themselves are true, one may doubt whether they are sufficient for such great mysteries and sacraments.

Therefore I am the more afraid in expounding it, lest I introduce something foreign or omit something proper, and thus, bound by the charge either of negligence or of rashness, I may incur with you, in place of favor, the danger of offense—although you yourselves have requested it. I have added at the side certain matters to this exposition which, if inserted into the text, might perhaps seem to some reader less fittingly joined. But I know a sufficient reason why it was appropriate for you to request this, and why it is not unfitting for me, so far as ability permits, to comply with the desire of those who ask.

## The Exposition Begins

[Col. 0413D] “My soul magnifies the Lord.”

If we wish to weigh the circumstances of the event, it will become clearer than light how worthy these words are of consideration. For a sacred interpretation is more suitably brought out into clarity when it is known either through whom the mystical account has been conveyed, or by what cause the reporter himself was moved either to be able or to wish to relate such things.

Let us therefore see how blessed Mary came to utter the words here set forth. We read in the Gospel of Luke (Luke 1) that the angel Gabriel was sent by God to Nazareth, a city of Galilee, to a virgin betrothed to a man named Joseph, of the house of David; and the virgin’s name was Mary, in order to announce the new coming in the flesh of the Son of God. Entering, he reverences the virgin with a new service of greeting, saying: “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you; blessed are you among women.”

When Mary heard this, she was troubled at the angel’s speech, not without great wonder; and she considered what manner of greeting it might be. But the angel, explaining the cause of such a greeting and so great a reverence, strengthened the sacred virgin—that is, soothed her with sweet words—saying: “Do not fear, Mary, for you have found grace with the Lord. Behold, [Col. 0415B] you shall conceive in your womb and bear a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. He shall be great and shall be called the Son of the Most High; and the throne of David his father shall be given to him, and he shall reign over the house of Jacob forever, and of his kingdom there shall be no end.”

And Mary said: “How,” she said, “will this happen, since I do not know a man?” To her the angel immediately explained the cause and manner of so ineffable a mystery: “The Holy Spirit,” he said, “shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you; therefore that holy thing which shall be born from you shall be called the Son of God.” And so that every uncertainty of faith might be removed, he displayed the efficacy of divine power by adding another miracle—wondrous indeed, though unequal to this one—saying: “And behold, Elizabeth your kinswoman has herself conceived a son in her old age; and this is the sixth month for her who is called barren, because no word shall be impossible with God.”

Immediately the virgin, full of faith and exultation, replied with great rejoicing: “Behold the handmaid of the Lord; let it be done to me according to your word.” Therefore, as soon as the Holy Spirit came upon the Virgin and, at the coming of the Son of God, filled the most holy dwelling-place with the grace of every virtue, there can be no doubt that the Virgin herself conceived a wondrous and inexpressible sweetness of heavenly joys and eternal delight, when that eternal light descended into her in all the splendor of its majesty, and he whom the world cannot contain placed his whole self within the virgin’s womb.

[Col. 0415C] Full, then, of such and so great a presence of divinity, who can say what she saw or what she felt? I boldly declare that not even she herself could fully explain what she was able to comprehend. Amid such wonders, therefore, how could a human tongue have remained silent unless that same Spirit who had filled the virgin had tempered the rushing torrent of his abundance with a most sweet embrace?

Already from afar the wisdom of God then cried out in that blessed soul: “The Spirit breathes where he wills, and you hear his voice; but you do not know whence he comes or whither he goes” (John 3). For you, he says, suddenly received the Holy Spirit entering into you; nor did your knowledge precede his coming, so as either to seek him before he came, to love him when he came, or to open to him as he entered. He slipped into you suddenly; he offered himself freely; he came unsought and poured himself in unexpectedly. You perceive the infusion, but you do not stretch yourself to the fountain of his immensity. Therefore you do not know whence he comes: for you can perceive how much has been given to you, but you cannot investigate from how great an abundance it has been given.

If, then, you could not go before him as he came into you, do not presume to anticipate his going forth through you; for you do not know whither he goes, just as you do not know whence he comes. Keep the secret; guard what has been entrusted; hide what has been committed to you. “It is not yours to know the times or seasons which the Father has placed in his own power” (Acts 1). He himself knows when, to whom, and how he may reveal the hidden things of his magnificence. You need only be ready to obey his command and render service at his bidding. Tempering herself, then, with such reflection, Mary wisely chose for the time to remain silent, until the giver of the gift should deign by his wisdom to become the author of its revelation.

[Col. 0416B] But because, taught by the same Holy Spirit, she had learned both to conceal her own gifts through humility and to rejoice through charity in the good things of others, she rose at once and, overflowing with such great grace, hastened to feast at the banquet of one below her. She went up into the hill country of Judea to see and congratulate Elizabeth, so that, believing, she might see in Elizabeth’s presence what she had heard concerning her, and receive it with fitting exultation.

But she who had now devoutly run to proclaim another’s blessings deserved to hear her own blessings proclaimed by another, so that her glory might also increase from the fact that she had not envied another’s exaltation. Thus Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, recognized the character and greatness of her visitor, and declared how unworthy she judged herself of that visitation, saying: “Whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me? For behold, when the voice of your greeting came into my ears, the child leaped for joy in my womb. And blessed are you who believed, because those things spoken to you by the Lord shall be fulfilled” (Luke 3).

Then Mary said:

“My soul magnifies the Lord.”

She could no longer contain herself when she saw the Spirit, whom she felt overflowing with such fullness within the hidden chambers of her heart, burst forth through the barriers of another’s mouth. Then, therefore, for the manifestation of the Spirit she opened her mouth; and, pouring forth the good word which she had conceived, she cried in praise of the Savior: “My soul magnifies the Lord.”

Let no one, then, think these words to be lightly esteemed. For things uttered from so deep a conception cannot worthily be penetrated without deep investigation. And would that, as we seek their hidden meaning, it might happen to us to proceed under the guidance of that Spirit by whom Mary, filled, deserved to conceive the Word of the Father and, by a word of exultation, to magnify the Father of the Word.

She says, then: “My soul magnifies the Lord,

and my spirit has exulted in God my Savior.”

Truly beloved and unique, brought by your royal Bridegroom into that wine-cellar, made drunk from the abundance of his house, and given to drink from the fountain of life—which is with him—you have poured forth the memory of the abundance of his sweetness and have exulted in his righteousness. You saw and tasted: you saw majesty and tasted sweetness. Therefore you gave outwardly what you had drawn inwardly.

[Col. 0417A] “My soul magnifies the Lord.” See what she says: “My soul,” she says, “magnifies; and my spirit has exulted.” Two and two: soul and spirit; magnifies and has exulted. The soul magnifies; the spirit exults. And again there are two: Lord and Savior; two words, one reality, and yet two: Lord and Savior. In “Lord” note power; in “Savior,” mercy.

Let us therefore consider the distinction of the words. First the soul magnifies the Lord; then the spirit exults in the Savior. She does not say that the soul exults. Nor did she say, “The spirit magnifies”; rather, she says, “The soul magnifies and the spirit exults.” Nor does she say, “It magnifies the Savior and exults in the Lord”; rather, “It magnifies the Lord and exults in its Savior.”

First let us distinguish why she separately used “magnifies” and “exults,” and why she first says “magnifies” and afterward “exults.” For nothing is without reason, since everything she said flowed from that innermost light of supreme truth, to which the virgin’s mind was most excellently joined. Nor could she, who spoke not by deliberation but by tasting, say otherwise; she was taught not by thought ranging through diverse things, but by devotion of mind adhering in contemplation to the one fountain of wisdom.

“My soul magnifies the Lord,” she says, “and my spirit has exulted.” For there are two things which the blessed spirits of angels and men draw from that fountain of good in eternal contemplation: namely, the incomprehensible majesty of God and his ineffable goodness. One of these produces chaste fear; the other gives birth to love. Because of majesty they revere God, and because of goodness they love him, lest love without reverence become unrestrained, or reverence without love become punitive. For, admiring, they love; and loving, they admire: thus love burns unquenchably through admiration, and admiration glows sweetly in love.

[Col. 0417C] On account of this reverence it is said that the pillars of heaven tremble before him, because even the powers of heaven cannot behold such majesty without wonder. The trembling of blessed spirits, however, is not a disturbance of tranquility, but an unceasing and life-giving attentiveness of perpetual contemplation. For because they never suffice perfectly to comprehend him whom they see, they always behold him above themselves; in this way they are, as it were, awakened through admiration, lest they grow dull before that which they can never comprehend.

Moreover, the more keenly they behold him, the more ardently they love him, because to see him is to be wise, and what is seen is sweetness. The more perfectly true sweetness is felt, the more desirably it is sought; for if that which is perceived is truly sweet, it must be sweeter if it is perceived more fully. Mary’s mind, then, had been raised to this light of contemplation. She expressed in her words, as wonderfully as she comprehended it ineffably, the sweetness of the heavenly homeland.

For when she declared that she magnified the Lord, she plainly showed that by inward vision she beheld that venerable majesty of the eternal Godhead, worthy of reverence from all. But when she asserted that she exulted in her Savior, she showed that she had received a taste of inward sweetness. Hence she confessed both Lord and Savior, so that, by the power through which he rules all his creation, he might be shown to be rightly feared even by those who do not love him; but by the goodness through which he mercifully saves some, he might be shown worthy of love.

[Col. 0418A] Certainly, since “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 24), it is perfect praise to confess him as Lord and Savior: truth is commended in “Lord,” and mercy in “Savior.” For truth belongs to the Lord and mercy to the Savior. For because he governs all his works with justice so great and so perfect that even what is found in them to have been done contrary to justice he does not leave disordered; and because what has been done wrongly can neither escape his judgment nor oppose the laws of the eternal ordering, truth preserves the course of justice.

But because he gathers some wanderers freely unto life and restores them to salvation in his judgment, he tempers justice with the gentleness of mercy. Therefore we magnify the Lord and exult in the Savior: for the justice of the Lord must be revered by every person, and the mercy of the Savior must be observed with exultation. Therefore Mary says: “My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit has exulted in God my Savior.”

Why does the soul magnify and the spirit exult? Perhaps the same thing has been repeated in another word. For in a human being soul and spirit are the same, although “soul” and “spirit” denote different things. “Spirit” is said with reference to substance; “soul,” with reference to giving life.

Nevertheless, since the occasion has presented itself, I think it not irrelevant to recall here the error of some persons. There are those who maintain that every human being has two souls: one rational, and one sensitive, lacking reason, such as the souls of brute animals. They attempt to establish this opinion by certain arguments and authorities. They say that the rational soul is infused only into a body formed in the womb, just as we read that in the first human being the body was first formed and then the breath of life was breathed into it. And Moses says in the Law: “If anyone strikes a pregnant woman and she miscarries: if the miscarriage has been formed, the striker shall render life for life; but if it has not been formed, he shall be fined money” (Exodus 21). Some of the holy Fathers are also found to have maintained this in their treatises.

[Col. 0418D] Therefore, since it is agreed that the rational soul is given only to a formed body, and since matter, like the body itself, moves and grows before it receives human form and is brought by the vital motion inherent in it to this very form, they think it must be granted without contradiction that, before the human body receives a rational soul, it has a sensitive soul by which it lives, is nourished, receives growth and form. Thus, they say, if the rational soul were not given to conceived and formed seed, a brute animal would be born from a human being in human form, living by that irrational soul which it has from its first conception, differing in nothing from other irrational animals except that it had derived its substance from human seed.

For since brute animals’ seed naturally has this property, that at the appropriate time it receives life from itself, it seems unworthy to deny this to human seed, which is known to be more excellent in its nature. After all this they also adduce in support of their assertion the fact that in Catholic Scriptures we frequently find “soul” and “spirit” named by a double term in reference to one person, and that in the Church’s daily prayers, when we render funeral observance for the faithful, we commend to the Lord the soul and spirit of the deceased without any suspicion of error.

[Col. 0419B] By this argument, then, they wish to prove that each person has two souls: one by which he lives, the other by which he understands; and that in the future both will be made blessed in the elect—the rational soul through the vision of the Creator, the sensitive soul through the incorruption of the body. Likewise, they say, in the reprobate both will be tormented: one by fire, the other by an evil conscience.

But the Catholic faith does not admit an assertion of this sort. Rather, it most truly testifies that one and the same soul both supplies bodily life in a human being through sensation and lives in itself through understanding. Nor, if a rational soul is not given to a human body before its formation, does it follow that its motion and growth before it receives human form must be attributed to some soul; for we plainly see shoots and grasses move and grow without a soul. Unless perhaps someone wishes to call vegetation itself and natural motion a soul. But although this power may in some respect be called soul, it must by no means be called a sensitive soul or one that produces animal life.

For it is ridiculous and wholly contrary to reason to say that a human body without a rational soul is born a beast, rather than that it neither lives nor is born if it has not been made alive by a rational soul. As for their claim that it would be unworthy for human seed, according to the natural conception of other animals’ seed, to be thought weaker for receiving life and less effective: how weightless this is becomes clear when we see that almost all brute animals surpass human beings in the strength of sensation. Indeed, this very fact more plausibly proves that seed receives life and sensation only from a rational soul: for it was just that brute animals, to whom nothing was to be given in intellect, should be given something more in sensation; and conversely, that the greater a deficiency human beings suffer in bodily senses, the greater their need should be shown to exercise reason.

[Col. 0419D] Nor is it the case that the terms “spirit” and “soul,” which we find sometimes in sacred Scripture in designating one and the same person, were used to signify different essences; they indicate different properties of the same essence. For one and the same spirit is called “spirit” in relation to itself and “soul” in relation to the body.

Thus those spirits who were first created to remain in their purity and not be joined to bodies may be called spirits but cannot be called souls, because they have a spiritual nature but do not animate a body. The spirits of brute animals, however, because they are essentially bodies and have no being outside bodily animation, are more properly called souls than spirits. The human soul, because it has being both in a body and outside a body, is properly called both soul and spirit. It is called soul insofar as it is the life of the body, but spirit insofar as it is a spiritual substance endowed with reason.

Therefore in this life the soul is lost so that the spirit may be saved, when this life is despised for God’s sake so that eternal life may later be granted by God. But because, as regards essence, what we lose is the very same thing as what we receive, the Lord in the Gospel by no means commanded us to lose the soul in order to receive the spirit safe; rather, he said that this same soul must be lost here in order to be received safe in the future (Matthew 10). By this he plainly signifies that whoever willingly despises for God’s sake this life, which now consists in the body’s animation by a soul that is temporally mortal, will in the future receive the same life of the body—not of the soul alone—as eternal and immortal.

[Col. 0420C] Thus too the holy Church, which most faithfully believes in the resurrection of the flesh, prays not only for the spirits but also for the souls of its faithful. It asks, namely, that at the visitation of the righteous they may receive, along with that blessedness which will arise from the vision of God for pure hearts, this also for the glory of eternal life: namely, through the resurrection of the flesh, what they now lay aside as corruptible through the death of the flesh may become immortal and incorruptible.

So much, somewhat aside from the subject but perhaps not without usefulness, may be said about the difference between soul and spirit. Let us now return, as we began, to the order of our exposition.

We ask, therefore, what this distinction of words means: whether it intimates something to us by saying not that the spirit but that the soul magnifies the Lord, and by testifying that the spirit—not the soul—exults in her Savior. Perhaps someone may think it attributable more to curiosity than to diligence to examine every individual point in this way and pass over not even the least without its own consideration.

I know that in Scripture many things are said by expression, or repeated by emphasis, in this manner for moving the affections. If someone says that the same was done here, there is nothing unsuitable in it. For “My soul magnifies and my spirit exults” is said as though it meant: “I praise God with my soul and spirit, that is, with my whole heart and whole will; and I exult with all my inmost being in his salvation, which I now see being prepared for the human race. For I now see assumed from me that which I believe must be offered for me.”

Yet I confess him as my Savior: although he has not yet offered the sacrifice of his flesh, he has nevertheless already assumed the flesh which, at the appointed time, he will offer as a sacrifice. Therefore he is Savior even now; and not only now, but Savior from eternity: he has now come to save through the flesh he has assumed, but he ordained from eternity to grant the salvation which he will manifest in his own time.

[Col. 0421A] Or, according to the distinction of the words, it is fittingly said that the soul magnifies God and that the spirit exults in its Savior. For in Scripture “soul” often denotes a certain affection and tenderness of mind. Therefore, when she asserts that she magnifies from her soul, she shows that she reveres God not with servile fear but with the affection of love. Again, when she says that her spirit exults in her Savior, she clearly declares that this is not a salvation in which the flesh rejoices, but rather an eternal salvation, prepared among invisible goods, in which the spirit exults.

Therefore, because that blessed soul had conceived the sweetness of chaste fear, she said that she magnified the Lord not in servile dread but in filial love. For in the soul, as has been said, the affection and devotion of one who loves is expressed: to praise from the soul is nothing other than to revere from affection and to hold in reverence from love. But because she had again drawn from that fountain of mercy assurance of eternal salvation, she exulted in spirit in her Savior.

Nor should we pass over in silence that, when she named the Lord, she added nothing; but when she called him Savior, she named him not simply Savior but her Savior. For almighty God, by the power through which he rules all his creation, is Lord of all; but by the mercy through which he restores only some, and not all, to life, he is not Savior of all. His dominion extends equally to all; his goodness distinguishes only some for salvation. Therefore lordship is not said specially of anyone, while the elect alone rightly glory in salvation from him as in their own particular gift.

[Col. 0421C] This is why in sacred Scripture he wished to call himself especially the God of certain persons: because, while he granted all things existence, he gave himself as their reward only to the good, that they might be blessed. “I am,” he says, “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob” (Matthew 22), because while the rest have from me merely that they exist, these, chosen by grace, have from me, in order that they may be blessed, that which they are—from him from whom they have their being. That is: I have given myself to them; and therefore I wish to be called their God, because I am theirs—received by them through grace, whom they could neither receive by nature nor deserve through sin.

Now they possess me; and behold, I am their inheritance. I am their God and Savior: the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, the God of Jacob. Blessed Virgin, therefore, seeing herself singularly chosen because she had received grace in a singular way, and confirmed, as it were, by a certain privilege of divine election, fittingly calls with confidence, joy, and exultation her own Savior him whom she had conceived as a Son for the salvation of the world.

“Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid.”

[Col. 0422A] This is the cause of her exultation: “Because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid.” It is as if she said: “Rightly I exult in him, because from him comes that by which I exult; and because I love his gifts for his own sake, I exult in him.”

Let us distinguish these two things. Some exult neither from God nor in God. Those who exult in the pleasure of the flesh, or who, as Solomon says, rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things (Proverbs 2)—these exult neither from God nor in God. Since that in which they exult is evil, it is plainly not from God that they exult. And since they exult from evil unto evil and establish their joy in wickedness, they do not exult in God.

There are others who misuse the gifts of grace they have received and turn what has been given for the salvation of the soul to the use of the flesh and the glory of the world. Having received God’s gifts, they rejoice and are glad that they possess what God has conferred—not that through it they may be helped to attain God himself, but that they may be seen to surpass others in receiving grace. Even though these appear to have from God something in which they rejoice, they do not rejoice in God, because they do not love what they have received from God either in God or for God’s sake.

But those who, having received grace, turn to the love of God the very thing which they receive from him are indeed shown to exult both from God and in God. We must therefore carefully consider, whenever we feel our mind touched by some joy, lest what elevates the mind through gladness either arise from evil or, though originating in good, drive the soul toward evil through its intention.

[Col. 0422C] Mary, then, to show what her habitual joy was, showed that this joy neither sprang from vanity nor was turned toward vanity. Rather, she declared that she loved God’s gifts in God, and that, because of the regard of grace by which she had been anticipated, she exulted in her Savior, saying: “My spirit has exulted in God my Savior, because he has regarded the humility of his handmaid.”

Certainly, in sacred Scripture God’s “regard” is commonly understood in three ways: according to knowledge, according to grace, and according to judgment. The Apostle says concerning the regard of divine knowledge: “All things are naked and open to his eyes” (Hebrews 4). Therefore God regards all things by knowledge, but he does not regard all by grace. For concerning the regard of grace it is said: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears upon their prayers” (Psalm 33). This is the regard which those do not deserve to whom it will be said at the end: “I do not know you” (Matthew 25).

Concerning the regard of judgment it is said: “The eyes of the Lord behold the good and the evil” (Proverbs 15). And again: “His eyes are upon [the Lord regards] every way of the children of men, and he considers all their steps. There are no darknesses and no shadow of death in which those who work iniquity may hide themselves” (Proverbs 5).

Thus, God’s seeing by knowledge is his ignorance of none of the things that are. His seeing by grace is his bestowal of the gifts of mercy. His seeing by judgment is his assigning each person, according to that person’s works, either to punishment or to glory. But since this passage concerns the regard of grace, let us consider more carefully how God regards a human being by grace.

[Col. 0423A] The very word “regard” indicates a certain intensification, so that “to regard” seems to be something more than “to see.” For to regard is, as it were, to visit those previously cast off and abandoned. God is said, as it were, to turn away from a person when, through the severity of judgment, he withdraws the gifts of his grace. But when, appeased through mercy, he restores what he had withdrawn, he turns again to that person through the regard of grace.

Mary therefore rightly testifies that the Lord regarded humility alone in her, because the divine favor which human nature lost in its first parents through pride, it recovered in Mary through humility. For because in her the Word of the Father assumed the substance of flesh which he would unite to himself, he regarded in mercy, as it were, the nature previously cast off, in order to raise it up.

God therefore regarded Mary’s humility: he gave her, as a reward for humility, to conceive his Son in her flesh and to bring forth from her flesh the true God and man, the Savior of all human beings, so far as lies in him. Immediately defining the power of this humility, she adds: “of his handmaid.” For because she humbly recognized herself to be what she was—a handmaid—she deserved sublimely to be what she was not: a mother.

But since we have said that in calling herself a handmaid she expresses the virtue of humility, we must distinguish the kinds of servitude in order that it may appear how this statement commends humility. Servitude varies in four ways: according to condition, necessity, fear, and love.

[Col. 0423C] According to condition, all things ought to be subject to divine service, because a work owes this by its condition to its maker: it must obey his ordinances and follow his institutions, so that, having been made by him, it proceeds only under him and according to him. According to necessity, however, wicked wills are said to serve God. Though they strive to oppose his commands, they are nevertheless constrained by his ineffable ordering, so that they cannot bring anything to effect without his will. Those unwillingly serve his ordering who are not willingly subject to his command.

The third servitude follows, which is performed through fear, when we fulfill divine commands not from love but from dread. The fourth servitude is when we willingly obey his commands because we love him who commands, and seek in our service no advantage outside him, except that, walking according to him, we may be able to attain him. For this is to do what he commands for his own sake: to do what he commands in order to attain him.

But of these four forms of servitude, the one especially commended here seems to me to be that according to condition. Our first parents refused to render this to their Creator in paradise when, raised up in pride, they disdained to be under him by whom they had been created, and perversely wished to be like him in majesty, though they were not equal in nature.

[Col. 0424A] Grace therefore fittingly corresponds to fault. Eve, through pride, failing to consider that she was God’s creature and God’s work, wished to make herself equal; but Mary, humbly submitting herself to her maker, called herself his handmaid. Therefore the former was cast off and the latter chosen. He despised the proud woman and regarded the humble one; and what the proud woman lost, the humble one received.

Therefore she says: “He has regarded the humility of his handmaid.” He regarded humility; he regarded humiliation. He regarded humility by rewarding the humble; he regarded humiliation by raising up the humiliated. Humility and humiliation are two things: humility is inward, in the virtue of the mind; humiliation is outward, in the abasement of human estimation.

Servants of God sometimes have humiliation together with humility. At other times they have humility but do not have humiliation. But they never have humiliation without humility. Those have humility together with humiliation who are humble before God and contemptible before human beings. Those have humility without humiliation who, though they do not outwardly appear contemptible before human beings, inwardly preserve inviolate before God the merit of humility.

For the former the world has been crucified, and they to the world: by humility they despise the world, and by humiliation they are despised by the world. For the latter, however, the world has not been crucified; yet they have been crucified to the world, because inwardly, by the virtue of humility, they despise the human glory offered to them which they did not seek outwardly.

Mary, then, who was humble before God and abased before human beings for God’s sake, testifies that she was regarded by God in both respects: both because her humility was made acceptable before God and because her humiliation before human beings was changed into glory. Hence it follows:

[Col. 0424C] “For behold, from this time all generations shall call me blessed.”

Until then she had borne among people the reproach of barrenness, because she preferred the integrity of virginity to the marriage bed. But that for which, in the preceding carnal generation, she bore what was like a sentence of curse, now wins for her the deserved praise of blessing from every generation: for to her alone among all women was granted both to have the fruit of fertility and not to lose the integrity of virginity.

For God regarded her humility and removed her humiliation; and therefore, she says, “from this time all generations shall call me blessed.” All generations which shall recover, through the fruit of my womb, the blessedness they were deprived of through the fruit of the forbidden tree—all shall call me blessed. Thus it is now a small matter that I endured in the past generation the reproach of barrenness, when I shall be called blessed by every generation to come because of the fruit of my fertility.

“From this time,” she says. It is as though she said to Elizabeth: “From the time when, through your mouth, he disclosed his mighty works which he has wrought in me, he will magnify those same works by making them known among all generations.”

For he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name. Great indeed was it that a virgin should conceive a son without a man’s seed. Great was it that she should bear in her womb the Word of God the Father, clothed in her flesh. Great was it that, while confessing herself a handmaid, she should become the mother of [Col. 0425A] her own Maker. Yet, although all these things are great, they are not impossible for him by whom they were made, because he is mighty. Therefore, “he who is mighty has done great things for me,” and things singularly great, because he is singularly mighty. Accordingly, she did not say, “He is able to do this or that”; but, she says, he is mighty, so that you may understand him to be almighty, who is called mighty without qualification because he can do all things. She therefore confessed him mighty, and said no more: for his power may be believed because it exists, but how great it is, or of what sort, cannot be comprehended. Thus she confessed only this, and did not presume to investigate that power, since it cannot be known how great it is—though this is most truly known of it, that it is immeasurable.

Let those therefore now go and glory in their own understanding who suppose that they can examine divine works by reason and confine his power beneath a measure. For [Col. 0425B] when they say, “He can do up to this point, and no further,” what else do they do but enclose his power—which is infinite—and restrict it to a measure? For they say: “God cannot do anything other than what he does, nor do better than he has done. For if he can do something other than what he does, he can do what he did not foresee; and if he can do what he did not foresee, God can act without providence, since he does everything which he foresaw that he would do, and does nothing which he did not foresee. Therefore, if his providence can neither be changed, so that something other than what was foreseen may occur, nor annulled, so that what was foreseen may not occur, then everything foreseen must occur, and nothing which was not foreseen can occur.”

Further, whatever is foreseen is certainly to be, and whatever is foreseen is undoubtedly to occur. But if it is impossible for anything to occur apart from providence—and everything foreseen to be must necessarily occur—then in no respect can anything occur other than what does occur. Further: if God can do whatever he does better than he does it, then in that very respect he does not act well, because he does not do in the best possible way what he does: for he would act better if he did what he does better. To do a thing and not will to do it better is to do evil, even while doing good. But a devout mind cannot endure that this be said of God. Hence it seems near at hand, and consequent, that he cannot do better than he does, because he acts in such a way that he does not act wrongly in acting as he does.

By arguments and reasonings of this kind some are led [Col. 0425D] to say that God is so bound and constrained by the measure and law of his works that he can neither do anything other than what he does nor do it better. And thus those who extend that infinite and immeasurable power of the Godhead only as far as something which truly has an end, and deny that it proceeds beyond it, are plainly convicted of binding that power beneath a limit and measure. For it is certain that everything made in number, weight, and measure has its lawful boundary and end; and therefore, if the Creator’s power and capacity are made commensurate with the measure of his work, that power itself is undoubtedly declared to be bounded by end and measure.

Therefore, lest we seem either without cause to withhold assent from arguments which appear reasonable, or to allow credulous people to receive falsehood as truth without examination, we must briefly answer the points just stated, for the present purpose.

First, one must consider whether God can, without any change or annulment of his providence, do something other than what he does. For it is evident that everything which occurs has from eternity been foreseen as going to occur, because what is going to occur is from eternity going to occur, although it itself is not from eternity. Yet we say that what is going to occur can fail to occur. And if what will occur did not occur—and it can fail to occur—it would never have been going to occur, nor would it have been foreseen. But because it will occur, it has always been going to occur and has been foreseen. No change or annulment of providence appears here: for just as, having been foreseen, it will occur, so, if it had not been foreseen, it would not occur. [Col. 0426B]

“But,” they say, “it has now been foreseen.” It has rightly been foreseen, because it is going to occur. Yet they say: “Providence can neither be changed nor annulled; but the event can be prevented, so that what is going to occur does not occur.
