If the event of the thing were prevented—which can happen—providence would be changed or annulled, which absolutely cannot happen.” But we answer them thus: if the event were changed—which can happen—providence would neither be changed nor annulled, because that absolutely cannot happen. Rather, what was never going to occur would never have been foreseen; and providence would stand in its determination that it should not occur, just as it now stands in its determination that it should occur—not changed, so that after one providence there should be another, but so that it should never have been another. Therefore God can do something other than what he has done, provided that in doing something else he himself does not become other; but whether he does the same thing or something else, he himself always remains the same. [Col. 0426C]

It remains now to inquire whether God can make something better than he makes it. Here those investigators of ours, who have exhausted themselves in investigating investigations, say that they bring forward something new—and truly new, though not so much true as new. They maintain that individual creatures, considered separately, fall short of perfection; but that the totality of all things is expressed in such a consummation of goodness that it cannot be better than it is.

Here I first demand an answer when they say that the totality of all things cannot be better than it is: in what sense are we to understand their claim that it cannot be better? Is it unable to be better because it is supremely good, so that no perfection of goodness at all is lacking to it? Or is it unable to be better because it cannot receive the greater good which it lacks? But if it is so supremely good that no perfection of goodness is lacking to it, then the work is plainly made equal to its Creator; and either what is inferior is extended beyond its proper boundary, or what is supreme is compressed within a limitation—both of which are impossible with equal absurdity. But if it cannot be better because it cannot receive the further good which it lacks, then this very inability belongs to defect, not completion; and it can be better if it is made capable of a greater good, because he who made it can also do this.

Therefore, it cannot be better by itself, but it can be better through God; for it cannot, but God can. And how much he can do cannot be stated. Therefore he himself cannot be better; but everything which he has made can be better, if he who can do so wills it. And what he has made can become better, not because he corrects something badly made, but because he advances what was well made to something better—not so that he himself, as regards himself, acts better, but so that what he made, while he repeatedly acts and remains unchanged, becomes better. Therefore he is supremely mighty, because he can do everything possible. Nor is he less powerful because he cannot do impossible things, since to be able to do impossible things would not be ability but inability.

Therefore Mary says: “For he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name.” She did not say, “He has done great things through me” or “in me,” but “for me.” For what was done in her for the salvation of all was, by the privilege of election, uniquely ordained for her glory. Therefore she says “great things,” and does not add what sort they were; for, although all God’s works exceed the capacity of human understanding, the sacrament of redemption especially—the mystery of the Word—is evidently ineffable above all things. For nothing more wonderful has ever occurred than that God should become man, and that incomprehensible nature should so unite to itself the substance of a body that it was no less present in it because it was immeasurable in itself, nor was it less in itself because it was wholly in that body. [Col. 0427B]

These, then, are the great things—great beyond expression—which were done in Mary for the salvation of all, and done for Mary’s singular glory. Therefore she says: “For he who is mighty has done great things for me, and holy is his name.” His name is holy in itself, and is sanctified in us when we are sanctified in his name. What is his name? His renown. His name is the knowledge of him. Faith in him is his name. This name is holy among the holy, because it is glorified and blessed by the holy; it is blasphemed by the perverse. “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you” (Rom. 2). Therefore, because he has done great things, his name has been sanctified; because, while the Word is wonderfully born in the flesh, the glory of God is manifested among human beings through the Word. “Father,” he says, “I have made your name known to human beings, and I have glorified you upon the earth” (John 17). Therefore he who is mighty has done great things, and holy is his name. [Col. 0427C]

And his mercy is from generation to generation upon those who fear him. “He has done [them] for me,” she says, yet not uniquely for me alone, but preeminently for one. Nevertheless, “his mercy is from generation to generation upon those who fear him.” No one is excluded from grace; rather, in every nation, whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him. “From generation to generation,” that is, to every generation. In this grace nothing distinguishes one person from another except the fear of God. Whether Greek, barbarian, Scythian; male, female, free, slave—let one possess the fear of God, and one shall be saved. “His mercy is from generation to generation upon those who fear him.”

Here again we must not pass over what ought to be said concerning fear. Sacred Scripture distinguishes four kinds of fear: servile, worldly, incipient, and filial. Servile fear is abstaining from evil in order to avoid punishment while retaining an evil will. Worldly fear is abstaining from good in order to avoid punishment while retaining a good will. Incipient fear is, in order to avoid punishment, cutting off not only a perverse deed but also wicked thoughts. Filial fear is firmly cleaving to the good because one does not wish to lose it. [Col. 0428A]

Of these four fears, two are evil—namely, servile and worldly fear—and two are good—namely, incipient and filial fear. Servile fear dreads punishment inflicted by human beings and therefore considers it enough to desist from an evil deed. It serves only outwardly and, intent on pleasing people, does not fear the guilt of conscience. Worldly fear, on the other hand, does not seek to please people, yet fears displeasing them; it too feigns what is not, being as deceitful in denying truth as the other is deceptive in concealing falsehood, and each offends against truth. The one does so because he timidly denies what is; the other because he perversely pretends what is not.

But incipient fear, because it strives to avert the punishment threatened by God, sees that it is by no means enough merely to refrain from unlawful action. For to him who looks upon the heart it is not enough, for approval, that the act be innocent, unless the very thought of the heart also appears sincere and undefiled before his eyes. Therefore, because such a person fears displeasing him who sees all things, he considers it necessary, in order to attain perfect innocence before him, to cleanse the whole person. Hence this is called incipient fear, because under it virtue begins through a good will and vice comes to an end; yet it is not perfection, because, while one thing is done and another intended, the good is not yet loved for its own sake. [Col. 0428B]

Then charity comes and enters through this fear. While fear shows what danger we must flee, it in some manner causes us to seek and desire a refuge. It therefore turns the heart toward God, so that in some manner it flees from him to him: that is, while taking care not to have him angry, it endeavors to have him gracious. Filial fear follows this, born from charity that has now succeeded it, so that fearing him is nothing other than no longer wishing to lose the good that has been tasted in charity.

This fear indeed still has some punishment joined to it while we walk in uncertainty and the condition of our changeable life can still incline in either direction. But when there is no longer any changeability, there will be no punishment arising from the uncertainty of apprehension. Then fear will in some sense be without fear, where we shall also be certain of stability; nevertheless, we shall not cease to show reverence to the Creator. Therefore, “his mercy is from generation to generation upon those who fear him.” Not only upon those who fear him with perfect charity, but also upon those beginning to fear and turning themselves through incipient wisdom: his mercy is from generation to generation upon those who fear him. [Col. 0428D]

He then begins to explain more fully this mercy bestowed on those who fear God, and by a clear narrative to set forth the order and manner of human redemption, saying:

He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thought of his heart. This is the mercy which God has shown to those who fear him: that he sent his Word into this world through assumed flesh, in order that through him he might overthrow the aerial powers by mighty strength and redeem the human race from their power. For they are the proud whom he scattered, driving them out from the hearts of human beings and plundering their spoils. For he destroyed the power by which they formerly ruled among human beings. “He has shown strength with his arm,” because through the humility of his Son he conquered the devil. Thus he showed strength with his arm. His arm is his Son. He displayed power in his arm, because through that which was made in him, that which was made by him was redeemed. He showed strength; he showed weakness; and that very weakness was strength, because through it the devil was conquered and humanity snatched from his power. [Col. 0429A]

“He has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thought of his heart.” What is “in the thought of his heart”? He scattered them in the thought of his heart—that is, in his profound counsel. It was a profound counsel that God should become man for the sake of man, and that the innocent should suffer so that the guilty might be redeemed. In all these things the counsel was profound, and the devil could not foresee it. But Leviathan was caught on the hook, and the wisdom of God struck down the proud one.

“The mystery,” says the Apostle, “kept silent through eternal ages, known to God alone” (Rom. 16), “which none of the rulers of this age recognized; for if they had recognized it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Cor. 2). This is “in the thought of his heart”: this God revolved in his heart—or rather, did not revolve, but possessed—and the devil did not know it. “The princes of Zoan have become fools; the wise counselors of Pharaoh have given foolish counsel. Where now are your wise men? Let them announce to you and make known what the Lord of hosts has purposed against Egypt. The princes of Zoan have become fools; the princes of Memphis have withered away; they have deceived Egypt, the corner-stone of its peoples. The Lord has mingled in its midst a spirit of dizziness” (Isa. 19). [Col. 0429C]

Thus, “he has scattered the proud in the thought of his heart, and he has shown strength with his arm,” because through the incarnation of his Son he both powerfully defeated the demons and wisely outwitted them. “He has shown strength with his arm, and has scattered the proud in the thought of his heart.”

We may also understand, not inappropriately, the proud to be the Jews, who boasted that they were of Abraham’s race, relied upon their own righteousness, and therefore were not subject to God’s righteousness. God then scattered these proud persons, having shown strength with his arm, in the thought of his heart; because through his Son coming in the flesh he taught that no one could be justified by works of the law, but only through faith which is from God. But the Jews who sought to defend the works of the law against God’s righteousness, and proudly despised Christ’s humble coming, he cast away from his grace, in which they seemed to stand; and he received the Gentiles, who humbly acknowledged their sins and preferred God’s righteousness. Hence the following is fittingly added:

He has put down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble. For he put down the mighty from their seat because he rejected the Jews, who appeared to be the children of the kingdom; and he exalted the humble—that is, Gentile people—because he received the Gentiles, who had been rejected, through humble confession into fellowship in the kingdom and adoption as children. Or, according to the earlier interpretation, he put down the mighty from their seat because he expelled evil spirits from human hearts; and he exalted the humble, namely those human beings whom he had formerly rejected because of pride, restoring them once humbled. [Col. 0430A]

Therefore he has shown strength with his arm; he has scattered the proud in the thought of his heart; he has put down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble. Yet I see that there is still something we may add to what has been said concerning the scattering of the proud. For if we interpret “in the thought of his heart” according to the earlier sense, it is clear that it was brought about by God’s lofty and inscrutable counsel that the Jews, who were chosen first, should later be rejected, and that the Gentiles, who had formerly been rejected, should afterward be received. This was done by so profound and unsearchable a counsel that God might enclose all under sin and have mercy upon all. Therefore the Apostle, astonished in contemplating this depth, cried out: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (Rom. 11). We may understand this, then, in the words: “in the thought of his heart.” [Col. 0430B]

And if we wish to apply yet another exposition, the interpretation will not be contemptible. For the mind of God’s heart is that living and enduring disposition of inward and hidden predestination. It is the book of life, in which are written the names of those who are saved and who are written for life in Jerusalem. Thus mind is the same as book: and what is written, as if to remain permanently in a book, is not erased when retained in the mind by memory. Accordingly, what is said here, “He has scattered the proud in the thought of his heart,” is expressed by the Psalmist in other words: “Let them be blotted out of the book of the living” (Ps. 68 [69]). But because the foreknowledge of divine predestination does not change, and to be erased or scattered from it is not to cease to be there, but never to have been there, he rightly adds: “And let them not be written with the righteous” (ibid.).

It should be known that someone is said to be written in the book of life in three ways: according to foreknowledge, according to cause, and according to operation. According to foreknowledge, those predestined for life are written in the book of life; they are never erased, because no one of those foreseen for salvation will be allowed to perish, although for a time one may be permitted to wander from the way of truth as though about to perish. [Col. 0430D] According to cause, those who walk in righteousness for a time are written in the book of life; and such people are sometimes persons who would be worthy of salvation if they remained such until the end. These, however, are erased when they abandon the righteousness they began and depart from the way of truth in which they had begun to walk, turning aside into errors. According to operation, or rather according to human estimation, those are said to be written in the book of life whose works appear, by human judgment, such that they seem worthy to be written in the book of life. When these in turn abandon the good things which they seemed to do, they are judged as though erased from the book of life.

Those, therefore, who are so erased from the book of life that they no longer deserve to be entered in it again, although for a time they appeared written either according to the cause of righteousness or according to the judgment of human estimation, nevertheless were never written according to foreknowledge. Since rational creatures, angels and human beings, had been inscribed by creation in the book of life for the rank of the heavenly homeland and inheritance above, but were cast down and deprived of their honor by the pride through which in each case they perversely sought to make themselves equal to their Creator, then indeed he scattered the proud in the thought of his heart, when he cast out from inward stability those who had swelled in pride concerning themselves and allowed them to fluctuate outwardly amid earthly desires. [Col. 0431A]

“He has scattered the proud in the thought of his heart; he has put down the mighty from their seat and exalted the humble.” First he cast down the angel, proud, from heaven, and humanity, proud, from paradise; afterward he restored humanity, humbled through repentance, to its former glory. And daily he puts down and humbles each proud person by withdrawing his grace; then, restoring the former grace to those same humbled persons, he exalts them. Of this also is what follows:

He has filled the hungry with good things, and sent the rich away empty. By “the hungry” he means those who know themselves to be in need of the true good; by “the rich” he wishes us to understand those who are proud and puffed up, and consider themselves to abound beyond others in gifts of grace. Therefore, just as the humble, thinking modestly of themselves, deserve to receive greater grace, so the proud and exalted, presuming upon themselves, lose even what they have received. [Col. 0432A]

He has taken up Israel his servant. He has taken up Israel his servant, namely his people, as a physician takes up the sick person: Israel his servant—that is, humble and innocent Israel—he has taken up in order to heal the infirm, redeem the captive, justify the ungodly, and save the righteous. He has taken up Israel whom he did not find Israel, but took up in order to make Israel. He has taken up Israel his servant.

Remembering his mercy. What he had long ago promised, but delayed for a long time, he at last fulfilled.

As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his seed for ever. Merciful in promising, truthful in fulfilling: because he promised without obligation and fulfilled without deceit. “As he spoke to our fathers, to Abraham and to his seed for ever.” [Col. 0432B]

[Col. 0431]

# QUESTIONS AND DETERMINATIONS ON THE EPISTLES OF ST PAUL. (G)*

## I. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS

Paul is an appellative name among Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins, though not with the same ending in each language (Rom. 1). Among the Hebrews it means “wonderful” or “chosen”; among the Greeks, “quiet”; among the Latins, “small.” This name was properly given to Paul as a mark of the twofold, or threefold, virtue indicated by the interpretations just given. Or the Apostle was called Paul from Sergius Paulus, the proconsul whom he converted in Cyprus. Or he had two names. [Col. 0431C]

### QUESTION I

The question is asked how Paul calls himself a servant, when elsewhere he says: “You have not received again the spirit of servitude in fear” (Rom. 8); and elsewhere: “He is no longer a servant but a son” (Gal. 4); and the Lord says in the Gospel: “I shall no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15). Was Paul not a friend?

**Solution.** Two kinds of fear produce two kinds of servants: namely, servile and filial. Paul, therefore, was a servant by filial fear and not by servile fear; and this servitude does not remove freedom or friendship, but rather establishes them. [Col. 0431D]

### QUESTION II

Why does Paul say that Christ was made from [Col. 0432C] the seed of David when we confess that he was born of the Virgin?

**Solution.** So that he might indicate that Christ was not conceived in the manner of other human beings, but from the Virgin by the operation of the Holy Spirit alone, without a man’s seed. Thus other human beings can generate other human beings, but cannot make them.

### QUESTION III

How did the Incarnation itself take place?

**Solution.** I say that the Word of God himself became flesh—that is, became man—yet was not changed or converted into man or flesh, but was clothed in flesh in order to appear to mortals. For this union was made in such a way that neither was the divine nature changed into the human nor the human into the divine; nor was a new nature or a new person made from the two natures. Rather, the two natures were ineffably united in Christ, so that the one assuming might confer upon the assumed, by grace, all that he had by nature; and all that belonged by nature to the assumed might become the property of the one assuming by gracious condescension. Hence he is called wholly God and wholly man, and conversely man is God and God is man—something which does not occur in the substances of a human being. [Col. 0432D]

### QUESTION IV

How can he here be called wholly God and wholly man, since the two natures are not parts of that person?

**Solution.** This is said because of a likeness: the two natures are united in Christ as parts are in a whole, but differently. For a whole has being from the conjunction of its parts, whereas the person of Christ does not have being from the union of humanity and divinity, since neither nature acquires any new being. That the natures are not parts of the person is evident from the fact that one of them is predicated of the person, as when it is said, “Christ is divine nature.” Likewise, the names of the natures are predicated of one another, as when it is said, “God is man” and “man is God,” which does not occur in an integral whole and its parts. [Col. 0433A]

### QUESTION V

How can “image” refer only to essence, when it is said relatively only of the Son?

**Solution.** “Image” sometimes signifies the divine essence, and then is predicated commonly of the three persons; it also signifies relation, and then is said of the Son alone.

### QUESTION VI

What is absent from the substance of a human being which is present in Christ’s substances?

**Solution.** Flesh is not soul, nor soul flesh; nor is man flesh or soul, as God is man and man is God, and Christ is both. This occurs because the union between God and man is greater than that between flesh and soul. For a soul united to flesh does not confer upon it everything which it possesses by nature, because flesh is incapable of many things that belong to the soul; whereas God, united to man, pours his whole self into him. [Col. 0433C]

### QUESTION VII

What is meant when it is said, “Man is God and God is man,” or “Christ is God, Christ is man”?

**Solution.** Modern doctors disagree among themselves in answering this question. Some say that the same thing is predicated of itself, namely, the person Christ. This is strange, since “God” and “man” signify different things, and “Son of Man” signifies something different from “Son of God,” as authority says. This also seems false to me, because the name “God” signifies the same thing when one says “man is God,” “Christ is God,” and “the Father is God.” If it is said that it does not follow that God, man, Christ, and God the Father are the same, then again: “man” and “God” are appellative names; how, then, do they properly signify this person, or when and by whom was such an imposition made?

Again, Christ is man, and the Virgin [Word] is man; is not the same thing predicated of both? If it is said that it is not, then they are not of the same nature, since the name of a nature is not common to both in the same signification. [Col. 0433D]

Others say that when it is said, “man is God,” what is signified by the name “God” is not predicated, but rather being personally united to God; and when it is said, “God is man,” having a man united in one person is predicated. But according to this view, neither is man truly God nor God truly man.

Others say that when it is said, “man is God,” the person of the divine nature is predicated of the person of the human nature; and when it is said, “God is man,” the person of the human nature is predicated of the person of the divine nature. Yet the person of the divine and human natures is the same, namely Christ; nevertheless, something different is understood when “man” is said and when “God” is said. These plainly grant that Christ is two things, one simple and the other composite; one eternal and the other temporal; and that Christ is, in respect of his humanity, something composite from flesh and soul, and in respect of divinity something simple. They also grant that divinity is not a part of this person but is the person itself, while flesh and soul alone are parts. [Col. 0434A]

### QUESTION VIII

Was Christ twice begotten?

**Answer.** He was born twice and begotten twice: once eternally from the substance of the Father, and again in time from the Virgin. He therefore has two births, two generations, and two filiations, eternal and temporal; yet he is not two sons or two beings born, but one and the same Son of God and son of man, though not by the same filiation. [Col. 0434B]

### QUESTION IX

Did person assume person, or nature person, or nature nature?

**Solution.** A person was not assumed; therefore neither did person assume person nor nature assume person. All grant that person assumed nature; but some doubt whether nature assumed nature. Yet without doubt divine nature assumed human nature, not into unity of nature but of person: that is, the union was so made that the one assuming and the assumed were one person, not one nature. Although authority often says this quite plainly, many deny it, saying: if what is assumed is a person, how has a person not been assumed?

But we say: although a person was assumed, God did not assume a human person but a nature, because he did not become of another person than he had previously been, just as he became of another nature than he had been, while retaining his own. For in assuming humanity he did not lose divinity. Thus it is granted that nature, not person, is assumed, not only by person but by nature. Those authorities which say that the Word alone was incarnate exclude only the other persons, not divine nature. [Col. 0434C]

### QUESTION X

What is predestination?

**Answer.** The preparation of grace. Predestination is also sometimes called the bestowal of grace itself. [Col. 0434D]

### QUESTION XI

Likewise, the question is asked: of what was predestination made—of person or of nature?

**Solution.** Of person, not according to the divine nature but according to the human. One may also say that nature, or the assumed man, was predestined to be so exalted that he should have no one above him.

### QUESTION XII

Should it simply be granted that Christ is a creature or a made thing?

**Solution.** This should not be granted without such a qualification as “according to the flesh,” lest we seem to agree with heretics who say that Christ is made according to both natures; and also because of the implicit negation contained in the word “creature,” for a creature is said to be what began to exist and did not always exist. For it does not follow: “Christ did not always exist according to humanity; therefore, he did not always exist.” But it does rightly follow: “He always existed according to divinity; therefore, he always existed.” [Col. 0435A]

### QUESTION XIII

Is Christ, according to his humanity, the Son of God, or God? They seek to prove this as follows: according to that whereby he is man, he is predestined to be the Son of God; but he is predestined, according to that whereby he is man, to be what he is; therefore, according to that whereby he is man, he is the Son of God.

**Solution.** It is not true that, if according to man he is predestined to be the Son of God, therefore according to man he is the Son of God—unless *according to* expresses person. But if it indicates cause or condition, it is not true, as appears in this parallel: “This man repents in proportion to the magnitude of his sin so that he may be saved; therefore, he is saved in proportion to the magnitude of his sin.” [Col. 0435B]

### QUESTION XIV

Is he a person according to that whereby he is man?

**Solution.** Some say: if *according to* signifies cause or condition, then according to that whereby he is man, he is not a person. They say: “If according to that whereby he is man he is a person, then he is either the third person in the Trinity or another person. But he is not another; therefore he is the third person in the Trinity, and thus according to that whereby he is man he is God.” Again, according to that whereby he is man, he is not distinguished from the Father or the Holy Spirit by a personal property, but only by filiation, which he had from eternity.

Others say that insofar as he is man, he is a person. Thus it correctly follows: “If he is man, he is a person.” But they say that this consequence is false: “If he is a person, he is either the third person in the Trinity or another person.” For the positing of the whole does not posit the part, as the removal of the whole removes the part; rather, the positing of the part posits the whole. But removing the part neither posits nor removes the whole. That what was assumed is a person is evident, since Augustine says that what assumed and what was assumed are one person. [Col. 0435C]

### QUESTION XV

Is Christ’s soul God?

**Solution.** This should not simply be granted, lest we seem to agree with those who said that the Word assumed flesh alone and that the Word itself animated the flesh in the place of a soul. For this reason the soul is not called God, because the term “soul” bears more strongly upon nature than upon person. [Col. 0435D]

### QUESTION XVI

Should it be granted that “that man existed from eternity”?

**Solution.** If the pronoun “that” indicates the person, it is true that that man existed from eternity. But if it indicates human nature, the statement “that man existed from eternity” is not true.

### QUESTION XVII

Is Christ’s soul a person? Some say no, while it is joined to flesh; but when separated, it is a person. Others say that Christ’s soul is the same person as the Word.

### QUESTION XVIII

Is what is signified by the name “Christ” universal? It seems so, because it is predicated of more than one thing when it is said, “man is Christ” and “God is Christ.”

**Solution.** It need not be granted on that account, since the predication in the two cases is not of the same form, although, according to some, there are also two things predicated of several things; nevertheless, it is not what is predicated of several things. Again, they seek to prove that it is what is predicated of several things, because the person which is said of the one assuming is also said of the assumed.

**Solution.** “Person” is, as it were, a comprehensive name, for two or more things are one person. Yet there are some who grant that what is signified by the name “Christ” is common to several things and signifies as much as this expression, “person of divine and human nature.” Nevertheless, Christ is not a universal, but, according to these persons, two singulars. [Col. 0436A]

### QUESTION XIX. Whether the assumed man is God

Answer. [Col. 0436B] Many say that he is not, whom authority plainly contradicts. For the Apostle says that “in him dwells all the fullness of divinity” (Col. II). And Ambrose: “Whatever the Son of God has by nature, the son of man has by grace.” Likewise the Lord, speaking of himself: “All power in heaven,” etc., “has been given to me” (Matt. XXVIII). If he has omnipotence, he is omnipotent; if he is omnipotent, he is God. Likewise John the Apostle says of him that he received the Spirit “not by measure” (John III). According to those who deny that the assumed man is God, the Spirit was given to him by measure, since he does not have everything that the Word has, to whom he is personally united.

### QUESTION XX. Whether that man can forgive sins, since he is omnipotent

Answer. That man [Col. 0436C] can forgive sins, not because he is man, but because he is God—just as he can reduce the world to nothing, if he should will it.

### QUESTION XXI. Whether a creature is equal to the Creator, since the soul of Christ, or the assumed man, has through grace everything that God has by nature

Answer. The creature is not equal to God, because it is one thing to be wisdom, another to be wise through wisdom; one thing to have something by nature, another by grace.

An objection is also made as follows: It has been said that whatever the Word has by nature, the man has by grace; but the Word has eternity by nature; therefore the man has the same by grace, and, if this is so, the man himself is eternal.

Answer. This term, “eternal,” denotes [Col. 0436D] a negation. For that is properly called eternal which always existed and did not begin to be. Therefore, because “eternal” does not simply predicate the person of the divine nature, but also indicates such a negation, the man must not be called eternal. Or it may be said thus: that man is the eternal God; he is not an eternal man.

### QUESTION XXII. Whether the assumed man is an adopted son or a natural son

Some wish to prove that he is an adopted son as follows: through grace alone he was predestined to be the Son of God; therefore he is a son of grace, and thus of adoption; therefore he is adopted.

Answer. That he is Son through grace alone belongs not to grace but to nature; that is, the assumed man is not an adopted son [Col. 0437A] but a natural son—not by nature, but by grace, through which he has everything that he possesses.

### QUESTION XXIII. How the Apostle shows affection toward the Romans, as the commentator says, by giving thanks to God, when thanks ought to be given to God for all good things which he gives both to good persons and to evil persons

Answer. He gives thanks not merely in respect of the gifts, but rather in respect of the Romans—that is, because the gifts have been bestowed upon them. But when someone gives thanks for gifts bestowed upon evil persons, he does this only in respect of the gifts, not of those upon whom they are bestowed.

### QUESTION XXIV. The commentator says that in the Romans the Apostle praises not faith but readiness of faith, which seems not praiseworthy, because one who easily believes easily ceases to believe

Answer. Readiness is twofold: one kind proceeds from frivolity of mind, and this is unworthy of praise; the other proceeds from strength of mind and close attention to reason, and this is worthy of praise.

### QUESTION XXV. The Lord forbids swearing by heaven or by earth in the Gospel (Matt. V); the Apostle swears not by a creature but by the Creator, which is more serious, when he says: “God is my witness” (Rom. I). Therefore he seems to be a transgressor of the commandment, and thus to sin unto death

Answer. The Lord forbids what is evil: namely, false swearing, or true swearing without necessity. He urged truthful speech; he permitted an oath when necessary, in which three things must be present: judgment, as regards the usefulness of discernment; justice, as regards whether it ought to be done; and truth, as regards knowledge. If any one of these is lacking, one incurs the guilt of perjury.

### QUESTION XXVI. What it is to swear by God

Answer. The sense is: “May God so help me, or not help me,” or, “As there is truth in God, so there is truth in this matter.” Whoever, so far as lies in him, nullifies this truth annihilates God’s truth, making God surety for them; but if it is not true, he in some manner imprisons God.

### QUESTION XXVII. Likewise, what is it to swear by a creature?

Answer. It is to swear by God, who made it. Hence Augustine says that one who swears falsely by a stone is perjured.

### QUESTION XXVIII. Whether an oath is good, evil, or indifferent

For if it is good, it ought not to be forbidden; if evil, it should never be made; if indifferent, how can it always be “from evil”?

Answer. It is not itself evil, but it is nevertheless an occasion of evil. Therefore the Lord advises avoiding it, lest by habitual use of it we incur perjury.

### QUESTION XXIX. How the Apostle shows his affection toward the Romans by saying, “I desire to see you, that I may have some fruit among you” (ibid.), when he seems to consider his own benefit more than theirs

Answer. He seeks not his own benefit so much as theirs, when he desires that they should bear fruit in good works, so that he too may gain some benefit from their progress.

### QUESTION XXX. If it is true, as many think, that a will accompanied by action is no more efficacious than a will without action, how does the Apostle say, “I desire to see you, that I may have some fruit among you,” since he would have had no more merit from the action than he had from the will alone?

Answer. It seems to us, however, that an action together with the will is a greater good than the will alone without action. But they say: he desired to come so that the will might increase together with the action and the merit become greater. What will they say concerning Christ’s passion? Did he not merit more by suffering than he had previously merited by desire alone? For they cannot say that his will was increased in the passion, so that his merit thereby increased.

### QUESTION XXXI. How the Apostle says that he is a debtor to Greeks and barbarians: did he not preach to them freely? Therefore, not as a debt

Answer. He does not say that he owes them anything because of their merit; rather, by reason of the office entrusted to him, he owes them the preaching of the Gospel. And with respect to them he preached purely gratuitously. Thus this debt does not take away grace, as he says elsewhere: “Necessity is laid upon me to preach the Gospel” (I Cor. IX). This necessity does not take away the will, just as this debt does not remove grace.

Again, it seems that there was something in them on account of which he owed this to them: namely, by the law of nature, by which he owed them what he would wish done to himself.

Answer. We grant that by natural law he was bound to illumine them with the light of truth; nevertheless, it must not simply be granted that he owed this to them. [Col. 0438C]

### QUESTION XXXII. Likewise, when it is said, “The righteous lives by faith” (Heb. X), it is asked why the efficacy of righteousness is attributed to faith and not to charity, since faith is sometimes present where there is no righteousness, whereas charity is nowhere without righteousness

Some answer by saying: Charity and righteousness are the same, and therefore neither is the cause of the other. Or otherwise: although charity is the cause of righteousness, nevertheless faith, which is the cause of charity, is suitably called the cause of righteousness, because whatever is the cause of a cause is also the cause of its effect.

And it should be known that it is one thing to believe that God exists (*credere Deum esse*), which is faith of cognition; another to believe God (*credere Deo*), which is called faith of assent; another to believe in God [Latin: *credere in Deo*], which is called faith of trust; another to believe into God (*credere in Deum*), which is to tend toward God through faith [Col. 0438D] and love.

Likewise, that which is believed is one thing; that by which one believes is another. Both are often denoted by the name “faith.” Again, that by which one believes is sometimes formed by charity, and then alone, according to some, is called a virtue. But when it is without charity, it is an unformed quality; it is neither a virtue nor does it justify.

To others it seems that wherever faith exists, even faith of cognition, it always justifies so far as lies in itself; yet its effect is sometimes impeded by an abundance of evil. Faith is the virtue by which things not seen are believed; or the certainty, above opinion and below knowledge, of invisible things pertaining to religion. Charity justifies, and faith, and grace, and God: therefore four things justify.

Answer. It is not true that there are four separately; for in faith and through faith charity justifies, and in charity grace, and through grace God.

### QUESTION XXXIII. How he says in the plural, “the invisible things of God,” when God is simple and one, and there is nothing in God which is not God, nor is anything here called an invisible thing of God which is not God

Answer. What is one and simple in nature does not come into our knowledge as one and simple, but as many. And this is rarely apprehended—namely, why it comes to us in this manner—because the inner eye is not yet able to attain that simplicity and ineffable unity which is God, in order to understand him as he is. Hence, when it understands God as good, wise, omnipotent, and the like, what is one in nature comes into the mind as if it were many. From this a higher question arises: whether those things which are understood by human reason as if they were many are distinguished in themselves, or in God, by some difference. They do not differ from one another substantially or personally. For example, the eternal reasons of things which existed in the mind of God certainly differ in some way; but in what way is not certain.

### QUESTION XXXIV. Likewise, because it is said, “His everlasting power also, and divinity,” it may be asked: since these two, God’s power and divinity, are invisible things, how are they distinguished from “invisible things”? For it cannot fittingly be said: “Animals live, and human beings and horses,” when human beings and horses are animals.

Answer. [Col. 0439C] Of the names said of God, some signify what God is not, such as “immortal,” “immeasurable,” “eternal,” and “infinite.” Some indicate what is in God, such as “wise” and “good.” Some by their predication suggest what God is, such as “goodness” and “wisdom.” Therefore, lest anyone should suppose that only those things which indicate what God is not—for instance, “immeasurable”—are beheld by the understanding from God’s creation, he added, “his everlasting power also,” etc.

Otherwise, according to others: by “invisible things” the Father is understood; by “power,” the Son; by “divinity,” the Holy Spirit. According to this, it seems that the philosophers possessed knowledge of the supreme Trinity through the things that were made. But Augustine, in his exposition on Exodus, says that the philosophers did not attain knowledge of the third person, but philosophized only concerning the Good (*peri tou agathou*, περὶ τοῦ ἀγαθοῦ), that is, the Father, and concerning intellect (*peri noun*, περὶ νοῦν), that is, the Son.

To this some reply that they did not possess, nor could they possess except by revelation, that distinction of the supreme Trinity which the Catholic faith confesses. For God is known in four ways: in two ways inwardly—namely, through natural reason, which, according to some, the Apostle indicates when he says, “What is known of God is manifest in them” (Rom. I); and through divine inspiration, which the Apostle indicates there when he says, “For God revealed it to them” (ibid.). He is known in two ways outwardly: through creation, as the Apostle indicates when he says, “The invisible things of God” (ibid.); and through Scripture, a mode sufficiently evident.

God therefore willed to remain hidden in some matters, so that faith might have merit; and to appear in some matters, so that unbelief might have no excuse. Note that in the magnitude of the universe divine power is indicated; in its beauty, wisdom; in its usefulness, goodness. Hence it is clear that not only in the universe as a whole, but in individual things, a certain image and trace of the Trinity shines forth. Nevertheless, care must be taken when likenesses are adduced, whether to demonstrate identity of essence, to suggest personal distinction, or to show that the incarnation belongs to the Son alone, although it is itself a work of the Trinity.

### QUESTION XXXV. Why is the Father understood by “invisible things” rather than the Son or the Holy Spirit, since they too are invisible?

Answer. Because nowhere is the Father read to have appeared in a visible form, as the Son did in the assumed man [Col. 0440B], and the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove and in tongues of fire.

### QUESTION XXXVI. Why is the Son understood by “power”?

Answer. Because he is the operative power of the Father, through whom all things were made.

### QUESTION XXXVII. Why is the Holy Spirit signified by “divinity”?

Answer. To show that he proceeds jointly from the Father and the Son, he bears the common name as though it were proper. Or, by “invisible things” the Holy Spirit is understood; thus “invisible things” is said in the plural because of the diversity of gifts. By “power,” the Father, to whose property power is usually referred. By “divinity,” or “deity,” the Son is understood. Thus different persons think differently.

### QUESTION XXXVIII. It is asked concerning what the Apostle says of the philosophers, that they were inexcusable: “Because, when they knew God, they did not glorify him as God” (ibid.)

For they seem to have had an excuse: such grace was not bestowed on them as would enable them to glorify God. Could they glorify God without charity? Can anyone have charity without faith? Could they love from that degree of knowledge which they possessed?

Answer. They were inexcusable because they did not do what they were able to do.

### QUESTION XXXIX. Likewise, it is asked whether, if they had done what they could, they would have been worthy of salvation had they departed this life in such a condition

For who is worthy of salvation without faith, or who can perish while having charity? Master Peter Abelard says that they were worthy of salvation, that is, worthy that there should be given to them the means by which they would be saved; for if they had done what they could, God would never have allowed them to pass away without faith.

Others say that they were inexcusable because from that degree of knowledge they could love, and that faith would immediately be given them from this state. But according to this, faith comes from charity, not charity from faith.

A third group think that they could not love from any degree of knowledge. Yet, if they had done what they could, faith would immediately have been given them, through which they would love God and thus glorify him. The objection is made to them: Could they have merited faith? Perhaps they will say that, although they could not merit faith, they could nevertheless become fit and capable of receiving faith from what they possessed. But how do they know that they would thereby become fit? Or, if fit, how do they know that faith would be given them? Were not the Tyrians and Sidonians fit? Yet preaching was not made to them.

Answer. We, however, believe that they could glorify God in part, although not yet perfectly. For if they attributed to God what they had received, and sought his glory rather than their own, they would glorify God in some respect; and in this they would love God, even if they could not do so perfectly.

Objection. From the knowledge they possessed, they could at least in part love God; therefore they could do this by charity which they had or which they did not have. But not by charity which they did not have; therefore by charity which they had; and thus they had love of God, and so were worthy of salvation.

Answer. [Col. 0441B] It must be granted that they could love God through the charity which they had; nevertheless, it must not simply be said that they had the love of God. Thus this sick and weak man carries a stone by means of the strength which he has; yet one must not simply say that he is strong or has strength. For we do not grant that those in mortal sin can perform no good work, as some think; rather, they do many good works, though works insufficient for salvation because of the greater evil which they possess.

### QUESTION XL. Whether natural reason can do anything by itself without the assistance of grace

Answer. Some say that natural reason can do many things by itself, as is apparent in the philosophers, who, relying on reason alone, knew many things not only in grasping truth concerning creatures [Col. 0441C], but also concerning the Creator: namely, that God exists, that he is one, and that he is three. Yet they do not seem to have attained this thought without the assistance of grace. Hence the Apostle says: “What is known of God is manifest in them”; and immediately adds: “For God revealed it to them.”

### QUESTION XLI. How then can it be without grace if God revealed it to them? Is this not grace?

Some reply thus: God is said to have revealed it because he made creatures such that the Creator himself could be known from them. Hence he adds: “For the invisible things of God,” etc.

### QUESTION XLII. Likewise, if natural reason has such power that it suffices for this degree of knowledge, it is asked wherein it was more effective before sin than now, or how it is now weaker than then

For just as then it knew that God exists, is one, and is three, so too now. And just as it cannot now comprehend the mystery of the incarnation without the assistance of grace, so neither could it then comprehend that mystery “hidden in God, who created all things,” as the Apostle says—as though nothing in creatures served as a means from which this could be known.

Answer. Before sin, reason grasped more easily and more perfectly what it now investigates with great difficulty, less perfectly, and from afar; it would also then have known many things which it does not now know.

An objection is made against those who say that natural reason can do something by itself: Does not the external eye see nothing without the illumination of supervening light, whether a ray of the sun or another [lacuna] and does not the inner eye likewise do nothing by itself without the illumination of that light “which enlightens every person coming into this world”? Therefore, what can natural reason do without grace, since such light comes from grace?

Some answer thus: In the first creation, the illumination of the supreme light was set before and offered to the inner eye; they ask how far, and to what end, it could attain by itself from such setting forth and offering, without some subsequently added grace. This illumination was not of the substance of reason nor of its nature, but was given to it gratuitously. Nevertheless, it may be said that it sees naturally, because aptitude and capacity for seeing were given to nature together with that light set before it, of which the preceding discussion spoke. Thus the eye of the mind can see nothing without grace of every kind; yet it can indeed see without a subsequently added grace other than that bestowed with nature, which subsequently added grace is most properly called grace.

### QUESTION XLIII. “God gave them up to the desires of their heart,” to “dishonourable passions,” and to “a reprobate mind”

From these authorities, and many others, such as: “He gave them a spirit of compunction, so that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not hear” (Rom. XI); “Pharaoh’s heart was hardened” (Exod. VII); and “He hardens whom he wills, and has mercy on whom he wills” (Rom. IX)—from these and countless other passages, certain evils seem to occur through God’s action.

Augustine too heaps together many passages to prove such a matter. Afterwards he infers: “From these things it is manifest [Col. 0442C] that God works in human hearts, inclining the good to good out of mercy, or inclining the evil to evil by his judgment, sometimes hidden, sometimes manifest, but always just.” Again: “Is it not just that one who is filthy should become filthier still?” (Rev. XXII). From whom comes this justice? Is it not from God, from whom comes everything just? Thus God seems to produce this.

Again, that sin which is the punishment of a preceding sin—from whom does it come? Everything just is from God, and that sin is a just punishment. Therefore it seems to originate from God.

Answer. To this some reply by saying that every sin is from God, not only that which is the punishment of another sin, but also that which is only fault. They grant that theft, robbery, [Col. 0442D] and adultery are from God, according to the prophet’s saying: “There is no evil in a city which God does not do” (Amos III). They also attempt to prove the same by this reasoning: Every essence is from God; but an evil will and an evil action are sins and have essence; hence, according to their opinion, it follows that sin is from God.

The following objection is made to them: What is it to make sin except to sin? What is it to make adultery except to commit adultery? To make theft except to steal? Therefore, if it is granted that God makes sin, it follows that God sins, steals, commits adultery, and kills—which it is wicked not only to say but even to think.

The objection concerning an evil will and a non-good action—that they are something and thus from God—is answered as follows. Sin is one thing in itself and another thing according to something else. Sin in itself is a certain disorder, such as the privation of justice; and this itself is nothing but the absence of justice. Hence it is not from God, since it is nothing. For God is not the author of that which is nothing.

An evil will and a non-good action are sin according to something else—namely, according to disorder. They are something, and are called sins not from what they have but from what they lack; for they are sins because they lack order or measure.

The prophet’s saying, “There is no evil in a city which God does not do,” is understood of the evil of adversity, not of the evil of perversity. Or perhaps we are not even compelled to understand this of the evil of adversity, if we consider the context of this Scripture more carefully. For the prophet has it thus: “There is no evil in a city which the Lord does not make known to his servants the prophets.”

Again, they object concerning the power of sinning, because it is from God; and it itself is sin, and thus sin appears to be from God.

Answer. This is nothing, because the power of sinning is neither sin nor a sufficient cause of sinning without the will.

### QUESTION XLIII. Again the question is asked thus: Whether every will is from God, since there is nothing which does not have being from God

Answer. It must not be granted that every will is from God because nothing exists without having being from God; for this would mean both good and evil will. The same is to be understood concerning action. For when one says “evil action” or “evil will,” the expression applies more to the quality than to the essence.

[Col. 0443C] Therefore, although it has that from which it is said to have being from God, since its quality is not from him, an evil action or will must not be said to be from God. Note that disorder is called the quality of an evil action because of a similar manner of answering; or “quality” is taken broadly for that which establishes what a thing is like, or what it is not like.

Again, this proposition, “The essence of this action is from God,” is understood in two ways: either that the action itself is from God, or that that from which it has being is from God.

Others, however, say that not every sin is from God, but only that which is the punishment of another sin occurs through God’s action. They say: If the statement “God gave them up to a reprobate mind” is referred to permission alone, it could generally be said of every sin that God produces it; but God is never said to give anyone up to any sin except that which is the punishment of sin. Again, if it is referred to the withdrawal of grace, it is clear from this that God produces it, since he withdraws grace. Again, since that sin necessarily follows the withdrawal of grace, who is its cause but the one who withdraws it? For if a house had some support without which it could not stand, and someone removed the support, who would be the cause of its collapse but the one who took away the support? Or if people were in a little boat at sea, and someone sank it, since they could not live without it, who would be the cause of their death but the one who sank it?

By these analogies, therefore, they attempt to maintain that God produces some sins, if not [Col. 0444A] all. But there does not seem to be a likeness between a house, which can merit nothing, and a human being through whose fault that without which he cannot stand is taken away.

A more fitting analogy would be this: if a house were about to fall, and someone put his hand beneath it and held it up to prevent its fall, then afterward, when reason required it, withdrew his hand, he would not be the cause why the house fell, but he would have been the cause why it had not fallen earlier.

Likewise, if someone were naked and another gave him clothing, and afterward the clothed man offended the one whose clothing he wore, so that the clothes were reasonably taken away, and he consequently died naked, who is the cause of death? Is it not the one who dies naked?

And if someone, for a cause requiring it, withdraws instruction from a person to whom he had previously provided it, he does this not by doing something, but rather by not doing what he had been doing. Thus we also say that, by withdrawing grace because our fault requires it, God is not himself, in our view, the cause why grace is withdrawn; nor did he do this by performing something, but by not doing what he had previously done.

Therefore it is on no ground to be granted that sin occurs by God’s operation, whether it is the punishment of sin or not. Accordingly, when Augustine says that God works in human hearts either by inclining them to good or to evil, “works” is said either by an analogy of expression to the verb “to withdraw,” which is construed with an accusative as though it signified doing something; or, better, “to work” is taken as meaning to act or not to act, as in: “For what I work, I do not understand” (below, ch. 7). Otherwise, if it were not understood thus, doing evil and not doing good would not be parts of working. Likewise: “He will render to each according to his works”: namely, for what he did and for what he did not do when he ought to have done it.

But the statement, “Let the one who is filthy become filthier still” (Rev. 22; below, ch. 2), is understood thus: the justice does not arise from the quality of becoming filthy, but from God’s judgment by which this occurs. Hence, if it is called just, the justice is not in the person himself but in God’s rule; it is not that the becoming filthy itself is from God or that God produces it. The same applies to every sin which is the punishment of a preceding sin. For such a punishment is called just not from its own quality, but from God’s judgment.

### QUESTION XLV. Whether the punishment itself which is also fault is from God

This appears to be so, because everything just is from God, and every such punishment is just. Therefore such a punishment seems to be from God.

Answer. It need not be said so, since it is just not from its own quality but from God’s law, as has already been said. For it is written: “God did not make death, nor does he delight in the destruction of the living” (Wis. I).

Or, even if it is granted that punishment is from God, fault is nevertheless not from God, although the same thing is both punishment and fault. For it does not have from God that it is fault, though in some way it has from God that it is punishment.

Since punishment is something in itself, it is said to be from God for three reasons: because of its matter, which God makes—for example, the matter of fire; because of its nature, namely, that such a thing cannot exist in such a thing without its suffering; this nature is from God; and because of God’s judgment, by which such punishment is inflicted for such fault.

Yet we do not call God the cause of that punishment; for this would be to say that God made the fault of that punishment, since he is not the cause of corruption. If corruption did not exist, the person being punished would suffer nothing. Thus a punishment of this kind, which is something, is said to be from God for three reasons: matter, nature, and judgment. But in two respects—namely, fault and corruption—it is not from God.

That punishment which is sin may be said to be from God for two reasons: because of God’s judgment, and because of the nature whereby no one can sin in this way without thereby being punished. But fault and corruption are in no way from God.

Therefore it must not be said that anyone is hurled into sin by God’s operation or impulse, not even into that sin which is punishment. Rather, the Scriptures which seem to imply this must be referred either to permission or to the withdrawal of grace.

Some also refer them to the opening of a way. For wickedness conceived inwardly cannot come out unless a way is opened for it. Thus Nebuchadnezzar had first conceived wickedness within himself, and God, by exposing the Jewish people to him, opened a way for him; and so he exercised the wickedness which he had previously held enclosed within himself.

Others refer them to the closing of a way: God has closed all other ways so that he may have no other way by which to go out. Hence God is said to hurl someone into sin because he does not close this way by which the person goes out, as he closes the others by which he does not go out. Thus it is clear that God is not the cause why he comes forth by this way, but the one who goes out himself is the cause. Yet God is the cause why he does not go out by another way; and why he goes rather by this way than another arises from both. God is the author of why he does not sin more grievously; but why he sins to this extent, and not less, is from himself.

For example, if someone were in a tower and wished to throw himself from a window, and another person closed all the windows except one, and that person threw himself through it: behold, the one who closes the other windows is the cause why he did not go through another window; he is not the cause why he went through this one, but the person who threw himself is. But why he went rather through this one than another is from both.

Some also refer these passages to occasion: when the Lord entered Jerusalem, the whole city was stirred, and wickedness previously conceived, having received an occasion, was aroused to envy and then to persecution.

Thus, according to some, the statement “He gave them up to the desires of their heart and to dishonourable passions,” etc. (Rom. I), is referred either to permission, to the withdrawal of grace, to the opening of a way, or to the failure to close a way. But we say rather that it refers to all these than to one individual cause, although not all concur everywhere. Nevertheless, three always concur: permission, withdrawal of grace, and failure to close a way; whereas the opening of a way and occasion are not found in every case.

### QUESTION XLVI. How God is said to give them up to dishonourable passions, when there they not only suffer nothing but even take pleasure

Answer. On account of the effect: because eternal punishment follows, sins of this kind are called passions. Or they suffer even in the present life. For they cannot sin in this way without suffering: their nature is injured, corrupted, deprived of some good, and made foul. Thus it is true that they already suffer in the present.

### QUESTION XLVII. Again, what evil does it bring upon the reprobate to be given up to a reprobate mind, since they will not repent?

For those who are blinded so as to call light darkness and darkness light seem to sin less through such blindness, since they do nothing against conscience. Thus what is in itself the greater sin is less for the one who commits it, because it is done less against conscience. Therefore, since these persons sin less against conscience on account of the reprobate mind, it seems advantageous to them to be blinded thus.

Answer. Such necessity of ignorance has no excuse, because it proceeds from a perverse will.

### QUESTION XLVIII. How God does not sin by working in their hearts so that they incline toward evil

Answer. If the foregoing is recalled to memory, the answer is clear: in doing this, he does not introduce wickedness.

### QUESTION XLIX. How it can be defended that God does not act cruelly in damning a person from whom all grace has been withdrawn and who, left to himself, cannot avoid sinning

For if he does not avoid what he cannot avoid, what fault is his? Or if he is damned for this reason, it seems that he is treated unjustly.

Answer. This impossibility is inexcusable because it proceeded from the fault and defect of his own will. For he first hurled himself down, although he now sins unwillingly; nevertheless, God justly damns him for his sins. For it is just that one who is filthy should become filthier still (Rev. XXII).

### QUESTION L. How God does not consent to sinners, since he knows evil and can prevent it, and the commentator says, “To consent is not to correct when one can”

Answer. God corrects and rebukes sinners in many ways: through natural reason, through written law, through his ministers, and through their own or others’ punishments. Therefore he must in no way be said to consent to sinners.

### QUESTION LI. Whether those who commit sins and those who consent to them sin equally

Answer. In matters of this kind, which can vary according to different causes, no general judgment can be given; for such matters must be judged according to intention.

### QUESTION LII. “According to your hardness, [you are] impenitent,” etc. (Rom. 3)

It is asked what it is to repent.

Answer. Repentance is compunction of mind concerning the past and a purpose concerning the future; or sorrow because one has done what one proposes not to do again. For what else is it truly to repent than to bewail things committed and, by settled purpose, not to commit again things requiring lamentation?

Repentance is also called satisfaction for sins. Hence a priest is said to impose a penance. Again, one repentance is late, another fruitless. Fruitless repentance is that which does no good, such as Judas’s and that of the foolish who say, “We fools,” etc. (Wis. V). Late repentance is that which is usually made too late, when there is no time.

Therefore a person truly [Col. 0447A] repentant is one who is contrite in heart, confesses with the mouth, and offers fitting satisfaction.

### Question LIII

When it is said, “on the day of wrath,” etc., the question is asked concerning the day of judgment: why is it called a day of wrath rather than of mercy? For just as the wicked will hear, “Go into eternal fire,” so the good will hear, “Come, blessed of my Father,” etc. (Matt. 25).

Solution. In calling it a day of wrath, we are advised always to fear that day and, through fear, to avoid the eternal fire. Note that “day” is said not of time, but of manifestation. Again, it should be noted that all will come to judgment, both good and evil. Of the good, some—namely, the very good—will judge; others, the less good, will be judged. Likewise, of the evil, some have already been judged, whose condemnation is already certain; others are still to be judged, whose condemnation is uncertain. [Col. 0447B]

### Question LIV

How it is to be understood of the saints that they will judge the wicked. Some answer that this means nothing other than that the excellence of their glory will appear, showing how great a punishment those deserve who persecuted them or failed to imitate them. Or they are called judges because, in the judgment itself, the eternal reasons according to which judgment will be made, and the merits of each person concerning which judgment will be made, will be disclosed to them. According to Daniel: “The court sat in judgment, and the books were opened” (Dan. 7), namely the books of reasons and merits. Therefore, those whose punishment or glory is not so plainly evident are to be judged on the day of judgment.

### Question LV

[Col. 0447C] Again, concerning the words, “according to your impenitent heart,” the question is asked about sin against the Holy Spirit: what it is and why it is said to be unforgivable. Is it because it cannot be forgiven? Or because it will never be forgiven, though it can be? Or because it is forgiven only with difficulty, rarely, and scarcely?

Solution. Some say that sin against the Holy Spirit is, out of envy, to speak against divine goodness. The stain of this sin is so great that those who sin in this way can never submit themselves to the humility of repentance. Others say that despair or impenitence is called sin against the Holy Spirit. Others say that it is to sow discord among brethren with the torches of envy.

Against those who say that this sin can be forgiven, the following objection is raised. If it is possible for such a fault to be forgiven, then no impossibility follows from that proposition; but Truth says that this sin is forgiven neither in this age nor in the age to come (Matt. XIV). Yet if it were forgiven, it would be false that it is not forgiven; and that is impossible, because Truth cannot lie. No one is certain concerning this sin. Nevertheless, this is known: if anyone has committed it, he will never obtain pardon. [Col. 0447D]

### Question LVI

How does he render to each according to his works, when one person’s works are good but his intention evil, and another’s works evil but his intention good? Since a work receives its name from the affection, will someone be condemned for good works because the intention is evil, or saved for evil works because the intention is good?

Solution. Intention alone is not sufficient in every case for works to be called good; it is always required that the works be good for the person by whom they are done. If the works are good in themselves but the intention is evil, he is punished for the evil intention, not for the good works; nor will he be rewarded for them, because through the evil intention they have been made useless to him. But for works to be evil for him, an evil intention is not required. Intention may be good or evil while the works remain evil. Whatever the intention may be, once the works are evil, they harm the one who did them. But in matters that are indifferent—that is, in themselves neither good nor evil—judgment must be made according to intention. [Col. 0448A]

### Question LVII

How is each person repaid according to his own works, when one does good throughout his life and falls at the end, while another does evil throughout his life and rises at the end through repentance? Will not the one who did good be condemned and the one who did evil be saved? How then is the repayment according to works?

Solution. The works of each person are called those with which he departs from this life; for these alone God will repay him. The good deeds done by the one who falls at the end are made dead and, through the evil that subsequently comes upon him, become no longer his own. So too, for the one who lived wickedly but rose through repentance at the end, by the good that subsequently comes upon him the evil deeds he did become no longer his own. Or judgment is made with regard to works, so that he may be punished less because he did good, or may have less glory because he sinned. [Col. 0448B]

### Question LVIII

Again, how is repayment according to works, when one has the will to act wickedly but lacks the means of accomplishing it, while another has the will to act well but lacks the means of carrying it out?

Solution. Their works are reckoned as such because they exist in their wills, and nothing on their part prevents them from being done. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: “Whoever looks upon a woman in order to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5). Nevertheless, we do not say that he is now punished as much as he would be if the deeds themselves had been carried out; rather, he is punished as for works, though not as much for the will alone. [Col. 0448C]

### Question LIX

A question is asked concerning an unbaptized child: how is recompense made to him according to his own works, when he dies immediately before doing anything?

Solution. The works of his parents in his conception and birth are reckoned as his own, and for them he will be condemned as though he had actually done them. Likewise, concerning a baptized child, we say that he is saved by the grace of baptism without merits of his own. [Col. 0448D]

### Question LX

A question is asked concerning one who suffers for Christ but does not act: how is anything allotted to him according to a work?

Solution. “Works” is taken both for sufferings and for deeds; thus a deed is taken both for what is done and what is not done. When what ought not to be done is done, it is called sin; but when what ought to be done is not done, it is an offense.

### Question LXI

Since guilt is temporal but punishment eternal, how does he repay according to works?

Solution. The guilt of the wicked, so far as they themselves are concerned, is eternal; for it was always in their will to remain in evil. Therefore, by God’s just judgment, they will be punished eternally. Or rather, their evil will, their liability for guilt, and the impenitence of their heart will be eternal in them. Hence the Lord will say to them: “Depart from me, all you who work iniquity” (Luke I). He will not say, “you who worked,” but “you who work.” For not repenting is sin, and they cannot repent. Thus they will sin eternally, and so the punishment will be everlasting for eternal guilt. [Col. 0449A]

### Question LXII

Again, since the good will receive more than they have deserved, and the wicked will be punished less than justice might permit, how is repayment according to works?

Solution. There is no equivalence between merit and reward; rather, the sense is this: whoever has merited more will receive more, and whoever has merited less will receive less, according to quality and quantity. For one person’s merit and reward may be equal and dissimilar, or similar and unequal in comparison with another’s merit and reward. Thus two martyrs, or two confessors, whose merit and reward are the same and equal, are equal and alike in justice and glory. But if a martyr and a confessor are equal, they are nevertheless dissimilar in quality, because this one is a martyr and that one a confessor, etc. [Col. 0449B]

### Question LXIII

A question is asked concerning the statement, “Tribulation and distress upon every soul,” etc. (Rom. 2). Will a human being be punished in the soul alone and not also in the body? Why then does he say “upon every soul,” rather than “upon the body,” when one has sinned in both?

Solution. There are certain sins of the soul for which it alone will be punished, such as anger, envy, and unbelief—the matter with which the Apostle is especially concerned in this passage. Therefore he mentions punishment of the soul, not punishment of the body. There are also sins of the body, for which the body itself will be punished, such as gluttony, lust, murders, and quarrels, which are performed through the body’s service. Hence it is evident that people will be punished in both, according to the words: “Crush them with a double destruction” (Jer. 17). [Col. 0449C]

### Question LXIV

A question is asked concerning the glorification of the body: what does it contribute to the human being or to the soul, since the sole blessedness of the human being is the vision of God, of which the soul alone is capable? Thus bodily glory seems to contribute nothing to glory.

Solution. The glorification of the body will increase glory and joy for the soul itself. For it will glory greatly when it sees the body, formerly so weak and frail, made so firm that it can endure no injury thereafter.

### Question LXV

A question is asked: since the soul’s glory is to contemplate God, to enjoy his vision, and to know all things in him—for “God will be all in all” (1 Cor. 15), being the mirror of every creature, just as every creature is now a mirror of God—how, this being so, can the glorification of the body be said to belong to it so that its blessedness is increased?

Solution. The soul will already know this glorification in God himself, and that contemplation will be a part of its blessedness. [Col. 0449D]

### Question LXVI

When the Apostle says, “God is no respecter of persons” (Acts 10), the question is asked what it means to respect persons. Does not the Apostle say, “Honor to whom honor; fear to whom fear” (Rom. 13)? Must we not show greater reverence to one person than to another?

Solution. He respects persons who honors and prefers one human being above others because of something that belongs to that person. God does not do this. For when we show fear or honor to those established in positions of dignity, we do so only for God’s sake, whose person they bear or whose ministers they are. [Col. 0450A]

### Question LXVII

“The doers of the law will be justified.” The question is asked whether fulfillment of the law justifies. This seems so from the words spoken when the lawyer asked the Lord, “What must I do to possess eternal life?” The Lord answered, “What is written? How do you read?” And he said: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind; and your neighbor as yourself.” And the Lord said to him, “Do this, and you shall live” (Luke 10). Behold, the commandment of the law, when observed, confers eternal life. Hence it is written that the law fulfilled justifies (Rom. 2).

Likewise, elsewhere, when the young man said to him, “What must I do to possess eternal life?” the Lord said to him: “Honor father and mother; do not kill; do not steal; do not commit adultery; do not bear false witness; do not covet your neighbor’s wife or property.” And the young man said, “All these I have kept from my youth.” And the Lord looked upon him and loved him (Matt. 19; Exod. 20; Mark 10; Luke 18), which he would not have done unless he had been just through observance of God’s commandments. But what follows—“If you wish to be perfect” (Matt. 19), etc.—belongs to the perfection of righteousness.

Likewise Paul says: “The commandment of the law, which was for life, was found to be for death to me” (Rom. 7). Likewise Bede: “The law, observed in its own time, conferred not only temporal goods but eternal ones also.” Thus it is manifest that the law fulfilled justifies. [Col. 0450B–C]

But the Apostle asserts that the law brought no one to perfection, saying: “No flesh is justified by works of the law,” and, “If righteousness is through the law, then Christ died in vain” (Gal. 2), and many other things of this kind. Therefore some say that those commandments whose fulfillment confers righteousness are commandments of the Gospel, even though they are written in the law. Whoever fulfills them immediately becomes an evangelical person and is not a person of the law.
