They also say that those commandments, fulfilled as they are understood in the law, do not justify immediately, but only make one fit to receive the faith of Christ, through which alone salvation is possessed. For they say that one who outwardly shows that he loves God and neighbor, even if inwardly he does not love from the heart, keeps the law insofar as the law is concerned. The law restrains the hand indeed, but not the mind.

The following objection is made to this solution: if through merely outward observance of those commandments persons become fit and worthy to receive the faith of Christ, faith is given not by grace but by merits. Again, if they are fit, how do they know that they will receive it? Hence they do not seem to resolve the preceding question appropriately. For what greater perfection is there than to love God with one’s whole heart and one’s neighbor as oneself?

Therefore we say that fulfillment of the aforesaid commandments justifies immediately; nevertheless, it is not the law that does so. The law does not suffice and is weak, without grace, even for its own fulfillment; it neither gives grace nor openly reveals faith in Christ, without which the commandments of the law are not fulfilled. It does indeed point out the homeland, but does not show the path by which one must go, nor the destination. Hence the Apostle says: “No flesh is justified by works of the law.” [Col. 0450D–0451A]

But someone will say: this authority plainly contradicts your solution. Are not these contrary: that righteousness consists in fulfilling legal commandments, as you asserted above, and that no one is justified by works?

Solution. The Apostle calls “works of the law” those works done through fear alone, the fear instilled by the law; from such works there is no righteousness. It should be noted that “law” is used in several ways. Sometimes it means the book of Moses; sometimes ceremonies and legal observances; sometimes the Ten Commandments written on the two tablets; sometimes the book of Psalms; and sometimes any observance whatever, as when one says, “This is the law of this or that thing.” Natural reason is also called law. In the New Testament likewise, law is understood in several ways: hence the law of faith, the law of the Spirit, the law of grace, the law of the flesh, the law of the members, the law of sin, and the law of death. [Col. 0451A–B]

### Question LXVIII

A question is asked concerning circumcision: to whom it was commanded and why; why it was in the genital parts and not elsewhere; why it was for males and not females; what efficacy it had; and why baptism succeeded it.

Circumcision is the cutting away of that little skin which covers the male organ; hence that skin is called the foreskin (*praeputium*), and the nations are called uncircumcised (*praeputiatae*) because they are without cutting (*putatio*), that is, incision. It was first commanded to Abraham; accordingly he and his entire household were circumcised. This command was not given universally or generally to everyone, but to the Jews alone. Hence it was said: “The soul that shall not be circumcised shall perish from his people” (Gen. 17). The people of God is the Jewish people.

This was commanded for a reason. God wished his people to be separated from others, and their hearts to be circumcised from vices and desires; and, in order to show this outwardly, he commanded them to be circumcised in the flesh—and in the genital parts rather than elsewhere. For since there are two principal means through which association is formed among people, namely marriage and food, God wished his people to be distinct in both. Thus he prohibited food common to the nations, namely pork. He likewise commanded circumcision in the genitals, lest they defile those sanctified parts by any union with unclean women, and that they might preserve their flesh from vices, as though it were the gate of our birth. And Gentile women, seeing that all their males were cut, would avoid marriage with them. It was commanded for males alone because no one who was without sin was to be born from male seed; but one was to be born from a woman. [Col. 0451B–D]

### Question LXIX

Again, a question is asked: what was its efficacy? Some say that it had the same efficacy that baptism now has, except that it did not send one into the kingdom. But if this is so, then in circumcision there was remission of sins, and therefore righteousness, and so righteousness from the law—which the Apostle denies.

Solution. We say that in circumcision there was remission not of all sins but only of original sin; but in baptism remission of all sins occurs, and in addition there is the bestowal of virtues. Whether baptism had this complete efficacy before the Passion is usually asked. Some say that it did not. Nevertheless, it may be said that after Christ’s death, to those purified before the cross, as much was bestowed through the sacrament of baptism as upon those who were baptized afterward. [Col. 0452A]

### Question LXX

Then the question is asked why baptism succeeded circumcision.

Solution. For three reasons: for pleasantness, for seemliness, and because circumcision itself was imperfect. For circumcision was harsh, and it is more honorable to be washed with water than cut with a knife. Baptism is also more universal: it is suited not only to men but also to women, and to Gentiles as well as Jews. [Col. 0452B]

### Question LXXI

A question is asked how the Apostle can say here that circumcision is profitable, when in what follows he says: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Gal. 5).

Solution. This is said according to the condition of different times. In the time of the law, observing it was beneficial; in the time of grace, observing it according to the letter is not beneficial—indeed, it is harmful.

### Question LXXII

A question is asked concerning what condition is meant when it is said, “What advantage then is there,” etc.

Solution. It is the former condition, in which the Jews were before the incarnation of the Lord.

### Question LXXIII

Again, the question is asked what relevance this has, since those to whom he was writing were not in that condition but in the state of faith.

Answer. It was so that we who have believed from among the Gentiles might not become proud against the Jews. [Col. 0452C]

### Question LXXIV

A question is asked whether the assumed man was a liar. It seems that he was, because he was a man, and every man is a liar. For someone is called a liar not because he lies or sins, but because he is mutable, never remains in the same condition (Job 14), and can fall away through sins. Some presume to assert all this also concerning the assumed man, arguing thus: if the assumed man could have been not assumed by the Word, he could have sinned; but he could have been not assumed; therefore he could have sinned. This seems to follow if the antecedent is granted; and everyone grants that he could have been not assumed.

Solution. It must not be granted that that man could have sinned. For when one says “that man,” the word “that” indicates a personal property, in which it is impossible for him to sin. But in the inference, when it is said, “If that man could have been not assumed, he could have sinned,” that personal property is not understood; rather, human nature is understood without reference to it.

Again, they attempt to prove the same thing in another way. When Christ came to Jerusalem, he could have gone into Galilee; and if he had then gone into Galilee, he would not now have suffered; and if he had not suffered, he would not have fulfilled the Father’s command, at whose command he suffered. But he could then have failed to suffer in Jerusalem, been disobedient, and thus sinned.

Solution. He could indeed have failed to go to Jerusalem in that way. Therefore, it does not follow that he could have failed to fulfill the Father’s command. For if he had not then suffered—which was possible, as he says, “I have power to lay down my life and power to take it up again” (John 10)—if, I say, he had not then suffered, it would not have been the Father’s command that he suffer there then. But these two things cannot coexist: that the Father commanded him to suffer then, and that he did not then suffer. This is the common solution. [Col. 0452C–0453A]

### Question LXXV

A question is asked concerning this hypothetical proposition: “If our iniquity commends the righteousness of God,” etc.—whether it is true, whether the consequent necessarily follows from the antecedent, and how it should be understood.

Solution. “Our iniquity commends God’s righteousness” may be understood in two ways. First, that by its own quality it makes God’s righteousness more commendable. This is false; and according to this understanding the inference would be valid: if this were so, God would be unjust to punish sins. It can also be understood to mean that, in comparison with our injustice, God’s righteousness appears more commendable. This is true; but according to this understanding the inference is not valid, nor does the consequent follow from the antecedent. For falsehood never follows from truth. [Col. 0453B]

### Question LXXVI

A question is asked how the words “Why am I still judged as a sinner?” should be understood: whose voice is this—of someone converted or unconverted? If a converted person speaks, he is not judged as a sinner; if one not yet converted speaks, God is not yet glorified in that person’s lie.

Solution. It is the voice of one who has been converted and has fallen again. [Col. 0453C]

### Question LXXVII

A question is asked whether God wills evil to be done, since he uses our evils for good and for his own glory, just as we misuse his goods to our own disgrace.

Solution. He does not will evil to be done. For it must not be granted that he wills evil either to be done or not to be done. If he willed evil to be done, he would be the author of evil, since for something to be done with his willing is nothing other than for it to be done with him as author. Again, if he willed it not to be done and yet it occurred, something would resist his will.

There are, however, some who say that God wills evil to be done; but according to them “will” is used in several ways, namely for permission, good pleasure, command, and prohibition. He wills evils to occur—that is, he permits them—not because he is their author.

### Question LXXVIII

Is it good for evil to exist?

Solution. “Good” is said in several ways: useful good, good by its own quality, etc. Similarly, “evil” is said in several ways: that which harms; that which is corrupted; a wicked act; and a wicked will, which is sin, the privation of every good. Every disorder is called sin. Thus a lyre-player is said to have erred if he continually strikes the wrong string. Therefore, when it is said, “It is good for evil to exist,” one must carefully consider what is meant by “good” or “evil.” [Col. 0453D]

### Question LXXIX

When he says, “We have charged all men with being under sin,” etc., this does not seem to be a necessary argument for showing that Jews do not excel Gentiles. For both were under sin, even mortal sin; yet it could have happened that the former were under a lesser sin and the latter under a greater one. Thus the former seem more worthy and fit to receive grace than the rest.

Solution. If both were under sin—namely mortal sin, which the Apostle indicates when he says “under sin,” as though oppressed and enslaved—it is evident that they deserved not grace but punishment. Therefore, if grace is bestowed upon them, namely faith and the other gifts, this is not from their merits but from God’s goodness alone. Thus, so far as they themselves are concerned, they do not excel.

Nevertheless, we do not deny that those under greater sin were less fit to receive grace; they were treated more mercifully than others who were under lesser sin. “Where transgression abounded, grace abounded still more” (Rom. 5), although the grace of the latter was not greater than that of the former in itself; nevertheless grace abounded according to the number of persons. In this place it need not be examined whether the Jews were subject to greater sin than the Gentiles. [Col. 0454A–B]

### Question LXXX

The statement, “There is none who understands or seeks God,” does not seem true. For many among that people had understanding of God—namely, that he is one, Creator, and omnipotent. If one is called non-understanding because one did not understand perfectly, then even people of grace, who do not yet understand perfectly except through faith, can be called non-understanding.

Solution. A person may be called one who does not understand because, although he knows God in majesty, he does not know him in humility and piety. Or someone is said not to understand God perfectly because, although he has some knowledge, he does not have it through the experience of charity. Or someone does not understand God perfectly—namely, that he alone is Creator of all things and also the author of all righteousness—which the Jews do not understand. Establishing their own righteousness, they are not subject to God’s righteousness. Indeed, in a sense they make themselves God when they say that they are justified by their own power without God’s grace, asserting themselves to be authors of righteousness—something God can do.

Hence the Apostle says that in the Gospel the righteousness of God, not of man, is revealed (Rom. 3). And elsewhere: “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law” (ibid.). If “the righteousness of man” is ever read, as David often says “my righteousness,” it must be understood as righteousness belonging to the human recipient, which is also God’s as giver. [Col. 0454B–C]

### Question LXXXI

A question is asked concerning the statement, “Whatever the law says, it speaks to those who are in the law,” etc. Even if it speaks to the Jews, does everything therefore concern the Jews because it was said to the Jews?

Solution. It is to be understood thus: it speaks to them in such a way that what it says concerns them. This again seems false, since many things are said in the law concerning the Gentiles. Therefore “whatever it speaks” must be understood without a qualification or distinction by which it is certain whether the speech concerns the Gentiles: thus, it speaks of those Gentiles, I say, who are *ex lege* (“from/by the law”; the sense is uncertain), so that what is said concerns them.

The following objection is made to this position. Were not David and many other righteous people in the law? If so, how does the statement “there is none who understands” concern them?

Solution. “To be in the law” indicates two things: to seek righteousness from the law and to rely wholly upon it, as do those who outwardly observe it from fear. In this sense David and the other righteous people were not in the law. For they did not seek to be justified by the law itself, but by faith in Christ still to come; thus they were people of the Gospel, not of the law.

Those also are said to be in the law to whom the law was given and who perform the works of the law. In this sense David and those like him were in the law, because the law was given to them and they observed it for the sake of those for whom the law was necessary, lest they despise the law through their example.

It should be noted that there are three classes of people: people of natural law, of written law, and of grace. People of natural law are those who have natural law alone, with nothing added. People of written law are those to whom the written law was given, with nothing added. People of grace are those to whom grace itself has been given.

Or otherwise: people of natural law are those who seek to be justified by their own powers; people of written law are those who rely upon the law, believing that the law justifies; people of grace are those who seek righteousness and salvation from no other source than grace alone. [Col. 0454D–0455B]

### Question LXXXII

When it is said, “No flesh is justified by works of the law,” a question is asked about Moses, David, and the other righteous people who lived in the time of the law: were they righteous by works of the law? This seems so, because they did those works from charity.

Solution. Those ancient people were righteous by faith in the One to come alone, and not by works of the law. Note that, according to some, “works of the law” means those instituted with the law and terminated with the law, namely ceremonial works. These were instituted not for justification but for signifying future things. According to others, works of the law are those done through fear alone and not love; it is evident that these do not justify. Hence the law is said to restrain the hand, not the mind. [Col. 0455B–C]

### Question LXXXIII

Why do works of the law performed with charity not justify as works of the Gospel do? Do not fulfilled moral commandments justify? From these points it appears that works of the law justify.

Solution. Not everything that we are bound to do by a commandment of the law is called a work of the law, but that which was instituted with the law and terminated with the law. Or, better: works of the law are those for whose fulfillment the law suffices, works done through fear alone of temporal punishment; these justify no one. [Col. 0455C–D]

### Question LXXXIV

A question is asked what difference there is between works of the law and works of the Gospel. For if works of the Gospel are done through fear of temporal punishment alone, they confer righteousness upon no one, just as works of the law do not.

Solution. Only outward matters belong to works of the law; hence the law forbids the hand. But inward matters also belong to works of the Gospel, such as affections and inward movements, in which righteousness consists. [Col. 0455D]

### Question LXXXV

A question is asked concerning the statement, “Through the law comes knowledge of sin,” etc.: knowledge of what sin was made through the law? For “sin” is used in several ways: sometimes for guilt, sometimes for punishment for sin. Thus God is said to bear our sins, that is, punishment for sin. Sometimes it means a sacrifice for sin; hence Christ “was made sin for us” (2 Cor. 5), that is, a sacrifice for sin. Sometimes it means satisfaction for sin or penance imposed for sin. Every disorder in anything is also called sin. Hence a lyre-player is said to have sinned if he repeatedly misses the same string. Again, “sin” means the deed of sin and the liability for sin; according to some, the latter differs from guilt, while according to others it is the same as guilt.

The question, therefore, is: knowledge of what sin was made through the law?

Solution. Some say that it was knowledge of the sin that is in the will, because before the law only sin in deed was believed to be sin, while concupiscence was not known to be sin. [Col. 0456A–B]

### Question LXXXVI

Again, why does the law not justify, when it manifests sin in this way? For what else does the Gospel do except manifest sin, teaching what must be pursued and what avoided—which the law also does?

Again, some wish to prove that the law leads to perfection from the Lord’s words when he answered the young man concerning a commandment of the law: “Do this, and you shall live” (Luke 10). Again: “You shall love the Lord your God,” etc. (Matt. 19). This is a commandment of the law, but when observed it justifies; therefore the law leads to perfection. Again Bede says: “The law, observed in its own time, conferred not only temporal but also eternal things.”

Solution. To answer all questions of this sort, we say that “law” means a commandment without grace, which never confers salvation; but “Gospel” means a commandment with grace, which justifies and leads to eternal life. [Col. 0456B–C]

### Question LXXXVII

“But now righteousness is apart from the law,” etc. The question is asked how both statements can be true: that God’s righteousness is manifested apart from the law, and that it is testified to by the law and the prophets.

Solution. The Apostle says that the righteousness of God is apart from the law; he does not say that it is manifested apart from the law.

### Question LXXXVIII

Again, when it is said, “The righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ,” the question is asked concerning this virtue of faith: can it be possessed equally by the good and the wicked?

Solution. Modern writers appear to disagree in answering this question. Some say that this virtue of faith is possessed only by the good and in no way by the wicked, for it is faith that works through love. Therefore, they say, where love is absent, faith is absent also.

Others, however, think that it is possessed equally by the good and the wicked. For what else is it to have faith than to believe the things that must be believed? But everything that this good person believes, that wicked person also believes. How then does he not have the same faith, especially when Augustine says that faith can be possessed without charity, and the Apostle says: “If I have all faith, so as to move mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing” (1 Cor. XXXI). How could he say this if faith could not be possessed without charity? [Col. 0456C–D]

### Question LXXXIX

“Justified freely by the grace of Christ.” How can he say “freely by grace”? Would not “freely” or “by grace” suffice? It seems that one of the expressions is superfluous.

Solution. “Freely” means without any merit of our own; “by grace” means through his gratuitous gifts. For he often bestows many things upon us indeed by grace, but not without all merit of our own; nevertheless, this does not occur without his grace. [Col. 0457A]

### Question XC

“Through the redemption which is in Christ Jesus,” etc. A question is asked why God redeemed humankind through his death, when he could have liberated it by a word alone.

Solution. Although another way was possible for God, none was more fitting for our misery, because in the same act he gave us a remedy and furnished examples of humility and love.

The remedy is seen in this: the devil laid hands upon him who was free from sin and in whom he found nothing that was his own. Therefore he deservedly lost those whom he seemed to hold by a certain right—those who believe in him who, through his death, became for all who obey him the cause of salvation. For he suffered not for himself but for us, granting us his merits, so that through them might be done for us what would have been done for him if he had needed it.

He moved us to humility in that, descending from the secret bosom of paternal majesty, he so emptied himself as to take the form of a servant (Phil. 3). He invited us to charity in that, although he is the Lord of glory, such and so great, he died thus for the ungodly and sinners.

Note that if he had redeemed humankind by a word alone, no wrong would have been done to the devil. Or if God had restored the human race through an angel, salvation would not thereby have been attributed to the angel. For God accomplishes many things through angels that should nevertheless be attributed not to angels but to God. But he redeemed us through himself and not through another because no other person’s merits could be so great as to suffice for the redemption of the whole world. [Col. 0457A–C]

### Question XCI

A question is asked whether God could have made a more fitting manner of redemption. If it is said that he could not, God’s power seems to have a limit and not to be infinite; if it is said that he could, how is this manner the most fitting?

Solution. Although in this respect he has a limit, it must not simply be granted that he has a limit. Or, although this manner is most fitting for our misery, it need not be the most fitting absolutely.

[Col. 0457D] ### Question XCII

A question is asked to whom our price was given: to the devil or to God?

Solution. It was given to God, not to the devil. For no wrong was done to the devil, since he was only, as it were, a jailer; nor would he have wished to receive it, so as to destroy humankind. It ought not to have been given to one unwilling, lest an injury be done to him.

### Question XCIII

A question is asked: from whom was humankind redeemed?

Solution. From the devil, from sin, and from torment. Moreover, humankind was reconciled to God; and this is the twofold efficacy of Christ’s blood.

### QUESTION XCIV

It is asked in what respect the devil’s power was diminished by Christ’s death. For just as before he had the power to tempt both good and evil persons, so he does now. Answer: It was diminished not in its essence but in its effectiveness [Col. 0458A], because he cannot prevail as much as before—especially since strength to resist has been given to humanity; and the stronger a person is in resistance, the weaker the enemy is in attack.

### QUESTION XCV

When it is said, “for the manifestation of the righteous,” etc., a question is raised concerning the righteous of old, who were held in hell: whether their sins had been forgiven through faith and repentance; and, if they had been forgiven, why they were held in hell. For without the remission of sins they were not righteous.

Answer: All their sins had been forgiven through faith and love, but they had not obtained the complete effect of remission. Remission has a twofold effect: namely, freedom from punishment and enjoyment of glory. Before Christ’s death they possessed only the first [Col. 0458B], because they did not suffer actual punishment; they had not yet received the second, because they did not see God.

Again, an objection is raised: Were they not righteous, and thus worthy of glory? Why, then, was that of which they were worthy not given to them?

Answer: Their righteousness was not such as would suffice to obtain life without Christ’s death; nor, indeed, were their sins simply forgiven, except under a certain expectation and pledge of the one who was to make satisfaction for them. Hence the Apostle says that Christ died not only for the remission of present sins, but also of earlier transgressions, because he is the lamb slain from the foundation of the world (Heb. IX).

### QUESTION XCVI

Could God condemn them to eternal punishment, when they were righteous, and could not justly punish the righteous? For God cannot do what is unjust [Col. 0458C]. And if he could not punish them, in what respect did he hold them?

Answer: It was necessary that satisfaction be made for original sin; and since they themselves could not make satisfaction, unless another made satisfaction for them, God could justly punish them. Yet one need not concede that he punished righteous persons. For that would be after Christ’s death. They are not to be called righteous simply, but only in comparison with Christ’s death; for they did not possess such actual righteousness as would enable them justly to claim eternal life, any more than we could without Christ’s death. Nevertheless Scripture calls them righteous because they had as much as God required of them, since Christ was to supply what was lacking to them.

### QUESTION XCVII

When it is said, “By what law? Of works?” etc., it is asked why the Mosaic law, the written law, is called the law of works, rather than the Gospel; whereas the law of the Gospel is the law of grace and the law of righteousness. For just as the former has works, so too does the latter.

Answer: The Mosaic law is called the law of works because it merely commands what is to be done, and does not confer the grace through which its commands are fulfilled. Therefore the commandment without grace is called the killing letter. The Gospel, however, does command what must be done, but in addition confers the grace through which what has been commanded may be fulfilled.

Or, for this reason: the written law is called the law of works because people under the law placed the entirety of their righteousness in the works of the law; whereas the law of faith or grace is so called because people of grace place the whole sum and efficacy of their salvation in grace alone [Col. 0459A], knowing that just as no one is saved by the righteousness of works, so no one is justified by works of righteousness. For righteousness does not arise from good works, but good works from righteousness.

### QUESTION XCVIII

“Is he not also the God of the Gentiles?” etc. The Apostle proves that God is the God of the Gentiles because he is their creator. But in that way he seems to be the God of stones.

Answer: He is indeed the creator-God of stones, but he is creator of the Gentiles in another way: he created them in his own image and likeness. Hence he is rightly called the God of the Gentiles, as one truly to be worshipped by them.

### QUESTION XCIX

Whether works preceding faith are wholly useless, or are useful in some respect. They seem to be of no use, because the whole life of unbelievers is sin.

Answer: Good works performed [Col. 0459B] before faith, although they do not avail to merit life, nevertheless avail toward receiving it, as some think; as appears in Cornelius.

### QUESTION C

“Do we then destroy the law through faith? By no means; rather, we establish the law.” It is asked how this can be true when elsewhere he says: “If I rebuild the things which I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor”; and, “Through the law I died to the law” (Gal. II). There he says that he destroyed the law; here he says that he does not destroy it, but establishes it.

Answer: “To destroy the law” is understood in two ways. Thus here the Apostle says that he does not destroy the law: that is, he does not show that the law was useless in its own time, of no value, or not to be fulfilled spiritually. Elsewhere he said that he destroyed it: that is, he preached that, after the fulfilment of truth, it ought to cease in respect of carnal observances [Col. 0459C].

### QUESTION CI

“Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Rom. IV). It is asked why he says “it was reckoned,” as though the righteousness he had through faith were not true righteousness, but something reckoned as righteousness. For if you owed me a horse, I could not fittingly say: “Give me a horse, and I shall reckon it as a horse.” But I could properly say: “Give me a donkey, and I shall reckon it as a horse.”

Answer: Had a human being not sinned, he would have possessed complete righteousness, consisting in complete fulfilment of God’s commandments: so that he would desire nothing at all contrary to reason, and would love God with his whole heart. But after sin, and because of sin, a human being could not possess this perfect righteousness [Col. 0459D], to which eternal blessedness is deservedly due. Yet through his grace God gives a person faith, and likewise through that same grace reckons it in place of that perfection—as though the person possessed perfection of righteousness.

### QUESTION CII

“But to the one who works, wages are not reckoned,” etc. It is asked what works are meant here: inward or outward works. Outward works include clothing the poor and other such things, which many do not perform, although they have time to work—for example, contemplative men. Thus, if the discourse here concerns works of this sort, they appear unworthy of salvation. Inward works include believing, loving, and praying, which are common to all believers, because without them there is no salvation. If these are meant here, how is faith without works reckoned as righteousness to one [Col. 0460A] who has no opportunity to work?

Answer: He is speaking of outward works, which are required of those who have the means of performing them; and, for those who lack the means to perform them, the will is reckoned as the deed.

### QUESTION CIII

“According to the purpose of the grace of God,” etc. Here there is customarily a question about grace and merit. For it seems that everything is so entirely from grace that merit contributes nothing; or, if anything is from merit, that it is not all from grace. Scripture testifies that everything is from grace. Hence the Apostle: “What do you have that you did not receive?” (I Cor. IV). “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Cor. XV). And: “Grace for grace” (John I).

What, then, is to be said? To say that merit is nothing is the error of the Manicheans, just as to assert that everything is from free choice is the error of the Pelagians.

Answer: [Col. 0460B] When it is said that everything is from grace, merit is not excluded, since merit itself is from grace. Therefore one must see what God’s grace works in us without us, and what it works in us not without us. Preventing grace, also called operating grace, heals free choice by freeing it from the yoke of sin; and this it does in us without us. Then the healed will is not idle and does not receive God’s grace in vain. It works not by itself but with grace; indeed, God’s grace cooperates with free choice, and is therefore called cooperating grace. The same work or merit is said to arise from grace and from the will, for they do not work separately but together.

Therefore, although everything is from grace, it does not follow that nothing is from merit or free choice. It is as if someone found a little child lying in mud [Col. 0460C] and unable to rise, raised him up, and then held his hand so that he might walk. The walking itself would arise from both; but the raising of him would arise only from the finder and not from the child. So too, our willing what is good arises only from preventing grace; whereas our doing what is good arises from subsequent grace—not, I say, only from it, but also from free choice healed and liberated through grace.

### QUESTION CIV

“Blessed are those whose iniquities have been forgiven.” A question is raised concerning what original sin is, a matter on which doctors discourse somewhat obscurely. Some say that original sin is liability to eternal punishment—that is, the debt and bondage by which we are bound over to punishment. But on this account original sin would not be guilt, but punishment. Yet authorities testify that it is guilt, which must be granted.

Others say that original sin is the tinder of sin (*fomes peccati*): concupiscence or concupiscibility; the law of the members, the law of the flesh, the sickness of nature, the tyrant dwelling in our members; an innate defect which makes an infant capable of desiring, and an adult desirous. By these and other names original sin is called [Col. 0460D].

### QUESTION CV

It is commonly asked why it is called original.

Answer: Because it is drawn from the defective condition of our origin.

### QUESTION CVI

Again, it is asked why it is imputed to descendants.

Answer: Because the intercourse of parents does not occur without lust [Col. 0461A], nor the conception of children without sin.

### QUESTION CVII

How is it removed in baptism?

Answer: It is wholly mitigated in respect of liability, and weakened in respect of act or inclination. Others say that original sin is the deprivation of a certain original righteousness which a human being would have had if he had not sinned. Therefore, because he is deprived of righteousness, he is also deprived of glory; and those punished for original sin alone will suffer no other punishment except that they will always lack the vision of God.

Again, since the soul is not derived by propagation, but only the flesh, it is asked how this sin is transmitted through flesh. For flesh without soul cannot have guilt, since guilt neither is nor can be except in a rational creature; for that which is not capable of righteousness is not capable of sin either [Col. 0461B].

### QUESTION CVIII

How then does that which cannot exist in flesh alone without soul pass through the flesh from parents in the propagation of offspring?

Answer: Sin is said to pass because its cause passes: namely, a certain defilement and impurity which the soul finds in the flesh when it is infused into it, and by which it is defiled. Thus, although the soul alone lusts, the soul is nevertheless not said to lust, because it lusts from the flesh.

### QUESTION CIX

Whether the soul is ever such as it was created by God to be. For if it was created clean by God, and from the time it was joined and united to flesh it was unclean, it follows that it is never such as it was created by God.

Answer: It may be granted that it was never wholly such [Col. 0461C] as it was created by God. It is as if I gave you a clean apple and you received it with unclean hands: it would be true to say that you never possessed such an apple as I gave you.

### QUESTION CX

It is commonly asked why the liability of original sin is imputed to souls created clean by God. Doctors say that this question is insoluble. Yet it may be said that it is not unjust that glory should not be given to a soul which lacks righteousness. For to be subject to the liability of original sin is to be deprived of original righteousness. What wonder, then, if such a fault is punished by such a punishment?

### QUESTION CXI

“And he received the sign of circumcision and the seal of righteousness,” etc. Circumcision has been discussed above [Col. 0461D]. But here it may be asked whether Abraham received any benefit from circumcision.

Answer: Doctors say that by it he was only shown to be righteous, not made righteous. Did it therefore have greater efficacy in his descendants than in Abraham himself? This seems so, since it was given to them as a remedy at least for original sin, whereas to Abraham himself it was given only as a manifestation of righteousness.

### QUESTION CXII

Again, it is asked whether remission of original sin was given through circumcision to those infants who were bound by no other sin, and how they were not thereby justified, and thus by the law.

The answer to this question is clear from what has already been said.

### QUESTION CXIII

A question is raised concerning infants who died before the eighth day [Col. 0462A], on which circumcision was performed: were they damned or saved?

Answer: The same judgment applies to those not circumcised as to those not baptized: namely, that they are damned by the liability of original sin alone. But if one asks concerning infants who died immediately upon being born, before circumcision, perhaps aid was given them by the faith of their parents.

### QUESTION CXIV

“For the promise was not through the law,” etc. It is asked how the Apostle can say that the promise was made to Christ not through the law but through the righteousness of faith. Was not a promise made in and through the law—namely, to Christ himself in David? Again, what does it mean for a promise to be made to Christ through the righteousness of faith?

Answer: The Apostle does not say that the promise was not made [Col. 0462B] through the law, but through the righteousness of faith. Rather, he says that the promise that he should be heir of the world was made not through the law, but through the righteousness of faith.

### QUESTION CXV

Again, it is asked how the promise was made to Abraham through righteousness. Was it by the merit of his faith? But if the promise was made through the merit of Abraham’s faith, then by the same merit came the fulfilment of that promise. How, then, is it by grace alone?

Answer: The text should not be construed thus: “The promise was made through the righteousness of faith.” Rather, thus: The promise was made to Abraham that he might be heir of the world through the righteousness of faith—through which he himself became the father of believers, and believers become Abraham’s children, that is, become righteous and heirs. The commentator says otherwise here than we do.

### QUESTION CXVI

Because it is said, “The law works the wrath of God” [Col. 0462C], it is asked how this should be understood. Is not the law good and wrath evil? How can what is good produce what is evil? Is not that whose effect is evil itself evil as well? How, then, can such a cause have such an effect?

Answer: The law does not work wrath immediately, by its own quality, and as an efficient cause; rather, it does so as if by occasion. For if the law had not been given, the wrath would not have been so great; it was increased by transgression of the law. For many things are said to effect something not because they produce it, but because it would not occur without them. Thus Christ is said to have been set not only for resurrection, as a cause, but also for ruin, by occasion (Luke II). And the Apostle is called not only an aroma of life, but also [Col. 0462D] an aroma of death (II Cor. II). By the same reasoning one must be alert in regard to similar cases.

### QUESTION CXVII

How does the Apostle prove that the law works wrath by saying, “Where there is no law, neither is there transgression”? For this too does not seem true. Where there is no law, can there not be transgression of the natural law or of the Gospel? How then is it true that where there is no law, there is no transgression? But if it is explained thus—where there is no law, there is no transgression of the law—then by the same argument it is proved that where there is no Gospel, there is no transgression of the Gospel.

Answer: By “law” the Apostle often means a commandment without grace; by “Gospel” he always means a commandment with grace. Hence it is clearly true that where there is no law—that is, no commandment without grace—there is no transgression [Col. 0463A]. Likewise, where there is a commandment with grace, there is no transgression, but fulfilment of the commandment.

### QUESTION CXVIII

Again, when it is said, “Who believed in hope against hope,” it is asked about Abraham’s faith, which the Apostle here praises and which is reckoned to him as righteousness: what it was, or what it concerned. For if the words of the Apostle and of Genesis are considered closely, it seems that the faith by which he believed God’s promise of offspring to him was reckoned to him as righteousness. But if this is so, then a faith other than faith in Christ is justifying faith. If, however, it is said that he then had faith in Christ, it is asked whether two faiths justify, or why righteousness is said to arise rather from that faith than from this one.

Answer: The Apostle commends Abraham’s faith by which he believed all things that were to be believed; and by that faith, among other things [Col. 0463B], he believed God to be truthful in the promise of offspring.

### QUESTION CXIX

How is Isaac’s begetting said to be against nature? What is nature? Is it not a certain power implanted by the Creator in creatures, through which like beings are begotten and propagated from like beings? Did not nature operate there? Was there not a certain proportioning in the acts of the parents and in the union of the flesh? How, then, was it against nature?

Answer: When the Author of nature operates in nature beyond nature’s customary course—that is, not according to lower causes but according to higher ones—then something is said to occur against nature. More properly, however, it would be said to occur above nature.

### QUESTION CXX

“Being most fully assured that whatever God has promised [Col. 0463C], he is also able to perform.” The commentator says that Abraham knew that God was omnipotent by the sight of divine power; and the Apostle says, “being most fully assured,” etc. This seems harmful to faith, because faith has no merit when human reason supplies empirical proof. Again, if he knew that God was God, what great thing was it if he believed him omnipotent? Or if he did not know him to be God, how did he believe him?

Answer: That vision of divine power which Abraham possessed did not arise from human reasoning but from the steadfastness of faith. Through it he was so certain as if he knew most fully, or saw.

### QUESTION CXXI

As to the question what was great about believing God omnipotent, since not only the good but also the wicked believe this [Col. 0463D], we answer: to believe it then was a great thing, when almost the whole world was wandering in the worship of demons and faith in one God had not yet been preached, or plainly set forth in Scripture, as it has now.

### QUESTION CXXII

“And not only was it written,” etc. It is asked how the Apostle can say that it was written for Abraham’s sake that faith was reckoned as righteousness. Does he obtain any benefit from its being praised in the Scriptures or imitated by us?

Answer: Perhaps the Apostle does not say that this benefits him. Rather, it should be understood thus: “And not only,” etc.—that is, this was written not only in order to show by what Abraham himself was righteous [Col. 0464A], but also to show us the one thing in which we too can be justified: namely, in the grace of faith, and nowhere else.

### QUESTION CXXIII

“He was delivered up for our offences,” etc. Authority says this. It is asked: By whom was he delivered up? It is certain that he was delivered by God the Father, by Judas and the Jews, and by Pilate. But it is asked whether what was done by God and by the Jews was good or evil. If it is said to be good, then the Jews did good. But if it is said to be evil, then God did evil. Again, did not the Jews do only evil and God only good? How, then, did God and the Jews do the same thing?

Answer: The work or deed of the Jews is taken equivocally for their action and for Christ’s passion. The action of the Jews was only evil; Christ’s passion [Col. 0464B], which followed from their action, was good. Therefore doctors sometimes unite God and the Jews in one and the same deed or work, because of Christ’s passion, which occurred both through the action of the Jews and through God; at other times they distinguish them because of the diversity of their actions. If, then, it is asked whether the work of the Jews was good, distinguish in this way: their action was evil; the passion which they inflicted was good.

### QUESTION CXXIV

Again, it is asked why the Apostle distinguishes thus, saying that Christ was delivered for our offences and rose again for our justification, when both his passion and resurrection free from sins and justify.

Answer: Although both are causes, they are not both figures.

### QUESTION CXXV

“And not only so, but we glory [Col. 0464C] in tribulations” (Rom. V), etc. How does the Apostle glory in tribulations, which are bitter and not to be sought for their own sake?

Answer: One should glory in them not on account of the tribulations themselves, but on account of their effect. But it is objected that by the same reasoning one ought to glory in sins, not for their own sake but for the good which they often produce, such as humility. Hence the Prophet says: “Before I was humbled, I went astray” (Ps. CXVIII).

Answer: Tribulations, by their own character, cooperate with inward grace toward attaining patience; sins do not. Rather, by his mercy God makes some good result from our evils.

### QUESTION CXXVI

When the Apostle says, “Hope does not disappoint,” it is asked what hope is, and whether it is possessed without charity.

Answer: Hope is the certain expectation [Col. 0464D] of future goods. It differs from faith in this: faith concerns past, present, and future things, both good and evil; hope concerns only future and good things. It seems, however, that hope is not possessed without charity. For to hope for future goods without good works and a good life—which are not possible without charity—is not hope but rather presumption, as Augustine says. Again, Augustine seems to assert that hope precedes charity.

Answer: One hope is the hope of pardon; another is the hope of glory. The first is possessed even by the wicked; the second perhaps only by the good.

### QUESTION CXXVII

“The charity of God has been poured forth,” etc. It is asked whether the charity by which God loves us is the same as that by which we love God.

Answer: Some say [Col. 0465A] that it is the same. Augustine, explaining this passage, opposes them and says that here the subject is the charity by which we love God; whereas there, “God is charity” (I John IV), the subject is the charity by which God loves us. He would not say this if it were the same charity.

Again, elsewhere he says: “I call charity the movement of the mind toward loving God for his own sake, and one’s neighbour for God’s sake.” God is not a movement; therefore charity exists which is not God. Again, charity can increase and decrease, whereas God cannot; therefore charity exists which is not God.

It must therefore be held firmly that the name “charity” is used equivocally of God, when it is said “God is charity,” and of a certain virtue, when it is said “charity is a certain virtue” or “the charity of God has been poured forth in our hearts.” The Apostle Paul almost everywhere uses this name to signify the virtue, which is not God but is from God. John uses the same name to signify God himself.

But Augustine says that fraternal charity, by which we love one another, is God. We grant this, saying that God, who is charity, also makes us love one another, but through charity as a means—just as he makes us believe through faith as a means. For the one from whom faith comes is the same one from whom charity comes, as Augustine says.

But an objection is raised: God, who is charity, is in us, and charity which is a virtue is also in us; therefore there are two charities in us, or we love God through two charities.

Answer: There are not therefore two. As the sun illumines us and the sunbeam illumines us, it does not follow that two things illumine us, because this would be separately and distinctly so. Rather, the sun illumines through its ray, and God illumines or enlightens us through charity as a virtue [Col. 0465C].

### QUESTION CXXVIII

Again, it is asked whether charity, once possessed, can be lost. Some say that it cannot, because it is written: “Charity never fails” (I Cor. XIII).

Answer: This is said of perfect charity; or it is said that charity never fails because it is possessed both in the present and in the future.

### QUESTION CXXIX

Charity is that fountain of which it is said: “Let your fountain be your own, and let no stranger share it with you.” It is asked: who are the strangers, if not the reprobate, who will hear, “Depart, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. XXV), etc.? But many belonging to their number love for a time, and thus strangers share this fountain [Col. 0465D].

Answer: They are called strangers according to foreknowledge—though the text is not now speaking of them—but according to their present unrighteousness: namely, all who do not now love, whether elect or not. Such persons, as such, do not share the fountain of love.

### QUESTION CXXX

How is it true that “Christ died for the ungodly”? Did Christ not die only for those to whom his death benefits? But it benefits only the godly; therefore he died only for the godly. It seems, then, that he did not die for the ungodly.

Answer: He died for the ungodly—that is, out of love for those who were formerly ungodly and became godly through faith. Thus it is true both that Christ’s death was for the ungodly and that it benefits only the godly.

### QUESTION CXXXI

“We were reconciled to God through the death of his Son” [Col. 0466A]. It is asked how this statement is to be understood. Before his death, was God angry with us as sinners, according to: “You hate all who work iniquity” (Ps. V), and was he appeased toward us through the death of his Son, beginning only then to love us? But if so, how did he choose us before the foundation of the world? Did he choose without loving? Or how did he give up his Son for us without being appeased?

Answer: God’s wrath is not an emotion of mind, but just vengeance. When such wrath is ended—which occurred through Christ’s death—God is said to be appeased toward us and we to be reconciled to him. Yet he did not love because he reconciled; rather, because he loved, he reconciled.

The justice by which Christ conquered has been discussed above [Col. 0466B], as has the manner of redemption. There is no need to repeat matters already dealt with. Let only Augustine’s words be briefly set down, in which he expresses it clearly. He says:

> This is the justice by which Christ conquered the devil. The devil, a lover of power and deserter of justice, killed Christ, in whom he found nothing deserving death. Therefore it is just that those whom he held should be set free, believing in him who was killed without any evil merit whatsoever. Christ did not choose to use power against the lover of power; rather, against the deserter of justice he chose to use justice, in order to teach us how we must fight against the same enemy: namely, not by power but rather by justice; and so we shall be conquerors.

### QUESTION CXXXII

“Therefore, just as through one …” It is asked why he says rather that sin entered the world through one man [Col. 0466C] than through one woman, when the beginning of sin was rather in the woman than in the man.

Answer: He followed customary usage, as Augustine says, because posterity is customarily named from the man, not from the woman. Or for this reason: man and woman are one flesh; therefore whatever was done by him or by her is said to pertain to the first human being. Or otherwise: if the man had not sinned, perhaps God would have provided him with another companion, from whom he would have begotten innocent offspring like himself; or God would have forgiven the wife’s sins on account of his merit. But because he sinned, sin is not improperly said to have entered the world through him.

### QUESTION CXXXIII

Again, it is asked why sin is said to have entered through a human being rather than through the devil [Col. 0466D], since it was first in the devil and entered even into the first human being through him. Thus it is written: “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. II).

Answer: Sin entered through the devil in one way and through a human being in another. Through the devil, it entered by imitation alone, not propagation. Through a human being, it entered not only by imitation but also by propagation.

One should know that the Pelagians said that original sin entered through Adam by imitation alone and not by propagation. If this were true, he would have called not a human being but the devil the author of sin. Hence they also said that original sin is not remitted to infants in baptism, because, according to them, none is contracted by those being born. But the Catholic faith does not hold this; it proclaims, and Scripture testifies, that just as [Col. 0467A] Christ, beyond providing an example for imitation, works illumination and justification inwardly and secretly, by which grace alone he incorporates into his body regenerated infants who cannot imitate him, so Adam, beyond providing an example for imitation, corrupted by the contagion of his concupiscence all who would be born from him through concupiscence.

### QUESTION CXXXIV

Julian asks thus: “The one who creates does not sin; the one who begets does not sin; the one who is begotten does not sin. Through what crevices, then, amid so many safeguards of innocence, do you imagine original sin has entered?”

Augustine answers him thus: “The Apostle says: ‘Through one man sin entered into this world’ (Rom. V). What could be sought more openly? What more insistently? What more plainly? Why seek a crevice [Col. 0467B] where one has a most open door?”

### QUESTION CXXXV

Again, it is asked whether original sin arises from will or from nature. If from will, the will is evil; if from nature, nature is evil.

Augustine answers: “Every evil work proceeded from an evil will as from a root. But no evil preceded the evil will itself; it first arose in an angel, afterward in a human being, each of whom was a good work of God. Thus evil arose in what was good; it had not an efficient cause, but a deficient cause.”

### QUESTION CXXXVI

Again, it is asked whether original sin arises from will.

Answer: It does indeed arise from the will of the first parents, and thus it may itself be called voluntary.

### QUESTION CXXXVII

“In whom all sinned,” etc. We did not yet exist; how, then, could we who did not yet exist sin?

Answer: We all sinned in him—that is, in him was done that by which we would all sin. Or thus: from him we derived the cause of sin. Or thus: we are all guilty of that sin which he committed [Col. 0467C].

### QUESTION CXXXVIII

It is also asked how all of us were one human being in Adam.

Answer: That is, we descend by propagation from him, who was one human being.

### QUESTION CXXXIX

Again, it is asked how so many and so great persons could descend from that small mass which was in Adam, or how so small a particle could be divided into so many parts that the body of each person is materially composed from it. This question is customarily asked concerning the seven loaves by which the Lord satisfied so many thousands without any addition of material (Matt. XV).

Answer: This occurred by the law of propagation. For the particle which was in Adam’s loins, once separated in the generation of his son, increased and multiplied in itself into the complete stature of a human being. From it, in the second generation, another small particle was again separated, which in itself again increased and multiplied. From this, once again multiplied, another was separated; and so thereafter, by the law of propagation, it grew into such a multitude without extrinsic addition or the transformation of foods into it. It is evident [Col. 0468A] that God can make any quantity of weight from one atom.

### QUESTION CXL

If, then, one atom were thus multiplied in itself into something great, containing infinitely many atoms, it is asked whether that atom would be all these atoms, or one among the number of the others, or whether those atoms are that one atom.

Answer: It need not be granted that it is all these atoms, but that it has been multiplied and increased into them; nor that all these are that one atom, but that they are from it, or were in it—as that grain grew into a tree. The tree is not the grain, but comes from it, or was materially in it. Such modes of speech must be noted carefully.

It should be observed that there are several kinds of change. Sometimes one essence is changed into another essence without a change of accidents, as in the sacrament of the altar [Col. 0468B]. Sometimes properties change without a change of essence, as when water was made wine. Sometimes change occurs only in quantity, into something greater, as in the seven loaves. But how Moses’ rod was changed into a serpent—whether only in properties, both substantial and accidental, or in essence—is not certain to me.

### QUESTION CXLI

It is written: “God did not make death.” Again: “Death and life are from God” (Wis. I). This appears contradictory, for nothing temporal is from God which he did not make. How, then, did he make death and not make it?

Answer: God did not make death, that is, the cause of death—namely, sin. But according to some, God made that punishment which is called death; and it too is numbered among good works [Col. 0468C], because it is just, and everything just is from God.

### QUESTION CXLII

“But not as the trespass, so also is the gift.” It is asked how the Apostle says that Christ’s gift abounds to more persons than Adam’s trespass, since more are not saved through Christ’s grace than are damned by Adam’s trespass.

Answer: This superabundance of grace is not to be considered in the number of persons. Rather, for those whom Christ’s gift benefits, it confers more good than Adam’s trespass inflicts evil on those whom it harms. For from Adam there comes not every condemnation, but only that condemnation suffered by those subject to original sin alone; besides this, those who have added their own transgressions are punished. But Christ’s grace not only frees from original sin, but also from sins added to it, advancing a person into justification and finally into eternal life.

### QUESTION CXLIII

Are actual sins derived from Adam’s sin? Some think so, because from the tinder of sin we are inclined toward sinning.

Answer: Such inclination is not an efficient cause, although it is a cause without which the effect would not occur, as some hold. But it is not even required, since it was present neither in the devil nor in the first human being before the fall, and yet sin existed in them without it. For it is not the cause of sin; rather, sin was its cause.

### QUESTION CXLIV

It is asked whether Adam’s other actual sins are imputed to his descendants.

Answer: The Apostle says that “in one trespass,” not “in trespasses,” many were made sinners. By this he indicates that not several sins, but one alone, is imputed.

[Col. 0469A] **QUESTION 145.** It is asked whether Eve’s sin too is imputed to us. **Answer.** Note the Apostle’s words, when he says, “in the trespass of one”; he does not say “of two.” Or, if it is imputed for the reasons stated above, he says that “through one man sin entered into the world,” or “in the trespass of one.”

**QUESTION 146.** It is asked whether the actual sins of immediate parents are imputed to their descendants. This seems so, because the Lord says: “I am the Lord thy God, a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation” (Exod. 20), etc. **Answer.** The sins even of immediate parents are not imputed to their children, unless the children themselves make their parents’ sins their own by imitation; nor are they then punished because of their parents, but because they themselves have sinned. According to another Scripture: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father” (Ezek. 18), etc. Teachers sufficiently explain the apparent contradiction between these two authorities.

**QUESTION 147.** But if it is asked why the sin of the first parents, and not that of immediate parents, is imputed: **Answer.** Because that sin stripped us; the other sins of others, finding us as it were naked and stripped, could not take anything from us. For original sin, as has already been said, deprives us only of a certain original righteousness.

**QUESTION 148.** Before sin, man could sin of himself and through himself; but he could not advance of himself and through himself without the help of grace. Therefore he was more inclined toward evil than toward good. But as yet he was [Col. 0469C] only such as God had made him. Therefore God made him more inclined toward evil than toward good. **Answer.** Before the fall man was not inclined to sin; nor did God make man such that he should be inclined to sinning, but such inclination afterward entered in through sin. Nor did he possess the power of sinning from God, but from his own nothingness; not from the good which he had received, but from its limit—not because he had received only so much, but because he had not received more, as has already been said above concerning this same matter.

**QUESTION 149.** “As through the disobedience of one,” etc. It is asked whether man could, by the good which he possessed before the fall, without the addition of other graces, obey and fulfil the command given to him. If it is said that he could, then from what he then had he could [Col. 0469D] advance—which almost everyone denies. Again, if it is granted that he could not obey without the help of grace, then what was his fault, if he did not do what he could not do without grace, and grace was not bestowed, nor was it his fault why it was not bestowed? **Answer.** He did not sin because he did not do what he could not do; but because he did not do it when he could.

**QUESTION 150.** Again, it is asked whether Christ, by obeying God the Father, merited anything. Some wish to prove that he merited nothing, because he did so neither according to his humanity nor according to his divinity. God, they say, cannot receive anything from anyone, nor acquire through anything that he does something else not previously due [Col. 0470A] to him; therefore he cannot merit anything. Likewise, insofar as he is man, he is good and loves; but he cannot fail to be good or to love. Therefore he is good or loves necessarily: how, then, can he merit? **Answer.** “To merit” has a twofold meaning. For someone is said to merit when, by a good work, he is made worthy of something of which he was not previously worthy. According to this meaning, it seems to us that Christ merited nothing either according to his divinity or according to his humanity, even in his death itself. But someone is also said to merit when he does some good that is worthy of reward. In this sense God too is said to merit when he bestows benefits upon us, for which we are bound to praise him eternally; and Christ, according to [Col. 0470B] his humanity, merited for us entrance into eternal life in his Passion. Indeed, he previously merited many things for us; but the Passion alone was not only precious, but the price of the world.

**QUESTION 151.** “The law entered in, that [sin] might abound,” etc. It is asked whether the law is a cause of evil, which it seems to be, because it is a cause of the abundance of transgression. **Answer.** “That” is sometimes causative, as, “I go to the market that I may buy a cloak”; sometimes operative, as, “He placed man in paradise that he might tend it,” etc.; sometimes consequential, as, “He went outside in order to die”; and sometimes it indicates occasion, as, “The law entered in, that sin might abound.” For the Jews received from the law a more abundant occasion of sin. The law was good, not the cause of evil; rather, their vice was the cause [Col. 0470C] of this evil—just as if I take from another’s learning an occasion to envy: it is not the cause of my grief, but my vice is.

**QUESTION 152.** “Where transgression abounded, grace also superabounded.” Did transgression not abound among the Jews because they transgressed the law? Yet grace did not also superabound, because they were blinded. How, then, is it true: “Where transgression abounded, grace also superabounded”? **Answer.** He does not say, “Wherever transgression abounded, grace also superabounded,” but simply, “where.” This must be understood with respect to those who believed: before they believed, transgression abounded in them, because besides their other sins they had the transgression of the law; but grace remitted everything and moreover bestowed faith and charity. This is not said [Col. 0470D] with respect to those who died in their sins, in whom transgression abounded and grace did not.

**QUESTION 153.** “What then shall we say? Shall we remain in sin, that grace may abound?” (Rom. 6). Concerning this it is asked what it means to remain in sin. **Answer.** Not to repent of sin, or, through a certain torpor of mind, to await grace while persevering in sin.

**QUESTION 154.** “All of you who have been baptized into Christ,” etc. It is asked which sins are remitted in baptism. **Answer.** Augustine says: not only past or present sins, but also future ones.

**QUESTION 155.** But it is asked how future [Col. 0471A] sins, which do not yet exist, concerning which no one repents, and for which one is not yet liable—for no one is yet guilty on their account—are, I say, remitted. **Answer.** Future sins are said to be remitted in baptism because they are avoided through the grace given there; or because afterward the recipient of this sacrament obtains pardon more easily.

**QUESTION 156.** Are sins remitted to one who approaches deceitfully? **Answer.** Augustine says that “yesterday’s day is forgiven,” and whatever fraternal hatred there was at the very hour of baptism; but they immediately return, because he does not repent.

**QUESTION 157.** It is asked how what Augustine says can be true. Is not one who does not repent a member of the devil? How, then, is he a member [Col. 0471B] of Christ? And if this is so, how have his sins been forgiven? He does not have faith; he does not have the Spirit of Christ. Therefore he is not a member of Christ, nor have his sins been forgiven. **Answer.** Some say that Augustine’s foregoing words should be understood thus: “Yesterday’s day is forgiven,” etc.; that is, baptism has such efficacy even in one who approaches with an uncontrite heart that, if the pretence did not remain in him, he would obtain pardon for all offences; and afterward he can obtain it if he chooses to repent of his pretence.

**QUESTION 158.** “Our old man was crucified,” etc. It is asked whether the old man and the outward man are the same, and likewise the new man and the inward man. **Answer.** They are not the same. For the outward man is called that which we have in common with animals; the inward man, that which [Col. 0471C] we possess in common with angels. But the old man pertains to both, for not only the outward man but also the inward man is old through fault. It is of this old man that the present chapter treats.

**QUESTION 159.** It is therefore asked what the old man is. Some say that the tinder of sin (*fomes peccati*) is so called; but it is truer that the tinder itself is called one part of oldness. It seems to us, however, that oldness is understood under two aspects: namely, fault and punishment. Punishment is either eternal or temporal; fault, however, is either original or actual. Again, original fault consists in the tinder itself, its act, and the liability of each. Actual fault, in turn, is either venial or mortal. Venial fault consists in three things: namely, [Col. 0471D] consent, act, and the liability of each. Mortal fault is similarly understood in the same three modes. Behold the number eleven of transgression, in which the old man is reckoned: one pair belongs to punishment; one triad to original fault, another to venial fault, and the third to mortal fault. Thus the three triads of faults together with the pair of punishments make eleven. It must therefore be seen in what respect the old man has been crucified. With respect to eternal punishment, he has been wholly destroyed in those who belong to Christ; with respect to temporal punishment, he has been weakened and mitigated. Likewise, with respect to mortal fault, he has been completely destroyed; with respect to venial fault, mitigated, though not yet wholly removed; further, with respect to the liability [Col. 0472A] of original sin, he is not imputed at all; but with respect to the act and tinder of original sin, he has been so crucified that he does not reign.

**QUESTION 160.** It is asked whether the tinder of sin in Abraham was crucified through Christ’s death. Some say that through faith in the then-future death of Christ it was weakened in him also.

**QUESTION 161.** Again, it is asked whether in the Apostle himself it was so weakened and crucified that he never consented to its movements. For how did he not consent to those movements when he committed venial sins? Again, were not the venial sins that he committed voluntary, and thus did he not will them? How then did the tinder of sin fail to draw the Apostle into consent to sin? **Answer.** Although the Apostle committed them voluntarily, he nevertheless did not will the sin. [Col. 0472B] For a sin is not called voluntary because someone willed it, but because it proceeded from some act of will. Nor did he consent to the tinder. For to consent is deliberately and knowingly to do what the movements suggested; and thus to consent seems also to be mortal.

**QUESTION 162.** “That you may obey its desires.” It is asked what difference there is between obeying desires and presenting one’s members to sin. **Answer.** To obey desires is mentally to consent to carnal pleasures. To present one’s members to sin, that they may be weapons of iniquity, is to carry out that iniquity itself in deed.

**QUESTION 163.** Hence it is asked why, after prohibiting the first, he prohibits the second. For, by forbidding obedience [Col. 0472C] to desires, he also forbids presenting the members to sin: whoever does not consent does not act. **Answer.** After forbidding consent, he also forbids the act, so that, if it should at some time happen that one consents in mind, such consent may nevertheless not proceed to action but may rather be cut off. Some, however, understand “obeying desires” as action and “presenting members to sin” as consent; and so, fittingly, after the prohibition of action follows the prohibition of consent.

**QUESTION 164.** “Sin shall not have dominion over you, because you are not under law but under grace.” Does not sin rule over many who are under grace? How then is it true: “Sin shall not have dominion,” etc.? **Answer.** To you who are obedient to grace, [Col. 0472D] power has now been given by which you can resist sin, so that it does not reign. Hence it is clear that if it ever regains strength so as to rule, this happens through our fault.

**QUESTION 165.** “I speak in human terms because of your weakness.” It is asked what the Apostle calls human: namely, something light and easy to do, which belongs to mature, not perfect, righteousness. **Answer.** He himself shows this by adding: “Just as you presented your members to serve uncleanness and iniquity unto iniquity, so now present your members to serve righteousness unto sanctification.” This is briefly and plainly to say: Serve righteousness with the same love with which you formerly, without compulsion and from pleasure alone, served uncleanness. This is called human because more is owed to righteousness than [Col. 0473A] to sin. For no one ever loved sin so much that he did not fear dying for it. But because we are inclined toward evil—which occurs without labor or any difficulty, and further with great sweetness and immoderate pleasure—while we are slow and sluggish toward good, which is accomplished only with great labor and immense difficulty, and often with little or no pleasure, because the way of virtues is steep and hard, narrow and constricted.

**QUESTION 166.** But it is asked how the Apostle calls it human to serve righteousness with as great a love and delight as we formerly served iniquity, since this seems to be perfect and complete. **Answer.** It is indeed true that when we see someone serve righteousness out of love, we call him perfect—especially in this time [Col. 0473B] when “the holy one has failed.” Yet with regard to truth itself, he is imperfect unless he despises for righteousness not merely other things but even death itself. Therefore it belongs to mature [or: adulterous] righteousness, and not to perfect righteousness, to perform the command out of love with a resolve to die for Christ, even though one does not yet possess such charity or constancy as would enable one to endure death itself. This degree is sufficient and required for salvation, because without it no one is worthy of glory. But it belongs to perfect and consummated righteousness to possess a virtue sufficient to endure death for truth and for love of righteousness. Peter seemed to possess the first degree when he said: “Even if I must die with thee, I will not deny thee” (Matt. 26). He had not yet obtained the second [Col. 0473C] degree, which he attained through the coming of the Holy Spirit.

**QUESTION 167.** “While her husband lives, the woman is bound by the law of her husband” (Rom. 7), etc. It is asked concerning David and the other righteous whether, while the law was living—that is, remaining in force—they were bound to observe the law; and whether they should be called adulterers because they were with another, that is, with Christ, in whom they believed and from whom they sought justification. **Answer.** The law was not indeed laid down for the righteous, since it is like a pedagogue for little children. Yet David and the other righteous were bound to observe the law for the sake of those to whom the law was necessary, lest they transgress it following their example. Nor should they be called adulterers because they were with Christ through faith and love; but [Col. 0473D] if, after despising the legal sacraments, they had presumed to introduce the sacraments of the New Testament already, then they would seem to be adulterers.

**QUESTION 168.** “For when we were in the flesh, the passions of sins,” etc. It is asked what he calls passions: whether the first movements or something else. **Answer.** It may be said that they are the inborn desires that are the cause of sin, and, in those who are not in Christ, also mortal sin. Or they may be the first movements, which are not imputed to the reborn; he calls them passions because they injure nature and deprive it of some good.

**QUESTION 169.** “What shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means!” It is asked whether the law itself causes sin or teaches it and thus is evil. **Answer.** It is not [Col. 0474A] evil but good; nor is it the cause of sin, although it may seem to be an occasion.

**QUESTION 170.** “For I did not know desire,” etc. It is asked of what desire the Apostle speaks here. Teachers say: of that which is forbidden in the Decalogue. Again it is asked what that is. For the term “desire” sometimes signifies the vice of desire, namely the tinder of sin; sometimes the first movement, which is called *propassio*; sometimes the second movement, called passion or pleasure; sometimes consent; sometimes outward effort. Which, then, does the law forbid when it says, “You shall not desire” (ibid.)? **Answer.** Modern teachers disagree in answering this question. Some say that the law forbids the first movements; others [Col. 0474B] say that it forbids consent; others explain it thus: “You shall not desire,” that is, recognize desire as evil and, as far as you can, avoid it; and so, on this account, nothing is forbidden. But whatever is contained in the Decalogue is either a command or a prohibition. Therefore something must be forbidden when it says, “You shall not desire.” To those who say that consent is forbidden, the following objection is made: the Apostle says, “I do what I do not will; but if this is so, I consent to the law not by doing, but by not willing” (ibid.).

**QUESTION 171.** It is therefore asked what that is which the law forbids and the Apostle did unwillingly. But these persons say that the law forbids consent. Yet it is clear that the Apostle did not consent, because if he consented to desire, he would in no way consent to the law, [Col. 0474C] but would act against it. Augustine, however, openly shows what it was that the Apostle did not will and yet did. Namely, he felt the movement of desire, but did not consent to it; indeed, he wished not to feel it. Hence it is clear that the law forbids the first movements of desire.

**QUESTION 172.** But it is again asked why God prohibited what no one has ever been able to avoid. The law seems not only useless but irrational, if it forbids what it is impossible to avoid. For this reason the aforesaid teachers do not wish the law to forbid the first movements. The following objection is made to them: Did not the law command that God be loved with the whole heart? But this command, as Augustine says, [Col. 0474D] no one can fulfil in the present life. Therefore, if something is commanded which no one here can perform, what wonder is it if something is forbidden which cannot be avoided?

**QUESTION 173.** It is therefore asked why God either prohibited what cannot be avoided or commanded what cannot be fulfilled.
