For he seems cruel or unjust. **Answer.** In order to humble the proud and enlighten the blind, and thus prepare them, made worthy, to receive grace. In forbidding what no one can avoid and commanding what no one can do, he showed what the perfection of divine righteousness is and what God can justly require from man. Moreover, he showed what man was before sin: namely, such that, with grace assisting, he desired nothing without any difficulty [Col. 0475A] and loved God with his whole heart; and what he was made through fault: namely, weak, carnal, unable not to desire or to love God perfectly. What, then, remains except that man, no longer presuming upon himself, flee to grace and say: “Lord, answer for me, for I am weak”? Therefore God commanded not cruelly but with great providential ordering what cannot be done except by the Mediator alone.

**QUESTION 174.** It is asked where the law so generally forbids desire. For no place is found where the law makes a prohibition except concerning a neighbor’s property or wife. **Answer.** The general is understood in the particular.

**QUESTION 175.** It is asked how it happens that we strive toward what is forbidden, and that what is prohibited pleases more [Col. 0475B] and becomes sweeter through prohibition itself. **Answer.** Human nature was so created that it naturally desires freedom; prohibition seems to diminish this and reduce it to servitude. Hence, as much as it can, immediately when a prohibition is imposed, it resists and strives against it.

**QUESTION 176.** It is asked in whose person the Apostle speaks when he says, “But I am carnal” (Rom. 7): in his own person or in a general one. For if he speaks in his own person, how does he say that he is carnal, when he was spiritual? But if he speaks generally, so that what he says applies to every righteous and unrighteous person of every time, how does it apply to the unrighteous to hate evil, will good, and consent to God’s law? **Answer.** Augustine says that he speaks in his own person, [Col. 0475C] calling himself carnal because of the movements which he felt; and at the same time he was spiritual, because he did not consent to those disordered movements. Yet it cannot be denied that he says certain things that do not suit his own person, such as: “I once lived without the law” (ibid.). Some say that he speaks in the general person of the righteous; but how can this apply to the righteous: “But I died” (ibid.)? We, however, say that the Apostle speaks in such a way that some things apply to the man of natural law, some to the man of written law, and some to the man of the law of grace. What applies to whom must be carefully observed; but our purpose is to pursue questions, not to expound the text.

**QUESTION 177.** “For what I do, I do not understand,” [Col. 0475D] etc. It is asked how he says that he does not understand what he does, when through the law he knew sin. **Answer.** “I do not understand” is used in place of “I do not approve.”

**QUESTION 178.** But when he says, “For I do not do what I will,” it is asked how he says that he does not will what he does. Is not what he does sin, and is not every sin voluntary? Thus he seems to will what he says he does not will. **Answer.** Willing is threefold: that of nature, of fault, and of grace. Thus the same person can will according to the flesh and not will according to the mind.

**QUESTION 179.** “But if I do what I do not will,” etc. It is asked what that is which the Apostle says he does not will and yet does, although the law forbids it. [Col. 0476A] **Answer.** To desire. For the law forbids desiring, and the Apostle wills according to the mind not to desire, yet according to the flesh he desired.

**QUESTION 180.** But it is asked how he says that he does and does not perform: for if he does something, he performs it; and if he does not perform it, neither does he do it. Can affirmation and negation simultaneously be true of the same thing? **Answer.** He does it according to the flesh and does not perform it according to the mind.

**QUESTION 181.** It is asked whether it follows that he does not perform simply, if he does not perform according to the mind, just as it follows that he does simply if he does according to the flesh. **Answer.** It is indeed true that a simple affirmation almost always follows a qualified [Col. 0476B] affirmation; but a simple negation does not usually follow a qualified negation. Therefore force must be placed upon the pronoun when it is said, “I do not perform [it]” (ibid.): as though, “I, the inward man, in whom the truth of man consists because [he is] the image of God.” Thus the negation that seems simple is not simple, but rather qualified.

**QUESTION 182.** “But the sin which dwells in me.” It is asked how sin, which is nothing but a privation of good, can be said to dwell in someone. **Answer.** By the term “sin” is meant the tinder of sin, which is called the law of the flesh or the law of the members, just as consent or action is called the law of death.

**QUESTION 183.** “I know that good does not dwell in [Col. 0476C] me, that is, in my flesh.” It is asked whether he says universally of every good, or indefinitely of some good, that it does not dwell in the flesh. But how can he say this of every good, when even corrupt flesh, subject to weakness, is God’s work and is not deprived of every good—especially since evil is not a thing existing through itself and cannot exist except in a good thing? Hence it follows that where there is no good, there can be no evil either; and where there is any evil, there must necessarily be some good. **Answer.** He says that health, or the integrity of nature, does not dwell in the flesh. Thus he fittingly proves that the tinder of sin—which is a privation of health or of the integrity of nature—dwells in the flesh. For where health [Col. 0476D] ought to be and is not, there is its privation, which the Apostle denotes when he says, “Good does not dwell in the flesh.”

**QUESTION 184.** “To will is present with me,” etc. It is asked what this will is which the Apostle says is present with him. **Answer.** It is nothing other than the natural affection of the soul, which is in the soul from creation and by which the soul naturally wills the good. But this affection always lacks effect unless it is assisted by God’s grace.

**QUESTION 185.** “To will is present with me, but I do not find the power to perform; because evil is present with me.” By these words the Apostle seems to suggest that, if evil were not present, not only willing would be present with him but he would also find the power to perform, since nothing would hinder [Col. 0477A] him from good or impel him toward evil. In this he suggests the first state of the first man before sin: willing good was present with him, but evil was not present. Therefore he could not say, “To will is present with me, but I do not find the power to perform, because evil is present with me.” It may be asked, however, whether he could perform, without the addition of greater grace, that good which he naturally willed. Was not Adam’s will before sin much more intense than the natural willing now possessed by pagans? Yet pagans, from the natural affection they possess, do many and great good things—though they are not worthy of eternal life because they are done without faith. How then could Adam before sin, from a greater will, not advance even a little, as nearly everyone maintains? [Col. 0477B] Again, if God did not confer greater grace, but left him in the state in which he created him, could God not justly require man perfectly to love him for the good already bestowed? But God could not justly require what man could not render. Thus it seems that before sin man could advance from the good already received, which many deny.

**QUESTION 186.** But someone will say: cannot God now justly require from man what man cannot render, as has already been said above? For unless God could justly require him to desire nothing contrary to reason and to love God with his whole heart, he would not have commanded man to do both. In the same way, it seems that before sin man could not render all that God could justly require. [Col. 0477C] **Answer.** Before sin man had not been made weak or incapable through any fault; therefore he could easily render what God could require. After sin, and through sin, he was made such that he cannot pay every debt which God nevertheless can require—and does require from those who presume upon themselves and do not flee to grace. It should be known that this passage, from “I am carnal” to “there is therefore now no condemnation” (Rom. 8), etc., is customarily read both of the man under law and of the man under grace. How it should or may be expounded of the man under grace according to Augustine has been stated. But how it is read of the man under law must be carefully considered. The man under law is one who, instructed by the law, knows sin and, unwilling though he is to resist it, [Col. 0477D] is conquered and succumbs and consents to the tinder; he is called carnal not merely because he feels the tinder, but because he also consents to it. Therefore, since consent belongs to reason:

**QUESTION 187.** It is asked how the following can apply to the man under law: “I will good, I hate evil, now it is no longer I who do it, and I consent to the law of God.” **Answer.** Although consent belongs to reason, nevertheless, because carnality drew it into consent, it is ascribed not to reason but to the flesh.

**QUESTION 188.** “That the justification of the law might be fulfilled in us” (Rom. 8). It is asked what he calls the justification of the law, since righteousness does not come from the law. **Answer.** He calls the law’s justification not that which the law bestowed, [Col. 0478A] but that which the law commanded and promised. It is fulfilled in us through the grace of Christ, who fully and perfectly fulfilled the law, gave us grace to fulfil it, and himself supplies what we do insufficiently and answers for us.

**QUESTION 189.** Whether walking according to the flesh, being according to the flesh, and thinking upon the things of the flesh are the same. **Answer.** They are not the same. To walk according to the flesh is to carry out in deed what the flesh desires. To be according to the flesh is to consent to desires or to be disposed toward carnal things. To think upon the things of the flesh is to delight in things which the flesh judges supreme, or not to perceive the things of God. For someone is called carnal in two ways: in life and in doctrine—either one who [Col. 0478B] indulges the flesh, or one who binds divine power to the natures of things, that is, who believes that God can do nothing except what he sees in the nature of things. Likewise, to walk according to the Spirit is to carry out in deed the things of the Spirit. To be according to the Spirit is to consent to the Spirit or to be disposed according to spiritual things. To think upon the things of the Spirit is to delight in spiritual things; according to these three, one is called truly spiritual. Someone is also called spiritual through understanding; one person is spiritual in life but not in understanding, another in understanding but not in life, another in both ways, another in neither, etc.

**QUESTION 190.** “But you are not in the flesh,” etc. It is asked how the Apostle says that they are not in the flesh, when he wrote to restrain [Col. 0478C] their proud contention. **Answer.** He says that they are in the Spirit and not in the flesh because they did not walk according to the flesh; or, better, among the Romans there were some who were spiritual and of perfect faith, and because of them he says, “You are not in the flesh.” There were also others among them who quarrelled with one another and were imperfect in faith; with reference to them he adds: “If indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you” (ibid.), exhorting them to perfection.

**QUESTION 191.** “But if Christ is in you.” It is asked what it is for Christ, or the Spirit of Christ, to be in someone. **Answer.** Augustine says: “Christ in a man is faith in the heart.” But on this account, wherever faith is, Christ is also; yet faith is in an evil person, therefore Christ or the Spirit of Christ is in an evil person. But Christ and the Spirit of Christ being [Col. 0478D] in someone are the same; and the Spirit of Christ is in no one except one in whom love is. **Answer.** Not everyone in whom faith is has faith in the heart; for faith is not said to be in the heart unless it rests pleasingly upon the heart, that is, unless it works through love. On this account, for Christ to be in someone and for the faith of Christ to be in that person’s heart are the same.

**QUESTION 192.** “The body indeed is dead because of sin.” It is asked on account of what sin the body is dead, that is, subject to the necessity of dying. **Answer.** On account of the liability of original fault. But since such fault—indeed every fault—is remitted in baptism, it is asked why such a penalty, imposed for such a fault, is not removed. **Answer.** Although the fault for which such a penalty [Col. 0479A] is imposed is remitted, such weakness remains lest people should hasten to receive that sacrament more for the usefulness of temporal advantage than for faith and love of the future life, and so being reborn in Christ would not benefit the soul. Or the body is dead because of sin (Rom. 8) that must be avoided. For the human spirit is such that, unless it were subject to weaknesses, it would be lifted up beyond measure and so would not be saved, which cannot occur without humility. Therefore our mortality, together with the other penalties, is not removed in baptism cruelly but mercifully; not through inability, but through great providential ordering.

**QUESTION 193.** “For you have not received the spirit of slavery,” etc. It is asked whether the spirit of fear and the spirit of adoption are the same. [Col. 0479B] **Answer.** The same Spirit is called by different names because of diverse effects. Note that a gift and the author of the gift are called by the same name.

**QUESTION 194.** It is asked how, speaking to the Romans, he says: “You have not again received the spirit of slavery unto fear,” etc. For the spirit of slavery had not previously been given to them as it had been to the Jews. **Answer.** “Again” does not denote a repetition occurring in the same persons but in different ones, as though he said: “The spirit of slavery unto fear was indeed given to the Jews at the giving of the law, and again to you has been given not the spirit of fear but the Spirit of adoption.” Fear is one thing when worldly, another when servile, another when initial, another when filial. According to some, worldly fear is when, while retaining a good will, we abandon good or commit evil [Col. 0479C] because of shame before others, lest we be considered contemptible; according to the same writers it is also called human fear. According to Cassiodorus, however, worldly fear is when we fear bodily dangers or losing worldly goods and therefore sin. This fear is evil and is abandoned with the world at the first stage; the Lord forbids it when he says: “Do not fear those who kill the body” (Matt. 10). According to the former authorities, servile fear is that which restrains the hand from an evil deed while the evil will remains.

**QUESTION 195.** It may be asked whether this is a gift of the Holy Spirit. If it is, it is good; but it seems evil, since it causes service because of punishment. **Answer.** It is good, having the good effect of restraining from an evil deed; but the fact that the evil [Col. 0479D] will remains does not come from it but from human vice. According to others, however, servile fear is that by which Gehenna is feared: through it good is done, but not well. According to the former writers this is called initial fear; according to the latter too it is the beginning of wisdom: it prepares a place for wisdom and leads to charity. Initial fear is also spoken of in another way: when that which was hard begins to be loved. This is, as it were, intermediate between servile and filial fear, having something of each. According to either opinion, filial fear is not that by which punishment is feared, but that by which one fears lest the bridegroom be offended or depart: lest we offend, lest we lack God. It is the companion of perfection.

### Question 196

But which of these fears is customarily asked to have been in Christ [Col. 0480A]? It is clear that worldly fear, since it is evil, was not in him; likewise neither servile nor initial fear, since neither could exist with perfect charity. Therefore either filial fear, or no fear at all, seems to have been in him. But filial fear is that by which we fear to offend: did Christ, then, fear offending or being separated?  

**Solution.** Filial fear was in Christ, not according to the effect it has presently in us, but according to that which it has in the angels or will have in the saints in the future; namely, as reverence, which is love joined with submission. Hence the Apostle says: “And he was heard because of his reverence” (Heb. 5). Again, did not Christ fear punishment, namely death, as it is said: “Jesus began to be afraid” (Mark 14)? By what fear, then? Was it filial, since no other fear was [Col. 0480B] in him?  

**Solution.** He began to be afraid by natural fear, which is not included in the foregoing division, because it exists equally in the good and the wicked. It is called natural not because it is innate with nature, but because through corruption it has in some manner grown into nature. Christ assumed it together with the other penalties.

### Question 197

Servile fear was given in the Law; but according to Augustine, servile fear is that by which Gehenna is feared. Therefore fear of Gehenna was given in the Law. But does not fear of Gehenna restrain not merely the hand but also the mind, whereas the Law restrains only the hand and not the mind? Again, Augustine says that servile fear is never present with charity; but does not everyone who fears eternal punishment possess fear of Gehenna? Yet someone who has incipient charity [Col. 0480C] still fears punishment; thus servile fear seems to exist with charity. I raise these questions not in order to solve them, but to stir the reader to inquire with me.

### Question 198

It is further asked concerning servile fear whether it makes one a servant of Christ or of the devil.  

**Solution.** It makes one the servant neither of God nor of the devil, but of punishment; for it in some measure takes away freedom and does not permit a person to do the work he wishes to do except because of punishment.

### Question 199

“But fellow-heirs with Christ,” etc. It is asked whether Christ is an heir, and, if so, according to which nature. For it seems that he ought not to be called heir according to his divinity, since an inheritance is the assured possession of a successor upon someone else’s death. But neither does the Father die, nor does the Son succeed him, since both are [Col. 0480D] eternal. How then is he an heir?  

**Solution.** Among us inheritance indeed exists through succession; but not so in God. For the Son has his being from the Father, and has from the Father all that he has (John 1), but not conversely. Therefore the Son is the Father’s heir. According to his humanity, however, he received the inheritance in that fullness from which we all have received.

### Question 200

It is asked what it is to be fellow-heirs with Christ.  

**Solution.** To share in the same inheritance. But on this account it seems false that we are fellow-heirs, because possession of the nations is Christ’s inheritance. Hence: “Ask of me, and I shall give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2). We are not participants in that inheritance [Col. 0481A], and thus are not fellow-heirs.  

**Solution.** The inheritance of Christ in respect of which we are fellow-heirs is eternal life, not possession of the nations.

### Question 201

“If indeed we suffer with him.” It is asked how one must suffer with Christ, who no longer suffers.  

**Solution.** We suffer with Christ in two ways: either by recalling to mind the pains which he endured for us and grieving sympathetically with him; or by enduring tribulations in likeness to him, with him and for his sake. “Compassion” sometimes names a natural affection, and sometimes the consent which is a virtue.

### Question 202

“The sufferings of this present time are not worthy,” etc. It is asked whether the merits of the saints suffice for attaining the future life. For if they have true [Col. 0481B] righteousness, they are worthy of the crown. But the Apostle himself indicates that the fathers of the New Testament are truly righteous, saying: “Henceforth there is laid up for me the crown of righteousness, which the just judge will render to me; and not only to me, but also to all who love his coming” (2 Tim. 4). Yet here he seems to say that the tribulations endured by the saints do not suffice to merit the future glory which is to be revealed. For this is what it means for sufferings not to be commensurate with future glory.  

**Solution.** The Apostle does not deny that the merits of the saints suffice for attaining glory; rather, they are not commensurate with meriting such surpassing glory, because God in his grace will add more than our merits have merited. In brief: our merits are very small [Col. 0481C] in comparison with the rewards. “For the creature was subjected to vanity.” Note that vanity is threefold: first, mutability; second, mortality; third, iniquity. And man is “all vanity,” that is, subject to every vanity.

### Question 203

“Not willingly, but because of him who subjected it in hope.” It is asked what the creature subjected to vanity does not will. If it does not will evil, its will is good; but then what follows is meaningless: “but because of him,” etc. If, however, it does not will good, it sins, since it ought to will the good.  

**Solution.** “Will” is used in several senses. Sometimes it means natural inclination, as in: “What I will, I do not do”; sometimes the consent which is said to deserve condemnation or reward; sometimes the flesh’s shrinking in horror, as in: [Col. 0481D] “Not as I will, but as you will” (Matt. 26). It is taken here in this last sense, and the meaning is: Although the punishment which I endure is bitter, nevertheless I delight in enduring it for Christ’s sake.

### Question 204

“The whole creation groans,” etc. It is asked how this can be true, since a stone is a creature and yet does not groan.  

**Solution.** “Every” here does not gather together the individual members of genera, but the genera of individuals. The meaning is: every creature, that is, the human being, in whom every kind of creature exists. For there are three kinds of creature: bodily, animate, and spiritual; all are in the human being, and thus every creature groans in the human being.

### Question 205

“Not only it, but we ourselves also,” etc. [Col. 0482A] Are not the good understood by the name “creation”? How, then, does the Apostle distinguish between the apostles, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, and creation, as though they themselves were not good?  

**Solution.** For the same reason that he distinguishes between creation and the children of God, although the children of God are creatures, he distinguishes between creation and the apostles, although they too are creatures. He makes a distinction that is not based on the diversity of another quality, as the glosses, carefully examined, make clear.

### Question 206

“Hope that is seen is not hope,” etc. It is asked what is signified by the name “hope” when it is said, “Hope that is seen,” and from what it is removed when it is said, “is not hope.” How can the name “hope” belong or be applied to that which is not hope?  

**Solution.** Just as “faith” is said equivocally both of that by which one believes and of that which is believed, [Col. 0482B] so “hope” is called equivocally both that by which one hopes and that which is hoped for. Thus hope that is seen—that is, the thing hoped for—is not the hope by which we hope, namely, that virtue. Or otherwise: hope that is seen, that is, hope concerning a visible thing, is not our hope, namely, that by whose merit we have already been saved.

### Question 207

“The Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings.” It is asked how the Spirit, who needs nothing and suffers no distress, can be said to intercede or groan.  

**Solution.** What the saints do with him as author is attributed to the Spirit. Therefore he intercedes or groans because he causes us to intercede or groan.

### Question 208

Does the Spirit ask for anything and fail to obtain it? Whenever we ask something in charity, does not the Spirit himself [Col. 0482C] ask within us? Yet we often ask for one who lies in sin and are not heard. Thus it seems that the Spirit, under whose teaching we pray, is not heard.  

**Solution.** There are two forms of righteous prayer: either when we ask for what ought to be asked, or when we ask where it ought to be asked. Sometimes, however, we ask where it ought to be asked, but not what ought to be asked. Then the Spirit teaches us how we ought to ask, but does not teach us what we ought to ask; and therefore we do not obtain it. But whenever we ask both what ought to be asked and where it ought to be asked, we obtain it.

### Question 209

“We know that all things work together for good to those who love God.” Do not some people love for a time and afterward fall, and thus are condemned? [Col. 0482D] Yet not all things work together for good to them; thus it seems that not all things work together for good to those who love God.  

**Solution.** He does not say simply that all things work together for good to those who love God, but to those who love God and are called saints according to his purpose. For some love God and yet are not called saints according to his purpose, just as some are ordained to life but do not yet love God. To neither of these do all things work together for good; rather, to those who love God and are called saints according to his purpose.

### Question 210

It is likewise asked how the sins of such persons themselves work together for their good.  

**Solution.** They rise again more humble and more instructed.

[Col. 0483A]

### Question 211

But if they had not fallen, and had then done good, would they not be better than they now are? For if this woman, corrupted as she was, had possessed together with the goods she now has also virginity, would she not be of a higher rank and of greater merit?  

**Solution.** It is indeed true that if Mary Magdalene had possessed virginity along with such great devotion, she would be of greater merit. Yet her fall contributed to a certain perfection; and perhaps, if she had not fallen so shamefully, she would never have loved the heavenly physician so greatly. Nevertheless, sin is not to be committed in order that grace may abound.

### Question 212

It is likewise asked how the sins of the wicked work together for the good of the good.  

**Solution.** Nothing happens in the world that does not contribute some usefulness [Col. 0483B] to the good of the universe; and thus all things—whether one’s own good or evil, or that of others—work together for good to the good.

### Question 213

Do all things work together for evil to those who are to be condemned? It is clear that their evils harm them; but one may ask whether the good things which they sometimes do work together for their evil. This seems so, because it is written: “It is better not to know the way of truth than, after having known it, to turn back” (2 Pet. 2).  

**Solution.** Not all things work together for evil to those who are to be condemned, because they will be punished less on account of the good things which they sometimes do. But the saying, “It is better,” etc., was not said concerning those condemned persons who were at some time righteous; it was said concerning heretics.

### Question 214

“Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined.” It is asked whether foreknowledge is the cause of predestination, [Col. 0483C] just as predestination is the cause of calling, calling the cause of justification, and justification the cause of glorification. This seems to follow from the presumed order. But since both are eternal, how can one be the cause of the other?  

**Solution.** Although both are eternal, one can nevertheless be the cause of the other. Thus the Son and the Holy Spirit are both eternal, yet the Son is the cause of the Holy Spirit. So, according to some, foreknowledge belongs to knowledge and thus to the Son; predestination belongs to election, and election to will, which pertains to the property of the Holy Spirit. Therefore, just as the Son is the cause of the Holy Spirit, so foreknowledge is the cause of predestination, which it precedes naturally, though not temporally.

[Col. 0483D]

### Question 215

Is foreknowledge and predestination the same thing in God? To resolve this question, it must be known that the divine *usia*—that is, essence—although one and simple, receives different names on account of diverse effects. For it is called wisdom, knowledge, foreknowledge, providence, disposition, and predestination. Wisdom and knowledge concern all past, present, and future good and evil things, and foreknowledge concerns the same things. Providence concerns things to be governed; it is sometimes taken as foreknowledge. Disposition concerns things to be made; predestination concerns those to be saved. Thus in God, as regards essence, foreknowledge and predestination are the same.

### Question 216

Would foreknowledge be in God if [Col. 0484A] there were no future things? They wish to prove that it would not as follows. If there were no future things, God would not foreknow any future things; and if this were so, foreknowledge would not be in God. But foreknowledge is divine knowledge, and divine knowledge is God’s essence. Thus it seems that, if there were no future things, God would not exist—far be it!  

**Solution.** Foreknowledge does not simply signify the divine essence, but indicates a relation in respect of future things. Thus the statement, “If there were no future things, foreknowledge would not be in God,” is understood in two ways. If it is said: “If there were no future things, foreknowledge would not be in God,” that is, if there were no future things, there would be no objects of divine knowledge from which that knowledge would be called foreknowledge, the understanding is true. But if it is understood thus: “If there were no future things, foreknowledge would not [Col. 0484B] be in God,” that is, the knowledge by which he foreknows future things would not be in God, the understanding is false.

### Question 217

Is God’s foreknowledge the cause of future things, or are future things the cause of foreknowledge? Nothing would be future unless God had foreseen it; thus foreknowledge seems to be the cause of future things. Hence Augustine says that God does not know all creatures because they exist; rather, they already exist because he knows them. But since he knows good and evil alike, it seems that foreknowledge is the cause of evils as well as goods. Yet Origen says: “A thing will not be because God knows it will be; rather, because it will be, God foreknows it.” This seems contrary to Augustine’s earlier statement.  

**Solution.** Sometimes knowledge is taken to mean good pleasure, and then it is the cause of future things—but only of good things. [Col. 0484C] Augustine took it thus above. At other times it signifies knowledge or cognition alone; then it is not the cause of future things, but stands equally in relation to good and evil. Origen took it in this sense. Thus foreknowledge is neither the cause of future things nor are future things the cause of foreknowledge, unless they are called a cause without which it would not exist.

### Question 218

Does foreknowledge entail a necessity of occurrence for future things? This seems so, because if God foreknew that something would be future, it cannot fail to occur; and if this is so, whatever he foreknew will occur necessarily. Again, it seems that God’s foreknowledge could be mistaken, because if what has been foreseen can occur otherwise than it does occur, it can occur otherwise than as foreseen. For if God foresaw that someone would read today [Col. 0484D], everyone grants that such a person, who is going to read today, can fail to read; and so the event can happen otherwise than it was foreknown.  

**Solution.** The common solution is that this and similar propositions can be explained by conjunction and disjunction. The conjunctive sense here is: “If God foresaw it, it must occur,” that is, it cannot be the case simultaneously both that God foresees it and that it does not occur; in this sense it is true. The disjunctive sense is: “This future thing cannot occur otherwise than in the manner in which it occurs and in which it is foreseen”; and this is false. Again, if it occurred otherwise than foreknown, divine providence would not be deceived, because then this would not have been foreseen, but something else, namely what would then occur.

The foregoing solution is challenged as follows: If God foresaw something, it will occur; [Col. 0485A] this conditional is necessary. Therefore, if the antecedent is necessary, so is the consequent. But the antecedent is necessary, because what has been foreknown cannot be not foreknown. Thus it seems that whatever is future is future by a certain necessity. This seems capable of another proof as well: from eternity God said through his eternal Word concerning every future thing that it will be. But it is impossible for God to lie. If what he said would be future did not occur, it would follow that God was a liar; and thus what is future will necessarily occur. Hence Augustine says: “As it is necessary that what was, was, so it is necessary that what will be, will be.” And elsewhere, speaking of God, he says: “Whose will is necessity, because, if he wills, it will necessarily be.”  

**Solution.** There are some who [Col. 0485B] concede that God can have not foreknown what he foreknew from eternity; and therefore they say that the antecedent of the preceding conditional is not necessary, and consequently neither is the consequent. But I do not see how what they say can be true. Let them also answer the second objection: how God is not a liar if what he foretold as future does not occur; or how God’s will is necessity; or how Augustine’s statement is true, that it is necessary that what is future will be. We, however, following Augustine, say that there is a twofold necessity: one considered according to lower causes, which is sometimes impeded by higher causes; and the other understood according to higher causes, which it is impossible not to be fulfilled. Of future things, some [Col. 0485C] occur equally according to higher and lower causes; others only according to higher causes. Whatever is future with respect to the necessity understood according to the totality of causes cannot be prevented from occurring. But ordinary speech is fashioned according to lower causes, because these are better known to us. Hence we often say that something can be and the same thing can fail to be, because these causes allow both. According to higher causes, however, only one thing can be: namely, what God wills, ordains, foreknew from eternity, and declared future through his Word. It cannot in any manner be prevented from occurring. Augustine, looking to these causes, said that what is future will necessarily be.

[Col. 0485D]

### Question 219

It is likewise asked whether God’s knowledge can increase or decrease. They wish to prove that it can as follows: God knows that this man will read, but he can fail to read; therefore God can fail to know that this man will read. Or thus: This man will not read, but he can read; therefore God can know that this man will read, though he will not read. But it can happen that he reads; therefore it can be known by God that he will not read.  

**Solution.** God’s knowledge is immutable and cannot increase or decrease. Nevertheless, some concede that God can know what he does not know, fail to know what he knows, and know more than he knows, because they do not know how to answer the foregoing objections. But we say that God cannot know what he does not know, fail to know what he knows, or know more than he knows. For if things which will never occur began to occur, they still would not begin to be known by God, who knows all things perfectly from eternity—not only things which at some time occur, but whatever can occur. [Col. 0486A] For he knows both by what causes they can occur and what they would be like if they occurred. He does not now have fuller knowledge of the world than he had from eternity; nor does he now have less knowledge of things that will never occur, though they could occur, than he would have if they did occur. Yet it is a great question whether there is anything of this kind that exists only in possibility and never in actuality. For what does not have a cause in God, how can it issue into actuality? But this must be discussed elsewhere; we have touched upon it incidentally here.

Answering the foregoing objections, we say that the statement, “God knows that this man will read,” posits both that this man [Col. 0486B] will read and that God knows it. Therefore, since he will not read, one must not concede that God knows that this man will read—not because God is ignorant of anything. For whether he reads or does not read, God does not thereby know more or less, or fail to know. The same judgment applies to similar cases. It should also be noted that when it is said that one who is going to read can fail to read, or that one who is not going to read can read, this is said according to lower causes. But if we look to higher causes, what will be shall determinately be, and not something else, nor can it fail to occur. Nevertheless, because ordinary speech is fashioned according to lower causes, which compel neither alternative but permit both, we say that either can be and not be, although in truth one future event, and not the other, is true [Col. 0486C].

### Question 220

Can the number of the predestined be increased or diminished? The same question is asked concerning the number of the reprobate. They wish to prove that it can. God can withhold grace from one to whom he gives it; if he did so, a predestined person would be damned. And he can give it to one to whom he does not give it; if he did so, a reprobate person would be saved. Thus one who is predestined can be damned, and one who is reprobate can be saved; and someone can pass from the number of the predestined to the number of the reprobate, and conversely.  

**Solution.** They solve this by analogy with the preceding questions, according to conjunction and disjunction. But we say that what is possible according to lower causes is perhaps impossible [Col. 0486D] according to higher causes. Again, the inference does not seem valid: “God can save or damn this person; therefore this person can be saved or damned.” God’s power does not entail our power. Thus, if God could have redeemed the human race otherwise, it does not follow that the human race could therefore have been redeemed otherwise than through the death of the Son of God. And if God had this in his power, does a human being therefore have it in his power to be saved otherwise? Could not God, if he wished, save Judas? Does it follow that Judas can be saved? It should be noted that lower causes are called those which God implanted in creatures in the first establishment of things, according to which like things arise from like things, so that from such a seed such a tree or fruit proceeds. Higher causes are called divine power, will, disposition, and predestination [Col. 0487A]. These sometimes work with lower causes and sometimes without them. They always have their effect, whereas lower causes do not always have theirs; indeed, they are sometimes impeded by higher causes.

### Question 221

“To be made conformed to the image of his Son,” etc. It is asked why the Son is called the image of the Father.  

**Solution.** Because he is most like him and is of the same essence.

### Question 222

But since the Holy Spirit is equally like the Father, being of the same substance, why is the Son, and not the Holy Spirit, called the image of the Father?  

**Solution.** Because image pertains more to the property of generation than of procession. For things that are generated are usually more alike than things that proceed.

[Col. 0487B]

### Question 223

Are there two images in the Son, because he is an uncreated image inasmuch as he is God and a created image inasmuch as he is human?  

**Solution.** There are not therefore two images, because the uncreated image and created image in Christ are not two images but one; just as he is Son of God and son of man, yet not two sons, but one Son of God and son of man.

### Question 224

“Those whom he called, he also justified,” etc. It is asked how the Apostle distinguishes between calling and justifying, since he justifies by calling.  

**Solution.** By calling he understands the infusion of charity; by justification, the grace that follows and preserves it.

### Question 225

“Those whom he predestined, he also called,” etc. It is asked whether all who are called are predestined [Col. 0487C]. This seems so, because calling is an effect of predestination. But some are called who are not chosen, because it is written: “Many are called, few are chosen” (Matt. 22). But only the chosen are predestined; therefore not all who are called are predestined.  

**Solution.** One calling is common, taking place by outward preaching and sometimes also inwardly by inspiration. Another is special, taking place according to purpose; by it no one is called except one who is chosen and predestined. But it was according to common calling that it was said: “Many are called, but few are chosen.”

### Question 226

“Who shall bring an accusation against the elect?” No one, because what God does not will another cannot do. But it is asked what it is for God to accuse someone.  

**Solution.** For God to accuse is to permit [Col. 0487D] a person to fall into sin. But for the devil to accuse is to cast someone into sin through temptation, and by casting him down to make him liable to accusation.

### Question 227

It is asked how Christ intercedes for us: by voice, by mind and desire alone, or in another way.  

**Solution.** Christ’s interceding for us is, through the merits of his obedience rendered in his humanity, to reconcile us to God the Father as we cling to him through faith and love.

### Question 228

It is also asked whether the saints, whose patronage we ask for ourselves, intercede, and how.  

**Solution.** The saints’ interceding for us is nothing other than God’s rewarding, for their merits, the good affections which we have toward them for God’s sake [Col. 0488A]. Therefore it makes no difference whether they hear us or do not hear us.

### Question 229

“Who shall separate us from the love of God?” etc. It is asked whether the Apostle was of such perfection that he could not sin mortally. For if he could not be separated from God, neither could he sin mortally; for this is what it is to be separated. But since elsewhere he says, “Lest the greatness of the revelations exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh” (2 Cor. 12), he indicates that if he could be exalted, he could also sin mortally and thus be separated.  

**Solution.** No other person could separate the Apostle from God; nevertheless, he himself could separate himself, because in this he merited: he could transgress and did not transgress. For when he confessed Christ before Nero, he could have denied him, if [Col. 0488B] he had wished. Therefore, what neither life nor death could do, he himself could do.

### Question 230

It is asked how the cause makes the martyr and not the punishment, since no one is a martyr without punishment, just as none is without a cause. For as punishment without cause does not suffice for the crown of martyrdom, so neither does cause without punishment.  

**Solution.** The statement, “The cause makes the martyr and not the punishment,” is to be understood as meaning “the cause alone.” But someone will say that, by the same reasoning, one may say, “Punishment makes the martyr and not the cause,” meaning “punishment alone.”  

**Response.** A cause without punishment is beneficial; punishment without a cause is not only not beneficial but harmful. And when punishment is beneficial, it derives this benefit from the cause. Therefore the former is more properly said than the latter.

[Col. 0488C]

### Question 231

“There is great sorrow to me and continual pain in my heart” (Rom. 9). It is asked why the Apostle says he grieves that, when he had formerly gone astray with the erring, he persecuted the Church. Since great benefit came from that persecution, ought he not to rejoice rather than grieve over it?  

**Solution.** The Apostle did not grieve over the good that followed from his evil, but over the sin that he himself committed, and it is always good to grieve over that.

### Question 232

“I myself wished to be anathema from Christ for my brethren.” It is asked how the Apostle wished to be separated from Christ: according to glory or according to righteousness. If according to glory, [Col. 0488D] he seems to have loved his brethren more than God, which must in no way be done. If he wished to be separated according to righteousness, this could not be wished without sin and offense against God; and no one can reasonably wish this.  

**Solution.** He did not wish to be separated from Christ in either sense; rather, by these words he showed his remarkable affection for the Jews. Moses used the same kind of expression when he said: “Either blot me out of the book of life, or forgive them this offense” (Exod. 32). Or it may be said that both Moses and the Apostle set in their desire and wish the salvation of such a great multitude above their own salvation. In this they did not put aside love for God; indeed, preferring God’s glory and honor to their own salvation, they preferred that God’s glory be magnified in so many saved persons rather than [Col. 0489A] diminished in one saved person. This perfection exceeds every perfection, because none greater can be conceived.

### Question 233

“What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God?” It is asked whether God is unjust in reprobating, hardening, and finally damning this person, who cannot act rightly without the grace of predestination, especially since he cannot merit predestination itself.  

**Solution.** Certainly there is no injustice with God. To make clear that there is no injustice in God, one must consider what predestination is and what its effect is, and what reprobation is and what its effect is. Predestination is the preparation of grace. By “grace” here are meant gratuitous goods by which we are justified in the present or crowned in the future [Col. 0489B]. But one must see what “preparation” signifies. It was said above that the divine *usia*, being one and simple, receives diverse names on account of the diverse effects of things; predestination is one of these names. Preparation, therefore, is nothing other than God himself preparing, distinguishing, establishing, proposing, or choosing within himself that he will bestow these gifts upon those persons in time. This purpose or preparation is the cause of the future goods by which we are adopted as children of God. Thus it has been said what predestination is and what its effect is: namely calling, justification, and glorification. But is reprobation something that existed eternally in God, or God himself, and that is a cause of future evils just as predestination is the cause of goods? If [Col. 0489C] this is granted, it follows that God is thus the cause and author of evils. Therefore it must be known that reprobation posits nothing, because for God to reprobate someone is nothing other than not to choose and not to predestine, not to prepare gratuitous goods. Its effect is hardening, which is nothing other than not giving grace; such is the cause, such is the effect. But there is no iniquity or injustice if God does not give something to one to whom he owes nothing. Therefore God is not unjust in reprobating or hardening anyone.

### Question 234

It is asked why God did not reprobate all, or why he did not predestine all; rather, why he predestined some and reprobated others.  

**Solution.** If he predestined all, [Col. 0489D] divine justice would remain hidden, because it would not be known what punishment is justly due to fault. If he reprobated all, God’s goodness would not appear. But divine wisdom judged it better that good and evil should exist than good alone, although wisdom itself made only good.

### Question 235

It is asked why God chose Jacob rather than Esau; the same may be asked concerning every elect and reprobate person. For it cannot be said that one is chosen and the other reprobated because of future good or evil merits, since then what is temporal would be the cause of what is eternal. Again, if it is said that Jacob was chosen by grace alone while Esau was reprobated because of original sin, one asks why Jacob was not reprobated for the same sin, or why Esau was not chosen by the same [Col. 0490A] grace.  

**Solution—if a solution should be called the showing that something is insoluble.** They say that it was done so because God willed it to be done. But if one asks why he willed it thus, the question is foolish, because it seeks a cause for the divine will, which has none; indeed, it is itself the first and principal cause of all things. But Blessed Jerome says that God did nothing merely because he wills it, but because there is reason for its being done thus. Therefore it is not improper to ask why he willed this and to answer: “The judgments of God are a great deep” (Ps. 35). Nevertheless, preserving reverence for mysteries and without the arrogance of assertion, we may say that he chose Jacob rather than Esau because he foresaw that greater benefit would come to the good of the universe from Jacob’s election than from Esau’s. But someone will say: “Therefore [Col. 0490B] what is temporal is its cause; the good which he then foresaw would be future is the cause of predestination.” To this we say that this is not true. Yet the cause, namely eternal reason, looks to that end: that it might choose the person from whose election greater benefit would result for the good of the universe. This reason is eternal, though it looks to the temporal good that would arise from Jacob’s election.

### Question 236

But again it is asked why greater benefit arose from Jacob’s election than from Esau’s.  

**Solution.** Because grace is more commended by Jacob’s election than by Esau’s. Again, it is asked why it is more commended by Jacob’s election than by Esau’s.  

**Solution.** Because Jacob was younger by birth. For if the elder by birth were chosen, it would seem that this occurred through the privilege of birth [Col. 0490C].

### Question 237

It is asked why Jacob was not older by birth and Esau younger, so that Esau at least might thus be chosen.  

**Solution.** This is to ask why Jacob is not Esau, and conversely; and therefore it is a question without reason.

### Question CCXXXVIII

From the things that occur in time the same difficulty arises: why God bestows grace upon this person rather than that is commonly asked, since they are alike, and neither can merit the grace without which he cannot be saved. For it seems that I ought not to be blamed if I do not do what I cannot do without grace, when grace has not been bestowed upon me; rather, blame should be assigned to him who does not confer upon me the necessary grace, since he cannot fail to confer it without loss to himself. [Col. 0490D]

**Solution.** Different people hold different opinions concerning grace. Some said that God cannot do anything except what he does; but it is clear that this is untrue. Others say: there is in this person a certain seedbed of virtue—which they call the root of charity—by virtue of which he is fitted, when grace is bestowed upon him, to merit eternal life; because this is absent in that person, he can merit neither charity nor eternal life. But since this is contrary to the Church, it should be altogether passed over.

Others say that God offers his grace universally to all: whoever receives it will be saved; whoever does not receive it will be damned. It is as though someone prepared good food for you in a tower and said, “Climb up to receive the food.” But because you cannot climb without a ladder or some such aid, [Col. 0491A] they say that another grace is necessary, so that you may ascend to that higher grace; then another grace is necessary to receive that one, and another for that, and so on to infinity. But these people attribute everything to grace and leave nothing to merit.

There are others who say that grace is offered even by being extended to a human being, so that he himself may receive it; yet, unless he receives it, he cannot be raised up. It is as when a rope is lowered to someone in a well, without which he cannot get out of the well; but if he stretches out his hand to the rope and takes hold of it, he is drawn out. Something thus comes from the human being, although merit cannot exist without grace. But because this view divides merit from grace, by maintaining that some good comes from the human being—at least that he raises his hand and grasps the rope—and because this cannot happen without grace, [Col. 0491B] this view too, along with the preceding one, must be avoided.

It may, however, be said that God’s grace is offered equally to the good and the wicked—that is, to the predestined and the reprobate—yet not everyone receives it or follows when it draws him. Indeed, the person into whom the ray of grace is poured closes his eyes, and thus repels the ray by which he is touched; consequently grace is deservedly withdrawn even from him, because he withdraws himself. For grace is like a ray of sunlight which presents itself to the eye: when the eye is touched by it, it exercises sight. The eye is of such a nature that sight is exercised through that ray when struck by the sun’s ray; without it there is no sight in the eye. Yet unless it were of such a nature, it would not see even when touched by the ray, just as a wall or a stone does not see even though flooded with the sun’s ray. Thus the soul [Col. 0491C] naturally possesses a capacity for meriting, but cannot exercise it unless flooded with the brightness of grace. When it is touched, it is moved and merits. Thus everything is from grace, yet merit is not excluded.

It is as if a child who cannot yet walk is led by someone and does walk. He could not do this by himself, nor even while another led him, unless he possessed the natural capacity to walk; nevertheless, his walking is said to come wholly from the one leading him. Thus, for the soul to merit, two things are required: grace and natural capacity. Yet the whole power of meriting belongs to grace alone, because natural capacity contributes nothing without grace.

### Question CCXXXIX

“Even for this very purpose I raised you up, [Col. 0491D] that I might show my power in you,” etc. It is asked whether God inclines a human mind in such a way that the person becomes worse.

**Solution.** Pharaoh was not made worse in that blinding than he had been before. Rather, through the signs set forth externally, the wickedness formerly conceived in his mind was stirred up and burst into action, just as the envy of the Jews burst forth when the Lord entered Jerusalem with such glory and brought to maturity the crime already conceived. Or God’s raising up is nothing other than permitting a person, by a just judgment, to be precipitated. This question has been discussed more carefully above.

### Question CCXL

“He has mercy on whom he wills, and he hardens whom he wills.” It is asked whether God’s will is, as it is the cause of mercy, also the cause of hardening; this seems so, [Col. 0492A] since the Apostle says, “He has mercy on whom he wills,” etc.

**Solution.** God’s will is the cause only of that which is something. Hardening does not posit something, but rather removes something. Yet the Apostle intends to show that God can justly give to whom he wills and not give to whom he wills not to give; for God acts not from necessity, but from will alone. That his will is the cause of good is evident from the Apostle’s earlier words: “It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who has mercy” [ibid.].

### Question CCXLI

But it may be asked how willing is not from the one who wills, since no one can do this without will.

**Solution.** A good will belongs to the human being as recipient, but to God as giver and author.

### Question CCXLII

“Does not the potter have power over the clay?” etc. [Col. 0492B] It is asked why this comparison is introduced. Does God make one vessel for honor and another for dishonor? Or does a dishonorable vessel derive its dishonorable character from God?

**Solution.** That one vessel is for honor comes from God; but that it is dishonorable comes from the vessel itself. Still, the comparison is sound, because, just as the potter makes one vessel for honor and another for dishonor, so God is said to form one vessel for honor and another for dishonor. Or, better: God is said to form one for honor and another for dishonor because, with God as author, even those things which are vessels of wrath or dishonor have being. Yet they are not vessels of dishonor from God, but through their own fault.

### Question CCXLIII

It is asked what it is to be written in the book [Col. 0492C] of life according to foreknowledge.

**Solution.** It is to be foreknown and preordained for life, just as to be written according to justice is to be in a state in which, if one should depart this life, one would be saved. Therefore some are written according to foreknowledge but not according to justice: those who do not yet possess virtue but are nevertheless preordained for life. Others are written according to justice but not according to foreknowledge: those who possess charity but are foreseen for death. Others are written according both to foreknowledge and to justice: those who possess charity and are predestined for life. Others are written neither according to foreknowledge nor according to justice: those who were never good and were not [Col. 0492D] predestined.

Those written there according to justice but not according to foreknowledge are said to be erased from it; but those written there according to foreknowledge are never erased from it.

### Question CCXLIV

It is asked whether those who are written in the book of life according to merit and not according to foreknowledge are written by disposition.

**Solution.** It may be said that they are written by disposition on account of merit, though not simply according to disposition; for if this were so, they could not be erased from it. With this qualification, they may be said to be written by disposition on account of merit: God disposed this, like every good thing.

### Question CCXLV

It is asked how the statement, “The elder shall serve [Col. 0493A] the younger” (Gen. 25), is to be understood as concerning foreknowledge.

**Solution.** The meaning is that this Scripture shows that God foreknew future things.

### Question CCXLVI

“But the righteousness which is from faith,” etc. It is asked what it means for righteousness to be from faith.

**Solution.** It means that righteousness is through grace, because one comes to faith not only by grace, but grace is also necessary after faith, so that faith may be fulfilled by good works; and their fulfilment is called righteousness.

### Question CCXLVII

Likewise, it is asked how the statement, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1), is to be understood as concerning judgment.

**Solution.** This prophecy shows to have been fulfilled what had been in God’s foreknowledge. Note [Col. 0493B] that the statement, “Jacob I loved, Esau I hated,” may be expounded concerning the eternal predestination of the one and the reprobation of the other, or concerning the bestowal of temporal grace or its withdrawal. Hence the gloss, “In Jacob he found nothing to love except the gift of his mercy,” is understood thus: from grace alone God determined to confer upon Jacob, in time, grace by which he would be saved. And the gloss, “In Esau nothing to hate except original sin,” means: God foreknew that, on account of original sin, grace by which Esau would be saved in time was not to be conferred upon him.

### Question CCXLVIII

Someone says: Why was grace not bestowed upon Esau because of original sin, when it was bestowed upon Jacob, though he had original sin? [Col. 0493C]

**Solution.** Because the same grace was certainly offered, but Esau withdrew himself from grace and closed his own eye; while grace removed sin from Jacob because he yielded to grace and followed it as it drew him, God working and disposing all things according to the good pleasure of his most just will.

### Question CCXLIX

“That he might show the riches of glory,” etc. It is asked whether the torments of the wicked benefit the good in the future life.

**Solution.** They say that they do benefit them, because God would never permit evils to exist unless they contributed some usefulness to the good of the universe.

### Question CCL

It is asked what benefit comes to the good from seeing the wicked punished. Do they therefore love or praise God more? Or do they delight in the punishment of the wicked?

**Solution.** They delight not in the punishment of the wicked, but in God’s justice; and their own [Col. 0493D] grace shines forth more clearly by comparison with the wicked, especially when they see that they have been delivered from the same punishments by mercy alone.

But someone will say: even if the wicked were not punished, would not the good know that they had been delivered from the same punishments, just as they know now?

**Solution.** Perhaps not so effectively; and in this respect they would love less. Again, if no one were to be damned, would not God render to the good according to their merits? Thus it seems that, even if all were saved, the good would not be less great than it is now—indeed, it would be greater—because the good would then rejoice more in their salvation than they now rejoice in their damnation.

Again, in the future life the good will either suffer with the wicked or not suffer with them. If they suffer with them, how are they blessed? If they do not suffer with them, they are cruel.

**Solution.** [Col. 0494A] Augustine resolves this question thus: it was better that there should be both good things and evil things than good things only, so that God might be praised more wonderfully from the very diversity.

### Question CCLI

“Pursuing the law of righteousness,” etc. Since the law does not justify, it is asked how it is called a law of righteousness.

**Solution.** Because it is a certain preparation for righteousness, it is called a law of righteousness.

### Question CCLII

“They stumbled at the stone of stumbling.” Since the Lord says in the Gospel concerning this: “Whoever falls upon this stone shall be broken; but upon whomever it falls, it will crush him” (Matt. 21), it is asked what it is to fall upon the stone.

**Solution.** It is to offend God through ignorance, just as to be crushed by the stone is to be punished eternally by Christ. Hence Christ is called the rock of scandal and the stone of stumbling [Col. 0494B] because, being humble, he was apt to be stumbled over by the proud.

### Question CCLIII

“I bear them witness that they have zeal, or emulation, for God,” etc. (Rom. 10). It is asked whether this zeal is good, what it is, and what its effect is. That it is good seems evident because the Apostle says this in praise of the Jews, and the interpreters also say that it is love of God. But if this were so, they would seem to possess something worthy of eternal life. Yet were not those who killed Christ worthy of death? How then did they have zeal for God—that is, love?

Again, if it was good, it had a good effect; but was not its effect what they did from that zeal? Yet this was mortal [Col. 0494C] sin—namely, the persecution of the martyrs and the killing of Christ. How, then, did good produce evil?

**Solution.** That zeal was a good inclination toward God, by which they were prepared to do what their conscience dictated must be done for God’s sake. Yet it was not so great as to make them worthy of eternal life, nor should it simply be called charity or love of God. If, however, it is sometimes called love of God, this is because they had it toward God. Its effect was not the persecution of the martyrs or Christ’s death, but the avoidance of contempt for God. For they were placed in such a strait that, whether they killed Christ or did not kill him, they sinned mortally. Yet they would not have sinned in the mere fact of not killing Christ, but because by not killing him they would have despised God. For one sin is often avoided through another. [Col. 0494D]

### Question CCXLIV

Again, in killing Christ they were not acting against conscience; indeed, they were doing what they believed should be done for God’s sake. How, then, were they sinning?

**Solution.** Although they were not acting against conscience, they nevertheless sinned mortally because they were blinded. For they did what their conscience ought to have told them not to do.

### Question CCLV

“Wishing to establish their own righteousness,” etc. It is asked how the righteousness of the law is called that of the Jews.

**Solution.** Because, in believing that they fulfilled it by their own powers, they made it their own righteousness; but not according to knowledge—that is, they did not exercise that good inclination as it ought to have been exercised according to the judgment of reason, and in this they erred. [Col. 0495A]

### Question CCLVI

“Christ is the end of the law.” It is asked how Christ is the end and fulfilment of the law, since the righteousness of the law is without aiding grace and had no merit before God.

**Solution.** Christ is not called the end or fulfilment of the law according to the manner in which it was kept by the Jews, but because he fulfils it spiritually in himself and in his own people.

### Question CCLVII

“But the righteousness which is from faith says thus: Do not say,” etc., “in your heart, Who shall ascend into heaven?” etc. It is asked how the Apostle introduced this authority. For it is taken from Deuteronomy, where Moses uses it in another sense. He forbade the Jews to say, “Who has ascended into heaven [Col. 0495B] to bring us the law?” or “Who has crossed the sea to transport the law?” or “Who has descended into hell to bring it forth for us?” because the word is near in your heart—that is, because they had the law presently at hand.

**Solution.** It is introduced suitably, even though the Apostle does not here express through it Moses’ literal sense. For just as this is literally a sin for the Jews, it may also be commanded to us figuratively that we should not ask, “Who shall ascend?” etc. Therefore the Apostle introduces Moses’ words under such a sense, and suitably represents Moses as speaking of it.

### Question CCLVIII

But someone will say: if Moses speaks in the law concerning the righteousness of faith, it seems that the righteousness of faith was in the law, and thus the law truly justified.

**Solution.** It does not follow that, because the law speaks [Col. 0495C] about the righteousness of faith, this righteousness was therefore in the law. Nor should it be accepted that Moses speaks of the righteousness of faith, unless “speaks” is understood as “signifies.” For in saying this, he figures the righteousness of faith as near—that is, not far from the nature of minds—because, as the gloss says, it is consonant with reason to believe.

### Question CCLIX

“The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart.” It is asked how this is true. Do we not believe many things which reason has not established? Hence it is written: “Faith has no merit when human reason supplies proof.”

**Solution.** If one considers how all things concerning Christ were predicted beforehand in the law and the prophets, and how they were fulfilled and confirmed by signs and wonders; how true, holy, devout, and powerful in deed and word he himself was in his own person, [Col. 0495D] what remains except to cry out: “Your testimonies have become exceedingly credible” (Ps. 92)? Reason is by no means permitted even to doubt a little. Or it is called consonant with reason because speaking and believing concerning what pertains to the soul’s salvation pleases reason itself; indeed, it desires this above all things.

### Question CCLX

“With the heart one believes unto righteousness.” The gloss says that a person can do the other things unwillingly, but cannot believe except willingly. But how is this true? Can no one hope or love except willingly? How then does it say that one can do the other things even unwillingly, since these are things other than believing?

**Solution.** By “the other things” it means external things. But again, it seems [Col. 0496A] false that someone does external things unwillingly; for if he did not will in any way, how would he do them?

**Solution.** “To will” is used in the sense of “to approve.” For we often do many things which we do not approve.

### Question CCLXI

“For everyone whoever calls upon [the Lord].” It is asked how this is true, since many call upon him and nevertheless are not saved. Hence the Lord says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 7). Is not saying this calling upon the Lord’s name?

**Solution.** To invoke is to call inwardly—that is, for God’s honor and on God’s account to desire knowledge; and this does not occur without faith, hope, and charity.

### Question CCLXII

“They could not believe, because Isaiah had foretold,” etc. It is asked concerning this prophecy whether [Col. 0496B] the prophet wished what he said to be fulfilled. If he wished it, he seems to have wished the blinding of the Jews to occur, for the prophecy was fulfilled in the Jews’ blinding.

**Solution.** It must not be conceded that he wished the Jews to be blinded, although he wished his prophecy to be fulfilled; just as Christ wished to be true what he said to Peter: “Before the cock crows, you will deny me three times” (Matt. 26), yet did not wish Peter to deny him. For many things are so connected that one cannot occur without the other, though we can will one without willing the other.

### Question CCLXIII

“Lord, who has believed our report?” etc. It is read in the Gospel concerning the Jews who did not believe, “that the saying of Isaiah might be fulfilled” (John 12). Hence they object thus: What fault was it of the Jews that they did not [Col. 0496C] believe, when the prophecy had necessarily to be fulfilled, and thus it was necessary that they should not believe?

**Solution.** God foretold the Jews’ sins through the prophet, but did not cause them. Foreknowledge of them does not impose necessity upon them. Thus, when it is said, “They did not believe, that the saying,” etc., it merely indicates that the prophecy was fulfilled in the Jews’ blindness and that it was foretold before it was fulfilled.

### Question CCLXIV

It is asked how the Jews sinned by not believing in Christ when it is written: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said: God blinded their eyes and hardened their heart” [ibid.]. Or, if they sinned in not believing in Christ, then they could believe and did not believe. If so, [Col. 0496D] how is this statement true: “Therefore they could not believe because God blinded,” etc.? How can it be true at once that they could believe and that they could not believe?

Again, he seems to place the cause of their unbelief in God, saying: “Therefore they could not [believe], because Isaiah said: God blinded their eyes,” etc.

**Solution.** It is true that they could not believe, as the Gospel says, and yet they sinned by not believing, because they came to that impossibility through the fault of their own will; therefore such an impossibility has no excuse. Both are true, then: that they could not believe and that they could believe, but not in the same respect. They could by nature, and could not by fault. For they were made such as to have the capacity not only to believe but even to see God [Col. 0497A] face to face; therefore it is said that they could believe by nature. But because by fault they became such that it was just before God not to have mercy on them, it was therefore said that, through fault, they could not believe. A similar manner of speaking occurs concerning the good angels: they are mutable by nature and immutable by grace.

What is said, “God blinded,” etc., must be understood thus: he permitted them to be blinded, not by imparting wickedness by which they might become worse, but by not conferring grace by which they might become better.

It should be noted that it is said, “They could not believe because they would not”: this exposition seems too general, for the same can be said of all who are in sins leading to death. Thus, according to this explanation, nothing special is said concerning the blinded. [Col. 0497B]

**Solution.** It may be said that the blinded deserve not to be willing to believe and that God should not have mercy on them, which not all who sin mortally do. Likewise, the further statement, “While they are proud,” etc., seems to be said too generally and simply, for this too can be said of everyone in general.

**Solution.** For “while” must be understood causally: by pride and other vices they deserve that it should be just for God not to have mercy on them.

### Question CCLXV

It is asked how this prophecy is introduced. Was it not spoken to those who belonged to the present state, though the prophecy had not yet been fulfilled? If so, how does he use this authority to argue against those then present about something still future? How did it pertain to those present then? [Col. 0497C] For the force of the proof seems to be this: all who were in the world heard Christ’s word, and therefore must be rebuked as hearers who did not believe. Again, if the prophecy had not yet been fulfilled, how can he use a verb in the past tense with a present meaning? If it is taken in a future sense, the Apostle’s proof seems absurd.

**Solution.** He spoke to those present, but not for the sake of those present only; rather, he set forth this prophecy also for all those of the future state. And he rightly rebukes those present in that time, because, although the prophecy had not been fulfilled in their time, what the prophecy foretold as future had nevertheless begun in them.

Note that some Scriptures seem to mean that Israel [Col. 0497D] did not know, while others seem to mean that it knew Christ; these appear contrary, but are not, because they are understood of different persons. For among that people some knew and others did not know.

### Question CCLXVI

“But if by grace, then no longer by works,” etc. (Rom. 11). It is asked: if everything is from grace, what is from merits? Or, if something is from merits, how is everything from grace?

**Solution.** Everything is from grace, though something is from merits, because merits themselves are from grace. Yet righteousness seems to arise from preceding merits, as in Cornelius, whose prayer obtained that he should be converted through Peter’s preaching and receive faith. Since this faith is from grace, grace therefore followed from works.

**Solution.** [Col. 0498A] It must not be said that grace or righteousness is from works, for this would mean that someone was justified from works without grace, which cannot be. Cornelius’s prayer that he might receive faith came from preceding grace; and for that grace a greater grace, namely justifying grace, was bestowed. For he was not without all grace when he believed in one God and, as the doctors say, possessed faith in the Incarnation; but he did not yet know that the Word of God had become incarnate, which he afterward learned through Peter’s preaching.

Note that there is one compunction of envy, by which a person is pierced and grieves and wastes away at the goods of others; another of guilt, by which a person is tormented in his own conscience, like Judas, who hanged himself with a noose because of his crime. Another is the compunction of grace: either that of beginners, who repent of evils [Col. 0498B] so as to abstain from them, or that of the perfect, who revere God out of love.

### Question CCLXVII

“What Israel sought, it did not obtain.” It is asked how this is true. Did it not seek external righteousness and obtain it? Therefore it obtained what it sought.

**Solution.** This is said because it lacked the end for which it acted. For it wished to be reckoned righteous before God, and this did not happen to it.

### Question CCLXVIII

“So that they may not hear, until this present day.” That the Jews of this time are blinded is plainly asserted here, and the saints say the same in many places, making the persecution of Christ the cause of the blinding, and still more their killing of James the Just. Yet it does not seem consonant with reason [Col. 0498C] that Jews now living should be punished for crimes which many of them disapprove and which their fathers committed.

**Solution.** Modern Jews too are not unjustly blinded, because, if they were given the opportunity, they would do to Christ’s members what their fathers did to Christ—and, if it were possible, to the head himself.

### Question CCLXIX

“I will magnify my ministry,” etc. It is asked what it is to honor one’s office.

**Solution.** A person honors his ministry when he expends something beyond what his office requires, as Paul did: by office he was required only to preach to the Gentiles, but he did more by preaching also to the Jews. But since Paul believed that some Jews could be converted to faith by his preaching and knew that this ought to be done for [Col. 0498D] God, he would sin if he did not do it; therefore he was obliged to do this. How then does he say that he honors his office, when he was also obliged to do what is added?

**Solution.** The obligation of office is one thing; the obligation of occasion another. Beyond the obligation of office Paul preached to the Jews and thus honored his ministry; yet he was obliged to preach to them with respect to the obligation arising from the occasion, since he knew it was to be done for God.

### Question CCLXX
