“For if their rejection is the reconciliation of the world,” etc. It is asked how the unbelief and blinding of the Jews were the cause of the salvation of the Gentiles. Would the Gentiles not have been saved unless the Jews had been blinded? Could God not save the Gentiles otherwise?

**Solution.** Their unbelief was not the efficient cause of the Gentiles’ salvation. Yet because [Col. 0499A] those who were blinded rejected the word of preaching, the Apostles received an occasion for preaching to the Gentiles. Thus the salvation of the Gentiles followed, God fulfilling his purpose through evils from which he draws a good effect.

### Question CCLXXI

“If the first-fruits are holy, so is the lump; and if the root is holy, so are the branches,” etc. It is asked whether this inference is true. Can the antecedent not be true without the consequent? How then is the inference true?

**Solution.** Although the consequent of each hypothetical statement is expressed simply, it is not to be understood simply, but with this qualification: naturally. For although the branches are broken off, they are nevertheless naturally good; and those few who have been converted to faith, if they have thus been steadfast, make it evident that those who will be converted at the end will be steadfast.

### Question CCLXXII

[Col. 0499B] But since the Jewish people is often called most hard in the Scriptures, how is it called naturally holy here, as though possessing an aptitude for holiness?

**Solution.** The Apostle deals with holiness understood as steadfastness in faith, not with an aptitude which they possessed for holiness.

### Question CCLXXIII

It may be asked: what is the first-fruits (*delibatio*)? The answer is: the tasting of a portion of some thing as a test of the whole mass. The mass is the multitude to be converted after the death of Antichrist. The Jews are called natural branches because they are born from the patriarchs, in whom was the origin of faith and from whom Christ was born according to the flesh.

Note that “nature” is called the customary course of nature, against which God often acts. Nature is also sometimes called the divine [Col. 0499C] disposition, against which God does nothing, but acts wholly in accordance with it.

### Question CCLXXIV

“For the gift and calling of God are without repentance,” that is, without change. God sometimes changes his sentence, but not his counsel. What is it to change a sentence? To do something which he did not seem about to do, or not to do something which he did seem about to do.

### Question CCLXXV

The interpreter says that, while the wicked act against God’s will, God’s will is fulfilled by them. But if God’s will is fulfilled by them, do they not themselves fulfil God’s will? And if so, how do they act against God’s will?

**Solution.** “Will” is used in two ways: for God’s command [Col. 0499D] and for his disposition. Thus, while they act against God’s command, they do what God has disposed to occur. For good things are often done through the wicked; and from evils which the wicked do, God always draws some good.

### Question CCLXXVI

“Whoever hears the Father comes to the Son. For no one comes to the Son unless the Father draws him” (John 6). It is asked what it is for the Father to draw a person to the Son.

**Solution.** It is to come, through the disposition which is from the Father, to knowledge of the Son in order to be saved by him. The Father draws to the Son when the Father reveals that the Son is equal to himself.

### Question CCLXXVII

“God has shut up all under sin, that he may have mercy upon all.” It is asked how this is to be understood. Is not shutting up under sin evil? How does God do this, or how [Col. 0500A] is it a cause of good?

**Solution.** God shut up all under sin, that is, he permitted them to be shut up. This is an occasion of good, not an efficient cause.

### Question CCLXXVIII

It is asked whether God brought about our salvation more by this way than by another—namely, by shutting up all under sin.

**Solution.** It so pleased God: that, seeing themselves unable to be justified, they might be humbled, seek grace, and thus ascribe everything to God. “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God,” etc.

Here a threefold kind of causes is commonly distinguished. Some are formal, others judicial, others final; some are causes according to which things occur, others through which, and others for which they occur. Judgments are judicial causes; counsels, final causes; and the causes through which things occur are formal causes, or wisdom and knowledge are formal causes.

### Question CCLXXIX

[Col. 0500B] The foregoing exclamation is commonly questioned. For the Apostle seems to exclaim somewhat without deliberation concerning the blinding of the Jews and the entrance of the Gentiles, saying, “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” although he knew how to give a reason for this, as when he says, “I do not want you to be ignorant of the mystery” [ibid.], etc., and afterward adds, “God has shut up all under sin, that he may have mercy upon all” [ibid.]. If he exclaims because human understanding is not sufficient fully to give an account of this, would it not follow by similar reasoning that he ought to exclaim over many other things?

**Solution.** He exclaims over this rather than another matter because in giving reasons for it one more readily errs and commits sin unto death.

### Question CCLXXX

“For from him, and through him, [Col. 0500C] and in him are all things.” It is asked whether sins, insofar as they exist, are from God. For if all things are from him, then sins are also; or else sins are not among all things.

**Solution.** Some say that sins, insofar as they exist, have being from God. But Augustine, in *On the Nature of the Good*, says that when all things are said to be from God, only things which exist naturally should be understood, not sins, which corrupt nature. Therefore sins are not from God in any respect.

### Question CCLXXXI

It is asked whether all things that have being from God ought to be called “of God.”

**Solution.** Only those which have being from the substance of God ought to be called “of God,” such as the Son and the Holy Spirit. They are so from God the Father that they are also of him, because they are consubstantial with him from his essence. [Col. 0500D] Creatures, however, are from God, not from God’s substance, but from nothing.

Note that by the three prepositions—“from,” “through,” and “in”—the Trinity of persons is here indicated; by the same pronoun the identity of nature is signified, a nature wholly present in each person. For in saying “from whom” he understands the Father; “through whom,” the Son; “in whom,” the Holy Spirit.

### Question CCLXXXII

It is asked, moreover, how, when he says “from whom are all things,” he understands the Father, since all things are from the Father just as they are from the Son and the Holy Spirit.

**Solution.** This is because of the Father’s primacy of authorship: all things have being from the Father in such a way that he does not have being from another. The Son and the Holy Spirit, although they are one principle of all creatures, nevertheless have a principle, or author—namely the Father [Col. 0501A] himself—from whom they have being. And they receive from the Father this very fact that they are the principle of all things, just as they receive from him all other things which they possess.

The interpreter says that in the Trinity there are the highest origin of all things, the most perfect beauty, and the most blessed delight—referring origin to the Father, beauty to the Son, and delight to the Holy Spirit. Thus these three—origin, beauty, and delight—are determinate, because each is assigned in a determinate way to a distinct person, as has already been said. But because the whole Trinity in turn is the supreme origin of all things, the most perfect beauty, and the most blessed delight, the same three are called infinite. And this, I think, is what is meant by the statement that the aforesaid three are both determinate from one another and infinite in themselves.

[Col. 0501B] **QUESTION 283.** Again it is said: In the Father there is unity; in the Son, equality; in the Holy Spirit, the concord of unity and equality. But since the same unity, equality, and concord belong to the three, it is asked why unity is said to be in the Father, equality in the Son, and concord in the Holy Spirit.

**Answer.** Preserving reverence for these mysteries, we say that unity is therefore said to be in the Father because, just as unity is the principle of numbers but does not derive its being from another number, so the Father, although he is the cause of all things, has no cause. Equality, moreover, is said to be in the Son because in him there is the first distinction and differentiation, the first plurality, and the second personal unity. So that this unity may be shown to be neither different from nor unequal to the Father himself, it is fittingly designated by the name [Col. 0501C] of equality. This declares that the Son has being from the Father alone in such a way that he is not the Father, nor different from him in nature, but is in all things equal and consubstantial with him. The Holy Spirit, however, is called the concord of unity and equality in order to indicate that the Holy Spirit is from both in such a way as to be equal to each of them. I say this while preserving the Catholic faith; and I would rather hear from another the hidden meaning of these words than say anything about them from my own inadequacy.

**QUESTION 284.** Again, one reads: “All things are one on account of the Father; all things are equal on account of the Son; all things are connected on account of the Holy Spirit.” How, then, should these words be understood? Are not the three persons one by the same unity, equal by the same [Col. 0501D] equality, and concordant by the same concord?

**Answer.** All things are one on account of the Father; that is, the three persons are one, possessing the same natural unity, which is customarily referred to the Father, though it is common to the three persons. The same must be understood concerning equality and concord. For the three persons are equal through the ineffable and natural equality by which they are thus united.

In creatures a trace of the Trinity shines forth, because they show in themselves that they possess unity, form, and order: for every thing is both one thing, is formed by some species, and keeps some order. Hence it was said: “He made all things in number, weight, and measure” (Wisdom 11). Number pertains to unity, weight to order, and measure to form. For of every thing it is true [Col. 0502A] that, from the moment it begins to be, it at once falls under number, because it is either one or many. Weight is said to pertain to order because individual things keep order according to the nature of their weight. There are two kinds of weights: one tends downward, as does the nature of lead; the other tends upward, as oil does. Again, order is considered according to place and time; hence angels receive their greater or lesser orders according to their affections and delights [“loves”]. The form of things, however, is a certain mode and measure of them.

**QUESTION 285.** It is further asked whether the Holy Spirit proceeds from himself or is sent by himself, as he proceeds from and is sent by the Father and the Son.

**Answer.** The procession or mission of the Holy Spirit is twofold: eternal and temporal. According to eternal procession, he proceeds only from the Father and the Son, not from himself. Temporally, however, he also proceeds from himself, because his temporal procession is an operation of the Trinity. The same should be understood concerning the temporal procession or mission of the Son. For just as he sanctified himself for us and did not betray himself, so he also sent himself—that is, he effected his own mission or incarnation, which is the same thing. But the Son’s eternal procession from the Father ought not to be called mission, but generation.

**QUESTION 286.** It is asked further how the Holy Spirit is the love by which the Father loves the Son and the Son the Father. Is not loving, for the Father, the same as being, and as that by which he has being and loves? If, then, [Col. 0502C] the Father loves by the Holy Spirit, how does he not have being from the Holy Spirit?

**Answer.** It is not said that the Father loves by the Holy Spirit, but that the Holy Spirit is the love by which the Father loves the Son, because the Holy Spirit is the divine nature and the Father loves by the divine nature. But if, by the expression “the love by which the Father loves the Son,” a personal property is meant, then it is not true that the Holy Spirit is the love by which the Father loves, just as the Holy Spirit is not the Father.

**QUESTION 287.** Hilary says: “Just as it is impious to proclaim two gods, the Father and the Son, so it is sacrilegious to proclaim a solitary God.” Again, the expositor says, speaking of the Trinity, that it is one singly according to substance [Col. 0502D]; this appears contrary.

**Answer.** Singularity sometimes excludes a plurality of persons, and in this sense it is sacrilegious to proclaim the Father and the Son a solitary God. At other times singularity is used for unity; and it is understood in this sense when it is said that, according to substance, it is one singly.

**QUESTION 288.** “Do not think more highly than you ought to think,” etc. (Romans 12). It is asked who thinks more highly than he ought. For no one in this life has such knowledge that he could not have more, and that he ought not even to desire more. How, then, does the Apostle command us not to think more highly than we ought, as though someone could, by inquiry concerning God, comprehend more than is necessary?

**Answer.** The Apostle does not prohibit inquiry into [Col. 0503A] truth, but forbids anyone through excessive investigation to fall into doubt concerning matters which must be believed firmly and without hesitation. Or he forbids someone to attribute to himself, with proud presumption, the understanding that he possesses. This is to be proud of one’s knowledge; for this is not wisdom but folly.

**QUESTION 289.** “He who shows mercy, with cheerfulness,” etc. It is asked, then, whether God punishes anyone without mercy; that is, whether he punishes those whom he punishes only as much as they have deserved to be punished. This seems so because “judgment without mercy will be for him who does not show mercy” (James 2). Yet again it is written: “All the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Psalm 42). Hence it seems that he does not punish even the wicked without mercy, according to the words: “He did not kindle all his anger” [Col. 0503B] (Psalm 77), that is, he did not punish them as much as they deserved, since he could justly have done more, had he wished.

**Answer.** God punishes no one without mercy, because he punishes no one as much as that person has deserved. Yet there is judgment without mercy for one who does not show mercy, because such a person is no longer corrected so as to attain eternal life. It is therefore true that, just as God will in the future grant the good more good from grace than they have deserved, so he gives the wicked less evil than they have deserved; and in both cases God is just and merciful.

**QUESTION 290.** It is asked why he says “judgment without mercy,” etc., of this matter rather than another, when this could be said of any crime.

**Answer.** Understand that it is said of this matter because many have fallen into this error: they believe that, for attaining eternal life, it is enough not to harm others and to turn away from evil, even though they do not give their own goods to the poor or perform works of mercy. Here the Apostle openly represses this error.

**QUESTION 291.** “Rejoice with those who rejoice,” etc. It is asked whether one ought to rejoice at temporal prosperity, for example at someone’s abundance of riches.

**Answer.** Since such things are given to the good and the evil, and more often to the evil than to the good, it does not seem that one should rejoice if they are given to anyone, nor grieve if they are taken away. God, however, must always be praised in his gifts.

**QUESTION 292.** “Weep with those who weep,” etc. It is asked concerning the weeping commanded by the Apostle whether it is reasonable, since one ought rather to rejoice than grieve concerning adversities that happen to good or evil persons. For adversities serve either for a greater crown to the good or for the correction of the evil. We also read that people wept imprudently at the death of martyrs, when it would rather have been right to rejoice than to weep, if the force of grief admitted reason.

**Answer.** One kind of weeping is that of natural affection; another is that of compassion. The former, which belongs to natural affection, is as it were natural and, according to some, does not merit reward. The latter, which belongs to compassion, does merit reward. For we ought to suffer with the weaknesses of our brethren, so that we may win those whose salvation we ought to desire and for whose salvation we ought to labor.

**QUESTION 293.** “Repaying no one evil for evil,” and “Love your enemies.” It is asked how the saints do not repay evil for evil, when it is written: [Col. 0504A] “The saints cry out: ‘Avenge, Lord, our blood’” (Revelation 6); and: “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance” (Psalm 37). Therefore, since good and evil alike desire that the Lord avenge them, in what are they distinguished?

**Answer.** The good do not rejoice in punishment as the evil do, but in God’s judgment.

**QUESTION 294.** It is asked whether Christ observes what the Apostle above commanded all, namely, that he repay evil for evil to no one. They wish to prove that Christ does not observe this. An evil person has deserved that evil be repaid to him for evil; therefore, unless God repays him evil, he will not render to him what he has deserved. Again, God renders something to him for evil—therefore either good or evil. If not evil, then good; and thus evil has deserved good. Again, does not God render punishment for guilt and [Col. 0504B] thus evil for evil?

**Answer.** Neither a good judge nor God repays evil for evil, because that would mean exercising vengeance with an evil intention. Hence one must carefully avoid drawing this conclusion in all the foregoing cases.

**QUESTION 295.** It is asked whether, according to what has been said, justice by which someone is hanged for theft and the like belongs to the Gospel. This seems so, since the Church hands him over to the ruler, and all the Church’s justice ought to be what is taught there. “See, here are two swords” (Luke 22). But if this belongs to the Church, as it seems to do, how can it be denied that the justice of the Gospel is more severe than the justice of the Law? For under the Law a tooth was commanded for a tooth, an eye for an eye (Matthew 5), whereas here a man’s head is given for a goat.

**Answer.** It is in no way the justice of the Gospel that a man should be killed for a horse or an ox. This is commanded nowhere in the whole Gospel; nor does the Gospel do this, but the Church merely permits it.

**QUESTION 296.** “Providing things good not only before God but also before men,” etc. It is asked what it is to provide good things before God.

**Answer.** It is to do in the secrecy of the heart—that is, to do for God those things which conscience dictates ought to be done.

**QUESTION 297.** But since God requires us also to provide good things before men, how does he distinguish between this and the former?

**Answer.** The meaning is this: the Apostle commands us also to do good things so carefully that the weak may not be scandalized, but may receive a good example for progress. In this very matter he also represses the proud presumption of some, who pay no attention to scandals affecting the weak, considering only what is permitted, not what is expedient.

**QUESTION 298.** “If your enemy is hungry, feed him,” etc. In the Law it is written: “You shall love your friend and hate your enemy” (ibid.). This seems contrary to the command: “Love your enemies” (ibid.), and to this: “If your enemy is hungry, feed him.”

**Answer.** To hate enemies is not a command in the Law, but a permission. And, according to some, loving enemies in the Gospel is counsel rather than command; thus there is no contradiction. Understanding this, David says: “If I have repaid evils to those repaying me, may I deservedly fall empty before my enemies” [Col. 0505A] (Psalm 7).

**QUESTION 299.** “There is no authority except from God,” etc. (Romans 13). It is agreed that the authority of the good is from God; concerning the authority of the evil, it is asked whether it is from God. If it is from God, it is good, because God is the author only of good things. But how is the authority of the evil good, when evil things are done through it, and when Scripture often calls it wicked and unjust? On the other hand, Scripture testifies that the authority of the evil is from God; how then is it evil?

**Answer.** The authority of the evil is good and from God; nevertheless, it is called evil on account of the malice of those who abuse it, just as the Law is indeed good but may be an occasion of evil, as may the light of the sun and many similar things.

**QUESTION 300.** It is asked what he calls authority.

[Col. 0505B] **Answer.** Some say that it is God’s ordinance, by which certain persons have authority over others. Others say that it is the persons themselves, established in high station as kings and rulers, who must be obeyed in all matters pertaining to authority. But if they command anything contrary to God, they are not to be obeyed.

**QUESTION 301.** It is asked whether the power to sin is from God. This is argued as follows: Pilate’s power, by which he was able to crucify the Savior, was from God, as the Gospel says (John 19); therefore the power to sin is from God. Again, on the contrary, because God is omnipotent, he cannot sin; therefore being able to sin is not power, nor is the power of sinning a power, but an impotence.

**Answer.** What is called “the power to sin” is a certain capacity to do something that cannot be done without sin, or a certain office by which someone may lawfully do what is not done without sin. Thus Pilate’s authority was indeed good, namely from God; by it he had authority to crucify Christ, just as from royal authority someone may exercise tyranny and, under the appearance of ordered authority, rage against his subjects. Yet to crucify Christ or exercise tyranny is not power but rather impotence, which is often called the power of sinning. It arises from defect or from a limit of good, and it existed even in the first man before sin.

**QUESTION 302.** “He who loves his neighbor has fulfilled the law,” etc. It is asked whether love of neighbor and love [Col. 0505D] of God are the same. If they are not the same, how is love of neighbor the fulfillment of the Law? How is the whole Law summed up in love of neighbor? How are the three commandments of the first table, which concern God, fulfilled by love of neighbor? Again, if this love and that are the same, why was one command given separately concerning love of God and another concerning love of neighbor?

**Answer.** Love is the name of a virtue, and in this sense it can be said that the love by which we love God and neighbor is the same. It is also the name of a movement of the mind, and in this sense love of God is one thing and love of neighbor another; love of God is greater and love of neighbor lesser, since love of God is contained in love of neighbor. For whoever loves God consequently loves his neighbor, and conversely; therefore one command is given in place of both [Col. 0506A] commandments. Love of neighbor is a movement of the mind toward one’s neighbor for God’s sake; how, then, can there be love of neighbor without love of God? Love of neighbor is a kind of matter in which love of God, which lies more hidden, is exercised; its effect appears in love of neighbor. Love of God is a movement of the mind toward God for his own sake.

**QUESTION 303.** But since love of God is worthier than love of neighbor, why did the Apostle mention love of neighbor rather than love of God, calling it the fulfillment of the Law?

**Answer.** Because love of neighbor appears more clearly in everyday life and conduct.

**QUESTION 304.** It is asked whether love of neighbor can exist without love of God. This seems possible, because someone may love his neighbor not for God’s sake but for some other reason.

[Col. 0506B] **Answer.** It must not be granted that someone loves his neighbor unless he loves him for God’s sake. To love otherwise is not to love but rather to hate, because “he who loves iniquity hates his own soul” (Psalm 10); and thus one who hates himself does not love another either.

**QUESTION 305.** Again, it is asked whether we ought mutually to love one another for eternal life. If this is granted, it seems that we act for our own advantage and are therefore hirelings. For Ambrose says that one who serves in hope and desire for the heavenly homeland is a hireling.

**Answer.** One’s neighbor ought to be loved for eternal life; nor is anything thereby preferred to God, because he himself is eternal life. In him there is nothing outside himself apart from himself. Therefore it is not fitting to extend Ambrose’s preceding words beyond their proper context, since they seem contrary to the Church’s usage. Yet he seems to mean this: if someone, thinking that eternal life were something separate from God, did good works while attending only to his own advantage and not because God willed it to be done, that person would be called a hireling.

**QUESTION 306.** It is asked whether all are to be loved equally.

**Answer.** Some say that all are to be loved equally in affection, but not in effect; indeed, some more and some less, according to what is written: “He ordered charity in me” (Song 2). Others hold that, even in affection, some ought to be preferred to others—for example, the better to the less good, and parents to strangers. Charity is therefore ordered both in affection and effect. This may occur in many ways: sometimes affection ought to be unequal; sometimes affection equal and effect unequal; and conversely.

**QUESTION 307.** It is asked where a command or teaching has been given concerning how a person ought to love himself.

**Answer.** When a person is taught how God ought to be loved, he is thereby taught how he ought to love himself. For what is it to love oneself except to love one’s own good? But what is the good of a human being except God? Whoever, therefore, loves God thereby loves himself; and insofar as he loves God, so far he loves himself.

[Col. 0507A] **QUESTION 308.** It is asked whether a person ought to love his neighbor as much as himself, because it is written: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Matthew 22).

**Answer.** According to some, when it is said, “Love your neighbor as yourself,” “as” indicates likeness, not quantity: that is, as you seek for yourself, so seek for your neighbor—that he may possess God; and, as far as you can, labor that he may do those things by which he is saved. What has already been said above concerning charity need not be repeated. For not all things can, or ought, to be said everywhere.

**QUESTION 309.** “Receive the weak in faith,” etc. It is asked in what sense he understands “weak.”

**Answer.** Here he understands weakness not according to firmness, but according to knowledge of faith.

[Col. 0507B] **QUESTION 310.** “He who is weak, let him eat vegetables. Let each be fully assured in his own mind.” It is asked how the Apostle advises that one who distinguishes foods be left to himself, when it is evil to distinguish foods and to judge one clean and another unclean. Rather, he ought to be drawn back from such error; for by granting this, the Apostle seems to encourage him in his error.

**Answer.** He permits the lesser evil in order to avoid the greater. For it would be a greater evil to eat against conscience than to abstain from certain foods while supposing that one ought to abstain from them. For whoever acts against conscience sins.

**QUESTION 311.** It is asked whether one who thus distinguishes foods sins. Does he not live according to the Apostle’s teaching? If so, how does he sin?

**Answer.** [Col. 0507C] Here the Apostle does not teach that this ought to be done as a good, but shows that it is a lesser evil. It is a lesser evil to err through good zeal than manifestly to sin against conscience. Therefore, lest he incur the greater sin, he should be tolerated rather than provoked. There are certain things prohibited even in the New Testament: for example, that no one eat animal blood or use animals that have been strangled. We also abstain from some things because it is unnecessary to use them, such as horseflesh—not because it would be equally good for food as beef, but because there is no need. We abstain from some things because they are harmful, such as snake, toad, and the like; these are poisonous and therefore kill those who eat them.

[Col. 0507D] **QUESTION 312.** It is asked how they distinguished foods. Did they posit some impurity in these rather than those, for which reason they refused to eat them? If so, they directed blame through the creature back upon God, and thus sinned mortally. But if they sinned mortally, how does the Apostle command that they be tolerated in death?

**Answer.** They erred and sinned, but venially, not mortally. For they abstained from certain foods not because they believed some impurity to inhere in them, but because, having been under the Law, they had become accustomed to abstain from them, and it was burdensome for them to abandon the custom.

**QUESTION 313.** It is asked to whom what the Apostle says here pertains.

**Answer.** What he says, “Receive [accept] the weak” [Col. 0508A] (Romans 14), appears to concern prelates. Again, in this chapter he seems to say certain things that concern the weak, such as: “Let not him who does not eat despise him who eats, and let not him who eats judge him who does not eat” (ibid.). For by these words he seems to instruct the weak.

**QUESTION 314.** “Before his own master he stands or falls.” When the Apostle says this, he seems to remove from us every judgment concerning goodness. For since a person is good by intention and charity alone, and these are not subject to human judgment, how can we judge anyone good?

**Answer.** The Church judges only what is manifest, not what is hidden. It does not judge that charity is in someone—for then it would judge to exist what it did not know to exist—but that the signs of charity present in him show that charity is in him. Likewise, when it judges or condemns someone, it does not judge that he is guilty of the crime of which he is accused, but that the evidences in the accusation concur against him, on account of which it gives a just sentence against him. If it is objected that the witnesses by whom he is convicted are false, and the accusation false, because he is not guilty of the alleged crime, we say that the accusation is true and the witnesses true, even if he is not guilty of that crime. For an accusation is called true—that is, irreproachable—when it is made according to judicial procedure. Likewise we say that the Church condemns one judged guilty, even though the crime for which he is accused is not in him, because we take him as convicted there according to judicial procedure.

**QUESTION 315.** “Doubtful matters must be interpreted in the better sense,” as the expositor says. It is asked, then, how we ought [Col. 0508C] to interpret ambiguous matters in the better sense. For when I am equally uncertain concerning a good act, whether it is good, and concerning an evil act, whether it is evil, I seem no less indiscreet in judging the former good than in judging the latter evil. But when neither is settled and certain to me, I ought to determine neither. How, then, should we understand the saying that ambiguous matters must be interpreted in the better sense?

**Answer.** Here “to believe,” “to judge,” or “to interpret” is taken to mean “to wish.” For the Apostle advises this: when we see ambiguous things being done, we should wish that they are done with a good intention and not an evil one. Since we cannot know with what intention they are done, we ought not judge what we cannot know.

[Col. 0508D] **QUESTION 316.** Again, the expositor says: “He who thinks an evil person evil is mistaken; but he who thinks an evil person good is not mistaken.” But is it not true that an evil person is evil, and false that an evil person is good? How then is one who thinks what is true mistaken, and one who thinks what is false not mistaken?

**Answer.** Without prejudice to a better opinion, we say that this should be understood thus: one who thinks an evil person evil is mistaken—he is delayed in his course—because he despises and scorns him, or at least loves him less. But one who thinks an evil person good is not mistaken; that is, he is not hindered or delayed in the path of conduct, because, in believing him good, he loves him more, and thus in some sense advances by erring.

It should be noted that some things are manifestly good and some manifestly evil, and we may judge concerning them, even if we do not know with what intention they are done. But there are also intermediate matters, which can be good or evil; it is dangerous to judge of these, and the Lord has forbidden it. These we ought to interpret in the better sense, as blessed Jerome says: “If you see a priest raising his hand over a woman, say that he does this to bless her.” This authority should be understood according to the preceding explanation. Yet we can rarely judge even concerning manifest goods, since almost nothing can be done by a righteous person that cannot also be done by an evil person, such as miracles, signs, and the like. He fasts, prays, and does other such things, which are signs of goodness. “Let each be fully assured in his own mind” (ibid.); that is, let him be permitted to remain in his own conscience, if the matter is not mortal, lest, when called away from it, he sin more gravely.

[Col. 0509B] **QUESTION 317.** “We shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ,” etc. It is asked how the Apostle says, “We shall all stand,” when elsewhere Scripture says: “You shall sit upon twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel” (Matthew 19). If the saints will sit at the hour of judgment, how will they stand? Or if they stand, how will they sit?

**Answer.** They are said to stand out of reverence for the supreme Judge, but to sit as those who will themselves judge.

**QUESTION 318.** “Nothing is unclean except for the one who considers something unclean.” The Apostle seems to suggest that the gravity of guilt must be assigned according to the degree and quality of conscience. Thus, if someone believes a venial sin to be mortal, by committing it against conscience he sins mortally—even if he merely lifts a straw from the ground when conscience dictates that this is a mortal sin. Thus it seems possible to conclude that every sin against conscience is mortal. For anyone who acts against his conscience, even by committing a venial sin, seems to despise God, because he places himself before God.

**Answer.** In a venial sin that is against conscience, some sin mortally and others venially. If someone commits such a venial sin against conscience while believing that he will be punished eternally if he commits it, he sins mortally and despises God. But if, through some weakness, conscience tells him that he is not damned for it, though he nevertheless acts contrary to it, he sins venially; he neither puts himself before God nor despises God. If someone objects that he sins against conscience and therefore approves the committed sin, and thus sins mortally, because authority testifies that “Everyone to whom sin is pleasing,” etc., sins mortally:

**Answer.** “To be pleasing” is taken in the sense of “to make habitual use of”; and whoever makes habitual use of any venial sin is guilty of death, as Augustine says.

**QUESTION 319.** “It is good for a man not to eat meat or drink wine,” etc. Jerome uses this argument against Jovinian: “It is good not to drink wine; therefore it is evil to drink.” But if drinking wine is evil, everyone who drinks wine sins, and the Apostle’s statement appears false: “I know and am confident in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean through him” (Romans 14).

**Answer.** According to [Col. 0510A] Jerome, drinking wine is called evil on account of occasion, because lust easily arises from drinking wine. The force of the argument is: if evil is avoided through abstinence from wine, an occasion of evil is easily taken through drinking wine. Therefore the Apostle says, “It is good for a man not to eat,” etc.; that is, it is good by abstinence from meat, wine, or any other food to prevent one’s neighbor from being offended. The Apostle could equally have spoken of beans, peas, and similar things.

**QUESTION 320.** “Everything that is not from faith is sin.” It is asked how “faith” is understood here: whether as the judgment of conscience or as the Catholic faith. The questions must therefore be considered according to both meanings.

Everything done against faith, that is, against the judgment of conscience, is sin. The judgment of conscience is that by which we believe something ought to be done for God. Nothing should be done against this—for example, if someone believes that a man should be killed if possible. If he does not do it, he sins even mortally, according to some. Others, however, think it is not mortal unless the person who believes this ought to be done for God also thinks that he sins mortally if he does not do it.

[Col. 0510B] **QUESTION 321.** It is asked, then, whether, when this person kills a righteous man with this intention, since he believes that he ought to do so, he merits by doing it. For whoever does for God’s sake what he thinks should be done for God’s sake merits; but this person does for God’s sake what he believes should be done for God’s sake; therefore he merits by this. That he ought to do this follows from the fact that, if he leaves it undone, he sins mortally.

**Answer.** Some plausibly say that he has brought himself into a narrow pass, and thus falls whether he goes forward or retreats: as when someone sees fire before him and perceives a precipice of water behind him, he encounters danger on either side. Others think that two elements are present: error and zeal. What belongs to error is evil, but what belongs to zeal is good and has merit. The will is good, but the thing in which it is exercised is evil. Therefore in the latter he sins, and in the former he merits.

**QUESTION 322.** “The whole life of unbelievers is sin,” as the expositor says. But do not unbelievers also perform certain good acts, such as sowing fields, building houses, and feeding their parents? Although these acts are not worthy of eternal life, they are nevertheless praiseworthy and in no way sins. How, then, is the whole life of unbelievers sin?

**Answer.** He calls “unbelievers” those who act against faith, not those who lack faith.

[Col. 0510D] **QUESTION 323.** Now let us pursue the other part of the question, according as “faith” is understood as the Catholic faith. Thus, when the Apostle says, “Everything that is not from faith is sin” (Acts 10), he seems to mean that no one lacking faith does anything beneficial to himself. This seems untrue, since Cornelius, though not yet possessing faith, was heard when he prayed; and elsewhere it is written: “Those who faithfully administer the affairs of Babylon will at some time deserve to be delivered from Babylon.”

**Answer.** The Apostle intends to say that nothing benefits one who lacks faith for attaining eternal life unless he comes to faith. Indeed, according to some, even all such persons’ good acts harm them, because good things mixed with evils are accustomed to harm, and the more a person abuses virtues, the more he offends. Hence Augustine: “The least good things are better than the greatest when they are mixed with evils.”

**QUESTION 324.** It is asked here, since everything not from faith is sin, whether a Jew sins by saying that Christ is God when compelled to say it. For in saying this he seems to lie, since he speaks against conscience; thus in saying it he seems to sin mortally.

**Answer.** It does not seem to sound well in the ears of the faithful that a Jew sins mortally by saying that Christ is God; nor do we say this, though some seem to assert it. For to lie is to say what the judgment of conscience dictates ought not to be said. Or, properly speaking, to lie is to say what is false with the intention of deceiving. Therefore, where there is no falsehood, there is no lie; nevertheless, someone can be guilty of lying even while speaking the truth. No virtue is genuine unless it is formed by knowledge of eternal truth. Nor, even in the best moral conduct—as is apparent in philosophers, who flourished in excellent morals—was there true virtue; rather, they shone with a false virtue because they lacked knowledge of eternal truth.

**QUESTION 325.** “For Christ did not please himself” (Romans 15). It is asked how this should be understood. Is not the will of the Father and that of the Son one? How, then, could he please the Father and not himself? Yet no one doubts that he pleased the Father in all things.

**Answer.** He did not please himself according to [Col. 0511C] the weakness of the flesh, whose affliction he did not reject, in accordance with what he says elsewhere: “I have not come to do my own will” (John 6); that is, he did not come to fulfill the inclination which he possessed from the nature of the flesh, but subjected it to the rule of reason, and this reason obeyed the divine will in all things.

**QUESTION 326.** “But the Gentiles, on account of mercy,” etc. God in a certain manner bound himself to the Jews by promise, whereas he came to the Gentiles by mercy alone. Yet he did both by grace: both promising himself to them and coming over to these. Nevertheless, because of the promises made to the Jews, truth is spoken of them; but mercy of the Gentiles, because what came to them and received them occurred by grace alone, not by God’s promise.

[Col. 0511D] **QUESTION 327.** But was not a promise made to the Gentiles when the Lord says in Hosea: “I will call my people ‘not my people’” (Hosea 2)? Again, Isaiah: “Rejoice, Gentiles, with his people” (Romans 15). Again: “Rejoice, barren woman who does not bear” (Galatians 4), etc.

**Answer.** A promise was not made to the Gentiles in the sense that the promise was directed to them: no writings concerning that promise were given to them. Or no promise was made to them that Christ would come to them and preach in his own person; for he came only to the Jews and preached to them. Hence the Apostle says that he was a minister of the circumcision.

**QUESTION 328.** “There shall be a root of Jesse, and he who rises to rule the Gentiles,” etc. It is asked why he is called the root of Jesse.

**Answer.** Because David proceeded from him [Col. 0512A], having been made king and having protected many by his power, just as a tree commonly protects by its roots, branches, and leaves.

**QUESTION 329.** It is also asked what kind of prophecy this was, since Isaiah began to exist after Jesse’s death. Does prophecy perhaps use the future for the past, as it often uses the past for the future?

**Answer.** This prophecy concerns the future, and its meaning is: “There shall be a root of Jesse,” etc.; that is, Jesse will be called a root, and from that root there will arise one who rises up, namely Christ.

### QUESTION CCCXXX

“I shall travel through you into Spain,” etc. The question is whether the Apostle was lying when he said that he would go through Rome into Spain, although it is established that, when he said this, he did not do so. For he did not then come to Rome. Perhaps, [Col. 0512B] as Jerome thinks, he crossed over to Spain by ship; hence it is said, “He shall plunder the sea,” which Jerome recalls as having been spoken concerning Paul alone: for he plundered for Christ the Spaniards surrounded by the sea, by converting them.

Answer. To lie, as Gregory says, is to state what is false with an intention to deceive. Since Paul did not do this, we do not say that he lied. He said this because he hoped that he could set out; nevertheless, the words he spoke signified something false. Yet he did not lie in intention: for he had resolved to do this, because he believed that it would indeed happen.

### QUESTION CCCXXXI

“According to the revelation of the mystery kept silent through eternal ages,” etc. (Rom. XVI.) [Col. 0512C] The question is how he calls them “eternal times” when he says “through eternal ages.”

Answer. Some understand “eternal times” as everything which preceded the creation of the world from the creation of the angels onward. In those times there was succession, but not passing away. Therefore, in a remarkable manner, there was there a certain immutability, and thus a certain eternity; and also a certain mutability, and thus a certain temporality. Yet nearly all say that the angels were not created before the creation of the world. Therefore perhaps he calls them eternal times as though saying that the mystery was kept silent and hidden from the beginning of the world.

### QUESTION CCCXXXII

“To God alone wise,” etc. The question is whether by the name “God” the Trinity is here understood, or the person of the Father.

Answer. Augustine says [Col. 0512D] that this is a name of the Trinity; according to some, it is a name of the Father. But on this account it seems that the Father alone is wise, which is contrary to faith. Therefore it must be known that “alone” is sometimes exclusive of a person, sometimes only of a nature.

### QUESTION CCCXXXIII

Moreover, when it is said, “God, Trinity, wisdom, wise,” the question is: by what wisdom? Is it the unbegotten wisdom, which is the Father; the begotten wisdom, which is the Son; the wisdom proceeding from the Father and the Son, which is the Holy Spirit; or wisdom which is neither unbegotten nor begotten nor proceeding?

Answer. The name “Trinity” signifies only as much as “three persons,” or Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. The Father is wise by unbegotten wisdom; the Son by begotten wisdom [Col. 0513A]; the Holy Spirit by wisdom proceeding from the Father and the Son. And unbegotten wisdom, begotten wisdom, [Col. 0514A] and proceeding wisdom are not three wisdoms, but naturally one wisdom.

## II. ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0513]

### QUESTION I

[Col. 0513A] “Paul, called an Apostle,” etc. (1 Cor. I.) This Epistle sent to the Corinthians, although it is arranged second in the collection of Epistles, was not written second by the Apostle. For both Epistles sent to the Corinthians were written before [Col. 0513B] that which is to the Romans. This is clear because in the Epistle to the Romans he says that he will proceed to Rome after he has delivered to the poor who are in Jerusalem the collection made by the Achaeans. He makes mention in these Epistles of making that collection.

But it is not without a rational cause that the Epistle to the Romans is placed before the others in the collection of Epistles, namely, because of the dignity of the Romans. Or rather, because in it the first vice is removed and destroyed, namely pride. The Corinthians, however, had been converted to the faith by the Apostle, but afterwards were overthrown and deceived in many ways by false apostles. They erred concerning the efficacy of the sacraments, and especially concerning the efficacy of baptism, thinking that baptism conferred by an evil person had no efficacy; that it was greater when bestowed by a better person, and less when bestowed by a less good one. [Col. 0513C]

They also thought too little of the Apostle and held him in contempt, because he had not come to them with words of human wisdom, but in the simplicity of faith, for the instruction of little ones. They also held unsound opinions concerning the resurrection, saying that it had already happened; indeed, some among them denied it altogether. Some also wished to keep the Law together with the Gospel as though necessary for salvation. They sinned also in marriage, as in many other matters, and caused schisms; and the Apostle intends to correct them in these things. For after pride has been cut down in us, it remains for us likewise to cut down the other vices.

From these things, therefore, it is apparent what is the subject matter of this Epistle, what its intention is, and what its method and order of treatment are. The particular subject matter of this [Col. 0513D] Epistle is the condition of the Corinthians as it was when the Apostle wrote to them from Ephesus. Its intention is to recall them from disputes to unity of faith. Its method is such that he instructs, corrects, strengthens, and praises according to the qualities of the persons. Its order is this: he first sets forth a greeting, according to the custom of letter-writers, lest he seem to have rebuked them at the outset. Then he puts their good qualities first, so that others may be conformed to them; and thus he comes to rebuking their dissension. He begins, therefore, with the greeting, saying, “Paul,” using a name of humility against pride; “Apostle,” a name of dignity and office.

### QUESTION II

“Through the will of God,” etc. The question is what he here calls the will of God. For the will of God is sometimes called his counsel, sometimes [Col. 0514A] his command, sometimes his disposition, sometimes his approval, and sometimes his permission.

Answer. He calls God’s will his good pleasure.

### QUESTION III

“Grace to you, and peace from God.” The question is what the grace of God is.

Answer. The grace of God is called [Col. 0514B] God freely giving; and grace, that is, divine inspiration—namely God’s operation—by which the mind is moved to love God and neighbour.

### QUESTION IV

“Awaiting the revelation,” etc. The question is whether every righteous person is immediately shown after death the fact of his salvation. It seems not; for since this revelation is full knowledge, which is eternal blessedness, it seems that if this is granted, no one is in the punishments of purgatory. For who can be at once in punishment and glory?

Answer. The perfect pass immediately to knowledge of the highest good, in which eternal blessedness consists. But the less perfect, before they attain eternal blessedness, pass through purgatorial punishments, though certain of their [Col. 0514C] eventual rest. Augustine makes clear that there are purgatorial punishments, saying: “The mildest purgatorial punishment is more grievous than any temporal punishment which exists among us.” Therefore punishment and glory cannot be together in such a fire.

### QUESTION V

The question is how the statement is to be understood: “The angels shall tremble on the day of judgment.” For if there will then be trembling in them, how are they blessed?

Answer. This trembling denotes reverence for higher power, not that the punishment of fear can exist where there is eternal blessedness. It should be noted that not every mortal sin is called a crime, but only that which is worthy of accusation and condemnation.

### QUESTION VI

“Unto the day of the coming of the Lord,” etc. The question is whether the Lord will come for judgment in the daytime, [Col. 0514D] since the time of his coming is often called “day.”

Answer. The time of the Lord’s coming is called “day,” not because of the illumination of the air, but because of the revelation of hidden things: for everything now concealed will then be disclosed. Whether he will come by day or by night is unknown. Nevertheless, the time of judgment is designated not only by the name of day, as above, but also by the name of night, as is written in the Gospel: “At midnight there was a cry: behold, the bridegroom comes” (Matt. XXV). But it is called night because it is exceedingly hidden; the day of judgment is called day because of the distinction between the good and the evil.

### QUESTION VII

“Now this I say: that every one of you says, ‘I am of Paul,’” etc. The question is whether the Apostle speaks truly when he says this, since [Col. 0515A] none of them said it. For they did not glory in the true apostles, but in false ones. Hence he will say later: “These things, brethren, I have transferred in figure to myself and Apollos” (1 Cor. IV).

Answer. The Apostle speaks truly, and the sense of the words is: “Now this I say, that every one,” etc.—that is, what I say is like what each one of you says. He did not wish to identify by their own names those in whom they gloried, lest he seem to envy them, and in order to show, by greater persons, that one ought not to glory in lesser ones.

### QUESTION VIII

Augustine says that Christ retained for himself the power of baptizing, which, had he wished, he could have given to his servants. The question, therefore, is what that power is which Christ retained for himself and could have [Col. 0515B] given to his servants, but nevertheless did not give. Is it the power of dipping bodies outwardly? But he gave this to the apostles, to whom he entrusted the ministry of baptizing. If, however, he calls the power of baptizing the power of washing souls inwardly, only God can possess this power, since it belongs to him alone to infuse himself into souls and wipe away the stains of sins. How, then, could he have given this to his servants?

Answer. Many labour over the answer to this question, not knowing what Augustine meant by the word “power.” But we say that he calls power a dignity: namely, that by the invocation of the name of Christ, or of the whole Trinity, baptism is given. He could have given this dignity to his chief servants, so that baptism might be designated by their names and called the baptism of Paul, the baptism [Col. 0515C] of Peter, and so that baptism designated by their names might have as much efficacy as baptism designated by the name of Christ himself. Yet he was unwilling to give this to them, lest anyone place hope in a human being.

### QUESTION IX

“Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” etc. It is customary to ask what it means to be baptized in Paul’s name.

Answer. The faithful have not been baptized in Paul’s name, because those who are baptized are not commanded to believe in Paul but in Christ; nor is Paul’s name invoked over them or over the element so that it becomes a sacrament, but the name of Christ, who alone baptizes in the Spirit.

### QUESTION X

“Lest the cross of Christ should be made void by wisdom of speech.” The question is how the cross of Christ would be made void by wisdom of speech.

Answer. The wisdom of the world, which is called wisdom of speech because it is commended by no power but merely by the arrangement of words, holds that natural ability suffices for knowing and free choice for living rightly. [Col. 0515D] If that were so, the cross of Christ would be made void—that is, Christ would have died gratuitously.

### QUESTION XI

“I will destroy the wisdom,” etc. Is not all wisdom from God? How then is it said, “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise”? Does God destroy what is from himself?

Answer. Their wisdom in them is not God’s wisdom, because they ascribe it to themselves and misuse it. Thus, while they think that they comprehend the highest things, they become vain in their thoughts and thereby incur condemnation through their wisdom. Therefore the prophet calls “the wisdom of the wise” their false opinion by which they believed that God could not do anything contrary to the customary course of nature, and by which they supposed that free choice sufficed for salvation. God destroys this wisdom by acting against it according to higher principles, accomplishing our salvation in the midst of the earth. [Col. 0516A]

### QUESTION XII

“The world did not know God through wisdom.” The question is how this statement can be true, since elsewhere it is written of the wise of the world: “When they knew God, they did not glorify him as God” (Rom. I). How can both be true: “the world did not know,” and “when they knew God,” etc.?

Answer. The statement, “When they knew God,” etc., is understood concerning the possibility of knowing him; but “the world did not know God” is understood concerning the actual exercise of knowledge. Or rather, “when they knew God” is understood of a few wiser and more excellent persons; but “the world did not know” is expounded of all, or of the greater part. Hence he here says “world,” a term by which the whole body or the greater part is usually understood.

Or “world” means the wise of the world; and although they knew God through the works of restoration, they knew him in power, not in piety; in majesty, not in humility. It should be noted that there are theophanies in creatures, that is, divine manifestations: as in the world, whose magnitude displays God’s highest power; while the fullness or beauty of the world displays God’s wisdom; and the usefulness of the world suggests his goodness. In power the Father, in wisdom the Son, and in [Col. 0516C] goodness the Holy Spirit are understood.

### QUESTION XIII

“He who glories, let him glory in the Lord,” etc. The question is what it is to glory in oneself or from oneself.

Answer. He glories in himself or from himself who thinks that what is from God exists from himself, and therefore attributes praise to himself; as far as lies within him, he takes from God what belongs to God. For God alone is the author of good things. Hence it follows that whoever says that any good thing is from himself in some manner makes himself God. He also glories in himself who, although he knows that what he has is from God, nevertheless turns to himself the end of it which he ought to refer to God.

### QUESTION XIV

The question is also what it is to glory in the Lord.

Answer. He glories in the Lord who considers himself worthy of glory by the grace [Col. 0516D] of God alone.

### QUESTION XV

“And I did not come to you in loftiness of speech or wisdom,” etc. (1 Cor. II.) The question is how the Apostle says that he did not come to the Corinthians in wisdom, but preached to them Christ, and him crucified—as though it were less difficult to understand that God, having assumed flesh, died than that God is one in essence and three in persons.

Answer. In Christ there are two natures, human and divine. Those things which belong to his human nature are more akin to us than those which belong to his divine nature; accordingly, they are more easily believed and understood by us. But those things belonging to the divine nature, such as the three persons, the same essence, and matters of that sort, are more remote [Col. 0517A] and therefore more difficult to understand. Hence he rightly said that he did not come to them in wisdom when he discoursed to them concerning Christ’s death, because he preached those lesser things and not the more sublime ones.

### QUESTION XVI

Is it not required, if someone is to be perfect, that he believe God to be one and three? Thus the Apostle seems to have handed down imperfect teaching to them by not preaching those more sublime things, and consequently to have deceived them.

Answer. Faith is spoken of in two ways: either when what must be believed is simply set forth; or when the distinction of the things believed is shown distinctly—what must be believed, how, and why. Thus the Apostle set before them generally, without distinguishing individual articles, what they ought to believe. For believers must first be initiated in this way, and afterwards those who make progress must be perfected. [Col. 0517B]

### QUESTION XVII

“We speak wisdom among the perfect.” The question is whom the Apostle here calls perfect. For some are perfect in faith and knowledge; others perfect in knowledge and less perfect in faith; others perfect in faith and less perfect in knowledge. Perfect in faith and knowledge are, for example, the apostles; perfect in knowledge and less perfect in faith are certain clerics, who are less steadfast in faith than country people; perfect in faith but not in knowledge are many country people, who have attained little knowledge and yet believe perfectly.

Answer. It seems to us that the Apostle spoke wisdom among those perfect in knowledge, because those who are perfect by faith alone seem incapable of higher things. Yet many things are often deservedly revealed to believers of that sort; [Col. 0517C] and therefore, according to some, he speaks to those perfect in faith.

### QUESTION XVIII

“Nor [the wisdom] of the rulers of this age, which is destroyed [who are destroyed].” The question is how the wisdom of the philosophers is destroyed, since it seems to be a comprehension of truth.

Answer. It is destroyed when it is shown to be false or nonexistent. For, as has already been said, they thought that God could do nothing contrary to nature. Thus, among the great and many things which they truly comprehended, they asserted many false things; and they attributed to themselves rather than to God the truth which they had from God. Hence their wisdom was turned into darkness.

### QUESTION XIX

“Which none of the rulers of this age.” The first question is whom he calls the rulers of this age.

Answer. Either the wise of the world, or demons, or also [Col. 0517D] experts in the Law.

### QUESTION XX

The second question is how it can be true that none of the demons knew him, since it is written concerning those who said: “Jesus, Son of David, have you come before the time to torment us?” (Matt. VIII.) And again: “Many demons were going out and crying, ‘This is the Son of God’; and he did not permit them to speak, because they knew him to be the Son of God” (Mark I).

Answer. The demons are said to have known because of their supposition: they supposed rather than truly knew that Christ was God. For God always left the devil uncertain, so that after certain humble things he would always do lofty things, and after sublime things would return to humble ones. Thus after that outstanding [Col. 0518A] miracle concerning Lazarus, when the devil thought without reservation that he was God, he allowed himself to be seized, bound, and scourged. The devil therefore again judged him to be a mere human being. But when he had already been led to the governor and the Jews themselves had become confirmed in evil, it was in some manner revealed to him that through Christ he would lose his right; and through Pilate’s wife he wished to persuade Pilate to release him.

### QUESTION XXI

Likewise, a third question is asked concerning the Jews: how can it be true that they did not know him, since it is written of them in the Gospel parable: “Behold the heir; come, let us kill him” (Mark XII)? And elsewhere: “Because they delivered him through envy” (Matt. XXVII). But if they knew him and nevertheless killed him, there was unbelievable cruelty in them. Again, if they knew him to be God, they knew him to be immortal and therefore incapable of dying. How then did they seek his death, if they knew that he could not die? [Col. 0518B]

Answer. Some say that the Jews knew Christ, which they could not deny. Or, in truth, some of them knew that he was the one promised in the Law and the Prophets. But they did not believe him to be God. Yet that they killed him whom they knew to be just was envy. Its nature is such that it seeks another’s disadvantage contrary to its own good. Therefore they were wholly ignorant of the dispensation of the divine counsel.

### QUESTION XXII

“That we may know the things granted to us.” The question is what it is to know the things given to us.

Answer. It is to know from whom they have been given, and not to be ungrateful to the giver. For he is said truly to possess who knows from where he possesses; he is said not to possess who does not know from where he has, and is ungrateful [Col. 0518C] to him from whom he has. For no one is blessed by God’s gifts who is ungrateful to the giver.

### QUESTION XXIII

“Comparing spiritual things with spiritual.” The question is whom he calls spiritual. For some are perfect in life but not in understanding; others in understanding but not in life.

Answer. Those whom he called perfect above he here calls spiritual.

### QUESTION XXIV

The question is whom he calls “natural.” For one may be natural according to life or according to understanding.

Answer. He calls natural one who is devoted to earthly wisdom and, contemplating earthly things, considers the things of God foolishness.

### QUESTION XXV

“But the spiritual person discerns all things,” namely, those necessary for salvation, “and he himself is judged by no one.” [Col. 0518D] For the natural person cannot understand what he does or why.

Objection. Peter was rebuked by Paul; therefore a spiritual person is judged by a spiritual person.

Answer. A spiritual person is judged by no one—that is, no one shows him to be condemnable and worthy of condemnation. For although he may sin in some respect, it is not thereby condemnable in him.

### QUESTION XXVI

“I could not speak to you as to spiritual persons,” etc. (1 Cor. II.) Was the Apostle not spiritual both in life and in knowledge, and thus able to speak spiritual things—which he in fact did? Hence above: “We speak wisdom among the perfect” (1 Cor. II). How then does he say, “I could not speak to you as to spiritual persons”?

Answer. He does not say this because he lacked inwardly the ability to teach greater things, but because they were not fitting hearers. Yet the same things are often said to a mixed body of perfect [Col. 0519A] and imperfect persons, although they are not understood in the same manner.

### QUESTION XXVII

“I planted, Apollos watered, but God has now given the increase.” The question is how the Apostle distinguishes between himself, God, and Apollos, since Paul or Apollos does nothing except from God and through God, and therefore whatever Paul or Apollos works, God also works.

Answer. The Apostle makes the distinction in order to show what God works through Paul, through Apollos, and by himself. The Apostle worked by preaching toward faith in Christ; and God did this through Paul. For the Apostle would speak outwardly in vain unless the Holy Spirit were inwardly working and moving the mind.

### QUESTION XXVIII

“He who waters and he who plants are one.” The question is how they are one, since they are divided both in substance and accident.

Answer. They are one, that is, indistinguishable. For Paul contributes no more from what belongs to Paul than Apollos contributes from what belongs to Apollos. In the bestowal of gifts, this man does no more than that one: God alone bestows gifts. Nevertheless, Paul labours more than Apollos, and a greater gift is bestowed through Paul’s office than through Apollos’s, because through faith, which comes from preaching, one comes to baptism. Or, through the sacraments themselves, no more is conferred from this person than from that, or through this man than through that one. [Col. 0519B]

### QUESTION XXIX

“For we are God’s fellow-workers,” etc. Does God need anyone? How then were the apostles God’s fellow-workers?

Answer. They were called God’s fellow-workers because God works through them, although he could have worked the same thing by himself. [Col. 0519C]

### QUESTION XXX

“As a wise architect I laid the foundation,” etc. The question is what he calls the foundation.

Answer. The faith of Christ which works through love, which they received through Paul’s preaching. If this foundation remains, no one can perish, although certain stains adhere which are cleansed by fire. For although they possessed certain worldly things here through desire, they did not nevertheless prefer these to God, but preferred God above all things. To prefer God to all things is, if the choice or alternative were given of dying or denying Christ, to prefer dying to denying Christ. One person builds this, another that, upon this foundation.

### QUESTION XXXI

The question is what is understood by wood, hay, [Col. 0519D] and stubble.

Answer. Some say that these three signify venial sin. But how do they build upon this foundation, when every sin rather belongs to destruction than to building? Again, how will one building these things be saved as through fire, since faith without works is dead? Again, if anyone has all faith so as to move mountains but does not have charity, it profits nothing (1 Cor. XIII). Therefore, if there is no salvation without charity, how can anyone be saved who builds only these three things upon this foundation?

### QUESTION XXXII

Others say otherwise: by wood, hay, and stubble are understood good works, but imperfect ones. According to this opinion, the question is how a good work will burn, or how it will [Col. 0520A] suffer loss.

Answer. A good work does not burn insofar as it is good; but insofar as it is imperfect, it will be cleansed of its imperfection, especially of certain carnal affections possessed by those who build such things, which seem to be venial sins.

### QUESTION XXXIII

“All things are yours; but you are Christ’s; and Christ is God’s,” etc. The question is according to which nature we are Christ’s—that is, whether we are his according to his human nature or according to his divine nature.

Answer. It may be said that we are his not only according to the divine nature, according to which he is our Creator, but also according to the human nature, according to which he is our Redeemer. He, however, according to both natures, belongs to God the Father, from whom he has whatever [Col. 0520B] he has, but in different ways. For insofar as he is God, he has by nature all that belongs to the Father; and insofar as he is human, he has all the same things, but by grace. This is the rule of right faith.

### QUESTION XXXIV

“I am conscious of nothing against myself,” etc. (1 Cor. IV.) The question is how the Apostle says that he is conscious of nothing against himself and yet is not thereby justified; while John says in his Epistle: “If our conscience does not rebuke us, we have confidence toward God” (1 John III). And Paul himself elsewhere says: “This is our glory, the testimony of our conscience” (2 Cor. I). Therefore we ought to judge ourselves righteous and derive glory from this if our conscience does not rebuke us. For what greater perfection of righteousness is there than to have so pure a conscience?

Answer. Something can always remain hidden from us. Therefore, for us to possess true righteousness, it does not suffice that our conscience not reproach us. Nevertheless, we may glory in having a clean and pure conscience. [Col. 0520C]

### QUESTION XXXV

Likewise it is asked how the Apostle was not conscious against himself, since he knew that he was not without sin. Thus John says: “If we say that we have no sin, we are liars, and the truth is not in us” (1 John I). And a child whose life on earth is one day long (Job II) is not without sin. Hence Paul himself says: “I do what I do not will” (Rom. VII).

Answer. The Apostle was of such perfection that whatever his conscience told him ought to be done, [Col. 0520D] he did it. Therefore, if ever, as a human being, he had sinned through ignorance, a sudden impulse (subreptio), or weakness, the power of divine love consumed it all like stubble.

### QUESTION XXXVI

“Do not judge before the time,” etc. It is one thing to judge doubtful matters, which is forbidden because it is condemnable; another to suspect, which belongs to human weakness and perhaps no one lacks it. But since the Apostle forbids judging and the Lord himself forbids the same in the Gospel, why does the Lord elsewhere say: “Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing” (Matt. VII)? He himself adds how they may be discerned, saying: “By their fruits you shall know them” (ibid.). From this he seems to imply that we ought to judge such persons.

Answer. [Col. 0521A] It is one thing to discern evil persons in order to avoid them; another to judge persons worthy of condemnation, when we do not definitely know whether they are good or evil.

### QUESTION XXXVII

It is likewise asked how false prophets can be discerned from their works, since they do all the same things as good persons—for works are understood by fruits.

Answer. False persons are tested and distinguished from true ones by the virtue of perseverance.

### QUESTION XXXVIII

The question is whether the Apostle speaks truly when he says, “Already you are filled” (1 Cor. IV), since he speaks ironically. This does not seem so, since the contrary is true.

Answer. Whenever this kind of expression occurs, what is said is false as regards the surface of the speech and the first signification of the expression. Yet the person speaking does not lie; rather, he speaks truly, which results from the nature of the trope. [Col. 0521B]

### QUESTION XXXIX

“Not that I may put you to shame.” Is it not good to bring about shame by speech, so that a sinner is put to shame and blushes at his fault and is thus corrected? How then does the Apostle say: “I do not say this in order to put you to shame”?

Answer. Shame is twofold. There is shame leading to death, by which some become worse; and there is corrective shame, when one blushes at sins through correction so as to abstain from them henceforth.

### QUESTION XL

“Shall I come to you with a rod, or in charity?” The question is how the Apostle makes this division when he says, “with a rod, or in charity.”

Answer. The name charity is here, from its accompanying context, restricted to pleasant and agreeable things [Col. 0521C] done from charity. At other times charity signifies all things, harsh and pleasant alike, which pertain to salvation.

### QUESTION XLI

The expositor says that sin is diminished in those punished by an inflicted penalty. But the question is how this can be true, since they endure inflicted punishment unwillingly and are thereby opposed to justice; thus they sin more, and their sin is increased by their being punished.

Answer. It may be said of such persons that, at least through the punishment they suffer, they avoid the sins into which they would fall if they lived longer. If they endured punishment voluntarily, even the sin already committed would be forgiven.

### ON 1 CORINTHIANS V

“I have judged to deliver such a man [Col. 0521D] to Satan,” etc. From this passage of the Apostle the Church derives the sentence of anathema, that is, separation. Separation is sometimes carried out in regard to known and manifest persons, sometimes in regard to unknown persons. But, whether concerning these or those, they must first be summoned before the Church. Some must also be awaited longer and warned more frequently, according to the diversity and quality of persons and sins—for example, if it is a king through whose anger slaughter threatens the Church.

But after they have been separated, if they are known, communion with them is in no way permitted. If they are unknown, one who communicates unknowingly does not sin. But if one suspects, then, if one can avoid them without scandal, one should avoid them; if one cannot, one should communicate. This punishment ought to be carried out for the sake of common benefit, both that person’s and that of others.

### QUESTION XLII

[Col. 0522A] The question, therefore, is whether excommunicating someone is good, which seems so because it is just.

Answer. It is good, that is, expedient, but it is not good in itself and by its own quality. But when something of this sort is called just, this is the meaning: it is repaid according to desert, not that it is informed by the quality of justice.

### QUESTION XLIII

Likewise, the question is whether being excommunicated is good.

Answer. According to the reasoning stated above, it seems to be good, because excommunication seems expedient not only for others but also for that person. For if he resisted the admonition of the Church, he would sin.

### QUESTION XLIV

The question, however, is: if it happens that one who has not deserved it is excommunicated, and someone is struck with the sentence of excommunication through the hatred or [Col. 0522B] envy of a prelate, ought he resist or yield?

Answer. If he can resist without scandal, let him resist and restrain by good zeal the pride of his prelate. If he cannot do so without scandal, let him yield and endure it patiently for God’s sake. Hence a prelate’s sentence is always to be feared, but not always to be observed. When someone is excommunicated, he is delivered into Satan’s power so that Satan may afflict his flesh and he may thus eventually come to his senses. Yet Satan does not always afflict him. For the cunning enemy spares one person in order to gain many, or in order to preserve that very person for himself.

### QUESTION XLV

“Purge out the old leaven,” etc. The question is what he calls the old leaven.

Answer. Empty boasting, or the oldness of life, which must be cleansed through [Col. 0522C] newness of life.

### QUESTION XLVI

“Such persons cannot gain them for Christ,” etc. This is from the gloss. The question is: since the human mind is more inclined toward evil than good, especially when it is persuaded to return to accustomed practices, why did the Apostle permit persons recently converted to the faith to share table fellowship and conversation with Gentiles, when Christians could more easily be brought by the Gentiles’ persuasion to idolatry than Gentiles could be brought to faith by Christians’ admonition?

Answer. In the primitive Church, those converted to the faith, fervent in charity, could not easily be torn from the foundation. Recognizing this, the Apostle permitted them fellowship with Gentiles only.

### QUESTION XLVII

“If one who is called a brother among [Col. 0522D] you is a fornicator,” etc. Since there is now so great a multitude in the Church, the question is whether we act contrary to the Apostle’s command when we eat with such people; whether all such persons ought to be expelled from the Church and cut off with the sickle of anathema.

Answer. This ought indeed to be done if it could be done without scandal. But because so many and such people would rather cause schism, since they reject correction and amendment, they are tolerated. And therefore nothing remains except that Rachel should weep for her children. It should be noted that one kind of fornication is bodily and another spiritual. Bodily fornication is every use of those members outside lawful use; spiritual fornication is that which separates the soul from God and takes her from her bridegroom as though she were a bride.

### QUESTION XLVIII

“Do you not know that the saints shall judge this [Col. 0523A] world?” (1 Cor. VI.) Here the Apostle shows that saints may judge concerning secular matters.
