But if this is so, how does he later add: “It is already altogether a fault in you that you have lawsuits among yourselves” (ibid.)? If it is lawful to judge, how is this a fault?

Answer. Saints may have legal cases under discipline, but they may not contend among themselves.

### QUESTION XLIX

The question is how it can be true that it is lawful to recover one’s own property, since the Lord says: “If anyone takes from you what is yours, do not demand it back” (Luke VI).

Answer. Although recovering one’s own property is not evil, it is an occasion of evil. Therefore the Lord counsels that one should not recover one’s own, in order to avoid disputes. This is what the Apostle says: “All things are lawful for me, but not all things are expedient” (1 Cor. X).

[Col. 0523B] **QUESTION L.** It is asked in what manner the saints are to judge in the future. It is said that this will be not only by comparison with their better conduct, but also by authority and power. Hence it is not without reason that one asks what that power is, since it is written: “The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5).  
**Answer.** As Daniel says: “The court sat, and the books were opened,” namely, the books of eternal reasons, according to which judgment will be made, and the books of consciences, concerning which judgment will be made (Dan. 7). These books of eternal reasons and of consciences will be open and manifest to those who are to judge with the Lord. According to some, this revelation of hidden things is their power and authority. According to others, the saints are said to judge with the Lord because, by comparison with them, the wicked will appear [Col. 0523C] worthy of condemnation. Hence one reads that the saints shall judge the nations.

**QUESTION LI.** It is asked whether what he says concerning judgments is a command, counsel, or permission. Counsel concerns the highest goods, as in: “Concerning virgins I have no command, but I give counsel” (1 Cor. 7). A command concerns intermediate matters, as: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery” (Exod. 20), etc. Permission concerns the lowest matters, as with taking food. It seems, however, to be a command: for if I do not reclaim what is mine, I encourage in his error the one who took it away. Therefore, for the sake of the common good, I ought to reclaim it; therefore I reclaim it by command, because every evil must be avoided by command.  
**Answer.** Reclaiming what is one’s own is permitted; not reclaiming it is counsel. The Apostle therefore shows what is lawful for the weak; [Col. 0523D] the Lord shows what is fitting for the perfect, namely, not to reclaim it. But to contend and conduct lawsuits before a judge—especially an unbelieving judge—is altogether sinful.

**QUESTION LII.** “He who clings to a prostitute becomes one body.” It is asked what this unity is and in what respect it is to be understood.  
**Answer.** He notes that such persons are not only one in bodily union, but also in the ardor of lust. It is most shameful thus to become one body with a prostitute when one ought to be one spirit, clinging to God.

**QUESTION LIII.** “For,” he says, “the two shall be one flesh.” It is asked how the Apostle introduces this authority, which concerns that marital union which is holy, in order to demonstrate this shameful union between the fornicator and the prostitute, since the union found there can in no way be this.  
**Answer.** The meaning is: if, in that marital union, the two become one body, much more does this become one flesh because of the greater pleasure of vice.

**QUESTION LIV.** “Bear God,” etc. What is it to bear God?  
**Answer.** To live soberly, justly, and devoutly. Therefore those bear God who live rightly in him. For this is to put on his image and the form of righteousness; just as those trample God underfoot who deny him by living wickedly. But those lay God aside who grow lukewarm in charity and become more lax and careless.

**QUESTION LV.** The gloss says: “It is more serious to sin against God than against one’s neighbor.” But do not those who sin against their neighbor offend God? [Col. 0524B] How then are the two distinguished?  
**Answer.** To sin against God is to offend God contemptuously in matters that pertain especially to him, such as sacraments, faith, and similar things. To sin against one’s neighbor is to injure that person in some way; this is less serious than the first. Or, to sin against God is inwardly to violate the mind; to sin against one’s neighbor is outwardly to injure a human being by word or example. Therefore not everyone who offends him is said to sin against God.

**QUESTION LVI.** “Now concerning the matters about which you wrote to me,” etc. (1 Cor. 7). He treats marriage in three ways: according to command, according to permission, and according to counsel. Let the careful reader distinguish each in its proper place. One must consider what marriage is, what its efficient cause is, for what purpose it is contracted, who are lawful persons, and what are the goods of marriage. Marriage, therefore, or matrimony, is the marital union of a man and a woman, between lawful persons, maintaining an indivisible partnership of life. This definition applies only to the marriage of believers. According to others: marriage is the lawfully contracted authority to have sexual union, arising from lawful consent. Its efficient cause is material consent expressed by words in the present tense. The consent which is in the soul ought to be shown before the Church, without which there is no marriage. Hence it is read: “Marriage is not made by the union of bodies, but by the will of souls.” The purpose for which it is contracted is the procreation [Col. 0524D] of children and the avoidance of fornication. Lawful persons are those whom neither a vow of continence, nor blood relationship, nor ecclesiastical order, nor disparity of worship, nor social condition, nor natural frigidity prevents. There are three goods of marriage: fidelity, offspring, and sacrament—that is, indissolubility. This indissolubility is twofold: that of the sacrament and that of marriage itself. For this third good, namely sacrament, is not itself marriage, although marriage itself is a sacrament, just as that other is. But whether both belong to the same thing may be asked; we postpone the solution here for brevity’s sake, following the traces of the source. For in the sacraments and teachings of the Fathers we treat these matters more carefully.

**QUESTION LVII.** “But I say this by way of indulgence.” What is, or what is called, indulgence?  
[Col. 0525A] **Answer.** Indulgence is a concession of a less strict manner of life, by which something is lawful that would be unlawful and sinful where no concession existed. For the carnal union of man and woman would be sinful unless it took place within the state of marriage; thus, by concession, what is unlawful becomes lawful. Such concession is usually made to avoid a more serious sin.

**QUESTION LVIII.** “But I would have you all be as I myself.” It is asked how the Apostle says that he wishes all to be chaste, when he knew that God does not will this. For if this were so, how would the human race be propagated?  
**Answer.** The condition is implicit, as though he said: “I wish it, and it is good,” or, “It would please me if all were such.” Perhaps, if all who now exist were good, the number of the predestined would be filled from among them.

[Col. 0525B] **QUESTION LIX.** “Let not a husband put away his wife,” etc. It is asked whether a husband may put away his wife if she has been convicted of adultery.  
**Answer.** He may put her away. Again, it is asked whether he or she, while the other is living, may be joined to another. Some say that this is not possible.

**QUESTION LX.** It is asked whether marriage remains after divorce. If it remains, then the husband has authority over his wife’s body, and conversely.  
**Answer.** It remains, and he has that authority; but he may not use this authority unless reconciliation has taken place.

**QUESTION LXI.** It is asked whether marriage exists among unbelievers, or between a believer and an unbeliever. This does not seem so, since it is written that no marriage which has not been made in God is valid.  
**Answer.** [Col. 0525C] They say that marriage exists among unbelievers, as between Priam and Hecuba, and between Philip and Herodias. Hence John reproved Herod for adultery: because it was not lawful for him to have his brother’s wife (Matt. 14). If there was adultery and marriage there, as Chrysostom says. [The conditional is incomplete in the source.]

**QUESTION LXII.** “But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart.” It is asked: if there is marriage between a believer and an unbeliever, how can the Apostle say, “If the unbeliever wishes to depart, let him depart,” and that the believer may be joined to another (1 Cor. 7), when above he says that the dismissed woman should remain unmarried? For if it is a true marriage, how can it be dissolved? If it is not a marriage, how does he urge them to remain together, since every union apart from a lawful one is fornication?  
**Answer.** The believer has authority [Col. 0525D] over the unbeliever’s body, but not conversely; because, as is read, injury against the Creator dissolves the right of marriage. Therefore the believer may remain and may depart. For even the marital debt that the unbeliever owed has previously been discharged; yet the believer has not lost the authority once possessed. But if the departing unbeliever joins himself or herself to another, that person commits adultery.

**QUESTION LXIII.** Regarding the marriages of the ancients, one commonly asks whether they were true marriages, and how one man, having several wives, conducted himself toward each under the marital law. How was there lawful consent maintaining an indivisible partnership of life?  
**Answer.** Some say that they were not marriages, but occupied the place of marriage. Others say that they were true marriages among some persons, and that they are marriages among Jews and unbelievers. [Col. 0526A] For one who says that such a marriage is not valid does not deny that it is a marriage, but maintains that it is not valid.

**QUESTION LXIV.** It is asked whether marriage is a greater good than virginity. It seems that it is, because there are greater anxieties, pains, and labors in marriage than in virginity, and reward will be rendered to each according to his labor.  
**Answer.** It does not follow that, if there is greater labor here than there, there is therefore greater glory. Virginity is in itself a greater good than marriage. Yet some married persons are not of less merit than certain virgins.

**QUESTION LXV.** “Do not become slaves of men.” Above he said: “Were you called as a slave? Do not be concerned about it” [Col. 0526B] (1 Cor. 7). How then does he here forbid us to be slaves of men?  
**Answer.** He warns that one should not serve human beings for the sake of human beings. This occurs when one places hope of salvation in them, like those who said: “I belong to Paul,” or “I belong to Apollos” (1 Cor. 1).

**QUESTION LXVI.** “But he who commits fornication sins against his own body,” etc. From these words fornication seems graver than other sins; for where there is greater pleasure and greater contempt, there is also greater offense.  
**Answer.** A certain pleasure, deriving from the punishment inflicted for original sin, is present in our members. Although this pleasure is greater than that of other sins, fornication nevertheless does not seem to be greater than all other sins in liability or guilt. Again, they wish to prove from Jerome’s authority that fornication is more serious than other sins. For he says: “As great as was the pleasure that preceded in the act, so great ought to be the bitterness of mind that follows in satisfaction.” Thus it seems that where the pleasure is greater, there is greater guilt.  
[Col. 0526C] **Answer.** This, I think, is not said in comparison with all other sins; rather, in each kind of sin, the magnitude of the crime is understood in accordance with the magnitude of the pleasure.

**QUESTION LXVII.** “Each person has his own gift,” etc. It is asked how this is true, since there are many to whom nothing has been given by which they can be saved.  
**Answer.** He speaks only of believers, among whom there are different degrees, such as continence, marriage, and virginity, in which they can be saved. It is as if he said: “Let the one unwilling to remain continent descend to the marriage [Col. 0526D] granted him by God, so that in it he may be saved.”

**QUESTION LXVIII.** “For the form of this world is passing away.” It is asked how this is true, since it is written: “The earth stands forever” (Eccles. 1).  
**Answer.** He does not say that the world passes away, but the form of the world—that is, the shape and appearance which it presently has—will change into a better form. If, however, it is read anywhere that the world passes away, this must be understood according to its form, not according to its substance, which will always exist.

**QUESTION LXIX.** “He who does not give [her] in marriage does better.” This is because of a greater capacity for meriting. But it is asked how there is a greater capacity for meriting in virginity than in marriage, since the struggle is greater here than there. For if the difficulty of meriting is greater in marriage, the reward seems greater.  
**Answer.** In virginity, [Col. 0527A] with less labor there is greater progress, and therefore greater capacity for meriting. In marriage there is great labor and little progress; in that state it is a great thing at least to stand firm.

**QUESTION LXX.** “But I think that I too have the Spirit of God.” It is asked what Spirit of God the Apostle says he had, so that the Corinthians should acquiesce in his counsel. If we say charity, this is insufficient: he could have charity and lack knowledge, as very many do. If knowledge, that also is insufficient: many have knowledge, but their lives do not correspond to their words. Therefore their counsel can rightly be disapproved.  
**Answer.** By the Spirit of God he means both knowledge and charity, because the Apostle excelled in both. Therefore his counsel [Col. 0527B] was to be accepted.

**QUESTION LXXI.** “Knowledge puffs up,” etc. (1 Cor. 8). This is so in itself without charity, not from its own quality, but by occasion, just as the law produces wrath. But the same seems capable of being said of charity. For many who persist in the progress of charity and other virtues sometimes grow proud and thus fall. Therefore, just as an occasion for sin is taken from knowledge, so it seems one may be taken from charity—which must not be conceded. For no one takes an occasion of evil from charity. “It does not act improperly; it is not puffed up” (1 Cor. 13).  
**Answer.** Knowledge is a thing such as can puff one up; yet it is from God, just as riches provide an occasion for evil and yet are from God. Likewise, wood is suitable for burning, but it is not burned unless fire is applied; [Col. 0527C] so too knowledge never puffs up unless the human heart is set aflame. But can charity ever be set aflame in this way? For can anyone possess charity and be proud?

**QUESTION LXXII.** “An idol is nothing.” It is asked how this is true, since every artifact is something. Augustine says: “Matter is from God, but human folly gave the form.” But again, since it is written: “Every substance, every form, every union, and every arrangement is made by God,” how is the form of an idol not from God, when it is something? Origen says: “An idol is nothing,” that is, it has no likeness of any thing that exists. Or: “An idol is nothing”—namely, what they suppose an idol to be, that is, a person made up of the image and [Col. 0527D] the presiding spirit. Or, better: “An idol is nothing in the world,” that is, among the things of the world it has no power to change them for better or worse. Therefore food sacrificed to idols may, so far as it is in itself concerned, be eaten, but not before a weak person, lest that person do it with reverence for the idol.

**QUESTION LXXIII.** “There is no God but one.” Is not the Father God, and the Son God, and the Holy Spirit God? And is the Father not the Son or the Holy Spirit? How then is there only one God? Again, the Father is unbegotten God and the Son begotten God: how then is there one God?  
**Answer.** God is one in nature, not in person. But what is the meaning of these words, “God is one in nature, not in person”? This is a great question among modern writers. Yet, to state what I think, many seem to me to incline toward the Sabellian heresy, through ignorance of the multiple meanings of the terms *unus* (“one”), *unum* (“one thing”), *singulus* (“single”), and *substantia* (“substance”). For these three terms are understood differently in theology and in ordinary speech; they must be treated separately.

**QUESTION LXXIV.** It is asked whether the Son or the Holy Spirit ought to be called our Father.  
[Col. 0528A] **Answer.** Not simply, lest the unbegotten person be understood; but this may be said with a qualification, namely, according to the grace of regeneration. For the whole Trinity, jointly through its grace, regenerates us as children of adoption.

**QUESTION LXXV.** Again it is asked whether God the Trinity is that Father who is eternally Father, or another.  
**Answer.** Not that one, nor another, but one and the same with the same.

**QUESTION LXXVI.** It is asked whether angels ought to be called gods, just as holy human beings are called gods, as in: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. 81 [82]).  
**Answer.** Angels should not be called gods, lest they appear to be worshipped with the service called *latria*. “God” is said in three ways: substantially, as of the Trinity; by adoption, as of the saints; and nominally, as of the gods of the nations.

**QUESTION LXXVII.** “Their conscience, being weak, is defiled.” It is asked how he can say that their conscience is defiled. For if they believed that they did this for God—namely, ate food sacrificed to idols with reverence—would they not sin if they abandoned this practice, since everything not from faith is sin? Thus Paul too would have sinned if he had not persecuted the Church at the time when he believed it ought to be persecuted for God.  
[Col. 0528C] **Answer.** Because they rendered to a creature what belonged to the Creator, they had no excuse on account of ignorance. Their minds were so perverse and blinded that they thought a wooden or stone image to be God. Hence the Apostle fittingly says: “Their conscience, being weak, is defiled” (1 Cor. 8), not that it is defiled on account of God. Note that, although a preacher may receive necessities from those subject to him, he should do so without scandal.

**QUESTION LXXVIII.** “Is God concerned for oxen?” [Col. 0528D] (1 Cor. 9). Is God not concerned for all things? And if for all things, how is he not concerned for oxen?  
**Answer.** One kind of care is providential care, which is generally exercised over all things. Another is the care of precept, which God does not have for oxen. For he does not give commands to human beings in order to teach them how they ought to feed oxen; he has this care only for human beings.

**QUESTION LXXIX.** “I became as a Jew to the Jews.” It is asked: how “as a Jew”? Was he truly a Jew?  
**Answer.** He truly observed Jewish rites, as Augustine says; not dispensatorily, as Jerome says. It would be dispensatory if it were evil, yet done temporarily for the sake of a greater good—namely, so that by that simulation they might be converted to the true [Col. 0529A] faith of Christ. Those two pillars of the Church differed on this matter. Yet we do not say that either of them lied, since believing this or that does not endanger faith. This controversy will be discussed in what follows.

**QUESTION LXXX.** “They all ate the same spiritual food” (1 Cor. 10). It is asked: how the same?  
**Answer.** The same in signification, or the same in effect. For, according to their view, that food had the same efficacy as this. Yet certain sacraments of the Old Testament receive their power and efficacy from the sacraments of the New Testament; thus manna, received by believers, had its power from the body of Christ, which is a sacrament.

**QUESTION LXXXI.** “Let us not tempt Christ, as [Col. 0529B] some of them did.” God tempts in order to prove; the devil tempts in order to cast down; a human being tempts in order to test and know. Thus temptation is threefold. The first is a testing, which is good, as in the case of Job. The second is deception, which is an experiment of the mind for the purpose of deceiving. The third is distrust and despair, as with the Jews who said: “Can God prepare a table in the wilderness?” (Ps. 77 [78]). It is asked, therefore, how the Jews are said to have tempted Christ, when they seem to have worshipped only God the Father and God the Trinity.  
**Answer.** The Jews are said to have tempted Christ because all the preceding things prefigured Christ. Hence this temptation is said to have been Christ’s rather than the Father’s, though it is not more the Son’s than the Father’s, even if it is so called.

[Col. 0529C] **QUESTION LXXXII.** “And they perished by the destroyer,” that is, by an angel striking them outside the boundaries of the promised land. If it is asked whether that angel was good or evil, we answer that the wicked are sometimes punished by good angels and sometimes by evil angels; but the good are punished only by evil angels.

**QUESTION LXXXIII.** “Upon whom the ends of the ages have come.” Were the ages ended at Christ’s coming? If they were not ended, how is there an end of the ages?  
**Answer.** They have ended in us, because various states of life preceded, all of which involved change and a certain expectation of Christ’s coming. But we await no other state of life, because between this life and the future one there is nothing intermediate. For those who still await the Messiah, however, the end of the ages has not yet come, as for the wretched Jews.

**QUESTION LXXXIV.** “God is faithful, who will not allow,” etc. It is asked how he can say that God does not permit anyone to be tempted beyond what he can bear, when many fall through temptation, separate themselves from God, are overcome by the devil, and are thus tempted beyond what they can endure.  
**Answer.** So long as they are with God, he does not permit them to be tempted beyond what they can bear. If some yield, it is because they do not wish to resist temptation though they can do so; therefore it is just that they be tempted so severely, as their fault requires. God sometimes permits someone to be tempted for testing and for preserving virtues. This is a temptation of providence, [Col. 0530A] as in Paul, to whom “a thorn of the flesh” was given (2 Cor. 12), to preserve humility.

**QUESTION LXXXV.** “The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ?” It is asked concerning the name of this sacrament: why is it called the Eucharist?  
**Answer.** The sacrament of Christ’s body and blood is called *eucharistia*, that is, “good grace,” because of its outstanding power. In this sacrament there is received not only an increase of virtue and grace, but he himself who is the fountain and source of all virtue and grace. There are three things in this sacrament: the visible species of bread and wine; the body and blood of Christ; and spiritual grace. The first is the sacrament of the second; the second is the reality of the first and the sacrament of the third; the third is the power of the first and the reality of the second. [Col. 0530B] Therefore the first is sacrament only; the second is both sacrament and reality; the third is reality only. The first sacrament thus has two realities: one signified and contained, namely the true body and blood of Christ; the other signified but not contained, namely the unity of the Church.

**QUESTION LXXXVI.** It is also asked why, after the sacrament of the typical lamb, the Lord gave his disciples the sacrament of his body and blood.  
**Answer.** To show that the legal sacraments, among which the chief was the sacrament of the paschal lamb, ought to cease and that the sacrament of the new law should be substituted, among which the Eucharist holds first place. He did this also in order to imprint this sacrament more deeply [Col. 0530C] and commend it more firmly to his disciples’ memory.

**QUESTION LXXXVII.** Next it is asked why he gave this sacrament under another species rather than under its own proper species.  
**Answer.** So that faith, which concerns invisible things, might have merit; for faith has no merit when human reason supplies proof. It was also so that the eye might not shudder at what the hand holds, and so that unbelievers might not mock us.

**QUESTION LXXXVIII.** Again, it is asked why under this species rather than another.  
**Answer.** Because the things of this species bear an explicit likeness to both realities of this sacrament. For just as bread is made from many grains and wine from many grapes, so Christ’s material body consists of many members, and his spiritual body of many believers. And just as bread and wine are the complete and principal refreshment of bodies, so in this sacrament there is the complete and principal refreshment of souls, because through the food of the flesh one comes to the taste of divinity.

**QUESTION LXXXIX.** Again it is asked: since the whole Christ is received under each species, why is he received not under one only but under two species?  
**Answer.** He is received under two species to show that he assumed the whole human being in order to heal the whole human being: he assumed body for body and soul for soul, and bread is changed into flesh and wine into blood. Therefore he is received under two species in order that the assumption of soul and body in Christ, and the liberation of both in us, may be signified.

**QUESTION XC.** Again, since flesh and blood are under each species, it is asked whether the substance of both species is changed into Christ’s flesh and blood.  
[Col. 0531A] **Answer.** Although both are under each species, the substance of bread alone is changed into flesh alone, and the substance of wine alone into the substance of blood alone. Nor should they be called two sacraments, but one. Nor is the sacrament said to be repeated for this reason, because the blessing is not repeated over the same species. Nor should other substances be offered in the sacrifice of truth, because Christ’s body and blood cannot be consecrated from other things than grain of wheat made into bread and wine.

[Col. 0531B] **QUESTION XCI.** It is asked why water is put with wine in the Lord’s cup.  
**Answer.** Water signifies the people. Therefore wine, by which Christ is signified, ought not to be offered without water, because Christ suffered only for the people; nor may water be offered without wine in any way, because the people are redeemed only through Christ.

**QUESTION XCII.** It is asked whether the sacrifice becomes invalid if water is omitted.  
**Answer.** If someone, without intending to introduce heresy, omits the water through forgetfulness or ignorance, it does not seem to become invalid. Hence the Greek Churches too do not add water. But water alone can in no way be offered in sacrifice, nor bread except from grain—that is, wheat—nor grain except when made into bread.

[Col. 0531C] **QUESTION XCXIII.** It is commonly asked whether water changes with wine into blood.  
**Answer.** Some say that it is changed; but it seems to us that it is not changed. We received this from Master Achard.

**QUESTION XCIV.** It is asked whether Judas received the Lord’s body in the dipped morsel.  
**Answer.** Not then, but earlier with the others.

**QUESTION XCV.** It is asked concerning the accidents which remain in species, taste, weight, and shape: in what subject they exist.  
**Answer.** Many doctors agree that they exist without a subject, just as the substances of flesh and blood are there without accidents of this kind.

**QUESTION XCVI.** It is also commonly asked concerning the breaking [Col. 0531D] and division which occurs there: in what thing it takes place, since there is no substance other than the substance of flesh and blood, which remains whole.  
**Answer.** Christ’s body remains whole in itself, and yet it is broken and divided in the sacrament.

**QUESTION XCVII.** It is asked whether a wicked person receives the true body of the Lord and the true blood.  
**Answer.** Such a person truly receives both, but to his own harm, because unworthily—for a person is unworthy who receives otherwise than Christ instituted, or who is in mortal sin.

**QUESTION XCVIII.** Again it is asked whether Christ is sacrificed daily.  
**Answer.** He who was killed once upon the altar of the cross is sacrificed daily in the sacrament in memory of his passion. This is not repeated because of his weakness, but because of ours: we sin daily, obtain forgiveness of venial sins, [Col. 0532A] and receive an increase of virtues if we participate worthily. An objection is made from Augustine’s statement that the good person receives the sacrament and the reality of the sacrament, whereas the wicked person receives only the sacrament and not the reality of the sacrament. Yet it has already been said above that the wicked person receives the true body and true blood; therefore the wicked person receives not only the sacrament but also the reality of the sacrament—which must unquestionably be believed.  
**Answer.** In the words cited, Augustine calls the true body and true blood of Christ the sacrament, and calls spiritual grace the reality of the sacrament; this grace only the good person, not the wicked, receives.

**QUESTION XCIX.** It is asked what sort of body Christ gave his disciples: mortal or immortal. If mortal, how could it be chewed or broken by teeth without injury? If immortal, then he gave such a body as he did not yet possess.  
**Answer.** We rightly say that he gave such as he willed, for nothing was impossible to him. Some nevertheless maintain that he gave a mortal body; we neither affirm nor deny this.

**QUESTION C.** It is asked what is the power of this sacrament.  
**Answer.** The remission of venial sins, the perfection of virtues; it was instituted for the increase of virtues and as a remedy for daily weakness.

**QUESTION CI.** It is asked whether one should communicate daily.  
**Answer.** Augustine says: “I neither praise nor blame receiving the Eucharist daily.” Yet if someone has an intention to sin, he is made more burdened by receiving than purified. And if someone is troubled by mortal sin, [Col. 0532C] let him make satisfaction with tears; if he has the will not to sin thereafter, let him approach confidently.

**QUESTION CII.** It is commonly asked whether immoral priests can confect this sacrifice.  
**Answer.** Although some are immoral in life, if they are within the Church by name and sacrament, they are believed truly to consecrate. But those who are excommunicated and openly marked by heresy do not seem able to do this. Three things must be observed in this sacrament: form, order, and intention—form instituted by the Lord; order, namely that the celebrant be a priest; and intention, namely that he intend to do this.

**QUESTION CIII.** It is asked whether the Lord’s body is touched or received by brute animals.  
**Answer.** It is received in no way by a mouse or any other little beast.

[Col. 0532D] **QUESTION CIV.** What then does the mouse receive when it eats?  
**Answer.** God knows—perhaps nothing but the accidents which are there.

**QUESTION CV.** “Do not eat, on account of the one who informed you, and on account of conscience,” namely that of the weak person, etc. It is asked how he can say: “Do not eat because of an unbeliever or a weak believer.” Is it not better to eat for the sake of both than to abstain? For if one abstains, the unbeliever is offended. The weak person, moreover, should rather be left to himself, as was said above: “Let the one who is weak eat vegetables” (1 Cor. 14). For one who thinks that you worship an idol if you eat things consecrated to an idol should be left to his own judgment. Although he thinks that you sin by eating, you nevertheless do not eat with reverence for the idol, [Col. 0533A] nor is he led away from faith by thinking this. Rather, through zeal for faith, he believes you err in eating and is therefore indignant.  
**Answer.** It is better to instruct the person who ate by abstaining than, by eating, to encourage him in error. Again, if you ate before a weak brother, he would be scandalized and perish through the scandal. Therefore one should abstain rather than eat.

**QUESTION CVI.** “Whether you eat or drink,” etc. It is asked how the command can be fulfilled that we do all things to God’s glory, since we do many things naturally and do not do them for the purpose of pleasing God.  
**Answer.** Let all our actions be done with such circumspection that nothing is done against God.

**QUESTION CVII.** “Just as I please all people in all things.” Elsewhere he says: “If I were still pleasing human beings, I would not be Christ’s servant” (Gal. 1). Was he not Christ’s servant while pleasing all people in all things?  
**Answer.** His saying, “If I were still pleasing human beings,” should be understood thus: if I pleased human beings, so far as I am concerned, by making human beings my cause and end, I would not be Christ’s servant. But one who pleases for the sake of truth does not make himself pleasing; rather, truth itself is what pleases.

**QUESTION CVIII.** “If anyone seems to be contentious, we have no such custom, nor does the Church of God.” Here we have authority that the customs of the holy Church are to be observed even if we do not know why they have been so established by it; for God does not permit his Church to err in those matters which pertain to him. Note: “Church” means both the gathering of believers and the house in which they assemble to receive the Eucharist, [Col. 0533C] not only in commemoration of Christ’s death, but also in order that we may conform ourselves to Christ in conduct and life.

**QUESTION CIX.** “A man is the image and glory of God, but a woman is the image and glory of man,” etc. It is asked how the man is God’s image and the woman is not, since in Genesis it is written of both that they were made in God’s image (Gen. 1).  
**Answer.** One image is common to man and woman, the one discussed in Genesis; another belongs to man alone and not to woman. The first consists in the natural power to know God; the second is understood thus: just as all things are from God, so all human beings are from one man. Or it should be understood morally: by the man, reason is meant; by [Col. 0533D] the woman, sensuality. In this sense, the man and not the woman is God’s image.

**QUESTION CX.** “There must be heresies,” etc. On the authority of the Church. It is asked who is to be called a heretic.  
**Answer.** A heretic, properly speaking, is one who, for the sake of some temporal advantage—and especially of glory or his own primacy—invents, or holds, follows, and defends false, new, corrupt sects alien from the truth which others have invented.

**QUESTION CXI.** “But let a person test himself,” etc. If someone is in mortal sin, let him not approach, but say: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Matt. 8). What is it, then, for someone to test himself except to see whether his conscience reproaches him for mortal sin and whether he intends still to remain [Col. 0534A] in sin? A priest ought to warn a person who is in mortal sin but not publicly known to be so not to approach; yet he cannot withhold communion from him. If, however, public report or a crime accuses him, he must not approach at all, lest the priest give it to him. For if the priest, induced either by favor toward him or by money, gives it to such a person, he kills Christ, so far as lies within his power. This is greatly to be feared.

**QUESTION CXII.** “There are varieties of gifts, but the same Spirit,” etc. (1 Cor. 12). Since the works of the Trinity are indivisible, it is asked why he attributes gifts to the Holy Spirit, ministries to the Son, and operations to the Father.  
**Answer.** In grace, benevolence appears most especially, and this pertains to the property of the Holy Spirit; therefore he attributes gifts to the Holy Spirit. In ministries wisdom shines, and wisdom is customarily referred to the Son. In operations there is power, which is especially the Father’s; therefore he refers operations to the Father’s authority.

**QUESTION CXIII.** “To one is given a word of wisdom,” etc. It should be noted that wisdom and knowledge are understood differently here than there: “O the depth of the riches of the knowledge and wisdom of God” (Rom. 11). When he says, “O the depth of the riches of the knowledge and wisdom of God,” he calls wisdom and knowledge the divine essence. But when he says, “To one is given a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge,” he calls wisdom knowledge of eternal things, and knowledge, knowledge of human things.

### Question 114. “But one and the same Spirit works all these things.”

It is asked why the Father is not called a gift, as the Son or the Holy Spirit is, although he gives himself just as the other persons do; for the Son or the Holy Spirit is given to no one without the Father. Solution: Because of the authority of the principle: lest he who is from no one be understood to be from another.

### Question 115. “For as the body is one,” etc.

It is asked whether only the good share in these gifts, or also the wicked. That even the wicked possess these gifts of the Spirit is evident from what is read in the Gospel: they will say to the Lord on the day of judgment, “Lord, did we not prophesy in your name and cast out demons?” (Matt. 7). To them the Lord will say: “Amen, I say to you: I do not know you,” etc. (Matt. 25). Likewise, when John the Evangelist saw a certain man who was not following the Lord casting out demons in Christ’s name, he wished to forbid him; but the Lord said to him: “Do not forbid him; he who is not with me is against me” (Mark 9).

From these passages it is evident that the wicked too often exercise these gifts; and thus it seems that they belong to Christ’s body and are its members. Yet, since they are wicked, they are members of the devil. Solution: The Apostle does not say that all who possess the gifts of the Holy Spirit stand in the unity of the body; or else “Church” is taken broadly, namely as the multitude of all who partake of the sacraments of the Church. Among these are certain rotten members, and many grains together with chaff, which are said to be in the body but not of the body. Hence John says: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2).

Note that the Apostle says that all the members of the body, although many, are one body. I say this because of certain persons unwilling to grant that all the parts of a whole, joined together, receive the name of the whole, although the Athanasian Creed also says: “Soul and flesh are one human being.”

### Question 116. “If I have all faith, but do not have charity,” etc. (1 Cor. 13)

Here the Apostle plainly shows that faith and the other gifts cannot be possessed without charity. First, then, it is asked what faith is meant here: Catholic faith or some other faith? It cannot be another faith, because mountains cannot be transferred from place to place by another faith, as by this faith of which he speaks here. Therefore he speaks here of Catholic faith. Hence it is clear that it can be possessed without charity, and thus can be possessed by the wicked—a point many deny.

According to these persons, however, Catholic faith is faith working through love. They may be asked whether they call faith working through love one thing or two. This whole cannot be one thing: for one who has faith in this manner not only believes, but also loves. These two cannot exist in the wicked; yet, insofar as faith is considered simply in itself, this whole may exist in a wicked person, even in the devil. For what does this good man believe which that wicked man does not believe? Does not that wicked man, or even the devil, believe that Christ died and rose from death, and the other things necessary to faith which must be believed?

But then the objection is made that the devil possesses Catholic faith and thus becomes a Catholic. Solution: “Catholic” is used in two ways: one who lives catholicly, by imitating Christ’s life, is called Catholic; and one who believes all things that must be believed is called Catholic, whether he has charity or not. Some grant that the devil too may, in the second sense, be called Catholic—a statement harsh to our ears, especially since the knowledge he has concerning Christ is more from the subtlety of his nature than from the inspiration of Christian faith.

### Question 117. “Charity is the proper fountain of good things,” etc.

It is asked whether charity can be possessed by those who are to be damned. Are not those persons strangers who do not share in the proper fountain of good things? Solution: Charity is called the proper fountain of good things because no one can simultaneously possess charity and be wicked.

### Question 118. “Charity never fails,” etc. [Col. 0535D]

It is asked whether charity, once possessed, is never lost. For if it never fails and is never lost, then those who are to be damned could never at any time possess charity. Solution: Charity is said never to fail because it is possessed here and in the future; yet, when possessed in the present, it is lost, and when lost is recovered again.

### Question 119. “Knowledge will be destroyed,” etc.

It is asked how he says that knowledge will be destroyed in the future. Shall we not have, in the future, knowledge of those things of which we now have knowledge? Indeed we shall have it, and much greater knowledge than we have at present. How, then, will knowledge be destroyed? Solution: Some say that knowledge will be stripped of its partiality and imperfection, so that it will no longer be partial and imperfect. But this is for it to be increased and perfected, not destroyed; for in the same way it could be said of charity that it too must be destroyed. For just as we know imperfectly, so we love imperfectly; and when that which is perfect comes, that which is partial will be done away with.

Solution: Some say that it is not knowledge, but its enigmatic and shadowy mode, that is to be destroyed. But again, by the same reasoning, charity too seems to be destroyed, since its mode of imperfection is to be done away with in the future. To this it is answered that it is true that the mode of imperfection will be removed from charity, but not every mode. For in the future one’s neighbor will be loved for his own sake and for God’s sake, as he is loved in the present. Others also say that the act of knowledge will be destroyed in the future. But charity which now exists—neither its act nor a certain mode of it—will be destroyed in the future. Faith and hope, however, will be wholly done away with; knowledge will be destroyed in part, for its act and mode will not remain.

### Question 120.

But there is another question that presses us more closely. It is true, and cannot be denied, that charity in the present is imperfect compared with the future. Yet the Apostle proves by this argument that prophecies will be done away with and knowledge destroyed: “We know in part, and we prophesy in part; but when that which is perfect comes, that which is partial will be done away with.” Therefore, since charity is partial, by a similar argument it too will be done away with when that which is perfect comes.

Solution: We say that knowledge or prophecy is called “partial” for one reason, while charity is called imperfect for another. Since some know and others do not know, prophecy or teaching has a place in this present life, where one teaches and instructs another. But in the future, when all will be taught by God, when all from the greatest to the least will know God fully and perfectly, human teaching will have no place, when no one will say to his brother, “Know God.” Therefore knowledge—that is, teaching—will be done away with.

But charity is not called partial in this way. It does not exist because some love and others do not love. Rather, it will exist much more truly when all love perfectly. Note that an *aenigma* is an obscure likeness; and just as in the present every creature is, as it were, a mirror in which God is seen, so in the future God himself will be the mirror of every creature, in whom all things will be seen more truly than in themselves. Hence, according to some, knowledge must be destroyed because this shadowy mode of knowing which we now possess will not remain when full knowledge comes.

### Question 121.

Faith and hope cannot be lacking to charity; but faith and hope can exist without charity. Yet some say, as was stated above, that faith cannot exist without charity; their error is destroyed here. For when he says, “If I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but do not have charity, I am nothing,” he plainly indicates that even perfect faith can be possessed without charity. And the commentator plainly rebukes them in the foregoing words, saying that faith and hope can exist without charity.

### Question 122.

It may further be asked how hope can exist without charity. Is not hope a confidence concerning future goods arising from preceding merits? But this cannot exist without charity. Thus it seems that hope cannot exist without charity. Again, if hope is, as others hold, the expectation of a future benefit, it will now be presumption rather than hope if I am certain that he will reward me, though there are no merits. It may be answered that hope is twofold: hope of reward and hope of meriting. Hope of meriting cannot exist without charity; but hope of reward can (not) exist without charity.

### Question 123. “He who speaks in a tongue speaks not to human beings but to God” (1 Cor. 14).

It is asked what it is to speak in a tongue. Solution: Some say that to speak in a tongue is to speak parabolically; others, to speak in an unknown language. Augustine says that the utterance of signs which the spirit forms in the human spirit is called speaking in a tongue. Hence the Apostle says: “The spirit speaks mysteries” (ibid.). For he says the same thing by “speaking in a tongue” and by “speaking in spirit.”

In the primitive Church the Holy Spirit formed, in the minds of the faithful for their conversion, signs of heavenly mysteries; and the Apostle calls the utterance of such things “speaking in tongues.” It should be noted that those who spoke in tongues sometimes understood and sometimes did not understand. But someone will say: If he who speaks in a tongue understands what he says, then this is no longer speaking in a tongue but prophesying. Solution: Although he himself understands, unless he expounds it to others, he does not prophesy but merely speaks in a tongue. Note that certain things are done in the Church for ornament alone, rather than chiefly from necessity; among these is speaking in tongues.

### Question 124. “You will be speaking into the air,” etc.

From these words some suppose that speaking in tongues means speaking in different kinds of languages. But this is not true. Rather, the Apostle introduces this comparison to show that speaking in tongues without interpretation has little usefulness, just as speaking in every kind of language would produce confusion rather than edification for those who understood none of them.

### Question 125. “If I do not know the force of the voice.”

It is asked what he calls “the force of the voice.” Solution: He calls the signification of the voice its force.

### Question 126.

It is also asked why this kind of utterance is called speaking in a tongue. Solution: This is so because what is in the tongue is in the voice and in utterance, whereas what is in the heart is in the intellect, since understanding is in the heart. Therefore, because this utterance exists only in utterance and not in understanding, it is called speaking in a tongue, and in spirit rather than in mind.

For spirit is a power of the soul lower than the mind, in which images of things are apprehended confusedly. It is the imaginative and confused apprehension of visible things, without discrimination of the properties of what is apprehended. Such was Pharaoh’s vision of cows and ears of grain: he saw only the images, while Joseph received from God, in the intellect, revelation concerning them.

### Question 127.

It is asked what words uttered in this manner signify, when someone speaks in a tongue in such a way that we put forward this example: “A sower went out to sow his seed.” For if this is the signification of the voice, it is itself true. It is therefore asked whether by these words that is said which they properly signify. If it is said that this is so, it follows that by them something false is signified.

To this some reply that, in such cases, one must not seek the signification of the voice but only that of the things, which belongs to allegory. Others say, speaking more freely, that it does indeed properly signify something false, yet a falsehood is not said by it, because the utterance does not end there. The first signification of the voice is not the end of the utterance, but the second, which is called allegorical.

It may also be said that the utterance itself signifies neither truth nor falsehood. For the things there signify only the truth which is mystically understood. Nor do I deny that there is a signification of the voice there, but only incomplexly: for this word, “man,” signifies a man, and so with the rest. But they do not signify complexly; they do not jointly signify so that truth or falsehood is signified, but so that they signify those things by which truth is signified.

Or it may be said that the proposition itself is employed, from the property of the things signified, to signify what is mystically understood—as this word “seed” signifies the word of God from the property of the thing which it signifies.

### Question 128. “Christ died for our sins,” etc. (1 Cor. 15)

It is asked whether Christ, according to the flesh, had a necessity of dying. The authority on that passage seems to maintain that he had such a necessity: “As it is appointed for human beings to die once, and after this judgment, so Christ was offered once” (Heb. 9): “so,” that is, with the same necessity and by the law of nature by which others die.

Again, the authority says, “He was offered because he willed it” (Isa. 53). Therefore, by will alone; how then by necessity? Solution: It is agreed that there was no cause of death in Christ, because there was no sin. Nevertheless, according to some, among the other penalties he voluntarily assumed even the necessity of dying. Thus this necessity does not impede his will: just as he assumed it when he willed, so he laid it aside when he willed. For, they say, unless some greater benefit had been conferred on the assumed flesh, it would necessarily have been subject to the law of nature. Some understand this necessity also by “mortality.”

### Question 129. “I am the least of the apostles,” etc.

It is asked how the Apostle calls himself the least of the apostles, when in merit he surpasses the merits of the others, for he labored more than all of them. Solution: He says this according to his former state, not according to his present state, in which he was not the least of the apostles but the greatest.

But the objection is made: he does not say, “I was the least,” but “I am the least of the apostles.” Therefore, since he is not among the least, but rather among the foremost, he seems to lie and thus to sin unto death, because “a lying mouth kills the soul” (Wis. 1). Solution: The meaning is: “I am the least of the apostles,” that is, I do not prefer myself to others, but rather others to myself. For he had all his own sins before his eyes—past or present, hidden or manifest—while he considered the simplicity and innocence of others. Thus, in this regard, he thought more humbly of himself.

For just as the proud person always notices whatever good things he possesses and the weaknesses of others, so that he considers himself alone great and despises the others, so the humble person sees his own weaknesses without interruption and weighs the good things of others. Hence the saints, though greater, regard themselves as humbler; nor is this a deceptive opinion, since they judge that the good things they possess are gifts not of their own but of God, while they know that the evils to which they are subject are their own.

### Question 130. “By the grace of God I am what I am,” etc.

It is asked of what grace he speaks. Concerning God’s operative and cooperative grace, or prevenient and subsequent grace, something has already been said above. For prevenient grace, or operative grace, is one and the same: it works in us without us, namely by preparing and healing free choice so that it may will the good. This is what the Apostle indicates when he says: “By the grace of God I am what I am.”

But subsequent grace, or cooperative grace, is likewise one and the same: it works in us not without us, following and assisting us so that we may not will in vain. This the Apostle indicates by saying: “And his grace in me was not empty, because I labored more than all; yet not I, but the grace of God with me.”

Therefore, from his saying, “I am what I am by the grace of God,” the error of the Pelagians is destroyed: they said that free choice sufficed to merit salvation. Again, by adding, “and his grace in me was not empty,” he shows that a human being can do something by free choice, which certain heretics deny when they say that a human being can merit nothing.

But the Apostle shows that a human being can do nothing from himself, but only from grace coming upon him. For grace must first go before the human being; then free choice, already anticipated by grace, must cooperate with that grace. Its nature is such that it can shine forth and cooperate, just as an eye touched by a ray of sun can see. Therefore, what a human being does is from the grace with which he cooperates.

For, as has already been said, a certain grace operates without human assistance because it pierces and stirs the mind. But without grace a human being cannot even consent to grace or accomplish anything else; rather, he relies upon grace as it draws and leads him, and thus, aided by grace, merits. From this it is evident that when a human being does something good, it is not from grace alone but also from free choice, although the whole is the work of grace, either operating by itself or with the human being. Thus some things are from grace alone, and some from grace and the human being.

### Question 131. “If there is no resurrection of the dead, neither has Christ risen.” [Col. 0540A]

It is asked whether this conditional statement is true and how it should be understood. Solution: It is true and is understood thus: if it were impossible for the dead to rise, as certain heretics said, it would also be impossible for Christ to have risen. Or, if the saints were not going to rise, it would not be true that Christ rose, because everything that he did in the flesh—dying, suffering, rising—he did for us.

### Question 132. “If Christ has not risen, our faith is empty.”

It is asked how the Apostle says that our faith is empty and that “we are more pitiable than all human beings” (1 Cor. 15), if there will be no resurrection of the dead or of bodies. For since the soul is immortal and alone capable of the vision of God, and thus alone can possess blessedness, can we not be blessed without the resurrection of bodies? And connected with this:

### Question 133.

It is asked what purpose the resurrection of bodies will serve, since bodies will not be needed there, where Christ will be all in all, nor can they receive blessedness, which will belong to the soul alone. Solution: One must carefully consider what is said and in what respect. For when he says, “We are more pitiable than all human beings,” he says this not with respect to the soul but with respect to the body. For in this life the Apostle suffered greater misery than others.

There will be a resurrection of bodies so that we may glory also in the second robe. For that brightness which will be in the body will augment blessedness itself, so that what previously served for misery may now be possessed for glory and beauty. The Apostle proves the resurrection of the dead from Christ’s resurrection, which occurred only so that the resurrection of bodies might be believed and might take place. “When he delivers the kingdom to God the Father” (ibid.), that is, when he brings the Church, in which he now reigns through faith, from the knowledge it has of the Son to the knowledge and vision of the Father.

### Question 134. “Until he puts all his enemies under his feet.”

It is asked how he says that Christ must reign “until he puts” all enemies beneath his feet (ibid.). Will he not reign eternally, especially after his enemies have been subjected? Solution: In similar passages, *until* is used in the sense of “for eternity.” For if he reigns when he has adversaries, it is evident that he will reign when all are subject to him, and so he will reign eternally.

### Question 135. “Then the Son himself also will be subject to him who subjected all things to him.”

It is asked according to which nature he says that the Son is subject to the Father. If according to the divine nature, he will thereby be lesser; but this is false, since according to divinity he is equal to the Father. Again, if this is said according to his human nature, then according to that nature all things are subject to him; and according to his human nature he is Lord of all. Therefore he is also Creator, and so according to the same nature he seems equal to the Father according to which he is less than the Father. Hence it is read: “Equal to the Father according to divinity; less than the Father according to humanity.”

Solution: This may soundly be understood according to each nature, divine and human. According to the human nature all things are subject to him; according to this nature he was raised to equality with the Father, when human nature was united in one person with the Word consubstantial with the Father. According to this nature he himself received fullness of gifts, “and of his fullness we all have received” (John 1); and thus we are subject to him.

Again, according to the divine nature, some understand the Son to be subject to the Father because he has being from him from whom he has whatever he has. So also: “My teaching is not mine” (John 7); and: “The Father is greater than I” (John 14), which some wish to understand according to the divine nature. In such expressions distinction is indicated, because the Son is from the Father, not the Father from the Son. Hence the Father is called the principle of the Godhead because he is from no one, while both the Son and the Holy Spirit are from him. For the Father is principle, not from a principle; the Son is principle from a principle; the Holy Spirit proceeds from both. Yet such matters should be spoken only in a fitting place and time, lest the weak incur scandal.

### Question 136. “In unequal brightness there will be equal joy.”

It is asked: if brightness is unequal, how can joy be equal? Will not the quantity of joy correspond to the quantity of brightness? Will not brightness itself be joy itself? Again, if one person is more blessed than another, one will have greater joy than another. How then will joy be equal? Again, will not the joy of all belong to each individual? How, then, will there be equal joy amid unequal brightness? If the same coin is given to all, how is there unequal brightness? If joy is equal, then Peter’s joy will be Martin’s joy.

Solution: Joy of experience is one thing; joy of will or affection is another. Peter’s joy in reward is joy of experience; Martin’s is not joy of experience but of affection. For Peter’s good pleases Martin as much as it pleases Peter himself; yet Martin does not feel and experience in himself as great a blessedness as Peter feels. Blessedness therefore differs in quantity, although it is the same in quality.

Thus, regarding the health of someone recovering from illness, I rejoice in affection as much as that person does, though not in experience, because I do not feel in myself the health that he experiences. As two people are covered by the same bedclothes, yet one is warmer, so in one vision of God one will rejoice more intensely than another. But no inferior person will envy one greater than himself, nor desire for himself the greater person’s greater joy, because each will have as much as he wills; otherwise he would not be blessed.

There will be life without death, knowledge without error, love without offense. There the end of our desires, namely God without end, will be seen; he will be loved without weariness and praised without fatigue.

### Question 137. “A natural body is sown,” etc.

It is asked whether the body has animality—that is, sensuality—from the soul, or the soul from the body. Solution: The body cannot possess animality except from the soul; nor would the soul be animal, that is, possess sensuality, if it were not joined to a body. Animality therefore appears to arise from the conjunction of both. Yet the soul alone senses through the body; the body receives this from it but does not itself sense.

For in the beginning the human being was so created that he was passible from creation, yet would never suffer unless he sinned. Hence he was also said to have been immortal before sin, because he could avoid dying: he could avoid sinning, because if he had not sinned, he would not have died.

### Question 138.

It is also commonly asked, since the human being before sin was called mortal and in a certain way immortal, whether he possessed both from nature, neither, or only one. Solution: With due reverence for the mysteries, and without prejudice to a better opinion, we say that before sin the human being was naturally mortal and passible, but would become immortal through the benefit of the tree of life. Therefore the doctors do not say simply that he was then immortal; rather, they add “in a certain way” and specify how. But they pronounce him simply mortal, in accordance with the statement: “The first human being was made into a living soul,” that is, into a soul which would nourish and enliven the body, not one which had no need of food.

### Question 139. “But this I say, brothers: flesh and blood cannot possess the kingdom of God; nor corruption incorruption.”

It is therefore asked what bodies we shall possess. Solution: After the resurrection we shall possess the same bodies which we now have, but changed not in substance but in quality: these are dissoluble, but those indissoluble; those of the good impassible, but those of the wicked passible. Hence the latter will be, as it were, in perpetual death.

The Apostle teaches that they will be indissoluble when he says: “Flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God” (ibid.). And he indicates that they will possess impassible bodies when he says: “But we shall all be changed” (ibid.).

### Question 140. “For the trumpet will sound,” etc.

It is asked what is signified by the name “trumpet.” Solution: The doctors say that the Apostle calls by this name some evident and glorious sign through which the mystery of the future resurrection will be fulfilled. This trumpet is elsewhere called a cry, elsewhere the voice of an archangel or the voice of Christ.

### Question 141. [Col. 0542D]

It is also asked whether the voice of the trumpet will be material in the future. Solution: It is evident that there will be a material voice produced through the ministry of an angel. For just as by a trumpet the Jewish people were summoned to feast or battle, so then they will be summoned to judgment; or there will be some evident sign accomplishing the same thing as is customarily accomplished by a voice.

### Question 142. “Death has been swallowed up in victory.”

It is asked what death, and in what victory, has thus been swallowed up. For by “death” are sometimes signified the devil, who is the author of death; sometimes sin, which separates from God; and sometimes the dissolution of soul and body. Solution: It may soundly be understood concerning the devil, sin, and the dissolution of soul and body. It is evident that in the victory of the Lord’s resurrection the devil has been swallowed up, so that he may not rule as before, when people were compelled by fear of death to every crime. But now the saints despise death. Most especially, in the future general resurrection of all, every death will be swallowed up, when this mortal nature puts on incorruption.

### Question 143. “But the strength of sin is the law.”

How this is to be understood can readily be discerned from what was said on the Epistle to the Romans. For when the law was given, carnal desire grew strong and transgression arose. The law, by forbidding, increases desire unless the Holy Spirit pours in charity.

### Question 144. “Therefore, brothers, be steadfast and immovable.”

It is asked in what these two differ. Solution: Be steadfast in faith, lest they be moved by the foot of pride; be immovable in temptations, lest, when the hand of sinners drives them, they abandon faith.

There are three kinds of temptations: one violent, another deceitful, and a third both violent and deceitful. The first comes through open persecutions; the second through false brothers and heretics; the third will come through Antichrist. Every kind of temptation is sent by the devil. Hence he is called a lion when he rages openly, and a dragon when he deceives secretly and covertly. Thus it is written: “Under his tongue are trouble and sorrow” (Ps. 10).

### Question 145. “Concerning Apollos, I make known to you that I urged him greatly to come to you, but it was not his will to come now” (1 Cor. 16).

It is asked which of the two acted unreasonably: Paul, in urging him to go, or Apollos, in not yielding? For it seems either that Paul did not request what was fitting, or that Apollos omitted what he ought to have done. Solution: It is true that both acted reasonably. For the Apostle requested that he do this; and therefore Apollos, because it was thus requested, saw that the Apostle’s request should rather be set aside, and so he did not yield.

### Question 146. “Greet one another with a holy kiss.”

It is asked why he added “holy.” Solution: There is a kiss of lust; there is a kiss of betrayal, such as Judas’s; and there is a kiss of holiness and concord, by which what is inward, namely the bond of charity, is made visible, etc. Therefore he says this in order to exclude the others.

## III. ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0543]

[Col. 0543C] **(2 Cor. 1.) “Paul, an apostle,” etc.**

This is the second epistle sent to the Corinthians. The Apostle sometimes writes two epistles and sometimes only one; but when he writes one, he says nothing diminished or imperfect, nor, when he writes two, anything superfluous, as may be seen here. For this following epistle is the completion and confirmation of the preceding one. In this second letter he urges those to correct themselves who had not yet been corrected by the preceding epistle. He notes that they were sparing in almsgiving. He commands that the corrected fornicator be received back. Hence the subject matter of this epistle, and also its intention, is evident.

Its subject matter is the particular condition of the Corinthians at that time. Its intention is to recall them to the unity and integrity of faith. In this particular condition he signifies and instructs the general condition of the Church, inviting all to the unity of faith.

In accordance with his custom and that of other writers of letters, he begins with greetings to those to whom he writes, seeking goodwill. Thus he says, “Paul, an apostle,” joining the name of humility and the name of dignity, so that humility, as the companion of dignity, may temper the excellence of dignity; without humility every virtue is empty and vain.

Likewise, “of Jesus Christ”: Jesus is the name of a person. Several have borne this name, such as Joshua son of Nun and Jesus the high priest, but only by appellation. Christ alone bears it substantively, because he possessed both the name and the reality: he truly was the Savior of the world. For Jesus means “Savior.” Christ, however, is the name of the person which embraces both natures. It is the name of an office, such as priest or soldier, and means “anointed.”

In the Old Testament two persons were anointed: the kingly and the priestly. But Christ was anointed with royal anointing, because according to his divine nature he could govern his own; according to his human nature he received the power of offering, since he offered himself to God the Father. Hence Christ is so called from the royal and priestly office.

The will of God is understood in many ways, as was said above; nor will it be superfluous to say it again. The will of God is called his disposition and good pleasure. Hence: “He has done all that he willed” (Ps. 134). The will of God is also called counsel or command. Thus it is said: “God wills all to be saved” (1 Tim. 2), that is, he counsels and commands them to do those things by which they may be saved, such as prohibitions or permissions and the like.

### Question 1. “When I wished this, did I use fickleness?”

It is asked, therefore, whether the Apostle lied by promising that he would come when he did not come. For he himself said, “I will come,” and did not come. Therefore with him there was “yes” and “no,” that is, affirmation and negation concerning the same thing, and thus a lie; and so he is guilty of lying.

Solution: A lie is a false signification of speech with the intention of deceiving. Therefore one who says what is false, but thinks it true, is not to be judged a liar, since he is deceived rather than deceiving. But whoever, with an intention to deceive, says what is true or false is guilty of lying. Hence it follows that someone who says the truth may be guilty of lying, or may lie; and that someone says what is false yet does not lie or become guilty of lying.

### Question 2.

It is asked concerning those who lie piously, whether they are guilty of lying, as were those Egyptian midwives. For with an intention to deceive they uttered falsehood. Solution: Those who lie in this way sin; and while providing for the lives of others, acting against their conscience they offend against truth and incur danger to their own souls.

### Question 3.

Likewise it is asked concerning those who say what is false in jest. Solution: Sometimes jesting in this way is evil, sometimes it is not; but if it is habitual, it is sinful.

### Question 4. “To some indeed an odor of death unto death,” etc. (2 Cor. 2)

It is asked whether the odor of death is good or evil, since the Apostle says that he is an odor, to some unto death and to others unto life. If it is good, how is it unto death? Again, if it is evil, how is it good to God? Solution: The Apostle was nothing but a good odor; yet by this good odor some died, that is, through envy they took occasion, just as the law is good yet an occasion of evil, namely of transgression.

### QUESTION V. “Not that we are sufficient,” etc. (2 Cor. 3)

The question is asked how the Apostle can say that we are not sufficient of ourselves even to think anything, when we can both think and do evil of ourselves. Likewise, since there are certain things that we can do naturally, which are neither for reward nor punishment—[Col. 0545C] things given to us from the first creation, such as raising, bending, or lowering a finger, and the like.

**Answer.** Here the Apostle is speaking of those goods which have merit before God, which can in no way be done without grace coming beforehand and helping. Hence: “His mercy shall go before me” (Ps. 58), and “his mercy shall follow me” (Ps. 22). For grace precedes the will, so that it may will; and follows it, lest it will in vain. Thus the Apostle here destroys the error of those who said that the beginning of a good act cannot naturally exist without grace, but that the completion of the good act comes from ourselves; this is what he refutes when he says: “But our sufficiency is from God.” For through free choice we have the capacity to act well; yet we cannot use this capacity unless grace assists us [Col. 0545D]. For free choice has been so cast down through sin that it cannot use its own power unless it is raised up and helped by grace—just as, although I have the ability to ride, I cannot exercise that ability without a horse.

### QUESTION VI. “The letter kills, but the spirit gives life,” etc.

It is asked how the letter is said to kill. Does it command such things as kill when observed? How then can the Apostle’s statement elsewhere stand, that the law is holy and the commandment holy, good, and just, if its precepts kill? Again, if it is said that the letter kills without the spirit—that is, without grace—the same seems capable of being said of the Gospel.

[Col. 0546A] Again, if the letter is said to kill because not everything in it can be observed literally, then one who observes it should not perish. The same may be said of the Gospel. For if this saying, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood,” etc. (John 6), is observed literally—that is, according to the sound of the words, so that we understand eating and drinking in that way—it is, here as elsewhere, foolish and damnable.

**Answer.** The letter without the spirit—that is, without grace—kills, because it is an occasion of death, just as knowledge without charity puffs up. But the letter of the Gospel is not without the spirit. Or, as was already said elsewhere: by “letter,” or “law,” is understood a commandment without grace; this always kills, because, by increasing concupiscence, it adds transgression. By the Gospel [Col. 0546B] is understood a commandment with the spirit, that is, grace. Hence the Apostle calls the law a ministry of death and the Gospel a ministry of righteousness.

### QUESTION VII. “And not as Moses put a veil,” etc.

A question is asked concerning the veil: does it blind?

**Answer.** One thing is the figurative veil, which is the reading of Moses; this was prefigured by the veil which Moses, when speaking to the children of Israel, placed over his face. Another is the veil of blindness, placed over the heart of the Jews. Both veils are removed through Christ. As a figure of this, the veil of the temple was torn in Christ’s Passion.

### QUESTION VIII. “But we all, beholding with unveiled face the glory of God, are transformed into the same image,” etc.

[Col. 0546C] It is asked what he calls “glory,” and what “image.”

**Answer.** He calls by the same name both the glory of God which we behold and the image into which we are transformed: namely Christ, who is the uncreated glory and image of God, just as man is the created glory and image of God.

### QUESTION IX. “Who is the image of the invisible God” (2 Cor. 4)

It is asked why the Son is called the image of the Father.

**Answer.** So that he may be shown to be from the Father in such a way that he is shown to be like and equal to him in every respect.

### QUESTION X.

If it is asked why the Holy Spirit, although he is from the Father and is like and equal in every respect, is not called the image of the Father as the Son is, the answer is that image, equality, and likeness belong more to the property of the Son than [Col. 0546D] to the property of the Holy Spirit. For things that are born, rather than things that proceed, are customarily like.

It should be noted that likeness follows upon image and equality: wherever there is image or equality, there is likeness; but the converse does not hold. Likewise, image does not entail equality, nor is it entailed by equality, since there can be image without equality and equality without image.

### QUESTION XI. “Having the same spirit of faith.”

The commentator says on this passage that times have changed, not faith, because whatever we believe, those ancients also believed, and conversely. Hence the following objection: Abraham believed that Christ was going to be born, whereas we believe that he has been born; but “going to be born” is different from “born” [Col. 0547A]; therefore he believed one thing and we another.

**Answer.** “Whatever we and the ancients believe,” etc., means that the same realities are the objects of our faith and theirs. Yet it does not follow that what is now past was past in their time, or that what was then future is future now.

Again, if it is objected: Abraham believed that Christ was going to be born; but now it is false that Christ is going to be born; therefore Abraham believed a falsehood.

**Answer.** As it appears to us, “what” is being taken in the sense of “of what kind.” When it is said, “Abraham believed Christ to be going to be born,” the meaning is: he had faith concerning Christ’s birth, which was then future. But in the minor premise, when it is said, “Now it is false that Christ is going to be born,” the meaning is: Christ’s birth is not future. Therefore it in no way follows from the two propositions that Abraham believed a falsehood.

### QUESTION XII. “But though our outward man,” etc.

It is asked whether the outward and inward man are two men; and whether the outward man is the same as the old man, and the inward man the same as the new man.

**Answer.** Just as the old and new man are not two men but one person, although he is called old in one respect and new in another, so the outward and inward man are not two men, but one and the same person so called in different respects. Nor is the old man the same as the outward man; nor is the new man the same as the inward man. For the old man consists in guilt and punishment, both of which are found not only in the outward man but also in the inward man. The new man [Col. 0547C], however, is understood in relation to righteousness and glory; these two also belong to the inward man. The outward man is whatever we have in common with brute animals; the inward man is what we have in common with angels.

### QUESTION XIII. “Who gave us the pledge of the Spirit,” etc. (2 Cor. 5)

It is asked how the Holy Spirit is called a pledge, and of what thing he is the earnest.

**Answer.** The Holy Spirit is love; and from the love which we have toward God we are certain of his promise. Since we have this certainty from the Holy Spirit, the Holy Spirit has therefore been given to us by God as, so to speak, an earnest and pledge. A pledge is certainty of a thing believed, promised, or to be believed.
