[Col. 0547D] “Therefore, knowing the fear of the Lord, we persuade people.” Fear is divided into five kinds, as was already said in the Epistle to the Romans; there is no need to depart from that discussion.

### QUESTION XIV. “For whether we are beside ourselves,” etc.

It is asked what transports of mind are.

**Answer.** There are two transports: terror, or attention to things above, so that in some manner lower things slip from memory. All the saints were in this transport of mind, to whom the mysteries of God surpassing the world were revealed.

### QUESTION XV. “Christ died for all.”

It is asked how Christ died for all, since his death does not benefit everyone: it does not benefit those to be condemned, but only the elect.

**Answer.** [Col. 0548A] According to Jerome, it is understood thus: for all who are to be saved. For universality is sometimes restricted, and this in several ways. Sometimes a universal sign gathers together the individual members of genera; sometimes the genera of individuals; sometimes neither, but the larger or more worthy part of the whole. Or, according to Augustine, Christ died for all because his death merited that all might be saved through him, unless something remained in themselves to prevent it; for it was sufficient for the salvation of all.

### QUESTION XVI. “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself.”

It is asked how the Father is said to be in the Son, or the Son in the Father; or how this saying [Col. 0548B] is to be understood: “He who sees me sees the Father also” (John 14).

**Answer.** One is said to be in, or seen in, the other because their substance is naturally one. I add “naturally” in order to exclude the Sabellian heresy. There is unity where there is no diversity, but complete sameness, equality, and identity. Hence Hilary says: “The Father is seen in the Son because of the united likeness of their nature.” Thus we detest the plague of the Arians, while nevertheless we also abhor the madness of the Sabellians; we confess God as three, yet one, and one, yet three.

Many in our day are Sabellians in understanding, though they confess three persons; for when it is said that the three persons are one substance, they understand nothing other than what Sabellius understood [Col. 0548C]. This happens because they fail to notice the multiple meanings of the term *substance*. Hilary says that when one says, “The Father and the Son are one substance,” such a statement contains both an awareness of faith and a ready-made deception. He then explains both, saying: “If you signify a singular God, Father and Son, the understanding is false. But if you say that Father and Son are one substance, or simply one, so as to understand one as equal and undifferentiated, equal in every respect and unlike in no respect, the understanding is true.”

By these words he most clearly distinguishes personal unity from natural unity: Father and Son are one in nature, not in person.

### QUESTION XVII. “Behold, now is the day of salvation,” etc. (3 Cor. 6)

[Col. 0548D] It is asked why the time of grace is called the day of salvation, when many were also saved in the time of natural and written law.

**Answer.** This time of grace is called the day of salvation because in this time the sacrifice has been offered through which alone entrance into the kingdom lies open, and through which those who went before also deserved salvation. It is also called the time of grace because greater powers have been given us through the manifestation of faith and love; hence the powers of the devil have been diminished; and because now all things are done freely, not for the sake of any earthly advantage; and because the things promised in other times are fulfilled in this time.

### QUESTION XVIII. “With charity unfeigned,” etc.

[Col. 0549A] It is asked what charity is called feigned.

**Answer.** Charity is feigned when it does not persevere; or when it is insufficient for salvation; or when it is simulated—that is, when some outward sign of love is displayed although it is not inwardly in the heart. Such charity is not charity.

### QUESTION XIX. “As dying, and behold, we live.”

It is asked, in light of these words, how the Lord’s yoke is sweet and his burden light, when the saints suffer so many and such harsh and difficult things; and how those who labor and are burdened, on coming to him, find rest, when they seem to pass not from labor to rest, but rather from rest to labor.

**Answer.** The Holy Spirit is present to the saints as they endure heavy and harsh things. In the corruption of the outward man, he renews the inward man [Col. 0549B] day by day; and, through the tasted experience of spiritual rest and the hope of future blessedness, he lightens every hardship. Thus, amid so many hardships, Christ’s burden is lighter. For the love of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ makes all savage and overwhelming things easy and almost nothing.

### QUESTION XX. “That there may be equality, as it is written: He who had much did not abound,” etc. (2 Cor. 8)

It is asked whether lesser persons who, like provincials, supply support to Christ’s soldiers are equal to them in merits; for the Apostle seems to intend this when he says, “that there may be equality.”

**Answer.** This equality is not equality of piety, but consists in the fact that each supports and is supported by the other. Lesser persons support the greater in carnal things and are supported by them in spiritual things. And greater persons—that is, spiritual persons—support lesser, carnal persons in [Col. 0549C] spiritual things, and are supported by those same persons in carnal things.

### QUESTION XXI. “For we provide things good not only before God,” etc.

It is asked how the Apostle distinguishes between before God and before human beings, since nothing can be done before God unless it is also done before human beings. Yet an outward work is not always required, namely when the means are lacking. But it is always required that the conscience be clean.

**Answer.** In order to show that the conscience cannot be clean unless good things are also provided before human beings, the Apostle distinguishes between these two matters.

### QUESTION XXII.

It is asked: What is it to provide good things before God?

**Answer.** It is to dispose the mind so that [Col. 0549D] nothing is done against God. This cannot be done unless scandal to the brethren is outwardly avoided. Or he distinguishes between the matters mentioned above in order to show that there are some things which, insofar as they concern God, may lawfully be done because they are good in themselves, although they appear otherwise to people, and which may therefore be omitted. Thus, what is both beneficial and fitting should be done: what is beneficial for our merit, and fitting as an example to others. Therefore, for conscience’s sake, we must provide good things before God. For reputation’s sake, we also provide good things before people; for one who, trusting in his conscience, neglects his reputation is cruel. Such a person does not care whether what he does pleases or displeases others, and omits nothing for fear of scandalizing the brethren.

### QUESTION XXIII. “He who sows sparingly shall also reap sparingly.”

[Col. 0550A] (2 Cor. 9) A question is asked concerning the poor, who sow sparingly or not at all: will they therefore also reap sparingly?

**Answer.** One who gives little does not sow sparingly if he would readily give more, had he more. Therefore, the person to be called one who sows sparingly is the one who has little love, whether he gives more or less; and this person will reap sparingly—that is, will receive a small reward in eternal life.

### QUESTION XXIV. “For we do not dare to insert ourselves,” etc. (2 Cor. 2)

That is, we do not arrogate authority to ourselves, but use authority given to us by God. It is therefore asked what it is to arrogate authority.

**Answer.** A person arrogates authority to himself who, though neither chosen nor called, takes honor to himself; who thrusts himself forward and wishes to rule without having received authority.

### QUESTION XXV. “But we do not glory beyond measure.”

[Col. 0550B] It is asked: What is it to glory beyond measure?

**Answer.** It is to glory more than one ought, or in what one ought not. This is what a person does who extends himself into that to which he has no right. To misuse authority is to flatter and to indulge the vices of sinners. To use authority is to rebuke sinners and do the other things that pertain to edification.

### QUESTION XXVI. “He who glories, let him glory in the Lord.”

It is asked what it is to glory in the Lord, since elsewhere he says: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6); and: “Not only do we glory in the hope of the children of God, but also in our tribulations” (Rom. 5). Is glorying in the Lord the same as glorying in the cross of the Lord and in tribulations? [Col. 0550C] What is it to glory?

**Answer.** To glory is to rejoice in praise and to judge oneself worthy of glory. To glory in the Lord is to attribute all confidence not to oneself but to the Lord as its author, and to exult in Christ with spiritual joy.

To glory in the cross of the Lord can be understood in two ways. One is rightly said to glory in the Lord’s cross when, with joy and hope of future life, he imitates the Lord’s Passion; and this is to glory in tribulations. A person is also said to glory in the Lord’s cross when he judges himself worthy of salvation only through the merit of the Lord’s Passion, saying with the apostle Peter: “Because there is no other name under heaven in which we must be saved” (Acts 4). I say these things without prejudice to a better opinion.

### QUESTION XXVII. “For I am zealous over you with the zeal of God,” etc. (2 Cor. 11)

[Col. 0550D] It is asked: What is zeal?

**Answer.** Zeal is a movement of the mind toward good or evil on account of another’s condition. When it is toward good, it belongs to love; when toward evil, to envy.

### QUESTION XXVIII.

It is also asked: What is it to be zealous with God’s zeal?

**Answer.** It is to love for the honor of God, or with the zeal that God inspires.

### QUESTION XXIX. “For I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.”

A question is asked about this betrothal by the Apostle: since not all who are in the Church are virgins, such as married people, how can he present as a virgin—as though one virgin—those who are not virgins, and moreover as chaste?

**Answer.** There is a twofold virginity: [Col. 0551A] that of body and that of mind. Virginity of flesh is an untouched body; virginity of mind is the uncorrupted integrity of the inner person. This latter is required of every believer, and without it bodily virginity is of no benefit. All are called one virgin because of the unity of integral faith, steadfast hope, and sincere love. She is chaste because she has no heat of evil will.

### QUESTION XXX. “Satan transforms himself into an angel of light,” etc.

It is asked whether it is dangerous to believe Satan to be an angel of light when he says or does things that accord with good things.

**Answer.** When he says or does things that are fitting, the error is not then dangerous. But when he begins to put forward his deceptions, lest anyone follow after him, vigilance is necessary; and this does not occur without God.

### QUESTION XXXI. “In hunger and thirst,” etc.

[Col. 0551B] It is asked where is God’s promise: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added unto you” (Matt. 6). For the promise seems to have failed, when the Apostle says that he labored in hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness.

**Answer.** That physician, to whom we have once entrusted our whole selves and from whom we have the promise of present and future life, knows when to supply or withhold these aids, as he judges beneficial for us.

### QUESTION XXXII. “Through a window in a basket, by the brethren.”

It is asked whether this deed was praiseworthy or blameworthy. It seems blameworthy to some, because he was not delivered by God’s help.

**Answer.** God’s assistance is not necessary before human assistance has failed; nor should anyone await [Col. 0551C] God’s help while he has something he can do, lest he seem to tempt God.

### QUESTION XXXIII. “And thus I escaped his hands.”

It is asked whether the Apostle acted by fleeing as a good shepherd or as a hireling. Did he not, when the wolf came, leave the sheep and flee? Thus it seems that he was not a good shepherd but a hireling.

**Answer.** When a particular shepherd is specially sought by persecutors, he may yield, avoid the rage of the persecutors, and by fleeing preserve himself for the benefit of the whole flock. Meanwhile, the others, who are not sought in the same way, should provide food to their fellow servants. But when a common danger threatens all, those who depend on others should not be abandoned by those on whom they depend.

### QUESTION XXXIV. “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows,” etc. (2 Cor. 12)

[Col. 0551D] It is asked how the Apostle could doubt whether he was caught up in the body or outside the body, since no one existing in this life can see God as he is. Hence God says to Moses: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). Again, if he was caught up outside the body—that is, if his soul was separated from the body—was his body during that time dead? Again, if he saw God by intellectual vision, then he truly saw him and possessed that knowledge in which supreme blessedness consists; and so he was in blessedness. But blessedness once possessed is never lost; or, if God took from him what he had already received, it seems that God acted unjustly.

**Answer.** Either could have happened: either his soul, separated from the body [Col. 0552A], saw God in itself; or the soul, freed from the body’s senses while remaining in the body, contemplated God in this way. Since either of these might rightly have occurred, the Apostle speaks doubtfully: “whether in the body or outside the body.” Therefore, whichever occurred, the authority of the saying “No human being shall see me and live” remains intact, because in either way he could have put off the human condition.

If he was outside the body, then his body was dead and separated from the soul, and was restored to life when the soul returned. But when he had full knowledge of God and was thus in blessedness, if that same glory was afterward taken away from him, this is neither strange nor unbelievable. For God could thus show beforehand to his beloved servant the future blessedness and joy which he was to receive, so that he might persevere more steadfastly in love and service to him and desire more ardently the very time of receiving it—just as, when transfigured on the mountain, Christ showed the glory of his humanity to his three disciples.

### QUESTION XXXV.

By the third heaven and paradise into which he was caught up, he understands the same thing: namely, full understanding or knowledge of divinity.

Note the fourfold account of the three heavens.

According to the first view, the first heaven is the aerial heaven, whence “the birds of heaven.” The second is the firmament, whence: “And he called the firmament heaven.” The third is the empyrean, which, as soon as it was made, was filled with angels, where angels and holy souls enjoy the contemplation of God.

According to the second view, the first heaven is bodily vision, by which [Col. 0552C] heaven, earth, and all things visible to the eyes are perceived. By the gift of God, certain things are sometimes seen by the same vision, such as Elisha’s fiery chariots (4 Kings 2), and Belshazzar’s hand writing on the wall: “mane [mene], thecel [tekel], phares”—“numbered, weighed, divided” (Dan. 5). The second heaven is imaginative or spiritual vision, by which not bodies but their images are seen, as commonly happens in dreams or ecstasy: Pharaoh’s ears of grain (Gen. 41), and Peter’s sheet (Acts 10). The third is intellectual vision, by which neither bodies nor images of bodies are seen, but incorporeal and immaterial things are perceived by the mind’s intuition, such as substance, divinity, and every affection of the soul.

The third view calls the three heavens the threefold hierarchy of angels according to Dionysius. The first in ascent contains angels, archangels [Col. 0552D], and virtues; the second, powers, principalities, and dominions; the third, thrones, cherubim, and seraphim. This third hierarchy in ascent, and first in descent, the Apostle calls the third heaven or paradise. When he says he was caught up to it, he shows that he saw God immediately, face to face.

The fourth view is that the first heaven is called knowledge of the heavenly bodies; the second, knowledge of heavenly spirits; the third, knowledge of divinity.

### QUESTION XXXVI. “I know such a man,” etc.

It is asked how he calls the person caught up “a man,” whether in the body or outside it, since a human being subsists in body and soul. How then does he say that a man can be caught up outside the body?

**Answer.** The true reality of a human being consists where the image and likeness of God are. Hence the saying: “The mind of each person is the person himself.” Therefore, by the name “man” he means the inward man.

### QUESTION XXXVII. “There was given to me a thorn of my flesh, an angel,” etc.

[Col. 0553A] It is asked by whom this thorn was given to him: by God or by the devil. If by God, how is it called an angel of Satan, as though sent by Satan? Again, if sent by the devil, how is the following statement true: “Lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me,” etc.? Did Satan therefore buffet the Apostle through an angel sent by himself in order that he might not be lifted up in pride?

**Answer.** He who afflicted the Apostle was sent both by God and by the devil, but by God for one reason and by the devil for another. He was sent by God so that the greatness of the revelations would not exalt him; by the devil, in order to draw him into [Col. 0553B] failure. He was also sent by God so that strength might be made perfect in weakness.

### QUESTION XXXVIII. “For which reason I asked the Lord three times,” etc.

The devil asked that Job might be tested and was heard (Job 1). The Apostle asked that Satan’s angel might depart from him and was not heard. Where, then, is divine justice? Was it just that the devil should be heard and not the Apostle?

**Answer.** God does not always hear according to their will those whom he has purposed to heal, but according to their healing. Yet sometimes in anger he hears some according to their will, as he did the devil.

### QUESTION XXXIX.

Again, since the Apostle knew that this weakness had been given to him for progress and for the preservation of humility, it is asked whether he reasonably asked [Col. 0553C] that such a temptation might depart from him.

**Answer.** Though he knew this, he nevertheless feared in human fashion that he might fall through affliction; [Col. 0554A] and thus he was humbled by fear. Humility expelled the disease of proud exaltation; and by this dispensation of divine providence that thorn was given him.

### QUESTION XL. “And they did not repent,” etc.

It is asked whether repentance is necessary for one who reforms his conduct for the better, and in what ways repentance is performed.

**Answer.** It is not enough to change one’s conduct for the better and withdraw from evil, unless satisfaction is made for guilt by the sorrow of repentance, the groaning of humility, and the sacrifice of a contrite heart. It should also be noted that repentance is performed in three ways: before baptism; after baptism for graver sins; and daily for lighter and frequent sins, according to the saying: “You have avoided great things; see that you are not crushed by sand.”

### QUESTION XLI. “We pray God that you do no evil” (2 Cor. 13).

[Col. 0554B] Here the Apostle indicates that one turns aside from evil only by God’s grace, saying: “We pray,” etc. For outward planting and watering avail nothing without inward growth, which God gives by grace alone. The question, therefore, is why Sacred Scripture often commands us both to turn aside from evil and to do good, when free choice is sufficient for neither of these, and when both are properly the work of grace alone.

**Answer.** The will does something, but does not act by itself. Therefore, when we are commanded to do this or that, we ought to acknowledge free choice; but when prayer is offered, the benefit of grace is sought. Concerning grace and free choice it has already been said above, and likewise what grace by itself accomplishes without the will [Col. 0554C], and what it does not accomplish without it; there is no need to repeat the same matters again.

## IV. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS

[Col. 0553]

[Col. 0553C] **(Gal. 1.) “Paul, an apostle,” etc.** The Apostle sends this Epistle to the Galatians. They had come from Gaul into a certain province of Greece and mingled with the Greeks. Hence that province was first called Gallograecia and afterward Galatia. Thus, although the Greeks are of keen intellect, these people are foolish and slower to understand, as Gauls are considered unteachable.

They were first instructed by the Apostle in faith [Col. 0553D] and evangelical doctrine; afterward they were subverted in many ways by false apostles, so that they believed Christ’s grace without the law of Moses to be insufficient for salvation. Hence it is clear what the specific subject matter is: the condition of the Galatians as it then stood; while the general subject matter is the common condition of the Church.

The Apostle’s intention in this Epistle is to call the Galatians, ensnared by the tricks of false apostles, back to the truth of Catholic faith and evangelical teaching. His method is as follows: he begins with a greeting, in which he briefly touches upon his own dignity and Christ’s grace against detractors and those who boast of the works of the law, commending his own person when the false apostles were disparaging him. After the greeting, he rebukes them for their fickleness; afterward, he commends his own person more fully. Then he disproves the law of Moses [Col. 0554C], teaching that it is not to be observed after Christ because it not only does not profit toward salvation and righteousness, but even harms. Afterward he commends the Gospel and faith in Christ, which suffice for salvation.

### QUESTION I. “Who gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from the present age,” etc.

Since the world or age is the work of God, who is the author only of good things, it is asked how the whole world can be said to lie in evil, or how the age can be called wicked.

[Col. 0554D] **Answer.** Not only places, but also times and instruments of evils, acquire the disrepute of the things done in them. Hence days are called evil and times dangerous. Forests full of robbers are also called evil; likewise the sword by which blood is shed and the cup from which poison is administered. Thus the world or age receives the name of wickedness because of the things done in it.

### QUESTION II. “But though we, or an angel, should preach to you beyond that,” etc.

Were there not many things which he had not yet preached to them, which ought to be believed and kept by little children who must be nourished with the milk of simple doctrine?

**Answer.** He does not say, “More than you have received,” but “beyond” [Col. 0555A] that; by this he means what is contrary. Hence he promised to come to some people so that he might supply what they lacked.

### QUESTION III. “If I were still pleasing people,” etc.

The question commonly raised here was resolved in the First Epistle to the Corinthians. But someone may say: Whatever may have been said elsewhere, I would like to hear how both statements are true: “If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ,” and “Please all people in all things” (1 Cor. 10). He himself does not wish to please people, so that he may be Christ’s servant; but he commands us to please all people. Does he not wish us not to be servants of Christ, since we cannot do both—please them and be servants of Christ? Hence it is written: “He scattered the bones of those who please people” [Col. 0555B] (Ps. 25).

The same question arises from different sayings of the Lord. In one place he says: “Let your light shine before people” (Matt. 5); and elsewhere: “Do not do your righteousness before people” (Matt. 6).

**Answer.** We are instructed by the words both of the Lord and of the Apostle in nothing other than not to place the end of good works in human praise, nor to desire such praise as though it were the reward of good works.

### QUESTION IV. “I persecuted the Church of God,” etc.

It is asked whether the Apostle sinned in persecuting the Church of God, since he had zeal for the law and believed that in doing this he was acting for God’s sake. For everyone is bound to do what conscience dictates ought to be done for God’s sake; and thus, if he did not do it, he would seem to offend God through contempt. Again, who can doubt that persecuting the Church is evil?

[Col. 0555C] **Answer.** Some say that whether he did this or that, he sinned. Others say that the zeal which the Apostle had was good, but that the deed itself—namely, the persecution of the Church—was evil and mistaken.

### QUESTION V. “But I saw none of the other apostles except James, the brother of the Lord.”

It is commonly asked why James the Less, son of Alphaeus, is called the brother of the Lord.

**Answer.** Some say that he was called the Lord’s brother because he was Joseph’s son by another wife, Joseph being thought to be the Lord’s father. But this is not established, since Joseph was believed to be a virgin; another explanation must therefore be sought.

It should be known, then, that Mary, the Lord’s mother, was the daughter of Joachim and Anna; she married Joseph, and thus Joseph was the Lord’s putative father. After Joachim died, Cleophas, Joseph’s brother, married the same Anna and begot by her a daughter whom he called Mary. She married Alphaeus, who begot sons: James, Joseph, Simon, and Judas. After Cleophas died, a certain Salomas took the same Anna as wife and begot by her a daughter named Mary, who married Zebedee and had by him sons—James, called the Greater, and John the Evangelist. Anna therefore had three husbands and three daughters.

It remains to be seen why James, son of Alphaeus and called the Less, is called the Lord’s brother. He was called the Less in comparison with the other James, who first attached himself to the Lord [Col. 0556A] and was therefore called Greater—not according to the time of birth, but of conversion. According to some, he was called the Lord’s brother because he was the son of his maternal aunt; or because of his likeness in holiness; or, more probably, because he was the grandson of Christ’s paternal uncle, namely Cleophas. For the Hebrews call brothers those joined by full consanguinity on the fathers’ side.

It should be noted that in Scripture “brothers” are so called in four ways: by nature, as Esau and Jacob; by nation, as all Jews call one another brothers; by kinship, as all those who belong to the same family, when a multitude spreads from one root—for Scripture calls Abraham, Lot, Jacob, and Laban brothers; and by affection, as all Christians are brothers, sharing the same grace and having the same heavenly Father.

[Col. 0556B] QUESTION VI. “You compel the Gentiles to live as Jews” (Gal. 2), etc. Concerning this rebuke, it is customary to ask whether it was genuine or merely dispensatory, and whether Peter sinned and was truly deserving of rebuke. Answer. In answering this question, those two illustrious lights, Jerome and Augustine, appear to disagree. Jerome says that the rebuke was dispensatory and not genuine, and that Peter neither sinned nor deserved rebuke. Augustine, however, maintains that the rebuke was genuine, not feigned, and that Peter truly deserved rebuke; he was not walking according to the truth of the Gospel—not because he became weak with the weak, but because by his example he compelled the Gentiles to live as Jews. Otherwise it would follow that Paul wrote falsely, which must in no way be believed.

[Col. 0556C] Likewise, concerning the abolition of the legal observances after Christ, these same two masters do not hold the same view. Jerome says that those legal observances are deadly after Christ. Augustine says that at that time, in the primitive Church, Jews were permitted to observe them, provided only that they did not place their hope in them. Before Christ’s coming they seem to have been necessary; at the very boundary between Law and grace they were indifferent, if hope was not placed in them; but now they are deadly. Note that a dispensation is a concession of an inferior state in order to avoid scandal, in which a lesser evil is done so that a greater may be avoided. With due reverence for mysteries, we prefer the judgment of blessed Augustine to that of blessed Jerome concerning the aforesaid rebuke and the abolition of the Law.

[Col. 0556D] Thus we answer blessed Jerome’s objections. The first is: “Christ is the end of the Law,” that is, its fulfilment and fullness, fulfilling and bringing it to completion in himself and in his own. Yet not in such a way that, after Christ’s advent, the Law could not lawfully be observed by anyone for any period of time. Again: “The Law and the prophets were until John.” Venerable old man Jerome, answer me with an unprejudiced mind: how is this to be understood, “the Law and the prophets until John”? Is it to be understood so that after John it was not lawful to observe the Law? That seems to follow from your argument. But did not Christ himself, even after John, observe the Law by celebrating the old Passover? Did Christ do what was unfitting? It must therefore be understood thus: “the Law and the prophets until John,” that is, from John onward the grace of the New Testament

[Col. 0557A] began both to be preached and to be bestowed; and from then the Old Testament began to cease. Again, at that time it was not heresy to observe the legal ceremonies, though now it would be—especially if anyone believed grace insufficient for salvation without the Law. Again: if they are to be observed, they confer salvation. Do we not observe certain things which do not confer salvation, but which we may use or not use at our discretion?

QUESTION VII. “No one shall be justified by works of the Law, except through faith in Christ.” It is asked how faith justifies and works do not, since God renders to each according to his works. Does not merit and reward, crown and righteousness, arise from works? If, therefore, the crown is from works, righteousness too seems to arise from the same. Answer. In the Epistle to the Romans this question has been discussed

[Col. 0557B] according to our capacity. For the present it is enough to say this: faith is said to justify because, from certainty concerning invisible things, eternal goods are loved; and love justifies. Thus we are said to be justified by faith because it is the first thing from which the rest are obtained. Nor, when he says that we are justified by faith, are good works rendered vain; rather, he says this because the works themselves arise from the grace of faith.

QUESTION VIII. “If I rebuild what I destroyed, I make myself a transgressor.” But someone will say: Did he not destroy the faith which he had been attacking, and rebuild it by preaching; and thus does he not appear to be a transgressor? Answer. Whoever destroys a false thing which can be destroyed, if he rebuilds it, is a transgressor. But faith cannot be destroyed, although

[Col. 0557C] it can be attacked. Therefore, although Paul had previously attempted to destroy our faith and afterwards to rebuild it, he was not a transgressor.

QUESTION IX. The same matter is objected thus: “If I rebuild what I destroyed.” Behold, he plainly says that he destroyed the legal observances; yet elsewhere he says: “Do we then destroy the Law? By no means! Rather, we uphold the Law” (Rom. 3). How then are both true? Answer. A person is said to destroy the Law in two ways. One destroys the Law by declaring it useless in its own state before the incarnation of the Word, and by asserting that it was not given by God; and in this sense Paul did not destroy the Law. A person is also said to destroy the Law by showing that after Christ’s advent it is not to be kept according to the flesh;

[Col. 0557D] and in this sense Paul destroyed the Law when he said: “If you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing.”

QUESTION X. Is Christ then a minister of sin, when the Law is good and the commandment good, righteous, and holy? How, if Christ ministers the Law, does he minister sin? Did God, when he gave the Law, minister sin? Answer. The Law is indeed good, yet it is an occasion of sin; and in this respect the minister of the Law is called a minister of sin.

QUESTION XI. “For through the Law I died to the Law,” etc.; that is, through the Law’s authority I abandoned it. But by what authority, it is asked? Answer. Moses says: “I will raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren, whom you shall hear as you hear me” (Deut. 18). And Jeremiah: “I shall establish a new covenant with the house of Israel.” And David:

[Col. 0558A] “And you did not require a burnt offering for sin; then I said: Behold, I come” (Ps. 39). It is also written in the Law: “You shall hate your enemy” (Matt. 5). Since no one can be saved while hating an enemy, it is plain that the Law justifies no one. Therefore one must flee from it to grace, which justifies. And because the Law restrained only the hand, not the mind, in external acts, and placed all its worshippers under a curse, it is evident that through it they themselves must die, so that they may live in God.

QUESTION XII. “Who loved me and gave himself for me,” etc. Recall that question concerning how the Father, the Son, and Judas concur in the handing over of the Son, discussed according to our ability in the commentary on the Epistle to the Romans. “For if righteousness is through the Law, then Christ died gratuitously”; but Christ did not die gratuitously—that is, without cause or benefit. Therefore righteousness is not from the Law. Reader, recall this authority whenever you need to prove that righteousness is not from the Law. I say this because there are authorities by which it seems possible to show that righteousness is from the Law, as was demonstrated above.

[Col. 0558B] QUESTION XIII. “Who has bewitched you so that you do not believe the truth?” etc. It is asked what bewitchment is. Answer. A magical deception by which certain things are shown to human eyes otherwise than they are is called a *fascinus*, or bewitchment; or, in common speech, bewitchment is that which harms infants. For some eyes are said to burn by their gaze, and this act is considered bewitchment. So envy harms not only the envious person, wasting away at another’s prosperity,

[Col. 0558C] but also those in whom certain goods are beginning to appear. Hence it is written: “The bewitchment of frivolity obscures good things” (Wis. 4).

QUESTION XIV. “Those who are of faith shall be blessed; those who are of works of the Law are under a curse.” It is asked what it means to be “of faith,” and what it means to be “of works of the Law.” Answer. Those are of faith whose being depends on faith—that is, who through faith tend toward true being, and who seek to be justified through the grace of faith. They alone will receive from God the blessing of eternal life. But those are said to be of works of the Law who seek to be justified by them; and therefore they are under a curse, as transgressors of the Law.

QUESTION XV. “Cursed is everyone who does not remain

[Col. 0558D] in all things written in the book of the Law, to do them.” It is asked whether God commanded in the Law anything that cannot be fulfilled. If the answer is “nothing,” how are all who are of works of the Law under a curse? Again, if God commanded something to a human being which he himself did not will that person to do, God appears unjust and cruel. Answer. Some say that nothing was commanded in the Law which a human being cannot fulfil. Against them the commentator says that God commanded many things which no one was able wholly to fulfil. Hence the apostle Peter says: “Why do you test God by placing upon us a yoke which neither we nor our fathers were able to bear?” (Acts 15).

QUESTION XVI. “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.” It is asked whether Christ is included under this universality of curse.

[Col. 0559A] But he is the one who is above all, God blessed for ever; through him every curse is removed, and he has blessed us with every blessing in the heavenly places. For he is the promised seed of Abraham, in whom the blessing of all nations is accomplished. How, then, can he be cursed? Answer. There is one curse of fault, which is far from Christ; another is a curse of punishment, which Christ voluntarily underwent, being made for us a curse—or sin, that is, an offering for sin—so that he might remove from the midst the curse of all, both of fault and of punishment. It may also be said that Christ was cursed with the curse of fault, not truly, but according to human opinion; hence, as a sinner, he was numbered among the wicked.

[Col. 0559B] QUESTION XVII. “For if the inheritance is from the Law, it is not from promise.” It is asked whether this inference is true. For it to be true, “the inheritance is from the Law” and “the inheritance is from promise” must be opposites; otherwise it would not follow: if from the Law, then not from promise. What, therefore, is it for the inheritance to be from the Law? What is it for it to be from promise? And what does he call inheritance? Answer. By inheritance he means eternal life. To be from the Law is to be from works of the Law, whose fulfilment a person seems sufficient to himself to accomplish, without needing God’s grace; this is for inheritance to be from merits. But for inheritance to be from promise is for it to be from grace. See, therefore, that to be from Law and to be from promise are opposites. Hence elsewhere the Apostle says: “If from works, then no longer from grace” (Rom. 11), that is, if from what is owed,

[Col. 0559C] then not from grace.

QUESTION XVIII. “Why then the Law?” Since the earlier saints, who were before the Law, were righteous through the grace of faith and obtained the promise, it is asked why the Law was given and what benefit it conferred. The Apostle gives the answer to this question when he says: “The Law was set in place because of transgression.” This can be understood in two ways: namely, the Law was set in place to restrain transgression, so that people might at least cease from transgressing through fear, and might someday do the same voluntarily; or the Law was set in place because of transgression, that is, in order to make people transgress, so that they might be humbled, seek a physician, and implore the help of grace. It was thus given to humble the proud, reveal weakness,

[Col. 0559D] and serve the hard-hearted as a scourge and as a sign of future things.

QUESTION XIX. It is asked why the Law was not given immediately after the fall of humankind; or why the Son himself did not come at once; or why he permitted so many people to perish. Answer. This was done by a great counsel: after the human fall, neither the Law was given nor the Son sent immediately. For unless human pride had first tested the powers of its own choice, it would have claimed sufficiency for freedom and judged the Law to have been given superfluously and the Son to have come in vain. Nor did all who then lived perish, just as not all who live now are saved. Therefore this was done so that a human being might recognize the sickness of his own weakness and implore the grace necessary for him. Under the natural law he was left to himself,

[Col. 0560A] so that he might thus test the powers of nature; and he was convicted of ignorance and confessed that the light of his eyes had failed. Yet he still believed himself to possess the power by which he could fulfil whatever was necessary for salvation. Hence he said: “There is no lack of one to fulfil it; there is a lack of one to command it.” As though he said: “I need knowledge, not power.” The Law was therefore given to enlighten ignorance, but not to aid weakness: it exposed sin, but did not destroy it. Once it was given, the sickness gained strength and desire increased—not through a fault of the Law, but through the fault of nature and the devil’s pressure—so that, once the insufficiency of both laws and human weakness were recognized, people might cry out to the physician and seek the help of grace. Thus, as weaknesses multiplied, they hastened to the physician, who, coming in the form

[Col. 0560B] of a servant, healed the wounds of the sick.

For he is that Samaritan who approached the wounded man who had fallen among robbers and bound up his wounds; whom the priest and Levite—that is, the Law and priesthood—passed by (Luke 10), because the Law brought no one to perfection (Heb. 7). He is Elisha, who, after sending a staff ineffective for salvation, came to raise the dead son of the Shunammite woman (4 Kings 4). He is the Angel of great counsel, who descended into the pool, and when the water was stirred one person was healed (John 5). He is the almighty Word who came from royal thrones while all things were held in the midst of silence (Wis. 18). Note that there are three silences. The first silence is ignorance of the sickness, which existed under the natural law. The second silence is despair of salvation,

[Col. 0560C] which existed under the written Law, and this is the middle silence. The third silence is the attainment of health, which will be in the glory of eternal blessedness. Therefore, while all things were held in the middle silence—that is, while they despaired of salvation—the Son of the supreme King descended from the light of heaven to the darkness of the world or of hell. Coming, he spoke peace, gave grace, offered mercy, and promised forgiveness. Thus, when the middle silence was broken, the sick began, with pure faith and true confession, as though with loud cries, to demand a remedy and hasten to the physician, through whom the sick might be healed and their wounds treated.

QUESTION XX. “The Law was placed in the hand of a Mediator.” It is asked why Christ is called Mediator. Answer.

[Col. 0560D] Because he mediates for us, that is, reconciles us to God.

QUESTION XXI. But since not only the Son reconciles us to himself, but also God the Father, as the Apostle says: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5), it is asked why the Son alone is called Mediator between God and human beings. Answer. The whole Trinity reconciles us to itself through the exercise of power; but the Son alone justifies and reconciles us through the fulfilment of obedience and the reception of the sacraments. Hence he alone is not improperly called Mediator.

QUESTION XXII. Since Christ, God and man, is mediator of God and human beings, it is asked according to which nature—divine, human, or both—he is Mediator. Answer. The authorities say that he is not mediator according to

[Col. 0561A] his being God, but only according to his being man, approaching us through mortality and God through righteousness.

QUESTION XXIII. “But Scripture has confined all things under sin.” It is asked what he calls Scripture. Answer. The Law, which elsewhere the Apostle calls “the letter,” he here calls “Scripture,” because it only commands and does not help. It convicts of sickness the sick person who seemed healthy to himself, and thus, by showing sins but not removing them, confines all things under sin. The Law was therefore given so that grace might be sought; and grace was bestowed so that through it the Law might be fulfilled. This agrees with what he says elsewhere: “God confined all things in unbelief, that he might have mercy upon all” (Rom. 11).

QUESTION XXIV. “As many of you as were baptized

[Col. 0561B] in Christ have put on Christ.” It is asked of one who comes deceitfully to baptism whether he is baptized in Christ and has put on Christ. If it is said that he is, it follows that he is conformed to Christ. But if he is not baptized, then, should he repent of his pretence, he could be baptized; yet this is not granted him. It is therefore clear that he is baptized. Answer. To be baptized in Christ and to put on Christ are understood in two ways: either by reception of the sacrament, which is common to the good and the bad; or by inward sanctification and conformity of life, which belongs only to the good.

QUESTION XXV. It is asked how Christ is the clothing of the saints, and whether the saints are Christ’s clothing. Answer. Christ is called the clothing of the saints, and the saints also the clothing

[Col. 0561C] of Christ—but in different ways. Christ is called the clothing of the saints through the overshadowing of the Holy Spirit, protecting them from the heat of vices. The saints, however, are Christ’s clothing, as though having him within themselves and surrounding him. They also honour him by their holy manner of life, just as the wicked, by living wickedly, blaspheme him.

QUESTION XXVI. “If you are Christ’s, then you are Abraham’s,” etc. Christ is called Abraham’s seed, and believers are called Abraham’s seed. Hence it is asked whether Christ and believers are called Abraham’s seed in the same sense. Answer. Christ is Abraham’s seed bodily, because he was born from Abraham’s stock; believers are Abraham’s seed spiritually—that is, righteous through

[Col. 0561D] faith, as Abraham was.

QUESTION XXVII. “We were enslaved under the elements of the world” (Gal. 4). If Jews too were enslaved under the elements, in what did they differ from pagans? Answer. Jews served God under the elements, not the elements themselves; pagans, however, rendered divine worship not to God but to the elements themselves.

QUESTION XXVIII. “When the fullness came,” etc. It is asked why the Savior’s coming is called the fullness of time. Answer. Because in this time the things foretold in previous times are fulfilled. More properly it would seem to be called “the time of fullness” than “the fullness of time”; and it is the same thing as “the end of the age.”

QUESTION XXIX. “God sent his Son,” etc. It is asked

[Col. 0562A] from where and to where the Son was sent. Hear: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16).

QUESTION XXX. But someone will say: “Was he not in the world, and was not the world made through him?” (John 1). Was he sent there where he had previously been? Answer. He was previously in the world through power and essence, but he began to be in the world in another manner, having become visible by assuming the form of a servant. Therefore, just as when he came forth from the Father he did not leave the Father, so he came into the world in which he had already been. Why the mission of the Son or of the Holy Spirit, though it is the work of the Trinity, is attributed to the Father has already been explained above.

QUESTION XXXI. “Made of a woman.” Since the Lord was born of a virgin, it is asked why the Apostle states that he was made of a woman. Answer. He uses the Hebrew

[Col. 0562B] manner of speech, which uses *mulier* (“woman”) for a female; thus Eve is called woman in Genesis even before she had experienced intercourse. Note that the commentator says that the Creator, who always existed, was made so that he might be a creature: he was made human so that he might become what he was not, not so that what he was might perish. I say this because certain persons deny that he was made anything.

QUESTION XXXII. “Made under the Law, that he might redeem those who were under the Law,” etc. Did he not redeem by his death both those who were under the Law and those who were without the Law? How then does the Apostle say that Christ was made under the Law in order to redeem those who were under the Law, as though he redeemed them through observance of the Law? Answer. He was made under the Law in order to fulfil it and, once fulfilled, cause it to cease; and thus also

[Col. 0562C] redeem the Jews from transgression of the Law. For unless he observed the Law in which the promise was made, who would believe that he was the seed of Abraham promised to Abraham, in whom not Jews only but all nations would be blessed?

QUESTION XXXIII. “That we might receive adoption as sons.” What does he call adoption: gratuitous goods pertaining to present righteousness, or those pertaining to future glory, through which we are made sons? Answer. Some think a distinction should be made between sons by adoption and sons by grace; but I judge them to be the same.

QUESTION XXXIV. “God sent the Spirit of his Son,” etc. Note that the Trinity is here plainly indicated. There are some who say that, just as the eternal generation of the Word

[Col. 0562D] is from the Father alone, so too is his temporal mission; for according to them, for the Father to send the Son is for the Son to be from the Father and to appear to us in assumed flesh. They make the same assertion concerning the Holy Spirit: just as his eternal procession is from the Father and the Son, and not from himself, so too is his temporal mission. But Augustine plainly says that the temporal mission of both the Son and the Holy Spirit is the work of the Trinity; hence the Son himself says that he was sent by the Holy Spirit.

QUESTION XXXV. “Crying: Abba, Father.” It is asked why the Apostle put two words having the same meaning; for one of them appears superfluous. Answer. He does this in order to indicate two peoples joined in one faith. For the Hebrew name signifies the Jews, while the Greek word signifies the Gentile people;

[Col. 0563A] the identical meaning of the two words symbolizes the unity of faith and Spirit.

QUESTION XXXVI. “Those who by nature are not gods.” Here he indicates that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit have one nature. For if the Son is not God by nature, then he is neither to be worshipped nor adored. But this objection is made against us: Is not Christ’s humanity worshipped and adored? Yet it is not God by nature. Answer. That which is assumed is adored not for its own sake but because of the one assuming it. Therefore we do not worship the Savior’s humanity alone and naked, but united to the Godhead.

QUESTION XXXVII. “Or rather, having been known by God.” Does not God know all things from eternity? How, then, is God said to know us then, as though for the first time, when we begin to believe in him? Answer. By a figurative expression,

[Col. 0563B] what we do with God as author is attributed to him. Thus he is said to intercede for the saints because he makes them intercede; so he is said to know us because he grants us knowledge of himself, and to rest because he causes us to rest in himself.

QUESTION XXXVIII. “How are you turning back again to weak and needy things?” The Galatians did not previously keep the Law; how then does he say, “You are turning back again to needy things,” etc.? Answer. In order to show that legal observance after Christ’s advent differs little or not at all from idolatry. Or he says this because they wished not only to keep the Law but also were returning to their former errors. Thus they had been ensnared by false teachers in a double error.

QUESTION XXXIX. “The seventh year of the seventh decade,

[Col. 0563C] which is called jubilee.” What does the commentator mean by this? Was not the fiftieth year called jubilee in the Law? How, then, was the seventh year of the seventh decade called jubilee? For the seventh of the seventh decade is the sixty-seventh year. Answer. At one time, oppressed by captivity, the children of Israel could not observe the jubilee year in its proper order. But in the sixty-sixth year permission to return was granted by Cyrus and Darius; some returned, and they observed the sixty-seventh year as a jubilee. But someone will say that they did not return from captivity before the seventy years were completed. Answer. They did not indeed return generally and wholly before the seventieth year; nevertheless, in the

[Col. 0563D] sixty-sixth year, as we have said, permission to return was granted to some. This is signified by the *Alleluia* sung on the Saturday after Parasceve [Good Friday], which is the sixty-sixth day of Septuagesima. But because some were still held in captivity, the tract follows, which is a sign of labor, just as *Alleluia* is a sign of joy. On the following Saturday, the second as well as the first *Alleluia* is sung, prefiguring the general return of the Jews when the seventy years are complete.

QUESTION XL. “If it could have been done, you would have plucked out,” etc. Could not what the Apostle says have been done? Answer. Sacred Scripture says that what is not justly done cannot be done. Thus Job says: “Would that I could kill myself” (Job 10). And the Lord says to Lot: “I cannot do anything

[Col. 0564A] until you enter there” (Gen. 19). He said that he could not do what he certainly could do by power, but not by justice.

QUESTION XLI. “Abraham had two sons.” Did he not have more sons by Keturah after Sarah’s death? How, then, does the Apostle say that he had two, as though he had no more than two? Answer. If he had more than two, then he had two; for he does not say “only two.” Yet he speaks of these rather than the others because Scripture treats each of these individually, indicating that something extraordinary was prefigured.

QUESTION XLII. “These are the two covenants.” Concerning this and similar expressions, it is asked how they are true. Is not a figure one thing and truth another; a signifier one thing and the thing signified another? How, then,

[Col. 0564B] is the name of the truth predicated of the name of the figure, when it is said, “These are the two covenants,” and “the rock was Christ” (1 Cor. 10)? Answer. In such passages the word “is” is used in the sense of “signifies.”

QUESTION XLIII. It may likewise be asked why Sacred Scripture uses the substantive verb in such a place. Would it not be clearer if it said, “These signify the two covenants,” and “the rock prefigured Christ”? Answer. To signify belongs to words; properly speaking, to be belongs to things. In theology, however, not only words have signification, but things too are employed as signs of other things; that is, certain things signify other things. Therefore, whenever Sacred Scripture wishes to show what thing signifies what other thing, it does not say, “this signifies that,” but “this is that,” as “the rock

[Col. 0564C] was Christ.” For if it were said, “the rock signifies Christ,” it would appear that the signification of the word *rock*, rather than of the thing which is a rock, was being shown.

QUESTION XLIV. Note that above he says that Ishmael was born according to the flesh, Isaac not according to the flesh but through promise. But was not Isaac, like Ishmael, born by the union of both sexes? How, then, was he not born according to nature or according to the flesh? Answer. Ishmael was born by the customary law of nature, namely, through the concurrence of natural causes. Isaac’s generation, however, was an operation not of nature but of divine power and grace. For nature grants no children through such intercourse as could take place between Abraham, an old man, and Sarah, an old

[Col. 0564D] and barren woman; but what nature denied, grace bestowed.

QUESTION XLV. “But just as then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was born according to the Spirit, or promise, so also now.” It is asked: Where is it found that Ishmael persecuted Isaac? For Genesis reads that the elder was playing with the younger (Gen. 21). What evil, then, did he do? What sin did he commit? How did he persecute him merely by playing? Answer. Sarah understood the elder’s play with the younger as mockery. Hence she said indignantly: “Cast out the slave woman and her son” (ibid.). And the Apostle calls such mockery persecution. Thus we too are more persecuted by mockers than by open persecutors.

QUESTION XLVI. “If you are circumcised, Christ will

[Col. 0565A] profit you nothing” (Gal. 5). Did not the Apostle circumcise Timothy? Therefore did he deceive him and make Christ profit him nothing? Answer. He says this of those who sought to be justified by circumcision; for that reason they had themselves circumcised, and thus fell away from grace, which they believed insufficient. But for those who received it from a certain reverence, yet did not place their hope in it, it was not harmful according to Augustine. According to Jerome, however, its reception harmed everyone unless a dispensation was made. This controversy has been more fully discussed above.

QUESTION XLVII. “I testify to every man who circumcises himself that he is bound to perform the whole Law.” If he fulfils the whole Law, can he even then attain righteousness? This seems to follow from these words; but

[Col. 0565B] elsewhere it is plainly stated that righteousness is not from the Law. Again, is not every person bound to fulfil the Law, at least according to the Spirit? Why then does he say that every person who circumcises himself owes this, but no one else? Again: is not everyone bound to love his neighbor as himself? But whoever loves his neighbor fulfils the whole Law. Do not these points show that everyone is bound to fulfil the entire Law? What then does he mean when he says: “I testify to every man who circumcises himself,” etc.? Answer. Whoever seeks to be justified through circumcision or the Law is bound, if he is to possess righteousness or be worthy of life, to fulfil whatever is commanded in the Law: namely, to desire nothing, and to love God with his whole heart. Perfect righteousness consists in these two things. If anyone possessed it, he would not need the grace

[Col. 0565C] of faith, any more than the angels of God do; but it has been granted to no one in the present life except the sole Mediator of God and human beings. Therefore, if anyone wishes to be justified or made blessed, he must flee to grace alone. For if he seeks to be justified in the Law, what is demanded of him cannot be discharged by a human being.

QUESTION XLVIII. “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has any power.” The commentator says that those who are in Christ Jesus must shun vices and seek virtues, but neither shun nor seek intermediate things, among which he includes circumcision. Hence it appears that circumcision neither benefits nor harms. But above it was said that circumcision not only does not benefit but even harms. And the Apostle says: “If you are circumcised, Christ will not profit you.” If, therefore,

[Col. 0565D] it takes Christ away from us, it harms greatly. Answer. Circumcision received simply, provided that it is not made a ground of salvation, appears indifferent; and thus it neither benefits nor harms. But if it is received with this intention and disposition, namely, that salvation is sought from it, it harms.

QUESTION XLIX. “The whole Law is fulfilled in one saying: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Since there are two commandments of love, namely, of God and of neighbor, it is asked how the whole Law is fulfilled in love of neighbor. Answer. Love of God is contained in love of neighbor. For who can love a neighbor for God’s sake unless he loves God? Again, no one can love a neighbor as himself unless he loves

[Col. 0566A] himself; and no one loves himself unless he loves God. For what is it to love oneself but to love one’s own good? But the true and highest good is Christ. Otherwise, whoever loves iniquity hates his own soul.

QUESTION L. It is asked who is one’s neighbor. Answer. Every human being. Therefore we are bound by commandment to love every human being and to render offices of piety to everyone in need.

QUESTION LI. “As yourself,” etc. It is asked whether we ought to love our neighbor as much as ourselves. This seems to be so, since it is said, “as yourself.” Answer. “As” is not a term of quantity but of quality: we are bound to do for others what we would reasonably wish others to do for us. Note: since both commandments of love are contained in each

[Col. 0566B] of them, often one rather than both is stated. For if both were stated together, it would appear that one could be possessed, or might be possessed, without the other.

QUESTION LII. “The flesh desires against the spirit.” It is asked how the flesh is said to desire, since the soul alone desires. Answer. What the soul does through the flesh is attributed to the flesh, just as the ear is said to hear and the eye to see, although the soul acts through such instruments.

QUESTION LIII. Since in substance soul and spirit are the same, by what does the soul desire against the spirit? Does it desire against itself? Answer. By “the flesh desiring” he means the carnal pleasure which the soul has through the flesh. By the name “Spirit” he means spiritual pleasure.

[Col. 0566C] Because of these two pleasures, the inward human being is divided and receives different names. According to the lower pleasure, it is now called flesh, now human being, now soul, or “animal” [soulish] or carnal; according to the higher, it is called spirit, or spiritual, or the new human being.

QUESTION LIV. “If you are led by the Spirit, you are not under the Law.” It is asked what it means to be under the Law. Answer. To abstain from every evil act from fear of punishment rather than from love of righteousness is to be under the Law. So too one is said to be under the Law who seeks to be justified by it and who is bound to fulfil the whole Law.

QUESTION LV. “Now the works of the flesh are manifest, which are fornication,” etc. It is asked how the Apostle

[Col. 0566D] enumerates among the works of the flesh certain things that are not vices of the flesh but rather of the soul, such as anger, envy, and so forth. Answer. By the name “flesh” he signifies the whole human being, who, living according to himself, fell into these things. For it is an error to believe that all vices arise from the flesh, lest the devil, who has no flesh, appear exempt from them.

QUESTION LVI. “But the fruit of the Spirit is charity.” The commentator says that the Apostle calls the works of the Spirit “fruits” because they are to be sought for their own sake. But Augustine says that virtues are to be sought only for the sake of blessedness, and that nothing is to be loved for its own sake except the highest good, whose enjoyment makes us blessed. What, then, is to be said? What position is to be held? Answer. Virtues are to be sought for their own sake because they delight

[Col. 0567A] their possessors with sincere delight; but not only for their own sake, also for the sake of blessedness, which is the supreme end.

QUESTION LVII. “If a person should be overtaken in some transgression” (Gal. 6), etc. It is asked what it means to be overtaken and what he calls a transgression. Answer. A person is overtaken when he falls into some transgression or sin because either he does not know what ought to be done or omitted, or, though he knows it, weakness nevertheless drives him to sin. A transgression is abandonment of good, just as sin is commission of evil; or a transgression is what is done ignorantly, sin what is done knowingly. Nevertheless, the terms are used interchangeably.

### QUESTION LVIII

“Each shall bear his own burden,” etc. The question is how both statements can be true: “Bear one another’s burdens,” etc. [Col. 0567B], and what is said here, “Each shall bear his own burden.”  

**Answer.** Some burdens concern shared weakness, of which he spoke above; others concern the account to be rendered to God for our deeds, of which he speaks here. It is therefore true that in the present life we ought to assist one another, and that those who are stronger ought to bear the weaknesses of others; yet in the future each shall bear his own burden—that is, for his own sin and not for another’s.

### QUESTION LIX

“Let us do good to all,” etc. The question is whether we are bound by precept to render offices of loving-kindness even to enemies. This seems so, since the Apostle says, “Let us do good to all”; and the Lord says in the Gospel, “Love your enemies; do good to those who hate you” (Luke 6). But Augustine says: “To love one’s enemies is not characteristic of so great a multitude as I believe is heard in the Lord’s Prayer, where it is said: ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors’” (Matt. 6). And Gregory says: “It is enough not to hate one’s enemies,” that is, to will their salvation, even if works of mercy are not bestowed upon them.

**Answer.** We are bound by precept to will the salvation of all. But, as regards the weak and less perfect, rendering offices of loving-kindness also to enemies is counsel; as regards the perfect, it is precept. One must therefore carefully observe what is said by way of counsel and what by way of precept.

### QUESTION LX

Likewise, since it is agreed that it is good to do good to evil persons, sinners, and ungodly persons, what does Scripture mean when it says: “Give to the merciful man, and do not receive the sinner; render vengeance to the ungodly and sinners; do good to the humble man, and do not give to the ungodly” (Ecclus. 12)?

**Answer.** The meaning of the foregoing authorities is that you should not do good to any sinner because he is a sinner, but because he is a human being. That is, we ought not to foster anyone’s fault, but his nature. In each person let us love what God loves and hate what he himself hates. But if we cannot assist all alike, both good and evil, we ought to bestow such good things as we can upon the servants of God; hence the Apostle says: “Especially those of the household of faith.”

## V. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE EPHESIANS

[Col. 0567]

[Col. 0567C] (Eph. 1.) “Paul, an apostle,” etc. He writes this epistle to the Ephesians. Paul did not establish them in the faith, but confirmed them after they had been established by the Apostle John. They persevered steadfastly in faith and good works; he exhorts them to advance in good, writing from Rome, from prison. Thus the subject of the Apostle in this epistle is the condition of the Ephesians as it then stood. His intention is to confirm them in the good things they possess, to urge them to higher things, and also to instruct them in humility and thanksgiving.

His method is as follows. According to his custom, he first offers a greeting; then he gives thanks, setting forth the many benefits of God bestowed by grace alone upon the human race, upon the apostles themselves, and upon the Ephesians themselves. Next he displays Christ’s dignity and preeminence. Afterwards he invites them to patience [Col. 0567D] and love, commending the unity of faith and of the Church and enumerating the gifts of grace. Finally, exhorting them to battle, he describes the armor of Christian warfare against the princes of darkness.

### QUESTION I

“Blessed be God, who has blessed us,” etc. Since “to bless” is said both of God and of man, the question is whether it is said in the same way and with the same meaning.

**Answer.** It is said differently of each. For God is blessed by man when he is exalted with worthy praises; but man is blessed by God when God grants him the gifts of his grace. [Col. 0568C]

### QUESTION II

The expositor says that the Apostle here sets forth two predeterminations: one concerning present righteousness, the other concerning the future crown. But since God’s predestination is one, and is God himself, how can two be spoken of?

**Answer.** They are not called two because they are not one, but because it has two effects: present righteousness and future glory. The following objection is made to this answer: if the number of predestinations is to be determined by the number of effects, then predestinations will be infinite, since the effects of predestination are infinite.

**Answer.** All instances of righteousness, because they differ in number and not in species, are called one effect; likewise all crowns, because they are distinguished not by species but by number alone, are called one effect of predestination. But because present righteousness and future glory differ not only in number but also in species, they are not improperly called two effects of predestination. It should be noted that there are many things of this kind which, though several in number and one in species, are not simply called several but [Col. 0569A] one, according to ordinary speech. Thus my faith and his faith, though two in number, are nevertheless not simply called two but one, because they are one in species. The same distinction must be made concerning grass, voice, understanding, sight, and many other things—letter, figure, element, vowel.

### QUESTION III

“As he chose us, that we should be holy,” etc. The Pelagian says that those whom God chose from eternity, he chose because he foreknew that they would be good through the choice of free will, not because he was going to sanctify them. But the Apostle destroys this heresy when he says: “He chose us that we should be holy and blameless”; he does not say, “because we were going to be holy,” but “that we should be.” For if what the Pelagian says were so, our justification would be the cause [Col. 0569B] of divine election, rather than divine election the cause of our justification; and thus what is temporal would be the cause of what is eternal, rather than the reverse. This cannot be.

### QUESTION IV

“In whom we have redemption,” etc. The question is whether he calls redemption and remission of sins the same thing. If they are the same, one of them seems to have been stated superfluously.

**Answer.** By “redemption” he means that price by which we were redeemed, through which we are given the ability to return; but remission of sins, conferred on us in baptism, is the effect of redemption itself.

### QUESTION V

“To restore all things which are in heaven,” etc. Since Christ did not die for angels, how were the things in heaven restored through Christ?

**Answer.** This is said because those who are saved by grace make up the diminished number of angels. Or, by “the things in heaven” he means souls already in heaven; by “the things on earth,” saints still living in this life. [Col. 0569C]

### QUESTION VI

“You were sealed with the Holy Spirit, who is the pledge of our inheritance.” The question is how the Holy Spirit is called the pledge of our inheritance. Is not a pledge something given temporarily for a price, and then taken back when the price is paid? Is the Spirit therefore taken away from us when the inheritance itself is given to us?

**Answer.** Here “pledge” is used for *arrha*, an earnest or deposit that is part of the price itself and is not taken away when the price is paid. Hence some manuscripts have “earnest” (*arrham*), not “pledge.”

[Col. 0569D]

### QUESTION VII

“Setting him at his right hand,” etc. God is spirit and is not bounded or enclosed by bodily form. How then is the Son said to sit at the Father’s right hand, when the Father has no right or left side because he has no body?

**Answer.** In Sacred Scripture, the right hand of God sometimes signifies eternal blessedness, sometimes equality of divine nature, and sometimes judicial power. Christ is at the Father’s right hand because he remains equal in the Father’s majesty, and because “the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). Therefore nothing bodily should be understood by God’s right hand, hand, arm, finger, eye, ear, and similar expressions; all must be understood spiritually.

[Col. 0570A]

### QUESTION VIII

“Above every name that is named, not only in this age,” etc. Are there not nine orders of angels—angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, dominations, thrones, cherubim, seraphim—and no more than these, all of whom are named in the present? How then does he say, “Set above every name that is named, not only in this age but also in the future,” as though some would be named in the future who are not named in the present?

**Answer.** The names of certain angels are given according to the offices they perform for us in the present: angels, archangels, virtues, powers, principalities, and dominations. They are therefore called names belonging to the present, because in this manner their designation concerns the present. [Col. 0570B] Hence they will be abolished in the future, when Christ delivers the kingdom to God the Father and God is all in all. But the designations of certain angels concern the future state, such as thrones, cherubim, and seraphim; therefore they will not be abolished even in the future. Yet above all these orders of heavenly spirits the humanity of the Savior has been exalted.

### QUESTION IX

“And he gave him as head over the whole Church.” The question is according to which nature, divine or human, Christ is head of the Church.

**Answer.** It may be said that he is so according to the divine nature, according to which he is the head, beginning, and author of all the faithful. The following objection is made: by the same reasoning he could be said to be head of a stone and of every creature, of which he is the author; and nothing would be said specifically of the Church. Therefore we say that Christ is properly head of the Church according to his humanity. [Col. 0570C]

### QUESTION X

Why Christ is called the head of the Church. Why he is called the head may fittingly be asked.

**Answer.** Christ is called the head of the Church because, just as all bodily senses are fully present in a human head—namely sight, hearing, smell or olfaction, taste, and touch—so in Christ is the fullness of all spiritual senses, namely the fullness of grace, “of whose fullness we have all received” (John 1). Hence we are called members, as though not all possessing every sense, just as the other members of the body have only one sense; none has all except the head.

### QUESTION XI

“We were by nature children of wrath” (Eph. [Col. 0570D] 2), etc. God is the author of nature; therefore, if we are children of wrath by nature, it appears that this is so with God as author.

**Answer.** In Sacred Scripture “nature” is taken in three ways: first, for that whole and unimpaired good in which man was created; in this sense it is said that every creature of God is good. “Nature” is also called the corruption of sin, in which every human being is conceived and with which he is born; and it is so understood here when it says, “We were by nature children of wrath.” For vice has become ingrained as nature. Therefore, because on account of the fault of original sin, with which we are born, we deserve Gehenna, we are called children of wrath by nature. Nature is also taken for the remnants of that natural good which remained in us after sin; and it is so understood [Col. 0571A] where it is read that “the Gentiles naturally do the things of the law” (Rom. 2).

### QUESTION XII

“To me, the least of all the saints, grace was given” (Eph. 3). Since the Apostle was not the least in number among all the saints, but indeed was one of the foremost among the apostles, how can he truly call himself least of all?

Seek the answer to this question at the passage, “I am the least of the apostles,” in the First Epistle to the Corinthians.

### QUESTION XIII

“The unsearchable riches of Christ,” etc. The question is how the Apostle understood or preached them if the riches are unsearchable. For unsearchable things are said to be those which cannot be comprehended.

**Answer.** Things unsearchable by their nature were made traceable by the grace [Col. 0571B] and revelation of the Holy Spirit, not only to the Apostle but also to the other faithful, whom that anointing itself teaches concerning all things.

### QUESTION XIV

“Of the hidden mystery,” etc. The question is: what things are called hidden?

**Answer.** In the world, the causes of all things that happen naturally are hidden. But in God alone are hidden the causes of all things that happen by grace. Something has already been said above concerning these two kinds of causes.

### QUESTION XV

“That it might be made known to the principalities and powers in the heavenly places through the Church,” etc. The question is whether the mystery of the incarnation was revealed to the heavenly essences before its fulfillment. Jerome [Col. 0571C] and Augustine seem opposed in their answers to this question. Blessed Jerome says that the angelic dignities did not fully understand the aforesaid mystery; hence they ask: “Who is this who comes from Edom?” (Isa. 63), and elsewhere: “Who is this King of glory?” (Ps. 23). But blessed Augustine says that the mystery of the kingdom of heaven was not hidden from the angels. Hence the text, “That it might be made known,” etc., is explained in different ways.

This apparent opposition between the aforesaid doctors may be resolved thus: the mystery in question was revealed to those of greater dignity, but not fully to the others, as blessed Jerome says. Many teachers unanimously maintain that angels grow daily in knowledge from the things that occur in the world. [Col. 0571D] We therefore hold this as virtually certain, since canonical Scripture seems plainly to suggest it.

### QUESTION XVI

“From whom every fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named.” From this passage we have that not only God is our Father, but angels and human beings also are called our fathers. Yet elsewhere the Lord says: “One is your Father, who is in heaven” (Matt. 23). If he is one, how are there many? Or if there are many, how is he one?

**Answer.** Just as God, who alone truly is and alone truly is good, imparts the name of his being and goodness to other things, so that they too are called beings and good, so he who alone is truly Father of all by creation and of the faithful by regeneration has granted the name of fatherhood to others. It must be understood that God the Trinity is Father of all [Col. 0572A] by creation and of the faithful by regeneration. But the unbegotten God alone is Father of the Only-Begotten by nature. Angels are called our fathers by the authority of example, by reason of benefit, care, and providence. Human beings are called fathers by nature, by the authority of example, by reason of benefit, care, and providence.

### QUESTION XVII

“What is the breadth, and length, and height.” The breadth may be understood as the breadth of love, the length as that of eternity, the height as that of power, and the depth as that of knowledge, according to an interpretation concerning God.

### QUESTION XVIII

“To know also the love of Christ that surpasses knowledge.” If Christ’s love surpasses knowledge, how can it be known? If it cannot be known, how does the Apostle pray that the disciples may know it?

**Answer.** What human knowledge cannot comprehend is known in part by grace; and the Apostle prays that this may occur. [Col. 0572B]

### QUESTION XIX
