“That you may be filled unto all the fullness of God,” etc. Shall we not have less than God himself? How then can we be filled unto all the fullness of God? How can anyone have God’s fullness and not be God full and equal to God?

**Answer.** The sense is: that you may be full of God, not full God. This is to be filled into every fullness: to possess in the present the fullness of virtues and in the future the fullness of glory. Paul does not pray that anyone may receive the fullness of the divine nature, but that we may be full of God both now and in the future.

[Col. 0572C]

### QUESTION XX

“One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4). How are these to be understood?

**Answer.** The Father, Son, and Spirit are one Lord in nature, not in person. Faith is one not in number but in kind, because it is similar in all, just as all who will the same thing are said to have the same will. Faith has already been discussed. Baptism is called one because it is equal and of the same essence, by whomever it is administered, and also because it cannot be repeated.

### QUESTION XXI

“He gave gifts to men.” But David says: “You received gifts among men” (Ps. 67). If he gave, how did he receive? Or, if he received, how did he give?

**Answer.** As God, he gave. He received not only in himself insofar as he is human, but also in his members, in whom he is; and it is of this reception [Col. 0572D] that the Prophet speaks when he says, “You received gifts among men.”

### QUESTION XXII

What gifts did he give when ascending?

**Answer.** The Holy Spirit, and also gifts which are not the Holy Spirit. When he gives these gifts, he also gives the Holy Spirit in them; he does not give the Holy Spirit separately from his gifts, which are not himself. Rather, by giving the Holy Spirit he gives gifts, and by giving the gifts of the Holy Spirit he bestows the Spirit himself. I say this because of those who refuse to grant that the Holy Spirit is given, since he is immutable, though they grant that his gifts are given. For the Holy Spirit is said to be given to us by the Father, the Son, and even by himself when he pours into our hearts through love this power [Col. 0573A] by which we love God and neighbor.

### QUESTION XXIII

Since Christ is God and human, the question is according to which nature he gave gifts.

**Answer.** According to the nature by which, as the expositor says, he ascended and descended; thus he gave according to his humanity, because the divinity, which is everywhere, neither descends nor ascends. But this seems contrary to what was said above, where I maintained that he gave as God, not as human. Therefore, when it is read that he gave as human, or according to humanity, it must be understood as meaning: he who is human gave, not because he is human, but because he is God.

### QUESTION XXIV

Whether and how the Deity descended. Another exposition likewise says that Christ descended according to [Col. 0573B] his Deity and ascended according to his humanity, which seems contrary to what was said above. It was said that the divinity which is everywhere neither descends nor ascends; yet here it is said that the Deity descended. What then must be held?

**Answer.** When it is said that God descended, this is understood of the descent of the incarnation, by which God became human. When it is said that the human being descended, it must be understood of the descent into hell, which was according to the soul alone—not according to the body, which lay in the tomb, nor according to the Deity, which was everywhere.

### QUESTION XXV

“To a perfect man,” etc. The question is: by what perfection?

**Answer.** Perfection may be understood either of the whole Christ—that is, body and head—or [Col. 0573C] of the individual members. Christ is complete in himself; in others he grows and advances, but in the future he will at last be perfected so that nothing may be added either in strength or in number. Each person also will then be a perfect man, both by the consummation of virtues and by bodily stature. Hence follows: “To the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ.” For each shall rise in that perfection in which he was, or to which he would have attained, at thirty years of age. Not all will be of the same size, nor of the size Christ had when he departed from this life.

### QUESTION XXVI

“Be angry, and do not sin,” etc. The Apostle permits anger, which cannot be avoided, but the Lord forbids anger, saying: “Whoever [Col. 0573D] is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (Matt. 5). It therefore seems that the Apostle permits what the Lord forbids. Again, it was said above that nothing is forbidden in the New Testament which cannot be avoided, just as nothing is commanded which cannot be fulfilled. This does not seem true if the Lord forbids anger and no one can avoid becoming angry.

**Answer.** The first movement of anger, which is not in our power, is permitted by the Apostle. But the Lord does not forbid the first movement, called *propassio* [an initial involuntary passion], but the will and intention to harm another. Therefore one thing is permitted by the Apostle and another forbidden by the Lord; the latter can be avoided with the help of grace.

### QUESTION XXVII

What are the gates of death and life? Note that desire and fear of the world are two [Col. 0574A] gates of death through which the devil enters, just as fear and love of God are gates of life through which Christ enters. Each stands at the door: Christ knocks, and the devil also; but the enemy is cast out and Christ is brought in.

### QUESTION XXVIII

“Do not grieve the Holy Spirit,” etc. The question is how anyone can grieve the Holy Spirit, since he is impassible and cannot receive in himself the passion of grief.

**Answer.** He employs a trope quite common in theology, by which things brought about in us with God as their author are attributed to God himself. Therefore, because those whom he fills with love, just as they rejoice in the progress of others, so grieve over the falls of those who lapse, the Apostle says: “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit”—that is, those in whom [Col. 0574B] the Holy Spirit dwells through love.

### QUESTION XXIX

“Forgiving one another,” etc. Scripture says that unless we forgive our fellow servants, God reclaims what he had forgiven. But the question is how God reclaims it. Will God punish again for sins for which satisfaction has already been made through contrition of heart, confession of mouth, and worthy fruits of repentance? Will he punish twice for the same thing?

**Answer.** In order that someone may produce worthy fruits of repentance, it is required that thereafter he not sin mortally. Hence whoever sins after repentance makes his previous satisfaction useless to himself.

### QUESTION XXX

What is it to punish twice for the same thing? To punish twice for the same thing is to punish again in another life for a sin deleted by repentance and not repeated. [Col. 0574C] God does not do this. But if someone doing penance is afflicted for a sin and repeats that same sin, then, if he is punished for it again in this life or another, that is not punishment twice for the same thing.

### QUESTION XXXI

“For an odor of sweetness” (Eph. 5), etc. If Christ’s death was a sweet odor to God, then God willingly accepted his death; therefore the Jews who crucified him did not sin, because they did what was good and pleasing to God.

**Answer.** The action of the Jews was evil, and what was done by them did not please God. But Christ’s suffering was good and the cause of our salvation.

### QUESTION XXXII

“The days are evil,” etc. Do not days have their being from God as author, as it is written: “Yours [Col. 0574D] is the day, and yours is the night” (Ps. 73)? How then are they called evil?

**Answer.** Days are called evil on account of human wickedness and misery; otherwise, as regards their divisions of hours, they are ordered and good.

### QUESTION XXXIII

“No one has hated his own flesh,” etc. Do not holy men hate, persecute, crucify, and mortify the flesh rather than nourish or cherish it? How then is it true that “No one has hated his own flesh”?

**Answer.** The saints hate and persecute not the flesh, but the vice of the flesh.

### QUESTION XXXIV

“For this reason a man shall leave his father.” The question is how this applies to the Son of God, who never forsook the Father but always remained inseparably with him.

**Answer.** Because the Son did not appear to us in that form in which he is equal to the Father, he is said to have forsaken or left the Father; yet he never departed from him. He came into the world and did not forsake the Father. [Col. 0575A]

### QUESTION XXXV

“He who loves his wife.” The question concerns what love is treated here. For if it is the love by which we love one another for God’s sake, the sense is: “He who loves his wife loves himself,” that is, he does what is useful to himself. On this basis he could say the same concerning any neighbor.

**Answer.** The Apostle says this because it is more incumbent upon a husband to provide for his wife than for another person. Therefore, if for God’s sake he procures her necessities and governs her, he also loves himself—that is, he does what is useful to himself—because by this he merits before God.

### QUESTION XXXVI

“Servants, obey your masters” (Eph. 6). Here the question is whether it is lawful for a Christian to have a slave, since the Apostle permits it. The Catholic Church also, and especially the Church of the Gauls, accepts it.

**Answer.** It would be better not to demand servitude of this kind. Nor does the Church accept it as a good, but tolerates it as an evil. [Col. 0575B]

### QUESTION XXXVII

“Children, obey your parents; and you, fathers, do not provoke your children to anger.” The question is why the Apostle commands parents to love their children [Col. 0576A] and children to honor their parents, when nature compels them to love one another.

**Answer.** Natural love has no merit unless it is done for God’s sake. Therefore he commands them to love one another for God’s sake, that they may thus have merit.

### QUESTION XXXVIII

“Our struggle is not against flesh.” Do not the saints fight against flesh and blood, against evil human beings, or against vices that arise from flesh and blood? How then does he say: “Our struggle is not,” etc.?

**Answer.** Our struggle is not only against flesh and blood, but also against demons.

### QUESTION XXXIX

“Against the rulers of the world.” Does not God, who made the world, govern and rule it, so that he is both maker and ruler? How then does the Apostle call demons rulers of the world?

**Answer.** Here by the name “world” he signifies lovers of the world. This is the world which lies wholly in the evil one; this is the world in which there is found nothing but the desire of the flesh, the desire of the eyes, and the pride of life. The Apostle calls this world darkness, adding “of this darkness,” and saying elsewhere: “You were once darkness, but now light in the Lord” (Eph. 5). [Col. 0576B]

## VI. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS

[Col. 0575]

[Col. 0575C] (Phil. 1.) “Paul and Timothy,” etc. The Apostle writes this epistle to the Philippians, who are Macedonians. Philippi is a metropolitan city in Macedonia, a province in Greece. Philip, the father of Alexander, built it and called it after his own name. Having received the word of preaching from the Apostle, these people were firm in faith and admitted no false teachers. He therefore fortifies them against a twofold warfare, namely that of tribulations and of false preachers.

Thus the Apostle’s intention in this epistle is to exhort the Philippians to patience against tribulations and constancy against false apostles. His method is as follows: according to his usual custom, he first offers a greeting. Then he gives thanks for them, imploring greater goods for them, that, increasing in virtues, they may attain perfection. Then [Col. 0575D] he urges patience in tribulations by his own example and that of Christ. Afterwards he admonishes them to guard themselves against the guiles of false apostles. Finally he inserts a moral admonition; and near the end he says that he rejoices over the gift which the Romans sent him through Epaphroditus.

### QUESTION I

“For what then? Provided that in every way, whether through occasion or through truth, Christ is proclaimed.” The question is how the Apostle permits evil persons to preach evangelical doctrine, when elsewhere it is written: “God said to the sinner: Why do you recount my righteous ordinances?” (Ps. 49), etc. Likewise: “Praise is not fitting in the mouth of a sinner” (Ecclus. 15). Likewise: “When a man’s life is despised, it remains that his preaching should be disregarded.”

**Answer.** In such cases the preacher is rebuked on his own account, not on account of others. For what he preaches does not profit himself but others; [Col. 0576C] hence praise of God in the mouth of sinners is not fitting. Hired laborers are therefore to be tolerated. Hence the Lord says: “The scribes and Pharisees sit on Moses’ seat: do what they say” (Matt. 25), etc. Therefore preachers who preach for truth’s sake are to be loved; hired laborers, who announce truth for occasion and temporal advantage, are to be permitted; thieves and robbers—that is, wolves—are to be guarded against—indeed, fled from.

### QUESTION II

“What I shall choose, I do not know,” etc. The question is how the Apostle can be uncertain whether to choose to remain in the flesh or to be dissolved and be with Christ (Phil. 1), when he knows that the stronger the struggle, the greater the crown. Did he not know that fighting has greater merit than resting?

**Answer.** Affection drew him toward both; therefore he says that he does not know what to choose. The Apostle’s uncertainty is thus one of affection, not ignorance. But then it is asked: how does he say that to be dissolved and be with Christ is much better?

**Answer.** Here “better” means more pleasant and more secure. [Col. 0576D]

### QUESTION III

“To you it has been granted not only to believe in him, but also to suffer for him,” etc. The question is whether suffering itself is good and whether it is a gift of God; if it is, it ought to be desired.

**Answer.** He from whom comes the faith of believers also gives the endurance of those who suffer. But punishment itself is not good in itself, is not to be desired for its own sake, and ought not to be reckoned among God’s gifts. Yet to suffer for Christ is good and desirable because it has great merit. Nor does the Apostle simply say, “To you it has been granted to suffer”; [Col. 0577A] rather, he says: “To you it has been granted to suffer for Christ.”

### QUESTION IV

“Who, being in the form of God” (Phil. 2). The question is what “form” denotes here.

**Answer.** Form is sometimes used for representation, sometimes for the truth of a thing, as here: “Who, being in the form of God,” that is, in the truth of the divine essence and equality of substance. For just as a human being begets a human being and a dog a dog [Note: [Col. 0577] “Not only is the comparison inadequate, but it is also baser and almost impious.” EDITION OF THE *PATROLOGIA*.], so God begot God, equal in all respects, not unequal. Hence the Son is said to be what the Father is. Since this can be understood according to person and nature, Augustine explains the meaning of the statement, saying: the Son is said to be what the Father is because, just as the Father is God, so also is the Son; just as the Father is omnipotent, so also is the Son; and just as the Father is immutable, so also is [Col. 0577B] the Son. For the Father and Son are one, and supremely one, because there is no diversity of nature or will between them. Scripture therefore says both that the Son is equal to the Father and that the Father is greater than the Son; the latter according to the form of a servant, the former according to the form of God.

### QUESTION V

“And he was found in appearance as a man,” etc. In how many ways does one thing come to be possessed by another?

**Answer.** A thing may accrue to another so as to be possessed in four ways: either so that it changes and is not changed, as wisdom; or so that it changes and is changed, as food; or so that it neither changes nor is changed, as a ring; or so that it does not change but is changed—not from its own nature, but from a certain prior form—as clothing when it is put on. It does not change the human being, but is changed; not from its own nature, but it receives the appearance and form which it did not have when laid aside. The incarnation is understood by this comparison and likeness. Thus the form of a servant came to the form of God in such a way that it did not change or transform it; rather, the form of a servant itself was changed, not from its own nature but into a more excellent and worthy state than it had previously possessed. [Col. 0577C]

Therefore Augustine adduces all this concerning appearance or habit (*habitus*) in order to show that when the Word became flesh, it was not changed or transformed into a human being, just as a human being is not changed into clothing when he puts it on. But what some add of their own—that just as a human being does not become something when he puts on his clothing, so neither did God become something when he took the form of a servant—this, I say, they do not have from Augustine’s words or from those of any other saint, since it is false. For if they wish to maintain the analogy drawn from clothing in every respect, they must concede that just as a human being does not become clothing when he puts it on, so God did not become human when he put on the form of a servant.

For if Christ is only what he was from eternity, he has no being in common with his mother; therefore he is not consubstantial with his mother, because nothing substantial is predicated of both. For when it is said, “Christ is a human being” and “the Virgin, mother of the Lord, is a human being,” the term “human being” does not signify the same thing in each statement according to these new heretics. These matters have been discussed more fully above in the Epistle to the Romans. [Col. 0577D]

### QUESTION VI

“Who humbled himself, becoming obedient,” etc. The question is whether Christ merited anything.

**Answer.** He merited for us, not for himself. For through his merit we were made worthy of eternal life; but by his death he acquired for himself nothing of which he was not previously worthy. Yet it may truly be said that through the humility of his passion he merited the glory of resurrection, namely impassibility and immortality. I do not say that Christ would not have become immortal and impassible unless he had died; rather, I say that such merit was worthy of such a reward.

[Col. 0578A]

### QUESTION VII

The question is how supreme blessedness and sorrow could coexist in the same soul; for before the passion both were in Christ. That blessedness was present in him according to the mind from the time that he became human must be believed; otherwise, I do not see how he could be true God. Likewise, that sorrow was present there is clear, since he himself says: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26).

**Answer.** Just as Paul had an inferior power and a superior power, so Christ had an inferior power, namely a movement or certain affection of the soul that recoiled from death; yet the higher reason flourished freely in its blessedness. For bodily affection in him did not, as it does in others, impede reason in any respect, so that he contemplated the divinity less fully. [Col. 0578B]

### QUESTION VIII

Likewise, the question is how he did not have greater blessedness after the resurrection, when he put on immortality and impassibility.

**Answer.** He did not then have more in respect to the mind, but then possessed more peacefully what he had possessed before—just as a king possesses his kingdom more peacefully and securely when the enemies who harass it have ceased. [Col. 0578C]

### Question IX

“Therefore God bestowed [on him],” etc. Did he not previously possess the name that is above every name? How then does he say, “Therefore he bestowed”? For this name was given him not only eternally by nature, insofar as he is God, but also, insofar as he is man, it was given by grace to the assumed man from his conception.  

**Solution.** A thing is said to come to be when it becomes known. What he possessed before, then first became known after the resurrection to human beings and demons.

### Question X

Likewise it is asked to whom this name was given [Col. 0578D]: to God or to man?

**Solution.** Augustine says that the name above every name was given to the man, and not to God (Philippians 2): namely, that he should be God and Son of God by the grace not of participation but of union, and that the assumed man should possess by grace all that the begotten God possesses by nature. Thus by grace the man possesses sonship—not as a son of grace, but as a Son by nature. Ambrose states differently: the name above every name was given to God, not to man.

### Question XI

But do Augustine and Ambrose hold contrary views on this point?

**Solution.** One thing is the gratuitous gift of which Augustine speaks; another is the natural gift [Col. 0579A] of which blessed Ambrose speaks. It was given to the man, from the moment of his conception, to be God through personal union. For when God became man by condescension, man became God by grace—not an adopted God, but natural God, eternal God, omnipotent God. But to the begotten God it was given eternally to be God by nature. Therefore there is no contradiction in meaning between the teachers of truth.

### Question XII

“We serve God in spirit,” etc. (Philippians 3.) It is asked by what kind of service.

Note that the service owed to God alone is called *latria*; hence one who renders God’s worship to idols is called an idolater, an abomination is called idolatry, an idol-house is called an *idolium*, and a sacrifice offered to idols is called an *idolothytum*. But the service by which we are commanded through charity [Col. 0579B] to serve one another is called in Greek *dulia*. Both kinds of service, however, are designated by the Latin word *servitus*.

### Question XIII

“A Hebrew of Hebrews; according to the Law, a Pharisee.” It is asked why they are called Hebrews.

**Solution.** Hebrews are named after Heber, not Abraham—as blessed Augustine at one time thought, though he later retracted it. This is evident because Abraham himself is called a Hebrew in one passage; this would not be so if the name had been derived from him. Moreover, Abraham means “father of many nations”; Hebrews means “those who pass over.” It is therefore evident that the Hebrews are not called after Abraham, but after Heber, who alone retained the Hebrew language at the division of languages [Col. 0579C].

### Question XIV

“According to the righteousness which is in the Law.” It is asked how he can say that he lived blamelessly according to the righteousness in the Law, when elsewhere he says that, while under the Law, he walked with others in the desires of the flesh, and therefore calls himself a child of wrath.

**Solution.** Both are true: he walked according to the desires of the flesh, and yet lived blamelessly according to the righteousness that was in the Law—a righteousness that makes one serve from fear of punishment, not love; that restrains the hand, not the mind. Such was the righteousness in the Law.

### Question XV

“Not having my own righteousness,” etc. Did God not give the Law and command obedience to it? [Col. 0579D] How, then, does he call the righteousness which is from the Law his own?

**Solution.** The solution to this question is contained above. While he was under the Law and sought to be justified by works of the Law, he made the Law’s righteousness his own by believing that he could fulfill that Law by his own powers.

### Question XVI

“In faith for knowing,” etc. This is understood of faith that has no time for works. But is not loving a work of faith? Yet faith without love, once someone is an adult, is never effective. How then does the expositor say that this must be understood of faith having no time to work—that faith itself is sufficient for knowing God and for other things?

**Solution.** This is said lest anyone think [Col. 0580A] that believing and having faith without works is sufficient for salvation when one has the opportunity to act well.

### Question XVII

“Whose names are written,” etc. It is asked what the book of life is.

**Solution.** The book of life is God’s predestination, in which all who are to be saved are written—either by predestination alone, or also by righteousness and predestination.

### Question XVIII

“Rejoice in the Lord always” (Philippians 4), etc. The expositor says that rejoicing in the world and rejoicing in God are opposites and cannot simultaneously exist in the same person. But is there not someone divided, who partly rejoices in the world and partly in the Lord, just as one partly loves the world and partly loves God?

**Solution.** A person is said to rejoice in that joy [Col. 0580B] which is recognized as predominating in him. The part of the inward person occupied by worldly joy is not possessed by the joy that is in the Lord, because they cannot exist in the same subject in respect of the same thing.

### Question XIX

“Let your petitions be made known to God,” etc. Does not God know all things fully and perfectly before they occur? How then does the Apostle say, “Let petitions be made known to God”?

**Solution.** The meaning is: Let your petitions be so earnest and not lukewarm that they are worthy to be heard and fulfilled. For when they are fulfilled, it becomes known to us that they have reached God.

### Question XX

The expositor says that angels offer [Col. 0580C] our prayers to God. It is therefore asked how this offering should be understood.

**Solution.** With due reverence for the mysteries, we say that our prayers are offered to God by angels only in the sense that, through them, they are made worthy to be heard by God. Angels are also intermediaries between us and God: just as they announce divine mysteries to us, so they are said to report to God the things that take place here among us.

### Question XXI

But since God’s perfection is sufficient for knowing all things, it is asked why angels report anything to him.

**Solution.** Not in order to teach him, but in order to consult his eternal and unchangeable truth, and to know what they ought to do, and what, to whom, and when they ought to announce.

[Col. 0580D] ### Question XXII

“I seek not the gift, but the fruit,” etc. It is asked what is the difference between a gift and fruit.

**Solution.** He calls a gift what is given, such as food, money, or clothing. But fruit is the intention of the giver. It is called fruit because an act is judged useful and fruitful according to it. Or he calls fruit the reward itself. Thus a good work is called a flower, from which the fruit of eternal life grows.

Note that the raven which fed Elijah signifies a gift, where there was a good work without a good intention. The widow who fed the same prophet signifies fruit: there was a good work with a good intention.

## VII. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS

[Col. 0581]

[Col. 0581A] (Colossians 1.) “Paul, an apostle,” etc. The Apostle writes this epistle to the Colossians, who are Asians. The Apostle himself did not preach to them; rather, his disciples did, namely Archippus and Epaphras. Archippus had undertaken ministry among them, whereas Epaphras was native to their community and, instructed by the Apostle, confirmed Archippus’s teaching. Later pseudo-apostles arrived and preached fleshly observances, and the Colossians became uncertain whom they ought to believe. Therefore the Apostle, whose authority was renowned, acts as a kind of arbitrator in deciding which side should rather be maintained, writing to them from Ephesus.

The Apostle’s purpose in this epistle, then, is to confirm the Colossians in the faith and teaching they received from his disciples and to teach that hope must not be placed in anything apart from [Col. 0581B] Christ. His manner of treatment is as follows: according to his custom, he begins with a greeting; then he gives thanks for their good qualities, commending their faith and love. He prays that they may be perfected in Christ, commends Christ’s benefits and primacy according to each of his two natures, recalls the dignity of his own ministry, and warns them not to be seduced away from Christ by philosophy or legal ceremonies. Finally, he gives moral instruction to all together and separately—to the sexes, ages, and conditions. At the end he admonishes Archippus to be diligent in his ministry.

### Question I

“Giving thanks,” etc. The expositor says that here the Apostle begins to show that the Law [Col. 0581C] does not benefit but harms. Was not the Law good, given by God, and did it not not merely fail to harm but benefit in its own state? How then is it true that it does not benefit but harms?

**Solution.** It is true that the Law benefited before grace; but after grace it was useless. This solution is challenged thus: Does not the Law now bear witness to the truth, and are we not enlightened through it in the knowledge of the Godhead? Therefore the Law benefits us even now, in the time of grace. How, then, is it true: “The Law does not benefit but harms”?

**Solution.** The Law, when read and understood spiritually, benefits and does not harm. But when observed according to the letter, it does not benefit but harms.

### Question II

“Who made us worthy to share in the lot of the saints.” It is asked what he calls the lot in which [Col. 0581D] we have become participants.

**Solution.** The Apostle here calls the future inheritance a “lot,” because it is given without merits by lot—that is, by divine grace and will.

### Question III

Likewise it is asked how the future inheritance is given to saints without merits, since they merit it through faith, love, and good works.

**Solution.** [Col. 0582A] This must be understood as “without merits preceding faith,” not as “without subsequent merits.” These subsequent merits are from grace and therefore are not excluded when future glory is said to be given by grace alone. We have already spoken of these matters above.

### Question IV

“He transferred us into the kingdom of the Son.” It is asked what he means by the kingdom of the Son of God.

**Solution.** The kingdom of heaven, or of the Son, is understood in several ways: as future glory, as in “Thy kingdom come” (Matthew 6); as the present Church, as in “When he hands over the kingdom to God the Father” (1 Corinthians 15); as faith in Christ, as in “The kingdom of God is within you” (Matthew 12); or as sacred Scripture, as in “The kingdom of heaven will be taken away from you and given to a nation producing fruit” (Matthew 21).

[Col. 0582B] ### Question V

“Of the Son of his love.” Is not the Holy Spirit the love by which the Father loves the Son and the Son the Father, and is Christ the Son of love? It would therefore seem that he is Son of the Holy Spirit—a conclusion faith does not admit.

**Solution.** When he is proclaimed Son of love, “love” is understood generally as the divine nature, substance, or essence. For he is Son of a nature, substance, and essence consubstantial and coessential with the Father. But what “love” signifies when it is said, “The Holy Spirit is the love by which the Father loves the Son,” and conversely, has been explained elsewhere. Redemption likewise, image, and the statement that Christ is called head of the Church have already been discussed; there is no need to repeat what has been done.

[Col. 0582C] ### Question VI

It is asked whether Christ, according to his humanity, was the head of the saints who preceded the Incarnation. It appears that he was. But how could one who did not yet exist according to his humanity be their head? Or, if he was, how could they have as their head one who was not yet head?

**Solution.** Christ can be called the head, even according to his humanity, of those who existed from Abel onward, because all who were saved were saved through faith in the one to come.

Note that Christ is proclaimed to be of the same nature as the Father where he is shown to be the Son of love. But where he is called image, not only identity of substance but also personal property is indicated. Where he is called firstborn of every creature, he is asserted to be coeternal with the Father. Where [Col. 0582D] it is read that all things were created through him, his omnipotence is declared. Where it is said that all things subsist in him (Colossians 1), his immensity is made manifest; his eternity is indicated in John, where it is written, “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1); his personal property, when it is added, “And the Word was with God” (ibid.); and identity of substance [Col. 0583A] when it is said, “And the Word was God” (John 1). Therefore the Son is coeternal, consubstantial, and co-omnipotent with the Father; distinct in person, yet with the Father the one principle of all creatures.

### Question VII

“And he, namely Christ, is the head of the Church.” It is said that the Church first began with Abel, who was the first righteous man. But was Adam not righteous? For it is believed that after his fall he was justified through repentance and faith. Why, then, is the Church not said to have begun with Adam?

**Solution.** The Church contracted the stain of original sin from Adam, but none from Abel; it is therefore better said to have begun with Abel than with Adam. Scripture mentions Adam’s sin, not his righteousness, and Abel’s righteousness, not his sin. Christ [Col. 0583B] is therefore always the head of all who have existed from the beginning, just as of those who followed him; through him alone we have access to the Father.

### Question VIII

“See to it that no one deceives you through philosophy and empty deceit” (Colossians 2), etc. Was not knowledge of natural things, handed down by philosophers, useful for knowing God’s invisible things? For by the visible forms of visible things—the doctrine of which is taught in mathematics—one comes to the invisible causes of visible things, which physics teaches; and through these one comes to know invisible substances and the invisible natures of invisible substances. How then does the Apostle call such knowledge empty deceit?

**Solution.** The Apostle does not criticize philosophers [Col. 0583C] because they investigated the natures of things, but because they attempted to confine God’s power, which is infinite, beneath natural causes, saying that God does nothing contrary to nature. Thus they called it impossible that God should become a creature, that a virgin should give birth, or that a dead person should return to life. The Apostle rightly rebukes this error of theirs, not their true knowledge of natures.

### Question IX

“In whom all the fullness of divinity dwells.” Since the fullness of divinity is one and simple, how can he say “all fullness of divinity,” when “all” ordinarily gathers a plurality?

**Solution.** “All fullness of divinity” is said in order that it may be understood that every mode of indwelling is there, including personal indwelling. Or otherwise: “all fullness” is said to indicate [Col. 0583D] that in him there is fullness not only of knowledge but also of power and goodness. This refutes the error of those who say that the assumed man possesses through grace all the knowledge which the Word has by nature, but not all power.

### Question X

“The fullness of divinity bodily.” Since divinity is incorporeal, it is asked how it can dwell bodily in Christ.

**Solution.** “Bodily” means completely, solidly, and truly, with reference to the legal figures, which were shadows of things to come and whose body—that is, fulfillment and truth—is Christ. Or otherwise: “bodily” does not signify the nature of an existing thing, but rather the mode of existing. For just as a body naturally exists in one place so that it cannot at the same time be in another, so the fullness of divinity exists in the assumed man, in a manner in which it exists in no other creature. It is in every creature by essence, in the righteous by grace, and in Christ alone according to personal property. To say that the Godhead dwells bodily in Christ, therefore, is to say that it dwells personally.

Just as a body is in several places simultaneously, not bodily but spiritually. In saying this, I do not deny that the truth and essence of the Lord’s body are simultaneously present at several altars; rather, I indicate that this mode of existence is not shared with other bodies, nor does it arise from the body’s nature, but is instead shared with spirit—not created, but uncreated. Both are wondrous and true: that a created spirit is somewhere bodily, and that Christ’s sacramental body is spiritually in several places [Col. 0584B].

### Question XI

“Blotting out the handwriting of the decree which was contrary to you,” etc. It is asked what he calls the decree and what the handwriting.

**Solution.** By “decree” he means either the Law of Moses itself or the commandment God gave to the first man in Paradise, saying, “Of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat” (Genesis 2). By “handwriting” he means the memorial of the violation of either decree. But the handwritings of all sins were blotted out by the shedding of guiltless blood.

### Question XII

“Which are a shadow of things to come, but the body is Christ’s.” It is asked how shadow, body, and spirit are distinguished.

**Solution.** Shadow is one thing, body [Col. 0584C] another, spirit another. These three are called by other names: figure, thing, truth. Thus shadow and figure are the same; body and thing are the same; spirit and truth are the same. Legal ceremonies were called the shadow and figure of things to come. The sacraments of grace are the body, or reality, of those shadows or figures. Spirit, or truth, means spiritual grace—that is, the grace conferred and signified by the sacraments of the New Testament. But the sacraments of the Old Testament signify spiritual grace only; they do not confer it. This is the difference between those sacraments and these.

It should also be known that what was commanded in the time of the Law is not commanded now, in the time of grace, but is only testimony to truth. Therefore it was then a sin not to [Col. 0584D] observe even one such command; now it is not a sin not to keep them—indeed, one who keeps them offends.

### Question XIII

“Put to death your members” (Colossians 3), etc. It is asked what, or which things, he calls members that must be put to death. Must the eye, hand, or foot be put to death?

**Solution.** Here the Apostle calls the concupiscence of the members “members,” as he himself adds and explains: fornication, etc.

### Question XIV

“Covetousness, which is the service of idols,” etc. Are not covetousness and idolatry different things? How then does he call covetousness the service of idols?

**Solution.** He compares covetousness to idolatry because their wickedness is not dissimilar. Just as an idolater worships a log, so a miser worships money. And just as an idolater strives to take from God his due honor, so a miser appropriates for himself alone things [Col. 0585A] that God created for all in common.

### Question XV

“Putting off the old man,” etc. It is asked what he here calls the old man.

**Solution.** Sometimes the old man means Adam, the first man, who by sinning clothed both himself and all his posterity in the garment of oldness. Sometimes every person who bears the image of the earthly man is called the old man. Sometimes the old man means oldness itself, consisting in guilt and punishment. Sometimes it is called the habit of vices, as here according to the expositor.

### Question XVI

“And put on the new man.” Likewise it is asked what he here calls the new man. For sometimes the new man is Christ, from whom [Col. 0585B] all newness comes; sometimes every person renewed in Christ is called the new man; sometimes it is the habit of virtues; sometimes, more particularly, the rational mind. But above it was said that the mind is called the inward man; here, however, it is said that the inward mind is called the new man. This seems contrary, since the new man and the inward man are different, as was already shown.

**Solution.** The expositor says that he calls the rational mind the new man, and this is not contrary to the statement above that the mind is called the inward man; for one and the same thing receives different names because of different properties.

### Question XVII

“Which is renewed in the knowledge of God according to his image,” etc. It is likewise asked how [Col. 0585C] the mind is said to be renewed according to the image of God, since it itself is the image of God. Can it be renewed according to itself?

**Solution.** The image which is renewed is the same image according to which it is renewed, just as we say that someone is dead according to the body—that is, bodily, not spiritually. Thus the mind is renewed according to itself, that is, in itself. In the Epistle to the Ephesians, however, it is said that this renewal takes place according to God; it is said to be according to God so that it may not be said to be according to a creature. Through such renewal it is made like and conformed to God; therefore it is said to exist according to that image.

Note that this image, which is renewed in the knowledge of God, is found equally in man and woman. It is different from that other image [Col. 0586A] of which it was said above, “Man is the image of God, and woman of man.”

### Question XVIII

“Forgiving yourselves, if anyone has a complaint against another.” The Lord commanded the same thing, saying, “Forgive your debtors” (Matthew 6). But what is it that we can forgive? Is it a debt that can be exacted from the one who has injured us?

**Solution.** It is to forgive an injury inflicted: in no way to demand satisfaction for ourselves on account of the injury. Some other matters concerning this have been stated by us elsewhere.

### Question XIX

The expositor says that one who abstains from unlawful things has praise, while one who restrains oneself even from lawful things has praise and reward—as though he said: the former avoids punishment; the latter also merits a crown. But does not one who abstains from unlawful things likewise receive not only praise but reward?

**Solution.** One who abstains from unlawful things always avoids punishment, but does not always merit a crown, except when tempted and attacked [Col. 0586B].

### Question XX

“Do all things in the name of the Lord.” By “all things” he understands only good things which are to be done by us. Therefore it is asked whether he commands all things that are to be done to be done for God. Am I bound by the commandments to give my cloak to a poor person whom I see is in need, and when I know that this pleases God? For if I leave him, I seem to despise what I know he wills to be done.

**Solution.** It must be understood thus: “Do all things in the name of the Lord,” that is, do nothing contrary to God, and in good things seek not your own glory but God’s. Yet we do not merit in everything we do, because some things are indifferent, such as sitting, standing, breathing, closing one’s hand, opening one’s eyes, and the like. But some actions are such that they have merit if done and are not sins if omitted: for example, giving a cloak to a poor person, selling everything, and giving to the poor. This belongs to the perfect, who follow Christ nakedly [Col. 0586C].

### Question XXI

“Tell Archippus: See to the ministry which you received in the Lord, that you may fulfill it” (Colossians 4). It is asked whether subjects may admonish their prelates.

**Solution.** Here is authority for subjects to admonish their prelates, lest they be negligent in providing for things pertaining to salvation.

## VIII. ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 0585]

[Col. 0585D] (1 Thessalonians 1.) “Paul and Silvanus,” etc. The Apostle writes this epistle to the Thessalonians. Thessalonica is the metropolis of Macedonia, which is a province of the Greeks. The Thessalonians, therefore, are Macedonians or Greeks. Converted by the Apostle, they could not be moved from the truth of faith either by tribulations or by false preachers. The Apostle praises them [Col. 0586D] because they had absorbed so great a spirit of faith that, in hope even of future things, they endured dangers with devoted spirit at the hands of their unbelieving fellow citizens for Christ’s name.

Yet some among them were idle and meddlesome; others held less sound opinions about the resurrection and therefore grieved too intently over the death of friends. The Apostle therefore corrects them in this epistle, admonishes the perfect not to yield to adversities or false apostles, and urges them to correct others. He wrote from Athens. The Apostle’s purpose in this Epistle is to correct the wicked and uncorrected, and to exhort the good to perseverance and to correcting others. His method is this: according to his custom he begins with a greeting; having given it, he gives thanks for their good qualities, recounting not only their faith and works, but also the manner of their conversion and their endurance of evils, in order to provoke perseverance. He also interweaves remarks about his own labors, the truth of the Gospel, his prudent conduct among them, and his strong desire to see them. Then he beseeches the disordered to refrain from luxury, idleness, and meddlesomeness, and confirms that the dead will rise. Near the end is moral instruction. Thus Paul and Silvanus say, etc. [Col. 0587B] Timothy, etc. Note that it was the Apostle’s custom to join to himself in the greeting those who had been with him among the recipients or were to be with him.

### Question I

“The living and true God,” etc. It is asked why he says “true.”

**Solution.** One God exists naturally; many are gods by participation. In distinction from them he is called the true God, namely, because he is God from himself and not from another. The others are gods not from what they are, but from what they have received.

### Question II

“For the wrath of God has come upon them” (1 Thessalonians 2). It is asked how God’s wrath and punishment came upon them for their sins—that is, before death. Is eternal punishment lightened by temporal punishment? If it is not lightened, God seems unmerciful, punishing here and there. Again, if eternal punishment [Col. 0587C] is lightened by temporal punishment, such punishment seems not to proceed from God’s wrath but from mercy; and therefore it should be called mercy, not wrath.

**Solution.** It is indeed great mercy of God to call people to repentance through temporal punishment. But because they refuse to repent, they turn God’s mercy into wrath against themselves, and the punishment inflicted—which could have been a means of salvation—becomes for them the beginning of eternal punishment.

### Question III

“We hastened to see your face with great desire,” etc. The expositor says that evils might befall them. But it is asked how the teacher’s presence could bring evils upon disciples, since good rather than evil would seem to arise from it. For he desired to see them because of the usefulness of his presence [Col. 0587D], namely, that he might strengthen them and supply what was lacking.

**Solution.** Their crown would be greater and their victory more praiseworthy if they stood unmoved while their master was absent. Yet the Apostle, in human fashion, feared that they might fall, and therefore desired to come to them.

### Question IV

“At his coming,” namely, the Lord’s. It is asked at what coming.

**Solution.** There are three comings of the Lord: one into flesh, one in spirit, and one in flesh. He came into flesh when he became man. He comes in spirit when he pours his Spirit into our spirit, healing and justifying it. He will come in flesh at the judgment. He also comes secretly to each person at death: to purify them or open the gate of the kingdom; but to the wicked, to punish them.

### Question V

“That you may not grieve as the rest [Col. 0588A] who have no hope” (1 Thessalonians 4). It is asked whether grieving and weeping over the death of friends is a sin, since the Apostle says, “That you may not grieve.”

**Solution.** When death takes a beloved person, it necessarily grieves the affection of love. Therefore it is not blameworthy to grieve at the necessity of losing someone, provided that we are consoled by hope of receiving them again. Hence the Apostle does not simply say, “Do not grieve,” but says, “Do not grieve as the rest, who have no hope”—as if to say: grieving is permitted, but with hope.

### Question VI

It is asked how the Lord wept for Lazarus when dead, though he was immediately to live at the Lord’s command.

**Solution.** He wept not for the dead man but for death, which Lazarus had not earned by sinning, and to which Lazarus was again to be recalled, and to the miseries of the world. Thus the Lord [Col. 0588B] was moved.

### Question VII

It is asked whether prayers, alms, and sacrifices of the altar benefit all for whom they are offered.

**Solution.** After death, the things just mentioned benefit only those who lived before death so as to be worthy for these things to benefit them after death. They do not benefit those who departed this life without faith working through love, because while living here they lacked the pledge of salvation—that is, the pledge leading to salvation.

### Question VIII

Since Christ can do all things, it is asked why he did not immediately grant immortality to his faithful, so that they would never experience death at all.

**Solution.** If this were so, a certain happiness would indeed be given to the flesh, but the strength of faith would be diminished. No one would then hasten to Christ’s grace for the sake of the future [Col. 0588C] life, but rather to escape the hardship of death; thus belief in Christ would in a certain way be soft and self-indulgent. Where, then, would be the glorious triumph of the martyrs?

### Question IX

“And those who have fallen asleep.” Since he calls Christ, who now lives, dead, why does he call faithful dead persons not dead but asleep?

**Solution.** He says that Christ died and rose again so that, hearing this, we may hope for the same—namely, that we shall rise through the power of the Godhead. But he calls the elect asleep because no one can be awakened from sleep as easily as God will awaken all of them from the sleep of death.

### Question X

“At the voice of an archangel,” etc. It is asked whether this voice [Col. 0588D] will be material.

**Solution.** Some say that it will be material, formed through the ministry of angels, just as the material voice heard at the Lord’s baptism was material. It is therefore called God’s voice because God will give it efficacy, so that through it the dead may rise. Others say that it will be some evident sign. An ambiguous solution for an uncertain matter: all things to come at the end are uncertain to us.

### Question XI

“Then we who are alive.” It is asked how the Apostle can say that those who died long ago will rise first, and then those found alive at that time, when elsewhere he says that the resurrection will take place in the twinkling of an eye and in a moment (1 Corinthians 15), where nothing is earlier or later, but all occurs at once.

**Solution.** It may be said that the resurrection of the dead is called simultaneous because [Col. 0589A] there will be only a short delay.

### Question XII

It is commonly asked whether those whom Christ finds alive will die, or pass to immortality without death.

**Solution.** We have nothing certain on this matter. Yet some hold that in the very rapture they die and return to life, since elsewhere the Apostle says, “In Christ all shall be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15), and elsewhere, “What you sow is not made alive unless it first dies” (ibid.). This should not seem incredible, since the common and general resurrection is believed to occur in a moment and in the twinkling of an eye.

### Question XIII

“We shall be caught up to meet Christ in the air.” It is asked whether this is said of all.

**Solution.** The good, as though light, will meet Christ in the air; but the wicked, as though heavy, will not meet Christ in the air but will cling to the earth, which they have always loved [Col. 0589B].

Note that there are four classes of those who will come to judgment. Some will come only to judge, namely the very good, not to be judged; their salvation is certain. Others are less perfect, and their salvation is not yet certain; they will come to judgment to be judged. Likewise there are two kinds of wicked. Some will come to judgment to be judged: the less wicked, whose condemnation is not certain. Others will come not to be judged [Col. 0590A], because they have already been judged, since their condemnation is already certain. Why then will they come? Surely not to judge! Why, then? To hear with the devil: “Go, you cursed, into eternal fire” (Matthew 25), etc. The manner of judgment has already been discussed in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: that is, how the saints will judge, whether by comparison alone or also by authority.

### Question XIV

“The day of the Lord will come like a thief in the night” (1 Thessalonians 5), etc. Since no one knows whether the Lord will come to judgment by day or by night, it is asked how the Apostle calls the time of the Lord’s coming a day.

**Solution.** In such a place “day” does not mean illumination of the air, as elsewhere; it means revelation, that is, manifestation, because then all things will be made manifest. For everyone will know why [Col. 0590B] the Lord saves or condemns him or another.

### Question XV

“Pray without ceasing.” It is asked how this commandment of the Apostle can be fulfilled. For who can pray always? Must one not sometimes sleep?

**Solution.** It is understood thus: do not omit prayer at the appointed hours. Or prayer is understood as holy desire and devout affection; and thus a righteous person never ceases to pray unless he ceases to be righteous. For one who always acts well always prays well.

## IX. ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS

[Col. 0589]

[Col. 0589C] “Paul and Silvanus” (2 Thessalonians 1), etc. The Apostle writes this Epistle to the Thessalonians. Because a more severe tribulation had arisen among them, he urges them to patience, showing God’s just judgment, so that the good may attain glory and the wicked punishment. And because in the first epistle he says certain things about the coming of the Lord and the resurrection of the dead, from which it was thought that the day of the Lord was imminent, he now writes a second epistle. In it he indicates, though obscurely—for he cannot do so openly—the abolition of the Roman kingdom, the appearance and condemnation of Antichrist, and the restlessness of certain brothers. He also writes that the day of the Lord is not imminent, as some seem to suppose on the occasion of the earlier Epistle.

The Apostle’s purpose in this epistle is therefore to move the good and quiet to patience, correct the disorderly [Col. 0589D], and make somewhat clearer what he had said obscurely in the former epistle. His manner is as follows: first he gives greeting, then thanks for their good qualities; afterward he admonishes them to patience and steadfastness. Then he asserts that Antichrist will precede Christ’s coming and, although obscurely, announces certain signs of Antichrist’s coming, treating of the abolition of the Roman kingdom and Antichrist’s destruction. Near the end he urges them to rebuke the meddlesome and idle.

### Question I

“In a flame of fire, inflicting vengeance on those who do not know God.” It is asked whether the Lord will come to judgment surrounded by [Col. 0590C] fire.

**Solution.** He is said to come in a flame of fire because he will appear terrible to the wicked, in order to burn and torment them. Fire will indeed precede his coming, by which the elements will be dissolved in order to be renewed.

### QUESTION II

It is asked how those living persons whom the Lord will find alive will be preserved.  
**Answer.** Just as the fire did not harm the three children in the furnace, so that fire preceding the Judge’s coming will not harm the good.

### QUESTION III

It is asked what punishments the souls of the impious now suffer in hell: material punishments, or only the torments of conscience?  
**Answer.** It is believed that they suffer material punishments, such as fire and cold. Hence it is said: “They shall pass from snowy waters to excessive heat” (Job 24) [Col. 0590D].

### QUESTION IV

Likewise, it is asked how they are tortured by these punishments, since spiritual things cannot be touched by bodily things.  
**Answer.** It can happen that they are punished by things which do not touch them; just as someone contracts great terror from something seen or imagined, even though he is not touched by it.

### QUESTION V

Likewise, when their bodies have been resumed and are thereafter to be immortal, how will they be punished in them, since they cannot be dissolved?  
**Answer.** The bodies of the wicked will indeed be immortal, but capable of suffering—that is, such bodies as those in which the wicked suffer, yet without injury to the natural size or essence of the bodies themselves [Col. 0591A].

### QUESTION VI

“Unless the falling away comes first” (2 Thess. 2), etc. It is asked: how will what is said concerning the falling away happen?  
**Answer.** This can be understood in four ways: either concerning the earthly Roman empire, or the spiritual dominion of the Roman Church, or faith, or Antichrist. Since another translation says, “the Renegade.”

Note that it is read that Antichrist will be born in Babylon, from the tribe of Dan, in accordance with Jacob’s words: “Let Dan be a serpent in the way, a horned serpent in the path” (Gen. 49). When he first manifests himself, he will come to Jerusalem and be circumcised, saying: “I am the Christ promised to the Jews.”

### QUESTION VII

[Col. 0591B] “Who exalts himself above everything that is called God,” such as the gods of the Gentiles or the saints; “or that is worshipped,” such as God the Trinity.

But it is asked how he can exalt himself above God the Trinity. Will not his greatest pride and exaltation consist in saying that he is Christ and thus equal to God? For he will not call himself greater. How, then, is he exalted above everything worshipped as God?

**Answer.** As it seems to me, this exaltation is to be understood in this respect: that the lawless one, the man of sin, the son of perdition, will cause the veneration and worship due to God the Trinity alone to be rendered to himself and not to God. It is read that, just as the fullness of divinity dwelt in Christ, so in Antichrist there will be the fullness of malice and of every iniquity and, so to speak, the fullness of devilishness.

### QUESTION VIII

[Col. 0591C] Hence it may be asked whether he will simply be a man, or whether the devil will assume him personally, as God assumed a man.  
**Answer.** The devil cannot so assume a man as to be personally united to him. He will therefore be a mere man; yet the devil will possess him in such a way as to fill him with every power of his wickedness and every iniquity, so that, wholly given over and devoted to him, he will will and be able to do nothing except what the devil wills and is able to do.

### QUESTION IX

“The mystery of iniquity is already at work.” The expositor says that the devil already works secretly in Nero and in other evil persons, though he will rage openly in Antichrist. Hence it is asked how he works secretly in Nero. Did Nero not deny Christ and openly persecute those who preached Christ?

**Answer.** He is said to work secretly in Nero because Nero did this through the deceitful prompting of certain persons. Or, better: the devil is said to work secretly in Nero not because that persecution was manifest, but because it is a shadow, figure, and image of that which will occur through Antichrist, which will be far more grievous than all that preceded it [Col. 0591D]. For he will reign for three years and a half; and, sitting in a tent on the Mount of Olives, he will be slain by the power of the Holy Spirit through Michael—whether the Lord himself or another angel, as the teachers say.

### QUESTION X

“Whom the Lord will destroy by the brightness of his coming,” etc. Will Antichrist not be slain before the Lord comes for judgment? For from the book of Daniel it is understood that the elect will be granted forty-two days for repentance after Antichrist’s death. Yet how long afterward the Lord will come is entirely unknown, not only to human beings but also to angels. How, then, does the Apostle say that the Lord will destroy him “by the brightness of his coming,” when he is to be slain before that coming?

**Answer.** Antichrist will indeed, as is believed, be slain before the Lord’s coming, through the separation of body and soul. Yet the Lord will destroy him, once resurrected with his whole body, by the brightness of his coming: condemning him and casting him into eternal fire, saying to him and the other reprobate: “Go, you accursed, into eternal fire” (Matt. 25) [Col. 0592A].

### QUESTION XI

[Col. 0592B] “According to the working of Satan,” etc. The expositor says: “yet not without awareness,” as are the insane, who bear no guilt for the evils they commit. Hence it may be asked: if Antichrist will do everything through the devil’s instigation, cooperation, and in some manner compulsion, why is it imputed to him rather than to the insane? Or, if the insane do this through the devil’s instigation, why is it not imputed to them? And how are they without guilt for the evils they commit, rather than that lawless one?

**Answer.** The insane, who are without awareness, should be said rather to suffer something than to do something; evils are done through them rather than by them, since they are not their authors, because they do not apply their will to them. But Antichrist will do everything under the devil’s instigation in such a way that he will apply his entire will and understanding to the same end; therefore everything will be imputed to him for eternal punishment [Col. 0592C].

### QUESTION XII

“With lying signs and wonders,” etc. It is asked concerning those signs which Antichrist will perform through the devil: are they called lies because they will not be real as they appear, but phantasmal—that is, because he will deceive mortal senses through apparitions? Or are they called lies because, by God’s permission, they will draw people into falsehood?

**Answer.** It seems probable to us that Antichrist will truly perform every sign which the devil can perform. But those things over which the devil has no power, neither will that lawless one truly perform; rather, by magical art alone he will deceive mortal eyes, so as to appear to do what he does not truly do [Col. 0592D]. Hence the Apostle says: “whose coming will be in every power,” with regard to those things which he will truly do, “and in every deception,” with regard to those things which he will not truly do. Yet all of them avail for the deception of the impious. What things the devil can do and what things are not subject to his power is not for our smallness to unfold.

### QUESTION XIII

“God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe a lie, that they may be judged,” etc. It is asked about those who, moved by the signs and wonders of that lawless one, will believe him to be good and the Son of God: do they have any excuse? For if they do not render him divine worship, when their conscience dictates to them that he must be worshipped as God, they will sin unto death; and thus they seem inexcusable.

**Answer.** The Apostle says that because “they did not receive the brightness of the truth, so as to be saved”—that is, Christ previously preached openly—God will send them an operation of error, so that they may believe a lie and be judged. Here he sufficiently teaches that, because of preceding sins, they will have no excuse, even if they suppose that, in believing in Antichrist, they are rendering service to Christ, that is, to the true God [Col. 0593A].

### QUESTION XIV

Augustine says that being able to have faith or charity belongs to the nature of believers; having faith or charity belongs to the grace of God. Hence it may be asked how this should be understood. Is not what is natural within our own power? But since we cannot have faith or charity without grace, how is being able to have faith the nature of believers?

**Answer.** To be able to have faith—that is, the capacity for having it—is natural; but to have the use of this capacity belongs to grace alone, not to nature [Col. 0593B].

### QUESTION XV

“Whoever is unwilling to work, let him not eat” (2 Thess. 3) [Col. 0594A]. It is asked what work is meant here. For if external work is meant, how does he command that one unwilling to work should not eat? Many are worthy to eat although they do not work.

**Answer.** Augustine says that the Apostle wishes the servants of God to work with their hands, so that necessity may not compel them to seek what they need. Yet those who postpone outward works for spiritual ones, when they have the means to live, do not act wrongly, since Mary chose the better part (Luke 10). But those devoted to idle curiosity and unwilling to work are rebuked, not those who abandon lesser goods for greater ones.

### QUESTION XVI

“If anyone does not obey our word by this letter, take note of that person, and do not associate with him, that he may be ashamed.” The Apostle says this because one who resists the Church’s admonition is to be excommunicated [Col. 0594B]. Hence it may be asked how this should be done. Certainly it must be done with great discernment, lest the Church suffer harm; nor should such punishment be exercised for a slight cause.

## X. ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY

[Col. 0593]

[Col. 0593C] “Paul, an apostle” (1 Tim. 1), etc. The Apostle writes this Epistle to Timothy, who was the son of a faithful woman and a Gentile father. Although he had not been circumcised and was himself a Gentile, and although the brothers in Lystra and Iconium bore good testimony concerning him, Paul wished him to travel with him; and for that reason he had him circumcised because of the Jews who were in those places.

He was trained both in the divine Scriptures and in the liberal arts. The Apostle made him a bishop. Therefore, having left him in Asia, he instructs him in this Epistle concerning the episcopal office: namely, how he should resist false apostles and instruct the Church; what kind of presbyters or deacons he should ordain; what widows he should honor; and how he should conduct himself in the Church or govern it. The Apostle’s purpose in this Epistle is to instruct Timothy concerning the office of episcopal dignity [Col. 0593D]. Its arrangement is as follows: first he greets him; then warns him to resist false teachers; afterward instructs him concerning the episcopal office, teaching what sort of presbyters and deacons he ought to ordain; then what sort of widows he ought to receive; afterward instructs him concerning the manner of rebuke; and at the end warns him to avoid profane novelties.

### QUESTION I

“Of God the Father, our Savior,” etc. Since the Son is frequently called Savior in Scripture—he alone having died for our salvation, not the Father nor the Holy Spirit—it is asked why the Apostle ascribes our salvation to God the Father here, saying: “Of God the Father, our Savior.”

**Answer.** God the Father, in that he deigned to send us his Son and to bestow the Holy Spirit in the sacraments of the New Testament, is the author of our salvation and is therefore called Savior [Col. 0594C].

### QUESTION II

“And of Jesus Christ, our hope.” Likewise, it is asked why he refers hope especially to the Son, saying, “and of Jesus Christ, our hope,” when we hope in and believe in the whole Trinity.

**Answer.** We refer our hope to Christ because he rose from the dead and ascended into heaven; through his resurrection we hope to attain the glory of the future resurrection.

### QUESTION III

“Grace, mercy, and peace,” etc. It is asked why, contrary to his usual practice, the Apostle places three things in this greeting, saying “grace, mercy, and peace.”

**Answer.** He wrote the preceding nine Epistles generally to churches. But he writes this one particularly to Timothy, his fellow bishop; therefore he gives three things. By mercy he understands what in the others he calls grace, namely remission of sins; by peace, tranquility and a foretaste of the future life; but by grace he understands the gift of the Holy Spirit, by which Christ’s ministers are armed [Col. 0594D].

### QUESTION IV

“That they should not give heed to fables,” etc. What does the Apostle here understand by “fables”? Does he in this place call the words of the Law and divine utterances by that name? Elsewhere he says: “Avoid profane and old-womanish fables” (1 Tim. 4).

**Answer.** Here he calls “fables” the teaching of those who preach that the Law together with grace is necessary. Or he calls “fables” the traditions which the Jews maintain without writing and which one transmits orally to another, calling them *deuterōsis*; in them they say and believe that God first created two wives, from whom they weave endless genealogies of human beings, producing fruitless questions [Col. 0595A]. Concerning such traditions, alien to the sacred Scriptures, the Lord says in the Gospel: “Why have you made void the commandment of God because of your traditions?” (Matt. 15).

### QUESTION V

“But the end of the commandment is charity, from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith.” Here the Apostle defines charity, as the expositor says. Hence it may be asked what definition is given here: is it “the end of the commandment,” or is it “from a pure heart and a good conscience and an unfeigned faith”?

**Answer.** The definition of charity is: to be from a pure heart, a good conscience, and an unfeigned faith.

### QUESTION VI

Likewise, it may be asked whether this definition applies to every charity. If it is granted, no one possesses charity unless he is perfect, since charity fulfills and perfects the Law; for charity is the end of the commandment, that is, its perfection and completion. “End” is here taken for completion; elsewhere it is taken for consumption, as when it is said, “the bread is finished,” and elsewhere for a boundary, as when it is said, “the field ends here.”

Likewise, who can have a pure heart and good conscience without charity? Does not purity of heart and a good conscience proceed from charity? How, then, does charity proceed from a pure heart?

**Answer.** It seems to me that the definition given here is that of perfect and completed charity, and so it does not apply to imperfect charity. Love is first given, which cleanses the heart; from it good works arise, and from these a good conscience is born. Finally, once the heart has been cleansed and a good conscience acquired, charity is perfected and completed—the end of the commandment [Col. 0595C]. I say this without prejudice to a better judgment.

### QUESTION VII

“The Law is good, if anyone uses it lawfully.” It is asked what it is to use it lawfully.

**Answer.** As the expositor says, that person uses the Law lawfully who, understanding it spiritually, recognizes through it the disease and seeks the physician; who knows that it was given for a time and abandons it for Christ. It should be noted that an unjust person uses the Law lawfully when he understands why it was given and, through fear of it, flees to Christ’s grace so as to become just. But a just person uses the Law lawfully when he imposes it upon the unjust as a terror.

### QUESTION VIII

[Col. 0595D] “The Law is not laid down for the just.” Did not David and the other righteous people who lived under the Law have to keep the Law? How, then, is the Law not laid down for the just?

**Answer.** The Law is not imposed on the righteous so as to rule them and restrain them by fear; the righteous person is not under the Law, but rather with it, as a friend of the Law.

### QUESTION IX

“Because I acted ignorantly,” etc. The expositor says that *because* can indicate either a cause or a consequence. But it is asked how ignorance, which is a fault, can be the cause of divine mercy.

**Answer.** There is a kind of ignorance arising from weakness. If someone acts against God out of good zeal arising from it, he merits, through the disposition he has, to be freed from that ignorance.

### QUESTION X

[Col. 0596A] “He came into this world to save sinners,” etc. It is asked concerning little children born of baptized parents whether they belong among the sinners whom Jesus came into the world to save. For they have no actual sin; and how can they contract original sin from parents who do not have it, since it has been remitted to them?

**Answer.** It must be known that original sin is remitted in baptism in such a way that it does not wholly cease to exist, but ceases to be guilt. The defect of corruption nevertheless remains even in baptized persons who beget children—not from that in which they have been reborn, but from the old condition of corruption through which original guilt passes to little children. Hence they too need a remedy. Thus the Physician himself says: “Allow the little children to come to me” (Mark 10).

### QUESTION XI

[Col. 0596B] “Of whom I am the first.” Were Cain and Saul not before Paul? How, then, was Paul first among sinners?

**Answer.** Paul was first not in chronological order, but in the magnitude of wickedness. An objection is made to this answer: Did Paul not sin through ignorance, while many others sinned knowingly? But it is a greater sin to sin knowingly than through ignorance. Therefore Paul was not first among sinners in the magnitude of wickedness, since others—especially those who sinned against the Holy Spirit—are much worse than Paul, even in his former condition, in which he was a blasphemer, persecutor, and insultingly violent person.

**Answer.** Considering the magnitude of his own offenses, Paul judged himself worse than all sinners, although it was otherwise in the eyes of God [Col. 0596C].

### QUESTION XII

“But to the King of the ages, immortal, invisible, the only God, be honor and glory for ages of ages. Amen.” The expositor says that the man assumed by the Word is King of the ages from the time when he was assumed by the Word. But if the assumed man is neither man nor God nor a person, as some have dared to profess, how is the assumed man King of the ages from the moment he is assumed, and not before?

But we say that the man assumed by the Word is man and God: he is the Word himself by whom he was assumed, and he began in time to be King of the ages when, namely, he began to be assumed by the Word. For when God began to be man, man also began to be God, as many authorities attest.

### QUESTION XIII

[Col. 0596D] “Who wills all people to be saved” (1 Tim. 2). Since God is omnipotent and no one can resist the divine will, how are not all saved, if God wills all to be saved? Or is it his will that the reprobate be saved?

Ambrose resolves it thus: God wills all to be saved, if they themselves will it. But do not many wish to be saved and nevertheless are not saved? How, then, is it true that God wills all to be saved?

Others therefore explain it thus: God wills, etc.—it would please him if all were saved; or, “all,” that is, some from every class of human beings. Or thus: he offers grace to all, through which they can be saved if they will. But how is this answer true? Are there not many people, both now and formerly, who did not hear even a word of preaching?

Or: “He wills all to be saved,” that is, he causes the saints to will that all be saved [Col. 0597A]. Or thus: “He wills all to be saved,” that is, no one is saved unless he wills it. In a similar way should be understood: “Who enlightens every person” (John 1), that is, no one is enlightened except by him; and “all are made alive in Christ” must be understood in the same manner. Thus diverse interpretations are given of an ambiguous expression.

### QUESTION XIV

“One mediator of God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus.” Something concerning the mediator has already been said above in part. Here it is enough to consider what the expositor says: that insofar as he is man, he is middle, not insofar as he is the Word. But is he not, insofar as he is the Word, middle between angels and God the Father, and also between angels and the Holy Spirit—although he is middle in one way between angels and God the Father and in another way between angels and the Holy Spirit and the Father?

**Answer.** It can rightly be granted that, insofar as he is the Word, he is middle between rational creatures and God the Father. But he is not mediator between God the Trinity and human beings insofar as he is the Word, but insofar as he is man: like God in righteousness and like human beings in mortality. For if he were mediator between human beings and God the Trinity insofar as he is the Word, then something would be intermediate between himself and another, because the Word would stand between himself and human beings; this must not be granted.

Someone will say: Christ is no longer mortal; how, then, is he middle between mortal human beings and the immortal God, if he is called middle because he is like human beings in mortality and like God in righteousness?

**Answer.** Christ still reconciles us to God the Father as the best mediator through what he did for us in the days of his flesh, that is, through mortality [Col. 0597C].

### QUESTION XV

“Adam was not deceived, but the woman.” It is asked which sinned more, Adam or Eve.

**Answer.** The teachers say that the woman not only sinned, but also caused the man to sin. An objection is made to this answer: Adam was deceived because he did not believe the adversary’s persuasion to be true; but the woman was deceived, believing what the serpent said to be true. It follows that he sinned knowingly and she through ignorance. But it is more grievous to sin knowingly than through ignorance. Therefore the man sinned more than the woman.

**Answer.** That ignorance had no excuse because it proceeded from fault; for she responded with doubt, saying: “Lest perhaps we die” (Gen. 3). But the man reflected upon God’s mercy and repentance, and therefore sinned less [Col. 0597D].

### QUESTION XVI

It is asked how it can be true that Adam “was not deceived.” Did he not believe that what was mortal sin was venial? Therefore he too was in some manner deceived.

**Answer.** He was not deceived first, nor in the same matter as the woman, as the authority says.
