But is one not deceived if one was not deceived first and not deceived in the same matter as the woman? For if someone was not wounded in the head, does it follow that he was not wounded? Does a simple negation follow from a qualified negation?

**Answer.** The teachers of the New Testament sometimes say that something was not, when the Scripture of the Old Testament does not say that it was. Hence, because Genesis, speaking of the woman’s deception, says nothing about any deception of the man, the Apostle says: “Adam was not deceived, but the woman.”

In the same manner of speaking, elsewhere the same Apostle asserts that Melchizedek had neither beginning nor end, neither father nor offspring, although in reality he had a beginning, end, father, and perhaps offspring. But because Scripture introduces him in such a way that it says nothing about his genealogy, birth, or death, the Apostle asserts that he lacked all the things mentioned above [Col. 0598A]. Ambrose likewise says that the man is blessed with the first woman and not with the second—as though to say: In Sacred Scripture we read the blessing of the man with the first woman, but we do not read where God blesses the man with the second.

### QUESTION XVII

“But the woman will be saved through the bearing of children.” If bearing children saves, what will the continent woman or virgin do? Will she not be saved because she has no children? Why does the Apostle elsewhere say: “She will be happier, whether widow or virgin, if she remains so”?

**Answer.** He does not place the cause of salvation in bearing children, but rather in faith and love; hence he adds: “if she remains in faith and love.” The sense is: even if woman was the cause of sin, nevertheless not only the continent woman or virgin, but also the married woman, will be saved, even if she never ceases from bearing children, but leaves this world while engaged in bearing children—provided they remain in faith and love [Col. 0598C].

Or it will contribute to an increase of her salvation if her children remain in faith and love through her teaching and diligence. Or, rather, it is understood mystically. Woman is a type of the flesh, which elsewhere is signified by the turtledove. Adam is a figure of reason, which is represented by the sparrow. The children are good works, understood through the young of the turtledove, who live only in the nest of the Catholic faith; outside it they do not flourish, indeed they are trampled down, because good works do not benefit pagans, Jews, heretics, or schismatics. Hence he says here: “If she remains in faith and love,” namely, the woman’s children, the young of the turtledove, good works.

### QUESTION XVIII

“If anyone desires the episcopate, he desires a good work” (1 Tim. 3), etc. But an ambitious person desires the episcopate. Can one infer, therefore, that he desires a good work?

**Answer.** “Episcopate” means attention to one’s own life and that of others; thus it is the name of a work, desired by the good person who, setting aside but not abandoning Rachel of beautiful face, enters with Jacob to Leah of bleary eyes because of her fruitfulness in children; who descends with Moses from the mountain of contemplation to the fields of action [Col. 0598D]. For no one should be so idle as not, in that very idleness, to consider the benefit of the neighbor; nor so active as not to seek contemplation of God.

“Episcopate” is also the name of a dignity, desired by the ambitious person, who wishes rather to preside than to be of benefit.

### QUESTION XIX

“One-woman man,” etc. It is asked whether a man who had a wife before baptism, put her away, was reborn in Christ, and afterward took a faithful wife should be called a monogamist and can be ordained.

**Answer.** Jerome says that such a man is not a bigamist and can be ordained; for after he is made new, neither fornications nor other previous acts are imputed to him. But Augustine says that he is not a monogamist and ought not to be ordained, although what he did previously does not harm him, because of the mystery which must be preserved in those being ordained, and which cannot be preserved in the case described [Col. 0599A].

### QUESTION XX

But do Jerome and Augustine hold opposing views in their answers to the foregoing question?

**Answer.** Jerome says that such a man is a monogamist with regard to merit, and that it is not a sin if he is ordained. Augustine, however, says that he is not a monogamist with regard to the force of the sacrament and cannot be ordained where the sacrament of monogamy is preserved. Nor is it required that it be preserved in every person ordained; otherwise a virgin could not be ordained, since he is not the husband of one wife. The Church is an assembly of many persons for the worship of one God [Col. 0599B].

### QUESTION XXI

“The great sacrament of godliness,” etc. It is asked what is here called a sacrament. Sometimes a sacrament is called a sign of a sacred thing, as the sacrament of baptism and of the altar; sometimes it is called something hidden and secret, or a mystery.

**Answer.** Christ, hidden according to his divinity, is called a sacrament; he is the cause of all religion and true worship. For who has ever been devout and faithful except after first receiving knowledge of this sacrament?

### QUESTION XXII

“That which was manifested in the flesh,” etc. It is asked what manifestation is meant here.

**Answer.** The manifestation effected by preaching, powers, and signs displayed in the assumed flesh [Col. 0599C].

### QUESTION XXIII

“Justified in the Spirit.” Does the discourse not concern the Word of God? Yet this was not justified, but rather was born just from eternity.

**Answer.** When the discourse concerns Christ, one must carefully consider what is said and in what respect. Therefore, “justified in the Spirit” is understood of Christ according to the assumed man, according to whom he is free from every sin and possesses complete righteousness.

### QUESTION XXIV

“He appeared to angels.” Here we have authority that angels advance in knowledge through those things which occur in the Church. We have already dealt carefully above with this subject in connection with the passage, “that the manifold wisdom may be made known,” etc.; and the expositor bears witness to the same point here [Col. 0599D].

### QUESTION XXV

“Nothing is to be rejected which is received with thanksgiving” (1 Tim. 4). It is asked whether this is contrary to legal teaching, which distinguishes certain foods, calling some clean and others unclean.

**Answer.** In the Law certain animals were called unclean, not by nature but by signification. Thus, if one asks concerning a pig and a lamb, both are clean in nature, since every creature is good; yet in signification the lamb is clean and the pig unclean.

### QUESTION XXVI

“Godliness is useful for all things, having the promise of the life which now is,” etc. It is asked what he calls the promise of the present life; for the promise of the future life is evident.

**Answer.** Sufficiency of temporal things and abundance of spiritual things. God promises both to his worshippers. Sufficiency of temporal things is promised where it is said: “Seek first the kingdom of God, and all these things shall be added to you” (Matt. 6). Spiritual abundance is promised where it is written: “Whoever leaves these or those things for my sake shall receive a hundredfold” (Matt. 19): that is, in the present life the delight of spiritual goods exceeds the abundance of temporal goods as much as one hundred exceeds one [Col. 0600A].

### QUESTION XXVII

“Which was given to you through prophecy,” etc. It is asked what he calls prophecy.

**Answer.** He calls prophecy the election by the saints who chose him as bishop. Or rather, the inspiration of the Holy Spirit, through which the Apostle knew that he was worthy of the episcopate [Col. 0600B].

### QUESTION XXVIII

“With the laying on of hands.” What is this?

**Answer.** He calls the laying on of hands the mystical words by which the one chosen for this work is confirmed, receiving authority, with his conscience as witness, so that he may dare, in the Lord’s stead, to offer sacrifices.

### QUESTION XXIX

“The laborer is worthy of his wage” (1 Tim. 5), etc. It is asked whether that which is given by the people to the preacher is a due and fitting wage; whether he sins if he preaches for it; and whether one who does this sells the Gospel.

**Answer.** Who would dare say that what Truth itself calls a wage is not a wage? Yet one ought not preach for such a wage, but in order to receive an eternal reward from the Lord [Col. 0600C]. Thus it belongs to necessity to receive the means of living; it belongs to charity—and indeed it is a duty—that those who receive spiritual things should supply bodily things. The preacher ought to receive in order that he may preach, not preach in order that he may receive.

### QUESTION XXX

“But those who sin, rebuke before all.” This seems contrary to what the Lord says in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, rebuke him between yourself and him alone” (Matt. 18). Does so good a disciple disagree with so good a Master?

**Answer.** Both are true. At times what the Lord said with his own mouth must be done, namely, when you alone know: for an occult fault must be rebuked secretly, as righteous Joseph did concerning Mary, when he alone suspected adultery. Otherwise, if you act differently, you will be a betrayer, not a corrector. At other times, however, what Truth said through Paul’s mouth must be done, namely, when the sin is committed openly. A public offense requires public satisfaction [Col. 0600D].

### QUESTION XXXI

“Use a little wine.” It is asked how he gave this advice.

**Answer.** He gives a particular counsel, that Timothy may regulate himself through sound teaching. For God wisely wills to be served: not that people should be made weak by excessive abstinence and afterward seek help from physicians.

### QUESTION XXXII

“Diseased about questions and disputes of words” (1 Tim. 6), etc. The question was whether anyone could be a slave, since all descend from the same fathers and Christ redeemed all. Likewise, the dispute of words was that Christ “made free,” because the Lord says: “If the Son has made you free, you shall be truly free” (John 8) [Col. 0601A]. These and similar statements seem to conflict with apostolic teaching, which exhorts slaves to be subject to their masters, and likewise with the Lord’s words: “Render therefore to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s,” etc. (Luke 20).

Such a controversy of words must be resolved thus: “If the Son has made you free, you shall be truly free” must be understood of spiritual freedom, not bodily freedom. But Paul speaks of bodily freedom and slavery, which spiritual freedom does not remove.

### QUESTION XXXIII

“The root of all evils is covetousness.” Elsewhere Scripture says: “Pride is the beginning of every sin” (Ecclus. 10). But here it says avarice or covetousness. If avarice is taken as a species for a genus, how can both statements be true? For if pride is the beginning of every sin, then it is the beginning of covetousness; and if covetousness is the root of all evils, then it is the root of pride. Thus the same thing is cause and effect of itself.

**Answer.** When it is said that covetousness is the root of all evils, or pride the beginning of every sin, it is false if the respective genera are understood as universal genera; but true if they are understood as genera of particular instances [Col. 0601B]. For there is no kind of sin which does not arise sometimes from pride and sometimes from covetousness. Some desire riches in order that by them they may attain the summit of honor; others seek rank in order to become richer.

### QUESTION XXXIV

“He alone is mighty.” Are not angels mighty, since they are also called virtues and powers?

**Answer.** God alone is mighty by nature, from what he is; angels are mighty by grace, from what they have received [Col. 0601C].

### QUESTION XXXV

“Who alone has immortality,” etc. Are not souls and angels also immortal by nature?

**Answer.** God alone has immortality, that is, immutability, because he neither could, can, nor will be able to sin. Neither angels nor the souls of saints have this immortality. Although they are immortal through grace, they are truly believed to be mutable by nature.

### QUESTION XXXVI

“Who dwells in inaccessible light.” The Prophet says: “Approach him, and be enlightened” (Ps. 33). Is not God himself the very light which he is said to inhabit? How are we urged to approach this light if it is inaccessible?

**Answer.** No one approaches it of himself, but only one to whom it is granted by his gift [Col. 0602A].

### Question XXXVII

“Whom no human being has seen, nor can see.” Did not Abraham see God, and Moses, and the other fathers? How then is it true that no one has ever seen God? Again, do we not also hope for the vision of him? But how can this be, if no one can see him?

**Answer.** God, in his own nature, is invisible to the bodily eye; but those visions were displayed to the holy fathers in a subject creature. Hence Moses, after those figures in which God was seen, said: “Lord, show me your face” (Exod. 33). In the future, moreover, God will be seen by the pure in heart, and now he is seen by the holy angels.

[Col. 0602B] ### Question XXXVIII

“Avoiding profane novelties of speech,” etc. It is asked whether every novelty of expression is to be avoided.

**Answer.** No; for not all are profane. Thus the very name *Christian*, *homoousion* [“of one substance”], “new commandment,” “new testament,” and “new song” are called novelties—not profane novelties, but sacred ones, suited to religion. But in the time of the heretics *hypostasis* denoted a profane novelty. The heretics used this term now in the sense of person, now in the sense of substance, in order to deceive the simple: if they granted that the Trinity was one hypostasis, they would infer, “Therefore they are one person”; but if they said that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were three hypostases, they would conclude, “Therefore they are three substances.” Now, however, [Col. 0602C] this word does not denote a profane novelty, because it has been restricted to the meaning of person. Accordingly, we now simply grant that the Trinity is three hypostases, and not one; something which formerly was not to be granted without qualification, when it still retained a multiple meaning.

### Question XXXIX

“And oppositions of knowledge falsely so called,” etc. It is asked what knowledge the Apostle calls falsely named. Is it logic? But if so, how does Augustine call dialectic the knowledge of knowledges, which not only makes one knowing but also demonstrates that one knows?

**Answer.** In my judgment, he calls sophistical art knowledge falsely so called; its oppositions are to be avoided by the devout and gentle, because they avail only for the overthrow of the simple.

## XI. ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY

[Col. 0601]

[Col. 0601D] “Paul, an apostle” (2 Tim. 1), etc. About to depart from the world, he writes this second epistle from prison at Rome to Timothy, worn out by weaknesses and adversities, exhorting him to labour steadfastly in the grace of God entrusted to him, to martyrdom in many ways, [Col. 0602D] and to persevere in the office of right preaching and holy conduct; and foretelling what will happen in the last times and concerning his own death.

The Apostle’s purpose in this epistle is to exhort Timothy to the diligent fulfilment of his office and to the palm of [Col. 0603A] martyrdom; and he adds some further matters concerning the episcopal office. Its arrangement is as follows: first he greets him; then he gives thanks for the good he possesses, where he shows his desire to see him. Afterwards he urges him to preaching and to endurance of martyrdom, by his own example and in other ways. Then he says what kind of people will arise in the last days. Finally, he speaks of the imminence of his own dissolution.

### Question I

“God has not given us a spirit of fear.” It is asked of what fear this is said.

**Answer.** Of the fear which the love of God drives out.

### Question II

“Which was given to us before the ages of the world,” etc. How could anything be given to us when we did not yet exist?

**Answer.** It was given—that is, foreseen as to be given. Hence he does not simply say, “was given,” but adds, “in Christ Jesus.”

[Col. 0603B] ### Question III

Again, it is asked why he does not simply say “before times,” but adds “of the world.” Are not all times worldly? In contrast with what, then, does he say “worldly”?

**Answer.** Some say that the angels were created before the creation of the world, and that those intervals which extended from the creation of the angels to the creation of the world are elsewhere called by the Apostle “eternal times”; in contrast with these he here says “worldly times.” But someone will say: does not time signify mutability and eternity immutability? How, then, can any times be eternal? How can they be mutable and immutable at once?

**Answer.** The aforesaid teachers understand it thus: in those intervals called eternal times there was succession, but no passing away; and thus there was a certain immutability, [Col. 0603C] and in this respect a certain eternity. Jerome appears to agree with this opinion. Almost all teachers, however, say that angels were created not before the world but with it; but what, according to them, should be understood by “eternal times,” let whoever follows their opinion see and investigate. To me, however, the opinion of the former seems preferable, with due reverence for mysteries. I say this while asserting nothing rashly.

### Question IV

“No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in worldly affairs” (2 Tim. 2), etc. Do not active men serve as soldiers for God, while nevertheless being involved in worldly affairs? How then does the Apostle say, “No one serving as a soldier for God,” etc.?

**Answer.** He calls affairs worldly when the mind is occupied with the care of collecting money; [Col. 0603D] no one can do this and serve as a soldier for God at the same time. Active men, however, do not attend to external matters in order to accumulate money, but only in order to provide necessary things for themselves and others.

### Question V

“Of the seed of David according to my Gospel, in which I labour even unto chains.” It is asked from what tribe Christ and Mary came. But from this passage observe that Christ was born of David, as he says at the beginning: “Of the seed of David according to the flesh.” And the archangel Gabriel says of the same: “The Lord God will give him the throne of David his father” (Luke 1).

I say these things because of those who do not wish the Lord’s mother to be of the seed of David, who was from the tribe of Judah, but claim that she was only from the tribe of Levi. Because Joseph, Mary’s husband, was of David’s family, they say that Christ is called to be from [Col. 0604A] David’s seed; and Origen, it is said, thought thus. Others say—and this also seems to us—that Mary too descended from David’s stock, and thus from the stock of Judah, not only from that of Levi. For the two tribes, royal and priestly, were intermingled; and therefore it is not surprising that the Virgin drew her origin from both, since she was to bear the true King and Priest.

“Do not contend about words.” Among the servants of God there ought to be not contention but discussion, and a modest inquiry into truth.

### Question VI

“Saying that the resurrection has already taken place.” It is asked of which resurrection the Apostle speaks: that of minds or that of bodies. For if this is said of the resurrection of minds, which occurs in baptism, how did those who said [Col. 0604B] it had already taken place overthrow the faith of some, when this is true and ought to be believed? Again, if they said this concerning the resurrection of bodies, how did they overthrow the faith of some by it, when it is evident to all that this is false?

**Answer.** This may be understood of both resurrections. For, by saying that the resurrection of minds had already occurred and that no other resurrection of bodies would take place, they deceived people, since they craftily denied the resurrection of bodies. Or they also overthrew faith by saying that the resurrection of bodies had already occurred, taking an occasion for their error from what is written in the Gospel: “Many bodies of the saints arose and appeared in the holy city” (Matt. 27). [Col. 0604C] They denied that the general resurrection which we await would take place.

### Question VII

“In a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver,” etc. It is asked whom he understands by vessels of gold and silver, and whom by wooden and earthenware vessels.

**Answer.** By vessels of gold and silver he understands the predestined; by wooden and earthenware vessels, the reprobate. Or by golden vessels are understood the good, whether predestined or not; by wooden and earthenware vessels, the evil, whether foreknown for life or reprobate. Thus, according to this opinion, among both kinds some are for honour and some for dishonour. According to the former opinion, however, only golden and silver vessels are for honour, while wooden and earthenware vessels are for dishonour.

“Avoid foolish questions and questions without instruction,” [Col. 0604D] etc. Here he indicates that not all questions are to be avoided, but only those in which there is no profit.

“Having an appearance of godliness, but denying its power.” Many people in this time are such as the Apostle here describes: they love themselves, not God; they possess the name and outward habit of holiness, while inwardly they are full of every impurity. He calls charity the power of godliness, of which it is written: “Love is strong as death” (Song 8). Contempt for the world necessarily precedes this.

### Question VIII

“All who wish to live devoutly in Christ will suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3). Does not the Church have a time of peace, in which many live devoutly and yet do not suffer persecution?

**Answer.** The saints suffer in many ways, in heart and body: [Col. 0605A] now from the devil, now from evil people, now from their own desires. The conduct of the weak is likewise a persecution to them. For these say with the Apostle: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is scandalized, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. 11). Therefore those who live devoutly in Christ are not without persecution, even in a time of peace.

### Question IX

“I have finished the course” (2 Tim. 4), [Col. 0606A] etc. Did not a fiercer and crueler enemy still remain before the completion of the course, namely Nero’s sword? How, then, was it true that Paul had finished the course before the triumph of his passion?

**Answer.** He says this not as an accomplished fact but in certain hope. For he who had made him victorious in the contest had already, by revelation, made him certain and secure concerning its completion.

## XII. ON THE EPISTLE TO TITUS

[Col. 0605]

[Col. 0605B] “Paul, a servant of God” (Tit. 1), etc. He writes this epistle from Nicopolis to Titus, left as bishop of Crete, who was excessively patient through humility and simplicity. He treats authoritatively and imperiously of the episcopal office, prescribing useful matters to him by his own authority. For a bishop ought to possess maternal tenderness and paternal severity, so that he may be strong toward the proud and gentle toward the modest, having neither a corner of fear nor the brow of arrogance.

He should burn and shine. Hence the vestment of the legal high priest included scarlet twice dyed, which has the appearance of fire. Fire does two things: it burns and shines. So likewise the bishop, by the sword of preaching—that is, by fiery speech—ought to burn by biting rebuke and fearful threat, and to shine upon the gentle by cherishing them and promising delightful things. Hence it is said of manna that it hardened [Col. 0605C] in the fire and melted in the sun.

The episcopal staff pricks at its lower end, and at its top stretches forward while turning back upon itself. Thus an ecclesiastical teacher ought with the sword of the word to prick—that is, sharply to rebuke—sinners, which belongs to the lower nature; and to direct those who have been corrected toward things before them, yet in such a way that he returns by self-examination to his own conscience, lest perhaps he possess in himself what he proclaims by reproaching others. Thus the shape of the staff signifies that the bishop ought to prick the rebellious and draw the gentle toward himself. Hence someone says:

> Its curved part draws the gentle; its sharp part pricks the rebellious.

The Apostle’s purpose in this Epistle, therefore, is to instruct Titus concerning the episcopal office, to admonish him to exercise it authoritatively, and to avoid heretics. Its arrangement is this: [Col. 0605D] first he greets him; then he instructs him concerning the episcopal office, teaching what he ought to do and what sort of bishops he should establish through the cities; then how he ought to instruct different persons according to sex, age, or condition; afterwards he warns him to avoid heretics.

### Question I

“Which he promised before the ages of the world,” etc. It is asked how God promised eternal life before all times, when human beings did not yet exist to whom he might promise it.

**Answer.** He promised—that is, he proposed unchangeably and eternally in himself that he would in time give eternal life to those whom he had already predestined.

[Col. 0606B] ### Question II

“Without crime,” etc. He does not say “without sin,” because, as the authority says, no one, however devoutly he may live, even if worthy of the name of just, is without sin. But someone will say: is there not in baptism and through true repentance a full remission of all sins? If this is so—indeed, since it is so—it is clear that one who is baptized and truly repentant is without sin. How then is it true that “no one is without sin”?

**Answer.** When it is said, “No one is without sin,” it is understood thus: no one, however good, can pass through this life without sin. Yet one can live without crime—that is, without a graver sin—and without accusation, that is, without a sin such as deserves accusation and condemnation: adultery, homicide, theft, and the like.

[Col. 0606C] ### Question III

“Cretans are always liars,” etc. It is asked why the Apostle interspersed in his teaching, which possesses divine authority, words from a Gentile and unbelieving author; and why, speaking to the Athenians, he said, “In him we live, move, and are” (Acts 17), and elsewhere, “I found an altar on which was written, ‘To an unknown God,’” which is certainly taken from Gentile writings (ibid.).

**Answer.** Divine authority may take from whatever source it wishes a testimony of truth which it judges necessary. It does not thereby approve all the other things found there or judge them to be true. As a figure of this, the Hebrews despoiled the Egyptians of gold, silver, and other things necessary for divine worship. And in the Law the Jews were commanded that, if they bought a Gentile slave, his hair should be shaved and the growth of his nails [Col. 0606D] cut off; then he was to be taken into domestic service. So, once the vain and superfluous superstitions of the Gentiles have been shaved away and cut off, whatever is found pure ought to be taken up for the service of God’s house.

It should be noted that divine authors employ testimonies of this kind in a meaning other than that in which their own author used them. Thus: “It is expedient that one man die for the people, [and not] that the whole nation perish” (John 11). Caiaphas understood it one way, the evangelist another. He whose power and strength caused an ass to speak with a human voice, using it as an instrument, used Caiaphas in uttering the aforesaid words.

[Col. 0607A] ### Question IV

“They profess that they know God, but deny him by their deeds.” Note that some profess God in words only, others also in deeds; some deny God in deeds only, while others deny him both in words and deeds. Those who profess God in words and deeds are good. Those who deny him in both words and deeds are unbelievers. But those who profess him in words and deny him in deeds—should they simply be called professors or deniers?

**Answer.** Listen: “You shall know them by their fruits” (Matt. 7); he does not say, “by their words.” Therefore all evil people deny God by their deeds; all are antichrists who deny Christ by their life. Antichrist has not yet come, and yet many antichrists are already in the world.

### Question V

“A heretical person, after a first and second correction, avoid” (Tit. 2), etc. [Col. 0608A] He calls heretical one who attacks the Law by means of the Law. But why should such a person be avoided? Would it not be better to confer with him often and call him back from error to truth?

**Answer.** Once he is incorrigible, it is better to avoid him, because, if he were corrected too often, it would become an exercise in evil.

### Question VI

“Being condemned by his own judgment.” It is asked how such a person is condemned by his own judgment; for he believes what he says to be true and thus does not judge himself condemned.

**Answer.** The Apostle seems to speak of one who sins knowingly, who recognizes error and knows truth, yet praises error and disparages truth. Such a person is condemned by the testimony of his conscience, as is evident to everyone.

## XIII. ON THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON

[Col. 0607]

[Col. 0607B] “Paul, a prisoner of Christ Jesus,” etc. He writes this Epistle from prison at Rome to Philemon of Colossae, who held no rank in ecclesiastical ministry but was a praiseworthy man among the laity. He sends him a familiar letter on behalf of Onesimus, his slave, who had fled after causing him loss, but who, having heard the Gospel from the Apostle, had been baptized. The Apostle both asks pardon for him and entreats forgiveness of his fault.

The Apostle’s purpose is to obtain Onesimus’s pardon from Philemon. Its arrangement is this: first he greets him with his wife and son; then he gives thanks to God for their good qualities, commending their faith and charity. Afterwards he entreats Philemon—although he could command him—to spare Onesimus and to give thanks to God because he has received him as such a one that he should consider him not a slave but a most beloved brother. Then he asks him to prepare lodging for him, as he hopes to come to him.

### Question I

“To Philemon, and Apphia, and Archippus,” etc. [Col. 0608B] It is asked why in this greeting he does not observe the rank of persons—that is, why he does not place Archippus, who was bishop of Colossae, before the others, but after them; and why he puts Philemon, who held no ecclesiastical dignity, first. Is it perhaps because this man was the father and that one the son?

**Answer.** He places the layman before the ordained man because the matter concerns household affairs.

### Question II

“Yes, brother, may I have joy of thee in the Lord,” etc. What is it to enjoy (*frui*)? Is it not to cleave to something for its own sake by love? But only God is to be enjoyed in this way, since God alone is to be loved for his own sake. How then does the Apostle say to Philemon, “Yes, brother, may I have joy of thee in the Lord”?

**Answer.** He does not say simply, “Brother, may I enjoy you,” but adds, “in the Lord,” thereby indicating that he has set the end of his love in the Lord. Or *frui* is said of using something with a certain delight, and may be understood here in that sense.

## XIV. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE HEBREWS

[Col. 0607]

[Col. 0607C] “In many and various ways” (Heb. 1), etc. Paul, the eminent teacher and Apostle of the Gentiles, wishing to honour his ministry—as he says in the Epistle to the Romans: “So long as I am the Apostle of the Gentiles, I will honour my ministry, trying whether in some way I may provoke my flesh to emulation” (Rom. 11)—writes this epistle to the Hebrew churches. He treats of Christ’s pre-eminence according to each nature, and of the uselessness of the Mosaic Law, establishing in many ways that faith in Jesus Christ, apart from legal observances, suffices for righteousness and salvation.

After Christ’s passion, legal observances [Col. 0608C] not only do not profit but even hinder. He excludes the opinion of certain Hebrews who confessed Christ but thought that legal observances ought to be kept; by their authority they had also led into this error some who had come to Christ from the Gentiles. Therefore the Apostle, providing for the Gentiles so that they may not henceforth be drawn into this error by the authority of the Hebrews, and also provoking the Jews to emulation, commends the grace of God bestowed through Christ, the true high priest, upon believers at this time, showing the Law to have been rejected.

The Apostle’s purpose [Col. 0609A] in this Epistle, therefore, is to show Christ’s pre-eminence and the sufficiency of faith, as well as the insufficiency and uselessness of the Law.

Its method of treatment is as follows. First, he proposes that the words of Christ are to be heard as are those of the prophets, and even more so, comparing him with the prophets and preferring him to them, because God has spoken in him as in the prophets and he is greater than they. Then he commends him in turn according to each nature, namely human and divine. Next he compares him with the angels and prefers him, interspersing much about his excellence according to each nature. Then he compares him with Moses and prefers him.

Then, with many arguments and authorities, he declares that the grace of faith is to be preferred to the shadow of the Law; and he shows the priesthood of Christ to be preferred to [Col. 0609B] the Levitical priesthood, the New Testament to the Old, and his one sacrifice to the many sacrifices of that Law, because there is shadow there, truth here. Finally he provides a description of faith, commending it by many testimonies; near the end he adds moral instruction.

### Question I

First it is asked why he did not prefix to this epistle, as to the others, his name, Paul; and why he also omitted the title of rank, Apostle.

**Answer.** Because he was odious to the Hebrews, to whom he seemed a destroyer of the Law, he suppressed his name, which was hateful to them, lest the prejudice attached to the name placed at the head of the work should exclude the usefulness of the reading that followed. Knowing their pride and showing his own humility, he did not wish to set forth the dignity of his rank by calling himself [Col. 0609C] an Apostle. Concealing the merit of his office, he, humble before the proud, did not call himself an apostle, lest the proud should take offence.

But someone will say: does not the Apostle write to believers who were in Jerusalem, to whom the name of Paul was not odious and who did not envy his rank as though he were proud? How then is it true that he omitted his own name or title of rank because it was odious to the Hebrews, when he was not odious but beloved by those to whom he wrote?

**Answer.** Among those to whom, as an eminent preacher of grace, he was very pleasing, there were some zealots for the Law, who believed and preached that the Law ought to be kept together with grace. To these Paul’s name was hateful. For they found no one so opposed to their false opinion as Paul; hence they persecuted [Col. 0609D] him as much as they could.

It should be noted that some said this Epistle was by no means the Apostle Paul’s, because his name is not prefixed to it as in all the others, and because it shines with a more splendid and eloquent style than the others; they claimed it was by Luke, Barnabas, or Clement. Jerome answers them thus: if it is not to be called Paul’s because it is not inscribed with his name, then neither is it to be called any of theirs—indeed, it is no one’s at all—since it bears no one’s name in its title; this was done for the reason already stated. And that it shines with greater eloquence than the others is not surprising, since it is natural for each person to be more capable in his own language than in a foreign one. Since he wrote this one [Col. 0610A] in Hebrew, but the others in Greek, what wonder is it if it has greater elegance?

### Question II

“In these days.” It is asked what days he means.

**Answer.** The Apostle calls the time of grace “days” because of the eminent teaching of faith and knowledge of salvation; hence elsewhere: “Behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Cor. 6).

### Question III

“Whom he appointed heir of all things,” etc. It is asked according to which nature Christ is here called heir of all things.

**Answer.** He may fittingly be called heir here according to his divine nature—that is, possessor and Lord of all things, namely of every nature. Or he is called heir of all things according to his humanity, namely of those to be saved, or of Jews and Gentiles. For he is the heir of the world, that seed in whom all [Col. 0610B] nations are blessed, to whom the Father says: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance” (Ps. 2).

### Question IV

“Through whom he also made the ages.” Did not God the Father make all things through the Son: visible and invisible, mutable and immutable? Why then does the Apostle not say, “Through whom he made all things,” but “through whom he also made the ages”?

**Answer.** These visible and mutable things are better known to us; and therefore we marvel more at God’s power in them than in things unknown to us. This is why he especially named the ages instead.

### Question V

“Who, being the brightness of glory,” etc. It is asked why he uses this comparison here and others elsewhere.

**Answer.** Wishing to show that, although the Son is from the Father, he is coeternal with him, [Col. 0610C] the Apostle uses a proportionate comparison from temporal things, saying, “being the brightness of glory,” as if to say: just as the brightness of fire, although it is from fire, is coeval with fire—and would be coeternal with it if the fire were eternal, for fire has never existed without brightness—so the Son, although he is from the Father, is coeternal with him, because the Father has never existed without the Son.

Again, wishing to show the identity of nature which the Son has with the Father, he uses a proportionate comparison from other things, calling the Son the image of his substance, because he could not show both things by the same comparison. For among creatures nothing is found which has being from another and is of the same nature or substance as that source, without being preceded by it. But the Son has being from the Father in such a way that he is coeternal with him, just as brightness is coeval with fire; [Col. 0610D] and he is of the same essence or nature with the Father. So too a man who begets and the man begotten from him: as a human being cannot beget anything other than what he is—that is, a human begets a human—so God generates nothing other than what he is, that is, God generates God.

Reader, carefully consider these words of the Apostle and the exposition of the saints upon them, and you will perceive how both the Sabellian and the Arian heresy are plainly destroyed here.

### Question VI

“And upholding all things by the word of his power.” It is asked how God is said to uphold all things by a word, since upholding does not belong properly to the Word. Likewise, whether he is under all things, rather than presiding over and surpassing them, so that he may be said to uphold them.

**Answer.** [Col. 0611A] He is said to uphold all things by a word rather than by power in order that, in upholding—that is, containing, governing, and preserving—he may be understood to endure no labour or difficulty. For he is more inward than every thing, because all things are in him; higher than every thing, because he is above all things; older than every thing, because he is before all things; and newer than every thing, because he is after all things—that is, after the beginnings of all things.

### Question VII

“He sits at the right hand,” etc. The expositor says that the assumed man was exalted to equality with the Father, which is understood by “the right hand.” It is therefore asked whether it should be granted that the assumed man is equal to the Father. But since the Son says, “The Father is greater than I” (John 14), which must be understood [Col. 0611B] according to what was assumed, how is the same thing equal to the Father, when according to it the Son is less than the Father?

**Answer.** That man, insofar as he is man, is less than the Father and not equal to him. But insofar as the assumed man is God, the Son of God is not less than the Father but equal to him. Therefore one must see what is said of what, and in what respect, whenever discourse concerns Christ. Yet there are many who do not grant that the assumed man is God, as has already been said above.

### Question VIII

“Having become so much better than the angels.” It is asked according to which nature he speaks here of Christ. That he is better than angels according to divinity is beyond question; yet he did not become better than angels but rather was born so. Therefore, because he says [Col. 0611C] “having become,” we are compelled to understand this of Christ according to his humanity—namely, that he became better than angels. But this seems contrary to what is found in the Psalm: “You made him lower than the angels” (Ps. 8). How can he, according to the same nature, be both better and lower?

**Answer.** He was made lower than the angels by the mortality and suffering of the flesh; yet he is greater and better than the same angels by the fullness of grace, from which the angels themselves receive.

### Question IX

“I have begotten you today,” etc. It is asked of what day he speaks.

**Answer.** Augustine says that this may be understood of that day on which Christ was born according to the flesh. Yet it may be understood more divinely of his eternal generation. Hence he says “I have begotten,” [Col. 0611D] lest it be understood as new; for “today” concerns the past, and thus eternity is indicated, in which nothing is past as though it had ceased to exist, nor future as though it did not yet exist.

### Question X

But it may again be asked how this can be expounded of Christ’s temporal generation, since God the Father did not beget Christ according to his human nature. For just as Christ has no mother according to divinity, so neither does he have a father according to humanity. Since, therefore, he is not his Father according to this nature, how can he be said to have begotten him according to it?

**Answer.** Begetting does not always signify natural generation, but sometimes a gratuitous generation, as in: “Of his own will he begot us by the word of truth” (Jas. 1). Therefore, because Christ’s [Col. 0612A] temporal generation was the work of the whole Trinity, it may fittingly be said that the Father begot him even according to his humanity. But someone will say: then Christ is a son of grace, and therefore adopted?

**Answer.** This is not true. By grace that man was made a son, not of grace but of nature.

### Question XI

“And again he says: ‘I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me,’” etc. It is asked how this authority applies to Christ, since neither the preceding nor the following words of the passage from which this authority is taken seem to allow it. For in the Book of Kings God the Father is introduced speaking to David: “You shall not build me a house, because you are a man of blood; but your son, who shall reign after you—[Col. 0612B] if he does wickedly, I will correct him with the rod of men and with the strokes [scourges] of the sons of men, and I will establish his kingdom for ever and ever, and I will be a father to him, and he shall be a son to me” (2 Kings 7), etc. All these things cannot be adapted either to Solomon or to Christ.

**Answer.** In divine Scripture, several things are often placed in the same sequence: some belong only to history; some only to the mystical sense; and some can be taken in both ways. Thus, in the passages mentioned above, some things refer to Solomon and others to Christ.

### Question XII

The same occurs in many other places. For if someone follows the historical sense, considering what precedes and follows where it is written, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isa. 7), it will seem to him more likely [Col. 0612C] that this authority refers to that young woman of Isaiah than to the Virgin, since there are things there which cannot in any way suit the mother of our Emmanuel and belong only to the historical sense. Yet a certain manner of expression and propriety of reference sufficiently indicate that all things refer to the same person: “Your son,” he says, “who shall reign after you,” etc.

**Answer.** One must know that there are three kinds of references. One is personal, as “Saul, who is also Paul”; another is general and simple, as “the woman who condemned, saved”; another is verbal, as “my hands, which made you, were nailed.”

### Question XIII

Again, it is asked according to which [Col. 0612D] nature the Father says, “I will be a father to him.” For according to the human nature he is not Father; according to the divine nature he was Father from eternity. How then does he say, “I will be his Father”?

**Answer.** A thing is said to come to be when it begins to be known. Therefore, because by the resurrection it became evident to all believers, and in the future will become evident also to unbelievers, that he is the Father and that he is the Son, he says, “I will be a father to him.” Or thus: “I will be a father to him,” that is, to the assumed man; and that man will be a son to me—not, however, according to humanity, but according to divinity.

### Question XIV

“And when again he brings the firstborn into the world,” etc. It is asked how the Apostle calls an entrance the coming which the Lord himself calls an exit, saying, “I came forth from the Father and came into the world” (John 16), [Col. 0613A] when he says, “And again, when he brings in” (Heb. 1).

**Answer.** With respect to the Father, within whom he was, the Lord’s coming is called an exit; but with respect to us, who were outside, it is called an entrance—or conversely.

### Question XV

“And let all the angels of God adore him,” etc. Concerning the assumed man it is customary to ask whether he is to be adored with the adoration called *latria*. For *latria* is offered only to God and not to a creature; but the assumed man is a creature, and so it seems that *latria* ought not be offered to him.

**Answer.** *Latria* is offered to that man not because he is man but because he is God; this has already been discussed above. The adoration offered to human beings or angels is called *dulia*.

[Col. 0613B] ### Question XVI

“Who makes his angels spirits,” etc. It is asked how he does this.

**Answer.** “Spirit” is the name of a nature, as “human being”; “angel” is the name of an office, as “soldier.” Therefore angels are made from spirits, just as soldiers are made from human beings; spirits are not made from angels, just as human beings are not made from soldiers.

### Question XVII

“And his ministers a flame of fire,” etc. It is asked how he makes the flame of fire—that is, the seraphim—his ministers, since the seraphim always stand in attendance. How, then, is that order said to minister if it always stands in attendance? For they are not said to minister except insofar as they minister.

**Answer.** It may be said that the seraph immediately receives from God what it reveals to an inferior being who is sent to us. Hence an inferior [Col. 0613C] is designated by the name of a superior whose office it performs, or rather from whom it receives its office. Thus Isaiah says: “One of the seraphim flew to me and touched my lips” (Isa. 6). Or it may be said that, when great things are to be done or announced, then those higher beings are sent; yet their office is not to minister, but rather to stand in attendance.

Note that nothing happens unless it happens either by God’s command or by God’s permission. By these words it is indicated that not everything that happens is God’s work; for what he merely permits, he does not do. I say this because of those who say that whatever exists, insofar as it exists, is from God. If this is so, the aforementioned distinction does not exist: some things happen by God’s command, others happen by God’s permission.

[Col. 0613D] ### Question XVIII

“Therefore he anointed you,” etc. The expositor says that Christ was anointed in order that he might love righteousness. But did he not love righteousness from the moment he existed, and was he not full of love before he was anointed? How then is he said to have been anointed in order that he might love righteousness?

**Answer.** By the oil of anointing is understood grace itself and virtue; by “loving” is indicated the very act proceeding from virtue. Therefore the anointing causally precedes the act of loving, not temporally. Or follow another exposition.

### QUESTION XIX. “Therefore he anointed,” that is, because you loved righteousness, he anointed you.

But did he not possess the fullness of anointing from his very conception? What anointing, then, did he receive as though as a reward because he loved righteousness?

**Answer.** By the oil of gladness, with which he was anointed as a reward for love, some understand the robe of the mature resurrection. [Col. 0614A]

### QUESTION XX. “God, your God, has anointed you,” etc.

The other, that is, the first occurrence of “God,” is in the vocative case, as though it said: “O God the Son, your God has anointed you.” But what God has a God? What God is anointed?

**Answer.** Christ is God and has God—not insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is man; and according to this he is anointed.

### QUESTION XXI. “They shall perish,” etc.

It is asked of which heavens it is said that they are to perish.

**Answer.** Of the aerial heavens, as the expositor says: they perished through the Flood and are to perish through fire. Hence it is asked: if they have already perished through the Flood, how are they again to perish through fire? If they have already perished, did they not cease to exist? And if they have already ceased, how will they again perish by fire?

**Answer.** They perished through the Flood, that is, they were changed for the worse; and those same heavens are to perish through fire, that is, they are to be changed into a better state. But concerning the earth and the higher heavens there is no question that they are to be changed for the better; hence Peter says: “We await new heavens and a new earth” (2 Pet. 3). Concerning water and air, however, it is doubtful whether they are to be changed to a better state, as earth and heaven are, because in the Apocalypse it is written: “And the sea was no more” (Rev. 21). And here it is written of the aerial heavens: “They shall perish.” Hence some think that water and air will lose those properties by which these names apply to them, and will lose the names themselves along with those properties. Yet they will not be wholly annihilated; rather, when the characteristics for which they were formerly so called have been removed and annihilated, they will no longer be called either water or air. [Col. 0614B–C]

### QUESTION XXII. “Are they not all ministering spirits?” etc.

It was said above that it is not the office of the higher orders to minister. How, then, are all ministering?

**Answer.** It may be said that all spirits minister to us: either immediately, as the lower orders do; or through others as intermediaries, as the higher and middle orders do. Or “all” does not include everyone, but only those of the lowest order, who are properly called angels. Their particular office is to minister, and therefore they alone are properly called ministering spirits.

### QUESTION XXIII. “What is man that you are mindful of him?” (Heb. 2), etc.

It is asked how this is to be expounded.

**Answer.** It is expounded in three ways. First: by “man” is understood the old man, and by “son of man” the new man. Second: by “man” is understood any good person, and by “son of man,” Christ. Third: by “man” and “son of man” the same person is understood, namely Christ. [Col. 0614D]

### QUESTION XXIV. “You made him a little lower than the angels,” etc.

Above he said that Christ was made better than the angels; here he says that he was made lower than they. We have already said how both are true. But here it is asked whether one should simply concede that Christ is lower than the angels. Some wish to prove it thus: Christ is everything that he was made; but he was made lower; therefore he is lower than the angels.

**Answer.** One should not simply say that he is lower than the angels. The phrase, “made a little lower,” is to be understood in this way: he was made lower in some respect, namely according to the weakness of the flesh and the suffering of death, as the authority says. Nor does it follow that, if he is lower in some respect, he is therefore simply lower than the angels. [Col. 0615A]

### QUESTION XXV. “You subjected all things beneath his feet” (Ps. 8).

“Everything” sometimes denotes universality, as in: “All the angels of heaven are righteous.” Sometimes it is restricted to a part by qualification, as in: “All mine are yours” (John 17). For God the Father says this to the elder son, that is, to the Jewish people. Therefore, by “all things” here one must understand not those things which belong to God according to nature, but only those things necessary for salvation. Sometimes “all” also has the force of a negation, as in: “All that I have heard from my Father I have made known to you” (John 15), that is, nothing except what I heard.

Hence one may ask how it is to be understood when it says: “You subjected all things.”

**Answer.** Some say that it is restricted to a part, and understand by “all things” only angels and human beings. But if the more excellent things are subject to Christ, how are the lesser not subject to him? For Ambrose says that, just as nothing is excepted from God’s work, so nothing is excepted from Christ’s power. And Augustine says: “No creature will remain unsubdued to him to whom the chief angels are subject.” The Apostle himself shows that nothing is excepted when he adds: “For in subjecting all things to him, he left nothing unsubdued to him.” [Col. 0615B]

### QUESTION XXVI. “But now we do not yet see all things subjected to him,” etc.

The Prophet says, “You subjected all things to him”; the Apostle, explaining this, added, “He left nothing unsubdued to him.” How, then, does he say here: “We do not yet see all things subjected to him”?

**Answer.** David, in his usual manner, uses the past for the future because of certainty, saying: “You subjected all things to him.” The Apostle, understanding this, said above that the world to come would be subject to him; and here he says: “We do not yet see all things subjected to him,” as though he said: the prophecy has already been fulfilled in part and remains to be fulfilled in part.

But someone may say: do not all things serve the divine dispensation, whose will nothing can resist? Thus, whether willing or unwilling, all things are already subject to him. How, then, does the Apostle say: “We do not yet see all things subjected to him”?

**Answer.** Subjection is one thing generally and another specially; likewise, one kind is hidden, another necessary, another voluntary. According to general, hidden, and necessary subjection, all things are already subject to God. According to voluntary subjection, not yet are all things that will be subjected already subject. Not yet does every tongue of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth confess that the Lord Jesus is in the glory of the Father (Phil. 2). Not yet have all his enemies been made the footstool of his feet (Ps. 109). All this will indeed occur in the future. Therefore the Apostle says: “We do not yet see all things subjected to him,” that is, voluntarily or openly.

Note that only God is greater than the human mind, not any angel. Angels may indeed be greater than human beings in respect to the body and to the soul burdened by the body’s corruption (Wis. 9); but not in respect to the mind’s own purity, in which it was assumed by the Word. [Col. 0615C–0616A]

### QUESTION XXVII. “That by the grace of God he might taste death for all,” etc.

Christ’s death did not benefit everyone. How, then, did he taste death for all?

**Answer.** Universality is here restricted to a part: namely, he tasted death for all the predestined. Or he is said to have tasted death for all because Christ’s death is sufficient for all, so far as depends upon him.

### QUESTION XXVIII. “It was fitting for him, for whom are all things and through whom are all things,” etc.

It is asked how it was fitting that God the Father should perfect through the suffering of death the author of the salvation of the faithful. In what does this fittingness consist, when it seems rather unfitting that the Lord of glory should die?

**Answer.** If Christ had not died, humankind would have perished. If that had occurred, God would not have been glorified by the whole universe; and this would have been unfitting, since all things were made for God’s glorification. Again, if Christ had not died, humankind would not have been saved, and thus the divine predestination would not have been fulfilled. It would have been unfitting for it to be rendered void.

Nor was it unfitting that the author of salvation should die for us, since he is our neighbor and brother; and it is fitting for a neighbor to provide, so far as he can, for the benefit of his neighbors. Hence follows:

### QUESTION XXIX. “For which reason he is not ashamed to call them brothers,” etc.

It is asked whether Christ is called our brother because he became a participant in our nature by taking the form of a servant (Phil. 2). But since the nature assumed by God is common to the good and the evil, it seems that Christ is not only the brother of believers but also of unbelievers.

**Answer.** Christ is called our brother not merely because he shares our nature, but also because we have received from the fullness of his grace. Therefore, for anyone to be called Christ’s brother, he must be joined to him both by nature and by grace. [Col. 0616B–C]

### QUESTION XXX. “And he himself,” namely Christ, “likewise partook of the same,” namely of the children, or of flesh and blood.

But it is asked: how did Christ partake of the children?

**Answer.** That is, he became a child consisting of soul and flesh, as the expositor says. Or: he partook of flesh and blood, that is, he became human; and this “likewise” means passible and mortal. [Col. 0616C–D]

### QUESTION XXXI. “That he might destroy him who had the dominion of death.”

Since death is a punishment justly imposed by God, and thus is not unfittingly said to be from God, it is asked how the devil is said to be the author of death. For the same thing does not appear able to be from both God and the devil.

**Answer.** Because death comes from the sin which the devil persuaded human beings to commit, he has—or is said to have—the dominion of death. Because he was the cause of death, he is called its author. Thus it is said that God does not make death, that is, its cause does not derive from God.

Note that this is the justice by which we were redeemed. Since the devil shed the blood of one who was not his debtor, he was commanded to give up his debtors; and because he shed innocent blood, in which he found nothing, he was commanded to withdraw from the guilty, whom he seemed to possess by a certain right. [Col. 0616D–0617A]

### QUESTION XXXII.

The expositor says that unless it were a human being who conquered the devil, humankind would be taken from him not justly but violently. But had the devil not wronged God, when he first deceitfully deceived the servant and afterward violently possessed him? What injustice, then, would God commit if by the word of his power alone he snatched humankind from the hand of this most unjust invader?

**Answer.** All God’s works are just; but in some of them power is manifest and justice hidden, while in others hidden power is present and justice manifest. Therefore, if Christ had employed manifest power and hidden justice in our deliverance, someone of less discernment might have thought that humankind was taken from the devil not justly but violently. But in order that “all iniquity might shut its mouth” (Ps. 106), our Lord employed manifest justice and hidden power in our redemption. [Col. 0617A–B]

### QUESTION XXXIII. “That he might free those who through fear of death,” etc.

It is asked to whose servitude those whom the Lord freed had been subject.

**Answer.** Before Christ’s coming, the devil obtained through death the effect of his wickedness. By fear of death he cast down those whom he was unable to cast down in any other way. For they gave everything for their life. Hence it is read in Job: “Skin for skin; all that a man has he will give for his life” (Job 1). Thus, conquered by the fear of death, they yielded and succumbed to temptation, until Christ came. By dying and rising again, he removed the fear of death from their midst. Hence the saints mock death and desire “to depart and be with Christ” (Phil. 1).

Or the fear of punishment may be understood, by which the Jews served under the Law. Christ, having rendered the Law inoperative through grace, freed them from the burden of the Law and from servile fear. [Col. 0617B–C]

### QUESTION XXXIV. “For surely it is not angels that he takes hold of,” etc.

It is asked whether God could have assumed angelic nature into the unity of his person, as he did human nature.

**Answer.** It seems to us that he could have done so, but did not will to do so. In this is understood the dignity of our race: for to humanity, which had received less than the angels at its creation, more was bestowed at its glorification through grace. For human nature does not adore angelic nature above itself; rather, the reverse is the case. [Col. 0617C–D]

### QUESTION XXXV. “Therefore he had to be made like his brothers in every respect.”

Was he not made like his brothers solely by grace in this: that he was born human, was brought up, suffered, and died? How, then, does the Apostle say that he “had to” be so, when this is not a debt but God’s gratuitous gift?

**Answer.** He does not simply say “had to,” but adds: “that he might become merciful” (Heb. 2). For he could not have mercy on us by dying unless he had first become passible and mortal. Or he says “had to,” that is, it was fitting that he be made like his brothers. For by bearing our weaknesses and death for us, he summoned us to humility and kindled charity within us. [Col. 0617D]

### QUESTION XXXVI. “For because he himself suffered and was tempted, he is able,” etc.

Was he not able to help the tempted before the Passion—indeed, before the Incarnation? For his power was not increased through the Passion. What, then, is meant by: “In that wherein he suffered, he is able to help those who are tempted”?

**Answer.** After the Passion, he knows well even by experience what is the temptation and tribulation of those who suffer. Hence he stretches out his hand to compassion with great eagerness. Therefore he is said to be able to do these things and to know them perfectly. For he knows who those are who suffer for him; he knows when, how, and to whom he ought to extend his hand. Hence the Prophet says: “The Lord has become a refuge for the poor, a refuge in times of need, in tribulation” (Ps. 9). [Col. 0618A]

### QUESTION XXXVII. “How much greater honor has the one who built the house than the house itself” (Heb. 3), etc.

Does not the one who manages a house often have greater glory in it than the one who built it? How, then, does the Apostle say, “How much greater,” etc.?

**Answer.** This is to be understood of the spiritual house, as though he said: Christ, as Lord and Creator, is greater than Moses, who is a servant and minister. [Col. 0618B]

### QUESTION XXXVIII. “According to the day of testing,” etc.

It is asked by whom testing is performed.

**Answer.** A human being tests in order to know what he does not know. In this sense, testing is a certain gentle preliminary movement of the mind toward an experience by which something previously unknown may be known. God tests in order to prove through affliction and tribulation, so that he may crown the one proved. The devil tests in order to cast someone down into sin; hence it is said: “And lead us not into temptation” (Matt. 6), that is, do not permit us to be cast down into sin. The flesh tests when we experience its disordered movements. The world tests when through its vanity it invites us to love itself. [Col. 0618B–C]

### QUESTION XXXIX. “Therefore I was offended,” etc.

Another translation has, “I was near.” How, then, if he was offended, was he near? And if near, how was he offended? If both readings cannot stand, which should rather be retained?

**Answer.** He was near by applying the scourges of correction, because it belongs to a neighbor to correct a neighbor. He was offended and angry because, even through scourges, they were unwilling to repent. Or he may be understood as angry with the good for forty years, because for so long he did not bring them into the promised land; yet the following text does not seem to approve this interpretation. But he may be understood as near to the wicked for forty years because he endured them for so long and did not utterly destroy them. [Col. 0618C–D]

### QUESTION XL. “If they shall enter into my rest.”

It is asked under what figure this was spoken.

**Answer.** The figure is called *aposiopesis*, and the sense is: “If this happens, anything whatever that is impossible will happen,” or, “Let no one henceforth believe me in anything.” Note that there are four sabbaths, or rests. The first is God’s rest, concerning which it is written in Genesis: “And God rested on the seventh day” (Gen. 2). The second rest is the promised land; the third, rest of mind; the fourth is eternal rest. The first and fourth belong to God; the second and third to humankind. The first is a figure of the fourth, the second of the third. [Col. 0618D–0619A]

### QUESTION XLI. “As I swore in my wrath,” etc.

It is asked why this is called God’s wrath, since it is clear that such a passion does not befall God.

**Answer.** He calls wrath God’s unchangeable sentence of eternal justice, by the figure called *anthropopathos*, which occurs whenever things that signify passion when said of human beings are figuratively attributed to God. Therefore God swears in wrath when he firmly determines to punish obstinacy in sin.

Note that there are four kinds of symbols, that is, signs—namely, things figuratively said of God. Some symbols are similar and taken from bodily things, such as fire, light, the sun, and the like. Others are similar and taken from incorporeal things, such as reason, understanding, spirit, and the like. Others are dissimilar and taken from bodily things, such as lion, bear, worm, and the like. Others are dissimilar and taken from incorporeal things, such as wrath, fury, pain, repentance, and the like. [Col. 0619A–B]

### QUESTION XLII. “That none of you may be hardened by the deceitfulness of sin,” etc.

It is asked what he calls the deceitfulness of sin.

**Answer.** The deceitfulness of sin is when someone presumes upon God’s grace and, secure in this confidence, lies in sins. Or it is when someone promises that he will amend himself in the following year, in order to sin more securely in the present—a thing done under the devil’s authorship. A threefold deceit may also be noted here: first, when we consent to a perverse impulse; second, when we break forth into an evil deed; third, when we delight in the habit of sin. [Col. 0619B–C]

### QUESTION XLIII. “But with whom was he angry forty years?” etc.

It is asked how this should be understood.

**Answer.** Forty signifies the completeness of years. Therefore he is said to have been angry with them for forty years because he is angry with sinners up to the end of their lives.

### QUESTION XLIV. “Although the works were finished from the foundation of the world” (Heb. 4), etc.

It is asked where mention is made of that eternal rest which is signified by the promised land. For there the Sabbath rest is treated: “And God rested on the seventh day from all the work which he had accomplished.” But mention of the rest of the land of Palestine seems to be made where it says: “If they shall enter into my rest.”

**Answer.** Where Sabbath rest or the rest of the land of Palestine is treated according to the letter, there also the true rest is treated anagogically, which is signified by those two. [Col. 0619C–D]

### QUESTION XLV. “God rested on the seventh day,” etc.

Scripture says that in six days God made all his works, so that afterward he made nothing new. But does he not create new souls every day? How, then, does he make nothing new?

**Answer.** God makes nothing except from matter made in the first creation, as with any bodily thing; or after the likeness of things then already made, as with incorporeal spirits, namely human souls.

### QUESTION XLVI. “Again he appoints a certain day, ‘Today,’” etc.

It is asked how, by introducing here the Apostle’s words, he compels the Jews to understand a rest other than that of the promised land, when he says: “Today, if you hear his voice,” etc.

**Answer.** Those to whom he wrote had faith and believed David to be a prophet. Accordingly, from the prophet’s words set down there, they had necessarily to understand another day and another rest besides the rest of the promised land; and thus the Apostle’s proof proceeds. [Col. 0620A]

### QUESTION XLVII. “For the word is living,” etc.

The expositor says that the Son of God sees how reason and sensuality agree in their distinctions. But do they not differ in their distinctions? How, then, do they agree in their distinctions? Can things agree and differ in the same respect?

**Answer.** He does not say that reason and sensuality agree in the distinctions by which reason differs from sensuality, or conversely. Rather, reason has distinctions by which it is distinguished within itself: when it thirsts after God, thinking about the divine *usia* [being/essence]; when it considers heavenly things below; when it contemplates the natures of invisible spirits; or when, on earth, it rightly treats matters that must be managed in worldly affairs. Likewise, sensuality has distinctions by which it is divided within itself: when, more given over to lower things, it is lower; or when recalled from them, it is more worthy.

The Son of God therefore sees how the higher distinction of sensuality agrees, by consent, with the distinctions of reason; or how the lower distinction of reason, oppressed and captive, sometimes consents to the lower distinction of sensuality.

Note that “soul” is used either for sensuality, or for carnal sins, or for carnal thoughts; likewise “spirit” for reason, or for spiritual sins, or for good thoughts. When it is said that the word of God reaches “to the division of soul and spirit” (Heb. 4), you will therefore find a threefold exposition in the gloss, corresponding to the threefold sense of soul and spirit. [Col. 0620A–C]

### QUESTION XLVIII. “Tempted in every way according to likeness, without sin.”

In that he was tempted, he knows how to sympathize; in that he was without sin, he can deliver. The expositor says that it is impossible for a human being to know afflictions unless he has experienced them. But do not many know, merely by seeing, the afflictions of others which they have never themselves suffered—even to the point of sympathizing with them? How, then, is it true that it is impossible for a human being, etc.?

**Answer.** One who has not experienced them does not know them as perfectly as one who knows through experience. The Apostle notes this mode of knowing when he says: “We do not have a high priest who [cannot sympathize, that is, knows …” [text incomplete]. [Col. 0620C–D]

### QUESTION XLIX. “And no one takes the honor to himself” (Heb. 5), etc.

Do not many very eminent people in this time put themselves forward, and sometimes—even uncalled—take honor to themselves by force? How, then, is it true: “No one takes the honor to himself”?

**Answer.** No one acting piously and religiously puts himself forward. Nor did Christ glorify himself, etc., since this glorification of the Son by the Father occurred according to his human nature.

### QUESTION L.

It is asked how this authority—“Today I have begotten you” [Col. 0621A]—which according to Augustine is expounded concerning eternal generation, is introduced by the Apostle in this place. How does the Father, saying, “Today I have begotten you,” testify that Christ, as man, is his Son and the redeemer of the world?

**Answer.** Jerome says that this authority is to be understood concerning Christ’s human generation as follows: “Today,” that is, in the time of grace and light, “I have begotten you,” that is, I have incarnated you; or, “I have begotten,” that is, I have shown you to be begotten. Thus this authority is fittingly introduced.

### QUESTION LI. “According to the order of Melchizedek,” etc.

The expositor says that Melchizedek was not temporal. But was he not merely a human being, and thus temporal, since every human being is temporal?

**Answer.** It was said that he was not temporal because Scripture [Col. 0621B] is silent concerning the beginning and end of his life, as a figure of Christ, who lacks beginning and end. Or he may be called a priest not temporal because of his priesthood, which remains in Christ forever.

### QUESTION LII. “He was heard because of his reverence,” etc.

It is asked what it means that Christ was heard because of his reverence. Was Stephen not likewise heard because of his reverence, as were the other saints? What, then, is great concerning Christ if he was heard because of his reverence?

**Answer.** It is not surprising if some things said of Christ are common to martyrs, since some things common even to Levitical priests are set down here. Yet it may be said that Stephen was heard because of Christ’s reverence rather than his own. For Christ entered through himself; others entered through him. Hence “from his fullness we have all received” (John 1). And thus something special is said of Christ when it is read that he was heard because of his own reverence: this is marked by the fact that he died and suffered without sin and out of charity alone. [Col. 0621B–C]

### QUESTION LIII. “He learned obedience from the things which he suffered,” etc.

We learn things that we do not know. Therefore, since Christ knew all things as God, how did he learn what he was not ignorant of?

**Answer.** This question has already been sufficiently treated above. For it was said that knowledge is twofold: one kind is knowledge by comprehension, the other by experience. He possessed the former, knowledge by comprehension, from eternity; the latter he learned in time.

### QUESTION LIV. “What are the elements of the beginning of the words of God?” etc.

It is asked what distinction there is among these three: elements, beginning, and word of God.

**Answer.** By “word of God” he means evangelical doctrine; by “beginning,” the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer; and the elements are the material contained in the Creed, such as the nativity, Passion, and the other articles of faith. [Col. 0621C–D]

### QUESTION LV. “Everyone who partakes of milk,” etc.

The expositor says: “One who does not grasp, ‘The Word was made flesh’ (John 1), how will he grasp, ‘In the beginning was the Word’ (ibid.)?” It is asked, therefore, how “The Word was made flesh” is easier to understand than “In the beginning was the Word,” when the former statement concerning the Word’s Incarnation is contrary to human reason, while the latter, concerning the Trinity of persons and unity of essence, can be investigated by reason, as is evident from the prophets.

**Answer.** The statements concerning the Incarnation are called easier because they were visibly exhibited; the latter are more difficult because they are comprehended by the intellect of only a few. [Col. 0621D–0622A]

### QUESTION LVI.

Again, it is asked how those to whom the Apostle speaks here needed to be taught what were the elements of the beginning of the words of God. Were they not believers? How did they not know the nativity, Passion, and other articles of faith, without which no one is a believer?

**Answer.** They knew these things, but not fully.

### QUESTION LVII. “Therefore, leaving the elementary teaching” (Heb. 6), etc.

Since the teaching of the beginning seems necessary to them, how does he say, “leaving the teaching of the beginning”?

**Answer.** The sense is: you ought not always to remain occupied with matters belonging to the beginning, but should press on toward perfection. [Col. 0622B]

### QUESTION LVIII. “Not laying again the foundation,” etc.

This appears contrary to the foregoing. For if they still needed teaching concerning the elements, a foundation was necessary for them.

**Answer.** The glosses suffice for this question, explaining how “not again” ought to be understood.

### QUESTION LIX. “From dead works,” etc.

He calls dead works mortal sins, or good works that have been made dead by a subsequent evil. It is therefore asked how it is true that no good goes unrewarded, just as no evil goes unpunished.

**Answer.** Such good works are called dead because they do not profit toward eternal life. Yet they will be rewarded in this respect: those who performed them will be punished less in the future. Or perhaps temporal benefit was given for them. Again, such good works are called dead because, according to some, they can be revived through repentance—not so that one will receive further reward for them, but because through good deeds previously done persons will obtain grace more easily.

But it seems to us that, after the sin by which they had been made dead has been removed through repentance, they are, as before they were dead, worthy of eternal life. [Col. 0622B–C]

### QUESTION LX. “Of baptisms,” etc.

It is asked how he says “baptisms” here in the plural, when elsewhere he says: “One Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4), etc. If it is one, how can there be many?

**Answer.** Just as faith is said to be one not in number but in kind, as the authority teaches, so baptism may be called one not in number but in kind, because it has one form; it cannot be repeated; and because there is one operation of the three persons therein. It is called plural in respect of the individual washings.

Or he says “baptisms” in the plural because there is baptism in potentiality and in blood.
