This does not mean that the sacrament of baptism is celebrated otherwise than in water; rather, the shedding of blood, faith, and repentance supply baptism’s place—only where an emergency of necessity, not contempt for religion, excludes the sacrament of baptism.

The following objection is made to this solution: “Unless one is born again of water and the Holy Spirit, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (John 3). According to this authority, it appears that no one is worthy of salvation without receiving this sacrament.

**Answer.** Doctors expound the Lord’s preceding words—“Unless one is born again of water,” etc.—thus: unless someone is born again by that Spirit and regeneration by which those who are born again of water and the Holy Spirit are born again, he cannot be saved. Yet people are born again by this Spirit in different ways: some through repentance, others through the shedding of blood, others through baptism.

Note that the foundation of Christian religion is divided into six matters, set down here by the Apostle: repentance, faith, baptism, laying on of hands, resurrection, and future judgment. These pertain to the instruction of neophytes. [Col. 0622C–0623A]

### QUESTION LXI. “It is impossible for those once enlightened,” etc.

Here the Apostle seems to deny repentance to those who have fallen grievously, as in the following passage, where he says: “For those who sin deliberately, there no longer remains a sacrifice for sin.”

**Answer.** It seems to us that in both places he describes sin against the Holy Spirit. Whoever has once fallen into its abyss cannot obtain repentance or salvation. But the doctors say that “impossible,” etc., here does not deny every renewal, but only repetition of baptism. Or it may be understood of the future state; certain glosses support this interpretation. [Col. 0623B]

### QUESTION LXII.

The expositor says that baptism avails even against subsequent sins. But it is asked how sins not yet committed can already have been forgiven.

**Answer.** Some say that baptism is said to avail against subsequent sins because, through the grace bestowed in baptism, future sins are avoided. But according to this solution, what does the following statement in the same gloss mean: “if repentance is performed concerning them”?

It seems to us that it should be understood thus: baptism avails against subsequent sins because through baptism’s power they can be wiped away with a lesser satisfaction. Thus, if a believer and an unbeliever commit the same sin, the repentance sufficient for salvation in the reborn person is not sufficient in the unbeliever or one not yet reborn. I say this without prejudice to a better opinion. [Col. 0623B–C]

### QUESTION LXIII. “The Lord entered through himself,” etc.

Since the Lord says in the Gospel: “Let your word be: Yes, yes; no, no; whatever is beyond this is from evil” (Matt. 5), it is asked how the Lord then swore to Abraham. Would Abraham not have believed God, or have believed him more slowly, had he made the promise without an oath?

**Answer.** The Lord did not swear for Abraham’s sake, since Abraham would have believed him firmly without an oath. Rather, he swore for the sake of those who would come after Abraham, who would either not have believed at all in the promise made to Abraham, or would have believed more slowly, unless it had been confirmed by an oath. Thus that oath was not from Abraham’s evil, but from the evil of those who were to come. [Col. 0623C–D]

### QUESTION LXIV. If it is asked, “Why did the Lord swear by himself?”

**Answer.** Because human beings customarily swear by one greater than themselves, while God had no one greater. Hence it is clear that those who swear by something inferior sin. For that by which they swear they somehow set above themselves. [Col. 0624A]

### QUESTION LXV. “An oath is the end of every controversy among them.”

What, then, shall we say about trials by fire, water, or other such things, which the Church seems to accept? Does not the end of controversy also consist in these?

**Answer.** These trials do not belong to the Church. Accordingly, the guilty are often acquitted by them, and the innocent are sometimes adjudged guilty by them. This would never occur if mother Church countenanced them. Hence in certain places she tolerates these practices rather than commends them.

But someone may say: the same judgment ought to be made concerning oaths.

We concede this. For the Church did not institute them, any more than it instituted the trials mentioned above. [Col. 0624A]

### QUESTION LXVI. “According to the order of Melchizedek” (Heb. 7), etc.

It is asked: in what way?

**Answer.** Christ is called high priest according to the order of Melchizedek in many ways. First, because Melchizedek alone was both king and priest, as Christ is. Second, because he was anointed not with visible oil, as Moses was instituted, but with the oil of gladness and purity of faith. He did not sacrifice animals; rather, by an offering of bread and wine he consecrated Christ’s sacrifice. So too Christ was anointed by the Father with the Holy Spirit, offered himself to God the Father upon the altar of the cross, and gave his true body and blood to the disciples at supper. And his priesthood remains forever in ritual and dignity. [Col. 0624B]

### QUESTION LXVII. It is asked what benefit Melchizedek’s offering of bread and wine conferred on those who received it.

**Answer.** Some say that it benefited only those who received it with faith, as much as Christ’s body now benefits. This does not seem true to us. For the sacraments of the natural law or of the written Law did not benefit, nor could they benefit, as much as the sacraments of grace. [Col. 0624C]

### QUESTION LXVIII. “Without any contradiction, the lesser is blessed by the greater.”

Is not a holy man often blessed by one of lesser holiness—for example, when a monk is blessed by some secular priest? How, then, is it true that the lesser is blessed by the greater?

**Answer.** One person may be less than another in excellence of merits and greater than that same person in dignity. Here, however, the question concerns superiority and inferiority according to dignity. Thus what is lower in dignity is blessed by that which is greater in excellence of dignity. Nor is every sort of blessing in view here, but only that which belongs to the consecrated. [Col. 0624C–D]

### QUESTION LXIX

“Through Abraham, and Levi, who received tithes, was tithed,” etc. Augustine says that, just as when Adam sinned those who were in his loins sinned, so when Abraham gave tithes those who were in his loins were tithed. But did Christ either sin when Adam sinned, or was he tithed when Abraham gave tithes, since according to the flesh he was in the loins of each? Therefore, since Levi and Christ were alike in Abraham’s loins, how was Levi tithed and Christ not? Or, if Christ was tithed as Levi was, how does the Apostle prove Christ’s priesthood to be greater than the Levitical priesthood by the fact that the Levitical order, in Levi, was tithed in Abraham?

Solution. There were some—and perhaps still are—who say that Christ’s flesh was preserved whole and incorrupt from Adam down to the Virgin; they should not be heard. Levi, therefore, was tithed and Christ was not, although both were there, because Levi derived from that source the thing which subjected him to tithing, namely guilt. Christ, however, derived nothing from it which would have made him subject to tithing; his flesh derived from it not a wound but the remedy for the wound.

The following objection is raised against this solution: All flesh that was in Isaac descended from Abraham according to the common law, namely through concupiscence; but Christ’s flesh was in Isaac; therefore Christ’s flesh descended from Abraham through concupiscence.

Solution. It must not simply be granted that Christ’s flesh thus descended from that source through concupiscence; for that would mean that Christ’s flesh came to be through concupiscence. It may, however, be granted by division: some flesh which afterward became Christ’s descended from that source according to the common law—flesh which, from the first man down to Mary, was under original sin.

### QUESTION LXX

“When the priesthood is transferred, it is necessary that a transfer of the law take place.” It may be asked how a transfer of the law necessarily follows from a transfer of the priesthood.

Solution. Since both were given together by the same giver under the same promise, what is asserted of one must necessarily be understood of the other. Or, the law is necessarily transferred when the priesthood is transferred because the priesthood is transferred precisely because no one was justified through its ministry, and so it was transferred because of its insufficiency and weakness; but the law is equally insufficient and weak. Hence the Apostle says: “The law brought nothing to perfection” (Hebrews). Therefore it too is transferred by the same necessity. Since neither could bring perfection, both are transferred. This was foreshadowed by the priest and Levite who passed by the sick man who had fallen among robbers and did not grant him the mercy of healing (Luke 10).

### QUESTION LXXI

“It is evident that our Lord arose from Judah” [Col. 0625D]. It is therefore asked whether his mother also came from Judah.

Solution. Recall the question which we set forth above on the Epistle to Timothy, prompted by Origen’s words saying that Mary was only from the tribe of Levi, and that the Lord was called of the tribe of Judah only because of Joseph. But, as I said, the two tribes—the royal and the priestly—were intermingled; the Virgin was from the tribe of Judah on her father’s father’s side, and from the tribe of Levi on her mother’s side.

### QUESTION LXXII

“The law brought nothing to perfection,” etc. Were not some persons perfect in the time of the law, such as David and many others? And, since they were righteous, they possessed that righteousness through obedience to the divine law. How, then, were they not righteous through the law?

Solution. The righteous of that time possessed righteousness not from the law but from faith in what was to come [Col. 0626A]; for the law exposed transgressions but did not remove them.

### QUESTION LXXIII

“To intercede for us,” etc. It is asked how Christ intercedes for us.

Solution. The expositor says, “by presenting himself”; this must be understood to mean that the merit of his Passion, which he displayed in his humanity, reconciles us believers to the Father.

### QUESTION LXXIV

“Who does not have daily need” (Hebrews 8). It is asked what benefit the sacrifices of the law conferred: did they grant remission of sins?

Solution. For certain sins, sinners were barred from entering; by sacrifices they were so reconciled that they were permitted to enter the Temple. But through such remission they were not made worthy of eternal life [Col. 0626B].

### QUESTION LXXV

“If then he were on earth, he would not even be a priest,” etc. It is asked how these words are to be understood.

Solution. The wording of this chapter is compressed and broken, and therefore creates obscurity. Accordingly, it is expounded in five ways, as is found in the glosses. Note that four things are considered in every sacrifice: to whom it is offered, by whom it is offered, what is offered, and for whom it is offered. The one and same mediator of both, reconciling us to God through a sacrifice of peace, would remain one with him to whom he offered; would make one in himself those for whom he offered; and would himself be both the one offering and that which was offered.

### QUESTION LXXVI

“Who serve the copy and shadow” [Col. 0626C], etc. It is asked what is here called a copy (*exemplar*).

Solution. The truth shown to Moses on the mountain is called the copy of the figures made in accordance with it. Again, the figures themselves are called a copy of the truth which was afterward fulfilled. Thus the figures, in different respects, may be called both *example* (*exemplum*) and *copy* (*exemplar*). Properly speaking, a copy is that in the likeness of which something is made; an example is that which is drawn from it.

### QUESTION LXXVII

“For if the former had been without fault,” etc. Is not the law good, holy, and given by God? How then is it not free from fault?

Solution. The old testament is said not to be free from fault in the same sense in which the law is said to work wrath: namely, because it does not justify, and because it commands what cannot be done without grace.

### QUESTION LXXVIII

[Col. 0626D] It is asked why we do not worship God according to the rite by which the Hebrew patriarchs worshipped him.

Solution. Because God commanded something different for us through the fathers of the New Testament. Nor are the things we observe contrary to the Old Testament; rather, they were foretold and announced in it.

### QUESTION LXXIX

Again, why do we retain the authority of that testament?

Solution. So that we may not extinguish the prophets and remove the testimony of truth from our midst. Therefore, when something is read that we do not observe, we must inquire only what it signifies, not condemn it; for by the very fact that it is now observed, it is shown not to have been condemned but fulfilled.

### QUESTION LXXX

Again, it is asked why the former is called the Old Testament and this the New, when the law is fulfilled [Col. 0627A] through the New Testament.

Solution. The Old Testament is called old because of the old injury which is not healed by the letter that commands and threatens. This is called new because of the newness of the Spirit, which heals a human being from the vice of oldness. Carefully note the difference between the two testaments: that one old, this one new. There is the letter, which by itself kills; here the Spirit, which gives life. That was written on tablets of stone; this on minds and hearts. That promises earthly things; this heavenly things. That has sacraments signifying salvation but not conferring it; this has sacraments conferring salvation.

Also note that “testament” is called both the temporal or eternal promise itself, and the writing containing that promise. Thus the Old Testament contains a promise [Col. 0627B] pertaining to the old human being; the New Testament contains the promise of the eternal inheritance pertaining to the new human being.

### QUESTION LXXXI

“For if the ashes of a heifer, sprinkled upon the defiled, sanctify” (Hebrews 9), etc. It is asked what he calls the defilement from which the sprinkled ashes of the heifer sanctify.

Solution. He calls it contact with the dead; or leprosy, from which those ashes cleanse—that is, from the penalty which under the law was due for such uncleanness. By this contact consent to sin is signified.

### QUESTION LXXXII

“And as it is appointed for human beings to die once.” The expositor says that Christ died by the same necessity and law of nature by which other human beings necessarily die in fact [Col. 0627C]. It is therefore asked whether Christ died of necessity and whether he had the necessity of dying. This seems evident from the authority cited above. But if by necessity, how did he die by will alone, as it is written: “He was offered because he willed it” (Isaiah 53)?

Solution. Some say that, among the other penal conditions which the Lord assumed with our nature without guilt, he also voluntarily assumed this penal condition, namely the necessity of dying. This neither excludes the will nor is excluded by it. Yet it must not be understood as though Christ could not, by the power of his divinity, lay aside this penalty without the dissolution of soul and body, and clothe the assumed nature with the robe of immortality; but if he conferred no more upon it [Col. 0627D] than had been conferred before death, he would necessarily die.

### QUESTION LXXXIII

“To those who await him for salvation,” etc. On this passage the expositor says that Christ died not by necessity but by will for the sin of those awaiting him for salvation; yet above it was said that he died by necessity. This seems contradictory.

Solution. Understand what is said here as follows. Christ died not by necessity—that is, there was no sin in him for which it was necessary for him to die. Hence, as if explaining what he had said, he adds: but he died for their sin, namely, for the sin of those who awaited him for salvation.

### QUESTION LXXXIV

“Otherwise they would have ceased to be offered” (Hebrews 10), etc. The legal victims, as the Apostle says, would cease to be offered if [Col. 0628A] they made people perfect. It is therefore asked why the saving victim of the New Testament, although it brings perfection and completes those who are sanctified, is offered repeatedly and does not cease to be offered.

Solution. It was indeed offered once, through the Passion of death, upon the altar of the cross in human form; nor is it offered again in that manner through death. Yet it is offered repeatedly in the sacrament, not because of its own weakness but rather because of ours, since we sin daily; and especially for the remembrance of Christ’s death, so that his love may be impressed more deeply upon our hearts through our remembrance of so great a benefit.

### QUESTION LXXXV

“But you have prepared a body for me,” etc. It is asked in what respect he prepared Christ’s body.

Solution. This fitness consists in two things: purity and mortality. Unless it were pure, the impure could not be redeemed through [Col. 0628B] it; unless it were mortal, it could not be sacrificed. Therefore the Lord’s body had to be pure through freedom from sin, and mortal.

### QUESTION LXXXVI

“Not forsaking your assembly.” It is asked whether the Apostle here condemns what the Lord permits when he says, “If they persecute you in one city, flee into another” (Matthew 10), of which he himself gave an example by fleeing into Egypt. Paul likewise is often found to have done the same. What then is it that he blames in those who abandon the assembly?

Solution. In this passage the Apostle blames those who, as though because of their own holiness, cannot live among other weak or imperfect persons. By abandoning the assembly they divide unity, and thus sin unto death [Col. 0628C]. When certain persons are especially sought by persecutors, then it is permissible to evade the fury of the persecutors, if this can be done without detriment to the assembly.

### QUESTION LXXXVII

“Those who sin deliberately,” etc. It is asked who are the deliberate sinners for whom no sacrifice for sin remains.

Solution. The gloss says that by “those who sin deliberately” he means those who remain in sin through a will to sin. Christ, who is the sacrifice for sin, does not benefit them; he benefits penitents alone.

### QUESTION LXXXVIII

But again it is asked why the Apostle says, “after receiving the knowledge of truth,” since Christ does not benefit those who remain in a will [Col. 0628D] to sin even before receiving knowledge of truth. Perhaps someone will say that such persons can benefit through the grace of baptism, so that no penalty of satisfaction is imposed at all, whereas after the grace of regeneration they cannot be renewed even through penitence. In saying this, we do not exclude penitence, as some wish to do, taking occasion from the Apostle’s words, “those who sin deliberately,” etc.

But some think that by “those who sin deliberately” he means those who knowingly attack the truth out of envy, hatred, or some similar cause and sin against the Holy Spirit, and therefore sin beyond remission; for this sin has forgiveness neither in the present age nor in the future, as the Lord says. This too seems indicated above, where the Apostle says: “It is impossible for those who were once enlightened” [Col. 0629A] (Matthew 12), etc. Subsequently, in this place, he adds: “Whoever has trampled the Son of God underfoot, and regarded the blood of the covenant as unclean, and insulted the Spirit of grace.” By these words the sin against the Holy Spirit seems plainly to be signified.

### QUESTION LXXXIX

It is asked why baptism cannot be repeated, whose repetition, according to some, is denied here by the Apostle.

Solution. Because baptism removes both guilt and punishment together. Therefore, if it were repeated, it would not only be cheapened but would also invite sin. But someone may say: by the same reasoning penitence too ought not to be repeated, lest it be cheapened or provoke sin.

Solution. The judgment concerning penitence, which restrains from sin by the infliction of punishment, differs from that concerning baptism, by which both guilt and punishment are wholly remitted [Col. 0629B].

### QUESTION XC

“And a certain fiery zeal.” It is asked what punishment he signifies here by fire.

Solution. Fire here signifies the intensity of eternal punishment, because no element has such efficacy as fire.

### QUESTION XCI

“Which will consume the adversaries,” etc. Will fire reduce Christ’s enemies to nothing?

Solution. Fiery zeal is said to consume adversaries because no part of body or soul will be free from punishment without being tormented by fire.

### QUESTION XCII

“Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord.” It is asked whether vengeance must always be reserved for the Lord. Is it not lawful for a human being [Col. 0629C] to take vengeance? Are robbers not lawfully hanged?

Solution. It is not lawful for a person to take vengeance for himself, nor should he desire it; but if vengeance must be taken, God alone and zeal for justice must be the cause. Whoever takes it otherwise sins mortally. In accordance with the saying: “Whoever takes up the sword shall perish by the sword” (Matthew 26).

### QUESTION XCIII

“Faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen” (Hebrews 11). Concerning this definition of faith, it is asked whether it applies to every faith and whether it can apply to faith alone. This definition seems to apply only to faith concerning future things; but since faith concerns present and past things, such as the Nativity and Passion, how is faith in the Passion the substance of things hoped for [Col. 0629D]?

Again, are not hope and charity a substance—that is, the thing and cause which makes hoped-for things subsist in us? How then is faith alone the substance of things hoped for?

Solution. As the gloss explains this definition, it seems not to apply to faith alone. Nevertheless, though part of this definition may appear applicable to other virtues, the whole does not. Faith alone is the evidence of things not seen, through which alone we are certain that eternal things exist; through hope, however, we trust that we shall possess them. Therefore faith is properly called the substance of future things, because through it we know that they exist. Faith concerning present or past things can also be called the substance of things hoped for—that is, the cause which [Col. 0630A] at times makes the things we hope for subsist in us—because through faith in the Passion one comes to future goods. It is also evidence of things not seen, so much so that those who saw him suffer believed something: namely, that Christ hanging on the cross was God.

### QUESTION XCIV

“From invisible things,” etc. It is asked what he calls invisible things.

Solution. Either the formless and invisible matter of the four elements, which is called *chaos* in Greek; or the invisible world, called the archetype, which was in God’s mind and according to whose pattern this perceptible and visible world was made.

### QUESTION XCV

“Abel, though dead, still speaks through faith,” etc. How does one who does not live speak [Col. 0630B]?

Solution. He speaks—that is, he provides matter for speech; he speaks because by his example he urges us to be righteous.

### QUESTION XCVI

“Without faith it is impossible to please God,” etc. It is asked what faith is meant. Is it faith in the Incarnation?

Solution. It is said that without it no one from the beginning pleased God.

### QUESTION XCVII

“One approaching God must believe that he exists,” etc. It is asked what faith he treats: perfect or imperfect faith. If imperfect faith, how could anyone please God through it? If perfect faith, how can it suffice for salvation to believe that he exists and is a rewarder of those who seek him? For these do not contain all the articles necessary for salvation.

Solution. He seems [Col. 0630C] here to lay down an order for the faith that must be held—that is, to show what one must believe first—not to set forth the sufficiency of faith.

### QUESTION XCVIII

It may be asked whether there was ever a time when merely believing this—namely, that God exists and is a rewarder, etc.—sufficed. This does not seem to be the case.

### QUESTION XCIX

“By faith Isaac blessed Jacob even concerning things to come,” etc. When he blessed him, did he understand what was signified by blessing the younger? If he did understand, then he knew that he was blessing Jacob, which the narrative by no means permits. For he even felt his hands to determine whether he was Esau; and afterward, when Esau came, he said: “Who was it that came deceitfully, to whom I gave the blessing? And he shall be blessed.”

Solution. [Col. 0630D] Although he did not understand then, he understood afterward and had faith in this matter: that the greater people would serve the lesser.

### QUESTION C

Again, it is asked how Isaac was deceived in giving the blessing.

Solution. He was not deceived in that he knew the effect which the blessing would have in the person whom he blessed; nevertheless, he did not yet know that the one whom he blessed was Jacob. Properly speaking, deception is usually understood in matters which ought not to be done. Is one to be called deceived who buys gold for bronze, or silver for tin? But if deception is taken broadly, for all things that occur otherwise than expected, then there was a certain deception here too.

### QUESTION CI

“And he worshipped the top of his staff” [Col. 0631A], or, as another text has it, “upon the top,” etc. It is asked what it means that Jacob worshipped upon the top of Joseph’s staff.

Solution. Perhaps he had taken the staff from his son when that same son was swearing; and while holding it after the words of the one swearing, before it had yet been returned, he immediately worshipped God. Thus Augustine resolves the matter. Or it may be said that he worshipped the top of his son’s staff, that is, Christ’s future kingdom among the Gentiles, which was signified by it, so that what is signified is understood under the name of the sign.

### QUESTION CII

Jephthah, etc. It is asked whether he made a rational vow and whether he sinned in fulfilling it by offering his only daughter to the Lord. If a dog had met him, would he have offered it to God?

Solution. It appears that he acted foolishly in making the vow, and more foolishly in fulfilling it [Col. 0631B]. Yet if he did this through a hidden prompting of the Holy Spirit, he is excused, like Samson, who crushed the Philistines with himself, because it is not lawful for one to lay hands upon oneself. Hence Jonah too said: “Cast me into the sea.”

### QUESTION CIII

It is asked why, in remembrance of the death of that girl, Hebrew virgins make lamentation every year.

Solution. As an example, lest anyone again make or do something so foolish that such sorrow may follow.

### QUESTION CIV

It is asked whether Abraham sinned in will by wishing to sacrifice his son, whereas, according to some—indeed, truly—Jephthah sinned by killing his daughter unless this was done by divine prompting.

Solution. Abraham is not merely free from blame for the crime of cruelty; he is even praised under the name of piety [Col. 0631C], because he wished to kill his son not wickedly but obediently.

### QUESTION CV

“Moreover, we have had instructors who were fathers of our flesh, and we reverenced them. Shall we not much more obey the Father of spirits and live?” (Hebrews 12.) If it is asked whether human souls are derived by propagation, note this authority carefully. It plainly proves that souls are not derived by propagation as flesh is; for if this were so, the Apostle would by no means distinguish between the fathers of our flesh and the Father of spirits.

### QUESTION CVI

“Watching lest anyone fall short of the grace of God,” etc. It is asked what it is to fall short of God’s grace.

Solution. It is to close the eyes of the mind to grace offered and reject grace, just as, with my eyes open to the ray of the sun [Col. 0631D], I can close them or keep them open at will. This belongs to free choice; and so grace does not exclude free choice, nor does choice itself exclude grace.

### QUESTION CVII

“He sold his birthright,” etc. It is asked what the Apostle calls Esau’s birthright.

Solution. Here he calls the birthright the honor and dignity of the priesthood. For before Aaron’s priesthood all firstborn sons were priests, as Shem was. This was a great dignity, because the firstborn received the larger portion of paternal property and inheritance, shone more splendidly in richer clothing, and received the blessing.

### QUESTION CVIII

It is asked whether Esau’s sin was [Col. 0632A] unforgivable, since the Apostle says that he found no place for repentance. Did he not repent? Indeed, he wept. How then is it true that he found no place for repentance?

Solution. He found no place for repentance, that is, for pardon and for the place of blessing through repentance—not because he did not repent, but because he did not repent as he ought. For those tears arose more from indignation against his brother and pain at the honor he had lost than from humility and true repentance.

### QUESTION CIX

“Jesus, mediator of the New Testament, and the sprinkled blood speaking better things than Abel.” It is asked in what respect Christ’s blood speaks better than Abel’s blood.

Solution. The gloss says: better because this blood, Christ’s, sought pardon [Col. 0632B], while that sought vengeance; this sought salvation, that condemnation. But someone may say: Did not the shedders of Christ’s blood perish, just as the shedders of Abel’s blood? Therefore Christ’s blood speaks vengeance, just as Abel’s blood does. How then does this speak better than that?

Solution. Christ’s blood not only cries for vengeance against those who despise it; it also speaks pardon to all, even persecutors, if they themselves are willing to repent. But Abel’s blood speaks only vengeance and pardon to no one. Or Christ’s blood speaks better than Abel’s—that is, makes us speak better: namely, that Jesus is the Son of God, by whom we have been redeemed—than Abel’s blood, which makes us say that Abel was a righteous man sacrificed as a figure of Christ. Note that Abel, who was the first to be killed unjustly, is set in place of all [Col. 0632C] others whose blood could procure no pardon.

### QUESTION CX

“Through this indeed they pleased God,” etc. It is asked whether Abraham and Lot knew that they were angels. If they knew, how did they render services of hospitality which are unnecessary except for human weakness? Again, if they did not know that they were angels but thought them merely human, how did they honor them as more than human?

Solution. At first they considered them human beings divinely sent, and persons in whom God was present; afterward they learned that they were angels.

### QUESTION CXI

It is also asked how angels could eat in bodies they had assumed. For they did not have those bodies united to themselves as human souls have bodies united to them [Col. 0632D]; hence those bodies were neither alive nor capable of sensation, and the angels could not be injured in them.

Solution. The angels did not eat in the manner of animals; rather, as fire consumes and reduces to nothing what is placed upon it, so that food was consumed by their operation, or they made of it whatever they wished.

### QUESTION CXII

Again, it is asked how, when three angels were seen, Abraham could worship one of them in faith of the Trinity and unity.

Solution. By divine revelation he recognized in them the mystery of the Trinity and unity.

### QUESTION CXIII

“Of what animals,” etc. The expositor says that by a double allegory he proves [Col. 0633A] that Christ’s body is not to be eaten by those who serve the tabernacle. But since there is one meaning in both narratives, how does he prove this by a double allegory? What is allegory? Is it not a spiritual meaning? Therefore, where there is one meaning, how is there a double allegory?

Solution. He says “by a double allegory” [Col. 0634A], that is, by an allegory arising from a double narrative. Or “allegory” denotes both the signifying thing and the thing signified; here it is used for the signifying thing. What then is “by a double allegory” except “by a double narrative,” namely one of the Old Testament and the other of the New?

## APPENDIX: EXEGETICAL DOUBTS ON HOLY SCRIPTURE

[Col. 0633]

THIRTEEN BOOKS OF LATER EXCERPTS CONTAINING ALLEGORIES OF BOTH TESTAMENTS.  
(The books of earlier excerpts appear below in the appendix to the dogmatic works.) (G)*

## PROLOGUE

Whoever applies himself to divine wisdom or knowledge is better able to know the fruit of reading by personal experience than by another’s instruction. For in it the reader’s mind possesses the good of honorable occupation, finds the diligence of meditation, the constancy of prayer, and the brightness of heavenly contemplation. There it is formed according to the pattern of holy imitation; instructed for the exercise of virtue; strengthened for the performance of good work. In it, the paint of falsehood having been rejected and the malice of wickedness driven away, it is led to a true—or perfect—knowledge of truth and to love of goodness. In it the mind is encouraged not to be broken in adversity; strengthened not to be dissolved in prosperity; and it takes remembrance from the past and caution for the future.

But whoever refuses to be nourished by the food of sacred Scripture already begins to lose the life of his soul, so that it may be said of him: “His soul abhorred every kind of food, and he drew near even to the gates of death” (Psalm 106). Receive, therefore, dearest brother, this second part of our excerpts which you requested, as a dish prepared for your soul, so that through it you may spiritually grow stout, become rich, and be enlarged. As in the preceding part, I have arranged for you in order, before the beginning of the book, the chapters of this part, for the clearer understanding of the whole work that follows.

## SECOND PROLOGUE

In the preceding work, after first setting forth an account of the origin and classification of the arts and of certain other matters, we arranged the rise, course, and fall of all kingdoms from the beginning down to our own time. In what follows, we shall elucidate the profound obscurities of allegories according to the course of the underlying narrative: first from the Old Testament, then from the New, insofar as seems sufficient for the present brevity. In this part of the little book you will find many things, according to the weakness of my understanding, necessary for your beginning, and in every way useful both for knowledge of truth and for love of virtue—provided, however, that you do not neglect to read what is written and commit it to memory.

The first book of the *Allegories of the Old Testament* treats the mysteries of events from the beginning of the world to Abraham, and contains eighteen chapters. [Col. 0635] The second treats the mysteries of events from Abraham to Moses, and contains nineteen chapters. The third treats the mysteries of events from Moses to Joshua, and contains twenty-two chapters. The fourth treats the mysteries of events from Joshua to Elkanah, Samuel’s father, and contains eighteen chapters. The fifth treats the mysteries of events from Elkanah to David, at the point where it is written: “The Lord has torn your kingdom from you today and has given it to one better than you,” and contains nineteen chapters. The sixth treats the mysteries of events from David to Solomon, and contains twenty-five chapters. The seventh treats the mysteries of events from Solomon to the Babylonian captivity, and contains forty-three chapters. The eighth treats the mysteries of events contained in Ezra, and contains sixteen chapters. The ninth treats the mysteries contained in the books of Esther, Tobit, Judith, and Maccabees, and contains four chapters.

# ALLEGORIES ON THE OLD TESTAMENT

## BOOK ONE: ON THE BOOK OF GENESIS—FROM THE BEGINNING OF THE WORLD TO ABRAHAM

[Col. 0635]

### CHAPTER I—On the Significance of Heaven and Earth

[Col. 0635A]

> [Note: [Col. 0635B] Note that there is found a certain *Summa* called Master Richard’s *Allegorical Summa of the Bible*, in which sayings of our Hugh are gathered far too briefly; [Col. 0636B] therefore, leaving it aside, attentive reader, devote yourself carefully to this most extensive garden of all allegories, and perhaps you will not regret so great a work.]

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth.” Heaven signifies things highest; earth, things lowest. Heaven signifies invisible things; earth, visible things. Heaven signifies angels; earth, human beings. Heaven signifies spiritual things; earth, bodily things. Heaven signifies angels by elevation of position and excellence of condition: by elevation of position, because it surpasses all visible and material creatures in height; by excellence of condition, because it precedes other things by its firmness and a certain permanence. Thus the angelic nature of heavenly spirits surpasses and outshines all creatures both by the dwelling-place of the heavenly homeland and by the dignity of its own condition.

Earth signifies the human being both by its position and by the lesser dignity of its condition: by position, because it is lower than heaven; by lesser dignity of condition, because it is more corruptible [Col. 0635B] than heaven. Thus human beings, in comparison with angels, are lower both in dwelling-place and in the condition of their bodily nature.

According to the foregoing interpretation, heaven also signifies prelates, the perfect, and contemplatives; earth signifies subjects, the imperfect, and the active. For prelates, the perfect, and contemplatives are superior to subjects, the imperfect, and the active, whether by the authority of office, difference of rank, or merit of virtue. Subjects, however, the imperfect, and the active are inferior to prelates, the perfect, and contemplatives.

Heaven, therefore: angels; earth: human beings. Heaven: prelates; earth: subjects. Heaven: the perfect; earth: the imperfect. Heaven: contemplatives; earth: the active.

### CHAPTER II—On Heaven, Earth, and the Works of the Six Days

[Col. 0636A]

“In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Genesis 1). Heaven is spirit; earth, body. For as heaven is higher and firmer than earth, so spirit is more excellent and more worthy than body. The world in its first confusion is the human being in his wickedness. For as light and the future order had not yet entered the primordial confused world, so in the person subject to wickedness neither does light shine through knowledge of truth nor does order exist through the arrangement of justice.

And God, as though in the midst of confusion, creates the primal light when he illumines the sinner, confused by diverse crimes, with the rays of inward light, so that the sinner may recognize what he ought to be and order himself toward the knowledge of right living. Thus the primal light signifies knowledge of sin.

The firmament [Col. 0636B] between the upper and lower waters signifies discernment between virtues and vices. The lower waters signify vices; the upper waters, virtues. And, as it were, a firmament is placed between both waters when, through the virtue of discernment, virtues are separated from vices and vices from virtues.

Then follows: “The gathering of the waters that were under the firmament.” The gathering of waters expresses the restraint of vices. For since vices cannot be wholly emptied out or eliminated from the inward recesses of human nature in this present life, on account of the impulses toward them originally implanted in us, they must be restricted and restrained as far as is possible through divine grace, and gathered into one, lest they flow everywhere, occupy and corrupt [Col. 0637A] the whole person, and hinder our senses from the inquiry into truth, our affections from the practice of virtue, and our limbs from the performance of good work.

For just as earth occupied by water could not sprout, so we, occupied by vices, are unable either to seek truth with our senses, practise virtues with our affections, or perform good works with our limbs. Therefore, when the waters are gathered into one, the air grows warm and the earth sprouts: because, when vices are restrained, a human being is warmed through recognition, shines through love, and the flesh bears fruit through good action.

The creation of the lights signifies perfect illumination through the contemplation of truth, once the clouded blindness of ignorance has been set aside. The sun may signify knowledge of those things that pertain to the divine nature; the moon, knowledge of those things [Col. 0637B] that pertain to the holy Church; and the stars, knowledge of those things that pertain to each faithful soul. Fish, which labor in the depths—that is, in the waters—signify the diligence of good action, which is tossed by the waves of this transitory life. Birds, which fly to the heights, signify contemplation of heavenly things, through which we are lifted from low things to higher ones. Animals signify the senses of our body, because they share in human senses. For animals are, as it were, created in us when the bodily sense previously corrupted through vanity is restored through divine grace.

Accordingly, when these things have been set in order, lastly man is made in the image and likeness of God: when, in this way, the virtues and good works have been arranged within us, he becomes conformed and similar to God through righteousness, [Col. 0637C] whereas formerly he was unformed and dissimilar through sin. Finally, when man has been formed, he is transferred into the paradise of delight, because the sinner, regenerated by grace in the world, is transferred into heaven by glory.

Therefore: heaven, the spirit; earth, the body; the creation of the primal light, knowledge of sin. The firmament between the upper and lower waters, discrimination between vices and virtues. The gathering of the lower waters, the restraining of vices. The bringing forth of plants, the performance of good works. The creation of the lights, perfect knowledge of truth. Fish, good action. Birds, contemplation. The creation of animals, the restoration of bodily senses. The formation of Adam, the perfection of the righteous person. Adam [Col. 0637D] in paradise, the righteous person in heaven. The primal light before the sun signifies the law before grace, John before Christ, beginning before perfection, grace before glory. For just as the primal light preceded the sun in time and yet was less in brightness, so the law is recognized as prior to grace, John to Christ, beginning to perfection, and grace to glory in order, yet far inferior in perfection. But in other orders of things it is found that some things precede and others follow: lesser things precede; greater things succeed.

## CHAPTER III.—On the upper and lower waters

The upper waters signify the good who are to be saved; the lower waters, the evil who are to be damned. Of the upper waters it is said: “Bless the Lord, waters that are above the heavens” (Dan. III), because the elect will [Col. 0638A] never cease eternally to praise the Lord’s name. Of the lower waters it is written: “Let the waters be gathered into one place,” because the reprobate, now scattered throughout the whole world, will be gathered into hell, to be punished forever.

Yet who are these waters? The unclean, fornicators, concubine-keepers, incestuous persons, adulterers, the avaricious, thieves, plunderers, drunkards, perjurers, murderers, envious persons, the wrathful, those stirred by hatred (I Cor. V), those who look upon a woman in order to lust after her, and those who say to their brother, “You fool” (Matt. V); and all who are separated from God and not justified through His grace, such as pagans, Jews, and false Christians. These will be gathered into one place, that is, into hell, which is a place in darkness where the fire is not extinguished.

## CHAPTER IV.—On the sun, moon, and stars

[Col. 0638B]

Holy teachers commonly understand Christ by the sun, the Church by the moon, and each of the faithful by the individual stars. Christ is understood by the sun because, just as the sun is perfect in itself and does not change, so Christ, because He is infinite, cannot be increased. The Church is signified by the moon because, just as the moon is brought to fullness through prolonged increase, so the body of the holy Church is brought to completion as its members, succeeding to it through grace, are added. And just as the moon receives light from the sun, so the holy Church receives life-giving power from Christ. The faithful are signified by the stars because they too are lights fixed in heaven. Thus Paul said of himself and the lights like himself: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. III). [Col. 0638C] And again: “You shine in the Church as lights in the world” (Phil. II). Therefore, the sun is Christ; the moon, the Church; the stars, the faithful.

## CHAPTER V.—On fish and birds

Fish signify the evil, because they remain in the place where they were created. Birds signify the good, because they rise to a higher dwelling-place. Thus the evil remain in the sin in which they were born, while the good ascend through grace to the glory for which they were reborn. The evil have the wings of sins; the good, the wings of virtues. The good sing divine praises in modulated voices; the evil—“in whose mouth there is no comely praise” (Ecclus. XV)—are silent.

## CHAPTER VI.—On the paradise of delight

The paradise of delight signifies the Church, in which [Col. 0638D] there are diverse delights and joys: some through the abundance of graces, some through the fragrance of virtues, some through the manifold diversity of good works, some in contemplation of the heavenly homeland, some in the melody of divine praise, some in the sweetness alike of divine and eternal recompense, and some in hope of future blessedness.

The fountain in paradise signifies Christ. For “the fountain of wisdom” is the divine Word, that is, the Son of God. Whoever finds this fountain of paradise—that is, the Word and wisdom of God—finds life and draws salvation from the Lord. The four rivers issuing from the fountain are the four Gospels of Christ, by which the garden of the holy Church is watered and made fruitful, so that it may grow and bear fruit. They fittingly traverse diverse lands, [Col. 0639A] because they gather into the unity of faith diverse peoples formerly intent on earthly things.

The tree of life likewise signifies Christ. For He Himself says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV). For if we feed upon Him, we shall have eternal life, as He Himself says: “He who eats my flesh” (John VI), etc. Therefore Christ is the tree; Christ is the fountain: the tree, because He satisfies us with the fruit of life; the fountain, because He gives us to drink the saving water of wisdom. But the tree of the knowledge of good and evil expresses God’s commandment. It is rightly called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, because if we keep it, we experience good, and if we transgress it, evil.

Therefore paradise is the Church; delight, grace; the fountain, Christ; the four rivers, the four Gospels. The tree of life also is Christ; but the tree of the knowledge of good and evil is knowledge [Col. 0639B] of the commandment; eating of that forbidden tree is transgression of the commandment.

## CHAPTER VII.—On the formation of the first man

The earth from which the first man was made signifies the Virgin from whom the second man was born. Virgin earth: the Virgin Mary. Just as the human body was made from earth by divine operation, so the Word is believed to have been incarnate from the Virgin by divine operation. The body of Adam, taken from earth, was without stain; and Christ’s body, animated from Mary, was immaculate.

Adam was made on the sixth day of the world; Christ was born in the sixth age, and suffered at the sixth hour of the day, on the sixth day of the week. Adam fell asleep so that Eve might be made from his side; Christ was put to sleep in death so that the Church might be redeemed by His blood. Adam was bridegroom, and Eve, made from [Col. 0639C] him, bride; Christ is bridegroom, and the Church, redeemed by Him, bride. Adam ought to preside over and govern Eve; Christ presides over and governs the Church. Therefore earth is Mary; the sixth day of the week, the sixth age, or the sixth day, or the sixth hour. Adam is Christ; Adam’s sleep, Christ’s Passion; Eve’s creation, the Church’s redemption. Moreover, in the likeness of Adam and Eve, Christ and the Church, God is the bridegroom of every faithful soul.

## CHAPTER VIII.—On Adam, Eve, and the serpent

Adam signifies the spirit; Eve, the flesh. For just as Adam rules Eve, so the spirit ought to rule its flesh. And just as Adam ought to have begotten children through Eve, so the spirit ought to bring forth good works through the flesh. The serpent signifies the devil; the apple, delight in earthly things. [Col. 0639D] For just as the serpent deceived Eve by an apple, so the devil enticed and seduced the unreasoning flesh by earthly delight. And just as Eve led Adam to eat the apple, so the flesh sometimes draws the spirit into the practice of sin; and so each is cast out of paradise, that is, from the state of its good: for the soul is both afflicted by an evil conscience and punished by penalty. Therefore Adam is the spirit; Eve, the flesh; the serpent, the devil; the apple, delight in earthly things; expulsion from paradise, the affliction of spirit and flesh.

## CHAPTER IX.—On the six days of divine work, and the seventh of rest

The six days signify the labor of good works; the seventh expresses the rest of eternal blessedness. For God completed His work in six days, and on the seventh day rested from all work. So too, in the present age we ought to labor in the performance of good works, so that in the future we may rest in the Sabbath of recompense. We have discoursed mystically on the work of creation, so that we may rest from the work which we have accomplished.

## CHAPTER X.—On Adam, Eve, and their sons

After Adam and Eve were cast out of paradise through the sin of disobedience, Adam knew his wife, namely Eve, and begot Cain; then he begot Abel, whom Cain killed. After this, Cain became a wanderer and fugitive upon the earth.

[Col. 0640A]

Adam, the parent of the human race, signifies God, who is Father of all visible and invisible things by nature, and Father of all the elect by grace: Father of the former because their Creator; of the latter because their Redeemer. [Col. 0640B] Eve signifies the Synagogue, to whom God had betrothed Himself. From her He in some sense begot Cain and possessed him as a son—that is, the ancient people—of whom He Himself says: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. IV). He also begot the innocent and righteous Abel, that is, our Lord Jesus Christ. Abel was righteous and innocent; Christ “committed no sin, nor was deceit found in His mouth” (I Pet. II). Abel was the first righteous person in temporal order; Christ the first righteous person in excellence of holiness. Abel offered God the flesh of a sheep; Christ offered His own immaculate flesh. God looked upon the sacrifice of righteous Abel, and likewise looked upon Christ’s Passion, which He undertook for the redemption of the whole human race.

Abel signifies Christ; [Col. 0640C] Cain, the Jewish people. Cain killed Abel, and the Jewish people fastened Christ to the cross. Cain became a wanderer and fugitive after fratricide; and after Christ’s Passion, the Jewish people were scattered throughout the world from their brother according to the flesh. Therefore Adam is God; Eve, the Synagogue; Cain, the Jewish people; Abel, Christ; the death of righteous Abel, Christ’s Passion; Cain’s expulsion from the Lord’s presence, the dispersal of the Jewish people. In likeness of Cain the persecutor and Abel the sufferer, the flesh persecutes the spirit, the impious persecute the righteous, vice persecutes virtue, malice persecutes kindness, and evils persecute goods.

## CHAPTER XI.—On Seth, Cain, and their sons

Those who were of Seth’s stock were called sons [Col. 0640D] of God; those of Cain’s stock, sons of men. Seth signifies Christ; Cain, the devil; Seth’s sons signify the elect; Cain’s sons, the reprobate. The elect are regenerated through grace, and the reprobate are rejected through sin.

The generations of the sons of God end in a man; because, by reason of his strength, he signifies virtues, since the life of the elect is perfected in the strength of virtues. The generation of the sons of men ends in a woman, who signifies softness, because the life of the reprobate ends in the softness of vices. The sons of God took the daughters of men. For often those reborn through baptism, and who seemed elect, join themselves to the delights and vices of the reprobate. From this union giants were born upon the earth; and the evil are defiled through lust and raised up through pride. Therefore Seth is Christ; [Col. 0641A] Cain, the devil; Seth’s sons, the elect; Cain’s sons, the reprobate; the daughters of men, carnal delights; the marital union, the dishonorable use of the world; the giants of the earth, the pride of life.

## CHAPTER XII.—On Enos, Enoch, and Noah

Enos, third from Adam, who began to call upon the Lord’s name, signifies those who are perfect in faith in the Holy Trinity. Enoch, seventh from Adam, who pleased God, signifies those sanctified by the gifts of spiritual grace. Noah, tenth from Adam, who found grace before God, expresses those who fulfill the Decalogue of the law through good action.

## CHAPTER XIII.—On the ark and the flood

All flesh had corrupted its way through unlawful marriage; and Noah found grace before the Lord. [Col. 0641B] And the Lord said to Noah: “Make yourself an ark of smoothed timbers, and you shall enter it, you and your sons, your wife and your sons’ wives with you; and you shall bring into the ark seven each of every clean living creature, but two each of the unclean. And I shall bring the waters of the flood, and destroy man and all things which I made for man, in which is the breath of life” (Gen. VI), etc.

Corruption of life signifies the commission of sin. The inundation of the flood signifies the disturbance, instability, fluctuation, and persecution of the present age. Noah signifies Christ, or any prelate, who insofar as he can makes the ark—that is, builds the Church—so that he himself and his sons, that is, his subjects, may be saved in it. The individual timbers are individual souls. They are fittingly smoothed when, through preaching, the bark and enormity of vices [Col. 0641C] and sins are cut away from them. And they are joined together when, through grace, they are united into the unity of faith, as though from diverse forests—that is, from diverse peoples and languages.

The ark is also said to have been coated with pitch. Pitch signifies charity. The holy Church is coated with this pitch inwardly when charity is preserved in the affections of hearts, and outwardly when it is shown in the performance of works. The compartments in the ark and its three stories signify diverse teachers and the diverse merits of those who live well. Its being said to be three-chambered signifies three orders in the holy Church: married persons, the continent, and virgins, who receive dwellings according to the difference of their names and works. Its being said to be two-chambered signifies the active and the contemplative, of whom the active are below and the contemplative [Col. 0641D] above.

The length of three hundred cubits signifies the three periods through which the present age runs—namely, the time before the law, under the law, and under grace—and perfect knowledge of the Holy Trinity. The breadth of fifty cubits, through the five bodily senses, intimates the performance of good works toward one’s neighbor. The height of thirty cubits signifies the loftiness of the three principal virtues: faith, hope, and charity.

The fact that creatures from every kind were brought into the ark signifies that people from every nation are led into the holy Church. Clean animals, brought in seven at a time, signify the good, who are justified through sevenfold grace. [Col. 0642A] Unclean animals, brought in two at a time, signify the reprobate, who through sin are divided from God and from themselves. For the number two, which first departs from unity and divides itself, is a sign of division. The animals below also signify the active; the birds above, the contemplative. Females signify the weak; males, the strong. Food signifies sacred Scripture, the spiritual food of souls. The door below signifies good action, through which we enter into the unity of the holy Church. The windows above signify contemplation, through which we behold or observe heavenly things. The mountains covered by water are holy prelates, whom persecution sometimes overwhelms. The cubit in which the ark was completed is Christ, who is the head [Col. 0642B] of the Church.

The ark was broad below because many are called; narrow above because few are elect. Broad below because there are many subjects; narrow above because very few are prelates. Broad below because there are many active persons; narrow above because there are few contemplatives. Broad below because there are many imperfect persons; narrow above because there are few perfect persons. The number of forty days during which the waters flooded, consisting of four times ten, signifies the present life, in which we are continually shaken by the waves of temptations and persecutions; yet we must fulfill both the Decalogue and the four Gospels. The mountains of Armenia signify the sublimity of eternal life. The ark rested upon the mountains of Armenia, and the holy Church will rest in the sublimity of eternal life.

[Col. 0642C] Therefore corruption of life is the commission of sin; the ark, the Church; Noah, prelates; Noah’s family, their subjects; the inundation of the flood, the temptations and persecutions of the age; individual timbers, individual souls; smoothing of the timbers, justification of souls; inward coating, charity in the affections of hearts; outward coating, charity in the performance of works; the compartments and three stories of the ark, diverse teachers and the diverse merits of those who live well; the twofold chambering, good action and contemplation; the threefold chambering, marriage, continence, virginity; the ark’s length, the three periods and perfect knowledge of the Holy Trinity; its breadth, the effect of good work toward one’s neighbor; its height, the excellence of the three principal virtues—faith, hope, and charity; animals, active persons; birds, contemplatives; food, [Col. 0642D] Scripture; the forty days, present life; the mountains of Armenia, the sublimity of eternal life; the withdrawal or drying up of the waters, the removal of temptations and persecutions.

## CHAPTER XIV.—A moral interpretation of the ark

The ark is the soul. We ought to be saved in the ark, returning to it and entering into it, as it is written: “Return to the heart, you transgressors” (Isa. XLVI). Its length is faith, by which it believes all things to be true that God has done from the beginning of the world, or will do until the end of the world, through Himself, through angels, and through human beings. Its height is hope, by which it is raised toward the goods to be hoped for, which will follow in heaven. Its breadth is charity, by which it extends toward the northern quarter through love of enemies, and toward the southern quarter through love of friends.

In this ark [Col. 0643A] is Noah: rational understanding and spiritual perception, desiring good wills. The animals are deeds carried out in earthly matters; the birds, thoughts; the flooding of waters, the onset of temptations; the mountains of Armenia, the height of divine contemplation.

## CHAPTER XV.—On the raven and the dove

The raven, sent out from the ark and not returning, signifies false Christians who, when they are sometimes sent outward on account of necessity, remain outside. For, clinging to visible things, they never return to inward rest, while outside they take delight in the fluctuation of temporal things. But the dove, which returned, signifies the good, who, when they go out for the necessities of their neighbors, return, since they find no rest outside; and they bring [Col. 0643B] an olive branch because they have performed a work of mercy.

## CHAPTER XVI.—On the colors of the rainbow

The rainbow, that is, the heavenly bow, has two colors. The first color is green; the second, red. Green signifies the judgment God made at the beginning through the water of the flood. Red signifies the judgment God will make through fire at the end of the world. For water is green and fire is red.

## CHAPTER XVII.—On Noah’s vineyard and his drunkenness

Noah planted a vineyard, became drunk, and was uncovered. When Ham saw this, he mocked; but Shem and Japheth covered their father. Therefore Ham deserved his father’s curse, while Shem and Japheth deserved blessing for themselves.

[Col. 0643C] Noah, who was tenth from Adam, signifies Christ, who fulfilled the Decalogue of the law, of whom it is written: “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. V). Noah indeed is interpreted “rest.” And Christ is our rest in the present through grace, in the future through glory. His vineyard was the Israelite people, as it is written: “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel.” When it ought to have borne grapes, it bore wild grapes and turned to bitterness (Isa. V). The vineyard released Barabbas and made its planter and cultivator, Christ, drunk with the wine of His Passion. He fell asleep in the sleep of death, and His vileness—that is, the mortality He had assumed from us and for us—was openly displayed.

Unhappy Ham, that is, the unbelieving Jewish people, mocked Him, saying: “He saved others; [Col. 0643D] Himself He cannot save. If He is the king of Israel, let Him now come down from the cross, and we will believe Him” (Matt. XXVII). But Shem—that is, the apostles and other disciples, and all from among the Jews who believed in Him—and Japheth, [Col. 0644A] that is, the Gentile people converted to faith, covered the father’s shameful parts with a cloak, because they showed Christ’s Passion to have been not a defect but the effect of all power and the true sacrament of human redemption. Hence Canaan, Ham’s son, is punished by a curse, because the Jewish offspring is condemned by the Jews’ curse. And Shem and Japheth, that is, the people converted from each nation, are enriched with everlasting blessing. And Canaan, Ham’s son, becomes a servant of servants, because the unbelieving successors of the Jews are servants of Christians, because Christians are servants of Christ, for whom to serve is to reign.

Therefore Noah is Christ; the vineyard, the Jewish people; drunkenness, the Passion; the sleep of death, nakedness; nakedness, the manifestation of true humility; Ham’s mockery, the disparagement by the Jews; Shem and Japheth, the two believing [Col. 0644B] peoples; the garment, the sacrament; the curse of Canaan, Ham’s son, the condemnation and dispersal of the Jewish nation.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—A moral interpretation of the same

Noah signifies prelates, who, when they preside well, are fathers, as it were, of as many sons as they are rulers of rulers. They plant a vineyard when they build the Church. They become drunk from its wine when, human weakness assailing them, they take at least a little glory in the success of virtues and the prosperity of their governance. Their shameful parts are uncovered when thoughts of human self-glorification, once conceived, are made known either through some boastfulness, through empty joy, or through some excess in human conduct.

[Col. 0644C] But Ham mocks their shameful parts, because all the reprobate, when they observe in any prelates failings arising from the weakness of their condition, do not cease to tear them apart and ridicule them with wicked speech. But Shem—that is, good contemplatives, in whose tents God dwells through inward rest—and Japheth—that is, good active persons, whom God enlarges through good action—strive to overlook and excuse the weaknesses of prelates, and thus, as it were, cover their father’s shameful parts with a cloak. Ham is cursed when the deeds of wicked subjects are consigned to the service of demons, who are servants of the devil. But blessing is granted to Shem and Japheth because the good are rewarded with the first blessing.

Therefore Noah is prelates; his sons, their subjects; Ham, the reprobate; Shem and Japheth, the elect contemplatives and active persons; the vineyard, [Col. 0644D] the Church; drunkenness, self-glorification; nakedness, disclosure of thought; mockery, disparagement; covering, excuse.

# BOOK TWO. ON THE REMAINING MYSTERIES OF GENESIS, FROM ABRAHAM TO MOSES

[Col. 0643]

## CHAPTER I.—On Abraham’s departure from his land

[Col. 0643D]

“Go out from your land and from your kindred, and come into the land that I shall show you; and I shall give it to you, [Col. 0644D] and to your seed.” Abram, whose name means “exalted father,” and who was afterwards called Abraham, that is, “father of many nations,” signifies Christ. [Col. 0645A] He is the exalted Father because He is the King of glory. His land is Judaea, and His kindred is the carnal Israelite people from whom He took flesh. The house of His father is the synagogue or the Temple.

He went out from all these things when He left Judaea, the Israelite people, and the Temple; and through the preaching of the apostles came into the breadth of the nations. There He pitched the tent, namely the holy Church, and built an altar through the faith of those who had gone before; and upon it He offers to the Father a sacrifice, the good action of His faithful people. There He is enlarged toward east and west, north and south, as it is written: “I shall call your seed from the east and from the west, and I shall say to the north, ‘Give,’ and to the south, ‘Do not hinder’” (Isa. XLIII). For Christ’s possession is in all parts of the world, because Christ’s faith is among [Col. 0645B] all nations.

Therefore Abraham is Christ; his land, Judaea; his kindred, the people of Israel; his father’s house, the Temple, from which He came; the tent, the Church; the altar, faith; the sacrifice, Christ’s good work; the enlargement, possession of the whole world.

## CHAPTER II.—Moral exposition of the same

“Go out from your land and from your kindred” (Gen. XII). Abram is any faithful soul, placed in Ur of the Chaldeans, that is, in the fire of vices. Its father is the devil, as is written of it and of other evil persons: “You are of your father, the devil” (John VIII). Its land is earthly delight, to which it clings. Its kindred is the demons, to whom through sin it is known to be related as if by blood. [Col. 0645C] Its father’s house is the wicked manner of life in which it first long remained under its father the devil.

The land to which it is invited is the spiritual life, to which the soul, pierced by the divine word, passes when it turns away from evil and does good. It pitches a tent there through honorable conduct; builds there a stone altar through firm faith; offers sacrifice through good conduct; and is enlarged on every side through the manifold exercise of virtues and performance of good works. Therefore Abram is the soul; its land, earthly delight; its father’s house, wicked conduct; its parents, demons. The land to which it comes is spiritual life; the tent, honorable conduct; the altar, firm faith; its sacrifice, good action; its enlargement, [Col. 0645D] exercise of virtues and performance of good works.

## CHAPTER III.—On Abraham’s sacrifice

Again the Lord said to Abraham: “Take a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old ram, a three-year-old she-goat, also a turtledove and a dove.” Taking all these animals, he divided them, but did not divide the birds (Gen. XV). The promised measure was set for Abraham’s seed, and this is its figure. By the heifer was figured the Jewish people, placed under the yoke of the law; by the goat, the same people as destined to sin; by the ram, the same people as destined to reign. These animals are called three years old because, through the courses of time from Adam to Noah, and thence to David, that people grew to maturity as though passing through a third age. [Col. 0646A]

By the turtledove and the dove are signified spiritual peoples in the Church: indivisible children of promise and heirs of the future kingdom. Their temporal age is not mentioned because, meditating upon eternal things, they have passed beyond temporal desires. But what does it mean that those three-year-old animals are divided, with their parts set opposite one another, except that carnal persons, even within the old people, are divided among themselves? The birds, however, are not divided because spiritual persons are undivided: they do not contemplate schism and are not seduced by heretics, but peace is within them, whether they withdraw from others like the turtledove or dwell among them like the dove.

## CHAPTER IV.—Moral exposition of the same

According to the tropological sense, Abraham is [Col. 0646B] any faithful soul that offers God a sacrifice, namely the fruit of righteousness. The animals are good works conducted in earthly affairs. It offers birds, namely contemplative thoughts, which fly upward through heavenly desires. The animals are separated because good works rendered to neighbors in earthly matters are divided among many affairs. But the birds are not divided at all, because contemplative thoughts are raised toward the sole intention of the vision above. The birds that lie in wait for the sacrifice are demons or unclean thoughts, which we ought to cast away by persistent prayer and the caution of discernment.

## CHAPTER V.—On the threefold circumcision

There are three circumcisions. One is merely outward in the flesh, and is a sacrament (Gen. XVII). The other [Col. 0646C] two are the reality and virtue of the sacrament. One occurs in the present, when the soul is circumcised through the putting away of iniquity; the other will occur in the future, when the body is circumcised through the putting away of corruption. Thus the first is in the flesh, the second in the mind, the third in the body.

In sacred Scripture, the number eight sometimes signifies the time of resurrection that follows the present life; at other times, the time of grace, in which eternal goods are promised to those serving God, as though after the Sabbath of the law. Rightly, then, was that first circumcision, which is the sacrament of the other two, commanded to be performed on the eighth day, so that it might be shown that in the time of grace hearts were to be circumcised through the correction of iniquity, and in [Col. 0646D] the time of resurrection bodies indeed through the putting away of iniquity and corruption.

## CHAPTER VI.—On Lot’s departure from Sodom

Lot was told that, leaving Sodom, he should ascend the mountain so as to be saved; but he asked for Zoar (Gen. XIX), and it was granted him. Yet he did not dare to remain in Zoar, but ascended the mountain. Sodom signifies the luxury of the present life. Lot signifies the soul predestined to eternal life. The angels are preachers, who announce salvation to it, saying: “Turn away from evil and do good” (Ps. XXXVI). They say, as it were: Leave Sodom and ascend the mountain; abandon worldly life and ascend to spiritual life; abandon luxury and take up continence.

But Lot, fearing to climb the heights, asks for Zoar, [Col. 0647A] because the faithful person, not presuming to ascend to the summit of spiritual life and continence, judges the married life to be loved, believing that in it he can save his soul. But at last he leaves Zoar and ascends the mountain, because the righteous person sometimes, seeing the fall, labor, and danger of married life, sets married life aside and ascends to the height of spiritual life and continence.

Lot’s wife, who looked back and perished, likewise signifies carnal persons who, although they sometimes leave their sins as to the act, nevertheless immediately return to the same sins in mind and will. And because they put their hand to the plough and look back, they are not fit for the kingdom of God (Luke IX). Therefore Lot is understood as the faithful soul; Sodom, worldly life; Zoar, married life; [Col. 0647B] the mountain, spiritual life; Lot’s wife, carnal persons who are in the Church.

## CHAPTER VII.—On God’s testing of Abraham

God tested Abraham, saying: “Take your only son, whom you love, Isaac, and go into the land of vision, and there offer him as a burnt offering on one of the mountains” (Gen. XXII), etc. Abraham signifies God the Father, and Isaac, Christ. The mountain on which he was to be sacrificed expresses the height of the Lord’s charity. The two young men waiting with the ass signify the unbelieving Gentiles and Jews who consented to the Lord’s death. The ass signifies the folly of both. For it is foolish to await one who is to come when it is proved by the testimonies of many prophets and the innumerable wonders of miracles that He has already come.

[Col. 0647C] The altar signifies the wood; the thorns signify the Lord’s cross. Isaac, who did not taste death in the sacrifice, expresses the divinity, which felt neither punishments nor pain in the Passion. The ram, which underwent death, signifies the humanity, which endured the bitterness of the Passion. The fire signifies the anguish of the Lord’s Passion, by which that immaculate Lamb was roasted, and God the Father was appeased concerning the transgression of the first parent and of the whole human race. Therefore Abraham is God the Father; Isaac, Christ; the mountain, divine charity; the two young men, unbelieving Jews and Gentiles; the ass, the folly of both in unbelief; the altar, the wood; the thorns, the destruction of the cross; Isaac, divinity; the ram, humanity; fire, the anguish of the Passion.

## CHAPTER VIII.—On Sarah, her death, and burial

[Col. 0647D] Sarah, whose name means “princess,” signifies the soul which presides over the people of its spiritual senses, virtues, pleasures, thoughts, affections, words, and actions, and over which it presides by governing itself well. Sarah’s death signifies the mortification of the soul and of worldly concupiscence. The cave in which she is buried signifies the spiritual life, which is hidden and is rightly called twofold because of good action and contemplation. Therefore Sarah is the soul; Sarah’s death, the mortification of the soul; the cave, spiritual life.

## CHAPTER IX.—How Rebecca was brought to Isaac
Sarah having died, Abraham sent his servant for [Col. 0648A] Rebecca, Isaac’s wife; and Abraham’s servant brought her upon a camel, and Isaac took her as his wife, etc. (Gen. XXIV). Abraham signifies God the Father, who is the father of many nations because he is the father of all by creation. Sarah signifies the Synagogue, to whom the Lord had betrothed himself in the Old Testament. Isaac, whose name means “laughter,” signifies Christ, who is our joy. Abraham’s servant represents the apostles, purified from original and actual sin by grace. Rebecca, brought from among the Gentiles by the servant, is the Church of the Gentiles, converted through the preaching of the apostles. The well from which Rebecca drew water is philosophical eloquence, from which the Gentile world at that time attempted to quench its thirst. The ornaments which the servant gave Rebecca signify the virtues [Col. 0648B] bestowed upon the Church through the preaching of the apostles. The camel’s hump, on seeing which Rebecca descended, represents the former enormity of sins and the pride of Gentilism, from which the holy Church, having recognized Christ’s majesty, humbled herself. The cloak with which she covered herself signifies the good work by which, after receiving faith, the holy Church adorned herself before God, angels, and human beings. The field into which Isaac had gone signifies the world; and the evening of the day, the end of the age. Isaac’s marriage to Rebecca signifies the marriage of Christ and the Church. Isaac prayed for barren Rebecca, and Christ intercedes at the right hand of God the Father for the Church. God granted conception to Rebecca, and God grants fruitfulness to the Church. Jacob signifies the good, who receive blessing, in the present through [Col. 0648C] grace and in the future through glory. Esau signifies the wicked, who are excluded from blessing in the present through fault and in the future through punishment. Therefore Abraham is God the Father; Sarah, the Synagogue; Sarah’s death, the unbelief of the Synagogue; Isaac, Christ; the servant, the apostles; the well, philosophical learning; the ornaments, virtues; Rebecca’s being brought, the conversion of the Church; the camel’s hump, the enormity of sin; the descent, the Church’s humility; the cloak, good work; the field, the world; evening, the end of the age; Isaac’s and Rebecca’s marriage, the union of Christ and the Church; Jacob, the good; Esau, the wicked.

## CHAPTER X.—On Abraham, Isaac, Their Servants, and the Wells

Abraham and his servants dug wells, and the Philistines quarrelled [Col. 0648D] and filled the wells with earth. Then Isaac dug a well over which they did not quarrel, and called its name “Breadth” (*Rehoboth*) (Gen. XXVI). Abraham, as stated above, signifies God the Father; Abraham’s servants signify the books of the prophets. Water is knowledge, which washes and gives drink: it washes away fault and gives grace to drink. Isaac signifies Christ; Isaac’s servants are the evangelists and apostles. The Philistines are the Jews, who contend over the wells of the Scriptures and fill them with earth because of their carnal and earthly understanding. The well which Isaac dug last and called Breadth, and which the Philistines did not fill, is evangelical teaching, spread throughout the world, which the Jews cannot take away. Therefore Abraham [Col. 0649A] is God the Father; Isaac, the Son; Abraham’s servants, the prophets; Isaac’s servants, the apostles and evangelists; and the wells they dug, the books they wrote; the well called Breadth, the preaching of the Gospel.

## CHAPTER XI.—On Jacob’s Blessing

The story is well known: Jacob supplanted Esau in his father’s blessing (Gen. XXVII). Isaac signifies God, from whom blessing descends upon the head of the righteous.
