Rebecca signifies mother Grace, who instructed Jacob concerning his father’s blessing. Jacob, younger in age, remaining at home and obtaining the blessing, signifies the Gentile people, who came to divine knowledge after the Israelite people and inwardly nurtures, with mother Grace, vows that render praises [Col. 0649B] to God. He is blessed by God in the world through grace, in heaven through glory. Esau, older in age, serving in hunting outside and losing the blessing, signifies the people of Israel, who came to the knowledge of God, who seeks righteousness outwardly in the letter and relinquishes the blessing of the heavenly inheritance. The skins with which Rebecca covered her son represent confession of sins. The food is the virtues with which God is fed, while they are exercised by the Gentile people through cooperating grace. The garments are the good works of the Law with which grace mercifully clothes the Gentile people, while the Israelite people stands and wanders outside. Wine signifies joy in the Holy Spirit. We give the Lord this wine to drink when we rejoice in the Holy Spirit. Therefore Isaac is God; [Col. 0649C] Rebecca, grace; Esau, the Jewish people; Jacob, the Gentile people; Esau’s outward hunting, observance of carnal ordinances and an understanding of the carnal letter. The kids’ skins, confession of sins; food, the exercise of virtues; wine, joy in the Holy Spirit; garments, good works; the field blessed by the Lord, the holy Church, in which, as blessed Gregory testifies, the flower of the vine gives fragrance through preaching, the flower of the lily through chastity, the flower of the violet through humility, the flower of the ear of grain through the maturity of good works, the flower of the olive through mercy, and the flower of the rose through patience. Esau hated Jacob: the Jews hate the Christian people gathered from the Gentiles, seeing it rule over them.

## CHAPTER XII.—How Jacob Went to Laban

[Col. 0649D] Having obtained the blessing, Jacob went to Laban, his uncle. He fell asleep in a certain place, with a stone placed beneath his head; and he saw a ladder raised to heaven, God leaning upon the ladder, and angels ascending and descending. Then he came into a field to a well near Haran, where flocks were pastured and watered. Then, having lived with Laban, he took Leah and Rachel, Laban’s daughters, as wives; and by them and their maidservants he begot twelve patriarchs and became wealthy with Laban (Gen. XXVIII).

Jacob, according to the tropological sense, signifies the spirit; Esau, the human body. Jacob signifies the spirit because the spirit is gentle when, guided by reason, it seeks only necessities. Esau signifies the body because the body is hairy when, urged by desire, it seeks superfluities. [Col. 0650A] Concerning their conflict it is written: “The corruptible body weighs down the soul, and its earthly dwelling presses down the mind full of many thoughts” (Wisdom IX). And again: “The flesh desires against the spirit, and the spirit against the flesh” (Gal. V). But the spirit, having received the blessing of grace, flees the sword-edge of bodily desire, as the Apostle commands, saying: “Flee fornication” (I Cor. VI).

Laban, whose name means “whitening,” signifies the Lord, who is supreme purity and whom the spirit of the righteous, when it flees carnal allurements, desires to approach and cling to. That spirit indeed sleeps well on the journey when, in its spiritual progress, it rests from the noise of the present age. And while asleep it contemplates heavenly things, because, when it properly closes its eyes to outward matters, it [Col. 0650B] merits inwardly to behold wonders concerning invisible things. It places its head not upon the ground but upon a stone, because it makes the firm faith of Christ the foundation of its virtues and works.

The field to which Jacob came is Holy Scripture, in which diverse shepherds—that is, diverse teachers—feed diverse flocks, namely diverse believers. Here, therefore, married persons, continent persons, and virgins are fed. Some are fed through history, others through allegory, and others through tropology. All receive there the nourishment of food who derive from it teaching for right living. The well from which the flocks were watered signifies divine wisdom, from which believers drink. The stone by which the mouth of the well was covered represents the difficulty of understanding. All teachers labour in Scripture so that, when the [Col. 0650C] stone—that is, the difficulty of understanding—has been removed, they may provide believers with drink from true and hidden wisdom.

In this field God meets the righteous person, taking him into his service and assigning him his two daughters: Leah, whose name means “labouring,” that is, the active life; and Rachel, whose name means “the principle seen,” that is, the contemplative life. He also gives Rachel a maidservant, namely steadfast reason, to serve her; and likewise Leah a maidservant, namely incorrupt sense-perception. For reason serves contemplation, and sense-perception action. Jacob increased in children and livestock with Laban; and the righteous person, dwelling with God, is enriched in spiritual perceptions, affections, thoughts, words, and works.

Jacob secretly [Col. 0650D] departed from Laban with his possessions; and the righteous person, sometimes examining himself less cautiously, secretly attributes to himself the virtues bestowed by God. Laban pursued Jacob fleeing to the mountain; and God pursues the righteous person who departs from him through vain thoughts into self-exaltation. Laban maintained that whatever Jacob had belonged to his own goods; and God shows a human being that whatever good he has is from God’s gifts. Jacob, returning from Laban, feared that he would be killed by his brother; and the human faculty of understanding, descending to lower things because of the weakness of mortality, fears being tempted by the body’s defect. Jacob did not wish to have Esau as a companion in life or a neighbour in his homeland; and the human spirit, enriched with spiritual gifts, despises having the fervour of the flesh either as a companion in work or as a relative in pleasure. Therefore Jacob is [Col. 0651A] the spirit; Esau, the body; Laban, God; the field, Scripture; the well, wisdom; Leah, good action; Rachel, contemplation; Jacob’s enrichment in offspring and livestock, the righteous person’s increase in virtue and good works.

## CHAPTER XIII.—On the Rods Jacob Peeled

Jacob peeled rods and placed them before the sheep in the watering-troughs; and, seeing the variegated rods at conception, they bore variegated offspring (Gen. XXX). Jacob signifies holy preachers; the water, Scripture; and the troughs, books. For just as Jacob watered the flocks entrusted to him from the water and troughs, so preachers and teachers refresh the believers entrusted to them from the whole body of Scripture and its various books. Variegated rods signify diverse sayings. These [Col. 0651B] sayings are compared to rods because, by many grave threats concerning transgressions of God’s commandments, they chastise us. The sheep are believers because of their innocence. Sheep, by beholding varied rods, bear varied offspring when each believer, through hearing diverse sayings, produces diverse manifestations of works. Therefore Jacob is the preachers; the sheep, believers; water, Scripture; rods, sayings; the variegation of the rods, the various differences of sayings; the sheep’s offspring, the manifold result of works.

## CHAPTER XIV.—On Dinah, Jacob’s Daughter

Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, went out to see the women of that region; and Shechem corrupted her, violating the virgin by force (Gen. XXXIV). As we find in the words of the saints, [Col. 0651C] Dinah signifies the soul overly intent upon external things. The region whose women Dinah wished to see signifies the world. The women represent souls softened by diverse vices. Shechem represents the devil, who corrupts through desire the soul that attends too curiously to worldly things. Therefore Dinah is the soul; that region, the world; Dinah’s going out, the soul’s curiosity; Shechem, the devil; Dinah’s violation, the corruption of the soul.

## CHAPTER XV.—The Story of Joseph

The story of Joseph is well known: he was sold by his brothers and exalted in Egypt (Gen. XXXVII). In this figure Jacob represents God the Father. He had flocks, namely the Israelite tribes, of whom it was said: [Col. 0651D] “But we are his people and the sheep of his pasture” (Ps. XCIV). Joseph signifies Christ, whom the Father loved and loves above all, because he is Son by nature while others are sons by grace; he by generation, others by adoption; he from eternity, others in time. The Father also clothed him in a many-coloured robe when he clothed him in the nature of our humility. Joseph saw and knew through dreams of sheaves and stars that his brothers would worship him.

The ten brothers feeding their father’s flock signify the Pharisees, who ought to have fed the Israelite tribes through the Decalogue of the Law. Shechem signifies the Law, to which God had sent the Pharisees with the tribes entrusted to them. Joseph’s brothers, abandoning Shechem with the flocks committed to them, turned aside [Col. 0652A] into Dothan, which means “defection”; thus the Pharisees, abandoning the Law with the tribes of Israel, descended into the falling-away of transgression. The envy of the ten brothers toward innocent and righteous Joseph is the Jews’ envy toward Christ. Joseph’s brothers stripped him of his robe, and the Jews stripped Christ of his humanity. They dipped Joseph’s robe in the blood of a kid; these men stained Christ’s humanity with his own blood poured out for the people’s sin. They placed Joseph in a pit; these men placed Christ in a tomb. Joseph came out of the pit; Christ rose from the tomb. Passing Ishmaelites bought Joseph; and the apostles, having no abiding city here but seeking the future one, left everything for Christ. The Ishmaelites led Joseph into Egypt, [Col. 0652B] and the apostles preached Christ throughout the whole world. Joseph was exalted in Egypt, and Christ was exalted in the world. Joseph filled the Egyptian king’s granaries with grain, and Christ filled God’s Church with Scripture. Diverse unbelieving peoples bought food with their money in the Egyptian king’s granaries; and diverse peoples, having become believers, now labour earnestly by their own zeal in the Churches of God. At last the brothers came to Joseph and recognized him; and at the end of the age, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, the remnant of Israel will be saved and will turn to Christ (Rom. XI). Therefore Jacob is God the Father; Joseph, Christ; the ten brothers, the Pharisees, namely those feeding the people under the Decalogue; Shechem, the Law; Dothan, transgression; the robe, humanity; the dipping in a kid’s blood, suffering for the [Col. 0652C] people’s sin; the cistern, the tomb; the Ishmaelites, the apostles; Egypt, the world; Joseph’s exaltation in Egypt, Christ’s exaltation in the world; the granaries, the Church; the grain, Scripture.

## CHAPTER XVI.—On Jacob and His Sons

Jacob is Christ; his sons are the twelve apostles. These are also the twelve springs in the wilderness which Israel found at Elim; the twelve loaves of the Presence; the twelve stones in the high-priestly garment; the twelve stones taken up from the Jordan; the twelve oxen beneath the bronze sea; the twelve stars in the bride’s crown; the twelve foundations; the twelve gates; the twelve months of the year; the twelve hours of the day; and the twelve fruits of the tree of life.

## CHAPTER XVII.—On Judah, His Sons, and Tamar

[Col. 0652D]

Judah went up to the shearers of his sheep and found Tamar sitting at a crossroads. Having given a ring, bracelet, and staff as a pledge, he slept with her; and the woman conceived and bore Perez and Zerah (Gen. XXXVIII). Judah signifies Christ; the sheep, Christ’s faithful people. Their shepherds are teachers, who feed Christ’s flock with the fat of wheat—that is, the word of God. Wool signifies good works; Judah gathers wool from his sheep when Christ receives from his faithful people their good works. Tamar in a harlot’s dress is the soul in sin. She properly turns aside to the crossroads when she approaches confession. The harlot sitting at the crossroads makes known her occupation or purpose; likewise the soul makes known its sin in confession. [Col. 0653A] Christ makes that soul pregnant, just as Judah did Tamar, when after confession of its sin he pours into it the gifts of the Holy Spirit. As a pledge of future recompense, he gives it a ring, signifying faith; bracelets, signifying good works; and a staff, signifying the rectitude of justice. Tamar made fruitful by Judah bore twin offspring; and the soul made fruitful by the Holy Spirit gives birth to the exercise of virtue and the performance of good works. Therefore Judah is Christ; the sheep, the faithful; the shepherds, teachers; wool, good works; Tamar, the soul; sitting at the crossroads, confession of sin; the ring, faith; the bracelet, good action; the staff, the rectitude of justice; impregnation, the infusion of grace; the bearing of twin offspring, the exercise of virtues and performance of good works.

## CHAPTER XVIII.—On Pharaoh’s Two Servants

[Col. 0653B]

Pharaoh was angry with two of his servants, one of whom was over the cupbearers and the other over the bakers; and he sent them to the prison in which Joseph was. There they saw dreams corresponding to their interpretation. The chief cupbearer was restored to his former rank, but the chief baker was hanged on a gibbet (Gen. XL). The king of Egypt signifies the Lord God, king of the whole world. Pharaoh’s house signifies Paradise, into which he placed the human being he had formed. The two servants represent two kinds of people, good and evil: the cupbearer, the good; the baker, the evil. The servants’ fault is original sin, through which, as all sinned in Adam, so all were expelled from Paradise in Adam. The prison signifies the misery of this world. [Col. 0653C] Dreams are consciences, which now, in the night of this age, anticipate their future recompense. Through a good conscience the good obtain good things, [Col. 0654A] because “the desire of the righteous shall be granted”; through an evil conscience, as though from an evil dream, the wicked obtain evil things, because “what the wicked man fears shall come upon him.” Joseph signifies prelates, who, from hearing consciences, both promise good to the good and threaten evil to the evil.

The three days are the three periods: the time of natural law, the time of written law, and the time of grace. The time of natural law was from Adam to Moses; that of written law, from Moses to Christ; that of grace, from Christ to the end of the world. After these three periods, as after three days, God will remove both good and evil from the prison of the present world. He will restore the good to the rank of heavenly blessedness, but will hang the evil in the torment of Gehenna. Therefore the king is God; his house, Paradise; the two servants, good [Col. 0654B] and evil; the servants’ fault, original sin; the prison, the world; Joseph, prelates; dreams, consciences; the three days, the three periods; restoration of the cupbearer, restoration of the righteous to the state of innocence and eternal blessedness; hanging of the baker, the eternal torment of the wicked; the birds are demons, which eat the baker’s flesh because they will be satiated with sinners’ punishments.

## CHAPTER XIX.—On the Spices with Which Jacob Was Embalmed

Jacob died and was embalmed with spices (Gen. XLIX). Jacob signifies the faithful soul, which dies to the world in order to live to God. Having died to sin through repentance, it lives to righteousness through grace. It is embalmed with spices—that is, with diverse virtues—so that henceforth it may remain incorrupt within itself and may become Christ’s sweet fragrance to others in [Col. 0654C] every place. The tomb signifies the hidden place of spiritual life, in which the faithful person is concealed, lest he be disturbed by the fluctuations of the present age.

# BOOK THREE: ON THE REMAINING BOOKS OF THE PENTATEUCH, AND FIRST ON EXODUS

[Col. 0653]

## CHAPTER I.—On the Birth of Moses and Israel’s Departure from Egypt

[Col. 0653D]

The story of Moses’ birth is well known (Exod. II ff.): how Pharaoh’s daughter found him beside the river, how she entrusted him to his mother to be nursed, and afterward adopted him as her own son. It is also known how God sent him to lead the children of Israel out of Egypt, after it had been scourged by ten plagues; how they crossed the Red Sea and the wilderness; and how, after forty years had been completed, they arrived at the land of promise.

Moses beside the river signifies any human being placed beside the stream of the present age. The king’s daughter signifies grace, which frees from the flux of the age anyone predestined to life and adopts him as a son, so that one who was formerly a child of wrath may afterward become a child of grace. She entrusted him to a Hebrew woman, namely to his mother, the Church, so that the Church might nurture one whom grace had regenerated [Col. 0654D]. This holy Church is rightly called a woman because she faithfully bears and nurtures many believers for her bridegroom Christ. And she is Hebrew—that is, “passing over”—because she has no abiding city here, but seeks the future one (Heb. XIII).

Moses, when grown up and instructed in knowledge, is sent into Egypt for the children of Israel; so every faithful person, nourished in righteousness and trained in knowledge of the Scriptures, is established by God as a preacher. Pharaoh, whose name means “denying him,” that is, the Lord, signifies the devil, who denied him when he said: “I will place my seat in the north, and I will be like the Most High.” Egypt means “darkness” and signifies the world, not insofar as human beings live in it, but insofar as they live badly in it. Its rulers are demons, who always obey his will.

The mud in which the children of Israel served Pharaoh signifies, because mud defiles, lust. [Col. 0655A] Straw, because it is light and quickly flies away, signifies vain glory. Brick, made from soft earth and hardened by the baking of fire, represents the hardness of the human heart baked hard through a long habit of either desire, lust, or avarice. Through all these things many today serve Pharaoh, although they are predestined to eternal life and will obtain the land of the heavenly homeland.

Egypt’s scourging signifies the destruction of the world, not insofar as it is governed by divine providence, but insofar as, through the ministry of preaching, it is weakened in its wickedness. The firstborn represent the principal vices. The firstborn are killed when, through God’s grace, the principal vices are destroyed. [Col. 0655B] The killing of the lamb signifies Christ’s passion, through which all the elect are freed from the devil’s slavery and from captivity in the present age. We mark both our doorposts with the blood of this lamb (Exod. XII) when we believe his passion in our heart and confess it with our mouth (Rom. X).

Wild lettuce signifies the bitterness of repentance. For when we participate in the sacrament of the Lord’s body, we ought to lament the crimes formerly committed under Pharaoh. Girding the loins signifies continence. Shoes, made from the hides of dead animals, signify remembrance of mortality. The staffs which they were to hold in their hands signify justice, for a staff has straightness. The haste of eating represents the speed of conversion. Egypt’s gold, which the children of Israel took, signifies, because it gleams, [Col. 0655C] philosophical wisdom. Silver, because it gives sound, signifies eloquence. The weapons with which the children of Israel are said to have been armed signify the virtues by which we arm ourselves against vices: chastity, by which we are defended against lust; humility, against pride; and likewise with the other virtues and vices. The unleavened flour which they took with them signifies simple and sound teaching, in no way corrupted by heretical depravity. The Red Sea signifies baptism consecrated by Christ’s blood. Pharaoh and his rulers were drowned in the Red Sea; and in baptism we are freed from the devil’s power and his dominion.

The wilderness into which the children of Israel entered after crossing the Red Sea signifies [Col. 0655D] the spiritual life which we ought to live after receiving the grace of baptism. This life is rightly called a wilderness because it is deserted by many and cultivated by few; for though many are called, few are chosen. Many are in spiritual life in name alone while, by their perverse will, they are in secular life. The Amalekites, who first met the children of Israel armed, and the kings who afterward fought against them, represent two classes of vices, carnal and spiritual, which fight through a double enemy, through human beings and demons. “For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood, but against the powers of these darknesses, against spiritual wickednesses in the heavens” (Eph. VI).

The Jordan, whose name means “descent,” signifies death, and the land of promise eternal blessedness. [Col. 0656A] At the crossing of the Jordan, the lower part of the water ran downward, while the upper part stood firm. So in death the lower part of the human being, namely the flesh, runs downward because it is earth and returns to earth; but the higher part, that is, the soul, stands firm, because, now receiving its own robe, it passes into eternity. Two goods are promised to us in the heavenly homeland: milk and honey. Milk, because it is from flesh, signifies Christ’s humanity; honey, because it congeals from heaven’s dew, signifies his divinity. Let us therefore receive the land flowing with milk and honey, because we are made blessed by contemplating Christ’s humanity and his divinity.

Therefore Egypt is secular life; the wilderness, spiritual life; the land of promise, heavenly life. Pharaoh is the devil; [Col. 0656B] his rulers, demons; mud, lust; straw, vain glory; gold, philosophical wisdom; silver, eloquence; brick, hardness of heart; Egypt’s river, the flux of the age. Moses is the preachers; the children of Israel, Christians; the killing of the firstborn, the destruction of principal vices; the killing of the lamb, Christ’s passion; wild lettuce, the bitterness of repentance; unleavened flour, simple teaching; the Red Sea, baptism; the people of Amalek, carnal vices or perverse human beings; Og and the other kings, spiritual vices or demons; possession of the land of promise, eternal blessedness; shoes, remembrance of mortality; staffs, justice; haste of eating, the speed of conversion; girding of the loins, continence; the two doorposts, faith and confession.

## CHAPTER II.—On Things That Spiritually Signify the Lord or Christ

[Col. 0656C]

There are certain things in the Old Testament that spiritually signify Christ: such as the Paschal lamb, the pillar, the rock, and certain others. The Paschal lamb signifies Christ, because just as the children of Israel were freed from the Egyptian king’s slavery by the killing of the lamb, so in the Lord’s passion the elect children were freed from the devil’s slavery. The pillar that went before the children of Israel signifies Christ, because as the pillar went before the people journeying to the land of promise, so Christ, “becoming obedient to the Father unto death” (Phil. II), goes before the Christian people, who are tending toward the homeland of heavenly life, by the example of his passion. [Col. 0656D] “Through many sufferings and tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven” (Acts XIV).

The cloud signifies Christ’s humanity; the fire, his divinity. The rock struck with the rod, which gave water to the people, signifies Christ, who, suffering upon the wood, bestowed upon us the grace of redemption. The ark signifies Christ. For just as the ark contains the two tablets of the Law, manna, and the rod, so “in Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” (Col. II), by which we are instructed in knowledge of truth; spiritual grace, by which we are fed; and justice, by which we are ruled. The two tablets signify wisdom and knowledge; manna, grace; the rod, justice. Christ instructs us by wisdom and knowledge, feeds us by grace, and rules us by justice.

[Col. 0657A] The four rings attached to the ark are the four books of the Gospels. These books are like circular rings because they promise us eternity, in which there is no end. The poles by which the ark was carried always adhere to the rings, because preachers ought always to remain in the four books of the Gospels through meditation and reading, so that by preaching they may carry the ark—that is, Christ—to the minds of their hearers. The mercy-seat signifies Christ. For just as the Lord was made propitious to the children of Israel from the mercy-seat, speaking to Moses there his commandments, so in Christ he was made propitious to humankind, forgiving its sins, as it is written: “God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (I Cor. V).

The table of the Presence signifies Christ. For on the table of the Presence there were loaves. And Jesus says: “I am the living bread that came down from heaven; and the bread that I will give is my flesh for the life of the world” (John VI). [Col. 0657B] The lampstand signifies Christ. For as the lampstand is an instrument of light, so Christ made the Father’s name manifest in the world, as he himself testifies when he says: “Father, I have made your name manifest” (John VII). The shaft of the lampstand signifies the holy Church, which is Christ’s body. The branches proceeding from it are preachers, who sound out to us the word of life. The cups, because drink is customarily poured into cups, are hearers of the word. The small globes also present on the branches signify the movement and swiftness of good work. The lilies, because lilies are green and white, signify the eternity and beauty [Col. 0657C] of eternal recompense.

Three branches proceeded from one side and three from the other, because both before and after Christ’s incarnation there were those who preached faith in the Trinity. The three cups, globes, and lilies upon each branch signify three periods: for the elect before the incarnation—in the time before the Law and under the Law, under the prophets—and after the incarnation, in the time of the primitive Church gathered from Israel, in the time of the Church gathered from the Gentiles, and in that of the Church yet to be gathered at the end from the remnant of Israel, are found, as cups, thirsting for the drink of grace; as globes, running on the way; and as lilies, awaiting the gift of recompense. The four cups in the shaft are the four books of the Gospel; the seven lamps, the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0657D] The altar signifies Christ. Sacrifices were offered upon the altar, and we ought to offer good works and the gifts of prayers upon Christ—that is, upon faith in him. The Lord says: “You shall make me an altar of earth” (Exod. XX). The altar of earth is Christ’s flesh from the Virgin Mary. The scapegoat, sent into the wilderness and taking away sins, signifies Christ. Offered on the cross, he was sent out of the world through death and took away the sins not merely of one people but of the whole world. The red heifer also signifies Christ. His flesh is rightly called a heifer because it is incorrupt, and red because it is suffused with the blood of suffering. We are cleansed by its ashes because through faith in his death we are justified. The bronze serpent likewise signifies Christ. Just as Moses raised [Col. 0658A] the serpent in the wilderness, so Christ was raised upon the wood (John III). Those who looked at the bronze serpent were healed from the bites of serpents, and those who look upon Christ with true faith are healed from demonic suggestions.

The cluster of grapes which two men, scouts, carried on a pole signifies Christ. For he is the fruit of life by which we are fed; he pours out for us first the wine of grace and then that of glory, by which we are made drunk. The two scouting men signify the prophets and apostles, who brought into this world for us, through their Scriptures, the secrets of the heavenly homeland and Christ. The wood of the pole signifies the wood of the cross. And just as the one who went ahead of the two men carrying the cluster did not see the cluster upon the pole behind his back, so the company of prophets going before Christ did not see him suffering on the cross. But the one who followed saw the cluster, because the choir of apostles, which remained in the world after him or departed the world after him, beheld him going before them in the flesh and suffering on the cross.

[Col. 0658B] The ten scouts who, by evil words, turned the hearts of the children of Israel away from entering the land of promise signify unbelieving Jews placed under the Decalogue of the Law, who refuse to seek heavenly promises through faith in Christ. The two scouts who faithfully exhorted the people to enter that land signify elect Christians placed under the two commandments of love, who desire with all their hearts to enter the joy of the heavenly homeland. Therefore the Paschal lamb is Christ; the pillar, Christ; the rock, Christ; the ark, Christ; the mercy-seat, Christ; the table, Christ; the lampstand, Christ; the altar, Christ; the heifer, Christ; the serpent, Christ; the goat, Christ; the cluster upon the pole, Christ upon the cross.

## CHAPTER III.—On Egypt, the Wilderness, and the Land of Promise

Egypt, which means “darkness,” signifies the flesh. For what is blinder, what is darker, than the flesh? Unless it is restrained by reason, it always seeks pleasant things and never useful ones. The wilderness signifies the mind, because it is abandoned by many and cultivated by few. Few indeed return to their heart from transgression in order to exercise the mind’s virtues. The land of promise represents God. For as temporal freedom exists in the land of promise, so eternal happiness exists in God. [Col. 0658D] Let us therefore depart from Egypt—that is, from the darkness of the flesh and from concupiscence—and through the wilderness, that is, through the mind, by exercising its virtues and advancing from virtue to virtue, let us tend toward the land of promise, namely God, in whom the fullness of every good is promised to us. Therefore Egypt is the flesh; the wilderness, the mind; the land of promise, God.

## CHAPTER IV.—On the Commandment of Love
“Love the Lord your God with all your heart,” etc. (Deut. VI). After man abandoned the Creator through the primal fault and entered into the misery of this world, he is subjected to many cares, occupied with activities, and wearied by labours. Yet among all the things in which man is stretched out under the sun, one is best and enduring: to serve God; for [Col. 0659A] all else is transitory, all else vain. Whoever does not serve God is vain and ought to be reckoned as nothing. His life is worth nothing; it would be better for him not to be than to be badly, and not to live than to live badly. And if such a person in this present life could possess Samson’s strength, Absalom’s beauty, Solomon’s wisdom, Hazael’s swiftness, Croesus’ riches, Alexander’s integrity, Octavius’ [Octavian’s] power—he who held the whole world in his power—and the length of life of Enoch, who was born at the beginning of the age and will not die until its end: if, I say, he possessed such and so great things in the present life, so that all things favoured him, they would profit him nothing, because he had not served God at all.

For when all these things had passed away, and finally he died, [Col. 0659B] his wretched flesh would be given to worms and his spirit to demons and to the torments of Gehenna, until on the day of resurrection all flesh is restored to its original state. Then, having taken up again the flesh through which he sinned, he will likewise endure eternal condemnation. Therefore it is best to serve God, because even if a person is deprived throughout his life of bodily and temporal goods, yet, if he serves God, he passes from the misery of the present life to eternal blessedness.

Since, therefore, among all the pursuits and attainments of this present age which the human race follows or obtains, serving God alone is the best and enduring good, we must seek by every means to know what it is to serve God; and, once it has been sought and found, we must persevere in it without ceasing. For only the one who perseveres in it [Col. 0659C] will be blessed.

Brothers, what it is to serve God is comprehended and explained in a brief, sweet, and pleasing statement. To serve God is to love God. Whoever does not love does not serve; whoever loves serves. Whoever loves little serves little; whoever loves much serves much; and whoever loves perfectly serves perfectly.

Whoever possesses temporal goods—lands, vineyards, flocks, herds, costly garments, houses, gold, silver, or a wife whom he loves greatly—if he finds that any one of these things, or all of them together, stands against the love of God, ought to leave all things and set all things aside for divine love. A person must also despise his own life for the love of God, if it should happen that he cannot preserve the one together with the other. Thus Peter did; thus Paul did; so did the other apostles and martyrs of Christ, who gave up not only their possessions but themselves also for the love of God. They too were human beings, and they left us an example of how we ought to act.

Therefore we ought to love God because he first loved us, bestowing his many gifts: giving some to us, promising others; and, so to speak, in all things earning from us the love with which he is to be loved. The least gift that God gave man, so that he might be loved by man, is this whole world. For God made the world—for man’s sake—heaven, earth, sea, sun, moon, stars, birds, fish, beasts, plants, trees, and everything that visibly exists. Since, therefore, among God’s gifts the world is the least gift, [Col. 0660A] how great, do you suppose, is the greatest?

The second gift of God, which God gave man, is that he made him in his own image and likeness: a great and altogether wonderful gift of God, that the creature should be made like and conformed to its Creator. The third gift is the grace which he bestowed on us in redemption, when he did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all (Rom. VIII). The fourth gift he keeps and promises us: namely, the glory to come, of which “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man, what God has prepared for those who love him” (I Cor. II).

Thus we may call the first gift the gift of creation; the second, the gift of nature; the third, the gift of grace; and the fourth, the gift of glory. For all these things we ought to love God. But with how much of ourselves ought we to love him? With all the heart, with all the soul, with all the strength, with all the mind. With all the heart—that is, wisely; with all the soul—that is, sweetly; with all the strength—that is, strongly; with all the mind—that is, mindfully. And in whatever other ways it may be said, for one cannot say too much of what cannot be loved too much.

“And your neighbour as yourself” (Matt. XIX). We ought to love our neighbour as ourselves in deed, word, and desire. In a deed is good work; in a word, sound counsel; in desire, pious longing. In all these ways let us love in this life the neighbour whom we shall have as a companion in our homeland.

## CHAPTER V. On the precepts of natural and written law

Under natural law there were two precepts and three sacraments. The two precepts were: “What you do not wish for yourself, [Col. 0660C] do not do to another”; and: “Whatever you want people to do to you, do the same to them.” The three sacraments are tithes, offerings, and sacrifices: tithes in portions; offerings in possessions; sacrifices in animals.

Under written law there were many precepts and many sacraments. Of the precepts of written law, some were changeable and others unchangeable. Changeable precepts are those established by God through dispensation. Unchangeable precepts are those which arise from nature and are either so evil that they can never be done without fault, or so good that they can never be omitted without fault.

## CHAPTER VI. On the two tables

The first table is so called because it contains the more excellent commandments, which concern love of God. The second [Col. 0660D] contains the lower commandments, immediately following these, which concern love of neighbour. Or the first table is so called because it contains the precepts that instruct us in good action.

On the first table there are three commandments, because what is believed by faith is the Trinity. On the second table there are seven commandments, because only in this present life—which revolves in the cycle of seven days—are the duties of humanity rendered to one’s neighbour. But three and seven make ten, because right faith and good action make a person perfect.

The first commandment of the first table pertains to God the Father, just as the first commandment of the second table pertains to one’s human father, so that in both cases fatherhood may be honoured by the authority of its primacy. In the first table there is a command and a prohibition; likewise in the second, [Col. 0661A] so that in each you may endeavour to do what you ought and avoid what you ought not to do. For if you offend in the latter, it is a sin; but in the former, an omission. To do what ought not to be done is a sin; not to do what ought to be done is an omission.

## CHAPTER VII. On the four Sabbaths

Scripture appears to commemorate four Sabbaths. The first is that on which God is said to have rested after completing his works. The second is that which the children of Israel were commanded to observe bodily. The third is that which the people of God are commanded to keep. The fourth is that on which, in the promise, God pledges to his lovers “Sabbath for Sabbath.”

There are now, therefore, two Sabbaths: one outward and one inward; one belonging to God and one to man. The Sabbath [Col. 0661B] of God, on which he is said outwardly to have ceased from work, is the sacrament of that inward Sabbath in which the holy mind, resting by a good conscience from the bondage of sin, rejoices in the joy of the Holy Spirit. Whoever keeps this Sabbath in the present life in such a way as to consent to no evils will attain in the life to come that eternal Sabbath of God, where he will feel no evils, as it is said: “And there shall be Sabbath from Sabbath, month from month” (Isa. LXVI).

## CHAPTER VIII. On theft, lying, and perjury

“You shall not commit theft” (Exod. XX). Theft is understood here as any unlawful appropriation of another’s property, whether secret or open. For he who prohibited theft did not permit robbery; since, as the saints testify, it is a greater sin to seize openly and violently than to take secretly, because it stirs up greater hatred and greater anger. Usury is also included under theft.

A lie is a false signification by speech with the intention of deceiving, either concerning something presently existing or something that will happen later. For if someone promises another that he will give him something, intending to give it, but later changes his mind and refuses to give it, it is a lie—not because his heart was double at the time of promising, but because the promiser subsequently made his heart double. Perjury is a lie confirmed by the invocation of a sacred attestation.

## CHAPTER IX. On the construction of the tabernacle and the offerings made in it

The tabernacle signifies the Church. The boards signify [Col. 0661D] souls. They are rightly said to be made of shittim wood, because souls are immortal by nature and incorruptible by grace. The silver bases signify faith, upon which the holy Church is founded or, once founded, stands firm.

These bases are not inappropriately many because God distributes to each according to the measure of faith. One person has great faith both in knowledge and affection; another has little in knowledge and affection; another great knowledge but little affection; another little knowledge but great affection. Two bases were placed under each board because faith consists in two things, knowledge and affection; or because we believe that God is the Creator of all things and the Redeemer of the elect.

In constructing this tabernacle we ought to offer gold, silver, [Col. 0662A] bronze, hyacinth, and so forth. Gold, because of its brilliance, signifies wisdom, which shines in the hearts of believers. Silver, because it is bright and has a sweet sound, signifies eloquence. Bronze, because when struck it gives out a loud sound, signifies preaching that resounds far and wide throughout the world. Hyacinth, which displays an airy or heavenly colour, signifies hope for heavenly goods, or heavenly conduct. Purple signifies bodily suffering, for which we ought to be prepared to suffer for Christ. Scarlet, because it resembles flame, signifies charity, which burns in the hearts of the saints. This scarlet is called twice-dyed because it is coloured through a twofold love, namely of God and neighbour. Fine linen, because it is white, signifies chastity. Hyacinth skins signify men living a heavenly life; shittim wood, men steadfast in faith. Oil, because it excels other liquids, signifies mercy, which surpasses or transcends the other virtues. Spices and incense signify the fragrance of a good reputation. Ointment denotes inward sweetness and richness, or pleasantness. Precious stones, because of their brilliance, signify the working of miracles, flashing far and wide. The court signifies the rudiments of beginners. A column signifies strong and perfect men. The ten curtains signify those who fulfil the Decalogue of the Law. The eleven goat-hair coverings signify those who practise severe penance for transgressing the Law. For eleven, which exceeds ten, signifies transgression of the Decalogue; [Col. 0662C] and because goat-hair coverings are rough, they signify the severity of penance. The loops by which the curtains were joined are the virtues of the saints by which they themselves are united. The golden rings indicate the everlasting splendour of future reward. The Holy Place signifies the present life; the Holy of Holies, eternal life. In the Holy Place is grace; in the Holy of Holies, glory. In the Holy Place is merit; in the Holy of Holies, reward. The veil signifies heaven because it separates heavenly from earthly things. Moses or Aaron signifies Christ because he builds and sanctifies the holy Church. Bezalel and Oholiab signify teachers and preachers. The various vessels are souls sanctified by diverse gifts and serving in offices and orders. The entrance of the tabernacle [Col. 0662D] signifies the vice of the age; the rear part of the tabernacle, the end of the world. The southern side signifies the Jews, illumined from ancient times by the rays of divine knowledge. The northern side signifies the gentiles, from the beginning far removed from the brightness of divine knowledge. The former were bright and warm through faith; the latter dark and cold through unbelief.

Therefore the tabernacle is the Church; the individual boards, individual souls; the bases, faith; the ten curtains, saints fulfilling the Decalogue; the eleven goat-hair coverings, the righteous rendering satisfaction through penance for transgressing the Law; the loops, virtues; the round rings, eternal rewards; the Holy Place, the present life; the Holy of Holies, eternal life; the veil, heaven; Moses or Aaron, Christ; Bezalel and Oholiab, teachers and preachers.

In constructing this tabernacle we ought [Col. 0663A] to offer gold through wisdom; silver through eloquence; bronze through preaching; hyacinth through hope for heavenly goods or through heavenly conduct; purple through suffering or compassion; twice-dyed scarlet through twofold love; fine linen through chastity; frankincense through prayer; oil through mercy; incense through a good reputation; and likewise all other goods of righteousness which we can possess. Very many things could be said concerning these matters, if they did not exceed the limited capacity of our understanding. But we have briefly touched on certain matters among them all, lest we seem to pass over everything. It does no harm that we frequently depart from the order of historical narration. Such transposition of order is no obstacle, provided the truth of history is preserved. Indeed, this kind of transposition sometimes produces greater understanding and memory.

## CHAPTER X. On sacrifices

Sacrifices also have their meanings. We ought to offer the Lord a calf, an ox, a lamb, and so forth. The calf, until it grows and comes forth into the strength of a bull, because at its age it can be guided at the will of its leader, signifies obedience, which proceeds according to the will of its superior. The ox likewise, because it parts the hoof and completes its work by ploughing, signifies a discerning and perfect soul and suitably represents action. The sheep, because it is an innocent animal, signifies innocence. The she-goat and he-goat, because goat-hair coverings in which penance is performed are usually made from their hair, signify penance. The lamb, because its fleece and body [Col. 0663C] are most clean, signifies purity. Likewise the dove, because it is simple and without gall, signifies simplicity; and the turtledove, because it is a chaste animal, chastity. Salt signifies wisdom, because as salt seasons foods, so wisdom seasons virtues and good works. Unleavened flour expounds simple teaching, pure from every heretical perversity. For as leaven corrupts flour, so heresy corrupts doctrine.

Let us therefore offer a calf through obedience; an ox through discerning action; a sheep through innocence; a lamb through purity; a she-goat and he-goat through penance for every fault; a dove through simplicity; a turtledove through chastity; salt and flour [Col. 0663D] through wisdom and doctrine. We ought to offer all these things without the leaven of heretical perversity and without the honey of worldly sweetness, because leaven, which signifies heretical perversity, and honey, which signifies worldly sweetness, were prohibited in the sacrifices of the Old Testament.

A sacrifice partly burned and partly reserved signifies a good beginning. A holocaust, wholly burned, signifies completion. In the same way, the morning sacrifice signifies a beginning; the evening sacrifice signifies completion. Sacrifices cooked by fire signify good works performed through the ardour of inward love. Those cooked by water signify works performed through the grace of compunction. A libation of wine signifies the intoxication of the mind bestowed through the consolation of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0664A].

We may also say that every victim signifies good conduct; the victim’s skin, the exterior appearance of that conduct; its head, the beginning; its tail, the end; its entrails, hidden virtue; the washing of the victim, the purity of an honourable life. We strip the skin from the victim and divide the victim limb by limb when, beneath the outward appearance of our conduct, we carefully examine each of our works by inward rational judgment according to place, time, manner, and intention, lest vice deceive us under the appearance of virtue or fault under the appearance of right action.

## CHAPTER XI. On the table of the Presence

The table of the Presence signifies sacred Scripture, which refreshes us with as many loaves as it instructs us with sentences. The four supports of the table are the four senses of Scripture—history, allegory, tropology, and anagogy—by which it is raised and lifted above earthly things. The rim signifies the preaching of Scripture. The circuit of the rim signifies perseverance in preaching. For the rim is, as it were, carried around in a circuit when preaching is nowhere brought to an end. The four rings are the four books of the Gospels. They are rightly called rings because they promise us eternity, in which there is no end. The pierced crown signifies the discernment of the mind; the golden crown placed above it, the splendour of reward. The twelve loaves signify apostolic teaching. The vinegar bowls signify sharp and frequent rebuke, namely against vices. The bowls, which held a larger measure, signify abundant and perfect knowledge and doctrine. [Col. 0664C] The cups, which held less, signify narrower knowledge and doctrine. The censers, because incense is customarily offered with prayer, suitably signify prayer.

Thus the table is Scripture; its rim, preaching; the circuit of the rim, continual zeal in preaching; the four rings, the four books of the Gospels; the poles, preachers; the twelve loaves, apostolic doctrine; the vinegar bowls, sharp rebuke; the bowls, abundant knowledge or doctrine; the cups, limited knowledge or doctrine; the censers, devout prayer.

## CHAPTER XII. On the journey of three days

“We shall go a journey of three days into the wilderness, and we shall sacrifice to the Lord our God” (Num. X). One day is hope; one day, faith; one day, charity. The first day shines; the second shines and is warm; the third shines and burns fervently. The journey of three days is the exercise of spiritual virtues, because one who completes the journey of these days offers a sacrifice pleasing to God; for whoever has these three virtues is pleasing to God in whatever he does or practises. [Col. 0664D] We ought, moreover, to offer a sheep through innocence, a lamb through purity, and the other things explained above concerning sacrifices. But all these things are abominations to the Egyptians, because all virtues and all good works are an abomination to demons and wicked people.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the two Testaments

The Old Testament signifies the New; the Law, grace. The Law was given through Moses; grace through Christ. [Col. 0665A] The Law was given on the fiftieth day after the Passover had been celebrated in the land of Egypt; grace was given on the fiftieth day after the Lord’s resurrection. The Law was given on a high mountain; grace was born above, in the upper room. The Law was given amid fiery flashes; grace was given in fiery tongues. The Law was given to twelve tribes; grace was given to twelve apostles. The Law was written on two tables; grace consists in the two commandments of charity.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the two tables, the two cherubim, and the two trumpets

The two tables of the Testament, on which the Law was written by the finger of God, signify the two Testaments. The two cherubim, because *Cherubim* is interpreted “fullness of knowledge,” signify the two Testaments, because [Col. 0665B] perfect knowledge is contained in them. Likewise the two silver trumpets signify the two Testaments, because by their preaching those predestined for life are summoned to the unity of the Church and to the height of eternal life.

## CHAPTER XV. On the anointing and garments of the priest

The anointing by which priests were consecrated signifies the grace of the Holy Spirit. Priests are consecrated by anointing when each of the faithful, anointed with the grace of the Holy Spirit, is justified. The inner linen garment, which is white and not visible, signifies purity of heart, known not to everyone but to God. The breeches, which bound and covered the thighs, fittingly signify continence of the flesh. The ephod, placed upon the shoulders, signifies endurance of present labours, because we customarily bear burdens on our shoulders. The outer and visible tunic signifies good action, by which we are defended and adorned before our neighbour. The belt by which the tunic was bound so that it might not fall around the priest’s feet signifies the readiness of that same good action. The breastpiece, which was around the breast—in which breast the heart is contained, where wisdom is—appropriately signifies wisdom and discernment. The turban, by which the hair of the head was bound, denotes sobriety in thoughts. For they bind the hair of the head, as it were, with a turban when they restrain the thoughts of the mind in sobriety. The plate on which the name of God is written signifies faith in God, through which he makes himself known to us. The bells, which sounded on the high priest’s garment, signify the sound of preaching. [Col. 0665D]

Thus the priest’s anointing is the grace of the Holy Spirit; the inner linen garment, purity of heart; the breeches, continence of the flesh; the ephod, endurance of labours; the tunic, good action; the belt, readiness in that action; the breastpiece, wisdom and discernment; the plate on the forehead, confession of holy faith; the bells, preaching of that same faith.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the foreskins of trees

“When you have entered the land and planted fruit-bearing trees in it, you shall remove their foreskins. The fruits which they produce shall be unclean to you; you shall not eat of them” (Lev. XIX). Fruit-bearing trees are works made perfect by virtues. Therefore we remove the foreskins of trees when, suspicious of the very weakness of our beginnings, we do not approve the first stages of our works. We regard as unclean the fruits they produce and do not make them fit for our food, because when the beginnings of a good work are praised, it is fitting that they should not feed the soul of the worker, lest, while praise is sweetly plucked, the fruit of the work be eaten prematurely.

## CHAPTER XVII. On priests to be rejected, from the book *Pastoral Rule* of blessed Gregory

The Lord said to Moses: “Speak to Aaron: No man of your seed who has a blemish shall offer bread to the Lord his God or approach his ministry” (Lev. XXI). Where he immediately adds: “If he is blind, if lame, if he has a small or large and crooked nose, if he has a broken foot, if he is maimed, if hunchbacked, if bleary-eyed, [Col. 0666B] if he has a white spot in his eye, continual scabies, an eruption on his body, or swollen testicles” (*ibid.*).

Blind, indeed, is the person who does not know the light of higher contemplation, who, oppressed by the darkness of this present age, does not perceive by love the coming light, and therefore does not know where to direct the step of his action. Hence, as Hannah prophesies, it is said: “He will guard the feet of his saints, and the ungodly shall be silent in darkness” (IV Kings II).

Lame is one who sees where he ought to go, but through weakness of mind cannot perfectly keep the way of life that he sees. Since a loose habit is not raised to the state of virtue, the steps of action do not effectively follow to that place upon which desire relies. Hence Paul says: “Lift up the slack hands and weakened knees, and make straight paths for your feet, so that no lame person may go astray, but rather may be healed” (Heb. XI).

A person of a small nose is one unfit to maintain the measure of discernment. By the nose we discern odours and stenches. Thus discernment is rightly expressed by the nose, through which we choose virtues and reject vices. Hence, in praise of the bride, it is said: “Your nose is like a tower which is in Lebanon” (Song VII), because the holy Church, by discernment, perceives from individual causes what temptations may arise, and from on high detects the coming battles of vices.

But some persons, unwilling to be thought dull, frequently exert themselves in certain inquiries beyond what is necessary and are deceived by excessive subtlety. Thus it is also added here: “with a large and crooked nose.” [Col. 0666D] A large and crooked nose is an immoderate subtlety of discernment; when it has grown beyond what is fitting, it itself confounds the rectitude of its action.

The one with a broken foot or hand is a person wholly unable to walk in God’s way and entirely destitute of good works; so that he does not at least hold to them as a lame person does, though with weakness, but is wholly alien from them.

The hunchbacked person is one oppressed by the weight of earthly anxiety, so that he never looks upward but attends only to things trodden underfoot below. Even if he should at times hear something concerning the good of the heavenly homeland, nevertheless, weighed down by the burden of perverse habit, he does not raise the face of his heart, because he cannot lift the condition of his thought, which the practice of earthly anxiety keeps bent. Concerning the likeness of such persons the Psalmist says: “I am bent down and brought low utterly” (Ps. CXVIII). Rebuking their fault, the Lord himself says: “The seed which fell among thorns are those who hear the word of God and, trampled by the cares and riches of the world, bear no fruit” (Luke VIII).

The bleary-eyed person is one whose intelligence indeed flashes toward knowledge of truth, but whose carnal deeds obscure it. In bleary eyes the pupils are sound, but, because moisture flows, the weakness of the eyelids causes them to swell; and thus, while the eyes are burdened by continual discharge, even the sharpness of the pupil is impaired.

There are some whose understanding is wounded by the activity of carnal life: through their natural ability they could see rightly and sublimely, but by habitual wicked actions they grow dim. Bleary-eyed, then, is the person whose natural ability has sharpened his understanding but whose continual bad conduct confounds it. [Col. 0667B] To him the angel fittingly says: “Anoint your eyes with eye-salve, that you may see” (Apoc. III). We anoint our eyes with eye-salve so that we may see when, in order to know the brightness of the true light, we aid our understanding with some remedy of good action.

The person who has a white spot in his eye is one who is prevented from seeing the light of truth because he has been blinded by the arrogance of wisdom or righteousness. The pupil of the eye, being black, sees; bearing a white spot, it sees nothing. Thus, if the mind of human thought understands itself to be foolish and sinful, it apprehends the knowledge of inward brightness. But if it attributes to itself the whiteness of righteousness or wisdom, it excludes itself from the light of higher knowledge; and it does not penetrate the brightness of the true light precisely because it exalts itself within itself through arrogance, as is said of certain persons: “While claiming to be wise, they became fools” (Rom. I).

The one who has continual scabies is a person over whom the wantonness of the flesh rules without ceasing. In scabies the inner heat is drawn to the skin; and this rightly signifies lust, because if the delight of the heart leaps forth as far as action, inward heat breaks out as far as the itching of the skin and now wounds the body outwardly: for when pleasure is not repressed in thought, it rules also in action. Paul was, as it were, seeking to wipe away the itching of the skin when he said: “Let no temptation seize you except what is human” [Col. 0667D] (I Cor. X). It is as though he said openly: it is human indeed to suffer temptation in the heart, but diabolical to be overcome in the contest of temptation and in action.

Whoever has an eruption on the body is devastated by avarice in mind. Unless it is checked in small matters, it undoubtedly expands without measure. An eruption also takes possession of the body without pain and, increasing without weariness to the afflicted person, disfigures the beauty of the limbs. So avarice, while it seems to delight the captive mind, ulcerates it; while it presents to thought things to be acquired, it incites it to hostilities. It produces no pain in the wound because it promises abundance to the fevered mind through fault. But the beauty of the limbs is lost because through it the beauty of the other virtues too is disfigured; and it roughens, as it were, the whole body because it undermines the mind through every vice, as Paul testifies when he says: “Covetousness is the root of all evils” (I Tim. VI).

The person with swollen testicles is one who does not practise shameful conduct in deed but is continually and immoderately burdened in mind by the thought of it. He is not indeed carried as far as wicked action, but his mind delights in the pleasure of lust without any spur of resistance. Swelling is a condition in which fluid from the inward parts descends to the genitals, which then swell painfully in disgrace. Thus the swollen person is one who, flowing in all his thoughts toward the wantonness of lust, bears the burden of shamefulness in his heart. Although he does not commit wicked acts in deed, he is nevertheless not uprooted from them in mind; [Col. 0668B] nor can he rise openly to the practice of good work, because a shameful burden weighs him down in secret.

Whoever, therefore, is subject to any of these vices is forbidden to offer bread to God; and surely one whom his own sins lay waste cannot cleanse the sins of others.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On victims, from the book of Isidore

The varieties of victims, and which should or should not be offered to God, are enumerated in Leviticus; but by comparison with sins they display human conduct. Therefore, if a man offers to God a peace-offering, whether in fulfilment of a vow or as a voluntary offering, he shall offer an unblemished animal, from either sheep or cattle, so that it may be acceptable: there shall be no blemish in it. If it is blind, broken, scarred, has pustules, scabies, or an eruption, you shall not offer these to the Lord, nor burn any of them upon the altar of the Lord. An ox or sheep with ear or tail cut off you may offer voluntarily, but a vow cannot be made from them. You shall not offer to the Lord your God any animal whose testicles are bruised, crushed, cut, or removed; nor shall you do this at all in your land. From the hand of a foreigner you shall not offer bread to your God, or anything else that he wishes to give, because all are corrupt and blemished: you shall not accept them, etc. (Lev. XXII).

First, a blemished or variegated animal is rejected from sacrifice: that is, those in whom there is a diversity of sins, and who are changed now by lust, now by greed, now by diverse crimes. A blind animal too is rejected: that is, one who neither sees the Lord [Col. 0668D] nor does his works. So also is a broken animal: one harassed and crushed by criminal vices. The one bearing a scar is rejected: one who does not mourn the wounds of his sins with fitting satisfaction, but still keeps inwardly the mark of the old disease through desires for pleasure. One with a tongue cut off is rejected: that is, one who does not confess God or meditate on the divine Law. One with pustules is rejected: that is, one who burns with the itching of lust and the heat of concupiscence. Likewise the scabrous one is rejected: that is, one who fulfils the sin of the flesh by the contagion of action.

Further, one having an eruption signifies an assembly of heretics, who frequently immerse themselves in the body of the Church and produce the lividness of an eruption. Those with an ear cut off are persons who do not obey the word of God and do not do what is commanded. The one with a tail cut off is the person who does not bring the good things he begins to completion in a persevering end. Finally, one whose testicles are bruised or removed signifies those who are made effeminate at all times through the practice of shamefulness. Those entangled in these crimes are rejected from God’s sacrifice; they are neither made companions of Christ’s passion nor of heavenly sanctification.

Nor may the bread of a foreigner be offered to the Lord: that is, the teaching of heretics or the superstitious studies of secular letters, which are outside faith and considered alien. Such offerings are rejected by the Lord, and this sacrifice is rejected by the catholic Church.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the firstborn of ox and sheep

“You shall not work with the firstborn of your ox, nor shear the firstborn of your sheep” (Deut. XV). To work with the firstborn of an ox is to display the beginnings of good conduct in the exercise of public action. To shear the firstborn of sheep is to uncover before human eyes our beginning good works from the covering of their hiddenness. Therefore we are forbidden to work with the firstborn of an ox and restrained from shearing the firstborn of sheep because, if we begin to perform something vigorous, we ought not quickly display it in public. But when our life begins something simple and innocent, it is fitting that it should not abandon the veils of its secrecy or show this to human eyes as though its fleece had been removed.

Thus the firstborn of cattle and sheep serve only for divine sacrifices, so that whatever vigorous or innocent thing we begin, we may offer it upon the altar of the cross for the honour of the inward Judge. It is received by him all the more willingly because, guarded more carefully from human sight, it is not stained by any desire for praise. [Col. 0669C] Often the beginnings of a new way of life are still mixed with carnal life; therefore they ought not quickly become known, lest, when the good things that please are praised, a mind deceived by its own praise be unable to detect in them the evils that lie hidden.

## CHAPTER XX. On the woman captured in war
If you go out to war against your enemies and see a woman beautiful in appearance and desire her, you shall shave the hair of her head and her nails; you shall clothe her in mourning garments, and she shall sit in your house mourning her father, her mother, and her paternal home; and after thirty days [Col. 0669D] she shall be your wife (Deut. 21). If we find among the Gentiles a beautiful woman—that is, a soul created beautiful by God—and wish to join her to our body, that is, to Christ, then, once the worship of idolatry has been laid aside, let her put on the mourning garments of repentance and bewail her father and mother, that is, every remembrance of the world and its fleshly allurements. [Col. 0670A] Then let her shave away with the razor of God’s word and teaching every sin of unbelief, which is dead and empty. For these are the woman’s hair of the head and nails. Thus, once purified by the water of the saving bath, she is joined to the holy servants of God, when she has nothing upon her head and nothing upon her hands, so that she bears nothing unclean or dead either in her thoughts or in her actions. But the command that, after thirty days, she is to be taken as a wife signifies faith and work by the numbers three and ten. Therefore, through faith in the Trinity and the work of the Law she is rightly joined to the faithful. Every soul that clings to the true Israelite, namely to the body of Christ, ought to be without stain through sincerity of faith and purity of actions.

Others have thought that this woman beautiful in appearance signifies some rational discipline [or branch of learning] [Col. 0670B] that is found wisely expressed among the Gentiles. Therefore, when we have found it, we must first remove and cut away from it every impurity of superstition, and then receive it into the pursuit of truth. For there is no wisdom among unbelievers to which impurity is not mingled.

## CHAPTER XXI. On not ploughing with an ox and an ass together

“You shall not plough with an ox and an ass together” (Deut. 22). By the name of the ox is understood the people from the circumcision, placed under the yoke of the Law; by the ass, the people of the Gentiles, belonging to the Gospel. He ploughs with an ox and an ass together who receives the Gospel in such a way that he does not abandon the Jewish superstitions and ceremonies which preceded it in shadow and image.

Likewise, by the ox are sometimes represented [Col. 0670C] the lives of those who live or work well; by the ass, the hearts of fools. As though it said: “Do not associate a fool with a wise person in preaching, lest through one who is unable to accomplish the matter you hinder the one who is capable.” Yet, if necessary, anyone may yoke an ox and an ass without loss to the work. But one makes a wise person and a fool companions—not so that one commands and the other obeys, but so that both alike proclaim the word of God with equal authority—not without scandal.

## CHAPTER XXII. On a garment woven of wool and linen

“You shall not wear a garment woven of wool and linen” (Deut. 22). For by wool simplicity is denoted, but by linen subtlety. A garment made of wool and linen conceals the linen within and displays [Col. 0670D] the wool on its surface. Thus he wears a garment woven of wool and linen who conceals the subtlety of malice within a speech of innocence. To mingle wool with linen garments is also to live disorderly: so that either a woman devoted to chastity possesses bridal clothing, or one who, not containing herself, has married lives under the appearance of a virgin.

# BOOK FOUR. ON THE BOOKS OF JOSHUA, JUDGES, AND RUTH

[Col. 0669]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0669D]

Having suitably set forth these matters briefly above concerning the Pentateuch, [Col. 0670D] let us turn our hand to the book of Joshua, in order to disclose its mystical meanings, partly according to our own [Col. 0671A] understanding and partly according to the words of the holy Fathers.

## CHAPTER I. On Joshua and the crossing of the Jordan

“Moses my servant is dead. Arise, and cross this Jordan, you and all the people with you, into the land that I shall give to the children of Israel,” etc. (Josh. 1). Moses, who gave the Law, signifies the Law. When Moses is dead—that is, when the Law according to carnal and old observances is dead, that is, fulfilled or ended—at once Jesus our Savior, who delivered his people from their sins—Jesus, I say, the Son of God—was manifested and chosen as leader over the people (Matt. 1), so that, after God’s enemies had been overcome, he might distribute God’s gifts among the people. For Joshua son of Nun, as Jerome says, overthrew the kingdoms of enemies across the Jordan as a type of the Lord, not only in his deeds [Col. 0671B] but also in his name. He divided the land among the victorious people and, through individual cities, villages, mountains, rivers, torrents, waters, and boundaries, described the spiritual kingdoms of the Church and of the heavenly Jerusalem. So too our Jesus Christ, having cast out the prince of this world and his soldiers, works in the elect, provided that the manifestation of the Spirit is given to each for usefulness: “To one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge; to another, faith; to another, the grace of healings; to another, the working of miracles; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of utterances” (1 Cor. 12). And afterwards, according to the diversity of gifts, there shall be given to each a diversity of heavenly [Col. 0671C] goods, and according to merits everlasting goods shall be bestowed.

The Jordan signifies baptism, because, just as the Israelite people entered the land of promise while the priests stood in the Jordan, so the Christian people, while priests administer baptism, enter into the joy and rest of the spiritual life. The upper part of the Jordan remained in sweetness; its lower part flowed down into the bitterness of the sea. So the baptized elect preserve the sweetness of grace, but the reprobate flow into the bitterness of vices, having lost grace’s sweetness. Joshua, preceding the twelve companies, signifies Christ, who goes before and leads us who hold and preach the truth of apostolic faith. For, as it were, twelve companies follow Christ when all believers, believing in Christ through the word of the twelve apostles, [Col. 0671D] imitate him.

The twelve stones which the twelve children of Israel took up from the Jordan signify the steadfastness of apostolic faith and life. The second circumcision performed through Joshua signifies spiritual circumcision after carnal circumcision. The Passover also, which the children of Israel celebrated after crossing the Jordan, signifies the eating of the true Passover and the true Lamb. We too take up twelve stones from the Jordan when we hold in mind the steadfastness of apostolic faith and life. We also ask whether the angel is ours or belongs to our adversaries when we discerningly examine what is good and what evil.

## CHAPTER II. On the sons of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh

[Col. 0672A]

The sons of Reuben and Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh go before the army of the children to fight; their fathers were firstborn among the sons of their mothers. And the righteous of old go before us, armed against our enemies and spiritual wickednesses with examples, virtues, and words. On this Origen says: “We see Isaiah, Jeremiah, and the others girded and ready to help us, wounding the fiercest enemies of our heart with the darts of their writings. Daniel too girds himself to help us when he instructs and forewarns us about Christ’s kingdom and the future deceit of Antichrist. Ezekiel is present, signifying for us heavenly mysteries in the fourfold eyes of the wheels. Hosea also teaches [Col. 0672B] the twelve companies of the host; and they go before us with their loins girded in the truth which they preach, for our aid.”

## CHAPTER III. On the overthrow of Jericho

The ark, while trumpets sound, goes around Jericho for seven days; Jericho is overthrown; Rahab is delivered with a scarlet cord placed in the window; and Achan is stoned for the theft of a golden bar and a scarlet cloak (Josh. 6–7). Jericho, which is interpreted “moon,” signifies the present age, which, like the moon, is brought to fullness and diminution, now raised up, now diminished and humbled by adversities. We see the cycles of the years through which the age rolls: in spring, when time alone opens the pores of the earth in likeness of the new moon’s first emission of light, the earth brings forth shoots. Then, just as we see the moon reach fullness through long and diverse successions, so we observe all that springs from the earth attain its maturity and perfection in summer through the life-giving force of heat and the growth-producing power of moisture. Afterwards, they are diminished like a waning moon, when, as their natural heat and moisture fail, they die in autumn. Finally, in winter they return, as it were, to a kind of interlunium, as, worn down by the harshness of cold, they again retreat to the hidden bosom of nature and withdraw themselves from our sight.

So too we see in human beings, beasts, birds, and fish: after they come into being, they first strive to reach perfection and then hasten through decline toward non-being. So, yes, so we see the glory of the present age now arise, now grow, now be exalted, now be diminished, now be reduced to nothing. The ark, which, as was said above, signifies Christ, is carried around Jericho for seven days, while Christ is preached in the world until the end of the age, which runs through a course of seven days. The bearers of this ark are the holy apostles and preachers, of whom it is written: “Their sound has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18). The bronze trumpets signify the strong and invincible authority of preaching. They hold them sounding in their hands when holy preachers fulfill in deed what they sound forth in speech. The walls of Jericho signify philosophical arguments [Col. 0673A] or the worship of idols, strengthened and exalted throughout the world; these fell through the circuit of the ark and the sounding of the trumpets, because they perished through Christ’s preaching resounding throughout the world. The men of Jericho are slain when people of the age, devoted to worldly affairs, are condemned forever.

Rahab the prostitute signifies the Church chosen from among the Gentiles, which was once enslaved and subject to many lovers, that is, many demons. In order to be saved, Rahab placed outside in the window the scarlet cord which she had in her house; and in order to be saved, the holy Church confesses with her mouth Christ’s passion, which she believes in her heart. Achan steals the golden bar and cloak and is stoned in the valley; and every false Christian or heretic who brings into the Church philosophical [Col. 0673B] wisdom, signified by the golden bar, and worldly worship, signified by the cloak, is condemned to hell. Gold, silver, and any metals from Jericho or from other cities, purified by fire, are taken up for the Lord’s use, because the wisdom or eloquence of philosophers, or any teaching of theirs, once purified from every defilement of error by the examination of sacred Scripture, is not rejected from the ministry of divine preaching.

He who rebuilds Jericho is cursed, and cursed is he who restores and rebuilds, by evil word or example, worldly malice which has been destroyed in the baptized. “He lays its foundation in his firstborn and its gates in the last of his children,” because through this sin he loses both the first gift of nature that he received [Col. 0673C] and the last gift of grace that he received, so that neither henceforth avails him for salvation. Moreover, all that belongs to him is consumed by fire, when his body, soul, and whatever he possesses in either are burned in the conflagration of Gehenna.

## CHAPTER IV. On the city of Ai

The city of Ai also signifies the world, not insofar as it is God’s creature, but insofar as the devil’s malice and the concupiscence of humankind abound in it. The men of Israel lying in ambush behind the city by night are the holy prophets of old, who lay hidden, as it were, in the night before Joshua’s coming to Ai—that is, before Christ’s coming into the world—because in the Old Testament, before the sun of righteousness rose for us, [Col. 0673D] “who enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1), they served the Lord in the shadow of the Law and in figures of the future Savior, preceding the Savior himself. But the king of Ai did not know Israel’s ambushes, because the obscure enigmas of the prophets and the secret mysteries of the legal figures were hidden from the devil, and he did not know the manner of redemption. Therefore, like the king of Ai, he rashly attacked the Redeemer’s presence in an attempt to overcome it.

Joshua feigned himself weak and powerless before the king of Ai and took flight; and so, by pretending to be defeated, he shrewdly conquered the king of Ai. Likewise, Christ, displaying the weakness of humanity, humbled the devil’s pride and wisely overcame his malice when he allowed himself to be tempted by the devil and, with the devil himself cooperating, to be crucified by his servants.

[Col. 0674A] The raising of the shield signifies the exaltation of faith. Ai too is consumed by fire when everyone who loves iniquity is burned in the flames of hell. The elders who were with Joshua and the other warriors represent the apostles and preachers. But the king and his army are killed when the power of the devil and his servants to do harm is divinely taken away.

## CHAPTER V. On the altar which Joshua built
