Joshua, after overthrowing the enemies, built an altar of stones which iron had not touched (Josh. 8). He wrote Deuteronomy upon it and divided the people for blessing and cursing. He set the nobler tribes for blessing and the less noble for cursing. The stones of which Joshua built the altar are the holy, steadfast in faith, who work through love. Iron does not touch them because no sin of cruelty corrupts them. When they come together in the unity of faith and the concord of charity, they make one altar.

[Col. 0674B]

Deuteronomy, which is interpreted “second law,” signifies the Gospel. The Lord wrote it upon this altar when he said: “You have heard that it was said to those of old, ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you: whoever looks upon a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. 5). Those who walked beside the mountain of blessing signify those who come to salvation, inflamed by love of the heavenly promise and without fear of the punishment of hell. But those who walked beside the mountain [Col. 0674C] of cursing signify those who fulfill what is written in the Law in order to attain salvation, not from love of blessing but from fear of future punishments. Yet it is clear that those are nobler who do what is good from desire for goodness itself and love of eternal blessing.

## CHAPTER VI. On the deceit of the Gibeonites

Meanwhile, the Gibeonites, terrified by fear, came to Joshua with fraud and cunning, clothed in old garments and shoes and begging to be saved. They immediately received salvation from Joshua. Yet, when he recognized their deceit, he made them hewers of wood and drawers of water (Josh. 9). In their figure are shown those who, coming from the world to the Church, have [Col. 0674D] faith in God, bow their heads to priests, minister to the saints, serve them, and render some usefulness. They are even ready for the adornment or service of the Church. Yet they persist in their former morals and manner of life, retaining the old person with his deeds and clothed in old vices, just as those men were covered with old garments and shoes. Because they believe in God, they seem devoted in their reverence for God’s servants and the Church; yet they have no amendment or renewal in their morals. Such people, therefore, display only some sign of salvation temporarily within the Church, but among the Israelites—that is, among God’s saints—they do not at all obtain either the eternal kingdom or [Col. 0675A] freedom.

The report that, while Joshua son of Nun fought at Gibeon, the sun and moon stood still until Israel’s enemies were destroyed (Josh. 10) signifies that our Jesus, much more now by his intervention, while we wage war against the nations of vices and struggle against “principalities and powers and rulers of this darkness, against spiritual wickednesses in the heavenly places” (Eph. 6), has the sun of righteousness continually at our side. He never leaves us and does not hasten to set, because he himself said: “I am with you always, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28).

The five kings signify the five senses, which attack the Gibeonites, that is, carnal people. They flee to a cave (Josh. 13) when, immersed in earthly actions, they bury themselves in [Col. 0675B] the body. Yet, while Joshua fights—that is, through evangelical preaching—they are overcome; and when the word of God enters us, that is, enters the cave of our body, they are all together slain. Then, when the nations have been destroyed or cast out, Joshua divides the land of promise among the peoples by lot. Thus Christ also cast from before his faithful, as it were, Gentile error and evil spirits, and divided the land within us by lot, “one and the same Spirit working all things and distributing his own gifts to each as he wills” (2 Cor. 12).

## CHAPTER VII. On the Levites

The fact that dwellings, as suburbs, and towns are assigned by Joshua to the Levites throughout all the tribes signifies that those who administer the grace of [Col. 0675C] teaching in the Church of God ought to receive from all those to whom they dispense divine things the earthly support which they do not possess, so that the apostolic command may be fulfilled: “If we have sown spiritual things for you, is it a great thing if we reap your carnal things?” (1 Cor. 9). And rightly they are said to be distributed throughout all the tribes, because they live by the provision of all.

But the fact that they receive forty-two cities (Num. 35) undoubtedly signifies the preaching of the saints itself. For they possess teaching which consists of the Decalogue of the Law and the fourfold number of the Gospel, as though they possessed forty cities. Two are added to these because, indeed, they proclaim everything they preach in both a moral and a mystical sense.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Canaanites made tributary

[Col. 0675D] Let us explain the fact that, when the land of promise is distributed to the Israelite people according to the command, an entire Gentile people of Canaanites is assigned to the tribe of Ephraim, but is said to have become tributary, as it is written: “The Canaanite dwelt in the midst of Ephraim, tributary” (Josh. 16). For what does the tributary signify except the subjection of servitude, and what does the Canaanite signify except vice?

For we often enter the land of promise through great virtues, because we often investigate inward matters concerning eternity. But when, after higher vices have been killed, we nevertheless retain certain small ones, we permit a Canaanite, as it were, to live in our land. Yet he becomes tributary because we turn this very vice, which we cannot subdue, to the use of our [Col. 0676A] humility, so that the mind may think humbly of itself and its own powers because it does not overcome even the small things it seeks by its own strength. Hence it is also well written: “These are the nations which the Lord left, that through them he might train Israel” (Judg. 3). Certain very small vices are retained in us so that our vigilant purpose may always exercise itself in conflict and may not grow proud of victory because it sees enemies living within itself, by whom it still fears being conquered. Therefore Israel is trained through the nations left behind, because when we live with certain vices, the exaltation of our virtue is restrained, and our mind learns from the small things resisting it that it cannot subdue greater things by itself.

## CHAPTER IX. On Joshua’s successors

[Col. 0676B] After Joshua’s death, the children of Israel consulted the Lord, saying: “Who shall go up before us against the Canaanite and be leader of the war?” (Judg. 1), etc. Just as Joshua signifies Christ, so Joshua’s successors signify the apostles and the other teachers and rulers of the Church, by whose discernment, foresight, and teaching the Church is governed, defended, and instructed in holiness. When the children of Israel sinned, the Lord delivered them into the hands of foreign kings; but when they repented, he raised up for them a leader to deliver them. So, when we sin, we give demons strength against us; but when we turn to God, he sends us teachers to show us the way of salvation and, after the enemies are subdued, restore the grace of freedom. These are signified by Othniel, [Col. 0676C] Ehud, and others.

We read of Shamgar that he killed six hundred men with one ploughshare. Thus we too ought sometimes, laying aside the hidden sword of excommunication and most sharp rebuke, to break open the hearts of hearers with the ploughshare of discerning exhortation and the moderation of a gentle word; and so to drive the army of demons from their borders and restore the Lord’s people to true freedom.

## CHAPTER X. On Deborah

Deborah, whose name is interpreted “speech,” signifies prophetic discourse. She dwells beneath a palm tree because she exhorts us toward the palm of the heavenly calling. This Deborah summoned Barak, whose name is interpreted “flashing,” and who signifies the Jewish people: [Col. 0676D] it flashed briefly in goodness, but, like a flash, quickly faded. She summoned him to war against Sisera, that is, against the devil. Yet victory is not ascribed to Barak, since Sisera is slain through Jael, a foreign woman; because, while the Jewish people does not resist the devil, the holy Church gathered from the Gentiles courageously kills him with the wood of the Lord’s cross, since it truly believes in him who hung upon the wood for our salvation.

So there are some endowed with certain gifts of grace, distinguished by learning and eloquence, who, though they ought courageously to resist the devil’s suggestions, grow slack in a womanly fashion; while others who are weak and possess less grace than they do vigorously repel those suggestions. So too, some cloaked in the habit of religion fall from the fervor of their begun devotion, while others who remain in secular dress [Col. 0677A] rise to it with all their strength.

Those whom Deborah rebukes for not having come from Israel to the war are all Christians and unbelievers who devote themselves to earthly things, rest in them, and never come to spiritual battle because they do not believe prophetic exhortations. “Why,” she says to Reuben, “do you dwell between two boundaries, so as to hear the bleatings of the flocks?” (Judg. 5). What are these boundaries between which the wicked dwell, except the boundaries of vices and sins? For they dwell between the boundary of pride and sloth, between the boundary of avarice and lust, of gluttony and robbery, and so with the rest. They dwell between boundaries when they are subject here to the defilement of flesh, there to the defilement of spirit; or indeed they dwell between boundaries because, “while professing to know God with their mouth, they deny him by their deeds” [Col. 0677B] (Tit. 1). Do not those people dwell between boundaries of whom it was said: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Mark 7; Isa. 29)? These hear the bleatings of flocks, that is, the tumult of vices or of people living carnally, who, like flocks—that is, brute animals—under the devil’s leadership run in herds and without sense toward torments.

Gilead rested beyond the Jordan, and Dan was occupied with ships. Asher dwelt on the shore of the sea and lingered in the harbors. The Jordan, which is interpreted “descent,” signifies humility. Therefore Gilead, which rested beyond the Jordan and refused to come with Deborah to the war, signifies worldly people who, proud of the abundance of passing things, rest securely in the vice of self-exaltation and disdain to come to spiritual battle. The sea signifies the world, and ships running on the sea signify worldly activities. Thus Dan, who was occupied with ships, represents those who attend to worldly activities and for that reason refuse to fight against spiritual enemies. [Col. 0677C] Asher, who dwelt on the shore of the sea and lingered in harbors, signifies those who, although through weakness of strength they cannot undertake worldly business, nevertheless labor, as far as they can, to be present with and attached to the world, worldly rumors, and worldly activities. Therefore Gilead, Dan, and Asher do not come to war with Deborah, because all who are proud, entangle themselves in worldly affairs, and love the world disdain to serve as soldiers for Christ.

[Col. 0677D] But Zebulun and Naphtali offered their lives to death. The leaders of Issachar were with Deborah. Those who were with Deborah in the Lord’s battle signify those who crucify their flesh in the battle of temptations through abstinence. “You who ride upon shining asses, who walk in the way, and sit in judgment, speak” (Judg. 5). What are shining asses except chaste bodies: asses because of the submission they render to the spirit, shining because of chastity? The way signifies Christ; judgment, discernment of good and evil. Therefore you who ride upon shining asses—that is, who preserve chaste bodies—who walk in the way—that is, who live rightly in Christ—and who sit in judgment—that is, who distinguish truth from falsehood and good from evil—speak. What should you speak? “Justice,” he says. For God said to the sinner: “Why do you recount my justices?” [Col. 0678A] (Ps. 49).

“The kings fought near the waters, yet took nothing as plunder” (Judg. 5). Kings fight near water when demons tempt holy persons who devote themselves to readings and meditations upon sacred Scripture. They carry away nothing as plunder because, defeated and confounded, they depart. Heaven also fights against them when divine aid is given to the saints in temptations against demons. The stars likewise fight against Sisera when holy angels, sent from heaven to help us, overcome the devil. Blessed is Jael—that is, the holy Church—among women, that is, among the other nations, with heavenly blessing in Christ. “To one asking for water, she gave milk” (ibid.). The devil seeks water when he desires that heretical teaching and worldly wisdom, [Col. 0678B] cold from the warmth of faith, be put forth and spread abroad. But the holy Church gives milk because she does not cease to preach simple teaching. Deborah, therefore, is prophecy; Barak, the Jewish people; Sisera, the devil; Jael, the holy Church.

## CHAPTER XI. Allegorical sense concerning the threshing floor

Teachers commonly understand the threshing floor of Gideon (Judg. 6) figuratively as the world, the fleece as blessed Mary, and the dew as grace. For the fleece was soaked with dew when the blessed Virgin conceived Christ. And then the threshing floor, when the holy Church, spread throughout the world, believed in him.

## CHAPTER XII. Moral sense concerning the threshing floor

We may also, according to the moral sense, understand [Col. 0678C] by the threshing floor on which Gideon purified wheat with a rod, the breadth of the heart; by the rod, the rightness of discernment; by the wheat, virtues; and by the chaff, vices. For we cleanse wheat on the threshing floor with a rod when in our heart we separate vices from virtues by the power of discernment. Thus in this case Gideon is every believer; the threshing floor, the heart; wheat, virtues; the rod, discernment; chaff, vices.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Gideon and the war against the Midianites

Gideon (Judg. 7) signifies Christ. The Midianites signify demons; vices, wicked people. But the three hundred men who fought with Gideon signify the apostles and successors of the apostles, the teachers and rulers of the Church, and all the elect marked with faith in [Col. 0678D] the holy Trinity. They rightly drink water without bending the knee, because, while they draw in the knowledge of the Scriptures, they do not bend down the uprightness of their state to low things. For those bend the knee while drinking water who both search the Scriptures and bend or bow shamefully toward the desire for earthly things.

The saints also hold trumpets in their hands, and jars with lamps. The trumpets signify the sound of preaching, the jars the frailty of bodies, and the lamps the brilliance of miracles. The saints sound the trumpets because they preach divine utterances without ceasing. They hold jars in their hands and break them because they willingly subject their bodies to abstinence, labors, and death for Christ. They hold lamps because they shine far and wide with miracles. Equipped with all these things, the saints [Col. 0679A] terrify and overcome demons, and become victorious.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Gideon, his wives, and his sons

Gideon (Judg. 8), as we said in the preceding figure, signifies Christ. Gideon’s many wives are the many churches, or the many nations adhering to Christ by faith; Gideon’s sons are individual Christians. The concubine by whom he begot Abimelech signifies the Synagogue. She is a concubine because she is sinful. Abimelech (Judg. 9) signifies Antichrist, who, having gathered together the nations that are lost, will persecute God’s Christian servants, just as Abimelech slaughtered his brothers. Jotham, the youngest, who alone escaped from among all his brothers and climbed the mountain of blessing, represents [Col. 0679B] those who ascend through grace to the mountain of spiritual life and thus escape the guilt of condemnation.

Let us also consider Jotham’s parable spoken against the men of Shechem: “The trees of the forest went forth,” he says, “to anoint a king over themselves” (ibid.), etc. What do we understand by the trees of the forest except any unfruitful nations and people set and hardened in sins, prepared for eternal fires? Oil signifies mercy, because, just as oil surpasses all liquids, so mercy surpasses all virtues. And we customarily attribute mercy to the Father, just as we say in blessing him: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies” (2 Cor. 1). Therefore, by oil or the olive tree the Father is fittingly represented. By the vine is signified [Col. 0679C] the Son, who said: “I am the vine” (John 15). But by the fig tree, which has sweet and pleasant fruit, is represented the Holy Spirit, of whom it is written: “How sweet, Lord, is your Spirit within us?” (Wis. 12); and Wisdom says: “My Spirit is sweeter than honey” (Ecclus. 24).

Thus the forest trees come to the olive, the vine, and the fig tree and seek a king when all the unfruitful say with deceitful lips to the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, “Lord, Lord.” But the olive, vine, and fig tree reject kingship over the forest trees, because the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit do not receive wicked and unfruitful people—unless they become fruitful—among the children of the kingdom. For he says: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ shall enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven” [Col. 0679D] (Matt. 7). As the men of Shechem accepted Abimelech, so the forest trees accept the bramble as king, because the wicked will submit themselves to the rule of Antichrist. But as those are consumed by one another’s fire, so these are condemned by a common guilt.

We may also understand by the oil or olive tree a faithful person excelling in the virtue of mercy; by the vine, someone outstanding in the virtue of wisdom; and by the fig tree, another preeminent in the grace of inward sweetness. Thus the trees come to the olive, vine, and fig tree to take one of them as king when any unfruitful assemblies seek to have as their prelate some merciful, wise, or leading man. But the olive, vine, and fig tree reject [Col. 0680A] such government because all the elect fear that, if they are established in authority over wicked people, they will be deprived of their own fruit through the wickedness of those people and will benefit them in nothing. Then the trees raise the bramble as king over themselves when the wicked demand as ruler another wicked person covered in the thorns of sins. These too are consumed by reciprocal fire when perverse subjects and their perverse prelate are disturbed by mutual fury and anger.

## CHAPTER XV. On Jephthah

Jephthah (Judg. 11), as teachers explain, signifies Christ. For just as Jephthah, expelled by his brothers, received leadership, so Christ, rejected by the Jews, received leadership over the people of the faithful. Just as Jephthah delivered the people of the faithful, [Col. 0680B] just as Jephthah delivered the people from the hand of the children of Ammon, so Christ delivers the elect from the slavery of demons. Jephthah sacrificed his daughter through victory, and Christ offered his own flesh.

## CHAPTER XVI. On Samson

Samson (Judg. 13) signifies Christ. Samson’s birth was announced through an angel, and the Savior’s birth was announced through an angel. Samson killed the lion, and Christ killed the devil. Samson drew a honeycomb from the jaws of the lion, and Christ drew humankind from the jaws of the devil. Wax is the heart; honey, the spirit. Samson took a foreign wife, and Christ took the Gentile Church. Samson struck down the Philistines, and Christ struck down spiritual and [Col. 0680C] bodily enemies. Samson, carrying the gates of Gaza, ascended the summit of the mountain; and Christ, having broken the gates of hell, ascended into heaven. Samson struck down more enemies by dying than he had done while living, and Christ likewise more by dying than by living.

## CHAPTER XVII. Moral application of the same

According to the tropological sense, Samson signifies every believer strong in faith, who kills—or conquers—the lion when he kills or conquers the devil; who draws a honeycomb from the lion’s jaws when he rescues himself or another from subjection to the devil; and who strikes down the Philistines when he casts spiritual and carnal vices out of himself. Yet such a great person is sometimes conquered and compelled to grind, [Col. 0680D] when, overcome by temptations, he is afflicted both in spirit and body. But, strengthened as his hair grows again, he kills more enemies than before, because, again fortified by gifts of grace, he attains an even greater triumph after his fall and at the end.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Ruth
The land of Moab signifies Gentile life; Ruth, the Church from among the Gentiles; the land of Israel, spiritual conduct; the kinsman who does not take Ruth, John the Baptist; Boaz, Christ; the field, the world; the harvests, human beings; the reapers, angels. Thus the mystery of human redemption was prefigured in the Old Testament by many riddling signs and figures.

## BOOK V. ON I KINGS—FROM ELKANAH TO DAVID

[Col. 0681]

### PROLOGUE

[Col. 0681A]

In what has preceded, concerning the book of Joshua and the book of Judges, we have clarified certain matters according to the sayings of the holy Fathers, and certain matters according to our own understanding. In what follows we turn our hand to the book of Kings, and in it likewise shall expound certain matters according to our limited ability and certain matters according to the words of the holy Fathers.

### CHAPTER I. On Elkanah and his wives

“There was a certain man of Ramathaim-sophim, of Mount Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah,” etc. (I Kings 1). Elkanah is interpreted “possession of God,” which is the Son of God, who says: “The Lord possessed me” (Prov. 8). He is rightly called “one man,” not numerically, but because he is never changed, nor becomes other than himself. He is from Ramathaim-sophim, [Col. 0681B] which is called “their heights,” that is, “watchtowers”: namely, the heavenly Jerusalem, from which he came, taught contemplation, and by his death made it possible to possess it.

Jeroboam means “merciful”; Elihu, “my God is he”; Suph, “pouring forth.” For mercy, coming to us in the Passion, says, “My God” (Matt. 27), where, emptying himself, he poured himself out: hence, “Your name is poured-out ointment” (Song 1). Poured out from his invisible realm to our visible one. An Ephrathite means “fruitful,” because he abounds in the gifts of the Holy Spirit.

And he had two wives, Hannah and Peninnah. Peninnah is the Synagogue, which at first was fruitful, bearing children to God through the Law, but now remains barren because of unbelief. Barren Hannah is the Church of the Gentiles, once barren in relation to the [Col. 0681C] spiritual Father, but now redeemed by Christ’s grace and bearing offspring for God. Hannah, whose name means “grace,” bore children to God through baptism and through the Holy Spirit. To Peninnah—that is, to the Synagogue—and her children he gave portions, that is, temporal goods, according to the saying: “He gave them the regions of the Gentiles” (Ps. 104). And because the oracles of God were first entrusted to them (Rom. 3), to Hannah—that is, the Church of the Gentiles—he gave one portion (I Kings 1), namely, understanding. Hence she went away sorrowful (ibid.), because the Lord had closed her womb: the time for mercy upon her had not yet come, so that she might be made fruitful by spiritual grace.

As Peninnah despised Hannah, so the Synagogue despised the Gentile world. Many among the Gentiles awaited the Redeemer’s coming, as is found in Job. And because they persevered in prayer, at last the Redeemer brought consolation to Hannah, who wept and [Col. 0681D] took no food. “Hannah, why do you weep?” etc. “Am I not better to you than ten sons?” etc. (ibid.). Her husband—that is, Christ—is better to the Church than the ten sons whom the Synagogue bore to God. “And her countenance was no longer changed in different directions.” For the Church was never changed by turning aside from faith and love of the Redeemer in divergent directions.

### CHAPTER II. Moral interpretation of the same

[Col. 0682A]

Elkanah means “possession of God,” and by strength of mind he is called a man; and “one,” not changeable or wandering, but steadfast and undivided. All are also fittingly called one when they possess one wisdom, confess one Jesus Christ, and are filled with one Spirit of God. Hence, “The fool changes like the moon” (Ecclus. 27). God is called one, not numerically, but because he is unchanging; hence it is written: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. 101). Hence also the Apostle says: “All indeed run, but one receives the prize” (I Cor. 9). Every one of the foolish is not one but many.

Elkanah is the preacher whom the Lord possesses. Peninnah and Hannah are the active [Col. 0682B] and contemplative life. Peninnah is fruitful in sons and daughters; the active life brings forth strong and weak works. Peninnah means “turning,” because the active person must diligently turn toward deeds by which he may benefit his neighbours. For the active life is to give the bread of teaching to the hungry, to correct one who errs, to call the proud back to the way of humility, to care for the sick, and to distribute to each what is expedient.

Hannah means “grace,” because contemplation is possessed through grace. It is barren because, since no one can penetrate it as it is, and no one can sufficiently proclaim what it perceives, it follows that no one, by preaching it, begets many children. The contemplative life is to keep in the mind the love of God and neighbour, to rest from outward things, and to cling to the Creator alone in desire, [Col. 0682C] so that one no longer wishes to act in external matters.

Whoever wishes to become God’s possession should take these two wives: first the active life, and then the contemplative. Above all, a teacher should pass from the embraces of Peninnah to those of Hannah, giving portions to each and linking virtues to virtues.

### CHAPTER III. On Hannah and Samuel

“And it came to pass after the cycle of days that Hannah conceived and bore a son, and called his name Samuel, because she had asked him from the Lord” (I Kings 1). Because Hannah devoutly asked before the Lord, she conceived and bore. The Church, praying through natural understanding, conceived in her heart the mystery of the Incarnation and brought it forth through the mouth of confession.

[Col. 0682D] Samuel—his name means “named by God,” or “asked of God”—Hannah’s firstborn, is a prophet. Who is this but God-and-man? Moreover, Hannah’s remaining behind and not going up with her husband until the child had been weaned teaches us that the Church advances no one to the priesthood while he remains a participant in the milk of infancy rather than in solid food and spiritual understanding. Hannah’s song after Samuel’s conception and birth [Col. 0683A] signifies the thanksgiving of holy Church, whether for the incarnation of our Redeemer or for the conversion and perfect justification of any sinner.

### CHAPTER IV. On Hophni and Phinehas, sons of Eli

Hophni (I Kings 2), “barefoot,” or “madness of conversion,” and Phinehas, “mute mouth,” signify the scribes and Pharisees. They are called sons of Eli because Eli bears the type of the priesthood. Since they did not receive what the Law and Prophets foretold, they turned to the madness of unbelief and deserved to have a mute mouth regarding confession of Christ. And because they would not raise up the seed of faith for Christ, their deceased brother, they deserved to be made barefoot and to be outside the lot of those of whom it is said: “Your feet shod in preparation for the Gospel of peace” [Col. 0683B] (Eph. 6).

And because they tried to claim the bride’s name for themselves by usurping the Church, rather than for Christ, they remained naked, stripped of every dignity and of the examples of patriarchs and prophets. Hence Shiloh—where the priests were—is interpreted “division,” or “his dismissal and petition,” because they asked Pilate to dismiss Barabbas for them. They were therefore rightly dismissed and abandoned by almighty God.

### CHAPTER V. Again on Eli and his sons

Eli (I Kings 2) means “foreign.” For one who does not correct those subject to him is alien to God. Hophni means “madness of conversion”; he is rightly so called because he delays changing for the better. Phinehas means “hardness of mouth,” or “obedient to the mouth.” We read of two priestly Phinehases: one, the righteous son of Eleazar; the other, the unrighteous son of Eli.

[Col. 0683C] Among priests today there are those who bear the type of each. Priests who guard their mouth lest anything crooked come forth from it are figured in Eleazar’s son. But those whose mouth is hardened, whether through ignorance or consciousness of sins, are figured in Eli’s son. Woe to the priests of our time, or of the New Testament, who, like Hophni and Phinehas, reject the Lord’s sacrifice; who do not obey paternal and divine correction, but daily entangle themselves miserably in sins, “walking in revelry and drunkenness, in beds and shameless acts, in strife and jealousy” (Rom. 13). For as bodily death followed their sin, so eternal death will follow the life of these men unless they repent.

### CHAPTER VI. On the camps of Israel and the Philistines

[Col. 0683D] “Israel went out to meet the Philistines in battle and encamped beside the stone of help. But the Philistines came to Aphek and drew up their line against Israel. When battle had begun, Israel turned its back before the Philistines, and about four thousand men fell scattered through the fields” (I Kings 4).

Israel means “the man who sees God” and “strong with God.” The Philistines are “those falling by drink,” namely demons: intoxicated with the cup of pride, they themselves fell and hasten to overthrow human beings. Against them Israel—that is, the faithful—encamps beside the stone of help, so that they may not fall but overcome. The stone of help is Christ, concerning whom it is written: “The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner” (Ps. 117).

[Col. 0684A] The faithful encamp beside him so that they may find him a helper, while they meditate on the Law of the Lord. But the Philistines come to Aphek, that is, to “new fury,” because when they see the faithful applying themselves more fully to the divine laws, unclean spirits set in motion sharper and new conflicts. Thus they easily overthrow as it were four thousand of them—that is, of the faithful who trust not in the Lord but in their own powers, glory in human wisdom, and therefore despise the grace of the Gospel.

### CHAPTER VII. On the ark of God and the deaths of Eli’s sons

“The ark of God was captured; and Eli’s two sons, Hophni and Phinehas, also died” (I Kings 4). The ark’s capture by foreigners signifies that the covenant would pass to the Gentiles. Eli dies, and his sons die, because the high-priesthood fails together with the old priesthood.

[Col. 0684B] But his daughter-in-law, Phinehas’s wife, was pregnant and near to giving birth. When she heard the report that the ark of God had been captured and that her father-in-law was dead, she bent herself, gave birth, and died. The priest’s wife did not perish before giving birth to a living child; nor did the Synagogue wholly perish before the primitive Church, which came from it, believed.

“Do not fear, for you have borne a son.” Believers console the Synagogue, but she, despairing, takes no notice. She does not reckon the new offspring a glory but a disgrace; hence it follows: “And she called the child Ichabod” (ibid.). The child was called Ichabod, Josephus says, because the name signifies “inglorious,” since glory was transferred from Israel when the ark was captured. Hence: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” [Col. 0684C] (Matt. 21).

### CHAPTER VIII. On the ark of God and Dagon

“The Philistines took the ark of God and carried it to Ashdod” (I Kings 5). Ashdod means “fire of the father,” or “burning.” The place where Dagon’s idol stood is well so called, because the ark of God’s arrival in Ashdod was a burning for the devil, father of all the wicked.

Dagon, meaning “fish of sorrow,” signifies the devil, who devours sinners in the sea of this age. In Job he is also called Leviathan and Behemoth (Job 40). “Dagon’s head and the two palms of his hands were cut off upon the threshold” (I Kings 5). Dagon’s head signifies the devil’s pride, from which sin began, because he established idolatry throughout the world. The two palms signify the operation of idolatry; [Col. 0684D] the threshold, the end of impious worship.

### CHAPTER IX. On the heavy hand of the Lord upon the Ashdodites

“The hand of the Lord was heavy upon the Ashdodites; he destroyed them and struck Ashdod and its borders in the most private part of the buttocks” (I Kings 6). Those who receive God’s covenant and love the rearward things of this life—which they ought to reckon as dung (Phil. 3)—were justly tormented in those rearward parts. For those who take up God’s covenant yet look back and do not strip themselves of former vanity are like those who placed the captive ark of God beside their idols.

And the old things indeed fall, even against their will: “All flesh is grass, and human glory like the flower of the field. The grass withered and the flower fell” (Isa. 60 [materially uncertain citation; cf. Isa. 40]). But the ark of the Lord—that is, the hidden covenant of the kingdom of heaven, where God’s everlasting Word is—remains for ever.

[Col. 0685A] The five golden hemorrhoids and five mice which the Philistines made after their plague and brought to the ark signify that fleshly persons devoted to the body’s five senses, when corrected by the Lord, acknowledge their crimes, confess that they have been justly struck, and, though compelled, are changed for the better. This is well signified by the five cities of the Philistines—Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, Gath, Ekron—which represent those who follow the acts of the outward person.

Ashdod means “fire of the father,” or “burning”; Gaza, “strength”; Ashkelon, “infamous fire” or “ignoble fire”; Gath, “winepress”; Ekron, “instruction of sorrow” or “of barrenness.” For every infamous and ignoble desire, inflamed by the devil, urged on by hostile powers, and as though pressed out in the winepress of wickedness, pours out wine of bitterness in corrupt teaching and perverse action. It must therefore tend toward death, where there is everlasting sorrow and perpetual barrenness.

The ark of the Lord was in the region of the Philistines for seven months. The number seven signifies the totality of times, which pass in the sevenfold number of days, and signifies that God’s covenant will remain among the Gentiles until the consummation of the age.

### CHAPTER X. On the two cows that brought back the ark

[Col. 0685C] “Taking two cows, they yoked them to a cart, shut up their calves at home, and placed the ark of God upon the cart. The cows went straight ahead by the road leading to Beth-shemesh; they proceeded along one road, going and lowing, and did not turn aside either to the right or to the left” (I Kings 6).

Beth-shemesh means “house of the sun.” If, therefore, we are tending toward the dwelling of the eternal Sun, let us not turn aside from God’s way because of fleshly affections. We must consider that the cows fastened to the cart under the ark of God go on and groan, yet do not bend their steps from the road. So God’s preachers, and all believers within the Church, ought to sympathize with their neighbours through charity, yet not wander from God’s way through compassion.

For the ark of God set upon the cart to proceed to Beth-shemesh is to draw near, through heavenly knowledge, to the dwelling-place of inward light. [Col. 0685D] We truly do this when we do not turn aside because of affection for those near to us. Thus those who carry the ark of God through inward knowledge, being placed beneath the yoke of the sacred Law, ought to proceed: so that their compassion for their neighbours’ necessities may not make them turn aside from the path of righteousness they have begun.

Their need ought indeed to hold our mind, but not turn it aside, lest that mind either be hard because it is untouched by affection, or, being touched too much, become slack in weeping.

### CHAPTER XI. That the children of Israel asked for a king

[Col. 0685D]

“The elders of Israel assembled and came to Samuel at Ramah, and said to him: ‘Behold, you are old, [Col. 0686A] and your sons do not walk in your ways. Appoint for us a king to judge us, as all the nations have’” (I Kings 8).

“There was a man of Benjamin named Kish, son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Bechorath, son of Zareth, son of Aphiah, a Benjamite, mighty in strength. He had a son named Saul. The asses of Kish, Saul’s father, had been lost; and Kish said to his son Saul: ‘Take with you one of the servants; arise, go, and seek the asses.’ He searched and came to Samuel, and Samuel brought him into the dining-room and gave him a place among those invited to the meal” (I Kings 9). “And Samuel took a little vessel of oil and anointed him king” (I Kings 10).

Saul, who was made king over Israel when God was offended, signifies the Jews. For as he became hard, proud, and severe, so as to press them down with a servile burden rather than set them free, so the Jewish people, although anointed [Col. 0686B] in priests and kings, nevertheless—because it was the son of the slave woman who bears children unto bondage—could never attain perfect freedom through that anointing, particularly because it refused to receive Christ the king, meek and humble, by whose rule it could have been freed.

Saul means “petition.” He was of Benjamin’s stock, in this genealogical sequence: son of Kish, son of Abiel, son of Zeror, son of Bechorath. These names aptly express the type of the Jews. Benjamin means “son of the right hand”; Kish, “hard,” “vomit of a man,” or “a vomiting man”; Abiel, “my father is God”; Zeror, “little” or “turbulent”; Bechorath, “firstborn son.”

Israel, therefore, God’s firstborn, whose Father [Col. 0686C] was God, was a son of the right hand, because it often prevailed over its enemies through God’s help. But since it was always ungrateful for God’s benefits and stiff-necked, it broke out into blasphemy, becoming small from great and turbulent from peaceful.

Saul’s seeking his father’s asses signifies that the Jews, following the folly of fleshly perception, seek the world’s luxury through wandering errors. For an ass is a brute and lustful animal. Coming to the prophet—that is, to Moses—they heard that the asses had been found: that is, they learned that they would eat the goods of the land. From him they were also promised both the oil of anointing and the governance of the kingdom, by which for a time they might deliver their brothers from their enemies’ hand.

[Col. 0686D] Samuel’s bringing Saul up to the high place and giving him refreshment there signifies Moses and the prophets inviting the Hebrew people by their teachings to higher things, so that, refreshed by spiritual knowledge, it might stand on the height of virtues and not relapse into vices. Samuel took a little vessel of oil. A *lenticula* is a square earthen vessel having an opening, by which the frailty of the kingdom is signified.

### CHAPTER XII. Again on Saul

According to another figure, Saul (I Kings 11) signifies Christ. Saul, seeking his father’s asses, was taken up as king; and the Savior, sent by the Father to the sheep that were lost of the house of Israel, was appointed king over all the people. For the asses signify the same thing as the sheep. Saul was anointed by Samuel, and the Only-begotten was anointed by the spiritual Father. [Col. 0687A] Saul towered above others from the shoulder upward, because Christ, our head, is above us.

### CHAPTER XIII. On Nahash king of the Ammonites and Jabesh-gilead

“Nahash the Ammonite went up and began to fight against Jabesh-gilead. All the men of Jabesh-gilead said to Nahash: ‘Make a covenant with us, and we will serve you.’ Nahash the Ammonite replied: ‘On this condition I will make a treaty with you: that I may put out the right eyes of all of you.’”

Nahash’s war and his army against Israel signify the devil’s and heretics’ war against the Church. Nahash means “serpent”; Ammon, “oppressing,” “straitening,” or “people of sorrow”; Jabesh, “dried up”; Gilead, “heap of testimony.” Nahash therefore signifies the ancient serpent, who is [Col. 0687B] prince of the Ammonites—that is, of heretics. They are fittingly called a people of sorrow, because they do not possess the joy of the Holy Spirit. He proposed a covenant with the people of the Church in order to put out all their right eyes and take away the sight of sound and orthodox faith. For he wishes to have them as confederates in such a way that, retaining the left eye, they think only what is corrupt and belongs to the left.

But the mind of the faithful, dried from every defilement of vice, gathers a heap of testimony—that is, the sayings of Holy Scripture—with which it may manfully resist enemies. Saul with three thousand defeats Nahash and his army when Christ, through faithful teachers distinguished by faith in the Trinity, routs the devil’s and heretics’ cunning devices and drives them from the Church’s [Col. 0687C] doors. “He struck them from the morning watch until the sun grew hot” (I Kings 11): that is, from the clear knowledge of faith’s beginning to the ardour of perfect love.

### CHAPTER XIV. On the three thousand chosen by Saul

[Col. 0687C]

“Saul chose for himself three thousand men of Israel: two thousand were with Saul at Michmash and on Mount Bethel, but a thousand were with Jonathan at Gibeah of Benjamin. He dismissed the rest of the people, each to his own tent. And Jonathan struck the Philistine garrison” (I Kings 15 [materially uncertain citation; cf. I Kings 13]).

The three thousand Israelites were rightly chosen to fight against the Philistines; for only those are fit to fight against the Church’s enemies who possess the perfect faith of the Trinity, [Col. 0687D] in which they can resist enemies from a superior position. He dismissed the remaining people to their station—that is, to their tents—when Christ left the remaining nations in sins.

And the people with Saul were afflicted; the Hebrews went down into the Philistines’ camp; others hid in caves; and all the people with Saul were terrified. The Philistines are heretics who, conspiring together against the Church with a common purpose, attempt to ravage it. Some join them in their united faith while afraid to confess the faith openly and so hide as though in caverns. Various sects, bound by one chain of impiety, range about to deceive. The horsemen are those puffed up with power who aid heretics. The common crowd, like sand, is the multitude gathered by heretical persuasion. The men remaining with Saul [Col. 0688A] are Catholics firmly adhering to Christ.

### CHAPTER XV. On the fact that no blacksmith was found in the land of Israel

“No blacksmith was found in all the land of Israel” (I Kings 13), for the Philistines had taken care lest the Hebrews perhaps make sword or spear. The devil, through pagans, heretics, and false Christians, strives to prevent there being teachers in the Church who make spiritual weapons and furnish them to us for battle. Pagans prevented Christians from being trained in the liberal arts; heretics also persuaded rulers that Catholic defenders of the Church should be driven into exile, so that they might more easily seduce the deserted people.

Even now, in the Church’s peace, [Col. 0688B] that same ancient enemy similarly strives to turn away from diligent teaching as many as he can of those who rule peoples, lest they bestow the gifts of truth upon their subjects, so that he may more easily deceive them unawares. “Through the devil’s envy death entered the world” (Wis. 2). Those who belong to his party imitate him. Hence the devil is bound by a double guilt: pride, by which he fell; and envy, by which he strives to cast down others.

The Philistines mean “double ruin”; the Hebrews, “those passing over”: “for here we have no abiding city, but seek the one to come” (Heb. 13).

### CHAPTER XVI. On Jonathan and his armor-bearer

[Col. 0688B]

Jonathan said to his young armor-bearer: “Come, let us cross over to the Philistines’ garrison.” Now between the ascents by which Jonathan tried to cross over to the Philistines’ garrison there were high rocks on either side, and cliffs steeply cut off here and there like teeth [Col. 0688C] (I Kings 14).

Jonathan means “gift of the dove.” These are those filled with the gift of the Holy Spirit, through whom the Lord scatters the assemblies of heretics and puts them to flight. His armor-bearer signifies spiritual disciples, who undertake not a level but a steep way. For priests cannot resist enemies unless they proceed along the narrow way, moving between both Testaments and between prosperity and adversity, as though between two rocks on the right and left, and with all their mind strive toward the heights of contemplation.

Jonathan, however, crosses over to the enemies only when provoked, [Col. 0688D] because Catholics do not initiate contention against heretics unless first provoked to conflict. Jonathan strikes down enemies in the cultivated field; teachers conquer heretics in meditation upon Scripture.

### CHAPTER XVII. On Jonathan and the honey he tasted

[Col. 0688D]

“Jonathan stretched out the end of the rod which he held in his hand, dipped it in a honeycomb, brought his hand to his mouth, and his eyes were enlightened” (I Kings 14). Jonathan, “gift of the dove,” here signifies those who, having received the grace of the Holy Spirit, prepare to despise the world’s enticements. For no one can fight manfully against spiritual Philistines—that is, demons—who cannot avoid the world’s sweetness.

His eyes were enlightened, not so that he might see—he had seen before—but so that he might discern, having touched what was forbidden. [Col. 0689A] For then that fall, as in Adam’s case, made him attentive and rendered him ashamed. By this deed everyone who wishes to serve as a soldier of God is warned that all the enticements of pleasures must be despised. “The lips of a harlot drip honey” (Prov. 5): that is, fleshly pleasure offers unlawful delight.

Jonathan is mystically understood to have tasted of this honey; detected by lot, he was scarcely freed by the people’s prayers. It is therefore plain that one overcome by worldly pleasure needs the intercession of the saints and the prayers of brethren. For the more obstinately someone resists the united counsel of ecclesiastical rule, the greater is the help of many that he needs, so that one who cannot be saved by his own merit may, reconciled through others’ devout prayers, be delivered from imminent danger. Therefore the people delivered Jonathan so that he would not [Col. 0689B] die.

Past good deeds are of great benefit. For unless Jonathan’s former good deeds had aided him, he would not have escaped the evils that threatened him. For God is not unjust so as to forget good works (Heb. 6).

### CHAPTER XVIII. On Saul’s rejection

“The word of the Lord came to Samuel, saying: ‘I repent that I have appointed Saul king.’ And Samuel said to Saul: ‘Though you were little in your own eyes, were you not made head of the tribes of Israel?’” (I Kings 15).

What is rejected by this rebuke except the pride of the king who had been raised high? Every prelate can and ought beneficially to apply it to his own correction. It is as though it were plainly said: When you regarded yourself as little, I made you great above others. But because [Col. 0689C] you regard yourself as great, you are judged little by me.

Therefore, when David was despised for dancing before the ark of the Lord with the power of his kingdom, he said: “I will play, and I will become more contemptible than I have become, and I will be humble in my own eyes” (II Kings 6). If, therefore, holy men think lowly things of themselves even when they perform mighty deeds, what will those say in their defense who swell with pride without any work of virtue?

Yet even if good works of every kind are present, they are nothing unless seasoned with humility. An admirable action joined to self-exaltation does not lift up but weighs down. Whoever gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind; and from the very source from which he appears to bear something, he is more grievously blinded. Therefore, in all that we do, let us retain humility as the root of good work. Let us look not at those over whom we are already superior, but at those to whom we are still inferior, so that, setting before ourselves the examples of better persons, we may always be able to ascend to greater things through humility.

### CHAPTER XIX. On the virtue of obedience

[Col. 0689D]

“Does the Lord desire holocausts and sacrifices, rather than that the Lord’s voice should be obeyed?” (I Kings 15). Since a suitable occasion has presented itself for displaying the virtue of obedience, it is pleasing to examine it a little more attentively and carefully, and to show how great is its merit. (Gregory, *Moralia*, book 25.)

For obedience alone is the virtue that implants the other virtues in the mind and preserves them once implanted. Therefore the first human being received a command to keep, so that, if he wished to submit himself obediently to it, [Col. 0690A] he might attain eternal blessedness without labor. Hence Samuel again says: “Obedience is better than sacrifice, and listening than offering the fat of rams” (I Kings 15), because “to resist is as the sin of divination, and to refuse compliance as the crime of idolatry.”

Obedience is rightly preferred to sacrifices, because in sacrifices another’s flesh is slain, whereas in obedience one’s own will is slain. Thus each person appeases God more swiftly insofar as, before God’s eyes, he sacrifices himself with the sword of the command by repressing the pride of his own choice. On the other hand, disobedience is called the sin of divination, so that the greatness of obedience’s virtue may be shown. What is thought of its praise is thus better made evident by its opposite. For if resistance is as the sin of divination, and refusal to comply as the crime of idolatry, [Col. 0690B] obedience alone possesses the merit of faith; without it anyone is proved faithless, even though he seems to be faithful.

Hence Solomon, in demonstrating obedience, says: “An obedient man speaks victories” (Prov. 21). An obedient person speaks victory because, while we humbly submit to another’s voice, we overcome ourselves in the heart.

But because at times the prosperous things of this world are commanded us, while at times adverse things are commanded, we must take the greatest care to consider this: obedience is sometimes nonexistent if it has something of its own; but at other times, if it has nothing of its own, it is very slight. For when worldly success is commanded, when a higher position is ordered, the one who obeys in receiving these things empties the virtue of obedience for himself if he also longs for them [Col. 0690C] by his own desire. For one does not guide oneself under obedience when, in receiving life’s prosperity, one serves the desire of one’s own ambition.

Again, when contempt for the world is commanded, when acquiring reproaches and insults is ordered, unless the mind itself also desires these things, one diminishes one’s own merit of obedience by descending unwillingly and reluctantly to things despised in this life. Obedience is indeed brought to loss when one’s own desires do not in some degree accompany the mind in accepting the reproaches of this age.

Thus obedience, in adversity, must have something of its own; and again, in prosperity, it must have nothing at all of its own. In this way, in adversity it is more glorious insofar as it is joined more closely to the divine order even in desire; and in prosperity it is more humble insofar as the present glory which it receives from God is more deeply separated from the mind.

[Col. 0690D] But we show the weight of this virtue better if we recall the deeds of two citizens of the heavenly country. Moses humbly refuses the leadership of the people, saying: “I beseech you, Lord, I am not eloquent—neither yesterday nor the day before, nor since you began speaking to your servant; for I am slow and impeded of tongue. Send whom you will send” (Exod. 4). Thus, setting himself aside, he asks for another. Paul likewise, gladly embracing the adversities of the world, boldly says: “I am ready not only to be bound but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of Jesus” (Acts 21).

## BOOK VI. ON I AND II KINGS—FROM DAVID TO SOLOMON

[Col. 0691]

### CHAPTER I. On the tearing of Samuel’s cloak

[Col. 0691A]

“The Lord has torn the kingdom of Israel from you today and has given it to your neighbour, better than you” (I Kings 15), or, according to another reading, “good above you.” Saul, to whom this is said, reigned over Israel for forty years, as long as David reigned, and heard this at the beginning of his reign. We should understand, therefore, that this was said to him because none of his offspring would reign, and we should look to David’s line, from whom Christ was born according to the flesh, to reign under the New Testament not carnally but spiritually. Of him it is said: “He will give it to your neighbour, good above you” (ibid.), that is, better; or “above you” because, since he is always good, it is written of him: “Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool [Col. 0691B] of your feet” (Ps. 109).

The expression “your neighbour” refers to kinship according to the flesh. For Christ is from Israel according to the flesh, as Saul also was. Thus this man, who was the first to lose the kingdom, figuratively bore the person of the people of Israel, from whom Christ took the kingdom as from his persecutor. Yet there was also an Israel in whom there was no guile, like a lily among thorns (Song 2), and like wheat among chaff: from Israel came the apostles, from Israel the martyrs, Stephen being first among them; from Israel came the Churches magnifying God.

### CHAPTER II. On Saul, David, and his harp
The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an evil spirit from the Lord troubled him. And Saul’s servants said to him: “Behold, an evil spirit from the Lord troubles you. Let our lord the king [Col. 0691C] therefore command, and let your servants who are before you seek out a man skilled in playing the lyre, so that, whenever the evil spirit from the Lord seizes you, he may play with his hand, and you may bear it more lightly” (1 Sam. 16).

The evil spirit from the Lord is the devil. Although he always seeks the affliction of the righteous, nevertheless, unless he receives authority from God, he has no power to bring a temptation to its point of action. Therefore the devil’s power, because it is from the Lord, can only be just; but his whole will is unjust. For of himself he unjustly desires to tempt; but God justly permits those who are to be tempted, and to the extent to which they are to be tempted, to be tempted. Therefore this spirit is called both “of the Lord” and “evil”: “of the Lord,” by permission of just power; “evil,” through the desire of an unjust will [Col. 0691D]. Thus he ought not to be feared, since he can do nothing except what he is permitted to do. For although malice is not from the Lord, no power exists except from the Lord.

David was indeed trained in musical songs. The rational and measured harmony of differing sounds, joined together in concordant variety, signifies the unity of the ordered Church, which daily resounds in diverse ways and is melodiously ordered with mystical sweetness [Col. 0692A]. David, still a boy, singing sweetly—indeed, powerfully—upon the lyre, restrained the evil spirit that troubled Saul: not because his lyre possessed such power, but because, through the wood and the stretching of the strings, it mystically bore the figure of Christ’s cross, which even then was putting demons to flight.

Tropologically, moreover, by this action we are taught to show compassion toward our neighbour. For often a proud rich man must be appeased by the gentleness of exhortation, because severe wounds are often softened by mild poultices, and the frenzy of madmen is often brought back to health when the physician uses gentleness. When concession is made to them in sweetness, the sickness of madness is alleviated. Nor should it be carelessly overlooked that, when the hostile spirit attacked Saul [Col. 0692B], David took up the lyre and soothed his madness. For what is signified by Saul, if not the pride of the powerful? And what is indicated by David, if not the humble life of the saints? Therefore, when Saul is seized by an unclean spirit, his madness is moderated as David sings; because, when the minds of the powerful are driven into fury by pride, it is fitting that they should be recalled to mental health by the tranquillity of our speech, as though by the sweetness of a lyre.

## CHAPTER III. Concerning the battle-line of Israel and the Philistines

Israel drew up its battle-line, and the Philistines also were ready (1 Sam. 17). The battle of the Philistines against Israel may fittingly be understood as the warfare of evil spirits against the Church of God. Goliath, however, signifies the devil’s pride, whom David—that is, Christ—overthrew in single combat [Col. 0692C] and delivered God’s people from fear of him.

David killed the lion and the bear: that is, the devil and Antichrist; the one now lying secretly in wait for human beings, the other later raging most openly. Pride challenged humility; the devil challenged Christ. David took up the weapons of war, which he could not carry because of his age, and laid them aside. And he took five stones from the stream and put them into the shepherd’s bag. Thus Christ, at the time of the New Testament, in order to disclose and commend grace, laid aside the bodily sacraments of the law. These were not imposed upon the Gentiles; we read of them in the old law and do not observe them, but understand that they were set forth and established for some signification [Col. 0692D]. He laid aside these weapons as the burdens of the old law, and took up the law itself. For the five stones signify the books of Moses.

He therefore took five stones from the stream (ibid.), that is, from the age; for the mortal age flows away. They were like stones in the stream—that is, among that first people. They were useless and idle, and profited nothing; the stream flowed over them [Col. 0693A], but David received grace so that the law might become useful. For the law cannot be fulfilled without grace. He took five stones and cast one. Five books were chosen, but unity prevailed, as the Apostle says: “Bearing with one another in charity, being diligent to preserve the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. For the fullness of the law is love” (Eph. 4).

David prevailed against the Philistine with sling and stone, and, having struck the Philistine, killed him. And because David had no sword in his hand, he took away the Philistine’s sword and cut off his head (1 Sam. 17). Christ likewise killed the devil with his own weapons when the magi believed—those whom he held in his hand and by means of whom he slaughtered other souls. For they turned their tongues against the devil, and thus Goliath’s head was cut off with his own sword.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the Philistines and Goliath again

[Col. 0693B]

The Philistines are demons; Goliath is their head, who could not be overcome before the Lord’s coming. Gath, Goliath’s city, is interpreted “winepress.” This is the world and hell, in which he trampled people down as those enslaved to sins. Goliath’s height is the pride of the devil, through which he gained dominion over his children, lifting himself up like a palm tree. Goliath’s weapons are the devil’s cunning devices for doing harm.

David was sent by his father to visit his brothers; Christ likewise was sent by God the Father to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. David brought his brothers an ephah of parched grain—that is, a measure of three modii—and Christ commended to believers the mystery of the Holy Trinity. David brought ten cheeses to the commander [Col. 0693C], and Christ delivered the Decalogue to believers.

## CHAPTER V. Concerning the love of Jonathan and David

Jonathan’s soul was bound to David’s soul, and Jonathan loved him. Therefore Jonathan stripped himself of the tunic with which he was clothed and gave it to David, together with his remaining garments, even to his sword, and his bow, even to his belt (1 Sam. 18).

Jonathan signifies those Jews who believed in Christ; for, having received the grace of the Holy Spirit, they left behind everything that they might have possessed in the world and followed the Redeemer himself for Christ’s love. Hence Peter says: “Behold, we have left all things and followed you” (Matt. 19). For just as Jonathan gave David his garments, from tunic to belt, so believers [Col. 0693D] devoted everything that they possessed to Christ’s service.

## CHAPTER VI. Concerning Jonathan and David hidden in the field

Jonathan came into the field according to David’s arrangement, with a young boy beside him. And he said to his boy: “Go and bring me the arrows which I shoot.” And when the boy had run, he shot another arrow beyond the boy (1 Sam. 20).

What does it mean that Jonathan, wishing to preserve David while he lay hidden in the field beside the stone, shot two arrows, which the young boy, not knowing what he was doing, gathered and brought back into the city? It means that the Father kept his only-begotten Son, whom he had determined to send for the salvation of the human race, hidden in the letter of the law, while the Jews did not understand. David [Col. 0694A] was therefore hidden in the field, and Christ was concealed in the world, of whom John says: “He was in the world, and the world was made through him, and the world did not know him” (John 1).

He sat beside the stone because he was written upon the tablets of the law, as in the words: “The Lord your God is one God, and you shall not take the name of your God in vain” (Deut. 15). Saul, proud and envious, hating David, who was simple and humble, judged him to be a son of death as he sat at the feast; and Jewish perfidy, amid the Paschal feasts, plotted the Lord’s death. When morning dawned, Jonathan came, and—together with the rest, as we have stated above—he shot an arrow and shot another. So too God the Father, when the morning of faith dawned, first brought forth the testimony of the law concerning Christ, and then sent the prophets.

Jonathan’s boy gathered the arrows [Col. 0694B] and brought them to his lord, wholly unaware of what was happening. So also the Jewish people, carrying the books of the law and the prophets and honouring them as though divinely written, did not know him whom Moses and the prophets had foretold.

## CHAPTER VII. Concerning David’s changing his countenance before Achish

David changed his countenance before Achish, and stumbled among their hands; he struck against the doors of the gate, and his saliva ran down upon his beard (1 Sam. 21).

Achish is interpreted “How is it?” and thereby ignorance is signified. For it is the expression of one who marvels and does not recognize; this was fulfilled in the Jews, who, when they saw Christ, did not recognize him, before whom [Col. 0694C] he changed his countenance and departed. For there were there carnal precepts of the law. There was sacrifice according to the order of Aaron; but he established from his own body a sacrifice according to the order of Melchizedek. Therefore he changed his countenance in sacrifice; he changed it in the commandments, giving another Testament and rendering void the carnal observance.

“He stumbled among their hands” (ibid.) when they seized and crucified him. “And he fell down at the gate’s entrance” (ibid.), that is, he humbled himself at the beginning of our faith. The entrance of the gate is the beginning of faith. The Church begins from faith and reaches unto sight. That saliva, as though of a madman, ran down over his beard, the Apostle explains when he says: “We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews indeed a stumbling-block, but to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. 1). Saliva [Col. 0694D] signifies weakness. “But what is weak in God is stronger than men” (ibid.). The saliva flows through the beard: for as weakness is displayed in the saliva, so strength is displayed in the beard. He therefore concealed his strength in the body of his weakness; and what was weakened outwardly appeared like saliva, while inwardly divine power lay hidden like a beard.

## CHAPTER VIII. Concerning those who came together to David

Those who were in distress, oppressed by debt, and bitter in spirit gathered to David; and he became their leader (1 Sam. 22). David—that is, Christ—becomes the leader of those oppressed by debt: namely, the tribute of sins, which they pay to the devil while they present their members to serve iniquity unto iniquity [Col. 0695A] (Rom. 6). They must be bitter in spirit, so that they may practise repentance in the bitterness of their soul and come to David—that is, to Christ, desired by all—that he may become their leader. For he is the one appointed by God judge of the living and the dead (Acts 10), the Prince of Peace (Isa. 9), whose kingdom shall have no end (Luke 1).

## CHAPTER IX. Concerning the Ziphites

The Ziphites went up to Saul at Gibeah, saying: “Is not David hiding among us in the fortified places of the forest?” (1 Sam. 24). “Ziphites” is interpreted “flourishing,” and they signify the Jews who, desiring the flower of an earthly kingdom, plotted the killing with their rulers. When they seized Christ betrayed by his disciple and delivered him to the governor to be crucified [Col. 0695B], they acted thus. So too the flourishing people of this age betray Christ in his members to the powers of this world.

## CHAPTER X. Concerning David’s cutting off the hem of Saul’s cloak

Saul entered a cave to relieve himself, and David cut off the hem of his cloak; and David’s heart smote him because he had cut off the hem of the king’s garment (1 Sam. 25).

What is signified by Saul except evil rulers? What is signified by David except good subjects? Saul’s relieving his belly, therefore, means that wicked superiors extend the malice conceived in their heart into deeds of evil odour, displaying their harmful inward thoughts by carrying them out in outward acts. Yet David fears to strike him: that is, devoutly minded subjects, abstaining from every plague of detraction [Col. 0695C], do not strike the life of their superiors with the sword of the tongue, even when they rebuke them for imperfection.

If, because of weakness, they can scarcely restrain themselves from speaking—yet they speak humbly, not of the greatest and outward evils of their superiors, but only of some lesser matters—they silently cut off, as it were, the hem of the cloak. For, while they secretly speak against the dignity set over them, even without harmful intent, they seem, as it were, to defile the garment of the king placed above them. Yet they return to themselves and most vehemently rebuke themselves even for the slightest contention of speech. Hence it is rightly written there: “After these things David’s heart smote him because he had cut off the hem of Saul’s cloak.”

The deeds of superiors ought not to be struck with the sword of the mouth [Col. 0695D], even when they are rightly judged deserving of rebuke. But if the tongue should slip against them even in the smallest matters, the heart must be pressed down through the affliction of repentance, so that it may return to itself; and, when it speaks against authority set over it, it must dread the judgment against itself of him by whom that authority was placed over it. For when we speak against superiors, we oppose the ordinance of him who set them over us. Hence Moses too, when he learned that the people were complaining against himself and Aaron, said: “For what are we? Your murmuring is not against us, but against the Lord” (Exod. 16).

## CHAPTER XI. Concerning Abigail’s words to David

“If a man should ever rise up pursuing you and seeking your life, the life of my lord shall be kept, as in a bundle of the living, with the Lord God. [Col. 0696A] But the life of your enemies shall be whirled around as by the force and circle of a sling” (1 Sam. 25).

With a most beautiful comparison she distinguishes the condition of the righteous and the reprobate. She calls the souls of the former living, thereby suggesting that those of the latter are, by contrast, overtaken by spiritual death, according to the saying: “The soul that sins, it shall die” (Ezek. 18). She compares these to a bundle, those to a sling-stone. A bundle is bound together so that it may remain whole and be preserved. A stone is put into a sling in order to be thrown away.

Thus, in this age, the elect are bound tightly by the pressures of tribulations, so that, admonished by these, they may be more closely joined to one another by mutual love; and, thus united in the unity of faith, they may be preserved for ever, mutually, by the hand of their Redeemer. But the reprobate, the more freely they are allowed to spread themselves abroad in this life in their own pleasures [Col. 0696B], are cast the farther away in the life to come from the glory of the divine vision; for they are driven away from the Lord’s hand.

Moreover, she wonderfully describes the almighty providence of the Redeemer when she says that the soul of the holy man is kept with him like a bundle of the living. For just as it is easy to preserve any bundle of grass or hay held in one’s hand, so the power of our Lord and Saviour guards the elect throughout the world, from the beginning to the end of the age, without effort, lest any one of them perish for any reason. Hence he himself says in the Gospel: “No one shall snatch them out of my hand” (John 10).

## CHAPTER XII. Concerning Abigail and Nabal

Abigail did not tell her husband Nabal anything, small or great, until morning. But at dawn, when Nabal had digested the wine [Col. 0696C], his wife told him these words (1 Sam. 25).

We correct the angry better if, in the very agitation of anger, we avoid confrontation. For while disturbed, they do not know what they hear; but when they return to themselves, they receive words of exhortation all the more willingly because they are ashamed that they have been so patiently endured. To a mind drunk with rage, every right thing that is said appears perverse. Hence Abigail laudably kept silent concerning his fault while Nabal was drunk, and laudably spoke when the wine had been digested. For this reason he was able to recognize the evil that he had said or done: because he did not hear it while drunk.

## CHAPTER XIII. Concerning the Amalekites

When David and his men came to Ziklag on the third day [Col. 0696D], the Amalekites had made an attack from the south upon Ziklag, burned it with fire, and carried away captive the women from it (1 Sam. 30).

We should consider what it means that the Amalekites invade Ziklag and take spoil. The Amalekites are called “the licking people.” What, then, is signified by the licking people except the minds of worldly persons? They “lick,” as it were, all earthly things by embracing them, while delighting only in temporal things. For the licking people make spoil, as it were, when those who love earthly things increase their gains from the losses of others. And they do this while David is absent, because they neglect to keep the Redeemer before the eyes of their heart.

David found on the road an Egyptian boy whom the Amalekite had left sick on the journey. He refreshed him with food, made him the guide of his route, pursued the Amalekite [Col. 0697A], and utterly destroyed him. What does it mean that the Egyptian boy grows weary on the Amalekite’s journey, except that a lover of the present age, covered by the blackness of his sin, is often left weak and despised by that very age, so that he cannot run along with it but lies inactive, broken by adversity? But David finds him, because our Redeemer, truly strong of hand, sometimes finds those whom worldly glory has despised and turns them to his own love. He feeds him with food because he refreshes him with knowledge of the word; he chooses him as a guide for the journey because he even makes him a preacher of himself.

And the one who could not follow the Amalekite becomes David’s guide, because the person whom the world abandoned as unworthy not only receives God into his converted mind, but also carries him through preaching even to other hearts [Col. 0697B]. With this guide, David finds the Amalekites feasting and destroys them; because Christ, through the preaching of those whom the world scorned to have as companions, destroys the world’s joy. Thus those who formerly could not run with worldly people in this world often overcome the minds of worldly people by preaching.

## CHAPTER XIV. Concerning the mountains of Gilboa

“Mountains of Gilboa, let neither dew nor rain come upon you” (2 Sam. 1). What wrong did the mountains of Gilboa commit when Saul died, that neither dew nor rain should fall upon them? But because Gilboa is interpreted “a flowing down,” and through Saul, the anointed one who died, the death of our Mediator is expressed, the mountains of Gilboa fittingly signify the proud hearts of the Jews. While they flow down into the desires of this world, they joined themselves to the death of the Anointed One—that is, of Christ [Col. 0697C]. And because the anointed king dies bodily among them, they are dried up from every dew of grace.

Of them it is pronounced that they cannot be fields of firstfruits (ibid.). For the proud minds of the Hebrews did not produce firstfruits; at the coming of the Redeemer, remaining for the most part in unbelief, they refused to follow the first beginnings of faith. The holy Church, indeed, made fruitful in its firstfruits by a multitude of Gentiles, will scarcely receive, at the end of the world, those Jews whom it finds, gathering them at the end as though they were remnants of crops. Of these remnants Isaiah says: “Though the number of the children of Israel be as the sand of the sea” (Isa. 10), “a remnant shall be saved” [Col. 0697D] (Rom. 9).

Yet the mountains of Gilboa may be cursed by the prophet’s mouth for this reason: that when no fruit arises from the parched earth, the landowners may be struck by the loss of barrenness, so that they themselves may receive the sentence of curse who, as their wickedness deserved, were found worthy to admit the king’s death among themselves.

## CHAPTER XV. Concerning the same

The devout prophet David figuratively mourns Saul and Jonathan (2 Sam. 1). Although they had been powerful and always prevailed over their enemies, wounded by enemies, they immediately fell wounded in the midst of battle. So Christians mourn those who, while resisting demons, slip upon the slippery ground of the age. For the mountains of Gilboa are interpreted “slippery.” And, abandoning hope of recovery [Col. 0698A], they kill themselves with the sword of their own despair, just as Saul fell upon his own sword.

But the Philistines—that is, the demons—strip virtues from the slain and ascribe the victory to their own virtue or strength; yet such things happen by God’s permission. But our David laments in his elect the fall of those who collapse, and forbids it to be published in the cities of the Allophyles—that is, he commands the faithful to guard themselves carefully. Let them have the shield of faith, the breastplate of righteousness, the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Holy Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. 6), with which they may resist adversaries and, not being shamefully overcome, give no joy to their enemies.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning David’s ascent to Hebron

David went up to Hebron, with his two wives. David also brought up the men who were with him, each one with his household (2 Sam. 2).

David’s ascent to Hebron with his two wives signifies the calling of the two peoples into the catholic Church. For Hebron is interpreted “marriage”; the Church alone is the bride of the heavenly king. David brought there each man with his household, because individual believers are called to that fellowship through evangelical preaching. “There is no distinction between Jew and Greek” (Rom. 10).

The number of days during which David stayed in Hebron, ruling over the house of Judah, was seven years and six months [Col. 0698B]. David reigned seven years and six months in Hebron, which is interpreted “marriage” or “everlasting vision,” because Christ reigns in the Church, which is his bride, throughout all the time of this life—which runs its course in the sevenfold number of days—according to the saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). And because, after the completion of six—that is, the perfection of good work—he will lead his elect to the second Sabbath, that is, eternal rest, where they will enjoy the perpetual vision of God [Col. 0698C].

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning Abner and Asahel

Abner spoke to Asahel: “Withdraw; do not follow me, lest I be compelled to strike you through to the ground.” But he despised to listen and would not turn aside. Therefore Abner struck him in the groin with the butt end of the spear and pierced him through; and he died in the same place (2 Sam. 2).

Asahel signifies those whom raging fury carries away violently into destruction [Col. 0698D]. They must be avoided in the very onset of their fury with greater caution in proportion as they are seized by greater madness. Hence Abner, whose name in our language means “lamp of the father,” flees; because the speech of teachers, which indicates the heavenly light, when it perceives a brother’s fury, refrains from hurling the darts of words back against one who is angry, as though it does not wish to strike its pursuer.

But when angry people moderate themselves by no consideration and, like Asahel, do not cease to pursue and rage, those who try to restrain the furious must not rise up into anger themselves. Rather, they must display whatever tranquillity they possess, and subtly utter certain things by which they may prick the mind of the raging person indirectly. Hence Abner pierced his pursuer not with the point but with the butt end of the spear. To strike with the point is to meet an attack with the open rebuke [Col. 0699A] of correction.
