But to strike a pursuer with the reversed spear is to touch a raging person tranquilly in certain respects, and, as it were, to overcome while sparing him.

Asahel immediately falls, because when agitated minds feel themselves spared and yet are inwardly touched by the reasoning of replies beneath tranquillity, they immediately fall from the position into which they had raised themselves. Thus those who recoil from the onset of their fury under the blow of gentleness die, as it were, without iron.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the long conflict between the house of David and the house of Saul

There was a long conflict between the house of David and the house of Saul. But David was always advancing and growing stronger in himself, while the house of Saul was daily diminishing (2 Sam. 3).

The house of David is the heavenly Jerusalem, which partly journeys on earth and partly reigns in heaven [Col. 0699B]. The house of Saul, the proud and impious king, is Babylon, which makes all nations commit fornication. There is a long conflict between them, because the one who is according to the flesh persecutes the Church, which is according to the Spirit. But the house of David rejoices in the progress and perfection of its children; the house of Saul, in its wickedness, is finally submerged in the depths of the abyss according to its deserts.

## CHAPTER XIX. Concerning the speech which Abner addressed to the elders of Israel

Abner spoke to the elders of Israel, saying: “Both yesterday and the day before yesterday you sought David, that he might reign over you” (2 Sam. 3).

Abner urges all Israel [Col. 0699C] to leave Ish-bosheth, Saul’s son, and come to David, because holy priests, who are called the father’s lamp, filled with the light of faith and knowledge, exhort all nations to despise idol worship, abandon the error of confusion together with its author the devil, and hasten to come to the true David—that is, Christ.

Joab, moreover, who spoke deceitfully to Abner and killed him by striking him in the groin, signifies the ancient enemy, who fraudulently overthrows the faithful and kills them through the contagion of lust. For Joab is interpreted “enemy” or “the father himself.” The devil is the father of all the wicked. Hence: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8). David is free from this killing, because God tempts no one (James 1), and he wills all to be saved (1 Tim. 2). But through the envy of the devil [Col. 0699D], death entered into the world (Wis. 2). Joab may also, in name and person, signify the Jewish people, who were always enemies of the preachers of faith and everywhere persecuted Christ’s faith.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning the sons of Rimmon and the death of Ish-bosheth

The sons of Rimmon the Beerothite, Rechab and Baanah, came into the house of Ish-bosheth during the heat of the day, while he was sleeping on his bed at noon; and the female keeper of the house, while cleaning wheat, fell asleep. They entered secretly and, taking ears of wheat, struck him in the groin (2 Sam. 4).

(Gregory, *Morals*, I.) The female keeper cleans the wheat when the guard of the mind separates virtues from vices by discernment. If she falls asleep, she admits ambushers to the death of her own lord; because, when the watchfulness of discernment ceases [Col. 0700A], it opens a way for evil spirits to kill the soul. Entering, they take away the ears of wheat because they remove the shoots of blessed thoughts; and they strike in the groin because they kill the strength of the heart by fleshly delight. To strike in the groin is to pierce the life of the mind by the pleasure of the flesh.

Ish-bosheth would by no means have succumbed to an unexpected death if he had not assigned a woman—that is, a weak guard—to the entrance of the house, that is, to the entrance of the mind. A strong and watchful understanding ought to be placed over the gates of the heart, one which neither the sleep of negligence overwhelms nor the error of ignorance deceives. Hence Ish-bosheth is rightly said to have been exposed to hostile swords by a female guard. Ish-bosheth means “man of confusion.” The man of confusion is one not fortified by a strong guard of the mind; for while he thinks that he performs virtues [Col. 0700B], unnoticed vices entering in kill him. Therefore the entrance of the mind must be fortified with every strength, lest enemies penetrate it through the opening of negligence or neglected thought.

## CHAPTER XXI. How David captured Jerusalem

David and all the men who were with him went to Jerusalem, to the Jebusite, inhabitant of the land (2 Sam. 5).

David’s driving the Jebusite out of Jerusalem signifies Christ driving contrary powers from the hearts of the faithful and remaining there. “Jebusite” is interpreted “trodden down”; Jerusalem, “vision of peace.” For Christ not only acquired for himself a trophy of glory by destroying through the mystery of the cross every dominion of the devil [Col. 0700C], but also gave his faithful power over every power of the devil. Hence: “Behold, I have given you power to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke 10).

David rightly dwelt in the stronghold of Zion after driving out the blind and the lame, and called it his city; for when Christ expels the crowd of evil spirits and vices from the soul, he dwells there. It is deservedly called the stronghold of Zion—that is, of watchfulness—so that it may rightly be said of it: “His place is made in peace, and his dwelling in Zion. There he broke the powers, the bow, shield, sword, and war” (Ps. 75).

Just as David took the stronghold after first removing the blind and lame who hated David’s life, so the Lord gained dominion in the Church of the Gentiles after first rejecting the scribes [Col. 0700D] and Pharisees, who, blind and lame, hated Christ’s soul—that is, attempted to take away his life. Pipes signify the false knowledge of the world and the doctrines of heretics; the Lord destroys these through Joab—that is, through preachers.

## CHAPTER XXII. Concerning Michal’s pride and David’s humility

Michal, Saul’s daughter, went out to meet David and said: “How glorious the king of Israel was today, uncovering himself before the maidservants of his servants; he was stripped naked as though one of the buffoons should strip himself” (2 Sam. 6).

(Gregory, *Morals*, XXVII.) It is pleasing to consider how great were the gifts of virtues that David received, and how strongly he preserved himself in humility amid them all. Whom would it not have exalted to break the jaws of lions, shatter the limbs of bears [Col. 0701A], be chosen while his elder brothers were passed over, be anointed for the governance of the kingdom while the king was rejected, strike down Goliath, feared by all, with a single stone, bring back numerous foreskins of slain Allophyles at the king’s demand, finally receive the kingdom promised to him, and possess the entire Israelite people without any opposition?

And yet, when he brings back the ark of God to Jerusalem, as though forgetting that he was set over all, he dances before the ark mingled among the people. Since dancing before the ark was, as is believed, a custom of the common people, the king turns himself about in a dance in divine service. Behold: he whom the Lord had singularly set above all despises himself beneath the Lord, both by doing lowly things and by displaying himself in the least things. He does not recall the power of his kingdom; he does not fear becoming contemptible in the eyes of his subjects by dancing; before the ark of him who gave him honour, he does not remember that he was set above others in honour [Col. 0701B]. Before God he performed weak or lowly acts, that by such humility he might strengthen the acts of strength which he had performed before men.

What others think of his deeds I do not know; I marvel more at David dancing than at David fighting. In fighting he subdued enemies; but in dancing before the Lord he conquered himself. When Michal, Saul’s daughter, still mad with the pride of royal lineage, despised him in his humility and said, “How glorious the king of Israel was today, uncovering himself before the maidservants of his servants, and stripped naked like one of the buffoons,” she immediately heard: “I will play before the Lord who chose me rather than your father.” And shortly afterward he also says: “I will play, and I will become more contemptible than I have become [Col. 0701C], and I shall be humble in my own eyes.” It is as though he openly said: “I seek to become contemptible before human beings, because by humility I seek to preserve for myself a kingdom before God.”

There are some who think humbly of themselves and, though placed in honour, reckon themselves nothing but dust and ashes. Yet they shrink from appearing contemptible before people, and, contrary to what they think inwardly about themselves, veil themselves outwardly in a kind of rigid elegance. And there are some who desire to appear contemptible before people and despise themselves by outwardly presenting themselves as abased; yet inwardly, before themselves, they swell as though on account of the very merit of their displayed lowliness, and are so much the more exalted in heart as they more greatly suppress outward appearance of pride.

David perceived both these great wars of pride with careful discernment [Col. 0701D] and separated them by wondrous virtue. That he thought humbly of himself and did not seek honour outwardly, he indicates when he says: “I will play, and I will become more contemptible.” And because, by presenting himself outwardly as contemptible, he did not swell inwardly, he adds: “And I shall be humble in my own eyes.” It is as though he openly said: “As I display myself outwardly in contempt, so I consider myself inwardly.”

What then are those to do whom learning exalts, if David—who knew that the Redeemer would come from his flesh and proclaimed his joys by prophecy—nevertheless pressed down the neck of his heart by the strong heel of discernment, saying: “And I shall be humble in my own eyes”?

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning Hanun and David’s servants

Hanun took David’s servants, shaved off half [Col. 0702A] of their beard, cut off their garments in the middle as far as the buttocks, and dismissed them. When this was reported to David, he sent to meet them. For they were greatly and shamefully humiliated; and David commanded them: “Remain at Jericho until your beards grow, and then return” (2 Sam. 10).

What do these words signify except the devil’s warfare against the Church? Hanun, whose name is interpreted “their sorrow,” signifies the devil, ruler of the Ammonites—that is, of evil spirits—the people of sorrow, always in distress, who desire to oppress or constrict human beings. He shaves half the beard of David’s servants when the devil, by corrupting, stains the speech or conduct of certain preachers. He cuts off their tunics to the groin when he reveals before human eyes the shameful deeds that he persuades them to commit.

These must remain at Jericho until their beards grow, lest they become a reproach and disgrace to the better persons and an anathema to all, until through good diligence the form of the beard—that is, the growth of virtues—arises in them and they are judged worthy to be presented to their king [Col. 0702B]. But our David does not allow his soldiers to remain unavenged. Gathering an army, he avenges the injury done to his own; and he not only now confounds his adversaries through the victory of his saints, but at the last judgment will hand them over, by a just sentence, to be tormented in everlasting fires.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning Rabbah and its king’s diadem
Joab sent messengers to David, saying: “I have fought against [Col. 0702C] Rabbah; the city of waters must be taken. Therefore now gather the remaining part of the people, besiege the city, and take it, lest, when the city has been devastated by me, the victory be credited to my name.” And when David had fought against it, he took it and removed the crown of their king from his head (2 Kings 12).

This victory of David, which Joab began and David himself completed, signifies the victory of our King. For the commander wages war against enemies when the order of preachers sets the shield of faith against the powers of the world. But the victory is referred to Christ, because to him is ascribed all authority and the power of the kingdom. For God is he who works in us both to will and to accomplish (Phil. 2). David takes the crown of the king of the hostile people and makes it his own diadem [Col. 0702D] when Christ, taking the kingdom from the devil, prepares for himself a glorious emblem. What, moreover, is better understood as the crown of the true David than the assembly of the catholic people, which nobly surrounds our king and head, namely Christ, with devoted faith and fittingly crowns him by worthy conduct? For every labor, struggle, and victory of the saints is directed to the honor of the heavenly King. Rabbah is a city of the kingdom of Ammon, now called Philadelphia, and its name means “many.” And in the Gospel it is said: “Many will come from East and West and recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 8).

## CHAPTER XXV. How David Numbered Israel

“The anger of the Lord again burned against Israel. And he stirred David up among them, saying to Joab: ‘Go, number [Col. 0703A] Israel and Judah.’” And he numbered the people. For this reason the Lord sent a plague upon Israel, and seventy thousand men of the people died from Dan as far as Beersheba (2 Kings 24). (GREGORY, *Morals*, 25.)

The actions of rulers are ordered according to the character of their subjects, so that often, because of the evil of the flock, even the life of a truly good shepherd incurs fault. That David who, with God as witness, was praised, that man conscious of God’s secrets, puffed up by a sudden swelling of pride, sinned in numbering the people. Yet the people received punishment while David sinned, because the life of rulers is ordered according to the deserts of their peoples. But the just Judge corrected the fault of the sinner by punishing those through whose fault he had sinned. Yet because he himself, namely, in freely growing proud, was not guiltless [Col. 0703B] of the fault, he too received the punishment of guilt. For the raging wrath which struck the people bodily also cast down the ruler of the people in inward sorrow of heart.

It is certain, however, that the merits of rulers and peoples are so mutually connected that often the life of peoples becomes worse through the fault of pastors, and often the life of pastors is changed through the merit of peoples. But because rulers have their own Judge, it is a matter of great caution for subjects not rashly to judge the lives of those who govern them. For it was not without purpose that the Lord himself scattered the money-changers’ coins and overturned the seats of those selling doves (John 2): clearly signifying that through teachers he judges the lives of peoples, but by himself examines the deeds of teachers. Yet the faults of subjects also, which teachers either overlook because they are similar to them or are unable to judge, are beyond doubt reserved for his judgment.

Therefore, while faith remains unharmed, it is a meritorious virtue to endure whatever belongs to one’s superior; nevertheless, it ought to be suggested with humility, if perhaps what displeases may be corrected. But one must take the greatest care lest an unregulated defense of justice pass into pride [Col. 0704A]; lest, while uprightness is loved incautiously, humility itself, the teacher of uprightness, be lost; lest anyone despise the one set over him because he happens to find something in that person’s conduct to criticize. The mind of a subject is subdued against this swelling of pride by the guard of humility if it constantly attends to its own weakness. For we neglect to examine our own powers truthfully; and because we believe great things about ourselves, we judge strictly those set over us. The less we recognize ourselves, the more we see those whom we strive to criticize.

These are evils often committed by subjects against superiors and by superiors against subjects. Those who preside judge all their subjects to be less wise than themselves; [Col. 0704B] and conversely, those who are subject pass judgment upon their rulers’ actions and think that, if it happened that they held authority, they could have acted better. Hence it commonly happens both that rulers see less prudently what ought to be done, because the very mist of pride darkens their eyes, and that someone who is subject, when he becomes a superior, does what he formerly criticized while subject. And because he does what he had judged, he should at least blush because he judged it.

Therefore, just as superiors must take care lest a higher position exalt their hearts through the opinion that they possess singular wisdom, so subjects must take care lest the deeds of their rulers displease them. But if the life of teachers is rightly criticized, subjects ought nevertheless to revere them even when they displease them. Yet this must be carefully considered: if one whom it is necessary to revere is blameworthy, do not desire to imitate him; nor, if you disdain to imitate someone, scorn to revere him. For a subtle path of uprightness and humility must be maintained: the blameworthy deeds of teachers should displease us, yet the mind of the subject must not depart from preserving reverence for authority. [Col. 0704C]

# BOOK VII. ON 3 AND 4 KINGS—FROM SOLOMON TO THE BABYLONIAN CAPTIVITY

[Col. 0703]

## CHAPTER I. On Solomon’s Various Foods and Horses

[Col. 0703D]

Solomon’s food for each day was thirty *cors* of fine flour and sixty *cors* of meal; ten fat oxen, twenty pasture-fed oxen, and one hundred rams, besides game—stags, gazelles, buffaloes, and fattened birds, etc. (3 Kings 4). Solomon—that is, “peaceful” both in name and in the most serene state of his kingdom—signifies Christ. Solomon’s food is Christ’s refreshment: he is fed by the faith and works offered to him daily by the Church. The thirty *cors* of fine flour signify faith in the holy Trinity. The sixty *cors* of meal signify the perfection of good work. For God completed the work of creation in six days. The ten [Col. 0704D] fat oxen figure the preaching of the Decalogue in the Old Testament; the twenty pasture-fed oxen, the doubling of that same preaching in the New Testament; the hundred rams, perfect ecclesiastical headship; the hunting of wild beasts and capture of birds, the conversion of nations of every kind—proud and savage alike.

“And he had forty thousand stalls for chariot horses and twelve thousand horsemen,” etc. Solomon’s horses signify Christ’s preachers, by whom Christ is borne throughout the world and in whom he fights against demons. The multitude of stalls signifies the multitude of books: he composed three thousand parables.

## CHAPTER II. On Solomon’s Wisdom, Officials, Subjects, and Wives

[Col. 0705A]

God gave wisdom to Solomon, and he was wiser than all human beings (3 Kings 4). In Christ are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge (Col. 2), and he is wiser than all angels. Solomon composed five thousand songs, and Christ bestowed upon humanity wisdom by which it may govern the five bodily senses. Solomon discoursed upon cedar and hyssop, beasts and birds, and creeping things; Christ knows all things, and no creature is invisible in his sight; and he has set forth for us in many ways the principles of all things.

Solomon’s twelve officials supplied food for his household, and the twelve apostles administer sound teaching. [Col. 0705B] Princes of diverse kingdoms were subject to Solomon; to Christ are subject the prelates of diverse Churches and all kings of the whole world. The queen of the South came to Solomon to hear his wisdom (3 Kings 10), and the Gentile world came to Christ to hear his wisdom. The queen of the South presented Solomon with many spices; and the Church, sanctified by Christ’s grace, presents Christ with virtues and good works fragrant far and wide through a good reputation. Solomon had, as it were, seven hundred queens and three hundred concubines; and Christ has faithful souls reborn through sevenfold grace and made illustrious through faith in the holy Trinity.

## CHAPTER III. On the Building of the Temple

Solomon built the Temple (3 Kings 6), and [Col. 0705C] Christ built the Church. In the construction of the Temple there were craftsmen: stonecutters and woodcutters (2 Chron. 3); but in the construction of the Church the craftsmen are preachers and teachers. Solomon sent three kinds of material for the Temple’s construction: stones, wood, and gold. The stones signify firmness of faith; the wood, the loftiness of hope; the gold, the brightness of charity.

In the fourth year of his reign Solomon began to build the Temple. Through the preaching of the four Gospels, the holy Church began to be gathered from Jews and Gentiles. Hiram sent Solomon cut cedar and fir wood from Lebanon to be placed in the house of the Lord (3 Kings 5), because converted Gentile society sent to the Lord men distinguished in the world, [Col. 0705D] yet cut down and humbled from the mountain of pride by the axe of rebuke, so that, instructed by the preaching of truth in the knowledge or rule of the Gospel, each might be placed in the structure of the Church according to his merit.

He also sent craftsmen—that is, philosophers converted to true wisdom—to be placed over peoples to govern them by the grace of learning: such were Dionysius the Areopagite in the apostles’ time, and later Cyprian, an outstanding teacher and most steadfast martyr. He also sent gold: men distinguished by wisdom and talent, on whose behalf he awaits the gifts of heavenly grace. Hiram sent Solomon wheat, namely the word of God; he sent oil, namely charity or the anointing of the Holy Spirit.

The three stories signify the three orders in the holy Church: married persons, the continent, and virgins. [Col. 0706A] Nothing was in the Temple that was not covered with gold, because there is nothing in the holy Church that is not covered by charity, if it is judged to be within her and not outside her. Its door was gilded because the Fathers of the Old Testament pleased God through charity. The Temple itself was gilded because this same charity has been poured out in our hearts. The inner house was gilded because charity reigns in the heavenly homeland. The statement that the upper chambers were straight and of gold refers to the same thing. The various carvings are the Church’s various virtues. The bronze sea signifies baptism.

Solomon built the Temple for seven years, and in the eighth year completed and dedicated it, because Christ gives life to the holy Church in the present age, which turns through the course of seven days, and after the resurrection glorifies her in the eighth number of blessedness. [Col. 0706B] The golden table is sacred Scripture, radiant with spiritual understanding. The various vessels of the Temple are diverse souls filled with the various gifts of the Holy Spirit. But the fact that the wood and stones were prepared at Tyre and placed in the Temple without the sound of hammers or tools signifies that we are reformed unto righteousness in the world through tribulations, and in the heavenly homeland are peacefully rewarded according to our merits.

## CHAPTER IV. On Israel’s Freedom and the Foreigners’ Servitude

Solomon made tributary all the people who were not of Israel; but he did not appoint any of the children of Israel to serve. Rather, they were his men of war, ministers, princes, and commanders (3 Kings 9). [Col. 0706C] Our Peaceful One makes tributary all the people who were not children of Israel when he employs in his own service those who are not numbered among the children but are in a servile condition. Although such persons oppose him in many ways, nevertheless they frequently serve the Church’s needs when in the present time they provide others with support from their possessions.

But those who are not children of the slave woman, but of the free woman—those whom the Son of God freed by his blood—he does not appoint to serve under constraint, because he compels no one to live according to Gentile rites and compels no one in New Testament times to observe the ceremonies of the old law. He appoints them to be warriors, to fight against spiritual wickedness with the shield of faith and the sword of the Spirit; and to become his ministers, that is, to render him spiritual service in good works; princes and commanders, so that they may rule themselves well and tame the lust of the flesh, or so that they may govern their subjects well and lead them in the paths of righteousness. [Col. 0706D]

## CHAPTER V. On Solomon’s Throne

King Solomon made a great throne of ivory and covered it abundantly with yellow gold. It had six steps; the top of the throne was rounded at the back; and there were, as it were, two hands on either side holding the seat. Two lions stood beside each hand, and twelve lion cubs stood on the steps on either side (3 Kings 10).

Solomon’s throne is the Church, in which our Peaceful One reigns and is known to render his judgments. It is fittingly said to have been made of ivory, since the elephant, whose bones yield ivory, is of great intelligence among four-footed creatures; it mates temperately with its female and does not use its wife when she is pregnant. This applies to the chaste, who follow Christ’s commandments through chastity. [Col. 0707A] He clothed her—that is, the Church—with gold, because he makes the splendor of his glory shine in her through miracles.

It had six steps. God completed the world’s adornment in six days; this number, by its perfection, signifies the perfection of good works. God rested on the seventh day; and because the world consists of six ages, during which it is permitted to labor, whoever desires the heavenly homeland should devote himself to good works and hasten to ascend. The roundness of the throne at the back signifies eternal rest, prepared for the saints after this life, so that whoever labors well here may be rewarded by enjoying everlasting repose.

The hands holding the seat signify the consolations of divine grace, which advance [Col. 0707B] the Church to the heavenly kingdom. They are on either side because both Testaments preach that no good thing can be accomplished without divine help. By the two lions are figured the Fathers of the two Testaments, who learned by strength of mind to exercise mastery over themselves and others. They stood beside the hands because the holy Fathers attributed to God, not to themselves, whatever good they did. Hence: “Not to us, O Lord, not to us, but give glory to your name” (Ps. 113).

By the lion cubs is signified the order of preachers, following apostolic teaching. They stand above the six steps on either side because, through the steps of good works, they strive to excel on both sides by teaching and example.

## CHAPTER VI. On Rehoboam

[Col. 0707C]

Rehoboam answered the people harshly, abandoning the counsel which the elders had given him, and spoke to them according to the counsel of the young men: “My father made your yoke heavy; but I will add to your yoke. My father struck you with whips; but I will strike you with scorpions” (3 Kings 12).

Rehoboam signifies bad rulers in the Church who, devoted to earthly desires and delighting in a multitude of attendants, do not have fitting concern for those entrusted to them. Rehoboam is interpreted “breadth of the people,” because such persons walk the broad and spacious way which leads many to death. Having abandoned the counsel of the holy Fathers, whose sayings and examples tend toward what is lofty, he obeys those enslaved to youthful [Col. 0707D] desires, who burden him with wicked praises and flatteries. Wisdom threatens such persons too, saying: “Woe to you, O land, whose king is a child and whose princes eat in the morning; and conversely, blessed is the land whose king is noble and whose prince eats at his proper time” (Eccles. 10).

## CHAPTER VII. On Jeroboam

Jeroboam said in his heart: “The kingdom of David will not return to me if this people goes up to offer sacrifices in the house of the Lord in Jerusalem; and the heart of this people will turn to their lord Rehoboam, king of Judah, and they will kill me and return to him.” Having devised a plan, he made two golden calves and said to them: “Do not go up to Jerusalem. Behold your gods, who brought you out of the land of Egypt” (3 Kings 12).

Jeroboam, [Col. 0708A] who separated the ten tribes from God’s Temple and led them into idolatry, signifies heretics who split the unity of catholic faith by heresies and thus subject it to the worship of evil spirits. Jeroboam is interpreted “one who judges apart.” For heretics seem to divide the people when they make followers of their error. They take ten divisions when they corrupt the ten commandments of the law by violating them. And one tribe remained with David’s offspring when the lot of the elect remained in the rule of catholic faith: “one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4).

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Passage, “I Will Cut Off Baasha’s Posterity”

“Behold, I will cut off Baasha’s posterity, and the posterity of his house” (3 Kings 16). The Lord cuts off the posterity of any wicked person when he punishes sins after the end of life; the Lord cuts off the posterity of his house when he condemns that person’s imitator to eternal torments. Whoever, therefore, perseveres in wicked works to the end of his life has his posterity cut off, because he will be cut down from the land of the living. [Col. 0708B]

## CHAPTER IX. On the Rebuilding of Jericho

Ahiel of Bethel built Jericho. In Abiram, his firstborn son, he founded it; and in Segub, his youngest son, he set up its gates (3 Kings 16). Ahiel means “living to God”; Bethel means “house of God.” Ahiel of Bethel, therefore, restores Jericho’s walls, which Joshua had destroyed and anathematized, when one who had assumed the habit of religion in the Church luxuriously returns to the crimes which the Lord Jesus forgave him on the day of baptism and to the pomps of the devil which he had formerly anathematized.

And when he prefers erroneous doctrines or pagan fables to the ecclesiastical truth in which he had been instructed, he repairs the ruins of Jericho as though going forth from Bethel. Thus he destroys both the foundations of faith from which he ought to begin good buildings and the barriers of good conduct by which he ought to be brought to completion. [Col. 0708C]

## CHAPTER X. On Elijah and the Brook Cherith

Elijah went away and sat by the brook Cherith, which is opposite the Jordan. Ravens also brought him bread and meat in the morning and evening, and he drank from the brook. But after some days the brook dried up (3 Kings 17).

Our hidden Elijah, Christ, drank from the brook [Col. 0708D] Cherith—which means “bald”—when, in the place of Calvary, where his strength was hidden (Hab. 3), he tasted the stream of our mortality. Ravens fed Elijah, bringing him bread and meat, when the Gentile world, coming from the blackness of sins and enlightened by Christ’s grace, offers to Christ, who hungers for our salvation, bread through faith and meat, that is, hope of the resurrection. This occurred in the morning, namely at the beginning of evangelical preaching; in the evening, when, preserving that same faith undefiled to the end of the world, the resurrection of the flesh is presented to the coming Judge.

After some days the brook dried up, because when the course of this present life is completed, death will be swallowed up in victory, and there will no longer be death, mourning, or crying, because the former things have passed away (Rev. 21).

## CHAPTER XI. On Elijah and the Widow of Zarephath

[Col. 0709A]

The word of the Lord came to Elijah, saying: “Arise, go to Zarephath of the Sidonians, and remain there, for I have commanded a widow woman to feed you” (3 Kings 17). The widow of Zarephath signifies the holy Church, which was, as it were, a widow while it awaited the coming of the Savior. Elijah comes to the widow when Christ comes to the Church through the mystery of the Incarnation.

The woman gathered two pieces of wood when the holy Church received faith in the Passion. The little meal signifies imperfect knowledge of divine things, and the small amount of oil expresses the insufficiency of grace. Elijah came, and the meal and oil sufficed, because at Christ’s coming knowledge was multiplied and the gift of grace was multiplied. The woman feeds Elijah when the holy [Col. 0709B] Church refreshes Christ through faith and good works.

The three years of famine signify the absence of faith in the holy Trinity. The six months pertain to good work, which had wholly ceased among human beings, as it is written: “There is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13). Elijah raised the widow’s son when Christ redeemed the human race. Abundance of rain also came through Elijah when through Christ the world was drenched with the dew of heavenly grace.

Thus: the widow is the Church; Elijah, Christ; the wood, the cross; the meal, knowledge; the oil, grace; the three years of famine, imperfect knowledge of the Trinity; the six months, the failure of good works; the raising of the son, the redemption of the human race; the abundance of rain, the fullness of grace.

## CHAPTER XII. On Elijah and the Prophets of Baal

[Col. 0709C]

Elijah repaired the altar, took twelve stones, built an altar from them, made a water-channel around it, placed wood upon it, offered a burnt offering to the Lord, and the people cried out: “The Lord himself is God” (3 Kings 18).

Our Redeemer, contending against the ruler of the world and his followers, cleanses the altar of the Lord which had been destroyed—that is, the hearts of believers—from the stain of iniquity, and consecrates an altar to God, said to have been built from twelve stones. For from those who follow prophetic faith or doctrine an altar most pleasing to God is constituted, on which the sacrifice of praise is offered as a sweet-smelling savor.

He made a water-channel from a contrite heart and a humbled spirit, producing rivers of tears [Col. 0709D] from fear of hell and desire for eternal life. There he also places wood, because he sets the sayings and deeds of the saints before believers as examples. He divided the ox limb by limb and placed it beneath the wood when he taught believers to conform all their actions to the example of the holy Fathers.

He commanded water to be poured over the burnt offering and the wood once, twice, and three times, because at every time it is necessary to temper our words, thoughts, and works by that same compunction of tears, and not to cease before the trenches of the water-channel are filled—that is, until future joy, succeeding present sorrow, is filled perfectly. Thus what follows will occur: “The fire of the Lord fell and consumed the burnt offering,” when the future judgment of the Judge, perfectly [Col. 0710A] examining our words, deeds, and whole life, will prove us as silver is proved by fire (Prov. 17), make us immortal and holy, and place us in the eternal—that is, everlasting—seat. Then, after the manner of the Israelite people, we shall sing in eternal rejoicing: “The Lord himself is God” (Ps. 94).

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Slaying of Baal’s Prophets

Elijah led Baal’s prophets to the brook Kishon, which means “their hardness,” and killed them there (3 Kings 18). Thus our Redeemer, when the day of judgment comes, will send his angels; they will gather every offense out of his kingdom and cast them into the lake of fire, where they will be tormented according to their hardness and impenitent heart (Rev. 20).

And there was a great rain. After Christ tasted death and ascended victorious over the world to heaven, [Col. 0710B] he sent from above to earth the rain of divine grace through the sevenfold Spirit, to cleanse us from sin and make us bear spiritual fruits.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Elijah’s Flight before Jezebel and the Juniper Tree

Elijah, fearing Jezebel’s threats, left his servant, went one day’s journey into the wilderness, and sat beneath a juniper tree (3 Kings 19). Holy men who are lifted to heavenly things by the raising power of the Spirit are, while they remain in this life, subjected to temptations lest they grow proud. Hence, after Elijah had advanced in so many virtues, he fled Jezebel—even though she was a queen, still a woman. He who raised the dead, foresaw the coming judgment, cried aloud, and performed other splendid works, was struck by fear: he fled death from a woman’s hand; from God’s hand he asked for death and did not receive it.

In Elijah’s virtues, power was strong; in his weaknesses, he recognized what he could do of himself. There he endangered what he had received; here he preserved what he had received. In miracles he was displayed; in weaknesses he was safeguarded. Elijah, the Lord’s prophet, illustrious in life and miracles, signifies every faithful person. Ahab, the wicked king and opponent of the Lord and his commandments, signifies the devil, who is king over all the children of pride. Jezebel, the shameless woman and Elijah’s constant enemy, expresses the uncleanness of the flesh, which always persecutes the righteous and opposes his deeds.

Threatened by her, Elijah—that is, the faithful person—is sometimes terrified, although he had previously shone with virtues and many good works. For he had destroyed the prophets of Baal—that is, he had cast every unbelief and heretical depravity out of his heart—and had merited to receive rain from heaven, that is, grace granted from above. Nevertheless, he fears lest an occasion arise and Jezebel—that is, lust—kill him. Obedient, then, to the apostolic counsel which says, “Flee fornication,” he also flees secular dress and abandons the manner of life of the world. He goes into the wilderness when he assumes the habit and life of religion. The wilderness is spiritual life and religion, because it is deserted by many and inhabited by few.

Elijah left his servant and entered the wilderness alone because it is right that every faithful person entering a spiritual way of life should abandon all childish, vain, and frivolous things [Col. 0711A] and do nothing childishly in eating, drinking, speaking, or any other action. By the juniper beneath which Elijah sat we may understand the austerity of some order, such as that of canon monks, regular clerics, or any other religious profession. For every ordered profession seems, like the juniper, to have certain thorns of austerity: the observances of the cloister, weariness of silence, fear of the superior, the discipline of chapter, abstinence from food, and other such things, which can prick through the hardships of their austerity. There are also other thorns of this juniper: namely, very sharp and troublesome thoughts or temptations which, like thorns, prick the tenderness of souls.

[Col. 0711B] There are four modes of temptation. One temptation is light and hidden; another light and manifest; another severe and hidden; another severe and manifest. A light and hidden temptation is when someone is tempted lightly, yet does not understand whether the thing concerning which he is tempted is evil. For example, when someone is lightly tempted concerning an office or prelacy, the temptation is light and hidden because he does not know whether what he desires is beneficial to him.

A light and manifest temptation is when someone is tempted lightly, and is manifestly tempted concerning evil. For example, when someone is lightly tempted concerning fornication, the temptation is light because he is tempted lightly, and manifest because it concerns something plainly evil.

A severe and hidden temptation is when someone is tempted severely, and yet does not know whether the thing concerning which he is tempted is harmful to him. [Col. 0711C] For example, when someone is severely tempted concerning a prelacy or another ministry, the temptation is severe because he is tempted severely, and hidden because he does not know that the devil’s deceit lies concealed there. For the devil tempts through exaltation so that a person may fall more deeply into condemnation through exaltation.

A severe and manifest temptation is when someone is tempted severely and manifestly concerning evil. For example, when someone is severely tempted concerning fornication, the temptation is severe because he is tempted severely, and manifest because it is plainly concerned with evil.

The Psalmist fittingly indicates these modes of temptation when he says: “You shall not fear the terror by night, the arrow flying by day, the pestilence that walks in darkness, the assault and demon at noon” [Col. 0711D] (Ps. 90). A light and hidden temptation is the terror by night. A light and manifest temptation is the arrow flying by day. A severe and hidden temptation is the pestilence walking in darkness. But a severe and manifest temptation is the assault and demon at noon.

These modes of temptation, therefore, are the thorns of this juniper—that is, of this religious order—which, in the manner of thorns, prick the tenderness of souls and sometimes wound the hearts of the good. This is not because the order becomes evil, but because the devil pricks the righteous more fiercely through temptations in proportion as he sees them pass by the habit and life of the order to more exalted and hidden things. Therefore, according to what has been said above, an order of religious is rightly compared to a juniper, because it is proved to prick by varied austerities and temptations.

Finally, Elijah comes to this shade of the juniper [Col. 0712A] when someone fleeing secular things submits himself to an order of some austerity. He asks that his soul may die when he desires utterly to die to the world and live to God. Yet he finds not the death he seeks, but the sleep he does not seek, because a religious person, often wearied by diverse temptations and adversities in spiritual life, becomes sluggish in advancing in virtues and good works.

The angel, Elijah’s guardian and awakener, is the superior who guards and exhorts the faithful soul subject to him. When he sees Elijah—that is, the soul entrusted to him—sleeping beneath the juniper, that is, growing sluggish under the order, he immediately rouses, feeds, and gives him drink. He does so when he admonishes him toward better things and teaches him from sacred Scripture the harder matters signified by food and the easier matters [Col. 0712B] figured by drink. Elijah, awakened, eats and drinks when, admonished, the subject patiently assents to the speaker’s words and does not contradict what is said.

But he sleeps again because sometimes a subject afflicted by much weariness grows lukewarm again after the first admonition and instruction. Yet Elijah is awakened and fed a second time by the angel when the subject is again admonished and instructed by a prudent and faithful superior: “Arise,” he says, “eat; a great journey remains for you.” It is as though he said: “If you trust in the order alone, know that it profits you nothing merely to abandon the world bodily, merely to display before human eyes the outward garb of religious life. Strive to advance further in virtues and to assist your neighbors through works of mercy. Read, meditate, chant psalms, pray, [Col. 0712C] work: a great journey remains for you, because you have advanced little as yet and have much progress still to make.”

Finally Elijah eats, drinks, and goes in the strength of that food for forty days and forty nights to Horeb, the mountain of God, when the subject, strengthened by sound instruction, advances through the exercise of virtues and performance of good works amid prosperity as though in days and adversity as though in nights; and, fulfilling the fourfold Gospel and the tenfold Law, comes to the summit of loftiness. There he is rightly said to stand at the entrance of the cave when he is ready, whenever the Lord calls him, to depart from the flesh.

## CHAPTER XV. On Elijah’s Vision upon the Mountain

[Col. 0712D]

“Behold, the Lord passes by; and a great, strong wind, overturning mountains and breaking rocks before the Lord. The Lord was not in the wind; and after the wind, an earthquake; the Lord was not in the earthquake; and after the earthquake, fire; the Lord was not in the fire; and after the fire, the whisper of a gentle breeze” (3 Kings 19).

The wind before the Lord overturns mountains and breaks rocks because the dread that rushes upon us at his coming both casts down the height of our heart and melts its hardness. An earthquake follows the wind when, after that dread, our heart is moved toward better things. Fire also succeeds the earthquake when, after amendment, divine love warms the heart. The Lord is said not to be in the wind, earthquake, or fire, but is not denied to be in the whisper of the gentle breeze. For when the mind is suspended in the height of contemplation, whatever it is able perfectly to behold is not God. But when it beholds something subtle, that is what it hears concerning the incomprehensible substance of eternity. [Col. 0713A] We perceive, as it were, the whisper of a gentle breeze when in sudden contemplation of bounded truth we delicately taste its savor.

Therefore what we know of God is true when we feel that we cannot know something of him fully. Hence it is fittingly added there: “When Elijah heard this, he covered his face with his cloak and went in and stood at the entrance of the cave.” After the whisper of the gentle breeze, the prophet covered his face with his cloak because, in that most subtle contemplation of truth itself, he recognizes how great is the ignorance that covers the human being. To draw a cloak over the face is to veil the mind, through consideration of its own weakness, so that it may not dare to seek higher things or rashly open the eyes of understanding beyond itself, but may reverently close them to that which it cannot grasp.

He who does this is described as standing at the cave’s entrance. For what is our cave except this dwelling of our corruption? Yet when we begin to perceive something of the knowledge of divinity, we stand, as it were, already at the entrance of our cave. Because we cannot advance perfectly, nevertheless longing for knowledge of truth, we now catch something of the breeze of freedom. Therefore, to stand at the cave’s entrance is, by restraining the obstacle of our corruption, to begin to go forth toward knowledge of truth. [Col. 0713B]

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Safeguarding of Humility
[Col. 0713C] Elijah said to the Lord: “They have destroyed your altars and killed your prophets with the sword; and I alone am left” (1 Kings 19). What was so difficult for the prophet in recognizing that servants of God remained in this world? Yet he who, in humility, knew even God’s hidden things, when puffed up did not know even what was plain. Hence it is certain that one illumines oneself by the ray of humility when one highly esteems the good qualities of others; for, while one sees outwardly, and in others, the deeds that one has oneself performed, one suppresses the swelling of pride that strives to burst forth inwardly from a sense of uniqueness. Thus, by the voice of God, Elijah, who thought himself alone, is told: “I have reserved for myself seven thousand men whose knees have not bowed before Baal,” so that he might know that he was not the sole survivor and reject the glory of self-exaltation [Col. 0713D] arising from his singularity.

## CHAPTER XVII. On Elijah’s Anointing of Elisha

Departing from the mountain, Elijah found Elisha son of Shaphat ploughing with twelve yokes of oxen; and he himself was one among the twelve yokes that were ploughing. When Elijah came to him, he cast his cloak upon him. At once he left the oxen and ran after Elijah, saying: “I beg you, let me kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you” (3 Kings 19).

Elijah, departing, found Elisha son of Shaphat ploughing with twelve yokes of oxen when our Redeemer, descending from heaven, by divine judgment won for himself a people still intent upon earthly occupations, and wrought salvation in it when he converted it to faith. For Elijah means “the Lord God”; Shaphat, “of one judging” or “of one declaring”; Elisha, “the salvation of my God.” The prophet cast his cloak upon him when the Lord clothed the people in the Catholic faith. Hence the Apostle says: “All of you who have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ” (Gal. 3). He left the oxen and ran after Elijah because, upon hearing the Redeemer’s voice, “Unless anyone renounces all that he possesses, he cannot be his disciple” (Luke 14), he immediately ceased to seek earthly gain and to serve secular desires, and thus preached the word of life to others. For this is what it means to kiss father and mother: to wish, by one’s speech, to correct whatever persons one can among Jews or Gentiles.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On Ben-hadad’s Battle against Israel

Ben-hadad, king of Syria, gathered all his army, together with thirty-two kings, chariots, and [Col. 0714B] horses; and he went up, fought against Samaria, and besieged it. And behold, one prophet said to Ahab: “I shall deliver this multitude into your hand.” Ahab said: “Through whom?” And he said to him: “Through the foot-soldiers of the provincial rulers” (3 Kings 20).

Ben-hadad signifies the devil, who gathers together diverse armies of malignant spirits to overthrow God’s people; yet he is conquered by the young men of Israel’s rulers—that is, by the good hearers of teachers—because they fulfill in deeds what they hear with the ear. The ancient enemy is put to flight, because those who perfectly possess the knowledge of both Testaments and preserve faith in the Trinity together with twofold charity are proved fit for service in the army of the supreme King. Ben-hadad, king of Syria, flees with [Col. 0714C] horsemen.

Ben-hadad—that is, the devil—is the prince of the wicked, whose eyes are lofty. Trusting in the horse of his pride, together with horsemen, that is, with all the proud, since he is “king over all the children of pride” (Job 41), he is overcome by Christ’s army and put to flight. The king of Israel strikes down horses and horsemen because the King of kings crushes spiritual wickedness by blotting out the sins of the human race.

## CHAPTER XIX. On What Was Said by the Servants of the King of Syria: “The Gods of Israel Are Gods of the Mountains”

The servants of the king of Syria said to him: “The gods of Israel are gods of the mountains; therefore they overcame us. But it will be better for us to fight them in the plains, and we shall overcome them” (3 Kings 20). Although the devil is often conquered by the saints, he nevertheless renews battle against them; and, while defeated in one way, he immediately attempts to conquer in another. For if the devil and malignant spirits are conquered in spiritual matters, they prepare war in bodily matters, striving to cast souls down from heavenly things to lowly things, in order to conquer them more easily. If they see people desiring heavenly things, they introduce earthly things to be loved; if people are guided by the prosperity granted through God’s grace, they strive to break them by adversity. But, like the Syrians, the demons were cast down precisely where they expected to prevail.

## CHAPTER XX. On Elisha and Elijah’s Cloak

Elisha stood upon the bank of the river Jordan and struck the waters with Elijah’s cloak, which had fallen to him; but they were not divided. He said: “Where is the God of Elijah, even now?” And he struck the waters, and they were divided this way and that, [Col. 0715A] and Elisha crossed over (4 Kings 2).

Elijah’s ascent signifies the Lord’s ascension. Elijah’s cloak signifies the Lord’s incarnation, through which he broke through the river of death and prepared for us a passage to life. Elisha retained this after Elijah’s crossing, because after Christ’s ascension the Church preserved faith in the incarnation, through which it strives to pass through the waves of this present life. But just as Elisha divided the waters only after invoking Elijah’s God, so the Church can perform no miracles except through invocation of Christ’s name. For it is God “who works in us both to will and to accomplish” (Phil. 2).

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Man of God Cursing the Boys at Bethel

Elisha went up to Bethel. As he was going up [Col. 0715B] by the way, little boys came out of the city and mocked him, saying: “Go up, bald man! Go up, bald man!” When he looked back, he saw them and cursed them in the name of the Lord. Two bears came out of the forest and tore forty-two of the boys to pieces (4 Kings 2).

Elisha means “the salvation of God.” The Jews mocked him—that is, Christ—as he was raised upon the cross at the place of Calvary. In mocking him they acted foolishly and childishly; but after Christ ascended into Bethel, that is, into the house of God, in the fortieth year he sent two bears from among the sons of the Gentiles, Vespasian and Titus, who overthrew them in a cruel slaughter; and their blood was shed there where they had hung the Lord.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the Water Given by the Lord to the Armies of Three Kings

[Col. 0715C]

The king of Israel, the king of Judah, and the king of Edom went to fight against Moab, and there was no water for the army (4 Kings 3). The three kings at war are the rulers of the faithful, who through faith in the Trinity fight with spiritual weapons against the prince of the world and his people—philosophers, heretics, schismatics, and all the wicked. Moab means “from the father,” and this suits those to whom the Lord said: “You are from your father the devil” (John 8). These oppose the Church with threats, persecutions, and deceit; but they are put to flight through Christ, who is our head, namely the head of Christians.

And Elisha said: “Make ditches and ditches in the bed of this torrent. For thus says the Lord: You shall see neither wind nor rain, yet the channel shall be filled with water, and you, your households, and your beasts shall drink.” He makes ditches in the torrent-bed who seeks the deep mysteries of the Scriptures; and these are filled with water without rain or wind, because divine power often grants wisdom to its investigators without human assistance. Hence John says: “You have no need that anyone should teach you; but as his anointing teaches you concerning all things” (1 John 2). Therefore humans and beasts will drink (Num. 20): that is, the intelligent and the simple will receive instruction.

“This is a small thing in the sight of the Lord; moreover, he will also deliver Moab into your hands, and you shall strike every fortified city.” For it is not enough for a man of God to know God’s hidden mysteries; [Col. 0716A] he must also preach them to other people and refute those who oppose them. To these is promised every victory over the enemy, so that they may strike every city. The secular city is worldly wisdom, in which philosophers and heretics trust; it is overthrown by preachers.

“You shall cut down every fruitful tree”: namely, the tree that bears not good fruit but deadly fruit, which at the future judgment, cut down, will become fuel for eternal fire. Springs of water are stopped up when heresiarchs together with their followers are condemned by Catholics. “You shall cover every choice field with stones”: choice fields are covered with stones when the beauty of heretical and philosophical speech is overwhelmed by the weight of anathema. Yet there remain walls of clay—that is, false arguments—which are reduced to nothing by slingers, that is, holy [Col. 0716B] preachers.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the Woman Who Cried Out to Elisha

A certain woman, one of the wives of the prophets, cried out to Elisha, saying: “Your servant, my husband, is dead; and you know that your servant feared God. And behold, the creditor has come to take my two sons into slavery for himself.” Elisha said to her: “What do you wish me to do for you? Tell me, what do you have in your house?” She said: “Your handmaid has nothing at all in her house except a little oil with which I may anoint myself.” He said to her: “Go and borrow empty vessels, not a few, from all your neighbours. Then go in and shut your door when you are inside with your sons; pour into all these vessels, and when they are full, you shall remove them” [Col. 0716C] (4 Kings 4), etc.

This woman is the holy Church, mother of the two peoples, Jewish and Gentile. Previously, by a perverse act, consenting to the persuasion of the crafty spirit, she had, as it were, received a coin of sin from the creditor and feared to lose the two sons whom she had begotten in faith. But obeying the prophet’s words, that is, the precepts of Holy Scripture, she filled empty vessels by pouring in the little oil which she had. For when the empty minds of many draw from the mouth of one teacher some small thing concerning love of the Trinity, they are filled to the brim by the overflowing grace of the ointment of divine love. Even now, many hearts which had previously been vessels are full with the anointing of the Spirit, though they seemed to have received only a scant infusion of oil. When this is given to one person after another and faith is received by hearers, the woman—that is, the holy Church—is delivered and no longer held under the debt of her creditor.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the Chamber Which the Shunammite Woman and Her Husband Built for Elisha

The Shunammite said to her husband concerning Elisha: “I perceive that this is a holy man of God, who passes by us and stays. Let us therefore make for him a small upper chamber, and put in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a lampstand, so that, when he comes to us, he may stay there” (4 Kings 4).

Elisha, whose name means “the salvation of God,” signifies Christ by the meaning of his name, the working of miracles, the practice of virtues, the performance of good works, integrity, holiness of conduct, [Col. 0717A] and the raising of the dead after death. The Shunammite woman, whose name means “captive” or “scarlet,” represents the soul which Christ redeemed from the captivity of the devil by his blood.

Elisha often came to the Shunammite woman, just as Christ often comes to the soul in many ways. He comes through contemplation of creatures; he comes through the working of miracles; he comes through inward inspiration; he comes through adversity; he comes through prosperity; he comes by threatening evils; he comes by promising goods; he comes by removing evils; he comes by conferring goods; he comes through knowledge of truth; he comes through love of virtue. Christ comes spiritually to the soul by visiting it, lodging with it, and giving it assurance; at times he passes by, withdrawing grace from it. For he withdraws grace in part so that the mind, which thinks excessively lofty thoughts of itself, may be humbled; but he returns again when he pours it in anew.

The husband of this woman, that is, of the rational soul, is understanding, which by powers and perception implanted in it by nature or bestowed by grace ought to govern the soul, counsel it, provide for it, rule and guide it, and beget from it offspring of virtues and good works. With this husband the soul takes counsel, saying: “I perceive that this man of God is holy, who frequently passes by us.” He is truly holy because he is the Holy of holies, and no one is holy except through him.

“Let us make for him a small upper chamber and put in it a bed, a table, a chair, and a lampstand, so that when [Col. 0717C] he comes to us he may stay there.” An upper chamber, because it is elevated, signifies a spiritual manner of life. Paul had well made such an upper chamber for this Elisha when he said of himself and those like him: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Phil. 3). Its being called small signifies humility. For “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (James 4). Therefore, if the faithful soul ever does great things, it considers them small in the sight of the Creator.

On a bed we customarily rest from labours and, in sleeping, disregard visible things. Thus contemplation is rightly represented by the little bed. For one who abides in it rests from the onslaught of temptations and the affliction of labours; intent upon inward things, one pays no attention to what is happening outwardly.

The table signifies Scripture. For just as a table is filled with foods, so Holy Scripture is filled with meanings and gives us one kind of nourishment through history, another through allegory, another through tropology, another through the Old Testament, and another through the New. The chair signifies instruction. Teachers who instruct others customarily sit. And fittingly the chair follows the table, because it is right that one who has learned Scripture by hearing or reading should impart to others through teaching the good which one has come to know.

The lampstand is an instrument of light. The lampstand has a foot below, a shaft raised upright upon the foot, a small sphere around the shaft, and above the sphere a point upon which the lamp is set. The foot of the lampstand has three branches equal in length, equal in size, of one form, and equally distant from one another. It therefore signifies faith in the holy Trinity. For such as is the Father, such is the Son, and such is the Holy Spirit. The shaft of the lampstand, in being straight, expresses the rectitude of equity; in being raised up, the elevation of good intention. The small sphere signifies the circumspection of the mind. For a small sphere is, as it were, placed upon the lampstand when a mind rightly watchful over itself bears itself about by circumspection. The point above signifies the subtlety of sound reason; the lamp placed upon it expresses Christ; the wax is his humanity; the light, his divinity.

The Shunammite woman, then, taking counsel with her husband—that is, the faithful soul through understanding—makes for Elisha, [Col. 0718B] that is, for Christ, an upper chamber through a spiritual manner of life, small through humility; she sets in it a bed through contemplation, a table through reading the Scriptures, and a chair through moral instruction. She also sets in it a lampstand, the instrument of the true light. Its foot she makes through faith in the holy Trinity; its shaft through the rectitude of equity and the elevation of good intention; its small sphere through circumspection of mind; its point through the subtlety of reason, which ought always to have a lamp upon it because it ought always to cleave to Christ. The soul that knows how thus to prepare lodging for Christ deserves to have Christ as its guest and, through him, to possess the Son.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the Raising of the Shunammite Woman’s Son

[Col. 0718C]

The Shunammite woman is the holy Church. The Shunammite woman lay at Elisha’s feet for the raising of her son (4 Kings 4), because the holy Church humbly prayed to the Lord in the patriarchs for the redemption of the human race. When the Lord gave the Law through Moses, he sent the rod, as it were, through a boy; but he could not raise the dead person through the rod, that is, through the terror of the Law, because the Law brings no one to perfection. He himself, coming upon the corpse, stretches himself out over it, because, “being in the form of God, he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. 2). He walks back and forth because he calls both Gentiles and Jews to eternal blessedness through faith. He breathes seven times upon the dead because by the operation of the divine gift he breathes into those lying in the death of sin the grace of the sevenfold Spirit. And immediately the child whom the rod could not raise returns to life through the spirit of love.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On What Is Written: “Death Is in the Pot”

There was a severe famine in the land, and the sons of the prophets were dwelling before Elisha. He said to one of his servants: “Set on the great pot and cook a stew for the sons of the prophets.” One of them went out into the field to gather wild herbs; he found something like a wild vine and gathered from it colocynths, filling his cloak with them. Returning, he cut them up into the pot of stew (4 Kings 4).

This famine signifies famine for hearing the word of God. The sons of the prophets are sons of preachers, who [Col. 0719A] dwelt before Elisha, that is, Christ or a holy prelate standing in Christ’s place. He gathers into the pot colocynths—that is, wild gourds—whoever, intent upon the letter of the Law, or devoted to philosophers, mixes the bitterness taken from the Law and the deadly matter taken from philosophers with evangelical truth. Cooking such a stew in the pot of the heart, that person prepares such teaching for hearers. For the Apostle says: “The letter kills” (2 Cor. 5). “The prudence of the flesh is death; the prudence of the Spirit is life” (Rom. 8). Knowing this, the faithful cry out, “Death is in the pot.” But flour is put into the pot when spiritual knowledge is added to such seasoning, so that, once the abundance of bitterness has been removed, the food may become wholesome.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On Him Who Brought the Man of God Loaves of Firstfruits

[Col. 0719B]

A certain man came from Baal-shalishah, bringing to the man of God loaves of firstfruits, twenty barley loaves, and new grain in his bag. He said: “Give it to the people, that they may eat” (4 Kings 4).

This man is the assembly of the Fathers. He is from Baal-shalishah because he preserves the number three in confession of the Trinity; for Baal-shalishah means “having a third.” This man offers the man of God loaves of firstfruits when, inspired by the Creator’s grace, he offers books composed concerning the origin of creatures. He offers new grain in a bag when he presents the New Testament in the writings of the Gospel and the apostles. Our Elisha commands his servant, that is, preachers, to distribute this to the faithful and bring forth new things and old from the treasury. “Give,” he says, “to the people, that they may eat” [Col. 0719C] (John 6). “For thus says the Lord: They shall eat, and there shall be some left over” (Matt. 8).

We read this mystery in the breaking of the five and seven loaves, when, after the crowds had been fed, they gathered twelve baskets or seven hampers of fragments. For no one so fully comprehends the mysteries of Scripture that, even after being satisfied, something does not remain over, in accordance with the Lord’s word.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the Captive Girl and Naaman the Syrian

Raiders went out from Syria and carried captive from the land of Israel a little girl who was in the service of Naaman’s wife (4 Kings 5). Raiders went out from Syria, which means “loftiness,” when Gentiles, entangled in greed and various businesses, wandered throughout the whole earth. They carried away captive from the land of Israel the girl [Col. 0719D] who testified concerning the prophet, because the report from Israel, carried abroad through merchants of the nations, reveals to the curiosity of humankind—which Naaman’s wife signifies—that the true prophet and Saviour remains in Judaea.

Hearing this, Naaman reported it to his lord, just as those to whom knowledge of the word has come suggest to those set over them the greatness of spiritual knowledge. The king of Syria sends letters to the king of Israel for the healing of his servant when the primacy of the Gentiles, hearing that the Lord is in Israel and foreseeing the salvation of its own people, sends an embassy to Judaea in order to receive faith in the Saviour through apostolic teaching. Hence Cornelius of Caesarea sent to Peter at Joppa.

The king of Israel tore his garments (Acts 10), because the priests, scribes, and Pharisees, the rulers of the Jews, seeing crowds everywhere flocking to the Redeemer, regarded this as blasphemy and tore their garments, as the high priest did in the Gospel (Matt. 26). “Let him come to me, and let him know that there is a prophet in Israel”; and “those whom the Lord foreknew, he also called” (Rom. 8). The Gentile people came to the house of holy Elisha, namely the Church, and through messengers, that is, evangelical preachers, received instruction to wash itself seven times in the Jordan, reborn from water and the Holy Spirit. The Jordan signifies baptism, because in it the Saviour consecrated baptism.

Naaman’s contempt for the Jordan washing [*lotionem*, “washing”] signifies the simplicity of the unlearned, who could not understand its spiritual efficacy, since “the natural man does not perceive [Col. 0720B] the things that are of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2). The servants, by better counsel, persuaded him to obey the prophetic command, because the Lord often reveals to the lesser person what is better, since “the Lord is no respecter of persons” (Acts 10). After he had washed seven times, his flesh was restored as before, because every person cleansed in baptism through invocation of the holy Trinity, or of the sevenfold Spirit, is restored to the infancy of an innocent life. For in baptism we are commanded to renounce Satan and confess Christ’s faith. Naaman denies that he will henceforth sacrifice to gods and promises that he will in all things serve God alone. He took a portion of holy land because the baptized ought to be confirmed in participation in the Lord’s body.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On Naaman’s Leprosy, Which Clung to Gehazi

[Col. 0720C]

Gehazi followed behind Naaman. When Naaman saw him running toward him, he leapt down from his chariot to meet him and said: “Is everything well?” He replied: “My master has sent me, saying: ‘Just now two young men from Mount Ephraim, from the sons of the prophets, have come to me. Give them a talent of silver and two changes of clothing’” (4 Kings 5).

Two originators are found of those who buy or sell spiritual gifts, namely holy orders and the goods of the Church: one in the Old Testament and one in the New. Gehazi is therefore shown to be the originator of sellers in the Old Testament, and Simon Magus is recognized as the originator of buyers in the New Testament. Their followers are separated from the Church to be tormented in eternal fires.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the Siege and Famine of Samaria

[Col. 0720D]

Ben-hadad king of Syria gathered all his army, went up, and besieged Samaria. A great famine arose in Samaria (4 Kings 6). Ben-hadad and his army are the devil and wicked spirits—pagans, Jews, and heretics—who are stirred up to wage war against the Church. Through such persons God’s people, established in Samaria—that is, in the keeping of the divine Law—are afflicted. Famine arises when teachers are not permitted to preach the word of God. But when Elisha reveals it—that is, when the Redeemer declares it through the Gospel—salvation, “which is far from sinners” (Ps. 118), is known to be near those who fear God.

For the Lord says: “Tomorrow a measure of fine flour shall be for one stater, and two measures of barley for one stater” [Col. 0721A] (4 Kings 7). A measure of fine flour is the perfect measure of divine wisdom found in the New Testament; two measures of barley are knowledge of the Law and the prophets. These are compared to one stater—that is, the Catholic faith—at the gate of Samaria, namely the apostolic preaching through which one enters the Church. When the storm of persecution, which takes place today, has ceased, the Lord will give tranquillity tomorrow—that is, in the future time—so that preaching may be perfectly fulfilled.

There were four leprous men near the entrance of the gate, who said to one another: “Come, let us desert to the Syrian camp.” The Lord had caused a sound to arise in the Syrian camp, and the Syrians had fled. When the lepers came to the beginning of the camp, they entered one tent, ate and drank, and took gold, silver, and clothing. They said to one another: “This is a day of good news. If we keep silent and do not announce it until morning, we shall be charged with wrongdoing.”

Lepers are those who, given over to various vices or entangled in errors, display on their skin the foulness issuing from an inward disease. When the Lord often converts such people to faith and cleanses them from vices, he makes them messengers of true salvation. Thus Matthew was made an apostle from being a tax collector. After his resurrection the Lord appeared to Mary Magdalene, from whom he had cast out seven demons. She went and announced it to those who had been with him, while they mourned.

The lepers were refreshed in the Syrian camp and carried away gold and silver when those despised by this world, devoting themselves to philosophy, acquire humility of thought and beauty of speech. Thus, being well furnished, they can serve the needs of the Church. They are aptly said to be four, so that, instructed by the four Gospels, they may preach the truth of faith in the four regions of the world.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On Jehu

Elisha’s servant said to Jehu: “I have a word for you, O commander.” Jehu said: “For which one of us?” He replied: “For you, O commander.” He rose and entered the chamber. Then he poured oil upon his head and said: “Thus says the Lord God of Israel: I have anointed you king over the people of God, Israel; and you shall strike the house of Ahab your master, that I may avenge from the hand of Jezebel the blood of my prophets and the blood of all the servants of the Lord” (4 Kings 6).

Jehu signifies [Col. 0721D] the rulership of the Gentiles. The Lord appointed it to destroy by just vengeance the sacrilegious city that killed the prophets and the Lord of the prophets, and persecuted his apostles; to overthrow the priesthood which it had vainly retained after Christ; to destroy the Temple; to cast the impious Synagogue, which always thirsted for the blood of the saints, down from the summit of its kingdom; and to kill its rulers.

## CHAPTER XXXII. How Joash Repaired the Temple

Joash said to the priests: “Let the priests receive, according to their order, all the money brought into the temple of the Lord by passers-by, which is offered as the price of a soul and which they bring into the temple of the Lord freely and by the choice of their hearts; and let them restore [Col. 0722A] the repairs of the house wherever they see that restoration is necessary” (4 Kings 12).

In accordance with this likeness, Christ our King commands that teachers should receive all the money of spiritual knowledge and good examples which is contributed to the Lord’s treasury by righteous passers-by, and that it should be applied through the offices of preachers to restoring the spiritual temple. Thus, wherever they find anything torn by error or vices, they may restore it, lest through the negligence of teachers a multitude of hearers perish.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Scribe, the High Priest, the Money, and the Workmen

The scribe of the Law and the high priest poured out and counted the money found in the house of the Lord, and gave it by number and measure into the hands of those who were set over the masons in the house of the Lord (4 Kings 12).

The scribe and high priest signify the apostles and the highest teachers, whom divine election established as leaders in the Church. Through their disciples they scattered seeds of the word throughout the world, so that fit workers of God’s will might arise among their hearers. Some fashioned timber when they strove to make themselves and those obedient to them fruitful wood in the house of the Lord. Others repaired the roof of the temple when they rebuilt those things that had been torn apart through heresy and schisms. Others hewed stones when they sternly rebuked the hard-hearted and unbelieving. Thus the restoration of the house of the Lord was completed in all things requiring expenditure, to fortify the house of the Lord, according to the saying: “To each one of us grace has been given according to the measure of Christ’s gift” [Col. 0722C] (Eph. 4).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Arrow of Salvation

Elisha said to the king of Israel: “Open the eastern window.” When he had opened it, Elisha said: “Shoot an arrow.” And he shot it (4 Kings 13). Thus Christ first urges his own to be illumined by the light of knowledge, and then to send forth the arrows of preaching. Elisha said: “The arrow of the Lord’s salvation against Syria: you shall strike Syria at Aphek.” According to this example, holy preaching is the surest destruction of spiritual enemies, if it is carried out perseveringly.

Therefore a ruler or teacher ought not, because of greed, to neglect the care of souls, but rather lead them through faith and piety to eternal rest, which Aphek signifies. For it means “he will contain” or “he will lay hold.” Hence the Apostle, having enumerated the vices that accompany greed, added: “But you, man of God, flee these things; pursue righteousness, piety, faith, charity, patience, gentleness; fight the good fight of faith; lay hold on eternal life” (1 Tim. 6).

Elisha said: “Strike the ground with the arrow.” When he had struck it three times and stopped, the man of God was angry with him and said: “If you had struck five, six, or seven times, you would have struck Syria unto complete destruction.” According to this deed, teachers are commanded to strike the earth—that is, carnal persons—with the arrow of preaching. But those who do this less diligently are deservedly rebuked by divine correction.

For what is it to strike the earth three times with an arrow except to impress faith in the Trinity upon carnal persons? But when a teacher has accomplished this and brought people to faith, it remains necessary to persist in instruction until he teaches them to rule the five bodily senses, which are signified by the number five; to devote themselves to good works, expressed by the number six; and to meditate diligently on spiritual knowledge, which the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit established in the sacred Scriptures and set forth in the twofold Testament for the salvation of the human race. Those who think that faith alone, without good works and meditation upon God’s Law, suffices them for salvation are rightly rebuked, for they do not act rightly, since, according to James, “Faith without [Col. 0723B] works is dead” (James 2).

## CHAPTER XXXV. On Israel’s Rejection

The Lord rejected all the seed of Israel, afflicted them, and delivered them into the hand of the king of the Assyrians (4 Kings 17). The king of the Assyrians, that is, the devil, together with his army, daily afflicts the people of the Church by besieging and ravaging them, removing them because of sins committed from their own dwellings—that is, transferring them from virtues and good works into a foreign land, namely the region of dissimilarity.

## CHAPTER XXXVI. On the Samaritans

While the Samaritans worshipped the Lord, they also served their own gods (4 Kings 17). They signify heretics, who possess certain sacraments in common [Col. 0723C] with the holy Church and rightly understand certain sayings of Holy Scripture; yet nevertheless they serve idols of their own errors or of unclean spirits.
