They seem to themselves to keep the fear of God rightly when, according to their own understanding, they think that they support the truth. But because they disdain to possess the unity of the Catholic faith, they truly show themselves to obey the wills of malignant spirits. And not only do the first inventors of error, signified by the fathers of the Samaritans, do this; their followers also, whom we understand to be denoted by the names of sons and grandsons, act similarly.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On Josiah and the Passover He Celebrated

Josiah cast out the idols of the land and all impurities, [Col. 0723D] and celebrated the Passover for the Lord (4 Kings 23). The fact that Josiah is read to have celebrated the Lord’s Passover after casting out idols and every impurity teaches us morally that we must first cleanse the ground of our hearts from every vice, correct our actions from every defilement of sins and from dead works, so that we may serve the living God; and thus celebrate a Passover pleasing to the Lord, “not in the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth” (1 Cor. 5).

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Tribute Paid by the People to Pharaoh under Jehoiakim

Pharaoh bound Jehoahaz at Riblah, in the land of Hamath, so that he should not reign in Jerusalem; and he appointed [Col. 0724A] Jehoiakim in his place. Jehoiakim exacted from every person, according to his means, both silver and gold from the people of the land, to be offered to Pharaoh (4 Kings 23).

The malignant spirit demands from the carnal people the tribute of service owed to him, so that they may be ready in every respect to obey him both in thought and speech. Jehoiakim exacts tribute at Pharaoh’s command because the devil, through teachers devoted to himself, demands that each person pay him, according to his ability, the tribute of sin; and thus, through wicked prelates, he daily prepares destruction for those subject to them.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the First Siege of Jerusalem
Nebuchadnezzar came to besiege Jerusalem; and he received Jehoiachin, who came out to meet him, took the golden vessels which King Solomon had made in the temple of the Lord, and carried off from Jerusalem to Babylon all the princes, mighty men, craftsmen, and smiths (4 Kings 24). Since the allegory of this most lamentable history accords greatly with the negligence of our own time, I do not think it should be passed over in silence. For it is evident that Jerusalem and the land of Israel signify the city of Christ, that is, the holy Church; while Babylon, and the Chaldeans or Philistines, signify the city of the devil, that is, the whole multitude of the wicked, whether human beings or angels.

Israel serves the Philistines or Chaldeans when any of the faithful, outwardly remaining in the Church only in name, are otherwise deceived by unclean spirits or persons, and bow the necks of their minds to avarice, luxury, or any other sin. Nebuchadnezzar carries the king of Jerusalem and all the mighty leaders of the army, to the number of ten thousand, into captivity when both teachers and those who seemed to serve the Lord with a manly spirit and faithfully to keep the Decalogue of the Law in love of God and neighbour, overcome either by the enticements of the world or by adversities, defile themselves with graver crimes or indeed fall into heresy.

But what are the weapons by which, resisting the devil, we defend the freedom granted us by God, except the sayings of the Scriptures? In them, by the examples of the Lord himself and of his saints, we learn more clearly than light in what order the wars of vices ought to be overcome. The Chaldeans deprive the children of Israel of these weapons when evil spirits, introducing worldly affairs, hold back the minds of the faithful from meditation upon the sacred Law, so that they may neither themselves gain confidence in resistance through its exercise, nor perhaps inflame others, who do not know the Law, to resist vices by exhorting or reproving them.

They take away the makers of weapons when they overwhelm in crimes those who know the sacred utterances to such an extent that they are utterly ashamed to speak the good things they have learned. They transfer every craftsman and smith from Jerusalem to Babylon when they turn aside from their purpose those who were accustomed to benefit many people through manifold works of virtue and to fortify the city of God against the outbreaks of temptations, compelling them instead to employ, at the will of the king of vices, the talent which they ought to have spent in defence of the holy Church. If, however, by “smiths” we understand not workers in doors or walls but setters of gold and gems, the exposition tends to the same end. For it is said of wisdom that “gold and a multitude of gems cannot be compared with it” (Prov. 3). Therefore we can understand its setters most fittingly as teachers. So long as they live or teach rightly, they devote the skill of their craft to adorning the holy city. But if they should go astray, by whom are they carried captive and transferred to Babylon except by the king of the Chaldeans? And because we understand the transfer of craftsman and smith from Jerusalem to Babylon as the burying in the earth of the talent of the word received from heaven—that is, the turning of spiritual knowledge toward works of sin—we must always take vigilant care that nothing of the kind be committed by us.

## CHAPTER XL. On the second siege of Jerusalem, and the famine

[Col. 0725B]

Now in the ninth year of King Zedekiah, in the tenth month, on the tenth day of the month, Nebuchadnezzar came with all his army against Jerusalem; they surrounded it and built siegeworks all around it. The city was shut up and besieged until the eleventh year of King Zedekiah, on the ninth day of the month. The famine prevailed in the city, and there was no bread for the people of the land.

What else do we understand in Zedekiah but evil rulers in the Church, who misuse divine favour and gift and falsely arrogate to themselves the name of righteousness? For the name by which the king was first called, Mattaniah, means “gift” or “present”; Zedekiah, “the righteousness of the Lord.” He is said to have reigned for eleven years, signifying that he was a transgressor of the Law, which is signified by the number ten. The number eleven, which exceeds ten, signifies a going beyond the Decalogue. But the number nine signifies imperfection in relation to the Law, just as eleven signifies transgression: the latter exceeds ten, while the former falls short of ten.

Nebuchadnezzar rightly besieged the city in the ninth year of Zedekiah’s reign, in the tenth month—that is, on the tenth day of the month—because when evil shepherds neglect to fulfil in deed and teaching the commandments of the Decalogue which they hold in knowledge, it is inevitable that the ancient enemy, together with his army, should surround the people entrusted to them with siege and, having built a fortification of error and vices, shut up the city by encircling it. Thus famine of the word of God prevails in the city, when the bread of doctrine is not freely distributed to the people of the land.

## CHAPTER XLI. On the breach in the wall and Zedekiah’s flight

[Col. 0725D]

The city was breached, and Zedekiah fled; and all the fighting men fled by night through the way of the gate which is between the two walls, beside the king’s garden (4 Kings 25).

The spiritual city is breached through the various temptations of evil spirits; and those who ought to have defended the city with weapons flee, surrounded by the night of ignorance and the darkness of sins. For “the hireling, who is not a shepherd, sees the wolf coming, leaves the sheep, and flees; and the wolf snatches and scatters the sheep” (John 10).

“Through the way of the gate which is between the two walls, beside the king’s garden.” By these words he covertly reproves the slothfulness of teachers, who, set between the two walls of the two Testaments, seek not to fight but to escape, and to flow away in pleasures—this being signified by the garden—rather than to withstand their enemies with the shield of faith.

Moreover, the Chaldeans were besieging the city all around. Zedekiah fled by the way which leads to the plains of the wilderness, because, with evil spirits surrounding the people, the ruler flees not to the mountains, of which it is written, “Mountains are around him” (Ps. 124), but to the plains of the wilderness, that is, to the expansiveness of luxury. Hence it is written, “Broad is the way that leads to death” (Matt. 7).

The army of the Chaldeans pursued the king, caught him in the plain of Jericho, and all the fighting men who were with him were scattered and abandoned him. For when virtues desert a person—which ought to have defended him—he is captured in the plain of Jericho, that is, in the failing of carnal perception. For Jericho means “moon” and signifies the waning of the flesh. The king of Babylon killed Zedekiah’s sons before his eyes and put out his eyes. For the king of Babylon is the devil, the possessor of deepest confusion. He first slaughters the sons before the father’s watching eyes because he often destroys good works in such a way that the captive mind itself sees with sorrow that it is losing them.

For the mind often groans, yet, overcome by the pleasures of its flesh, it loses the good things which it loves even while grieving for them. It considers the losses which it suffers, yet does not raise the arm of virtue against the king of Babylon. But while it is struck through the perpetration of wickedness while still seeing, it is brought by the habit of sin to the point at which it is deprived even of the light of reason. Hence the king of Babylon first destroys the sons and then tears out Zedekiah’s eyes, because the evil spirit first removes good works and afterwards takes away the light of understanding as well.

Zedekiah rightly suffers this at Riblah. For Riblah means “these many things.” At times the light of reason is shut off for one who is burdened by a perverse habit and by the multitude of his iniquity.

## CHAPTER XLII. On Nebuzaradan

Nebuzaradan, commander of the army and servant of the king of Babylon, came to Jerusalem; he burned the house of the Lord, the king’s house, and the houses of Jerusalem, and burned every house with fire (4 Kings 25).

Nebuzaradan, whose name means “winnowing fan,” comes when some evil spirit attacks the people of the faithful and, inflamed by desire, overthrows the king’s house and the houses of Jerusalem—that is, rulers and those who seemed to abide in the vision of peace. He burns every house when he kindles each person’s conscience with the flame of unlawful love. He destroys the walls around Jerusalem when, in those who despair, he dissolves the intentness of prayer and the pursuit of virtues, which he knows to prevail against him, lest through hope of pardon they run to divine aid and seize the defences of a reformed life.

Leading the people into captivity, he left among the poor of the land vine-dressers and farmers. This is because, by taking captive through vices those who could have been useful by word and example, he entrusts agriculture to the foolish and dull, so that not the wine of spiritual grace and the grain of sound teaching bear fruit in the vineyards and fields of the peoples, but rather the thorns and briars of vices grow up.

## CHAPTER XLIII. On Judah’s removal

And Judah was removed from its land (Isa. 66).

Judah is removed when those who seemed in the Church to possess confession of God’s name are, through crimes and manifold sins, transferred from the land of virtues and brought into the kingdom of confusion and error. Whoever persist in evil service under that dominion will not deserve, under Jesus’ guidance, to return to the land of Judah and rebuild there the temple of the Lord. After the misery of this present life they will be handed over to the prison of everlasting death, where “their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched.”

But let it be granted to us, in the pilgrimage of this passing age, to practise true repentance for what we have committed, so that, after the course of seven days—or, as it were, after seventy years—we may be freed from this captivity and from every power of the king of Babylon, that is, the devil; and, aided by the sevenfold Spirit, may be able to enter the heavenly Jerusalem and contemplate the face of our Creator for ages of ages.

# BOOK EIGHTH. ON THE FIRST TWO BOOKS OF EZRA

[Col. 0727]

## CHAPTER I. On Cyrus, the liberation of the captives, and the restoration of the temple. On First Ezra

[Col. 0727B]

In the first year of Cyrus king of Persia, that the word of the Lord spoken through the mouth of Jeremiah the prophet might be fulfilled, the Lord stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of Persia; and he caused a proclamation to be made throughout all his kingdom, even in writing, saying: “Thus says Cyrus king of Persia: The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he himself has commanded me to build for him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judah. Who is among you of all his people? May the Lord his God be with him. Let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judah, and build the house of the Lord God of Israel” (1 Ezra 1).

Just as Cyrus, after destroying the empire of the Chaldeans, freed the people of God, sent them back to their homeland, commanded the rebuilding at Jerusalem of the burned temple, and ordered this also by letters, so Christ, after destroying the kingdom of the devil, gathered into the Church his elect who had been scattered under the devil’s tyranny. The Church, justified in the present by faith, has peace with God and hastens through him toward the vision of everlasting peace. For Jerusalem is called “vision of peace.” He also caused the burned temple to be restored when, bringing back to salvation those who had lost faith through the devil’s snares, he makes them worthy of his dwelling.

He also sends the holy Scriptures throughout the whole world, by which he proclaims faith in his name and hope of salvation to all who belong to his kingdom, that is, to the elect. In the sacred Scriptures, each one of the elect and the whole Church are customarily called the house or temple of God, because he is accustomed to dwell in the hearts of those who believe, hope, and love in him. Hence it is written: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my words; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

## CHAPTER II. What it signifies that the Jews are freed after seventy years

That the Jews are freed after seventy years and rebuild the house of God and the holy city signifies this: certain persons who have been separated from communion with the Church through their sins are joined to the number of the faithful; again, through the gifts of the Holy Spirit they perform good works; and thus they receive fellowship with the faithful—the house, namely, and city of God, from which they had been cast out.

It should be noted that the house of the Lord rebuilt after its burning, the city restored, the people sent back to their homeland after captivity, and the holy vessels brought back all proclaim the same return of a penitent person to the Church.

## CHAPTER III. On the number of vessels brought back from Babylon

This is the number of vessels brought back from Babylon: thirty golden bowls; one thousand silver bowls; twenty-nine knives; thirty golden cups; four hundred and ten second-quality silver cups (1 Ezra 1), and so forth.

Bowls are open and shining vessels: they are the hearts of the simple, who harbour no deceitful thought but utter with a pure tongue what they hold in their hearts. Knives, used for suitably cutting or dividing the parts of victims, so that after everything had been divided according to reason one part might be consumed on the altar, one given to the priests, one to the Levites, and one to the offerers, signify those who possess discernment, who know perfectly how to distinguish concerning the saving sacrifice, which is Christ: what ought to be said to all, what to the more perfect, and what, exceeding the measure of the human condition, should be entrusted to the fire of the Holy Spirit. Golden cups are those who shine with the brilliance of greater wisdom; silver cups, those who, splendid in the gracefulness of teaching, explain more plainly what they know.

## CHAPTER IV. On the number of those returning from Babylon

The people who returned from Babylon were counted according to their lineage (1 Ezra 2).

For this reason Scripture carefully distinguished from which lineage the captives, released, returned to their homeland: that we might be reminded by it with what certainty the Lord records the total number of his elect in the book of life and, as though in another heaven, marks down how many souls each of the faithful has converted by word or example, rewarding them with a sure recompense.

## CHAPTER V. On the number of animals

Their horses were six hundred and thirty-six; their mules, two hundred and forty-five; their camels, four hundred and thirty-five; their asses, six thousand seven hundred and twenty (1 Ezra 2).

Among the people who came up from captivity, even the animals by which they were assisted are listed, and their number is indicated just as is the number of the people. For there are many in the Church who are slower in understanding or less spiritual; when they devoutly obey spiritual teachers and bend the back of their minds to bear the burdens of their brethren’s need, they are rescued with the rest of the elect from the confusion of diabolic captivity and press on toward the walls of the heavenly city. Their number is now continually preserved in the memory of God. Hence: “Your eyes saw my imperfection, and all shall be written in your book” (Ps. 138). And elsewhere: “You will save human beings and beasts, O Lord” (Ps. 35).

## CHAPTER VI. On the offering of the leaders

The chiefs of the fathers gave toward the expenses of the temple forty-one thousand gold solidi, five thousand minas of silver, and one hundred priestly garments (1 Ezra 2).

The chiefs of the fathers offer, according to their means, gold, silver, and priestly garments toward the expenses of the works of the temple when holy men contribute to the building up of the faithful, by living well, whatever wisdom, eloquence, and good action they have received. The weight of gold and silver is fixed, and the number of priestly garments is fixed, so that we may know that God knows thoughts, words, and deeds, and rewards them worthily.

## CHAPTER VII. On the foundation of the temple

Therefore, when the temple of the Lord had been cleansed, all the people cried out with a great cry in praise of the Lord because the foundation of the temple of the Lord had been laid. But many of the priests, Levites, chiefs of the fathers, and elders who had seen the temple before it was founded, and this temple before their eyes, wept aloud (1 Ezra 3).

In the building of the spiritual temple, tears and joy arise together among the leaders. Teachers rejoice at the salvation of penitents; but they grieve because the penitents have committed wicked deeds requiring repentance. The penitents themselves exult in their salvation because by repenting they have risen from the death of the soul; they grieve because by sinning they had perished. The newly baptized rejoice that the grace of the Saviour has gathered them together; they sorrow that they perished with the human race in the first parent and, as though the temple of God had been corrupted by enemies—that is, the state of body and immortal soul—were transferred into Babylon, namely the confusion of this present exile.

But because, as the progress of the good increases, the envy of the wicked increases, and the trials of the perverse do not cease amid the growth of the godly—who try to injure the saints either by feigning good or openly introducing evil—the following is rightly added.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the enemies of Judah and Benjamin

The enemies of Judah and Benjamin heard that the children of the captivity were building the temple for the Lord God of Israel. Approaching Zerubbabel and the chiefs of the fathers, they said to them: “Let us build with you, for we seek the Lord our God as you do” (1 Ezra 4), and so forth.

By the enemies of Judah and Benjamin he means the Samaritans, whom, after the captivity of the ten tribes, the king of Assyria transferred from diverse peoples of the nations into their cities and lands. Afterwards they observed in part the Law of God which they had received, but no less also the idols they had formerly served. These people, who abhorred being seen as worshippers of God, promise help in the work so that, once admitted into partnership, they may be able to inflict harm.

They therefore represent false brethren, that is, heretics and bad Catholics, who are enemies of Judah—that is, of confession and praise, which the Church offers through right faith and worthy action—and of Benjamin, that is, “son of the right hand,” while they separate their hearers from the faithful, who are to receive at the Judge’s right hand blessing and the eternal kingdom. They say therefore, “Let us build with you,” and so forth, when heretics desire that authority to preach among Catholics be granted to them. They promise that they maintain with Catholics the same purity of right faith and action, so that, having received authority to preach, they may sow tares amid the good seed; Paul is surnamed *spermologos*, that is, “seed-word speaker” (Acts 17).

For they entered the land of the children of Israel not under Joshua’s leadership, not subject to Jerusalem’s rule, but brought into its land by a faithless king, namely by the enemy of God’s people—not to serve the Lord but the opposing king. Thus heretics and false Catholics, when by perverse living or teaching they attack the peace of the Church, are strangers to the kingdom of Jerusalem and belong rather to the lot of the Gentiles, whose idols they serve. They enter the boundaries of the holy Church not under the leadership of Jesus Christ but under that of the devil, whom the king of Assyria signifies, just as Simon Magus received baptism in the Church not for his salvation but in order to investigate more intimately the Church’s secrets. The outcome showed this: when he could not disturb the Church in the role of a false brother, he disturbed it most fiercely in the role of an utterly open enemy.

## CHAPTER IX. On the dedication of the house of the Lord

The children of Israel—the priests, Levites, and the rest of the children of the transplantation—celebrated with joy the dedication of the house of God (1 Ezra 6).

The temple is rightly dedicated with joy by the priests, Levites, and the rest of the children of the transplantation, because when sinners are corrected there is joy in heaven before the angels of God (Luke 11), among the teachers who laboured for their salvation, and among all who have migrated in mind and deed from the confusion of sins to the height of virtues, that is, to the land of promise. Priests, Levites, and all the people rejoice at the dedication of the restored house, because all the teachers of the Church rejoice over sinners reconciled through repentance.

## CHAPTER X. How Ezra signifies Christ

Ezra signifies Christ, who renewed holy Scripture, brought captives back to Jerusalem, exalted the house of the Lord with greater gifts, appointed leaders and governors beyond the river Euphrates who knew the Law of God, corrected the children of the transplantation concerning foreign wives, and cast out from the assembly of the transplantation both the children of such women and their mothers.

For Christ renewed the sacred Scripture, which the scribes and Pharisees had corrupted through traditions or taught to be understood only according to the letter. He showed it to be full of spiritual meaning, and, after sending the Holy Spirit, caused the New Testament to be written through the apostles and apostolic men. He led the people out of Babylonian captivity and brought them, freed, into Jerusalem, the land of promise, because, having once suffered upon the cross, he redeemed the world by his blood; descending to hell, he led true Israelites from there to the walls of the heavenly city and brought them to the joys of their promised inheritance. Daily he summons the faithful, gathered from the turmoil of the world, to the fellowship of the Church and the everlasting kingdom.

He increased the ornaments of the temple with gold, silver, and precious vessels which the people of Israel and the Persian rulers sent through him, because, leading into the Church those who believe in him from each people, he does not cease to adorn and glorify her by the brightness of their faith and works. He appointed leaders and rulers over all the people beyond the river who knew the Law of God, because in the Church—which, washed by the river of baptism, has crossed beyond the Babylonian river, that is, the disturbance of the age, through the purity of faith—he set apostles, evangelists, pastors, and rulers.

He corrected the children of the transplantation concerning foreign wives because he forbade those who renounce the world by the profession of faith to serve the world’s enticements. He expelled such children and their mothers from the assembly of the transplantation lest, when grown up, they should follow their mothers’ unbelief rather than their fathers’ faith. For he taught that our works which seem good, if mixed with carnal delights or deriving their origin from the contagion of human favour, must be rejected and do not suit those who wholly abandon the world and pass with their whole mind to heavenly things. Such persons ought not to be weakened by temporal flatteries, but exercised by adversities and prepared for eternal rest.

## CHAPTER XI. On the circumspection of teachers

Nehemiah says: “I came to Jerusalem and was there three days. I rose by night, I and a few men with me; and I told no one what God had put in my heart to do in Jerusalem. No animal was with me except the beast on which I rode. I went out by night through the Valley Gate, before the Dragon Fountain and to the Dung Gate; and I considered the broken wall of Jerusalem and its gates consumed by fire” (2 Ezra 2), and so forth.

He goes over the various places of the ruined city in inspection and carefully considers how each should be restored. It also belongs to spiritual teachers frequently to rise by night and, while the others are at rest, with diligent indignation to inspect the state of the Church, so that they may vigilantly investigate how to correct and raise up what has been soiled and cast down by the filth and battles of vices.

The wall of Jerusalem lies broken down when the conduct of the faithful is defiled by earthly and low desires. Its gates are consumed by fire when the chief virtues and principal works through which a believer ought to enter into life are destroyed by the heat of temptation and the burning of vices. This wall and both sets of gates are rebuilt when, through teachers’ diligence, the conduct of the faithful is raised from earthly affections and there is urgently shown what are the perfect virtues and the greater works by which one enters into life.

## CHAPTER XII. A general interpretation of the whole building

It would take long to discuss mystically each individual structure or act of building, which the learned reader can also recognize for himself. Yet this must be noted: those who build the gates and towers through which citizens may enter or enemies be kept out are the prophets, apostles, and evangelists, through whom is supplied to us the pattern of faith and right action by which we enter the Church, and from whose words we learn to refute the adversaries of truth.

Those who build up the rest of the city are the pastors and teachers, whom the Apostle placed second; through their industry the Catholic faith, built up to this day throughout the whole world as though by great architects of the Church, is preserved. And as Nehemiah, enumerating in order all the city’s builders, commends them to lasting memory, so Christ, the comforter of our poverty, writes in heaven the names of all who build the Church among the elect.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the anger of Sanballat and the Samaritans

When Sanballat heard that we were building the wall, he was very angry (2 Ezra 4).

Plainly this is the anger of heretics; these are the words of those who call themselves Samaritans, that is, keepers of God’s Law, though they are opposed to God and his laws, having been separated from the house of David—that is, from the unity of Christ and the Church—through heresies, schisms, and evil works. They fear the building of walls lest their impiety be overcome.

“And, greatly moved, he mocked the Jews.” This is the mockery of all those who “profess to know God, but deny him by their deeds” (Titus 1). And he said before his brethren and the assembly of the Samaritans: “What are these feeble Jews doing? Will the nations let them alone?” (2 Ezra 4).

The Samaritans served the Lord in such a way that they did not renounce their own gods. Today they are imitated by those who are Christians in such a way that “their god is their belly” (Phil. 3), and who either follow avarice, “which is idolatry” (Eph. 5), or, enslaved to the other enticements of the world, serve the creature rather than the Creator (Rom. 1). Such people, therefore, like heretics, do not wish the walls of the Church to be renewed, lest, as the condition of godliness grows, they be compelled to abandon their impiety. Such persons customarily call the Jews—that is, the confessors of faith—feeble and easily overcome by the nations, although in the daily conflict of souls they love vices more than they desire to win the palm of virtue’s victory.

## CHAPTER XIV. On the caution of the builders

Half of the young men did the work, and half were ready for battle (2 Ezra 4). Of the builders on the wall, and those carrying and loading burdens, each did the work with one hand and held a sword with the other. Each of the builders had his loins girded with a sword: not only did half of the young men do the work and half stand ready for battle, but the young men who did the work were girded with swords.

So great was the cunning of the ancient enemy, so great is the fury of his malice against the Church, that not only the preachers of truth but God’s people themselves must always be watchful against him and stand, as it were, in battle line. Builders gird their loins with the sword when those who labour at good works and care to order by regular discipline those entrusted to them—for this is to place living stones fittingly in the building of the holy Trinity—strive to restrain within themselves the laxity of luxury by the sharpness of God’s word.

## CHAPTER XV. How they observed the Sabbath

“We shall not accept from them on the Sabbath the goods for sale and all things brought in by the peoples of the land to sell on the Sabbath day” (2 Ezra 10).

We too must always observe the spiritual Sabbath: we must always rest from servile work, that is, sin; we must always be still and see that he is God (Ps. 33), so that, after such a Sabbath, freed from the sins of conscience, we may attain the Sabbath of future glory. But the peoples of the land seek to profane the Sabbath by bringing in merchandise on the sanctified day when unclean spirits try to stain purity of heart and introduce the enticements of vices for the price of our consent, in order to defile the day of greatest sanctification—that is, to obscure the light of devout action or thought by errors. But we must wholly avoid such commerce, with the walls of our city shut—that is, by the guarding of a more perfect life.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the twofold dedication of the city

The holy city, once completed, is dedicated (1 Ezra 12) when, at the end of the age, the full number of the elect having been gathered, the universal Church is brought into heaven to behold her Creator. Whenever in this life we are raised by longing for that life, we rejoice as though at the future dedication of our city.

Thus the dedication may be understood as twofold: first, in the hope of those who desire it and cleanse the eyes of their heart so that they may see God; then, in the reality itself, in the enjoyment of the divine vision by the blessed, in spiritual bodies among the angelic hosts.

# BOOK NINTH. ON THE BOOKS OF ESTHER, TOBIT, JUDITH, AND MACCABEES

[Col. 0733]

## CHAPTER I. On the mysteries contained in the book of Esther

[Col. 0733C]

“In the days of Ahasuerus, who reigned from India to Ethiopia over one hundred and twenty-seven provinces” (Esther 1), and so forth.

Ahasuerus, a powerful and wealthy king, signifies Christ both by the interpretation of his name and by the exaltedness of his power and the greatness of his riches. By the interpretation of his name, because it means “door”: Christ said, “I am the door” (John 10). By the exaltedness of his power, because “all power in heaven and on earth has been given to Christ” (Matt. 28). By the greatness of his riches, because “whatever the Father has is his” (John 17).

In the third year of his reign he made a great banquet for his princes and servants. The history of this banquet displays the pomp of wealth and royal luxury; but allegorically it signifies here the spiritual riches which Christ dispenses to each person. For Christ, in the third year of his reign—that is, in the third period of this age—revealed the mysteries of his incarnation and displayed most abundantly the spiritual banquet of preaching and of his body and blood. The first period was before the Law, the second under the Law, the third under grace.

He made this banquet for his princes and servants, that is, the apostles and all purified from sin; for the strongest, namely those who had conquered the evil one; for the renowned, that is, those who shall be called children of God; and for the governors of provinces, that is, the prelates of churches. He made the banquet for all to whom he granted the gift of spiritual grace.

“For a long time, one hundred and eighty days” (Esther 1): one hundred on account of eternal life, since one hundred is a perfect number and passes from the left hand to the right; eighty because there are eight beatitudes to which this banquet leads. The seven days during which the banquet was prepared signify the present time, which revolves in the number of seven days. The court of the garden in which the banquet was prepared signifies the present Church, in which we are justified for the joy of future glory. The ornaments of the court signify the adornment of the Church in the condition of this present age. The vessels through which drink was brought are the holy preachers, through whom heavenly grace is administered to us.

“And there was none to compel the unwilling, because the king had decreed that each should take what he wished.” Preaching must be moderated in this manner: it should benefit all, injure none, and pass among vices like a two-edged sword. It should cut away pride without increasing timidity; it should impose care upon the idle and sluggish without increasing restless and curious persons in their troublesome activity.

Queen Vashti made a banquet for the women in the palace where the king was accustomed to dwell. Proud Queen Vashti is the Jewish people, which reigned so long as it surpassed the other nations in the worship of God. She made a banquet for women when through the Law she provided refreshment for holy souls. She made it in the palace where the king was accustomed to dwell, that is, in Jerusalem, in which God had imparted knowledge of his power.

Therefore, on the seventh day, when the king was more cheerful and had grown warm with wine after drinking, he commanded his seven eunuchs to bring in the queen, so that she might display her beauty to all peoples and princes. The seventh day is the time of the revelation of the sevenfold grace, when the fullness of time came and God sent his Son into the world and revealed with more abundant grace the mysteries of the Law by which he had formerly nourished the faithful.

Then he commanded the seven eunuchs—that is, the preachers filled with the sevenfold Spirit, who made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven—to bring in Queen Vashti, that is, the Jewish people, through spiritual understanding, because she was still outside through the letter of the Law. This was so that she might display her beauty to all—that is, that she might be an example to all for faith and good action. For she was exceedingly beautiful, on account of the prerogative of the fathers and her knowledge of the Law and the prophets.

He commanded that she be brought in with a diadem placed upon her head, that is, with the honour of religion. But Queen Vashti refused to enter because the Jewish people, rejecting God’s grace, disdained to come by faith.

The seven wise men of the king are all teachers filled with sevenfold grace and divinely instructed through it for every work to be done. Memucan, the last of the wise men, who pronounced the judgment that Vashti should be deposed and another set in her place, signifies Paul, who said, “I am the least of the apostles” (1 Cor. 15), and who said to the Jews opposing his preaching: “Since you judge yourselves unworthy of the kingdom of God, behold, we turn to the Gentiles” (Acts 13).

With Vashti repudiated, beautiful young women were sought for the king [Col. 0735C] and placed under the charge of the eunuch Hegai, that they might receive from him what was necessary for their use (Esther II). Thus, with Judaea repudiated, persons from various parts of the world are brought through preachers into fellowship in royal dignity, dispensing the word of God; and they are placed under the charge of Hegai—whose name means “festive,” and who is guardian of the royal women—that is, they are entrusted to pastors, to whom the care of the souls of the faithful is given, so that by word and example they may provide whatever they see to be necessary for the practice of godliness. Whoever pleases the most high King by right faith and a pure conscience shall enter in to him, Vashti having been repudiated. Many young women are sought, many brought to the court of the king, but one is chosen, one is crowned queen: because for all the Churches of the faithful there is one faith, one [Col. 0735D] baptism, one God, and one Father of all (Eph. IV). The adornments of the young women signify the spiritual adornments of faithful souls.

There was a Jewish man in the city of Susa named Mordecai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, of the stock of Jemini, who had been carried away from Jerusalem at the time when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon carried away Jeconiah king of Judah. He was the guardian of the daughter of his brother, Hadassah, who was also called Esther; she had lost both parents and was exceedingly beautiful and fair of countenance. Esther means “hidden”; Hadassah, “mercy.” She is the Church of the Gentiles, which, nurturing the chastity of faith in the hidden place of the heart, found mercy and grace before the eyes of God, the Synagogue having been repudiated—the Synagogue which in Hosea is called “without mercy” (Hos. [Col. 0736A] I). Spiritual Mordecai nourishes her and adopts her as a daughter: he is the teacher of the Gentiles in faith and truth (I Tim. II), and he is of the stock of Jemini, that is, of the stock of Benjamin. Spiritual Nebuchadnezzar, the king of confusion, carried her away from the natural law and the worship of the one God into the confusion of idolatry; but divine mercy called her back to the way of truth through preachers.

Esther pleased the king, and the things necessary for her use were given to her. Likewise, the Church pleased Christ, and sound teaching, knowledge of the Scriptures, and an upright life were given to her. Esther received for her service seven most beautiful young women; and the Church received faithful souls regenerated and refined by the grace of the Holy Spirit, who follow her footsteps in faith, teaching, and good works, of whom it is said: “The young maidens loved thee exceedingly” [Col. 0736B] (Song I). Esther was unwilling to reveal her country to the king; and the holy Church covers before God her former guilt by good works. Mordecai cared for Esther’s salvation; and the Apostle Paul, along with the whole company of teachers, cares for the salvation of the Church through his teaching.

Bagathan and Thares, the king’s two eunuchs, who were gatekeepers and presided at the first threshold of the palace, wished to rise against the king and kill him. This did not escape Mordecai; he immediately reported it to Queen Esther, and she to the king in Mordecai’s name, who had brought the matter to her. The matter was investigated and discovered, and both were hanged on a gibbet. In the two eunuchs schismatics and heretics may be denoted: carrying in their hearts the poison of deceit and malice, they devise plans against the truth in order to take it away from believers and [Col. 0736C] to kill Christ—that is, faith in Christ—in the faithful themselves. But holy teachers expose their wickedness, so that the innocent may be saved and they punished by just retribution.

Ahasuerus exalted Haman (Esther III). By proud Haman, the enemy of Mordecai and of the holy nation, the Jews and the powerful of this present age may be signified. For as Haman, sending letters, strove to seal them with the king’s seal so that his wish might more easily be fulfilled, so the Jews take as testimony in confirmation of their heresy the books of the divine law, in which is the seal of the supreme King—that is, the grace of the Holy Spirit—rejecting fellowship with the Gentiles and Christ’s Gospel as though contrary to the divine commands [Col. 0736D]. The powerful of the age also, abusing benefits conferred by divine mercy, disdain to have as companions in grace those whom they have as companions in nature; and they strive to transfer to themselves the honor and reverence due to God alone. Those who refuse to agree, however, they persecute with hatred and torments. But by a just judgment the wicked are caught in their own snares; the righteous person is delivered from distress, and the ungodly is given in his place.

That night the king passed without sleep, and ordered the annalistic histories of earlier times to be brought to him. While these were being read in his presence, they came to the place where it was written how Mordecai had reported the plot of the eunuchs Bagathan and Thares, who wished to assassinate King Ahasuerus (Esther VI). [Col. 0737A] The king passed the night without sleep, because “he who keeps Israel will neither slumber nor sleep” (Ps. CXX). For God, remaining immovable in himself, beholds the course of times and the actions of human beings; no thought is hidden from him, to whom all things are present. Hence the Apostle says: “For in him there is not ‘is’ and ‘not’; but in him ‘is’ was” (II Cor. I). Mordecai’s deeds are recalled before the king because the good works of holy teachers are never consigned to oblivion before God; rather, “the righteous shall be in everlasting remembrance” (Ps. CXI).

At the king’s command Haman took the robe and went before Mordecai—whom he himself had wickedly prepared a cross for—mounted upon a horse, proclaiming: “This honor is due to whomever the king wishes to honor.” Thus the teachers of the Church, illumined by the cultivation of every virtue and by the beauty of wisdom, are honored with the diadem [Col. 0737B] of royal dignity. As members of the supreme King, they mount the royal horse—that is, the people of the faithful—in whose hearts the King of angels dwells. Hence the prophet Habakkuk: “Thou mountest upon thy horses, and thy chariots are salvation” (Hab. III). To these, spiritual Haman, the enemy of God’s people, though unwillingly renders service, when persecutors of the Church are compelled to bear witness, being unable to conceal what is manifest.

Mordecai returned to the gate of the palace. But Haman hurried to his own house mourning, with his head covered. This is “the change of the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. LXXVI). He who seemed to himself more glorious and powerful than others appears beneath others, more worthless and inferior, according to the saying: “He hath put down the mighty from their seat, and hath exalted the humble” (Luke I). Likewise Isaiah [Col. 0737C] says: “Lebanon shall be turned into Carmel, and Carmel shall be regarded as a forest” (Isa. XXIX). Thus the pride of the Synagogue was brought low and the humility of the Church exalted; thus the persecutors of the Church and of the faith were reduced to nothing, while the confessors of Christ were exalted throughout the whole world. The head was turned into the tail, and the tail into the head, because “everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke XIV), and so forth.

Esther fell at the king’s feet and prayed that he would order Haman’s malice and his most wicked schemes, which he had devised against the Jews, to be made void (Esther VIII). Thus the holy Church daily implores almighty God, through faith and the mysteries of the Incarnation, for the deliverance of her children: that the boldness of enemies may be restrained and the innocence of the faithful set free. [Col. 0737D] Therefore Mordecai was exalted, and his race, because the elect are exalted both in the present through grace and in the future through glory. Haman was punished, and his race, because all evil persons are rejected in the present through guilt and will be punished in the future through penalty. Therefore the joy and exultation of the Jews signifies the eternal gladness of the blessed.

## CHAPTER II. On the mysteries contained in the Book of Tobit

The Book of Tobit is wholesome on the surface of the letter. It abounds especially in examples and counsels for moral life. But allegory surpasses history as greatly as fruit surpasses leaves. For it contains the greatest mysteries of the Church. Tobit himself signifies the people of Israel, who, while others were given over to idolatry, served God by right faith and works. Hence it is said:

[Col. 0738A] “While all were going to the golden calves which Jeroboam king of Israel had made, he alone avoided fellowship with them all and went to Jerusalem, to the Temple of God, and there worshipped the Lord God of Israel. When he had become a man, he took as wife Anna from his own tribe, and begot a son by her, giving him his own name” (Tobit I). Thus the people of Israel multiplied in Egypt, received the Synagogue established by Moses through legal ceremonies, and begot a son by her, because it knew that Christ was to be born from its own race. Hence it is written: “God shall raise up for you a prophet from among your brethren” (Deut. XVIII); and again: “Of the fruit of thy womb I will set upon thy throne” (Ps. XIII). It gave him its own name by believing and confessing what the Father says of him: “I will make him my firstborn” [Col. 0738B] (Ps. LXXXVIII). For this is Israel’s own name. Hence it is written: “Israel is my firstborn son” (Exod. IV).

When he came to Rages, a city of the Medes, and had ten talents of silver from those possessions with which he had been honored by the king, he saw amid the great multitude of his kindred the needy Gabael, who was from his own tribe, and gave him the stated weight of silver under a written bond. Thus, through the seventy interpreters, God’s people entrusted to the Gentiles the knowledge of the Law contained in the Decalogue, in order to free them from the famine of God’s word. It gave it under a written bond—that is, on condition of repayment—when he who had received it should be wealthy, or when he who had given it should demand it back. The Gentiles received God’s word and exercise it, as it were, in trade, even after Christ’s coming, when they seek its spiritual meaning. At the end of the age they will repay it to the lender, receive believing Jews, entrust them to Christ’s mysteries for salvation, and disclose the hidden things of Scripture. [Col. 0738C]

When the angry Sennacherib was killing many of the children of Israel, Tobit buried their bodies. But when it was reported to the king, he ordered him to be killed and took all his possessions. Tobit, however, fleeing naked with his wife and son, lay concealed, because many loved him. Thus the devil wished to destroy God’s people by spiritual death through idolatry, but was unable to take away all their riches of virtues, because among them were many holy people who cared for its life and salvation. He fled with his son and wife, because he did not abandon either faith in the Lord’s Incarnation or the condition of the Synagogue, as appeared more clearly than light in the struggles of the Maccabees [Col. 0738D]. When the king was killed, all Tobit’s possessions were restored by his sons, because, when the devil—who begets, as it were, a most wicked offspring—was repeatedly overcome by his own crimes, prosperity returned to God’s people. We still see the condition of the Church tossed by such alternations.

It happened one day that, wearied from burial, he came home, threw himself down beside the wall, and fell asleep; and hot droppings from a nest of swallows fell upon his eyes while he slept, and he became blind (Tobit II). The blinded Tobit signifies the people of Israel. For “blindness in part hath happened to Israel” (Rom. XI). He was blinded when weary from burial. For whoever perseveres tirelessly in good works does not lose the light of faith. So also, spiritually, the person who neglects to watch, to stand firm, to act courageously, and to be strengthened, sleeps from weariness. [Col. 0739A] To him it is said: “Arise, thou that sleepest, and rise from the dead” (Eph. V). Swallows, because of their light flight, signify frivolity and pride; their filth blinds those over whom it has dominion. He sleeps beneath a swallow’s nest who incautiously subjects himself to frivolity, wantonness, and pride. This blindness prevailed especially among the people of Israel when the Lord’s coming in the flesh was near, while they labored under the yoke of Roman servitude and violated the precepts of the divine law by evil living.

It happened that Sarah, the daughter of Raguel in the city of the Medes, herself heard reproach from one of her father’s maidservants, because she had been given to seven husbands, and a demon named Asmodeus had killed them as soon as they entered to her (Tobit III). Sarah signifies the multitude of the nations, whose teachers knew only the life of this age [Col. 0739B], which revolves in the number of seven days, and knew nothing of eternal life. Therefore, snatched away by the devil and, as it were, enslaved to idolatry, they were killed, until Christ came, the true bridegroom, who espoused her to himself in faith, having overcome the enemy—as Tobit espoused Sarah, the devil having been bound, with the angel present and cooperating. In the angel is signified the Savior’s divinity, as his humanity is signified in Tobit.

Nor is it surprising that we say one person of Christ is figured through two persons, angel and man. For in the expositions of the Fathers we read that his one person is figured in Isaac and the ram: in his humanity he is slain like a sheep; in his divinity he remains impassible with the Father, just as Isaac returns home unharmed with Abraham. If, indeed, the ram signifies Christ’s humanity and Isaac his divinity, [Col. 0739C] why should not man more aptly signify the humanity and the angel the deity?

The prayers of Tobit and Sarah, both of them, were heard before the glory of the supreme God, and the angel Raphael was sent to heal them both. Raphael means “God’s medicine” and signifies Christ, who says of himself: “They that are whole need not a physician, but they that are sick” (Matt. IX). He freed both the Jewish people from the darkness of unbelief and the Gentile people from slavery to idolatry; of him it is written: “His name shall be called the angel of great counsel” (Isa. VI).

The angel appeared to Tobit and offered himself as a companion (Tobit V); and the Son of God assumed humanity, visibly conversed with human beings, and [Col. 0739D] saved the human race. Tobit brought the angel to his father, and the Lord, through the miracles which he performed in the flesh, showed the Jewish people—from whom he took flesh—that he is the Son of God and the angel, that is, messenger, of the Father’s will. To them he also proclaimed the joy of everlasting salvation, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven draweth near” (Matt. III). And to those despairing of the light of heaven he says: “I am the light of the world; he that followeth me walketh not in darkness, but shall have the light of life” (John VIII).

The angel promises Tobit that he will lead his son to the city of the Medes and bring him back. Christ promises believing Jews—although many are blinded—that he will reveal to the Gentiles the mysteries of his Incarnation and disclose them more fully to the Jewish people at the end of time, accompanied and assisted by faith in [Col. 0740A] his divinity. In leading him to the Medes he says: “I have other sheep, which are not of this fold” (John X). Of bringing him back the Apostle says: “Until the fullness of the Gentiles should come in, and so all Israel should be saved” (Rom. XI).

Tobit asked the angel who and whence he was. “I,” he said, “am Azariah, son of the great Ananiah.” Azariah means “helper,” Ananiah “God’s grace.” Christ makes known to his faithful that he is he of whom it is said: “Thou art my helper and my deliverer, O Lord; delay not” (Ps. LXIX). And: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth” (John I). When all things that were to be carried on the journey had been prepared, Tobit bade farewell to his father and mother, and the two went together. Thus, upon the Lord’s appearing, all things [Col. 0740B] necessary for our redemption were prepared, by which the Church’s faith and life are nourished and strengthened until the journey of this age is ended: namely, his virtues, teaching, temptation, passion, resurrection, ascension, the sending of the Holy Spirit, the faith of believers, and the persecution of unbelievers. After these things had been accomplished in Judaea, the mediator between God and human beings proclaimed, through the apostles, to his Jewish fellow-countrymen and to the Gentiles the joys of heavenly salvation and peace. To those who were willing to believe and receive, he gave them through himself; and thus through the apostles he reached the salvation of the Gentiles.

Tobit set out, and a dog followed him (Tobit VI). Thus, when the Lord came to save the Gentiles, preachers followed in his footsteps because they fulfilled what he commanded. Hence it is written: “Go ye [Col. 0740C] and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII). The Lord himself first filled the house of Cornelius with the Holy Spirit, and then Peter sprinkled him with water (Acts X). Preachers are called dogs because they defend God’s house, his possessions, and his spiritual sheep from thieves, bestial spirits, and heretics.

Tobit set out and stayed beside the river called Tigris; and Christ, coming into the world, remained beside the river of mortality. Tobit went out to wash his feet; and Christ went out from the Father to wash his elect from the defilements of sins. The fish wished to devour Tobit; and the devil attempted through his agents to destroy Christ. [Col. 0740D] Tobit feared the fish; and Christ, because of the weakness of the flesh, feared the death impending upon him from the Jews through diabolical suggestion and cooperation. Tobit seized the fish and drew it onto dry ground; and Christ overcame the devil by his power and holds him bound. Tobit disemboweled the fish; and Christ revealed the devil’s hidden wickedness to all the elect. Tobit set aside the fish’s heart, gall, and liver as useful for various remedies; and Christ caused the devil’s malice, rage, and various counsels to be written for the benefit of readers. Whatever Tobit took from the fish he roasted; and Christ does not cease to kindle with the grace of the Holy Spirit those elect whom he separates from the devil’s body by preaching.

Tobit said to Raguel: “Today I will neither eat [Col. 0741A] nor drink here until thou confirm my request and promise to give me Sarah thy daughter.” Hearing this, Raguel was afraid, knowing what had happened to the seven men, and began to fear lest perhaps the same should happen to this man also (Tobit VII). Thus, when the people of the Gentiles heard God’s word and were admonished by the apostles to give Christ a wife from their own stock, they could not receive the ordinances of the new faith without fear or examination. For they had had many teachers, all as it were comprehended in the number seven, who knew only this life and said nothing certain of eternal life; therefore, without hope of immortal life, the destruction of eternal death carried them away. But when truth taught inwardly and sounded outwardly through the mouths of teachers, they finally understood that it was just for those who spoke foolish things to perish foolishly.

[Col. 0741B] Tobit, brought into the bridal chamber, took from his bag a portion of the liver and placed it upon live coals. Then the angel Raphael seized the demon and bound it in the desert of upper Egypt (Tobit VIII), and so forth. When the Lord is to receive the Church from the Gentiles, at the beginning of her espousal he commands her to renounce the devil and all his pomps, and to confess faith in the Trinity for the remission of sins. This is to burn the inward parts of the fish upon live coals. The desert and Egypt signify the hearts of unbelievers: deserted by God because they are unworthy of his dwelling, and, according to the interpretation of “Egypt,” darkened by the shadows of their unbelief. Rightly, moreover, whoever is deserted by God is filled by the demon. But the angel [Col. 0741C] bound the demon who wished to kill Tobit in the desert because, the devil having been restrained from the faithful, he permitted him to rule only over unbelievers. In them he holds him bound, because he is not even permitted to harm them as much as he attempts.

It happened about cockcrow that Raguel summoned his servants, and they went together with him to dig a grave. For he feared that the same thing had happened to him as to the other seven who had gone in to her.

When they had prepared the pit, Raguel returned to his wife and said to her: “Send one of the maidservants to see whether he is dead, so that I may bury him before daylight.” And she sent one of her maidservants. [Col. 0741D] Entering the chamber, she found them safe and unharmed, sleeping peacefully, and so forth. The sound of cockcrow is that of preachers who, after the darkness of errors, announce the coming day of light. Among the Gentiles were those who doubted whether God had truly conquered the ancient enemy; therefore they judged it better to block up and conceal faith in his name. But afterwards, when the light of truth was recognized, as dawn came before and the crowing became more frequent—that is, the voice of preachers—they truly recognized Christ, the enemy overcome, to be the bridegroom of the holy Church.

Raguel rejoices at Tobit’s life and at his daughter’s union. He kills two cows and four rams, and prepares a feast for all his neighbors and friends. The people of the Gentiles rejoice in faith in Christ and in the calling of their people, advancing in the Lord’s faith, so that [Col. 0742A] from among them there would be teachers who afterwards became martyrs. The cows are those who bore the yoke of the Gospel and begot, by preaching, others to bear it. The rams are like fathers and leaders of peoples. Hence it is written: “Bring unto the Lord, ye sons of God; bring unto the Lord the sons of rams” (Ps. XXVIII). They are fat, refreshed by the grace of heavenly love. Hence it is said: “My soul shall be filled as with marrow and fatness” (Ps. LXII). Raguel adjured Tobit to remain with him two weeks. So let us also pray Christ to remain with us until, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, we attain the perfection of rest and are freed from sins in deed and from evil thoughts in mind.

Tobit sends to Gabael and invites him to [Col. 0742B] his wedding; being invited, he comes (Tobit IX). Thus the new people is gathered daily in the Church. This may, however, be understood especially of those who received the letter of the law through the seventy interpreters and therefore received the faith more quickly.

Raguel gave Tobit Sarah and half of all his possessions—in male and female servants, camels, livestock, cows, and much money—and sent him safely and rejoicing to his father (Tobit X). Thus at the end the teacher of the Church will send Christ, together with the Church herself full of the riches of virtues, to the Jewish people—from whom the Son of God took flesh—to illuminate faith and enrich the substance of good works.

The angel said to Tobit: “If it please thee, let us go ahead, [Col. 0742C] and let the household follow our journey at a slow pace” (Tobit XI). Thus, after the people of the Gentiles has been enlightened, divine grace goes before to enlighten the blindness of the Jews, so that in their books they may recognize Christ as true man and true God. Then, as though seeing the angel and his son whom they had long not seen, they may greatly rejoice and finally join themselves in the communion of mysteries to the Church gathered from the Gentiles.

The dog which had been with him on the journey ran ahead and seemed to rejoice by wagging its tail. Thus teachers rejoice in the effect of their work when they understand that Judaea is to be gathered again by the Lord. They rejoice in the reward of eternal life, then proclaim that the hearts of all the elect are to be gladdened by the same reward, and show that the grace of the Holy Spirit will immediately come. The blind father rose up and, stumbling with his feet, began to run. Thus, having heard the word of salvation from teachers, the Jewish people will arise from the long blindness of its unbelief and run in love to the Lord; but, stumbling in the steps of works, it will do so until it is reborn and instructed in Christ, and receives the light of faith and action. [Col. 0742D]

Tobit took the fish’s gall and anointed his father’s eyes, waited about half an hour, and the whiteness began to come out of his eyes like the membrane of an egg. Tobit took hold of it and drew it from his eyes. Immediately he received sight, and he, his wife, and all who knew him glorified God. Tobit said: “I bless thee, Lord God of Israel, because thou hast chastened [Col. 0743A] me and thou hast saved me.” Thus, after the Jewish people has recognized the exceedingly bitter malice of the ancient enemy, it will receive the light it had lost. The whiteness signifies the folly of the Jewish people pleasing itself, having zeal for God but not according to knowledge. Of them it is said: “Seeking to establish their own righteousness, they are not subject to the righteousness of God” (Rom. X). For a black pupil sees; a white one is dark. And in those who seem wise to themselves and say, “Are we blind also?” (John IX), truth is not. Those conscious of their ignorance, who say, “Lord God, enlighten my darkness” (Ps. XVII), are enlightened by the Lord.

Therefore the Jewish people still has a veil before the face of its heart, so that it does not understand Christ’s grace; it has whiteness because it seems to itself white and righteous. [Col. 0743B] It is like the membrane of an egg because it endures blindness of mind under the most foolish hope that Christ is still to be born, will free the Jews, and will give them a great empire. But when the veil has been removed, they will recognize that Christ has already come and redeemed the world by his blood. Hence it follows that, when sight was restored, Tobit and his wife glorified God.

“I am Raphael the angel, one of the seven angels who stand before God. It is time for me to return to him who sent me” (Tobit XII). As the angel was about to return to heaven, he explained more openly who he was, why he had come, and to whom he was to return. Christ disclosed his nature more fully to that people as it advanced, showing that he is in the Father and the Father in him. The angel returns to the Lord; Tobit remains with [Col. 0743C] his father; and Christ is understood by his faithful as equal to the Father in divinity and consubstantial with human beings in humanity.

Opening his mouth, Tobit blessed God (Tobit XIII), confessed his truth and mercy, and taught that God’s benefits must always be proclaimed and his scourges feared. Filled with the spirit of prophecy, he sings much concerning the heavenly Jerusalem. So also the Jewish people converted at the end of the age will have many teachers and prophets who will kindle the minds of peoples with heavenly desires by proclaiming the joys of the celestial homeland.

After the death of his father and mother, Tobit departed from the city of Nineveh and returned to [Col. 0743D] his parents-in-law; he found them safe in a good old age (Tobit XIV). Christ does this daily when, leaving evil people, he turns to enlighten the hearts of the good. They are found in a good old age because they have long devoted themselves to good works. But he passes by others who, though long-lived, are neither mature in counsel nor venerable with the gray hair of good action, but bent beneath the weight of sins. Hence Isaiah: “The child of a hundred years shall die, and the sinner of a hundred years shall be accursed” (Isa. LXV)—that is, one who, though living long, does not abandon the frivolity of his mind.

All his kindred and all his descendants buried the younger Tobit. Tobit’s burial signifies the faith of the world, into whose rest our Lord will enter with his body, which is the Church, while angels rejoice over fellowship with human beings [Col. 0744A] and place individuals in different dwelling-places according to the diversity of their merits.

## CHAPTER III. On the mysteries contained in the Book of Judith

Nebuchadnezzar king of the Assyrians, who reigned in the great city of Nineveh, fought against Arphaxad and conquered him in the great plain called Raga. Then Nebuchadnezzar’s kingdom was exalted and his heart lifted up (Judith I), and so forth. When the devil subjects a multitude of the lost to his own will, his heart is lifted up. Attributing this to his own power rather than divine permission, he burns all the more fiercely for the destruction of the greater number of the lost, the more he believes that he prevails through evil suggestion. Hence it follows: “And he sent to all who were in Cilicia, Damascus, [Col. 0744B] and Lebanon; and to the nations in Carmel and Kedar; and to the inhabitants of Galilee in the great plain of Esdraelon; and to all who dwelt in Samaria and beyond the Jordan as far as Jerusalem; and throughout all the land of Jesse, until one comes to the mountains of Ethiopia.” The devil sends envoys through various provinces when he disperses crowds of evil spirits throughout the world to deceive the nations. He spares neither rank nor honor, for he desires to draw all to hell and make them companions in perdition. Nor does he allow the faithful—signified by the name of Jordan and by Jerusalem—to remain secure. It is not enough for him to swallow the heathen unless he can also devour Christians. Hence Job: “He shall swallow up the river, and shall not wonder; and he shall trust that Jordan may flow into [Col. 0744C] his mouth; and his food is choice” (Job XL). Yet, though he overcomes many, he is scorned by many. Hence it is said: “All with one voice spoke against him.”

Then the angry Nebuchadnezzar called Holofernes, commander of his army, and commanded him to subject all the land to his empire (Judith II). This Holofernes signifies the rulers of the Gentiles who persecute the Church, or Antichrist, the son of perdition, into whom the whole of Satan will enter so that he may do what his fathers did not do and may not regard the God of his fathers, who will rise against every kingdom. He will come with a great multitude in order to crush and kill, and will set his tent upon the renowned and holy mountain, where he will be broken by divine power and fall. This is the beast to which, according to the Apocalypse, the dragon will give his strength and power (Apoc. XIII), so that all may worship the dragon who gave such power to the beast.

When Holofernes had passed the borders of the Assyrians, he came to the great mountains of Ange, which are on the left of Cilicia; he ascended all their strongholds and took every fortification. He destroyed the exceedingly powerful city of Melothi and plundered all the children of Tharsis. The various provinces and place-names contained in the history signify distinctions of persons and ranks of dignity, from which the devil claims a great portion for himself. He does not fear the difficulty of battle, but strives by great power to bring about great ruin.

[Col. 0745A] Then kings and princes of all the cities and provinces—namely Mesopotamia, Syria, Sobal, Libya, and Cilicia—sent their envoys, who came to Holofernes and said: “Let thy indignation against us cease. It is better that we live and serve the great king Nebuchadnezzar and be subject to thee than that, by dying with our destruction, we suffer the losses of our servitude [facimus]” (Judith III). Mesopotamia means “exaltation”; Syria, “high”; Sobal, “vain”; Libya, “those entering”; Cilicia, “assembly” or “mourning.” Therefore the princes of those regions who sent envoys to Holofernes for peace signify carnal persons who seek reconciliation with persecutors so that they may escape the danger of death and the loss of pleasure. Of these it is said: “Whosoever will be a friend of this [Col. 0745B] world is constituted an enemy of God” (Jas. IV). For in them the care of this world and the deceitfulness of riches choke the word, and it bears no fruit. These bear the names of the provinces: they are lifted up in pride and follow vanity. They enter the earth by two ways, and will be joined to the assembly of mourners, or of those paying in hell the penalties of their luxury, where “they shall be transferred from snowy waters to excessive heat” (Job XXIV), and “their worm shall not die, and their fire shall not be quenched” (Isa. LXVI).

Then, hearing this, the children of Israel who dwelt in the land of Judah were greatly afraid at his approach (Judith IV). Thus, in time of persecution, the saints fear lest the devil and the persecutors directed by him should do to the Church and its faithful what they do to other nations. [Col. 0745C] They fear lest the Church be overcome in its weaker part and thus suffer some loss. They send to Samaria—that is, to those who ought to guard themselves and others—counsels of salvation, lest by an entrance through perverse pleasure they give enemies access to the depths of the heart. They send round about, that they may diligently prepare and guard themselves on every side. They occupy the mountain summits when they ascend to and fortify the subtlety of intellects and spiritual perceptions. They surround the villages with walls when they strengthen in faith and virtues the faithful entrusted to them. They gather grain in preparation for battle when they apply themselves more zealously to every reading and meditation upon Holy Scripture. The priest of the Lord, Eliakim, also writes to all, [Col. 0745D] when the spiritual prelate instructs everyone to hold the mountain ascents—that is, the steepness of virtues—and to guard the narrow path—that is, to observe carefully the subtle perceptions of the soul. The children of Israel perform all that has been commanded them when the elect obey the commands of their superiors.

Hearing that the children of Israel were preparing to resist, Holofernes called all the princes of Moab and the leaders of Ammon and said to them: “Tell me, who is this people that occupies the mountains?” (Judith V). Thus persecutors customarily ask one another who these faithful people are, of such great constancy that they presume to resist them in word or deed. Then Achior, leader of all the children of Ammon, answered and said: “If thou deign to hear me, my lord, I will speak the truth about this people in thy presence.” By [Col. 0746A] Achior, heretics are signified. Although they do not hold the way of truth in every respect, they nevertheless proclaim in their teaching many true things consistent with our faith. They fight against the Church; yet, overcome by reason, they do not wholly conceal the truth. For heretics mix good things with evil, since if they always spoke falsehoods, they could not remain concealed. Like one who offers a drink of poison, they touch the rim of the cup with honey, so that the sweet thing may be tasted first and what is deadly may not be feared.

Then Holofernes ordered his servants to seize Achior and take him to Bethulia, etc. (Judith 6). Thus the highest rulers of the world command the persecutors of the faithful who are subject to them to seize any confessors of Christ and heralds of truth, so as to hand them over to the children of Israel—that is, to the elect [Col. 0746B]—whom they themselves suppose destined for destruction. And they proceed across the plains, because they desire to draw such persons, through unlawful desires, onto the broad way that leads to death. Against them come forth slingers—that is, holy preachers—standing in the mountains, that is, in the steepness of the way that leads to life; by open preaching they hurl forth the words of Holy Scripture. But those men, leaving Achior, bind him to a tree, because through diverse tribulations they make him a sharer in Christ’s Passion. And the leaders returned to their lord, because persecutors of the faithful always become worse through the increase of their crimes. Then the children of Israel, coming down from Bethulia, came to Achior; when they had released him, they brought him to Bethulia. Thus the teachers of the Church release one bound to a tree when they teach their catechumens [Col. 0746C] to fear neither persecutor nor death; they release one bound to a tree, as it were, when they rescue a timid mind from dread of the cross and train it to suffer.

This is better accomplished if, following the example of the leaders Uzziah and Charmis, who strengthened Achior and poured forth devout prayers with all the people, the masters of the Church commend their hearers to the Lord in devout prayers together with the other faithful, so that by His gift they may possess what human weakness does not deserve. Then Uzziah, having taken counsel, received him into his house and made him a great supper. And, having summoned all the elders, when they had ended the fast together, they were refreshed. He makes a great supper after the fast has ended who refreshes a soul long languishing and fasting from the bread of God’s word [Col. 0746D] with evangelical teaching and the fare of virtues at a banquet. Hence all the elders are summoned together, so that by their exhortations and examples neophytes may be strengthened to receive and preserve the faith.

Moreover, while Holofernes was making the circuit, he discovered that the spring which flowed in supplied their aqueduct from the south outside the city, and he ordered their aqueduct cut off (Judith 7). Thus persecutors of the faithful remove, by prohibition and threats of death, the teaching of the Gospel which, flowing from the living spring, teachers enlightened by the grace of the Holy Spirit introduce through the channel of their mouth into the city of the holy Church, so that they may kill by deprivation of spiritual drink. Then all the men and women, [Col. 0747A] young people and little children, gathered around Uzziah and all together said with one voice: “May God judge between us and you, because you have done evil to us by refusing to speak peaceably with the Assyrians; and for this reason God has sold us into their hands.”

These represent carnal persons who say, “Lord, Lord,” while their heart is far from God (Isa. 29). Thus there will be bad fish in the Lord’s net until the shore of the future judgment: people who bear the hardships of this present life heavily, who choose to enjoy present pleasures rather than have heavenly goods kept for them in the future, who afflict their teachers with importunate complaints and compel them to indulge their worldly luxury. Hence it follows: “And when, wearied by these cries and exhausted by these weepings, they had fallen silent, Uzziah arose, bathed in tears, and said: ‘Take courage, brothers; let us wait these five days for mercy [Col. 0747B] from the Lord.’”

Thus the idle teacher asks for a reprieve, as it were, of five days through the five bodily senses by which the present life is conducted: he indiscriminately promises bodily comfort to his hearers, as though the generosity of the supreme Giver were in his own power, whereas the measure of giving belongs rather to the giver than to the recipient. But if the comfort of this present life is withheld, they abandon their subjects, so that, by yielding to persecutors, they may avoid bodily punishment.

Judith—that is, the Church—rejects and despises this agreement (Judith 8). For Judith, whose name means “confessing” or “praising,” signifies the Church, which confesses God in true faith and never ceases to praise Him in all His works. Her husband was Manasseh [Col. 0747C], who died in the days of the barley harvest. Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, is aptly called Manasseh, that is, “forgetful” or “one who has forgotten,” because by the consolation of the future life He makes us forget our former affliction. In those days of the barley harvest—that is, of the election of the Jewish people—He entrusts and sends forth His apostles to preach and to gather a sheaf of believers.

The heat of persecution came upon the head—that is, upon the Divinity; for the head of Christ is God (1 Cor. 11). For the Jews are especially scandalized because He said that He was the Son of God (John 10). Hence it is written: “He makes himself God.” His bride, after the Bridegroom has been taken away, devotes herself to fasting and prayer until the end of the age and does not deign to be defiled by the errors [Col. 0747D] of heretics. To her her husband had apportioned the riches of spiritual wisdom and virtue, and he gathered a household into the multitude of the nations.

Judith said to the elders: “What is this word to which Uzziah agrees, that he should hand over the city to the Assyrians if help does not come to us within five days? And who are you who put the Lord to the test? This is not speech that provokes mercy; rather, it stirs up anger and kindles wrath. You have fixed a time for the Lord’s compassion and have made it subject to your own decision!” We ought to prescribe neither time nor measure to the Lord, but rather leave all things to His judgment.
