Hence one of the Fathers is recorded as having said in prayer: “Son of God, have mercy upon me as You will and as You know.” We ought only to seek the kingdom of God, and the rest will be added to us (Matt. [Col. 0748A] 6). Let the present life be for the faithful a matter of use, the future one a matter of enjoyment. Let temporal things belong to the journey; let eternal things be desired at the destination.

Judith’s oratory (Judith 9), into which she entered to pray, signifies the secrecy of the heart into which we ought to enter when we pray to the Lord. Sackcloth signifies the severity of repentance; ashes, remembrance of frailty and death; prostration, the effect of humility.

Judith’s beauty (Judith 10) figures the spiritual beauty of the holy Church, and her adornment proclaims the adornment of the holy Church, which she possesses through the practice of virtues and the performance of good works.

Holofernes burned with desire for Judith and wished to violate her in his lust [Col. 0748B] (Judith 12). The persecutors of the Church desire to corrupt her integrity. Judith was not defiled by Gentile food in the camp of Holofernes; likewise the holy Church, dwelling among pagans, is not contaminated by the filth of idols. Judith cut off Holofernes’ head with his own sword; likewise the holy Church destroys her enemies through their own malice.

After the victory Judith celebrated joy with her companions (Judith 13), and the holy Church, having overcome vices and her enemies, will celebrate joy with the angels. The rout or destruction of the enemies signifies the destruction and condemnation of the ungodly. Abra, Judith’s maid, figures faithful young women who serve the holy Church. “Blessed be the Lord, who created heaven [Col. 0748C] and earth, who directed you to the wounds of the head of the prince of our enemies; because today He has magnified your name so greatly that your praise shall not depart from the mouth of people who remember the power of the Lord forever.” The praise of the Church will not depart from the mouths of those who remember her: she securely endures present tribulations through love of God and neighbor, full of faith and firm in hope, while looking to the greatness of heavenly rewards, where she will be joined to the blessedness of the angels.

After the victory all the people came to Jerusalem to worship the Lord; and, as soon as they had been purified, they all offered holocausts, vows, and their promised offerings (Judith 16). Having gained victory over his enemies, every elect person, purified from every stain, hastens to enter [Col. 0748D] the heavenly city of God, where there is the true vision of peace, and where he may render his vows to his Creator.

## CHAPTER IV. On the mysteries contained in the Book of Maccabees

“And it came to pass, after Alexander son of Philip, the Macedonian, who first reigned in Greece, had gone forth from the land of Kittim and struck Darius king of the Persians and Medes, that he fought many battles, captured all their strongholds, killed the kings of the land, passed on to the ends of the earth, took spoils from a multitude of nations, and the earth was silent before him. He gathered power and an exceedingly strong army; his heart was exalted and lifted up; he gained possession of the regions of the nations and of tyrants, and they became tributary to him. [Col. 0749A] After these things he took to his bed and knew that he would die. He summoned his noble servants, who had been brought up with him from youth, and divided his kingdom among them while he was still alive. Alexander reigned twelve years and died. His servants took possession of the kingdom, each in his own place. After his death they all placed diadems upon themselves, and their sons after them for many years; and evils multiplied in the earth. From them came forth a root of sin: Antiochus the Illustrious, son of King Antiochus, who had been a hostage at Rome. He reigned in the one hundred and thirty-seventh year of the kingdom of the Greeks. In those days lawless men went out from Israel and persuaded many, saying: ‘Let us go and make a covenant with the nations around us, because since we withdrew from them, [Col. 0749B] many evils have befallen us.’ The proposal seemed good in their eyes. Some of the people volunteered and went to the king, and he gave them authority to observe the ordinances of the Gentiles. They built a gymnasium in Jerusalem according to the laws of the nations; they made themselves foreskins, withdrew from the holy covenant, joined themselves to the nations, and sold themselves in order to do evil. And Antiochus went up against Israel and came up to Jerusalem with a heavy multitude” (1 Macc. 1).

The blessed wars of the Maccabean brothers must not be passed over in silence. For their glorious struggles signify the contests of the saints against their spiritual enemies. For whom does Alexander the Great—who subjected almost the whole world to his dominion, and to whom such a desire for rule was given that, so far as he was able, he spared no kingdom—whom, I say, does he signify except the devil, who said: “I will ascend into heaven; above the stars of God I will exalt my throne; I will sit upon the mount of the covenant on the sides of the north; I will ascend above the height of the clouds; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. IV). By his pride, cunning, and the multitudes of angels who were proud with him, he subjected to himself the human race in its first parent.

Alexander [Col. 0750A], dying, left his empire to his attendants; and the devil, seeing at the coming of the Mediator of God and humankind, the man Christ Jesus, that his dominion was being diminished, inspired the wicked rulers of this present age with his malice to persecute believers. From these shall go forth the root of sin: King Antiochus, Antichrist, the son of perdition. The more powerful he will be, the more destructive he will be in persecution. False Christians, heretics, and persecutors of the Church, who daily persecute her, belong to the service of this wicked king. For false Christians are those who make a covenant with the nations, because in their crimes they agree with the nations and by their perversities oppose the faithful.

Therefore Antiochus the Illustrious, the root of sin, together with his rulers, will persecute the holy city Jerusalem [Col. 0750B], because Antichrist with all the wicked will persecute the Church. But Mattathias with his sons resists manfully, and Christ with His elect prelates powerfully defends the Church. Let us see, then, what weapons our Maccabees use to fight their enemies, overcome them, and drive them from their borders. What are these weapons except virtues and good works? They have the shield of faith, the helmet of hope, the breastplate of charity, the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God (Eph. 6). They also have the spear of prayer, raised upward toward the Lord and directed against the enemy; greaves in their travels through diverse places; the bow and arrows through preaching; the bridle through temperance; and spurs through vigils and fasts.

In this spiritual [Col. 0750C] warfare, the body is the horse and the spirit the soldier. Whoever is not armed with the aforementioned weapons is not a soldier of Christ, because without them he cannot belong to Christ. Whoever is not His soldier is His enemy, as He Himself testifies: “Whoever is not with me is against me” (Luke 11). Let everyone strive to be armed with these weapons; let him strive to fight with Christ, so that after victory he may deserve to be crowned by Christ.

# ALLEGORIES COMPRISING NINE BOOKS ON THE NEW TESTAMENT

Four of these explain allegories of the four Gospels; the remaining five contain elucidatory annotations upon the text itself, or determinations of doubts concerning it.

[Col. 0749]

The first book, therefore, concerns the mysteries contained in the Gospel of the most divine John, because, as will be clear at the end of the prologue, he wished to begin with it. The second concerns the mysteries contained in the Gospel of Matthew, with certain additions. The third book concerns the mysteries in the Gospel of Mark. The fourth book concerns the mysteries in the Gospel of Luke. The fifth book contains elucidatory annotations on the Gospel of John. *(It is not by the compiler of the Excerpts.)* The sixth contains elucidations of Paul’s Epistle to the Romans, which we have divided into the customary chapters so that anyone may very easily find the passage sought. The seventh contains elucidations of the same author’s First Epistle to the Corinthians, divided into chapters for a similar reason. [Col. 0751] The eighth explains the Second Epistle to the Corinthians, divided in the same way. The ninth contains very acute questions and highly learned determinations of difficulties occurring in all the epistles of Saint Paul.

# [ALLEGORIES ON THE GOSPELS AND THE EPISTLES OF PAUL]

[Col. 0751]

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 0751]

The first parents of the human race, by their first sin, made themselves and their offspring liable to death and condemnation. But divine providence, which had made the human being in its own image and likeness, purposing to restore him to blessedness, first granted him the helps of salvation through the sacraments of redemption until the coming of the Redeemer. But when the fullness of time had come, God sent His Son (Gal. 4) into the world, so that through the assumed humanity He might redeem humankind and call redeemed humankind back to the kingdoms of heaven, as had been prefigured from the beginning by manifold figures and foretold by many oracles of the prophets.

For the writers of this dispensation divine wisdom chose four Evangelists, so that the human being, composed of four elements and four humors, dispersed through the four regions of the world, might by the teaching of the four Evangelists be able to reach one dwelling-place in heaven and the blessedness of angels. The prophet, taught by the Holy Spirit, describes these four Evangelists by the forms of four living creatures: “The likeness of the faces of the living creatures: the face of a man, the face of a lion, the face of an ox, and the face of an eagle” (Ezek. 1).

By the face of a man Matthew is signified, who begins his Gospel with Christ’s humanity, saying, “The book of the generation” (Matt. 1), etc. By the face of a lion Mark is signified, who says at the beginning of his Gospel, “The voice of one crying in the wilderness” (Mark 1), etc. For the lion roars in the wilderness; so John, whom Mark mentions at the beginning of his Gospel, roared in the wilderness of Judaea in order to awaken the Jews, oppressed by spiritual sleep, saying: “Prepare the way of the Lord; make straight the paths of our God” (Isa. 40), as the prophet Isaiah says. The face of an ox, or calf, belongs to Luke, who begins with the priesthood of Zachariah, saying: “There was in the days of Herod the king a priest named Zachariah” (Luke 1). By the face of an eagle John is signified, who, soaring to the heights, says: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1), etc.

The face of a man belongs to the humanity; the face of a calf, to the Passion; the face of a lion, to the Resurrection; and the face of an eagle, to the Divinity and Ascension. But the face of a man and that of a lion are said to be on the right, because Christ’s birth and resurrection are a universal joy to all. The calf is said to be on the left, because Christ’s death was sorrowful to the apostles. The eagle is described not beside them but above, because it signifies the Ascension and declares the Deity. Although there are four living creatures, the eagle is mentioned above all, because John, by seeing the Word in the beginning, surpasses both the others and himself.

We may therefore refer these faces to Christ, who was born as a human being, suffered as a human being like a calf, rose again like a lion, and ascended like an eagle. Every perfect person also is a human being in reason, a calf in sacrifice, a lion in strength, and an eagle in contemplation. For the things said of the four living creatures apply to all perfect persons. Saint John likewise in the Apocalypse describes the holy Evangelists by these same faces. Therefore, desiring to draw a few drops from the fullness of the Gospels, we begin our exposition where Christ, the author of good things, began the working of His miracles.

# BOOK I. ON THE MYSTERIES OF THE GOSPEL OF SAINT JOHN

[Col. 0751]

## CHAPTER I. On water changed into wine

[Col. 0751A]

“A wedding took place at Cana of Galilee, and Jesus was there with Mary His mother” (John 2). Cana means “zeal” and signifies the fervor of love. Galilee means “a passage made” and signifies the Church, or the honorable conduct of spiritual life in the wilderness. For in the holy Church, or in [Col. 0752A] honorable conduct of spiritual life, putting transient things behind us, we shall pass over to eternal things. Weddings take place at Cana of Galilee when, within the holy Church or good conduct, faithful souls are joined to Christ through the fervor of love.

There [Col. 0753A] Jesus the Savior—that is, He who saves His people from their sins (Matt. 1)—turns water into wine when He converts the ungodly and makes them godly: when He makes the lustful chaste, the drunkard sober, the miser generous, the prodigal temperate, the furious gentle, the proud humble, the wrathful mild, and the persecutor patient. He turns water into wine when He removes guilt and bestows grace. By water the wicked are signified; by wine, the good. For the wicked are cold like water because of their malice; and just as water flows and runs down into the sea, so they flow and run down, through the corruption of vices, into eternal bitterness. But the good, like wine, are inwardly warm through grace, and outwardly give others drink, warm them, and make them drunk through teaching.

[Col. 0753B] Some, however, are so malicious in perversity that they are not merely cold like water through malice, but hardened like ice through hardness of heart. They are slowly thawed from their perversity so as to be changed into the pleasantness of wine. Yet nothing is difficult for the Lord Jesus, because at His will even their hardness is dissolved, and at His command every grace is bestowed. The six water-jars are the five senses of the body together with the one simple sense of the soul. The jars are also said to be made of stone, because before grace our senses are hardened by sin. We fill these six water-jars with water when, through the tears of our compunction, we perfectly wash all our senses from past sin. By such water the Jews—that is, the true confessors of Christ—are purified: those who confess Him not only with the voice of their mouth [Col. 0753C] but also in the truth of their heart by the work of their hands.

The jars hold two measures when we have sinned by pleasure and consent; but three measures when we cleanse by tears not only wrongful pleasure and consent, but also the evil deed. Finally, water is changed into wine because joy in grace follows weeping for sin. Every human being first puts forward good wine, because people who love the things belonging to earth seek delights in the present; then comes what is worse, because in the future they will receive bitter things. God keeps the good wine, because the good things He gives us in time are few in comparison with the future goods He will give us in eternity.

## CHAPTER II. On the same mystery

[Col. 0753D]

“Fill the water-jars with water” (John 2). Galilee means “a passage made.” Therefore the present life is Galilee, passing from present things to future things. Weddings take place in Galilee because, through the passage of time, is signified the enduring union of the Church’s love with Christ and of the soul’s love with God. The six water-jars are the six ages of the world: the first, from Adam to Noah; the second, from Noah to Abraham; the third, from Abraham to David; the fourth, from David to the Babylonian captivity; the fifth, from the Babylonian captivity to Christ; the sixth, from Christ to the end of the world.

In human life there are: infancy, the first age; childhood, the second; adolescence, the third; youth, the fourth; mature adulthood, the fifth; and old age, the sixth [Col. 0754A]. The first, infancy, is overwhelmed by a kind of flood of slippery forgetfulness, so that it is not seen afterward and leaves no traces behind. The second, childhood, first emerging from the flood of forgetfulness into awareness, is raised up through pride and divided and scattered through desire. The third, adolescence, is first circumcised through the restraint of discipline; then it is formed by precepts and governed by counsel. The fourth, youth, is now compelled to serve and made subject to rule, so that through fear of man it may speak of the divine. The fifth, mature adulthood, comes through fear of man to the divine. The sixth, old age, if it is sated with these things, is drawn by desire for future things.

Thus the human race was first overwhelmed by the Flood; second, [Col. 0754B] raised up in the building of the tower and scattered by the division of languages; third, circumcised in Abraham, formed by precepts in Moses, and governed by counsel under the judges; fourth, subjected to dominion under kings; fifth, obedient to religion under high priests; sixth, illumined by true goodness under grace. These six water-jars, whether in the course of this present age or in human life, are all filled with water, because the world is full of judgment and “Your judgments are a great deep” (Ps. 35). God has done many things from the beginning of the world and does not cease to work until its end. All these are judgments, and nothing happens without cause. But so long as a human being cannot say, “Your judgments are pleasant” (Ps. 118), the water has not yet been changed into wine.

When the old wine fails, the jars are filled with water: that is, when carnal pleasures fail in human life [Col. 0754C], divine consolations take their place. At first these impart less savor to beginners, but become sweeter to those who make progress; for then water is changed into wine, when God’s work, which previously has no flavor to one laboring, becomes sweet in the mind of one illumined by spiritual understanding.

## CHAPTER III. On the expulsion of buyers and sellers from the Lord’s temple

The Jewish Passover was near, and Jesus went up to Jerusalem. He found in the temple people buying and selling oxen and sheep, and money-changers seated there. Having made something like a whip of cords, He drove them all out of the temple, along with the sheep and oxen; He poured out the money-changers’ coins and overturned their tables. And to those [Col. 0754D] selling doves He said: “Take these things away from here, and do not make My Father’s house a house of trade” (John 2).

We keep Passover when we pass from vices to virtues. Jesus comes for this purpose when He daily visits the Church and examines the conduct of each person, casting out those who among the holy either do good hypocritically or evil openly. By the oxen that plow are signified the preachers of heavenly teaching. Those sell them who preach not for the love of God but for temporal gain. Innocent sheep offer their wool for clothing; by them are signified works of mercy and purity. They are sold when they are done for human praise. The Holy Spirit appeared in a dove; hence by the dove is understood the Holy Spirit [Col. 0755A], whom simoniacs sell. Those lend money in the Church who serve not heaven hypocritically but earthly things openly. All these are expelled from the portion allotted to the saints: those who do good hypocritically or evil openly. The cord of sins now lashes them for correction, though the uncorrected will at the end be bound by it. He also drives out the sheep and oxen because He shows their life and teaching to be reprobate. He overturns the money and tables because, at the end, the very things they loved will be destroyed.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Samaritan woman

Jesus came to a city called Sychar (John 4), etc. The coming of Jesus signifies the assumption of flesh. Sychar, which means “enclosure” or “branch,” signifies the Gentile people. For the Gentile people [Col. 0755B] were shut up under sin and are a branch cut off from the wild olive and grafted into the olive tree. Jacob’s well, which was there, signifies natural reason, arising from no other source than the cause of all good things, namely God. Thus it is aptly said: “Jacob’s well was there,” that is, infinite reason proceeding from the Father’s height.

Jesus, weary from the journey, sat above the well. Jesus’ journey is the dispensation of the Incarnation; His sitting, the condescension of humility; His weariness, the weakness of the flesh; the sixth hour, the sixth age; the well, the depth of this world; the Samaritan woman, the Church. The woman came, then, not yet justified but about to be justified. She had not yet laid aside the water-jar of desire, and she drew the stream of pleasure from the depth of the present age. Jesus said to her, “Give me a drink.” Jesus asks the primitive Church from among the Gentiles [Col. 0755C] for the drink of faith, by which He may be believed to be the Redeemer. He asks for the drink of reason, that He Himself may be sought out as Creator. And while He asks drink from her, He makes her drunk with the drink of heavenly grace.

The apostles buy food in the city when, by their preaching in the world, they acquire faith among the peoples and good works for the honor and will of the Savior. “Go, call your husband.” The woman answered: “I have no husband.” Jesus said to her: “You have rightly said, ‘I have no husband.’ For you have had five husbands, and the one whom you now have is not your husband.” The five husbands are the five senses of the body. They are rightly called the husbands of the soul because they are naturally joined to it, so that by their union it may have the fruitfulness of good works and bring forth offspring. These senses die one by one in the soul when they are corrupted by successive wrongdoing [Col. 0755D]. When these husbands have died—that is, when the senses have been corrupted by wrongdoing—human nature joins itself to a sixth, not a husband but a fornicator and corrupter: namely, worldly error.

Christ therefore found the Samaritan woman, that is, the Church of the Gentiles, not joined to any lawful husband—that is, to sound understanding—but joined to her corrupter. But the Lord, wishing to call her back to truth, taught her next, lest she—because she had heard that the fathers worshiped on that mountain and that the Jews then worshiped in Jerusalem—should suppose, I say, that worship was to take place only on that mountain or in Jerusalem. He said: “Woman, believe me: the hour is coming, and now is, when [Col. 0756A] you will worship neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem; but true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth.”

Immediately the disciples came. The disciples come from the city to the Lord with food when, from this world, they produce for Him among the Gentiles the fruit of good works through their preaching or teaching. They marvel that He speaks with a woman, because they are astonished at God’s mercy, that the grace of God is bestowed even upon the Gentiles. The woman—that is, the Gentile people—having been converted and received through faith such great knowledge of truth, left behind her water-jar by renouncing desire; and through good works and remission of her sins she went into the city—that is, into the multitude of unbelievers—and said to those people through preaching: “Come and see a man who told me everything [Col. 0756B] that I did.” For the Church converted from the Gentiles desires the salvation of all and summons all whom it can to the divine vision. And they went out from that city and came to Him. Thus, because they heard the voice of preaching, those who will share in eternal blessedness went out from the perversity of their former life and came to the knowledge of truth.

Let the children of the Church learn to imitate their mother. Let them learn to bring unbelievers to God not by arms but by words; let them learn not to take perishable goods from them by force, but rather to confer on them through love both perishable and enduring goods. “Rabbi, eat.” And He answered: “I have food to eat that you do not know. My food is to do the will of Him who sent me.” The will of His Father is the conversion and justification of humankind, because Christ refreshes Himself when He teaches unbelievers the truth.

[Col. 0756C] “Lift up your eyes and see the fields, for they are already white for harvest.” As the apostles offer bodily food, He teaches them what food He Himself hungers for: namely, the salvation of human beings. “Lift up your eyes and see,” that is, consider with understanding, that when the winter of unbelief has passed, the warmth of faith is present and hearts are ready for you to gather works of righteousness from them. “So that he who sows may rejoice together with him who reaps.” Both were necessary: sowing and reaping. For in this the saying is shown true: “One is he who sows and another he who reaps” (John 4). Unless they had been prepared by the prophets, they would not have heard the apostles; for the apostles would not have been believed unless the prophets had preceded them.

[Col. 0756D] “I sent you to reap that for which you did not labor. Others labored, and you entered into their labors.” The patriarchs and prophets had many labors, and in them all was prophecy of Christ; many also suffered, as though in the cold of sowing. It is as if He said: I make you harvesters where others have sown—that is, in Judaea, where the first harvest was gathered. From there some will go forth to sow throughout the whole world. Hence another harvest, as it were arising from grains, will be gathered at the end of the age by the angels who are harvesters.

Many Samaritans from that city believed in Him. Those believe in Him who acknowledge Him not only through belief but also love Him in affection. And He remained there two days. He remains two days with those whom He instructs in the two commandments of love and to whom He shows Himself, as it were, in the light of two days [Col. 0757A].

## CHAPTER V. On the son of the royal official healed by the Lord

There was a certain royal official whose son was sick at Capernaum (John 4). This royal official signifies the assembly of patriarchs and prophets; Capernaum, the world; the official’s son, the people subject to sins and to be saved by grace. Patriarchs and prophets are aptly signified by the name of royal official, because they knew how not only to govern themselves rightly in life but also to govern others by word and example. “Lord, come down”—as though the assembly of the ancient fathers said: “Lord, come down through the assumption of human flesh, so that You may save by the Passion of Your death the people—who will become a son through faith—dying through wrongdoing.” And just as the faith of the official obtained [Col. 0757B] the salvation of his son, so the faith of the fathers prevailed for the salvation of the human race.

The official’s servants, who meet him and announce his son’s recovery, are preachers laboring in the conversion and justification of human beings, rejoicing and celebrating with the Lord over their salvation. It is rightly said of the healed son that the fever left him at the seventh hour, because in the distribution of the sevenfold Spirit the Gentiles and all those predestined to life are released from sin. The royal official and his entire household believe when the assembly of the fathers, together with the other faithful, is illumined by divine grace.

In the same way, a royal official intercedes for the healing of his sick son when any prelate pours out prayers for his subordinate, corrupted by diverse temptations, to be healed by the Lord. The sick person is healed when one corrupted by sin is recalled through grace to righteousness [Col. 0757C].

## CHAPTER VI. On the sheep-pool
Jesus went up to Jerusalem. Now in Jerusalem there is a sheep-pool, called in Hebrew Bethsaida, having five porticoes (John 5). The sheep-pool—that is, the pool for sheep—in which the sheep offered in sacrifice to the Lord were washed, signifies a holy and religious manner of life. In it the soul, which ought to be a sheep by innocence, must be washed by repentance, so that it may be offered to the Lord through good works. This pool has five porticoes, on account of the bodily senses, through which all our action is brought to its perfect effect. But within these five senses of ours lies a great multitude of the sick [Col. 0757D], because the corruption of the bodily senses is manifold. Sight is corrupted by seeing vain things; hearing, by hearing vain things; taste, by greedily eating pleasant things; smell, by smelling vain things; touch, by doing slippery deeds.

Whoever delights in spectacles of vanity and in the manifold appearance of temporal things; whoever looks upon a woman in order to lust after her (Matt. 5); whoever sees gold, silver, costly garments, and such things, and unlawfully desires what he has seen, has a multitude of the sick in his sight. For as many unlawful desires as he has in his sight, so many sick persons he contains in that same sense. Whoever delights in the empty melodies of various sounds or voices, or in enticing songs; whoever lends his ear in order to drink in blood—that is, by willingly listening to slanders—has within the range of his hearing a multitude of the sick [Col. 0758A]. Whoever satisfies the desire of his palate and belly with delicate foods, diverse flavors, and drinks keeps a multitude of the sick within the circuit of this portico. Some strive to satisfy their sense of smell with diverse perfumes and the fragrances of various spices. Others serve the pleasures of touch through the delights of diverse things. But each sense keeps as many sick persons as it suffers corruptions of desire.

The water in which the sick were healed signifies compunction. The angel who stirred the water signifies the Holy Spirit. The angel of the Lord came down into the pool, the water was stirred, and one person was healed. So whenever the Holy Spirit comes down into us and enters us, he awakens [Col. 0758B] the grace of compunction, and our sense is healed from whatever infirmity of corruption holds it. The statement, “and one person was healed,” indicates that whoever is joined to the unity of holy Church immediately merits the grace of spiritual health.

The lame are those who do not direct their path along righteousness. The blind are those who know neither God nor his commandments. The withered are those who do not stretch out their hands in good works or in the distribution of alms. Therefore many are infirm, but one is healed, because only the person who remains in the unity of holy Church, who worships one God, is justified. The fact that some of those sick persons, after being put into the pool by a human being, were healed, whereas this man obtained health through the Lord alone, without human cooperation, signifies that at times we obtain salvation through the cooperation of preaching [Col. 0758C] or human intercession, while at other times we are justified by inner inspiration alone.

“Take up your bed and go.” The man who had been ill carries his bed home when the soul, healed by the forgiveness of sins, returns to inward watchfulness over itself together with its body, lest it again admit anything by which it may be struck.

## CHAPTER VII. On the five loaves and the two fish

When he had lifted up his eyes and seen that a very great multitude was coming to him, he said to Philip, “Where shall we buy bread for these people to eat?” etc. “There is a boy here who has five barley loaves and two fish,” etc. (John 6). The five barley loaves are [Col. 0758D] the five books of Moses, in which the pith of spiritual understanding is contained beneath the husk of the letter. The two fish are the books of the prophets and the Psalms. Of this food the Lord says: “What is written concerning me in the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms” (Luke 24).

The Lord broke this food for the apostles to set before the people when he opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures. They, however, set the food they had received before others when they preached throughout the world that the Scriptures of the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms must be understood and observed spiritually. Those who eat also recline upon the grass when, nourished by preaching or reading, they subdue their flesh with fasts and vigils, lest it rule over them. The five thousand are found to be such on account of the five bodily senses [Col. 0759A], which those set over them govern well and perfectly, and through which they act.

Finally, those who eat are satisfied when hearers are instructed through preaching and reading in everything pertaining to faith and good works. “Apart from,” he says, “women and children.” Women, the weaker sex, and children, that is, the younger age, are unworthy of the number. They signify those weak in faith and not yet fit for battle. Women and children may also signify the reprobate, who, although they eat with the elect by hearing preaching, nevertheless stand outside the number of the elect because of the perversity of their conduct.

“And they took up twelve baskets full of the fragments that remained.” The remnants are the subtler and more hidden teachings of spiritual understanding, which the unlearned cannot grasp [Col. 0759B]. They ought not to be carelessly left behind, but diligently sought by the apostles and their successors. Servile tasks are performed with baskets; and “God chose the weak things of the world to confound the strong” (1 Cor. 1). Let us also strive to set before others, through preaching, the bread of divine knowledge which we have received, lest through our negligence they fail on the way or perish from hunger.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the woman caught in adultery

The scribes and Pharisees brought to Jesus a woman caught in adultery, set her in the midst, and said to him: “Teacher, this woman has just been caught in adultery. Now Moses commanded us in the Law to stone such persons. What then do you say?” (John 8). This woman signifies the Gentile Church [Col. 0759C], violated by the devil through the worship of idols. The Jews wish her to be stoned because, envying her participation in heavenly grace, they wish her to be condemned.

“They said this to test him, that they might be able to accuse him.” The hostile Pharisees test him concerning justice, to see whether he would speak against it. For they knew that he was gentle and a preacher of mercy, and that this was why he pleased the people. Hence they thought he would say that the adulteress ought to be dismissed; then he would be called an opponent of the Law of Moses and of God its author, and thus would be liable to death together with the adulteress. But if he said, in accordance with the Law, that she should be stoned, they would mock him as one without the gentleness that he preached and for which he was loved.

But he is caught by neither calumny. Preserving gentleness, he gives the answer required by true justice: “Let him who is without sin [Col. 0759D] be the first to cast a stone at her.” But he, bending down, wrote with his finger upon the ground. The Law was written by the finger of God upon tablets of stone because of the hardness of that people. Now, bent down in human form, he who is guardian, giver, and judge of the Law writes upon the ground. In this he teaches us not rashly to judge anyone on the basis of evils we have heard, but first to examine ourselves inwardly with the finger of discernment, as he says there: “Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her”; as though he said: First be righteous, and afterward punish the guilty.

For the Law commands the guilty to be punished, but not by persons guilty of like offenses. Behold complete justice: that a righteous person should punish evil people and evil deeds. Therefore let them either dismiss the guilty woman or undergo punishment with her. And again, bending down, [Col. 0760A] he wrote upon the ground. He wrote again upon the ground, turning his face aside in another customary manner, so that those whom he foresaw would leave sooner than ask further questions might be free to depart. He teaches us, moreover, that as before correcting another person, so afterward we should humbly investigate ourselves, lest the same thing or something similar be in us.

But when they heard these things, they went out one by one, beginning with the elders; and Jesus alone remained, with the woman standing in the midst. Thus, when the Jews abandon Christ through unbelief, the Church of the Gentiles stands in faith, perseveres in expectation of divine mercy, has her guilt forgiven, and receives grace. In the same manner the Lord daily receives the adulteress when through grace he receives any soul corrupted by the devil through sin.

## CHAPTER IX. On the blind man given sight

[Col. 0760B]

As Jesus was passing by, he saw a man blind from birth (John 9). This blind man signifies the human race, blinded in its first parents through original sin. “I must,” says the Lord, “work the works of him who sent me while it is day.” Not only then, when Christ was in the world, but always until the consummation of the age, he is with the elect through faith, and it is a time for working. “Night comes, when no one can work.” That night is the darkness of hell, in which no one is permitted to work, just as it was not permitted to the rich man in flames; it is only a time for receiving.

He spat on the ground, made clay from the spittle, anointed the man’s eyes with the clay, and said to him: “Go and wash in the pool of Siloam” (which is interpreted “Sent”). So he went and washed, [Col. 0760C] and came back seeing. Therefore the neighbors, and those who had seen him before because he was a beggar, said: “Is this not the man who used to sit and beg?”

The saliva is divinity; the earth, humanity; the clay formed from both, the union of the two natures. Siloam, which is interpreted “Sent,” signifies Christ, in whom the blind man anointed with clay is washed when the sinner is renewed in baptism through faith in his divinity and humanity. Blindness is removed when sin is blotted out. Finally, the washed man sees clearly when every reborn person believes, loves, or contemplates the good things of the heavenly homeland. Thus this blind man is the human race; blindness is sin; the clay is the mystery of the Incarnation; the anointing and washing are faith together with baptism; the reception of light is contemplation of the heavenly brightness. But the Jews cast out the man who has received sight when [Col. 0760D] they despise the Christian people. And Jesus receives the enlightened man because he prefers the Christian to the Jew.

## CHAPTER X. On the grain of wheat

“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the ground and dies, it remains alone” (John 12). It is evident to everyone concerning a grain of wheat that, when it falls into the ground, unless it dies—that is, unless it is moistened by the moisture of the earth, ceases to be what it formerly was, and through the alteration of growth becomes something else—it remains alone and bears no fruit. But if it has died, that is, has been decomposed by the richness and moisture of the earth, it immediately puts forth a blade, strengthens a stalk, forms ears, awns, husks, and grains, and bears much [Col. 0761A] fruit.

For, as is said in another parable, “thirtyfold, sixtyfold, or a hundredfold” (Matt. 13), so Christ, falling into the earth through humanity, bears much fruit by dying through his Passion. For his birth would have bestowed nothing upon us unless, by dying, he had been able to redeem us. Concerning this fruit and increase the Psalmist says: “I am alone until I pass over” (Ps. 140). For he was alone until he passed over, because until he tasted death he did not accomplish the fruit of human redemption. But by dying he multiplied fruit from himself, because he redeemed all those predestined to eternal life.

This fruit signifies the patriarchs, prophets, evangelists, apostles, martyrs, confessors, virgins, and all elect souls: all who from the beginning were to be justified through [Col. 0761B] the grace of redemption, and all who at the end will be made blessed through the glory of recompense. Saint John the Evangelist also describes this fruit when he says: “I heard the number of the sealed: one hundred and forty-four thousand sealed from every tribe of the children of Israel” (Rev. 7). And afterward: “After this I saw a great multitude which no one could number, from all tribes and peoples and tongues, standing before the throne.”

By the one hundred and forty-four thousand sealed from every tribe of the children of Israel, he signifies those whom divine Providence, having predestined them to life before the Redeemer’s coming, prepared for salvation through the preceding sacraments of redemption. But by the great multitude which no one could number, which he saw from all tribes [Col. 0761C], tongues, and peoples, he indicated those whom heavenly grace justifies and saves after the Redeemer’s coming. This multitude is rightly said to be one which no one could number, because few were justified before Christ’s coming in comparison with those justified after his coming. Before his coming, indeed, God was known only in Judea. But now all nations clap their hands and rejoice in God with a voice of exultation (Ps. 75). O how wonderful! (Ps. 45). This is the grain that produces thirtyfold fruit among married persons, sixtyfold among the continent, and a hundredfold among virgins.

## CHAPTER XI. On casting the net into the sea

Jesus said to his disciples: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find [fish]” (John 21). Twice in the holy [Col. 0761D] Gospel we read that the Lord commanded nets to be cast for fishing: namely, before the day of his Passion and after the Resurrection. But before our Redeemer both suffered and rose again, he commands the net to be cast for fishing, yet does not command whether it ought to be cast on the right or the left. After the Resurrection, however, appearing to the disciples, he commands the net to be cast on the right.

In that fishing so many and such great fish were caught that the nets were broken; in this one, however, many were caught and the nets were not broken. Who does not know that the good are symbolized by the right hand and the evil by the left? Therefore, that fishing, in which it is not specifically commanded to which side the net should be cast, signifies the present Church, which gathers good and evil together and does not choose [Col. 0762A] whom it draws, because it does not know whom it can choose. But this fishing, performed after the Lord’s Resurrection, was cast solely to the right, because only the Church of the elect will attain to behold the glory of his brightness; it will have nothing of the work of the left.

In that fishing, the net is broken by the multitude of fish, because now so many reprobate persons enter the confession of faith together with the elect that they even rend the Church itself by heresies. In this fishing, however, many and great fish are caught, and the net is not broken, because the holy Church of the elect, resting in the unbroken peace of its Author, is no longer torn by any dissensions.

Therefore they cast the nets, and they were no longer able to draw them because of the multitude of fish. “Bring some of the fish which you have now caught.” Simon [Col. 0762B] Peter went up and drew the net onto land, full of one hundred and fifty-three great fish. This number is not devoid of a great mystery; rather, the depth of so great a mystery awaits our attentive consideration. For the Evangelist would not have stated the total number so carefully unless he had judged it to be full of sacramental meaning.

For you know that in the Old Testament every work is commanded through the precepts of the Decalogue. In the New, however, the power of this same work is given to the multiplied faithful through the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit. Announcing him, the prophet says: “The Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and strength, the Spirit of knowledge and piety; and the Spirit of the fear of the Lord filled him” (Isa. 11). But one receives activity in this Spirit who acknowledges faith in the Trinity: who believes that the Father, the Son, and that same Holy Spirit are of one power, and confesses them to be of one substance.

Therefore, because the seven gifts mentioned above are more abundantly given through the New Testament, while the ten commandments are given through the Old, all our virtue and activity can be fully comprehended through ten and seven. Let us therefore take the triangular number of seventeen, and it comes to one hundred and fifty-three. This number indeed is not devoid of a great mystery, because in the Old Testament we read that the fiftieth year was commanded to be called the jubilee, in which the whole people was to rest from every work. But true rest is in unity. For one cannot be divided; where there is the rupture of division, there is no true rest. Let us therefore take the triangular number of fifty [Col. 0762D] and one: it makes one hundred and fifty-three.

Therefore, because all our activity and virtue, performed in faith in the Trinity, tends toward rest, we multiply seven and ten by three, so that we arrive at fifty-one. And our true rest is then attained when we acknowledge the very brightness of the Trinity, which we firmly maintain to exist in the unity of divinity. We multiply fifty-one by three, and we have the total number of the elect in the heavenly homeland, as it were the number of one hundred and fifty-three fish. It was fitting that the net cast after the Lord’s Resurrection should catch as many fish as signified only the elect citizens of the heavenly homeland. And though they were so many, the net was not broken.

The Evangelist adds a necessary point [Col. 0763A], saying: “And though they were so many,” or “so great”—as he says above, “full of great fish”—the net [Col. 0764A] “was not broken”; that is, they were great, but there were no heresies among them.

# BOOK TWO. ON MATTHEW

[Col. 0763]

## CHAPTER I. On the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount and the eight beatitudes according to Matthew

[Col. 0763B]

Seeing the crowds, Jesus went up the mountain, etc. (Matt. 5). The fact that the Lord, when about to teach his disciples the number eight by which one reaches the eight beatitudes, went up a mountain indicates to us that whoever dispenses the word of sacred Scripture ought not to remain in the valley of perversity or on the plain of unrestrained dissipation, but should ascend the mountain of spiritual conduct through the practice of virtues and the performance of good works. And as it is written: “Go up onto a high mountain, you who bring good news to Zion” (Isa. 40). Thus ascent of the mountain signifies exalted conduct; the Lord’s sitting, the authority of teaching; the opening of his mouth, the effect of preaching.

[Col. 0763C] “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” etc. Some are rich in spirit; others have, in a manner of speaking, nothing of spirit; others are poor in spirit. The rich in spirit are the proud. Those having nothing of spirit are excessively fainthearted. The poor in spirit are the humble. The proud do what ought not to be done through self-exaltation. The fainthearted omit what ought to be done through faintheartedness. The humble omit what ought not to be done, and do what ought to be done through humility. Poverty of spirit, therefore, having nothing of deficiency and nothing of excess, leads by the royal road to heavenly blessedness.

“Blessed are the meek.” The meek are gentle and patient, who harm no one and yield to the wicked. Yet there are some who wish to be so meek that they care nothing for another’s life, admonish no one toward good, and correct no one for evil. But such gentleness is not greatly to be praised, because it suffers a defect where it ought to exercise the effect of virtue. Therefore people ought to be meek in such a way that they harm no one, patiently bear evils brought upon them, and neglect neither their own life nor that of another; so that, if need be, they may offer exhortation to the good toward better things and correction to the evil for evil. “There is a measure in things” (Horace, *Satires*, book I, satire I, 106); for just as a person ought not to be excessively harsh, so neither ought one to be excessively gentle, but should attain the land of blessedness between right and left through discerning meekness.

“Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted.” Mourning commonly occurs over the loss of loved ones, as when someone loses those dear to him: a father, mother, son, or some relative. Alas! How many mourn bodily losses but disdain to mourn [Col. 0764B] spiritual losses! When someone becomes ill or dies, friends mourn; but when someone sins damnably, when he commits fornication, when he says to his brother, “You fool,” they do not mourn. O insane health! O blind sight! O dead life! Over things that ought not to be mourned, or only slightly mourned, they mourn grievously; and they do not mourn spiritual losses, which ought to be grievously mourned, but even laugh over them.

Of these, I say, Isaiah prophesied: “Woe to those who call good evil and evil good, who put darkness for light and light for darkness, bitter for sweet and sweet for bitter” (Isa. 5). Let us not mourn, brothers, the loss of loved ones, but let us mourn the loss of good works and the loss of virtues. Let the corrupted person mourn the loss of virginal integrity; let the malicious mourn the loss of piety; [Col. 0764C] let the proud mourn the loss of humility; the angry, the loss of inner tranquility; the avaricious, the loss of generosity; the drunken, the loss of sobriety; the slothful or weary, the loss of spiritual exercise; the envious, the loss of charity.

For blessed are those who now mourn through repentance, because they will be comforted through pardon, then through righteousness, and finally through glory. We may therefore say that there are three kinds of those who mourn spiritually and fruitfully before the eyes of the Creator. Some mourn for forgiveness of sin; some mourn from the sweetness of grace divinely bestowed upon them; others, inflamed by greater fervor, mourn from desire for future glory. And in all these ways blessed are [Col. 0764D] those who mourn, because “those who sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Ps. 125). And God “will wipe every tear from the eyes of the saints, because there shall be no more mourning, nor crying, nor any pain, because the former things have passed away” (Rev. 21).

“Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they shall be satisfied.” All people hunger and thirst; but some hunger and thirst for evil, others hunger and thirst for good. Some hunger and thirst for gold, silver, costly garments, estates, lands, vineyards, houses, horses, and innumerable possessions. All these things, however, are good in themselves; yet in a certain sense they are called evil in this respect, because evil people hunger and thirst for them uselessly, as the Lord called mammon—that is, riches—unrighteous (Luke 16), not because the things constituting riches are unrighteous, but because they are acquired through unrighteousness.

Others hunger and thirst for powers and honors; others, for pleasures; others, for greetings in the marketplace, the chief places at banquets, seats [Col. 0765A] in synagogues, and to be called Rabbi by people (Matt. 25). But such persons cannot become blessed, because they cannot be satisfied. For the entire world could by no means suffice a person for whom God, the Lord of the world, does not suffice. The eye is not filled by seeing, nor the ear by hearing (Ecclus. 1), nor can a person be satisfied in the other senses by their pleasures. King David understood this well. Although he had food and drink not merely for necessity but, if he wished, even for excess, he nevertheless said: “I shall be satisfied when your glory appears” (Ps. 16). Therefore let us hunger and thirst not for transient or earthly things, but for righteousness, because through hunger and thirst for righteousness we shall reach the satisfaction of eternal glory.

[Col. 0765B] “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy.” If you wish to receive mercy, show mercy. “Forgive,” he says, “and you shall be forgiven.” For “with the measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you” (Mark 4; Luke 6). Blessed also are the merciful, who stand by others in their miseries and protect and defend them according to their ability.

“Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God.” Pure in heart are those defiled neither by the dust of useless thought nor by the mire of shameful delight. Pure in heart are those untouched by the mist of earthly ignorance and uncorrupted by the heat of foul desire. Let us therefore cleanse our hearts from every ignorance through inquiry into truth, and from every perverse [Col. 0765C] desire through love of virtue, so that we may deserve to see God in the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.” Peacemakers are those who know how to make and preserve peace within themselves: who raise up virtues, drown and extinguish opposing vices, prudently and powerfully drive out whatever perverse thought, word, or deed they discover in themselves, and permit no disturbance to remain in the kingdom of their rule. If adversity comes upon them, they nevertheless preserve their peace and judge all things with tranquility of heart.

Peacemakers are those who, when evils are inflicted upon them by evil people, return no evil, but are peaceful with those who hate peace; who preserve peace not merely in themselves, but also bring others at variance with one another back to the unity of peace. These shall be called children of God, because God is supreme peace and judges all things with tranquility of mind: children of God and brothers of Christ. These are children by grace; Christ is Son by nature. “Heirs of God, and joint heirs with Christ” (Rom. 8).

“Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.” Many suffer persecution, but some on account of guilt and others on account of righteousness: evil people suffer on account of guilt; good people, on account of righteousness. A thief is hanged for guilt; a righteous person cannot be hanged except on account of righteousness and innocence. But someone will say: No one can now attain [Col. 0766A] blessedness through persecution, because all things now stand in peace and holy Church suffers adversity almost nowhere.

And I say that temptations and persecutions are everywhere, because daily, in the inner precincts of holy Church, Cain persecutes Abel, Ishmael Isaac, Esau Jacob—that is, the impious person persecutes the righteous. And if anyone does not suffer persecution from outsiders, he nevertheless suffers it from false brothers. For “all who desire to live piously in Christ suffer persecution” (2 Tim. 3). Therefore, because persecutions do not cease, patience is necessary to us, that we may obtain the promises. But woe to those who lose patience, because they also lose the crown of patience. Let us not therefore murmur if we are afflicted in a few things, because we shall be rightly ordered in many things (Wis. 3).

[Col. 0766B] Therefore, through poverty of spirit one reaches the kingdom of heaven; through meekness, or gentleness, the land of the living; through mourning, true consolation; through thirst and hunger for righteousness, the satisfaction of heavenly delight; through mercy practiced in time, eternal mercy; through purity of heart, the vision of God; through peace, divine sonship; through present persecution, eternal tranquility and rest in the kingdom of heaven.

“Blessed are you when people revile you and persecute you,” etc. Above he spoke to all the elect. Now he turns his address to the apostles, though these words also apply to other elect persons, showing the apostles in these words how much they would suffer for his name. O how few there are who attend with the eyes of the mind to these words of the Lord and seek blessedness through their admonition! How many, for a slight verbal injury, return blows if they can; and if they cannot accomplish what they attempt, nevertheless threaten even greater things!

How well the holy apostles had impressed these words upon their hearts, since they went away rejoicing from the presence of the council because they had been counted worthy to suffer dishonor for the name of Jesus (Acts 5). It should be noted, moreover, that he says, “lying, and on my account.” For if people, when they revile us, speak evil truthfully, this no longer has such merit. And if we endure blasphemies on account of our own cause and guilt, not on account of God, we have no merit.

“Rejoice and exult.” In many things we are deceived, brothers. For when worldly things smile upon us, when the crowd exalts us with praises, we rejoice and exult, whereas we ought rather to weep and grieve, because prosperity entails greater danger than adversity, and praise than reproach. But let us rejoice, because sound joy and sound exultation are shown to the apostles when they are told that they ought to rejoice and exult amid insults and persecutions. He adds the reason, saying: “For your reward is great in heaven.” This reward, brothers, is abundant, great, precious, and lasting. It is so abundant that it cannot be numbered; so great that it cannot be comprehended; so precious that it cannot be valued; so lasting that it cannot end.

## CHAPTER II. On the Lord’s Prayer according to Matthew and the seven petitions contained in it

[Col. 0767A]

Among all that human frailty can do in order to please God, prayer is especially powerful, if it is made with a pure conscience and humility of heart. For if the conscience is polluted by the poison of an evil will or deed, or if our heart is filled with empty self-exaltation, our prayer is not received by God and our mind is not heard. “Whoever turns away his ear from hearing the Law, his prayer shall be an abomination” (Prov. 28).

Therefore Christ Jesus, man and mediator of God and humanity, providing for human salvation and mercifully making provision for it, among the other words of his most sacred teaching established a form of prayer and taught [Col. 0767B] how we ought to pray to the Father, saying: “When you pray, do not be like the hypocrites, who love to stand praying in synagogues and at street corners. And when you pray, do not speak much, as the Gentiles do; for they think that they shall be heard because of their many words. Therefore pray in this way: Our Father, who art in heaven,” etc. (Matt. 6).

This Lord’s Prayer is known to contain seven petitions. The first petition is: “Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name”; the second: “Thy kingdom come”; the third: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth”; the fourth: “Give us this day our daily bread”; the fifth: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors”; the sixth: “And lead us not into temptation”; the seventh: “Deliver us from evil” (ibid.).

### First Petition: “Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name” [Col. 0767C]

Behold, beloved, on almost every day clergy and people, men and women—but especially on feast days—flock together to the churches. Each, according to his means, adorns himself in better clothing before the eyes of men; securely, as though children of God, they enter the house of God together; they bend the knee, beat their breasts, spread out their hands, open their mouths, and pour forth prayers, saying: “Our Father, who art in heaven.” Yet—what cannot be said without deep sorrow—many enter the house of God in order to pray to God, and few are heard. Many call God Father in this prayer who are not his children, but children of that father of whom it is written: “You are of your father the devil” (John 8).

They are not children of God because they have lost his grace; they are children of the devil because he has begotten and nourishes them through sin. The children of the devil are—as we are accustomed to say in other statements—unclean persons, fornicators, adulterers, robbers, the avaricious, cursers, usurers, and those corrupted by any other damnable sins; those who say to their brother, “Fool”; those who look upon a woman in order to lust after her (Matt. 5); and all who, even if not by a perverse deed, are nevertheless alienated from God by a perverse will.

Therefore, brothers, whoever calls God Father in the Lord’s Prayer, whoever desires to be heard by him, should live in such a way that God may recognize him by grace as his own Son—he who is the Father of all by nature. Otherwise, when he is judged, he will go forth condemned, and “his prayer shall become sin” (Ps. [Col. 0768A] 108).

“Our Father, who art in heaven.” Whoever says “Father” seeks benevolence; whoever says “our” excludes pride; whoever says “who art in heaven” displays reverence. Whoever says “Father” seeks benevolence, because he calls upon one who is merciful. Whoever says “our” excludes pride, because he does not arrogate to himself something private or exclusive, but declares it to be shared also by others. Whoever says “who art in heaven” displays reverence, because by faith he proclaims God to be ruler not only in the lower regions but also in the highest.

“Hallowed be thy name.” There are many divine names. What name, then, do we ask to be hallowed when we say, “Hallowed be thy name”? The name of God is faith, through which he becomes known to believers. “Hallowed be thy name,” that is, your faith, which is knowledge of you.

But you say: God’s name is not to be hallowed, but is holy; for all the Scriptures cry out, all resound: “Holy is thy name” (Ps. 110). The name of God, brothers, is holy; yet it can still be hallowed more fully in certain hearts. It can be hallowed in the hearts of pagans, in whom it has not yet been hallowed through faith. It can be hallowed in the hearts of Jews, in whom it has not been hallowed through the perfection of faith. It can be hallowed in the hearts of false Christians, in whom it has not yet been hallowed through love. It can also be hallowed more fully in the hearts of the elect, through a greater perfection of faith and a greater love of God and neighbor. For the more perfectly the elect person loves and believes in God, the more fully he hallows and shows hallowed within himself the name of the Father.

Let us therefore say: “Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name” in the hearts of pagans; hallowed be it in the hearts of Jews, so that the former may believe in you and the latter may believe in you more perfectly, and that both may love you. Hallowed be it in the hearts of false Christians, so that, as they possess knowledge of you through faith, they may likewise possess love through the affection of charity. Let it still be hallowed in the hearts of the elect through a greater brightness of knowledge and a greater sweetness of love. Therefore: “Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name.”

### Second Petition: “Thy kingdom come”

What do we ask when we say, “Thy kingdom come”? Does God not have a kingdom? Is God not king? If God is not king or has no kingdom, what does the Psalmist mean when he says: “God is King of all the earth; sing wisely” (Ps. 4:6 [citation as printed])? Therefore God is king and God has a kingdom. Why, then, do we ask that his kingdom may come?

We do not ask that it may come in that in which it already exists, but in that in which it is not yet manifest. For many are still to be born who are predestined for his kingdom, but who have not yet been manifestly shown to all to belong to his kingdom. Therefore, may your kingdom come, O heavenly Father: that those predestined for your kingdom may be generated through the nature of the flesh, regenerated through the grace of baptism, and made righteous; and that through the charity of righteousness they may be manifest to all as children of your kingdom.

May your kingdom also come, so that at the end of the age, on the day of judgment, [Col. 0769A] in the general resurrection, grain may be separated from chaff, fish from serpents, lambs from goats, wheat from tares (Matt. 13; Matt. 25). And may your Church, which is your kingdom, pass, at your summons, from the oppression of this present age into the glory of the heavenly homeland.

Again, may your kingdom come, so that, as you reign in those already justified, so you may reign in those still to be justified; and as you reign in those who are good, so, once the power of demons has been expelled, may you reign also in those who are still evil. Therefore, may your kingdom come.

### Third Petition: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth”

We know that in heaven none of the saints or angels departs from God’s will; no one contradicts him. How, then, can it happen that God’s will is done on earth as it is in heaven? How can no one on earth sin, whether through ignorance or human frailty, when an infant of one day is not without sin upon the earth, and “we all offend in many things” (James 3)?

But it must be understood that the word “as” does not denote equality of quantity but sameness of quality; it indicates likeness, not equality. If someone built a small house according to the form and arrangement of a larger house, we would not say of the small house, “This one is as large as that larger one”; but we would say, “This one is such as that one is”—similar in kind, not equal in size.

Therefore, O Father, may your will be done in heaven by angels, saints, and those already glorified through the first robe; and likewise on earth by human beings who are to be justified and glorified. As they do your will in heaven, may these do it on earth: if not according to equality, yet according to likeness; that is, if not according to their perfection, yet according to imitation of their perfection.

May your will be done not only in the elect through the performance of good works, but also in the reprobate through the ordering of evils. For although you are not the author of evils, you are nevertheless the disposer of evils; and although many evils lie under your power, you leave none of them unordered. Thus your will is done in all things: in the good through action, in the evil through ordering.

“Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth”: as cherubim and seraphim, thrones and dominions, powers, principalities, angels, archangels, [Col. 0769D] patriarchs and prophets, apostles and martyrs, confessors, virgins, and all elect souls freed from the bonds of their bodies and glorified before you do your will in heaven, so may all bishops, presbyters, and the whole clergy; all kings, princes, and the entire people; males and females, great and small, good persons and also evil persons converted from evil to good, do it on earth according to the grace granted them by you and according to their capacity.

May your will be done not only in rational creatures through knowledge and love of you, but also in irrational creatures through their existence and multiplication. May your will be done not only in sentient things through the fertility of propagation, but also in insentient yet living things—done, I say, through the growth of their sprouting [Col. 0770A]. Finally, may your will be done not only in things living in whatever manner, but also in things subsisting in whatever manner, yet according to your good pleasure.

Again, “thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth”: as it is done already in those who have been justified, so may it be done in those still to be justified. Again: as reason, aided by your grace, dictates what ought to be done, so may the flesh, without resistance and without failure, carry out what has been dictated. Therefore, “thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.”

### Fourth Petition: “Give us this day our daily bread”

God made man from a twofold substance, namely corporeal and spiritual. Therefore, because he is composed of two substances, a twofold bread is necessary for him: one for the body, the other for the spirit—corporeal bread for the body, spiritual bread for the spirit. The body is fed by the produce of the field; the spirit is fed by sacred teaching.

We ask God for bodily bread, because unless God gives rain and causes the earth to sprout, we could not have this bread. We ask God for spiritual bread, because unless God gives it, we would not have that either. Bodily fathers ought to distribute bodily bread to their children; spiritual fathers—namely prelates and teachers—ought to distribute spiritual bread. Hence it is now required among stewards that one be found faithful (1 Cor. 4).

For who in our times is the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord has set over his household to give them food in due season (Matt. 24), who distributes the bread of teaching faithfully and prudently—faithfully in relation to God, prudently in relation to human beings? Faithfully in relation to God: namely, that he may dispense the word of God with such faith, fear, concern, earnestness, and diligence as God commanded. Prudently in relation to human beings: that he may instruct each person according to the capacity of each.

But—what cannot be recalled without profound grief—as blessed Gregory says, the world is full of priests, and yet, if there is someone willing to hear what is good, there is no one to speak it. What will certain priests of our time do? What will they say on the day of judgment, on the day of calamity coming from afar? They have received priestly orders, yet they are not ashamed to live disorderly lives. With the people entrusted to them—wholly ignorant and corrupted by wicked habits—they delight [Col. 0770D] to sit at crossroads; to speak and hear idle, even harmful words; to swear arrogantly; and to slander not only the living but even the dead.

They demand, in season and out of season, the revenues of churches entrusted to them; with the whole gaping appetite of their hearts they covet offerings; sometimes they demand them imprudently with their mouths; when they arrive, they receive them with both hands. Some devote themselves to feasts and drinking parties; they entangle themselves in beds and shameless acts. And many things done by them in secret, as the Apostle says, are shameful even to mention (Eph. 5).

They clothe themselves in the wool and feed on the milk of the Lord’s flock, while the sheep die from the scarcity and famine of God’s word. Time runs on, the yearly cycle passes, and not one word proceeds [Col. 0771A] from their mouths by which the flock entrusted to them may be instructed, reproved for evil, recalled to good, and confirmed therein. Yet every day, imagining that they render service to God, they howl—or rather hiss—the words of divine praise; and by their vocal sound and bodily movement they scandalize, rather than edify, those who hear and see them.

Therefore feed them, Lord; feed your own sheep. May your anointing teach them concerning all things, so that your Spirit may pour teaching into them through inward inspiration (1 John 2), teaching which the mute mouth of such priests does not distribute. Such priests ought to reflect that the prophetic rebukes spoken against them apply to themselves: “As is the people, so is the priest” (Isa. 24). And again: “The priests did not say, ‘Where is the Lord?’” (Jer. 2). “And those who held the law did not know me” (ibid.). Elsewhere it is written of such persons: “Mute dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56); and, “Most shameless dogs, they knew not fullness” (ibid.).

Let no one, therefore, expect to receive the bread of sacred teaching from priests of this kind, because such priests either do not know how to teach, or are ashamed to teach, or despise teaching. What, then, are the sheep entrusted to them to do? They should recognize that in other places there are learned priests who live holy lives; they should go to them and humbly ask them to teach them and to give counsel concerning their souls.

There are also certain false preachers, sown by the devil like tares in the Lord’s field. They travel through the whole world in their phylacteries and pronounce blessed, with lying words, the unlearned populace burdened with diverse sins, saying: [Col. 0771C] “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace (Jer. 8). But what does Scripture say? “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and destroy the way of your paths” (Isa. 3). And again: “Those who call blessed and those who are called blessed shall be cast down” (Isa. 9).

Therefore: “Give us this day our daily bread”—bodily bread and spiritual bread. Bodily bread: that you may cause the earth to sprout, to produce its fruit and bring it to maturity. Spiritual bread: that you may inspire the prelates and teachers of your Church diligently to distribute to us faithfully and prudently the teaching entrusted to them. And if they do not care to break this bread for us, feed us yourself through the hidden inspiration of your Holy Spirit, so that inwardly through you we may receive the bread of which we are deprived outwardly through their silence. Therefore, “give us this day our daily bread.”

### Fifth Petition: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors”

How fearful and perilous this prayer is for many, brothers! For it brings many more loss than increase, more harm than gain. There are some who, hardened through great and long-standing malice and the wickedness of hatred, desire to strangle, slaughter, or injure in every possible way those who have become their debtors through some injury done to them; and neither for fear of God nor at the prayers of men are they willing to accept satisfaction or make peace.

Of such persons it is written: “Their grape is a grape of gall, and their cluster most bitter; their wine is the gall of dragons and the incurable venom of asps” (Deut. 38). Though they are such, they nevertheless flock confidently to church and, praying before God and his altar, say: “Our Father, forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors.” But what wretched folly, what unhappy presumption! A man is said to provoke God’s wrath against himself by his prayers when he cherishes wrath against another human being and asks mercy from God (Ecclus. 28).

There are also certain imperfect persons, to whose imperfection, as blessed Augustine says, divine mercy condescends by allowing them at least then to forgive their debtors their debts when those debtors ask them to grant forgiveness—as the Lord is said to have done to his wicked servant, as it is written: “Wicked servant, I forgave you all the debt because you asked me” (Matt. 18; printed “Marc. XVIII”).

But whoever, when asked by his debtor, disdains to forgive the debt of any injury, asks the Lord in vain to forgive him the debt of his own sin; indeed, he rather aggravates that debt before the eyes of the Judge than lightens it. Although imperfect persons are permitted to seek what is their own, to receive satisfaction for an injury done to them, and to be asked by their debtors for forgiveness, nevertheless, if it happens that none of these things is done, they should restrain all anger of their own heart and drive the darkness of hatred from themselves, mindful of what is written: “The anger of man does not work the righteousness of God” (James 1); and again: “He who hates his brother is a murderer, and every murderer has no share in the kingdom of Christ and of God” [Col. 0772C] (1 John 3).

But it belongs to the perfect, with a pure heart and cheerful countenance, to forgive everyone everything, without restitution of goods, without satisfaction for injuries, and without any petitions from their debtors; moreover, to give what is theirs and render offices of charity. Let each person, then, look to himself in this prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors,” so that he may strive to grant others the kind of forgiveness that he desires to receive from God. Otherwise, according to my counsel, let him remain silent and by no means say this prayer: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.”

Therefore forgive us, O Father, our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And if through some frailty, or even corruption, you see that we do not forgive as we ought, grant us grace to forgive according to your will, and thus to obtain your forgiveness. Grant that we may love human beings in such a way as not to love their errors; that we may love in them their nature without loving their sin; that we may love what they are without loving what they do wickedly. “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.”

### Sixth Petition: “And lead us not into temptation”

Since it is written, “God is not a tempter of evils; he himself tempts no one. But each person is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire” (James 1), what do we ask when we say, “And lead us not into temptation”?

The sense, therefore, is: Do not lead us into temptation—not that you may never permit us to be assailed by temptations, but grant that we may be proved through temptations and not rejected. Temptations greatly benefit the elect, who attain the crown through victory in temptation, as the apostle James testifies, saying: “Blessed is the man who endures temptation, because, when he has been proved, he shall receive the crown of life which God promised to those who love him” (James 1). And at the beginning of the same Epistle: “Count it all joy, brothers, when you fall into various temptations, knowing that the testing of your faith”—which takes place through temptations—“produces patience” (ibid.). And of patience it is written: “In your patience you shall possess your souls” (Luke 21).

There are four kinds, or modes, of temptation, as we have already said elsewhere: one temptation is slight, another hidden, another severe, another manifest. There are three things that tempt us: our flesh, the world, and the devil. The flesh tempts us through gluttony and lust; the world tempts us through prosperity and adversity—through prosperity in order to deceive us, through adversity in order to crush us. The devil attacks us in every way and strives to draw us into every wickedness.

Therefore: “Our Father, lead us not into temptation”; that is, do not permit us to be tempted beyond what we are able to bear, but with the temptation also provide an outcome, so that we may be able to endure it (1 Cor. 10). Therefore, lead us not into temptation.

### Seventh Petition: “Deliver us from evil”

There are many evils to which the human condition is subject and whose danger it is entirely unable to escape by itself. Considered generally, we can distinguish them in six ways.
