One evil is that of the body, another that of the soul. Again, one evil is sin, another evil is punishment. Again, one evil belongs to the present age, another evil to the future.

From all these and from others—which are comprehended through these and contained under them—we ask to be delivered when we pray, saying: “Deliver us from evil,” as though we said: Deliver us, Father, from every evil; for unless you deliver us, we cannot be delivered without you, whether from one evil or many, from a great evil or a least one. Therefore deliver us, Father, from evil.

### Conclusion of the Foregoing Petitions

“Amen” means “truly” or “may it faithfully be done,” and concludes all the foregoing petitions. “Amen,” as though we said: O our Father, who art in heaven, may all the things which we have asked above truly come to pass in us and in others. Truly may your name be hallowed. Truly may your kingdom come. Truly may your will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth. Truly give us this day our daily bread. Truly forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. Truly lead us not into temptation. Truly deliver us from evil.

This, brothers, is a prayer to be said continually, since the Savior himself taught it and commanded us continually to pray to the Father by it. None is loftier than this; none more useful. There are some who, like the pagans, boast that they pour out many words, read many psalters, chant various hours, and continue long prayers, while they speak to the Lord with their mouths but their hearts sometimes wander to the ends of the earth. Let such remember the Scripture which says: “This people honors me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. 29).

Nor, in saying this, do we blame the diligence of holy prayer or persevering devotion, which we greatly praise when the length of prayer is accompanied by the fervor of inward love.

## There follows another exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, added here from elsewhere

### Chapter III. On the seven mortal sins, against which the petitions of the Lord’s Prayer are effective

There are seven principal vices which infect rational nature and corrupt its integrity as it were by the leaven of their admixture. A vice is a corruption of natural affection contrary to order and beyond measure. When this is received through consent, it is sin; merely experiencing it without consent is punishment, not fault.

Indeed, in those not regenerated, vice has no excuse at all: even where consent does not follow, the mere fact that something moves contrary to reason is liable to condemnation. Hence the Apostle says: “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8).

The first vice is pride; the second, envy; the third, anger; the fourth, acedia; the fifth, avarice; the sixth, gluttony; the seventh, lust. Pride is love of one’s own excellence. Envy is resentment at another’s happiness. Anger is an irrational disturbance of the mind. Acedia is distaste for inward good. Avarice is an immoderate desire to possess. Gluttony is an excessive appetite for eating. Lust is an immoderate desire to satisfy sexual appetite.

These, then, are the seven vices from which all corruption of the rational soul flows. For whatever corrupts integrity is a vice. But the integrity of bodily nature is one thing; that of incorporeal nature another. Again, among bodily natures, some have existence but lack sensation; others have both sensation and existence. In that which lacks sensation, corruption entering in violates unity; but in that which has sensation, corruption entering in damages health.

The integrity of spiritual nature consists in truth and goodness: in truth when it is known, and in goodness when it is loved. Corrupted knowledge through ignorance introduces into the rational soul a kind of ugliness; corrupted love through desire is the soul’s deformity; but purity of love is its health. Therefore it is a greater vice not to love the good than not to know the true, because what follows the will is justly reckoned as fault. You can know or fail to know unwillingly; but you cannot love or fail to love except willingly. Therefore only that which is according to the will is imputed as merit: toward good if it is right, toward evil if it is perverse. Hence all merit consists in affection; neither righteousness nor fault can be found except in the affection of the rational will.

### Chapter IV. That these three sins—pride, envy, and anger—are especially opposed to divine goodness

[Col. 0775A]

The corruptions of this affection, then, are seven. The first is pride, that is, love of one’s own excellence. It deforms affection itself because, while it draws it away to a part, it cuts it off from the whole. Every good, indeed, comes from the highest good, and is less in itself than in that from which it comes. Whoever delights in some good outside the highest good, by perversely choosing a part, justly loses the whole.

Thus pride, as though cutting off a part from the whole, takes beauty away from rational affection; the other attendant vices inflict pain. For in all the rest there is the punishment of the first vice, because what is sinned in pride as its precursor is punished in the others that follow after pride. In pride good is loved as one’s private possession: for a person rejoices to possess what another does not possess, or to possess what another does not possess. Therefore, because it loves excellence as private possession, it is called love of one’s own excellence.

In loving private possession, it hates sharing, and envy, the daughter of pride, is born. Envy is hatred of another’s happiness, and it springs from pride. For you could not be displeased that another had something unless you had first wished to have it alone. Therefore another’s happiness wounds and weighs heavily upon you, because in it your own deficiency is shown to you. Through it you are convicted of not being what you either rejoiced to be or desired to be.

Thus in pride you delight unjustly; in envy you are rightly tormented. In pride you perversely approve of what you are; in envy you unjustly disapprove of what another is. Therefore the wound of pride corrupts the more ruinously because its malice can be felt the less; and the more sweetly it enters, the more deeply it penetrates. Envy, however, because it brings pain along with its wound, is sometimes recognized as evil precisely because it is experienced as not only perverse but bitter. Envy is recognized to possess something of justice in this: one who acts unjustly is justly punished.

After it comes anger, that is, an irrational disturbance of the mind, which likewise bears its punishment with it. For if another’s happiness causes pain when it is seen, it causes far more pain when it is opposed. This is the irrational disturbance of mind called anger, when you disdain to suffer an evil inflicted upon you. Thus, stirred by impatience, you are disturbed because you do not endure adversity.

There is a good anger by which you disdain to do evil; but there is an evil anger by which you disdain to suffer evil. The former rejects fault; the latter does not receive justice. Therefore evil anger is disturbed when adversity confronts it, and impatience agitates the tranquility of the mind. The soul no longer wishes to stand fast in enduring a punishment that is just, just as earlier it had refused to stand fast through self-restraint against a fault that was unjust. Thus it increases misery by receiving bodily torment in addition to the mind’s pain.

These vices, therefore—pride, envy, and anger—are especially opposed to God. Pride denies God; envy accuses him; anger drives him away. Whoever boasts in singularity denies a superior; whoever envies the good things of others accuses their giver; whoever admits disturbance into his heart expels the lover of peace. Yet all together blaspheme: pride says that God is not good; envy and anger say that he has not acted beneficently—the former because he bestowed good on another, the latter because he inflicted evil upon it.

Thus these three vices appear especially to concern injury against God, in that through them the rational mind perversely abandons its own good, which is God: through pride, inwardly separating itself from him; through envy, not seeking him outwardly with devout regard; through anger, driving even the memory of him from its recollection.

### Chapter V. That the remaining four vices—acedia, avarice, gluttony, and lust—avenge injuries done by us to God

[Col. 0776B]

There follow four other vices, by which God avenges upon man the injury done to himself; for the sinful soul, abandoned by God, is punished by these vices as though they followed in punishment.

Among these four vices the first is acedia, that is, weariness of mind, born from distaste for inward good. Having lost its good, the mind remains solitary and abandoned, and is changed into bitterness and pain for itself. Then follows avarice, that is, an immoderate desire to possess, which compels a mind deprived of inward good and insufficient to itself to seek external things.

Acedia, then, causes pain to the soul; avarice causes labor. The former afflicts through sadness; the latter, dividing the soul through varied desires, stretches it out into laborious efforts. After avarice follows gluttony. For the mind, poured out through desire for external things, is first received by gluttony, which, under the pretext of necessity, flatters it more familiarly. Because gluttony introduces superfluity after necessity, it is a vice: it deforms appetite by drawing it beyond measure; afflicts it by extending it in immoderate desire; and defiles it by infecting it with shameful pleasure.

Finally lust succeeds. For flesh inflamed by excess in food immediately boils over into sexual desire. In it likewise there is shamefulness insofar as it exceeds measure; and there is greater shamefulness insofar as its act is excused by no necessity. The desire for eating is sometimes natural; the movement of lust is always fault. Nature cannot subsist without food, but it can subsist without intercourse.

Therefore reason, following after, moderates the appetite for eating, which arises from nature, lest it become evil. But the appetite for intercourse, even if restrained from action, is nevertheless a vice in that it does not arise from prior reason. Therefore, in the former case, arising is natural and exceeding the measure is vice; but in the latter, even its arising is vice where its action is not rational. This vice arises in us irrationally from the tinder of sin, is restrained by reason, and excused by grace, as it is written: “There is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus” (Rom. 8).

Nevertheless, whatever moves against justice is altogether sin; but that which is excused by grace is not condemnable. Therefore the Son of God assumed our nature with punishment but without fault. He is read to have endured hunger at times, but it is most truly affirmed that in that same nature he never at all experienced any stimulation arising from the tinder of sin. For a desire whose action could not have been rational would not have been entirely without vice; and it ought in no way to have existed in him who came not to receive sin but to take it away.

Accordingly, the appetite for eating, insofar as it is appetite, is natural; insofar as it is disordered, it is vice. But the appetite for intercourse is rightly condemned in its very existence unless it is excused by reason preceding and grace following. No reason, however, is shown to precede unless a rational act follows, because what is beyond the necessity of nature ought neither to be done nor desired.

### Chapter VI. That pride is checked by lust; and that seven petitions in the Lord’s Prayer are opposed to the seven sins named

[Col. 0777B]

Therefore, just as pride, the first of these vices, draws the soul down from the heights, so lust, the last, fixes it in the depths, as it is written: “I am sunk in deep mire, and there is no firm ground” (Ps. 68). Rightly, then, the uncleanness of lust is opposed to the glory of pride; and where the exaltation of the spirit precedes, the shamefulness of the flesh follows. Thus one who perversely considers within himself what gives him cause for glory may also justly find within himself what gives him cause for shame.

These are the seven vices that corrupt the entire integrity of the soul. Against them, for healing, are set the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit, as seven particular antidotes; yet these are obtained through the preceding sevenfold petition. For God had given certain goods freely to the human being when he was created, without being asked; but because humanity ungratefully cast these away, it is fitting that it should not receive the second goods until, humbled, it seeks them by desire and supplication. Therefore petition comes first, so that the bestowal of what the will seeks may follow.

These seven petitions are contained in the Lord’s Prayer, each to be opposed to one of the seven vices. Against pride is opposed the first petition: “Hallowed be thy name.” Against envy is opposed the second petition: “Thy kingdom come.” Against anger is opposed the third petition: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.” Against acedia is opposed the fourth petition: “Give us this day our daily bread.” Against avarice is opposed the fifth petition: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors.” Against gluttony is opposed the sixth petition: “And lead us not into temptation.” Against lust is opposed the seventh petition: “Deliver us from evil.”

### Chapter VII. On the seeking of benevolence at the beginning of the Lord’s Prayer
But it should be noted that in this Lord’s Prayer, before the petitions themselves, there is prefixed, as it were, a certain winning of goodwill, when it is said: “Our Father, who art in heaven.” For the one who prays seeks compassion from those set over him by calling upon a father. For if he is a father, he loves his children and is moved by compassion to hear those crying to him and [Col. 0778A] grant what is asked. Therefore, whoever says “Father” signifies confidence of being heard. But whoever says “our” shows humility, not presuming individually upon a good bestowed in common. And whoever says “who art in heaven” hears what he ought to ask, lest, by seeking things not to be requested, he offend the ears of compassion. For why should he ask for earthly things, when he confesses that he has a Father in heaven? For things must be sought there, where the Father dwells.

Say therefore, “Father,” that you may have confidence in asking; say “our,” lest you exalt yourself individually over a common good; say “who art in heaven,” that you may understand what you ought to ask for. You have God as Father; you have man as brother, so that, in striving toward Him, you may not be divided from the latter. Let love draw you toward Him; let pride not divide you from the latter. Therefore you cry, “Our Father,” that you may understand [Col. 0778B] that you have brothers and are not alone in this good that has been given by grace to all.

One man said, “My Father” (John 5); and indeed he would not have said this had he not been more than man. For where he was man, he had to say, “Our Father”; where he was God, he had to say, “My Father.” For where he was God, he was alone, one, the only-begotten; therefore he said, “My Father.” But where he was man, he had brothers and was not alone. Therefore here he said, “Our Father,” and elsewhere: “Go, tell my brothers” (Matt. 28); and again: “I will declare thy name to my brothers” (Ps. 21).

Therefore: “Our Father, who art in heaven.” A Father in heaven, compassionate and exalted, loving and powerful: if thou art Father, thou wilt help; if thou art in heaven, thou canst. Therefore thou wilt and thou canst; hence we who ask do not hesitate: thou wilt and thou canst. “Our Father, who art in heaven,” forgive what we ask, because what we ask is right: first, what concerns thine honour; afterwards, what concerns our salvation. What concerns thine honour: “Hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come; thy will be done, as in heaven, so also on earth.” What concerns our salvation: “Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation. But deliver us from evil.”

Therefore hear us, because thou hast said: “If you ask anything in my name, it shall be given you” (John 16). For we ask in thy name; we ask what pertains to thine honour; we ask what pertains to our salvation. First for thee, [Col. 0778D] afterwards for ourselves. For thou art Lord; and therefore, by right, thy cause ought everywhere to hold the first place. Therefore we discharge the debt of reverence by supplicating, so that our salvation may prove more effectual before thy mercy: a salvation which, even when acting for itself, does not hesitate to place itself after thine honour.

Our petition brings nothing that ought to displease the ears of thy majesty. We set the honour of God before our own advantage and unite with it the salvation of our neighbour. Do not therefore reject our prayer, in which love of thee as God and of our neighbour is commended to thee. In it, asking not a private but a common good, we love our neighbour as ourselves; and, preferring thy glory, we hold thee, our God, above ourselves. These things have been said as a commendation in this winning of goodwill.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the First Petition of the Lord’s Prayer, against Pride

[Col. 0779A]

“Hallowed be thy name.” This is the first petition, by which we ask that God’s name may be hallowed: first in us, then through us. What is the name of God? Perhaps, on hearing “the name of God,” you think of—or suppose that one ought to think of—some sound. If therefore it is a sound that is to be hallowed, what sound can be conceived worthy to claim sanctification uniquely for itself, since there are many names by which God is named by us, just as he has deigned to make himself known to us in many ways?

Or perhaps all these names contain one name: that God is named in us? That is, one apprehension, one knowledge, one faith, by which he has been revealed to us and is known by us. This is the [Col. 0779B] name by which God is named and made known: his renown, his knowledge, his faith. Thus we say, “That man is of great name,” and “That man has a great name among the people”: of great name, that is, of great renown. “God is known in Judah; his name is great in Israel” (Ps. 75). Therefore, in knowledge itself is his name; for he is named where he is known.

What then do you ask when you say to God, “Hallowed be thy name”? God has already been named to you; his name has reached even to you; his name is with you. Just now, when you entered the Church, you heard Scripture cry out: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth” (Gen. 1). God was named to you, and you learned that he himself is Creator of all. Hear again: “How good is God to Israel, to those who are upright in heart” (Ps. 72). In what way good? “Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob, whose hope is in the Lord his God, who made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them” (Ps. 145). Therefore the God who created heaven and earth is himself the God of Israel and the God of Jacob; for Israel himself is Jacob.

If then the God of Jacob made heaven and earth, the sea and all that is in them, therefore he who in the beginning made heaven and earth is the God of Israel and the God of Jacob: there, Creator; here, helper; there, great; here, good. “How good!” “Blessed is he whose helper is the God of Jacob.” Good unto so great a good, good unto blessedness; therefore supremely good, because good unto the supreme good. But perhaps he is good only to Israel, and Jacob alone is blessed, whose God is his helper. Hear again: “Blessed are all who fear [Col. 0779D] the Lord, who walk in his ways” (Ps. 127). Therefore the same God who in the beginning made heaven and earth, and the same one who afterward gave the law, is one and the same who, coming at the last, bestowed grace. First he created; afterward he restored; at the end he made blessed. Not one and another, although one thing and another.

In all these things God has been named to you; his name has sounded in your ears, and his renown has become celebrated with you. Henceforth you cannot excuse yourself on the ground of ignorance. You have heard his name; but beware lest you take the name of your God in vain.

What is it to take God’s name in vain? To hear and despise; to recognize and not revere; to know and not love. Pray therefore that his name may be hallowed [Col. 0780A] with you, for in itself it is always holy. Whatever can be said of him is wholly holy; but it is not so to you if you do not love, if you do not revere. For in your estimation he is not holy, if you do not judge him holy. If therefore you hear and despise, his name is not hallowed in you. You take holiness away from him in yourself—you cannot take it away in him. You do as much as you can; and if you could do more, you would do more.

Therefore God will judge the disposition of your malice. For you are proud, and resist as far as you can; you harden your soul so as neither to fear nor revere him, whose goodness, though you do not receive it, you nevertheless do not escape his power. Pray therefore that he may incline your heart to reverence for him; and, as he has enlightened it unto knowledge, so may he awaken it unto love, so that you may be humbled beneath his mighty hand (1 Pet. 5), and may both revere greatness and love goodness. Thus, when humility comes upon you, pride will fall, and you will begin, joyful and gentle, to sing to God: “Lord, I cried to thee, and thou hast healed me” (Ps. 29).

But after God has hallowed his holy name in you and made you hallow it, do not stop here; let not your own salvation suffice you. Extend the affection of love, and cry to him for others: “Hallowed be thy name.” Let it be hallowed by all and glorified by all, “so that, according to thy name, thy praise may reach the ends of the earth” (Ps. 47). Thus, “Hallowed be thy name.” “Not unto us,” he says, “O Lord, not unto us, but unto thy name give glory” (Ps. 113). This is “Hallowed be thy name.” For it is hallowed when it is glorified. [Col. 0780C] “Hallowed be thy name.”

## CHAPTER IX. On the Second Petition, against Envy

“Thy kingdom come.” This is the second petition, set against the vice of envy, in which the desire for a brother’s salvation is commended. For what is the kingdom of God except the salvation of human beings? The kingdom is not here meant in that sense in which God presides over all by power and turns all things at the nod of his might according to the decision of his will. For this kingdom neither comes through increase nor departs through diminution, because divine power cannot be increased, being full, nor diminished, being eternal.

But that kingdom by which he presides over devout minds subjected through love comes only insofar as human salvation increases. In these minds, whenever that which was perversely striving against justice is brought into order, through grace inspiring conformity to the nod of the divine will, then indeed a kingdom is prepared in them for God who comes, so that he may dwell in them: now directing all their movement toward justice; later, when the course of this mutability has ended, bringing all their desire—every contradiction having been lulled—to the peace of eternal tranquillity.

Therefore the kingdom of God is that by which he presides inwardly through grace, rules the wavering minds of human beings, and bends them to follow the laws of eternal justice, not by force but by love: so that under him through devotion, after him through imitation, they may be directed toward him through glorification. Therefore, as in the first petition we ask for God’s glory, so in the second [Col. 0781A] we request our neighbour’s salvation. The former is against pride; the latter against envy. There we subject ourselves to one above us through humility; here we join ourselves to our neighbour through love. “Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come.”

## CHAPTER X. On the Third Petition, against Anger

“Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” This is the third petition, set against the vice of anger. For one who assents to the divine will does not wish to contend, but humbly submits himself to the just ordering, so that even in what is done against his own will he may not be stirred against his Judge by any fault of impatience or murmuring. Since he recognizes that he has committed forbidden evils, he patiently bears the evils inflicted upon him. And though in bearing them the flesh may suffer disturbance through the impatience of murmuring, reason nevertheless remains tranquil through consideration of justice and disposes itself to obedience.

For the will of the spirit, conformed to the divine will through justice, disapproves what it feels moving in its flesh against truth and desires that it too may be calmed into assent to truth, saying: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” For this heaven—that is, reason, conformed to heavenly things through the love of justice—strives in nothing against God’s will; and what it feels moving in the opposite direction, it restrains by the vigour of that same justice, lest it run loose, as it is written: “Not my will, but thine be done” (Luke 22).

For just as the humanity in the God-man, according to the property of the mortal nature which he bore, naturally willed one thing below through the inclination of flesh fleeing pain, [Col. 0781C] and approved another thing above through the judgment of reason loving justice; so we must restrain, by the judgment of reason, what we perceive moving in us from vice against God’s justice, saying: “Lord, let not our will be done, but thine.” For our will is the will of our flesh: whether it is moved by weakness of nature, it is ours because it is in us; or whether it is moved by the vice of sin, it is ours because it is from us. The former is ours because we bear it; the latter ours because we made it. For we made sin; we bear nature.

Therefore what moves from nature, though it is sometimes restrained, is never imputed. But what moves from sin is both blameworthy in its arising and to be restrained lest it act. Yet what we desire according to the weakness of nature, although it is not sin, we must nevertheless sometimes restrain, because, when God’s justice requires one thing for punishing sin and weakness another for sustaining nature, we must patiently bear injury to nature for the fulfilment of justice. But what we desire from vice must both be lamented because it arises and restrained lest it be completed, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “Let not sin reign in your mortal body” (Rom. 6).

Therefore, in order that the kingdom of sin may be destroyed also in the earth of our flesh and the kingdom of God may come, we must pray that, as in heaven, so also on earth his will may be done; for then his kingdom also comes on earth, if a movement that is not from justice, subject to reason, does not rule but serves. But when a human being has subjected the heaven of his soul [Col. 0782A] and the earth of his flesh to the kingdom of God, then, extending himself forward in the affection of love, he ought to pray that what is accomplished in him through grace at work may, by grace likewise bestowed, be accomplished outwardly: “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.”

As angels obey in heaven, so may human beings obey on earth. Or, if those human beings who are on earth have through grace become heaven and have been lifted in mind to heaven, so that thy will is done in them, may those who still cling in mind to earth and are earth imitate them, and go before in heart to the place which they are to follow in body. Thus, “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.”

Behold, Lord, we grant that thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth. We do not resist, struggle, or fight against thee. Until now we wished to do one thing and planned to accomplish another; but now we consider that thy will is almighty. Therefore, if we struggle against it, either we shall be corrected by thy power, lest we accomplish what we wickedly will, or we shall be allowed by thy patience to perish. Therefore, Lord, we do not contend with thee: “Thy will be done.” We know, Lord, that whether we will or will not, thy will shall be done. Therefore: “Thy will be done.” We concede what we are altogether unable to prevent, lest perhaps, if we will otherwise, the effect be denied and the inclination condemned.

Therefore we join our will to thine, so that thou mayest reward devotion, because we praise and love thy power. We pray thee to do what we do not doubt thou art able to do: by thy good will restrain our perverse wills, and do not permit that which we will wickedly, but which thou in goodness dost not will, to come to pass. [Col. 0782C] Even if it should come to pass, thy will would not be less powerful; ours would be more wretched. Therefore, Lord, “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.” For we now trust thy goodness so greatly that concerning ourselves we believe thee more than ourselves. Therefore, “Thy will be done.” For we can will even our own evil; thou canst not, since neither ignorance deceives thee nor malice corrupts thee. Therefore, Lord, “Thy will be done, as in heaven, so on earth.”

## CHAPTER XI. On the Fourth Petition, against Acedia

“Give us this day our daily bread.” This is the fourth petition, set against the vice of acedia. Here the bread of life is requested by those hungering for justice. Bread is refreshment: give bread, give refreshment. “Give us this day our daily bread”: our bread, thy bread; thine, because thou givest it; ours, because we receive it; thine, because it comes from thee; ours, because it is granted to us. It springs from thee, and therefore is thine; it is granted to us, and therefore is ours.

For thou art that land of the living from which the bread of life springs, which strengthens the human heart (Ps. 103). Therefore, O land, give bread, give refreshment, feed thy inhabitants. If we dwell in thee, let us be fed from thee. We have already begun to remain; we have already begun to rest, because we have already begun to assent. Behold, we do not recoil through any contradiction; we have sung, “Thy will be done.” Behold, therefore, we remain: “This is my rest for ever and ever” (Ps. 131). But we cannot remain unless we eat. Give us therefore bread: “Give us this day our daily bread.”

Behold, we are not anxious about tomorrow; we ask only today’s provision. “Give us this day our daily bread.” We do not wish thy manna to decay with us. We gather what is sufficient, and we gather no more than we are able to use. “Give us this day our daily bread”: according to the present illumination, grant refreshment. As much as thou hast enlightened, so much refresh; as much as thou hast granted us to know, so much grant us to love. We do not wish thy love in us to exceed knowledge, because what is not done according to knowledge [Col. 0783A] (Rom. 10) is blameworthy, even though it appears to arise from zeal for justice. Therefore those are rebuked who had zeal not according to knowledge, who wished to extend refreshment beyond illumination. They ate food at night which ought to have been taken only in the day. Therefore they wandered and became drunk, so that they did not understand what they were doing.

For this reason: “Give us this day our daily bread.” Give bread, give refreshment; thy word is refreshment for the soul. “Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word which proceeds from the mouth of God” (Matt. 4). Therefore the word feeds as bread feeds, because the word itself is bread. Give therefore thy word, that thou mayest refresh our souls. What is thy word? Truth. Send thy truth into our heart, that thou mayest refresh us. Send truth, and with truth love. Let the Son come; let the Holy Spirit come with the Son; let both come, so that the refreshment may be full: truth enlightens, love refreshes. For love itself is refreshment.

“Give us this day our daily bread.” See what he says: “Give us this day our daily bread.” He seeks refreshment on the present day. For today is present, just as yesterday is past and tomorrow future. Seek the day within; if you recognize refreshment within, you have bread within, you have the day within. For external bread and the external day—although these also are from God and ought to be sought from God—are now passed over, because the intention is directed to what is better. Seek therefore the day within; seek the bread within. For if the one refreshed is within, within is that by which he is refreshed, and within is the time when he is refreshed.

The hungry person cries here and seeks his refreshment lest he fail. The soul cries; it is the one that hungers; and would that it hungered, and hungered for that which, when fully attained, it will hunger for no longer. Therefore the soul hungers. What is it to hunger? To desire. The soul hungers; the soul desires. What does it desire? Bread. What bread? Truth. This is its bread; no other creature can receive this bread, except the rational creature alone. Therefore it says: “Our bread.” For this we were made; for this we were created. Therefore it says, “Give, because thou hast created us, so that we may not live without this bread.”

“Give us this day our daily bread.” What is “this day”? On the present day. Attend: the rational soul was so created that it might be enlightened by truth and that the light of truth itself might never be darkened in it. If, therefore, it had remained in the light of truth, it would have had one day, and that day would have been eternal, having neither yesterday nor tomorrow. But now, because it falls away from truth, [Col. 0784A] the light of truth departs from it and does not always remain with it. Therefore its days pass, and after light darkness succeeds, when through sin truth is abandoned; and after darkness light returns again, when the soul lying in sin is visited through grace.

Therefore, when grace is present, it is day, because the soul is enlightened when it is visited. This is “today,” when refreshment is sought, because the soul, anticipated by grace, is aroused to desire. Note that this bread is called daily because, according to the number of spiritual illuminations, the refreshment of inward sweetness is multiplied.

But it must be considered how this petition is said to pray for the healing of the vice of acedia, although the one praying is described not as disgusted, but as hungering and desiring. Yet it must be understood that, unless the mind of the one praying had first been aroused by grace to desire the good, it would never have strength to pursue its evil. Therefore, by that desire through which it is set aflame by grace against its evil, it afterward prays for the healing of its evil desire; for unless it sensed in some measure what it had lost, it would not grieve over what it suffers.

Thus one cannot pray against pride unless one possesses humility at least in desire; nor against envy unless one possesses kindness at least in disposition. Thus we pray with gentleness against anger, with desire against acedia; praying against avarice, we are kindled with a desire to forgive; supplicating against gluttony, we are inflamed with an appetite for self-restraint. Finally, unless love of chastity were present in desire, no one would pour out prayer against the shameful pleasures of lust. Therefore we are first aroused that we may will; afterward we pray that we may be able more fully, as it is written: “My soul has desired to desire thy justifications at all times” (Ps. 118).

Thus, “Give us this day our daily bread”: give, for we give thanks for the past and supplicate for the present. It is not ours to inquire how future things will happen, but thine to provide. Therefore we do not pray for tomorrow, which we do not know whether it will be granted us; yet we hope that thy bounty will not fail us then either, if it be thy will that we should reach it. For it is written: “Jesus Christ, yesterday and today, the same also for ever” (Heb. 13). Therefore: “Give us this day our daily bread”: thou who hast created, feed; thou who hast given the beginning, grant nourishment. For if thou forsakest us, to whom shall we look? Therefore: “Give us this day our daily bread.”

## CHAPTER XII. On the Fifth Petition, against Avarice

“Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.” This is the fifth petition, set against the vice of avarice. For the spirit that so faithfully sets forth the condition, “Forgive as we forgive,” had conceived a desire to forgive. For we are ready to forgive; therefore we confidently accept the condition. Thou hast already touched our hearts by thy grace, so that we love forgiveness. Therefore we perceive the goodness of mercy and desire help, that we may fulfil what we approve.

For the mind, inclined by the desire of virtue to spare, desires and longs to forgive, so that forgiveness may also be granted to itself. Therefore it readily offers itself for the condition, not through presumption of virtue, but through desire for goodness. For here desire moves prayer, in which the virtue of forgiveness has been conceived; and by the very effort of devotion it asks help toward perfection. Therefore it cries, “As we forgive.” “We, Lord, by the bounty of thy grace, offer what is ours; add what is thine. For we know that no good is perfected without thy cooperation. Therefore we gladly offer the desire which we have already received, that thou mayest grant the disposition of virtue which we have not yet received but desire, and for which we pray in desiring.”

Therefore, when we say to thee, “We forgive,” [Col. 0785B] we do not boast of the fullness of virtue, but rejoice in the beginning of good desire. Therefore behold, we forgive: we are ready to forgive, ready to pardon. We forgive so as not to demand again; we forgive so as not to be angry. For the heart speaks to thee, Lord; the soul confesses to thee. Therefore we forgive from the heart, because thou wouldst not regard as acceptable whatever were done outwardly if the conscience did not also approve what the tongue says. Therefore we forgive our debtors: we forgive, so as not to seek vengeance; we forgive, so as not to retain malice.

Therefore do thou forgive as we forgive: forgive, so as not to retain for hatred; forgive, so as not to exact for punishment. For it is too little for us not to be punished unless we also deserve to be loved. Therefore we also love enemies, since we were all thine enemies so long as we loved iniquity and did not keep thy will. Therefore, Lord, because we fear thy just anger, we flee to thy gracious condition. For thou hast said: “Forgive, and you shall be forgiven” (Mark 11). Therefore, Lord, we hold thee to thine own condition, by which thou wast pleased freely to bind thyself to us, because thou hast loved our life more than our death. Therefore thou hast willingly promised—though no obligation compelled thee—to forgive our debts if we were not avaricious in exacting those owed to us.

Therefore, Lord, considering the abundance of thy merciful compassion, we do not dare to neglect such great mercy. For thou pressest our malice from every side: on one side by thy free goodness, by which thou promisest pardon to those who forgive; on the other by thy deserved indignation, by which thou thunderest wrath against those who do not forgive. Therefore, Lord, behold, thy mercy conquers us, by which thou deignest so graciously to yield thine own right for our sake.

For what is all that one human being can do against another compared with injury done to thee? What great matter is it if an evil person wrongs an evil person? But where compassion itself is injured and goodness embittered, that is a greater iniquity. Therefore the sin of one human being against another is not altogether sin, because what one evil person does unjustly, another evil person suffers justly. But when we sin against thee, Lord, our iniquity is multiplied, because what we do out of malice, thou sufferest without fault. Therefore our debts against thee exceed [Col. 0786A] every measure; nor can that in which one human being offends another be compared with our guilt, in which our pride assails thy mercy with condemnable presumption.

Yet, Lord, in free kindness thou forgivest greater things, to provoke us to forgive lesser things; and not without reason. For thou art great, we are small; and therefore thou workest great things, so that we may emulate, insofar as we can, thy surpassing goodness. Therefore we forgive our debtors. We are not eager to exact, nor avaricious to retain. We forgive our debtors: we forgive not only vengeance to thee, but also malice to them. We leave vengeance to thee, that thou mayest nevertheless punish them; we leave malice to them, so that we do not hate. Therefore forgive us our debts, as we forgive [Col. 0786B] our debtors.

First, “Give us this day our daily bread”; afterward, “Forgive us our debts.” First give bread, afterward forgive debts. First refreshment, afterward remission. For if thou waitest to give refreshment until it is unnecessary to ask for remission, and delayest food until disease ceases, thy sick people do not recover. Therefore, Lord, although “it is not good to cast the children’s bread to the dogs” (Matt. 15), nevertheless, because thou savest humans and beasts—“O God, how thou hast multiplied thy mercy” (Ps. 35)—look upon the wretched and refresh the weak, so that we may first recover through thy nourishment for pardon, and afterward, healed and justified by thy refreshment, advance to glory.

Therefore once more now, “Give us this day our daily bread,” and afterward “Forgive us our debts,” so that, with grace breathing upon us, we may be kindled to love and through love renewed unto remission, as it is written: “Her many sins have been forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke 7). Therefore first give bread, give refreshment; pour in love and grant remission. Give daily bread to the sick, whom thou wilt give everlasting bread when they are well; give now, so that it may often be sought again, but afterward thou wilt give so that it is never interrupted; give now gradually for sustenance, but afterward continually for fullness; give now for healing, afterward for glory. Thus, first: “Give us this day our daily bread”; and afterward: “Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors.”

## CHAPTER XIII. On the Sixth Petition, against Gluttony

[Col. 0786D]

“And lead us not into temptation.” This is the sixth petition, set against the vice of gluttony. For one prays not to be led into temptation or seduced by seductive allure, which, approaching more familiarly under the cover of necessity, knocks close at hand upon the mind’s steadfastness, gently entices, and provokes excess of superfluity. This evil is specifically called temptation because the other vices lie far from human nature; and therefore, the less they offer a semblance of reason, the less they bring temptation.

For to tempt is cunningly to test and, as it were, by first putting forward certain flattering attempts, before violent assault to discover what may be thought of something uncertain. Therefore where there is undisguised violence, it is not so much temptation as oppression; if it prevails, it is called invasion. The appetite for eating, then, because it rules through an inborn necessity, urges all that it introduces more effectively the less it can be repelled, even when, because of what is blameworthy within it, it cannot be approved.

For even when it counsels superfluity, though reason restrains it from excess, it is not restrained from what is owed to necessity. Thus even when we recognize that it wishes, through the immoderate ardour of desire, to pass beyond the bounds of necessity, we nevertheless serve it out of necessity for the sustenance of nature. Therefore, because it is admitted in the performance of the duty owed to necessity, knocking nearby it gently suggests, together with what is sweet to weakness, even that which is not granted to necessity.

This is temptation, which false reason strives to justify: because what is owed to necessity is reasonably admitted, that also which ought rightly to be reckoned superfluity is not guarded against. Thus vice tempts gently, touching through necessity, in case by that necessity itself it may soften the mind toward superfluity. This is temptation in the proper sense. When the other vices attack, they can oppress; but because they have no rationale for doing so, they cannot, as it were, tempt. For this reason it is specifically named temptation, because it cunningly persuades what is not permitted. Since it is inevitably approached through natural necessity, the prayer does not ask what is impossible, namely, that one should not come to it, but only that one should not be led [Col. 0787C] into it.

“Lead us not,” it says, “into temptation.” For thou art our guide upon this way by which we run toward thee; we shall not reach thee unless we are led by thee. Therefore thou art our guide: guide well, because thou art truth; guide toward the good, because thou art life. If, following thee, we go astray, thou wilt be blamed, since thou oughtest to provide guidance. Many things occur on the way of this life that seek to seduce; but it is thine to direct us, lest we be seduced, as it is thine to defend us, lest we be oppressed. See therefore, Lord, that thou fulfil what is thine. Thou hast promised guidance to those running toward thee. Guide us, then, and direct us, lest the error of our temptation here be imputed to thee, if thou allowest us through superfluity to enter into that temptation to which thou leadest us by necessity.

Therefore, Lord, lead us not into temptation; for we shall impute it to thee if thou permit it to happen. We have here something to set against thee, if we are forsaken by thee. Therefore here we presume something further against thy majesty: thou hast so made us that we cannot live without that through which we cannot be safe. Therefore, if thou joinest us to it, guard us from it. Otherwise, Lord, thou thyself leadest us in, if we are deceived by that which we can neither reject because of thee nor avoid without thee.

If therefore, Lord, thou leadest us in, it would not be fitting for thy goodness if our destruction were turned into an accusation against thee. Therefore, “Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.” For we ask both: that thou guard us from future things which we cannot avoid without thee, and deliver us from past things which we did not do through thee. Therefore, “Lead us not into temptation; but deliver us from evil.”

## CHAPTER XIV. On the Seventh Petition, against Lust
Deliver us from evil. This is the seventh petition, which is set against the vice of lust; gluttony, which precedes it, is the tinder of the lust that follows. Therefore, after gluttony, we rightly turn in prayer against lust: “Deliver us from evil.” For we are held captive, and cannot escape from the violent hand of vices and from the slavery of sin unless you rescue us: “Deliver us.”

See to what an end our pride has come. You made us so that we might rule over every one of your creatures; you subjected us only to yourself, the Lord of all creatures. But pride came and persuaded us to raise our necks [Col. 0788B] against you; thus we departed from you, Lord, and behold, left alone without you, we who refused to serve the Lord of all have become slaves of vices. Thus, Lord, our folly avenges your injury: you take vengeance upon us through our own miseries. Therefore deliver us from evil.

Behold, we captives cry out to you, whom we despised when free. Behold what a Lord we despised! Behold what a tyrant we served! Shamefulness holds us captive, so that our presumption may be put to shame. Therefore, Lord, deliver us from evil. Our misery is your glory: such have we become, we who abandoned you, the Lord of all. Behold, we cry to you because, taught by our evils, we have learned that we can do nothing without you. Therefore, Lord, deliver us—you who alone are able—deliver us from evil.

This is evil, Lord, [Col. 0788C] and it is not like other evils: it pursues more cruelly, harms more deeply, wounds more effectively. It flatters in order to deceive; it seduces in order to destroy; it feigns sweetness in order to pour in bitterness. Therefore, Lord, it is conquered with greater difficulty and uprooted more slowly, because it fights against us by means of our own desires; and, with its flattering sweetness, it penetrates the will itself unto death, and in order afterward to rule over the whole of nature, bends reason itself—which governs everything—by a certain violent persuasion of destructive love.

For this reason it is evil: “Deliver us from evil.” For it lies that it is good while it delights; but we, having experienced its wickedness, recognize it as evil. Therefore, deliver us from evil. If it is anger, it torments; if envy, it wastes away; and every individual vice [Col. 0788D] does not conceal its own malignity. For harmful things are easily recognized when they are felt to be bitter. Therefore, when this or that is named, what it itself is may be understood as evil. For each thing has within itself something by which it cannot be concealed. But this evil is not understood unless something more than what it itself is be said of it. Therefore we say that it is evil, because perhaps it would not be perceived unless it were called so.

For sensation has a deceptive experience in it and is deceived within itself unless it is taught from outside itself. Therefore let him learn by hearing that it is evil, who perhaps could judge it to be good by feeling it: “Deliver us from evil.” We now know that it is evil; therefore we beg to be delivered, because it is evil: “Deliver us.” For knowledge has been enlightened so as to recognize it, but strength has not yet been strengthened so as to [Col. 0789A] overcome it. How greatly, then, it ruled when it was still unknown—now it can no longer be hidden, yet it still cannot be overcome. Hear us, therefore, as we confess, and help our weakness: “Deliver us from evil.”

[Note: [Col. 0789] Here was inserted the little work *On the Seven Sevens*, which we have placed among the genuine works. EDITORS.]

## CHAPTER XV. On the prudent man and the hearer of God’s word

“Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them shall be likened to a prudent man who built his house upon a rock” (Matt. 7).

The wise man is Christ, who is the power of God and the wisdom of God, and who built his house upon a rock because he built his Church upon himself. Thus, whoever hears the words of God and does them builds his house upon a rock, because he builds the structure of faith, virtues, and good works upon firmness.

The rain descends—that is, the assault of an aerial [Col. 0789B] storm; lightning comes—that is, human power and persecution; and winds blow—that is, the perverse prompting of demons and evil persons. They rush upon that house through importunate temptation; but it does not fall through the deliberation of any wicked consent.

The fool builds upon sand because, despising heavenly things, he never ceases to yearn for earthly ones. The evils mentioned above come, and his structure is shaken by unforeseen temptation; it falls through the perpetration of some sin, and its ruin is great. For, shaken by temptation, he is hurled from temptation into delight, from delight into deliberation, from deliberation into action, from action into habit, [Col. 0789C] from habit into despair, and from despair into eternal damnation.

There are, moreover, three kinds of persons who build. There are those who love God alone: these build gold, silver, and precious stones. In love of virtue, gold; in knowledge of truth, silver; in the cooperation of good work, precious stones. There are others who love something besides God, yet nothing contrary to God and nothing more than God. In these the foundation indeed remains, because love of God is not destroyed; yet, from attachment to things loved alongside God, some corruption is contracted, and wood, hay, and straw are built upon it. In wood is the sin of an unlawful deed; in hay, the sin of wrongful delight without a deed; in straw, the sin of unlawful thought. There are others [Col. 0789D] who love certain things contrary to God; and in them the foundation is utterly destroyed, because love of God cannot exist where he is not either alone or supreme. Thus it belongs to the first to be saved and praised; to the second, to be rebuked and delivered; to the third, to be accused and condemned.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the cleansing of the leper

“When Jesus had come down from the mountain, crowds followed him; and behold, a leper came and worshipped him, saying: ‘Lord, if you will, you can cleanse me.’ And stretching out his hand, he touched him, saying: ‘I will; be cleansed.’ And immediately his leprosy was cleansed” (Matt. 8).

The mountain in this place signifies the sublimity of the divine majesty; the plain, however, the humility of the Incarnation. For the only-begotten Son of God was on the mountain before the Incarnation; but, taking our flesh, he descended to the low places—remaining on the mountain in the form of God, appearing in the plain in the form of a servant.

The leper whom the Lord healed in the level plain signifies the human race, dispersed across the plain of the world. It was truly leprous, because it was contaminated not only by original sin but also by many actual sins. For it was polluted by diverse cults of idolatry; it was defiled by many crimes of shameful acts. But the Lord touched the leper when he joined his divinity to human frailty; and he cleansed the leper when, dying on the cross, he expiated the guilt of the human race. [Col. 0790B] He touched leprosy and remained clean, because he took the true form of humanity and did not contract guilt.

This leper is the human race, which, so long as it was leprous, was separated and far removed from God and from the city of God, that is, Jerusalem—which is our mother above. But the Lord, as was said above, healed the leper and made it a citizen of his city. The Lord likewise does not disdain to perform this same miracle daily through his grace.

For there are many within the bounds of the holy Church who are ugly with the leprosy of vices and polluted, as it were, by the contagion of sins. For all unclean fornicators, men with concubines, incestuous persons, adulterers, the greedy, usurers, false witnesses, perjurers, those who say to their brother, “You fool,” those who look upon a woman in order to lust after [Col. 0790C] her, and anyone who, though not evil in deed, is nevertheless evil in will—all such persons, I say, who are separated from God through guilt, are judged by priests who know and observe God’s law to be leprous, and are separated from the assembly of the faithful, not bodily indeed, but spiritually.

Therefore, whenever the Lord justifies anyone of this sort who is ungodly, he rightly cleanses a leper. So long as a person is ungodly, he is leprous; when he is justified, he is cleansed. Whoever is now separated from the assembly of saints through guilt, unless meanwhile cleansed through grace, will be removed farther away in the future through punishment.

But just as damnable sins are signified by leprosy, so venial sins are signified by scabies: such as [Col. 0790D] a useless thought, an occasional idle word, laughter, and things of this kind. And it should be noted that no one is driven from the city on account of scabies; no one is judged to be separated from the citizens. For even if, because of our frailty, we sometimes commit venial sins, we are by no means separated from the fellowship of the faithful on that account. Nevertheless, we ought to cure this scabies; we ought also, insofar as we can and the Lord helps us, to drive these venial sins from ourselves, although to some they seem so slight that they are not thought worthy of cure.

For any sin, although it seems very small to human beings, can become great before the just Judge if it does not displease us. For, as we have heard from others, blessed Augustine says: “No sin is mortal while it displeases; no sin is venial while it pleases.” Let us therefore strive to avoid not only great sins but also small ones, lest, if we despise the small, we gradually slip into mortal sins.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the disciples’ passage through the grainfields

“It happened, as Jesus was walking through the grainfields, that his disciples began to go along and pluck ears of grain” (Matt. 12).

The disciples pass through the grainfields when prelates survey their subjects with pious concern and diligently consider how they may draw each person toward the kingdom of heaven. And when they desire to draw them to blessedness, they hunger, as it were, for their salvation. [Col. 0791B] They pluck ears of grain when, through preaching, they separate the minds of hearers from love of temporal things. They rub the ears when they strip them of the chaff of their old life. They eat the grains when, having purified them from superfluity and roughness, they unite them to the truth of holy Church and incorporate them into it.

And they do this on the Sabbath, because, resting from earthly activities and devoting themselves to God, they both seek heavenly rest by their works and promise it by their preaching.

Otherwise: they walk through grainfields because they investigate the sacred utterances. They hunger when they desire to learn better meanings in them. They pluck ears of grain when they gather from the Scriptures those things that seem more useful to them. They rub what they have gathered when, beneath the chaff of the letter, they seek the grains of spiritual understanding. They eat the grains when, through spiritual understanding, [Col. 0791C] they strengthen virtues and works. And they do this on the Sabbath because they have leisure to see that the Lord himself is God. The Lord of the Sabbath approves this, but the foolish defenders of the Sabbath reject it, because they love only the surface of the letter: they do not know the refreshment of the mind or the rest of souls.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the unclean spirit departing from a person

“When an unclean spirit has gone out of a person, it walks through dry places, seeking rest and not finding it” (Matt. 12).

The unclean spirit is the devil. It is a spirit by nature, unclean by guilt; a spirit by condition, unclean by iniquity. The unclean spirit departs from a person when, through grace, it is driven from that person [Col. 0791D] in baptism. Having departed from the person, it roams through dry places seeking rest when, driven from someone by exorcism or baptism, it investigates for habitation the hearts of any faithful persons who have been cleansed from the softness and moisture of unstable thought. But it finds no rest at all in dry places, because the heart of every faithful soul never rests from thinking, speaking, and doing what is good.

Then it says, “I will return to my house from which I came out.” And it comes and finds it vacant, swept clean, and adorned. Vacant: that is, ceasing from good work; swept clean: that is, cleansed from vices by exorcism and the water of baptism; adorned: that is, covered with simulated virtues. Then it goes and takes with it seven other spirits more wicked than itself, and, entering, they dwell there. The seven spirits signify the whole multitude of demons, [Col. 0792A] who dwell in the wicked through the seven principal vices and draw them to damnation.

The unclean spirit returns with seven spirits more wicked than itself and inhabits its house, vacant, swept clean, and adorned, when the devil, with the whole multitude of vices, again enters through guilt a soul once his own, baptized but idle from good work and covered with simulated virtues. It enters fittingly with spirits more wicked than itself when it seeks to hold more wickedly, and to defile with graver crimes, a soul taken from it by baptism and recovered through guilt than it did before baptism. “And the last state of that person is worse than the first,” because through contempt for the grace which, by living badly, he drives [Col. 0792B] away from himself, he deserves worse punishments.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the strong man and his vessels

“No one can enter the house of a strong man and plunder his vessels unless he first binds the strong man” (Matt. 12).

The strong man is the devil; the stronger one who comes upon him is Christ; the strong man’s house is the world; the vessels are human beings; the binding of the strong man is the restraining of the devil, so that he may not tempt us beyond our strength. The plundering of the vessels is the conversion to faith of those who come to it. The stronger one bound the strong man, entered his house, and plundered his vessels when Christ, coming into the world in the flesh and restraining the devil from issuing temptations, converted to his faith persons possessed by the devil.

## CHAPTER XX. On the sower and the seed

[Col. 0792C]

“The one who sows went out to sow his seed” (Matt. 13).

The seed is the word of God; the sower, Christ; the field, the world; the path is a heart worn down and dried up by the frequent passing of evil thoughts, so that it cannot receive or germinate the seed of the word. The birds by which the seed is snatched away are demons, through whom the word is taken away lest it bear fruit. They are called birds of heaven because they are of a heavenly and spiritual nature, or because they move through the air.

The rock is an untamed and hard heart, penetrated by no ploughshare of true faith; in it there is neither true love nor perseverance in virtue. Thorns are riches, which tear the heart with many cares and choke the seed of the word. Good soil, [Col. 0792D] is a gentle and teachable heart, which truly bears fruit when in it the perfect fullness of good works grows. The fruit of the seed is a person’s justification.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the enemy who oversowed tares

“The kingdom of heaven is like a man who sowed good seed in his field. But while people were sleeping, his enemy came and oversowed tares” (Matt. 13).

In these words of the Lord, which are easier and more evident than the rest, we judge that we should not linger long but pass through them briefly. This man who sowed good seed is Christ; the field, the world; the seed, the word of God. The enemy is the devil; the tares are the doctrines of heretics, or any sins whatsoever.

“But while people were sleeping, the enemy came and oversowed tares.” The sleeping of people signifies the death of the apostles or the sluggishness of prelates. After the death of the apostles, indeed, heretics arose; with the devil’s assistance they scattered corrupt doctrine throughout the field of the world. When prelates too sleep through sluggishness, demons arise, and perverse people also arise; they cast upon good hearts the seeds of evil thoughts or suggestions. Upon some they sow lust, upon others avarice, and they cast the diverse seeds of sins into different persons. And from evil seeds—that is, from evil suggestions—evil crops arise, that is, evil people.

“Do you wish,” the servants say, “that we go and gather them?” And he says: “No, lest perhaps, in gathering the tares, you uproot the wheat.” Spiritual men, seeing heretics or any perverse persons spring up and grow in the Lord’s field, would, if they knew it pleased God, wish to remove them from the midst of the righteous, because they seem in some respects to harm the righteous. But, having consulted divine justice as to whether they ought to do this, whether God wills it, and whether it is human beings’ office to remove evil people from the earth, they recognize that in this life one does not know what those who are now evil will become, or what their error contributes to the good. Therefore they are not to be removed, lest good persons be killed—persons whom they may perhaps become—or lest their removal harm the good whom they benefit.

But then they recognize that evil persons are appropriately removed, when there is no longer time to change their lives or to benefit others; and thus that they are to be removed by angels, not by human beings. “At harvest time I will say to the reapers: Gather first the tares and bind them in bundles to be burned; but gather the wheat into my barn.” The time of harvest is the day of resurrection, when the reapers, the angels, will bind bundles of evil persons to be burned: binding the unclean with the unclean, the avaricious with the avaricious, and likewise the ungodly with those like themselves, so that those who were companions in guilt may be tormented together in punishment. But they will gather the wheat into the barn, because they will assign to the good the blessed dwelling places of heaven.

## CHAPTER XXII. On the mustard seed

“The kingdom of heaven is like a mustard seed, which a man took and sowed in his field” (Matt. 13).

[Col. 0793D] This man signifies God; the field, the world; the mustard seed, faith, which seems small because of the scandal of the cross, but is fervent because of the heat of love. This seed—that is, the Catholic faith—becomes a great tree: it has a trunk through hope, branches raised high through love of God, and spread wide through love of neighbor. In its branches dwell the birds of heaven, namely the saints, who fly on the wings of virtues toward the rewards of heavenly goods.

Thus every upright person sows a mustard seed in the field when, because of the scandal of the cross, he deposits in his own heart the divine preaching which the reprobate regard as insignificant. It grows into a great tree when it receives strength through the exercise of virtue and branches through the multiplication of good work. In its branches, [Col. 0794A] the birds of heaven rightly make their dwelling when spiritual perceptions seek residence in it through the elevation of a good conscience.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On the leaven hidden in three measures of flour

“The kingdom of heaven is like leaven which a woman took and hid in three measures of flour, until the whole was leavened” (Matt. 13).

Above he treated of faith; here he treats of love. The woman signifies divine wisdom; the leaven, love; the flour, hearts; the three measures, three kinds of people: people of the natural law, people of the written law, and people of grace. The woman therefore hides leaven in three measures of flour until the whole is leavened, because divine wisdom places love within the hearts of the three kinds of people. The whole will be leavened when [Col. 0794B] the number of the elect is completed at the end of the age.

Sometimes leaven signifies good, sometimes evil. Good, as in this passage: “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven”; evil, as in: “Purge out the old leaven” (1 Cor. 5). By this woman we may understand the soul; by the three measures, the soul’s three powers—reason, anger, and desire; by flour, thought; by leaven, as above, love.

Thus a woman hides leaven in three measures of flour until the whole is leavened when any faithful soul deposits the fervor of love in the thought of the three natural powers. The whole, therefore, is leavened when the threefold thought of the three powers is converted into the flavor and fervor of love; and through [Col. 0794C] reason we possess discernment of good and evil; through anger, hatred of vices; through desire, love of virtues.

## CHAPTER XXIV. On the treasure hidden in a field

“The kingdom of heaven is like a treasure hidden in a field, which a man who finds it hides; and because of joy over it he goes, sells all that he has, and buys that field” (Matt. 13).

The field is Scripture; the treasure, divine knowledge; the finding of the treasure, the revelation of good; the hiding of the treasure, concealment of good from the devil’s knowledge and from the desire for human favor. Whoever, for the sake of sacred Scripture, true knowledge, and divine love contained in it, abandons all other things opposed and alien to them, sells everything and buys the field.

## CHAPTER XXV. On the merchant seeking good pearls

[Col. 0794D]

“The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant seeking good pearls; but when he had found one precious pearl, he went away, sold all that he had, and bought it” (Matt. 13).

The good pearls are the Law and the Prophets; the one precious pearl is knowledge of the Savior. The person who, like Paul, renounces the old observances in order to gain Christ sells everything and buys this pearl. Likewise, the person who for love of heavenly things despises earthly things sells everything and buys the precious pearl.

## CHAPTER XXVI. On the net cast into the sea

“The kingdom of heaven is like a net cast into the sea, gathering fish of every kind; when it was full, they drew it out, sat down upon the shore, selected [Col. 0795A] the good into their vessels, and threw the bad away” (Matt. 13).

This net is evangelical preaching, which, cast into the sea—that is, into the turbulence and bitterness of the present age—gathers a multitude of fish, that is, people of every kind, and draws them to the seashore, that is, to the end of the present age. The filling of the net is the completion of evangelical preaching.

It gathers from every kind of people: from the Jews, to whom Christ preached; from the Romans, to whom Peter and Paul preached; from the Indians, to whom Thomas preached; from the Persians, to whom Simon and Jude preached; from the people of Lesser India, to whom Bartholomew preached; from the Syrians, to whom Philip preached; from the Asians, to whom John preached; from the Achaeans, to whom Andrew preached; from the Ethiopians, to whom [Col. 0795B] Matthew preached; and from the Alexandrians, to whom Mark preached; and thus from other nations to which the sound of preaching came, whether through the apostles or through the apostles’ disciples and successors. “Their sound has gone out into all the earth” (Ps. 18). For in taking people from all nations, evangelical preaching draws fish of every kind.

Otherwise: it gathers fish of every kind because it gathers people of every kind of sin. It gathers unclean sinners: fornicators, adulterers, incestuous persons, usurers, and all others who are separated from God by lesser or greater sins and scattered through many iniquities. It gathers all of them, justifies those gathered, and excludes no one who, having heard it, wishes to enter it.

This net contains many fish, both diverse good and evil ones; but while the net is being drawn to shore, these frequently change into those. For good people sometimes become evil through sin, and evil people sometimes become good through grace. Nor can it yet be judged who is to be chosen for the vessels and who cast out, until the shore is reached—that is, the end of the age. Then the true judgment that separates good and evil will be manifest, because the angels will select the good into vessels—that is, into eternal dwelling places—and cast the evil out into eternal torments.

But all who will not receive the Christian faith are outside this net, like Jews and pagans. Such persons have already been judged not only by judgment according to foreknowledge [Col. 0795D] and judgment according to cause, but also by judgment according to action; they are still to be judged by judgment according to recompense.

Judgment according to foreknowledge is that by which we were judged before we existed. Judgment according to cause is that by which we are judged from the time that we are good or evil. Judgment according to action is that by which we are judged, through manifest action, to be good or evil when previously, according to cause, we were hidden. Judgment according to recompense is that by which we receive as reward according to what we were and did in merit.

Of these four judgments, two are hidden and two manifest. Hidden are judgment according to foreknowledge and judgment according to cause. Manifest are judgment according to recompense and judgment according to action. [Col. 0796A] Two also belong to God: namely, judgment according to foreknowledge and judgment according to recompense. Two belong to humanity: judgment according to cause and judgment according to action. But those who utterly reject the Christian faith have already been judged by the three preceding judgments—namely, judgment according to foreknowledge, judgment according to cause, and judgment according to action—but are yet to be judged by judgment according to recompense.

## CHAPTER XXVII. On the Canaanite woman and the healing of her daughter

“Jesus withdrew into the region of Tyre and Sidon. And behold, a Canaanite woman came out from those borders, crying: ‘Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David’” (Matt. 15).

The Gentile woman, who comes to the Lord in faith, signifies the Church of the Gentiles. She prays for her demon-possessed daughter, [Col. 0796B] that is, for her own people not yet saved, so that, freed from the devil’s deceits, it may serve the true divinity in freedom.

The territories of Tyre and Sidon, in which the woman prays to the Lord, signify the unanimous faith in Christ of the two peoples, Jews and Gentiles, who have been converted. But this woman, according to Matthew, is rightly said to have come out from the borders of Tyre, while according to Mark she is said to have entered the house, come to God, and fallen at his feet. From both accounts it is gathered that only those pray faithfully and rightly for persons in error who leave the former dwellings of their unbelief and transfer themselves, in humble and pious devotion, into the house of the Lord—that is, the Church.

“It is not good to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs.” The table is Scripture; [Col. 0796C] the bread, knowledge; the children, Jews; the dogs, Gentiles. It is as if he said: It is not good that the benefit of miracles, which belongs to the Jewish people who possess knowledge of God, should be bestowed upon your Gentile daughter, who lacks knowledge of God. But the Gentile woman, through her humble reply, obtained for her daughter the benefit of healing.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. On the lunatic delivered from a demon

“A man came to Jesus, falling upon his knees before him and saying: ‘Lord, have mercy on my son, because he is lunatic and suffers badly’” (Matt. 17).

A lunatic is one who changes from vice to vice with each passing moment, does not persist in what he has begun, but declines from good and increases in evil—now carried into the fire of lust or anger, now cast into the water of fluctuating desire. [Col. 0796D] Mark says of him: “And when the spirit saw him, immediately it convulsed him; and, thrown to the ground, he rolled about foaming” (Mark 9). While the boy approaches the Lord, he is thrown down, because converts are usually attacked more grievously by the demon when they come to the Lord, either so that they may be brought back to vices or so that the devil may avenge himself for his expulsion. Thus, at the beginning of the nascent Church, he brought many and grave conflicts against those whom he saw being withdrawn from his kingdom.

## CHAPTER XXIX. On the king who settled accounts with his servants

“The kingdom of heaven is like a king who wished to settle accounts with his servants” (Matt. 18).

This man is God, who has servants—that is, human beings—created in his image and likeness and bound to serve him. The settling of accounts is the distribution of the divine examination; debt is sin; debtors are sinners. The more a person has sinned, the more he owes; and whoever has sinned less owes less.

The servant who owed ten thousand talents is the one who has transgressed the ten legal commandments and has nothing from which to repay, because he has nothing in himself from which he may become righteous and fulfill the commandments of the Law. The Lord commands that he, his wife, and his children be sold, with all that he has, when he commands him, on account of his unjust will and abominable deeds, to pay penalties together with all his contrivances.

Foreseeing this, the debtor—that is, the sinner—sometimes comes forward in humility and asks by humble prayer that patience be shown him through divine mercy; and he promises that he will repay everything through the satisfaction of repentance. [Col. 0797B] In this action the Lord forgives him the debt, because he forgives him the sin.

But this man, to whom the Lord forgives so great a debt, casts his fellow servant into prison for a hundred denarii, when he utterly excludes from every mercy another person who has offended him slightly in word or deed. Therefore the Lord, justly angered, hands him over to torturers until he pays the entire debt, because he compels him to undergo the eternal punishments which he had earlier deserved for transgression of the Law.

“So also my heavenly Father will do to you, if each of you does not forgive his brother from your hearts.” Some are altogether unwilling to forgive, because they retain malice in their hearts and, when able, exact vengeance in deed. Others, although they forgive with respect to vengeance, nevertheless retain conceived hatred with respect to malice. But whoever desires the Lord to forgive him must forgive his brother in both ways: neither exercising vengeance in deed nor retaining malice in the heart.

## CHAPTER XXX. On the laborers in the vineyard

“The kingdom of heaven is like a householder who went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard” (Matt. 20).

The householder is God; the vineyard, the Church; the laborers, prelates; the hours of the day, the age of the world. The hiring of laborers is the appointment of prelates or the sending forth of preachers; the late hour of the day, the end of the age; the wage of the denarius, the reward of the kingdom of heaven.

Likewise, the householder is God; the vineyard, the soul; the laborers, our faculties; diligence in work, the exercise of virtue; the hours of the day, the ages of human life; evening, the end of life. [Col. 0797D] The recompense is eternal blessedness.

On the cultivators of this vineyard and their reward, a certain versifier says:

> The vineyard was cultivated; the cultivators seek their rewards.  
> The labor was not equal, yet the gifts were equal.  
> He who comes last when summoned by the steward  
> receives as much as one who came before.

Thus God shows that, whenever we may wish to undertake the work, we may be certain of the reward.

## CHAPTER XXXI. On the son who refused to enter the vineyard

“A certain man had two sons. Coming to the first, he said: ‘Son, go today and work in my vineyard.’ But he answered and said: ‘I will not’; afterward, however, moved by repentance, he went. Coming to the other, he spoke similarly. But he answered and said: ‘I go, sir’; and he did not go. Which of the two did the will of his father?” (Matt. 21).

The son who refused to enter [Col. 0798A] his father’s vineyard is the Gentile people, who at first despised serving God. The son who promised to enter is the Jewish people, who first pledged their service to God.
