But the one who had first refused afterward entered, because the Gentile people, moved by repentance through the preaching of the apostles, submitted their necks to God’s service. And the first son did not fulfill what he had promised, because the Jewish people did not remain in God’s service.

## CHAPTER XXXII. On the king who made a wedding feast for his son
The kingdom of heaven is like a man, a king, who made a wedding feast for his son. And he sent his servants to call those invited to the wedding feast, but they would not come (Matt. 22). The kingdom of heaven is the present Church, the congregation of the righteous. The king is God the Father, who rules all things. The wedding of the son is the incarnation of the Word. Those invited are the Jews. [Col. 0798B] The servants sent on account of the invited guests are the prophets and apostles. “My oxen and fattened animals have been killed, and everything is ready: come to the wedding feast.” The oxen are the fathers and warriors of the Old Testament, who drove enemies from their borders by the horns of authority granted to them. The fattened animals are the preachers of the New Testament, rich in the fullness of spiritual grace and seeking the joys above on the wings of contemplation. They are called “killed,” either because they have been set at rest from what they once were, or through the death of the flesh. The oxen and fattened animals signify that both the prophets earlier and the apostles later suffered at the hands of unbelievers; they are now examples to us of what we ought to believe.

“But they, neglecting this, went away: one to his farm, another to his business. And the rest seized his servants, insulted them, and killed them.” Those who refused to come to the wedding feast [Col. 0798C] signify those among the Jews who refused to believe in Christ or despised him. Some of them went to their farm, while they devoted themselves to earthly work; others to their business, while they pursued greed. Those, however, who killed the king’s servants represent those Jews who persecuted the prophets, apostles, and other preachers. When the king saw that his servants had been killed, he was angered; and, sending his armies—that is, the Romans, Titus and Vespasian—he destroyed those murderers, namely the Jews, and burned their city, namely Jerusalem.

“Go out to the ends of the roads.” The ends of the roads are the errors of the nations, which lie outside faith, hope, and charity, the roads leading to the homeland. “And whomever you find”—that is, persons of every condition—“call by preaching to the wedding feast,” [Col. 0798D] that is, to faith in the Lord’s incarnation. And the servants—that is, the apostles—went out from Judaea into the roads, that is, the sects of the nations, and gathered into the unity of belief the bad, that is, false Christians, and the good, that is, the elect. The wedding feast was filled with those reclining at table: that is, all who were called through preaching entered the profession of the Catholic faith.

“The king came in to see those reclining.” The king enters the wedding feast to see those reclining when God, in the present life, illuminates the consciences of those designated by the Christian name and carefully weighs and judges what each one does. “And he saw there a man not clothed in a wedding garment.” The wedding garment is the work of charity. Whoever does not possess this garment, having his hands and feet bound—that is, being utterly deprived [Col. 0799A] of the power to act well—is cast into the outer darkness, which is the darkness of hell. The text adds what he will suffer there, who despised to live well here: “There will be weeping”—namely, of eyes now wandering in the vanity of the world—“and gnashing of teeth,” of those now delighting in gluttony. Many are called by preaching, but few are chosen for the kingdom through the holiness of a good life.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. On the Day of Judgment

“As it happened in the days of Noah, so it will be in the days of the Son of Man: they ate and drank, took wives and were given in marriage, until the day when Noah entered the ark; and the flood came and destroyed them all” (Matt. 24; Luke 17). Noah builds the ark when the Lord gathers the faithful into the Church; when it has been completed, [Col. 0799B] he will enter it when, on the day of judgment, he illumines it by his presence. But while the ark is being built, the wicked indulge in luxury; and when it is entered, they are punished with eternal damnation.

“It was likewise in the days of Lot: they ate and drank, bought and sold, planted and built. But on the day Lot went out of Sodom, God rained fire and sulphur from heaven and destroyed them all.” Lot, whose name means “turning aside,” is the people of the elect. While it dwells in Sodom—that is, among the reprobate—as a stranger, it turns aside from their crimes as far as it can. When Lot goes out, Sodom perishes, because at the consummation of the age the angels will go out, separate the wicked from among the righteous, and cast them into the furnace of fire (Matt. 13).

## CHAPTER XXXIV. On the Ten Virgins

[Col. 0799C] “The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and bride” (Matt. 25). The ten virgins are all believers who perform good works; the lamps are works; the oil is grace or a good conscience. The five foolish virgins signify those who, in the good things they do, seek not a good conscience but human praise. The wise virgins are those who, in the good things they do, seek not human praise but a good conscience. The bridegroom’s delay is the postponement of judgment; the virgins’ sleep is human death; midnight is the unexpected occurrence of the resurrection; the cry announcing the bridegroom’s arrival is the evangelical trumpet on the day of judgment; the preparation of the lamps is the recollection and reckoning of works.

But [Col. 0799D] the lamps of the foolish are extinguished, because at the coming of judgment they are darkened within and receive no reward, because they have received praise. “Give us some of your oil”: that is, bear testimony to our works. “Go rather to the sellers.” This is not advice, but an indirect recollection of their fault: “Go to the sellers,” that is, you will now see what those who were accustomed to sell you praise can do for you. The sellers are flatterers who give praise in order to receive some reward. But while the foolish virgins seek a good conscience too late, the wise enter with the bridegroom into the wedding feast; for, once the reprobate have been cast out to damnation, the elect will enter with Christ into blessedness. “And the door was shut,” that is, the entrance to the kingdom of heaven. “Lord, Lord, open to us.” After late repentance, [Col. 0800A] after fruitless tears, they vainly knock, left outside. “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.” It is as though he said: “Therefore I abandon you, because I do not recognize you by the merit of your life.” Behold how great is the severity, after his judgment, of him whose mercy before it is ineffable. “Watch therefore, because you know neither the day nor the hour.” Behold the point of the parable. Its point is that we should open the eyes of our hearts to the future; escape evils by abandoning sin; and obtain good things by pursuing righteousness.

## CHAPTER XXXV. On the Man Who Entrusted His Possessions to His Servants

“A certain man, about to depart on a journey, called his servants and entrusted his possessions to them” (Matt. 25). This man is Christ; the servants are Christians; the departure is the Ascension; the possessions are gifts; the five talents are outward [Col. 0800B] knowledge acquired through the five senses; the two talents are understanding and good action; the one talent is understanding alone; the multiplication of talents is the exercise of virtues and the performance of good works for one’s own justification and the benefit of another.

The servant who hid his lord’s money in the ground signifies false Christians who have received natural ability but spend it on earthly and transitory things; who fear to take up the paths of the higher life; and who are ashamed, contemptuous, or negligent of multiplying by preaching the wisdom or knowledge divinely received. “I reap where I did not sow and gather where I did not scatter.” It is as though he said: “I require the fruit of action and preaching not only from those to whom I granted the grace of acting and preaching, but I also condemn for barrenness and unfruitfulness those to whom I granted no grace.” [Col. 0800C]

“Wicked and slothful servant”: servant, because you ought to have served me by acting and preaching; wicked, by doing evil; slothful, by refraining from good. “You ought to have entrusted my money to the bankers, and on my return I would have received what is mine with interest.” The bankers are those who, having heard preaching, strive to multiply in deed and word what they have heard. It is as though he said: “Having received my grace, you ought to have applied yourself to good works and preaching. Had you done so, you would have gained for me not only yourself but many others also by your example and word. But because, through your sloth, by which you ceased from good, and through your wickedness, by which you did evil, you inflicted on me the loss not only of your own justification [Col. 0800D] but also of another’s, therefore I rightly accuse and condemn you for your wickedness and sloth.”

“Take the talent from him, and give it to him who has ten talents. For to everyone who has, more will be given, and he will abound,” etc. To one who has merit, reward will be given: “will be given” with respect to recompense; “will abound” with respect to blessedness. “But from him who does not have, even what he seems to have will be taken away.” For every false Christian, in condemnation, will not even be allowed to retain the name of Christianity. And, as he is now stripped of the inward truth of the sacraments, so then he will be stripped outwardly of their external shadow. Let human conscience therefore take care for itself now, in time, so that afterward it may rejoice in eternal reward. Let it expend the talent of heavenly gift in such a way that it receives not damnation but salvation at the [Col. 0801A] end.

Let no one say: “It is enough for me to attend to myself and provide for myself; I shall give an account for myself. I do not wish, in seeking another’s salvation, to put myself in danger. I am not learned in the Scriptures or fluent in speech. I know little; God will never accuse or condemn anyone merely because he does not preach, for so small a thing.” For in respect of every person whom one can benefit by word, one causes God loss by one’s silence; and for each such person one will, not unjustly, give an account at judgment. Therefore let one who knows much say much; let one who knows little say little; and let each say as much as he knows. Whoever knows even one Gospel or one example of virtue should impart to others through preaching whatever he has received through knowledge. Let him consider neither sex, age, person, [Col. 0801B] time, nor place, but preach to all, always and everywhere: to men, women, old people, young people, rich, poor; in prosperity and adversity; by day and night, in the morning, at noon, in the evening; in church, in the street, on the road, in the field, on land, at sea. Let him always and everywhere speak the good that he knows, if someone able to hear is present.

For there are many who always look for more distinguished persons in all these situations, and refuse to preach to their opposites, as if the Lord God regarded higher things and did not care for lower things; although sometimes what seem lowest to human beings are held highest by God. There are also those who preach to a more numerous crowd but do not care to speak to a few. They bind themselves to greater guilt before God because, whether through embarrassment, pride, or the pomp of wealth, they wholly refuse to impart the word of God. [Col. 0802A]

Whoever expends in preaching the talent of known good gains profit for the giver of the talent, if not in another, yet in himself. For even if the hearer does not abandon evil and do good, the speaker nevertheless delivers his own soul by what he says; ignorance does not excuse the hearer, and for that reason the divine judgment condemns him more justly. Yet no one can excuse himself from this distribution of the talent, because there is no one who cannot by his word spur another toward better things.

Those who have been marked out for the ministry of preaching, who receive the resources of that ministry and live from them delicately and luxuriously, and yet do not know the divine Scriptures—these, I say, must be reproved for torpor, idleness, or contempt. For although the churches are filled with libraries, homiliaries, expositions, and treatises, they themselves devote no diligence to reading or meditating upon the Scriptures. Let the useless, unlearned, and ignorant ministers of certain churches therefore be ashamed; let them shake off their torpor, read books, expend their talent, and redeem the time, because the days are evil. [Col. 0802B] Finally, in every way by which we can amend ourselves or help others, we ought to dispense and, by dispensing, multiply the Lord’s talent, since we shall render an account of it in strict judgment.

# BOOK III. ON MARK

[Col. 0801]

## CHAPTER I. On the Man with a Withered Hand

[Col. 0801C]

Jesus entered the synagogue, and there was there a man with a withered hand. He said to him: “Stretch out your hand” (Mark 3). This man signifies the human race, hindered from every good action through original sin. The Lord healed his hand when he granted it the grace to act well. For he stretches out, as it were, a withered hand when he receives the lost capacity for good work.

Otherwise: this man signifies the greedy, who, unwilling to give, wish to receive. They are told to stretch out their hand, so that “the one who steals may steal no longer” (Eph. 4), but rather labor by working, so that he may have something to give to one suffering need.

## CHAPTER II. On the Demoniac Possessed by a Legion

As Jesus came out of the boat, a man in an unclean spirit came from the tombs to meet him; he had his dwelling among the tombs (Mark 5). This demoniac, possessed by a legion, signifies the people of the nations, long possessed by the entire host of demons. For the Gentile people was held by all demons as long as, through its manifold worship of idolatry, it served them all. For the Gentiles, as [Col. 0802C] the Apostle says, “exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds, quadrupeds, and serpents; because they exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshipped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for the ages. Amen” (Rom. 1).

The chains or fetters by which he was bound and which he broke signify the precepts of the natural law or the ordinances of Gentile laws, by which they ought to have been restrained from evil. But the bound demoniac broke chains and fetters, because the more the Gentile people was bound by this or that commandment prohibiting evils, the more furiously it broke them by transgression. And he dwelt among tombs because he lived amid dead and stinking works. Paul describes this breaking [Col. 0802D] of chains and fetters thus, saying: “Their women exchanged natural intercourse for that which is against nature; likewise the men also, abandoning natural intercourse with women, burned in their desires for one another, men committing shameful acts with men and receiving in themselves the due recompense of their error. And since they did not see fit to retain God in their knowledge, God gave them over to a reprobate mind, to do things that are unfitting: filled with all iniquity, wickedness, sexual immorality, greed, and malice; full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, malignity; whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God, insolent, proud, haughty, inventors of evils, disobedient to parents, foolish, disorderly, without affection, without covenant, without mercy” (Rom. 1). [Col. 0803A]

Behold how the legion possessed the man, how he broke chains and fetters, how he lived among the tombs. He is rightly said to have cried out night and day among the tombs and mountains and to have cut himself with stones, because, in both adversity and prosperity, the Gentile people openly displayed itself in shameful conduct and tore itself to pieces through the worship of stony gods.

The herd of swine feeding near the mountain, into which the legion entered after being driven from the man, and which it hurled into the sea, represents the multitude of unbelievers and all unclean people. They rightly feed near the mountain while, lifted up by pride, bent low like swine, they know nothing of things above and brutishly immerse themselves only in transitory things. And while they defile themselves with the pollution of flesh or spirit, like swine they seek their food in mud. Alas, how manifold is this herd of swine: namely, human beings living shamefully and brutishly, and imitating swine that seek their whole good in the lowest things! For, to say nothing of Jews and pagans, who could number the multitude of false Christians [Col. 0803C] who, though they have received baptism, nevertheless, by doing evil and thus insulting the Spirit of grace, have driven him out of themselves and defiled themselves with dreadful crimes? Yet these can figuratively be called two thousand: two, because they are divided from good; thousands, because they are perfected in evil.

Therefore, when the legion is driven from the man, it enters the swine: demons, expelled by the grace of the Redeemer from those predestined to eternal life, rule over evil people living wickedly and intent upon earthly things. Yet they do not do this unless Jesus allows it, because they do not presume even to tempt the wicked unless divine power permits it. The herd of swine is hurled by the legion into the sea when the whole body of the wicked is brought by demons to the bitterness of hell. [Col. 0803D]

The people of that city saw the man freed from the legion, sitting at Jesus’ feet, clothed and in his right mind, and they were afraid. Sitting at the Lord’s feet signifies humility and the imitation of good works; being clothed, good conduct; soundness of mind, justification. “And they begged Jesus to depart from their territory.” So Peter, mindful of his frailty, said: “Depart from me, Lord, for I am a sinful man” (Luke 5). Thus these people, still weak, feared him and begged him to depart from their territory.

Jesus said to the freed man: “Go home to your own people and tell them how great things the Lord has done for you, and how he has had mercy on you.” By this example everyone is taught first to proclaim to his own people the salvation granted to himself and to urge them to receive the same salvation. He is more especially bound to them by the relationship of the flesh, and perhaps they will believe him more quickly than a stranger. But how many are enclosed within the bounds of the Church and do not follow this example! Many inquire about their relatives: whether they are physically healthy; whether they have food or clothing, houses, fields, horses, flocks, herds, gold, silver, temporal peace, or the favour of the powerful and rich; and so they are concerned for their friends about things pertaining to the body, [Col. 0804A] but take no care for what pertains to the salvation of souls. It is to be feared that such people have relapsed into their former vices and themselves lack the salvation which they do not care to preach even to their own.

For those who are spiritual seek the things of the Spirit. They diligently ask about their own people whether they are pure from vices, free from sins, rich in virtues, full of good works; whether they have the peace of God with all people (Gal. 6); and whether they do good to all, especially to those of the household of faith. These imitate the freed man, who, at the Lord’s command, endeavoured to announce to others the salvation accomplished in himself and preached throughout the Decapolis. The Decapolis, a region of ten cities, signifies the holy Church, which keeps the Decalogue of the Law. And he proclaims the salvation accomplished in himself in the Decapolis when, by good words and deeds, he demonstrates to the faithful of the holy Church that he has been delivered from the devil.

Let us also strive, if we have not yet been delivered, to be delivered from the devil. And if we know ourselves already delivered, let us preach to others the salvation which we rejoice to have obtained, mindful of what is written: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Luke 11); and again: “Let the one who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22). [Col. 0804C]

## CHAPTER III. On the Disciples Resting in a Deserted Place

Jesus said to his disciples: “Come away by yourselves to a deserted place and rest a little” (Mark 6). There are two lives: the active and the contemplative. The active is in labour; the contemplative, in rest. The active is in public; the contemplative, in the desert. The active is concerned with a neighbour’s need; the contemplative, with the vision of God. We are therefore admonished by these words of the Lord occasionally to rest from activity and pass into the secret place of contemplation. This contemplation is rightly called a desert because it is abandoned by many and inhabited by few. [Col. 0804D] There we rest a little, because in our frailty we cannot long adhere to the divine vision, nor can we long neglect care for our neighbour’s need.

“For many were coming and going, and they had no opportunity even to eat.” Thus in our own days many come and many go. Many come through faith, but many go back through wickedness. The thief came; Judas went away. And we have no opportunity to eat when, occupied with good or evil people through preaching or some ministry, we have no leisure to read and meditate upon the Scriptures. Let us therefore sometimes board the boat with the apostles and go away into the desert, so that, ceasing from speech and ministry, crossing the worldly waves through the faith we have in God, [Col. 0805A] we may at least for a short time devote ourselves wholly to reading and meditation, prayer and divine contemplation. For, as we read in the books of blessed Gregory, no one ought wholly to set aside a neighbour’s need for contemplation of God, nor, because of a neighbour’s need, despise contemplation of God.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Boat at Sea

“When evening came, the boat was in the middle of the sea, and Jesus alone on land” (Mark 6). Evening signifies the ignorance of the present life; the boat, the holy Church; the sea, the instability of this age; the land, heavenly solidity; the fourth watch, knowledge of the four Gospels; the disciples’ labour at rowing, [Col. 0805B] the labour of the righteous in acting well; the wind is the devil; the wind’s opposition, the devil’s temptations.

Jesus walks upon the sea when he treads down, suppresses, and humbles the swelling of the present age. He sees the disciples’ labours when he mercifully attends to the manifold tribulations of the righteous in their midst. “And he intended to pass them by,” so that, troubled for an hour but immediately afterward delivered, they might marvel more at the miracle of their deliverance and give greater thanks to their deliverer. For divine compassion often seems to abandon the faithful in tribulation and temptation. Hence it is written: “Why have you cast me off? Why do I go mourning while the enemy afflicts me?” (Ps. 42). But the Lord is immediately at hand and says: “Take courage; it is I. Do not be afraid.” Of this consolation it is said: “When you pass through [Col. 0805C] water, I will be with you, and the rivers shall not cover you” (Isa. 43). He enters the boat with them when, entering the holy Church through grace, he fortifies the faithful against every adversity.

## CHAPTER V. On the Healing of the Deaf and Mute Man

Jesus, leaving the region of Tyre, came to Sidon through the midst of the territory of the Decapolis. They brought to him a deaf and mute man and begged him to lay his hand upon him (Mark 7). The human race, as one man corrupted by diverse plague in the first-created human, lost sight when it lost the brightness of divine contemplation; hearing, when it lost the virtue of obedience; smell, when it lost the virtue of discernment; taste, when it lost the savour of inner sweetness; touch, when it lost the gentleness [Col. 0805D] of inner delight; speech, when it lost the confession of divinity; its hand, when it lost the performance of good work. It lost, as it were, the functions of its individual senses and members when, through original sin, it lost the exercise of all virtues and the performance of good works. It is bent over when, abandoning what is highest for what is lowest, it bends down. It is swollen with dropsy when it is distended by desire for external goods; it is filled with a demon when it openly gives itself over to demonic service. The various miraculous actions signify restorations of the various virtues and acts in the human race.

“Jesus, leaving the region of Tyre.” Tyre means “narrowness” and signifies Judaea, to which the Lord said through the prophet, indicating that he would abandon it: “The bed is cramped, so that one must fall off” (Isa. 28). [Col. 0806A] Sidon means “hunting” and signifies the fierceness of the Gentiles and the Gentile nations. The region of the Decapolis, on account of the number ten, represents the ten commandments of the divine law. The Sea of Galilee, which means “a migration accomplished,” signifies the restless changeability of the nations which had perfectly migrated from evil to good through abandoning idolatry.

Thus Jesus, leaving the regions of Tyre and Sidon, coming through Sidon to the Sea of Galilee amid the territory of the Decapolis, healed the deaf and mute man when, abandoning the straits of unbelieving Judaea, restraining the fierceness of the nations, and calming their instability through preaching the Decalogue, he cured the harmful silence and deafness [Col. 0806B] of the human race. And he laid his hand upon him when he gave him power to obey his commands and confess the Catholic faith. The persons who bring him are apostles and preachers, who pray for the healing of the sick man as often as they humbly pray for the salvation of unbelievers.

The Lord leads the sick man to be healed away from the crowd when, justifying any impious person, he separates him from the society and company of unbelievers and evildoers. He puts his fingers into the sick man’s ears and, spitting, touches his tongue when, through the Holy Spirit, he grants him grace to obey his commands and wisdom to confess and preach. By groaning, he gave us only an example of groaning for others. Finally, the sick man’s ears are opened for hearing and his tongue is freed for speaking when a person justified by grace listens with the ears of the heart to divine commands and confesses and preaches what he has learned. [Col. 0806C] We are therefore taught by this example to endeavour daily, through our preaching, to bring all sinners to the Lord and continually pray to him for them.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Seven Loaves, a Few Small Fish, and Four Thousand People Fed

We read in the Gospel (Mark 8 and Matt. 15) that the Lord fed four thousand people from seven loaves and a few small fish. In this passage the seven loaves signify the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; the little fish, the examples of the ancient Fathers who lived under the natural or written law. Those who ate are described as four thousand because of the perfection of the four Gospels, or because of the exercise of the four cardinal virtues. The Lord therefore feeds four thousand people from seven loaves and a few small fish when, through the gifts of the sevenfold Spirit and the examples of the preceding fathers—rescued from the waves of this age and consecrated by divine blessing—they provide us refreshment lest we fail on the course of this age. [Col. 0806D]

He feeds, I say, four thousand people when he perfects, instructs, and justifies the elect, embraced in faith by the four Gospels and exercised in the four principal virtues, through spiritual gifts and the examples of the fathers. Note that the fish are said to be few because righteous people of old were exceedingly rare. They remain with the Lord for three days because, established in faith in the holy Trinity, they desire to receive spiritual food from God. “Some of them have come from far away.” Whoever hastens to the Lord’s service having experienced no carnal corruption has not come from far away. Likewise, one who has been polluted by no unchastity or crimes, but has experienced marriage alone, has not come from far away. But those who defile themselves with many and great crimes and afterward return to God come from far away.

“And if I send them away hungry, they will fail on the way.” Converted sinners fail on the path of the present life if they are dismissed in their conscience without the nourishment of doctrine. The seven baskets filled with fragments are spiritual persons, who collect and preserve loftier matters exceeding the capacity of lesser people. [Col. 0807A] “And he dismissed them.” The Lord dismisses those who have been refreshed when, having instructed them in spiritual teaching so that they may perform what they have learned, he leaves them to their own free choice and does not compel any of them to serve him.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod

“Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod” (Mark 8). The leaven of the Pharisees is the pretence of religion, the tenacity of avarice, and the intemperance of desire. The leaven of Herod is murder, adultery, and reckless swearing. Whoever mixes their perversity into his own works does not at all beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and Herod.

## CHAPTER VIII. On a Hand or Foot Causing a Person to Stumble

“If your hand or your foot causes you to stumble, cut it off [Col. 0807C] and cast it away from you” (Mark 9; Matt. 18), etc. We should understand action by the hand; bodily movement by the foot; intention of heart by the eye. There are many whom their own hand causes grievously to stumble. Those who rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things (Prov. 9), because they delight in vices and evil works: their own hand miserably causes these people to stumble and delays their entry into the kingdom of heaven.

There are also those who delight in bodily movement and wandering: they traverse cities, castles, towns, villages, travel round the land and walk through it; they are never in one place or at rest, never able to restrain their feet from running to and fro. Hence, concerning such a traveller, a certain versifier says:

[Col. 0807D]

> While he was in the world, he lived by travelling through the world.  
> This is his last day; this is also his first rest.

What, then, do such people suffer—people who fly through regions not for prayer or temporal necessity, but solely from curiosity—except a stumbling through this foot, that is, through this wandering which greatly pleases them? What, I say, except that they are hindered from entering life?

The eye also causes to stumble those who, in what they do, do not seek to please God or benefit souls, [Col. 0808A] but seek to exalt either themselves or their carnal friends according to the vanity of the present age, and strive to obtain for themselves or their associates some transitory advantage. But such an eye—that is, this intention, which affords vain pleasure—prepares nothing but an obstacle to entrance into the kingdom of heaven. Let us therefore cut off, root out, and cast away from us this hand, that is, action; this foot, that is, movement; and this eye, that is, intention. For it is better to enter life with good action, movement, and intention alone than, mixing good with evil and thus having, as it were, two hands, two feet, and two eyes, to enter Gehenna.

## CHAPTER IX. On the Paralytic Let Down through the Tiles before Jesus

[Col. 0808B]

They came to Jesus, carrying a paralytic borne by four people (Luke 2; Matt. 2). This paralytic signifies a soul enfeebled by vices and sluggish in the softness of the flesh. The four bearers are teachers, who lift up and carry such a soul while they administer to it the teaching of the four Gospels or the preaching of the four principal virtues. The house in which Jesus was staying signifies the protection and sublimity of Holy Scripture. The crowd that did not allow the paralytic to be brought in signifies the multitude of useless thoughts that denies the sinful soul the sight of God. But the roof is uncovered when the lofty and mystical [Col. 0808C] sense of Scripture is opened; and the paralytic is brought before Jesus.

Then, where his sin is forgiven, he is called “son,” commanded to take up his bed and go away. For after a person truly returns to the knowledge of God, God heals him by grace from all in which he has sinned, calls him son by adoption, and commands him to take up his bed through subjection of the flesh and to go through good action. “Rise,” he says, “take up your bed, and go to your house.” It is as though he said: “Raise yourself from carnal desires through repentance; rule your flesh through continence; and go through good action to your house”—that is, to an honourable manner of life.

People are afflicted with bodily troubles for five reasons: either for increasing merits, as Job; or for preserving humility, as Paul through the angel of Satan; or for correcting or recognizing sins, as Miriam, Moses’ sister, and this paralytic, who could not be healed unless his sins were forgiven; or to make God’s glory manifest, as the blind man of whom it is said, “Neither he nor his parents sinned, but that the works of God might be manifested in him” (John 9); and Lazarus, whose sickness was not unto death but for God’s glory (ibid.); or as the beginning of eternal damnation, as Herod. [Note: [Col. 0807] “The Exposition on the Canticle of Blessed Mary” which the Rouen edition presents here is found below among the genuine exegetical works. EDITORS.]

# BOOK FOUR. ON LUKE

[Col. 0809]

## CHAPTERS I–II. On the Man and Woman Healed

[Col. 0809A]

We read in the Gospel that the Lord cast an unclean spirit out of a man and immediately healed a woman—Peter’s mother-in-law—from fevers (Luke 4). Morally understood, the man delivered from a demon signifies one cleansed from an impure thought; and the woman subsequently healed from fevers signifies the flesh restrained from the heat of desire by the precepts of continence. And the healed woman ministers to the Lord when the members of the flesh, which previously served uncleanness, serve righteousness.

## CHAPTER III. On the Patch, the New Garment, and the Wineskins and Wine
No one puts a patch from a new garment onto an old garment; otherwise he tears the new one also, and the patch from the new will not match the old [Col. 0809B] (Luke 5). The new garment is a good work; the old garment, sin. Whoever joins any good work to the sin in which he remains loses what he does, and the tear becomes greater; for it would have been better for him not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment delivered to him (2 Pet. 2). And no one puts new wine into old wineskins; otherwise the new wine bursts the wineskins, and it will itself be spilled, and the wineskins will perish. But new wine must be put into new wineskins, and both are preserved. Old wineskins are sinful people, imitating the old man with his deeds. New wineskins are people renewed through grace, imitators of the new man who was created according to God—that is, [Col. 0809C] Christ. Old wine is guilt; new wine, grace. Thus at times new wine is put into old wineskins, and the wineskins burst and the wine is spilled: because those who receive the grace of God, but after receiving grace wish to remain as formerly enslaved to sin, themselves become worse than they had been through contempt for grace—and grace is taken from them.

Alternatively: No one puts new wine into old wineskins; that is, God does not grant grace to sinners unless they are first renewed from their old condition. Otherwise the wine bursts the wineskins and is itself spilled; that is, if sinners themselves presume to receive the sacraments in which grace is contained and conferred, they themselves become worse through their presumption, and grace is by no means allowed to be present with them. But [Col. 0809D] new wine must be put into new wineskins, and thus both are preserved: because, when grace is granted to a good person, he both preserves the grace he has received, and the preserved grace justifies him. And no one who drinks old wine immediately wants new; for he says, “The old is better.” For as long as anyone delights in guilt, grace does not please him [Col. 0810A]. But after he has properly tasted new wine—that is, the sweetness of grace—he prefers the new to the old, that is, grace to guilt; grace which the unchangeably and supremely good God bestows.

## CHAPTER IV. On the Election of the Twelve Apostles

The Lord chose twelve apostles (Luke 6), to preach by making known to others the mysteries of the sacred faith. Twelve consists of four times three and three times four. Therefore the Lord chose twelve apostles so that through the four quarters of the world they might preach faith in the Holy Trinity and summon believers to the glory of heavenly blessedness.

## CHAPTER V. On the Tree and Its Fruit

“There is no good tree that produces bad fruit, nor a bad tree producing good fruit” (Luke 6). The tree is [Col. 0810B] the soul; the good tree, a righteous soul; the bad tree, a wicked soul; fruit, a work; the fruit of the righteous, righteousness; the fruit of the ungodly, guilt; knowledge of the tree from its fruit, knowledge of a person from his action; cutting down the bad tree, the condemnation of the sinner; the axe, Christ; the handle, humanity; the iron, divinity; the edge of the axe, the judgment of divine power.

## CHAPTER VI. On the Centurion’s Servant

Jesus entered Capernaum. Now the servant of a certain centurion was ill and about to die, and he was precious to him. And when he had heard about Jesus, he sent Jewish elders to him, asking him to come and heal his servant (Luke 7). The centurion signifies the Gentile world; the centurion’s servant, the Gentile people; the Jewish elders who were sent, the company of the apostles or of other believers from the Jews [Col. 0810C] converted to the faith and interceding for the justification of the Gentiles; the centurion’s approach and humility are the conversion and humility of the Gentile world; the effect of the healing, the grace of justification. And the Lord fittingly says of the centurion: “I have not found such great faith in Israel,” because few from Israel believed in him, while many from the Gentiles received faith in him.

## CHAPTER VII. On the Woman and Simon the Leper

A certain Pharisee asked Jesus to eat with him (Luke 7). The Pharisee, proud of his own righteousness, is the Jewish people; Mary Magdalene, who was a sinful woman, is the Gentile Church given over to idols; the pouring out of tears, confession of crimes; [Col. 0810D] the wiping, satisfaction; the ointment, the renown of a good work; the spreading of its fragrance, the extension of good repute.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Two Debtors

There were two debtors to a certain moneylender. One owed five hundred denarii and the other fifty. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave them both [Col. 0811A] (Luke 7). The two debtors are the two peoples, who owe God their Creator the coin—that is, their soul—marked with the image of the King and entrusted to them for safekeeping. The debt of each people is multiplied by five, because there are five bodily senses which we use in this life and by which we ought to cultivate the image of the Creator that we have received. But the Jew owes less, since the Decalogue of the Law is given through a servant; the Christian owes more, since through the Son the grace of life is entrusted to him. Therefore the Jews’ debt is increased by the number ten, the Christians’ by the number one hundred. But because neither is saved by his own strength, but by God’s grace through faith, it is rightly said: “Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave them both.” Therefore the Church from the Gentiles loves more than the Jew, because in its present [Col. 0811B] state greater grace is conferred upon it, and also because it is drawn out of greater foulness in respect to its past. He owes more who receives more.

## CHAPTER IX. On Jairus, Ruler of the Synagogue, and the Woman with the Issue of Blood

There was a certain ruler of the synagogue named Jairus; and seeing Jesus, he fell at his feet and begged him, saying: “For my daughter is at the point of death; come, lay your hand upon her, that she may be healed and live” (Luke 8). Jairus is interpreted “enlightened” and signifies the Jewish people, enlightened in the ancient fathers, prophets, Moses, Samuel, David, and others. The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue is the Synagogue, ordered by the institution of the Law, as though the only daughter born to Moses. In her twelfth [Col. 0811C] year—that is, as the time of puberty approached, when she ought to have borne spiritual offspring to God—she was dying, stricken by sudden sickness. But while the Lord was proceeding to the ruler of the synagogue’s daughter, the sick woman suffering from an issue of blood anticipated the healing. For the salvation of humankind was so ordered that first some from Israel, then the fullness of the Gentiles, should enter, and thus all Israel should be saved (Rom. 11).

Therefore the bleeding woman healed by God is the Church from the Gentiles, polluted by the great outflow of carnal pleasures and separated from the assembly of believers. When Christ had determined to save Judaea, she, by certain hope, anticipated the salvation already prepared for others; and she had spent much upon physicians—that is, theologians, prophets, and teachers of secular laws—who promised to give useful precepts for living [Col. 0811D]. Demons also, as though counselling human beings, claimed that they should be worshipped as gods. The more the Gentiles expended the powers of their natural ability in listening to these, the less they were able to be healed. But when they heard that the Jewish people were sick and that the true physician had come from heaven, they began both to hope for and to seek a remedy for their sickness.

And it should be noted that the girl was twelve years old and the woman had suffered an issue of blood for twelve years; that is, when this one was born, the other began to be ill. For in one and the same age of the world, the Synagogue began to be born in the patriarchs and the Gentiles began to be defiled by idolatry. Therefore she came up from behind in the crowd and touched his garment, and immediately the flow of her blood ceased [Col. 0812A]. The Church of the Gentiles came from behind because it did not see God present in the flesh; but afterward it came to the grace of faith and knowledge, and by touching his garments—that is, by sharing in his sacraments—it deserved to be healed from sins. The flow of blood (Matt. 9) signifies the origin of sin and the beginning of unclean thought, from which every sin is born. But the Lord cleanses not only evil deeds, but also evil words and wicked thoughts, from the source of uncleanness by evangelical sacraments, as though by his garments. That the crowd is said indeed to press upon him, while one woman alone was healed, signifies that many are called but few are chosen (Matt. 22).

When the woman is healed, the girl is reported dead, because once the Church of the Gentiles has been stripped of the stain of vices, the Synagogue is immediately destroyed by the death [Col. 0812B] of unbelief and envy: by unbelief, indeed, because it refused to believe in Christ; and by envy, because it was grieved that the Church believed. The girl will be raised when, after the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, all Israel will be saved. While raising the girl, the Lord kept only a few and expelled the others, because divine mysteries are not to be revealed to unbelievers, nor divine miracles to mockers. In the moral sense, the Lord heals the woman daily when he cures by grace a soul corrupted by various vices. The crowd too is expelled so that the girl may be raised; for unless the multitude of worldly concerns is driven out of the heart, the soul lying dead within is not raised. For while it scatters itself among many thoughts, it in no way gathers itself for consideration of salvation.

## CHAPTER X. On the Three Dead Whom He Raised

[Col. 0812C]

We read in the words of the Gospel that the Lord raised three dead persons: the girl in the house (Luke 8), the young man in the open country (Luke 7), and Lazarus in the tomb (John 11). The three dead persons signify three kinds of sinners. Those are dead in the house who still keep in their heart a wickedness conceived without outward manifestation in deed. Those are dead in the open country who display, by action and in the open field of the senses, the sin conceived by consent. Those are dead in the tomb who, long defiled by evil habit, through their infamy also corrupt others. The raising of the dead is the justification of sinners. And each is raised by grace the more easily [Col. 0812D] the less he has been made dead by guilt; and he is cleansed by a smaller satisfaction of repentance the less he has been corrupted by iniquity. Hence the Lord is read to have raised by his word alone, with few witnesses present, the girl lying recently dead in the house. But in raising Lazarus, four days dead in the tomb, he is reported to have groaned, been troubled, wept, and cried with a loud voice—not because raising Lazarus was any less easy for the Lord than raising the girl, but because the Lord’s deeds are examples of other things.

## CHAPTER XI. On the Seventy-Two Disciples

The Lord appointed another seventy-two (Luke 10). As the apostles are the model of bishops, so the seventy-two disciples are the model of presbyters [Col. 0813A] of the second order. Seventy-two are sent to preach the Gospel to the same number of nations of languages, so that, just as the first twelve apostles were appointed on account of the twelve tribes of Israel, so these also might be sent to instruct the other nations. By sending them two by two, he indicates that no one ought to undertake the office of preaching who does not have charity toward another. He sends them before his face into every city and place where he himself was to come, because where the words of preaching run ahead, the Lord comes to the dwelling-place of the mind.

And he said to them: “The harvest indeed is plentiful, but the laborers are few.” The harvest is the multitude of believers; the laborers, the apostles and their followers. And although this harvest is sown by the word of God, it nevertheless requires the labour and careful service of the laborer, lest the birds of heaven scatter the seed that has been sown [Col. 0813B]. But because the laborers—that is, the preachers—are few, one must continually ask that the Lord give the grace of preaching to believers and send them to tend his harvest. Hence it is added: “Pray therefore the Lord of the harvest to send laborers into his harvest.” For how will they preach unless they are sent? (Rom. 10). Again: “Behold, therefore, I send you as sheep among wolves” (Matt. 10). As wolves lie in wait for sheep, so heretics lie in wait for believers. And as a wolf circles the sheepfold by night, not daring to enter, testing the dog’s sleep and the shepherd’s absence as signs of negligence, so a heretic seeks to deceive believers in the night of his temptation, not entering the Church openly, and intending either to kill negligent shepherds or send them into exile.

A wolf cannot readily bend its stiff body; so a heretic, by the stubborn resolve of his heart, is not usually recalled from error. Hence the Apostle: “Avoid a heretical person after a first and second correction” (Titus 3). A wolf is carried along by its own impulse and is therefore often outwitted; so a heretic makes an attack and often remains empty-handed when he cannot do harm. If a wolf sees someone first, by a certain force of nature it takes away his voice; if a person sees it first, he puts it to flight. So the person whom a heretic anticipates by crafty argument is rendered mute, lest he confess the word of God. But if anyone has recognized the inventions of the heretic’s fraud, the heretic suffers the loss of his voice. Like the wolf, so the heretic: first, because each attacks the throat and inflicts a wound upon the vital parts. We may also understand by wolves any persecutors who, after the manner of wolves, try to tear believers to pieces.

[Col. 0813D] “Carry neither purse nor bag nor sandals.” The whole confidence of the preacher ought to be in God, so that, even if he does not provide for himself the expenses of this present life, he may know with fullest certainty that they will not be lacking; lest, while his mind is occupied with temporal matters, he preach eternal things less fully. Therefore he should carry no purse. In the mystical sense, money shut up in a purse is hidden wisdom which is not distributed for Christ. By the bag are figured the burdens of the world; by sandals, the examples of dead works. The preacher should not carry the burden of worldly affairs nor look to examples of foolish deeds, lest he think to fortify his works as though with skins from dead animals. And “greet no one [Col. 0814A] on the way.” He who preaches salvation to his hearers not from love for the eternal homeland but from desire of rewards, as it were greets on the way, because he wishes salvation for his hearers from an occasion rather than from intention. For everyone who greets on the way does so because of the occasion of the journey, not from an intention of obtaining salvation.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Man Who Fell among Robbers

“A certain man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho” (Luke 10). This man, who went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers, as we read in the homilies, signifies the human race. Having descended from the heavenly city in the first parents and fallen through sin into the misery of this world and exile, it was stripped through the deceit of the ancient enemy of the garment of immortality and innocence, and grievously wounded by the vices of original [Col. 0814B] sin. God made man, as we have said elsewhere, in his image and likeness (Gen. 1): in his image, according to reason; in his likeness, according to love, so that by both he might cleave to God and, cleaving to him, might be blessed. But the devil, envying human blessedness, inflicted upon man in original sin two principal evils contrary to the two goods just mentioned. In that man had been made in the image of God according to reason, he wounded him through ignorance of good. But in that man was made in the likeness of God, he wounded him through desire for evil.

Man was stripped, wounded, and left half-dead because, although the divine likeness that consists in love can be wholly corrupted in human nature, the divine image that consists in reason cannot be wholly erased [Col. 0814C]. For although a person can be so affected by malice that he loves no good whatever, he cannot be so blinded by ignorance that he knows no truth whatever. He was therefore rightly left half-dead: although he has been corrupted in large part because of primordial sins, he has not been utterly blinded. For even after the wounds he lived in that some small spark of understanding remained to him. Therefore the hostile sword did not utterly destroy man, since it could not completely efface in him the dignity of natural good.

The Psalmist also set forth the meaning of this teaching, saying: “Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me” (Ps. 50). By the clean heart he signifies in himself the divine [Col. 0814D] likeness; by the right spirit, the divine image. By asking that a clean heart be created in him but a right spirit renewed, he fittingly indicates both that the divine likeness can be wholly corrupted and that the divine image cannot at all be completely erased. For where no good remains, good, if it is restored, is created; but where some good remains, it is renewed. Purity of heart consists in perfect love of God; rectitude of spirit, in sound reason.

That, according to the preceding distinctions, the divine image and divine likeness in us may be understood in this way, teachers explain in their exposition of another verse, where it is written: “The light of your countenance, O Lord, has been marked upon us; you have given gladness in my heart” (Ps. 4). By the light marked upon us, or in us, they distinguish the divine image in us, which they locate in the discernment of reason; and by gladness, the divine likeness, which they define as the delight of love [Col. 0815A].

The priest and Levite, who, on seeing the stripped and wounded man, passed by, represent the ancient fathers, who passed through the state of this present life by living holy lives, but did not heal the human race wounded by sin. The Samaritan passes by when Christ, through his humanity, hastened through the moments of this life. He poured wine and oil upon the wounded man when through his preaching he offered him both gentle consolation and severe rebuke. Binding up his wounds, he lifted him onto his beast when, hanging on the cross in the flesh he had assumed, he expiated that man’s guilt by his death. He brought him to an inn when he placed him within the holy Church. The inn signifies the Church, because, as beasts leave their filth in a stable, so sinners who formerly lived brutishly lay aside their sins through confession and satisfaction in the holy Church. On the following day he brought out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper to care for him, when, after the mystery of redemption had been accomplished, he distributed to all who ought to govern the Church knowledge of both Testaments and the grace of preaching [Col. 0815B]. “And whatever you spend in addition, I will repay you when I return.”

Prelates ought to spend something beyond what is required in caring for the sick, so that they may endeavour not only to preach what is contained in the two Testaments, but may also labour to devise many other things in accordance with what is written and make them known to others by preaching. But on the day of judgment, when the Lord returns, he will render a reward according to merit. Yet, since in this care the Lord demands even our own contribution, what shall we say, what shall we do, who rarely or never expend what belongs to him? For if we never relate even the plain letter to those to whom we owe instruction, what will become of us, who ought continually to preach to them even the countless interpretations devised, with grace assisting, through our own study and labour—or at least heard from others and most carefully stored in our hearts [deposited] [Col. 0815C]?

We may therefore say that in this figure Jerusalem is heavenly contemplation; a certain man, human nature; Jericho, worldly misery; robbers, demons; descent, sin; garments, immortality and innocence; wounds, vices; Levite and priest, the ancient fathers or ministers of the old priesthood; the Samaritan, Christ; the beast, the flesh; oil, gentle consolation; wine, severe rebuke; lifting up, redemption; the inn, the Church; innkeepers, prelates; the two denarii, knowledge of both Testaments.

## CHAPTER XIII. On Martha and Mary, Sisters of Lazarus

Jesus entered a certain village, and a woman named Martha received him into her [Col. 0816A] house (Luke 10). These two sisters signify two spiritual modes of life. Martha signifies the active devotion of work, by which we are joined to our neighbour in charity; Mary, the religious attention of the mind joined in love to God’s Word, by which we sigh in love for God. The active life gives either bodily bread to the hungry or instruction to the ignorant, corrects the erring, recalls the proud to humility, and dispenses to each what is fitting. The contemplative life retains love of God and neighbour, rests from outward action, clings to the desire of the Creator alone, and, trampling all cares underfoot, burns to see the Creator’s face and desires to be joined to the heavenly citizens who rejoice in eternal incorruption in God’s presence.

“And she had a sister named Mary, who also, sitting at the Lord’s feet, [Col. 0816B] listened to his words.” Mary sits because the contemplative person, after the tumults of vices have been calmed, already enjoys inward repose of mind in Christ. Martha stands because the active person toils in laborious conflict. “At his feet”: for the more humbly she sits, the more fully she receives, just as water flows to the valley from the heights of hills. “She listened to his words.” Mary was intent upon how she might be fed by the Lord, while Martha was intent upon how she might feed the Lord. The one prepares a banquet; the other already delights in the Lord’s banquet. “Lord, do you not care that my sister has left me to serve alone?” She speaks on behalf of those who, still ignorant of divine contemplation, consider only the work of brotherly love that they recognize to be pleasing to God. Therefore they judge it beneficial that all who wish to be devoted to Christ should be devoted to this work.

“Martha, Martha.” The repetition of the name is a sign of love, or perhaps of stirring her attention so that she might listen more carefully. Martha’s part is not blamed, because it too is good; but Mary’s part is praised. Why it is best is then added: “It shall not be taken away from her” [Col. 0816C]. For contemplation begins here and is perfected in the heavenly homeland; because the fire of love, which begins to burn here, will burn more intensely in love when it sees him whom it loves. Contemplation, therefore, shall not be taken away, for it is perfected when the light of this present age is withdrawn. The active life fails with the body, because in the eternal homeland it will not give bread to the hungry—for no one will be hungry—nor perform the other works of mercy, which will not be needed. Therefore the active life is taken away with the present age; rightly, therefore, all the merits of righteous acts and all pursuits of virtues are placed beneath contemplation.

## CHAPTER XIV. On Girding the Loins

“Let your loins be girded and lamps burning in your hands” (Luke 12). The girding of the loins is continence of the flesh; the burning of lamps, the performance of a good work. “And be yourselves like people awaiting their lord when he returns from the wedding.” The lord went to the wedding when, after the resurrection, the new man united the multitude of angels to himself. He returns from them when he is made manifest to us in judgment. We rightly await his return when, in expectation of his coming, we prepare ourselves in all things [Col. 0817A], so that when he comes and knocks, we may open to him immediately. He does not wish to open to the knocking Judge who, fearing to see angry the one whom he has despised, is afraid to depart from the body. He opens who cheerfully and confidently receives the Judge and rejoices in approaching death.

“Blessed are those servants whom the Lord, when he comes, finds watching.” He watches who keeps the eyes of his mind open in the true light, so that he may avoid the darkness of negligence; he also performs what he believes. “Amen I say to you, that he will gird himself,” preparing himself for recompense, “and make them recline,” that they may be refreshed in eternal blessedness; “and, passing” from judgment to kingdom, “will serve them,” because he will satisfy them with contemplation of his divinity. “And if he comes in the second watch, and if he comes in the third watch, and finds them so, blessed are those servants.”

[Col. 0817B] He calls them watches by comparison with those who keep guard at night, because in the night of this world we must always be vigilant against enemies and await the coming light, that is, the coming of the Judge. The first watch, therefore, is the guarding of childhood; the second, of youth; the third, of old age. But if anyone neglected to keep watch in childhood, let him nevertheless not despair, but come to his senses in youth, or at least in old age, because the Judge patiently awaits our delays still longer. He also introduces the comparison of outward losses in order to shake off the mind’s sloth, so that by these the soul may be aroused to guard itself. Hence it is added: “But know this: if the master of the house knew at what hour the thief was coming, he would certainly watch and would not allow his house to be broken into.” While the master of the house does not know, the thief breaks into the house, because while the spirit sleeps instead of guarding itself, unforeseen death breaks into the dwelling of the flesh and drags it to punishments. But he would resist the thief if he watched, because, cautiously anticipating the Judge’s secretly coming advent, he would meet it with repentance. “And you be ready.” After the comparison he adds the exhortation, that we may all be ready without spot or wrinkle, because we do not know at what hour he will come [Col. 0817C].

## CHAPTER XV. On Going on the Way with One’s Adversary

“When you go with your adversary to the ruler on the way, make an effort to be freed from him, lest perhaps he drag you to the judge, and the judge hand you over to the officer, and the officer cast you into prison” (Luke 12). Our adversary on the way is the word of God, opposed to carnal desires in this present life. He is freed from it who humbly submits to its commands. Otherwise the sinner, guilty through contempt for the word, will be held in the Judge’s examination. The Judge will hand him over to the officer—that is, to the devil—because he will permit the devil to draw his soul to punishment; and the officer himself will thrust it into Gehenna. “I tell you, you will not leave there”—that is, never—“until you have paid even the last quadrant” (Matt. 5; Luke 12): that is, until you are punished even for the least sins, and always pay penalties by suffering for sins, never obtaining pardon [Col. 0817D].

## CHAPTER XVI. On the Fig Tree Planted in the Vineyard

“A certain man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard; and he came seeking fruit on it and did not find any” (Luke 13). This vineyard was the Israelite people, in which the Synagogue was planted like a fig tree [Col. 0818A]. The cultivator of the vineyard is Moses and the prophets. The three years are three periods: the time of natural law, the time of written law, and the time of grace. Digging is preaching; applying manure, remembrance of sins. Cutting down the fig tree is the casting down of the Synagogue.

In the moral sense, this tree is every unfruitful soul, surrounded by the leaves of virtues through the appearance of good works, but deprived of the fruit of true righteousness. The three years signify knowledge of the Holy Trinity; digging around the tree signifies removal of earthly desire by the digging tool of preaching. The manure expresses sins of the flesh, which are placed at the root of the tree when the conscience is touched by the memory of known wickedness; when it repents of this, it returns, as though by touching manure, to fruitfulness in work [Col. 0818B]. The cutting down of the unfruitful tree is the judgment of condemnation. The cultivator of this tree is the preacher, who ought always to intercede for such a soul, that God may grant it time for repentance and for producing the fruit of righteousness—as the prophets and apostles, since they understood that some from the Synagogue were to be saved, frequently prayed for it.

## CHAPTER XVII. On the Woman Who Had a Spirit of Infirmity for Eighteen Years

“Behold, a woman who had a spirit of infirmity for eighteen years” (Luke 13). This woman is human nature; the spirit of infirmity, love of earthly desire; the eighteen years of sickness express transgression of the Law, which is completed by ten, and despair of resurrection, which is signified by eight [Col. 0818C]. She was bent over through sin and could not at all look upward through righteousness. For one who loves and thinks earthly things does not look upward to heavenly things. When Jesus saw her through predestination, he called her through preaching and said: “Woman, you are released from your infirmity,” that is, you are absolved from your guilt. And he laid his hand upon her through spiritual grace; she was made erect through justification and glorified God through thanksgiving.

The ruler of the synagogue, indignant, is the Jewish people zealous for the letter of the Law, not understanding that the Sabbath must be observed by abstention from servile work, not by refraining from healing infirmity or ceasing from divine praise. “Hypocrites, does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or [Col. 0818D] ass from the stall and lead it away to water?” The ox, which knew its owner, and the ass, its lord’s manger (Isa. 1), signify the Jewish and Gentile peoples, each of which, released from the bonds of sin, laid aside the thirst and heat of this world by drinking from the Lord’s fountain. Thus in these two animals the Lord declares the calling of the two peoples, despite the opposition of the Jews.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the Healed Dropsical Man

It happened, when Jesus entered on the Sabbath the house of a certain ruler of the Pharisees to eat bread, that they were watching him. And behold, there was a certain dropsical man before him (Luke 14). Ὕδωρ (*hydōr*) means “water”; hence *hydropsis*, dropsy: a watery subcutaneous disease arising from a disorder of the bladder, with swelling distension and foul breath. It is characteristic of the dropsical person that [Col. 0819A] the more he drinks, the more he thirsts. But the vice which this man has in his body the Pharisees carry in their minds. Therefore he is healed bodily before them, that by this example they may learn to be healed spiritually.

The rich, greedy, and covetous person is compared to a dropsical man; for just as the dropsical person, the more he drinks, the more he thirsts, so the wretched greedy and covetous person, the more he accumulates transitory things, the more he pants, inflamed by covetousness to gather greater things. He rightly gives off foul breath while he spreads everywhere the ill repute of his wickedness. Anyone given over to pleasures of the flesh is also likened to a dropsical man, because the more anyone tastes the foul sweetness of desire for the flesh, the more he desires to be defiled by that desire. Therefore the dropsical man is healed from his infirmity as often as either a fleshly person is cured of lust or a greedy person of covetousness [Col. 0819B].

## CHAPTER XIX. The Guest at a Wedding Must Not Recline in the First Place

“When you are invited to a wedding, do not recline in the first place” (Luke 14). The wedding signifies the union of Christ and the Church. He gives place to a more honored person invited afterward who, made more secure by confidence in his long-standing manner of life, is surpassed in the promptness of life by those who have followed Christ after him. And he occupies the last place with shame when, recognizing that others are better, he humbles whatever lofty thought he had entertained about his own work. Therefore recline in the last place: that is, “the greater you are, humble yourself in all things” (Ecclus. 3). So that he who invited you may say to you: “Friend, go up higher” [Col. 0819C], because God gives grace to the humble (Jas. 4), which he takes away from the proud. Then you will have glory before those reclining with you—that is, those resting in the same faith or in the same blessedness.

## CHAPTER XX. On the Man Who Made a Great Supper and Invited Many

“A certain man made a great supper and invited many” (Luke 14). This man is God; the supper, heavenly blessedness; the servants, holy preachers; the hour of supper, the time of grace; the invitation, preaching; those invited to supper who refuse to come, the reprobate clinging to earthly things. He who bought an estate signifies the covetous; he who bought five yoke of oxen, the five bodily senses intent upon external things; he who took a wife, those given over to pleasures of the flesh. But the yokes of oxen are said to be five because the bodily senses, being present in both sexes, are doubled [Col. 0819D].

“Go out quickly into the streets and lanes of the city.” The streets are the broad ways of open iniquity; the lanes of the city, the associations of shameful conduct. The poor, weak, blind, and lame who are brought in are those regarded by lovers of the world as vile and judged useless. But, called through preaching and justified through grace, they are known before God to be glorious and exalted. “Lord, what you commanded has been done, and there is still room.” And the lord said to the servant: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel whomever you find to enter.” Those compelled to enter are those who, broken by adversities, are corrected from their wicked ways and brought back to the love of God [Col. 0820A]. We may understand by the first to come to the supper those chosen from the Jews; by the second, those chosen from the Gentiles; and by those who refused to come, those who perish from both peoples.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Lost Sheep and Drachma
Who among you, having a hundred sheep, if he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness and go after the one that was lost until he finds it? etc. (Luke 15). This man is God; the sheep are rational creatures; the ninety-nine sheep are the nine orders of angels; the hundredth sheep is human nature; the seeking of the hundredth sheep is the divine incarnation; the restoration of the sheep is human redemption; the friends and neighbours are the angels; the friends’ and neighbours’ rejoicing at the finding of the sheep [Col. 0820B] is the angels’ exultation over human salvation. Or what woman having ten drachmas, etc.? The woman is divine Wisdom; the ten drachmas are the nine orders of angels together with human nature. For the woman possessed ten drachmas when God created human beings and angels in his image. But she lost one when humankind departed from the likeness of the Creator. Yet Wisdom kindled a lamp to seek it when it appeared in the flesh, for the lamp is light in an earthen vessel: that is, the Word in the flesh. When it shone among human beings, it overturned the house, because it troubled human consciences through reflection on their guilt. Thus the drachma is found when the likeness of the Creator is restored in a human being.

## Chapter XXII. On the Prodigal Son

[Col. 0820C] A certain man had two sons; and the younger of them said to his father: “Father, give me the portion of the estate that falls to me” (Luke 15). This man, God the Father, had two sons because he is the Creator and author of the two stocks of the human race, namely Jews and Gentiles. The elder son remained in the worship of the one God; the younger has until now forsaken God in order to worship idols. The estate is everything by which we live, understand, think, and speak; God gave these things equally to all. Hence it is written: “He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world” (John 1). Therefore the younger asks that his share of this estate be given to him when a human being, delighting in his own rational faculty and seeking to govern himself by free choice, seeks to depart from the dominion [Col. 0820D] of his Creator.

Thus this man is God; the two sons are the two peoples; the elder son is the Jewish people; the younger, the Gentile people; the estate, natural goods; the younger son’s departure, the error of the Gentile people; the distant country, idolatry; the prostitutes, pleasures of the flesh; the dissipation of the estate, corruption of nature; one of the citizens, one of the demons; the son’s famine, lack of knowledge of the true God; the husks of the swine, the filthy fictions of poets and the teachings of philosophers polluted by diverse errors, which are food for unclean spirits; the son’s return, the conversion of the Gentile people; the father’s coming to meet him, the effect of divine mercy; the ring, faith; the first robe, innocence; the shoes, preaching; the fatted calf, Christ; the slaughter of the calf, Christ’s passion; the feast, participation in grace; [Col. 0821A] the music and dancing at the son’s return, thanksgiving for the conversion of the Gentile people.

The elder son remains in the field while the Jewish people search in the books of the Old Testament for the perfection of righteousness and knowledge. The father’s invitation to the elder son to enter signifies that, when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, then all Israel will be saved (Romans 11). God also receives a returning son daily whenever he accepts any penitent sinner. He does all the things mentioned above when he restores to that person the grace which he had received in baptism and lost through sin.

## Chapter XXIII. On the Rich Man and His Steward

A certain man was rich and had a steward; and this steward was accused before him of having squandered his goods (Luke 16). The rich man is called God the Father; [Col. 0821B] the estate is human nature; the steward is the spirit of the inhabitant—the human intellect, affection, sense, and appetite; the rich man’s goods are the Lord’s gifts, both those which we possess by nature and those which we possess by grace.

The many goods which God placed as furnishings of this estate are: buildings, signifying the manifold honourableness of good conduct; calves, the beginning of goodness; oxen, its completion; bulls, the generation of virtue; cows, the fruitfulness of good will; heifers, the incorruption of spiritual integrity; sheep, the gentleness of innocence; lambs, the brightness of purity; goats, the loftiness of contemplation; bees, the taste of inward sweetness. Yet even swine, although [Col. 0821C] God forbade their flesh for food, are sometimes found there through the stealthy intrusion of an unclean thought. They too, insofar as they contribute to humility of mind, greatly assist in the increase of justification.

There is also found in this estate—that is, in human nature—barley, signifying knowledge of the Old Testament; wheat, knowledge of the New. There are many fields, through the breadth of the faculties and affections, and various ploughs, through the many exercises of virtues and actions. O how good, how rich is this estate, in which God has placed so many and such great goods! Let the steward beware lest he squander his goods. The squandering of goods is the loss of gifts; the corruption of virtues is the removal of good works.

It should be noted that it says: “as though he had squandered his goods.” For we cannot truly squander the Lord’s goods. Although human nature may be so affected by wickedness as to love no good thing, it nevertheless cannot be so blinded by ignorance as to know no truth. [Col. 0821D] Stewardship is one’s manner of life; the loss of stewardship occurs in a person’s death; the accounting for stewardship is the just examination of one’s past life; the rich man’s speech with the steward is the Lord’s speech with the human spirit.

“What shall I do,” says the steward, “because my master is taking stewardship away from me?” The steward’s distress is the fear of the human spirit. “Sit down quickly and write.” The debtors of the servant are the human intellect, affection, sense, and appetite, perverted through sin. The farther intellect, sense, affection, or appetite departs from the good, the more it owes to God. The debtor’s sitting is the sinner’s humiliation; writing down the debt is consideration [Col. 0822A] of sin; remission of the debt is forgiveness of sin.

Therefore let this steward—that is, the human spirit—fear and provide wisely for itself, so that it may meanwhile lighten these debtors’ burden of the debt of sin through repentance, in order that at the end the Lord may praise it without end for such prudence. For, once stewardship has been lost, it will not be able to dig, and it will be ashamed to beg, because after this life no one is granted either the ability to work or the confidence to entreat God. The debtors released from their debt also receive the steward into the house after his stewardship, when the senses and affections, relieved from sin through repentance and forgiveness and enriched with heavenly rewards, make the human being joyful in the heavenly dwelling.

## Chapter XXIV. On the Rich Feaster and Lazarus the Beggar

[Col. 0822B] A certain man was rich, and he clothed himself in purple and fine linen, and feasted splendidly every day (Luke 16). This rich man signifies the Jewish people, who outwardly possessed a rule of life and employed the delights of the law received for splendour, not for usefulness. Lazarus, full of sores, signifies the Gentile people, who, when converted to God, confess their sins. For the poison that lay hidden within is discharged outwardly, as though the skin had burst, when hidden evils are exposed through confession.

“And he desired to be filled with the crumbs which fell from the rich man’s table, and no one gave to him,” because the proud Jewish people scorned to admit any Gentile to knowledge of the law. Since it possessed the teaching of the law not for charity but for self-exaltation, it swelled, as it were, with received wealth; and because words flowed from it through knowledge, crumbs, as it were, fell from its table. But on the contrary, dogs lick the poor man’s sores, because preachers, when by speaking they rescue people from sins, restore them to health as though by touching sores, just as a dog heals wounds of the flesh by licking them. Hence Lazarus is interpreted “well helped,” because these men assist him in rescue who heal his sores by the rebuke of their tongue.

And it came to pass that the beggar died and was carried by angels into Abraham’s bosom. Abraham’s bosom is the rest of the good poor, whose is the kingdom of heaven (Matthew 5), into which they are received after this life. The rich man also died and was buried in hell. The burial of hell is the depth of punishments which, after this life, devours the proud and the merciless. [Col. 0822D] But lifting up his eyes while he was in torments, he saw Abraham from afar and Lazarus in his bosom. The unbelievers see from afar when, placed in the depths before the day of judgment, they observe the faithful resting above them, though they cannot behold them after their joys. What they desire is far away, because they do not attain it by merits.
