“Father Abraham, have mercy upon me, and send Lazarus that he may dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, because I am tormented in this flame.” The unbelieving people held the words of the law in their mouth, which they scorned to observe in deed. Therefore it burned more fiercely in that place where it showed that it knew what it refused to do. He who has been given over to eternal punishments desires to be touched by the tip of a finger when he wishes that even the least works of the righteous might be shared with him.

“Son, remember that you received [Col. 0823A] good things in your lifetime, and Lazarus likewise evil things.”

Note that this rich man did some good, since he received a transitory good in this life; and Lazarus did some evil, but the fire of poverty purged Lazarus’s evils. “Son, you received good things in your lifetime,” because you regarded all your joy as transitory prosperity. The righteous also possess good things in the world; but because they do not receive them as recompense and burn with holy desires for eternal things, the present things seem scarcely good to them. “Remember, son.” Behold, they call the rich man a son, yet this does not free him from torment, because the preceding fathers of this people see that many have strayed from their faith, yet deliver from torments by no compassion those whom they nevertheless acknowledge as sons according to the flesh.

“For I have five brothers.” The Jewish people, now for the most part condemned, knows that its followers whom it left upon the earth are given to the five books of Moses understood carnally, or to the five bodily senses. Thus it expresses by the number five the brothers whom it left behind, because it knows that they do not rise to spiritual understanding. “If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone should rise from the dead.” The Lord rose from the dead; but because the Jewish people refused to believe Moses, it scorned to believe him who rose. And because it refused to understand Moses’ words spiritually, it did not come to him whom Moses foretold. Hence Truth says: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would also believe me” (John 5).

## Chapter XXV. On the Ten Lepers Cleansed

It came to pass, as Jesus went to Jerusalem, that he passed [Col. 0823C] through the midst of Galilee and Samaria. And as he entered a certain village, ten leprous men met him (Luke 17). The ten lepers signify those who live contrary to the precepts of the Decalogue and defile themselves through evil actions in diverse and damnable sins. Such people come to Jesus through faith, since he entered the village of this world through the incarnation; they stand at a distance through humility and cry out through repentance of heart: “Jesus, master, have mercy on us.” As they go to show themselves to the priests through oral confession, they are healed from the leprosy of past wickedness, as it is written: “I said: I will confess my injustice against myself to the Lord; and you forgave the impiety of my sin” (Psalm [Col. 0823D] 31).

The nine who, having received healing, neglected to return to give thanks signify those who, after receiving remission of their crimes, scorn to render thanks for grace by fulfilling the Decalogue. The one who returned and gave thanks signifies the unity of the universal Church, which never ceases to give thanks for the benefit of grace.

## Chapter XXVI. On the Two in the Field, of Whom One Will Be Taken and the Other Left

“There will be two in the field: one will be taken and the other left; two women grinding at the mill: one will be taken and the other left; two in bed: one will be taken and the other left” (Luke 17). By those who are in the field, we may understand lay people living freely in the world. For just as the person who is in the open field has the power to turn wherever he wishes, so lay people, using their possessions freely, have power to do what they wish: they eat when they wish, drink when they wish, and so with the rest. Therefore, because of this great freedom granted them, they may appropriately be said to be in the field.

By those women who will be grinding at the mill, we may understand those who have charge of ecclesiastical affairs. They are rightly denoted by the feminine gender because, through their weakness and frailty, they cannot ascend to the height of the contemplative life and are permitted only to handle outward business. As they take care of all committed to them, they draw the mill around, as it were, through the circuit of their labour.

By those who are in bed, we may understand those who, resting from outward actions, ought to devote themselves solely to heavenly works and to apply themselves to divine contemplation. For the bed signifies rest. The first are in the field on account of freedom; the second in the mill on account of labour; the third in bed on account of rest. But of all these, one will be taken and the other left. The grain will be taken, the chaff left; the wheat taken, the darnel left; the lamb taken, the goat left; the fish taken, the serpent left; the good person, through grace, taken in the present, the evil person left through sin; the good person taken in the future for glory, the evil left for punishment; the good taken for blessedness, the evil left for condemnation.

Meanwhile, while this present life continues, good people are always joined with evil people in every manner of life: there are two together in the field, at the mill, and in the bed, good and evil. Therefore let each person now consider what sort he is, and make himself such as ought to be taken, not left.

## Chapter XXVII. On the Pharisee and the Tax Collector Praying

Two men went up into the temple to pray, one a Pharisee and the other a tax collector. The Pharisee, standing, prayed thus within himself: “God, I thank you that I am not like other people” (Luke 18). There are four forms of pride: when someone thinks that the good he possesses comes from himself; or, if he believes it given by God, thinks it given to him for his merits; or when he boasts of possessing what he does not possess; or when, despising others, he seeks to appear uniquely to possess what he does possess. The Pharisee suffered from this plague. Therefore he went down not justified, [Col. 0824D] because, attributing the merits of good works uniquely to himself, he preferred himself to the tax collector, saying: “God, I thank you.”

Behold, the Pharisee has an eye open for displaying abstinence, for giving mercy, and for returning thanks to God; he has none for guarding humility. And what does it profit if an entire city is guarded but one opening is left through which enemies may enter? The Pharisee signifies the Jewish people, who exalt their own merits from the laws of justification and depart through pride. The humbled tax collector signifies the Gentile, who, standing far from God, confesses his sins and draws near to God by lamenting, and is exalted.

## Chapter XXVIII. On the Blind Man beside the Road Given Sight

It came to pass, as Jesus approached Jericho, [Col. 0825A] that a certain blind man sat beside the road begging. When he heard the crowd passing by, he asked what this was. They told him that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by (Luke 18). This blind man signifies the human race, which, shut out from heavenly brightness, suffers the darkness of its condemnation; but it is healed as the Lord draws near to Jericho. Jericho is interpreted “moon,” by which the decline of our mortality is understood. Therefore, when the Word of God assumed the weakness of our flesh, humankind returns to knowledge of divine things.

The blind man sits beside the way when he begins to believe in him who says: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 12). He begs when he asks. Hence it follows: “And he cried out.” Jesus, passing by, hears the blind man; standing still, he gives him sight. For through his humanity he has compassion on the cries of our blindness, but through the power of his divinity he pours into us the light of grace. “And those who went before rebuked him, that he should be silent.” Those who go before Jesus signify the tumult of carnal vices, which scatter a person’s thoughts and disturb the utterances of prayer, lest Jesus may come to illuminate the human heart.

But now the believer, sensing himself to be burdened by the phantasm of former vices and the voice of his prayer to be impeded so that he cannot pray for himself, cries out more ardently. And Jesus said to him: “Receive your sight; your faith has made you whole.” And immediately he saw and followed him, glorifying God. The one who understands and performs the good follows Jesus passing by. Such a person not only advances in God but also kindles others to praise God. Hence it follows: “All the people, [Col. 0825C] when they saw it, gave praise to God.”

## Chapter XXIX. On Zacchaeus

Behold, a man named Zacchaeus; and he was chief of the tax collectors, and he was rich. And he sought to see who Jesus was, but could not because of the crowd, for he was small in stature (Luke 19). Zacchaeus, whose name is interpreted “righteous,” signifies believers from among the Gentiles, who were lowly and insignificant through preoccupation with temporal affairs but were sanctified by God. They desire to see the Saviour entering Jericho when they wish to participate in the faith which he brought to the world. But the crowd—that is, the habit of vices, which rebuked the blind man crying out—also hinders the one receiving Jesus.

Yet, just as the blind man overcame the crowd by crying out more loudly, so the small man, abandoning earthly things and climbing the tree of the cross, rises above the obstructing crowd, crying with the Apostle: “Far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6). The sycamore is a tree like the mulberry in its leaves, but surpassing it in height; it is interpreted “foolish fig,” that is, the cross, which nourishes believers like a fig-tree but is ridiculed as foolish by unbelievers. The small man climbs it when anyone humble and conscious of his own weakness glories in the power of the cross. Through this praiseworthy foolishness he sees the Lord passing near: for, although he does not yet attend to the light of heavenly wisdom as firmly as it is in itself, he nevertheless attends to it fleetingly and, as it were, in passing.

But the Lord is refreshed while remaining in the house when, dwelling through the Spirit in the Gentile people converted to faith, or in any faithful person, he is satisfied by their good works. [Col. 0826A] Zacchaeus also gives half of his goods to the poor when, because he is converted to God, he keeps for himself only what is necessary for the body and distributes the rest to the poor. Finally, he repays fourfold for his fraud when, for every sin, he fulfils the precepts of the four Gospels or practises the four cardinal virtues.

## Chapter XXX. On the Lord Weeping over Jerusalem

Jesus approached Jerusalem, and seeing the city he wept over it, saying: “If only you also had known” (Luke 19). What the Lord did once according to the history, the Church does daily through its elect. She laments the reprobate all the more, who do not know why they should be lamented, because they rejoice in the worst things [Col. 0826B] (Proverbs 20). If they foresaw their own damnation, they would lament themselves with the tears of the elect. In their perversity they have their day here, in which they have peace from the abundance of temporal things; and punishments are now hidden from their eyes because they refuse to foresee the things to come which disturb temporal happiness.

But a day will come when hostile demons will surround with a rampart the souls departing from their bodies, dragging them into fellowship in their own damnation. They will surround and press them in on every side when they unfold before their eyes the iniquities not only of their deeds, but also of their speech and thought. They will be thrown to the ground when the flesh is reduced to dust. Their children also will fall, when on that day all their thoughts perish (Psalm 145). [Col. 0826C] These thoughts too are denoted by stones, when it adds: “There shall not be left in you one stone upon another.” For when a perverse soul adds a more perverse thought to a perverse thought, it builds stone upon stone, as it were. But when the soul is carried away for vengeance, such a construction of thoughts is destroyed.

This occurs because it did not know the time of its visitation. God sometimes visits a perverse soul through a command, sometimes through a scourge, sometimes through a miracle. But because, in pride, it scorns these things and is not ashamed of its evils, at the end it is handed over to enemies, with whom it is joined in fellowship of damnation at the eternal judgment.

## Chapter XXXI. On the Vineyard and the Husbandmen

A certain man planted a vineyard and leased it [Col. 0826D] to husbandmen; and he went away for a long time. At the appointed time he sent a servant to the cultivators, that they might give him some of the vineyard’s fruit (Luke 20). “The vineyard of the Lord of hosts is the house of Israel”; the labourers hired to cultivate the vineyard at the first, third, sixth, and ninth hours are the tenants. He who is present everywhere went away when he left free choice to the vine-dressers.

The first servant sent is understood to be Moses the lawgiver, who for forty years sought from the cultivators the fruit of the law which he had given. But they sent him away beaten and empty-handed, because “they provoked Moses in the camp, and Aaron, the holy one of the Lord,” and Moses was distressed on their account because they embittered his spirit (Psalm 105). Of them he himself says: “Their grape is a grape of gall, and their clusters are most bitter. Their wine is the gall of dragons” (Deuteronomy [Col. 0827A] 23 [citation as printed]).

The second servant is the prophet David, who after Moses invited the vineyard’s tenants to the practice of good works by the melody of psalmody and the sweetness of the harp. But they also sent him away dishonoured and empty-handed, saying: “What portion have we in David? Or what inheritance in the son of Jesse?” (3 Kings 12). Yet, lest this vineyard be wholly uprooted, he prays for it thus: “Lord God of hosts, turn again; look down from heaven and see, and visit this vineyard” (Psalm 79).

The third servant was the choir of prophets, who corrected the people and foretold the evils threatening the vineyard’s tenants. But they persecuted and killed them also. Jeremiah laments the barrenness of this vineyard, saying: “I planted you as a choice vineyard; how have you turned into a corrupt foreign vine?” “What shall I do? I will send my beloved son; perhaps, when they see him, they will respect him.” When the tenants saw him, they thought within themselves, saying: “This is the heir; let us kill him, that the inheritance may be ours” (Jeremiah 2). Thus the Jews seek to seize for themselves from Christ the inheritance of the Church when they attempt to extinguish the faith which is through him: “not subject to God’s righteousness, but seeking to establish their own” (Romans 10). “And casting him out of the vineyard, they killed him.”

[Col. 0828A] Mark reverses this order, saying: “They killed him and cast him out of the vineyard” (Mark 12). In this their obstinacy is indicated: after the resurrection, they refused to believe the apostles who preached, but, casting him out like a worthless corpse, handed him over to the Gentiles for reception. But the Lord destroyed the evil tenants miserably when he left the unbelieving Jews in their unbelief and scattered them far and wide through Roman rulers.

According to the moral sense, the vineyard is leased when the mystery of baptism is entrusted to the faithful to be exercised in works. Three servants are sent to receive fruit when law, psalmody, and prophecy exhort to right action; but they are insulted, beaten, or cast out when the word heard is scorned or blasphemed. Moreover, the one who kills the heir sent is the person who scorns the Son of God and offers insult to the Spirit by whom he was sanctified. The vineyard is given to another when the grace rejected by the proud enriches the humble. The scribes seek to lay hands upon him, but are restrained by fear when any false person is either ashamed or afraid to attack the Church’s unity because of the multitude of good people.

# Book V. On John  
*(Not by Hugh, indeed not even by the compiler of the excerpts.)*

[Col. 0827]

## Chapter I, or Prologue

[Col. 0827C]

Among all writings, Sacred Scripture excels, and its excellence is evident from its very name. For it is called sacred because it instructs us unto holiness. It is divided into two parts, the Old Testament and the New. But just as Sacred Scripture surpasses other writings, so the New Testament surpasses the Old. For the Old encourages desire for temporal things, whereas the New encourages desire for eternal things. Accordingly, the former is called Old either because it draws one toward the desire for temporal things, saying, “You shall do this and that, and you shall eat the good things of the earth”; through this desire we are made conformed to the old man, namely Adam; or because it was not to endure, but another was to succeed it. Hence it is said: “When new things come, you shall cast away the old” [Col. 0827D] (Leviticus 26). The New Testament, however, is called New because it creates desire for eternal things, which are always pleasant and delightful and therefore new, since they never grow old; or because it is to endure and no other ought to succeed it.

But just as Sacred Scripture surpasses other writings, and the New Testament is worthier than the Old among the sacred writings themselves, so the Gospel is more excellent among the writings of the New Testament. Hence it also bears this name. For by reason of its excellence it possesses as its own the name that is common to the others: it is called Gospel. For Gospel is “good proclamation.” This proclamation is more excellent in evangelical teaching than in the others, both because of the fulfilment and presence of the thing proclaimed, because of the manifestation of faith, and because of the delight of the future life.

Because of fulfilment: since in the Old Testament it was said, “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son” (Isaiah 7), while in the New its fulfilment is announced where it says, “She gave birth to her firstborn son” (Luke 2). Because of the manifestation of faith: since there faith in Christ was preached obscurely, but here openly. There they saw with veiled face, in an enigma; here with unveiled face and manifestly. Hence it is said: “Many kings and prophets desired to see the things which you see, and could not” [Col. 0828D] (Luke 10). Because of the delight of eternal life: because the New Testament promises eternal things, which are pleasant and delightful. For from the faith taught by the Gospel one comes to love, which gives eternal life.

This evangelical teaching is neither restricted by too small a number nor expanded by a superfluous multitude—as would be the case if either only one person had written, or infinitely many. For if only one had written, it would be believed less. Hence it is said in the law: “By the mouth of two or three witnesses every word shall stand” (Deuteronomy 17). But if infinitely many had written, it would be held cheaper because it was so commonly disseminated. Therefore it is contained in a definite and fitting number. There are only four Gospels. This number is prefigured in many other places, but especially in Ezekiel by the four living creatures (Ezekiel 1).

Yet among these four the Gospel of John excels, as was also shown in those prophetic living creatures. For John is compared to the eagle, which flies higher than other birds and fixes its sight upon the sun with eyes unstruck by its rays. He flies with the Lord to heaven by beholding his divinity more highly than the others. Hence Augustine says that he began so loftily that, had he thundered more loftily, not even the whole world could have contained him, when he said: “In the beginning was the Word,” etc. But the others walk with the Lord on earth, since they treated of his humanity.

It is also evident from the order itself that his Gospel is more worthy than the others. For John is last in the order of writing and first in perfection of doctrine. He is last in the order of writing because for a long time he preached faith in Christ without the assistance of Scripture. But when Domitian exiled him to the island of Patmos, he was comforted by frequent revelation and wrote the Apocalypse. Then, after Domitian’s death, with the permission of Nerva and the entire senate, he returned to Ephesus. But during his absence many heresies had sprung up in his church. Therefore, at the bishops of Asia’s request that he write against those heresies, he wrote the Gospel during the said three-day fast. In it he not only plainly cuts off the heresies that had sprung up, but also supplies what the others had omitted.

For he had read the others’ Gospels and approved the truth of their history; [Col. 0829C] but he saw that some things were lacking, especially the Lord’s deeds before John’s imprisonment, which he himself supplies. Many heresies had arisen in that Church. Some said that Christ had not existed before Mary; he destroys this error by saying: “In the beginning was the Word.” Others said that the same God was now Father, now Son, now Holy Spirit; he refutes them by saying: “And the Word was with God,” as one person is with another. Others also said that Christ existed from eternity but was not God; John again confounds them by saying: “And the Word was God.” Still others said that Christ had not a real but a phantom body; he likewise overthrows them by saying: “And the Word was made flesh.”

He is also first in perfection of doctrine because he treats of the eternity of the Word—that is, of divinity—which is most perfect. Hence he himself says: “This is eternal life: to know you, the only God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John 17). Christ’s humanity is milk for infants, but his divinity is food for the mature. Therefore one must ascend through the humanity to the divinity by the steps of doctrine.

John therefore has a common subject matter, Christ; his purpose is to teach faith in Christ. His special subject matter is Christ’s divinity; his special purpose is to cut off the heresies that had sprung up, and to add the matters omitted by the others: Christ’s miracles, and especially those which the Lord performed before John’s imprisonment; and to show [Col. 0830A] the identity of the divine essence and the distinction of the persons.

His method is as follows: first he treats of the eternity of the Word, of the identity of the divine essence, and of the distinction of the persons; then he narrates miracles performed before John’s imprisonment; afterward he also recounts matters common to the others, until he comes to the Lord’s discourse which he delivered to the disciples at the supper, a discourse he describes with the greatest care and subtlety. For in it the Lord taught most plainly about his divinity, namely the identity of his essence with the Father and the distinction of his person—a discourse which none of the others dared to approach.

As for the claim that he then slept upon the Lord’s breast and, carried away in ecstasy, understood the things that the Lord said: I neither deny nor affirm it. But what is signified by the statement that he reclined and slept upon the Lord’s breast is that he drank more deeply than the others from Christ’s divinity. He then treats of Christ’s passion and resurrection, and thus concludes his Gospel.

## Chapter II

“In the beginning was the Word” (John 1). John, intending to write a Gospel concerning the divinity of the Word, began in this way in order wholly to remove and cut off the heresies and errors which existed or might exist concerning Christ’s divine nature. For there are two natures in Christ, namely human and divine. The other three had sufficiently removed the errors that might arise concerning his human nature, because they had treated Christ’s humanity adequately. Therefore John says, in order that the same may be done concerning his divinity: “In the beginning,” etc.

“In the beginning” means: in the Father. For the Father is principle not from a principle; the Son is principle from a principle, though without beginning.

But it is asked whether it may be said of the Holy Spirit that he is “principle from a principle” and that he is “in the beginning.” To this we say that, when it is said, “The Son is principle from a principle,” this means only that he is from the substance of the Father. The same may truly be said of the Holy Spirit, because he too is from the Father’s substance; and in this respect he is likewise in the Father, because he is from him. Yet we do not have the usage of such expressions as, “The Holy Spirit is principle from a principle,” or “is in the beginning,” or “is in the Father”; the wording is lacking, though not the ground for the wording, and therefore we do not accept it.

Or, if expressions such as “principle from a principle,” “to be in the beginning,” or “in the Father” signify a person, so that they designate that the Son is begotten from the Father, then they can in no way apply to the Holy Spirit.

Again, when it is said that the Father begets the Son, it is asked whether one may say in this way, “a person begets a person.” Although there may be a true sense in these expressions, this must nevertheless be observed: the names *Father* and *Son* have been transferred in order to denote that generation; but *person* is a name of distinction, adopted in order to establish personal distinction. Hence that generation is improperly indicated by it.

And it should be noted that later the Son is said to be in the Father essentially, where it says: “The Father is in me, and I am in the Father” (John 14), which means: I and the Father are altogether of one and the same essence.

Likewise, it is asked why the Son is here called the Word. “Word” signifies two things, just as the Greek *logos*, to which it corresponds: namely, a concept of the mind and an utterance of the mouth. For the mind first conceives inwardly what it afterward discloses by an utterance of the mouth. Thus also the Father begets the Son from his own substance; through him, while ordering all things, he made himself known, and by incarnating him in time he presented him visibly to the world, and thus made himself especially known to the world. Therefore, because through him he ordered all things from eternity, and through him, coming in the flesh, made himself known to the world, the Evangelist suitably calls him the Word in this place.

This word, “was,” is substantive; it denotes the essence [Col. 0831B] of the Word without temporal motion—that is, without connoting or determining time. For sometimes it connotes time, as when one says, “A man is”; sometimes it does not, as when the divine essence is being discussed, as here: “In the beginning was the Word,” etc. It is called substantive because it indicates simply and solely the substance of a thing, with no participation in accident. Other verbs, however, are adjective, because through them an accident is shown to inhere in a subject; but this verb simply indicates that the substance is [the subject]. Hence, even if some thing were stripped of every accident and remained only what it is, this verb would apply to it. Therefore it properly belongs to God, whose being is simple and true.

Moreover, “was,” the imperfect past, is used here more suitably than “is” [Col. 0831C] or “was” in the perfect, in order to signify the generation of the Word: so that, since the imperfect past signifies the beginning of a thing but not yet its completion, that generation may be shown to have been from eternity and not yet completed—that is, not terminated. Yet I do not say this as though that generation were imperfect, for there can be nothing imperfect there, but that it is not terminated. For the Father always fully begets the Son, and the Son is always perfectly begotten by the Father. Hence the Father is Father from eternity, and the Son Son from eternity; for neither can exist without the other. Therefore, according to Ambrose, it is better said, “The Father begets the Son,” than “begot,” lest that generation seem to be finished.

Augustine also shows both that it has existed from eternity and that it is always perfect, referring the words, “This day I have begotten you” [Col. 0831D] (Ps. II), to the eternal generation of the Son. For he says that the present-time adverb and the past-tense verb are quite appropriately placed there: by “today” the eternity of that generation is signified, while its perfection and completion are shown by the past verb. Therefore, from the statement that the Word was in the beginning, it is shown that he existed from eternity; that he is himself the beginning of all things; and also that he is another person than the Father—though these points appear more clearly in what follows. The Father is the principle of the Word, and he is also the principle of all things. Such a manner of speaking is found among authors; therefore it will be said below whether the Father can be called the principle [Col. 0832A] of the Son in the same way in which he is called the principle of other things.

“With God”: as one person with another. For the Son is not the same person as the Father, nor is the Father the same person as the Son. This is against those who said that he is Father when he wills, Son when he wills, and Holy Spirit when he wills. Here “God” is a personal name. But when the other personal names precede or follow this name, “God,” it is customarily understood of the Father’s person. Yet when it is placed as the subject, “And God was the Word,” it is the same as if one said, “The Word was God”;” and the name “God” is placed in the predicate to designate the divine nature, which is common to the whole Trinity. This may properly be done in this way, although in the preceding clause it is personal.

[Col. 0832B] This also opposes those heretics who said that the Son existed from eternity and was coeternal with God, but was nevertheless not God. And by the statement that he was in the beginning with God, those heretics are refuted who said that Christ did not exist before Mary, as also in the preceding words; likewise those who thought that the Son surpassed creatures only in dignity, not also in existence. But the Son precedes creation both in dignity and in existence.

“All things were made through him,” etc. Having shown the eternity of the Word, he says that all things were made through him. There are three kinds of works, all of which are done through him. Some are things which God created from nothing, such as the four elements—not from pre-existing matter and form, as the Platonists imagine. With respect to these he is properly called Creator, for those things are properly called created which are made from nothing.

[Col. 0832C] There are other things which he himself directly composed from matter and form: for example, human beings in the beginning, and the other animals formed from the earth. Hence it was said in Genesis: “Let the waters bring forth fish and flying creatures, and the earth trees and things of this kind” (Gen. I). For at that time there was no nature from which such things could be formed; rather, God then implanted nature so that like things might be born from like things. With respect to these works God is properly called Former. Hence, “He formed Adam from the mud of the earth.”

The third kind consists of works of nature: as a human being from a human being, a dog from a dog, a tree from a tree. Yet God makes these too, through the mediation of nature. There are also miraculous works, of which something will be said elsewhere. There are likewise works of the craftsman who imitates nature. [Col. 0832D] All these are done through the Son of God. For God bestowed the capacity for doing such things. Hence he himself is the author of all things.

But it is asked concerning an evil will and an evil action whether they are done through him. If this is affirmed, then evil and sin too seem capable of being said to be done through him, since both an evil will and an evil action are sin. Such expressions—that God is the author of an evil will or evil action—must not be accepted, because the Church condemns such language. For according to ecclesiastical usage, they imply that people derive wickedness from God, which is false. Nevertheless truth requires one to say that God is the author and cause of every essence of will and action.

[Col. 0833A] For in an act of homicide, what is there of which God is not the cause? That I raise my hand to strike comes from nothing other than the capacity which God gave me; nor does the act of striking itself come from elsewhere. But if this act—my raising my hand to strike a poor person—is considered insofar as it is an act, nothing is found in it for which it is not from God any more than in my raising my hand to support a poor person. Yet sin is not anything of which God is the author, for sin itself is nothing. Hence some define it in this way: by a negation that removes something and posits nothing. Sin is not doing what one believes ought to be done for God, or not refraining from what one believes ought to be refrained from for God’s sake.

[Col. 0833B] Others say that it is the privation of a good, or the privation of a due end, or the perversity of the will. Privation occurs when an action or will is directed to something other than that to which it ought to be directed by its proper end. For it ought to be directed to the honor of God; when this does not occur, it is perverted and becomes sin.

But since a will informed by an evil end is evil, yet in itself—that is, insofar as it is something—it seems good, it follows that the same will is good and evil in different respects, and therefore that contraries are in the same thing. Augustine says that here the rule of the dialecticians fails, since every evil is a corrupted good. Yet it may be said that good and evil are not contraries in every sense. For when this will is said to be good because it has being from God, “good” here means what is beneficial or what bears likeness to its Creator.

[Col. 0833C] Hence every individual thing created by God is called good, and all things together are said to have been “very good” (Gen. I). For if in each created thing there was something of divine beauty, much more did the Creator’s beauty appear in all things most fittingly ordered together. Thus, when the will is called good in this sense and evil in the sense that it is directed to an evil end, good and evil are not contraries. Therefore we do not accept the expression that the same will is good and evil, because from the form of the expression good and evil would be understood in contrary senses—namely, that the same will was directed both to good and to evil—which cannot be.

It is therefore clear that God is the author of all things, as their highest cause and origin, from whom all things proceed, whether they are made through him without any intermediary, or through some intermediary, whether nature or a capacity bestowed by him. Hence some refer the Evangelist’s statement, “All things were made through him,” to works which he himself performs directly or through the mediation of nature. [Col. 0833D] But they refer what follows, “Without him nothing was made,” to things done by us. Ambrose also, writing to Bishop Gratian, and John Chrysostom make this division: “Without him was made nothing that was made,” because of certain heretics who, taking occasion from these words, said that the Holy Spirit was made, since after mentioning the Father and the Son the Evangelist immediately added: [Col. 0834A] “All other things were made.” The usage of the Church, however, has a different division.

The Apostle also says of an idol that it is nothing (1 Cor. VIII). An image is called, according to its origin, a representation of an existing thing or of something whose likeness is found among things. But an idol is a representation of a non-existent thing, such as goat-stags, chimeras, and the like. Hence, because it represents what is nothing, it too is called nothing, the effect being transferred from its cause. Or an idol means that fiction of the mind by which we imagine that wood is God, or that God presides over it. Since this is nothing but falsehood, the idol is nothing. Accordingly it is said: “Destroy the idol of your heart.” Or “the idol is nothing” there means that it has no efficacy, so that foods are made holy or defiled by it.

“What was made, in him was life.” Lest anyone consider God according to created things—so that, as mutability exists in them, so it might also exist in the Creator—he shows that God created all mutable things immutably. For it is said to him: “[lacuna] and, remaining unmoved, you give motion to all things.” For just as, when a craftsman conceives something in his mind, the likeness remains and is not changed when the thing is moved, so God, Creator of all things, comprehended from eternity in his wisdom all things that he would make, but immutably.

[Col. 0834B] Therefore there is not a complete likeness between the mind of the craftsman and the divine mind, because in the craftsman’s conception there is motion, since there is before and after, and therefore variation. But in the divine comprehension there is no motion, no variation, since God himself is that comprehension. [Col. 0834C] Hence it is said that he “orders all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII), that is, without motion or labor. On account of this sweetness, what was made is said there to be life.

For the Father has life in himself, and gave the Son to have life in himself. Hence the life which is in him differs from the life of a human being, which is the soul, and from the life of the soul, although it is itself the soul’s life: for it has the movement of living in itself and does not derive it from another creature. Yet the soul itself is inferior to the life which is God in three respects: it is mutable, it has a beginning, and it can have an end. But the life of God is unchangeable and has neither beginning nor end. Therefore this alone is true life.

[Col. 0834D] Hence the Evangelist will say: “What was made, in him was life”; that is, God, from whom are all things, immutably brought to completion in time what he had eternally foreseen. For God, through wisdom—which he himself is—disposed all things from eternity, and brought to completion in time the things so disposed. Hence all things have both life and being from God’s wisdom. Thus they are rightly said there to be life, because they derive life from it.

Or there was life there because, according to the wisdom of God, which is the life of all things, everything that was made was made. For this was God’s exemplar, according to the likeness of which the entire world was made; and this is that archetypal world, in likeness to which this sensible world was made. Nor should one say that there are certain ideas in the divine mind situated below the Creator and above creatures. For there is nothing in God which is not God. Nor can there be a variety of properties [Col. 0835A] there, where there is nothing but being. For for God, being and living are the same. Hence his essence is simple, lacking parts and properties.

It is asked whether these expressions should be admitted: “A stone was life in God”; “a human being was life in God.” Certain authorities seem to intend this. But such figures of speech ought not to be extended, although in a true sense one could say, “A stone was life in God,” that is, God foresaw from eternity that the stone would exist.

“And the light shines in the darkness,” etc. This light is the wisdom of God, which shines inwardly through knowledge and outwardly through the representation of creatures. Hence whether one enters or goes out, one finds pasture. This light shines in darkness, that is, in sinners, who are dark, as Paul says: “For the invisible things of him, from the creation of the world, are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made” (Rom. I). But the darkness did not comprehend it.

[Col. 0835B] How is it said that they did not comprehend it, when the Apostle says what we have just cited? And again: “What is known of God is manifest in them” (ibid.). For philosophers comprehended the Trinity of persons and the unity of the divine essence. Yet it is nevertheless fittingly said that they did not comprehend that light, because they did not enclose it inwardly by love. They therefore comprehended it by knowledge, but did not comprehend it by love. For comprehension of that light is twofold: by knowledge or by love. But they did not love; rather, “although they knew God, they neither gave thanks nor glorified God, but became vain in their thoughts” (ibid.).

Or it may be said thus: “The light shines in darkness,” that is, it appears in the wicked, as in Nero and others, by showing how great a punishment is prepared for their followers. Hence the Apostle says: “The wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness,” etc. (ibid.). [Col. 0835C] Yet others do not comprehend it so as to flee that wrath by their example and guard themselves.

“There was a man sent from God,” etc. Having corrected the errors entertained concerning Christ’s divinity, the Evangelist also wishes wholly to cut off every heresy that could be entertained concerning his humanity. For some said that human nature had been so ruined in Adam that it could not be repaired. Therefore, to remove this and other such heresies, the Evangelist descends from the lofty flight of contemplation of the divine nature to the humility of the truth of human nature; and to manifest this he says that John the Baptist was sent. Thus this is connected with the preceding passage: “The darkness did not comprehend the light; but, in order that it might be comprehended, there was a man sent from God,” etc.

Some come; some are sent. Those who come either come of themselves, seeking what is their own rather than what is God’s; or they are sent by the devil, when they come at the devil’s prompting, whether to disturb the peace of God’s Church, to introduce error, or for something similar. Of those who are sent, some are sent by human beings, others by God.

[Col. 0835D] By God, as the apostle Paul, chosen by God and not by the other apostles. By human beings, as those sent by the apostles to preach. But being sent by a human being does not exclude being sent by God; indeed, they are chosen by God through human beings, just as others are converted by God through preachers. But this John was sent by God, not through a human being, but through divine inspiration.

“There was John.” Things done by divine disposition are more properly said to be than to come to be. For this name was imposed not according to human will, but according to God’s disposition. “This man came,” etc. Since it was stated first, “There was a man sent,” in which the election of divine grace is indicated, he adds, “He came,” in which free choice is denoted. Moved and stirred by prevenient grace, free choice must consent to grace and cooperate with it; otherwise merit does not exist. Therefore, so that the Evangelist might indicate these two matters—their conjunction and the priority of grace—he first said “sent” and then added “came.”

[Col. 0836A] The Son of God is called light because he kindles us in the love of God; as he is called Word because of the knowledge of the Father which he gives us, and life because of creation. “The true light.” For there is an illuminated light and an illuminating light. Illuminated light is such as the apostles, of whom it is said: “You are the light of the world” (Matt. V). Illuminating light is that which shines of itself, and which is true light—that is, Christ.

But since Christ is called illuminating light, it is asked according to which nature he is called light. For just as in a human being there are two natures, body and soul, according to either of which something is said of the human being—for example, that he is white according to body and rational according to soul—so also in Christ there are two natures according to which speech is customarily made concerning him.

[Col. 0836B] If it is said that he is illuminating light insofar as he is God, this is true; but then, in the respect in which the man assumed is here preferred to other human beings, he is not preferred insofar as he is human. But if he is said to be illuminating light insofar as he is human, then insofar as he is human he is God, and thus insofar as he is human he is equal to the Father. This is false, because insofar as he is human he is less than the Father.

It must instead be said that he is illuminating light insofar as he is human because, insofar as he is human, he has the fullness of gifts, and we all receive from that fullness; thus we are illuminated by him. For insofar as he is human he grants us from his fullness, yet insofar as he is human he is not God; for according to that nature he is not God but human.

“He enlightens every human being”: not because all are enlightened, but because whoever is enlightened is enlightened through him. Or “human being” calls the higher nature in a human being, namely reason; or “every human being” means someone from every kind. “He came into the world,” that is, he appeared in the flesh.

[Col. 0836C] “And the world did not know him.” It did not possess knowledge of love, although it possessed discriminating knowledge, as stated above. “He came into his own,” that is, into our common nature: for he took flesh that was capable of suffering and mortal, but free from sin. Or, “into his own,” namely the kingdom of the children of Israel, to whom he said that he had been sent; but his own did not receive him, except for a few. “But as many as received him, he gave them power to become children of God.”

To receive him by faith and to have this power—that is, to be able to become children of God—seem to be the same thing. [Col. 0836D] Hence it is asked why he first said “received” and then added, “He gave them power to become children of God,” as though they could receive faith of themselves by free choice, and did not have that power except by grace. To this we say that receiving, or having, and having power to become children of God are the same. Yet “they received” is suitably placed first so that free choice may be shown to have force for meriting. But lest it be thought that it can be bent toward good without prevenient grace, “he gave them power to become children of God” is suitably added. For faith and love are given to us by grace, through which we become children of God both by imitation and by participation in blessedness.

“To believe in his name” is to possess the knowledge of faith unto his praise and honor. “Who were born not of bloods,” etc. He determines how people can become children of God: not by carnal generation, through which all are corrupted, but by spiritual regeneration, which occurs through faith. For through faith in Christ we are renewed and depart from oldness.

[Col. 0837A] “And we saw his glory,” etc.: glory, that is, himself appearing gloriously in flesh at the Transfiguration, or his glorious resurrection, or the full knowledge which was in him. Hence he also possessed perfect blessedness: “For this is eternal life, to know you, Father, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII). “Glory as of,” etc. Here “as” is not comparative but confirmatory. For he is truly the only-begotten Son of God. “Full of grace and truth,” that is, truly possessing fullness of grace. For in him was the fullness of all gifts.

“John bears witness concerning him.” The Evangelist inserts testimonies by which both natures of Christ may be proved, though they pertain especially to proving Christ’s divinity. He proceeds quite artfully, now inserting testimonies and now returning to the narrative. “He cried out,” that is, he preached openly. For in the Law there was some knowledge, but obscure and veiled under figures. John, however, declared openly: “This is the Christ promised in the Law.” “And from his fullness we have all received.”

[Col. 0837B] It is asked whose fullness this is; but there is no doubt that it is Christ’s. Yet according to which nature? According to his divine nature, he had it naturally from eternity; but in time he received it according to his human nature. Therefore this fullness belonged to Christ according to his human nature. Hence it is asked how it existed in him according to his humanity: whether according to his human nature he had as great a fullness as according to his divine nature.

Some wish to infer from this authority and certain others that Christ’s soul had as much knowledge as God. For it is said that whatever the Son of God had by nature, the son of the Virgin had by grace. Hence they say that that soul has as much knowledge by grace as the Son of God has by nature; nevertheless it is not equal to him in knowledge or [Col. 0837C] in anything else, since soul has it in one way and God in another. For God has it by nature, but the soul by grace. Equality, however, is customarily considered according to quantity and not according to quality; thus, if this person has as much wealth by acquisition as that one has by inheritance, he may be called equally rich.

“Grace for grace”: because from the grace which he gave in order to enable us to merit, he will finally give eternal life; and thus everything is from grace, both our meriting and our attaining the fruit of merit. Yet I do not exclude free choice, which does not reject grace when offered but consents to it. It can indeed consent of itself, but does not consent without the assistance of grace. Or, in return for the grace of election, he gives the grace of love and action.

“The Law was given through Moses; truth came through Jesus Christ.” For what Moses taught, he was altogether unable to fulfill; hence he gave what he himself could not do. But Jesus Christ fulfilled in deed what he taught, whence it is said: “What Jesus began both to do and to teach” (Acts I).

[Col. 0837D] In Moses, indeed, figures came beforehand; but in Christ came the fulfillment of the figures, and therefore truth came through him. “No one has ever seen God.” For no one in the flesh has been able to see God as he is. Hence he appeared to patriarchs and prophets through creatures or certain signs. To Moses also, when he asked that God show himself to him, he replied: “Stand in the cleft of the rock, and you shall see my back parts” (Exod. XXXIII). In the cleft of the rock—that is, in the cross of Christ—you shall see the back parts, that is, the assumed flesh, which is Christ’s lower nature.

Paul likewise, when caught up to the third heaven and seeing those secret things which no human being sees, was above human nature. Hence he himself says: “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (2 Cor. XI). But that vision in which God will be seen face to face will be in the future. Thus, when he is now said to appear in some creature, this means nothing other than that through some creature subject to him he manifests his will.

[Col. 0838A] “He has declared him.” The prophets narrated, but none of them declared him; he himself, coming in the flesh, declared him. For he said many things about himself which others had not said, and he spoke more plainly than others. This he was well able to do, since he is in the bosom—that is, in the secret—of the Father: that is, begotten from the Father’s essence. Hence he was able fully to declare that generation, since through that generation he is equal to the Father.

“And the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us.” For that union was a permanent state in him. Once he assumed it, he never laid it aside. And he was found in habit as a human being. Christ never laid aside the human being he assumed. For from the moment he assumed him, he always had him united to himself in one person; for even in death he had the human being united to himself, that is, soul and flesh. Then too he was human in the same sense, because he had human nature united to himself. Therefore one should not ask whether at that time the human being was dead or alive.

“I am the voice of one crying,” etc. John acknowledges himself to be the heralding voice of Christ, which none of his predecessors could say. For the voice is the interpreter of the mind and is fruitless unless the word follows it. Thus John too is a voice—that is, the herald of the mind, namely Christ, who is the wisdom of the Father and the mind—and that voice would be wholly useless unless the Word followed it.

[Col. 0838B] Or John is called a voice, which none of the others could be called, because just as there is nothing between voice and word, so between John and the Word of God there was no intermediary. “And those who had been sent,” etc. There were three sects of Jews: Essenes, Sadducees, and Pharisees. The Essenes retained nothing as private property, but worshipped the rising sun. The Sadducees—that is, “the righteous”—denied the resurrection, asserting that souls perish together with bodies. The Pharisees, skilled in the Law and distinguished from the common people by the superiority of their knowledge, displayed their own righteousness. These often listened to John, because he preached the resurrection of bodies, which they too believed would occur, though carnally.

“He stands [or: let him stand] in your midst,” etc. The middle is that which is equally distant from either extreme. Thus Christ was distant from them, because he was without sin; and for that reason they did not know him. Or “middle” means common and lowly. Therefore, because the Lord appeared in common and lowly nature, they could not know him. Hence Christ was in the midst because he was mediator of God and human beings; this could not be if he were only God or only human. And because he was God and human, they did not know him.

[Col. 0838C] “Whose sandal strap I am not worthy,” etc. He is not worthy because it is not his office to preach but to baptize, or to usurp the bridegroom’s name. The custom of the Law is alluded to. For it was the custom in the Law that if a man having a wife died without leaving offspring, his nearest kinsman should take her and raise up offspring for his brother. If he refused, another should take her, remove his sandal at the gate, and spit in his face; afterward his house was called “the house of the unsandaled one,” to his disgrace.

“The next day,” etc. For this relative term, “next,” can be referred either to the preceding day, on which the Pharisees came to John, or to the subsequent word “man”: “A man came,” that is, one having greenness, whence there can be hope of fruit. For where there is no greenness, there can be no hope of fruit. But in Christ there was greenness, from which we all have borne fruit.

Christ is baptized by a servant, lest superiors disdain to be baptized by inferiors. Yet he did not wish to be baptized by him alone, lest he seem to have received something from John’s baptism. For John’s baptism bestowed nothing upon anyone, but merely introduced an observance and custom.

[Col. 0838D] “He saw the Spirit descending like a dove,” etc. It is asked what this dove was. It is clear that it was then created; but after completing its office it was immediately reduced into the matter from which it had been formed, like the star which appeared more conspicuously at the Lord’s birth. And it was truly a dove, just as that was a real star. But that the Holy Spirit descended means nothing else than that the dove descended, signifying the Holy Spirit. For the dove is a gentle creature and without gall, and through it the benevolence of the Holy Spirit is signified. Nor should one believe that God was in that dove otherwise than in other creatures.

“And I did not know him,” etc. It is asked what John understood that he had not understood before. Augustine says that he had not previously understood that Christ would reserve to himself the power of baptizing and would not confer it upon any of his ministers. He could have given it to one of his ministers if he had wished, but he did not wish to do so, lest there be thought to be as many baptisms as ministers—if one spoke of the baptism of Peter, Paul, and others—and lest its efficacy be attributed to a human being rather than to God.

[Col. 0839A] But it is asked what this power is, which he could have given to servants if he had wished. Is it the ability to immerse? But ministers immerse; therefore that ability is not this power. If it is said that it is the power of forgiving sins, he neither gave this to servants nor could he give it. Rather, it is the power which he could have given had he wished: that by invoking the name of Peter or another servant, the sacrament might be efficacious for the forgiveness of sins, just as it is by invoking the name of the Trinity. But Christ retained this power for himself and did not wish to give it to any of his own, for the reasons stated above.

Or John had previously not known that Christ himself would redeem the world through his own death; or he did not know him to be both human and God. “And remaining,” etc. The dove sat upon him so that it might thereby be shown that the fullness of the gifts of the Holy Spirit always remains in him. The Holy Spirit is in others now remaining and now departing; but in him he was always present.

[Col. 0839B] A dove, if it finds a branch outside the ark that bears fruit, brings it to the ark; but how can it be green outside the ark? For who can possess the fruit of faith unless introduced into the Church through baptism? It may be said that, once a person is already in the waters of baptism, he immediately receives greenness by the power of the sacrament, so that he may be brought into it. For immediately after receiving baptism he is among the members of the Church.

Or many, before they come to faith, faithfully administer Babylon’s affairs; and because they conduct themselves well in what belongs to another, they deserve to be entrusted with care for what is their own. Therefore, on account of this good work and good disposition of mind, more is revealed to them and they become participants in the Church, [Col. 0839C] as is read concerning Cornelius, whose prayers were heard so that Peter might be sent to him and reveal the faith to him (Acts X); yet he did not previously possess the disposition which is charity.

On the next day, after the Pharisees came to John. “Rabbi,” which is interpreted “teacher.” The question is who said this—whether the evangelist or someone else. It is clear that John wrote in Greek. But *rabbi* is Hebrew, which the evangelist, writing in Greek, translated when he said, “which is interpreted διδάσκαλε [teacher].” The Latin was supplied by the one who translated from Greek into Latin. Andrew was one of the two disciples who came to Christ at John’s command; the other was John himself, the evangelist. But disciples customarily put their own name forward when they say anything [Col. 0841A] great about themselves, lest they have an occasion for self-exaltation; conversely, they name themselves when they say humble things about themselves. Nor is Paul to be blamed for saying great things about himself when he says, “Are they Hebrews? So am I,” etc. (2 Cor. 11). Yet at times fools must be endured, lest we too seem impatient; at times they must be repelled, lest we be thought to agree with them.

“But Jesus looked at him.” Concerning this look, some entertain an error. They say that God sees in one person a certain seedbed—namely, an aptitude given at creation—by which this person is more fitted to believe and obey than that one; and that this is why one is chosen more than another. Thus certain signs of future goodness appear in this people which do not appear in that people. But that this is false is clear both from many other considerations [Col. 0841B] and especially from the Lord’s saying: “Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida; for if the things done in you had been preached in Tyre and Sidon, they would long ago have sat in ashes and sackcloth” (Luke 10). Hence it appears that that land would have been more suited to cultivation than the land of the Jews. From this it is also clear that God does not attend, in his calling, to a greater aptitude of hearts. Rather, from the fact that he converts what is less suited to himself, grace appears greater and more glorious than those make it appear who assert that it works from such aptitude. Therefore there is nothing in the heart on account of which God chooses; rather, God works his grace in the secret place of the heart, by which it is moved to repentance and love, and thereby merits eternal salvation.

And this is precisely to look into [Col. 0841C] the secret place of the heart: to work secretly by grace in the heart, so that it may be moved from error to the knowledge of truth and thus become worthy of life.

“Can anything good come out of Nazareth?” Its vigor is the efficacy of the mystery. Nazareth is interpreted “flower” or “shoot.” Now, in a flower there are three things: it comes forth from the tree without injury; it contributes to the tree’s beauty; and it bears the hope of fruit. So too Christ came forth in birth from Aaron’s rod—that is, from the Blessed Virgin—without any injury. And this was to her adornment: for because of him she is called blessed among women, while he himself is “beautiful in form beyond the sons of men.” In him indeed is for us the hope of the fruit of eternal life.

“In whom there is no guile.” Guile exists when one thing is done and another is feigned within: that is, when one thing is thought within [Col. 0841D] and another is displayed outwardly, as was the case with the Pharisees. But this Nathanael was not such a person; rather, if any fault was within, he confessed it outwardly.

“When you were under the fig tree,” etc. Some say that this was literally so: he, being a teacher of the Law, went out to meditate upon the redemption of the human race and sat beneath some fig tree. Others say that this is to be referred only to that fig tree from whose leaves Adam and Eve made themselves loin-coverings after sin. For all of us, they say, were there—that is, in Adam; and therefore we sinned in Adam and were corrupted there. But how could we have been there, or have been corrupted there, when we were not yet anything at all? They say, however, that the entire human race was materially there, and that each person [Col. 0842A] was some part of Adam’s body. But this cannot be so, since not even as many atoms could have been in Adam as there have subsequently been human beings. Indeed, according to this opinion, every part of this body would necessarily have been one part of Adam’s body.

But we say that all this is false: for neither were we all there, nor did we all sin or become corrupted there. What the authority says—namely, that all sinned in Adam—is true in this sense: all contracted from there the cause of sin. And in the same sense the whole of human nature was corrupted there: for there sin was committed, on account of which all posterity was corrupted. The propagation of the human race always descends through corruption in generation. For every human being is generated in corruption [Col. 0842B]. And we contract this through Adam, from whose origin we all descend: he was our origin, and from him we draw our origin.

What is said here—“When you were under the fig tree, I saw you”—is understood thus: “When you were under the shadow of the Law or of death, I saw you by my providential ordering.” For from eternity he had disposed either concerning his salvation or concerning his calling.

“You will see greater things than these,” etc. Because they believed him to be the Messiah, they were given to know more concerning him—namely, that he was God and not merely man, as the Jews still believe concerning the Messiah, that he will be a mere human being. “Amen, amen” is a Hebrew word and means “truly” or “let it be”; nor was it changed by any translator, lest, if changed, it lose its force. It is as it were God’s oath. In this Gospel alone [Col. 0842C] it is found doubled. “You will see heaven opened,” etc. This is that greater thing which the Lord promised they would see. In this knowledge of both natures is shown.

“And on the third day a wedding took place,” etc. (John 2). That is, the third day from the first, or from the calling of those disciples. “What is there between me and you, woman?” This is not the speech of one denying or despising his mother—whom he himself commands to be honored, as heretics say, who maintain that Christ had a phantom body—but of one showing that what she asked could not be done from what he had received from her, namely, his humanity, but only from his divinity.

“My hour has not yet come.” From this again heretics wish to establish that he was subject to the fatal necessity of death, namely, that he would die by necessity [Col. 0842D]. There was indeed an hour of death fixed in the divine ordering, but by no fatal necessity. For he received death when he willed; hence he himself says, “I have power to lay down my life, and to take it up again” (John 10). It is as if he said: “From what I have from you, I cannot perform miracles; but what I have from you will appear when, as I hang upon the cross, I commend you as mother to my disciple.”

“Two or three measures apiece.” Because some held two, some three. This is not an expression of doubt. In Greek, “measure” is called *metron*, whence μετρήτη, *metrete*; or this may be referred to the mystery.

“Master of the banquet.” A *triclinium* is called the place where there are three couches, that is, three rows of reclining diners, as in the monks’ refectory; the chief and highest person among them—that is, the one set over them—is called the master of the banquet (*architriclinus*) [Col. 0843A].

“This Jesus did as the beginning of signs.” How is this said to have been the beginning of signs, when earlier, at twelve years old, he sat in the Temple, asked questions, and answered? And when he went down into Egypt, all the idols are said to have fallen? But this was the beginning of those signs narrated here, or of those written in the Holy Scriptures.

“Take these things away from here, and do not make my Father’s house a house of trade.” Who are those who must be cast out of the Church? Are they only buyers and sellers? Yes, only they, if under them are included all who seek in the Church their own interests, not those of Jesus Christ. But you will say: “Is it not lawful for me to buy the use of that prebend? I am not buying the office, but the use of the benefice [Col. 0843B].” But this cannot be done. For on what basis do you share in the same refectory, counsel, and ecclesiastical service? By election, or by purchase? Thus, in buying what you desire, you buy also what you do not care about—namely, God’s grace—which is not permitted. So likewise it does not seem to be approved that anyone should be received among monks, canons, or any religious persons with money. Either money is the cause, or it appears to be.

“But Jesus did not entrust himself to them.” For one who easily believes easily withdraws; hence: “Would that you were cold or hot,” etc. (Rev. 3). Yet communion of the body and blood of the Lord is not to be entrusted to catechumens.

“Amen, amen, I say to you: unless someone has been born again [Col. 0843C] anew, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3). It is as if he said: “Although you believe through the signs you have seen and have faith, nevertheless faith does not suffice for your salvation without receiving baptism.” Hence the question arises whether someone can be saved without receiving this sacrament, since the Lord says, “Unless someone is born again of water and the Holy Spirit,” etc. It is clear, however, that the shedding of blood takes the place of baptism; likewise true contrition of heart, when there is no time to receive it. Therefore the saying, “Unless someone is born again,” etc., must be understood thus: unless someone is prepared to be reborn, or unless someone has faith in baptism.

Again, the question arises whether everyone who receives it is reborn. But if everyone is, then so too is this heretic and the person who approaches deceitfully. But if he is reborn by the Holy Spirit, then he is inwardly cleansed [Col. 0843D], and thus his sins are blotted out. Again, Christ baptizes there; therefore he too is baptized by Christ and thus, as it seems, cleansed inwardly.

But it is not true that sins are forgiven in baptism to one who approaches deceitfully or harbors brotherly hatred. Yet he is baptized, and Christ baptizes: that is, he receives the sacrament, and Christ effects it, giving it force and efficacy so that sins may be blotted out through it, unless the recipient impedes it. In the same sense it may also be said that the person who has outwardly received the sacrament—by which he could be inwardly cleansed unless he himself impeded it—has been born again of water and the Holy Spirit. Nevertheless, in no way should it be conceded that he has been born again in spirit—that is, inwardly cleansed.

“What is born of flesh is flesh [Col. 0844A], and what is born of spirit is spirit.” That is, just as what is born from flesh bears the likeness of flesh, so what is born from spirit bears the likeness of spirit and retains its resemblance. For just as the Spirit is invisible, so too are his gifts and effects. Hence the person born from the Spirit is spirit. The soul is born from the Spirit when the Holy Spirit illumines it by his invisible grace and, having put off its oldness, cleanses it into newness of life. Thus, united to him, it becomes not only spiritual but even in some manner spirit, when, despising all else, it clings to him alone and enjoys his gifts. Therefore the carnal person does not know such a generation. Hence it is said to such a person: “You hear his voice, but you do not know whence it comes or where it goes.” For the carnal person does not know whence—that is, from what mercy [Col. 0844B] and hidden justice of God—the voice of the Spirit comes, nor where it goes—that is, to what end it leads.

“If I have told you earthly things,” etc. “Earthly” means small things, those said concerning Christ’s humanity, in comparison with those believed concerning his divinity; for example, that God is three in persons and one in essence.

Concerning his humanity, Christ had said above: “Destroy this temple, and in three days I shall build [raise] it.” But the question arises how believing the Trinity of persons and unity of essence is greater than believing that the Word became flesh and the like, when reason supports the former. For philosophers too grasped those things by natural reason; whereas these are entirely contrary to natural reason—namely [Col. 0844C], that God was born and died, and the like. But these are called lesser because they are visible and were visibly displayed to all; those are greater because they can be comprehended only by the intellect of the wise and have been made known to few. Or he indicates the order by which one must advance to the perfection of faith. First one must believe that Christ was born, suffered, rose again, and ascended into heaven; so one arrives at faith in the Trinity of persons and unity of essence.

“And no one has ascended into heaven except he who descended from heaven,” etc. This was said according to that figure of speech in which it is said that only the king came or only the king is received, although he comes or is received with his soldiers. Thus it is true that Christ alone ascended, because he was the first and because no one ascends except through him [Col. 0844D]. For the head ascends with its body. Hence in the ascension of the head the ascension of the body is also understood. Christ ascended according to his human nature, just as he descended according to his divine nature.

“And just as Moses,” etc. (Num. 21). Moses raised up a bronze serpent on a pole in the wilderness; the children of Israel who looked upon it were healed when wounded by fiery serpents, or, if unwounded, remained safe. The bronze serpent raised on the pole is Christ lifted upon the cross. He was bronze, that is, strong, for destroying death, since in him there was no cause of death. Again, the bronze serpent was real, but had the likeness of a serpent, because Christ assumed our nature not as sinful, but as having the likeness of sinful flesh [Col. 0845A]. Those who look upon him—that is, who have faith in his passion—are healed from the fiery bites of serpents, that is, from the wounds inflicted by enemies, namely demons, which are incitements to vices.

“God so loved the world that he gave his only-begotten Son.” Here “world” means human nature, for whose sake all other things were made. Therefore, because of its dignity, he calls it the world, just as elsewhere it is called “every creature,” on account of the same excellence of nature. God so loved this world that he gave his only-begotten Son. That is, from the gracious kindness of his own love, he eternally ordained to incarnate his Son and thus redeem the human race through him.

But when God the Father gave the Son, to whom did he give him? Did he give him to me and you? To Judas and the Jews? To Pilate and the devil? Certainly he gave him to us, whom he redeemed through him [Col. 0845B]. But he exposed him to the devil and to the will of the Jews, because he permitted them to have this power over him, to kill him, so that by his death he might rescue humankind from the devil’s power. Therefore he gave him to us for our redemption when he permitted him to be killed by the devil; or “gave” means that he determined to give him.

“The one who does not believe has already been judged.” How can he say that one who does not believe has already been judged, as though unbelief itself were damnation? It must be understood thus: from not believing here follows not knowing in the future, which is a most grievous punishment. But will there not be other punishments there besides being deprived of the vision of God? For the prophet says: “Their worm shall not die, nor shall their fire be extinguished” (Isa. 66). From this it is understood that material punishments will exist there. Yet this alone is said to be there—namely, not knowing—because every punishment terminates in this, and because it is the consummation of every punishment. Therefore it is rightly said to be the only punishment there [Col. 0845C]. For the most grievous torment will consist in never attaining what they desire, just as one is oppressed by hunger more severely the more one hungers. This applies also to children, but not so severely, Augustine says, that they would prefer not to be rather than to be.

“Therefore a question arose from John’s disciples,” etc. The question concerns John’s baptism: how it differed from Christ’s baptism, what benefit it possessed, and what John said—that is, what rationale he put forward—in introducing a new rite. The difference between Christ’s baptism and John’s is clear: John only immersed; Christ himself, by immersing, cleansed inwardly. Hence Christ’s baptism is called a baptism of remission, while John’s baptism is called a baptism of repentance—either because he admitted none except the penitent, or because immediately after baptism he imposed penance.

But was John not Christ’s minister? Certainly. Therefore Christ baptized through him, as through others, and so, while Christ baptized, he remitted sins. This is indeed true; but the baptism by which sins were remitted was not John’s but Christ’s. Once Christ’s baptism began, John’s baptism ceased [Col. 0846A]. Yet it had this benefit: it accustomed people to baptism, so that when Christ’s baptism came they would not shrink from it.

But what did he say in introducing a new rite? He said that he baptized in the name of the One to come: not that his baptism cleansed from sins, but that it was a sign of the future baptism by which sins would be taken away. Christ was then called “the One to come,” although he had already come, because it later became known that he was the Christ. At that time he was known by few; hence some thought John himself was the Christ. Thus he who had already come by birth was still to come into public recognition.

But once Christ was baptizing and removing sins through baptism, did those who were circumcised sin, or those who were baptized and circumcised at the same time? It must be understood that there was an intermediate period, as it were, between the time of the Law and the time of grace: from the first institution of Christ’s baptism until that general and manifest institution when it was said, “Go, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). During that time, if someone was only circumcised, or if the status of baptism was revealed to him and he was only baptized, either was saved. But if it was not revealed to him and he received both, he did not sin. After the manifest institution of baptism, however, it was unlawful to combine them [Col. 0846B].

“He who comes from above [heaven] is above all.” Christ came from above according to both natures. According to the divine nature this is clear. But how according to [Col. 0846C] the human? He came from above even according to that nature because he assumed flesh that did not descend through concupiscence, but was without sin. Hence he is said to have come from the height of human nature—not because Christ’s flesh had been kept in Adam before sin, and afterwards always remained incorrupt, but because he assumed it incorrupt as human nature was incorrupt in Adam before sin. Or he came from the height of human nature before sin because, as was said, it did not descend into Christ through concupiscence; for it belonged to the integrity of human nature before sin that propagation should take place through concupiscence.

“For God does not give the Spirit by measure.” God gave the Spirit without measure to his Son according to his humanity [Col. 0846D], because he gave him as much as could be bestowed upon a creature. Thus the fullness of the gifts of the Holy Spirit was bestowed upon human nature, so that it was personally united with the Word; nothing more could be bestowed upon it. Therefore the Spirit was bestowed upon him without measure, because he was given all that could be given. The gloss says that, just as the Father begot the whole Son from his whole self, so he gave the whole Spirit to the incarnate Son. Did he also give it to the Word assuming flesh? But if he gave it to him, then the assuming Word received something from him and so did not always possess it. But it is clear that the Word eternally possessed whatever the Father possessed. Therefore he gave it to the incarnate Son, but not to the Word assuming flesh.
