The Father also begot the whole Son from his whole self, because the Son is the same as the Father: Father and Son are altogether of the same essence [Col. 0847A]. For charity, as Augustine says, is the consubstantial bond of Father and Son. Hence they are one. This charity is the Holy Spirit, who is the love of Father and Son; but this exceeds our understanding—namely, how they are one by a bond and how they are one through this.

“Behold, you have been made whole; sin no more” (John 5). From this it is inferred that the Lord forgave him his sins by healing him, although the person being healed did not know him. Hence it seems that someone can be cleansed from sins and be worthy of eternal life without faith in Christ. But “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11). It must be said that this sick man did indeed possess a good disposition, by which he deserved to be freed from the illness that held him because of preceding fault [Col. 0847B]. This disposition, inspired by God’s grace, was improved through God’s action; nevertheless, it would not have sufficed for salvation if he had then departed from life. Thus “Sin no more” means: do not persist any longer in sin.

“My Father works until now, and I work.” Because the Jews said that Christ was a transgressor of the Law, and therefore opposed to God, since he worked on the Sabbath when God rested on the seventh day from all the work that he had completed, the Lord therefore shows false what they supposed—namely, that God had then ceased from work in such a way as to work nothing further. Therefore we must consider the ways in which God works.

There is the work of creation and the work of formation [Col. 0847C], in which God worked during the six days. To create is properly to bring from non-being into being, as God worked in the four elements. There is also the work of formation, by which, after creation, he gave to things created from nothing the form of their arrangement. From these God rested on the seventh day, no longer creating or forming new things. There are also the works of governance, preservation, renewal, propagation, and multiplication. By these God either governs created things by arranging them; preserves them in being so that they do not fail; renews them by imparting powers; propagates like things from like things through the mediation of nature; or multiplies what has been propagated by his goodness.

The work of repairing the human race is especially attributed to the Son, because the Son is God’s wisdom [Col. 0847D]. In the redemption of the human race, God’s wisdom appears more than his power. Thus, although the other works are attributed to the powerful Father, this work is rather attributed to the wise Son. Hence he says, “My Father works until now.” It is as if he said: “Until now the Father has been made known through the elements and creatures of the world; but now he will be made known more fully to the world through me incarnate.” For in the flesh he made both himself and the Father—who is the same as he—to be known to human beings. The Father cannot be known except through the Son.

“The Son cannot do anything from himself.” The Son refers to the Father the things he does, since he has being from him. Hence he says that he can do nothing from himself [Col. 0848A], as though he did not have this from another; or, as man, he can do nothing from himself.

Again: “The Son cannot do anything except what he sees the Father doing.” The Son’s seeing the Father doing is nothing other than the Son’s being from the Father, through whom the Father orders all things. The same is also for him to hear from the Father the things that he speaks. For the Son himself is the Father’s wisdom, which enlightens every person coming into this world (John 1). But from what is added, “These things he likewise does,” he is proved equal to and consubstantial with the Father. For someone can do the things God does, but not in the same manner; the Son alone does them in the same manner. A human being does not possess in himself the power of acting, but from God; the Father, however, can order and govern all things from himself [Col. 0848B], and so too the Son possesses from his own essence the ability to do all things. For by being the Father’s Son, he is God; and by being God, he can do all things through himself. Hence from eternity he orders all things with the Father. Therefore he alone does in the same manner all the things which the Father does. “In the same manner” means without distinction. For there is no difference in the operation of Son and Father, since the Son’s operation is the Father’s operation.

Again, the Father is said to show the Son what he himself does. This is what was said above: the Father orders and works all things through the Son. For he shows them to him because, in begetting him from his own essence, he gives him being, and through him orders all things. This is to show him what he himself does.

“For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son.” The question is what it means for the Father not to judge but to have given all judgment to the Son. Later he will say in what respect he has given judgment to the Son: because he is the Son of Man. The Father is said to judge no one because the person of the Father will not appear in judgment, but the person of the Son will. The Son will appear in judgment in the humanity he assumed. And because through him, appearing in the flesh, that separation of good and evil will take place, judgment is said to have been given to him because he is the Son of Man [Col. 0848C]. For he does not have this power of judging from being human, but from being God—unless “because he is human” means “because he who is human,” so that it does not denote a cause.

Or the Father is said to have given all judgment to the Son because judgment consists in discrimination, which belongs to wisdom, and the Son is the Father’s wisdom. Therefore, because the effect of wisdom will appear more in rendering judgment than the effect of power, judgment is attributed rather to the person of the Son than to the person of the Father. For although the works of the Trinity are common to the whole Trinity, Scripture more commonly attributes to the Father works in which divine power is preeminent; to the Son those in which wisdom is preeminent; and to the Holy Spirit those in which divine kindness and love are preeminent.

But because the Son has everything he has from the Father, the Father is said—as the Son himself testifies—to have given him all judgment, from whom he also has being. And because this effect of wisdom will be manifested through the Son appearing in the flesh, he later says, “Because he is the Son of Man.” For through the Word, the Son of God, comes the resurrection of souls; through the Word made [Col. 0849A] flesh, the Son of Man, comes the resurrection of bodies. Or, from what he accomplished in the flesh, he merited that his own body should be glorified in rising again, and that the same glory in bodies should be given to others who imitate him.

The question is how Augustine says that the resurrection of souls comes through the Word, the Son of God, but that of bodies through the Son of Man. The resurrection of souls takes place when, with the darkness of ignorance and blindness expelled, they return to the knowledge of their Creator through illumination by the light of God’s wisdom. Through the assumed man, however, the Word of God could die and rise again. By dying and rising, he bestowed faith upon us; through this faith we attain the resurrection of immortality and impassibility, insofar as the resurrection of the good alone is under discussion. In this sense it is clear why he distinguishes the Son of God from the Son of Man. For insofar as he is the Son of God, he works only in hearts, not insofar as he is human. But for the resurrection of bodies he has worked not only according to that nature by which he is God, but also according to that by which he is the Son of Man: by dying and rising, as stated [Col. 0849B]. Thus the Son of God is rightly said to bring about the resurrection of souls, and the Son of Man that of bodies. Or the Son of God brings about the resurrection of souls because he works invisibly in souls, bestowing the grace by which they rise; but the Son of Man brings about that of bodies because he himself will visibly appear in judgment, when all will rise together in the flesh, whether to glory or punishment.

“If I bear witness concerning myself, my witness is not true.” Does not the Son bear witness concerning himself, and the Father concerning the Son, and the Holy Spirit? How, then, does he say, “If I bear witness concerning myself, my witness is not true”? This is what he means: “If I, as man, bear witness concerning myself that I am God according to my human nature, or if I ascribe this to myself and not to another, my witness is not true.” For the Son refers to the Father whatever he has, as has been said.

“The works themselves which I do bear witness concerning me.” How did his works make known that he was the Son of God? Did not others also perform the same works? Even Antichrist, when he comes, will perhaps perform many more miracles. But it is clear that, although others have performed or will perform the same works, they do not do so in the same way. For he performed them in the power of the Father, which he could not do unless he were God [Col. 0849D]. Hence he himself says: “So that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins,” he said to the paralytic, “I say to you, rise” (Matt. 9; Mark 2). Thus his rising should be proof of divine power; no one else could say this in order to prove this. For Satan or Antichrist will be able to do nothing in God’s power. Nor will he be able to do anything by the fact that he is God.

“Do not think that I shall accuse you before the Father. There is one who accuses you, Moses, in whom you hope.” The question is how Moses accuses the Jews and Christ does not accuse them. For if Moses accuses them because they did not believe his words and teaching [Col. 0850A], Christ likewise accuses them because they did not believe his teaching. But it is clear that, although they believed the words of neither, they are held guilty before the Father by Moses, whose teaching they have transgressed, not by Christ, whose teaching they had not accepted. No one is held guilty before others if he fails to perform an office that he has not undertaken; but they had received Moses’ law and promised to keep it, and because they became its transgressors they are rightly said to be accused by him. They are said to hope in Moses because they think the carnal observances of the Law sufficient for righteousness.

“Therefore they gathered and filled twelve baskets with fragments,” etc. (John 6). From the multiplication of the loaves a question arises. It is asked whether they were multiplied in themselves or by some addition. For if they were multiplied by addition, not all who ate, indeed only few of them, were satisfied from those five loaves. Yet some who hold this opinion say that all were fed from those five loaves because this multiplication and feeding occurred under the form of those loaves [Col. 0850B]. But some authors and teachers maintain that they were multiplied in themselves; yet they do not know how this happened, just as they say they cannot know how an acorn grows into so great a tree. Some ask how it could happen that those loaves should become so large: whether parts became parts, or whether the whole became the whole, so as to become of such quantity.

[Col. 0850C] “What sign do you perform, that we may see and believe you?” Because the Jews had heard that manna had been given through Moses to the fathers in the wilderness, which they considered a greater miracle than what the Lord had done in feeding five thousand, they ask him for some special sign by which they may know that he is the Son of God. Therefore, showing the difference between the bread he gives and the bread they ate in the wilderness, the Lord says: “I am the bread of life.” For he is the food by which the hungry mind is refreshed. This happens when true faith embraces him. For from faith we love; through love we are united to Christ, who is our life. Therefore this spiritual bread, tasted by faith, profits daily toward life even without sacramental reception. Of it we say: “Give us this day our daily bread” (Luke 11). For while it is the “today” of the present life, we need this bread [Col. 0850D]. Hence Augustine: “Why do you prepare tooth and stomach? Believe, and you have eaten.”

“Everything that the Father gives me comes to me; and the one who comes to me I shall not cast out.” By sending his Son, the Father made him known to the world and caused people to believe in him; by his faith those who believe in him are made his. Therefore the Father is said to give to the Son—that is, to draw to knowledge and love of the Son. Likewise the Son, by making the Father known, draws to him those to whom he reveals him. The Father and Son have reciprocal knowledge: the Father cannot be known except through the Son, nor the Son except through the Father. For once one of two correlatives is known, the other also must be known [Col. 0851A].

But lest anyone think it of little benefit to be given to the Son by the Father, he adds: “And the one who comes to me I shall not cast out.” We are cast out through sins: here, when grace is withdrawn from us as our merits require; and in the future, when we are tormented by the fire of eternal burning. But the one who clings to Christ by faith will not be cast out either here or in the future. Hence a crown is promised to the one who perseveres. For the head cannot be deprived of its members by excluding them from itself.

“Not to do my own will,” that is, insofar as I am human, or a will that I do not have from another. He then shows what the Father’s will is, saying: “This is the will of my Father,” etc. His will is that we believe—that is, have faith—so that through faith [Col. 0851B] we may come to knowledge and thus obtain life. Therefore our salvation is God’s will. The Son came to fulfill this will. “And I will raise him up on the last day.” Human nature united to the Word brings about the resurrection of bodies. How this is to be understood has been explained above.

Many of his disciples, on hearing this, said: “This saying is hard; who can listen to it?” Some, not understanding Christ’s preaching, were scandalized by it and ceased to believe in him, so that it might give you an example not to desist from preaching even if some are present who do not grasp what is said and are made worse by what they hear. But it is asked how he had love of neighbour, when he knew that they would by no means understand words so spoken, but would rather be scandalized [Col. 0851C] by them. Would it not have been better for these things to be said in such a way that they could be understood by them, so that they might be edified by them rather than scandalized and ruined through not understanding them? But it must be understood that they were not worthy for it to be said to them otherwise. Hence elsewhere the Lord says: “To you it has been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God; but to the rest, in parables, so that seeing they may not see and hearing they may not understand” (Luke VIII). This indeed happens because of the fault of those for whom preachers are “the odour of death unto death.” Hence, as follows, many of the disciples went back because of this.

“The flesh profits nothing,” etc. Christ’s flesh is the vessel of the Spirit, who is the Word; and participation in it, in faith, is for us a cause of salvation. Yet in itself it profits nothing; nor does it refresh the body as other food does, but the mind.

“Your fathers ate in the wilderness,” etc. It is asked of what eating he speaks here: of spiritual or bodily eating? Yet many who ate Christ’s flesh bodily died eternally; but those who ate spiritually, both groups were saved—not through the manna, but through the thing signified, which is Christ’s body. Or “eating” may be taken equivocally. And it should be noted that not everyone who receives Christ’s body eats it: for to eat here is to be united to him through faith. Thus some receive and eat; some receive but do not eat; some eat but do not receive. [Col. 0852A] Augustine says of these: “Why do you prepare tooth and stomach? Believe, and you have eaten.” But some neither receive nor eat. Of those who do not receive, some refrain out of reverence; theirs is the saying: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Matt. VIII). Others refrain from despair and contempt; concerning them one must despair.

Christ’s body is received under the species of bread and wine. For there are there some things which are only sacraments; some which are sacraments and the reality of the sacrament; and some which are only the reality of the sacrament and not sacraments. Bread and wine are changed into Christ’s body. For he is received whole under either species. Water is mixed with the wine to show that the Gentiles, as well as the Jews, belong to Christ, by whose death both were redeemed. Whether this water [Col. 0852B] is changed into blood, we do not know.

Jesus therefore said to the Twelve. He names the Twelve because the number is sacred and enduring, although not in all those who were then twelve. For Judas, one of them, did not endure; but Matthias was afterwards put in his place. Thus the number endured, although not in the same persons.

Now the feast-day of the Jews, the Feast of Tabernacles, was near (John VII): σκῆνος, *skēnos*, means a dwelling and a tent; πήγνυμι, *pēgnymi*, means “I fasten.” Hence *scenopegia*: the setting up of tents. For the representation of that manner of dwelling in the wilderness, where they had remained in tents, they set up tents and stayed in them for seven days.

“But your time is always ready.” [Col. 0852C] For in this life a human being is always prone to commit evil for which he may be condemned; but the time had not yet come for the Lord to pass to immortality and impassibility. For immortality and impassibility cannot be possessed in this life. “My teaching is not mine,” that is, mine as man; or, as has often already been said, it is not mine as though not received from another.

“I have done one work, and you all marvel.” It should be noted that the Lord did no work for which he could be reproved, even if he owed anything to the Law. For the Law did not forbid refraining on the Sabbath from things pertaining to human salvation. Thus the Jews themselves circumcised on the Sabbath, lest a man perish.

[Col. 0852D] “But when Christ comes, no one knows where he is from.” They themselves raise this objection concerning Christ. Yet it is asked: since they knew from the Scriptures both the place and the origin of the Lord’s birth, and accordingly told Herod that Christ would be born in Bethlehem of Judah, and knew that he would be born from David’s house, how could they say, “When Christ comes, no one knows where he is from”? But it seems that they could well know that Christ would be born and that he would be born from David, and yet not know whence he was—that is, from which particular persons he would be born—whereas they said that they knew whence he was.

“Let him who is without sin among you be the first to cast a stone at her,” etc. (John VIII). Here Christ seems to take all judgment away from human beings, since no one can live without sin. If, then, only he [Col. 0853A] who is without sin can cast a stone at the adulteress, and no one except Christ can be without sin, it is clear that judgment of this sort has been removed from everyone; hence judgment seems to be left to Christ alone. But it is plain that the judgments of the Church are Christ’s when they are made reasonably—not for the sake of men or of any advantage, but solely for God’s sake. For when a judge hangs a robber, he does not take vengeance for himself, but for the Lord. In this way judgment must be left to him alone who is without sin.

Some say, however, that even one who has authority to judge cannot judge another if he himself is blameworthy, especially if he is guilty of a similar fault. We, however, say that the power of judging is not taken away so long as he is received by the Church. Yet such a person is not fit to pronounce judgment upon others. Therefore, that he judges belongs to his office; that he is such a man belongs to his fault. Or: “Let him who is without sin kill the adulteress,” that is, remit adultery; this Christ alone could do, and therefore could justify the adulteress. “Let every word stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses.” “Whoever commits sin is the slave of sin” (II Cor. XIII). That is: one who delights in sin, or who commits it by habit, is the slave of sin, because he serves the sin by which he is driven. Though such a person enters through receiving the sacraments, he does not remain in the house for ever unless he becomes free from being a slave; and this is accomplished through Christ.

“He was a murderer from the beginning and did not stand in the truth.” It is asked of what truth he speaks here: of that which is blessedness, or of that which is true knowledge [Col. 0853C] of things? For if he had possessed the knowledge that makes blessed, he would never have fallen; indeed, like the others who turned to God, he would have been confirmed in good. But if he had true knowledge of things, as some say, then he knew what he owed to the Creator and what to the creature, and thus knew himself to be inferior to the Creator. Therefore he knew that he ought to serve and love him. If he did not do so, he sinned; and so he sinned before he wished to be equal to his Creator.

But the saints say that there was no interval between creation and the fall. If this is so, he had not yet possessed either that true knowledge of things or that knowledge which makes blessed. Therefore it seems one must say that he “did not stand in the truth” which he had been created to possess, not because he had never possessed it, but because he would immediately have possessed it had he stood.

There are two fears. One restrains from evil through avoidance of Gehenna, and charity casts this fear out. There is another which remains: it is with charity, and it fears not punishment but separation. For one who loves greatly continually reveres and fears, from love itself, lest he offend and be separated. Nor does he have this reverence in order to avoid punishment, but in order to avoid separation, though he cannot be separated without punishment. Just as God is to be loved not for the rewards he will give those who love him, but for his own sake—although rewards always follow his love.

“Who sinned, this man or his parents?” (John IX). It is asked concerning the punishment inflicted upon this man blind from birth, since [Col. 0854A] every punishment arises from sin. For if no sin preceded, this man seems to have been punished unjustly. But it is plain that original guilt preceded in him, and this punishment resulted from it. Thus he too was justly punished; and the purging of this punishment served God’s glory. For God was manifested through his healing.

“If anyone does his will,” etc. As if he said: “If he has wished to believe, he will understand”; for faith is illumination of the mind. Whoever has faith working through love has love; and if love, understanding. For love itself is knowledge. Some have greater faith and less knowledge; others less faith and greater knowledge; others greater faith and greater knowledge. But it is asked whether simple persons possess knowledge of faith, since it is said: “Give an answer concerning your faith to everyone who asks” (I Pet. III). And again: “He who believes readily is diminished in faith” (Ecclus. XIX). But it is also said: “The oxen were ploughing and the asses feeding beside them” (Job I); this means that the simple and the lesser are saved in the faith of their prelates. Therefore discernment of faith is not required from everyone. Yet each must have faith and give an answer to one who asks, namely, by being ready to confess the faith with others and by knowing it.

Or, anyone has all the articles of faith, even if not in himself, at least in another who belongs to the same body. Again, “He who believes readily shall be diminished in faith”: this means that one who believes because he has been moved by miracles or some such impulse, rather than by the judgment of the mind, is not firm in faith, since he may be moved by every wind of doctrine; hence Jesus did not entrust himself [Col. 0854C] to them.

“But the hired man flees,” etc. (John X). It is asked why the hired man is rebuked. Did not Christ flee his persecutors? Did not Paul and the other elect flee the fury of persecutors? But it must be observed that one thing is to flee for one’s own sake, in order to protect oneself; another is to yield to persecutors for the sheep’s sake, so that by fleeing one preserves them rather than abandons them. Thus, though one who flees in this way is absent bodily, he is present in mind. Thus Paul says: “Though absent in body, yet present in spirit, I have already judged, as though present, him who has so acted: in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when you are assembled and my spirit with the power of the Lord Jesus, to deliver such a man to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved” [Col. 0854D] (I Cor. V), etc.

“As the Father knows me, and I know the Father.” He shows the bond of charity between himself and the Father. Thus he and the Father are one. For he alone knows the Father *as*—that is, so perfectly—as the Father knows him; he is proved to be of the same knowledge and power as the Father, and thus the same God with him. For no one except the Son knows how he is from the Father, or how the Father begot him. Hence he said above that the Son has declared what no one except him could do. Others declared it through him. “And I lay down my life for my sheep.” Did not Peter and the other elect do this also? Therefore, just as he is called the good shepherd, they too can be called good shepherds. [Col. 0855A] Yet others did not lay it down as he did, because he laid it down through himself, while they did so only through him. Thus others can be said to lay it down, but not as he does.

“I will lay down my life, and take it again.” Here is overthrown the heresy of some who say that Christ had no soul apart from the Word; and likewise that of those who said that he had an irrational soul. For if he had no soul, how could he lay it down or take it up again? Or how would the Father love him, because he laid it down in order to take it up again, unless by laying it down he could merit something? To merit is, however, to love by grace.

But when he lays down his soul—that is, when the soul is separated from the flesh—it is asked whether the divinity remained separated from one of the two, or from neither. Certain authorities seem to maintain that it was separated from one, with some supporting argument. For Ambrose says on the text, “My God, my God, look upon me: why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. XXI): “The man cries out, about to die through separation from the divinity.” Athanasius likewise says: “Whoever does not believe that the man was assumed anew, let him be anathema.” Augustine also says that the soul was the bond between the Deity and the flesh. For through the soul the Word was united to the flesh. How, then, could those united things remain joined when the bond had been dissolved?

But these authorities must be interpreted. For the statement, “The man cries out, about to die through separation from the divinity,” means that the divinity handed him over to the will of those killing him and left him so as not to preserve him from death. Again, “Whoever does not [Col. 0855C] believe that the man was assumed anew, let him be anathema,” means: whoever does not believe that he returned to life again—that is, rose from the dead—let him be anathema. Again, regarding the bond: it is clear that, though the bond is separated, the extremities can nevertheless remain connected through it, as appears in a pair of compasses. Thus, when the soul was separated from the body, the divinity was separated from neither: neither from the soul nor from the flesh.

Hence Jerome says: “He never laid aside the man whom he assumed.” Augustine likewise says: “The soul was separated from the flesh; the divinity from neither.” Accordingly Christ then lay in the tomb, Christ was then in hell, Christ was in heaven. For just as one says, “Peter lies in Rome,” because Peter’s body is there, and “Peter is in heaven,” because Peter’s soul is there, so the body lying in the tomb was called Christ, the soul Christ, and the Word Christ. The Word was then also man, for he never laid aside the man he had assumed. He had man—that is, soul and flesh—united to himself in one person.

But was Christ then a dead man? Certainly he was. For I confidently say that Christ was then a dead man, since I proclaim that Christ was then dead. Therefore Christ was then body, soul, and Word, as conversely. Since, then, the man had died, he was not thereby no longer man; that is, he did not therefore cease to have soul and flesh united to himself. Nor does it follow, if he was then man, that he was then mortal or immortal. For a proper conclusion cannot be inferred from a figurative expression.

[Col. 0856A] “The works which I do in the name of my Father bear witness concerning me.” Could others, such as Peter and Paul, say this same thing—namely, “I do works in the name of my Father”? Certainly not. For although Peter worked in the name of the Father, he could not say, “in the name of my Father.” For the Father is called Christ’s Father differently from the way he is called the Father of others. He is Father of the Son because he begot him from his own substance; he is Father of others because, as Creator, he gives them being.

Again, demons and evil men perform the same works that Christ did: for example, the Egyptian enchanters made real frogs, as Moses did. How then do the works bear witness that he is God? But it is clear that he performs works as Creator; [Col. 0856B] whereas the magicians, through malign spirits, joined the elements in such a way that frogs were born from them. Yet the demons and magicians themselves did not produce that mixture of elements; rather, they knew that it had been given them by God, as subtle and spiritual beings, so that if the elements were combined, such animals would result. But neither humans nor demons can perform works in such a way that they are adduced as proof that they themselves are gods. Christ alone could do this. Hence he says: “That you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins, I say to you, arise” (Matt. IX), as though putting forward this sign to prove that, as God, he could forgive sins. This is what he means: “The works which I do in the name”—that is, in the honour or knowledge—“of my Father,” as of the one who begot me, “bear witness concerning me.”

“My Father, what he has given me, is greater than all; and no one can snatch [them] from the hand of my Father.” He shows that no one can snatch them from his own hand. For the power which he has from the Father is greater than all. By it he bound the strong one and plundered all his goods. For the Son has the same power as the Father; but because whatever he has, he has from the Father, he says: “What the Father has given me”—namely, by begetting me—“is greater than all.” Or, that the wording may cohere more closely according to that nature in which he above called himself shepherd, door, and doorkeeper: he can also say that what the Father gave him is greater than all. For by grace the Word of God assumed a human being; and likewise by grace the assumed human being is the Son consubstantial with the Father. Thus even in this respect he is greater than all. In this respect, indeed, he is our Redeemer. Hence no one can snatch from his hand—that is, make those whom he has prepared for salvation perish. [Col. 0856D] An evil human being or the devil may suggest evils to those who cleave to Christ; but they can by no means snatch them away, that is, violently carry them off to perdition.

“I and the Father are one.” Not “one person” (*unus*), but “one thing” (*unum*), because the former refers to person and the latter to nature or essence. For the Father and Son are of one essence. In this the Arians are confounded, who said that the Father was one thing, the Son another, and the Holy Spirit another. So too are the Sabellians, who said that the same one is now Father, now Son, now Holy Spirit—Father when he wills, Son when he wills, Holy Spirit when he wills. This is clearly false, since the Father is other than the Son and the Son other than the Father.

[Col. 0857A] “Is it not written in your Law: ‘I said, You are gods,’” etc.? Since the Jews could not comprehend so great a splendour—namely, how he was God essentially—he avoids their calumny by interposing a cloud and shows that he ought not to be stoned because he said that he was God and the Son of God. For in the Law—as also in the Psalms, which are called “Law,” because law binds so that not everything may be done at pleasure—it is said: “I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High” (Ps. LXXXI).

It should be noted that “God” is said by nature, by estimation and opinion, and by participation. By nature, as Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, who are one God by nature; by estimation, as idols; by participation, as elect human beings. Thus, when the Lord said that he was God by nature—which the Jews did not understand, when they wished to stone him for it—it is asked how he frees himself from the accusation by this answer, namely: “I said: You are gods,” etc., since here “God” is said by participation but there, whence the accusation arose, God is said by nature. Nor does this citation seem relevant in any way. For the Law also commanded that if any human being made himself God, he was a blasphemer and was to be stoned.

But it is plain that the Law commanded nothing against Christ. For what is commanded in the Law is that if a merely human being [Col. 0857C] makes himself God—that is, claims for himself what he is not—he is a blasphemer and is to be stoned. One is said to make oneself wise when one arrogates to oneself what one is not. If Christ had done this, he would indeed have been a blasphemer and worthy of stoning. But he was not merely human, since he was human and God; nor did he make himself God when he was not God. Rather, he confessed himself to be God, as he was.

But because the Jews were literalists, following the letter rather than the sense, he answered them in this way, satisfying them as to the word: “I said: You are gods,” etc. As though he said: “You ought not be troubled by the word through which I said that I am God and also the Son of God, since your Scripture is said to use this very word of all the elect: ‘I said: You are gods, and all of you sons of the Most High.’”

“The Father is in me, and I in the Father.” That is, I and the Father are of the same essence. The Son is said here to be in the Father differently from the statement, “In the beginning was the Word” (John I), that is, the Word was begotten from the Father.

God is said to be in his creatures in three ways. In all things he is potentially and essentially—which are the same, since divine power is divine essence, and conversely. But what it means for God to be essentially in all creatures is asked. Some say that it should not be asked, since it cannot be known in this life. But if I believe it to be so and do not know what it is, this faith is blind—not the faith of prelates, but of asses feeding beside oxen.

God cannot be in creatures as something is said to be in a place. [Col. 0858A] He is indeed in all creatures, not locally, but through himself, governing and preserving them in being without any intermediary. For just as the soul is whole in every part of the body—this can be proved from the fact that it senses everywhere, vivifying and governing the body itself; when it departs, the body is dead and reduced to dust, from which it is clear that the soul is the body’s life—so God, by his whole essence, is in every creature, giving it being. If he departed from it, it would without doubt be utterly reduced to nothing, just as a body whose soul is its life is reduced to dust when the soul departs.

How God governs or preserves a creature, or how the soul governs and preserves the body, I do not know; but I know that in this way God is essentially in his creatures. God is also said to be in certain beings through indwelling grace, as in a rational creature, human or angel. He is also said to be in a creature through personal union, as he was only in the assumed human being—that is, in Christ. According to the manner in which he is in some through indwelling grace, he is said to be in human beings as in a vessel, because he fills with virtues those in whom he is thus present, as a vessel is filled with what it contains.

This may also be expounded thus: “The Father is in me, and I in the Father,” because whatever is in the Father by which he may be shown to be God, etc., that same thing is in the Son, because they are of the same power, knowledge, essence, and deity.

“Are there not twelve hours in the day?” (John XI), etc. The Lord introduces this comparison to show [Col. 0858C] that they ought rather to follow him and be illuminated by him than that he should follow them. For “day” here means the sun shining upon the earth; the “hours” are the very air illuminated by the sun. They do not illuminate the sun but are illuminated by it.

“Lord, if you had been here,” etc. This means that, if he had been bodily present, he could have shown mercy from an affection of pity so that Lazarus would not die. Though absent in body, he did not have this; present in the affection of pity, he wept.

“And Jesus wept.” It is asked whether these tears were real or not; and if real, whether they were reasonable. It is certain, however, that they were real, for from them his true humanity is proved. [Col. 0858D] He wept, as Jerome says, not because Lazarus was dead, but because he was about to be recalled to the misery of this life. This perhaps should be understood thus: from the affection of true pity which, as true man, he then possessed, he bewailed the miserable lot of the human condition, to which Lazarus was about to be recalled—not because this recall harmed the one recalled. But in Lazarus the compassionate Lord testified with tears to the misery of humankind, with which he sympathized and grieved from the natural affection of the human mind. For this reason, seeing the city, he wept over it, saying: “For if you too had known” (Luke XIX).

“And immediately he who had been dead came forth, his hands and feet bound with strips,” etc. We read that the Lord raised three dead persons: a girl in a house with few witnesses admitted; a young man at the gate with many seeing; and a third in a tomb, already four days dead and foul-smelling. By these are signified those who die through delight consenting—for not every delight is a sin unto death, but only that which involves consent; those who, after consent, proceed to the act; those who proclaim their crime in speech; or those who, through deed and evil habit, have now almost wholly rotted away. [Col. 0859A] Yet all are raised by the Lord, though some are awakened from the death of the body of vices more easily and others more difficultly.

In Lazarus’s resurrection it is also intimated how the disciples, and their successors in the Church, namely prelates, can loose and bind, although different persons hold different views about this. Some say that priests do nothing else in loosing and binding than the priests in the Law did concerning those cleansed of leprosy: they show them as loosed or bound. God alone forgives sins, just as he binds on account of them. Others say that priests forgive sins by virtue of the office they possess. For although sins are forgiven to a sinner at whatever hour he groans, nevertheless, because something still remains to be paid from the debt, sins are also said to be forgiven through the imposition of satisfaction made by a priest, just as in baptism are washed away those sins already forgiven through true contrition of heart. Thus, by binding persons to penance, they loose sins.

They remit, however, when they restore to the Church’s sacraments those previously cast out who repent, [Col. 0859C] and so loosen their hands for action and their feet for walking freely in the Church.

“But one of them, named Caiaphas, being high priest that year, said to them,” etc. It is asked what this priest spoke through the Holy Spirit. Did the Holy Spirit move his heart to give this counsel of killing Christ? If so, then he gave good counsel, and the Jews ought to have carried it out. But one must by no means say either that he gave good counsel or that the Jews did not sin in killing him. Yet the Evangelist says that, because he was high priest that year, he prophesied that Jesus would die for the people.

Some say that it was from the Holy Spirit that he uttered these words, which could bear both meanings: the counsel which he gave from himself and the prophecy which he uttered unknowingly. Thus he gave evil counsel, which he expressed by those words; and unknowingly prophesied, the Holy Spirit inspiring prophetic words by which he also signified that prophetic meaning, namely, that Jesus would die for the people of the whole world.

“Leave her, that she may keep it for the day of my burial” (John XII). What does this mean: “That she may keep it for the day of my burial,” when another Evangelist says, “She has anticipated anointing my body” (Mark XIV)? What does “that she may keep it” mean? It means: that from what she now does to me, it may be shown how great an affection she has, since, when I lie in the tomb, she would do the same thing in devotion, though not in deed. Or: leave her to keep it, in devotion, for anointing my buried body—what she could do in deed. [Col. 0860A] For the affection she had in anointing him alive, she had for anointing him dead, if it had been permitted. This is the same as: “She has anticipated anointing my body,” because she rendered in service to him alive what she would have rendered to him dead in devotion—or in the act itself, if she had been permitted and able.

For she did not then know that he would die, so as to do the same thing then, because after he was dead she could not. Again, it is asked whether it would have been better for that ointment to be sold for the use of the poor or for the Lord’s body to be anointed with it. We answer: that woman stirred up greater devotion in herself, and thus profited more by bestowing it on the Lord’s body itself than she would have by distributing it among the poor. Because of this devotion pilgrims visit the thresholds of the saints. Hence the Lord himself commends her act and declares it worthy of lasting fame.

“He who hates his life in this world,” etc. That is, one who hates his life to the point of not living in worldly desires; or conversely, one who so loves it as to live in them. The latter loses it when assigned to eternal torments; the former keeps it to possess eternal life. Or, one who so hates it that he would rather lose it here than deny Christ keeps it. But one who so loves it in this world as to prefer this life to Christ loses it in the future.

“Now is the judgment of the world; now shall the prince of this world be cast out.” It is asked how the prince of this world, that is, the devil, has been cast out. For he still reigns in many. The evil are more numerous than the good. I ask, therefore: since he still exercises his power over so many, how is he said to have been cast out through Christ’s death? But it is clear that through Christ’s death strength has been conferred on us by which we can resist the devil and prevent him from doing anything. [Col. 0860C] For, as blessed Augustine says, he is strong only because we are weak. Hence, because through Christ we have been made strong, he remains stripped of all strength. He exercises the power of his tyranny only over those who cast away the weapons conferred upon them and make themselves weak.

“That the saying might be fulfilled which Isaiah the prophet spoke.” This saying must be fulfilled, but it cannot be fulfilled unless they sin; therefore they must sin. But this is false. For when I say that prophecy must be fulfilled, I mean that it cannot happen that this whole thing was prophetically foretold and does not occur. It does not follow that this other thing must happen, namely that they do not believe or that they sin.

“He blinded their eyes and hardened their heart,” etc. It is asked who is the author of this blinding. For God is said to have blinded them. Hence Augustine: “God inclines human minds either to good or to evil, by his judgment—sometimes hidden, sometimes manifest, but always just.” God is said to blind them or hand them over to desire because, their previous merits demanding it, [Col. 0861A] he withdraws grace; once it is withdrawn, they rush into greater sins. Therefore God does nothing to make them blinded, but through their own hardening and abundance of iniquity they deserve to be cast down in this way. Thus, for God to cast them down and blind them means nothing other than that he justly withdraws grace from them, lest they be further raised by the assistance of which they have made themselves unworthy.

Nor should it be said that, when grace is withdrawn, he makes them fall. Rather, when that grace which they deserved to have taken away is withdrawn, they fall through their own malice, and by falling thus they deserve that grace for rising again should no longer be given to them. Hence it is also said here:

“Therefore they could not believe.” For no one of those who do not believe can merit that grace be given to him; but some of them merit that grace not be given to them—not all, however, because if this were so, no one could be saved. Therefore no one who is blinded can believe or be saved. Yet God cannot save such persons either. I do not mean that God cannot remove a city and thereby save them; rather, it is unjust to save such persons, and therefore God cannot do this. For God cannot act unjustly.

“The things, therefore, which I speak, as the Father told me, so I speak.” Christ enters the door through himself; and as he enters the door through himself, so he speaks through himself, because in speaking he manifests himself and makes his faith known, just as he enters through himself—that is, through preaching faith he introduces himself into the hearts of believers. Christ speaks in two ways: inwardly through inspiration and outwardly [Col. 0861C] by the voice of the flesh.

But perhaps it will be asked why Christ needed to speak outwardly in this way, when without outward speech he could move inwardly and confer the grace of understanding and belief. Likewise, why are angels sent to disclose God’s will to human beings, when he could inspire through himself? It is also asked what benefit there is in prayers made aloud; and what Paul’s preaching contributes. Why should Paul’s preaching be spoken of rather than Paul’s baptism? Does Paul contribute more by preaching than by baptizing?

But it is clear that, through the Lord’s words then sounding outwardly and now written or heard in some manner, the hearts of believers are more moved and stirred to devotion. Yet what is heard or seen outwardly profits nothing unless grace inwardly enlightens the mind. Likewise the preacher’s words, though they do not enlighten, nevertheless stir persons to receive the grace prepared for them; only when it is received or infused are they enlightened. For we must cooperate with grace, without which we can neither understand nor be justified. We say the same concerning angels and prayers.

What is done outwardly, such as preaching, is indeed grace—that is, an outward sign employed. Yet this grace has no effect without the inward grace; indeed, it sometimes produces blinding, as in Pharaoh. But of the inward grace it is said that it is never possessed without benefit.

“Before the feast-day of the Passover, Jesus knew that his hour had come” (John XIII), etc. As the time of his passion approached, the Lord, wishing to fulfil that for [Col. 0862A] which he had come—namely, by death to pass to the Father, and thus by his example to teach others to pass away from love of the world—instructed his disciples by example and word. He clearly showed both that he was God, that he had come in the flesh for the redemption of the world, and that he would die. This is also noted where it follows: “Having loved his own, he loved them unto the end,” that is, unto death, namely, so that he might die for them. For no greater love—that is, manifestation of love—can exist than that one should die for one’s friends (John XV).

If I do not wash you, you will have no share with me. From this some wish to maintain that original sin is not remitted except in the washing of the feet after baptism; they say that the author of this view was Ambrose, bishop of Milan. Hence in certain churches the feet of those who have been baptized are washed [Col. 0862B]. For by the feet they say that sin arising from the flesh, as from a lower nature, is signified. But this ought not to be said. For original sin was not then present in Peter; for perhaps it had been remitted in him both through circumcision and through baptism—although one may nevertheless say that its form was displayed in him. It is better to understand by the feet, by which we walk, the impulses of the flesh by which we are moved to sin. These must be washed by the Lord even after baptism and the reception of the other sacraments of the Church. Unless this is done, they cannot be cleansed through baptism and the other sacraments of the Church, nor can they have a share with the Lord. And this is what follows: He who is clean has no need except to wash his feet.

Therefore, if I, Lord and Teacher, have washed your feet [Col. 0862C], etc. He teaches that he has left them an example: just as he forgave them their sins, so they too should forgive one another’s sins. But since this is commanded in this passage, and since the Lord’s Prayer commands us to forgive those who sin against us, the question arises: what ought a human being to forgive—guilt or punishment? Yet it is clear that one cannot remit guilt. Nor does it belong to one to remit punishment. For if this were commanded, all justice and judgment in the Church would perish, whereas God says: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Deut. 32). Therefore we say that a person ought to dismiss from the heart the malice [malevolence] which he might contract from an injury done to him, so that on his own account he wishes no evil to happen to the offender. Hence another Evangelist says: “Unless each of you forgives from his heart” (Matt. 18) [Col. 0862D]. That is, unless he wishes to exact nothing on his own account. For if vengeance is exacted by a judge, it is exacted not for a human being but for God. Whoever takes it for himself sins. But one who retains malice or bitterness toward the person who inflicted the injury attends to himself rather than to God, when, on his own account, he wishes some evil to happen to that person.

This is what it is to forgive a debt: namely, to forgive the one who injured oneself in such a way that, so far as one is concerned, the offender owes one nothing. By this same manner of forgiving, the one who has done wrong is recalled to repentance.

“He who receives anyone whom I send receives me,” etc. Christ is received in the apostle, because the apostle is received only for Christ’s sake. Hence it is meritorious to receive Christ in anyone, whether the one received belongs to Christ or does not. For whoever receives a prophet in the name of a prophet will receive a prophet’s reward—not from the prophet. But if someone were so simple-minded as to receive Antichrist as Christ, then, if the error arose from piety, God would reveal it to him. Hence the Apostle says: “If you think otherwise in anything, God will reveal this also to you” (Phil. 3) [Col. 0863A].

When Jesus had said this, he was troubled in spirit. The Lord was truly troubled—by will, indeed, not by necessity. Not, as some say, by will in such a sense that he could not naturally be troubled and suffer; rather, he was troubled because he possessed a nature capable of being troubled, saddened, and suffering. Yet he voluntarily assumed all these things belonging to our weakness, because there was in him no reason why he should endure them, since he was without sin [Col. 0863B]. Thus they were voluntary, because there was no cause in him for assuming them except will alone. For will did not give him the capacity to be troubled; rather, it was the nature of our flesh, which he assumed.

“He is the one to whom I shall offer the dipped morsel.” Here the Lord did not openly reveal Judas, but said this secretly to John alone, the others not hearing.

“And after the morsel Satan entered into him.” Judas did not receive the Lord’s body in the morsel; nevertheless, because he used that good thing badly, he deserved to be abandoned more fully to himself and thus to be more completely possessed by the devil. For in bold and shameless presumption he approached as though he were clean, to receive that good thing from the hand of the Lord whose death he was plotting [Col. 0863C]. That morsel signified some good thing.

“A new commandment I give you: that you love one another,” etc. It is asked whether this commandment suffices for salvation, and why it is called new, since it seems to have been given in the Law. We say that this commandment suffices for salvation. For love of God is included in this commandment. Mutual love of neighbors cannot be commanded unless love of God is commanded; nor can one love one’s neighbor unless one loves God. For the question here is not love arising from a lawful or unlawful carnal affection, but that love which puts a person to death to the world and joins him to God, and which exists solely for God’s sake. Hence it is said here: “As I have loved you,” that is, love one another toward the same end—to salvation—for which I loved you [Col. 0863D].

Likewise God cannot be loved unless one’s neighbor is loved. For it is impossible for anyone to love you unless he loves whatever you love. If he hated something that you loved, he would disagree with you in this and so offend you; but one cannot love and offend at the same time. This commandment is rightly called new. For by it whoever is renewed is renewed. It is new again because it was not expounded in the old Law. There the mystery lay hidden. And since there it is neither commanded nor expounded, it is rightly called the new commandment of the new Law, because here it is both commanded and plainly expounded. For although the Law says: “You shall love the Lord your God with your whole heart and with your whole soul, and your neighbor as yourself” [Col. 0864A] (Deut. 6), it does not there say: “As I have loved you.” Although what cannot be fulfilled apart from this is commanded there—and thus it may be said to be contained and hidden there—it is not said to be commanded or to exist there. The precepts of the Old Testament did not renew, but made people conformable to the old man.

“I will lay down my life for you.” Peter’s saying this was an impulsive utterance arising from the fervor of love: he promised that he would do what he was not yet able to do. Hence the Lord immediately afterward showed both that he would someday lay down his life for love of him, and that he would shortly deny him. In that denial he lost charity. For, as the gloss says, by denying life he killed his soul. Whoever says either that Christ is not God or that he himself is not Christ’s disciple denies Christ’s faith, and thus Christ himself [Col. 0864B]. That Peter denied Christ is clear from the fact that the Lord foretold that he would do so. Therefore those who absolve Peter of lying prove Christ a liar, by saying that Peter did not do what Christ foretold he would do.

“The cock will not crow,” etc. It is asked why another Evangelist says, “Before the cock has crowed twice, you will deny me three times” (Mark 14), whereas this Evangelist says simply: “The cock will not crow until you have denied me three times.” Two answers are given. Either Peter had already, in intention, committed that threefold denial before the cock crowed, because he was ready to deny as often as he should be questioned; or that threefold denial began before the first crowing of the cock and was finished and completed before the second [Col. 0864C]. Thus this Evangelist says: “The cock will not crow until you have denied me three times,” that is, until you have denied me—a denial which will be threefold. What the other Evangelist says is evident.

“In my Father’s house are many dwelling places” (John 14). By “dwelling places” he means the differing rewards which already existed with the Father in predestination, corresponding to differing merits.

“If otherwise, I would have told you, because I go to prepare a place for you.” He wishes to make them more certain that those dwelling places are prepared. Thus he proves this by an impossibility, saying: “If otherwise,” that is, if they were not prepared, “I would have told you this: that I go to prepare.” But it is impossible that I should have told you, “I go to prepare predestination,” since predestination remains eternal and immutable [Col. 0864D]. Therefore they must be prepared as I say. But because they still had to be prepared in another way, he adds: “And if I go away and prepare a place for you, I shall come again and receive you.” He went away by dying, rising, and ascending. By this departure from them he greatly kindled their hearts and raised them from earthly things to the things above, where he had ascended. For things that are loved are more ardently desired when they are not seen than when they are present. Thus, by departing, he prepared through action what had been prepared from eternity through predestination.

Thomas said to him: “Lord, we do not know where you are going.” Some of the disciples did not know that he was God, but thought him a mere man; Philip was among them [Col. 0865A]. Hence the Lord rebukes him in what follows. Others believed him to be God; Thomas was among them. Thus the Lord proves that Thomas knew what he himself did not know that he knew. For a person can know something, and yet, before testing it, not know that he knows it. Therefore the Lord says that he knows what he himself said he did not know.

“And he will do greater works than these.” This is expounded in many ways; one interpretation is as follows. Whoever believes in Christ, the Lord will justify through him sinners—an act of justification greater than the creation of angels. For although both are acts of equal power, the former is an act of greater mercy. Mercy is needed only where there is misery. Since there was no misery in the angels, no mercy was needed there [Col. 0865B]. But in us there was and is misery, which Christ came to remove in mercy. In relation to us, therefore, God’s mercy in the justification of the ungodly is greater than in the creation of the righteous. No effect falls upon God himself.

“And whatever you ask the Father in my name, this I will do.” Some righteous people ask and are not heard, as Paul, praying that Satan’s angel might depart from him, was not heard. Some wicked people pray and are heard, as the devil in Job’s affliction. What then does the Lord mean when he says, “Whatever you ask in my name, I will do for you,” when the Church often seems to pray in the Lord’s name and yet is not heard—for a king, for the sick, or for the repose of the dead who are damned? To ask in the Lord’s name is to ask for what pertains to salvation, whether of the person praying or of the person for whom prayer is made [Col. 0865C]. But no one can pray thus except by speaking in God’s Spirit, that is, unless he has charity. Hence the Apostle says: “No one speaking in God’s Spirit can say, ‘Jesus be accursed’” (1 Cor. 12).

Here, however, it is promised particularly to the apostles that whatever they should ask for the aid of their preaching, tending to the benefit of planting the Church, he would do for them. More generally, whatever is asked for salvation is asked in the Lord’s name. The Lord has always heard this petition, because it never returns empty. Either it obtains what it asks, or through the petition one advances in some respect—as Paul, through that experience, learned that tribulation contributes to the increase of the crown [Col. 0865D]. Thus the Lord always does what is asked in his name, because he always hears prayer so that it advances in some respect.

It should be noted that some who pray for others are heard because of themselves, since they are worthy, although those for whom they pray are unworthy—as Moses prayed for his wicked people. At times both those who ask and those for whom they ask are worthy, as when someone worthy of salvation is saved. At times those who ask are unworthy, but those for whom they ask are worthy, and so they are heard not for their own sake but for the others’. Reason requires this, even if examples are not at hand, though it may be shown by analogy. For Satan’s petition was not granted for his own sake, but for the benefit of others. So the wicked are sometimes heard when praying for the good, not for their own sake but for theirs.

[Col. 0866A] “For the Father is greater than I,” etc. From this the heretic wishes to maintain that the Son is not equal to the Father, since the Son himself declares that he is less than the Father. But if he is lesser, then he will be a son by grace rather than by nature. Yet this is excluded by what precedes: “I go to the Father.” For insofar as he goes, he is less than the Father, while in the nature of divinity he is equal. Thus that this man is the Son of God is by grace; but he is not a son of grace, rather a Son by nature. Yet that the assumed man is the natural Son is by grace. Therefore one must not say separately, “The Son is less than the Father”; for the authority of the statement would be curtailed if it were uttered thus.

“As the Father has loved me, so I have loved you” (John 15). It is asked of what love he speaks: “As the Father has loved me,” etc.—whether of the love by which he loved him according to his divine nature, or that by which he loved him according to his human nature [Col. 0866B]. But it cannot be that, as the Father loved him in nature, so he loves us, for then we should be equal to him. The meaning, therefore, is: As the Father loved me, the man assumed by his Word, by grace, so I love you by grace, not because of your merits. For the assumed man is by grace the Son of God by nature; yet this was bestowed upon the man by grace.

What follows, “Remain in my love,” can be understood either as: remain in the love by which I love you—that is, do not reject the grace that I have bestowed on you—or: remain in the love by which you love me, that is, persevere in good affection.

“That my joy may be full.” Let no one suppose that the Lord’s joy ever increased; rather, as it is said, “Jesus advanced in age and wisdom” (Luke 2), so it is said concerning his joy [Col. 0866C]. For he advanced in age, that is, in accordance with the progress of age; and he also advanced among human beings in teaching and wisdom.

“No one has greater love than this: that one lay down his life for his friends.” Above he commanded love; now he shows how great love ought to be. But it is asked of what love he speaks, beyond which there can be no greater. For it does not seem possible to say this of inward affection, since one person dying for Christ may have greater affection than another, and indeed someone who does not die may have it. Thus some say that this concerns the manifestation of affection, rather than affection itself. For there can be no greater sign of love [Col. 0866D], nor does anyone have anything further that he can do. This is the thing that a human being holds dearer than all else. Hence when one gives what is held dearest, one gives what it is most difficult to lose. Therefore a human being has nothing more to give. Hence the Law says: “Skin for skin, and all that a man has he will give for his life” (Job 2). For we give tooth for tooth and eye for eye (Matt. 5) in order to preserve life.

From this it is also clear that there can be no greater love even in respect of inward affection. For what greater affection can a person have than to be willing to die for a friend? This is the greatest thing that anyone can do. Yet although this is the greatest in one person, this person’s greatest is less than another’s greater. For one embraces death with a greater affection than another; one cannot have as much affection as another [Col. 0867A]. Just as no one can do more than love with all the heart, soul, and strength, and yet one loves more than another because this person’s whole heart is greater than that person’s whole heart, though both love with their whole heart. For to love with one’s whole heart is to love even unto death: namely, to love God more than oneself and lose one’s life in order to gain Christ, so as to be able to say with Paul: “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1).

Augustine nevertheless says that this commandment cannot be fulfilled in this life. He said this because in this life it cannot be otherwise than that the flesh weighs down the soul and resists it in some respect, until this mortal puts on incorruption; thus he understands “with all the heart” equivocally. Therefore, though Christ’s death and Peter’s death benefited us both in effect and in affection, Peter’s death cannot be equated with Christ’s death, because Christ’s death redeemed us. Peter’s death encouraged faith, but did not redeem [Col. 0867B]. Hence we say that Christ’s love in death was greater, even in manifestation, than Peter’s death or that of anyone else. For he manifested more, because by his death he redeemed us.

“I will no longer call you servants,” etc. It is asked how he can say that he will no longer call them servants but friends, when he himself at the reward says, “Well done, good servant,” etc. (Matt. 25). Thus he calls the righteous servants, while here promising not to call them servants. Blessed Augustine says that, just as there are two fears, so there are two kinds of servants. There is servile fear, by which one is a servant; but such a person does not know what his Lord does. For even if he sometimes does something good, he does not know that it is done by the Lord, but attributes it to himself. There is another fear, a chaste fear, which remains for ever and ever [Col. 0867C]. This preserves charity; charity expels the former fear. By this fear servants are friends, to whom the Lord reveals his secrets and says: “Enter into the joy of your Lord” (ibid.). Thus the apostles had formerly been servants through fear of punishment; shortly, when they were to receive the Holy Spirit more fully, they were to be called friends, not servants.

A friend is called, as it were, the guardian of the soul (*animi custos*), one to whom the secrets of another’s mind are open. “If you had been of the world,” etc. The apostles were in the world, that is, among the wicked; but they were not of the world, that is, they were not among the number of the wicked. Hence, conversely, John says of the wicked that they are not of the good: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1 John 2) [Col. 0867D].

“The world would love what was its own,” etc. Does not the world sometimes hate the world, as the prodigal hates the miser? Why is this? Because it hates what is contrary to itself: vice is contrary to vice. Yet it does not hate what is apparent. For the prodigal does not hate the miser because he is wicked, but because he is contrary to himself. Therefore it loves in him what is its own, namely, that he is wicked; but it hates in him what is contrary to its own wickedness.

“If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin.” Would the Jews have had no sin if Christ had not come and spoken to them [Col. 0868A]? He does not mean that they would have had no sin if he had not come, but that they would not have had the sin of unbelief. For their failure to believe in Christ would in no way have been imputed to them if he had not come. But if they were not bound by this sin, would they be saved without faith in Christ? No; indeed, they would be condemned for other sins. But if they had no other sin, some of those who lived before Christ’s coming would not be condemned because they lacked faith in Christ, since they would have an excuse concerning this; for without a preacher they could not believe it, nor could they understand Christ’s incarnation through natural reason.

For what sin, then, would they be condemned? To say that they are condemned without sin is to say that God is unjust [Col. 0868B]. To this we reply that God would by no means allow such a person to be condemned; rather, if he were clean in other respects, God would reveal Christ’s faith to him. Nor could it occur that someone lacked sin unto death and did not have faith in Christ. For while this sin remains, the others remain—that is, none can be remitted; but when this sin departs, the others depart—that is, when it departs through acquired faith, the person now has that through which he can be free from other sins. For faith is the first entrance to salvation. Hence “one who approaches God must believe” (Heb. 11).

Thus, as it is said that “those who sinned under the Law will be judged by the Law” (Rom. 2), that is, they will be grievously punished eternally for transgressing the Law; and “those who sinned without the Law will perish without the Law” (ibid.), that is, they will perish not for transgressing a Law which they had not received, but will be punished more lightly—as Tyre and Sidon will fare more lightly on the day of judgment than this generation (Matt. 11) [Col. 0868C]. Those who had not yet heard or received faith in Christ were not to perish for unbelief; but those to whom it was preached and confirmed by the power of miracles, when they ought to have believed and refused, were held by the sin of unbelief. On that account they were to be condemned more severely than if they had not heard Christ’s faith proposed to them and had not, through wickedness and envy, despised it.

“He who hates me hates my Father also,” etc. Augustine says concerning the passage in Matthew, “Either he will endure the one and despise the other” (Matt. 6), that no person’s conscience can hate God. But in the *Retractations* he retracts this statement and says that he regrets having said it. For this had not yet come to mind: “The pride of those who hate you rises continually” (Ps. 73). Therefore we say that many hate God, whom, because they know him to be the avenger of crimes, they would wish not to exist; for whoever fears someone wishes him to perish. These are those who love sins, yet would not wish sins to be sins or evils; and thus they would wish the order and nature of things to be changed [Col. 0868D]. Of these it is said here: “He who hates me hates my Father also.”

But Augustine raises the question how they could hate him when they did not know that they hated him. The gloss beginning, “We can love or hate those not seen,” pertains to the solution of this question [Col. 0869A].

“If I had not done among them the works that no one else did,” etc. It is asked what works the Lord did, which no other did, by which they could believe him to be God. This cannot be said of works not performed in the presence of the Jews, such as his birth from a Virgin or his resurrection from the dead. They had not seen these, and so could not believe through them. It is therefore said of the multitude of healings which he had performed before and among them, such as no one else had performed among them; or it is said because of his manner of acting, because he acted by himself as one possessing power, whereas all others acted through him. For if miracles are true, they are done from him and through him; otherwise, they are illusory.

[Col. 0869B] “But the hour is coming when everyone who kills you will think that he is offering service to God” (John 16). This is added for consolation. As though he said: Do not despair because of tribulation. For through your tribulation and death the Church will multiply so greatly that the Jews will think they are offering service to God when they kill you, lest God’s Law and Temple be abandoned by all. But it is asked whether those who ignorantly persecuted the saints sinned, when conscience told them that this should be done for God. For the Apostle says: “Everything that is not from faith,” that is, contrary to conscience, “is sin” (Rom. 14). Therefore, if they did not kill them when conscience told them that it ought to be done, they sinned. To this we answer, as we have often said, that whether they acted or refrained contrary to conscience [Col. 0869C], they sinned unto death—as it is said: “Woe to the little vessel: whether it strikes the stone or the stone strikes it.”

“Because they have not known the Father or me.” Above, speaking of the Father, he said: “Whom you say is our Father” (John 8); here he says that they have not known him.

“And when he comes, he will convict the world concerning sin,” etc. The Spirit is said to convict and to give charity because, in his sending, charity was bestowed upon the apostles—not by the Spirit alone, but by the whole Trinity. Through the charity bestowed in the Spirit’s mission, when fear had been cast out, they convicted sinners of their unbelief. But it is asked how blessed Augustine can say here that, while this sin of unbelief remains, the others remain [Col. 0869D], when the same could be said of any sin: while it remains, the others remain.

Some nevertheless say that a person can repent of one sin in which he is involved, even while persisting in another; and the following authority seems to support this: “The Lord rains upon one city and not upon another, and one part of a single city has been rained upon, while another part has not” (Amos 4). This means that one sin is remitted while another remains. But James says: “Whoever offends in one point is guilty of all” (Jas. 2). Reason itself also requires that one who persists in one sin cannot repent of another. For if repentance is sorrow for sins committed arising from love, then one who repents of one sin while persisting in another does not have love. This is clear because, in intending to remain in sin, he despises [Col. 0870A]. It is manifest that such a person cannot truly repent, nor can he do anything beneficial to himself while he remains such.

Therefore we shall say of the authority which seems to intend otherwise that it must be interpreted differently. There are some who are so compuncted over certain sins that they burst into tears. Of them Jerome says: “A tear wipes away the sin which shame prevents one from confessing,” that is, which is so great that shame itself compels one to burst into tears. This must not be understood as though it could be wiped away by a tear without confession, when shame prevents confession. There are other sins over which people do not repent so much as to come to tears. This is what is meant by: “One part has been rained upon, another part has not”; for over these sins one is so compuncted as to shed tears, but over those sins one does not grieve enough for weeping to follow [Col. 0870B].

Since, then, while any sin remains the others remain, how does Augustine say specifically of this sin of unbelief that its continuance makes the others remain? We say that this is said by way of comparison. No sin is so much the cause why the others remain as this one, because the other sins arise from weakness, whereas this one arises from wickedness. Or it is because, while this sin remains, a person cannot be raised even to a small good; but while the others remain, one can in some way be moved toward good. For one can have some compunction by which one is moved toward good, even though it does not benefit one unto life.

“Concerning righteousness, because I go to the Father,” etc. The world is convicted of the sin of unbelief and again of righteousness—not its own righteousness, but that of believers. This seems to be the same as being convicted of sin: namely, being convicted because it remains in unbelief, and again being convicted because it does not wish to be justified by believing. But it is one thing to remain in unbelief and another not to imitate others in faith [Col. 0870C]. Hence some are convicted because they do not believe; others are convicted because they do not imitate others in faith. For the highest righteousness is to imitate by faith what is not seen.

“I still have many things to say to you,” etc. We cannot determine what these many things are. This is said on account of that future revelation which will occur in eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0870D] “He will teach you all truth”—both concerning the present and concerning the future.

“Spirit of truth,” etc. This is the source of the controversy between Latins and Greeks. The Greeks accuse us of anathema. For since the Creed does not contain the words, “The Holy Spirit proceeds from the Son,” and since it is written there, “If anyone adds anything else, let him be anathema,” they judge us guilty of anathema because we add this. But we have in many places that the Spirit is from the Son as well as from the Father. For the Apostle says: “God sent the Spirit of his Son into your hearts” (Gal. 4). And again: “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ” (Rom. 8). Here also we say that Christ says: “I shall send him to you.” But how would he send him unless he gave him? And how would he give him unless he were his? Therefore we say that he belongs to both and proceeds from both. Yet we add nothing else, because nothing contrary is added. “Else” is understood in this sense also in Paul: “If anyone preaches to you another gospel, let him be anathema” (Gal. 1).

“He will receive from what is mine,” etc. From this the heretic wishes to maintain that the Holy Spirit is less than the Son, because the receiver is less than the giver. This is resolved by what is said, “from what is mine,” that is, from the Father, from whom the Son also is. Hence it is more evident that he is equal than inferior [Col. 0871A].

“All that the Father has is mine.” But the Father has this: that he begot the Son and has a Son; the Son, however, does not have this. We reply that every good of the Father is a good of the Son. Thus this good of the Father—namely, that he is Father or possesses a Son—is a good of the Son. For to say that the Son has this, that the Father himself is Father, means nothing.
