“A little while, and you will no longer see me,” etc. If this “little while” refers to the whole span of this life, how can he say that they will not see him, when many believers to whom he says this saw him after the Ascension, such as Paul, Stephen, and others? This is resolved by a single word: they no longer saw him mortal.

“Until now you have asked nothing in my name,” etc. The apostles had asked nothing in the Lord’s name: either believing and loving in the name Jesus, which is signified in this name; or “in the name,” that is, in that purer awareness and firmer knowledge which they would later possess, once deceptive imaginings had been cast off and the Holy Spirit sent [Col. 0871B]. For previously they were carnal and, as it were, old vessels to which new wine would have been inappropriately entrusted.

The images in question are likenesses of bodies: for example, when one supposes that, as a ray of sunlight penetrates the air, so God penetrates all things; or that, as water fills every cavity and pore of a sponge, so he fills all things, as though he had parts and admitted of greater and lesser. Therefore, in order that God may be seen purely, all such imaginings must be expelled and transcended, and God himself contemplated in himself—not by an imaginative thought, but by pure understanding. Yet the knowledge possessed here is only a kind of shadow in comparison with that future vision, when we shall see God immediately as he is. For now we see “through a mirror, in an enigma,” but then we shall see “face to face” (1 Cor. 13) [Col. 0871C].

I do not, however, say that the knowledge of God possessed here does not arise from these visible things. For invisible things are perceived through visible things (Rom. 1). But I say that no form of visible things must be attributed to God. Therefore no one who asks in such knowledge—which is to ask in his name—can be rejected. For if one asks only for what is for one’s salvation, one is not mistaken in such a petition: “The spiritual person judges all things and is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2). This petition was sometimes made in affection, sometimes also in words.

[Col. 0872A] “I have spoken these things to you in proverbs,” that is, obscurely in proportion to their limited capacity at that time. Hence, when the Spirit came, these were no longer proverbs but intelligible words.

Jesus spoke these things, and, lifting up his eyes, etc. (John 17). According to some, the discourse ends here and the prayer begins. “Father, glorify,” etc. With his passion imminent, the Lord prays within his disciples’ hearing in order to teach them, with tribulation impending, to have recourse to prayer. The glorification of the Son by the Father occurred chiefly in the resurrection, faith in which the Son brought about together with the Father. Yet, in order to distinguish the person of the Father from the person of the Son, it is said that the Father raised the Son from the dead. The glorification of the Father by the Son occurred when, after the Holy Spirit was sent, they had firm faith that Christ was God and the Son of God, equal to the Father [Col. 0872B]. Thus through the incarnate Son the Father was made known to the world. This knowledge is not yet complete, but will be completed in the future, when it will itself be supreme blessedness.

It is asked concerning the statement, “You have given me authority over all flesh”: according to which nature did he receive this authority, by which he can save and give eternal life? The authorities say that he received and possesses this authority according to his human nature, just as he himself says after rising: “All authority has been given to me,” etc. (Matt. 28). So also we say that according to his human nature our Redeemer is Lord and is to be adored. But if he possesses this authority according to his human nature [Col. 0872C], then according to this lower nature he is equal to God—which cannot be. We say that according to his lower nature he possesses this authority—namely, to save and forgive sins—far more excellently than others possess their own authority, because he is united with the Son of God in one person.

This should nevertheless be noted: *secundum* (“according to”), when used in this way, sometimes indicates a cause, as when I say that according to his humanity he is less than the Father or suffered; at other times it designates the person existing in that nature, as when I say that according to his human nature he is Redeemer or has the power to save. That is, he who exists in human nature, or the man himself. Yet it must be noted that he redeemed through human nature and received according to human nature. For it was granted to the man that the one who redeemed and grants eternal life should be united with the Word [Col. 0872D].

“I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world.” Not merely that you are God and Father of all through creation, but that you are my Father through generation. For he manifested to the world this distinction of persons. The Father begot from his own substance a Son equal to himself: distinct in person, indeed, but the same God in substance; for the Father and the Son are of the same substance.

And all that is mine is yours. Above he said, “All things that the Father has are mine,” speaking of those things that pertain to the Godhead; but here he says that all his things are the Father’s [Col. 0873A], speaking, namely, of creatures given him by the Father. “That they may be one,” etc. It is as though he said: Just as we are one in substance, so may they too be one in love. For it would be pointless to pray that they should be one in the nature of humanity, since they were already one in nature in that way. Therefore, when the gloss says, “that they may be one in their nature,” it is to be understood thus: that they may be one—that is, harmonious in charity, by which charity they may cleave to God, from whom they are born, that is, from whom they have being. Hence *nature* means “that which is”; whence everything naturally tends toward being. They therefore are one in nature, yet they ought to cleave through love to him who is Being and from whom they have being. For they cannot be essentially one human being, as the Father and the Son are one. But just as it is said that the multitude of believers [Col. 0873B] “were of one heart and one soul” (Acts 4), so here it is prayed that they may be one—a union to be accomplished by the bond of charity.

“Sanctify them in truth,” etc. “Who will believe through their word,” etc. It is called *their* word because it was first entrusted to them, and first made known and preached by them. Moreover, in this word which sounded from their mouths, that Word which abides eternally became known; it poured itself into the hearts of believers and elect persons and, by its grace, enlightened them for believing and loving. Thus he says: “Who will believe through their word, that they may be one in us”—that is, that through charity they may cleave to us; and this charity comes from the faith by which they believe us to be one. For love is born from faith.

[Col. 0873C] “That the love with which you loved me may be in them, and I in them.”

“They led him first to Annas” (John 18), etc. The Lord was led first to Annas, contrary to the order of Caiaphas’s rank, who was high priest that year, so that everything might be done disorderly by him. For nothing is done in order where the killing of the Savior is being plotted.

“Are you also one of the disciples of this man?” Here it is asked whether Peter sinned by denying him, even if he loved him in his denial. Some indeed wish to defend Peter not only from sin, but even from denial. But he can be defended from neither. Yet it is asked whether, when he denied him, he had charity or not. Some say that at that time he loved no less than before [Col. 0873D], just as a father who gives up his son to death for himself does not then love him less than before. Yet he prefers the son to die rather than himself. But if Peter loved in such a way that he preferred himself to Christ, he had charity in no way at all, since charity consists in a person loving God more than himself. Therefore either he had not previously had charity, or else he lost then the charity which he had earlier possessed. But nearly everyone acknowledges that he had possessed charity before. Thus, out of an excessive affection and ardor of charity, he promised both to lay down his life and not to deny him even unto death. But it is said that he never had so great an ardor as would enable him to undergo death for Christ. If danger were imminent, he would rather deny Christ than undergo death for him; [Col. 0874A] therefore he seems never to have had charity.

But we say that there are many who have charity in affection and intention only, and many also in affection and in persevering constancy. Those, however, who have it in intention—namely, so that they intend that they would rather die than deny Christ—fail when they come to the test. For they cannot endure what they promised. They resemble Peter, who, as Jerome says, was like a bird without wings when he promised to die for Christ. For a bird without wings wants to fly but cannot. Peter therefore had such an affection before his denial; had he persevered in it, he would never have denied Christ out of fear. But because he did not possess the virtue of constancy along with this affection, when danger threatened [Col. 0874B] he failed through fear of death and lost the affection of charity which he had previously had. Thus, by denying him, he sinned mortally; this sin was wiped away by the bitter tears of contrition.

“And I have spoken nothing in secret.” It is as though he said: I spoke nothing for the purpose of keeping it hidden; rather, I spoke everything so that it might at the appropriate time become public and be proclaimed from the rooftops.

“If I have spoken wrongly,” etc. He seems to resist the one striking him when, as if reproaching him, he says, “Why do you strike me?” Yet he spoke the truth and nevertheless was ready not only to offer the other cheek, but to expose his whole body to punishment.

Jesus answered: “You say so.” First, there is a question about Pilate’s utterance when he said, “Then are you a king?” [Col. 0874C] He said this as a question and, it appears, affirmed nothing. But because the Lord, for whom it is impossible to lie, says that Pilate said that he was a king, we say that someone often asks in such a manner that, by the very manner of questioning, he seems to assert what he asks. Pilate therefore employed this manner in questioning, either because he believed it or because the Holy Spirit, using him as an instrument, caused the question to be expressed so that the matter was asserted by the manner of speaking.

But the Lord answers Pilate with a verb in the present tense: “You say [*dicis*].” To the high priest, however, he says in the past tense: “You have said [*dixisti*].” For by the priest the Jewish people are signified, who in the Law had long since asserted Christ to be king. By Pilate, however, the Gentile people are understood, who [Col. 0874D] were shortly to say this—namely, that Christ is king of heaven and earth. Hence he says, “You say.” It is as though he said: Soon it will come to pass that you say that I am king and recognize it through the power of miracles.

“You would have no power over me unless” (John 19), etc. First it is asked here whether Pilate sinned, when he strove as far as he could to rescue the Lord from their hands. Since, therefore, he delivered him to death and could do no more than he did, why should we call him guilty of Christ’s death? But it must be said that he ought on no account to have exercised authority over the Lord, nor, out of any fear, to have yielded to the Jews as they pressed him from envy. Because he did so, [Col. 0875A] he sinned.

Next it is asked whether Pilate’s power came from God and whether he used it in the killing of the Lord. It is manifest, as the Apostle says, that every power is from God, whether of good persons or evil; therefore Pilate’s power too was from above—that is, given by God—and therefore good. If, then, he used it in crucifying the Lord, he did not sin in that very act. But we say that he had a good power from God; yet in killing the Lord he did not use it, but misused it. Nevertheless, he had from that power the ability to misuse it in this way. Thus, a king exercising tyranny does not do this by royal authority, because that authority extends only to just things. Yet because he possesses royal authority, he can exercise tyranny. The power he has makes it possible for him to misuse that power. Thus Pilate would not have had [Col. 0875B] power—because he was able to misuse it against the Lord—unless it had been given him from above; that is, he could not have committed this wickedness against the Lord unless he had received from God the power which he had. Or, Pilate would not have had this power over the Lord—that the Lord should be placed before him as an accused person—unless he had received it from above.

But because Pilate had this power at all, however slight, under the authority of a superior—namely, under Caesar—the Lord therefore adds:

“Therefore he who delivered me to you has the greater sin.” For Pilate did this under the compulsion of fear of a higher authority, while the Jews acted solely from envy; and the one who sins from envy sins more grievously than the one who sins from fear. Therefore the Lord says that the Jewish people [Col. 0875C], who delivered him to Pilate, have the greater sin in delivering him than Pilate in acting. Yet Pilate himself is not free from sin, although he sinned less from fear than they did from envy.

“Now it was the Preparation of the Passover, about the sixth hour.” Mark says that they crucified him at the third hour. Here, however, it says that it was the sixth hour when Pilate sat upon the judgment seat, delivering the Lord to be crucified. Jerome reconciles them thus: the immolation of Christ began at the ninth hour of the night, when in the house of Annas he was judged worthy of death; and from that hour of the night until the third hour of the day six hours are counted. At that third hour of the day—the sixth hour of the Preparation—the Lord was crucified. For, as Jerome says, [Col. 0875D] it could not have been that at the sixth hour—from whose beginning until the ninth hour, that is, the end of the sixth, darkness lay over the whole earth—all those things occurred which happened after the Lord had been placed on the cross: namely, that they mocked him and offered him a vessel of vinegar, and so forth. For, seeing the earthquake and the darkness, they returned, beating their breasts.

“And it was written in Hebrew,” etc. The title was not written three times; rather, the three languages were contained in its several parts, as Jerome says. Thus: Malchus of the Jews, *exomoloson* [reading and sense uncertain].

“Woman, behold your son.” No one should understand this as though, pointing to himself, he said, “Behold your son.” Rather, [Col. 0876A] he says this of John, just as afterward he says to the disciple, “Behold your mother”—as though to say: the one for whom you are to provide care as for a mother. “Now a vessel full of vinegar had been placed there,” etc. Either by some chance, or perhaps by divine providence, a vessel containing vinegar was there.

“For they did not yet understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead” (John 20). From this passage, and from Peter’s saying to the Lord when he foretold his Passion, “Far be it from you, Lord!” (Matthew 16), it appears that the Apostles did not yet have faith in Christ’s death and resurrection, without which they could not have charity. We say that in Christ’s death they lost charity as well as faith, when they abandoned him and fled. But before his death, even when Peter said, “Far be it from you, Lord!” he had both charity and faith [Col. 0876B]. He said it from an excessive ardor of love. For out of the ardor of love he could not bear to hear of the death of him whose eternity he had confessed, saying: “You are the Christ, the Son of the living God” (John 11). Thus, in trying to prevent his death, he indeed erred out of piety, but did not sin. He also believed and had faith, but amid a certain enigma and obscurity of the mysteries. For he believed that what the Lord said concerning his death was true; but because the Lord was accustomed to speak to them in parables, he thought that he meant something else. Yet in no respect did he disbelieve what the Lord said. This is like the faith of a simple and unlearned person who believes whatever his superior believes, although he himself does not know how to distinguish its meaning. He acknowledges as true whatever is said in the Gospel, and yet does not know what [Col. 0876C] has been said.

“Whose sins you forgive,” etc. After breathing upon them and giving the Spirit, he says: “Whose sins you forgive are forgiven them,” etc. Hence it is asked what sins the Lord gave them power to forgive. For if, as some say, they received power to remit only the punishment of sin, this seems a small thing. For it is not much either to remit or to avoid this temporal punishment to be endured for sin. Peter is also told: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matthew 16). Some wish to understand this as follows: Whatever you show on earth—where the Church can only bind—to be bound shall be bound also [Col. 0876D] in heaven. For they say that the office of the apostles and their successors is to show persons as loosed, just as it was the office of priests under the old Law to show persons as cleansed. But merely to show this is indeed a small thing, and to have no effect in loosing or binding is nothing.

Therefore we say that the Lord principally granted the apostles the power to effect remission of sins—not merely of punishments but also of guilt; not merely of temporal punishment but also of eternal punishment—and granted it not only to them but to all their successors who hold their place on earth. Yet it remains true that God alone forgives sins, just as he alone justifies, although he justifies believers. For no one other than he performs what he accomplishes through his ministers [Col. 0877A]. Nevertheless, the ministers are truly said to do what the Lord does and ratifies by their ministry. Therefore, whenever priests, using the power delivered to them, forgive sins, those sins are forgiven also by God; and whenever they retain sins—that is, separate persons from the Church of believers and condemn them to death—those sins are retained.

I say, however, “using the power delivered”: for there are some who indiscriminately loose or bind. Of these it is said in the prophet: “I will curse your blessings and bless your curses” (Malachi 2). For, as is said elsewhere, “they put to death souls that were alive, and gave life to souls that were dying” (Ezekiel 13). Therefore, if a prelate, constrained by some necessity, binds a person who is nevertheless not guilty, or looses one who is not inwardly loosed [Col. 0877B], he acts rightly and does what it is his duty to do. Hence God also looses and binds—i.e., ratifies—what has thus been done by the prelate. Yet God does not loose the former in his soul, nor bind the latter in his soul; neither does the Church, whose judgment is always true. For the Church does not judge the former guilty, but to be bound, so that the rigor of the Church and the rule of justice may be preserved.

Therefore it is true what is said: “Whose sins you forgive,” that is, whose sins are forgiven through you, “are forgiven also before God.” This is stated generally and was both said and given not only to the apostles—as some say, claiming that this was the apostles’ prerogative—but to all their successors.

If someone says that sins are forgiven before God in true contrition of heart before the penitent person [Col. 0877C] comes to the priest, and that therefore they need not be forgiven by the priest, we say that this is not so. Rather, God first forgives them as soon as the person truly groans in repentance; he likewise forgives them in confession through the ministry of the priest, and also in carrying out satisfaction. For a debt is said to be forgiven as long as something remains to be done concerning the debt; and when the debt for sin is forgiven, the sin itself is rightly said to be forgiven too.

This is clear also in one who approaches baptism in true contrition of heart. Before he receives baptism, through faith and true repentance his sins have been forgiven; by baptism they are forgiven. Yet this forgiveness is not different from the former, nor repeated, but the same and continuous forgiveness.

“Put your finger here,” etc. It is asked whether the Lord [Col. 0877D] showed wounds or scars after the resurrection. It is clear that he showed scars only; these will appear glorious even on the day of judgment, perhaps more glorious than the other parts of the body, because in them the Lord displayed a greater proof of obedience. Certain authorities nevertheless seem to maintain that he showed his opened side.

“Jesus indeed performed many other signs,” etc. Here the book ends according to the author’s intention. Yet afterward he adds certain things for the reader’s greater instruction. For great mysteries of faith are contained in the matters which he adds.

“I am going fishing” (John 21), etc. It is asked how [Col. 0878A] Peter, after he had known that the Lord had risen, returned to fishing, when he had often heard from the Lord and perhaps read: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God” (Luke 9). But we say that he did not look back, because he did not return to worldly covetousness. Thus, although he had left boat and nets so that he would no longer use them to seek profit, he was nevertheless permitted to use them again to supply necessity. He was not permitted to use them for worldly greed.

“Come, dine,” etc. The Lord truly ate with the disciples after the resurrection, just as did the angels received by Abraham; yet the food was not incorporated into him, but was consumed by chewing, like the flesh of burnt offerings through fire.

[Col. 0878B] But this raises a greater question: how did the Lord prove to them the true resurrection of bodies by actual eating, since in the resurrection they will need neither food nor drink, as the Lord himself had previously said: “They neither marry nor are given in marriage; they are as the angels of God” (Matthew 22). For bodies there will be spiritual, not animal. A body is called animal when it needs nourishment. But it must be said that, although they had heard this, they had not understood it or retained it in memory. The Holy Spirit sent from heaven suggested to them many things which they had not understood and which they had forgotten, as the Lord says: “He will bring all things to your remembrance” (John 14), etc. Therefore, that they might believe more firmly, he ate with them to strengthen their faith in his resurrection, which they would have doubted unless he had established it by so many proofs [Col. 0878C].

“Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” etc. Jerome says that the Apostle Paul was both an apostle and a virgin and, as he himself says, labored more than all; accordingly, Jerome says that Paul was of greater merit than any of the others. If so, he also loved more than all the others. How then does the Lord say that Peter loves more than the rest? The answer is easy: he loved more than the other apostles who were present there.

“Another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish,” etc. The Lord showed Peter by what death he was to die and also taught how he would undergo the unpleasantness of death, saying: “He will lead you where you do not wish.” On this passage the expositor says that Peter was led unwillingly to that unpleasantness, but was brought forth willingly. For when Peter was led to death, he recoiled from death itself by the natural weakness of human nature; thus Peter, in the affection of the flesh, refused to undergo death and was led unwillingly. Yet in the Passion itself, through the ardor of charity, he lost this very horror; beyond this, the punishment itself pleased him and became sweet. Thus it is written of Stephen that the stones of the torrent were sweet to him. So he was brought forth willingly even in the affection of the flesh, not merely by the voluntary rational desire which he always had—that is, he was consummated in death [Col. 0878D].

In this passage it is also asked about Christ’s will when his Passion was impending. For he prays thus: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me. Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will” [Col. 0879A] (Matthew 26). From this they argue: Christ wished death to be removed from him; therefore he did not wish to die. But again, whatever the Father wished, he also wished. Therefore, since the Father wished him to die, he too wished it. Thus he did not wish what he wished—a statement not to be made.

It must therefore be said that there were three wills in Christ. Inasmuch as he was human, there was in him a will of the flesh: movements, namely, toward hunger, thirst, and sorrow, which he assumed for us not by necessity but voluntarily. These movements are sometimes called will; hence on account of these natural appetites we say also that brute animals want to eat and the like. But although these movements of our weakness were in Christ, they were otherwise in him than in us: [Col. 0879B] in us they are immoderate, but in Christ they were moderated.

But since this natural movement in Christ was that he should not die, it is asked whether that movement was rational or irrational. We can say that it was neither rational nor irrational, but natural. Therefore it was good in him. But if it was good, why did he not consent to it? It is clear that the will of reason, by which he subjected himself to the Father’s will, was better; therefore it was to this that consent should rather be given. These natural appetites in Christ are thus called will, according to which it is said that he wished the cup of death to pass from him.

There was also in him the will according to the purpose of reason, which belonged to Christ’s soul; according to this will he is properly said to have willed something. Thus whatever he willed with this [Col. 0879C] will, he also did. For it was in all things subject to the divine will and consented to it. By this will, therefore, he wished to die for our redemption. There was also a third will in Christ, regulating both the others: namely, the will of the Word, which was eternal.

When, therefore, Christ prays thus, “Father, if it is possible,” etc., he does not pray that the cup should pass from him; for if he prayed this, it would also happen. For he was heard in everything whatsoever he prayed, because of his reverence; for he was worthy to be heard. Rather, he prays that the Father’s will may be done, although the flesh itself recoiled from death. It is as though he said: Father, although the flesh shrinks from dying, nevertheless let not what the flesh desires be done, but what you will. For the prayer ends and is directed toward this.

Or, as some say [Col. 0879D], in saying this Christ prays—or rather, by using this form of prayer, instructs us what we ought to do when we pray: namely, always to set the divine will before our own. Hence some religious have the custom always to add to their petitions, “Nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will.” Whether this is said in this manner, therefore, or as was stated above, Christ had no will contrary to reason or to the divine will [Col. 0880A]. For only that will which is accompanied by deliberation is properly called contrary to the will.

“The disciple whom Jesus loved,” etc. Here Augustine asks how it can be that John, loving less, is loved more, while Peter, loving more, is loved less. That Peter loved more is manifest from the Lord himself asking him, “Do you love me more than these?” For he who asked knew this to be true; otherwise he would not have asked. Likewise, when it is said of John that the Lord loved him, a certain special privilege of love is attributed to John. Here, as Augustine says, there is manifest mercy and hidden justice.

Yet it may be said that the Lord loved John more familiarly than the others; hence [Col. 0880B] Augustine says that he loved John more. Nevertheless, Augustine transfers the discussion from persons to two lives: the active and the contemplative. He says that the active life loves more and is loved less. Since it is engaged in the miseries of this life, it more ardently desires liberation from them than the contemplative life desires to pass from the repose and vision in which it is now to that vision of peace where there will be complete perfection. Yet it is loved less by the Lord, because the Lord will wholly remove these miseries when he wipes every tear from the eyes of the saints (Revelation 21). The contemplative life, however, is loved more because the Lord will not take away the vision of repose which it has here, but will perfect it. Nevertheless, it loves less here than it will love in the future, because it does not yet know that future repose by experience; for now it sees “through a glass darkly,” but then it will love more when it sees God as he is (1 Corinthians 13) [Col. 0880C].

“If I wish him to remain,” etc. From these words the disciples thought that John would not die. He himself shows that this is not to be understood in that way when he says, “And Jesus did not say,” etc. Yet some think, from the fact that the earth bubbles up with a certain spring over the mouth of him lying in the tomb, and because this seems to occur from his breath proceeding from retained spirit, that he still lives. Augustine refutes this as follows: since, according to Paul’s testimony, it is better for the righteous to depart and be with Christ (Philippians 1), it would have been a small gift for Christ to give his beloved one merely not to die. Therefore it seems more likely that he has died and that his soul, separated from the body [Col. 0880D], enjoys eternal blessedness with Christ than that he should lie thus in sleep.

“I suppose that the world itself could not contain the books that would be written.” These words in Sacred Scripture appear, by hyperbole, to exceed all credibility. For the increase of things is sometimes indicated in this manner by this figure of speech. Yet the words, in their proper meaning, do not exceed credibility.

## Sixth Book of Allegory on Paul’s Epistle to the Romans

[Col. 0879]

[Col. 0879D] “God made all things in weight, number, and measure” (Wisdom 11). Weight is considered according to order. [Col. 0880D] Order is understood in two respects: place and time. Therefore God made all things in weight—that is, where [Col. 0881A] and when they ought to be; in number—that is, as many as they ought to be; and in measure—that is, as great and for as long as they ought to be. For measure is understood both according to magnitude and according to time.

(Romans 1.) “Concerning his Son, who was made for him from the seed of David according to the flesh,” etc. Christ consists of two things, namely human substance and divine substance, neither of which is the other; therefore, is not man God, nor God man? Solution: the first proposition concerns natures; the conclusion concerns the person, and therefore there is no valid argument. Thus a ring, insofar as it is gold, is a work of nature; insofar as it is a ring, it is a work of craftsmanship; yet a work of nature is not a work of the craftsman. Or: Christ is equal to the Father insofar as he is God [Col. 0881B], and less than the Father insofar as he is human; therefore he is equal to, and less than, the same person.

“By the resurrection of the dead,” etc. Jerome: “He never put off the man whom he assumed.” Therefore Christ was human in the same way in death as before death. But before death he was human, consisting of body and soul. Therefore in death he was human, consisting of body and soul. But in death the soul was separated from the flesh; therefore nothing consisted of those two. Solution: Christ was human in death in the same way as before death, but not in every respect in the same way. In death he was human because he had human nature—namely, body and soul—united to himself, although the soul was then separated from the flesh, because the Word was separated from neither. Before death, however, he was human not for this reason alone [Col. 0881C], but as Peter and Paul were—that is, consisting of body and soul. If, therefore, it is asked whether Christ was human in death, answer thus: “He was then human,” meaning “having human nature united to himself,” is true. But “human,” meaning “consisting of soul and flesh,” is false. Nor was he then mortal or immortal, but rather dead.

Again, if the soul was the bond between flesh and the Godhead, how, when it departed from the flesh, was the Godhead united to the flesh? Solution: Just as two people are joined in love by means of a third, yet remain joined when that third departs.

“The righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith unto faith.” Faith is so called because it is fulfilled by works. For one does not obey faith who contradicts faith by works. “Because when they knew God,” etc. There is a threefold knowledge: one preceding faith, of which it is said, “Faith comes by hearing” (Romans 10); this is understanding of words. Another follows faith: this is understanding of mysteries, of which it is written, “Unless you believe, you will not understand” (Isaiah 7). A third expels faith and will exist in the future, of which the Apostle says: “Then I shall know even as I am known” (1 Corinthians 13).

“They changed the glory of the incorruptible God.” Glory is a reputation extending most excellently, supremely, and widely.

“Therefore God gave them over,” etc., “receiving in themselves the recompense of their error.” The following objection is made against those who say that every punishment is from God: every sin corrupts [Col. 0882A], injures, and punishes nature; therefore, insofar as it is sin, it punishes; insofar as it punishes, it is a punishment; and insofar as it is a punishment, it is from God, as they say. Therefore every sin, insofar as it exists, has its being from God—which is not true.

For just as God does not perform evil—namely, an evil act or an evil will, for these are works of human beings—so neither does he cooperate with one performing evil. For if, when someone sinned, God performed that act which is evil, how would he not cooperate with the sinner? It must not be granted that sin is something which is from God; neither an evil act nor an evil will is from God. But “All things were made through him” (John 1) must be understood of natural things.

Punishment is sometimes called the matter itself in which someone is punished, such as fire; sometimes the action of the punisher; sometimes [Col. 0882B] the pain of the sufferer.

“In the likeness of the image of man.” Augustine says that, without impiety, the earth—that is, Christ’s humanity—is adored. Must it then simply be granted that a creature is adored, since it is a creature? Solution: This creature is adored; yet it must not be granted that a creature is adored. For man is adored not because he is man, but because he is God-man. Again, we adore Christ’s cross; how then do we not adore a creature? Solution: We adore the cross—that is, the one affixed to the cross. Yet in order that the mystery of the cross may be held in greater reverence, we bend the knee before the cross.

“They, knowing the righteousness of God,” etc. Justice is the will to render to each person what is his own. According to some, this “his own” is to be referred [Col. 0882C] not to the recipient but to the giver; this does not please us. According to Justinian: Justice is the constant and perpetual will to render to each person his right. God’s justice is God’s ordering, by which such a punishment is due to such a sin, and such a reward to such merit. The righteousness of God is also called the grace by which he freely justifies the ungodly; in this respect God is not just, but appears so. God’s justice is also called God’s essence, which is God himself.

“They did not understand that those who do such things are worthy of death.” “Not to understand” sometimes means to be ignorant; sometimes not to retain in memory; sometimes not to carry out in practice what one retains in memory; sometimes not to approve. “Not to know” is used in the same ways.

[Col. 0882D] There is death of the soul, namely sin; death of the body, namely the separation of the soul from it; and eternal death.

There is life of the soul, namely righteousness; life of the body, namely the soul; and eternal life.

The debt owed by prelateship is one thing; the debt of charity another.

“But also those who consent to those who do them.” A person consents to sin who either does not prevent sin when he ought and is able, or does not correct a deed when he ought and is able.

*Par* (“equal”) is used for “common,” as there will be equal joy amid unequal glory.

(Romans 2.) “According to their works.” This *according to* refers to two things: quantity and quality. Quantity is considered in two respects, namely magnitude [Col. 0883A] and multitude. Similarly, quality is considered in two respects: the quality of the work and the quality of the doer. Works evil by their own quality harm the one doing them, whatever the intention with which they are done. But one who does good things with a bad intention does not sin because he does them, but because he does not do them well; and perhaps he would sin more if he did not do them.

A comparison of thing with thing is sometimes made according to substance, as when it is said: “Man is better than every other creature.” Sometimes a comparison is made according to an extrinsic cause, as when the Lord of the vineyard compared and made equal the workers of the eleventh hour with those who had come early in the morning (Matthew 20): to both he gave a denarius; to both he rendered justice, not according to the quantity [Col. 0883B] of labor, but according to the fairness of the agreement.

The eternal Judge made an agreement with all. To those sinning mortally, he promised eternal punishment; to those doing good for God’s sake, eternal reward. Let no one complain if each person is recompensed according to the fairness of the agreement.

Fortitude is the deliberate undertaking of dangers with perseverance.

“To those indeed who by patient continuance in well-doing,” etc. Some are patient in good; some in evil. Some are impatient in good; some impatient in evil. Patient persons in good are those who persevere in good and cannot be turned from it. Patient persons in evil are obstinate in evil. Impatient persons in good [Col. 0883C] are those who easily withdraw from good, or who do some good with grumbling. Impatient persons in evil are those who quickly repent, or who rebuke offenders with a certain impatience and beyond measure.

“But to those who are contentious.” One kind of contention is venial, such as that of the disciples; another is investigative, undertaken for the purpose of seeking truth; another is condemnable, such as that of which the Apostle speaks, namely the opposition to truth through the presumption of loud assertion (1 Timothy).

Some do not assent to the truth because of the greatness of love, such as Peter, who could not believe that the Lord would die (Mark 8); others do so from envy and blindness of mind, like those of whom the Apostle speaks here.

[Col. 0883D] “For not the hearers of the Law are just,” etc. Hearers of the Law are called those who possess the Law but do not observe it even according to the letter. Hearers of the Law are also called those who observe it according to the letter but attend to nothing else in it. Again, “the work of the Law” is called what the Law itself teaches one to do according to the surface of the letter. The work of the Law is also called that for which the Law was instituted—namely, the work of faith; whoever perform this work of the Law are justified. This is the end of the Law: to believe in Christ and cleave to him through love.

“The Gentiles naturally do the things of the Law”: that is, they do so not aided by the Law, but by natural reason alone, restored by grace. Therefore this *naturally* [Col. 0884A] excludes the Law, not grace. That is: Gentiles without the Law, but not without grace, perform the work of the Law.

“Their conscience bearing witness to them.” Conscience is spoken of now in relation to good, now in relation to evil. It is called an evil conscience because it is bitter, because it bites back; just as punishment is evil because it is grievous. Where there is no knowledge, there is no conscience.

And you know his will. Note that God’s will is sometimes directed both to a thing and to the actual occurrence of the thing, as in the case of good things that come to pass; sometimes to the thing but not to its actual occurrence, as when it is said, “God wills the salvation of all human beings.” Some say that God “wills” means that he permits evils to be done. But does not God forbid evils to be done? How then does he permit what he forbids? Solution: [Col. 0884B] When it is said, “God permits evils to be done,” the meaning is: he does not prevent their being done. But if one says, “He permits evils to be done,” meaning that he grants or authorizes them, this is not true. It seems to some that one ought not to concede that God wills a human being to sin, or to be disobedient to him, or to be contrary to his will—though some do concede all these things.

“Having the form of knowledge,” that is, fullness, or form but not reality; an image but not truth. “You commit sacrilege.” Sacrilege is the violation of a sacred thing, such as a temple, whether material or spiritual, and, generally, of whatever pertains to the worship of God.

“Circumcision indeed profits,” etc. Circumcision is threefold: the first is that of the flesh; the second, that of the heart; the third, that of flesh [Col. 0884C] and heart. The first had its proper state in the time of the Law; the second, in the time of grace; the third, in the future. The first was a sign of the second, and the second of the third. Therefore, when the discussion concerns circumcision of the flesh, as when it says, “Circumcision profits,” etc., one asks what this has to do with the present state of those to whom the Apostle was writing. Solution: Much indeed, because Jews converted to the faith still gloried in their former condition. But just as in, “If you love me, keep my commandments” (John XIV), this does not mean that love can exist without keeping the commandments, but that keeping them is a sign of love, so some understand this of circumcision of the heart: “This circumcision profits,” etc.

(Rom. III.) “But God is true,” etc. He is *verax*—truthful—in effect; he is *veritas*—Truth—in essence. Again, *truth* is sometimes a name of essence, as in: “The Father is Truth, the Son is Truth, the Holy Spirit is Truth.” Yet the Son is often called the Truth of the Father because through him the Father has become known as truthful. Or the Son is called the Father’s Truth because he possesses the true nature of the Father; and this is against the Arians.

“Upon all who believe in him,” etc., because it is freely bestowed from above. Faith, righteousness, and every virtue are not earned from lower things; they are given freely. A person earns merit not by them, but through them.

A human being is not bound by the law of nature to die for his neighbour; otherwise no one below perfection could possess charity.

“Excluded,” etc. To exclude is understood in two ways: [Col. 0885A] either as to repel, or as to place outside what is shut in—that is, to make manifest.

Authority is a saying or deed worthy of imitation.

“For we judge that a human being is justified by faith without works of the Law.” He does not speak doubtfully, but makes an assertion with discernment. There is no judgment without discernment; it is free when directed toward good, oppressed when directed toward evil.

“Is he the God of the Jews only?” One asks why the Law was given more to the Jews than to the Gentiles, since God is the Father and Creator of both. Solution: The Law was given to the Jews for the sake of the Gentiles, because it was to pass from the Jews to the Gentiles.

[Col. 0885B] “We establish the Law,” that is, we set an end to it, so that it may cease; or, we establish it—that is, we give it the condition it ought to have, namely a spiritual one.

(Rom. IV.) “Wages are not reckoned according to grace.” Not every good thing that we do is to be attributed to grace in such a way that the merit of free choice is abolished; that is the error of the Manichaeans. Nor is it to be attributed to human merit in such a way that grace is excluded; Pelagius erred in this. We do indeed concede that everything is from grace, but not from grace alone when something is from merit—yet in such a way that that very thing is from grace. For every good merit that comes from free choice is from grace; but not everything that comes from grace is also from human merit. A human being naturally wills the good, but lacks its effect without grace; just as the eye, though it naturally possesses the power of seeing, [Col. 0885C] cannot exercise it without the coming of light. By free choice a human being can do good and evil; but free choice is a natural power, whereas the ability to do evil is a natural incapacity. How, then, does the ability to do evil pertain to free choice? How can the same thing be an effect both of power and of incapacity? Some say that the ability to do evil does not pertain to free choice. According to them, it is thus defined: Free choice is discernment of good and evil, with the capacity to do good and refrain from evil. But it seems to us that free choice is the faculty of discerning, choosing, and carrying out. I say this with reference to the first state; through sin this faculty has been utterly destroyed as regards execution, [Col. 0885D] but greatly diminished as regards discernment and choice.

They say that circumcision in the time of the Law had as great an efficacy as baptism now has. The following objection is made to them: One who is baptized is reborn in the Holy Spirit, which we do not believe occurred in circumcision. Again, in baptism there is remission of all sins; moreover, power is given to act well, to advance in the good, and to persevere in progress. In circumcision there was only remission of all sins; therefore it did not profit as much, nor have as great an efficacy, as baptism has. Those to whom every sin was forgiven were worthy of salvation not merely because of what they possessed, but rather because of what they were to possess through the grace of Christ. For the liability of original [Col. 0886A] sin was not remitted in such a way that it ceased entirely, but in such a way that it was sustained until Christ.

Abraham was called the first way of believing, because faith first shone forth in him.

The fulfillment of the Law was impeded by the multiplicity of its commandments, their great severity, and their slight usefulness. The fulfillment of the Gospel is aided by the brevity of its commandments, their greater sweetness, and their supreme usefulness. For what is briefer than: “Believe, and you shall be saved” (Rom. X)? What is sweeter than charity? What is more useful than highest blessedness? Before God, he is counted a father who seeks to beget children more for God than for himself.

(Rom. V.) “Let us have peace toward God.” There is peace in God, and peace toward God. Peace in God will be in the future, when God shall be all in all; peace toward God [Col. 0886B] is in the present. Hence the prophet says: “Peace upon peace”: as though saying, peace in exchange for peace, just as grace in exchange for grace.

“We glory in tribulations.” If the flesh conquers the spirit, it too will be punished for its victory together with the conquered spirit. If it yields to the spirit, it will together with it be rewarded with the robe of immortality and the crown of glory. One asks how one ought to glory in tribulations, when the Lord says: “Father, take this cup away from me” (Luke XXII). Solution: Tribulation occurs in three ways: as punishment, as correction, and for the increase of one’s crown. Again, three things must be considered in tribulation: its bitterness, cause, and end. Therefore, if righteousness is in the cause, one ought to glory in the punishment—not on account of the punishment, but on account of its cause and end.

[Col. 0886C] The exercise of tribulation turns the disposition for patience into the habit of patience; and thus tribulation produces patience—not the disposition, but the habit.

“And testing, hope.” Testing is sometimes used for purification, as in, “He tested [*probavit*] as gold in a furnace,” that is, purified.

Hope concerns a future good, with knowledge of the good [a good conscience].

A friend is loved in God, that is, because he is in God. An enemy is loved unto God, that is, so that he may have God.

Our goodness is nothing other than the affection of a mind cleaving to the highest goodness.

The grace of God is customarily referred to the Holy Spirit; [Col. 0886D] thus what is done by God’s grace alone and wholly is often said to be done by the Holy Spirit.

Every sin may broadly be called impiety, because it is at variance with goodness and piety.

“In whom all sinned.” One asks how all sinned in Adam, since they were not in him according to the soul, to which sinning belongs. Solution: Because they were in him according to the flesh, from which the soul draws the cause of sin; therefore all are said to have sinned in him. The flesh of all was wholly, though not in so great an amount, in Adam; it was multiplied in itself into such a multitude without alteration through food or drink.

“Until the Law sin was in the world.” One asks how the reign of death began to be destroyed through the Law. For once the Law was given, the reign of death seems to have been increased, [Col. 0887A] because “the Law entered in, that the offence might abound.” Solution: Some say that the reign of death began to be destroyed through the Law by knowledge of sin and fear of punishment, or that it was destroyed in idolatry through the Law.

If Christ is not one person, or is merely some human being, as some say, how does the Apostle speak of “the grace of one man”?

According to some, original sin means the liability for sin; according to others, ignorance and concupiscence; according to others, original unrighteousness; according to others, the tinder of sin.

If the first parents had not sinned, their children would have possessed original righteousness, by which they would have been worthy of life; the deprivation of this righteousness is called original sin according to Master Acardus.

[Col. 0887B] If sin did not exist, the soul in its earliest age would have the use and exercise of reason, because it would have no impediment; otherwise infants would be born lower than brute animals, as they now are. For in brute animals of that age there is a greater liveliness of the senses than in infants. Nature, when examined, proves both points.

In baptism original righteousness is conferred—not that righteousness which infants would have had had there been no corruption of sin, but that which is understood in participation in Christ’s merits. Thus the deprivation of that primordial righteousness is removed in baptism: not in such a way that its habit is conferred, but in such a way that it is not imputed. But this original righteousness, which is given in the sacrament [Col. 0887C] of regeneration, has as much value for merit as that first righteousness, and perhaps more; for our infants who die immediately enter into joy.

The soul has corruption from the body, which, like the body, is from Adam. Therefore the soul is rightly said to have sin from Adam, because that very corruption is the reason why the soul is subject to sin. In this manner, although the soul is not propagated by descent, it nevertheless draws sin from descent. Some say that original sin is forgiven in baptism only as regards the debt of eternal damnation, and remains even after baptism as regards guilt, according to the saying of the Apostle: “Now it is no longer I who do it, but sin that dwells in me” (Rom. XVII [probably VII]). Behold, the Apostle calls this [Col. 0887D] sin. But it seems to us—indeed, to almost everyone—that after baptism it is not guilt or sin.

“Christ merited,” meaning that he acquired something not previously due to him, is not true. “Christ merited,” meaning that he performed a work of virtue worthy of recompense, is true. The saints merit through the torments they suffer, although all is from grace; just as they merit through loving and performing good works, although this too is wholly from grace. Therefore, if one reads that Christ alone merited, let it be understood as when it is said that God alone is good and God alone does wonders.

Christ did whatever he did by free choice, although he could not sin; he did it not by necessity, for that would have been as though under compulsion.

There is merit by which we merit what we do not yet possess; [Col. 0888A] and there is merit by which we merit to retain what we already possess.

It may be granted that Christ merited immortality, that is, he rendered such obedience as was worthy of such recompense. One asks whether Christ merited equally for us in all his works. This seems so, because every work that he did was informed by equal charity; and thus it seems that he merited as much for us in his birth as in his Passion. Therefore we were redeemed at his birth, and thus before his death—which is not true. Solution: Although Christ’s charity did not receive increase in itself, it did receive it in effect. Thus God is said to love one person more than another because of a greater or lesser effect. In this manner one may say—and it is true—that [Col. 0888B] he merited more for us in his death than in his birth; and we were redeemed in his death, not in his birth.

“There is none righteous,” etc., must be referred to the greater part, and not universally to all.

Causal expressions sometimes indicate a cause, sometimes a consequence, and sometimes the occasion of something.

“Where the offence abounded,” etc. This “where” refers not to persons but to time. “To complete its course by night” (Wisdom VIII) is for sin to reign in a mortal body. Although Jew and Gentile commit the same sin, the Jew sins more than the Gentile when the Law has been given, and the monk more than the layperson in the same act.

[Col. 0888C] (Rom. VI.) “For we who have died to sin,” etc. Those have died to sin in whom sin is dead, at least so that it does not rule. Those live to sin in whom sin reigns and rules.

“We were baptized into his death.” “Into his death” means into faith in his death, or into the efficacy of his death, or you were baptized in likeness to Christ’s death. A person is baptized into Christ in two ways: either so as to be in Christ as a good person, or so as to be able to be in Christ as a pretender.

“Through the glory of the Father,” that is, the power of the resurrection, in which the Father, glorifying his Son, is glorified by the same Son.

He calls the body of sin the whole mass of vices, of which [Col. 0888D] the devil is the author. Or two things are understood in the body of sin: nature and guilt. Therefore, the Apostle commands that what is in the body from sin be destroyed, not that which is from nature.

When some evil is done through the service of our members, then our members are weapons fighting for unrighteousness; when some good is done through their service for God’s sake, then our members are weapons of righteousness fighting for God.

Then the tinder of sin, or the devil, rules us, when it draws us into mortal sin.

A commandment concerns things without which there is no salvation. A prohibition concerns things with which salvation cannot exist. Permission is the granting of a less strict life. Counsel is an exhortation to a better life.

[Col. 0889A] The principle of justice requires that a reward be rendered in proportion to the amount of merit. But Christ’s death is a merit for which we are debtors. Yet we cannot render anything equal to this merit in quantity, even by dying. Let no one therefore say that he owes no more than he can pay. Thus God’s acceptance of less than the debt is grace, without which no one is saved. For if someone rendered to God as much as he owes, he would not need grace. There is no mercy where as much is rendered as is owed.

(Rom. VII.) “And you also have died to the Law,” etc. It may be said that David in this respect lived to the Law, namely, that he was bound to observe it according to the letter; and in this respect had died to the Law, namely, that he did not seek to be justified by it. Likewise, he was with Christ through faith and grace. He did not yet, [Col. 0889B] however, observe the ordinances of grace and the sacraments of the new Law.

“That we might bear fruit unto death.” The Law of Moses is called the law of death because of transgression, which is the cause of death, or because it put sinners to death.

“That we may serve in newness of spirit, and not in oldness of letter.” He serves in newness of spirit who serves in those things which renew the human being and render him conformed to Christ. He serves in oldness of letter who serves in those things that make the human being old and conformed to Adam—one who keeps the Law according to its surface.

“Therefore the Law is holy, and the commandment holy.” Since it binds, the Law may be called a prohibitory commandment, as well as a commandment in matters that are enjoined.

“Good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh,” [Col. 0889C] etc. Such and so great is the union of soul and body that what belongs to one is attributed to the other, as sensuality to the soul and personhood to the body. “To will is present with me” by the endowment of nature; “but to accomplish” I do not find by the gift of grace.

“For I delight in the Law of God according to the inward human being.” Natural reason cannot be wholly extinguished in the present life. It is the eagle that flies above; the child who, while the other children are endangered, is not endangered. A person of the Law delights in God’s Law more by reason’s approval than by love’s delight.

The law of sin is said to be in the members through whose service it is fulfilled: as in the eyes, through which one sees [Col. 0889D] what one desires, and in the tongue by lying.

If anyone serves the Law of God with the mind, that person is God’s servant in mind; and if the same person serves the law of sin with the flesh, that person is sin’s servant in flesh. Since it is the same person who serves in both ways, it seems that the same person is both servant of God and of sin. Solution: If someone serves the law of sin in the flesh, that person is not therefore simply a servant of sin. For one is called the servant of that person whose will one gladly does. Thus, in those who partly love God and partly the world, one must see which love preponderates in them, and judge accordingly whose servants they are. “I see another law,” etc. There are three evil laws: the law of the members, the law of sin, and the law of death. “For the law of the Spirit of life.” There are three good laws: the law of reason, the law of Moses, and the law of the Spirit of life.

[Col. 0890A] Those who are according to the flesh savor the things of the flesh, and things that pertain to the spirit are tasteless to them. The word of doctrine and edification is bitter to them; tales, rumours, and words of dissipation they gladly embrace.

“The prudence of the flesh is death.” Prudence of the flesh is that which, setting aside the things that pertain to God, busily pursues worldly affairs. Wisdom of the flesh is that which believes possible nothing except what is accustomed to occur according to the usual course of nature.

We ought to provide the flesh with necessities, lest it fail; and cut away superfluities, lest it rage. But one who indulges the flesh according to pleasure makes a god out of a beast of burden.

(Rom. VIII.) “If by the Spirit you mortify the deeds of the flesh, [Col. 0890B] you shall live.” Hypocrites mortify the flesh by the flesh; saints mortify the flesh by the Spirit. The horror of death’s bitterness in Christ was greater than in anyone else, because he perfectly foreknew how great the bitterness of death is.

“You have not received the spirit of bondage.” Servile fear restrains the hand from an evil deed through fear of temporal punishment. Initial fear restrains one from an evil deed and evil will through fear of Gehenna. Filial fear restrains from every evil through love of righteousness. It is asked whether initial fear makes one a servant or a son. Since it restrains from evil through fear of punishment, it seems servile. Again, since everyone who restrains himself from an evil act and evil will is good, it seems [Col. 0890C] filial. For every good person is a son. Again, every person is either servant or son. Solution: Initial fear can coexist with servile and with filial fear. A person first fears temporal punishment, and then also Gehenna; finally, he begins to love the good. One is said to have servile fear who, solely through fear of temporal punishment, does not commit a criminal act. Again, there is someone who fears Gehenna and loves the good, but not yet perfectly.

“Heirs indeed of God, but co-heirs with Christ.” We are Christ’s inheritance and his co-heirs: his inheritance, because he shall possess us eternally; co-heirs, because we shall possess the Father’s kingdom together with him.

“If indeed we suffer with him.” To suffer with Christ is to suffer in the flesh in likeness [Col. 0890D] to him, or to be pierced in soul by remembrance of his death, or to relieve, according to one’s means, the needs of his members.

“They are not worthy to be compared,” etc. One asks whether eternal blessedness can be merited. How can what is temporal be worthy of that which is eternal? Solution: Temporal merit can be worthy, but not commensurate with an eternal reward, because more shall be given in the reward than was present in the merit.

A comparison is sometimes made between thing and thing according to what is in them; sometimes according to equity; sometimes according to agreement. According to what is in them, as when a horse is compared with a horse, silver with silver. According to equity, as when someone is hanged [Col. 0891A] for a sheep, according to the equity of secular justice; and when God punishes someone eternally for the sin of a single moment. This equity consists, or is understood, not in comparing the quantity of guilt with the punishment, but rather in considering contempt of God and transgression of the divine commandment. The same occurs in rewarding the good.

There is comparison according to condition or agreement, as when I promise you a mark of silver for the work of the slightest labour; and this comparison is not unsuitably applied to the punishment of evils and the reward of goods. For God has proposed this agreement to all: “If you do this, you shall receive this.”

[Col. 0891B] “The whole creation groans,” etc. Creation is referred to the Creator. Therefore, not inappropriately, all those who are referred to their Creator through faith and love are understood here by the name *creation*.

Christ delays, but he is not late. For that person is said to be late who delays beyond the due time. Hence, “Though he delay, wait for him, because he will surely come and will not be late” (Hab. II). “For creation was subjected to vanity unwillingly.” Creation grieves that it is subjected to vanity, for it would wish to cleave unchangeably to truth. Great is the vanity of the body; but much greater is the vanity of the spirit, which through so many temptations and wandering thoughts almost always vanishes away.

[Col. 0891C] If creation is subjected to vanity unwillingly and sorrowfully, then it earns no merit by enduring—which is false, since, as the Apostle says, it is subjected in hope of recompense. Solution: It wills and does not will this, but not in the same respect.

“And travails until now.” I do not believe there is pain greater than that of a woman in labour, nor a greater desire.

“Not only that, but we ourselves, having the firstfruits of the Spirit,” that is, not only the lesser members in the Church, but we apostles also groan.

“The adoption as sons of God,” etc. Have we not already been adopted as sons of God? Are we not already sons of God? How then is it said of the saints that they await [Col. 0891D] the adoption as sons of God? Solution: Adoption has already begun in us through hope, but it shall be completed through sight. Hope is certainty of obtaining a future benefit.

“We do not know what we ought to pray for.” Everyone who asks for what should be asked, and in the manner in which it should be asked, is always heard for his benefit. But we do not know what or how we ought to ask except through the Holy Spirit.

Ignorance comes from the corruption and weakness of the flesh.

“To those who love God all things work together for good.” One asks concerning a person who, having been at a high degree of charity, declines through sluggishness to a lower one, and thus dies [Col. 0892A] in charity: how does that decline work together for that person’s good? For it diminishes the crown and reduces the reward. Solution: Had the person not thus declined, excessive progress would have produced pride; and thus such a decline works together for good.

It must not be said that all good things which the wicked do work together for evil to them, since Augustine says that it was useful to have been good for one day. “Those whom he foreknew,” etc. All things are foreknown by God before they come to pass. Yet those things are said to be foreknown by God with a certain prerogative which he approves as future, just as he is said to know what he approves. All whom he thus foreknew, he predestined.

“To be made conformed to the image of his Son.” Christ is the image of the Father, that is, an expressed likeness, wholly similar and equal. The saints are conformed, that is, according to their measure following Christ’s footsteps in purity of life, obedience, and humility, so that he may be the firstborn. Christ, as born of the Father, is called Only-begotten; as having brothers, Firstborn. “Those whom he predestined, these he also called,” etc. God can foreknow what he has not foreknown, will what he does not will, and be able to do what he does not do. The past tense is divided on account of its certainty, which no other tense can have.

“He also intercedes for us.” Christ intercedes for us by the presentation of his humanity—that is, by the merit of obedience which he rendered in his humanity. This obedience is so pleasing to the Father that, by its merit, forgiveness of sins is granted to us.

[Col. 0892C] “Neither death,” that is, the threat of death; “nor life,” that is, the promised preservation of life: that is, neither fear of death nor love of life shall be able to separate us from Christ’s charity.

Nothing rules a person so much as that person rules himself. For a person can compel and change his own will, which nothing else can do to him. Hence the Apostle, whom nothing could separate from Christ, could himself separate himself from Christ; lest this happen, he disciplined his body.

(Rom. IX.) “I speak the truth in Christ Jesus.” There is one who speaks the truth and yet incurs the guilt of lying: though speaking what is true, that person does not have it in his conscience.

“I was wishing to be anathema.” “I was wishing” is used in the sense of “I wish,” as Aimo reads.

[Col. 0892D] “For this is the word of promise,” etc. It should be known that God’s promises or prophecies are made in three ways. Sometimes they are made with an unchangeable declaration, as in: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive” (Isa. VII), etc. Sometimes with a certain threat, as: “Yet forty days, and Nineveh shall be overthrown” (Jonah III), where the condition, though not stated, is nevertheless understood: unless it turns from its way, Nineveh shall be overthrown. Sometimes they are made with the free will of those to whom they are addressed—that is, so that it lies within their own choice to receive or reject the promise made—as here: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (Gen. XXII). This promise was offered to all [Col. 0893A] in such a way that each might accept or reject it according to his own choice.

“In Isaac shall your seed be called,” that is, in the sons of grace, who are signified through Isaac, so that God’s purpose might remain—that is, be fulfilled.

One may ask whether the original or the final cause is sought when it is said: “Why did God choose Jacob rather than Esau?” But there is no cause of God’s will, which is the cause of all things. Again, if the final cause is sought, the answer is that Jacob’s election serves to confirm faith and commend grace; for we must believe that what occurred in two brothers occurs likewise in two peoples.

That God reprobated someone from eternity means nothing other than that he preordained that, in time, he would withdraw grace from that person on account of guilt. [Col. 0893B] But someone says: Therefore a temporal guilt was the cause of eternal reprobation. Solution: It may be said that the cause of eternal reprobation is temporal. Temporal guilt was indeed not its original cause, but rather its final cause, in which it terminates rather than begins.

Concerning two people lying equally in sin, to whom God’s grace is equally proposed and offered, one asks: how does it happen that one consents to it while it is rejected by the other? Solution: Both were given grace by which each could consent; yet one person’s mind was moved and consented. This was possible by the good of nature, because willing was present to that person; what that person could not accomplish before grace, that person, stirred by grace, accomplished and rose. The other, though able, did not consent, but freely rejected the grace offered [Col. 0893C] to him. This is apparent in a ray of sunlight and in two persons fallen into a pit. Whoever opens his eyes sees, though not without the brightness of the sun. Whoever closes his eyes does not see. Likewise, whoever grasps my hand is drawn by me out of the pit; but whoever neglects to do so and does not strive with the help offered does not come out.

“The elder shall serve the younger.” This was fulfilled not in those persons, since it is not read that Esau served Jacob, but in their children, namely in the time of David and Solomon; or “to serve” is used in the sense of “to benefit.” Jacob was chosen without merit; Esau was not reprobated or condemned in time without merit.

The beginning and completion of every good is not from the human being, but from God.

[Col. 0893D] “Scripture says to Pharaoh,” etc. What does the example of Pharaoh have to do with Esau, since the latter is reprobated only for original sin, while the former is also commonly considered in relation to actual sin? Solution: Analogies and examples are introduced so that what is less certain may be seen through what is more certain.

“He hardens whom he wills.” God is said to harden whom he wills because he freely, not under compulsion, withdraws the grace that he withdraws; once it is withdrawn, the person becomes worse.

“You who answer God.” “Answer,” that is, contradict, because it is the part of one answering to contradict.

“Vessels for honour” are vessels upon which food is placed at table. “Vessels for dishonour” are vessels for the kitchen or for excrement.

[Col. 0894A] “Into vessels of mercy, which he prepared for glory.” God acts mercifully toward the wicked by granting them time for repentance; yet he would seem to act more mercifully toward them if they departed sooner, because they would sin less.

The Manichaean heresy attributed every good to grace in such a way as to abolish free choice; the Pelagian heresy asserted that good could be done by human beings without grace. But the teachers overthrow both errors. When Ambrose says that God chose Paul knowing that he would correct himself, he does not mean that future merit was the cause of God’s foreknowledge, but demonstrates that free choice cooperates with God’s grace; this is against the aforesaid heresies.

[Col. 0894B] “God shall make a shortened word upon the earth” (Isa. I). The “shortened word” may be called the incarnate Word, who is shortened in humility and fulfills—that is, completes—the Law.

(Rom. X.) “The desire indeed of my heart is for them unto salvation.” Will is sometimes taken for the inclination of sensuality; to distinguish it from this, one speaks of the will of the heart or of reason. That person sins against the Holy Spirit who envies the Holy Spirit because he works good through this person or that. Therefore it would be unjust for God to forgive such a person this kind of sin. But God cannot do what is unjust. “They have zeal for God, but not according to knowledge.” Good zeal for God is an ardour of mind by which one thinks that, for God’s sake, something [Col. 0894C] should be done or omitted; it is sometimes accompanied by knowledge and sometimes without knowledge. Here knowledge is called the knowledge of faith. Those who sin in ignorance obtain pardon more easily than those who sin knowingly. Hence the Apostle says: “I obtained God’s mercy because I acted ignorantly” (I Tim. I); and this is so because the saints read it causally. Yet it indicates not an efficient cause but something providing an opening. “For Christ is the end of the Law.” There is an end of consumption, as bread is “finished,” that is, consumed; and an end of completion, as cloth is “finished,” that is, completed. Christ is the end of the Law by completing it. “The Law and the Prophets were until John” (Luke XVI), that is, until grace; once grace came, the Law was no longer to be kept further.

[Col. 0894D] “For everyone who believes unto righteousness.” There is one who believes not unto righteousness: one who has a faith not working through charity, and is therefore not justified by faith.

“He shall live in it,” that is, he shall have sustenance in it, according to: “If you do this, you shall eat the good things of the earth” (Isa. I).

“This is the word of faith which we preach,” etc. The word of preaching so accords with reason that, when it is preached to reason, reason immediately rests in and consents to it, because nothing desires so intensely as that to which nothing else in the world suffices. Thus, when it hears what it supremely desires, it is either altogether blind and devoid of reason, or it consents to it.

“Whoever calls upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.” [Col. 0895A] Not everyone who calls, invokes. Calling is an outward sound of words, concerning which it is said: “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord’” (Matt. VII), etc. Invocation, however, is an inward cry—that is, the devotion of the soul sighing to God for things that ought to be sought; concerning this Moses is told: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exod. XIV). “How beautiful are the feet,” etc. By feet, actions are sometimes understood and sometimes dispositions, as in “their feet were straight feet” (Ezek. I). Sometimes feet stand for the word of preaching, as in “he subjected nations under [his] feet” (Ps. XLVI).

“Of those who evangelize peace,” that is, reconciliation between God and human beings.

“But not all obey the Gospel.” Some reject faith entirely, as Jews and unbelievers do. Some obey only with the mouth. Some obey with mouth and deed but not heart, as hypocrites do. All these do not obey the Gospel; only those obey it who believe in their heart, confess with their mouth, and fulfill in deed what they believe.

“Who has believed our report?” God speaks inwardly to the faithful soul in two ways: either by revealing knowledge of truth, or by inspiring love of virtue.

“Who” now indicates impossibility, now difficulty, now rarity. External hearing is the cause of faith for many, but not an efficient cause; it provides an opening. “For neither the one who plants is anything, nor the one who waters, but God who gives the increase” (I Cor. III). The word preached by the apostles is Christ’s word because it was uttered by his mouth; or it is Christ’s word because he himself reveals it inwardly in the heart.

[Col. 0895C] “Into all the earth,” etc. This authority began to be fulfilled among the Jews in the time of the apostles. Some hold that the leaders of the Jews knew Christ to be the Son of God, but could not acquiesce in this knowledge because of envy; rather, knowingly and against conscience, they opposed him. Others think that they knew him to be a just man and one promised in the Law, but not the Son of God. For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory (I Cor. II).

“Isaiah is bold, and says.” A person is called bold who dares both what should and what should not be dared, and in this sense the term is used negatively. Sometimes boldness denotes confidence of mind, a virtue by which an unjustly threatened punishment is not feared.

[Col. 0895D] “I appeared openly to those who did not ask me.” One appears who comes suddenly and unexpectedly.

All day long I stretched out my hands, etc. When “whole” is used for every part, this word “whole” should not be used with the name of the whole, as when one says, “He acted the whole day”: here not part of the day, but the entire day ought to be understood. Yet we often speak thus: “I wait for you the whole day,” where not the entire day but a large part of it is meant.

He stretches out his hands who bestows benefits. This the Lord did for the Jews all day long—that is, throughout the entire time of grace.

(ROM. XI.) God did not reject his people whom he foreknew. As there is a twofold calling, so there is a twofold foreknowledge: the general, which belongs to all; and the special, which belongs only to the good.

“They have dug down your altars, and I alone am left” (III Kings XIX). This must be understood of those altars which the faithful had built for themselves, not daring to go to Jerusalem because of the idolatrous kings after the division of the kingdom.

“He gave them a spirit of compunction.” Then the soul possesses the southern land, that is, the dry land, when the sun of righteousness by his presence dries up within it the moisture of sins. The lower spring and the upper spring are added (Joshua XV), when a twofold compunction is given: both from remembrance of sins and from longing for the homeland. Evil compunction is envy, which is a torment. The Sicilian tyrants found no greater torment: envy is the stepmother of another’s happiness.
