“Let their table become,” etc. As we are bodily refreshed at a table, so we are spiritually refreshed in Scripture, where various dishes are set before us.

“Into a stumbling-block.” *Scandalum* signifies now offence, now ruin, now quarrelling.

“But if the first portion is holy, so also is the lump.” The first portion is a small tasting of some thing, by which the whole mass is tested. The lump is the race itself; the root, the fathers; the branches, the children; the olive tree, the Jews; the wild olive, the Gentiles; the richness, the apostles. Thus the lump is consecrated, even if not wholly in itself, yet according to election; and the branches are holy, though not all of them.

“You were grafted contrary to nature.” It is difficult to define nature; for definitions are dangerous, as someone says: “Whatever is apart from sin is either the work of God acting without nature, or the work of nature cooperating with God, or the work of an artisan imitating nature.” Again, God works some things according to nature, others above nature, but nothing contrary to nature. For God’s power is so great that from any nature, without it, he can make whatever pleases him.

“So that you may not be wise in yourselves.” He is called wise in himself who believes that the wisdom he possesses comes from himself, or was given to him on account of his own merit; or who abuses wisdom given to him, exalts himself, and despises others on account of his wisdom.

“Until the fullness of the Gentiles should enter.” *Donec* (“until”) denotes both a cause and an end—that is, it is used causally, as here: “I did not do this until you did that,” as though your action were the cause of mine; and finally, as here: “I shall wait for you until you come.”

“Fullness” here signifies a multitude, not universality.

“As regards the Gospel, indeed, enemies for your sake; but beloved as regards election, for the fathers’ sake.” It must not be understood that the same persons are enemies and beloved. For the relation refers not to the same persons, although it refers to the same people; as in: “The woman who condemned, saved.” And: “He who walked upon you with his feet, who brought you forth from the rock in the wilderness.” Here it indicates not the substance of the water but its nature. Thus all the elect are loved by the Lord; so I too love all who love me, though I do not know them all; and so the Apostle loved all the elect.

“For the gifts and calling of God are without repentance.” Repentance is used for change, because what we previously did and regret having done, we change by repentance; as here: “It repents me that I made man” (Gen. VI), that is, “I shall change the work which I made because of human wickedness.” Augustine says that God changes his sentence, not his counsel. By “sentence” he means punishment and vengeance due to us for sin; by “counsel,” the eternal disposition.

“O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” Where we cannot fix the eye of reason, let us fix the eye of wonder and the eye of faith.

It is one thing to resolve something so as to remove a doubt, and another to comprehend a depth. “Depth” denotes both loftiness and profundity. Profundity is from eternity; loftiness stretches into eternity.

He calls the eternal disposition “judgments”; his operations, “ways.”

“For ever and ever.” A *saeculum* (“age”) is so called from following, because one follows another. “Age of ages” means eternity, because it follows all ages, and nothing follows it. *Amen* is an adverb of wishing or confirmation.

(ROM. XII.) “That you may present your bodies as a living, holy sacrifice.” We ought to provide for the flesh so that it may serve, not rage; that it may be a handmaid, not a mistress. Let it become a sacrifice through the mortification of vices, yet live through virtue. [Col. 0897C] It is asked why the Apostle commands bodies, rather than souls, to be offered in sacrifice. Solution: sacrifice begins from the spirit and is completed in the body.

“And do not be conformed to this age.” From Adam we were made old, deformed, and unlike God; through Christ’s grace we are renewed and reformed, and conformed to God. In this conformity we progress daily through the pursuit of reading and good meditation, prayer and good works.

“What is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God.” The will is good in faith, pleasing in hope, perfect in charity. Or the will is good in subjection to superiors, pleasing in subjection to equals, perfect in subjection to inferiors. Or good in married persons, pleasing in widows, perfect in virgins.

“To all who are among you.” God alone truly “is,” because he is unchangeable by nature. Hence those alone who desire to cling to God are not improperly said to be.

“Through the grace given to me.” Peter, eminent and powerful in virtues, was fittingly given to the Jews, who seek signs. But Paul, to whom heavenly wisdom was given above the rest, was given to the Gentiles as apostle and teacher because, as he himself says, “The Jews ask for signs, and the Greeks seek wisdom” (I Cor. X).

“Not to think more highly than one ought to think.” Since no one is so wise that in the present life he cannot and ought not to become wiser, who thinks more highly than he ought? Solution: he thinks more highly than he ought who strives by his own reason to comprehend matters above human reason—matters which ought and can be believed, but cannot be known. He also thinks more highly than he ought who exalts himself and despises others. He thinks according to the measure of faith who thinks or does nothing except what he believes ought to be thought or done.

“To each as God has apportioned.” God did not give gifts to Christ as man by measure, but the fullness of all gifts. Grace is given to each also for the benefit of others, so that what one cannot do by himself he may do through another. “Whether prophecy,” etc. Prophecy is divine inspiration, declaring future events with unchangeable truth. Or, according to Gregory: [Col. 0898B] “Prophecy is the manifestation of hidden things brought about through the Holy Spirit.” He has prophecy according to the proportion of faith who, in preaching, moderates his words according to what he believes necessary for his hearers.

“He who gives, in simplicity.” He gives in duplicity who gives to one from whom he hopes for greater things. Hypocrites give in duplicity, namely for the sake of glory. They give in duplicity who give in hope of present and future reward. He has a simple and pure intention in giving who gives for this reason alone: because he believes it pleases God.

“He who presides, with diligence.” Love expels negligence; fear, presumption. A prelate should not swell with his dignity, but fear the account he must render.

“He who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.” He who gives alms to one in need should not think that he diminishes his goods; for he sows, intending to receive a hundredfold, provided that he does this from charity. Likewise, one who forgives should do it with a cheerful mind. He should not reproach one seeking pardon for injuries inflicted. For this is to shame a penitent rather than to restore peace.

“Not slothful in diligence.” Some are diligent in heart and slothful in work; therefore he says, “not slothful in diligence”: that is, be diligent in heart, yet not slothful in work.

“Fervent in spirit.” Charity is impatient; for everything it does seems little to it. Hence: “Would that you were either hot or cold; but because you are lukewarm, I shall vomit you out of my mouth” (Apoc. III). Hot is he who is fervent in charity; cold, one wholly unbelieving or lying in grave sins; lukewarm, one who does neither great evils nor great goods: thus the saints expound it. How then does he prefer someone to be cold rather than lukewarm? Is it not a greater evil to be in mortal than in venial sins, and thus better to be lukewarm than cold? Solution: in those words he considers not the thing as it is, but the opportunity arising from the thing. For it often happens that those who are in the depths of vices, once converted to God, attain a greater perfection than those who are lukewarm.

The word of God should not be scattered everywhere indiscriminately, but a suitable time must be observed. “Continuing steadfastly in prayer.” Perseverance in prayer consists in constancy and devotion.

“Pursuing hospitality.” He pursues hospitality who receives those who ask and compels those who do not ask; and diligently inquires or seeks, lest they remain outside.

“Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse.” It is read in the Acts of the Apostles that Paul cursed someone as follows:

“May the Lord destroy [strike] you, whitewashed wall” (Acts XXIII). Did he therefore do what he prohibited when he said, “Do not curse”? Solution: saints, compelled by zeal for justice, do such things; therefore they have the action of cursing, not the will to curse, and consequently, as it seems to us, they do not incur the guilt of cursing.

“Weep with those who weep.” One ought to weep over the failing, fall, and sin of others; not mock those who fall; and one ought to weep over the delay of glory. Other tears have no good merit.

“Do not be wise in your own eyes.” He is wise in his own eyes who, although foolish in the eyes of others, seems wise to himself, and who relies wholly on his own judgment. Hence, when his opinion is rejected, he immediately becomes angry.

Prudence without simplicity is cunning, just as simplicity without prudence is foolishness.

The prudence of the serpent is to preserve the head in which is the venom by which it lives; the simplicity of the dove is that, when injured, it does not retaliate.

“Give place to wrath.” He gives place to wrath who patiently hears injuries inflicted upon him; who, when provoked, does not answer but keeps silence.

“Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord.” Whoever avenges himself, so far as he is concerned, deprives the judge of his proper authority.

It is asked whether divine justice and human or secular justice are contrary. This seems so, since divine justice absolves through a priest one confessing sin, while human justice hangs one confessing his sins. Solution: vengeance taken upon a thief according to human justice is exercised for the common good with some charity, and therefore belongs to divine justice.

“If your enemy is hungry, feed him,” etc. It is enough not to hate enemies, as Augustine says; this must be understood of outward effect, not inward disposition. For we are bound to will their salvation and, if we can, to assist those suffering the distress of hunger. “Overcome evil with good.” He fights lawfully who perseveres in the contest, who resists the stirrings of gluttony or anger and all unlawful things.

(ROM. XIII.) “There is no authority except from God.” We have from ourselves the will to sin, but authority from God; this must be understood as that by which we bring our will to effect, namely, our limbs and the power of our limbs, which we have from God. Some say that the power to sin is not a part of free choice, since it is not in angels or in God. These say that demons do not have free choice. Others think otherwise. The parts of free choice are the ability to abandon evil and the ability to do good. Hence, according to them, the devil does not have free choice because he cannot abandon evil or do good.

Authority is an ordering established by God in the human race, by which some ought to preside over others. Four things are required for authority to exist: institution, matter, order, and limit. It must have its institution from God or from human law; otherwise prelacy is not authority but violence. It must have matter in subjects, by defending the good and punishing the wicked. It must have order—that is, the equality of justice—so that it does not depart from justice but exercises authority through love of it. It must have a limit, so that it is not extended beyond what it ought to be and does not invade what belongs to another’s jurisdiction. Therefore, when a prelate departs from justice, he is not to be obeyed but resisted—not by inflicting evil on him, but by preventing him from carrying out evil. For in matters belonging to authority we owe him obedience, not in matters belonging to tyranny.

“To whom tribute, tribute,” etc. *Tributum* (“tribute”) is so called from tribunes, that is, it was what subjects paid to tribunes. *Vectigal* (“customs-duty”) was paid on goods carried in conveyances.

“Owe no one anything, except to love one another.” The debt of love discharges a person from every debt, though no one can be released from it. It should always be paid so that it is always owed, and owed so that it is paid.

According to Augustine, charity is the rational movement of the will toward God for God’s sake, and toward one’s neighbour for God’s sake. But God is not a movement of the mind; therefore is charity something that is not God? Augustine seems to mean that all are to be loved with equal affection, but not with equal outward effect. Jerome appears to say the contrary: “After God, the Father of all, let one’s father according to the flesh also be loved.” Again, the objection is made thus: should not one who pleases God more be loved more? But suppose another is better than my father; then I am bound to love him more than my father. Solution: understand Augustine thus: all are to be loved with the same—that is, common—affection, but not with equal affection. What he says elsewhere, “Let us love our brothers as much as ourselves,” means: let us wish them as much good; and, even if not with so great an affection, [the comparison is] in respect of likeness, not quantity. The second objection can be answered thus: it sometimes happens that we are bound to love someone more in outward effect than another who is better than he, though we may rightly love that better person with greater affection. For we are bound to love more in effect those whose care has been entrusted to us. Similarly, I am bound to love my father more in effect than another, although the other is better.

“He who loves his neighbour has fulfilled the law.” He is perfect who does not offend in speech or word (James III); yet he is not perfect because he does not offend in speech. Rather, not offending in speech is added upon the accumulation of perfection. Thus we say that a man is old when he enters his hundredth year; nevertheless, his hundredth year did not make him old, but old age grew from the preceding years. Likewise, of one who has many castles we say that he would be rich if he had that one also; yet he would not be rich because of that one unless he had the others too.

Some say that it is a greater good not to offend in speech than not to commit murder. Against them it is argued thus: if, of two things, one is more to be desired than the other, its contrary is more to be avoided than the contrary of the other. Hence, if committing murder is more to be avoided than offending in speech, not committing murder is more to be desired than not offending in speech. Thus being healthy is more to be desired than being swift; therefore being ill is more to be avoided than being slow. Again, loving God has greater merit than loving an enemy; yet, according to some people’s argument, failing to love an enemy is not a greater offence than failing to love God.

It is asked whether love of God can be possessed without love of neighbour; some seek to prove that it can as follows. If no one existed except one person, he could love God without loving his neighbour, just as Adam loved God before Eve existed; yet he did not then love his neighbour, since no one but himself yet existed. Solution: the statement “love of God can be possessed without love of neighbour” is affirmative and false. For it posits that a neighbour exists and that love of God can be possessed without love of that neighbour. Love of God is, as it were, the form and cause of love of neighbour; love of neighbour is, as it were, the matter of love of God. Love of God is hidden; love of neighbour appears outwardly, and in it love of God is made manifest. Therefore the Apostle says that love of neighbour is the fullness of the law.

“You shall love your neighbour as yourself”: that is, toward that end for which you love yourself when you love yourself rightly, namely, in God and for God’s sake.

According to Augustine, to love God with the whole heart is to love him with the whole intellect; with the whole soul, with the whole will; with the whole mind, with the whole memory: so that you direct all thoughts, your entire life, and your whole memory to him from whom you have what you direct. Hence it is evident that this commandment cannot in every respect be fulfilled in this life. Therefore he says: “So long as anything of carnal concupiscence remains, God is not loved in every respect with the whole soul.” He consequently asks: [Col. 0901D] Why, then, is this perfection commanded to man, when no one possesses it in this life? He answers thus: one does not run rightly if one does not know the goal toward which one must run. For we love in part as we know in part. Yet we cannot complain of the yoke of this commandment as though it were an unbearable burden, since its fulfilment is not demanded from people of grace.

Some say that every commandment of the Decalogue is among those without which there is no salvation; but this is one of them; therefore without fulfilling it there is no salvation? Solution: it is certain that salvation comes from Christ’s grace alone, and either this is not among those commandments, or salvation exists without some one of them. Again, they object to us thus: fulfilling every commandment has merit; therefore this commandment will have merit in the future, when it is fulfilled there and not here. Solution: insofar as we love, we keep this commandment, and by keeping it we merit; to fulfil it belongs to reward, and pertains more to blessedness than to virtue. Again, they say that in the present no one can merit a reward proportionate to the fulfilment of this commandment. But we say this is false. It is written of Abraham: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness” (Gen. XV). Thus the saints, through the charity by which they love God above all, merit God, and thus merit a reward proportionate to the fulfilment of the aforesaid commandment. They say that this commandment can be fulfilled in the present. Augustine says that it cannot. Hence he asks why it is commanded and answers not as they do, but otherwise. But what they object—[Col. 0902B] “I cried with my whole heart, and I sought you with my heart” (Ps. CXVIII)—does this mean that, if for a time, therefore at every time, one is worthy of salvation? Or if the Prophet thus cried or cries, is therefore every human being worthy of life? Master Acardus expounded it thus: “I cried with my whole heart,” that is, insofar as it is mine; for insofar as concupiscence possesses it, it is not mine. Thus they explain: he loves God with the whole heart who turns his whole intellect toward him; with the whole soul, who subjects his will in all things to God’s will; with the whole mind, who directs to God’s honour everything that he remembers having done. Does not the righteous person often think vain thoughts? How then does he love God with his whole heart? Or how is he then worthy of salvation, since, according to their opinion, no one is worthy of eternal life who does not fulfil this commandment?

“The night has passed.” “Night” sometimes means the darkness of the air from the absence of the sun; sometimes adversity; sometimes sin; sometimes the whole time from Adam to Christ; and sometimes all time is called night in comparison with the brightness to come.

“Let us put on the armour of light.” The armour of light is the virtues.

“Not in revelries.” *Comessatio* (“revelry”) is said to come from *comis*, that is, villages, because people were accustomed to feast in them; and from eating, or perhaps from a table contributed by many, which many evils accompany.

“And drunkenness.” The drunkenness with which Joseph was drunk with his brothers (Gen. XLIII) was not one of excess but of abundance, as Augustine says: just as the earth is said to be drunk, that is, sufficiently watered.

“Not in beds.” *Cubilia* (“beds”) properly belong to beasts because of their foul desires; thence, because of the stench of lust, the beds of the luxurious are called by this name.

“And indecencies.” *Impudicitia* is shamelessness, and is used for incontinence.

“Not in contention and envy.” *Aemulatio* is used for envy.

“But put on the Lord Jesus.” Those put on Christ who, neither through love nor fear, conceal the truth where danger threatens justice.

(ROM. XIV.) “Receive the weak in faith.” Here is the order of life and doctrine: first we should love ourselves, by casting aside evil works and doing good; [Col. 0903A] after that, our neighbour, in whom the fulfilment of the law is contained.

“But he who is weak, let him eat vegetables.” By vegetables is meant food from the eating of which no one is scandalized.

“For God is able to make him stand.” God is able even to make the devil stand.

If man had not sinned, poison could not harm him.

Things are called ambiguous which can be done with a good or evil mind, as the authority says; but according to this it seems that all external goods and evils ought to be called ambiguous, since they can be done with a good or evil mind. Solution: those things are called ambiguous which have neither an evident appearance of good nor an evident appearance of evil [the source sentence breaks off].

“None of us lives to himself, and none dies.” He lives to himself who seeks his own advantage only in his own life. He lives to the Lord who strives to seek his neighbour’s advantage and to do the Lord’s will. He dies to himself who seeks his own glory in his death. He dies to the Lord who glorifies the Lord in his death. Or he says this because it is not in a human being’s power to live or die, but in the power of the Lord, who rules our death and life by the fact that he died and rose for us. “We shall all stand before Christ’s tribunal.” A tribunal is the seat of judges; a throne, of kingship; a chair, of teachers.

“As I live, says the Lord.” “As I live” is an oath in the Old Law, as in the Gospel: “Amen, amen.”

“To me every knee shall bow.” The bending of knees signifies the subjection of all.

[Col. 0903C] “Therefore let not our good be blasphemed.” He calls our good the faith which a Jew blasphemes when he sees a Catholic eating clean and unclean things; the Apostle warns that this should not occur.

“Everything not from faith is sin.” Some say that for unbelievers even doing good things is sin; this seems false to us, since Jerome says: “God does not reject the good life of many.” Not everything done against conscience is condemnable.

(ROM. XV.) “But I say that the Gentiles glorify God for mercy.” The Apostle says that the Gentiles glorify God for mercy because a greater and more manifest grace of God was shown to the Gentiles. Nor does he say this as though Jews ought not to do the same. “There shall be a root of Jesse, and one who shall arise to rule the Gentiles.” Jesse is the root; David, the tree; Mary, the branch; Christ, the flower. Or Christ is called the root of Jesse.

“That you may abound in hope and in the power of the Holy Spirit.” Charity is, by a certain prerogative, called the power of the Holy Spirit, as though the mother of the other virtues.

[Col. 0904A] “Sanctifying the Gospel of God.” Those who preach good things but by the example of an evil life make them contemptible contaminate the Gospel, so far as they are concerned. Hence Gregory: “When a person’s life is despised, it remains for his preaching to be despised.” The Gospel is sanctified by giving an account of what it teaches and by the example of one’s life. At first the grace of miracles was necessary for such people. Through Christ we give thanks to the Father; for without him we are not worthy even to praise God.

“Of signs and wonders.” *Prodigium* (“wonder”) is said as though from *porro digium*, “a sign pointing forth.”

“If I may first enjoy you in part.” To enjoy (*frui*) is to use with delight.

“And deliver to them this fruit.” Almsgiving is called fruit because it produces both greater grace in the present and recompense in the future.

“Assist me in your prayers,” etc. What the merits of one cannot accomplish, those of many can; and it is impossible—that is, very difficult—for the prayers of many not to obtain their request. “Impossible” is sometimes understood in this sense. Hence Cicero says: “Friendship alone is the thing which brings impossible things within possible power.”

The Apostle practised the trade of tent-making: *scena* means a tent or a shade. He therefore made and sold awnings or tents and lived from this; and it is said that he divided the night into three parts: in the first he slept; in the second he prayed; in the third he worked. By day he gave himself only to preaching.

(ROM. XVI.) “That you may mark those who cause dissensions,” etc. “To observe” is taken in a good and a bad sense: in a good sense, as here, “Observe the Sabbath”; in a bad sense, as “they observed,” that is, laid snares.

“Contrary to the doctrine.” *Praeter* is used in the sense of “against.” “By smooth words they deceive.” A flatterer is a pleasant enemy; truth is bitter to the wicked and unlearned. Hence the Apostle: “Have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?” (Gal. IV). And the comic poet:

“Compliance breeds friends; truth breeds hatred.” (Terence, *Andria* I.1.41.) And thus it breeds enemies.

“I want you to be wise in good and simple in evil.” He is wise in good who uses well the wisdom given to him. Heretics veil falsehood under an appearance of truth. Those are simple in evil who do not return evil for evil: they behave as if they know nothing. Those are double in evil who return evil for evil, making two evils out of one.

## BOOK SEVEN. ON PAUL’S FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0903]

[Col. 0903D] There are two kinds of pride. The first is when we are proud of things that are in us, or that we believe to be in us. [Col. 0904D] The Epistle to the Romans attacks this pride, and therefore it is placed first in the body of the Epistles. There is another kind, when we are proud of things that are in others, or that we believe to be in others—for example, nobility of birth. The Epistle to the Corinthians attacks this pride, and therefore it is placed second. There are two kinds of humility: first, that we believe nothing to come from ourselves of which we ought to boast; second, that we believe nothing to come from others of which we ought to boast. Or this epistle is placed second because it is nearer to the Epistle to the Romans and is found more similar to it in the depth of its mysteries.

(I COR. I.) “Paul, called an apostle of Jesus Christ through the will of God,” etc. In a greeting he sometimes gives titles of dignity, so that, upon hearing the name of teacher and apostle, they may yield to his correction. Sometimes he gives titles of humility, in order to invite them to it. Among [Col. 0905B] those to whom he appeared contemptible and lowly, he calls himself Paul—that is, “wonderful.” “With all who call upon the name of the Lord.” There are those who call but do not invoke. Of them the prophet says: “This people honours me with their lips, but their heart is far from me” (Isa. XXIX). Some invoke in order that they may obtain things outside themselves, such as those who seek riches from God with the whole affection of their heart. Others invoke inwardly: they worship God freely, seeking from him nothing other than himself.

“You have been made rich in all things.” A person is rich in some matter not when he has sufficiency in it, but abundance—namely, when he can impart it to others.

“In all speech,” that is, in the Old Testament; [Col. 0905C] “and in all knowledge,” that is, in the New Testament.

“It has been reported to me that there are contentions among you.” Each of us ought to take care that, if we cannot ourselves correct the sins of brethren which are known to us, we should report them to our prelate. By doing this we do not incur the name of accuser, but avoid the guilt of one who consents.

“Was Paul crucified for you?” The supreme Shepherd alone gave his soul for the sheep for their redemption. Other good shepherds give their souls for their sheep, not for redemption but for confirmation.

When the Church suffers persecution generally, prelates ought not abandon their inferiors, [Col. 0905D] but should be the first to receive the persecutor’s sword. For the life of prelates ought to be an example and rule for the life of their subjects. But if the pastor alone is sought, let him withdraw, following Paul’s example.

“Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?” Since baptism is given in the name of the Trinity, it is asked how the Apostle can say that some were baptized in Christ’s name. Solution: the individual persons are understood in each individual name, and the names of the individual persons in the individual names. But in the primitive Church there was doubt whether Christ was God. Therefore, especially in order to commend the greater authority of his name, the apostles preached his name, so that he might be believed by all to be God, as he truly is. But now that faith has been commonly received, the form of baptizing handed down by Christ must be observed: in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. If it is asked what that name is: solution, “name” means knowledge, that is, faith; yet he says better “in the name,” because “with the heart one believes unto righteousness, and with the mouth confession is made unto salvation” (Rom. X).

“Not in wisdom of speech,” etc. By “wisdom of speech” he means worldly wisdom, which is adorned with elegance of words and does not rest on the foundation of truth. It is rebuked because it thinks God’s power bound to nature. Thus it says: “It is impossible for God to die; for a virgin to give birth”; and so, as far as it can, it empties Christ’s cross.

“For since in the wisdom of God the world did not know God through wisdom.” The world did not know God “through wisdom,” that is, on account of its own wisdom; “in the wisdom of God,” that is, through God’s wisdom. That is, the wise of the world could not know God in the incarnate Son because of their wisdom—indeed, because of the pride of their wisdom—and therefore it pleased God to choose the foolish and unlearned for this knowledge.

“But we preach Christ crucified, and the power and wisdom of God.” Christ becomes wisdom and righteousness to us when through him we are enlightened and justified. It must not be understood that the Apostle preached Christ as merely man to those among whom he “decided to know nothing except Jesus Christ, and him crucified” (I Cor. II), but also as God, and all things necessary to salvation. Otherwise the preaching would be insufficient.

(I COR. II.) What then does he mean when he says: “I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ, and him crucified”? Solution: he says this because among those less capable he wholly kept silent about the mystery of Unity and Trinity, preaching only that Christ is the Saviour and the other things which simpler people can grasp.

“Which God predestined before the ages.” Although predestination belongs only to rational nature, nevertheless “to predestine” is sometimes used for “to prepare.”

“Which none of the rulers of this age knew. For if they had known,” etc. The Gospel passage is raised as an objection: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him” (Matt. XXI), which the Jews are understood to have said of Christ. And what Pilate said to them: “Behold your king” (ibid.). It can be said that, although the demons knew Christ to be God, they did not know that through him they would lose the power they had over the human race.

Some explain, “Behold the heir,” as “he who makes himself heir”; and “Behold your king,” as “he who makes himself your king.” According to these, the Jews did not truly know Christ. But it seems to us that some of them truly knew him, namely, as the one promised in the law and as truly just. For no one envies evil, but only good. Yet those Jews envied him; how then did they not believe him good? Again, when he preached that he was God, they either believed him true—and thus knew him—or false, and thus did not consider him good. How, then, did they envy him? Moreover, in the Gospel of John, when the Lord had said, “For judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see, and that those who see may become blind” (John IX), and the Pharisees answered, “Are we also blind?” Jesus said to them: “If you were blind, you would not have sin; but now you say, ‘We see,’ and your sin remains” (ibid.). But we shall say that those who see do not see when they do not assent to what they see and understand. Just as the intensity of love does not readily allow one to believe evil heard about a friend, so the burning of envy does not allow one to assent to good heard or seen in someone. Among the Jewish people in Christ’s time there were five kinds of persons: openly good, such as the apostles; secretly good, such as Nicodemus; others who thought him a deceiver, thinking that they rendered service to God by killing Christ and his followers—of these the Apostle says, “For if they had known,” etc., and Peter, “I know that you acted through ignorance” (Acts III); others were learned in the Law and knew that he was the Christ promised in the Law, but could not assent in faith because of the torches of envy. There were still others who neither believed nor disbelieved that he was good, but doubted—perhaps those who said: “If he is the Son of God, let him now come down from the cross, and we shall believe him” (Matt. XXVII).

[Col. 0907C] “But we have received the Spirit who is from God.” He has the Spirit who gives thanks to God for gifts freely given, uses them for good and for God’s sake, and understands what has been given to him by God.

The natural person does not receive the things that are of the Spirit of God. “Natural” is said in three ways: either of one who has vegetative life from the soul—whence man was made into a living soul—or of life, or of the mind’s sensation, as has been said elsewhere.

But the spiritual person judges all things, and he himself, etc. The spiritual person discerns what is necessary for salvation and what is opposed to it.

The spiritual person is judged by no one unto condemnation. Yet a spiritual person may indeed be rebuked by another spiritual person, as Peter by Paul. [Col. 0907D]

(I COR. III.) I gave you milk to drink, not solid food. Where perfect and imperfect persons are together, higher matters should not be withheld on account of the imperfect, nor lesser matters on account of the perfect, since one and the same word is nourishment of milk for some and strengthening solid food for others.

Neither he who plants, etc. The preacher’s tongue labours in vain unless the grace of the enlightener works inwardly.

We are God’s fellow-workers. God works through us, and we cooperate with him; and thus we are made worthy of reward.

You are God’s cultivation. We cultivate God, and God cultivates us; and both benefit us, not him.

Other foundation, etc. He has Christ as his foundation who has it in his will and purpose that, if necessity pressed him, he would rather cleave to Christ than deny him. For he does not have Christ as his foundation who has no purpose of abstaining from every mortal sin. [Col. 0908A]

But if anyone builds upon it, etc. Works done from necessity or desire, signified by wood, hay, and straw, are said to be built upon the foundation because, being laid upon it, they do not destroy the foundation—not because they adhere to the foundation. Yet the Gloss says that these things are not to be understood of evil deeds; hence we say that by wood, hay, and straw imperfect works are understood.

If anyone’s work is burned up, etc., he himself will be saved, etc. Since sorrow over things lost is sin, the question arises: how can it purify, when it rather defiles? Solution: such sorrow is sin in those who do not have Christ as their foundation in place of their earlier delight; it is purification in those who love Christ above all things. In whatever a person sins, in that he is punished. Such sorrow, although it displeases the good person, is not therefore evil, though it is bitter. [Col. 0908B]

For the day of the Lord will reveal it, etc. It is read that such great fear will seize everyone on that day that all would die again, unless they were immortal.

Let him become foolish, that he may be wise. He becomes foolish in order to be wise who regards the wisdom of this world as foolishness before God.

The Lord knows the thoughts of men, that they are vain. Those thoughts are here called vain by which the wise of this world try to prove that God can do nothing contrary to nature.

[Col. 0908C] For all things are yours, but you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s. Christ served us, not as a servant, but as the supreme Lord. But you belong to Christ by creation and redemption—not to Paul, not to Peter.

(I COR. IV.) Let a man so regard us as ministers of Christ and stewards of the mysteries of God. The Apostle rebukes the Corinthians for their contempt of him, not because he grieves at being despised, but because in their contempt of him he grieves that they sin.

The Apostle dispenses mysteries—that is, the hidden things of God—and ecclesiastical ministries, assigning this rank of dignity to some and that one to others.

Not everyone who is a steward shares in salvation. But those who regard stewards of ministries as the authors of graces make the Church of God a church of men. [Col. 0908D]

It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you, etc. Is not one cruel who disregards reputation? How then did the Apostle regard being judged by others as a very small thing? Solution: the sense is, Your judgment neither exalts nor depresses me; whether your verdict is given for me or against me.

You reign without us; and would that you did reign. Those reign in the present who rule the motions of the flesh, and who so do good works that they become secure in the hope of the future life.

But not many fathers. “Father” is said by nature, by care, and by reverence.

Shall I come to you with a rod, or in charity? The Apostle does not distinguish between charity and correction—for it is the greatest charity to correct those who err—but between different ways of coming in charity: whether by sparing or by rebuking, where charity is present, though it does not appear to be so. [Col. 0909A]

(I COR. V.) Purge out the old leaven. New leaven is the fervour of charity, which each person ought to mix into three measures of flour—that is, into faith in the Trinity. Old leaven is perverse doctrine. Hence the Lord says: “Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees” (Mark VIII). Old leaven is also called the swelling of pride, which made us conformable to the old man; and every sinner who corrupts others.

A little leaven corrupts the whole lump. If you do not rebuke a brother who sins, when you know that he sins, you will be corrupted, and the lump in you is already damaged. But as hard flour is cleansed of bran by the grinding of millstones, so we are cleansed of the bran of sins by the harsh mortification of the flesh, when, joined together by the compunction of tears, we are strengthened in mutual love. [Col. 0909B]

That you may be a new lump. That is, that you may persevere—as you are, as you were made in baptism.

For Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. “Passover” is sometimes the name of the lamb sacrificed at Passover, as there: “Where do you wish us to go and prepare for you to eat the Passover?” (Matt. XXVI). Sometimes it is the name of a passage or crossing, as here: that we may pass from Egypt into the land of promise, from vices to virtues, from the world to the Father. Sometimes “Passover” means the very solemnity of the seven paschal days. [Col. 0909C]

In the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. Sincerity is purity from vices; truth is found in good things.

Or a fornicator, etc. To commit fornication against God is to prefer something to divine love. A fornicator is so called either simply, or as one against whom sentence is pronounced in judicial order. You may admonish one publicly confessed, but you cannot prohibit him otherwise.

(I COR. VI.) Indeed, it is already altogether a fault among you that you have lawsuits with one another. A lawsuit cannot be brought against anyone without sin, for either your sin or his is its cause. And from a small cause and lawsuit a mortal sin often arises: from the cause comes the lawsuit; from the lawsuit, discord; then hatred; then murder. Yet even the perfect may recover what is theirs, so that the robber may be corrected, not so that the bosom of avarice may be filled. He who cleaves to a prostitute becomes one body of the devil with the prostitute. He who cleaves to God becomes one spirit with him. This union is not an identity of substance or person, but a participation in blessedness. Therefore one should not ask whether that spirit is created or uncreated. [Col. 0909D]

Flee fornication. The vice of fornication is conquered best by fleeing. Therefore let no one trust in advanced age or a firm purpose of mind. Flee the material, flee the place, and flee everything that furnishes you an occasion for fornication. One whose face you frequently behold ministers to you perilously.

He who commits fornication sins against his own body—that is, by acting against the dignity of the body, which is greatly enervated and weakened by such an act. [Col. 0910A]

(I COR. VII.) Because of fornication, let each man have his own wife, and each woman her own husband.

Marriage is the lawful and voluntary union of a male and a female, celebrated with solemnity. “Lawful” refers to the persons; “voluntary” excludes forced unions; solemnity excludes clandestine ones. Of marriages, one kind is ratified but not lawful; another lawful but not ratified; another ratified and lawful. Ratified but not lawful is that which is made secretly. Lawful but not ratified is when blood relatives are joined without the Church’s knowledge. Ratified and lawful is that contracted before the Church between lawful persons.

[Col. 0910B] Marriage, which would have been an office for the healthy, is now a remedy for the sick.

One error concerns the person, another fortune, another status, another quality. A woman with whom it is known that there has been no carnal intercourse does not belong to that sacrament which is great in Christ and the Church (Eph. V), although she belongs to that which is greater in God and the soul. The first is marriage; the second, the office of marriage. To that sacrament which is in God and the soul belongs the marriage of the Blessed Virgin and Joseph, the holier inasmuch as it was freer from carnal intercourse. Marriages contracted with others after the pledge of betrothal has intervened cannot be dissolved. A marriage which is at any time dissolved was never true, as between blood relatives, whose union is considered a marriage while it is unknown that they are blood relatives, and whose children are received as legitimate heirs. For if there were true marriage between such persons, there would at some time also be a sacrament, which cannot be separated from marriage, any more than faith and offspring can. But if there is a sacrament, then while both live marriage cannot be contracted with another man or woman. Hence some maintain that there can be no true marriage between a believer and an unbeliever, or between two unbelievers, since it can be dissolved. Others think differently. For many authorities assert that marriages exist between unbelievers. But this, some say, is so as regards use and form, not as regards the truth of marriage. [Col. 0910C]

[Col. 0910D] The Apostle gives that one reason alone for which he permitted marriage, saying: “Let each have his own wife because of fornication,” though there are many other more honourable reasons. But I say this by way of concession. If marriage belongs among those things that receive concession, it seems to be sin. For to whom is concession granted, except to sin? To this it is said that marriage is good, but its act is not done without sin. Hence David: “In sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. L). Such intercourse neither is nor can be carried out, even between the righteous, without disordered pleasure, which is sin and an effect of original sin. This seems contrary to Augustine’s statement that intercourse undertaken for the purpose of procreation is blameless and alone is marital. Solution: such intercourse, although it is sin, is not imputed, nor does one who knows his spouse for that reason alone need any satisfaction. Concession, or permission, occurs not only where something greater can be commanded or required, but also where a person can be moved toward something greater. [Col. 0911A]

It is better to marry than to burn. Burning corrupts and deforms the material in which it occurs; so too the heat of lust found in fornication corrupts nature and stains it with the blot of infamy. Thus one burns who is overcome in fornication: that is, he is corrupted inwardly and afflicted outwardly with the mark of disgrace.

If any brother has an unbelieving wife, etc. If there is no marriage among unbelievers, or between a believer and an unbeliever, as some maintain, how does the Apostle permit the believer not to depart from an unbeliever willing to cohabit? Carnal intercourse between such persons will be either lawful or fornicatory. If fornicatory, it is mortal sin; therefore it should not be permitted. To this the aforementioned reply that many things had to be said according to the condition of the primitive Church which cannot be applied to the present. Hence, if someone were now converted from Judaism to faith in Christ, he would not be allowed to live with his former spouse, but might unite himself with another under the New Law. But intercourse between unbelieving spouses, or between a believer and an unbeliever, is, according to some, neither lawful nor fornicatory—just as was that between Abraham and Hagar, and between Jacob and the maidservants of his wives. But to us it seems that in all these cases it was lawful. [Col. 0911B]

[Col. 0911C] Otherwise your children would be unclean. He calls unbelieving children unclean and believing children holy.

The question is raised concerning a woman who has the gift of continence and believes that she has it: does she sin if she marries? This seems so, since she does not use the gift given to her for the purpose for which it was given. Likewise, one may ask concerning anyone who has a more excellent grace and remains in a lesser state in which, nevertheless, he merits eternal life. Solution, without prejudice to the better opinion: I say that she does not sin if she has not yet made a vow of the higher state. For every human being owes God more than he can repay. Hence, since God deals mercifully with all, receiving less from each than is owed, he renders a reward beyond the measure of merit. Jovinian sought to prefer marriage to virginity because there is greater labour in marriage than in virginity, and God will render to each according to his labour (Matt. XVI), and each will receive a reward according to his labour (I Cor. III). Solution: it is not true that where there is greater labour there is greater merit. Martha’s labour was greater, but Mary’s rest more fruitful. Again, continence belongs to counsel; marriage to permission. Therefore the former has greater merit than the latter. Again, John’s celibacy is not preferred to Abraham’s marriage. This authority seems to mean that virginity ought not to be preferred to marriage. Solution: individual privileges do not make a common law. It does not follow that, if John’s celibacy is not preferred to Abraham’s marriage, this person’s celibacy cannot therefore be preferred to another person’s marriage. If you consider the dignity of the states, John’s celibacy was more excellent than Abraham’s marriage, although John’s person was not greater in merit than Abraham’s person. [Col. 0912A]

The time is short. Because whatever has an end is nothing in comparison with eternity.

Let those who have wives be as though they had none. He has a wife as though not having one who renders the marital due rather than exacting it, and who is chiefly occupied with the things that are God’s.

And those who weep, as though not weeping. It is shameful for one who awaits eternal joy to weep over temporal distress.

And those who use this world, as though not using it. He uses the world as though not using it who does not place delight and hope in the world’s goods, but uses them so as to attain those things which are to be enjoyed. [Col. 0912B]

But I want you to be without anxiety—namely, evil anxiety. Evil anxiety is intense and troubled care which does not permit the mind to remain in the things of God. Good anxiety is that by which one is concerned not only to fulfill God’s commands, but also to add something beyond them. But you will say: how can anyone add beyond what he owes, when Augustine says that we cannot render as much as we owe? Solution: one thing is the debt of necessity; another is the debt of recompense, by which we are bound to God for all that he has done for us, whether in creating or redeeming us.

He is anxious about the things of the world, how he may please his wife; and he is divided. Care and anxiety over necessities, and provision due to wife and children, divide one from God. [Col. 0912C]

Let her marry whom she will, only in the Lord. And if not everything is done for God’s sake, at least let nothing be done against God.

The question is raised about second marriages, and beyond that about several marriages: how is marriage present there, since the sacrament of Christ and the Church does not seem to be present? For the Church is one, Christ does not die, and he is not united to another. Solution: succession does not remove the sacrament, since it is only one person with one person, not several at once with one person. An objection is made from Jacob’s several wives, because on this account the sacrament does not seem to have been present there, since several wives existed at the same time for one man. Solution: the Church is one, but consists of different nations; in figure and sign of this reality the ancient Fathers had several wives. But one woman could not have several husbands at once. [Col. 0912D]

But I think that I have the Spirit of God. The word “I think” is not always used doubtfully, but sometimes affirmatively; by this word the unbelief of those to whom the discourse is directed is often rebuked.

(I COR. VIII.) Concerning things sacrificed to idols, etc. Goods must be used in such a way that they are an example of good, not an occasion of destruction.

An idol is nothing in the world. An idol is nothing—that is, it has no power able to sanctify or defile foods sacrificed to it. [Col. 0913A]

Since their conscience is weak, it is defiled, etc. The mind is weakened when it begins to hesitate; it is injured when it becomes erroneous; it is defiled when it is subjected to the worship of demons.

Therefore, if food causes my brother to stumble, etc. Not whenever someone is scandalized by our words or deeds do we cause our brother to stumble. Many were scandalized by Christ’s words, yet he scandalized no one. Therefore he scandalizes his brother who says or does something in that brother’s presence whereby he is offended, though he can abstain from it with a safe conscience. For a prelate who offends a brother by rebuking him does not sin.

If those who knew that an idol was nothing did not eat meats sacrificed to idols out of hatred and detestation of the idol, then, although the weaker thought, because of such abstainers, that those meats were thereby defiled, they would not sin; indeed, they would do well. [Col. 0913B]

(I COR. IX.) For though I was free from all, etc. Did not the Apostle owe it, by the debt of charity and the office imposed upon him, to benefit all? How then was he free from all? Solution: he was free from all—that is, subject to no party—yet he subjected himself to the parties of all by will, not by necessity.

I became to the Jews as a Jew. But did Paul not rebuke Peter for this? It is not unfitting to say that holy teachers held contrary views where there is no danger to faith. Did Peter not err when Paul withstood him to his face? Such an error is venial, because it is not against conscience and charity is its cause. [Col. 0913C]

Though I myself was not under the law. An objection is raised from what is said elsewhere: “God sent his Son, made under the law” (Gal. IV). Therefore, if Christ was under the law, how was Paul not also? Christ was made under the law, not under the dominion of the law, but by fulfilling the rites and observances of the law, so that after him no one believing in him would be bound to observe them.

To the weak I became weak through compassion; to all, all things through conformity of conduct.

Those who run in the stadium. A stadium is one hundred and twenty-five paces, namely one eighth of a mile; it is called from standing, because Hercules ran that far in one breath and stopped. [Col. 0913D]

(I COR. X.) They all ate the same spiritual food. The ancient Fathers ate the same spiritual food as we do: the same, I say, not in matter or efficacy, but in signification.

It is read concerning manna that it tasted in each person’s mouth as he wished; so too Christ’s body tastes to each what he wishes—that is, it gives the virtue and grace he desires most. Some understand by the blood under the species of wine charity or faith. This gloss must be noted: “and it effected the same thing for believers.” For the sacraments of the New Testament have greater efficacy than those of the Old; it therefore attributes this efficacy not to the power of the sacraments but to faith.

If you make the same objection concerning ours, because they do not benefit those without faith: it is true. Yet they have greater efficacy and benefit those who have faith more than the former do. Just as these weapons are effective only in the hand, and those likewise; yet these more than those. It is read that Abraham believed the same thing that we believe; but he believed Christ would come, while we believe that he has come. But is “will come” not one thing and “has come” another? Why then do we believe one thing and he another? Again, what Abraham believed ought not now to be believed, because it is false—namely, that Christ will come. Solution: the propositions “Abraham believed Christ would come” and “we believe he has come” are indeed different; nevertheless, the article of faith is the same which we and he believe, namely Christ’s birth. What then does it mean that Abraham believed Christ would come, except that he believed in Christ’s birth, which at that time was future? [Col. 0914B]

He does not believe perfectly who neglects to approach the sacrament of baptism or of Christ’s body. All these things happened to them in a figure, etc., upon whom the ends of the ages have come. The end of a figure is the manifestation of truth. The ends of the ages are the truths, manifested in our days, of all things which were figurally prefigured in the preceding ages. Let no temptation seize you except a human one. Of temptations, one is of testing, another of deception, another of presumption, another of weakness. The Gloss says that suffering for Christ is a human temptation, because in sufferings inflicted for Christ a person is tested through the weakness of the flesh. When the devil tempted God, he uttered words outwardly (Matt. IV); he showed the matter of temptation, but he could not bring it about that an illicit thought should touch his mind. That whole temptation was outward. [Col. 0914C]

God is faithful, who will not permit, etc. God is called faithful by fulfilling promises; but a human being is called faithful by participation in faith and the performance of works.

Beyond what you are able. Sometimes temptation is less than our strength, and then it is disgraceful if we are overcome. Sometimes it is equal, and then, if we are overcome, it is culpable. Sometimes temptation is greater than our strength. But if we stretched the grace already received to the measure of our ability, that grace itself would immediately receive increase. God provides against temptations in three ways: sometimes by removing the temptation altogether, sometimes by lessening it, and sometimes by granting greater strength. [Col. 0914D]

You cannot be partakers of the table of the Lord and the table of demons. One may share sacramentally in the sacrament of the Lord’s altar and in the table of demons, but not spiritually. By virtue of the sacrament, faith may also be called an altar, and unbelief the table of demons.

Whatever is sold in the meat market. A *macellum* is the place where meats are slaughtered, and is thus named. “Dinner” is called *ἀπὸ τοῦ κοινοῦ*, “from what is common,” from *coenus*, “common,” because the ancients commonly ate at the ninth hour.

Do all things to the glory of the Lord. If this is a command, then one sins mortally who does anything—even moving a finger—not to the glory of the Lord. It seems to us that it is an admonition that we do nothing against God or with scandal to our brothers. [Col. 0915A]

As I too please all men in all things. How does the Apostle say that he pleases all in all things, when in many things he displeased many? Solution: he says this because he did those things which ought to please all, namely by avoiding scandal to his neighbour and seeking the salvation of all.

(I COR. XI.) Every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonours his head. He proves that men ought not to cover their heads in prayer or teaching by the reason of creation, of order, and of mystical signification.

The head of every man is Christ. The whole Trinity may be called the head and principle of man as regards man’s creation. Yet Christ is specially called man’s head because head and members ought to be of the same nature. The head of Christ is God: as regards Christ’s humanity, the whole Trinity may be called Christ’s head, but in this respect head and member are not of the same nature. Therefore the Father is Christ’s head as regards Christ’s divinity, not because Christ, insofar as he is equal to the Father, owes subjection, but because what he has, he has from him. Therefore a woman ought to have a veil. What sort of veil the Apostle means is ambiguous. [Col. 0915B]

Every woman praying or prophesying. Whether women were formerly permitted to expound Scripture and otherwise teach in church is not established; but that they are not now permitted is clear. Abbesses are permitted to explain Scripture and preach to their sisters, which, I think, the Apostle does not prohibit. The Apostle proves that a man ought not to cover his head because he is the image and glory of God. By the same reasoning neither ought a woman, since she is the image of God, to cover her head. Solution: here man is called the image of God, that is, a form. For as all things are from God, so all human beings are from man; and as God rules over all through power, so man rules over all through intelligence. But because the woman has a head, man, between herself and God, she ought to cover her head. Yet it is objected that by the same reasoning a man ought to cover his head, because between himself and God he has as head Christ the man. Solution: this head does not cover but uncover; it does not overshadow but enlighten. In sign of this, a man ought not to cover his head. [Col. 0915C]

[Col. 0915D] I hear that there are divisions among you—that is, heresies. A heresy properly exists where something contrary to faith is taught. Yet the Apostle calls schisms heresies where the unity of peace is torn apart. For all schismatics are heretics. Nor is it a lesser sin to tear apart the unity of charity than the unity of faith.

There must be heresies, as the Apostle says; therefore it is useful and good that heresies exist. Again, if it is good for heresies to exist, then we ought to will them to exist; and it is good that evils exist and happen, and that human beings sin. Solution: in expressions of this kind there commonly is and ought to be a twofold judgment. Sometimes we judge an expression according to the quality of the thing; sometimes according to its consequence—that is, according to the opportunity it provides for what follows. Therefore, when the Apostle says that heresies must exist, he considers the good that follows, not the quality of the thing. For the same reason Augustine says, “It is good that evils exist,” and “God is he to whom our evils are goods.” The teaching of blessed Augustine and of other doctors would never have shone so brightly had it not been brought to light through the attack of heresies. [Col. 0916A]

To eat the Lord’s supper, etc. It is read that Christ’s flesh is offered for the health of the body and his blood for the health of the soul; but do not both work the salvation of both? Solution: it is true that flesh and blood work salvation for both body and soul; yet flesh is referred to the body and blood to the soul.

The body of Christ received at the altar signifies the body of the Church. The blood received there signifies charity, in which, as in blood, is the life of this body—that is, the Church. [Col. 0916B]

It is clear to every believer that the substance of bread passes into the body and wine into the blood. Hence the question is raised whether this statement is true: “The substance of bread will be Christ’s body,” or “Some substance not born of the Virgin will be Christ’s body.” The statement is similar, but not altogether the same: “Some substance which was not from eternity is God,” namely human substance. Solution: the substance of bread, while remaining the substance of bread, will never be Christ’s body; but when changed into it, it will without doubt be so. Likewise, the substance which was not from eternity is God not by nature but by union. Concerning those accidents which were in the bread before consecration, one must hold that after consecration they exist without a subject, although this is contrary to their nature. For the order of nature is not to be sought where everything done is above nature. Likewise, although Christ’s body is already indivisible in itself, it is divided in the sacrament; nor do I say that it is so divided in the sacrament as not actually to be divided itself—held by hands, seen even by bodily eyes, crushed by teeth. Therefore it remains undivided and is divided, but in different respects. Just as God, remaining immortal, died, though in different respects. One of the portions remaining outside the chalice signifies our head now glorified; another signifies those members already joined to their head in glory. The third, which is now mingled with the blood, signifies those who are still held subject to the sufferings of this life. [Col. 0916C–D]

Drink from the cup. In Sacred Scripture the cup sometimes signifies Christ’s blood, as: “This cup is the New Testament.” Elsewhere it signifies punishment and death, not only of Christ and the saints but also of the wicked.

He eats judgment unto himself. Not fear. He who places Christ in an unclean vessel does him a greater injury than one who afflicted him on the gibbet of the cross. If anyone is in mortal sin and receives Christ’s body, he eats and drinks judgment unto himself. But if he does not find himself in mortal sin, because he is not without daily sins, let him repent of these and say: “Lord, I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof” (Matt. VIII).

[Col. 0917A] But someone says: Is such a person not worthy? Otherwise he eats and drinks judgment unto himself. And if he is worthy yet says that he is unworthy, he lies and thus becomes unworthy. Solution: the Apostle did not lie when he said, “I am not worthy to be called an apostle” (I Cor. XV), and yet he was worthy. Precisely because he says himself unworthy—which is true as regards his own merits, if the excellence of so great a sacrament is considered—God through his grace and mercy reckons him worthy.

(I COR. XII.) Though the members of the body are many, they are nevertheless one body; so also is Christ. He calls the head together with the members “Christ” because of the ineffable union of head and members. Then Christ will be a perfect man when all members are joined to him. We were all made to drink in one Spirit. The Holy Spirit is called a drink because he gladdens and intoxicates the mind; and what material wine does for the body, the Spirit does for the world. [Col. 0917B]

(I COR. XIII.) Charity hopes all things. Augustine: “It is not unequal charity, but unequal capacity, in one who gives much or little.” Hence some maintain that wherever charity is equal, persons are equal in merits even if their works of charity are unequal. But on this account good works seem to contribute nothing, although it is true that God will render according to work. Again, in his passion Christ merited what he had not merited before; therefore merit increases where there is no evidence of charity.

Those do not have equal charity who do not act equally, if they have equal capacity to act, as some maintain. Yet this seems false, since a contemplative man has greater charity than an active man, and yet cooperates less. Charity never fails, though knowledge will be destroyed: for we know in part, etc. The knowledge which we now have of God, and that which we have of creatures, is an image and a shadow of that which we shall have concerning God and from God. That knowledge will be in truth; this is in an image. This is in shadow; that in light. Therefore that will be other than this. This will perish and cease when that appears, as a shadow perishes when light approaches. This is called “in part” because now we know God only through creatures as intermediaries—so say some. But according to the same persons, charity is not called “in part” because even now we love God immediately. [Col. 0917C–D]

But now remain faith, hope, etc. There is a hope preceding charity, concerning the obtaining of pardon; and a hope following charity, concerning the possession of the crown.

(I COR. XIV.) If I come to you speaking in tongues, what shall I benefit you unless I speak to you either in revelation, or in knowledge, or in prophecy? For three reasons the prophets, Christ, and the Apostles spoke in parables and veiled meanings: so that those who are unworthy may not understand; and such things are also covered lest they become cheap. “In other tongues I will speak to this people, and not even so will they hear me.” They ought, because of the novelty of the miracle, to believe and be more attentive; yet even so they do not believe.

Therefore tongues are for a sign, not to believers but to unbelievers. Tongues are a sign of unbelief, lest what is holy be given to dogs. By unbelievers he means not all without faith, but those obstinate against faith. If anyone is ignorant, he shall be ignored. It seems harsh that the unlearned should be rejected by God because they do not know that women ought not to speak in church and that prophecy ought to be preferred to tongues. Solution to these and similar matters: this is dangerous not for everyone, but for prophets and spiritual persons. [Col. 0918A]

(I COR. XV.) For I am the least of the Apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, etc. There is a great question how the Apostle speaks truth in calling himself the least of the Apostles when he was among the greater. Solution: some say that whenever saints use words of humility, they thereby signify that they hold an office by which they are bound to serve others. You will find the solution to this question treated more fully in our *Questions on the Epistles of Paul*. Another glory of the sun, another glory of the moon, and another glory of the stars. In the future there will be a twofold participation in joy: according to experience and according to affection. Glory will differ according to experience; joy will be equal—that is, common—according to affection. Or it is equal because whatever one rejoices over, another also rejoices over.

Ignorance is of one kind through contempt, of another through weakness, of another through deficiency of reason. By the sun are signified those having the number one hundred; by the moon, sixty; by the stars, thirty. It will rise in glory, etc. The glory of bodies will proceed from the blessedness of souls, greater or less according to diversity of merits. Nor is this surprising: for, as Solomon says, “A rejoicing heart makes the face cheerful” (Prov. V), and the brightness of the sun illuminates a glass body. But that in the highest good one will rejoice more and another less will not arise from that good—which will be whole, not divided into parts, in all—but from this: one will be more capable of the highest good and another less capable. There is a natural body and there is a spiritual body. First that which is natural, then that which is spiritual. A natural body is one that has vegetative life from the soul in such a way that it also needs external food for sustenance; such was Christ’s body before the resurrection. Then comes the spiritual body. Therefore those err who say that Christ’s body, from the moment it was assumed, was immortal and impassible. [Col. 0918B–D]

A spiritual body is one that does not require bodily food for its support. The good in the future will be both immortal and impassible; the wicked, immortal but passible. “Death has been swallowed up in victory.” The death of the body has as yet been swallowed up only in Christ, namely through the resurrection. In the present life, the death of the soul is swallowed up in us through Christ’s resurrection. In the future, the death of the flesh will be swallowed up in us. “The sting of death is sin,” etc. A sting is a barb which, by its thrust, pierces the skin; and therefore sin is called the sting of death, because through sin death entered and found an entrance; or because impulses entice the soul and incite it to sin. Therefore original sin is called the sting.

## BOOK EIGHT. ON PAUL’S SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS

[Col. 0919]

[Col. 0919A] **(2 Cor. 1.)** “Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God.” Evil persons are chosen by God’s will and through election become good, as Paul did. Evil persons are also chosen by God’s will—if not for their own good, yet for the good of others—as Judas was. Good persons too are chosen by God’s will, those who by merit of life and knowledge are ordained to govern the Church. In these days, it is the ruler’s will concerning those to be chosen that is awaited, not God’s.

“Blessed be God and Father of our Lord.” As the assumed man was assumed by grace, and by grace the natural—not adoptive—Son of God was made, so it appears that God the Father is Father of the assumed man by grace; nevertheless, not an adoptive Father but a natural Father.

God is Christ’s Father by generation; ours by mercy. [Col. 0919B] “In whom we hope, because he will still deliver us.” To hope *from* someone is to expect some help from that person, which is permissible even from a human being. To hope *in* someone is to place in him one’s whole hope of salvation and assistance; this is lawful only in God.

“While you also help through prayer for us.” There are three things which commonly hinder a petition: namely, that the person who asks is unworthy, or the person for whom he asks, or the thing which he asks. Again, sometimes an unworthy person asks and is heard, as Satan; sometimes a worthy person is not heard, as Paul; sometimes a worthy person asks for the unworthy and is heard, as Moses for the children of Israel.

“Our glory is this: the testimony of our conscience.” One may ask how the Apostle glories in the testimony of a good conscience, when, according to the same Apostle, one must glory in God alone. Solution: [Col. 0919C] to glory in the testimony of a good conscience and to glory in God are not different things; indeed, they are joined. For a good conscience imitates God and clings to him; otherwise one ought not to glory in it.

“That in simplicity of heart and sincerity of God,” etc. Simplicity is doing something solely from zeal for justice and for God; and, lest error be mixed with it, it must be sincere and discerning.

“Since I did not wish this, did I use fickleness?” Other writings judge utterances according to the meaning of the words; Holy Scripture, however, according to the intention of the speaker. Thus the former call anyone a liar who is known to state something false; Holy Scripture judges only that person to lie who speaks [Col. 0919D] against his own conscience. For what is lying except going against one’s own mind?

Someone says: “The Apostle did not fulfil what he promised; therefore he either deceived or was deceived.” Solution: The Apostle James teaches that, in utterances concerning a contingent future, a condition must be added or understood—namely, “if God wills” [Col. 0920A]—which the Apostle did not express in words but nonetheless had in mind.

It is asked concerning the Jews whether, in denying that Christ is God, they lie, since they do not speak against their conscience. Solution: They have been blinded, and therefore in denying these things they are guilty of lying.

“And he gave the pledge of the Spirit in our hearts.” A pledge makes the seller certain that he will receive the price; so charity makes one certain of eternal glory and is therefore called a pledge.

**(2 Cor. 2.)** “That you should rather forgive and comfort him.” Forgiveness must be granted to a penitent when, burdened by weakness, he cannot perform the imposed penance, or lest he despair because of excessive harshness.

“That we may not be outwitted by Satan.” The devil causes a prelate whom he cannot seduce through consent to sin to rage against his subjects through excessive severity under the appearance of correction. [Col. 0920B] A subject, on the other hand, is outwitted when he falls into worse things through despair or sets against him the brow of disobedience.

“To some indeed an odor of death,” etc. The wicked make the fragrance of life into a fragrance of death for themselves.

“Adulterating the word of God.” Those are called adulterers of God’s word who strive not to beget children in faith, but to fulfil temporal gratification.

**(2 Cor. 3.)** “The letter kills,” because it punishes without mercy; “the spirit gives life,” by sparing and remitting guilt.

“Beholding with unveiled face the glory of the Lord.” We behold the Lord’s glory in two ways: either in creatures, by attending to his power, wisdom, and goodness; or by faith and reason, contemplating him in himself.

“We are transformed into the same image.” [Col. 0920C] God’s image in us has been deformed through sin; but by grace we are re-formed into that same image—that is, into its integrity—or transformed into the image for which we were made, so that we may become like it.

The lower waters—that is, the affections of the flesh—must be gathered into one place and brought under the command of reason. The upper waters—that is, the desires of the spirit—must not be gathered into one place, because charity ought not to be restrained but extended to all.

**(2 Cor. 4.)** “In the face of Christ Jesus,” that is, before Christ, who is the face of the Father, because through him knowledge is obtained.

The necessity of compulsion is one thing; the requirement of due obedience another.

**(2 Cor. 5.)** “We groan, longing to be clothed upon with our habitation [Col. 0920D] which is from heaven; because we do not wish to be unclothed, but further clothed.” The affection of reason is one thing; the affection of the flesh another. By the affection of the flesh, the Apostle wished to pass to immortality without death; by the affection of reason, he wished to be dissolved and to be with Christ. The affection of the flesh is not meritorious—that is, neither good nor evil—because it is natural. With such an affection [Col. 0921A] we flee all bitter things and things contrary to the flesh, and on days of abstinence desire food before the hour.

“If indeed we are found clothed and not naked.” Clothed, namely, with faith, as the Gloss says. Therefore faith will remain when the body is laid aside. No: but he calls the object of faith “faith.”

“That each may receive the things proper to the body,” etc. This is true even of children, who believed or did not believe through others. Therefore the baptized will receive according to what was done in their body—that is, according to what was done by others in their body. But what will the unbaptized receive, since they themselves did nothing in the body, nor was anything done by others in their body, for which they might be condemned? Solution: Some say that they too had disordered impulses, for which they are condemned.

“We persuade people by the fear of the Lord.” Why fear rather [Col. 0921B] than love? Solution: This is said of filial fear, which nevertheless seems to belong more to precept than to exhortation. Yet it is with this fear as with faith: it cannot be compelled, but only urged.

“For whether we are beside ourselves, it is for God; or whether we are sober, it is for you.” Whatever we do is either for God’s honor or for our neighbor’s benefit. In some things, however, God’s honor appears especially, as when wisdom is preached among the perfect; in others, the neighbor’s benefit, as when milk is supplied to little ones.

An excess of mind is called ecstasy, namely when the mind is carried above itself. This happens sometimes through the swelling of pride; sometimes through the greatness of pain or fear, or also joy; and sometimes through rational contemplation, namely when the mind is carried by desire to heavenly things, retaining no [Col. 0921C] memory of lower things. Holy men devote themselves to this.

“For indeed God was in Christ reconciling the world.” God was in Christ: divinity in the assumed man.

**(2 Cor. 6.)** “Do not receive the grace of God in vain.” Augustine says: “It is beneficial even to have been good for one day,” which seems contrary to: “It would have been better not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to have turned back,” because one is condemned for ingratitude and contempt. Solution: these authorities concern different persons: the first, sinners who are not unbelievers; the second, those who after faith return to unbelief.

“Our mouth is open to you, O Corinthians.” Ignorance closes some people’s mouths; fear or [Col. 0921D] love closes others’; perverse life closes others’; acceptance of gifts closes others’.

“Come out from among them and be separate,” etc. We commit a greater evil in separating from the good than we contract by association with the wicked.
