This is not said universally of everyone, but of prelates and the perfect who sin grievously by leaving subjects and imperfect persons among the wicked whom they ought to strengthen by their presence. Lesser persons and subjects, because they fear that evil conversations may corrupt good morals (1 Cor. 15), do not seem to sin if they separate themselves even locally from the wicked, although some good persons may be among them.

Those who live in the world, as the authority says, do not possess merits sufficient for eternal life; but through the merits of those whom they support by alms [Col. 0922A] they obtain what they cannot obtain by themselves. But how? If they do not have charity, they do not seem able to be saved through others’ merits. For without charity no one is worthy of salvation. Solution: this was said of those who are not yet able to escape the habit of sinning. Through the merits of others they will obtain salvation: first grace, by which they may be delivered; afterward charity, by which they may be worthy of glory.

**(2 Cor. 8.)** “For if willingness is ready, it is accepted according to what one has, not according to what one does not have.” Concerning two persons unequal in resources, one may ask whether they merit equally if they give equally and with equal disposition. This seems so, because God weighs not one’s wealth but one’s disposition: not how much [Col. 0922B] one gives, but out of how much. These two, however, are equal in disposition; therefore, according to the common opinion of all, they are equal also in merit.

Again, an objection is made as follows. Everyone is bound to act according to his means; therefore one who has more is bound to give more; therefore he sins if he does not contribute more. Solution: it may be said that one who has more is bound by a debt of perfection, not of salvation: that is, this is required of him in order that he may be perfect, not in order that he may be saved—that he act according to his means. It may also happen that one who has more, although he does not give more, nevertheless merits equally, because, just as he gives from charity, so he retains from charity, in order to give to others who are more needy.

Nor is there any inconsistency in the fact that, although they give with equal disposition, they do not merit equally. The contrary occurs [Col. 0922C] when some persons commit a sin with equal pleasure, yet one is held more guilty than another—for instance, if a layman and a monk commit fornication with equal pleasure.

“For we provide what is good not only before God but also before people.” It belongs to a prudent person to act in such a way as to please in God’s eyes and so that people find nothing reprehensible in his actions. Yet we cannot prevent people from disparaging our good works; but that arises not from the quality of the works, but from the perversity of people.

Augustine says: “One who, trusting in his conscience, neglects his reputation is cruel.” But what does he call reputation except human praise? We ought not only to neglect this but [Col. 0922D] also to flee it. Solution: the person who neglects reputation is one who acts so as to cause scandal to brethren, although he could lawfully refrain from doing so. But the saying that we must flee human praise is to be understood with respect to ourselves.

**(2 Cor. 9.)** “He who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly.” How will one who receives eternal life and God himself in reaping reap sparingly? Solution: this is said because, just as there is diversity of merits, so there will be a difference of rewards, so that one who has merited less receives less.

**(2 Cor. 10.)** “Those who think that we walk according to the flesh.” A person walks according to the flesh who follows fleshly desires, acts and is acted upon according to the wisdom of the world, and thinks that the Law must still be observed according to the flesh. [Col. 0923A]

“And being ready to avenge all disobedience.” Readiness to avenge every disobedience consists in three things: namely, life, knowledge, and authority. How can one whose life is disobedient and criminal judge another’s disobedience and crime? Knowledge is required so that one may know how to temper correction according to person, place, and time, [Col. 0924A] lest the offender be overwhelmed; authority is required so that one may be a judge appointed to this office. It should be noted that sometimes the person exceeds the authority, as when someone exercises tyranny, taking an opportunity from authority itself; sometimes authority exceeds the person, as when an unworthy person is initiated into holy orders.

## SECOND PART OF THE GENUINE EXEGETICAL WORKS

[Col. 0923]

## COMMENTARY ON THE CELESTIAL HIERARCHY OF ST. DIONYSIUS THE AREOPAGITE, ACCORDING TO THE TRANSLATION OF JOHN SCOTUS, ADDRESSED TO LOUIS, KING OF THE FRANKS, SON OF LOUIS THE FAT, WHO CAUSED THE CHURCH OF ST. VICTOR AT PARIS TO BE BUILT. TEN BOOKS.

## BOOK ONE

**CHAPTER I.** On the difference between worldly and divine theology, and their demonstrations.  
**CHAPTER II.** What is the subject matter of the hierarchies, and their arrangement.  
**CHAPTER III.** On the three hierarchies.  
**CHAPTER IV.** Why Dionysius the Areopagite undertook to treat theology after accepting the Catholic faith.  
**CHAPTER V.** What hierarchy is, and its arrangement and origin.

## CHAPTER ONE. On the Difference Between Worldly and Divine Theology and Their Demonstrations

[Col. 0923B] “The Jews seek signs, and the Greeks wisdom” (1 Cor. 1). For there was a certain wisdom which appeared to be wisdom to those who did not know true wisdom. The world discovered that wisdom, began to be puffed up, and swelled with pride, thinking itself great in it. It presumed and said that it would go further, toward supreme wisdom, trusting in its own wisdom as though it could be a road to that wisdom. It climbed and was lifted up, so as to reach lofty things in heart. It made for itself a ladder, the appearance of the creature, striving toward the invisible things of the Creator.

Then the things of God that were manifest [Col. 0924B] came forth for illumination and were made known, so that they might be tested by an impure heart. For the things that appeared were known, while other things were unknown; and by means of those things that were manifest they thought to enter into the things that had been hidden. They fell in mind beyond the truth that was possible for them, into the lies of their own fabrications, where they found no further object to grasp.

Therefore God makes the wisdom of this world foolish, because the wisdom of God could not be found in it; and he showed another wisdom, which appeared to be folly but was not, so that true wisdom might be found through it. Christ crucified was preached, so that truth might be sought through humility. But the world despised the physician [the little one (*modicum*)], and could not recognize the truth.

For it wished to contemplate the works of God which he had made wonderful, but would not venerate those which he had set forth for imitation. It did not attend to its own sickness, so as to seek medicine with devout piety; rather, presuming upon a false health, it gave itself to investigating what was outside itself with empty curiosity. It seemed to progress beyond itself, but failed within itself and did not find him who was above it. It formed opinions about him which it had conceived in a proud heart, lest it seem ignorant of the truth; it followed the path of error into one thing after another, into very many things opposed to truth, and finally into things unseemly [Col. 0925B] for the Godhead and deformed in relation to supreme majesty, so that its error might become manifest.

For at first there was truth, and it appeared great; but finally falsehood succeeded, when truth ought to have been brought to completion. Something like a light was displayed in one part, so that something could be seen there; but opposite it there were thick darkness and the deep gloom of ignorance, where the snare of error was laid to capture the proud. They saw where the light was; where the darkness was, they could not see. There they were caught in the snare because of the boldness of their presumption, by which they had hurled themselves toward it.

These things are manifest. How many memorials of outstanding intelligence those men left behind! With such extensive investigation they pursued the secrets of nature and the hidden things of created realities that we may judge their achievement itself worthy to be preferred to every pursuit. [Col. 0925C] We read their arts, studies, disciplines, and many precepts of reasoning, which they, by the sense and intelligence given them, examined, discovered, wrote down, and handed on to posterity to be read: logic, ethics, mathematics, and physics—concerning forms of reasoning; life and morals fitting to the order of nature; and the arrangement, order, causes, and outcomes of all things.

They became strong in this sphere, so as to grasp truth; for even this truth was to be dispensed through them, though it did not lead to life for them, since they were not children of life. Therefore it was given to them for our sake, for whom completion was reserved and a beginning prepared, that they might discover [Col. 0925D] that truth which the children of life had to receive in the service of supreme truth. The labor was assigned to them; the fruit was reserved for us.

In all these matters they acquired the light of understanding, keenness of intelligence, and power of perception as preliminary instruction, by which they subtly examined the force of creatures and the manner of lower nature according to the form of implanted reason. Finally, to complete wisdom—as they thought, though in truth they were to lose it and not find the true wisdom—they devoted themselves to theology, concerning divine things and the investigation of invisible things.

For there they began to fall into the falsehoods of fabricated notions. They adopted visible forms as images of divine things, in order to see invisible things by means of visible things. There was something similar there, but it showed from afar what was sought and did not bring light to clouded eyes. [Col. 0926A] For nature, created for service, displayed its Creator; but the likeness was foreign to the excellent and ruling Majesty. Nor could that nature which had to be taught find an evident declaration in all these things, because it was not itself sound enough for the object to shine clearly before contemplation.

For it did not possess the patterns formed by grace for the healing of inward sight; nor did it know the ark of wisdom and of hidden treasures, the flesh of the eternal Word in the humanity of Jesus. Rather, using natural instruction alone and bringing a cloudy, ambiguous light to a bleary gaze, it contemplated in the appearance of created things.

Therefore they erred and became vain when they wished in mind to pass beyond what alone they had received to know; and, groping by conjectures toward things that could not be seen, they who thought they saw were found blind. [Col. 0926B] These are the images of errors which their theology—for thus they called the study through which they thought to investigate divine things—proclaims as venerable in their vanity and deception. In them they utter so many lies contrary to truth, rectitude, and what accords with good nature that they themselves too are compelled to blush at them.

It was fitting, indeed, that those proud of their knowledge of the lowest things should be confounded in the highest; and that those who despise the humility of faith in the Savior’s death should admire its loftiness in the knowledge of the Creator.

For two images had been set before humanity, through which it could have seen invisible things: one of nature and one of grace. The image of nature was the appearance of this world; the image of grace was the humanity of the Word. In both God was shown, but he was not understood in both. Nature, indeed, displayed the craftsman in its appearance, but could not illumine the eyes of the beholder. The Savior’s humanity, however, was both medicine, so that the blind might receive light, and instruction, so that those who saw might recognize the truth.

“He made mud from spittle, anointed the blind man’s eyes; he washed, and saw” (John 9). And what afterward? Then he said to the man who saw but did not yet know: “I am he; and he who speaks with you is the Son of God” [Col. 0926C] (ibid.). Thus he first illumined and afterward disclosed himself. Nature could disclose, but could not illumine. The world proclaimed its Creator by its appearance, but did not infuse into human hearts understanding of the truth.

Therefore through the images of nature the Creator was only signified; but in the images of grace God was shown as present, because in the former he acted so that he might be understood to exist, while in the latter he acted so that he might be recognized to be present. This is the difference between the theology of this world and that which is called divine theology.

For it is impossible for invisible things to be demonstrated except through visible things; and therefore every theology must use visible demonstrations in declaring invisible things. But worldly theology, as we have said, took up the works of creation and the elements of this world created according to appearance, in order to make its demonstration through [Col. 0927A] them. Divine theology, however, chose the works of restoration according to the humanity of Jesus, and his sacraments which have existed from the beginning, with natural things also subordinated according to their measure, in order to fashion instruction through them.

But, as we have said, a greater manifestation of divinity is displayed in the sacraments of grace, the flesh of the Word, and his mystical working than is proclaimed by the natural appearance of things. Consequently worldly theology, employing a demonstration of little clarity, could not bring forth incomprehensible truth without contamination by error, whereas divine theology is known to proclaim it by a simple and pure affirmation.

Now it must be said what theology is, beginning at a higher level in order to make the matters to be discussed evident. All philosophy is divided into three principal parts: [Col. 0927B] logic, ethics, and theory. To enumerate here the fourth part, which we added in its proper place, would be superfluous.

Philosophy, then, contains three parts. The first, logic, undertakes the force and method of reasoning and the judgment of truth and falsehood. The second, ethics, establishes a right manner of living and a form of discipline according to the precepts of the virtues. The third, theory, alone chooses to investigate truth in everything that is and is not.

Theoretical philosophy has three parts: first, mathematics; second, physics; third, theology. In these the contemplation of truth climbs, as by certain steps of contemplation, to the highest point. Mathematics contemplates the visible forms of visible things. [Col. 0928A] Physics investigates the invisible causes of visible things. Theology alone contemplates invisible substances and the invisible natures of invisible substances.

In these there is, as it were, a progression and advancement of the mind ascending to know truth. Through visible forms of visible things one arrives at the invisible causes of visible things; through the invisible causes of visible things one ascends to invisible substances and to the knowledge of their natures. Here is the summit of philosophy and the perfection of truth, beyond which nothing higher can exist for a contemplating mind.

Therefore the wise of this world, as we have already said, became foolish here: proceeding by natural instruction alone according to the elements and appearance of the world, they lacked the patterns of grace. Although their appearance was humble, in these a clearer demonstration of truth was afforded. Thus God made the wisdom of this world foolish (1 Cor. 1), because it could not recognize the truth, since in its instruction it disdained to retain the pattern of humility.

Let this now suffice concerning theology for the sake of Dionysius’s *Hierarchy*, regarding which we undertook to say some things for purposes of explanation. For every hierarchy is subordinate to theology; and it was necessary to preface the introduction to the reading of the *Hierarchy* with some remarks on theology, in order to define its subject matter, which consists wholly in invisible substances and their likewise invisible natures, while using visible evidence for its own demonstration.

## CHAPTER II. What Is the Subject Matter of the Hierarchies, and Their Arrangement

[Col. 0927]

[Col. 0927C] Dionysius the Areopagite, made a Christian theologian from a philosopher and describer of hierarchies, displays the order of divine arrangement in the governance of all things: how God made rational creatures participants in his power, establishing sacred magistracies, powers, and principalities in heaven among angels and on earth among human beings, so that they might rule his creatures.

For it was fitting that that part of his work should become a participant in his power in his ordering which, in its creation, had received a share in his likeness; so that what alone had been made in the likeness of its Creator might alone retain his image in its own ordering. Therefore God himself, the creator of all things, whose ineffable majesty and unfailing power were able by themselves alone to govern what they alone had created, wished to have participants and fellow-workers in governing the things made by him—not that he himself might be aided by their service, but that they might be exalted by sharing his power.

Therefore the Lord alone and prince of all established dominions and principalities beneath himself and in accordance with himself, for the fulfilment of service. The order of the universe required that his works be completed through orders and arrangements, with command flowing from the highest throughout all things. Thus the majesty and authority [Col. 0927D] universally, most omnipotently, supremely, and ineffably adored in the Lord and governor of all have been distributed by shares, divisions, ranks, and orders among those who have become participants in grace, companions and associates of glory and majesty—descending from him, looking back to him, and arranged beneath him, who is the source, cause, and first principle of all:

> “One work and one maker; one empire and one ruler, one prince and one commonwealth; one Lord and Father, from whom is all fatherhood in heaven and on earth” (Eph. 3); “one who is all things in all; and all things one in one.”

For the highest good, through participation in graces and distribution of gifts, is divided among all the participants in its bounty while remaining one in itself; and all those who participate in the one are gathered to the form and true simplicity of that unity. [Col. 0928D] They could not have become participants in power unless they first became through grace sharers in virtue. Nor could they do with him what he can do unless they first deserved to be from him what he is.

The omnipotent Creator is called governor of all things made by him not by an extraneous usurpation or a merely nominal designation, but because, by power inherent in himself and goodness implanted within him, he cherishes and nourishes all things, governs and orders the universe. This same goodness and power he dispensed in many ways through orders and ranks to those ruling under him, according to the measure of participation and the principle of ministry: bestowing greater and surpassing gifts upon those more excellent and set above by authority; granting lesser charisms to lower and subordinate ranks, and freely granting to those set over their subjects service that does not oppress.

These are distributions of lights descending into all things, to which it has been granted to partake [Col. 0929A] of them from the Father of lights and the sun of righteousness, having been made clear mirrors so that they may shine and illumine. Those subject to them shine, and those set over them illumine. There is one light and one good; yet there are many shining things and many participants in the one good and one light. Insofar as they participate in the one, they are gathered into one, brought back to one, and conformed to one.

These are the hierarchies—that is, sacred principalities—which the highest hierarchy formed after itself and established beneath itself to rule and preside over its works according to the appointed orders, [Col. 0930A] under one principle and one power, from which comes every power, every virtue, and every spiritual light that shines spiritually and illuminates all things that spiritually shine.

This is the admirable height, sublimity, and dignity of rational creation: that it has deserved to rule among the works of its Maker, having received power from him and holding authority with him. Because this power is variously and manifoldly distributed from one power and one authority, according to the measure of gift and participation, for the adornment and beauty of the works which wisdom has ordered, many virtues and many powers come into being.

But lest multiplicity should again generate schism and division, and the world should fight against itself under contrary dominion, there is one principle and one governor of all, from whom they have what they are, under whom they govern what they can do, and to whom they refer all that they accomplish, so that unity may remain in all things and peace may endure in the kingdom of God, who creates all things and rules all things. [Col. 0930B]

## CHAPTER III. On the Three Hierarchies

[Col. 0929]

[Col. 0929C] There are three hierarchies. In describing them, Dionysius, theologian and narrator of the sacred hierarchies and powers which are in heaven and on earth, expounded a completed work.

The first, principal of all, the form and supreme exemplar of the rest, is the ineffable power of the Trinity: simple, one, and uniform, without rank, difference, or comparison; supreme, eternal, perfect, and true; omnipotent by its own power in creating and governing all its works; receiving nothing external and losing nothing of its own.

The second hierarchy is formed in angelic nature through adoption, participation, and condescension. It is from the first, beneath the first, and second in relation to the first; exalted in likeness, it has rank, admits difference and comparison, and is second after the supreme Trinity in emulation, divided into three divisions. [Col. 0930C]

The third and last hierarchy is ordered in human nature, imitating the second in the first place and the first in the second. Through the intermediate it receives and reflects the supreme image and surpassing likeness, so that the whole may be from one, the whole directed to one, and the whole one.

Theology undertook to expound first the angelic hierarchy as the exemplar of human hierarchy, in likeness to which every hierarchy among human beings has been made and formed; after it, the human hierarchy which exists according to its likeness; and in the third place it establishes the supreme, ineffable, and most exalted hierarchy, so that it may become clear to human minds through the nearer illumination of the preceding hierarchies, although it is very intelligible and obscure.

## CHAPTER IV. Why Dionysius the Areopagite Undertook to Treat Theology After He Had Accepted the Catholic Faith

[Col. 0929]

[Col. 0929D] The theologian Dionysius, seeing that the wisdom of the world was puffed up against the humility of the Christian faith, and that the cross of Christ and the works of the Word’s humanity in the flesh—made a remedy—were despised as though unworthy of God, unsuitable to the supreme majesty, and impossible to truth; seeing also that the Word of preaching was judged foolish for the redemption of humankind, and that those who proceed by the teaching of nature according to the elements of this world judged false the things accomplished for human salvation in the death of the Redeemer—sets himself against it in order to empty the glory that belongs to the wisdom of this age. He shows that the wisdom of Christian faith is humble indeed in the Redeemer’s death, but sublime [Col. 0930D] in the knowledge of the Creator; and that the sacraments of redemption, which appeared contemptible according to the appearance of this world and the estimation of those who knew only worldly things, are exalted, venerable, and above this world’s wisdom and reasoning, and are effectual as doctrine for demonstrating the highest truth.

Accordingly, he declares divine theology—because it has used these exemplars in demonstrating invisible things—to be worthy of God and consonant with truth; whereas the theology of the world, which followed the elements of created nature according to fleshly reasoning, could not apprehend God’s truth. Thus, to speak in an enigma, Goliath, struck on his head by one despised and [Col. 0931A] small, falls prostrate: for the wisdom of this world, swelling itself on high, is convicted in its very summit of manifest error by the humility of Christian truth. God is shown to have been found by the humble and revealed to the humble, and to have bestowed the cross of Christ upon believers—something which the wisdom of the world could not bestow upon those who are proud and self-confident.

For this reason we set our theology, and the knowledge of lofty, sublime, and invisible things, against those who mock and accuse the humble faith, so that, if they can, those who despise these things may glory in like things of their own. And if by their wisdom, reasoning, and understanding—which they do not fear to prefer to our faith—they have discovered such things and known comparable things, let them examine their theology and the things they have said about God, which are shameful, [Col. 0932A] ridiculous, unsuitable, and false, so that they may acknowledge faith and embrace truth. For this reason God willed to live in human nature, so that human life might be in heaven; and for this reason he endured human things, so that the human being might deserve to know divine things. This is the sacrament of God’s humility, the sacrament of faith, and the sacrament of truth. The proud in heart did not know it, puffed up by their own understanding and by their wisdom, which was of the flesh and could not find God’s wisdom—so that that which was thought wisdom might be found to be folly, and was not wisdom. In this we have been exalted above them: the wisdom of God, believed by us in the flesh, is despised by them; in glory and majesty it is acknowledged by us and unknown by them.

## CHAPTER V. What hierarchy is, and its arrangement and origin

[Col. 0931]

[Col. 0931B] What it was necessary to set forth beforehand concerning Dionysius’s theology, for the description of the hierarchies and for understanding what is to be said, I have completed in the preceding chapters, as far as the occasion and my mind’s suggestion allowed. It now remains to consider what the theologian has said concerning them. Since the very surface of the reading is covered by a great depth of words, and is necessarily concealed beneath a certain lofty, elevated, and involved manner of speech, proportioned to the greatness and excellence of the most secret things, it must first be opened by a measured, ordinary explanation that is easy to understand. Perhaps this will be the more suitable exposition for those being introduced to so great a subject, since minds to be exercised in the meditation of matters so great and sublime ought not to be occupied with verbal wrappings. Although these are fitting veils placed over venerable secrets for those entering upon them, nevertheless, when the face is unveiled for contemplation of what lies within, they must be removed from the midst in the freedom of the Spirit, in order to disclose the mysteries. This, then, is what we now undertake, and this is enough for us in what we shall say. Whatever may be added beyond this will be an overflowing gift.

Hierarchy, translated from Greek, is called “sacred principality”; and there are three hierarchies, that is, three sacred principalities, which we shall describe as mentioned above. The first and highest hierarchy is the power of divinity. The second and middle one is angelic power, made in the likeness of the first power and established beneath the first power. The third and last hierarchy is [Col. 0931D] human power, made in the likeness of the angelic and established beneath it, and through this middle hierarchy beneath the first and highest one. By these hierarchies—that is, sacred principalities—the whole world is governed. Among them is the highest power, which only commands; the lowest, which is only commanded; and the middle, which commands the inferior and is commanded by the superior.

The highest and first power therefore established after itself the second and third powers in angels and human beings, so that they might be both conformed to it through participation in its virtue and its co-workers through fellowship in power. It divided the gifts of powers and, according to the divisions of gifts, distributed the offices of powers. It gave many gifts and established many powers; yet all gifts are from one, and every power is under one; and there is one in all things, all things are directed to one, and all are in one.

The theologian first sets forth the angelic hierarchy; secondly, he treats the human; thirdly, as it were at the conclusion and consummation, the divine and highest. He subdivides the angelic hierarchy itself into three hierarchies and distinguishes each of the three by three orders, so that the number of nine angelic orders may be completed. He establishes every hierarchy as possessing one power, one office, and one dignity; and in each hierarchy he establishes first, middle, and last orders. The first [Col. 0932C] orders illuminate; the last are illuminated; the middle are both illuminated by the first and illuminate the last.

After this he proceeds, concerning the last hierarchy, to the divisions of gifts, distributions of powers and dignities, offices, orders, and operations, arranged in likeness to the angelic hierarchy. Finally, ascending—as far as is possible for a human contemplator—to the divine, simple, and superexcellent hierarchy, and ending in it, these matters attain their consummation.

Its origin is this: since the supreme Good is one, it is wonderfully multiplied and varied for the beauty and loveliness of its division and outpouring among all who are worthy to participate in it, so that all may be one in it. For its gifts are lights; and lights make shining things, both things illuminated and therefore shining, and themselves illuminating; and shining things become light, and illuminating lights. They are lights, and everywhere one light; things shining are one in the one light; the one is multiplied in many, and the many are united in one. Theology therefore begins from this, because shining and illuminating lights are reflections of the divine; and in them is seen the shining and illuminating light which remains in itself incomprehensible and inaccessible. Therefore, that it may be seen, it goes forth into these lights and pours itself into them, so that they may apprehend, receive, and see it in themselves, shining from it. For those that do not shine from it cannot see or apprehend it, because without light not even light itself can be seen.

These, indeed, are beautiful images of light for an invisible outpouring, so that invisible things may be seen through visible things. For that Good and the light itself are not this light; yet in a certain respect it is light, and may truly be called light. When it is called light, truth is spoken, for it is light and an image of that light. And what exists in this light exists in that Good, because this light is good from that Good, and everything is in it because everything is from it. For when it began to exist from it, it did not cease to exist [Col. 0934A] in it; rather, it proceeded from it and remained in it. Thus the image serves, and the creature shows forth the Maker, because it was made for this purpose: that he might be seen in it.

For this reason gifts are illuminating lights; and participating lights are illuminated, themselves illuminating, and like the illuminating light. In being illuminated they become participants in grace; in illuminating they become partners in power. Every hierarchy consists in these two things and is perfected by grace and office, virtue and ministry—all of which are theologically shown by likenesses, figures, and various enigmas drawn from visible things.

## BOOK II

The titles of the fifteen chapters of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite’s *Celestial, or Angelic, Hierarchy* addressed to Timothy follow. After them the text of each chapter according to John Scotus will be supplied, and after the text, our Hugh’s exposition.

> [Note: [Col. 0933C] Compare the exposition and interpretation of the same book by John Scotus, which Henry Joseph Floss of Bonn edited from manuscript codices in a text much more corrected and enlarged than before, *Patrologia*, vol. CXXII, [Col. 0934C].]

[Col. 0933]

**CH. I.** That the divine illumination, coming forth in various unforeseen ways according to goodness, remains simple; and not only this, but also unifies those illuminated.  
**CH. II.** How beautifully divine and celestial things are manifested through dissimilar symbols.  
**CH. III.** What hierarchy is, and what is understood through hierarchy.  
**CH. IV.** What the appellation of angels signifies.  
**CH. V.** Why all celestial essences are commonly called angels.  
**CH. VI.** What is the first ordering of celestial essences, what the middle, and what the last.  
**CH. VII.** On the seraphim, cherubim, and thrones, and their first hierarchy.  
**CH. VIII.** On dominions, virtues, and powers, and their middle hierarchy.  
**CH. IX.** On principalities, archangels, and angels, and their last hierarchy.  
**CH. X.** Repetition and collection of the angelic ordering.  
**CH. XI.** Why all celestial essences are commonly called celestial virtues.  
**CH. XII.** Why, among human beings, high priests are called angels.  
**CH. XIII.** Why the prophet Isaiah is said to have been purified by a seraph.  
**CH. XIV.** What the traditional angelic number signifies.  
**CH. XV.** What are the formative images of angelic powers, and what follows.

## TITLE OF CHAPTER I. That divine illumination, coming forth in various unforeseen ways according to goodness, remains simple; and not only this, but also unifies those illuminated

### TEXT

[Col. 0933B]

> “Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James 1). But every procession of the manifestation of lights, set in motion by the Father and coming to us excellently and abundantly, in turn fills and converts us, restoring us as a unifying power, to the unity and deifying simplicity of the Father who gathers us together. For all things are from him and unto him, as the divine word says (Romans 11). Therefore, invoking Jesus, the paternal light, which is the true light “that enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John 1), through whom we have gained access to the principal light, the Father (Ephesians 2), we shall, as far as possible, look upon the illuminations handed down by the Father in the most holy utterances. And from these we shall consider, as far as we are able, the hierarchies of the heavenly minds symbolically and anagogically manifested to us.
>
> And, with the immaterial and unshaken eyes of the mind beholding the principal and super-principal brightness of the divine Father, which reveals to us in figurative symbols the most blessed hierarchies of angels, we are again restored from it into its simple ray. For the ray itself is nowhere and never separated from its own singular unity. Yet, for the anagogical and unifying proportioning of the things foreseen, it is excellently and beautifully multiplied and proceeds forth; while it remains securely fixed within itself, uniformly, in unchangeable likeness. It proportionately extends toward those who look upon it, insofar as is permitted, and unifies them according to its own simple unity.
>
> For the divine ray cannot otherwise shine upon us except when, anagogically veiled by a variety of sacred coverings, it has been prepared for us in a manner naturally adapted and proper to us by paternal providence. Therefore the perfect ordering of sacred things, judging our most holy hierarchy worthy of a supramundane imitation of the celestial hierarchies, handed down those immaterial hierarchies variegated in material figures and formed compositions, so that we ourselves might rise proportionately from the most sacred forms to simple and unfigured heights and likenesses. For our mind cannot ascend to that immaterial imitation and contemplation of the celestial hierarchies unless it employs the material guidance suited to it: taking visible forms as images of invisible beauty; sensible delights as figures of invisible distribution; material lights as an image of immaterial splendor; the manifold sacred disciplines as images of intellectual contemplative fullness; the orderly dispositions found here as images of states united and ordered toward divine things; the reception of the most divine Eucharist as participation in Jesus; and whatever else has been handed down supramundanely to the celestial essences but symbolically to us.
>
> Therefore, for the sake of our rational deification, the merciful source of perfection, revealing the celestial hierarchies to us and making our hierarchy their fellow-minister in virtue and in likeness to their God-formed sanctification, portrayed the supracelestial minds in sensible images in the sacred compositions of Scripture, so as to lead us back through sensible things to intelligible things, and from sacredly figured symbols to the simple summits of the celestial hierarchies.

### EXPOSITION

[Col. 0935C]

The first book of Dionysius the theologian, the Areopagite, entitled *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, that is, *the Celestial Principality*, is composed of fifteen chapters. In these he carefully enumerates, through the individual orders, ranks, distributions, and distinctions, the gifts, offices, virtues, and operations of the celestial spirits. The title of the first chapter is: “Because every divine illumination, variously and unforeseenly coming forth according to goodness, remains simple; and not only this, but also unifies those illuminated.”

For grace itself is divine illumination, and the gifts of grace are lights illuminating those who partake of them. All grace descends from one fountain, and every illumination from one light. There are many rays, but one light: the one light spreads itself out to illuminate many; many who have been illuminated shine, yet only one light is seen; and they become one light in one light. By such a likeness theology shows how the one Good offers itself to many for participation, so that those who derive one likeness from it may be one in it.

The theologian then proceeds to show that the invisible operations of grace and the distributions of invisible gifts cannot be shown or understood except through visible signs and likenesses; and that every visible form and sensible nature bears some likeness for the manifestation of invisible things. For just as every good comes from [Col. 0936A] the supreme Good, so in every good, according to the emulation of participation, the supreme Good can be contemplated. Theology therefore fittingly conforms every sensible species, form, and quality to the signification of invisible things. Such is the meaning of the first chapter.

“Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights.” By apostolic authority and divine theology he first proves that every good is from the supreme Good; then he adds his own judgment that every good looks back and is returned to the supreme Good, because, as it is divided among many by participation, so many are united in one likeness and imitation. The best gifts are gifts of nature; the perfect gifts are gifts of grace. The Father of lights is the author and bestower of gifts.

[Col. 0936B] “Every best gift therefore, and every perfect gift, is from above, descending from the Father of lights,” because every good thing—whether that which nature, originally created good, received at first, or that which it later deserved to obtain when glorified through grace—was given by the one author of nature and bestower of grace. To descend, as it were, was for these gifts to come from the fountain of supreme fullness to the participation of inferior beings. For every creature is by nature inferior to the excellence of the Creator; and therefore every good infused by the Creator’s gift into a creature is rightly said, as it were, to descend to lower things.

It descends because it pours itself into a subject nature, lower in dignity. It also descends because it distributes itself from perfect and consummate fullness into participation that is only partial. Yet this is so without the descending gift becoming a servant or the divided gift diminishing. Rather, remaining what it is in itself and in the one from whom it comes, it gives itself, so far as they are able, to those to whom it comes, giving them both what they receive as being and whatever degree of being they have deserved in what they are.

Thus all goods are from one Good, and all goods are in one Good. The Good itself, from which all goods come, is good and is light; it is the author of the goods that come from it and Father of lights. The goods themselves are lights: they illuminate those capable of shining and become shining lights from the light that illumines them. This Good leaves nothing that it has created alien from itself; yet it illumines only those whom it created for itself and formed according to itself. For only those receive light which can shine from light, in whom the incoming light finds things not unlike itself; and, when infused, it lifts them into a more perfect conformity with itself and into a more perfect outward image.

[Col. 0936D] These alone, therefore, receive the best gifts and perfect gifts. For every creature—except that which bears the image of the Creator and is capable of likeness—if it is good in its own kind because it received being from the Creator, was neither best when it was given nor perfect in consummation. But the rational creature, which alone was made in the Creator’s image, received gifts and endowments: best gifts when it was created in relation to lower things, and perfect gifts when it was raised toward the highest things. For nothing better was given to another nature than what this creature received at first, nor anything more perfect than what it later deserved to become. For it was first created good beyond all other things, and afterward made perfect in the image and likeness of the one by whom it was made.

Therefore the best gifts and perfect gifts descending from the Father of lights attain only to the height of rational creaturehood, which alone has been made sublime. At first, when the best gifts were granted, and afterward, when it was glorified, it became perfect—after a fashion similar and coequal to the highest. For these best gifts and perfect gifts are lights descending from the Father of lights; he is the light from whom they descend, and those into whom they descend become lights. For the Father of light could not beget anything other than what he is; nor can the recipient of light become anything other than light. If, therefore, he who begot the light is light, and he who received the light is light, then in some manner the begetter and the recipient are found to be the same. Yet the former is believed to be this by nature; the latter is known to be this by grace.

[Col. 0937B] The one light therefore poured itself out by participation into many lights, in order to reform many illuminated beings to one light, so that, as many received it by participation, all might appear one in its form. Thus, after the theologian had shown by divine authority that every good is from the supreme Good, he immediately adds his own judgment: that every good is directed to the supreme Good; that it is poured out from it by the division of participation, and united to it by likeness of conformation.

[Col. 0937C] “Every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights.” In this he proves that every good comes from the supreme Good. After this he adds that every good has conversion, return, and end in the supreme Good: “But every procession of the manifestation of lights, set in motion by the Father and coming to us excellently and abundantly, in turn fills and converts us, restoring us as a unifying power, to the unity and deifying simplicity of the Father who gathers us together.”

The Father’s movement is the inclination of paternal kindness. For it is by kindness and mercy alone that the Father is moved to pour out his lights upon us. He is moved not by disturbance of himself but by compassion for us; moved not by shaking himself, but by gathering us; not by emptying himself, but by filling us. He is moved, then, in order to come to us, but is not moved so as to withdraw from himself. He is moved so that he may begin to be for us what he was not, but is not moved so that he may cease to be for himself what he was.

Thus the Father of lights is moved over us; and once the Father has been moved, his lights descend into us and, by proceeding into us, are manifested through us—first to us, and afterward through us to others. This whole procession of the manifestation of lights—that is, the procession by which lights are manifested, for they would not be manifested unless they proceeded—goes forth from the Father when moved. This entire procession of the manifestation of lights coming into us accomplishes this: it fills us, assuredly with nothing other than itself; and, by filling, restores us anew by renewing us, just as it established us by creating us. It restores us as a unifying power which gathers what has been scattered, harmonizes what is diverse, and makes one out of many. Thus, restoring and reforming us, it converts us, who previously had been turned away by dissimilarity, divided by multiplicity, and perverted by crookedness. It converts us, I say, to the unity and deifying simplicity of the Father who gathers us.

[Col. 0938A] For the Father’s light, invisible in itself, proceeding into us and coming forth for manifestation, finds us empty and void of the true Good. Pouring itself into us, it fills us according to each person’s capacity and receptivity; and when it has filled us, it converts us, so that we may not be at variance with the Father, but may look toward him in the same likeness and image by which we do not differ from him. It fills by illuminating and converts by making lights. We are filled in receiving light; we are converted in becoming lights ourselves from the light received. For in it we are one with the light, and in the light we are one, because we are light; and there is unity in one likeness, one light, one brightness, and one illuminating and shining light.

Since, therefore, every good is from the supreme Good and every good is directed to the supreme Good—for from it we receive that by which we are one with it—there would be nothing in us by which to look toward it unless what belongs to it had first become ours through it. “For all things are from him and unto him, as the divine word says.” That is: as the authority of the divine word testifies, things proceed from him and are converted unto him; from him as beginning, unto him as end.

We may also understand the Father’s movement, not unsuitably, as the beginning of our contemplation. For when a mind accustomed to its own darkness strives to contemplate inward brightness, it cannot bear the force of the unfamiliar radiance, as though with trembling and wavering lights; it is repelled by the first rays that meet its sight. The light appears to it as though trembling, and the light itself seems to move, whereas rather its own darkness alone is moving and fleeing the presence of the flashing light. Here the light’s movement seems to be the movement of the light, though it is the fleeing darkness. After this movement lights are poured forth and proceed to manifestation—lights which could not have been seen while the darkness stood still. They fill us with light, so that we may shine and be lights, as is the light that illumines us, in order that all things may be from it and unto it: receiving from it the beginning of their existence and in it the end of their consummation, as the divine word testifies through the Apostle Paul: “For from him, and through him, and in him are all things; to him be glory for ever. Amen” (Romans 11).

[Col. 0938D] “Therefore, invoking Jesus, the paternal light, which is the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world, through whom we have gained access to the principal light, the Father, we shall, as far as possible, look upon the illuminations handed down by the Father in the most holy utterances; and from these we shall consider, as far as we are able, the hierarchies of the heavenly minds symbolically and anagogically manifested to us.”

In the preceding chapter he briefly summarized the subject of the work to follow: every good is from the supreme Good, and every good is directed to the supreme Good. Now, before entering the text of his subject matter, he invokes Jesus, who is the paternal light, through whose mediation all spiritual illuminations and gifts of grace are bestowed on those to be illumined. Thus, when he has himself been illumined and aided, he may, according to the traditions of the divine utterances—which were also handed down by the Father for illuminating human hearts—both truly know and worthily describe the invisible illuminations and sacred dispositions of the celestial spirits.

“Therefore, invoking Jesus”: as if he said, “Every illumination is indeed from the Father, but no illumination can be possessed without Jesus the mediator. Therefore we, who ask to be illumined, invoke Jesus,” so that we may deserve to be illumined. Then follows concerning Jesus Christ himself: “who is the paternal light.” Instead of saying, “who is the paternal light,” a reference has been made to the following phrase: “which is the paternal light.” Or: “invoking Jesus, the paternal light,” namely, the light which is true and eternal and possesses immutable being, and is light from what it is. It is unlike illuminated lights, which are lights not from what they are but from what they have received.

[Col. 0939B] It is also understood to be the true light, because it shines from what it is and not only shines for itself but illumines others: “which enlightens every human being coming into this world.” This does not mean that all are illumined, but that among all persons no one possesses from himself a reason why he should deserve illumination rather than another. For this illumination is of grace, not nature; a gift, not a debt; the benefaction of the giver, not the reward of the recipient.

Or this light enlightens every human being coming into this world insofar as all have been made naturally capable of reason and have received the light of understanding. Or again, this light enlightens every human being coming into the world, not because, as has been said, all are illumined, but because all—whether illumined or not—have no other source from which they can be illumined. For illuminating belongs only to light, just as being illumined belongs only to one who receives light. Hence, while receiving light belongs to all, illuminating all belongs to light alone.

[Col. 0939D] It follows: “Through whom we have gained access to the principal light, the Father.” Through Jesus the light we have gained access to the Father, the light. Jesus is light, and the Father of Jesus is light. The Son, light, was begotten from the Father, light; and Father and Son are one light. The Father is called the principal light not because he is a greater or better light—for the light is the same—but because he is light not from light. The Son is light from light; the Father is light not from light. Yet Father and Son are one light, as Father and Son are one God. Therefore the Father is the principal light because the Son, light, is from the Father, light.

This may also be understood otherwise: the Father is called the principal light because I see that the Son himself is in a certain respect light in which he cannot be equal to the Father. For the Father of Jesus is God and God alone; but the Son is God, not God alone, but both human and God. Jesus is light in that he is God, and is the same light as God the Father. But in that he is human, he is light because Christ’s humanity itself was light insofar as it showed truth and revealed the principal light, the Father. Yet the light of Jesus’ humanity was less than the light of his divinity; in the light of humanity Jesus was inferior to the Father, but in the light of divinity he was the same as the Father.

[Col. 0940A] Through him, then, we came from the light of humanity, in which the Son alone was present, to the light of divinity, in which Father and Son were present. Therefore through the Son we gained access to the Father—not to the Father alone, but to the Son and the Father.

I also see another access through Jesus to the principal light, the Father. Jesus is the Father’s wisdom; that wisdom revealed the Father, and the Father’s wisdom went forth while the Father remained hidden. The Father remained invisible, while his wisdom became visible so as to lead us to the invisible Father. Having become visible, it did not cease to be invisible, because it came where it had not been and did not depart from where it had been. First it went forth through the creaturely world and manifested itself in its works. The invisible became visibly seen in what was visible, and a certain light was displayed to lead to a greater light. The first light was wisdom, and the second light was Wisdom. Jesus became for us the way to the Father, from the lower light to the principal light.

Then Wisdom came a second time and went forth, as was said, through the flesh. It became light in an earthen vessel so as to illumine us, accustom us to the greater light, and lead us to the Father’s principal light. Thus also we gained access through Jesus to the principal light of the Father.

“Therefore, invoking Jesus, the paternal light, which is the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world, through whom we have gained access to the principal light, the Father.” The sentence remains incomplete here until it is completed by what follows; its meaning is this: invoking Jesus, we shall, as far as possible, look upon the illuminations of the most holy utterances—that is, the most holy utterances handed down by the Father, which illumine us by the teaching of truth and the understanding of mysteries. For the illuminations of the divine utterances were handed down by the Father in order that we might be illumined by them, until we become capable of contemplating the principal light. And while they illumine us, we now know heavenly secrets which we are not yet able to comprehend by understanding.

[Col. 0940D] We may also understand the illuminations of the most holy utterances as the descriptions of sacred discourse and configurations drawn from visible forms, in which Scripture shows us, by means of a proposed likeness, the state of invisible things and the reason and manner of heavenly mysteries. Through visible signs the human mind is more suitably instructed and illumined for the knowledge of invisible things. Therefore, almost everywhere in sacred discourse, visible forms are employed for signification when the human mind is instructed about matters hidden from human understanding, so that through what it knows it may grasp and understand what it does not know. Invoking Jesus, who illumines hearts inwardly, we ought to examine these illuminations set before us outwardly for instruction, and according to their demonstration learn heavenly secrets.

This is what follows: “And from these we shall consider, as far as we are able, the hierarchies of heavenly minds symbolically and anagogically manifested to us.” The order, then, is first to examine the illuminations of holy Scripture while invoking Jesus, through whom inward illumination is given and without whom outward illumination is empty. Then, with Jesus illuminating us, we consider from the illuminations of sacred Scripture the sacred principalities and powers of heavenly minds—that is, celestial spirits—which would otherwise be wholly invisible and unknown to us if they were not revealed through the traditions of sacred Scripture.

[Col. 0941B] This is what he says: “We shall consider as far as we are able,” or “as far as we can.” For our ability is small and slight compared with the magnitude of such things. “We shall consider hierarchies,” that is, the sacred principalities of heavenly minds, namely angelic spirits. These hierarchies, I say, are manifested to us—that is, shown or revealed by the illuminations, namely the demonstrations of sacred discourse, symbolically and anagogically.

A symbol is the comparison of visible forms for the manifestation of invisible things. Anagoge is the ascent or elevation of the mind to contemplate higher things. He here indicates a twofold mode of divine revelation, infused into the minds of theologians and prophets through visions and demonstrations, which the Greeks call *theophanies*, that is, divine appearances. For sometimes invisible things were shown through signs resembling sensible things; sometimes they were contemplated in higher things purely through anagoge alone, that is, the ascent of the mind.

From these two kinds of visions, two kinds of descriptions were likewise formed in sacred discourse. In one, the truth of hidden things is shadowed forth by forms, figures, and likenesses. In the other, it is expressed nakedly and purely as it is, without covering. Therefore, when what is hidden is manifested by forms, signs, and likenesses, or when what is manifest is described in this way, the demonstration is symbolic. But when something is shown by pure, naked revelation, or taught by plain and open narration, it is anagogical.

“And the principal and super-principal brightness of the divine Father, which reveals to us the most blessed hierarchies of the angels in figured symbols, when we behold it with the immaterial and unquivering eyes of the mind, restores us again through itself into the simple ray of that brightness.”

Here he plainly teaches through what stages the procession of divine illumination reaches us, and again by what advances our mind is led back to the contemplation of the highest brightness. For the divine light first descends into the angelic nature [Col. 0942A], and from that nature pours itself into our understanding and participation through divine revelations and manifestations, and through the mystical narrative of sacred Scripture. But the human mind, ascending again by the same stages to things above, considers, by sacred examination of the divine discourse, the heavenly mysteries and that illumination of divine brightness which is in the angels. Gradually growing from this into knowledge of invisible things, it finally becomes able to contemplate the very splendor of the supreme light. Thus comes about what was said at the beginning: one light divides itself for the illumination of many, in order that it may reform all things illuminated into the sight and likeness of one brightness.

Therefore, having learned from the sacred traditions of the divine discourse the brightness of the heavenly spirits, he shows how contemplation of the supreme light follows upon this knowledge, saying: “And the principal and super-principal brightness of the divine Father, which reveals to us the most blessed hierarchies of the angels in figured symbols, when we behold it with the immaterial and unquivering eyes of the mind, restores us again through itself into the simple ray of that brightness.”

The order of the words is: We, beholding with the immaterial and unquivering eyes of the mind the principal and super-principal brightness of the divine Father—which brightness reveals to us the most blessed hierarchies of the angels in figured symbols—are again restored through it into its simple ray. For, beholding the brightness of the Father, we are restored, that is, re-formed again: we are turned back by a returning movement to that from which we came, into his simple ray [Col. 0942C], so that in one light we may be one—we who shine from the one light—and that there may be no discord among those who shine, just as there is no diversity at all in lights.

The Father’s brightness is called principal and super-principal because it is not only superior to all things that shine in dignity or causality, but also loftier in nature. And because this brightness is not bodily but spiritual, and shines spiritually, it can therefore be seen only by immaterial—that is, incorporeal—eyes. These eyes must also be unquivering: that is, sound, clear-sighted, and un-dazzled, lest, looking upon so great a light with bleary vision, they bring darkness upon themselves from that very brightness.

It is fitting that, after contemplating through sacred Scripture the brightness of the angels, we are illuminated toward the brightness of the divine Father; for that angelic brightness itself is disclosed to us, through the revelation of sacred Scripture, from the brightness of the Father descending through them into us. This is what he says: “Which reveals to us the most blessed hierarchies of the angels in figured symbols,” that is, in signs and configurations figured according to visible forms: namely, principalities, dignities, and powers.

The orders and powers of the angels, and their divine operations, are wholly invisible; and unless they are shown through visible signs and likenesses taken from visible things, they cannot at all be understood by those who know only visible things. Therefore, the Father’s brightness, desiring to restore us to its principal light, first rouses us through the illuminations of sacred Scripture to contemplate the brightness of the angels [Col. 0943A], and, having illuminated us through that brightness, finally reforms us toward knowledge and light of its own brightness, so that we may be one in it, since we have received unity from it.

This brightness of the Father diffuses and penetrates all things through the emission and illumination of one simple ray, since the Father begot one Wisdom, through whom he made all his works. For the Word of the Father is light from light: one Word and one ray. The Word itself is wisdom, and wisdom itself is proceeding light, from which it is known: one from one, and therefore one ray from one brightness. Those who are illuminated are re-formed to it, so that they may shine from it and be light with it, just as it is light. And although there are many illuminated lights, shining variously and dissimilarly, there is nevertheless one light [Col. 0943B] illuminating in all the illuminated.

This is what follows: “For the ray itself is neither anywhere nor ever forsaken by its own singular unity.” For although the wisdom of God variously and dissimilarly pours itself into minds to be spiritually illuminated, according to the capacity and ability of those receiving it, yet it remains one and simple in itself. It is neither greater in those who abound from it nor less in those who are granted union with it according to a lower grace of participation; but it is wholly in the whole and wholly in each, transcending the highest and condescending to the lowest, offering itself for participation by many, while remaining one in itself.

Therefore it divides itself among many participants, yet through participation in itself restores the many participants to unity. For we can be gathered together in it [Col. 0943C], but it cannot be divided in us. Indeed, this ray—that is, wisdom itself, illuminating and proceeding from the principal light, the Father, and extending even to illuminate all things—is never forsaken by its own proper unity, because it is always with him; nor is it ever elsewhere, because it is everywhere in him. For even when, at different times, it presents itself differently to minds requiring illumination, it remains the same and unlike nothing else. And when it shows itself present at once in different places and to different fellowships of participation, it is not manifold.

“It is excellently and beautifully multiplied and proceeds toward the anagogical and unifying harmony of the things which have been foreseen; and it remains securely fixed within itself, uniformly, in the unchangeable likeness of its nature; and, as far as is lawful, it proportionately extends and unifies those who look toward it in itself according to the simple unity of itself.”

It is as though he said: The ray of divine brightness, which illuminates those who shine spiritually, though it remains one in itself, is nevertheless variously multiplied by participation and the distribution of gifts, because it is distributed and multiplied in many diverse ways. This multiplication and variation is the beauty of the universe; for unless individual things were beautifully diverse, the universe as a whole would not be supremely beautiful. No one thing among all diverse things could contain that whole which was beauty; and therefore supreme beauty was distributed among individual things through varied participation, so that it might be perfect in the universe as a whole [Col. 0944A].

This distribution is multiplied excellently and beautifully: excellently in the universe as a whole and beautifully in individual things; or excellently according to the disposition of the participants. For it is excellently multiplied so that the good perceived by many may be greater; and it is beautifully multiplied so that the adornment of the universe may be greater, because it is infused into individual participants in varied and diverse ways. Thus from the numerical multitude among participants comes the consummation of the good, and from the unequal distribution among participants comes beauty.

Or the multiplication of the simple ray by which we are illuminated may suitably be understood according to the many and diverse figures and likenesses of the divine discourses. Taken according to our condition, these declare to human minds in manifold ways the divine wisdom [Col. 0944B], which in its purity and simplicity is altogether incomprehensible, although it is always one and the same. It is therefore multiplied because it is declared in many ways: excellently indeed in relation to itself, and beautifully in relation to us. It is excellently multiplied because through this multiplication of declarations it is known more perfectly; it is beautifully declared because it is manifested by the beautiful and fitting appearance and diversity of the forms which declare it.

And this multiplication occurs for the harmony of those things which have been foreseen—that is, of the elect and those provided for life—so that they may be harmonized and united in concord of participation, like many limbs in one body, and so that this very diversity of gifts may mutually confirm the fellowship of unity and peace [Col. 0944C]. Thus no member may presume to separate itself from the cohesion of the whole body, since it possesses, in the society of the others, the fullness of the good which it possesses less fully in itself. For since each has what another does not have, each has in another what it does not have in itself, or has more in another than it has in itself. Therefore individual members mutually incline toward one another and preserve concord and peace among themselves. This concord and peace is harmony, by which they agree with one another so as to stand as one and be re-formed toward one.

For this reason he calls the harmony of those foreseen both anagogical and unifying: unifying, indeed, that they may stand as one; anagogical, that they may be re-formed toward one [Col. 0944D]. Unifying, because it gathers the dispersed into one; anagogical, because it leads the cast-down upward. Unifying through love of neighbor; anagogical through love of God. It is therefore beautiful in gathering and excellent in elevation.

Thus the ray of divine illumination, multiplied either through the distribution of spiritual gifts, by which it is inwardly participated in, or through the variety of mystical manifestations, by which it is outwardly declared in sacred Scripture, proceeds—that is, advances—into hearts to illuminate them: either filling them from within by inspiration or pouring itself into them from without through instruction in the sacred word. Yet it remains securely within itself, so that, while it offers itself for manifold and varied participation by minds to be illuminated, it does not flow out beyond the simplicity [Col. 0945A] of its unity.

For its unity always remains within itself because coessential immutability fortifies and preserves it. Though a multitude of participants comes to share in it, the diversity of participation cannot prevail to divide it. It therefore remains securely within itself, so that it may always be the same and not pass out of what it is into what it is not; but it is uniformly fixed in its unchangeable likeness, that it may not differ from itself, as though made unlike itself.

Nor does it merely remain one itself: it also extends itself to those looking toward it and turned toward it, as far as is lawful—that is, as far as is permitted and possible for them. That is, it stretches itself out so as also to come to those who are far away, without departing from itself. It extends itself proportionately [Col. 0945B], so that some receive more and others less according to the dispensation of the distribution of gifts or the receptive ability of the participants. Those who are nearer receive more abundantly from it; and so each receives more as he draws nearer, and less as he withdraws farther away. Nevertheless all receive, each according to his own share.

This is what he says: “It extends itself proportionately.” Yet because it extends itself to all and pours itself into all, it illuminates all and makes them lights from its own light. By this it makes them one, just as it itself is one. And this is what he says: “It unifies them according to the simple unity of itself.” For the illumination of all is one, the likeness is one, and the form is one, in which all who are illuminated by it are one from it [Col. 0945C] and one with it, because the illuminated are lights, just as it is light.

Yet those who are one from it are one by unification, not by unity. For, being one from many, they are one in one. They are themselves many, and therefore are not one in what they are; but because the many are in one, from one the many are one, and they are one by unification, not by unity. But it itself is one not by unification but by unity, because it is one from what it is, which is one. Therefore he called the unity simple, because it is one from one, and is itself the same one from which it is. Thus unity in one is simple; but unification is manifold in one, because those are one from one, and one in one, whereas here there is one from many, because many are in one and one is in many.

He then adds the reason why the divine ray—that is, divine wisdom, which is one from the Father and simple with the Father—is variously multiplied through likenesses and forms of manifestations in sacred Scripture: namely, because the invisible wisdom of God could not otherwise become known to us unless it conformed itself, by way of likeness, to forms of visible things which we know, and through them expressed for us, by signifying, its invisible things which we do not know. Therefore the divine ray, which is one and simple in itself, is multiplied by a variety of significations and manifestations when it comes to us, because it cannot be grasped in its own purity and simplicity.

[Col. 0946A] “For it is not otherwise possible for the divine ray to shine upon us unless it is anagogically veiled by the variety of sacred veils, and naturally and fittingly prepared, through paternal providence, by those things which are according to us.”

The sacred veils in which the divine ray shines upon us are the mystical descriptions in sacred Scripture which introduce visible forms and likenesses of invisible things for their disclosure. By such veils the divine ray itself is anagogically veiled. For anagogy, as was said, is called the ascent or elevation of the mind to the contemplation of heavenly things. It is therefore veiled anagogically because it is veiled in order to shine more fully; it is covered so that it may appear more clearly. Its shadowing, therefore, is our illumination; and its veiling [Col. 0946B] is our elevation.

Just as weak eyes freely behold the sun when it is covered by a cloud, though they cannot look upon its flashing light, so it is impossible for the divine ray to shine upon the bleary eyes of the mind unless it is veiled by the variety of sacred coverings and prepared, through paternal providence, naturally and fittingly by things which are according to us. Unless paternal providence had mercifully provided this for us by its ineffable goodness, its light could not shine upon our eyes at all. Therefore it provided for us paternally and compassionately, preparing that light for us and adapting it to things, likenesses, and forms suited to us; and so it showed it to us prepared [Col. 0946C] and adapted naturally and fittingly—that is, according to our nature and the particular character of what belongs to our nature. It conforms itself to our things so that through our things it may become known to us, and so that what is connatural and proper to us, when set forth for demonstration, may be understood by us more readily.

“It is for this reason that the all-perfect ordering of sacred things, judging our most holy hierarchy worthy of a supramundane imitation of the heavenly hierarchies, transmitted the aforesaid immaterial hierarchies in material figures and formal compositions, rendering them manifold.”

It is as though he said: Because invisible things are suitably demonstrated through visible things, divine Wisdom, which orders all things according to the likeness of the angelic hierarchy invisibly ordered in heaven, visibly formed the human hierarchy on earth. Thus there might also be among human beings sacred powers and principalities, by which human life, proceeding in time, might be governed, so that the invisible ordering of the angels might become known from the visible ordering of human beings.

This is what he says: “For this reason the all-perfect ordering of sacred things”—that is, the supreme hierarchy, the ineffable Trinity itself, from which and according to which all sacred things, that is, all sacred ordinances, are arranged—judged our most holy hierarchy, that is, the human hierarchy, worthy of the supramundane—that is, spiritual or intellectual—imitation of the heavenly hierarchies, that it might imitate them spiritually and be ordered according to them.

And therefore, rendering manifold—that is, variously and multiply declaring—those already mentioned immaterial [Col. 0947A], that is, spiritual and angelic hierarchies, in material, that is, bodily and visible figures, or figures drawn from visible things, and in formal compositions, that is, expressions suited and appropriately formed according to reason, it transmits—that is, institutes—our most holy hierarchy. This was done so that the principle of visible demonstrations leading to invisible truth might here also be maintained: so that we may ascend from the most sacred formations set forth outwardly for demonstration to unfigured heights and likenesses—that is, to things simple and spiritual.

We ascend, I say, proportionately to ourselves: that is, illuminated through outward things, according to the proportion and measure of spiritual gifts, into knowledge of invisible things and toward the sublime, simple, and ever-constant truth [Col. 0947B]. For the heights and likenesses themselves are the invisible powers: heights in dignity, likenesses in immutability, unfigured in simplicity. Toward knowledge of them, according to the differences of our advances and the increases of illumination, we ascend proportionately to ourselves through stages of spiritual progress within us and through differences of gifts among us.

For according to that proportion in which we now receive the gifts of grace differently, we subsequently pass, either here through contemplation of the mind or there through recompense, into the number of the angels. Thus we ascend proportionately to ourselves when, according to the differing ways in which we are now ordered through gifts of grace and degrees of dignities, we are raised to participation in invisible truth through secret and invisible advancement [Col. 0947C].

But that truth is figuratively and materially figured and formed in us through the offices of spiritual dignities, degrees, and distributions of orders, according to visible habits, actions, and signs, which are set forth in our hierarchy, as it were, for disclosure. All these exist in the heavenly and angelic hierarchy, according to simple truth, in a sublime way surpassing our nature, purely and uniformly, without signs or figures. In accordance with this excellence theology calls the angelic orders themselves heights [Col. 0947D] and likenesses: either because they do not differ from themselves through any changeability, or because the things which are in them according to simple truth appear to be, as it were, certain likenesses and exemplars of the things which exist through figures and images.

For unless there were some likeness between these and those, there could be no disclosure from these to those. But now, since divine wisdom formed these visible things in the first creation for the emulation of invisible things, in the second ordering it also established from these visible things signs and exemplars of manifestations for the rational mind ascending to knowledge of invisible things.

“For it is not possible for our mind to ascend to that immaterial imitation and [Col. 0948A] contemplation of the heavenly hierarchies unless it employs the material guidance that belongs to it.”

He calls the imitation or contemplation spiritual and incorporeal—that is, non-material—because everything bodily is composed of matter. Spiritual nature is rightly called immaterial, because it neither comes from matter, so as to be from something else, nor can be matter, so that something else may be from it.
