By material guidance he understands bodily signs, through whose guidance, as it were, the human mind is directed from visible things to imitation and contemplation of invisible things: to imitation through the exercise of virtue, and to contemplation through knowledge of truth.

Note also the new construction and new comparison in his use of “guidance by the hand” (*manuductio*). The human mind, enveloped in the darkness of its ignorance, cannot emerge into the light of truth unless it is directed and, like a blind person using a guide by the hand, proceeds where it does not see [Col. 0948B]. The very guidances and directions which the mind uses in striving toward invisible things are taken from visible signs and manifestations formed according to visible things.

The all-perfect ordering of sacred things arranged and ordered all this. In Greek it is called *hierothesia*, that is, “the placing of sacred things”: namely, the supreme Trinity, from which and according to which all sacred things are arranged and ordered in heaven, on earth, and elsewhere. By another name it is called *teletarchē*, that is, “the principle of purification,” because from it comes every cleansing and the beginning of purification—not only that evil things may become good, but also of illumination [Col. 0948C] and deification, so that things already good may become better.

Therefore the supreme priesthood, or supreme fatherhood, which cleanses, sanctifies, and illuminates all things, instituted and ordered this: that in the first place the angelic nature should be formed invisibly according to it, and in the second place human nature should be re-formed to the same image, aroused through visible things. For the human mind cannot be led back to knowledge or imitation of invisible things unless it is taught through visible manifestations, because visible things themselves were so made by God that, according to the likeness and emulation which they received from invisible things, they can suitably declare those invisible things, so that our mind, employing their guidance, may be directed to those things [Col. 0948D], assessing and considering them according to these, by the likeness of their manifestation.

As follows: “The mind itself reckoning visible forms to be imaginations, or images, of invisible beauty;” “sensory delights to be figures of invisible distribution”—understand: the mind itself reckoning them so; “material lights to be an image of immaterial radiance”—again understand: the mind itself reckoning them so; “the unfolded sacred disciplines to be according to the intellect images of contemplative fullness”—here more must be understood: our mind reckoning them to be images; “the ordered ranks of the dispositions that are here to be images of habits united to divine things”—again understand: our mind reckoning them to be images [Col. 0949A]; “the reception itself of the most divine Eucharist to be an image of participation in Jesus”—again understand: our mind reckoning it to be an image.

The summary of the whole chapter, then, is this: Because our mind cannot ascend to imitation and contemplation of invisible things unless it is guided through visible things, it must be guided in such a way that it knows how to reckon and judge invisible things from the visible, according to the likeness and signification which visible things bear to invisible things. He shows by adding certain distinct examples what likenesses of visible to invisible things our mind should reckon and judge. It is as though he said: The truth of invisible things was demonstrated through visible things because our mind cannot ascend to the truth of invisible things themselves unless it is instructed by the consideration of visible things [Col. 0949B], so as to reckon visible forms to be imaginations of invisible beauty.

Since the beauty of visible things consists in their forms, he rightly says that invisible beauty is demonstrated through visible forms, because visible beauty is an image of invisible beauty. Yet, because in visible things form is one thing and essence another, all visible things are changeably beautiful, since whatever is numerically diverse and mutable in nature cannot subsist together inseparably. But invisible things, in which form is not one thing and essence another, because everything which is is one, simple, and identical with its being, are beautiful by the fact that they are. Their beauty is not compounded from many things coming together into one, as visible nature seems to be, whose form is spread out according to spatial extension and arranged through figures fitted together from many things [Col. 0949C].

Therefore the beauty of visible nature is one thing and that of invisible nature another: the latter is simple and uniform, whereas the former is manifold and composed by varied proportion. Yet there is some likeness of visible beauty to invisible beauty, according to the emulation by which the invisible artificer established each, in which, as though in certain mirrors of diverse proportions, they fashion one image. Accordingly, from visible beauty the human mind is suitably aroused to ascend to invisible beauty; led as it were from like to like, it easily understands inwardly and invisibly what kinship visible things which it grasps outwardly possess with invisible things [Col. 0949D].

For, looking toward invisible things by the invisible light implanted within it, our mind readily judges visible forms to be images of invisible beauty, responding through a certain friendly likeness to the invisible thing which it possesses inwardly, and finds them acceptable according to approval and affection. For what is in the mind is invisible, just as the mind itself is invisible. Yet it—the invisible mind—conceives from visible things joy, love, and affection; and it loves some things from among them as though similar, friendly, and kindred, willingly yields itself to them, and exults in them. But it rejects, hates, and avoids others; it removes itself far from them in love and affection [Col. 0950A], and judges them alien to itself, unsuitable, and possessing no likeness with it.

In this way our mind is taught from its own nature that visible things have kinship and likeness with invisible things; and that visible things themselves are images and representations of things which cannot be seen visibly, because things not seen are understood through them. For, in some respect, everything that there invisibly subsists in immutable nature is received here visibly and sensibly by mutable nature so as to lead us to invisible things.

Here there is appearance and form which delights sight; melody’s pleasantness which charms hearing; sweetness of scent which refreshes smell; sweetness of taste which fills the sense of tasting [Col. 0950B]; and bodily softness which cherishes and gently receives touch. But there, appearance is virtue and form is justice; sweetness is love and scent is desire; song is joy and exultation; and touch is the finding of the beloved, desired, and sought good. All these things are there, and there they are true; and they bear some likeness to these things, which are not true, insofar as they are understood by us.

From these things our mind ascends to knowledge and imitation of those things, reckoning visible forms—whether nature displays them as implanted according to the first creation, or sacred Scripture providentially sets them forth in signification for making a disclosure—to be images of invisible beauty; and sensory delights, that is, sensible sweetnesses, to be figures and likenesses [Col. 0950C] of invisible distribution: that is, of the sweetness invisibly distributed, or bestowed in diverse ways, so that one receives more and another less according to the measure and gifts of the grace-giver.

Likewise, it reckons material—that is, bodily—lights to be an image of immaterial radiance, that is, spiritual light. Again, it reckons sacred disciplines—that is, teachings investigated and scrutinized by intellectual effort—to be images of contemplative fullness: that is, the full and perfect contemplation which is perceived and imparted according to the intellect alone, invisibly. For all the knowledge which we now learn from sacred Scripture through the labor of reading or meditation is only an image, as it were, of that full [Col. 0950D] and perfect knowledge which we shall afterward draw from immediate contemplation. Hence the Apostle also says: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face” (1 Cor. XIII). What wonder, then, if sensory things which appear outwardly are called images of invisible things, when even our knowledge itself, which is believed to be spiritual and invisible in comparison with those things, is judged to hold the place of an image and likeness in relation to those things?

“And the ordered ranks of the dispositions which are here, of habits united to divine things.” Again understand: our mind reckoning the ranks of dispositions “which are here,” that is, externally present, to be images of habits united to divine things. There is a certain habit of a good mind united [Col. 0951A] to divine things, as though gathered into one from the manifold rifts of desires, and ordered so that it may proceed rightly: united through love, and ordered through discernment; united to one and ordered in one.

The ranks of dispositions which are outwardly administered in the degrees, offices, and ministries of the holy Church are images of this invisibly ordered and subsisting habit. For just as in the one Church diverse orders and arrangements, by furnishing and cooperating with one another, produce one peace and concord in the whole, so in the one soul many virtues, cooperating and furnishing aid to one another, compose one form of perfection. And in each of us the disposition of the outward person, the order of living, and the manner [Col. 0951B] of acting disclose the form and habit of the inward person.

“And the reception itself of the most divine Eucharist, as participation in Jesus.” Again, understand what was said above: our mind judges the very reception of the most divine Eucharist to be an image of participation in Jesus. For the reception itself of the most divine Eucharist—that is, the most holy reception of the body and blood of Jesus Christ, which we now handle sacramentally and visibly upon the altar—is an image and form of that participation in Jesus by which either we are now joined to him in spirit through love, or later, when appearing in the same form of glory, we shall be united to him in complete likeness.

Here, indeed, it must be noted that some have supposed that they could find in this passage a support for their error. They say that in the sacrament of the altar the reality [Col. 0951C] of Christ’s body and blood is not present, but only its image and figure, because Scripture says that what is received in the Eucharist of the altar is an image of that which will be received in participation in Jesus. Surely they would not have fallen into this snare of error if they either received God’s sacraments with upright and humble faith, or handled the holy Scriptures with a fitting understanding. But now, because in God’s sacraments they prefer their own judgment to faith, and in the holy Scriptures disdain to maintain a sound method of interpretation, it comes about that the very word of truth makes them more blind, while, wrongly understood, it supplies error in place of truth. Yet this is not a defect of Scripture, but the blindness of those who read and do not understand [Col. 0951D]; nor a confusion in God’s sacraments, but the perversity of those who presume.

Here they have erred dangerously, preferring one ambiguous statement to so many manifest sentences and unquestionable assertions; and in that statement choosing falsehood rather than truth—not because that was said there more plainly, but because it was believed by them more readily. What then? Is the sacrament of the altar not reality because it is a figure? Then neither is Christ’s death reality because it is a figure; nor is Christ’s resurrection reality because it is a figure. For the Apostle plainly declares that Christ’s death and resurrection are figure, image, likeness, sacrament, and example, saying: “Christ died for our sins and rose again for our justification, that, having died to sins, we might live unto righteousness” (1 Cor. XV) [Col. 0952A]. And the Apostle Peter said: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow his footsteps” (1 Pet. II). Therefore Christ’s death was an example that we might die to sin, and his resurrection an example that we might live unto righteousness. Was it therefore not reality? Then Christ did not truly die and did not truly rise, if his death or resurrection was not real. Far be it! For it is written of him: “Surely he himself bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (Isa. LIII). Therefore Christ’s death was real and yet was an example; Christ’s resurrection was real and yet was an example.

Why, then, can the sacrament of the altar not be both likeness and reality? It is likeness in one respect and reality in another [Col. 0952B]. For although it is one sacrament, three distinct elements are set forth in it: the visible species, the reality of the body, and the power of spiritual grace. One thing is the visible species, which is seen visibly. Another is the reality of the body and blood, believed invisibly beneath the visible species. And another is spiritual grace, received invisibly and spiritually together with the body and blood. What we see is the species of bread and wine; but what we believe beneath that species is the true body and true blood of Christ Jesus, the body that hung upon the cross and the blood that flowed from his side. It is not merely that body and blood are signified through bread and wine; rather, under the species of bread and wine the true body and true blood are consecrated. The visible species [Col. 0952C] is the sacrament of the true body and true blood; while the body and blood are the sacrament of spiritual grace. And just as a species is seen there whose thing or substance is not believed to be there, so the thing whose species is not seen is believed to be truly and substantially present there. For the species of bread and wine is seen, while the substance of bread and wine is not believed. But the substance of Christ’s body and blood is believed, though its species is not seen.

Therefore, what is seen according to the species is a sacrament and image of that which is believed according to the reality of the body; and that which is believed according to the reality of the body is a sacrament of that which is received according to spiritual grace. Thus the sacrament of the altar and the divine Eucharist are, in the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, both image according to the species of bread and wine in which it is seen, and reality according to the truth of its substance, in which it is believed and received there [Col. 0952D]. And again, what we now receive upon the altar—Christ visibly according to the sacramental species, and bodily according to the reality of flesh and blood—is sacrament and image of the fact that we ought to receive that same Christ invisibly and spiritually in the heart, according to the infusion of grace and participation in his Spirit.

Therefore the most divine Eucharist, which is handled on the altar visibly and bodily, both according to the species of bread and wine and according to the reality of Christ’s body and blood, is sacrament, sign, and image [Col. 0953A] of the invisible and spiritual participation in Jesus, accomplished inwardly in the heart through faith and love. For the wisdom of God, which manifests itself through the visible, wished to show that it is itself the food and refreshment of souls; and therefore it set forth the assumed flesh as food, that through the food of flesh it might invite us to taste Divinity. But lest again human weakness shrink from contact with flesh in receiving it, it veiled that flesh under the species of accustomed and principal food, and set it forth thus to be received: so that sense might be sustained by the one thing and faith built up by the other. Sense is sustained by the one, in receiving only what is usual and familiar; but faith is built up by the other, in recognizing, in what it sees, the nature of that which it does not see.

The species of bread and wine is accordingly set forth in order to teach [Col. 0953B] that in receiving Christ’s body and blood there is full and perfect refreshment from Christ’s Divinity. Complete refreshment, moreover, consists in food and drink; and bread and wine are the principal substance of food and drink. The species is set forth from the principal substance of refreshment, so that in it the reality of the body and blood may be received and signified, as he himself testifies: “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (John VI). Yet that reception of body and blood, because it alone, without spiritual effect, does not confer salvation, is shown by the same Savior when he says: “The flesh profits nothing; it is the Spirit that gives life” (ibid.). Thus the power and fullness of spiritual refreshment which is in Christ’s body and blood is signified by the species of bread and wine [Col. 0953C], but is accomplished in the reception of grace and in the infusion of inward and eternal refreshment.

Thus, since three things are there in one, in the first is found the sign of the second; in the second, the cause of the third; and in the third, the power of the second and the reality of the first. These three are in one, and are one sacrament. It is therefore clear that reception of the most divine Eucharist is sacrament and image of participation in Jesus, because what we visibly receive as his sacrament is a sign that we ought to be united to him spiritually and invisibly. The Eucharist itself—that is, “good grace”—namely the most divine sacred offering, is called most divine because it makes divine, and makes participants in Divinity, those who partake of it. And because it is both sign and reality, in which Christ’s true flesh is received under the species of bread, and because by worthily receiving his flesh one is granted reception, participation, and fellowship in his very Divinity [Col. 0953D], it is most worthy, most holy, sanctifying all things, and holy.

“And whatever other things are delivered supermundanely to the heavenly essences, but symbolically to us.” After offering certain examples to show the likeness of visible things to invisible, he now concludes generally concerning the whole, saying: “And whatever other things are delivered supermundanely to the heavenly essences, but symbolically to us.” It is as if he said: Our mind ought to judge that the visible things mentioned above [Col. 0954A] have, according to the examples given, a likeness to invisible things; and not these alone, but whatever else has been delivered to us symbolically or to the heavenly essences supermundanely.

For not only these visible things set forth—forms, delights, lights of instruction, orders, and the sacred Eucharist—possess a likeness to, and manifestation of, invisible things; but all other visible things whatsoever, set forth for us, who are to be taught visibly, in a symbolic—that is, figurative—manner, for the signification and declaration of invisible things. Nor do these visible things alone, symbolically delivered to us, possess a manifestation of invisible things; those things also which are delivered to the heavenly essences—that is, to angelic spirits—supermundanely, that is invisibly and spiritually and not [Col. 0954B] according to the species of this world, are signs of invisible things and images of those things which subsist, beyond all understanding and sense, in the exalted and incomprehensible nature of Divinity.

This is what he says: not only those things delivered to us symbolically are signs of invisible things, but also those delivered supermundanely to the heavenly essences. For the angelic spirits themselves have their signs and manifestations through which they are taught immaterially, invisibly, and simply concerning God’s invisible things, exceedingly hidden and secret, concealed within. These signs, with regard to us and the visible things among us, are considered entirely invisible; but with regard to that exceedingly invisible, inaccessible light and incomprehensible Deity [Col. 0954C], they are, as it were, outward and proceed from within into manifestation. For this reason, these signs themselves, which come upon minds or souls divinely illumined, are called *theophanies*, that is, divine appearances; because in them, as they come into manifestation, that which is wholly hidden of God is disclosed.

These, then, are what are delivered supermundanely to the heavenly beings: not according to the manner of manifestation found among us, but breathed into them invisibly and simply. Much ought here to have been said concerning that mode of contemplation by which theophanies—that is, divine appearances—divinely breathed into illumined minds come upon them and, by wonderfully hidden, secret, and singular instruction, make them wise concerning God’s hidden and invisible things. This is especially so because here also some are found to have become vain in their reasonings, proclaiming God to be wholly incomprehensible and inaccessible to the rational mind, except insofar as it is taught concerning him by certain theophanies—that is, divine appearances—or divine likenesses set forth for contemplation [Col. 0954D]. They place these as certain images of hidden Divinity, intermediate between rational minds and God: higher indeed than the mind, but lower than Divinity. They hold that God is seen only in these, and only thus seen, since he cannot be seen in himself by any mind or soul.

But these are their idols and phantasms of vanity. While they try to assert that in these alone the light of Divinity is visible and apprehensible [Col. 0955A], they are shown to deprive holy minds of the true knowledge and vision of Deity. For what is it that God is seen only in them and not outside them, except that he is never truly seen and that truth is never seen? If the image alone is always seen and truth never seen, because the image is not truth even when it is an image of truth, then indeed truth is not seen. Let them therefore remove their fantasies, by which they strive to darken the light of our minds; nor let them shut off our God from us by the idols of their imaginings. For just as nothing besides him can satisfy us, so nothing can bring us to rest short of him.

Let us, therefore, understand theophanies in another manner, one consistent with truth. Just as there are two things, light and the body which receives light, and from these two one luminous thing is produced [Col. 0955B]—and the luminous thing itself is in a sense an image and likeness of light insofar as it shines as the light itself shines—so our God is light, indeed true light; and pure and cleansed rational minds receive that light. From it they become luminous; and they are not images of light insofar as they exist, but insofar as they shine from light, as light itself shines. These luminous beings are theophanies of light, in which the light is seen; for light would be seen by no one unless someone were illumined by the light. Indeed, whoever sees light in himself sees himself as luminous; and he certainly would not see himself if he did not shine, nor see himself shining.

Thus we do not establish another thing between our God and ourselves, but make a direct way both for ourselves to him and for him even to us, so that we may be in him and he in us [Col. 0955C]. There must be nothing other than him in which we are made blessed, just as there could be nothing other than him from whom we were created. Therefore let us interpret the foregoing theological statement in a more suitable sense. For, after saying that certain invisible things are manifested through the visible images which have been defined, he now appends a general statement about these invisible things, saying: “And whatever other things,” and so forth. It is as if he said: Not only those invisible things whose signs have been set forth have come into manifestation, but also all other invisible things which are delivered—that is, set forth and made manifest—to us, namely to human beings, symbolically, that is figuratively and through sensible manifestations [Col. 0956A], while to the heavenly essences, that is angelic spirits, they are revealed supermundanely and spiritually by bare and simple truth impressed upon them.

“Therefore, because of this our rationally accommodated deification”—that is, the divinity that is rationally accommodated (*corrationalis*) to us, namely suitable or fitting to us. For it is fitting that through things known to us we should become participants in divine things. “Therefore because of this,” as though he said: Since the human mind cannot be taught about invisible things except through things visible, known, and akin to itself, therefore “the merciful principle of perfection”—that is, God, from whom all perfection has its beginning, just as it receives in him its consummation and end, by grace and mercy alone—wished to recall us to his knowledge and restore us to likeness [Col. 0956B]. He did so by “manifesting to us the heavenly hierarchies,” that is, angelic powers, “and also perfecting our hierarchy as their fellow-minister,” namely as a fellow-minister of the heavenly hierarchies, so that it may be conformed to them both in dignity and in divine ministry, preserving in us the likeness of their God-formed sanctification, so that we may be like their sanctification, which is conformed to God; “according to our capacity,” that is, according to our possibility—so far as we, who are human, mortal, and still subject to sin, can be like them.

He “described the supercelestial intellects,” invisible spirits unknown to us, through sensible images, that through what is known we might learn what is unknown. He made this description [Col. 0956C] “in the sacred compositions of the utterances,” that is, in the descriptions of sacred speech; these compositions set before us figures and likenesses for the manifestation of invisible things. He did this “that he might lead us back through sensible things to intellectual things,” that is, through visible things to invisible. And that he might lead us also “from sacredly figured symbols,” that is, from sacred figures and figures of sacred things, “to the simple summits,” that is, to the simple and spiritual excellences to be known, “of the heavenly hierarchies,” namely angelic powers. For this reason he described them to us through visible signs: that he might make them intelligible to us and conform us to their imitation.

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0955]

## TITLE OF CHAPTER II: That divine and heavenly things are beautifully manifested even through dissimilar symbols.

## TEXT

[Col. 0955C]

It is necessary, then, I think, first to explain what we understand the contemplation of every hierarchy to be, and what benefit each hierarchy has brought to those who praise divine things. Then we must praise the heavenly hierarchies according to their manifestation in the Scriptures; and, following this, say by what kinds of divine formations the sacred descriptions of the Scriptures figure the heavenly orders [Col. 0956C], and to what truth one must ascend through the forms. This is so that we too may not, in an unclean manner and like many others, imagine heavenly and Godlike minds to be certain many-footed and many-faced beings, fashioned into bovine and cattle-like forms (*pecudalitatem*; variant *pecuinitatem*), or into the savage image of lions, or the hooked-beaked form of eagles, or the threefold fluttering motion of birds’ wings; and so that we may not imagine certain fiery wheels above heaven, material thrones necessary for Divinity to recline upon [Col. 0957A], certain many-coloured horses, armed commanders-in-chief, and whatever other things have been delivered to us in the sacred Scriptures, fashioned in the variety of symbolic forms that make things manifest (Ezek. I; Rev. IV; Isa. VI; Dan. VII; Zech. I; Rev. VI; Ezek. XXIII; Job XVI; Wisd. V; Josh. V; 2 Macc. III).

For theology has made a most artful use of sacred poetic formations in dealing with unfigured intellects: revealing our mind, providing for it a return appropriate and connatural to itself, and reforming it toward the holy, elevating Scriptures. But if anyone thinks that sacred compositions should indeed be received as representations of realities which are in themselves simple, unknown to us, and incapable of contemplation [Col. 0957B], yet considers the descriptions of holy intellects in the sacred Scriptures unsuitable and says that it is harsh to speak thus of this theatre of angelic names; and if he says that the theologians, when coming to corporeal construction in regard to bodily things, ought universally to have formed and manifested them by figures proper to corporeal things and, as far as possible, akin to them—using among us the most precious forms, somehow immaterial and exalted essences—and ought not to have placed the lowest earthly multiplicities around heavenly and Godlike simplicities: this, indeed, would appear to be more sublime and would not draw supermundane manifestations down into unsuitable dissimilarities. It would also not, at once, do injustice to the divine powers and mislead our minds equally by entangling them in impure compositions [Col. 0957C]. Perhaps, moreover, people would suppose that supercelestial things are filled with certain lion-like and horse-like multitudes, with lowing speech of praise, with the winged plunging of angels, with other animals, and with baser materials, as though confined to what is incongruous, ignoble, and passible, while wholly Godlike things are described through every manner of bright likeness in the revelatory Scriptures.

But the investigation of truth, I think, shows that the most sacred wisdom of the Scriptures (Ezek. XXVIII; Job XXXVIII) has made full provision for both concerns in its formations of heavenly minds: so that it neither does injustice, as someone might perhaps say, to the divine powers, nor fastens you in a passible way upon the base lowliness of images. Since the forms of the formless and the figures of what lacks figure are fittingly arranged [Col. 0957D], one might say that there is more than one reason: our analogy is unable to extend directly to invisible contemplations, and requires returns proper and connatural to itself, which present to us passible formations of formless and supernatural contemplations. But it is also most fitting to the mystical Scriptures to conceal divine things, which are incomprehensible, through enigmas and to make the sacred, hidden truth of supermundane intellects inaccessible to the many. For not everyone is holy, nor is knowledge for all, as the Scriptures say (Matt. VII; 1 Cor. II).

But if someone considers the ugly causes of the imagery dishonourable, saying that such shameful forms are referred to Godlike and most holy orders, it is enough to answer him: the mode of holy manifestation is twofold. One mode proceeds, as it were, fittingly through images of similar sacred figures; the other is shaped through constructions of dissimilar forms into what is wholly incongruous and unbecoming [Col. 0958A]. Thus the mystical traditions of the revelatory Scriptures praise the blessed Divinity, worthy of worship and above essence, sometimes as reason, intellect, and essence, declaring its divine rationality and wisdom, its truly existing substance, and its true causality for substances; they form it as light and call it life, remaining in these marvellously purer formations, having in some manner proved them superior to deficient material forms. And in this way they offer divine things a likeness to truth. For it is beyond every essence and life: no light characterizes it, and every likeness of reason and intellect falls incomparably short of it.

At other times, however, the Scriptures praise it supermundanely through dissimilar manifestations (Rom. XI; 1 Tim. VI; Ps. CXL), calling it invisible, infinite, and incomprehensible, and signifying what it is not rather than what it is. This, I think, is more powerful with reference to it. For, as the hidden and priestly tradition has introduced, we truly say that it is not any one of the things that are. Yet we do not know its superessential, invisible, ineffable, and boundless infinity [Col. 0958C]. If, then, negations in divine matters are true, while affirmations are inadequate, manifestation through dissimilar formations is more suited to the obscurity of the mysteries.

And so the sacred descriptions of the Scriptures do not disgrace heavenly adornments by manifesting them through dissimilar constructions of forms; rather, through these they show their supermundane excellences above all material things. Indeed, I do not think that any sound-minded person would deny that dissimilar likenesses lead our mind upward more effectively. Through the more precious sacred formations one may fittingly be deceived, imagining heavenly essences to be golden in form, or certain shining men clothed in beautiful garments, gleaming harmlessly with whiteness and fire, or in whatever similar figurative forms theology [Col. 0958D] has fashioned the heavenly intellects. In order that those who understand nothing higher than visible goods might not suffer this, the restorative wisdom of the holy theologians descended wonderfully to unbecoming dissimilarities. It did not permit our material nature, lingering among shameful images, to remain at rest; but it purified and raised it up, suggesting to the soul through the ugliness of the compositions that supercelestial and divine spectacles are in no way truly similar to material things—especially to such shameful things—as neither justice nor truth allows.

But one must also understand this: nothing that exists is altogether deprived of participation in the good; for, as the Truth of the Scriptures says, “All things are very good” (Gen. I). Therefore it is possible to draw good contemplations from all things and, from material things, to form the dissimilar likenesses spoken of for invisible and intellectual realities [Col. 0959A], since intellectual beings possess in one manner what sensible things possess in another. For fury in irrational creatures arises from a passible movement and their furious impulse is filled with every kind of irrationality. But in intellectual beings anger must be understood differently: it signifies, I think, their vigorous rationality and their unwavering [the text reads *immanem*, perhaps for *immanentem*] abiding in divine and immutable foundations.

In the same way, we say that desire in irrational creatures is an unreasoning and material quality, naturally arising from movement or habit: an uncontrolled inclination toward mutable things and an irrational continuance in bodily pleasure, compelling every animal, according to sensation, toward what it desires [Col. 0959B]. But when, applying dissimilar likenesses to intellectual beings, we ascribe desire to them, it must be understood as divine love: the desire, beyond reason and intellect, of immateriality; an unbending and need-free longing for superessentially pure and impassible contemplation; for that pure, most exalted, invisible, form-giving beauty of eternal, true, and invisible communion. It possesses, as it were, power in self-sufficiency and conversion; it is troubled by no power, through the unconfused and immutable love of divine beauty and the universal return to what is truly to be desired.

Likewise, in irrational animals or animate material things we properly call irrationality and insensibility a defect of reason and sense; but in immaterial and intellectual essences we confess them to be holy and fitting excellences, as surpassing our transient and bodily reason and the material sense of mind alien to incorporeal things [Col. 0959C]. Therefore it is not discordant to form heavenly figures even out of lowly material elements. For material things themselves, possessing subsistence from the truly Good, contain through their whole material arrangement certain images of intellectual beauty; and it is possible through them to be led back to the first immaterial forms, receiving dissimilar likenesses, as was said—likenesses that are not alike in the same manner, but are fittingly and beautifully defined according to the proper characteristics of intellectual and sensible things.

We shall find the mystical theologians wonderfully adapting such imagery not only in descriptions of the heavenly orders, but sometimes even in divine manifestations themselves. At times they praise Divinity through precious lights: as the sun of righteousness, as the morning star rising holily in the mind, and as light shining invisibly without circling (Mal. I; Rev. II). At other times they use intermediate things: as fire shining without harm, as water giving the fullness of life, and, speaking symbolically, as entering the womb and as rivers overflowing and flowing back without measure. At other times they use lowest things: as sweet ointment and as a cornerstone (Exod. III; John I). They also apply an animal form to it, fitting to it the character of lion and panther [Col. 0960A], clothing it with a leopard’s skin, and portraying it as a raging bear (Cant. II; Isa. XXVIII; Hos. V). Further, at what seemed lowest and most contemptible of all, the divine wise men [the text perhaps intends “divine Wisdom”] handed down that Divinity itself fashioned itself in the form of a worm (Ps. XXI).

Thus all the theologians and prophets, through hidden inspiration, distinguish the Holy of Holies from things holy and undefiled, and honour the holy figuration that is dissimilar, so that divine things may not be rightly received by the impure, nor those devoted to contemplation of marvellous images remain fixed upon the figures as though they were realities. They honour divine things, therefore, through true negations and through diverse likenesses drawn from the lowest things in composite imagery. There is consequently nothing incongruous if they also form the heavenly essences through unsuitable and dissimilar likenesses [Col. 0960B], for the reasons stated.

For perhaps we should never, through need of ascent, come by diligent inquiry into divine things to the question itself, unless the ugliness of the revelatory deforming of angels compelled us, refusing to let our minds remain in constructions of dissimilar forms, but forcing them to deny material passibilities and accustoming them, through visible things, to stretch themselves purely toward supermundane heights.

So much has been said by us concerning the material and unsuitable descriptions of angelic images in the divine Scriptures. Next we must distinguish what hierarchy itself is, in our judgment, and what benefit is derived from hierarchy by those who receive a share in it. May Christ be my guide—if it is permitted me to say so—the inspiration of every hierarchical manifestation [Col. 0960C]. But you, child, according to the holy ordinance of our priestly tradition, listen yourself in a holy and fitting manner. Become divine through divine instruction concerning marvellous things; keep within the secrecy of your mind the holy things that surround you, guarding them as unified things from the impure multitude. For, as the Scriptures say, it is not permitted to cast before swine the undefiled, light-bearing, and beneficent adornment of the pearls of invisible things (Matt. VII).

## EXPOSITION
First I said—and now I say, lest I keep you waiting—that I have undertaken your request concerning Dionysius’s *Hierarchy*, not in order to pursue an investigation of profound matters, but only to uncover and bring into the light the hidden meaning of the words [Col. 0960D]. This is more fitting, first of all, for beginners; especially because we recognize that the matters we judged should be discussed are exceedingly great and beyond our capacity.

The title of the second chapter is this: “That divine and heavenly things are fittingly manifested even through dissimilar symbols.”

We have already said above what a symbol is: namely, a comparison—that is, an adaptation of visible forms proposed for the disclosure of an invisible thing. For example, when we wish visibly to express the natures of heavenly spirits, we combine human faces and birds’ wings into one composite figure, so that, through the face of a human being—who alone among visible creatures uses reason—it may be understood that the invisible spirits too are rational and wise; while through the wings the agility of their nature and their swift motion toward all things may be expressed [Col. 0961A].

Therefore, because in the first chapter he discussed every hierarchy in general terms, briefly setting forth, as it were, the outline of his subsequent work for instructional purposes: first, because every good is multiplied from the highest Good by participation, and every good is united to the highest Good by likeness and conversion; then, because Scripture fittingly adopted visible signs for the disclosure of invisible things—now, in the following chapter, as the title itself announces beforehand, he shows that divine things, namely those which are in the highest hierarchy, and heavenly things, namely those which are in the angelic hierarchy, are fittingly—that is, appropriately and suitably—manifested, represented, and signified so as to become clear.

Both are fittingly manifested [Col. 0961B], not only through similar symbols—that is, not only through beautiful and decent figures and forms appropriate to their majesty and purity, or resembling them—but also through dissimilar symbols: that is, through forms and descriptions which appear foreign to their excellence and unworthy of their purity. This may seem less fitting to some. Yet to those who consider carefully it is found to have been established by great reason and necessary dispensation.

By reason: so that, when we see these foreign things adopted for their representation, we may recognize that even those things which seemed in some respect proper are foreign and dissimilar to the highest truth. By dispensation: so that, when the devout mind sees things which it cannot tolerate as belonging to divine realities in a proper sense attributed to them by way of signification [Col. 0961C], it may be unable to doubt that other things too which appeared worthy, and for that reason might be believed true and proper, are figurative and have been brought to the truth by likeness.

Thus similar symbols are proposed in representation in order to display the truth of invisible things through a resembling appearance; dissimilar symbols, however, in order to show, by their signification, that one must leave the figure behind and proceed to truth, not remain in things which could not be true. Accordingly, however much similar symbols excel in appearance, dissimilar symbols surpass them in signification. For although the former have a more beautiful appearance, the latter possess a clearer meaning. The former display truth; the latter compel one to depart from falsehood. The former signify truth in such a way that an untaught mind may easily be detained in them [Col. 0961D]; the latter instruct in such a way that they do not allow the minds of those who consider them to be deceived into revering themselves.

Although the former are signs of truth, they might perhaps sometimes cause themselves to be received as truth because of their excellent appearance, unless there were signs of the latter kind, in which truth is not believed to reside, even though truth is signified through them. For truth is one thing, and a sign of truth another: a sign is not truth, even when it is a sign of truth and is true. Therefore those signs possess the more evident demonstration which both, through likeness whereby they approach truth, make truth itself manifest, and, through dissimilarity whereby they stand at a distance from truth, show that they are not truth but nevertheless signs and an image of truth.

This, then, is what he intends to demonstrate in this chapter, as its title expresses: that divine and heavenly things are fittingly and appropriately demonstrated not only through similar forms and representations, but also through dissimilar ones [Col. 0962A]. And that no injury, as some have thought, is done to divine and heavenly beings if they are sometimes represented in the sacred Scriptures through lowly forms, seemingly remote from their excellence and unworthy of them—as when in Scripture God is compared to a cart and angels to oxen, and so forth.

“It is necessary, therefore, as I think, first to set out what we judge the contemplation of every hierarchy to be, etc.”

He modestly qualifies his assertion, as is fitting for a prudent man; nor does he seem to presume beyond human capacity in matters sublime and remote from human sense, saying, “As I think” [Col. 0962B]. He himself knew what he was saying, since he had been taught it by Him who had seen and knew. Yet he retained modesty of expression, in order to show that these things must be sought and found with humility, not arrogance.

“It is necessary, therefore, as I think, first to set out what we judge the contemplation of every hierarchy to be.” Here he first proposes, by way of introduction, five general matters for readers to consider, which he will explain separately in the chapters that follow.

First: the general definition of every hierarchy.  
Second: the usefulness of each hierarchy.  
Third: the praise of the heavenly hierarchies according to the visible forms found in sacred discourse [Col. 0962C].  
Fourth: the character of the forms and descriptions themselves through which the heavenly powers are signified.  
Fifth: what truth the human mind ought to conceive, in the invisible realities themselves, from those things which are visibly proposed for the declaration and praise of invisible things.

That is: first, to consider what hierarchy is; second, what benefit it provides—that is, what usefulness belongs to each; third, how the excellence of invisible hierarchies is shown through visible signs; fourth, to know the character of mystical signs and demonstrations; fifth, to separate what is signified from the sign, truth from figure.

“It is necessary first to set out what contemplation”—that is, what definition—“we judge every hierarchy to be”: in other words, how hierarchy ought generally or universally to be defined [Col. 0962D]. He calls a definition a “contemplation” because the definition of a thing is, as it were, a mirror in which the nature of that thing is seen, just as in a mirror the image of the nature of a body placed before it is seen.

A general definition is one which applies universally and is found throughout the whole. For someone who says that angelic principalities are hierarchy speaks truly; yet he does not define universally, since hierarchy is also found among human beings. Likewise, someone who says that hierarchy is order speaks truly, because where there is authority there is order. Yet he does not say the whole, since not every order is hierarchy, because not every order is authority. Therefore a general definition is one which applies to everything and contains the whole [Col. 0963A].

Accordingly, the author called this general definition of hierarchy the contemplation of every hierarchy, since it both applies to all and contains the whole. Since he himself will set it forth and explain it later, we ought not to anticipate it here.

Then he adds another of the things which must be sought or explained: namely, what each hierarchy benefits its divine praisers—that is, what or how much each hierarchy, namely sacred authority, benefits its own divine praisers: those established and ordered in it who praise God, or celebrate and frequent divine praises. For all hierarchies, whether higher or lower, have been ordered and instituted for divine praise, so that God may be praised by all: “from whom and through whom are all things and all things in all” [Col. 0963B] (1 Cor. 15). Those who are more excellent praise more; and those who praise more are rewarded more sublimely.

Thus every hierarchy benefits its own divine praisers according to what it has received through the distribution of grace and the gifts of divine generosity, so that one may be more exalted in knowledge or more fervent in love. For gifts are according to grace, merits according to gifts, and diversity of rewards corresponds to diversity of merits. Therefore every hierarchy benefits God’s praisers in reward to the extent that it has conferred gifts; because every dignity and authority increases in the fruit of recompense according to the grace of ministry and office by which it was able to proclaim and increase God’s praise, honor, and glory.

Even the heavenly powers themselves, for whom the very reward is to praise God, receive benefit, each according to its own order and dignity in its principalities and hierarchies [Col. 0963C], in proportion as it rises more or less toward the praise of the Creator through the gift of cooperating grace.

Then, he says, “it is necessary”—that is, after the divine definition of every hierarchy and its usefulness have been set out—it is necessary to praise the heavenly hierarchies, that is, the angelic principalities: to describe and demonstrate their praises according to the manifestation of those hierarchies in the discourses, namely according to the way their praises are made manifest in the discourses, that is, in the divine Scriptures. For sacred discourse proposes figures and demonstrations by which the powers and praises of angelic authorities are declared; and the author says that these are to be examined and considered for the manifestation of the angelic hierarchy [Col. 0963D].

He continues: “And, following upon these things”—that is, consequently after the matters mentioned above, or in the matters which follow—“it is necessary to say by what divine formations the sacred descriptions of the discourses, namely the divine discourses, represent the heavenly orders.”

It is as though he said: First it is necessary to consider how the divine discourses proclaim the heavenly powers as praiseworthy through formations of description. Then one must consider what the descriptions and formations themselves are like, which divine discourse employs figuratively in declaring those heavenly powers. Finally, it is necessary to consider to what truth one must ascend through the forms [Col. 0964A].

For it does not suffice merely to attend to what is visible, unless we also know what invisible truth we ought to conceive from what is visibly demonstrated. If we think that only what is visibly seen in the representation exists, we shall never become participants in truth. Therefore let us distinguish sign from truth, and know that one thing is set before the outward sense for instruction, another reserved inwardly for the mind’s blessedness.

For this reason one must say to what truth we ought to ascend from these visible forms of representation: lest we too, like many people, suppose that all these things which are figuratively proposed in the Scriptures as signs of heavenly realities exist there exactly as they are mystically represented here by likenesses, forms, and figures pertaining to bodily and sensible things [Col. 0964B]—things which do not at all belong to divine and spiritual realities.

This is what follows: “So that we too may not, like many people, impurely suppose heavenly and Godlike minds to be certain many-footed and many-faced beings, formed with the animal nature of oxen or the bestial image of lions; or shaped after the appearance of eagles with curved beaks, or the threefold movement of birds’ wings. And so that we may not imagine certain fiery wheels above heaven; material thrones needed by the Divinity for reclining; certain many-colored horses; armed commanders-in-chief; and whatever else has been handed down to us from the discourses in a sacred and figurative manner through a variety of manifestative symbols.”

Thus we must not suppose, as many suppose, that heavenly and Godlike minds—that is, invisible and incorporeal spirits, having the likeness and form of God rather than of bodies—are many-footed [Col. 0964C], as they are described figuratively in sacred discourse under the figures and forms of living creatures. In Ezekiel, Isaiah, Zechariah, Micah, and other prophets, angelic spirits are represented through four-footed animals, birds, and similar things.

Nor should we suppose that certain of these spirits are many-faced—that is, have many countenances or faces—as is written in Ezekiel of the holy living creatures: “Each had four faces” (Ezek. 1). Although this may fittingly be referred to the holy Evangelists, apostles, or any righteous persons, it may nevertheless not unfittingly be understood also of the holy angels who announce the incarnation of the Word, his passion, resurrection, and ascension, and who, in all these things, serve the incarnate Word in the ministry assigned to them.

He continues: “And [formed] with the animal nature of oxen.” We must understand: nor should we suppose certain beings formed with the animal nature of oxen—that is, in the likeness and form of oxen, which is animal and not angelic—as in Ezekiel the form of an ox or calf is expressed in the representation of the living creatures. Or again, we must not suppose those spirits formed according to the bestial image of lions [Col. 0965A], that is, according to an image or likeness of lions which is bestial and unworthy of a spiritual and rational nature, as in Ezekiel the face of a human being and the face of a lion are mentioned in the representation of the living creatures.

“And [formed] after the appearance of eagles with curved beaks”: again, we must understand, we ought not to suppose them so formed. In saying “with curved beaks,” he explicitly arouses fitting ridicule, as he does elsewhere, against those who think such things are assigned to spiritual nature in a proper sense. It is known that in Ezekiel’s vision the face of an eagle is also mentioned.

He continues: “Or represented with the threefold movement of birds’ wings.” Again, we must understand: nor should we suppose this. For just as it is written in Isaiah concerning the One seated on the throne and the temple: “Seraphim stood above it; six wings to one and six wings to the other. With two they covered the head, with two they covered the feet, and with two they flew, one toward the other” [Col. 0965B] (Isa. 6). And elsewhere: “For with two they covered their bodies” (Ezek. 1). Here, indeed, in the division of the six wings into pairs, a threefold or tripartite movement is found. For six wings joined two by two make three pairs of wings.

He continues: “And let us not imagine certain fiery wheels above heaven.” The negative particle must be supplied from above: namely, that we should not imagine certain fiery wheels above heaven, nor material thrones as though needed by the Divinity for reclining, since the divine nature, which alone supports all things, needs no support. We have testimony concerning fiery wheels and thrones in the book of Daniel [Col. 0965C] (Dan. 7), and in Isaiah (Isa. 6), and in Micah concerning the high and exalted throne of the One who sits upon it.

He continues: “And certain many-colored horses”—as white, black, black, and variegated horses are read in Zechariah (Zech. 6), and likewise in the Apocalypse (Rev. 6)—again, we must understand: let us not imagine them. “And armed commanders-in-chief”: likewise, let us not imagine leaders and generals of the army bearing weapons or clad in arms, as we read in Zechariah and Micah. Likewise, the Lord is described as seated upon a high throne, with the host of heaven at his right and left; and in the book of Kings, fiery chariots, horses, and horsemen were shown in the mountains to Elisha and his servant coming to their aid (4 Kings 6).

They are called *archistrategi*—commanders-in-chief—as though leaders or commanders of the forces of princes [Col. 0965D]. The compound name comes from ἀρχός (*archos*), “chief” or “ruler,” and στρατηγός (*strategos*), “leader and commander of an army.” Thus *archistrategi* are understood as leaders of the forces of princes: those who exercise authority over the princes themselves or furnish them with leadership from above.

Therefore all these things, taken by likeness from things belonging to us and attributed to those heavenly spirits in order to signify things invisible in them, must be understood so that we do not suppose that these things exist in them in this way, but strive through these visible things to perceive other things in them which are invisible to us. For corruptible appearance does not reach their purity; and therefore it is, in some sense, an impure supposition which without discernment attributes to that excellent nature, in a proper sense, things so lowly and unworthy [Col. 0966A].

Whether these things, then, or any others have been handed down to us from the discourses—that is, the Scriptures—in a sacred and figurative manner, that is, by the formation or representation of a sacred thing, amid a variety of manifestative symbols, namely sacred figures and descriptions through which secrets and hidden things are disclosed, let us understand them all in such a way that we believe, according to their likeness and signification, that the things of which they are made are wholly true; yet let us think that none of these things exists in those realities in a proper sense.

He continues: “For theology has made very artful use of sacred poetic formations in the case of intellects without figure [Col. 0966B], unveiling, as has been said, our mind, providing for it a reduction proper and connatural to it, and adapting to it the holy anagogical Scriptures.”

This answers what he said above: that one must consider the kinds of formations by which sacred Scripture represents the heavenly orders. It is as though he said: The formations of the heavenly orders in sacred discourse must be diligently examined because they were made in order to unveil—that is, illumine—our mind toward knowledge of invisible things through visible and familiar realities.

“For theology,” that is, divine Scripture, “has made very artful,” prudent, or considered use “of sacred poetic formations”: namely, descriptions of forms or figures proposed to represent sacred or holy things; poetic formations, that is, formations devised or invented by reason and set forth through the likenesses of mystical tradition, for signifying intellects without figure [Col. 0966C]—spirits existing in their simplicity without shape or bodily form.

“Unveiling, as has been said, our mind” from the lofty veil of ignorance, so that it may contemplate heavenly things with naked and uncovered face; “and providing for it,” namely for the mind, “a reduction proper and connatural to it,” so that it may be guided toward knowledge of invisible things through those things which are proper and connatural to it; and “adapting,” fitting, or tempering “the holy anagogical Scriptures to it,” namely to the mind, so that things first conformed to us might descend to us, and afterwards, by drawing us back, might raise us as enlightened persons to higher things [Col. 0966D].

Theology therefore acted with great art: speaking to us, it took up what belongs to us and, having admonished and instructed us through our own things, raised us to its own.

But if someone perhaps thinks this commendable insofar as theology adopted beautiful and decent forms drawn from things belonging to us for the signification of visible things, while judging blameworthy and incongruous the fact that it also applied unseemly and unworthy likenesses to such purity and majesty, the response must be that theology adopted not only similar but also dissimilar forms for the representation of divine things, in order that, through what is visibly said of them in a figure as dissimilar and almost foreign, even what might have appeared proper might be recognized as figurative and foreign to proper reality [Col. 0967A].

This is what follows: “But if anyone thinks that sacred compositions ought indeed to be accepted, as concerning subsistences simple in themselves, unknown to us, and incapable of contemplation.”

That is: it is fitting that sacred compositions, namely sacred representations or formations made concerning divine and invisible things, should be accepted, since they concern realities which subsist as simple and uncompounded, without bodily representation or form, and are therefore unknown and incapable of contemplation for us, who know only how to contemplate and think of bodily things. Unless they are shown through visible signs and demonstrations, they cannot be perceived by the human heart.

If, then, anyone thinks it fitting [Col. 0967B] and necessary for such reasons that sacred compositions should be accepted, but only if they were formed beautifully and decently and suitably to such purity, while now judging unseemly and incongruous whatever descriptions of holy intellects—that is, spirits—have been made “in the sacred discourses”; and if he also judges all this invention of angelic names a theatrical fiction—as though angels, oxen, lions, eagles, horses, wheels, chariots, thrones, and the like were introduced and named—which in his estimation seems theatrical and worthy of theatrical recitation and mockery:

Yet for us, who think devoutly and believe rightly, it is harsh to speak in this way—or it is harsh to say all this: that all such harsh and incongruous expressions and descriptions constitute, as it were, a theater of angelic names. Or, if he judges that what Scripture represents ought thus to be called a harsh—that is, discordant and inappropriate—theater of angelic names; and if he says further that theologians, coming down to bodily production, that is material representation, ought universally—that is, altogether—to form and make manifest incorporeal realities, namely heavenly and invisible things, as far as possible by proper and kindred representations [Col. 0967C]: that is, by suitable and similar representations taken from among visible things, either from the most precious things among us, namely those which are most precious among us, or from things in some manner immaterial—that is, things which appear in some way immaterial and incorporeal, such as light, fire, radiance, heat, and the like.

Although these are material and bodily, they nevertheless approach spiritual nature closely in subtlety and purity. If, therefore, he says that theologians ought to have drawn figures of utterly incorporeal things from those most precious, in some manner immaterial, and eminent essences, so that truly incorporeal things might be signified through things nearly immaterial and incorporeal; and if he further says that earthly and lowest—that is, final, inferior, or contemptible—multiformities, namely figures composed of many varied forms, ought not to have been set about Godlike simplicities, that is, spiritual natures [Col. 0967D]: because these are Godlike in glory, such earthly and lowest things, and because they are simple in essence, multiformities ought not at all to have been attributed to them.

And if he says further: “This indeed”—that is, if figures of invisible things were drawn from precious and eminent essences, and earthly and lowest forms were not set about or fitted to Godlike simplicities—“would be more elevated for us”: that is, would advance us more sublimely toward knowledge of spiritual things. Or: “This indeed would be ours,” because it would be bodily and material, “and would be more elevated,” that is, nearer to divine and spiritual things, so that it would be reasonable on both accounts: that it could not instruct through what was ours, namely familiar and known to us, and correspond to the excellence and dignity of spiritual things through what was higher and more worthy [Col. 0968A].

And such representations would not lead supermundane, namely heavenly and spiritual, manifestations down into unsuitable dissimilarities as these descriptions do, because they derive likenesses unsuitable and dissimilar to spiritual things from earthly and lowest essences. Nor would this—that is, if the figures of spiritual realities were made only from beautiful and decent forms—injure the divine powers by attributing to them unsuitable forms, which would be unjust. Nor, likewise, would it deceive our mind as this ugly and unseemly formation deceives it, causing it, when it involves itself in these impure compositions made unworthily concerning those powers, to think foreign and unworthy things about them [Col. 0968B].

Perhaps yet another evil may result from these ugly compositions: people may suppose that the superheavenly realms are filled, or full, of certain lion-like and horse-like multitudes, with a lowing discourse of praise and the precipitous flight of birds. For figures of lions, horses, oxen, and birds—whose acts are to roar, neigh, and fly, and which cannot praise God except by lowing or roaring—are attributed to angels.

And they may suppose that the heavenly realms themselves are filled not only with these but also with other still more ignoble animals and materials—worms, coals, and the like—which are found said figuratively of spiritual realities: as though the heavenly realms were disclosed, that is, laid open and exposed, to what is unfitting, ignoble, and perhaps capable of being admitted into them; or even to what is passible, that is, corruptible [Col. 0968C].

All these things, then, might be supposed when the likenesses of manifestative discourses are described, likenesses which the discourses clearly—that is, manifestly—propose for disclosure in ugly forms. If this whole argument seems persuasive to anyone—the sentence remaining suspended thus far and only then drawing its conclusion—he thinks that only beautiful and excellent forms ought to be employed for signifying spiritual and divine things. Yet if someone diligently seeks the truth, he will recognize that the wisdom of the divine discourses has fittingly employed both kinds.

This is what follows: “But, as I think, an inquiry into truth shows that the most sacred wisdom of the discourses has provided very carefully for both in forming heavenly minds, or spirits, so that it should neither inflict injury—as someone perhaps might say—upon the divine powers [Col. 0969A], nor fasten us passibly upon the lowliness of vile images.”

That is: through those lowly representations it should neither injure divine powers, namely spirits which are divine, sacred, and incorporeal—though someone perhaps might call this injury and think it should be called so, whereas it is not injury—nor through the same representations “fasten us passibly upon the lowliness of vile images,” namely upon the vileness of lowly, or the lowliness of vile, images.

The wisdom of divine discourse provided and guarded against both: that through these humble representations it should neither injure divine beings nor shape our minds toward base thoughts or false suppositions.

First, then, a necessary and fitting reason is shown why bodily and visible figures and forms are applied to manifest divine and invisible realities. Someone might perhaps say that the cause is not single but twofold: not only because those realities could not otherwise be made manifest to our mind through these visible things, but also because divine secrets had to be veiled and concealed from impure minds and ill-disposed persons in the figures and enigmas of mystical descriptions [Col. 0969B].

Thus, he says, someone may state the cause of mystical descriptions. Although he himself could have stated it certainly and truthfully, he modestly attributes it to another, lest he seem to commend his own authority.

This, then, is what he says: “For since forms have been fittingly provided for the formless, and figures for those without figures, someone might say that there is not one cause: our analogy. For since.” Contrary to Latin usage, he has piled up conjunctions according to the idiom of the Greek language; or *quia* may be read in place of *quod*, so that the sense is this: someone might say that there is not one cause, namely our analogy—that is, that our analogy alone is not the cause of the fact that forms of the formless and figures of those without figures have been fittingly—that is, appropriately—provided by sacred discourse [Col. 0969C].

In other words: forms and figures have been attributed in sacred discourse to those heavenly spirits which in their own nature have neither bodily forms nor figures. Someone might say that the cause of this is not merely analogy: namely, our condition, which cannot otherwise attain knowledge of invisible things and cannot immediately—that is, without some intermediary—extend through intellect to invisible contemplations, namely contemplations of invisible things.

By “our analogy” I mean a condition which also requires reductions proper and connatural to itself: that is, to be led toward knowledge and contemplation of invisible things through what is proper and connatural to it, namely visible and bodily things. These bodily things offer, that is, set forth, formations of the formless: namely spiritual contemplations, supernatural contemplations exceeding our nature and wholly incomprehensible to us unless they were shown and suggested to us through these passible formations [Col. 0969D].

He calls human condition “analogy,” because analogy is a property according to reason and proportion found among many similar things in one respect; just as grammarians customarily identify analogies of words according to the likeness of many falling under one property. The analogy of human nature—that is, its condition, property, or proportion—is its capacity to do and know what belongs to a human being, and what the human being has received to be and to do.

It is beyond our analogy—that is, beyond our proper proportion and equality—to investigate heavenly things unless we are instructed through visible things known to us. This analogy, therefore, namely the human condition, was one reason why sacred discourse proposed visible signs of invisible things for the instruction of human minds [Col. 0970A].

But this was not the only cause. Another was that “this also is most fitting for mystical discourses”: namely, to conceal and make inaccessible to many the sacred and hidden truth of supermundane intellects, that is, invisible spirits, through incomprehensible divine enigmas. For this reason enigmas, parables, and figures are placed in the mystical discourse of the Scriptures: lest the truth of spiritual things be open to carnal and impure spirits, and so that it may at once exercise the diligent and devout by its very depth. Yet the author judges this cause worthy of mention only in addition.

Divine mysteries are therefore veiled so that they may not be open to all, because not all are worthy of knowledge of truth. “For not everyone is holy, nor is knowledge for everyone, as the discourses say.” Since not every human being is holy, truth ought not to be made manifest to all; for if it were disclosed to everyone, many would gnaw at it by contradicting it in malice or defile it by impure living [Col. 0970B].

Hence it is said: “Do not give what is holy to dogs” (Matt. 7), namely to those who gnaw at the truth set before them with the teeth of malice; “nor cast pearls before swine” (ibid.), namely before those who, so far as lies in them, defile what is offered by evil living. Such people are not holy—that is, not worthy of sacred things—and knowledge is not theirs, “as the discourses say,” namely the sacred Scriptures.

For the Apostle says that “faith is not for all” (2 Thess. 3), because that knowledge of truth by which God is devoutly believed by holy and righteous people is either not received by the perverse or is not held by them worthily [Col. 0970C].

“If anyone judges the grounds for the description of images to be unbecoming, saying that such ugly forms are unworthily referred to godlike and most holy dispositions, it is enough to say to him: How is the mode of holy manifestation twofold?” At last he now answers the question raised above, which maintained that base and abject forms are not suitably attached in sacred discourse to sacred and divine things. He says: “If anyone judges the grounds for the description of images to be ugly”—that is, if anyone judges the grounds for describing images to be ugly, that is, unsuitable—saying that it is unbecoming for such shameful forms to be referred, that is, fitted, to godlike and most holy dispositions, that is, orders—if anyone, I say, judges and speaks thus, “it is enough to say to him how the mode of holy manifestation is twofold.” That is, such an opinion and objection is adequately answered by showing that the holy manifestation made through the Scriptures has a twofold mode.

“One mode is, as it were, consequent,” that is, fitting and becoming, in which the signs follow the truth signified through a similar property: because of similar images of fitting sacred figures, that is, figures proceeding to make manifestation, or arising—that is, apt and corresponding—to what they signify. “But the other mode is fashioned in a wholly inconsequent manner,” that is, discordantly, unsuitably, and unbecomingly, because the figures themselves and the signs themselves which manifest truth do not appear to speak it. This is what he says: “Because of unlike constructions of forms.”

It follows: “Accordingly, the mystical traditions of the manifesting sayings, praising the adorable blessedness of the superessential divinity, sometimes praise it as reason, intellect, and essence, declaring its divine rationality and wisdom, its truly existing subsistence, and the true cause of the subsistence of those things which are.”

It is as though he said: Since there is a twofold mode of manifestation in sacred discourse—one fashioned through similar signs, the other through dissimilar signs—therefore the sacred sayings themselves also represent the majesty of the divine nature sometimes through similar and sometimes through dissimilar forms. Through similar forms, indeed, they do so sometimes by things taken from bodies and sometimes by incorporeal things. By bodily things, as when they call it reason and intellect; by bodily things likewise, when they call it light and splendour, and other things of this kind. At other times, however, they manifest the divine nature through dissimilar forms, likewise taken from incorporeal or bodily things. From incorporeal things, as when they attribute to it anger, zeal, and repentance; from bodily things, when they assign to it, in signification, the forms or figures of beasts or of any other bodily things.

This, therefore, is what he says: “Accordingly, the mystical traditions of the manifesting sayings praise the adorable blessedness of the superessential divinity, sometimes indeed as reason, intellect, and essence, declaring its divine subsistence as truly existing and the true cause of the subsistence of all things that are.” For it truly subsists in itself, and makes all subsistent things subsist, insofar as they call it essence; although in its majesty it subsists above every reason, intellect, and essence, as a subsistence above all things, neither intelligible nor comprehensible.

It follows: “And they fashion him as light and call him life.” That is, the mystical traditions call the adorable blessedness so, although it itself subsists as light above every light and life above every life. Sacred discourse therefore fashions the divine majesty figuratively in so many and such great ways.

“Yet these marvellous forms remain purer than the others which appear unsuitable and unworthy; and these so great and marvellous forms are in some way shown to excel the other material forms.” It is as though he said: Although every form or representation is found inferior to that excellence, nevertheless, in comparison with other forms, forms so beautiful and fair are proved to excel. Thus when the divine nature is called reason, intellect, essence, light, and life, even though in these forms too likeness fails in expressing the ineffable truth.

Hence he says: “Though even thus the likeness to the divine truth fails.” That is, these more excellent likenesses also fail—even at such a height of excellence—in divine likeness; they fail, namely, to express the truth, as must be understood. For everything which is here in a sign is less than that which is there in truth.

“For,” namely, the divine nature, “is above every essence and life, with no light characterizing,” that is, figuring or expressing it; and it excels every reason and intellect, which are incomparably left behind, or below, its likeness. Hence it appears that, if its likeness is so much superior to reason and intellect, neither reason nor intellect can advance so as to equal that likeness.

It follows: “But at other times it is praised supermundanely by the sayings themselves through dissimilar manifestations, which call it invisible, infinite, incomprehensible, and that which is signified not from what it is but from what it is not.”

It is as though he said: It is manifested not only through similar and excellent representations, approaching its image; but at times it is also praised “supermundanely,” that is, mystically, spiritually, and above the appearance of this world, through dissimilar manifestations alien to its nature. For when it is praised by beautiful forms, it is praised according to the appearance of this world—that is, it is spoken of according to something which itself exists, through which it is praised. But when it is praised through dissimilar and alien forms, it is praised supermundanely, because it is said neither to be the same thing nor to be according to that thing, but to be wholly other and above that through which it is praised. Therefore it is praised supermundanely by the sayings themselves through dissimilar forms.

I mean the sayings—or the forms themselves—calling the divine nature invisible, infinite, and incomprehensible: first infinite in itself; then invisible to us; and afterwards incomprehensible to us. The sayings call the divine nature many other such things also, from which not what it is but what it is not is signified. For when God is called invisible, infinite, and incomprehensible, not what he is is stated, but what he is not: he is not visible, because he cannot be seen; he is not bounded, because he is enclosed by no place and limited by no time; nor is he comprehensible, because, although he is believed to exist, the measure of what he is cannot be grasped.

Thus one who calls him invisible does not say that what he is does not exist, but that what he is not does not exist. Likewise, one who calls him infinite and incomprehensible does not say what he is, because he affirms no thing; but says what he is not, because he denies some thing.
