For what he does not affirm is that which cannot be spoken; and what he denies is that which can be understood.

It follows: “For this, I think, is more powerful in respect of it.” Namely, that by which not what it is but what it is not is signified is more powerful—that is, more effective, more proper, and more expressive—in respect of it. For one who says what it is not says what can in some manner be understood; but one who says what it is says what cannot in any manner be comprehended. In regard to expressing truth, it is therefore more powerful and more excellent to say what God is not than what he is.

“For, as the hidden and priestly tradition has introduced, we truly say that it is not anything according to any of the things that are; but we are ignorant of its superessential, invisible, ineffable, and limitless infinity.”

It is as though he said: As the authority of sacred Scripture bears witness, introduced from concealment into manifestation and handed down for correction and instruction. Therefore, as that tradition itself—hidden with respect to the mysteries of hidden sacraments, and priestly with respect to the dignity and holiness of the divine writings themselves and to its own sanctifying power, since it was handed down by divine and prophetic priests and divinely sanctified for the sanctification of those through it—has introduced, we have learned that among all things which are there is nothing such that we may truly say the divine nature is it. No created kind approaches its likeness so closely that it displays, explicitly and properly, what truly is in it.

Or we have learned that it is not truly what we say it is according to something—that is, according to one of the things that are. For whatever truly is according to one of the things that are cannot be spoken of as the whole; and therefore, when we say that it is something according to the things that are, we do not yet disclose by expression what it truly is. But we are ignorant of its superessential, invisible, ineffable, limitless infinity. What is infinite cannot be assessed by human knowledge; because it is ineffable, it is not spoken; because it is invisible, it is not known; and because it is superessential, it is not comprehended.

The human mind can therefore grasp something about it, but not it itself; the human tongue can say something about it, but not it itself. Yet what is said about it must not on that account be judged false, since it is only about it and is not itself what is said; nor is what is thought about it vain, since it is only about it and is not itself what is thought. For truth is spoken and truth is thought, and this leads toward it, although it abides more sublimely and excellently in itself.

It follows: “If, therefore, negations are true in divine matters but affirmations are unfitting, manifestation through dissimilar forms is more suited to the obscurity of mysteries.”

It is as though he said: Since we more expressly and properly say that God is not any thing, while truthfully saying both that he is something and that he is not something, it is evident that in divine matters—that is, in those things said of God and attributed to God—negations are true, that is, proper; whereas affirmations are unfitting, that is, improper and incoherent, because they attempt to join and fit unlike things together according to that mode of speaking in which human speech cannot otherwise form an account of God.

But if negations in divine matters are true, that is, proper, and affirmations unfitting, that is, improper, then it is evident that manifestation made through dissimilar forms is more suited to the obscurity of mysteries to be revealed than manifestation through similar forms. The former, by removing things as if by negation, strives to show what God is not; the latter, by positing things as if by affirmation, attempts to show what he is.

“And so, sacred descriptions do not fill the heavenly adornments of the sayings with ugly forms, while manifesting them through dissimilar constructions of forms and through these displaying the excellences of the supermundane above all material things.”

“And so”: since dissimilar figuration in divine matters is more proper according to that mode in which nothing among all things that are is properly named of God, therefore in this mode the ugly—that is, deformed—forms proposed in sacred discourse do not “fill,” that is, assert as filled, the heavenly adornments, that is, the heavenly orders or dispositions. Rather, they manifest those adornments through dissimilar constructions, that is, combinations of forms unlike and alien to their excellence; and through these constructions they display the excellences of supermundane—that is, heavenly and invisible—things in relation to all material things. That is, they show that these supermundane and spiritual things excel all material things. For in attributing unlike figures to them, they show that even those things which appear to be said of them according to likeness do not rise to their proper nature.

It follows: “Moreover, I do not think anyone of sound understanding will deny that dissimilar likenesses lead our mind back more effectively.”

It is as though he said: Dissimilar figurations are credible not only because they display the excellences of supermundane things, but also because they draw our mind back from material and bodily things more than similar figurations do and do not allow it to rest in itself. Hear a great mystery.

What God is is above all things; and when the question is asked what he is, this cannot be said because it cannot be thought. For whatever can be thought ascends into the human heart and is grasped by the human heart, whether in things seen according to appearance, in things represented by imagination, or in things inwardly perceived through experience and truth. The human heart grasps only things it knows or things according to what it knows. It knows what it receives outwardly through sense and what it feels inwardly through experience; and everything it grasps it either grasps in these or conjectures according to them. But what is neither in these nor according to them the human heart cannot grasp.

But what God is is none of these things, because he is not a creature; nor is he according to them, because he is Creator. Therefore what God is can neither be found among these nor understood according to them. For if he were understood according to them, he would be brought down into likeness with them, and what is in him would be found among them. Yet whatever is in creatures is more closely related and akin to other creatures, because they are made, than a work is to its maker and a product to its fashioner.

Every time compared with eternity, and every space compared with immensity, is found to be less than any span of time compared with a moment, or any extent of magnitude, however great its increase, compared with the proportion of an atom. So what God is, compared with creation, is found to excel by more than the highest created thing excels the lowest or most remote made things. Therefore God cannot be thought as to what he is according to these things, because he is other, and otherwise, and far off, remote, and dissimilar; and what he is cannot be said.

For if any one of these things is said, he is other; if he is said according to any one of them, he is otherwise. What, then, should be said that God is? If heaven is said, he is other. If earth is said, he is other; and whatever is in heaven or on earth is not what God is. Therefore what God is is other. And what is this? Only this can be said: that he is other; and what he is cannot be said.

We therefore have something to say: “God is not this”; but we do not have something to say: “This is God.” For everything we have is not God, and among all these things we neither possess nor find what God is. For every such thing is other than God, because everything made by God is not God; and neither eye nor mind sees or grasps except this, or according to this, which is not God but is from God.

A human being has human sense and perceives according to human sense either what is outside, according to the flesh, or what is within, according to the mind; and the human being has nothing beyond this. The eye of flesh concerns what belongs to flesh; the eye of mind, what belongs to mind. What is beyond? “No human being knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being which is in him” [Col. 0976A] (1 Cor. 2). So no one knows the things of God except the Spirit of God; and whoever has the Spirit of God perceives through the Spirit of God the things of God.

There are three eyes: the eye of flesh, the eye of reason, and the eye of contemplation. The eye of flesh is open; the eye of reason is weak-sighted; the eye of contemplation is closed and blind. By the eye of flesh the world and the things in the world are seen. By the eye of reason, the mind and the things in the mind. By the eye of contemplation, God and the things in God. By the eye of flesh, a person sees what is outside himself; by the eye of reason, what is in himself; by the eye of contemplation, what is within him and above him.

Therefore, what God is cannot be thought by human beings or by human reason, which perceives only what it knows or according to what it knows, whether what is within itself or outside itself. But those who have the Spirit of God in themselves also have God. They see God because they have the illuminated eye by which God can be seen; and they perceive not in something else, nor according to another thing which he is not, but him himself and in himself, as he is present.

Yet this cannot be said, because it is ineffable; it cannot be thought, because it is unthinkable. It is perceived but not expressed. Therefore everything said about God as being is said according to that which can be said and thought, because it cannot be said otherwise; and everything that can be said and thought is less than and beneath what God is. This very thing which is said is said inadequately, and what God is itself is not said. For whoever says something says it according to something, and thinks what he says and according to what he says.

You name God and form two syllables, and suppose that you have said all that he is. What have you thought? For what you have thought, that you have said. “I have thought,” you say, “what is above all things.” What is this? If you can think what it is, you can say it. But if you cannot think it, you cannot say it; for what cannot be thought cannot be said.

You have said “God”: and what is God? What do you think, or of what sort do you think, when you say “God”? What the word sounds like means “one who looks,” or “one who runs,” or “fear,” or whatever else you may suppose about it as best you can. Therefore, when you say “God,” you say one who looks upon, contemplates, and considers all things. And what is this? How does God look upon things, and how does he see? What is his seeing except his being? And what sort of thing is this?

But if you understand “one who runs,” because he penetrates, apprehends, and contains everything that is, then for him to run is to stand still. And who can grasp this? Or if you interpret the word as “fear,” and assert that God is to be thought under that name when “God” is said, who can explain how fear is God? But if you think that he is called fear because he is feared, how is what is not seen feared? How can what cannot be thought be seen? And how can what cannot be known be feared?

See, then, what you say when you say “God,” or what you think when you say “God.” “I think,” you say, “of the Creator of all things when I say God: the one who made all things and was not himself made.” Therefore, when you say “God,” you think of the one who made all things. You think of what he made, and do not think of what he himself is who made them. You have not yet reached what you undertook: to think and understand what God is.

Everything you say is less than this, and all of it is not himself of whom you speak; yet you speak this of him, not so as to arrive at him, but so as to draw near to him. For it is a great thing for a human being now to go toward him, even if arrival is not granted. But it will be granted afterwards, when that which is perfect comes, and the human being begins to see as he is seen—not the image in a mirror, but truth face to face.

For now, in the meantime, everything is an image, and the image itself is far from truth; yet, as an image, it does what it can: it turns the mind but does not bring it to the end. This alone can exist in us, and we can have this alone in it, because the image cannot show more, nor can we comprehend anything else. Yet there is a certain image more sublime and nearer to truth, so that it can more readily be called truth by us, because there is nothing above it by which truth can be displayed more expressly.

For it is said that God is fire; and the figure is evident, since in strict propriety God is not fire, because fire is a body and God is not a body. It is also said that God is light; and here likewise an image of truth appears, other than the truth, because God is not light in propriety of nature, though he is named light figuratively. All these things are visible and are far from God in the proper character of their nature, even though they are fitted only according to likeness—and that likeness itself is slight in relation to the excellence of majesty.

There is, however, another incorporeal nature nearer to God, between which and God no other nature stands; and this comes nearer to likeness, though it too is far from truth. Accordingly, from this highest nature known to us a lofty likeness of God is fashioned for us when God is called spirit, wisdom, reason, and love. For the soul is spirit, and the angel is spirit, and in spirit itself there are reason, wisdom, and love.

We know what spirit is to the degree that we know the soul and the angel; and through the soul we know the angel to the degree that we know ourselves—though even this is slight knowledge and can scarcely be called knowledge. Therefore when we hear that God is spirit, we think of soul and angel and suppose a likeness: that God is something such as the soul and angel are, because soul and angel are spirit. Yet we do not know how far this is from the truth of incomprehensible excellence.

For one who called a body spirit would speak falsely, because a body is not spirit and spirit is not body. Whoever said this would rightly be reproved and judged opposed to truth. Yet one who says that God is spirit is thought to have spoken truly. No one accuses him of falsehood, although body and spirit are nearer in nature and condition to each other than spirit and God. For here both are creatures, both comprehensible, both mutable, and both finite. There, however, one is eternal and the other temporal; one immense and the other comprehensible; one always remaining the same and the other mutable; one falling under knowledge and the other unthinkable.

Yet because nothing else can be said, this is said, lest nothing be said where something must be said, although what God is cannot be said—or, if it can be said, cannot be understood. Thus this is said; truth tolerates this said of itself and commends it to us as truth, because we cannot yet grasp truth itself, until the figure passes away and truth is manifested, above and beyond all this, nakedly and openly, as it is in itself.

Therefore figures still remain. Some of them are far away and plainly show themselves to be only likeness; others are proper and are accepted almost as truth, although they are only signs of truth and not truth. Where nothing higher is available to lead to truth itself, truth permits us these and does not count our incapacity against us. But if forms are near and similar, yet are not the nearest, and something higher appears for manifesting truth, truth does not allow itself to be reduced to them in strict propriety, because it displays itself more perfectly in the other thing, by which it proves that here it is only by likeness.

But in that supreme thing above which there is nothing higher, no other thing appears by which the figure may be tested; and therefore it must be received as it is, because no other is given until that which is perfect comes. Every figure, then, displays truth more evidently in proportion as it more openly proves itself, through unlike likeness, to be a figure and not truth. In this way dissimilar likenesses lead our mind back more effectively to truth, because they do not allow it to remain in likeness alone.

Therefore, he says, “I do not think anyone of sound understanding will deny” that dissimilar likenesses lead our mind back to truth. For “it is liable to happen that people are deceived through more precious sacred forms,” that is, it may readily follow, arise, or occur that human thoughts are deceived by those representations of sacred things which are represented as more precious in sacred discourse. They may suppose “that some heavenly essences are golden in form,” as they are represented by likeness in certain places of Scripture; and they may suppose also that in heaven there are certain flashing men clothed in beautiful garments, as angels are read to have appeared in splendid garments and with shining countenances, “shedding harmless whiteness and fire”—that is, sending forth or pouring out brightness and light: whiteness with respect to their garments and fire with respect to their flaming and burning faces; harmlessly, that is, without injury.

In this very divine miracle lies the constant principle that in divine and heavenly natures, which are here shown through appearance, things are otherwise there according to truth: where the appearance of visible nature is seen, its effect is not found.

It follows: “And by whatever other similar imagined forms theology has figured the heavenly intellects,” that is, represented spiritual natures in expressions framed according to imaginable things, it is consequently possible for people to be deceived from these higher things, supposing heavenly essences to exist in their own nature as such things.

To prevent this from happening to “those who understand no goods higher than visible goods”—that is, those who think that no goods exist higher or better than visible goods—“the restorative wisdom of the holy theologians wonderfully descends to unseemly likenesses.” That is, the holy theologians, who through their wisdom restoring and reforming us to the knowledge of truth handed down divine sayings to us, with wonderful discernment descended to adopt unseemly likenesses, so as to fit them to divine and heavenly natures and, through them, to show that other things also said magnificently and beautifully of these natures must be referred to likeness and not to proper reality.

This, therefore, is what the wisdom of the holy theologians did: “not allowing our material element, remaining among ugly images, to rest; but cleansing and lifting upward the power of the soul, and suggesting through the deformity of the combinations that the superheavenly and divine spectacles are neither truly nor rightly proved to be similar to such very material things.”

It is as though he said: In descending to unseemly likenesses, the wisdom of the theologians wonderfully provided for our restoration by not permitting our material element—that is, our carnal sense, clinging to material things—to rest, remaining, I say, among ugly images. That is, it does not allow it, insofar as it would wish, to remain so that it thinks only of these things and accepts them alone as though true; for it would do so if it were allowed to rest in them and were not compelled by the ugliness of the images themselves to go forth in search of other beautiful and true things.

Or: it does not allow our material element to rest and remain among ugly images—that is, it does not permit it either to rest or to remain, but drives it out by the ugliness of the images themselves and advances it to higher things. It cleanses and lifts upward the power of the soul, namely, the intellectual power of the soul which bears upward and strives toward higher things. It cleanses it from the admixture of images, so that it may become accustomed to contemplate spiritual and invisible things purely and simply; and it suggests—that is, warns and persuades—the soul, by the deformity of the combinations themselves, that superheavenly and divine spectacles are not greatly similar, according to their truth, to material things, especially to things so ugly, as though it were neither right nor true to maintain that those things are like these.

Or it suggests, by the deformity of the combinations, that spiritual and invisible natures are not in their proper reality as they are displayed in visible appearance and image; and it further suggests that superheavenly and divine spectacles are not greatly—that is, not very—similar according to their truth to material things so ugly.

It follows: “But it is also necessary to understand this: that nothing which exists is universally deprived of participation in the Good. For, as the truth of the sayings declares, all things are very good.”

Above he showed that dissimilar representations are suitably employed for the manifestation of divine things so that, from things which plainly appear dissimilar, those things too which seemed similar may be recognized as outside strict propriety. Now he shows that dissimilarities are also not unsuitably assumed for this reason: even those things which appear dissimilar from the truth of divine and spiritual things possess something in common with them, in which they may be called similar. For nothing in the whole universe fails to draw participation from the highest Good; and thereby, insofar as it participates in that Good, it fittingly presents its image and likeness.

Accordingly, one must not consider only the former reason, but must also understand that none of the things which exist is universally deprived of participation in the Good. For “as the truth of the sayings declares”—that is, as the true sayings declare—“all things are very good.” Thus it is written in Genesis: “God saw all things that he had made, and they were very good” (Gen. 1). If, therefore, all things were good, good was in all things; all participated in good; and all possessed from the Good something similar to the Good, through which the Good itself might be understood and known in them.

Hence it follows: “It is therefore possible to understand good contemplations from all things, and to form”—or fit—“to invisible and intellectual things the likenesses called dissimilar,” namely, those which we called dissimilar above. I say “form” them “from these material things,” that is, bodily and visible things. Yet this must be done so that those things attributed to invisible realities according to the likeness of visible things are recognized to subsist differently in visible things and differently in invisible things. This is what he says: “In another manner being possessed by intellectual things,” namely, those things which are differently apportioned among sensible things.

It follows: “For rage belongs to irrational creatures through a passionate movement, and their raging motion is filled with every kind of irrationality.”

He now proves by certain examples that things transferred from the nature of visible realities to invisible realities subsist differently here and there, such as rage, desire, and the rest, which are transferred by likeness from visible to invisible things. It is as though he said: Things fitted from visible to invisible realities must be believed to have one manner in visible things and another manner in invisible things, as can plainly be understood in what follows.

For “rage” belongs “to irrational creatures,” that is, to those who proceed and act irrationally, whether because they lack reason or because, possessing reason, they do not proceed according to reason. Rage belongs to them through a passionate movement, that is, one born from a dominant affection—impetuous and fervent; and their raging motion is filled with every kind of irrationality. For that movement is called rage which, wholly outside reason, burns and is carried along by the mere impulse of passion.

“But in intellectual beings the irascible must be understood in another way,” [Col. 0981A] namely, so that the irascible in them signifies their manly rationality and their mighty repose in divine and immutable foundations. For when rage is named in a spiritual and heavenly nature, it does not signify impulse or movement, but repose and immutability.

This is understood by considering dissimilar and opposite things. Just as rage in the former seeks by impulse and vehemence to repel an approaching disturbance, so there an unmoved repose, persisting without any shaking, is not troubled by any disturbance which comes upon it. For this reason he calls that repose “mighty,” that is, strong, robust, and untroubled: it repels every motion without motion and suppresses every violence without its own shaking or disturbance.

Yet this repose does not arise from themselves, but from the divine and immutable foundations to which they adhere—that is, from divine love and contemplation—by which they are established in eternity, so that henceforth they can in no way be moved. And because this repose is not one of necessity, as though they were held unwillingly, but of will, so that they are not deserted as tireless lovers, he joins manly rationality to repose. He shows that by illuminating reason they manfully reject the evils which they discern, and by affectional love they rest in the goods which they perceive: so that repose may be fortified by reason, lest it admit an affection for evils; and reason may be guarded by repose, lest in opposing itself through hatred of evil it overstep the bounds of tranquillity.

Thus rage, when fitted to divine things, signifies this manly reason and this mighty repose—free, unrestrained, and admitting no disturbance. For, as we have said, just as rage here repels an oncoming disturbance through madness, so there rational and voluntary repose, through immutability, receives no shock.

It follows: “In the same way we say that desire in irrational beings is a certain unreflective and material susceptibility, implanted without restraint by natural movement or by habit in mutable things, and an irrational continuance of bodily pleasure, compelling every living creature together toward what is desirable according to sense.” Having shown what fury signifies when attributed to sensible and material things [Col. 0981D], and likewise what it signifies when applied to immaterial and invisible natures, he now proceeds to show the difference in desire, whether it is spoken of bodily things or named among spiritual and divine things.

Defining the desire of bodily beings, he says that it is a certain susceptibility or passion—that is, a dominant affection—unreflective indeed, because it is not guided by reason but drawn by a rash appetite toward those things in whose enjoyment it is affected; and material, that is, arising from flesh and from carnal sensation, appearing in things carnal and sensible. I call it a susceptibility implanted either by natural movement, namely when its appetite is according to nature, or by a habit held without restraint in mutable things, when its desire is carried outside or contrary to nature [Col. 0982A]; and an irrational continuance of bodily pleasure. We are to understand that he calls desire itself an irrational continuance—that is, a prolonging, intensity, or outpouring—of bodily pleasure: pleasure arising from the body and tending toward bodily things, and compelling every living creature, through the violence of its appetite, toward that which is desirable according to sense. Such, then, is the desire that we understand to belong to bodily beings.

“But when, clothing non-intellectual and spiritual beings in dissimilar likenesses,” or vesting them—“we adapt desire to them”—then we must understand this desire not as before, but rather as divine love [Col. 0982B], and as a longing for immateriality or incorporeality and for divinity existing beyond reason and intellect; since it can be loved more than it can be investigated or understood; and as inflexible, because it is always directed toward one thing; and as needing nothing, because that which is loved is present. I mean a desire for contemplation that is superessentially chaste and free from passion: that is, contemplation of that reality which they contemplate beyond essence, passing in mind beyond every essence and nature. Love for this reality is chaste because it brings no corruption upon its lover, and passionless because, sweetly refreshing the one who desires it, it does not afflict him.

“And we must also understand desire itself to be a longing tending toward that pure and most sublime brightness, and toward the invisible and form-giving beauty of the eternal, true, and invisible communion” [Col. 0982C]. That beauty is called form-giving because it conforms to itself those who turn toward it, so that they become beautiful, loving true beauty—not as in the flesh and according to the flesh, where a lover of beauty may be ugly and the possessor of beauty may be found not good; but there the one who loves possesses, and begins to be what he loves to possess. Such love and such longing, therefore, must be understood as the desire of spiritual and divine beings.

It follows: “And it receives, as it were, a power in sufficiency and in conversion; and by virtue of its unmixed and immutable love of divine beauty, and of its universal recall to that which is truly to be desired, it is afflicted by nothing.” As though he said: This desire, or chaste longing for eternal and invisible goods, because it is inflexible, as was said, and needs nothing, thereby receives or takes, in its sufficiency and conversion toward God and divine things, a certain power or excellence and firmness, so that it cannot at all be afflicted by any opposing force, violence, or strength [Col. 0982D].

For no one can be harmed or afflicted except in that which he loves. Therefore, one who loves only that which cannot be taken away cannot at all be harmed: he desires nothing else beyond it, having sufficiency in it, nor is he anxious over its loss, since he possesses it immutably. Since, therefore, it is sufficient, it suffers no want; and since it is inflexible, it cannot endure violence. This is conferred upon it through an unmixed and immutable love of divine beauty and a universal recall to that which is truly to be desired. For because God’s love in them is unmixed—or, to put it differently, unblended and pure—their desire is not divided among different things. And because it is immutable, it is not turned away from the same object. And because they are universally recalled and gathered into that which is truly to be desired, they are disturbed by no outward violence. For if they were not recalled and gathered with their whole desire to loving the truth, they could undoubtedly be harmed and afflicted wherever their minds clung to mutable and transitory things. But now, because they are wholly there where all things stand immutably [Col. 0983A–B], they too, through the adhesion of love, cannot experience the mutability of affliction.

It follows: “But irrationality and insensibility themselves, in irrational animals or in animate material things, we properly call a deficiency of reason and sense; whereas in immaterial and intellectual essences we reverently and fittingly confess them to be their pre-eminences, as belonging to beings above the world, surpassing our transitory and bodily reason, and the material sense of our mind, alienated from incorporeal things.”

By the examples set forth he shows that things said alike of visible and invisible beings are not said alike or in the same manner. As though he said: Not only fury and desire must be understood differently here and there [Col. 0983C]. Irrationality, which signifies an exaltation beyond reason, and insensibility, which shows an excess beyond sensation, when named here—that is, among irrational and senseless things—show a deficiency of reason and sensibility. But when they are said there—that is, among divine and intellectual natures—they signify something beyond reason and sense, not through defect but through advancement. For an excess beyond reason and sensibility takes place either upward or downward: one falls away from reason and sense through deficiency, so as not to possess them; or transcends them through advancement, so as to possess more.

Thus in Sacred Scripture we find holy men, inspired by the Spirit of God, sometimes undergoing ecstasy, that is, a going-beyond of the mind [Col. 0983D]. Being led beyond human reason and sense, they went beyond reason and sense in this respect: attaining what was higher than reason, they began to be made alive and enlightened by it. In those persons, therefore, there was an excess in what they received in addition; just as in these there was an excess because they lost that very thing. Accordingly, in irrational animals and in inanimate materials we properly call irrationality and insensibility a deficiency of reason and sense. But whenever we name irrationality and insensibility in immaterial and intellectual essences, we confess not their deficiency but rather their pre-eminence, as belonging to beings above the world.

We confess this reverently and fittingly [Col. 0984A], that is, attributing nothing irreverent or unfitting to them; but, as befits the pre-eminences or excellences of supramundane—that is, spiritual—essences, which surpass our transitory and bodily reason: reason which can neither rise beyond transitory things nor comprehend anything wholly outside bodily things. They also surpass the material sense of our mind, alienated amid bodily things: a sense vigorous only toward material things, and through material and bodily things alienated from immaterial and incorporeal realities, unable to perceive them. Since they are established through excellence of contemplation above such reason and such sense, they are rightly said to be alien to such reason and sense, so that their very insensibility and irrationality may not be understood as stupor or ignorance, but as another kind of knowledge of truth and perception of good, not such as is found in us or according to us [Col. 0984B].

It follows: “It is therefore not discordant to form likenesses appropriate to heavenly beings even from the lowly parts of matter; for matter itself, possessing its subsistence from the truly Good, has through all its material arrangement certain images of intellectual beauty; and through them it is possible to be led back to the first immaterial forms, receiving likenesses, as was said, dissimilarly and defining the same properties not similarly, but compactly, beautifully, and according to the properties of intellectual and sensible things.”

He adds another reason to the preceding one why likenesses are fittingly drawn from visible things to invisible things, even according to things that appear contrary: not only because things said here and there are understood to subsist differently, but also because whatever exists here has in some respect a likeness to what subsists there. For both these and those are what they are from the one Good; and according to the image which these possess of it, they also display a figure and likeness of those things.

This is what he says: “It is,” that is, it is possible, “to form for heavenly essences likenesses not discordant, even from the lowly parts of matter,” that is, of bodily substance; since matter itself, possessing subsistence from the truly Good, has certain images of intellectual beauty throughout all its material arrangement [Col. 0984C–D]. Through these images the mind can be led back to those first immaterial forms, that is, to the forms of immaterial and spiritual essences, which are first in relation to these things, because these are according to them, directed to them, and exist for their sake. I say that one can be led back from these to those, provided that the likenesses themselves are received dissimilarly: namely, that what exists here and is said of those things is understood to exist and subsist there in another way; and that the same properties are defined not similarly.

Yet they are to be defined compactly—that is, fittingly and aptly—and beautifully, that is, becomingly, according to the same properties, in both intellectual and sensible things. He calls it a likeness when descriptions of invisible things are taken from visible things through external forms, figures, or qualities; but a property when the likeness is derived from an inward nature [Col. 0985A]. Whether, therefore, likenesses are proposed to be transferred externally from visible things to the nature of invisible things, or properties are assumed internally from the same visible and material things for the demonstration of invisible things, the comparison and adaptation must be moderated in both cases. Thus the likenesses that appear to be proposed alike in both realms must nevertheless be received dissimilarly and understood to exist differently here and there; and the properties which seem to be attributed alike to both must be defined differently in the former and in the latter, and understood to be different, so that to each may be attributed what is fitting and appropriate to it according to its nature [Col. 0985B].

It follows: “We shall find that the mystical theologians adapt these things wonderfully not only to explanations of the heavenly arrangements but sometimes even to divine manifestations themselves.” He mentioned the same thing above: namely, that mystical theologians—that is, theologians who relate mystical and secret things—adapt and fit these likenesses and properties taken from visible things not only to explanations of heavenly arrangements, that is, of heavenly orders of angelic spirits. In other words, they propose these likenesses and properties of visible things not only to explain or demonstrate heavenly arrangements and angelic ordinances [Col. 0985C], but sometimes also to divine manifestations themselves: that is, they employ them to make divinity itself known and manifest.

“And sometimes indeed they praise divinity itself by precious lights,” comparing it with precious lights and displaying its praise through that thing which among visible things is precious and beautiful. For example, when they call it the sun, they do not mean this visible sun, which illumines bodily eyes even for the perpetration of wickedness, but the Sun of righteousness, which enlightens spiritual eyes for the knowledge of truth and virtue. Likewise, when they call it “the morning star,” whose rising drives away darkness, they do not mean a star ascending to illuminate this visible world, but one rising in the rational mind—which alone can receive this light—unto sanctification [Col. 0985D]. Likewise, when they call it “an uncircumscribed light shining invisibly,” they do not mean this visible light, which may be darkened by darkness, surrounded, confined in a place, and restricted by a boundary.

Thus mystical theology praises the excellence of divine majesty by the species and forms of the highest and most precious things. “But sometimes, indeed, from intermediate things”—that is, from things which in the order of creation are neither highest nor lowest—theology praises divine majesty: for example, when it calls it fire, not such bodily fire as, though useful in giving light, harms by burning and consuming, but “fire shining harmlessly” [Col. 0986A], illuminating without burning, kindling without consuming. Likewise, when it calls it “water that gives the fullness of life”: water that gives fullness of life and fills with life those who drink and bear it; and water that, “symbolically,” that is figuratively, “enters into the belly and overflows in rivers flowing back without measure.” All these things are said of it not properly but only figuratively. In all these matters mystical theology praises the majesty and goodness of divinity.

“Sometimes, however, it praises it even from the lowest things”—that is, from inferior and earthly things—and makes its praise known figuratively, as when it calls it “sweet ointment,” and likewise “a cornerstone” [Col. 0986B]. It adapts to it, by likeness, forms even of weak things, so much so that it sometimes seems in describing it to descend even to unsuitable and contrary forms. Yet this is done by a fitting and necessary dispensation, according to the reason mentioned above. “They even clothe it in a beastly form.” As though he said: The theologians take likenesses from lower things not only in explaining divinity, but—even more remarkably—they descend to contrary and dissimilar forms which, if understood properly, would be wholly unworthy of its majesty.

“For they even clothe it in a beastly form; they adapt to it the species,” that is, the appearance, form, or figure, “of a lion and of a panther [Col. 0986C]; and they vest it”—namely divinity—“in a leopard’s form,” that is, the form of a leopard. “And they vest it”—again, divinity—in a raging bear: that is, with the appearance of a raging bear; or they call it “a raging bear,” so that incongruity may be evident in both cases, when they attribute deformity to beauty and cruelty to gentleness.

It follows: “I will add what has appeared to be the most lowly of all and more expressive.” As though he said: Though great unworthiness may seem present in the preceding examples and others of that sort, yet in what I now add a far greater affront appears. “I will add”—that is, I shall venture, and seem to speak boldly—by adding even this to divine significations: “that which has appeared to be the vilest of all.” And thus, according to the reason stated above, by which dissimilar symbols make a fuller disclosure, it is proved to signify more than the rest [Col. 0986D].

Perhaps, however, no human being would dare adapt this to divine majesty unless the Wisdom of God itself had voluntarily deigned to assume it. “For those wise in divine things have handed down that it clothes itself in the form of a worm.” As it is written: “I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the rejection of the people” (Ps. XXI). Unless it had first said this of itself, who would dare say it of it? Since nothing seems more lowly and humble than a worm, who would presume to bring the highest Majesty down to this attribution [Col. 0987A], unless it had first clothed itself in such a form by its own dispensation? Therefore it first deigned to say this of itself, knowing that human conscience would not dare of itself to say it of its Creator.

“Thus all the divine sages and prophets by secret inspiration distinguish the Holy of holies from holy things that are undefiled.” Theosophers, that is, those wise in divine things and those made prophets by secret inspiration, all do this when they wish to signify invisible things through visible forms and through the properties of visible things: they distinguish, as we showed above, “the Holy of holies from holy things that are undefiled.” The undefiled holy things are symbols of divine things taken from beautiful and becoming forms; the Holy of holies are the divine realities themselves which are figured through these symbols [Col. 0987B].

Therefore, by attributing dissimilar figures to divine things, the theosophers also separate from their excellence and majesty similar formations, even those which appeared worthy. For by adapting to their signification things that are undoubtedly alien, they show that other things too, which might appear true, are not similar according to their proper nature. Thus in one and the same matter they separate figure from truth in similar images, while in dissimilar images they honor the figure with fellowship in truth: for those images, when shown to be other, are distinguished; and these, when adapted by likeness, are honored. For it was fitting that everything made should be shown, in comparison with the excellence of the Creator, neither equal in the highest things [Col. 0987C] nor dissimilar in the lowest. Since it is made, it cannot be comparable in equality; and since it was made by him, it cannot be wholly dissimilar to him by whom it was made.

It follows: “So that divine things may neither rightly be received by the unclean, nor those devoted to contemplation of marvelous images remain in figures as though they were true.” This, therefore, is accomplished by dissimilar figures: that in considering them those unclean in heart and unworthy of knowledge of the truth may be more fully blinded, while those devoted to contemplating marvelous images—that is, sacred representations wonderfully made—may be more fully exercised. Thus a just ordinance is fulfilled in both cases [Col. 0987D]: truth, while concealing itself in manifestation as though in a lowly garment, both provokes the unworthy to contempt of it and invites the worthy to desire and seek that aspect of it which lies hidden. Thus they are not content with what they behold outwardly, but, repelled by the very deformity of the external presentation, do not remain in figures as though they were true; for a sign cannot be the truth, even when it is a sign of truth.

It follows: “Accordingly, they honor divine things by true negations and by diverse likenesses of images composed from the lowest things.” As though he said: Since negations made concerning divine things signify their truth more expressly, and dissimilar formations of images demonstrate their purity more clearly [Col. 0988A], holy theologians do no injury to divine things either by making true negations concerning them or by attributing dissimilar formations to them. Rather, they honor divine things by true negations, through which they show their excellence to be so great that what they are cannot in any way be expressed, even if in some way what they are not may be said. They honor them also by likenesses differing from their sublimity through lowly formation: likenesses of images compounded from the lowest things, that is, composed and joined from the lowest—that is, inferior and base—species of corruptible things.

It follows: “There is therefore nothing incongruous if, for the causes stated, we form heavenly essences from unsuitable and dissimilar likenesses.” As though he said: Since divine things are honored by true negations and by diverse formations, there is nothing incongruous—that is, unsuitable—if theologians form, that is, represent, heavenly essences from dissimilar and unsuitable likenesses: through representations in figures dissimilar from their nature and in a sense unsuitable. I say that this is not incongruous for the reasons stated above [Col. 0988B].

“For perhaps we certainly would not have come, through need, to inquiry leading upward by diligent investigation of divine things, unless the deformity of the manifesting formation of angels compelled us.” As though he said: We would not have come, through our need, to this inquiry—that is, to investigation of the composition of visible images—or to anagogy, that is, inquiry into invisible truth. I say, through our need: we who, knowing the truth, have no need of such inquiries. We would not have entered upon this inquiry unless deformity compelled us, for the sake of others who might otherwise be scandalized if they were not instructed [Col. 0988C].

First observe the doubling of the negation by which the point is expressed. In this too it is evident that deformed formations in divine matters are useful: we would not investigate divine truth so diligently unless the deformity of the manifestations compelled us—that is, forced us. This is what he says: “Perhaps we certainly would not come to inquiry leading upward,” that is, contemplation of things above, through need for understanding the truth. We would not come, I say, by diligent investigation of divine things, “unless it compelled us”—that is, forced us—“to enter inquiry through need, and through inquiry into anagogy”: namely, the very deformity of the manifesting formation of angels; that is, unless the deformity of the formation through which angels are manifested in Sacred Scripture compelled us [Col. 0988D].

I say: it does so “not permitting our mind to remain in the dissimilar fabrications of forms,” that is, in the deformed compositions of representations which are dissimilar from the truth of spiritual things. Unless, therefore, the very deformity of representations compelled our mind from visible figures toward the search for truth, our mind would remain in those things outwardly presented, believing and venerating them alone; it would not recognize its need, so as to suppose that other things beyond these must be desired and sought. But now the intervening deformity compels the mind to leave the figure for truth: the mind, I say, unable to remain in things which in themselves are unworthy and incongruous with divine truth [Col. 0989A].

It struggles to deny to divine things these “material possibilities” which are outwardly proposed in signs; and, because it thus reverently rejects them, it becomes accustomed purely to extend itself through visible things, being stirred up “toward supramundane heights”: that is, angelic excellences, which rise above and surpass all worldly things. For unless, stirred from these things, it wholly left them behind through progress in contemplation, it could not purely behold those things which it strives to contemplate [Col. 0989B].

It follows: “So much has been said by us,” etc. He connects what precedes with the following discussion. “So much indeed”—as much as we have said thus far—“has been said by us concerning descriptions of angelic images,” that is, descriptions of angels made by visible forms and images drawn from visible things. These descriptions are “of the divine utterances,” that is, made through divine utterances and set forth in divine utterances. They are also material descriptions, formed according to the nature and likeness of material and bodily things; and they are unsuitable because of the incongruous and ugly representations attributed to those excellences [Col. 0989C]. It was on account of such things that the inquiry discussed thus far was proposed.

“But next we must distinguish what we judge hierarchy itself to be, and what benefit those who receive hierarchy derive from hierarchy itself.” “Next,” he says, that is, after the foregoing, we must distinguish what we judge hierarchy itself to be, by proposing its definition taken generally. “Next” we must also distinguish “what benefit those who receive hierarchy derive,” that is, what advantage they receive from hierarchy itself, the hierarchy allotted to each of them.

“And in saying this I pray,” he says, “that Christ, if I may say ‘my Christ,’ may be the guide of my discourse.” For it is a great thing, and seems almost close to presumption, that a sinner should receive the reward of the righteous and that one cast down should trust in familiarity with the Most High. Therefore I say: let “Christ”—and, if I dare more, let me say “my Christ”—be the guide of my discourse [Col. 0989D–0990A]. Without him discourse cannot be right, because he is the Word; nor can understanding be true, because he is Wisdom. For all who know true things know through him; and he is the inspiration of “all hierarchical manifestation,” because, as Wisdom, he inspires the minds of holy theologians and reveals to those whom he wills, in the ways he wills, the entire principle of hierarchical order, whether in heaven or on earth.

“But you, O child,” etc. He speaks to Timothy, Paul’s disciple, to whom he is said to have written these things. He calls him “child,” either because he was older than Timothy, or because he stood to him in the office and dignity of teacher and master. “But you, O child, listen.” As though he said: Because the matters to be spoken are great, listen reverently and fittingly, as befits the holy things that are to be spoken [Col. 0990B].

I say, listen according to the holy legislation of our priestly tradition, which commands us not to dispute or resist in teaching, but to listen reverently and humbly. Or, listen to the things spoken “according to the holy legislation of our priestly tradition”: that is, according to the holy law, namely Sacred Scripture, brought to us by God through priestly tradition, that is, through the tradition of holy and sanctifying persons. Thus, “you who have become divine in the divine teaching of marvelous sayings, listen to marvelous things spoken”: you who have become divine through divine teaching, which makes divine those who hear and do it; or, having become divine in the divine teaching of marvelous sayings, listen to the things I propose to say [Col. 0990C].

And do not merely listen, so as reverently to receive what is spoken, but also, “covering in the secrecy of your mind the holy things from the unclean multitude”—that is, from those unclean both in conduct and divided in their desires—“guard them as uniform,” that is, undivided and untouched, lest you imprudently expose them to be torn apart and polluted. “For, as the sayings declare, it is not lawful to cast among swine the unmixed, light-bearing, and beneficent adornment of invisible pearls.” These are that unclean multitude signified by swine in Sacred Scripture: those who pollute the Word of God by evil living. The invisible pearls are spiritual understandings: understandings which adorn character, shine through pure truth, are unmixed through the abundance of grace, and are beneficent toward those who approach them with reverence and honor [Col. 0990D].

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0989]

### TITLE OF CHAPTER III. What hierarchy is, and what benefit comes through hierarchy.

### TEXT

[Col. 0989D]

“Hierarchy, according to me, is a divine order, knowledge, and activity, assimilated, so far as possible, to the divine; and, in proportion to the illuminations divinely bestowed upon it, ascending into likeness to God [Col. 0990D]. Divine beauty, as simple, is unitive; as good, it is perfective. It is altogether pure from every dissimilarity; it distributes to each according to the worthiness of his own light; and it perfects through the most divine rites, according to the unchangeable formation, suitably ordered, of those perfected toward itself.

“The interpretation of hierarchy, therefore, is a likeness and union with God, so far as possible, having him as guide of every holy activity and knowledge; looking immovably toward its most divine beauty, and, so far as possible, being re-formed by it; and perfecting its own worshippers as divine statues, most clear mirrors, and pure receptacles of the principal light and divine ray, filled with the sacred brightness bestowed upon them, and in turn abundantly communicating it to those who follow, according to divine laws.

“For it is not lawful for the perfecters of holy persons, or for persons sanctly perfected, to perform anything at all outside the +mysteries of sacrifices or sacred ordinances [Col. 0991B]; nor can they subsist otherwise if they desire its divine brightness, look reverently and fittingly toward it, and are re-formed according to the upward-leading capacity of each of the holy intellects.

“Does not one who speaks of hierarchy therefore declare, in general, a certain sacred arrangement: an image of divine beauty, which through hierarchical orders and knowledges performs in sacred rites the mysteries of its own illumination, and is assimilated, as far as possible, to its own principle? For the perfection of everyone who receives hierarchy is this: to ascend, according to his proper proportion, to imitation of God and—to state the most divine thing, as the sayings declare—to become a co-worker with God (1 Cor. III; 3 John I; Matt. V), and to show the divine activity shining forth in himself, so far as possible [Col. 0991C].

“For the order of hierarchy is that some be purified and others purify; some be illuminated and others illuminate; some be perfected and others perfect; each, in whatever manner belongs to him, in a deifying union. The divine blessedness, so far as it may be spoken of among human beings, is pure from every dissimilarity, full of eternal light, perfect and without need, and at once the source of every perfection: purifying, illuminating, and perfecting; rather, beyond purification, beyond light, and prior to perfection; perfect through itself, the principle of perfection, and the cause of every hierarchy and of every sacred thing according to transcendent eminence [Col. 0991D].

“It is fitting, therefore, I think, that those being purified should be wholly perfected by the Pure and freed from every confusion of dissimilarity. Those being illuminated should be filled with divine light and restored, in the most chaste eyes of the mind, to contemplative aptitude and power. Those being restored from imperfection should become participants in the perfective knowledge of sacred things that have been fully examined. Those who purify should communicate to others, from their own purity, the greatness of purification. Those who illumine, having minds more full of light, possessing the capacity both to participate in and distribute light, and filled most richly with holy love, should convey all their surpassing light to those worthy of light. Those who perfect, as instructors in perfective tradition, should perfect those to be perfected by the most sacred teaching through knowledge of the sacred things contemplated [Col. 0992A].

“Does not every order of hierarchical arrangement, therefore, according to its proper proportion, return to divine co-operation through that grace which perfects and the God-given power which naturally and supernaturally belong to divinity, are superessentially enacted by it, and are manifested by hierarchy for the possible imitation of souls that love God?”

### EXPOSITION
Up to this point the theologian has set forth the points that had to be said universally for those being introduced to the knowledge of the hierarchies, according to the rationale of visible demonstrations proposed for the signification of visible things. Now, entering upon the principal exposition, he first defines what hierarchy is—not universally, however, but only with reference to that hierarchy which consists among angels and human beings, the meaning being thus restricted. “Hierarchy,” he says, “is, in my view, a divine order, knowledge, and activity, assimilated to God as far as possible, and ascending proportionately, through illuminations divinely bestowed upon it, to likeness to God.”

His words “in my view” must be understood as though he had said, “according to my judgment.” For he modestly qualifies his assertion, lest he seem to presume more than is right upon his own opinion. Then he sets forth three chief elements in the definition of hierarchy, which complete the definition itself: order, knowledge, and activity. If any one of these three is absent, there is no hierarchy.

First comes divine order, because authority does not exist unless it has been ordered by God. Hence he says, “divine order.” For “all authority is from God,” and whatever is from God is good and ordered; therefore, whoever resists authority ordered by God resists God (Rom. 13). Hierarchy, therefore, is a divine order—that is, authority ordered by God and arranged according to God. It is from God by ordination, and according to God by imitation; and therefore it is a divine order: from God, that it may exist; according to God, that it may be of such a kind and degree as it is.

Further, since every authority ordered by God is ordered to accomplish and complete something, “knowledge and activity” follow order in the definition. Knowledge, indeed, by which they understand what must be done; activity, by which they accomplish what they have understood must be done. In order there is office; in knowledge, discernment; in activity, ministry. Activity without order is presumption; order without activity is negligence; but without knowledge activity is blameworthy and order useless. For these reasons, therefore, hierarchy is divine order, knowledge, and activity.

By hierarchy I mean, in order, knowledge, and activity alike, something assimilated to God—that is, imitating conformity to God insofar as this is possible for it—and ascending into likeness to God proportionately through illuminations, that is, according to illuminations divinely bestowed upon it. Each hierarchy, namely, accomplishes its work in its own order according to the mode and measure of grace divinely infused into it, and ascends to the imitation of God, so that by right discernment and good action it may imitate him. For every hierarchy emulates the divine likeness in both respects: both insofar as it is arranged by him and insofar as it acts according to him. This definition, as we have said, embraces only the angelic and human hierarchy, which were made in likeness to the highest and eternal hierarchy and imitate it by being ordered according to it.

It follows: “Divine beauty, as simple, and as good, as consummating, is universally pure from every dissimilarity; but it distributes its own light according to the worthiness of each; and it brings to perfection, in the most divine sacrifice, according to the compact and unchangeable formation toward itself of those perfected.”

The meaning is this: divine beauty, which we call the highest hierarchy and according to which the other hierarchies were made, is universally—that is, altogether—pure, being always simple in unity, best in goodness, consummating in perfection. Where unity is, diversity is not; and where diversity is not, no dissimilarity can be. Likewise, where perfection is, there is no gradation; where there is no gradation, there is no difference; and where there is no difference, there is no dissimilarity. Therefore divine beauty, which is the form and exemplar of all things well and beautifully ordered, because it is one does not admit plurality; and because it is best and consummate—not merely consummate, but the consummator of all things to be consummated and the cause of consummation—it does not admit diversity, and thus knows no dissimilarity whatever. It is one in simplicity and the same in perfection.

Yet, though it is such in itself that it is neither divided by plurality nor made inferior by diversity, in those who become participants in grace it distributes its own light, granting that light in diverse ways according to the worthiness of each participant: giving greater gifts of grace to the higher and lesser gifts to the lower, so that in them it may be beautifully multiplied which in itself truly remains one.

Divine beauty is itself also perfecting, because it perfects and makes participants in its lights consummate. It is perfecting, I say, in the most divine sacrifice, by which it perfects those who are to be perfected according to the unchangeable formation, compactly conformed toward itself, of those perfected. By “most divine sacrifice” he means divine illumination itself, grace, and propitiation, by which all who must be purified and saved are cleansed and made clean—not only from the corruption of evil, that they may become good, but also from deficiency in good, that they may be better attendants.

This, therefore, is the supreme offering and *teletargis*, that is, the sacrificial victim of principal purification: namely, divine grace, which is offered to us and offered for us. It is offered to us for purification; it is offered for us for propitiation. It is offered to us, that we may possess it; it is offered for us, that through it we may be pleasing. It is offered to us by infusion; it is offered for us by cleansing. It is offered to us when we begin to be what we were not; it is offered by us when we display and present what we are.

Therefore this *teletargis*, that is, the victim of principal purification and the most divine sacrifice, without which all victims and all sacrifices can neither have efficacy nor profit, is that by which divine beauty perfects and makes perfect those who are perfected toward itself—that is, re-formed into its own likeness, harmoniously, so that they do not differ from it—according to the unchangeable formation of those perfected toward itself. That is, according to its likeness, which, once received, they preserve unchangeably, so that they do not fall away from it.

For divine beauty, which is one in itself and perfect, cleanses and perfects those who are to be perfected toward itself through the victim of principal purification—that is, through the infusion of its grace, which from its own fullness it has poured forth for those to be cleansed and perfected unto participation—according to the mode, measure, and capacity of each, which they have received by the gift of that same grace, according to their unchangeable formation toward it. This formation is called unchangeable either because, as we have said, it turns those who are formed and re-formed toward immutability, or because it remains unchangeable in that from which it proceeds, even though it is changed in those to whom and in whom it is.

It follows: “The interpretation [intention], therefore, of hierarchy is likeness and union with God, insofar as possible.” What is called *skopos* (σκοπός) in Greek, and what the translator calls “interpretation,” is more properly termed intention or direction. For the intention or direction called *skopos* is a fixed aiming toward an end. Every activity tends toward some end and tends by some direction; and *skopos*, that is, direction or destination, is that by which it tends.

Every hierarchy, therefore, has a *skopos*, that is, a direction by which it advances in fulfilling its ministry: namely, divine imitation and likeness. As it has been ordered by God in office and dignity, so it should advance according to him in ministry and operation, presuming to do nothing beyond the mode and measure assigned by him and owed to its order. Thus the interpretation—that is, the definition, or rather the direction and contemplation—of hierarchy, toward which every hierarchy ought to intend and by which it directs itself, is likeness and union with God: that is, imitation and identity with God, so that it may in nothing stray or decline from the likeness in which it has been placed, but may emulate him in all things insofar as possible.

Likeness to God is to imitate him; union is simply to follow him. This is the *skopos*, that is, the direction or destination, of every hierarchy: that it may advance according to him toward him, having him as guide of all holy knowledge and activity, following him in judgment and action—illuminated by him to know the truth and assisted to carry out good work. “Having him as guide,” presiding within in the showing forth of truth and going before without in the example of good action.

“And, while defining itself unchangeably toward his most divine beauty, it reforms, insofar as possible, and perfects as divine images its own praisers.” The hierarchy itself, namely, defining itself unchangeably—that is, turned or directed invariably and inflexibly through its own *skopos* toward the most divine beauty of God himself—imitates and follows him, so that it may be conformed to his beauty and most divine comeliness, according to which every hierarchy has been beautifully and fittingly arranged in its own order and rank. Insofar as possible, it reforms its own praisers—that is, those who praise God within it and have been disposed and ordered for God’s praise. It reforms them, I say, in that it makes them imitators of God and turns them in their ministry toward his likeness. By turning and reforming them, it perfects divine *agalmata*—that they may themselves be divine *agalmata*, that is, holy images, receptacles of divinity, and most bright mirrors; divine *agalmata*, indeed, by bringing divine light to perfection, but most bright mirrors by shining from the light received.

It also perfects its praisers as “pure recipients,” or receptacles, “of the principal light and the divine ray”—that is, of the light which illuminates immediately and descends upon the first beings to be illumined. Thus, having received the light, they may be filled with the sacred brightness bestowed, that is, infused, into them; and may themselves show forth that brightness “again,” that is, in a second place, showing it forth in those that follow, abundantly according to “divine laws.”

The sense is this. Because hierarchy, according to the disposition by which it imitates divine beauty, makes all its praisers—whether higher or lower—such as are worthy both to receive divine light and to shine from that light, it also brings certain persons in particular to such purity that they are capable of principal light and are illumined immediately by God; then they pour forth their light upon those who follow them and stand below them in dignity. They minister a second participation from the abundance of their first reception, but only while preserving the divine law, in which it is prescribed for each person what, how much, and to whom he ought to impart from the gift of grace granted him.

That this must not be done apart from divine law—that is, apart from that divine dispensation by which gifts of grace are distributed to participants in the bestowal according to a fixed measure and proportion, and offices are assigned so that each may know what and how much he may lawfully do according to his appointed ministry—he shows when he adds:

“For it is not lawful for the perfecters of the holy, nor for those perfectly made holy, to do anything whatever beyond the proper mysteries of sacrifices and sacred ordinances.”

As though he said: for this reason those who are higher in the order of hierarchies, according to divine laws, pour their lights into those beneath them: because it is not lawful—that is, not permitted at all—for either the perfecters of the holy, that is, those who bring others to perfection in holiness, or those perfectly made holy, that is, those brought to perfection in holiness by others, to do anything beyond their proper mysteries of sacrifices—that is, their proper gifts of grace—and their proper sacred ordinances, that is, the sacred orders assigned to each individually.

For to act without grace is vain; to act outside or against order is perverse. Each has proper gifts, according to which he is able to act, and proper orders, according to which he ought to regulate his activity. Therefore everyone must strive to recognize the grace he has received, lest he begin to presume in what he cannot do; and to heed his own office and order, lest he dare to transgress in what he ought not do.

The apostle Peter admonishes us carefully to preserve this order of divine dispensation, saying: “As each has received grace, ministering it to one another” (1 Pet. 4). The apostle Paul rebukes those unwilling to maintain this divine ordination and dispensation, saying: “Are all apostles? Are all prophets? Are all teachers? Do all work miracles? Do all have the grace of healings? Do all speak with tongues? Do all interpret? Strive after the better charisms” (1 Cor. 12).

Therefore it is not lawful for those who have become participants in divine grace, whether they received it immediately from God or through a human being, to do anything beyond their proper gifts and offices, so that divine beauty may be preserved in all things and the order of the highest dispensation may endure.

He calls “perfecters of the holy” those who have received such great grace from God that they bring others also to perfection in holiness by enlightening and teaching them. “Those perfectly made holy” are those who, enlightened and taught by their superiors, are brought to perfection in holiness.

By “mysteries of sacrifices” he means gifts of grace, which are called mysteries because they are secretly inspired, and sacrifices because they are given for the cleansing and expiation of those receiving them. Or by “ministries of sacrifices” he means the performance of holy works and the administration of divine sacraments. These are sacrifices because they are offered through the performance of action, and mysteries through the sacraments of signification, because through that which is visibly enacted outwardly in the sacrament, the invisible power of truth is signified.

Thus it is not lawful, beyond one’s proper mysteries of sacrifices—that is, one’s own gifts or ministries—for either the perfecters of the holy, those who administer grace received for the perfecting of others, or those made perfect themselves, those who are perfected unto the perfection of holiness through grace received, to do anything. Nor is it lawful for either group to do anything beyond their sacred ordinances—that is, beyond what pertains to their sacred orders—so that each may presume to do only what is shown to belong to the order and office assigned him.

It follows: “Nor can they subsist otherwise, if they desire his divine brightness and look reverently and fittingly toward it, and are re-formed according to the analogy of each of the holy intellects.”

As though he said: not only are they obliged to observe sacred mysteries and sacred ordinances; it is also necessary, because they cannot subsist otherwise in that state in which they imitate divine beauty unless, by preserving their orders, they advance according to divine laws. Therefore, if they desire the divine brightness of their Creator and look toward it in order to receive it, by holy affection and fitting disposition, and are re-formed to his likeness by imitating and following it—each of the holy intellects, that is, of the angels, “according to the analogy of each,” that is, according to the mode and measure of the capability which each possesses in accordance with its own order, rank, and property—they can in no way remain in the good they desire unless they advance according to divine laws, preserving their ordinances and carrying out their own ministries.

It follows: “Does not one who speaks of hierarchy thereby universally declare a certain sacred disposition, an image of divine beauty, sacrificing the mysteries of its own illumination in hierarchical orders and knowledges, and assimilated, insofar as is permitted, to its own principle?”

Since, he says, every hierarchy must desire divine likeness and cannot subsist otherwise unless it perseveres in imitation of it, one who speaks of hierarchy declares a certain sacred disposition, which is an image of divine beauty—that is, of divine loveliness. It is a disposition, I say, sacrificing mysteries, that is, performing or offering mystical works or divine ministries, according to its own illumination in hierarchical orders and knowledges. This means according to the proper illumination of each, insofar as each has been given to act in accordance with its own order, rank, and gift of illuminating grace. By acting, it is assimilated, insofar as permitted—that is, insofar as is possible to a creature according to its own mode and dignity—to its own principle, from which it was made to be something and according to which it was arranged to be such as it is.

“Does not one who speaks of hierarchy universally declare a certain sacred disposition?” That is, he declares one so constituted in every one of its orders and ranks, because it has been disposed and ordered as an image of divine beauty in hierarchical orders and knowledges, and sacrifices the mysteries of its own illumination, so that in all its disposition, order of dignity, knowledge of discernment, and imitation in work, it emulates its own principle.

A person sacrifices the mysteries of his own illumination when, from the hidden gift of inspiration, he presents a good work. He likewise sacrifices the mysteries of his own illumination when, pouring grace received into others, he multiplies the talent entrusted to him. He likewise sacrifices the mysteries of his own illumination when he administers only those things that accord with his own order and office.

“For the perfection of each who obtains a share in hierarchy is this: to ascend, according to his own analogy, into imitation of God; and, more divinely than all [or: most divinely], as the divine utterances say, to become a co-worker with God and to show the divine activity shining forth in himself insofar as possible.”

Therefore he says that one who speaks of hierarchy signifies a general disposition imitating divine beauty in its own ordering, because this is the perfection of each order or person among all who obtain a share in hierarchy: to ascend, according to one’s own analogy—that is, one’s own mode and measure—into imitation of God; and, as the divine utterances say, to become a co-worker with God in the most divine manner of all. That is, the utterances say that nothing is more divine; or, to become a co-worker with God in the manner which makes persons more divine than anything else does. And it is to show in oneself divine activity shining forth: namely, that one may pour into others through the example of one’s work what one first merited to receive through the gift of hidden inspiration.

Thus the perfection of hierarchy consists in this: that those who are cleansed may cleanse; those who are illumined may illuminate; and those who are perfected may perfect. “For this indeed is the order of hierarchy: that some be cleansed and others cleanse; some be illumined and others illuminate; some be perfected and others perfect; each in whatever manner belongs to deiform union.”

First they are cleansed, afterward illumined, and then perfected. For unless cleansing came first, illumination would not follow; and unless there were illumination, consummation would not come. Just as one who has not been cleansed cannot be illumined, so one who has not been illumined cannot be consummated, because knowledge of truth illuminates only the clean, and perfection in virtue comes near only to those illumined by truth.

But there are higher and exalted beings, themselves approaching divinity and receiving from it immediately both cleansing, that they may be clean; illumination, that they may be bright; and perfection, that they may be holy. And from them in turn, according to the order of divine dispensation, cleansing, illumination, and perfection pass to those who follow them and are subject to them in order. Thus, according to this mode, each union—that is, every order and distribution, in whatever way deiform—has deiformity or likeness to God in being cleansed, illumined, and perfected, so that each, in its own mode and measure, may possess deiformity and likeness to God: cleansed by purification, illumined by truth, and perfected by goodness.

[Col. 0998D] It follows: “Divine blessedness, insofar as one may speak of it among human beings, is at once pure from every dissimilarity, full of eternal light, perfect and at once needing no perfection; cleansing, illuminating, and perfecting.”

He now wishes to show that the good which exists in a creature, whether cleansed, illumined, or perfected by grace, subsists by nature in the Creator himself, from whom it comes.
