His divine blessedness is clean without cleansing, shining without illumination, and perfect without receiving. For it is not cleansed in order to be clean, nor illumined in order to shine, nor does it receive in order to be perfected. Rather, possessing all things in itself, it needs nothing external; and, ministering what is its own, it fills things which are needy in themselves.

“It is pure,” he says, “from every dissimilarity together.” This, then, is why it is rightly called clean: it has no dissimilarity whatsoever. Where purity is, dissimilarity is not, because it is wholly the same thing and a concordant unity. Corruption introduces dissimilarity and makes something other than what it was, when it recedes from its being and fails so as to become other than it was. Therefore, what is always the same admits no dissimilarity, and what remains unchangeable admits no corruption. For this reason divine blessedness is clean, incorruptible, and foreign to every dissimilarity, subsisting in what it is and preserving incorruptibly what it has.

It is also full of eternal light, yet not as something illumined, because it is itself light; nor as beginning to shine, because it is eternal; nor as increasing in light, because it is full. It is likewise perfect and at once in need of no perfection—that is, in need of nothing belonging to perfection—because it has and possesses all things, and is itself wholly what it possesses. Consequently it cannot be greater, because it has all things; nor lesser, because it has them unchangeably and eternally.

And though it is such in itself that it needs neither cleansing, being pure; nor illumination, being full of light; nor perfection, being consummate, it nevertheless cleanses, illumines, and perfects all who deserve to be cleansed, illumined, and perfected, whether they receive grace immediately in the first place or participate through those who merited first to receive it.

All this—namely, that divine blessedness is called full, full of light, and perfect—must be said “insofar as one may speak among human beings,” that is, according to the manner in which that which is ineffable can be spoken by human beings. For with regard to the ineffable purity of highest truth itself, the divine nature ought rather to be called holy cleansing, illumination, and perfection. Thus, to call it pure is understood to be too little; it is rather cleansing itself. To call it illumined is too little; it is rather illumination itself. To call it perfect is too little; it is rather perfection itself. Yet even this is still inadequate unless it is conceived as cleansing beyond every cleansing, illumination beyond every illumination, and perfection beyond every perfection.

Therefore he says: “Cleansing, illumination, perfection—above cleansing, above light, perfected beforehand,” or more-than-perfect, that is, above perfection. For everything said in this way is said in relation to something, from which he who supremely is is far removed, and therefore he is above all that is. Hence it is cleansing because it admits no defilement into itself and removes defilement or corruption from those who receive and suffer corruption; and yet it is above cleansing, because corruption does not touch it.

It is illumination because it shines in itself and makes dark things bright from itself; and it is above illumination because, irradiating and penetrating all things, it does not go forth from itself. It is perfection because it lacks nothing in itself and gives from itself what is lacking to those who have less; yet it is perfected beforehand, or more-than-perfect, because it wholly subsists in the singularity of the good and in undivided participation, so that its good is neither lesser because it is one nor multiple because it is participated.

For this reason “it is perfect through itself,” because it received what it has from no other; and it is “the principle of perfection through itself,” because in giving what it has to those being perfected, it does not lose it. And it is “the cause of every hierarchy and of every sacred thing according to transcendent exaltation.” It is principle because all things are from it; cause, because all things are through it and for it; and form, because every hierarchy in its order of dignity and every sacred thing in the ministry of action is dispensed according to it. From it, by predestination; through it, by creation; for it, by glorification; toward it, by conversion, so that it may imitate it and be beatified in it.

It follows: “It is necessary, therefore, as I think,” and so forth. [Col. 1000B] After showing that divine blessedness is the form and cause of every sacred authority and disposition, and that it is clean, shining, and perfect—clean and pure because it lacks every dissimilarity and confusion; shining because it contains in itself the fullness of eternal light; perfect because, possessing all things, it needs nothing—he now infers that those also who have been ordered in sacred dispositions to its likeness and imitation ought likewise to be clean from every contagion and confusion, shining with truth and perfect in goodness. Thus they too may cleanse, illumine, and perfect others by teaching and example, rising in both respects to the image and likeness of their Creator: both insofar as they themselves are clean, bright, and perfect, and insofar as they cleanse, illumine, and perfect others.

“It is necessary,” he says, “that those to be cleansed”—that is, whether those who receive cleansing in the first place or those who receive it through others—“be made wholly pure and freed from every confusion of dissimilarity,” introduced either by ignorance of truth or desire for evil.

“Those to be illumined, however, must be filled with divine light,” as persons to be brought by the most pure eyes of the mind “to contemplative disposition and power.” That is, they must have, in the eyes of their mind—made chaste and clean by the preceding cleansing from sin and error—“a contemplative disposition and power”: disposition through purity of mind, and power through stability in contemplation, so that they may contemplate divine things, apprehending them truly and retaining them perseveringly.

“Those to be restored from imperfection must become participants in the perfecting knowledge of things sacred that have been examined,” so that, following with love and apprehending by participation those true goods and sacred things which they investigate by perfect knowledge, they may be perfect in participation through perfect goodness, just as through perfect knowledge they have been perfected in cognition.

“Cleansers, moreover, must communicate cleansing to others by the greatness of their purification from their own purity.” That is, cleansers, whose ministry is that through them others may be cleansed from error and fault, must be such that by the greatness of their cleansing—that is, by the cleanness they possess in themselves—they impart cleansing to others through their own purity, making pure the lives of those to be cleansed not by another’s example but by their own.

“Those who illumine, however, must carry their surpassing light upon those worthy of light,” since they have brighter minds both for participation in light, through which they themselves receive light, and for distribution of light, through which they pour the light received into others to illumine them. They have these things “properly,” that is, singularly and excellently, because those who ought to illumine others must shine more than others; and they must be filled “most richly,” that is, abundantly, with holy brightness, so that from the abundance of their reception they may give each what is needed.

For one who must teach all must possess knowledge of all, because one who does not know the grounds and benefits of all things cannot minister to each what is expedient. They ought to carry their light upon others in such a way that by the excellence of their life they commend what they teach by word, as though shining on high and pouring forth lights upon those who remain lower in manner of life.

Those who perfect, moreover, must perfect those to be perfected by most sacred teaching through knowledge of sacred things that have been examined, as teachers of perfecting knowledge. One truly examines sacred things who knows a disposition by experience; one truly examines sacred things who has perceived inward goods by tasting them. Therefore one possesses most sacred teaching who teaches what he savors, instructs what he feels, and teaches not merely to know the true but to apprehend the good and love the just.

This tradition is called perfecting because this alone brings a human being to perfection: when he apprehends through the pursuit of good work the goods which he could not know through understanding. With such teaching, therefore, perfecters ought to perfect those to be perfected, so that they may be holy and perfect in goodness, imitating him to whose form and likeness they are re-formed, both by imparting and by receiving the participation of divine grace—imparting it to inferiors and receiving it from superiors.

Whence it follows: “Does not, therefore, each order of hierarchical disposition, according to its own analogy—that is,” its mode, measure, and order—“be led back to divine cooperation: acting and accomplishing through grace and power given by God, which naturally and supernaturally belong to divinity and, having been superessentially accomplished by divinity itself, were afterward manifested to hierarchy for the possible imitation of souls”—that is, spirits—“that love God?”

For unless those goods which are in God by nature descended to these beings through grace, they would not be like him; and unless they themselves acquired by acting what he possesses not by acting but by possessing, they would not be his imitators. Finally, unless those goods had been brought from his hidden invisibility into manifestation, they would in no way have been imitable by the capacity of a creature; nor would there be dignity according to him unless grace had gone forth from him.

See what love accomplishes. The hidden divine things are said to be made manifest and possible to imitate only to souls that love God. For rational souls perceive inward and eternal goods through love alone: through love and tasting, that they may understand them; through following, that they may apprehend them. Unless they loved, they would not understand, because these things are understood only when loved. Again, unless they loved, they would not seek; and unless they sought, they would not find, because they are not found if they are not sought.

Hence it is written: “I shall no longer call you servants, because a servant does not know what his lord does. But I have called you friends, because I have made known to you everything that I heard from my Father” (John 15). And again: “Father, I give you thanks, because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Luke 10).

See, therefore, how love alone reveals the hidden things of God, and likewise brings within possibility what is ineffable, superessential, and supernatural to every creature according to the incomprehensible sublimity of God. “If anyone loves me,” he says, “he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

Thus every order of hierarchical disposition is perfected through grace and power received from God by love alone, by acting and imitating God. In this way those things which belong to divinity naturally begin to be present in them through activity and imitation, because they are from divinity; and supernaturally, because they are the same as divinity: naturally, because they are coeternal; supernaturally, because they are consubstantial. For what is always present is natural; but what is the same is supernatural, because it is nature itself and is itself nature.

It follows: “And things enacted by it superessentially, and disclosed to the hierarchy for the attainable imitation of souls that love God.” These are the things which belong to divinity supernaturally, which were enacted by it superessentially, and finally disclosed to the hierarchy for the attainable imitation of souls loving God. He wishes certain invisible and ineffable goods to be understood—goods which were with God and in God, and had not yet come to knowledge through participation, so as to be known and possessed except by him alone whose they were and in whom they were. Afterwards they were made by him, when it came about that they should be made in us; and they were made superessentially, because they were first made by him for us, in order that afterwards through him they might be made in us.

They were made for us by predestination, in order that they might be made in us by reception; they were made for us when they are bestowed, in order that they may be made in us when they are received. They are made above us when they begin to come to us; they are made in us when they begin to be possessed by us. They are made unto us when they descend from him; they are made in us when they are bestowed through him. These, therefore, are the things which belong to divinity before us supernaturally, and which have been made superessentially by it for us, and finally disclosed in us through it. “They have been disclosed,” he says, “to the hierarchy,” that is, to the sacred order which is ordered and proceeds according to God; and this was done [Col. 1003A] “for the attainable imitation of souls that love God,” that is, so that souls loving God may be able to imitate him; for unless they had been disclosed, they would not be imitable. For unless they were known, they would not be sought; and unless they were sought, they would not be known.

This must be carefully observed: these goods are said to have been disclosed not to each individual separately, but to the hierarchy, that is, to the community. Yet they are exercised by each person [Col. 1004A] in the community through the zeal of imitation, because grace is poured out upon all and works in each. Outside unity no one can receive it, and within unity what is given to one cannot suffice for another. Therefore they are disclosed to the hierarchy so as to lead souls loving God to attainable imitation.

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 1003]

## TITLE OF CHAPTER IV. What the designation of angels signifies.

## TEXT

[Col. 1003B]

Therefore, what hierarchy is, as I think, has been well defined by us; next the angelic hierarchy must be praised, and the marvelous formations fashioned for it in the Scriptures must be contemplated with supramundane eyes, so that through mystical formations we may ascend to their most Godlike simplicity. And at the same time we shall praise, in divine worship and most perfect thanksgivings, the principle of the knowledge of every hierarchy: first of all declaring this truth, that the superessential divinity, by universal goodness, brought into being the essences of the things that are, establishing them in being. For it is characteristic of the cause of all things and of the goodness which is above all things to call the things that are into communion with itself, insofar as this is determined for each of the things that are according to its proper analogy.

Therefore all things that are [Col. 1003C] participate in the providence flowing from the superessential and most causative divinity. For perhaps they would not exist unless they received the essence and principle of the things that are. Thus all existing things participate in its being. For the being of all things is the superbeing of divinity; living things participate in the same life-giving power that is above every life; rational and intellectual beings participate in the same wisdom, perfect in itself and pre-perfect, which is above every reason and intellect. And it is clear that those essences which have received innumerable gifts from it are near to it.

Therefore the holy orders of the heavenly essences, through participation in the tradition of hierarchy, have been made superior to things which merely are and to things which live irrationally—according to which irrational living things we ourselves are rational. For, invisibly looking in a supramundane way toward the divine likeness [Col. 1003D] and desiring to be conformed to it, they possess more abundant and beautiful communions with it. For they attend to all life. Therefore they are first, manifoldly, and ever directed toward the highest good, so far as is permitted, in conformity with divine and unbending love; they receive the principal illuminations immaterially and purely, are ordered toward them, and possess all intellectual life. Therefore they are first and manifoldly made participants in God, and first and manifoldly revealers of the divine hiddenness.

For this reason they alone beyond all things have been deemed worthy of the designation “angel,” because they first bring forth within themselves the divine illumination and through themselves convey to us the manifestations that are above us. Thus, indeed, as theology says, they have been bestowed upon us through angels. Angels also led our glorious fathers, both before the Law and after the Law, back to the divine: introducing what was to be done; recalling them from error and an unclean life to the straight way of truth; or prophetically revealing sacred orders of supramundane mysteries, hidden visions, or certain divine fore-proclamations [predictions] (Gen. 19, 22, 31; Judith 6; Dan. 7; Matt. 2; Acts 10; Rev. 4).

But if anyone says that certain saints also received theophanies immediately from that source, let him learn this too wisely from the most sacred [Col. 1004C] Scriptures: no one has seen, nor will see, the hidden reality of God (Num. 12; 1 Tim. 6). Theophanies were indeed made to the saints, [but] according to manifestations fitting for God and through certain sacred manifestations of visions proportioned to those who beheld them. Theology itself, therefore, most wisely disclosed that the vision described within it is rightly called a theophany: a divine likeness of the formless, presented as it were in a form, by the leading back of those who behold it toward the divine—because through it a divine illumination is made for those who behold, and because these divine realities themselves sanctify and perfect them.

Our glorious fathers, however, attained and accomplished these divine visions through the intervening heavenly powers. Does not the tradition of the Scriptures also say that the sacred legislation was given by God himself to Moses, so that it may truly teach us that it is divine and sacred characters? [Col. 1004D] (Deut. 9.) But theology also wisely teaches that it comes to us through angels, as the divine legal order legally establishes this: namely, that through the first the second are led back to the divine. For this law is established from the superessential principle of the ordering of all things not only among souls set above and below, but also among those of equal power. That is: in every hierarchy there are first, middle, and last orders and powers; and those nearest the bottom have more divine teachers and guides for their leading into the divine, illumination, [Col. 1005A] and communion.

I see, moreover, that angels first taught the divine mystery of Christ’s humanity, and that thereafter through them the grace of knowledge descended to us (Matt. 1; Luke 1–2). Thus the most divine Gabriel taught Zechariah, the high priest, the mysteries: namely, that a child would be born to him beyond hope through divine grace, that this child would be a prophet, and that he would divinely and savingly reveal to the world the manly operation of Jesus’ divinity (Luke 1). He likewise taught Mary how the divine mystery of the ineffable divine formation would take place within her (ibid.). Another angel taught Joseph how the promises divinely made to the progenitor David would truly be fulfilled (Matt. 1; Luke 2). Another announced the Gospel to the shepherds, as persons purified by the return and silence of many; and with him a multitude of the heavenly host delivered to those on earth that highly praiseworthy doxology.

I shall also look to the most excellent manifestations of the light of Scripture. For I see that Jesus himself, the superessential essence of the superheavenly essences, in coming immutably to what pertains to us, did not withdraw from the human order which he had himself ordered and assumed; but, in obedience, he submits to the ordinances of the Father and God through angels. Through these intermediaries Joseph is told of the flight of the Son into Egypt, ordained by the Father, and again of the return from Egypt to Judea (Matt. 2). Through angels we see him ordered under the Father’s legislation (Luke 22). Indeed, I venture also to say—as is expressly known from our priestly traditions—that an angel strengthened Jesus himself; or that Jesus himself, coming through our saving, beneficent, and revealing dispensation, is called the Angel of Great Counsel. For, as the angel himself said, whatever he heard from the Father he announced to us (John 15; Isa. 9).

## EXPOSITION

After demonstrating, by giving and expounding the general definition, how hierarchy is to be understood according to the angelic and human order—for the divine, being infinite, cannot be defined—he now begins to treat the angelic hierarchy specifically. First he shows how the names of angels, given by human beings and according to human ways of speaking, are to be understood in that spiritual and heavenly nature.

He connects what precedes with the ensuing discourse, saying: “Therefore, what hierarchy is, as I think, has been well defined by us; next the angelic hierarchy must be praised, and the marvelous formations fashioned for it in the Scriptures must be contemplated with supramundane eyes.” It is as though he said: After we have, according to our judgment, adequately shown what hierarchy is from the definition proposed, it follows that we should praise the angelic hierarchy—that is, show how greatly it is praised in the sacred Scriptures, or demonstrate how praiseworthy it appears from what is said of it. To demonstrate this, it is fitting that we contemplate with supramundane eyes—that is, spiritual eyes, eyes that see spiritually—the marvelous works, that is, compositions or adaptations of forms, attributed to it in the sacred writings [Col. 1006A] in order to disclose its invisible nature. For this reason things visibly presented must be contemplated with spiritual eyes: lest one think that only what is seen exists, and lest the mind remain fixed upon what it outwardly beholds. Rather, through what is outwardly set forth for demonstration, it is invited to contemplate something truer and more exalted.

Therefore it follows: “That through mystical formations we may ascend to their,” namely the angels’, “most Godlike simplicity.” “For this reason,” he says, “the marvelous works fashioned from forms must be contemplated with supramundane eyes, so that, stimulated by these mystical formations considered outwardly, we may inwardly ascend to the most Godlike simplicity” of the angels themselves. For the very truth of mystical formations, through which they are outwardly displayed, is a kind of multiplicity in angels. But their unity of spiritual and unchangeable nature is simple. Therefore they do not possess Godlikeness in their multiplicity but in their simplicity, because in the aspect in which they are displayed through visible forms they assume a likeness to corporeal nature. But in the aspect in which they are understood as spiritual beings and of incorporeal nature, they look to the image and likeness of God. This likeness is called not merely Godlike but “most Godlike,” because, although the same likeness is also found in human beings, it is believed to be more excellent in angels.

It follows: “And at the same time we shall praise, in divine worship and [Col. 1006C] most perfect thanksgivings, the principle of the knowledge of every hierarchy.” In praising the angelic hierarchy, he says, we shall at the same time praise the divine and supreme hierarchy, which is the principle of the knowledge of every hierarchy—that is, the knowledge possessed by every hierarchy and through which every hierarchy is ordered, because every hierarchy is both ordered through it and illuminated by it. “We shall praise,” I say, “the principle of the knowledge of every hierarchy,” though not by definition and demonstration as we do the angelic hierarchy, nor by definition and comprehension as we do the human hierarchy—the former being invisible and shown through visible things, the latter being visible and known in itself. Rather, we shall praise it by divine worship and most perfect thanksgivings.

For what is beyond thought is not praised by demonstration, nor is what is incomprehensible praised by comprehension. Therefore God, who cannot be investigated or comprehended, can be praised only by worship and thanksgiving. If, then, you cannot praise him by speech, praise him by living. What the tongue cannot explain, a good life commends; he who is not investigated through knowledge is reached by good will. Therefore, if you do not comprehend him, by living according to him strive toward him: this is to praise by divine worship. Again, if you cannot speak him, you can speak of what has been given by him; commend his excellent gifts and proclaim him to be ineffably good. This is to praise by most perfect thanksgiving. Thus we shall praise our principle by divine worship [Col. 1007A] and most perfect thanksgivings.

In this praise of our principle, the first thing to be recalled is how divine goodness, diffused toward all things, first brought created things into being; then established them under itself to govern them, and refashioned them toward itself to nourish them. This is what he says: “First of all,” that is, before all things, it is necessary “to declare that truth,” namely, how the superessential divinity “by its universal goodness brought into being the essences of the things that are, establishing them”—that is, after creation, arranging and ordering them, or setting them beneath itself and ordering them according to itself.

“For it is,” etc. It is as though he said: For this reason divine goodness calls back and refashions toward itself the things it created, because it belongs to it by its innate kindness to call into its communion those which received being from it, so that they may be blessedly in being—insofar, that is, as each one according to the order and condition of its nature can be capable of participating in it. “For this is,” he says, “the characteristic of the cause of all things and of the goodness above all things”: that is, of the goodness which is the cause of all things, because all things were made through it and it is above all things because it draws to itself what it has made. This is its characteristic: to call the things that are into communion with itself; that is, as it is determined or apportioned to each of the things that are according to its proper analogy, namely, its measure, mode, and order.

For the beauty of the universe is perfected in this very fact: not all things are recalled to communion with divine goodness in one and the same way, but each in varied and manifold ways according to its own order and rank. Thus, in that they are not abandoned, the work of goodness is completed; while in that they are variously ordered, the work of wisdom is completed for the ornament and beauty of all things.

“Therefore all things that are participate in the providence flowing from the superessential and most causative divinity.” Since, he says, it is characteristic of divine goodness to call all things back to participation in itself, so that those which proceeded from it to receive being may endure by turning toward it, therefore “all things that are participate in providence”: that is, in the good provided and the grace provided, flowing [Col. 1007D] from divinity itself as from the fountain and first principle of all goodness. It is superessential because in the excellence of its nature it surpasses all essences and subsisting natures; and it is most causative, that is, the cause of all causes and the first cause, because from its goodness proceeds every good which it offers to all created things, for them to participate in so that they may endure.

“For perhaps they would not exist unless they received the essence and principle of the things that are.” From this, he says, one can prove that all things which are participate in divine providence: they could not otherwise subsist unless they subsisted by participation in the divine goodness itself, from which they received all being and in which all things subsist. For unless all things that are had received their beginning from divine goodness, they would not have begun; and unless they had their essence in it, they would not remain in what they are. Therefore it is the principle of all things, by receiving and participating in which they begin; and it is the essence of all things, by receiving and participating in which they subsist.

Hence follows: “Therefore all existing things participate in its being.” It is as though he said: Since nothing can subsist without it, it is evident that all things which subsist participate in its being. Thus the one and same divine nature, existing in itself, is, in respect to its effect, power, and operation, both the principle from which all subsisting essences and natures created by it receive being, and the essence in which they subsist. It is also life—not the life of all things, since not all things live, but the life of all living things, by and through which they are enlivened and live. It is also wisdom, not of all existing or living things, since not everything existing or living is wise, but the wisdom of all wise beings; and it is intellect and reason, by and through which they are enlightened, are wise, understand, and discern.

This is what he says: “For the being of all things is the superbeing of divinity,” because through the being of divinity, which is above every being, whatever is has being and subsists. But living beings, which receive from it not only being but also life, are enlivened and live by participating in the same life which is above every life [Col. 1008C] and in the same life-giving power. “But rational and intellectual beings,” by participating in “the same” wisdom itself, existing “above every reason and intellect, perfect in itself and pre-perfect”—that is, wisdom perfect above all things—reason, understand, and are wise. They reason by inquiry, understand by knowing, and are wise by participation, so that the one and same divine goodness may be essence to subsisting things, life to living things, and wisdom to wise things. From this it is clear that those created things are nearer in likeness and truth to the creating nature which have received more abundantly from it as gift.

[Col. 1008D] This is what follows: “And it is clear that those essences which have received innumerable gifts from it are near to it.” That is, they are near to the divine nature and close to it, immediately joined with it—those essences, or natures, which, after receiving being itself, have received from it innumerable or manifold gifts of powers. In the first rank among these are reckoned those heavenly and spiritual natures of angels, which are not only rational through the subtlety of wisdom, because they discern by intellect, but also intellectual through the subtlety of spiritual nature, because they are perceived in their own nature by intellect alone and do not touch bodily sense. Thus they have been made superior to all things that are because they live, and superior to all things [Col. 1009A] that live irrationally because they discern.

This is what he says: “Therefore the holy orders of heavenly essences”—that is, the holy ranks of heavenly spirits—“have been made, through participation in the tradition of hierarchy”—that is, participation in the grace handed down to the hierarchy ordered according to God—“superior to things which merely are,” because they live, “and superior to things which live irrationally,” because they discern; according to which irrational living things we human beings are and are called rational animals.

Nor, he says, is it surprising that angelic spirits are made superior in dignity not only to existing but nonliving things and to living but nondiscerning things, but also to rational corporeal beings. For rational corporeal beings, that is, human beings, although they are refashioned toward the divine likeness, look toward it only when instructed and stirred through corporeal intermediaries. But angelic sublimity, placed above all corporeal things and invisibly and immediately conformed to the divine likeness, with no other creature placed between itself and God, is more abundantly and manifoldly conformed to it, drawing grace from it and contemplating it more closely as the nearest reality.

“Invisibly,” he says, means without material and corporeal instruments and visible signs, conforming themselves to divine imitation—the orders of the heavenly essences themselves. “And looking toward the divine likeness in a supramundane manner” means looking spiritually, through imitation and conformity; “they possess more abundant and beautiful communions with it,” that is, they receive from the divine likeness more manifold perceptions of spiritual gifts. In these they have communion with it, because by receiving and sharing its good in these spiritual gifts they possess it and possess it with it: beautifully, purely, without corporeal defilement or material contact, being simply assumed into it.

“They attend to all life,” that is, to the highest life in which all life is, which wholly is life and lives not from another but is life. Thus they receive from the highest life all life, so that because they immediately receive within themselves the fullness of life, life never fails in them.

[Col. 1009D] It follows: “Therefore they are first and manifoldly, and ever directed toward the highest good, so far as is permitted, in conformity with divine and unbending love; they receive the principal illuminations immaterially and purely, are ordered toward them, and possess all intellectual life.” They, he says, are directed toward the highest good: first, because immediately; manifoldly, because perfectly; and always, because without interruption—“as far as is permitted,” that is, lawful or possible for a creature—to conformity with divine and unbending love, namely, love by which the creature loves God unbendingly or unchangeably and, through unbending and divine love, turns and is refashioned toward God.

“They also receive principal illuminations,” that is, illuminations given first and principally: immaterially, without a body, and purely, without defilement. They receive them immaterially, without visible signification, and purely, without the contamination of error. “They are also ordered toward them,” namely, toward receiving illuminations, so that difference of reception corresponds to difference of order; or they are ordered toward them in justice, subjecting and adapting themselves in every way to the divine will, so that they receive the illumination of grace without impediment precisely because they do not dissent from its truth through desire for wickedness.

They also “possess all intellectual life,” because what they are is life, and their spiritual substances have living as their very being. For in them there is not one thing which gives life and another which is given life, but the whole is one and the same. Therefore they are said to possess all life, or to be all life, because all that they are is life—just as the highest life itself, in which they are and in which they live, is all life, because it lives from itself and is life, and all that it is, is life.

It follows: “Therefore they are first and manifoldly made participants in God, and first and manifoldly revealers of the divine hiddenness.” These heavenly orders, he says, “are made participants in God,” that is, so that they participate in God and divine grace: first, because no creature precedes them; “and manifoldly,” because no creature is above them. “First,” because before all; “manifoldly,” because more than all. They are “revealers of the divine hiddenness,” that is, of divine grace breathed invisibly and secretly into them, because they afterwards disclose and communicate to others what they themselves receive inwardly by hidden inspiration. Or they are revealers “of the divine hiddenness,” that is, of hidden and invisible divinity, because the invisible things of God come forth into manifestation in them and through them: divine brightness first shines in them and afterwards, through them, illuminates the subordinate ranks placed under their care.

For this reason, he says, “they alone beyond all things have been deemed worthy of the designation ‘angel,’ because they first bring forth within themselves the divine illumination and through themselves convey to us the manifestations that are above us.” Because divine light first pours itself into [Col. 1010D] them and then descends through them to enlighten us, they have beyond all things been deemed worthy of the designation “angel.” For *angel* means “messenger.” Those who convey to others by ministering the grace they have received are nothing other than messengers of the author and giver of that grace. Yet some messengers are prior and others later. The angels who first receive divine grace and afterwards convey it to human knowledge are, as it were, the first messengers of that grace. Human beings, when they convey grace received by preaching and proclaiming it to others, are indeed called messengers, but they are not first messengers, since they received what they announce from others who were first illuminated and announced it before them.

For this reason those heavenly and invisible spirits are called angels both by a singular dignity and by a proper designation: because what they behold within themselves from the invisible light of divinity is first disclosed to them by hidden inspiration, and what they bear in themselves to make it known to us is first poured into us through them. For they first bring forth divine illumination within themselves as though giving birth from the hidden conception of divine light. They do not draw it from without, but inwardly conceive the light of eternal brightness, so that what they see within themselves may come forth from within toward themselves and may be poured out through them toward us. Thus, receiving divine illuminations first within themselves and through themselves, they afterward convey to us the manifestations of the same illuminations which are above us.

“For thus,” he says, “the divine manifestations were bestowed [Col. 1011B] upon us through angels, as theology,” that is, sacred Scripture, “testifies. And angels led our glorious fathers, both before the Law and after the Law, back to the divine: introducing what was to be done; recalling them from error and an unclean life to the straight way of truth; or prophetically revealing sacred orders of supramundane mysteries, hidden visions, or certain divine fore-proclamations.”

Thus, he says, as theology—that is, sacred Scripture—testifies, divine manifestations were bestowed upon us through angels. For both before the Law was given and after the Law was given, that is, under Law and grace, angels led our glorious fathers—namely, the elect and just, whose children we are by imitating their life—back to the divine, that is, to divine knowledge. They introduced what was to be done, that is, led them to live justly and piously; and they recalled them from error and an unclean life to the straight way of truth, teaching them to believe rightly, so that their faith might be right and their life pure.

Or they revealed sacred orders of supramundane mysteries: that is, heavenly secrets concerning the blessed life, the joys of the heavenly homeland, and the invisible ordering of blessed spirits—how all are happy in one good, yet not equal; how the superior are set over others without pride, and the inferior are subject without misery. Or they revealed sacred orders of supramundane mysteries, that is, divine secrets: namely, how that which God has ordained to be done by an invisible and secret dispensation must visibly and temporally be fulfilled by human beings. Or they revealed certain hidden visions signifying something concerning the past, present, or future. Or they revealed certain divine fore-proclamations made prophetically: that is, divine proclamations in which something was prophetically announced before it happened. Thus they ministered knowledge of future things to those who spoke, or understanding of what had been said to those who heard; and in all these ways, instructing holy men either in right faith or in good conduct, they led them back to divine knowledge and participation.

It follows: “But if anyone says that certain theophanies came immediately [Col. 1012A] from that source to some persons, let him learn this too wisely from the most sacred Scriptures: no one has seen, nor will see, the hidden reality of God.” If anyone, he says, against what I have said—that divine revelations come to human knowledge through angels—should say that, even without angels as intermediaries, certain holy fathers at times received revelations from divinity itself, let him also learn from the most sacred Scriptures that no one has seen or will see the hidden reality of God itself.

Therefore, if anyone—that is, any person—says that some holy persons received theophanies, that is, divine appearances, immediately from the divine secret, descending first upon them with no other creature intervening, let him also learn wisely from the most sacred Scriptures how “no one” has ever “seen, nor will see, the hidden reality of God”: namely, the divine nature, which is hidden and removed from every sense. No one has seen, I say, what this hidden reality itself is. That is: even if he saw it in a figure, he did not see it in essence; he did not see it in its species, even if he saw it in signification.

When he has learned this from the most sacred Scriptures, let him understand that the human mind cannot of itself approach immediately to contemplate inaccessible light, unless it is aroused and raised up by theophanies, that is, divine appearances. “Theophanies, however, were made to the saints [but] according to manifestations fitting for God, and through certain sacred manifestations of visions proportioned to those who saw them.” Theophanies, he says—that is, divine revelations or revelations of divinity—were made to the saints, not in such a way that the human mind, placed in mortal flesh and confined within human sense, might immediately approach the incomprehensible nature. Rather, they were made through certain sacred manifestations: either visible forms outwardly applied to the senses; or images, corresponding to visible things, inwardly impressed upon the mind; or in some other higher and more excellent way spiritually impressed on human reason. These manifestations were adapted with such fitness that they were suitable both to God, of whom they were made, and to those who saw them, according to each person’s proportion and capacity.

[Col. 1012D] This is what he says: theophanies were made to the saints according to certain sacred manifestations fitting for God and through manifestations of visions proportioned to those who saw them. They were so proportionately adapted to the ability of those seeing them that the less perfect received heavenly truth through a lower and less perfect kind of vision, whereas the more excellent knew divine secrets in a more sublime manner. Yet, in either case, whatever concerning God could come to human knowledge was less than God himself and in a certain way beneath him.

Thus it is written: “The things beneath him filled the temple” (Isa. 6), because whatever the human mind can comprehend in this life of the knowledge [Col. 1013A] of God cannot be equal to his ineffable majesty. Nevertheless, divine Scripture customarily calls those manifestations by which God reveals himself to human minds *theophanies*, that is, divine appearances. For although what is seen is not God by nature, it is according to manifestation, because God is made manifest through it and in it.

This is what follows: “Theology itself, therefore, most wisely disclosed that the vision described within it is rightly called a theophany: a divine likeness of the formless, presented as it were in a form, by the leading back of those who behold it toward the divine.” “Theology itself,” he says—that is, divine Scripture, which wisely brings divine secrets into human knowledge—“disclosed that it is rightly called a theophany,” namely, the vision described in it: a “divine likeness of the formless,” that is, spiritual natures having no corporeal form, expressed in a visible form or in a representation derived from visible things.

It disclosed, I say, that it is rightly called a theophany by the leading back of those who behold it toward divine things: because through it those who behold are led back to know divine things, as though divine illumination were made through it for those who behold; and because these divine realities themselves sanctify and perfect them. That is, it is called a theophany not only because it manifests divine things to those who behold, but also because it makes the beholders themselves divine.

It follows: “Our glorious fathers, however, attained these divine visions through the intervening heavenly powers,” [Col. 1013C] that is, through heavenly powers acting as intermediaries, through whom these visions were brought to human knowledge. Our glorious fathers attained, obtained, and perfectly understood these visions.

Then follows: “Does not the tradition of the sacred oracles also say that the holy giving of the law was bestowed upon Moses by God himself, so that it may truly teach us that it is divine, and that its characters are sacred?” Does not, he says, “the tradition of the oracles,” that is, the authority of the Scriptures, say that “the sacred legislation,” that is, the giving of the sacred law, “was bestowed upon Moses by God himself,” mentioning, namely, no mediator in the giving of the law between God and Moses, but attesting that God himself spoke directly to Moses? Thus it also teaches us that the law has sacred and divine [Col. 1013D] characters, that is, signs of sacred and divine things, so that by those things visibly done in the giving of the law it shows that certain invisible things were signified and displayed, as it is written: “You shall therefore make the tabernacle according to the pattern which was shown you on the mountain” (Exod. XXVI). According to this manner, then, the visible manifestation itself and the material address, by which the invisible God willed to show himself to human beings, is said to be God or to be of God, because in it the invisible God came forth into manifestation and brought what was hidden of himself into knowledge. Yet in that visible manifestation he accomplished all things through the intervening ministry of angels, so that what was made visible might be called both God’s, by its primary authority, and the angels’, by their subordinate operation.

Hence follows: “Theology also wisely teaches this: that it comes to us through angels.” Theology, he says, not only testifies that the legislation was bestowed immediately upon Moses by God, but also teaches that it, namely the law, comes to us—that is, is set forth for our understanding—through angels. Thus it is plainly demonstrated that this legislation belonged both to God, from whose authority it proceeded, and to the angels, whose ministry it also employed. “As though,” he says, “the divine legal order itself legally established this: namely, that through first things second things should be led back into the divine.” Thus, he says, Scripture shows the legislation as ordered by God through angels, as though the legal order itself, divinely established, had legally laid this down—that is, instituted or decreed it—namely, that second things be led back into the divine through first things. For when the divine law is said to have proceeded first from God to the angels and then through angels to human beings, it is plainly shown that through first and higher beings, second and lower beings are led back to divine knowledge. This must be understood not only between God and angels, or between angels and human beings, but also among the angels themselves, since the higher lead the lower back to divine knowledge. For among the angels themselves there are orders, some higher and some lower; and those who are higher draw more abundantly upon the light of divinity and pour it forth for the illumination of those who follow them.

Even within the orders themselves, [Col. 1014C] where many are equal according to a similar arrangement, this definition of the law is maintained: some are first, some second, and some last in receiving divine grace; and even those equal in rank are not equal in their reception of grace. This is what he says: “For not only among the superordinate and subordinate souls,” that is, spirits, “but also among those of equal power, the law itself is defined from the supra-essential principle of the ordering of all things: namely,” that is, “through every hierarchy,” meaning every sacred ordering, “there are first, middle, and last orders and powers.” And within the orders and powers themselves there are always more divine teachers and “guides by the hand” in divine things, [Col. 1014D] so that they may teach and lead others “into divine leading, illumination, and participation”: into leading through conversion, into illumination through knowledge, and into participation through reception.

Then follows: “I see also that angels first taught the divine mystery of Christ’s humanity; afterwards, through them, the grace of this knowledge descended to us.” From this, he says, it is clear that things sent by God to human beings are announced through angels, since angels taught the very divine mystery of Christ’s humanity, both those who foretold and believed it and those who saw and received it. And afterwards—that is, consequently—the grace of this knowledge descended to us through those angels. Thus, just as [Col. 1015A] Christ’s birth was announced through angels, so also the birth of his forerunner is read to have been announced through the angel Gabriel.

“Thus,” he says, “the most divine Gabriel taught Zacharias the high priest the mysteries: namely, that a child would be born from him contrary to hope,” because his mother was barren and his father old, and that by divine grace he would be “a prophet of the manly divine operation of Jesus, to be manifested divinely and savingly to the world.” It is as though he said: The most divine Gabriel taught Zacharias the high priest that the child to be born from him would be a prophet of Jesus’ manly operation: manly, because it was displayed in the nature of humanity, in which he assumed the sex of the flesh; and divine, because it was perfected through the power of divinity, by which he also created his own flesh. This operation, I say, was to be manifested through him [Col. 1015B] to the world divinely and savingly—that is, for the salvation of the world, which would come from God.

The same most divine Gabriel also taught “Mary how the divine mystery of the ineffable divine formation would be accomplished in her.” That is, the divine operation would ineffably, beyond the customary course and law of nature, take flesh from the flesh of that virgin without admixture of male seed, and wonderfully fashion it as the garment of the eternal Word. “But another of the angels instructed Joseph how the promises divinely made to his forefather David would truly be fulfilled.” That is, how the things promised by God to his forefather David would be fulfilled.

“Another angel, moreover, evangelized the shepherds as purified by a return from the multitude and by silence; and with him a multitude [Col. 1015C] of the heavenly host delivered to those on earth that most praiseworthy doxology.” Another angel, he says, in turn evangelized the shepherds, as people purified and made clean by “a return from the multitude,” that is, by separation or withdrawal from the crowd, uproar, and noise; and purified also by silence, that is, by tranquility of mind and inward peace. Thus they became worthy in this very respect of the Gospel and of evangelical speech: separated from the multitude, returning to themselves, and established in silence and tranquility of mind, they had become capable of receiving the spiritual announcement. Hence, as grace gradually increased after the proclamation by one angel, a multitude of the heavenly host is heard, delivering to human beings on earth, namely to people of good will, that most praiseworthy doxology—that is, the hymn of glory.

[Col. 1015D] Then follows: “And I will look also to the most excellent appearances of the light of the oracles.” It is as though he said: Not only in those things concerning the incarnation of the Word which were announced to human beings through angels does it appear that knowledge of divine things descends to human beings through angels as intermediaries and ministers; the same may also be seen in the person of the incarnate Word itself. Although he commanded angels by the majesty of his divinity, he nevertheless willed that those things which had to be done in time concerning his humanity should be administered through angels. In this he graciously assumed the condition of humanity itself: though lacking every necessity, he submitted himself to angelic arrangements solely by dispensation, as an example of humanity and a lesson in truth.

“I will look,” he says, “also to the most excellent appearances of the light of the oracles,” that is, to the appearances of Jesus Christ himself, when Jesus himself, who is the true light, appeared visibly in assumed flesh. These appearances of the light are most excellent above all other appearances of the oracles, that is, above all appearances related in the sacred sayings; for never before did God manifest himself to the world so excellently as when he himself appeared visibly in assumed flesh. Therefore, he says, I shall look to these appearances of light, highest above all appearances of the oracles, in order to prove in them also that divine mysteries are dispensed to human beings through angels. For if angelic dispensation was not rejected in relation to that [Col. 1016B] human being who is above human beings, how much more is it shown to be necessary in those who are subject to sin and placed in the darkness of ignorance? In that human being, therefore, who is the head of human beings, we may recognize what we ought to think concerning other human beings, his members.

“For I see,” he says, “that Jesus himself, coming immutably to that which is according to us from the supra-essential essence of the supra-celestial essences, did not recoil from the human ordering which he had himself ordained and assumed.” Jesus himself, he says, who according to his divinity—in which all things subsist—is the essence even of supra-celestial essences, that is, angelic spirits, who transcend not only earthly purity but also [Col. 1016C] heavenly subtlety; and is not merely essence, because they subsist in him, but supra-essential essence, because they do not attain equality with him: this Jesus, whose ineffable majesty and divine power both bears the angels through grace and surpasses them by nature, came to that which is according to us, that is, to the assumption of flesh, which belonged to our nature and was like us. And he came immutably—that is, without diminution or alteration of his divinity—and did not recoil from the human ordering, that is, from the ordering or law due to humanity.

This ordering, I say, was first ordained by him when he first formed humanity; afterwards it was assumed by him when he took the form and nature of humanity. If, however, he had assumed human [Col. 1016D] nature and rejected the human condition, he would have recoiled from human ordering. For in his case recoiling would have meant refusing in condition to endure what he had assumed by nature. But now, coming to human nature through the assumption of flesh, he did not recoil from human ordering, through the preservation of humility. “Rather, obediently, he is subjected to the ordinances of God the Father,” administered through angels concerning his humanity; and through those same “intermediate” angels—that is, by means of those angels—Joseph, as the guardian of his infancy, is told of the divinely ordained “departure” of the Son of God “into Egypt,” and again of his conveyance, or return, from Egypt into Judaea.

“And we also see,” he says, [Col. 1017A] “that he himself was ordered through angels under the paternal legislation.” We see him ordered through angels, that is, disposed, “under the paternal legislation,” meaning under the legal commands received for observance by those whom he had as fathers and forebears according to the flesh. Under these legal commands, therefore, he was ordered through angels when, according to the precepts of the paternal law, the Lord of angels was circumcised on the eighth day and on the fortieth day presented in the temple with gifts and sacrifices, observing the law given through angels.

Then follows: “For I persist in saying to one who knows what has been expressly set forth in our priestly traditions, even concerning the angel strengthening Jesus himself.” It is little, he says, merely to say that Jesus in his humanity was ordered under the paternal laws by angels: in that same humanity, as he approached his passion, he was also strengthened by an angel. I persist in saying something which perhaps, if it had not been said beforehand, would not at all seem credible. I persist in speaking of an angel strengthening Jesus himself. I persist in saying what I myself cannot utter without wonder, though I certainly believe and study it; and if I were to say it to one ignorant of these things, I would not dare say it at all. I persist in saying something so great that the knowledge of the small cannot comprehend it, so marvelous that the faith of the small cannot believe it: namely, an angel strengthening Jesus himself. I persist in saying something which, if it were thought to be spoken by me, would not be believed.

But to you, who know what has been expressly set forth—that is, plainly declared—in our priestly traditions, that is, in the Scriptures [Col. 1017C] handed down to us by priestly, sacred-ministering, and sanctified men, I dare confidently to declare the truth, hesitating in no way concerning your firm faith, which receives no scandal and has discernment of what was done and what was said. To you therefore, O son Timothy, as one who knows what is expressly set forth in our priestly traditions, I confidently “persist in speaking even of the angel strengthening Jesus,” so that it may appear beyond doubt how greatly humanity, according to divine ordering, is subject to angelic dispensation: in the human being, who willed at the time of the passion to be strengthened by an angel—not seeking help, however, but forming an example; not being under necessity, yet showing the condition.

[Col. 1018A] Therefore I “persist” in speaking to you “of the angel strengthening Jesus himself.” Or I also persist in saying this to you: that Jesus himself, coming through our saving, beneficent, and revelatory ordering, is called the angel of great counsel. That is, Jesus himself is called “the angel of great counsel,” “coming”—that is, insofar as he came to us—through our ordering, namely according to what he had ordained, or what had been ordained, concerning his coming in our nature. This ordering was saving, beneficent, and revelatory: saving in redemption, beneficent in the bestowal of grace, revelatory in glorification. It was saving because he redeemed from death; beneficent because he bestowed upon the redeemed gifts of grace for justification; revelatory because he first set God visibly before those to be justified in humanity, and afterwards leads those justified, through the vision of his humanity, to the contemplation of divinity.

[Col. 1018B] According to this “revelatory ordering,” therefore, “Jesus, coming, is called the angel of great counsel,” because, “as the angel himself says, whatever he heard from the Father he announced to us.” If, then, an angel is called a messenger, the Savior himself is rightly called a messenger, since he announces to us the will of God the Father and, by breathing through his Spirit upon our minds, reveals inward goods. In this also the dignity of angels is plainly displayed: the Savior himself, conveying to us the Father’s commands, is called an angel. For since the culmination of our salvation through redemption is accomplished not without an angelic designation, it is evident that all other things pertaining to the same salvation are also dispensed by angelic administration. These things, then, have been said concerning the angelic designation.

## TITLE OF CHAPTER V  
Why all heavenly essences are commonly called angels, while the individual orders have their own special designations, except for the first and second orders.

[Col. 1017]

## TEXT

[Col. 1017D]

This, then, so far as concerns us, is the reason for the designation “angel” in the oracles. But, as I think, we must investigate why theologians call all heavenly essences together angels; while, when they come to manifest the ordering of those supra-mundane realities, they name one order in particular the angelic order, which completes and terminates divine and heavenly matters. Before it, however, they arrange the archangelic ranks, principalities, powers, authorities, and whatever essences the revelatory traditions of the oracles recognize as established above these.

We say, moreover, that throughout every holy ordering the higher orders possess both the illuminations and powers of the lower orderings; but the last orders do not participate in those above them. Therefore theologians call the most holy orders of the highest essences angels, for they too are revealers of divine illumination (Heb. I). But they have no reason to name the final order of heavenly souls principalities, thrones, or seraphim. For it does not participate in the highest powers. Rather, as this final order leads our divine high priests back to the splendors of divinity known to it, so the altogether sacred powers of the essences before it lead it back; and they are subject to the divine ordering that perfects the angelic hierarchies. [The printed reading *adhuc immundae*—“still unclean”—is materially uncertain and appears corrupt.] Unless perhaps someone should also say that all angelic designations are common, according to the subjection of all heavenly powers to the God-formed and God-given light and their pre-eminent participation therein. But, so that the matter may be more carefully judged by us, we shall consider the holy and beautiful properties of each heavenly ordering, as expressly set forth in the sacred oracles.

## EXPOSITION

“This, then,” etc. In this fifth chapter it is investigated why all heavenly essences are called angels. This question seems to arise because in sacred Scripture some heavenly spirits are said always to stand before God and always to see his face, while others are said to be sent forth to accomplish outward ministries. Hence it seems to follow that those who always stand before the divine countenance do not go out to announce external matters, whereas those sent forth do not stand immovably, or immutably, before the divine presence.

For it is written in the book of the prophet Daniel: “Thousands of thousands ministered to him, and ten thousand times a hundred thousand stood before him” (Dan. VII). In this distinction, those who stand before him seem to signify those who do not go out to external matters, while those who minister signify those who, by going out to external tasks, do not always stand before him. Therefore, because the lower and final orders go out to external affairs, whereas only the higher and more excellent orders attend without interruption upon divine contemplation, those who stand before him are said to be fewer, but those who minister more numerous.

For although there are nine orders of angels, only two—angels and archangels—have received their designation from the thing itself, because they are specifically sent in accordance with the distribution of their office. Angels are called messengers, and archangels chief messengers, because the former announce lesser things and the latter greater things, as befits the dignity of their ministry. Yet because in Holy Scripture we read that some from the higher orders were sent—as in Isaiah, where one of the seraphim is recalled as flying to the prophet and touching his lips with a coal which he had taken from the altar with tongs (Isa. VI)—and because the Apostle in the Epistle to the Hebrews testifies that all are ministering spirits sent for the sake of those who receive the inheritance of salvation (Heb. I), a great difficulty of uncertainty arises for us, and it is not easy to determine what ought rather to be asserted on this matter.

The author resolves this question as follows. He testifies that the name angels belongs only to the lower orders, which by office properly have to announce external matters. But because the divine secrets which are externally conveyed to human knowledge by these lower orders are announced to them by higher orders, the name angels is communicable also to the higher orders. Though they do not go out to announce things externally, by receiving from above, according to the law of divine ordering, those things which must be announced externally, and by announcing and conveying them to the lower orders which follow after them, they participate in every power, grace, and property of the lower orders. Therefore the designations of the lower orders also pass to the higher. But not every power, grace, and property of the higher orders is communicable to the lower; and for that reason their designations likewise cannot, by a similar principle, be universally carried down to the lower.

Sometimes, however, lower orders, when through the nature of their office they receive a property belonging to higher orders, also take their names in carrying out that office. This explains what we mentioned above: the angel who came to kindle and purify the prophet’s lips is called a seraph, because in the quality of that work he exercised the property of one who kindles or inflames. The Apostle’s statement that all are ministering spirits and sent into ministry is understood in this way: as we said above, even those higher orders are not inappropriately said to be sent, because, although they do not go forth to external matters, they nevertheless bring them to the lower and following orders by announcing what must be announced outwardly.

Others think that all heavenly orders, both higher and lower, are sent outward at particular times, places, and for particular causes; but those who have this properly by office are specifically called angels or archangels. For the Apostle seems to assert, in the testimony mentioned above, that all are sometimes sent, saying: “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent into ministry for the sake of those who receive the inheritance of salvation?” The Psalmist also seems to assert that certain higher beings are sometimes sent outward, not by office but for an incidental reason, when he says: “He makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a burning fire” (Ps. CIII).

Thus some attend by office, while others go out to fulfill external matters; yet those who attend are sometimes sent into ministry and, when they receive the property of lower beings, they also take their designation in that sense. Nevertheless, when they go out to external matters, they do not depart from inward contemplation, because wherever they go they behold him who is present to them. Before examining the words of the book, then, we thought it necessary briefly to mention this question so as to make what follows clearer—defining nothing rashly, but reverencing a mystery which perhaps it is a pardonable weakness not to know, but a condemnable presumption rashly to assert.

Yet this should be known: the author seems rather to give his assent to the view that only some, not all, heavenly orders are sent to external affairs; and nevertheless, because of participation in the same property by which higher orders share the grace and power of lower orders, the names of the lower are also assumed by the higher. So too, at times lower orders, when through the nature of their office they assume the property of higher orders, take their names in that sense. Now to the text: “This, then, so far as concerns us, is the reason for the angelic designation in the oracles.”

“This,” he says, “is the reason for the designation ‘angel’ which we mentioned above”: namely, that divine secrets are announced to us through them; and therefore, because they convey divine commands to us by announcing them, they take the name angels “so far as concerns us,” that is, insofar as, or because of what, they do in relation to us. But because it has not yet been established by manifest reasoning or authority whether this task—bringing forth to human knowledge the announcements of the inward teacher—belongs to all, we must now inquire, he says, why in sacred Scripture the name angels is attributed commonly to all heavenly powers.

This is what he says: “We must investigate, as I think, why theologians call all heavenly essences together angels; while they name in particular the angelic order which comes to manifest those supra-mundane orderings, completing and terminating divine and heavenly matters.” It is as though he said: What remains to be investigated is why theologians universally call all those heavenly natures angels, although they specifically call angelic one order of those spirits who come to us to manifest those supra-mundane orderings—that is, spiritual, divine, and invisible orderings—“completing and terminating divine and heavenly matters,” that is, bringing to completion and fulfillment the things divinely arranged in the heavenly and hidden ordering.

For the divine command, descending from the highest point, is conveyed through the higher orders to the lower until it finally comes to human knowledge and is fulfilled in action. Hence that heavenly order to which the command of divinity descends last through the powers set above it, and which then announces it outwardly, is said to terminate it completely, or bring it to completion, because through its announcement the command is conveyed to the place where it must be fulfilled in its final visible operation. Therefore this is the question: why, although this last order is specifically marked by the angelic designation, all orders of heavenly essences are called angels.

“But before it they arrange the archangelic ranks, principalities, powers, authorities, and whatever essences the revelatory traditions of the oracles recognize as established above these.” It is as though he said: Theologians place the angelic order itself, last and final, nearest to human affairs, bringing forth divine visions by its final announcement and completing them. Before it, however, they place in order what is set above it—that is, “archangelic ranks,” the ordered and beautifully arranged choirs of archangels, who are both higher in dignity than angels and prior in announcing. Then these theologians establish not only above angels but also above archangels principalities, powers, and authorities, and other essences—that is, whatever spiritual natures the revelatory traditions of the sacred oracles make known. These essences are established above the angels, or above all the aforementioned orders, so that they are not only higher in dignity but stronger in the firmness of perfection and more stable toward eternity and immutability.

Then follows: “But we say that throughout every holy ordering the higher orders possess the illuminations and powers of the lower orderings; but the last do not participate in those above them.” It is as though he said: Since in this ordering of heavenly spirits some are higher and others lower, the higher possess every illumination and power of the lower, but the lower do not possess every illumination and power of the higher orders. Therefore the names of lower orders are sometimes transferred to higher orders, since they participate in the properties denoted by the same names. But the names of higher orders cannot in the same way be assumed by lower ones, because the properties denoted by those names do not universally pass to them.

This is what he says: “Throughout every holy ordering,” namely of heavenly spirits, “the excellent,” or higher, “orders possess” all the illuminations and powers “of the lower orderings,” that is, of subordinate orders. But the last, namely lower and subsequent in rank, do not participate in all—understand, all the illuminations and powers—of those who are more excellent than themselves. By illuminations we understand knowledge of truth; by powers, love of goodness and perfection in action.

Then follows: “Therefore theologians call the most holy orders of the highest essences angels, for they too are revealers of divine illumination.” Since he has said that the higher orders possess all the properties of the lower, theologians therefore call the most holy orders of the highest essences—that is, of the most excellent spirits—angels, because they participate in the angelic property. Although they do not go out to announce external matters, they reveal divine illumination as though announcing it, by pouring into the orders which follow them that illumination which they receive from above.

“But they have no reason to call the final order of heavenly souls principalities, thrones, or seraphim.” “They have no reason,” he says—the theologians—to call the final order of heavenly souls, that is, the last order of heavenly spirits, namely angels, “principalities,” that is, rulers, or thrones, or seraphim, because this final order of angels does not participate in the highest powers. Therefore angels cannot be called principalities, thrones, or seraphim, as principalities, thrones, and seraphim are called angels. The higher orders universally participate in the angelic property, whereas angels do not universally participate in the illuminations and powers of the higher, and possess even those especially by which the higher received their special designations only in part; they do not, however, possess the dignity and defining property of those designations.

For not everyone who possesses some power or property by participation should immediately be designated according to that property, unless they possess it either uniquely among others or excellently beyond them. Not everyone who has some wisdom is immediately called wise, nor is someone who has done something right at once called just. Only the one who possesses wisdom and justice uniquely or excellently ought to be called wise and just by a proper and explicit designation. Thus those heavenly orders of holy spirits have their proper designations, by which is indicated not what they have received uniquely, but what they possess excellently.

For seraphim, because from love of their Creator—as those near and close to him—they burn within themselves and kindle others from themselves, are interpreted as “burning” or “kindling,” not because they alone have this uniquely among all the others, but because they possess it with the others and beyond them in excellence. For all burn with love of God; nevertheless, those had to be called burning in particular who both first receive the fire of this love and, burning more strongly, send forth the flame of charity to kindle the others also.

Likewise cherubim—a name interpreted as “fullness of knowledge”—because they possess a greater knowledge of God than the others, alone receive their name from that which, though possessed with the others, they have merited to apprehend more excellently than all others. Thrones too are so called not because God sits and discerns his judgments in them alone, but because they received this gift more excellently than the others and therefore draw their special designation from it. In this manner the same must also be understood concerning the remaining orders: each is believed to receive its proper designation from that which it is shown to possess more excellently by the gift of grace.

But a question arises which is not to be dismissed, and which would bring great confusion to the mind if it were not examined by the application of reason. For if, as has been said, in that heavenly ordering each individual order derives its distinctive name from that property in which it is proved to excel the others, while the higher orders universally and more excellently possess all the illuminations and powers of the orders subject to them [Col. 1023D], then nothing distinctive remains for the subordinate and subsequent orders from which they may obtain a name proper to themselves and distinct from the rest. We must therefore consider more carefully how both propositions may simultaneously be true: namely, that the higher orders universally and more excellently possess the illuminations and gifts of the orders below them, yet that each retains something proper and special from which it may be designated by its own distinct name.

For the Seraphim express through their name a singular love; the Cherubim indicate a more excellent knowledge; and the Thrones show a greater power of discernment. Yet it is certain that those who love more ardently perceive more deeply and discern more subtly. For those who look more closely at hand undoubtedly recognize more clearly [Col. 1024A]. How, then, is the order of the Cherubim said to be named from the privilege of a singular grace, if another order possesses more excellently the gift from which that order itself receives its name?

Perhaps this question may not unfittingly be resolved in the following way—provided that the secret of truth is not violated by any rash presumption. It may be that, although the higher orders possess all the gifts of virtues more excellently, they derive their name only from those gifts which are more sublime among the gifts of virtues; and that they leave the others, which follow in order of dignity, to supply names for the orders following them, so that the first receives its designation from the first gift, the second from the second, and the third from the third.

We know, indeed, on the testimony of Scripture [Col. 1024B], that among all gifts of virtues charity excels.
