Accordingly, it was fitting that the order which is most eminent of all should take from charity alone its distinctive name, although it possessed the other gifts of virtues more excellently as well, and could have taken its designation and title from them. But since knowledge of truth is recognized as next in dignity after love of virtue, the angelic spirits who are second after the first are rightly named from this dignity.

Judgment in discerning truth, however, seems still to involve a verdict that is, as it were, doubtful, and appears in some manner suspended by a less perfect knowledge. Therefore, because it looks toward that highest knowledge of truth after full contemplation—in which truth is not sought but possessed [Col. 1024C]—it gave its name to the third order after the two preceding ones. This, however, must be understood according to human experience, for whose sake these names were given to the spirits themselves. For there judgment is not the determination of ambiguity, but the discernment of truth; nor is anything hidden examined where all things are manifest, but what is certain is assessed according to merit.

Accordingly, even in this judgment we consider knowledge of truth to be prior; for wisdom judges simplicity and unity, whereas judgment, by the force of discernment, is shown to look toward diverse and contrary things. Hence the more excellent designation ought to be taken from wisdom, by which the more excellent order [Col. 1024D] was to be designated. Though that order, as being more sublime and perfect, possessed both wisdom and judgment more fully, it nevertheless took its name from wisdom alone, leaving the designation of judgment to the order following after it.

According to this consideration, therefore, whoever wishes to interpret the names of the angels need find no inconsistency if the higher orders possess all gifts of virtues more perfectly, while the lower orders nevertheless possess their own names from certain gifts in particular.

Concerning the orders of angels themselves, there is one common opinion regarding the first and the last. For no one acquainted with the testimony of the holy Scriptures can be ignorant that the Seraphim are placed in the highest position, then the Cherubim after them, and then the Thrones. Likewise, ascending from the lowest, it is manifest that Angels and Archangels are placed first [Col. 1025A].

Some arrange the following four orders in this way: descending from the Thrones, they place first Dominions, then Principalities, then Powers, then Virtues, so that the nine orders are divided into three triads. The first and highest contains Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones; the second and middle includes Dominions, Principalities, and Powers; the third and lowest arranges Virtues, Archangels, and Angels together. Thus, ascending from the lowest, Angels are counted first, then Archangels, then Virtues, then Powers, then Principalities, then Dominions, then Thrones, then Cherubim, then Seraphim.

But the Theologian places Angels first, then Archangels, then Principalities, and assigns these to the first triad. In the second he places first Powers, then Virtues, then Dominions. In the third, ascending from lower to higher, he judges that Thrones are to be placed first, then Cherubim, then Seraphim [Col. 1025B].

But in this threefold distinction into three groups, one must chiefly observe that the three highest orders—namely Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones—by virtue of their singular excellence and the force of their names, seem to look only toward things inward. For to love, to know, and to judge belong to those who preside over inward things and are turned toward the interior. The three last and outermost orders, however, by the property of their names [Col. 1025C], are shown to be ordered only toward outward things according to the office of their ministry: Angels and Archangels, because they outwardly announce to human beings what must be done and made known; Principalities, because by invisible power they administer and arrange what must be managed concerning human beings.

The middle orders, however, seem, both in their arrangement and in their office, to move between invisible and visible things, and to administer, according to their dignity and office, what must be conveyed from the higher to the lower. Among these, Dominions are first: by their singular excellence they give form to the invisible command among the Virtues by command alone. Virtues are second: they carry out the command by executing the injunction in [Col. 1025D] the Powers. Powers are third: they bring the conceived mandate to completion in the Principalities, Archangels, and Angels subject to them for action.

Those who place Virtues after Angels and Archangels understand them to be the spirits through whom signs and miracles are more frequently performed. In this too the character of the final ordering is preserved, whose ministry we suppose to be ordained only for administering outward matters. They say that Powers are those spirits who have adverse powers subject to them and freely restrain them according to the authority given them, lest they be able to harm as much as they wish. Principalities, they think, are those spirits set even over the good spirits of angels: when they command what must be done, they rule those subject to them in carrying out the divine ministries and stand above them [Col. 1026A]. Dominions, they say, are those who surpass even Principalities by a more excellent power, so that they have subject to them those who have deserved to command others in fulfilling ministry.

We have thought that these matters concerning the orders and names of angels should briefly be set forth in advance as necessary for the forthcoming exposition, so that, having been stated once, the reader may apply them in what follows to each point as reason and occasion require, when matters concerning them—and perhaps matters obscure without them—are to be mentioned. Let us now return to the exposition of the sequence of the text itself.

Above, he said that theologians have no reason to name the angelic order *archai* [Principalities], or Thrones, or Seraphim, because the angelic order itself [Col. 1026B] does not participate in those most exalted virtues, and therefore cannot participate with them in name when it does not participate in the proper quality denoted by the name. He now proves the same point in the following words: namely, that the angelic order does not participate in the most exalted virtues. “It does not,” he says, “participate with them; rather, what it participates in, it participates from them.” For it is one thing to participate in fullness and another to receive participation from fullness.

Thus the angelic order is subject to the most exalted virtues in such a way that it does not participate with them but from them. For just as it leads back, through illumination and instruction, those among human beings who are led toward divine knowledge, so it itself receives divine illumination from the virtues that stand before it.

[Col. 1026C] This is what he says: “Just as it,” namely the angelic order, “leads back our divine high priests,” that is, holy men who immediately received sacred divine things from angels and handed them down to us, “to the divine splendors known to it,” that is, to the divine knowledge which it itself has received and bestows when received, “so also the virtues of the essences that are before it”—that is, before it or above it—“lead it back; I mean pure virtues,” that is, most holy or altogether holy, so that by their preeminent holiness they may be a pattern of perfection to those beneath them.

And they too are “holy virtues for the divine,” namely, for imparting—that is, for giving knowledge of divinity—“to the disposition that completes the angelic hierarchies” [Col. 1026D], that is, to the disposition which perfects, or contains and brings to completion, the angelic hierarchies. That is, it is the final disposition, in which the angelic order is completed insofar as it is perfect, while, insofar as it is last, the hierarchies of all spirits are terminated.

Here one must certainly beware the execrable error of the translator, who supposed the heavenly virtues to be called impure. For the Greek *πανιερόν* (*panieron*), which means “most holy,” “entirely holy,” or “universally holy,” he thought should here be understood as *ἀνιερόν* (*anieron*), that is, “unsacred,” “not holy,” or “without holiness.”

It follows: “Unless indeed someone should also say that all angelic names are common, according to the subjection of all the heavenly virtues to the Godlike and God-given light, and their preeminent communion” [Col. 1027A].

“The lower orders,” he says, “cannot assume the names of the higher, because they do not participate with them in the same excellence of virtues—unless someone should wish to say that all names of angels ought to be common, because all alike receive in subjection one light given by God; and from that received light all become conformed to God and share one preeminent communion in one light.”

“Unless,” he says, “someone should also maintain that all angelic names are common, according to the subjection of all heavenly virtues to the Godlike light—or toward the reception of the Godlike light given by God—and according to the preeminent communion of spiritual or special grace; so that, just as one [Col. 1028A] grace diffuses itself for the participation of all, one designation might reasonably be bestowed upon all.”

“But, that the question may be more carefully judged by us, we shall consider the holy and beautiful properties of each heavenly disposition expressed in the sacred utterances.”

“That we may be better able,” he says, “to judge whether angelic names ought to be common or not, we shall consider the holy and beautiful properties of each sacred heavenly disposition as expressed in the sacred utterances.” For, upon careful consideration of the properties of each, it may perhaps be recognized whether the communion of names can be the same. Although one grace is indeed infused into them, it is not given in one measure and proportion.

## TITLE OF CHAPTER VI. What is the first disposition of the heavenly essences, what the middle, and what the last.

[Col. 1027]

## TEXT.

[Col. 1027B]

I say that only the contemplative Prince of their perfection knows accurately how many and what kinds are the adornments of the superheavenly essences, and how the hierarchies are perfected according to them; and that even they themselves do not yet know their own powers and illuminations, or their own sacred and superadorned ordering. For it is impossible for us to know the ministries of the superheavenly minds and their most holy perfections, unless someone tells us whatever mysteries the Divinity, knowing them well as its own, has taught us through them. Therefore we say nothing by our own motion. But whatever concerning angelic contemplations has been contemplated by the holy theologians, we shall expound in teaching it, insofar as we are able.

Theology has called all the heavenly essences by nine manifesting names [Col. 1027C] (Colossians 1). Our divine and holy perfecter divides these into three threefold dispositions. The first, he says, always exists about God and is assigned to be united to him attentively and immediately before the others. For the manifestation of the divine utterances declares that the most holy Thrones, and the keen-sighted and winged orders called Cherubim and Seraphim in the Hebrew tongue, are placed immediately about God according to a proximity exalted above all others.

Therefore our common teacher says that this threefold adornment is, as it were, one hierarchy, equally ordered and truly first; than which (Ephesians 3; Colossians 1) there is no other more Godlike or more immediately intent upon the illuminations of divinity that operate beforehand in it of themselves [Col. 1027D]. He says that the second is completed from Powers, Dominions, and Virtues. And lastly, he sets forth the disposition of the third of the three heavenly hierarchies: Angels, Archangels, and Principalities (1 Thess. 4).

## EXPOSITION

The title of the sixth chapter is: “What is the first disposition of the heavenly essences, what the middle, and what [Col. 1028B] the last?” For in this chapter he treats of the threefold ordering of the nine orders. The first, which is also the highest, contains three orders: Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones. The second, which is also the middle, likewise contains three: Dominions, Virtues, and Powers. The third, which is also the last, likewise contains three: Principalities, Archangels, and Angels. In these the arrangement of the nine orders is completed.

But, intending to treat of matters so sublime and removed from human understanding, he first modestly confesses his ignorance. He shows that those heavenly secrets are unknown not only to human beings, but cannot be wholly comprehended perfectly as they are even by the angelic spirits themselves; and that only the divine power from which they are knows perfectly what they are.

[Col. 1028C] This is what he says: “How many and what kinds are the adornments of the superheavenly essences, and how the hierarchies are perfected according to them—I say that only the contemplative Prince of their perfection knows accurately.” That is, only divine wisdom knows: the wisdom from which they have their beginning in order to exist, and toward which they look in contemplation in order to be perfect.

“I say,” therefore, “that divine wisdom alone knows how many and what kinds are the adornments of the superheavenly essences,” that is, of invisible natures. For, as they were created by God, they themselves cannot comprehend perfectly what they are. Therefore, he says, “I also say that even they do not know their own powers and illuminations, and their own sacred and superadorned ordering” [Col. 1028D]. Thus divine wisdom alone, which made them, perfectly comprehends both what it made them and how it ordered them. In this it is plainly shown how greatly the immensity of the Creator surpasses every capacity of the creature, since the creature itself is by no means sufficient even to comprehend the Creator.

It follows: “For it is impossible for us to know the ministries of the superheavenly minds and their most holy perfections” [Col. 1029A]. Nor is it especially surprising if we cannot know concerning them what they themselves cannot comprehend concerning themselves, since even what we know about them we can know only as given and administered by God through them. Therefore it is impossible for us to know anything about them except what divinity has taught us through them.

“Unless,” he says, “someone should tell there whatever mysteries the Divinity, knowing them well as its own, has taught through them.” It is impossible for us to know unless someone says that we know only where we have been instructed through them, whatever mysteries—that is, secrets—divinity has taught us through them, as those who know their own ministries well. They therefore know their own ministries well insofar as suffices for our instruction; and do not know them well insofar as full and perfect comprehension is concerned [Col. 1029B].

It follows: “Therefore we say nothing by our own motion; but whatever concerning angelic contemplations has been contemplated by the holy theologians, we shall expound in teaching it, insofar as we are able.” Since, he says, we can know nothing concerning them by ourselves unless we have learned it from them, we do not speak from ourselves in the matters we wish to say concerning them—that is, we say nothing from our own motion, perception, or thought. Rather, whatever the holy theologians have discerned by contemplation concerning the angels, we teach by following their authority as far as we can.

“Theology has called all the heavenly essences by nine manifesting names” [Col. 1029C]. Theology, he says, called all the heavenly essences—that is, spirits—by nine manifesting names: it distinguished them by nine manifest and evident appellations, distinguishing Angels, Archangels, Principalities, Powers, Virtues, Dominions, Thrones, Cherubim, and Seraphim by their proper titles.

“These,” he says, “our divine holy perfecter divides into three threefold dispositions.” By his divine and holy perfecter, or teacher, no one is more plausibly understood than the Apostle Paul, by whom he had been baptized and instructed in the Catholic faith. Paul was caught up to the third heaven, into the paradise of God, and there heard secrets which it is not lawful for a human being to speak. It is thought that he revealed, by transmitting them to the memory of posterity, whatever concerning these matters was useful or possible to be known in this mortal life, not only to this holy man but also to others who had surpassed human understanding through the Spirit of God [Col. 1029D]. Relying, therefore, upon Paul’s authority and supported by the testimonies of the holy Scriptures, he brought knowledge of heavenly things down to earth.

“These,” he says—that is, these essences or nine orders—“our divine holy perfecter divides,” that is, distinguishes, “into three threefold,” that is, ternary, “dispositions. And he says that the first is always about God, and is assigned to be united to him attentively and immediately before the others.” He says that the first disposition always exists about God [Col. 1030A], never going forth toward outward things, and is assigned—that is, ordered and arranged—to be united to God himself: to be united attentively, always directing itself toward him; to be united before the other heavenly virtues which follow after it; and to be united immediately, since none stand before it.

“For the manifestation of the divine utterances declares that the most holy Thrones and the keen-sighted and winged orders called Cherubim and Seraphim in the Hebrew tongue are placed immediately about God according to a proximity exalted above all others.”

Thus our perfecter and teacher says that the manifestation, or authority, of the divine utterances teaches or bears witness that the most holy Thrones, and the keen-sighted and winged orders called Cherubim and Seraphim in the Hebrew tongue, are so placed: Cherubim are keen-sighted because of contemplation; Seraphim winged because of love. These orders, I say—Thrones, Cherubim, and Seraphim—he says are placed immediately about God according to the proximity they have to God, a proximity raised above and more excellent than that of all other orders [Col. 1030B].

“Therefore our common teacher says that this threefold adornment is, as it were, one hierarchy, equally ordered and truly first.” He says, therefore, that these three orders constitute one hierarchy, first in relation to the others and equally ordered in itself. Although in this hierarchy they excel one another in singular grace, all are in some sense equal in one arrangement; and in one respect they are equal because all look immediately upon God: the first in love, the second in knowledge, the third in discernment.

“Than which hierarchy there is no other more Godlike or more immediately intent upon the illuminations of divinity that operate beforehand in it of themselves.” No other hierarchy, he says, is more Godlike than this one, nor comes nearer to the likeness of God, nor is more intent upon the illuminations of divinity that operate beforehand in it alone, because it is before the others; and operate of themselves, because not through others. For divine illuminations operate in this hierarchy alone before the others, because all who follow this hierarchy are illuminated by those divine illuminations; and divine illuminations operate in this hierarchy alone of themselves, because through this hierarchy all the other hierarchies [Col. 1030C] are subsequently illuminated by divine illuminations.

“He says that the second hierarchy is completed from Powers, Dominions, and Virtues”—though with the order reversed, so that Dominions are understood to be first, Virtues second, and Powers third. “And lastly the disposition of the threefold heavenly hierarchy of Angels, Archangels, and Principalities.” One must supply from the preceding words: he, our teacher, says that the last disposition of the threefold heavenly hierarchies consists of Angels, Archangels, and Principalities.

If it is asked why Paul, when distinguishing and enumerating the ordering of angels in his Epistles, did not preserve this order, although elsewhere he affirmed that this was their order, it may be said that there he wished to explain not so much the order of the heavenly dispositions as their number. This is especially so because in one place he enumerates only some of them, whereas elsewhere he explains those whom he had there omitted without repeating the others [Col. 1032A]. From this it is clear that, if he had been attending to both order and number, he would have tried to set them all out together in one sequence of discourse. And perhaps there is some other reason which may suitably answer this objection.

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 1031]

## TITLE OF CHAPTER VII. On the Seraphim and Thrones; that is, on the first hierarchy of angels.

## TEXT.

[Col. 1031B]

Receiving this order of the holy hierarchies, we say that all the names of the heavenly intellects declare the Godlike property of each. And we know that the holy designation “Seraphim,” which is Hebrew, signifies either those who kindle or those who warm; and that “Cherubim” signifies a multitude of knowledge or an outpouring of wisdom.

Therefore the first of the heavenly hierarchies is beautifully sanctified by the most excellent essences, having the order highest of all—that is, placed immediately about God; and the theophanies and perfections which first operate are principally conveyed to it as being nearest. Thus those who warm, and the Thrones, and the outpouring of wisdom are named according to the manifestation of their Godlike dispositions [Col. 1031C].

For the designation or name “Seraphim” teaches that they possess a motion always moving about divine things—unceasing, warm, keen, and intensely ardent; a motion intent, perhaps inward, and always inflexible; a power that brings those beneath them back and acts as an exemplar, as though reheating and awakening them to a like warmth; a heavenly and fiery, wholly burnt-offering-like purification; an unveiled and unquenchable property, always light-bearing and illuminating in this manner, pursuing and disclosing every dark obscuration.

The Cherubim themselves possess knowledge and naked openness, are receptive and contemplative of the highest impartations of light, are filled with the first operative power of divine beauty and the bestowal of wisdom, and communicate abundantly to those below the outpouring of wisdom bestowed upon them [Col. 1031D].

The designation of the highest and compacted seats teaches their complete elevation above every dishonor of subjection; their supramundane upward bearing toward the highest; their ineffable elevation beyond every extremity into the most sublime; their unchangeable and stable establishment with all their powers about the truly Exalted One; their receptivity, in all impassibility and immateriality, to the divine advent; their God-bearing character; and their ministerial openness to divine receptions.

This, so far as concerns us, is the explanation of the names themselves. But we must say what hierarchy we judge theirs to be. I believe we have already sufficiently said that the contemplation of every hierarchy depends ineffably upon a God-imitating Godlikeness, and that every hierarchical action is divided into sacred participation and the transmission [Col. 1032B] of pure purification, divine light, and perfecting knowledge.

Let us now proceed fittingly to speak of the most excellent intellects, and of how their hierarchy is now disclosed by the sacred utterances. In the first essences, which are placed after the divinity that gives them being and are ordered, as it were, in its vestibules—transcending every created visible and invisible power—we must recognize a hierarchy proper to them and altogether equally ordered.

We must therefore judge them to be pure, not as freed from unclean stains and defilements, nor as receptive of material imaginations, but as cleansed of every diminution; as higher and placed above all the most Godlike powers by a loftiest purity surpassing every firmly established temple; as ineffably admitted by their own self-motion, according to the unturning order of those who love God; as wholly ignorant of insult in those beneath them; and as possessing an unfallen and immutable, most pure establishment in their own Godlike particularity [Col. 1032C].

Again, we must judge them contemplative, not as being led back to the divine by a variety of sacred, symbolic theory, whether sensible or intellectual, but as filled with the higher light of every immaterial knowledge and, so far as is permitted, made full by contemplation of formative, principal, superessential, and transparently radiant beauty. Likewise they have been made worthy of communion with Jesus: not by representing divine likeness in sacredly invented images, but by drawing near to him truly in the first participation of knowledge of his deifying lights, since likeness to God has been bestowed upon them substantially.

They participate, as possible, in the operative power of his deifying and human virtues. Likewise they are perfect, not as illuminated by an analytic knowledge gathered from a variety of sacred things, but as filled with first and surpassing deification according to the most excellent knowledge, possible among angels, of divine works [Col. 1032D]. For they are sanctified not through other holy essences but by divinity itself; they are immediately stretched out toward it in all-surpassing power and order; they are established in an altogether most pure strength; they are led, so far as is permitted, to contemplation of immaterial and invisible beauty; and, as the first essences about God, they are turned toward the knowable principles of divine works and sanctified most excellently by the Prince of perfection himself [Col. 1033A].

Thus the theologians plainly declare both that the subordinate dispositions of heavenly essences are beautifully instructed in deifying knowledge by those firmly established above them, and that those higher than all are illuminated, so far as is permitted, in instruction from divinity itself. For they introduce some of them as being sacredly instructed by those before them that the Lord of the heavenly virtues and the King of glory has been received into heaven in human form (Ps. 23). But they introduce others as questioning Jesus himself, learning from him knowledge of his divine action on our behalf, and being immediately taught by Jesus himself as he bestows upon them the manifestation of his human loving-kindness: “For I speak of righteousness and judgment of salvation” (Isa. 63).

I marvel, however, that even the first of the heavenly essences, which together surpass all others so greatly in divine illuminations, reverently seek the resolution of intermediate questions. For they do not ask directly, “Why are your garments red?” Rather, they deliberate among themselves before asking, thereby showing that they learn and seek deifying knowledge, but do not leap over the illumination imparted through the divine procession [Col. 1033B].

Is the first hierarchy of the heavenly intellects, then, sanctified by the Prince of perfection himself because it immediately reaches out toward him? It is purified, illuminated, and perfected by the most holy purification, abundant light, and prior perfect completion proportionately filling it: purified from every diminution; filled with the first light; and perfected by sharing in the first-given knowledge and understanding.

It comprehends—and perhaps I shall not say this without reason—that purification, illumination, and perfection are the reception of divine knowledge: purification, because it removes ignorance through the knowledge of perfect doctrines imparted according to order; illumination, by that divine knowledge through which it purifies what it had not previously contemplated but makes manifest through a higher illumination; and perfection, again, through the very light, according to the stable possession of knowledge of most luminous doctrines [Col. 1033C].

This, therefore, so far as our knowledge reaches, is the first disposition of the heavenly essences: standing in the circle of God and immediately about God, simply and unceasingly circling his eternal knowledge, according to the most excellent, ever-moving establishment possible among angels. It sees many blessed contemplations in purity; it is illuminated by simple and immediate splendors; it is filled with divine nourishment; it receives many things by the first-given outpouring and by the one familiar and unifying unity of divine refreshment; it is rendered worthy of much communion and cooperation with God, attaining, so far as possible, likeness in good dispositions and actions; and it knows many divine things in a surpassing manner, sharing in divine knowledge and understanding as is permitted [Col. 1033D].

Therefore theology handed down its praises to those on earth, in which the eminence of its most excellent illumination is wonderfully revealed. Some proclaim it in sensible speech like the sound of waters: “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place.” Others cry out that most praiseworthy and most devout theology: “Holy, holy, holy, Lord God of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory” (Ezek. 1; Ezek. 3; Isa. 6; Rev. 4).

We have already, insofar as possible, explained these most exalted hymns of the heavenly minds in the work concerning the divine praises, and there enough has been said concerning them, as far as pertains to us. From this, it is sufficient for the present merely to recall that the first disposition has been illuminated, so far as is permitted, with theological knowledge by divine goodness. Through this, as a Godlike hierarchy, it afterwards handed itself on to the others, briefly introducing the statement that the most devout, supremely blessed, and altogether blessed divinity ought fittingly to be known and praised as blessed, so far as possible, by the intellects that receive God [Col. 1034A].

For they are, as it were, Godlike divine places of divine repose, as the utterances say (Pss. 9, 46, 79; Isa. 66). And because the Monad and Unity, substantially three, extends its goodness in providence through the superheavenly essences down to the furthest parts of earth and to all things that are, it surrounds and contains all things as the super-principal principle and cause of every essence, with a containment immeasurably beyond all essences [Col. 1034B].

## EXPOSITION

The title of the seventh chapter is: On the interpretation of Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones; and on the first hierarchy, which is theirs. For after he has enumerated the orders of the heavenly hierarchies [Col. 1034C], he now begins to treat of the interpretation and meaning of their names. First he discusses those counted in the first hierarchy—Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones—demonstrating their power according to the property of their names.

“Receiving this order of the holy hierarchies.” “Receiving and approving,” he says, “this order of holy hierarchies which we set forth above, we consequently say that all the names of heavenly intellects declare the Godlike property of each.” For all the names of the holy intellects, that is, spirits, declare the Godlike property of each order. The name declares what is proper and singular to it, bestowed in Godlikeness through the excellence of its gift. For every grace reforms the soul into the likeness of God; yet what has been bestowed upon each within that one form is proper to it. And just as it is distinct in gift, so it ought to be distinguished in name [Col. 1034D].

Then follows: “And indeed, knowing that the designation *seraphim* is Hebrew, we explain it as ‘those who kindle’ or ‘those who make warm’; while that of *cherubim* [we explain as] ‘a multitude of knowledge’ or ‘an outpouring of wisdom.’ We say,” he says, “that all the designations of the heavenly intellects declare the deiform property of each one.” [Col. 1035A] We, I say, knowing the designation *seraphim*—which is Hebrew, that is, so called in Hebrew—explain it as “those who kindle” or “those who make warm”; and likewise, supplying “designation,” we explain the designation *cherubim* as “a multitude of knowledge” or “an outpouring of wisdom,” so that in the very expression of these spiritual names the grace of their gifts may be declared—gifts which, though not individually unique, nevertheless consist in excellence.

[Col. 1035B] “Thus the first of the heavenly hierarchies is fittingly sanctified by the most excellent essences, possessing a rank higher than all others; that is, it is placed immediately about God, and the theophanies and perfections which operate first are conveyed to it more principally, as to that which is nearest.”

This, he says, is fitting and appropriate: that the first hierarchy should contain the more excellent spirits, since it is itself higher in rank than every other hierarchy and is nearer to God, being placed immediately about him—that is, with no other hierarchy standing between it and God. And because it is nearest to God, the theophanies—that is, divine appearances, manifestations, or illuminations—whose operation is first, namely from the Creator into the creature and not through a creature (for these are the first operations of divine illumination into a creature; operations through creature into creature are secondary)—and also the perfections of spiritual gifts, are conveyed more principally into that first hierarchy than into those which follow and are subject to it. For the latter receive every participation in spiritual grace [Col. 1035C] only through its mediation.

“Therefore they are called those who make warm, and thrones, and an outpouring of wisdom, by a name that manifests their deiform dispositions.”

Since divine illuminations and perfections are conveyed more principally into that hierarchy, the orders established in it receive names expressive of their deiform dispositions: some are called those who make warm, such as the seraphim, because they receive and impart the fire of love; others, mighty in the judgment of truth, are called thrones; still others, shining and enlightening by the knowledge of understanding, are called “an outpouring of wisdom,” such as the cherubim. For from the very name of their designation the power of their deiform disposition is made manifest, so that they may be known to be endowed with divine likeness by the same distinctive [Col. 1035D] and singular designation by which they are marked. For that the distinction of name in each order denotes a certain singular and proper disposition of participation in God is proved by the following statement:

“For the designation, or manifestation, of the seraphim teaches that their movement about divine things is always mobile and unceasing, warm, sharp, and exceedingly fervent; that it is ever intent, perhaps inmost, and inflexible; that it is exemplary of a movement which draws up and activates those below them, as though reheating and reviving them to a like warmth; and that it possesses a heavenly fiery and wholly purifying property, unveiled, unquenchable, ever luminous and illuminating, pursuing and revealing every dark obscuration.” [Col. 1036A]

If I may say what I feel, I first confess this: I have heard words either not spoken to a human being, or not spoken by a human being. For it seems to me so great a thing even for them to be spoken through a human being that nothing greater could be given to a human being. And perhaps, because these words arose from things that could be heard, they ought not to have been spoken. For he who suggested or taught these things had reached even to the third heaven, had entered Paradise, and there had heard from God certain words concerning the Word—wholly secret, bordering upon silence—such as no human ear could reach: words which no one could hear unless he knew them. For they were heard within, where they were spoken; nor could they go out where the human being was.

Therefore they could be heard inwardly and within by him who was within, indeed very deeply within; [Col. 1036B] but they ought not to have been spoken to those who were outside. Yet lest those outside should be left wholly abandoned if they were not called by him who was within, words were born from words, as words were born from the Word: from words that had to be kept within, words that could be uttered outside; great things from immeasurable things, obscure things from hidden things, profound things from impenetrable things—whether, when heard by us, they are understood, I do not know.

These are the very words which the disciple of the Master, and master of disciples, has set before us to investigate—or rather, to marvel at. For the first disciple of the Word heard words from the Word; and that man, made a teacher by other words, had a disciple and made him a teacher. When at last this descended to our hearing, a voice as it were from heaven resounded upon earth, [Col. 1036C] and has already filled our ears with astonishment; yet it has not illumined our hearts with manifest truth. Therefore those who were human beings and could not yet receive divine things said that thunder had occurred, because they were only struck with awe and were not instructed. Others, somewhat illuminated but not yet perfected, supposed it was an angel; they did not understand God.

Thus we too have heard the thunder of the heavenly voice and have begun to marvel, but not yet to be illumined. Yet if our wonder should become an awakening, by that wonder we shall be converted, so that by conversion we may be illumined. Then those words will become sweet—not merely to be wondered at, but to be loved—when they begin to be heard and known, if only we are made receptive to them by grace. [Col. 1036D] For unless they are loved, they are not understood; nor are they loved unless they are tasted. What then? Why have we heard them if we do not understand? Or how do we understand if we do not love? For my own part I answer: if I do not presume upon love, I do not depart from wonder. Perhaps by wonder itself I shall awaken to knowledge; and if I am not sufficiently stirred to knowledge, I shall be prompted to love. Meanwhile love itself will be refreshment, until contemplation arises from it, through which illumination comes.

What is that of the angels: “always mobile and unceasing about divine things; warm, sharp, and exceedingly fervent, in a movement ever intent, perhaps inmost, and inflexible”? If we say that this is love, perhaps we shall seem to have said too little—[Col. 1037A] to those who do not know what love is. For whoever says “love” never says too little, unless perhaps he means a small love. But this author did not mean to speak of a small love, since he said so many things concerning love.

“Mobile,” he says, “and unceasing, warm, sharp, and exceedingly fervent.” Mobile, because it is life; unceasing, because it is everlasting; warm, because it is love; sharp, because it is wisdom. Is this enough? He has spoken of life, named it everlasting, set forth love, and added wisdom. All this is in one love, and is one love.

Do you wish to know that love is life? Hear that beloved one and lover, commending love: “He who does not love,” he says, “remains in death” (1 John). Therefore love is life. And what kind of life? “Love never fails” (1 Cor. 13). [Col. 1037B] If love never fails, then love is everlasting life.

And what of love? Where shall we be able to show that warmth and fervour in love? Where has love had fervour and heat—or rather, where has love ever been without heat and fervour? What did those who were walking and loving, kindling and fervent, say concerning Jesus, whom they had heard but did not recognize on the road? They were walking and moving, driven by the impatience of love; for if they had stood still, they would not have loved. For love is mobile, as it is warm, lest true love grow numb. Thus they walked in love’s mobility and burned in its warmth, saying: “Was not our heart burning within us concerning Jesus while he spoke to us on the way?” (Luke 24).

Because they were walking, they possessed mobility; and warmth, because they were burning. [Col. 1037C] But they did not possess sharpness, because they did not recognize him. Therefore, because they had not sharpness, they heard: “Foolish ones, and slow to believe all that the prophets have spoken” (ibid.). Thus they were dull and slow to know, but not lukewarm or sluggish in loving. Yet because they first loved and afterwards knew, sharpness came to be in their love as warmth was. First warmth, then sharpness. Therefore he did not say “sharp and warm,” but “warm and sharp”; just as first “mobile,” then “unceasing”: mobility awakens one to inquiry, unceasingness confirms one in perseverance; warmth gives life to perception, while sharpness penetrates unto comprehension.

For sharpness signifies a certain impetus of love and the force of burning desire, [Col. 1037D] carrying itself into the beloved, entering and penetrating, so as to be where that which is loved is—together with it and in it—so that it may not merely be warmed by it, but that its sharpness may pass into it. For one could be warm and, as it were, be warmed from a distance; that would suffice for someone content to love the beloved while absent and neither see it present nor possess it in its fullest presence. But that was not the love of a perfect hierarchy, nor was it greatly lovable, unless it made itself sharp, passed through all things, and penetrated until it reached the beloved—or rather, went into the beloved.

For if you do not go into the beloved, you still love from outside and do not possess love’s sharpness. But you have [it], and remain numb, divided, and outside the beloved, so that you do not become one. But love wishes to make you one with it; and therefore it penetrates all things and draws as near as it can to that one reality.

[Col. 1038A] Consider now how those of whom it is said, “Wherever the impulse of the spirit was, there they went” (Ezek. 1), possessed love’s sharpness. That impulse itself was sharpness; just as fluidity, in another passage, is called the sharpness of love. And I think that it was the bride herself who spoke, and that something hard or harsh ought not to have been introduced to one who was fearful and timid. Therefore “fluid” was used instead of “sharp,” as an endearment of love. For fluidity itself penetrates as sharpness does, and does not cease until it reaches the inner parts. Thus she says: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke; I sought him” (Song 3). For she sought him because she had melted toward him. [Col. 1038B] Had she not melted toward him, she would not have run after him; she would have stood hard and would not have entered.

But now she has melted and begun to run; yet she did not immediately find him, until she arrived. Therefore here too unceasingness was necessary, so that she might enter and penetrate and say: “I have held him and will not let him go, until I bring him,” she says, “into my mother’s house and into the chamber of her who bore me” (Song 5). “I shall bring him into my mother’s house, into the chamber of her who bore me.”

Thus he will enter into you, so that you may enter into him. For then you enter into him when he enters into you. When his love enters and penetrates your heart, and his love reaches the inmost part of your heart, then he enters into you; [Col. 1038C] and you also enter into yourself, so that you may enter into him. Therefore bring him into yourself; and do not bring him in merely in any manner, so that he remains or lingers outside within you—at your gates, in your courts, before the door of your house, or even only in your house. For this is neither much nor great for great love, unless he comes as far as the bridal chamber, enters the inner chamber, penetrates to the depths, and rests in your inmost places.

I shall say something further: perhaps he does not even love the chamber of the father unless he is brought into the chamber of the mother, where love is more tender and endearments sweeter, so that he may find in you nothing hard or rigid from masculine harshness. Rather, let everything melt and soften in the fire of love. Then no hardness will resist, so that love may reach the depths and possess the sharpness by which it penetrates all things. [Col. 1038D] This had to be said concerning love’s sharpness and fluidity, that you may understand how great is the power of love and affection—if indeed this can be understood, since love surpasses knowledge and is greater than understanding.

For more is loved than understood; love enters and draws near where knowledge remains outside. Nor is this surprising: love always ventures further and is always confident; love presses itself forward without hesitation. Therefore it has a sharp and fluid power that penetrates all things and follows the impulse of its burning desire, unable to dissemble until it reaches the beloved; and even then it thirsts still more to enter into the beloved, to be with it, and to be so near that, if possible, it may be the very same as he is.

[Col. 1039A] Is it not very sharp to penetrate all these things and enter into the depths, so that no power can repel it until it reaches where it loves? “Who,” says the Apostle, “shall separate us from the love of Christ? Tribulation, or famine, or the sword?” (Rom. 8)—and the many other things that could have impeded it had love not resisted them. But love, because it possessed sharpness, could not be held; it passed through and penetrated, escaping freely and running toward its desire.

If, then, such is love’s warmth and sharpness, what do you suppose the following term, “exceedingly fervent,” is? It must have something further, since it is added as an increase upon the preceding powers. The thing itself also warns us to conceive something greater in what is “exceedingly fervent” than in what is warm and sharp.

[Col. 1039B] For you know how a thing that boils is thrown outside itself by a certain violence of its heat and burning, lifted above itself, and made to move greatly by the hidden agitation of the heat it has conceived. The inner heat of hidden burning, which moves it, is not seen; but what is moved by it is seen. And from what we see, we conceive and understand the great force, robust power, and mighty violence of that which is hidden and unseen.

Who could worthily bring the analogy of visible things to the majesty of invisible things? Examples are set before us: boiling is shown to us from heat and moisture—or rather, in moisture through heat. [Col. 1039C] We see how heat gradually enters moisture without commotion, so that, having entered it, it casts it out forcefully and violently. It insinuates itself invisibly in order to raise it visibly, as though it did not wish it to remain there, since it hastens to expel it with the vehement force, as it were, of indignation.

Thus warmth is moved toward sharpness, and then sharpness advances toward exceeding fervour. For what was first sharp and fluid in love, able to penetrate other resistances, now becomes exceedingly fervent, boiling and unable to remain in itself. Love is sharp when it despises everything by passing through it; it is exceedingly fervent when, in despising itself, it even leaves itself behind. For one who seeks only what he loves despises even himself in comparison with it. He would not truly seek that alone if he loved himself together with it. But only great and singular love can bring this about: that through love of that alone which is loved, even the lover is despised, as though detached from himself.

[Col. 1039D] Thus, in a wonderful manner, while through the fire of love the lover is raised into him who is above him, he begins to be driven out from himself by the force of love and even to depart from himself. How, then, does one’s heart boil and seethe when, through the conceived fire of heavenly love, one is carried in thought and desire toward desiring that one alone who is above, is cast outside oneself, and lifted above oneself, and does not think of oneself while loving that one alone? Thus we understand love’s mobility, unceasingness, warmth, sharpness, and exceeding fervour.

[Col. 1040A] But how can we ascribe these things to those supercelestial natures, for whom life and essence are the same, because they have no essence other than life? What is their unceasing motion about divine things, and their warmth, sharpness, and exceeding fervour? What are those divine things about which they move unceasingly, grow warm, become sharp, and are exceedingly fervent? For one who is in a circle has not yet entered, because he either grows lukewarm from what is warm or grows numb from what is sharp. If, then, they possess sharpness, how are they in a circle?

Perhaps because those divine things of which Scripture speaks are within every creature, and are altogether so secret and hidden that, even if they can be touched, they cannot be penetrated. But there are other divine things which come into manifestation and in some fashion present themselves to knowledge, either by coming forth inwardly to the mind or by proceeding outwardly as far as sense. The Apostle indicates that some divine things are altogether within, concealed and hidden, while others have gone outward and been manifested, saying: “What is knowable of God is manifest in them” (Rom. 1).

For when he says, “what is knowable of God,” that is, what can be known concerning God, he plainly shows that among the things which are God’s and are in God, something is manifest and something hidden. That which is manifest can be touched by knowledge; but that which is wholly hidden can be penetrated by no reasoning. There are, therefore, certain divine things and things of God set forth for manifestation, which can in some respect be penetrated and comprehended; while others are so deep, hidden, inward, and wholly impenetrable that no intellect can search them out and no wisdom investigate them. With regard to these, it is already a great thing when one is granted to touch them, even if one is not granted to penetrate them; and when one arrives at them by penetrating, they themselves are not penetrated, but remain impenetrable and incomprehensible. Of them, only what is outside is displayed to the arriving intellect for knowledge; what is always within is not opened for comprehension.

Consider now and see whether the things visibly made by God do not teach you concerning God’s invisible things. For what is less readily investigated by reason alone is sometimes made knowable by the light of examples. See, therefore, what bodily sense can do in the world, so that from this you may understand, as far as possible, what mental sense can do in God. When we touch the visible world with the eye of the flesh, we perceive those things which are outward in it; but by that same sense we cannot penetrate to those things hidden within it. And if some things once hidden are at times opened, many others still remain hidden which cannot be comprehended: either because their immensity exceeds sense, their subtlety escapes it, or their obscurity does not admit sense to them.

So understand that the sense of the rational mind, by which we perceive divine things, if it is ever admitted to touch God, perceives only what is, as it were, outward in him; it does not comprehend those inward things that remain secret and hidden. He said, however, that this is outside him, not outside us, because everything in God is inward in relation to every creature. Yet, in comparison with those things which cannot be comprehended at all, that which is disclosed to even the most secret and subtle intellect concerning him is in some manner called outside him, or in him outward.

Therefore by love’s sharpness they penetrate to him; yet because of his incomprehensible majesty they remain about him, so that they do not enter into the whole, even though they penetrate as far as something. It should also be noted that they are said to be about him, not in some single part. For they encompass by desire what they do not penetrate by understanding, leaving nothing unexamined of all that can be known, always seeing and always thirsting to see. They are stable, lest they depart; mobile, that they may desire without ceasing. They are in a circle because they do not enter into all that he is. They are in a circle because they draw immediately near. They are in a circle because through contemplation and love they survey all that in him is knowable.

Thus their mobility about divine things, their unceasingness, and the warmth, sharpness, and exceeding fervour of their unceasing, intent, perhaps inmost, and inflexible motion may fittingly be understood. Yet we must not pass over the fact that he called the motion of invisible natures unceasing, intent, perhaps inmost, and inflexible, using the language of doubt in one point only, when he said “perhaps”; as though he asserted the rest without hesitation but did not dare establish this one point except with the qualification of doubt.

The motion of those spirits drawing near to supreme divinity is therefore called unceasing, inmost, and inflexible, because, tending from themselves toward God by love’s desire, it is mobile always, so that it never rests in itself; intent, so that it may proceed toward him; inmost, so that it may not flow away toward outward things; and inflexible, so that it may not turn aside toward other things outside itself and apart from him. Why, then, does he not simply say “inmost,” but, as though doubting whether it was so or should be said so, adds “perhaps”?

Perhaps because he thought that only that should be understood and called truly inmost beyond which there is nothing more inward. An inmost motion, therefore, is only one that either proceeds from what is inmost or goes all the way to what is inmost. Since the divine nature alone is inward to every nature, it alone is inmost in relation to every nature; its motion without motion toward the creature alone is called inward in the thing itself, because it proceeds from that than which nothing more inward can be found.

But a creature’s motion toward the Creator, however secret and penetrating, cannot properly be called inmost, because it proceeds from that which is outward in relation to him toward whom it proceeds. And although it is led to touch him who is inmost, a way is not opened to it all the way to his inmost depths. Therefore, because in some respect it comes outwardly from the creature going forth, and remains outwardly without attaining to penetrate the Creator’s inmost depths, it should not simply be called inmost. Nevertheless, because it proceeds from a more inward nature toward the inmost one, it may fittingly be called inmost in a certain respect. For this reason he aptly says “perhaps inmost,” indicating that it could be called inmost in one respect, though it was not inmost in every respect. It may be called inmost by property, not by comparison: inmost in relation to that from which it proceeds, but not in relation to that toward which it proceeds.

Then follows: “And exemplary of drawing up and activating those below them.”

In the preceding enumeration he expressed the power of true love toward God, as far as it is—I do not know—but I think, as far as it can be said. Now he subsequently shows the power and effect of that same love toward one’s neighbour. There he displayed its movement and turning toward higher things, by which they thirst for their Creator; here he expounds its movement and turning toward lower and neighbouring things, by which they do not withdraw from one another.

Thus the motion of love which there is called intent, inmost, and inflexible toward higher things is here called exemplary of drawing up and activating those who are beneath. For that motion which in relation to what is higher is contemplation is, in relation to what is lower, action. It tends toward what is higher in order to rest in it; it tends toward what is lower in order to draw it up to itself. Love moves upward in order to remain there; downward in order to return.

Therefore, in those above, the motion of love is said to draw those below upward and to activate them. It draws them upward insofar as, setting them ablaze with the same fire of love, it turns them toward their Creator. It activates them insofar as, enlightening them with the brightness received, it conforms them to his will. It is drawing upward in relation to those subject to it because it draws them toward what is higher. It is activating because it orders them among lower beings. It draws them upward so that they may tend toward God; it activates them so that they may proceed according to God.

Thus the form of love is exemplary of the upward-drawing and activating motion of those who are subject—that is, of the motion which draws those subject to it toward what is above them and trains them for action within themselves. By the example of those above, it shows those below with what affection of love they ought both to proceed according to God and to long for him. Or it may be read, “exemplary for those subject to them,” that is, what is set before those subject to them as an example, with “upward-drawing” and “activating” taken adverbially; the sense remains the same.

See, then, how love expands itself in those blessed spirits near to God, who burn as though from close by and are more intensely fervent, desiring to embrace all things. The fire of love is drawn back toward higher things while, thirsting through love of God for its own good, it moves also toward lower and subject beings, desiring to gather them as participants in its good and companions with itself. Thus those who love give to those subject to them a form for loving; those burning in themselves kindle others also with the flame of love.

For this reason their love became an example for those beneath them in tending toward higher things and proceeding according to those above, “as though reheating and reviving them,” namely those subject to them, “to a like warmth,” so that they may burn similarly, though not equally. When he says “reheating and reviving,” this is not to be understood as though they had first been extinguished and dead and were again kindled and made alive. Rather, through love descending from above, they are stirred anew to love and seek the same things which are above. Thus through the fire of love they are, as it were, reheated and revived: in them the kindled flame of love is drawn back to love again those things from which it had arisen first and principally in those who loved them before, and then in subsequent and subject lovers.

All these things, therefore, are taught by the designation or manifestation of the seraphim. For in being called *seraphim*, that is, “those who kindle” or “those who make warm,” the term is a designation for them and a manifestation for us: for in its sound their designation is expressed, while in the interpretation of the word the property of their designation is manifested to us. They would not be manifested unless they were designated. Those who are known to themselves by contemplation become known to us by designation. Thus with regard to the word itself it is called a designation for them; with regard to our interpretation of the word, it is called a manifestation for us.

The designation or manifestation of the seraphim, therefore, teaches all these things: namely, their mobile and unceasing movement about divine things; also the warmth, sharpness, and exceeding fervour of their intent, inmost, and inflexible motion; and also the exemplary quality in them, drawing up and activating those beneath them, which they provide from themselves to those subject to them for their upward drawing and action, so that they may be reheated and revived into a warmth and fervour like that of the higher beings.

The designation of the seraphim also teaches their “heavenly fiery and wholly purifying, unveiled and unquenchable” property: first, what descends upon them from heaven or divinely; then what proceeds from them, so that they may burn and kindle others, be purified and purify, be unveiled and unveil.

The same designation of the seraphim teaches also their ever-luminous and illuminating property, ever remaining so—that is, remaining in one and the same manner, without variation or change—and pursuing every dark obscuration so that it may not approach them, and revealing it so that it may not remain hidden outside them. All these things, therefore, are taught by the designation or manifestation of the seraphim.

And all these things, as we have said, are in one love and are one love: a love given to them from above and derived through them to those beneath them. By this enumeration the author distinguishes a threefold power of this love in those highest spirits: above them, in them, and below them. Above them it is mobile; in them, life-giving; below them, operative. Above them, it acts through desire; in them, through perception; below them, through affection. Above them, it seeks; in them, it perceives; below them, it gathers. Above them, in what they desire; in them, in what they perceive; below them, for the sake of those whom they draw with themselves toward what they perceive in themselves and toward what they desire above themselves.

Because of such wonderful operations of love he said so much about it, in which perhaps he would have said everything if everything could have been said. But we fear both alternatives, if we should be either negligent or fastidious. It is hard for us, in a matter so sweet, to deny anything we have received; and again it seems rash to add anything which we ought not. What, do you think, is love? When will it all be said? See: we have spoken of their “mobility,” “unceasingness,” “warmth,” “sharpness,” “exceeding fervour,” “intentness,” “inmostness,” “inflexibility,” “exemplary quality,” “upward-drawing,” “activating,” “reheating,” and “reviving.” This seemed much, and perhaps enough—unless other wonders, I know not whether still more wonderful, were to follow.

“Heavenly fiery,” he says, “and wholly purifying.” Two things must be noted: that he called it fiery, and that very quality heavenly. For there is also a fire from earth, but it is not like that which is heavenly fiery. Earthly fire burns, consumes, lays waste, and destroys; nor can it have fellowship with another thing. Those who approach it are harmed; and if they touch it altogether, they begin at once to be consumed. But what is heavenly fiery burns sweetly. It indeed kindles, but does not consume; and if it consumes anything, it does so not to harm but to purify. For it consumes that which would harm, if it were not consumed.

Therefore after “heavenly fiery” follows “wholly purifying,” because that fire purifies wholly and entirely: not only from the corruption of evil, but also from the deficiency of good. Some things had contracted the corruption of evil; others had not yet received the perfection of good. Both had to be purified: the former from corruption, the latter from imperfection. Those on earth needed purification from corruption; those in heaven, from imperfection. The latter were not perfect in their first condition; the former became corrupted after their first condition. The latter were purified from imperfection when they were perfected in glorification; the former were purified from corruption when they were freed from sin.

Thus the purification of the latter was not the correction of an evil they did not possess, but the completion of a good which they possessed in a lesser measure. The purification of the former was first correction, then completion. Such purification, therefore, we understand in that spiritual and heavenly nature. Yet if anyone understands purification in those beings, not as a purification from corruption, since they were always pure, but as perfect purity in which no corruption could exist, that too will be understood fittingly.

Therefore that “heavenly fiery” quality by which they are inflamed, so that they burn and are purified either from imperfection into completion or into full purity against every corruption, is “wholly purifying”: that is, universally purifying or purifying in its entirety, because it purifies the whole and purifies wholly, so that no corruption may be present and no perfection lacking. For a holocaust is that which is wholly set on fire and wholly burned.

## Book Seven

Exposition of the remaining part of the seventh chapter of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite’s *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, the text of which has been set before us.

[Col. 1045]

[Col. 1045A] Long inactivity calls for a new beginning. A little above, we entered upon a discussion of the names of the angels, where the author shows why such names or appellations are assigned to the individual orders of angels. Concerning the first and highest order, called Seraphim, we have, according to our capacity, pursued the reason for this appellation, which theology has supplied. It remains now to consider also the explanation which he gives of the name of the following order. He had previously said that the name, or manifestation, of the Seraphim teaches “their mobility, unceasingness, heat, keenness, and exceeding ardour,” together with what follows these terms. Now, however, he adds and says that the name, [Col. 1045B] or manifestation, of the Cherubim teaches “their knowing power and their vision of God,” and so forth. For he says: “The Cherubim themselves truly.” Two things must be supplied from the preceding passage: “name” and “teaches.” It is as though he said: The very name of the Cherubim teaches—that is, in their being called Cherubim, which is interpreted “fulness of knowledge,” their “knowing power” is taught and signified: namely, the knowledge, acquaintance, and understanding which they possess. By this name also their “vision of God” is signified: that is, the vision of God which is in them, because through the light of wisdom bestowed upon them they clearly contemplate the majesty of their Creator.

Also signified is their “receptivity of the highest gift of lights”: that is, that they have received most highly [Col. 1045C] and most perfectly the lights divinely given. For in being signified by their very name to possess fullness of knowledge, they are surely shown to have received the light of that wisdom from elsewhere; since, according to the Apostle’s saying: “If they had not received it, they could not have possessed it at all” (1 Cor. 4). In possessing it, reception is indicated; in possessing fullness, their advancement is indicated. The order is that they first receive the divinely given light of wisdom and then, enlightened by that same light, see and know God, the author of light. They are therefore well illuminated who are illuminated so as to see and know him by whom they are illuminated. Many are illuminated in order to see other things, yet do not see him through whom they see. But it is no great thing to see a work, if you do not know the maker. A created form cannot make one blessed if one does not attain to the beauty that produces it.

Therefore the name Cherubim teaches “their knowing power, their vision of God, and their reception of the highest gift of lights.” Note the unusual compounds in the terms *deividum* (“God-seeing”) and *luminundationis* (“light-inundation”).

The name [Col. 1046A] Cherubim also teaches their contemplation, namely, of divine beauty in the first operative power; that they are filled with wisdom-imparting tradition; and that they communicate the wisdom bestowed in abundant outpouring to the second orders. Distinguish it thus: the name Cherubim teaches contemplation of divine beauty in the first operative power. For in their being called Cherubim, that is, “full of knowledge,” it is shown that through the light of wisdom given to them they contemplate divine beauty. Surely, whatever else they might know, they would not be full of wisdom if they did not know divine beauty, from which and in which all things are beautifully and rationally ordered. Since, therefore, they are full of wisdom, they undoubtedly contemplate divine beauty.

Nor do they contemplate it in just any way, [Col. 1046B] but in the first operative power: that is, being first and principally illuminated by God, they may thereafter illuminate those below them. For divine power operates first, principally, and of itself in those who are nearest; then through them in the others who follow. This, therefore, is what the name Cherubim teaches: that contemplation of divine beauty exists in them through the first operative power, because God first works in them so that afterwards he may work through them.

It also teaches that they are filled with wisdom-imparting tradition; that is, it teaches that they are filled with divine grace, which is distributed through the wisdom-imparting bestowal of the Creator, more to some and less to others, according to participation. Thus their remarkable excellence is shown, because they are declared to possess not a portion but the fullness of that good which the wisdom [Col. 1046C] of the Creator has bestowed differently for the beauty of the universe.

The phrase may also be divided otherwise, so that the name Cherubim is said to teach that their contemplation is filled—that is, that their contemplation is filled with divine beauty and with wisdom-imparting bestowal in the first operative power. Moreover, divine beauty and wisdom-imparting bestowal may fittingly be understood to mean that divine wisdom produces greater beauty in its works precisely because it has arranged for its gifts to be shared by all not in one and the same manner. These highest spirits are filled with this beauty and bestowal because they have merited to possess in fullness the gifts which are given in part to those below and subject to them.

It follows: “And communicative of the wisdom bestowed in abundant outpouring upon the second orders.” Again, something must be supplied from above. The name Cherubim teaches their communicativeness—that is, their communication or participation [Col. 1047A] in the wisdom bestowed in abundant outpouring: namely, that in communicating they partake not sparingly but abundantly in the outpouring of wisdom given to them. This outpouring was first abundantly made in them, so that afterwards it might be made through them to the second orders; in order that the light of wisdom first abundantly infused from above into them might subsequently be poured through them into the second—that is, the following—orders, to enlighten them. Thus the name Cherubim teaches this fullness, dignity, and excellence in the gift of wisdom and the light of truth.

It follows: “But the name of the highest and compacted thrones teaches their complete elevation above every shame of subjection; their supermundane upward bearing to the highest; their ineffable establishment beyond every extremity in the most exalted and around the truly lofty, immovably [Col. 1047B] and firmly with all their powers; their reception of the divine advent in all impassibility and immateriality; and their God-bearing character and ministerial openness to divine receptions.”

After explaining the names of the Seraphim and Cherubim, he turns to explain the name of the Thrones. It is as though he said: Just as the name Seraphim signifies the ardour of love, and the name Cherubim the brightness of knowledge, so likewise the name Thrones signifies loftiness of dignity, because the invisible Creator, seated in them, orders all things subject to him by judging through them. On account of this dignity and excellence of divine judgment exercised through them, he called the Thrones “highest and compacted seats”: highest [Col. 1047C] because of dignity; compacted because of truth. For it is evident that thrones are the seats of those who reign and judge. Loftiness belongs to the ruler, but truth to the judge. He therefore rightly called them highest seats, because the one who reigns in them has no superior; and compacted seats, because the one who judges in them does not depart from truth.

What is “compacted”? Properly and suitably joined together. Observe the joining of God’s seats. The joining of God’s seats is the fitting coherence of judgments. Every judgment draws one conclusion from another: punishment from guilt, glory from righteousness, reward from merit, and the quality of recompense from the quality of the work. It finds guilt and adjudges punishment. It finds righteousness and adjudges glory. This seat is well joined; it is compacted. It agrees well and coheres fittingly: punishment with guilt, glory with righteousness. If glory were joined to guilt and punishment to righteousness, they would not agree with one another, nor would judgment have a compacted seat. The compactness of the seats, therefore, is the truth of judgments.

It should be known, however, that every lower judgment, when it comes into question or contradiction, customarily receives from a higher judgment either testimony or confirmation. But the highest judgment, since it has nothing above itself from which it might be confirmed, is rightly called God’s seat—not only compacted through truth but highest through dignity. If, however, we read not “compacted” but “lifted up,” which can likewise be understood from the ambiguity of the Greek term, this signifies that those heavenly spirits over whom God presides in judging have merited to be uniquely lofty [Col. 1048A] in glory, not through elevation of nature but through the uplifting of grace.

Let him say, therefore: “But the name of the highest and compacted seats,” that is, of the Thrones—again “name teaches” must be supplied from above—teaches this: namely, that the Thrones themselves are raised, or have been raised, completely above every shame of subjection; that is, above every shameful subjection. For the more perfectly they are subject to God who presides, the more truly they have merited through him and in him to be exalted above all other things. Therefore, since Thrones signify not subjection but dominion, when God’s discourse calls those heavenly spirits Thrones, it thereby shows that they rule perfectly and are free from every subjection.

Thus the name Thrones teaches that they have been raised above every [Col. 1048B] shame of subjection. It also teaches their upward bearing—that is, their elevation to the highest—and this supermundanely: that is, spiritually or invisibly, through an elevation spiritual and invisible and transcending every worldly and visible height. The name Thrones therefore teaches not only that through dominion they are set over those below them, but also that through exaltation they are raised to the highest, so that nothing lies between them and him who is highest.

It follows: “And, beyond every extremity, ineffably established in the most exalted and around the truly lofty, immovably and firmly with all their powers.” The name of the Thrones teaches their establishment—that is, their placing or stabilization—made immovably and firmly, with all their powers: that is, with every kind of power and unshaken strength. It has been made, I say, ineffably far beyond every extremity—that is, beyond every limit—in the most exalted and around the truly lofty. For where would God’s seat be if not where God sits? God dwells, reigns, sits, and rests where his Thrones and his seats are. See how far they are from us: how far supreme majesty is from every subjection, and eternal immutability from every corruption. Where majesty is, there is a throne; where immutability is, there is a seat. The throne signifies immutability. Therefore God’s seats are [Col. 1048D] placed in eternity itself, in immutability itself. And who can say how far this is from every extremity?

What is extremity? An end: where there is an end, there is an extremity. There is an end above and an end below. In both respects a creature has an end. The end below is where defect ceases, lest that which is something should go into nothing. The end above is where advancement comes to a stop, lest that which is great should extend itself beyond measure. How greatly, then, do those surpass the lowest things who ineffably transcend the highest?

We may still interpret these extremities otherwise, not inappropriately. All visible things are external things; for just as, for one ascending upward from the lowest things, that is highest beyond which there is nothing higher, so, for one proceeding outward from the innermost things, that is outermost beyond which there is nothing more external. Thus the divine seats, insofar as they are called Thrones, are shown to be raised in supreme excellence above the subjection of the lowest things through dignity; and insofar as they are called seats, they are shown to be immovably placed in the innermost region, through stability, beyond every fluctuation of external things. Yet they cannot be equal to the ineffable height above them, beneath which they are raised; nor, gathered inwardly, can they be compared with the simple unity around which they are placed. Therefore they are called seats because they are beneath the one who presides above them through ineffable majesty, and around the one who rests inwardly through immutable unity.

This, therefore, is what the name Thrones teaches. Nor does it teach only this, but also “reception of the divine advent”: namely, that they receive the divinity coming upon them from above in all impassibility and [Col. 1049B] immateriality—that is, incorruptibly and purely. Since they receive it in purity, they receive it immaterially; and again, because they receive it as sweetly flowing in without toil and weariness, they receive it impassibly. Those who advance to knowledge of hidden divinity through effort and labour receive the divine advent passibly. Again, to those for whom hidden divinity offers itself to be known through outward signs and bodily figures, it comes in a certain manner materially. Therefore, because those highest spirits neither advance by effort to receive knowledge of divinity nor are instructed by material figures, they are rightly said to receive the divine advent both impassibly and immaterially.

[Col. 1049C] It follows: “And God-bearing, and ministerially open to divine receptions.” Again, “the name Thrones teaches” must be supplied from above: namely, their God-bearing character—that they bear God presiding within them—and their ministerial openness to divine receptions: that they open themselves ministerially, that is, obediently, and willingly make themselves fit to receive within themselves God as he comes. Thus their will responds in subjection to divine operation, and their sacred ministry is shown to be not a matter of compulsion but of love.
