This is the proper order. First, God’s seats are raised through dignity; then they are established through stability; afterwards they receive and bear within themselves God as he comes. Finally, because they are rational vehicles, they join desire and will to their ministry, so that the work may be one of blessedness.

It follows: “This, indeed, is the explanation of their names as far as concerns us.” He connects himself to what follows. Having discussed the names of the three orders, he now proceeds to define and explain their hierarchy, that is, their sacred power. “This indeed”—namely, what we have said above—“is the explanation of their names,” namely, of the three orders. It is, I say, “as far as concerns us”: that is, as it seems to us; or, the explanation of their names is “as far as concerns us,” for our sake, so that they may be made known to us through names, not for their own sake, since they can be known to themselves even without names.

It follows: “But we must say what hierarchy we suppose them to have.” It is as though he said: Thus far we have spoken of their names; now we must speak of their sacred power, what we suppose it to be. “For I think we have already sufficiently said that the contemplation of every hierarchy depends ineffably upon God-imitating, Godlike form; and that every hierarchical action is divided into sacred participation and the impartation of pure purification, divine light, and perfecting knowledge.”

The sense is this: I think that we have already sufficiently said that the contemplation of every hierarchy—that is, the general definition of hierarchy—depends ineffably upon Godlike form, that is, upon likeness to God; a likeness, I say, that imitates God, that is, a likeness consisting in imitation of God. I think, he says, that enough has already been said concerning what hierarchy is in its general definition: namely, Godlike form, that is, conformity or likeness to God, which exists in those who imitate God. For above, in the third chapter, he gives this universal definition of hierarchy: “Hierarchy is, so far as possible, likeness and union with God.” Therefore I think that enough has already been said about what hierarchy is, insofar as this pertains to its general definition.

Likewise, I think that enough has already been said about the division of every hierarchical action: that every hierarchical action is divided into sacred participation and the impartation of pure purification, divine light, and perfecting knowledge. For every action of sacred power [Col. 1050C] consists either in receiving from a superior or in imparting to inferiors purification, illumination, and perfection. The grace is threefold, and is exercised in two ways: by receiving and by imparting. First comes purification unto purity; then illumination unto truth; then perfection unto goodness. For this is perfecting knowledge, which perfects and makes perfect when truth is perceived from the habit of virtue.

“But now let us proceed worthily to speak of the most excellent intelligences, how the hierarchy in their case is already manifested by the Scriptures.” It is as though he said: Since we have above sufficiently supplied both a universal definition and a division of hierarchy, let us now proceed worthily to speak of the most excellent intelligences—that is, the highest spirits, the Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones, in whom the first angelic hierarchy is ordered. Let us proceed, I say, to state how the hierarchy according to them—that is, their hierarchy—is manifested by the sacred writings. For the order of reasoning requires that, after the general definition and division of hierarchy, discourse should descend to its particular treatment.

First, therefore, concerning the first hierarchy, which consists in those three highest orders, we must inquire what kind of hierarchy the sacred writings show it to be. And lest anyone perhaps suppose that their sacred power is different because their orders are found to be different, he says that in all three there is one altogether similar hierarchy, insofar as all are united in the first place to the supreme and principal hierarchy and immediately receive from it the dignity of their sacred power.

This is what he adds, saying: “In the first essences, placed after their divinity which gives them subsistence and ordered as though in its very vestibules, surpassing every created invisible and visible power, one must suppose there to be a hierarchy proper to them and altogether uniform.”

The first essences are those highest and principal three orders of angels, which are first among all creatures and are established immediately after the divinity that gives them subsistence—that is, makes them subsist—and ordered as though in its vestibules: that is, so near that whatever lies beyond them is only divinity itself, and divinity itself is all that is there. In those first essences, then, thus placed and ordered, nearest to divinity and surpassing and transcending every created invisible and visible power—that is, every power belonging to visible or invisible creation—we must suppose there to be hierarchy, that is, sacred power: one proper to them, that is, distinct and different in itself from that of others, yet altogether uniform, that is, similar and equal among themselves.

For in the sacred power which they possess, just as they surpass all others, so they are wholly equal to one another: each has no superior in what he immediately receives from the supreme divinity, and all alike are first dispensers in what they bestow upon inferiors from divine participation. In this respect, then, the hierarchy is one and similar in the three.

It follows: “We must therefore suppose them to be pure, not as freed from unclean stains and defilements, nor as receptive of material imaginations, but as cleansed from every diminution and higher than all; established above every divinely strengthened temple according to the loftiest purity, in all their powers most conformed to God; received ineffably through their own movement and by themselves, and through the same movement according to the unturning order of those who love God; wholly ignorant of insulting those subject to them, but possessing the purest establishment of their own Godlike distinctiveness, beyond falling and therefore unchangeable.”

Above he said that in those three most excellent orders of angels there is one altogether similar hierarchy, that is, sacred power. He now consequently adds that those things which belong to hierarchical action, that is, the operation of sacred power, exist perfectly in them: purification, illumination, and perfection. Every sacred power ordered beneath the supreme power exercises these in two ways: by receiving from a superior and by imparting to inferiors.

He says, therefore, that these first essences, in which the first hierarchy is ordered, have purification: they receive it from the superior divinity in order to be purified, and confer it upon inferiors in order to purify them. But they receive purification not as though needing to be freed from some uncleanness or corruption, but as needing to be perfected from every imperfection and diminution. This is what he says: We must suppose them to be pure—namely, those first essences—pure, I say, yet not as though freed from any unclean stains and defilements, because they never possessed any uncleanness or defilement; nor pure as though receptive of material imaginations, since they receive no material imaginations whatever and therefore do not need to be purified from them, since they do not have them at all. Rather, they are pure as cleansed and free from every diminution and imperfection.

By unclean stains and material imaginations, he has plainly expressed two kinds of spiritual defilement: one in evil desires; the other in vain thoughts. Evil desires defile the purity of the heart like mud, while vain thoughts, like dust sprinkled over it, cloud its brightness. Therefore, since those most pure essences of the highest spirits receive no corruption either in evil desires or vain thoughts, they do not require cleansing either from unclean stains or from material imaginations. They are thus to be understood as pure, not as purified from corruption, but as cleansed from imperfection; and not only free from imperfection, but also, through the excellence of perfection, higher than and established above all other perfected beings.

[Col. 1052C] This is what follows: “And higher.” We must supply, “we must suppose the first essences to be,” “and established above every divinely strengthened temple”: that is, above every rational creature in which God dwells and which, by him dwelling within it, is strengthened unto the supreme good. Those first essences are established above all these according to their most excellent purity: that is, a purity more excellent than that of all the rest, a purity existing in all their powers—that is, in every kind of power—which are most conformed to God, that is, approach conformity with God more than the powers of others do.

Thus we must suppose those first essences both to be pure and, by the excellence of their purity, higher than all the rest and established above them. We must also suppose that they have been received ineffably into participation in purity itself in God through their own movement and by themselves, that is, without an intermediary; and through the same movement, that is, without deviation, always directed toward the same thing, according to the unturning—that is, the unturningness—of the order which loves God. For those who never grow lukewarm in love are never bent or turned away from their purpose.

It follows: “And wholly ignorant of insulting those subject to them”—we must supply, “we must suppose them to be.” For just as they receive God’s purity from above without diminution, so they offer it below for participation without arrogance, thereby imitating God himself, “who gives abundantly to all and does not reproach” (Jas. 1).

[Col. 1053A] Therefore, he says, “we must suppose them to be ignorant of insult toward those subject to them; but rather to possess an establishment of their own Godlike distinctiveness, beyond falling and therefore unchangeable.” By their own Godlike distinctiveness he means the excellent and singular beauty of divine conformity which exists in those highest essences. They are placed and founded in it so purely and perfectly that their establishment is beyond falling, one over which falling cannot prevail; and it is rightly beyond falling because it is unchangeable or immutable.

The sum of this chapter, therefore, is that those first and principal essences receive their purification or purity without diminution, offer it for participation without arrogance, and possess it incorruptibly without mutability. These things have been said concerning their purification.

Afterwards he joins the discussion of illumination, saying: “And again contemplative of sensible symbols, and speculative concerning intelligible things; not as brought back to the divine through the variety of sacred-scriptural contemplation, but as filled with the higher light of all immaterial knowledge and, so far as is permitted, full of contemplation of formative, principal, superessential, and three-shining beauty; likewise made worthy through communion with Jesus; not forming in a representational manner the Godlike likeness in sacredly made images, but as truly approaching it itself in the first participation of knowledge of its deifying lights; and because a likeness [to God] has been bestowed on them substantially by God. Such beings participate, insofar as possible, in the pre-operative power of his deifying and human powers.”

All this is said concerning illumination. It is as though he said: We must suppose not only that those first essences possess purification and are pure, but also that they possess illumination and are contemplative of sensible symbols and speculative concerning intelligible things. Sensible symbols are material signs, whether in creatures, the Scriptures, or divine sacraments, set forth to show invisible realities. The highest angelic spirits recognize, by contemplation through divine illumination, their mystical meaning and invisible truth. Through the same illumination they also speculate concerning intelligible things—we must understand symbols—namely spiritual theophanies, that is, divine manifestations, through which the hidden and invisible nature of divinity is inwardly revealed to them.

Or the passage may be read thus: We must suppose the essences to be contemplative of sensible symbols and speculative concerning intelligible things, and not—supply, “symbols.” For outwardly, among sensible things where material signs exist, there are symbols; inwardly, among intelligible things where there are not signs but truth, there are no symbols. Therefore in sacred sensible symbols they contemplate signs of truth; inwardly, however, in intelligible things they contemplate naked truth without signs. Thus we must suppose them to be contemplative of sensible symbols and likewise speculative concerning intelligible things, but not as though brought back to the divine—that is, to divine knowledge—through the variety, that is, the manifold teaching, of contemplation, namely of sacred-scriptural contemplation, because it writes and speaks of divine and sacred matters.

Taught through the simple illumination of divine contemplation, not through the varied and manifold teaching of the Scriptures, they contemplate all sacred figures and sensible signs: those set forth in either the Old or New Testament for the showing of invisible things, such as the tabernacle of the covenant, the ark of the covenant, and other such things; visible forms of creatures through which invisible things are shown; and mystical revelations made through sensible forms. They contemplate all these sacred symbols. And they speculate not only concerning these outward things but also concerning intelligible things, which shine inwardly through pure and naked truth.

Yet we must not suppose that they have been brought to speculation and divine knowledge of all these things through the variety of sacred-scriptural contemplation—that is, through the manifold teaching of the divine Scriptures. This teaching is necessary only in order that human minds, estranged from God, may be brought back to knowledge of truth and gathered into unity out of their varied dispersion. Therefore we must not suppose that those highest essences have knowledge of all these things as instructed through scriptural teaching, but rather as filled with a higher light—that is, a more excellent knowledge—of every immaterial, that is, spiritual, science. For higher and more worthy is the light of knowledge which is poured inwardly through invisible inspiration than that which is possessed outwardly through instructional teaching.

We must therefore suppose those highest essences to have knowledge of visible and invisible things, as filled with such a light; and also as full of contemplation of beauty that is formative, principal, superessential, and three-shining. “Full,” I say, insofar as is permitted: that is, insofar as the creature is allowed. It signifies divine beauty, which is formative because it has formed according to itself all things made by it; principal because, though it is the form of all things, it has not itself received form from another; and superessential because it not only precedes all things by form, as the exemplar of all, but also transcends them in essence, as creator of the universe.

It follows: “And three-shining”—we must suppose them to be “full of contemplation” of this beauty. The three-shining beauty signifies the same divine beauty, which shines in three, though it is not itself threefold: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are three persons, but God is one, divinity one, nature one, essence one, beauty one. You see the Father: you see that beauty shining in the Father. You see the Son: you see that beauty shining in the Son. You see the Holy Spirit: you see that beauty shining in the Holy Spirit. It therefore shines as though threefold, because it shines in three, though it is not itself threefold but one—the one beauty which shines. The Father is distinct in person: there it shines. The Son is distinct in person: there it shines. The Holy Spirit is distinct in person: there it shines. Yet, just as the divinity and nature of Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one, so their beauty is one. Therefore, he says, “we must suppose them to be full of contemplation of three-shining beauty.”

What wonder, then, if those highest essences perfectly know the visible and invisible divine works, since they are full, as far as is possible to a creature, of contemplation of the Creator himself?

It follows: “Likewise made worthy through communion with Jesus”—we must supply, “we must suppose them to be.” Note the compound *dignefactas*, “made worthy.” They have merited not only to receive contemplation and knowledge of divinity, but also to be made worthy, both by knowing and by participating, through communion in that salvation accomplished in the humanity of Jesus. For they shared in Jesus: by foretelling the mystery of his incarnation before it occurred; by ministering when it occurred; and, after it was accomplished and humanity restored to eternity, by rejoicing together in the same fellowship of blessedness.

Afterwards he adds, showing that, illuminated immediately by divinity itself, they receive divine contemplation without any intervening figures. Just as above he showed that they read and draw their knowledge of all visible and invisible things not through outward teaching but inwardly in God’s own wisdom, so now he shows that they receive this same divine contemplation not through intervening forms or images, but immediately, nakedly, and purely from divinity itself in the first place.

“They do not,” he says, “form the Godlike likeness representationally in sacredly made images; but rather they form it as truly approaching it itself”—namely, the Godlike likeness or divinity—“approaching it,” I say, “in the first participation of knowledge of its deifying lights,” that is, its deifying illuminations. The Godlike likeness is divine contemplation itself, because, while those enlightened through it become shining, they receive in some way the likeness of the illuminating light itself.

In this Godlike likeness they neither form themselves nor acquire it for themselves through sacred images fashioned and made—that is, composed to show spiritual realities—as do human beings, who are instructed through visible and material demonstrations in sacred discourse toward knowledge of invisible things. Thus those highest essences are not illuminated in divine contemplation by mediating things of this sort. Rather, they truly approach it itself: that is, they approach truth itself not through something else but through truth itself, because nothing stands between them and truth. Therefore they approach in the first participation of knowledge, because in the first place they participate in knowledge of its deifying lights: they immediately contemplate, know, and understand its deifying—that is, God-making—lights, because these lights make those illuminated by them through divine likeness into gods in some manner.

“**And because that which is like God has been given to them substantially.**” Therefore, he says, they truly approach the Godhead, and do so in the first participation, because that which is like God has been given to them—that is, because God’s likeness has been granted them substantially. For they are like God not through something else or through another; rather, they possess this because they receive the Godhead itself substantially, nakedly, and purely. Or: that which is like God has been given to them in the most immediate subjection, because they are subject in the nearest rank, so as to receive God’s very likeness in first participation.

“**They share, insofar as possible, in the pre-operative power of His deifying and [Col. 1056B] human powers.**” He concludes what was said above. Since such beings—that is, these highest essences—are filled with contemplation of the principal beauty, they share in the deifying powers; and since they have been made worthy by communion with Jesus, they share in the human powers; and since they participate in the first and nearest rank, they share in the pre-operative power of God—that power, namely, which first works in them and afterwards works through them.

Or he calls the human powers of Jesus those powers which He displayed from His humanity, that is, from mercy or loving-kindness. The sense is: since they share in His powers in the contemplation of majesty, so also they share in cooperation in loving-kindness. They share by contemplation in His majesty; they share [Col. 1056C] by the ministry of cooperation in our redemption. Thus they share in His deifying and human powers, insofar as this is possible to them according to the measure of grace given. Thus far he has spoken of their illumination. Now, in the third place, he adds something concerning perfection.

“**But they are perfected likewise, not as illuminated by sacred variety into analytic knowledge, but as filled with a first and surpassing deification, according to the most excellent knowledge of divine works possible among angels.**” It is as though he said: they should not merely be considered pure and illuminated, but also perfect in knowledge received through the habit of virtue. Yet they are not illuminated or instructed [Col. 1056D] in analytic—that is, resolving—knowledge or discipline by sacred variety, namely, by the manifold teaching of Holy Scripture. For, unlike human beings, they are not taught outwardly through a multiplicity of discourse, so that matters hidden and difficult may be resolved for them by disputations and distinctions in knowledge and discipline. Rather, they receive illumination through simple inward contemplation, so that nothing capable of being known is hidden from their knowledge.

They must therefore be considered perfect, not as though illuminated toward resolving and explicable knowledge through the variety of sacred discourse, but as filled with a first and surpassing deification—that is, divine illumination—by which they are enlightened before all other heavenly essences according to a knowledge of divine works [Col. 1057A] that is most excellent, as excellent as it can be among angels.

“**For they are sanctified not through other holy essences, but by the Godhead itself; they are immediately extended toward it; they are established in a power and order surpassing all things, and in a wholly most pure steadfastness; they are led, insofar as is permitted, to contemplation of immaterial and invisible beauty; they are bent toward knowable principles of divine works as the first essences and those about God; and they have been sanctified most highly by the Prince of perfection himself.**”

He proves that these highest essences receive divine illumination before and above all other heavenly essences, because they are sanctified not through other holy essences but by the Godhead itself; and they are immediately extended toward it through love and [Col. 1057B] exaltation, according to a power and order—that is, the grace and dignity—which they possess above all others. Thus, immediately joined to the Godhead, they receive from it alone purification, illumination, and perfection.

This is what he means when he says that they are “established”: they are made steadfast in a wholly most pure power, or inflexibility—that is, in a strong, unbending, incorruptible chastity. They are also led through illumination, insofar as is permitted—that is, lawful or granted—to contemplate the immaterial and invisible beauty of the Creator. They are bent, as though in soft wax; or they are formed, instructed, and perfected toward the knowable principles of divine works, as first essences [Col. 1057C] and those standing nearest about God, sanctified in the highest manner by the Prince of perfection himself, namely the Godhead.

“**This, therefore, the theologians also plainly declare: that the subordinate dispositions of heavenly essences are fittingly instructed in deifying knowledges by the orders set over them; but that those higher than all are illumined for doctrine by the Godhead itself, insofar as is permitted.**”

By authority he proves what he had said: namely, that the highest orders of angels are illuminated by the Godhead alone, while the lower are instructed by the higher. For the theologians—that is, the prophets and holy persons who have spoken of heavenly and divine matters—plainly declare that the subordinate dispositions, namely the lower orders of heavenly essences, [Col. 1057D] are orderly, beautifully, and suitably instructed in deifying knowledges by those “firmly established,” that is, by the orders set over them; while those higher than all are illuminated for doctrine by the Godhead itself, insofar as is permitted—that is, insofar as is possible for them.

“**For they introduce some of them as being sacredly instructed by their predecessors that the Lord is the Lord of heavenly powers and the King of glory received humanly into heaven.**”

He gives an example in which lower heavenly essences are taught by higher ones: namely, where the theologians introduce some of them as instructed by those preceding or superior to them, so that they might know that God is the Lord of heavenly powers and that the King of glory, according to His humanity, has been received into heaven. Thus [Col. 1058A] it is written that, when the Savior, according to the flesh He had assumed, ascended into heaven, certain angels, still ignorant of the exaltation of His humanity and therefore wondering and saying, “Who is this King of glory?” were told by others more fully illuminated: “The Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory” (Psalm 23 [Vulgate numbering]). This proves that some are sometimes instructed by others.

“**But they introduce others as questioning Jesus himself and learning for our sake the knowledge of His divine action; and they show Jesus himself immediately teaching them and, before all others, revealing to them His human loving-kindness: ‘For I set forth righteousness and the judgment of salvation.’**”

This example, taken from Isaiah, proves that the highest angelic orders [Col. 1058B] are illuminated to the knowledge of truth by God alone. The theologians introduce certain heavenly essences themselves as questioning—that is, putting a question—to Jesus himself, and as learning, not from another but from Him who is God, knowledge of His divine action performed for our sake. He calls the passion and death which Jesus underwent for us His divine action. This action is called divine because it was possible to God alone to destroy by death the power of death.

Thus they introduce heavenly essences as inquiring of Jesus himself concerning this action when, seeing the garment of assumed flesh stained with the blood of passion, they say: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” (Isaiah 63). And afterwards: “Why, [Col. 1058C] then, is your garment red, and your clothing like that of those who tread the winepress?” (ibid.). Thus they introduce them as questioning and desiring to learn.

They also introduce Jesus himself as immediately teaching them through himself and revealing to them His human—that is, merciful—loving-kindness which He showed to us. He gives them this revelation, bestowing before all others knowledge of His work. “I,” he says, “set forth righteousness and the judgment of salvation” (ibid.). “Righteousness” and “the judgment of salvation,” that is, of the Savior or salvation, signify the redemption of the human race. In it there was righteousness, insofar as the Creator recalled His creature from an alien dominion; [Col. 1058D] and judgment, insofar as He powerfully expelled the devil, an invader of another’s right, from the human being whom he possessed. He says that He “sets forth” this righteousness and judgment because He fulfilled it—with labor and as it were by a certain contest—in what belonged to the sufferings of assumed flesh.

“**But I wonder that even the first among the heavenly essences, and those together surpassing all others in divine illuminations, reverently desire questions as though they were intermediate.**”

This refers to the assertion that the highest essences are immediately illuminated and instructed by God. For it appears contrary to this that in this passage they are found seeking knowledge not only from their superior but also from one another, and as though wishing to learn. But it should be understood that this questioning [Col. 1059A] is not an inquiry for instruction but a profession of ignorance. They ask in order to show that they do not know and that they need to be taught. Where all ask, they surely indicate that they must be taught from elsewhere. Therefore they ask among themselves in order to be taught from above themselves.

Since this mutual questioning seems to be an inquiry into instruction and knowledge from one another, although they are certainly instructed by the superior alone, he says: I wonder that those first and principal heavenly essences—that is, those that surpass all other heavenly essences together in divine illuminations—reverently desire questions, that is, ask questions desiring knowledge, humbly, like persons lowly and inferior, as though not attending to the excellence of their own illumination. And [Col. 1059B] this is what he means by “as though intermediate”: either as though they had some intermediary between themselves and God and needed to be instructed by others; or “as though intermediate,” because they are not truly intermediate, since they do not put their question to others, nor yet truly immediate, since they direct their question not to their very principle but to one another.

“**For they do not ask Him first: Why are your garments red?**”

He proves that they truly question as though intermediate, because they direct their words not first to Jesus himself but to one another, saying: “Who is this who comes from Edom, with dyed garments from Bozrah?” For, he says, they do not ask Him first—that is, they do not begin their question from Him—“Why are your garments red?” in which case they would direct their speech immediately to Jesus himself [Col. 1059C]; but first they ask among themselves, as though through an intermediary: “Who is this?” and so forth. Hence it is remarkable that these highest essences, though first and nearest to the Godhead, ask questions as though intermediate.

“**But they deliberate among themselves before asking, showing that they learn and desire deifying knowledge.**”

He now resolves the question why those highest essences, though nearest to God, ask questions among themselves: namely, because they deliberate among themselves before asking, lest by too hasty a question they leap over or anticipate that illumination which is produced in them through divine procession—that is, through the divine grace [Col. 1059D] proceeding into them to illuminate them. By this very deliberation concerning their question they also show that they desire deifying knowledge. For in asking, they signify that they desire knowledge; but in first discussing the question among themselves and deliberating, they show that they do not dare to anticipate the divine procession into themselves.

This is what follows: “**But they do not leap over the illumination bestowed through divine procession.**” For they desire knowledge and therefore ask; but, not leaping over divine illumination until it spontaneously offers itself by proceeding into them, they deliberate among themselves. They do not dare first to ask Jesus until He offers himself, saying: “I am he who speaks righteousness.” Only then, [Col. 1060A] having taken confidence, do they direct the question to Him: “Why is your clothing red, and your garment like that of those who tread the winepress?”

“**Is, then, the first hierarchy of heavenly intellects, sanctified by the Prince of perfection himself in that He immediately extends Himself into it, proportionately filling it with most holy purification, abundant light, and a perfection surpassing all perfection, purified, illumined, and perfected?**”

The sense is this: Is not the first hierarchy of heavenly intellects purified, illuminated, and perfected? It is sanctified by the Prince of perfection himself—that is, by the Godhead itself, which is prince and principle of all sanctification. It is sanctified, I say, in that the Godhead immediately extends itself into it, illuminating, irradiating, or filling it proportionately—that is, with a differentiated participation from the illumination of the rest—with most holy purification, abundant light, and a perfection surpassing all perfection, [Col. 1060B] that is, a supereminent consummation or perfection.

It is “purified,” “illuminated,” and “perfected,” so as to be pure from every diminution or imperfection; to be full of the first light, namely that which shines first into it before the others; and to be perfect, participating in perfect knowledge and in cognition first given to it.

As for his use of “sanctified”—or, perhaps more suitably though less customarily translated, “pontificated”—by the Prince of purification himself: he signifies the Godhead, as we have said, which in Greek is called *teletarchia*, that is, “Prince of purification” or [Col. 1060C] “sanctification.”

“**And, gathering this together, perhaps I shall not speak without reason.**”

As though one were to ask what this purification is, he replies that the reception of divine knowledge in the rational soul is both purification, illumination, and perfection. It is purification because it cleanses ignorance; illumination because it illuminates by divine knowledge; perfection because, by illumination, it consummates knowledge of perfect teachings or disciplines according to an enlightened habit. This is what he says: “Gathering together”—that is, briefly bringing the foregoing into one—I may perhaps say not without reason that the reception of divine knowledge is purification, illumination, and perfection.

[Col. 1060D] He gives the reason why it is called purification, illumination, and perfection: “**Cleansing ignorance, indeed, by the knowledge of perfect doctrines bestowed according to order.**” It is called purification because it cleanses ignorance by knowledge bestowed—that is, through the bestowed knowledge of perfect doctrines. It is bestowed “according to order,” that is, according to what the dignity and excellence of each order requires.

“**But illuminating by that divine knowledge itself, through which it also cleanses that which does not contemplate beforehand.**” It is called illumination because it illuminates each hierarchy by divine knowledge, through which divine knowledge it also cleanses that hierarchy. It cleanses, I say, the hierarchy which does not contemplate before it is purified, as it is written: [Col. 1061A] “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matthew 5).

“**Which it manifests through a higher illumination, and again perfects by that very light, according to the habit of knowledge of most luminous doctrines.**”

The reception of divine knowledge manifests that hierarchy through a higher illumination. For it shows that hierarchy to be higher than all the rest precisely by illuminating it with the higher and more excellent light of divine cognition.

“**And again perfects by that very light, according to the habit of knowledge of most luminous doctrines.**” He does not distinguish illumination and perfection sufficiently clearly, since he appears to assign both to cognition and knowledge. Yet this is the difference: illumination properly belongs to that knowledge which builds up understanding, while perfection belongs to that knowledge which displays the form of good character and the habit of virtues. Some matters are investigated only for knowledge in understanding; others pertain especially to understanding in action. Illumination is necessary for the former; perfection for the latter. [Col. 1061B] For the knowledge of truth does not make one perfect unless the habit of virtue follows.

For this reason he calls “most luminous doctrine” that which consists in the habit of virtue, because experience is the teacher of understanding, and the person who knows virtue best is the one who has learned it not merely by hearing, but also by tasting and doing it. In experience and the habit of virtue, the knowledge of truth is perfected, which begins in illumination concerned only with understanding. Since all this is acquired through the reception of divine knowledge, it is fittingly called purification, illumination, and perfection.

[Col. 1061C] “**Therefore it is, so far as our knowledge extends, the first disposition of heavenly essences: standing in the circuit of God and immediately about God, and simply and ceaselessly circling His eternal knowledge, according to the most excellent and ever-moving position possible among angels.**”

He draws an inference from what has been said. It is as if he said: since that hierarchy of highest spirits is first and principally purified, illumined, and perfected by the Godhead itself, it is therefore the first and principal [Col. 1061D] disposition, or principal order, of heavenly essences, standing immediately in the circuit of and about God. It stands through the immovability of contemplation; it circles through the life-giving and unceasing desire of eternal love. It is unceasing because it does not fail in love; simple because, while circling, it does not depart from unity.

The unity in the middle is the simplicity of the Godhead; they are in a circuit and around it insofar as they immediately draw near to it. They are also in a circuit because they too are, in a certain sense, outside its ineffable and hidden incomprehensibility, which they do not wholly penetrate. Yet they encircle and desire it, strive toward its inner things, and, approaching through knowledge and love, become nearest according to the most excellent position [Col. 1062A] which they hold beside God—most excellent, I say, as compared with that found among all the other angels. And I call this position ever-moving because they do not withdraw in contemplation and always draw near in desire.

For all these reasons, this disposition is principal among all the other heavenly essences—principal, I say, so far as our knowledge reaches, that is, so far as it can be comprehended through our knowledge. He continues in praise of this hierarchy, accumulating one after another many exalted, sublime, and divinely admirable matters, some profound and known only to the pure.

Such, he says, is that disposition or order of the first hierarchy: nearest in position, most ardent in desire and intention. Although it cannot penetrate all that belongs to God, which is incomprehensible, it nevertheless never ceases, through eternal love, to encompass all that can be grasped and comprehended by a creature. But lest this should seem a pursuit of labor rather than of blessedness—if it always encompassed and never attained, always sought and never received, always desired and never tasted—he adds the fruit of inquiry and the effect of desire, saying:

“**Seeing many blessed contemplations purely, illuminated by simple and immediate splendors, and filled with divine nourishment; filled by a great first effusion, and made worthy by the sole, proper, and unifying unity of divine refreshment, and worthy of abundant communion with God and cooperation toward it, insofar as possible, through likeness of good dispositions [Col. 1062C] and actions; knowing many divine things in a supereminent manner, and made a participant, insofar as is permitted, in divine knowledge and cognition.**”

He has said, as well as he could, that three surround the Trinity: the Seraphim by love, the Cherubim by knowledge, and the Thrones by dominion. Here is the whole Trinity. Dominion is in the Father, wisdom in the Son, and love in the Holy Spirit. The Seraphim seemed to have been set above, because charity surpasses all things; but behold, we also see that the throne is the Father’s, the Thrones are joined with the Father, and love is assigned to the Holy Spirit. If you think the Thrones subject because they are named after Seraphim and Cherubim, think them also preeminent because they pertain to the Father, who is named before the Son and Spirit. But in [Col. 1062D] the Trinity there is no rank. Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are one God. Unity cannot be inferior to itself.

Therefore that hierarchy of highest spirits, first and principally formed by the supreme and supereminent dominion of the Godhead according to that most excellent likeness by which it imitates simple unity, has no rank within its dominion, although it has a difference according to the measure of participation and distribution of grace, since a creature cannot be equal to the Creator. Therefore there is one dominion of the three, by which they are universally set above all subject things after the supreme and supereminent dominion of the Godhead; they are not subject to one another. Therefore all together hold the first place, and each surrounds in nearest position [Col. 1063A] such that one neither intervenes before another by position, nor anticipates another by participation, nor surpasses another in dominion. Thus that disposition is properly the first, standing in the circuit of God and immediately about God. And what is the fruit of such great familiarity?

Hear what follows: “**Seeing many blessed contemplations purely, illuminated by simple and immediate splendors, and filled with divine nourishment.**” Do not therefore wonder if they thus encompass God and do not allow themselves to be drawn away. Something there draws them. What is it? You await a statement of what it is that stirs the affection of those who desire so greatly and provokes their love. But how do you suppose we can speak of what they do not penetrate? They have not yet entered, but stand [Col. 1063B] in the circuit. It is a great thing for them to approach it, to see, touch, taste, and experience what the sweetness of the good is like when exposed without obstacle to those who love it. Yet they neither enter nor penetrate so as to comprehend and grasp completely how great is the immensity of the hidden reality.

How then do you suppose that one can explain outwardly what even those within remain outwardly in relation to? Therefore we cannot express that good which holds those blessed souls immovable near itself through the joy of eternal contemplation, so that they do not flow away toward perishable things, and again draws them to itself by moving them through desire, so that they seek it in unceasing love. Yet, lest we wholly pass over in silence what cannot at all be spoken, hear what holds them near itself and draws them to itself.

It is a certain good, great above [Col. 1063C] all these goods which you know—wholly other, not only by difference but by supereminence. Yet, so that it may be suggested and made known to you, as far as possible, through these goods that you know, let us say that that good is light and sweetness. Why light? Because it makes the eyes clear. Why sweetness? Because it refreshes. These are two great goods among us, and no others greater than these are found, nor any more conducive to our joy or blessedness: light and sweetness. One is for illumination; the other for refreshment.

If you are illuminated but not satisfied, that is a great good but not a complete one. If you are satisfied but not illuminated, that likewise is a great good but not a perfect one. Refreshment makes pleasant what is within; illumination presents pleasantly what is outside. Both are required for full joy. For if you are refreshed in one respect and afflicted in another, joy is not perfect when mingled with sorrow.

Seek, therefore, refreshment, so that what is in you may be pleasant to you; seek illumination also, so that what is outside you may be pleasant to you. Refreshment seems indeed more necessary, just as the good within you seems more properly your own than the good outside you. Yet how much pleasure does illumination through contemplation add? “Sweet is the light, and pleasant to the eyes is the sight of the sun.” Look upon this world, which presents many pleasing spectacles. All these things were made through the wisdom of God. Everything you see came forth from that place where is the reason and cause of all things. If, therefore, [Col. 1064A] it is so beautiful to see the ordering and form of a work, how pleasant and delightful do you think it is to contemplate the wisdom of the maker?

But do not think, because one wisdom is named, that those who see it contemplate some solitary and tedious object. It is one, but not one in that manner. How do you suppose the wisdom of God is one? Perhaps as you call one essence, one species, one form, one place, and one time: all these are one in number. What is “in number”? By distinction. What is “in number”? By smallness. What is “in number”? By imperfection. For thus you count this and that: when you count, you say “this and not that.” Therefore whatever is numbered by unity is separated by unity; and by that same unity it is shown to be diminished from all those things from which it is shown to be distinct [Col. 1064B] by that unity.

Do you suppose the wisdom of God to be one in this way? Then you number it and rightly say, “This is it, and not that.” If it is this and not that, then it is not the whole; something is outside it which is not in it. If all is in it, it is all; how then do you say, “This and not that is it”? Do not number it. Scripture tells you: “His wisdom has no number. All things that are from it were made in number, weight, and measure; but it is not under number.” In it there is true unity without smallness and universality without multiplicity; it is not under weight, being beyond estimation, nor under measure, being incomprehensible.

What then do you suppose it is to see the wisdom of God? When you see this world, how many things do you see in it? [Col. 1064C] And all this comes from there; and the whole is there, where the wisdom of God is. And why do I say “all this”? For it is too little to say that in the wisdom of God there is nothing else. If God understands His work but does not understand himself, what wisdom is that? For God is more than what is made by God. If therefore He knows what He has made but does not know what He himself is who made it, He is ignorant of what is greater, and there is no perfect wisdom in Him.

If your heart can take in and comprehend the things you make and set forth in work, arranging all things by reason speaking inwardly, and conceiving beforehand in reason all that you will do, so that when these things issue into work they do not depart from reason, how can everything [Col. 1064D] made fail to be in the eternal reason of the Creator?

Again, if it is too little for a rational mind to see and comprehend outward things unless it also contemplates inward things, which are far greater and more wonderful, and recognizes that what it itself is is greater than everything outside itself, then the eternal craftsman cannot, in that wisdom by which He sees all that He himself has made, be ignorant of that which is greater than all—the selfsame maker. Consider, therefore, what this wisdom is, in which are all things made, and besides and above all things, that which is greater than all: He by whom all things were made.

What kind of form do you think this is, in which there is such beauty? When, therefore, you hear the wisdom of God named, think of this whole reality: it is all in that wisdom; and to see it is to see all this. In it are seen all things made; [Col. 1065A] and in it is seen He by whom all things were made. Therefore those highest spirits, who immediately draw near through the excellence of surpassing grace, are illuminated by it to contemplate it itself; and in its contemplation they see what was made through it, what is in it, and Him who made through it, in whom it is.

These, therefore, are the contemplations which the first hierarchy sees purely, illuminated immediately by simple splendors. These contemplations are many because all things are seen there; and blessed because He who made all things is seen with all things. For that which is seen in Him is not seen apart from Him, because what is seen is one—namely, He himself—and in that one all things are seen, in whom all things are one and the one is all things.

See how [Col. 1065B] many are the contemplations where none of all things is hidden; how blessed the contemplations where all things are seen in the highest good; where seeing and possessing, loving and tasting the good, are the same; where nothing is seen except truth and nothing loved except goodness. For there are two things: knowledge and love. One belongs to illumination; the other to refreshment. Knowledge illumines; love satisfies. Knowledge of truth and love of goodness: in these blessedness consists, namely in knowing and loving the good. “Taste,” Scripture says, “and see that the Lord is sweet” (Psalm 33 [Vulgate numbering]). In “taste” is love; in “see” is knowledge. It distinctly commends these two, namely knowledge and love.

“**Seeing many blessed contemplations purely, illuminated by simple and immediate splendors.**” This was said concerning illumination and knowledge.

“**Filled with divine nourishment; filled by a great first effusion, and by the sole, proper, and unifying unity of divine refreshment.**” This was said concerning love and refreshment. He commends each in many ways. First, he commends knowledge in many blessed contemplations purely seen through illumination by simple splendors. What are simple splendors? Pure illuminations. Through pure illuminations one comes to pure contemplations. Pure illumination occurs when truth is apprehended through itself; pure contemplation occurs when truth is seen in itself. When [Col. 1065D] truth is learned through an underlying image or figure, there is no pure illumination; when truth is known in an underlying image or figure, there is no pure contemplation. For simplicity cannot exist except where there is only one thing; nor purity except where there is truth. Simplicity is in the one alone; purity in the true. Therefore those who contemplate immediately and approach truth through themselves alone possess simple illuminations and pure contemplations.

“**Filled with divine nourishment.**” What is divine nourishment? Divine refreshment. And what is that refreshment except love of God? Therefore, after saying that the supereminent angelic disposition was filled with divine nourishment, he added: “filled with the unity of divine refreshment.” What is divine refreshment except divine nourishment? [Col. 1066A] Therefore the unity of refreshment and the unity of nourishment are one refreshment and one nourishment. Thus at God’s table only one dish is set forth. But do not despise it: there is abundant satisfaction. “I shall be satisfied,” says the Psalmist, “when your glory appears” (Psalm 16 [Vulgate numbering]).

There are many things in this world, and all these cannot satisfy the human heart. But there is one good with God, and only when it is received is satisfaction found. Therefore satisfaction lies not in multiplicity but in unity. When is there satisfaction? When “enough” is satisfaction. Suppose you possess some of the many things in the world which you love: you will see that it does not suffice. Let more come: you will still not say, “It is enough.” Let everything be added: you will find yourself still in need and not yet sufficiently supplied. Therefore satisfaction cannot exist in all these things, where there cannot be enough.

But that one good will come, and there will be satisfaction because there will be enough. Do not wonder. All these things are many, but they are not much; that one is one, and is much. Therefore that sinful woman, because she had many things to be forgiven, loved not many things but greatly. She left many things and chose much. She was wise: she did not attend to the heap but weighed the value. In many things there is little; in one there is much. Therefore attend not to number, but seek the fruit. God has prepared one good for you. Do not fear when you hear “one”: it is one good, but in that good is every good. He has prepared one refreshment, one food, one dish, one bread; but do not despise it. Hear what is written: “Having every flavor and [Col. 1066C] every delight of sweetness” (Wisdom 15).

This is the divine nourishment, and the great effusion—or abundant outpouring—by which that blessed society is filled, having been given it in the first rank. There is also the unity of divine refreshment, by which unity alone—that is, by a singular, proper, and unifying unity—it has specially been made worthy. That one and simple divine refreshment is called singular because it is not received together with alien delight or an extraneous sweetness; proper, because it is prepared only for friends and familiars; unifying, because it makes one with itself all those to whom it grants that it may be received and shared.

It follows: “And filled with much communion with God and cooperation [with Him].” The disposition, or hierarchy, of the first celestial essences [Col. 1066D] is understood to be filled. I mean, it was made worthy of that communion and cooperation with God, insofar as this was possible for it, through likeness to good dispositions—that is, virtues—and actions. For through good dispositions it was made worthy of communion; through good actions, worthy of cooperation. And the order is right. First it is illuminated by the brightness of knowledge; afterward it is refreshed by the sweetness of love, so that it both communes with God in virtue and cooperates with Him in action, as it is written: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him” (John 14).

It follows: “And knowing many divine things in a supereminent manner, and made a participant, insofar as is lawful, in divine science and knowledge” [Col. 1067A]. That is, this hierarchy knows many things concerning the divine—many things concerning God—in a supereminent manner, that is, more excellently than the other hierarchies; “and it was made a participant,” that is, it became a participant in divine science and divine knowledge, insofar as this was lawful for it, that is, granted to it.

It follows: “Therefore theology also handed down its praises to those who are on earth, in which the eminence of its most exalted illumination is wonderfully made manifest.” As though he said: Because the hierarchy of the first essences is of such great excellence, theology—that is, divine Scripture—therefore handed down its praises or laudations to those who are on earth, that is, to human beings. In these laudations [Col. 1067B] the eminence of its most exalted illumination is wonderfully manifested. As though he said: Because its sublimity is so great, theology disclosed to human beings its laudations, by which it praises God, so that through the excellence of its praise the eminence of its illumination might be made manifest.

It follows: “For some of them, uttering it sensibly, resound like the voice of waters: ‘Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place.’” As though he said: Truly excellent are the laudations of this hierarchy which divine Scripture makes manifest, because others of it—that is, certain ones from it—sounding sensibly, resound or echo, or cry out, like the voice of waters: “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place.” Or it may be read thus: Theology handed down its praises sensibly—that is, speaking of spiritual things [Col. 1067C] through likenesses of sensible and bodily things—that “some of them,” that is, some from its number, “resound like the voice of waters: ‘Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place.’” This testimony is taken from Ezekiel, where the prophet recalls a voice of great commotion arising behind him. Although that voice is not there said to have been uttered, this author nevertheless testifies without ambiguity that it was produced by the spirits of the highest celestial orders.

It follows: “But others proclaim that most praiseworthy and most merciful theology: ‘Holy, holy, holy: Lord God Sabaoth. The whole earth is full of his glory’” (Isa. 6). This testimony is taken from Isaiah, where two flying seraphim are recalled as proclaiming to one another [Col. 1067D] this theology—that is, this divine utterance or laudation.

It follows: “But these most exalted hymnologies of the celestial minds we have already, as far as possible, unfolded in those writings which concern the divine praises. And concerning these things, sufficient has been said there, insofar as concerns us.” He says that he has unfolded or expounded the aforementioned hymnologies—that is, the divine praises of the celestial minds, namely of the celestial spirits—as far as was possible for him, in other writings composed by him concerning divine praises. And he testifies that sufficient has there been said concerning these hymnologies—in those writings, that is—insofar as his own capacity extended. This work [Col. 1068A], which he claims to have composed concerning divine praises, is not found among those of his writings which are available to us. Nevertheless, from this statement we may know that he wrote concerning divine praises, since in the book *On the Divine Names* he introduced certain passages from the amorous hymns of Saint Hierotheus, in which something is discussed concerning the aforesaid praises.

It follows: “From these it is sufficient, for present purposes, merely to recall that the first disposition, insofar as is lawful, was illuminated with theological knowledge by the divine goodness, through which, as a God-formed hierarchy, it afterward handed itself down also to others.” As though he said: From these divine praises, sufficiently expounded in the aforementioned book [Col. 1068B], it now suffices, for present purposes, only to recall or point out this: that the first disposition, that is, the first hierarchy of angels, was illuminated with theological—that is, divine—knowledge by divine goodness itself. Note the construction in the phrase “illuminated with knowledge.” For one similarly says, “I am instructed in a discipline,” or “I am taught a discipline.” He says, therefore, that the first disposition was illuminated by divine goodness alone unto knowledge; through which knowledge, namely, that disposition handed itself down afterward—that is, subsequently—to the other hierarchies which follow after it. “It handed down,” I say, “itself as a God-formed hierarchy,” that is, as possessing conformity and likeness to God and imitating God in this: that, illuminated by Him, [Col. 1068C] it illuminates others and sets itself before them as a kind of form and exemplar of divine conformity.

Thus it now suffices to say concerning the aforesaid praises that, in them, the first disposition of angels, praising its Creator, handed itself down as a pattern of praise to the hierarchies following after it, “introducing indirectly,” that is, suggesting or intimating to them, “that thing by saying it briefly.” For it introduced or suggested something as though hidden and manifest to few. And it suggested, by speaking briefly, another thing which it suggested. Rightly indeed it was suggested only obscurely, because it was invisible; and it was said only briefly, because it was ineffable. For however much it might be expounded for knowledge, that which was impenetrable would remain hidden; [Col. 1068D] and however far it might be extended in speech, that which was boundless would be brief in comparison with itself. Yet it suggested, intimated, and expounded it, so that through it that which it had perceived without any intermediary might come to the knowledge of others. What did it suggest?

Hear: “It is right that the most merciful, supremely blessed, and altogether blessed Divinity should be blessed by intellects receiving God, insofar as it is possible for them to know and praise it. For they are, as it were, God-formed divine places of the divine rest, as the oracles say.” He expounds the aforementioned testimony taken from Ezekiel: “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place.” The first hierarchy, he says, crying out, “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place,” teaches that it is right—that is, just, due, or fitting—that the most merciful, supremely blessed, and altogether blessed Divinity should be blessed by intellects receiving God, and blessed insofar as it is possible for it to be known and praised. It is just, he says, that the Divinity which in itself is always most merciful—ready, that is, to bestow and not needing to receive—and which is supremely blessed and altogether, or most strongly, blessed, that is, whose glory within itself is so great that it can neither be increased by another’s benefit nor more highly commended by another’s praise—it is right, he says, that although it is thus perfect in itself, so as to need neither blessing nor praise, yet rational intellects, that is, hearts, should bless and praise it insofar as they can know it [Col. 1069B] and praise it according to the knowledge they have received. For although its glory is perfect from itself, we nevertheless ought not to cease from blessing and praising it. Even if we do not perfect it by blessing and praising, we are nevertheless perfected by it.

Or what he says may be understood otherwise: that it is just that the Divinity which is supremely blessed in itself should be blessed by intellects receiving God. As though he said: Although God’s praise is supremely perfect in itself, this nevertheless is rightfully ascribed to His praise: that by grace He deigns to dwell in hearts made by Himself. Thus it is right that the Divinity, supremely blessed in itself, should also be blessed and held blessed for this: that it offers itself to be received by minds that are to be made blessed, and deigns to dwell in them as in its own place. For He does not dwell in them as though seeking a support, or as something about to collapse unless it has a prop. God does not seek a place for Himself as though He could not exist unless contained; rather, He seeks, as it were, a receptacle into which He may pour Himself. That receptacle surely could not be blessed unless it were filled by Him. Therefore this is added to every praise of Him: that, supremely blessed in Himself, He makes others blessed from Himself. Let Him be blessed by them, and blessed also on their account. Let Him be blessed by them insofar as He reveals Himself to them as one to be known and praised; let Him be blessed on their account insofar as He is manifested in them.

It follows: “For they are, as it were, God-formed divine places of the divine rest, as the oracles say.” He gives the reason why, from what has been said—“Blessed [Col. 1069D] be the glory of the Lord from his place”—he understands that glory ought to be blessed by intellects receiving God: because, he says, these intellects receiving God are themselves divine places. For *theodochos* (θεοδόχος) is said in Greek, that is, “a receiver of God.” By this name every pure mind, whether human or angelic, may be signified. For God dwells and rests in both. Therefore they are, as it were, God-formed divine places.

He gives, as it were, a reason why they are called divine places. The same cause explains both why they are places and why they are God-formed. For because they receive light, they become a place of light; and again, because they receive light, they become shining and are made conformed to the light. They are therefore divine places, being [Col. 1070A] God-formed and possessing the likeness of God from the God dwelling within them. Again, because they are divine places, it is clear that they are places of divine rest; for they could by no means be divine places unless they were places of rest and peace, as the oracles say: “In peace his place has been made” (Ps. 75).

It follows: “And that the Monad and Unity are substantially three; and that, extending its goodness from the celestial essences down to the furthest parts of the earth, it is providence over all things that are, as the super-principal principle and cause of all essence, and as the superessential, immeasurable containing embrace of all things.” He adds this in explication of the following passage, which had been taken from Isaiah. As though he said: Just as that first celestial hierarchy, crying, “Blessed be the glory of the Lord from his place,” taught that God is to be blessed and glorified not only in Himself but also in His saints, so likewise, by proclaiming “thrice holy” and adding not “lords” but “Lord Sabaoth,” it signified that there are three persons in one Godhead—not three gods, but one God.

This is what he says: “And because the Monad and Unity are substantially three.” As though he said: Not only did that first celestial hierarchy indirectly introduce to the hierarchies following after it what was said above concerning the glory of the Lord to be blessed from His place; it also introduced this: that the Monad and Unity—that is, the Divinity, which is truly one and a simple nature—is substantially three persons; that is, the three persons are one essence or substance, and the one essence is three persons, because God is one in essence and three in persons.

Certainly, although *monas* and *unitas* seem to mean the same thing, they are used together because of the Greek. In Greek there are two names, *monas* and *henas* (ἑνάς). Although they have one interpretation among us—for each means “unity”—nevertheless this distinction seems to obtain: *monas* signifies rather that unity which is spoken of with respect to distinction, whereas *henas* indicates that which is marked by simplicity. For everything simple is one; but not everything one is simple. For “one” is said also by collection, by composition, and by likeness. Since none of these is wholly what it is one, they are not truly one, and they borrow the name of unity only by likeness, not by propriety. [Col. 1070D] But of the divine nature, for which to be one and to be simple are the same, all that it is is truly one. Therefore it rightly ought to be called not only Monad but also Henad, because its unity subsists in the ever-true simplicity of the same and undivided substance.

Let him say, therefore, that in true Godhead Monad and Unity are substantially three: because, just as the trinity of persons in God does not divide the unity of essence, so the unity of nature does not confuse the trinity of persons. But the three are substantially one, for those three have one substance.

It follows: “And extending its goodness from the celestial essences down to the furthest parts of the earth as providence over all things that are.” And this also, he says, [Col. 1071A] the first hierarchy intimated to those following after it: that the true Unity and supreme Trinity extends, or causes its goodness to penetrate, from the celestial essences down to the furthest parts of the earth—that is, from the highest things to the lowest. I mean goodness existing as providence over all things, because it provides for all and leaves nothing alien to itself, since it is the super-principal or superessential principle of every essence and the cause of all things, because all things were made from it and unto it; and because it is the encompassing embrace of all things—that is, their encompassing—because it surrounds, embraces, and contains all things superessentially, with an immeasurable containment which comprehends the whole and remains itself incomprehensible. Therefore, because it is the principle from which all things were made, the cause through which all things were made, and the encompassing containment in which all things subsist, the whole earth is full of its glory; for all things that have been made through that goodness are filled and nourished by it, so that they may subsist in it.

# BOOK EIGHT

[Col. 1071]

## TITLE OF CHAPTER VIII: Concerning dominions, powers, and the hierarchy which is intermediate between them.

## TEXT

[Col. 1071B]

We must now proceed to the intermediate disposition of the celestial intellects, examining, as far as possible, with supermundane eyes those dominions and the truly powerful contemplations of the divine powers and virtues. For every designation of the essences above us signifies their God-imitating, God-formed properties. Therefore I consider the manifestive designation of the holy dominions to declare a certain free elevation, liberated from every pedestrian diminution; a dominion liberally severe, in no way at all bent by tyrannical dissimilarities, set above every slavery that diminishes, superior to every subjection and removed from every dissimilitude; ever desiring lordship, and, insofar as possible, excellently and beautifully conforming both itself and those after it to the likeness of that power which naturally subsists; turned toward none of the things that seem vain, but toward the universal Being properly so called, and made ever a participant, insofar as possible for it, in the God-formed likeness of lordship itself.

But I consider the designation of the holy virtues to declare a certain strong and unchangeable manliness in all their operations according to their God-likeness; not feebly weakened for any reception of the divine illuminations bestowed upon it, powerfully led back into imitation of God; not abandoning its God-formed motion through any weakness of itself, but bearing itself firmly upward to the superessential and power-making might, made, insofar as is permitted, an image like that might; powerfully turned toward it as the principal might, and proceeding God-formingly toward secondary things by giving power [and giving].

But I consider the designation of the holy powers to declare an order equal in power to the divine dominions and virtues, well ordered and unconfused concerning divine receptions; an order of supermundane and intellectual authority, not tyrannically cast down through its ruling powers upon inferior things, but powerfully led back to divine things after being well ordered, and God-formingly leading back those after it; made like, insofar as is lawful, to the power-making causal Power, and revealing it, insofar as possible, to the angels by a ruling power in the orders well arranged through it [Col. 1072B].

Possessing these God-formed properties, the intermediate disposition of the celestial minds is purified, illuminated, and perfected, as has been said, by the divine illuminations bestowed upon it secondarily through the first hierarchical disposition and conveyed through that intermediate one by a second manifestation. Therefore, by making a symbol from one saying coming through another angel heard by another angel, we shall form a symbol of the perfection which is supremely perfect and, by procession, hidden in the things which follow. For the wise concerning our sacred offerings say that the self-luminous fullnesses of divine things are more perfect in themselves than through other participations of contemplation. Thus I also consider the immediate participation of the angelic orders first extended toward God to be the perfecting cause, by mediation, of the perfected.

For this reason, in our priestly tradition the first intellects are named the perfecting, light-giving, and purifying powers of those below, as beings led back through them to the superessential principle of all things and made participants, insofar as is lawful for them, in mystical purifications, illuminations, and perfections. For this has been altogether divinely promulgated by the divine ordering: that secondary things participate in divine illuminations through primary things [Col. 1072D].

You will find this expressed repeatedly by the theologians. For when the divine and paternal kindness, nurturingly correcting Israel for its sacred salvation, delivered it to avenging and savage nations for correction, then by every kind of providential leading toward what was better released it from captivity and mercifully restored it to its former beneficence, one of the theologians, Zechariah, saw one of the first angels, as I suppose, and those about God—for, as I said, this designation “angel” is common to all—learning from God Himself the consolatory words concerning this, as was said [Col. 1073A]. He saw another of the subordinate angels coming to meet the first, as though to receive and perceive illumination; then instructed by him in the divine counsel as by a high priest, and turning to teach this to the theologian: that Jerusalem would be fruitfully inhabited by a multitude of human beings (Zech. 1).

Another of the theologians, Ezekiel (Ezek. 8), says that this was most sacredly promulgated by the glorious Divinity established above the cherubim. For Israel itself, as has been said, *dux exercitus humanitas* [“the humanity of the commander of the army”; the Latin syntax is corrupt], leading through disciplines toward what is better, is answered by divine justice correcting it; it justified those who had been corrected. This is taught by the first one after the cherubim, girded about the loins with sapphire, who was clothed in a long robe according to the hierarchical symbol. The divine ordering commands the remaining angels, who had axes, to be taught the divine judgment concerning this by the first one (Ezek. 10). To him indeed it said: “Pass through the midst of Jerusalem and give a sign upon the foreheads of the corrected men”; to the others: “Go out into the city after him and strike, and let not your eyes spare”; and to all: “Do not approach any upon whom is the sign” (Ezek. 9).

What perhaps might someone say concerning the angel who said to Daniel, “The word went forth”; or concerning the first one himself receiving fire from the midst of the cherubim (Dan. 9)? Or concerning that fuller indication of angelic order in the same prophet: that the cherub sends fire into the hands of the one clothed in the holy robe (Ezek. 10)? Or concerning the most divine Gabriel calling and saying: “Make him understand the vision” (Zech. 1)? Or concerning whatever else has been said by the sacred theologians about the God-formed ordering of the celestial hierarchies? To this ordering, the ordering of our hierarchy, insofar as possible, is assimilated, formed into angelic beauty as far as it possesses this in images, and led back through it to the superessential source of every hierarchy.

## EXPOSITION

The eighth chapter concerns dominions, virtues, and powers, and the hierarchy intermediate among them. In the preceding chapter he treated [Col. 1073D] of the three first orders—seraphim, cherubim, and thrones—and of their hierarchy, that is, their sacred power, which is the first and chief in the celestial disposition and is ordered immediately after God. Now, therefore, he proceeds to discuss the three following orders, namely dominions, virtues, and powers, and their hierarchy—that is, their sacred power—which is established second or intermediate in the celestial disposition, after the first and before the last. Concerning this hierarchy, then, he proceeds in the same manner as he did concerning the higher order: first showing the cause or rationale of the designation assigned to the orders of this hierarchy, then expounding more fully the power of that sacred authority.

[Col. 1074A] “We must now proceed,” he says, “to the intermediate disposition of the celestial intellects, examining, as far as possible, with supermundane eyes those dominions and the truly powerful contemplations of the divine powers and virtues.”

The connection is with his preceding statement, as though he said: After the exposition of the highest hierarchy, the order of treatment requires that we proceed to the intermediate one—that is, to the exposition of the intermediate hierarchy of celestial intellects, namely angelic spirits. Then he explains by name which are the angelic orders in which that intermediate sacred power consists, to whose exposition he says that he must proceed, adding: “the dominions, examining those with supermundane eyes, as far as possible, and the truly powerful contemplations of powers and virtues.” “We must proceed,” he says, “we who examine in that hierarchy the dominions and the truly powerful contemplations of powers and virtues,” that is, the powers and the virtues. For these are the three orders of the second hierarchy. Whoever desires to expound their sacred power must carefully examine their virtue and functions. Therefore, he says, they must be examined “with supermundane eyes,” that is, spiritual eyes. For these things are not seen with bodily eyes.

Thus, “we examining those,” namely the celestial dominions, and “examining the contemplations,” that is, speculations or contemplations, “of powers and virtues.” What he says concerning his investigation of the speculations or contemplations of the powers and virtues may be understood either as meaning that he will investigate their dignity through the speculation or contemplation he has of them, or that he testifies that he will examine and investigate their very contemplation, by which they contemplate God and perceive divine things. He calls them truly powerful contemplations, or powerful speculations, because they examine those who are truly powerful. For by “a powerful contemplation” he means the contemplation of powerful beings. He calls them truly powerful because they are powerful in goodness and truth. For to be able to do evil is not truly to be able, but rather not to be able, as it is written: “Why do you boast in malice, you who are mighty in iniquity?” (Ps. 51). Therefore he also calls the powers themselves divine, because they can do all that they can do from God and in God.

It follows: “For every designation of the essences above us signifies their God-imitating, God-formed properties.” As though he said: I rightly called the powers and virtues divine, because their very designation teaches this. Just as every designation of the essences above us—that is, the celestial essences—signifies their God-formed properties; and they are God-formed because they imitate God. For whatever form the celestial essences have, they do not possess from their own quality but from imitation, because it is not nature but grace that confers upon them likeness to God.
