It follows: “Therefore I consider the manifestive designation of the holy dominions to declare a certain free elevation, liberated [Col. 1075A] from every pedestrian diminution; a dominion liberally severe, in no way at all bent by tyrannical dissimilarities, set above every slavery that diminishes, superior to every subjection and removed from every dissimilitude, ever desiring lordship; and, insofar as possible, excellently and beautifully conforming both itself and those after it to the likeness of that power which naturally subsists; turned toward none of the things that seem vain, but toward the universal Being properly so called, and made ever a participant, insofar as possible for it, in the God-formed likeness of lordship itself.”

All these things are taught by the designation “dominions.” For in being called dominions, they are signified to possess and do all these things that have been said of them. This is what he says: “I consider the manifestive designation of the holy dominions,” that is, the designation by which their virtue, excellence, and dignity are manifested and declared—I consider, he says, that this designation declares all these things. What things? Hear: “For they are many.” Therefore I said “all these things”: they are many for us, though few for them.

“I consider,” he says, “the designation of the holy dominions to declare a certain free elevation,” that is, a freedom alien from every depression, “anagoge,” that is, their excellence, sublimity, or upward leading, by which they are raised to the highest point, so that they are subject to none below the highest. I also consider that this designation declares that their anagoge or excellence is in no way at all bent by any tyrannical dissimilarity—that is, by any tyrannical dissimilarity, or according to any tyranny wholly unlike their dominion. As though he said: Just as by universal excellence they are elevated above every subjection, so they are inclined by no tyranny toward oppressing those subject to them.

It follows: “A dominion liberally severe, set above every slavery that diminishes.” From the preceding words one must understand, “I consider the designation of the dominions to declare their dominion”—a dominion liberally severe, that is, kindly severe: possessing severity in power and liberality in kindness. It is severe because power is exercised from above; it is liberal because freedom is not taken away from one below. Therefore it is a dominion liberally severe, set above every slavery that diminishes [Col. 1075D], that is, subject to none for a servitude which diminishes freedom; superior to every subjection; removed from every dissimilitude, that is, from every inferiority or imperfection which might make it unlike its Creator; and ever desiring lordship—that is, by likeness to lordship and conformity to its Creator, looking toward, tending toward, or cleaving to Him. And it conforms both itself and those after it so that each, insofar as possible, may imitate divine power excellently and beautifully.

Therefore, he says, “I consider their designation to declare a dominion conforming itself and those after it to divine power, and turned toward none of the things that seem vain, but toward the universal Being properly so called.” He uses “things seeing” (*videntium*) for what he ought to have called “things seen” (*visorum*), according to a very common Greek usage, because it is derived from the verb δοκοῦμαι, that is, “I see” or “I seem,” since the verb is common. The meaning, then, is this: I consider it to declare one turned not toward any of the things which appear vain—that is, which, considered in themselves, appear lowly and transitory—but rather turned toward the universal Being properly so called, that is, toward that which is properly and universally: namely God, to whom being belongs properly because He subsists through Himself, and universally because He grants being to all things.

It should be known that ὄν (*on*), among the Greeks, when written with ὄμικρον, the short or small *o*, is neuter and means “that which is”; but when written ὤν with ωμέγα, the long or great *ō*, it is masculine and means “he who is.” Thus *on* is the Creator and principle of all things: He who is, and that which is properly in Himself and universally toward all things. He says that this dominion is turned toward that principle and made a participant—that is, made a partaker—of the God-formed likeness of lordship, which it always, that is, unchangeably, retains; made, I say, insofar as is possible for it. Up to this point he has shown what the designation of dominions signifies; now he proceeds to show what the designation of virtues signifies.

It follows: “But I consider the designation of the holy virtues to declare a certain strong and unchangeable manliness in all their operations according to their God-likeness, not feebly weakened for any reception of the divine illuminations bestowed upon them, powerfully led back into imitation of God; not abandoning its God-formed motion through any weakness of itself, but bearing itself firmly upward to the superessential and power-making might, made, insofar as is permitted, an image like that might, and powerfully turned toward it as the principal might, proceeding God-formingly toward secondary things by giving power.”

“I consider,” he says, “the designation of the holy virtues”—understand “to declare”—a certain manliness strong and unchangeable in all operations: a manliness bestowed upon them according to their God-likeness, because they are like or conformed to God in this, that they have merited to receive a strong and unchangeable manliness or power for doing all things. For divine power is strong in acting, so that it is not broken by the difficulty of any work; and unchangeable in perseverance, so that it does not languish or grow weak through length of duration. In this, then, the virtues are God-formed and therefore alike: that they have a strong and unchangeable strength for doing all things.

Nor do they have only a manliness strong and unchangeable for doing all things beneath them; they also have a manliness or power not feebly weakened [Col. 1077A] for the reception of the divine illuminations bestowed upon them. For they are strong in carrying out works, and they are also strong in receiving gifts; because, although their power is weak when compared with divine power, it is nevertheless not weakened when conformed to the divine. It is weak by condition, in that it cannot receive all that belongs properly to the Creator; but it is not weak by corruption, in that it receives all that is due to a creature. Therefore it is not feebly weakened: though it does not have power equal to the Creator’s, it nevertheless has strength sufficient for a creature.

Therefore it has a manliness strong and unchangeable for carrying out what is to be done, and not weakened for receiving gifts; and it is powerfully led back—that is, turned or reformed—in imitation of God, so that it may imitate God. It is led back indeed by illuminations, into imitation by operations. And it has a manliness which does not abandon its God-formed motion through any weakness of itself. He calls “God-formed motion” the fact that these celestial virtues move unceasingly to imitate God: either by desiring to receive from above what He has, that they may be the same with Him; or by doing below what He does, that they may not depart from Him.

Thus they have a manliness which does not abandon God-formed motion, but through that God-formed motion firmly bears or lifts itself up to the superessential and power-making might of the Creator; and thereby is made an image like the power of that Creator, insofar as is permitted—that is, insofar as it is granted or possible for them. For in this, that their manliness through God-formed motion is lifted up to the Creator’s superessential and power-making might, it is shown to become an image and likeness of that divine power.

Therefore, he says, I consider their manliness made an image like divine power and turned toward that divine power as toward the principal power; while toward secondary things it gives power and proceeds God-formingly. Thus, he says, the designation of virtues teaches that their manliness is turned toward the higher power of God, so that it may receive God-likeness from it as from the first source; and it also teaches that it proceeds toward secondary things—that is, toward the following orders—so as to proceed to them God-formingly, giving them power and, in that power, conformity to God, so that it may both receive that God-likeness from what is above and impart it to what is below: receive it by gift, impart it by example.

“Next: ‘I consider the [designation] of the holy Powers to signify an order equal in power to the divine Dominions and Virtues; well adorned and unconfused in its reception of divine things; an order of supramundane and intellectual power, not tyrannically precipitated by its powers of command toward things below, but powerfully turned toward divine things after those which are well ordered; which, after itself, leads others back in a godlike manner; which is assimilated, so far as is lawful, to the power-making causal Power; and which reveals that Power to the angels, by a ruling power, in the orders well adorned through it.’” After the designation of the Virtues he passes to that of the Powers. By “the [designation] of the holy Powers” (the word *designation* being understood), I consider him to declare an order equal in power to the divine Dominions and Virtues—that is, an order of equal power with the Dominions and Virtues—well adorned and unconfused in the reception of divine things, that is, in receiving divine gifts. For the gifts of God which it receives for the adornment of spiritual beauty it preserves, humbly remaining in its own rank and order without confusion.

I also consider the designation of the Powers to declare an ordered supramundane and intellectual power: a power, I say, not tyrannically precipitated toward things below with powers of command, that is, with violent strength; but rather powerfully led back or turned toward divine things after those which are well ordered, that is, after the Virtues which are ordered before it. And it declares a power which leads back in a godlike manner—that is, according to divine likeness—those things which are after it, namely the orders of angels which follow it. For just as it is itself turned, through the mediation of those above it, toward likeness to God, so through its mediation the things below it are recalled to that same likeness of God.

He continues: the Powers are assimilated, so far as is lawful—that is, permitted or granted—to the power-making causal Power, because it can do all things and is the cause of all things. And I mean a power revealing that divine Power, so far as it is possible to reveal it to the angels. How does it reveal it? By ruling power. Where does it reveal it? In the orders well adorned through it—that is, in the subsequent orders which it adorns, revealing the divine Power to them by its own example.

“Next: ‘The middle disposition of the heavenly minds, possessing these godlike properties, is purified, illuminated, and perfected, as has been said, by the divine illuminations bestowed upon it in the second place through the disposition of the first hierarchy, and conveyed through that middle hierarchy in a second manifestation.’” The middle disposition of the heavenly minds, he says—that which has hitherto been discussed and consists of Dominions, Virtues, and Powers—possessing these godlike properties, namely those mentioned above, is purified, illuminated, and perfected, as was said above concerning the first hierarchy. It is purified, I say, by divine illuminations bestowed upon it in the second place, through the first hierarchical disposition.

The first hierarchical disposition consists of the three first orders: Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones. It receives divine illuminations immediately from the Godhead in the first place. When those illuminations are afterwards conveyed, in a second manifestation, through that middle hierarchy to the second hierarchy, the second hierarchy itself is purified, illuminated, and perfected in the second place by those same divine illuminations.

“Next: ‘Thus, by a saying uttered by one angel and then coming to be heard by another angel, we shall make a symbol of perfection far beyond all perfection, hidden in itself and proceeding into what follows.’” By example and authority he proves what he had said: namely, that the middle disposition of angels is illuminated by the first, or through the first. This is what he means by, “We shall make a symbol,” that is, an example or demonstration, of divine perfection, far beyond all things perfect and hidden in itself as it proceeds into what follows. For although it is hidden and invisible in itself, yet by its procession it goes forth and is manifested in those that follow: either in those immediately after it in the first rank, or in those who follow after them.

Of such divine perfection—perfect and hidden in itself, yet proceeding into those that follow by the bestowal of grace—we shall make a symbol by a saying, that is, a word or discourse uttered by one angel and subsequently reaching another angel and heard by him. For in the fact that one angel spoke and another heard, one communicated teaching and another received it, a symbol was made—that is, a demonstration or proof—that divine perfection proceeds to be shared from the prior and higher beings to the following and lower.

“For the wise concerning our sacred rites say that the self-luminous plenitudes of divine things are more perfect than those who participate contemplatively through others.” It is as if he said: It is not surprising that, among angels, one taught and another was taught, since one is more learned than another. For those who are wise concerning our sacred rites—that is, our sacrifices or sacraments—say that the plenitudes of divine things, namely those angels who are full of divine gifts or illuminations and shine by themselves, are more perfect than others in contemplative participations. He has used the genitive for the ablative. Those, he says, who are wise or skilled in our sacraments testify that those angelic spirits who receive divine contemplation immediately through themselves are more perfect than the rest, who share that same contemplation through the mediation of those above them.

“Next: ‘So I consider the immediate participation of the angelic orders which are first stretched out toward God to be more perfect than participation through the mediation of those who are perfect.’” Since the wise, he says, testify to this, I too consider the immediate participation of the angelic orders first stretched out toward God—that is, those angelic orders which, in the first and chief place, are directed toward God and immediately participate in him—to be more perfect: that is, I consider them more perfect in participation than those perfected through mediation, namely than those who participate in the perfect through mediation.

“Next: ‘For this reason the perfecting, light-giving, and purifying powers of the first intellects are called, by our priestly tradition, [the powers] of those below them, as of beings led back through themselves into the superessential principle of all things, and made, so far as is lawful for them, participants in mystical purifications, illuminations, and perfections.’” It is as though he said: Because the higher spirits are more perfect than the lower and subsequent ones, therefore the first intellects—that is, the highest orders of angels—are called by our priestly tradition the perfecting, light-giving, and purifying powers of those below them. For through them the lower are perfected, purified, and illuminated. They are called powers “of those below,” as of beings led back through themselves—that is, by themselves—into the superessential principle of all, namely God; and as of lower beings made participants, so far as is lawful for them, in mystical purifications, illuminations, and perfections. Thus they are purified, illuminated, and perfected through those higher beings.

“Next: ‘For this has been divinely promulgated by the divine ordinance in every respect: that secondary beings participate in divine illuminations through the first.’” This, he says, has been divinely promulgated, or made manifest, universally in the divine ordinance: that secondaries everywhere participate in divine illuminations through first beings.

“Next: ‘Moreover, you will find this often expressed by the theologians.’” What I say, namely that secondaries participate in divine illuminations through first beings, you will find expressed—that is, clearly set forth and noted—in the sacred Scriptures by the theologians, that is, by those who reasoned and wrote concerning divine things.

“Next: ‘For when the divine and paternal philanthropy, chastising Israel for its sacred salvation as a nurse does, and delivering it to avenging and savage nations for correction, with an all-embracing transfer of its providential dealings toward the better, released it from captivity and mercifully restored it to its former beneficence: one of the theologians, Zechariah, saw one of the first angels, as I suppose, among those around God—for, as I have said, this designation “angelic” is common to all—learning from God himself consolatory words concerning this matter, as was said. He saw another of the subordinate angels coming to meet the first, as though to receive and perceive illumination; then instructed by him in the divine counsel, as by a high priest; and he saw this angel turn and teach the theologian that Jerusalem would be inhabited fruitfully by a multitude of people.’”

He proves the example which he had given. In the prophet Zechariah one reads that an angel, having received a command from God, went out and gave a command to another angel who met him: he was to run and announce to the prophet that Jerusalem would still be inhabited without walls. This is what he means by “when the divine and paternal philanthropy,” that is, the paternal mercy of God, “chastising as a nurse does.” That is, like a nurse who scourges a small child in order to correct him, God chastised Israel with the scourge of Babylonian captivity for its sacred salvation: so that while for a time he outwardly destroyed it bodily, he might inwardly save it by restoring it to holiness.

Thus the mercy of God, chastising Israel paternally and delivering it for correction—that is, delivering it to the Chaldean nations in order that it might be corrected—delivered it to nations which were avenging and savage. They avenged God’s injury, yet they did so not with zeal for justice but with the fury of cruelty. He delivered Israel over for transfer: that it might be transferred from its homeland into exile, from its own land into a foreign land, from Jerusalem into Babylon, from the vision of peace into the captivity of confusion. This transfer was all-embracing—that is, universal or general—of all providential dealings toward the better, namely toward the salvation of the predestined.

For in that captivity and restoration, performed bodily in one people, a pattern was displayed of all the elect who were to be freed from the captivity of sin. Therefore, when divine mercy, delivering Israel in such a transfer with paternal purpose, afterwards released it from captivity and mercifully restored Israel itself to its former beneficence, then one of the theologians, namely Zechariah, “saw one of the first angels”: that is, one of the foremost angels, one of those excellent, superior angels who stand about God.

He says, “one of the first, as I suppose,” for theology does not say that this angel was one of the first. But I suppose that he was one of the first because he did not receive an order from another before him, but gave a command to the second. Therefore, he says, “I suppose” that this one was among the first angels. How can he be among the first angels, when those first are not angels, since only the last and lowest are called angels? I do not use “angel” in that sense. Rather, since, as stated above, this designation “angelic” is sometimes common to all, I now call the highest orders angels.

Thus Zechariah, one of the theologians, saw one of the first angels learning consolatory words from God himself concerning this affair of Israel’s captivity and restoration, as was said in the prophecy of Zechariah himself. He also saw another of the subordinate angels coming to meet the first angel—that is, going out or preceding him, running ahead before being called—as though ready and devoutly prepared in himself to receive and perceive the illumination which he was to receive from him. Then Zechariah saw that second angel instructed in counsel by the first angel, as by a high priest, that is, as by one superior and bestowing sacred things. He also saw the same second angel subsequently turn to teach the theologian: turning from the first angel, to whom he had been attending, toward the theologian, namely Zechariah himself, in order to teach him the divine counsel which he had learned from the first angel; while the first angel had learned it from God.

This was the counsel which he announced: “Jerusalem shall be inhabited fruitfully,” that is, abundantly, “by a multitude of people.” Another translation says: “Jerusalem shall be inhabited without walls” [Col. 1082A]. The sense is the same: after the slaughter wrought in the captivity, by divine grace that people was to be multiplied so greatly that the multitude of inhabitants could not be enclosed within the circuit of Jerusalem’s walls.

“Next: ‘The other theologian, Ezekiel, says that this was most sacredly promulgated to the Cherubim by the glorious Godhead itself, established in unshakable firmness.’” By the testimony of another theologian he proves what he said: namely, that divine counsels, received immediately by the first angels, are then conveyed through lower angels even to the minds of theologians. This is what he says: “The other theologian, Ezekiel,” says that this divine counsel was most sacredly promulgated by the glorious Godhead itself, firmly established in majesty and eternity, to the Cherubim. From whom was it afterwards made more fully manifest to the subsequent orders?

“For the philanthropy which is commander of the host, as has been said, leading Israel toward the better through disciplines, condemned the guilty and justified the corrected; and this is answered to the correcting angels by divine justice.” Philanthropy, he says—that is, mercy, the commander of the host or mistress of discipline—leading Israel toward the better through disciplines, condemned the guilty and justified the corrected. This judgment, he says, is answered from divine justice to the correcting angels sent to punish: divine mercy brought in the scourges in order to condemn the reprobate and justify those corrected.

Or divine justice answers the correcting angels what is just: that the reprobate be condemned and the corrected justified. Or, to the correcting Chaldeans—that is, the persecutors through whom God scourged and corrected his people—divine justice answers that they should receive according to their deserts; but divine mercy justified the corrected Israelites.

“This is taught to the first one after the Cherubim, girded about the loins with sapphire, who was clothed in a robe reaching to the feet according to the hierarchical symbol.” This divine counsel of condemnation and justification, he says, is taught to the one placed first after the Cherubim, who was clothed in the robe reaching to the feet according to the hierarchical symbol. For the appearance, after the Cherubim, of a certain one girded about the loins with sapphire and clothed in such a robe was a hierarchical symbol—that is, a hierarchical figure—because hierarchy uses visible figures to demonstrate invisible things.

And not only was the divine counsel taught to him who was first after the Cherubim, but also to those who followed. For this is what he adds: divine ordinance commands the other angels who had axes to be taught by the first one concerning this divine judgment. Concerning this counsel or work, divine ordinance commands the Cherubim that “the other angels be taught by him” who was first after the Cherubim: so that the divine command might descend first to the Cherubim, then through the Cherubim to the nearest one clothed in the robe reaching to the feet, and finally through him reach the subsequent angels who were prepared with axes.

“Next: ‘For to him indeed it said to pass through the midst of Jerusalem and place a mark upon the foreheads of the men who had been corrected.’” Or “to him,” that is, to the Cherubim, divine ordinance said that he should command his follower to pass through the midst of Jerusalem, and so forth. Or “to him,” namely to the one following after the Cherubim, it said through the Cherubim, “Pass through the midst of Jerusalem,” and so forth.

And it gave a command not only through the Cherubim to that one, but also to the others following after him. This is what follows: “Go out into the city after him and strike; and let not your eyes spare. But do not draw near to any upon whom is the mark.” All these matters drawn from prophetic visions serve to show that the first and highest angels are instructed by God himself, the second by the first, and the third by the second.

“Next: ‘What, perhaps, might someone say about the angel who said to Daniel, “A word has gone forth”? Or about that first one himself who received fire from the midst of the Cherubim? Or about this further feature of the same account, which gives a fuller display of angelic order: that the Cherubim put fire into the hands of the one clothed in the holy garment? Or about the angel calling the most divine Gabriel and saying to him, “Make him understand the vision”? Or about whatever else the sacred theologians have said concerning the godlike adornment of the heavenly hierarchies, to which the ordering of our hierarchy, so far as possible, is assimilated—possessing angelic beauty in its forms, shaped through it and led back to the superessential [principle] of every hierarchy?’”

In these prophetic testimonies, as we said above, he intends to prove only this: that among angels some teach others, and that lower angels receive command and instruction from higher angels; likewise, when human beings are instructed by angels, lower beings receive knowledge from higher. For what could anyone say concerning the angel saying to Daniel, except that an inferior is instructed by a superior and receives teaching? Or what could anyone say concerning that first one, mentioned above after the Cherubim, who was clothed in the robe reaching to the feet and received fire from the midst of the Cherubim, except likewise that one is shown to receive from another what he cannot possess in himself?

Or what else is that further feature of the same vision or example, which affords a fuller and more abundant demonstration of angelic order—that is, showing that among angels some orders are appointed above others—namely that the Cherubim puts fire into the hands of the one clothed in the holy garment, unless it plainly shows that dispensation occurs through one to another?

The testimony from Ezekiel’s vision, from which this is taken, is inferred rather than expounded: because the fact that this first one after the Cherubim, clothed in the holy garment or robe reaching to the feet, is commanded to receive fire from the midst of the Cherubim makes it reasonably believed that he received the same fire from the Cherubim itself. What, then, could anyone say of this except that the divine bestowal is plainly shown to pass from some to others?

Or again, what could anyone say of the angel calling the most divine Gabriel and saying to him, “Make him understand the word [the vision],” except that according to the ordering of the same disposition divine command descends through some to others, and that those who are higher command lower beings concerning what is to be done, just as they indicate what is to be known? Of these, then, and of all other things whatever which sacred theologians have said concerning the godlike adornment of the heavenly hierarchies, what could anyone say except what has been stated above?

The ordering of our hierarchy—that is, the human or ecclesiastical hierarchy—is assimilated to that adornment of the heavenly hierarchies; and so far as it is able to be assimilated, it shall possess angelic beauty through that likeness, so far as it has it in *characters*, that is, figures and likenesses. For as much as it now possesses in the figure of likeness, so much it shall afterward possess in the height of glorification. It now has a character and sign in a figure; then it will possess the reality and truth in glory.

Some have attempted to interpret these *characters* in an alien manner, setting before those who contemplate in that future glory of heavenly blessedness certain fantasies and images of errors in place of God, while asserting that God in his substance is never visible to anyone. But we do not await blessedness in the contemplation of figures, to whom the truth itself has been promised.

Therefore the disposition of our hierarchy, formed after the angelic adornment, will possess in glory as much beauty as it now possesses likeness in characters and figure. It is now formed through that adornment: that is, both according to that angelic adornment and, through the mediation of the same angelic adornment, led back to the superessential [principle] of every hierarchy—that is, restored to the likeness of God, who is superessential to every hierarchy. For from him every hierarchy has not only its form but also its substance; for he has not only instituted but also created every hierarchy, that it might be after him in likeness and beneath him in creaturely condition.

# BOOK NINE

[Col. 1083]

## TITLE OF CHAPTER IX: Concerning Principalities, Archangels, and Angels, and their final hierarchy.

## TEXT

[Col. 1083D]

“The remaining adornment for our contemplation, completing the angelic hierarchies, is that disposed by the godlike Principalities, Archangels, and Angels. First, I consider it necessary to state, so far as it is possible for me, the meanings of their sacred designations. For the designation of the heavenly Principalities reveals their godlike princely leading, together with sacred order and most fitting princely powers; their universal conversion to the super-princely Principle; their hierarchical guidance of others; their formation, so far as possible, after that princely Principle itself; and their manifestation of its superessential ordering and of the adornment of princely powers.

“The designation of the holy Archangels is indeed equal in power to the heavenly Principalities. For, as I said, there is one hierarchy and disposition of them and of the Angels. Yet because there is no hierarchy which does not possess first, middle, and last powers, the holy order of Archangels is admitted as sharing in the hierarchical middle of the extremes. For it shares with the most sacred Principalities and with the holy Angels: with the former, because it is turned in a princely manner toward the superessential Principle and, so far as possible, re-formed after it, and because it unifies the Angels according to its well-ordered, orderly, and invisible leadings; but with the latter, because it belongs to a prophetic order, receiving divine illuminations hierarchically through the first powers, announcing them in a godlike manner to the Angels, and through the Angels manifesting them to us according to the sacred proportion of each who is divinely illuminated.

“For the Angels, as we have already said, completely bring to completion all the dispositions of heavenly minds, according as they are to be completed. For they possess the angelic property among the heavenly essences; and they are more suitably called Angels among us than are the prior orders, inasmuch as their hierarchy and adornment are concerned more with what is manifest.

“For the most excellent disposition, as has been said, must be understood to order the second as that which first approaches, in due order, the hidden [reality]. The second, completed by the holy Dominions, Virtues, and Powers, presides over the hierarchy consisting of Principalities, Archangels, and Angels: more manifestly over the first hierarchy, but more hiddenly over that which follows it. The manifestive disposition of Principalities, Archangels, and Angels directs the human hierarchies in sequence, in order that there may be ascent, conversion, communion, and unity toward God according to order; and likewise the procession from God, most excellently bestowed upon all hierarchical beings and communicatively coming upon them, with most sacred adornment.

“Accordingly theology assigns our hierarchy to angels, naming Michael the ruler of the Jewish people (Dan. 10), and different [angels] over the other nations. For ‘the Most High established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God’ (Deut. 32). If anyone should ask how the Hebrew people alone was led back into divine illuminations, one must reply that the right dominions of the angels over other nations must not be blamed for their error regarding non-existent gods. Rather, those nations themselves, through their own inclinations, fell away from the right leading toward the divine, through self-love, pride, and the worship of things that seemed to them divine and rational. The Hebrew people itself is said to have suffered this: ‘You rejected the knowledge of God,’ he says, ‘and went after your own heart’ (Hos. 4; Jer. 2).

“For we do not possess a compelled life; nor are the divine lights of provident illumination revealed by the mere power of providential beings. Rather, the dissimilarity of intellectual visions either makes the gift of light from the superabundant paternal goodness wholly unshared, because it is not distributed for their reformation, or makes the participations diverse—small or great, obscure or clear—of the one, simple, ever unchanging, superabundant fountain-ray.

“Further, among the other nations also—from which we too have looked toward the great and abundant sea of divine light, prepared and open to be handed down to all—not certain foreign gods, but the one Principle of all ruled; and angels, exercising priestly office in each nation, led their followers back to him. Melchizedek must be understood as the high priest who was most dear to the Lord of beings—not of non-beings, but of the truly existent, most high God. For thus the God-wise writers simply called Melchizedek not merely a friend of God but also a priest (Gen. 14), evidently to signify to the wise that he not only converted those under him to the God who truly is, but also, as high priest, led others back to the true and sole Godhead.

“And we shall remind your supremely priestly understanding that, when an angel ruled Pharaoh among the Egyptians (Gen. 41), and another proper ruler presided over the prince of the Babylonians, ministers and leaders of the true God were appointed over those nations, in accordance with the divisions of all providence and lordship. By the manifestation of angelic vision, angels continually revealed from God through angels to the holy men Joseph and Daniel (Dan. 2).

“For there is one Principle and one providence of all. It must in no way be thought that the Jews fully declared the Godhead, whereas angels ruled other nations separately, with equal honour, in opposition, or as certain gods. Rather, that utterance must be understood according to its sacred meaning: not as though God endured our guidance to be shared with other gods or angels, being content with rule over Israel and leadership of the Israelite nation.

“But [it means] that the one and highest providence simultaneously distributes all human beings for salvation through the restorative guidance of their own angels, while Israel, almost alone beyond all others, was turned toward the illumination and knowledge of the God who is. Hence theology, signifying that Israel had been made God’s own possession for the service of the true God, says, ‘The Lord’s portion was made’ (Ps. 134; Deut. 32; Isa. 19). Showing also that he distributed the other nations individually to certain holy angels so that they might know through them the one Principle of all, it says that Michael led the Jewish people (Dan. 10), plainly teaching us that there is one providence of all, superessentially set above all invisible and visible powers together. And all angels ruling over the individual nations, following him as their own Principle, extend every power toward him by an essential will.

## EXPOSITION

“The remaining adornment for our contemplation, completing the angelic hierarchies, is that disposed by the godlike Principalities, Archangels, and Angels.” The words are plain. The adornment completing the angelic hierarchies, he says, disposed by the godlike Principalities, Archangels, and Angels, remains for our contemplation. That is, it now remains for us to contemplate or consider the adornment—that is, the beautiful disposition—of the angelic hierarchy, which is, as it were, the conclusion and end of the two preceding [hierarchies], and in which three orders are disposed: Principalities, Angels, and Archangels.

[Col. 1087B] He continues: “First, I consider it necessary to state, so far as it is possible for me, the meanings of their sacred designations.” I consider it necessary, he says, first to state the meanings of their designations, so that their properties may be made manifest through the interpretation of their designations. Thus he considers it necessary first to explain why in this final hierarchy some are called Principalities, others Archangels, and others Angels: because their respective properties are made manifest from the distinctness of their designations.

This is what he adds: “For the designation of the heavenly Principalities reveals their godlike princely leading, together with sacred order and most fitting princely powers; their universal conversion to the super-princely Principle; their hierarchical guidance of others; their formation, so far as possible, after that princely Principle itself; and their manifestation of its superessential ordering and of the adornment of princely powers.”

He explains what the individual designations in this final hierarchy signify, and first treats the designation of Principalities. He shows that the designation itself reveals their godlike princely leading—that is, the princely guidance which they possess after the likeness of God. For just as God is the one and supreme Prince of all, so they are princes and leaders of the angels and human beings subject to them.

This leadership, therefore, their designation reveals together with sacred order and most fitting princely powers, because they possess this leadership both from sacred order and from princely powers. They are leaders and princes of others both because they have been appointed to this office and because they surpass the rest in princely powers.

He continues: “And their universal conversion to the super-princely Principle.” The designation of the Principalities, he says, also reveals that the powers which they possess are universally turned toward the super-princely Principle, namely God. Their designation also signifies that they guide other powers—that is, the powers of others—to that same princely Principle, so far as possible causing those powers to be formed after it or conformed to it. They guide them hierarchically, that is, according to the mode and measure of their pre-eminence.

For they lead their own powers to their Principle by universally turning them; they lead the powers of others to their Principle by taking precedence hierarchically. For they have the power to lead only insofar as they ought to precede or preside. Therefore they lead hierarchically, because where they are not prelates, they cannot rightly be leaders. Their designation therefore reveals that they possess principality after the likeness of God, by office and power; that they turn their own powers toward their Principle and guide the powers of others; and that the adornment of these princely powers—that is, the disposition of the Principalities themselves—manifests the superessential ordering of that first Principle. For the designation of Principalities itself indicates that the first Principality is manifested in their pre-eminence, because in ruling they both imitate and manifest it.

It follows: “The very designation of the holy archangels is indeed of equal power with the heavenly principalities. For, as I have said, there is one hierarchy and one ordering of them and of the angels.” The designation itself—understood as “of the holy archangels”—“is of equal power,” that is, signifies an equal or equivalent power, “with the heavenly principalities,” because there is one hierarchy and one ordering of the three orders, [Col. 1088C] namely, of the angels, of the archangels, and of the principalities. And although, from the fact that there is one hierarchy, there is also one and equal authority among the three, nevertheless, because there is no hierarchy that does not have first, middle, and last orders, the archangels, placed midway between the principalities, which are first, and the angels, which are last, share in the property of both. This is what he says: “But since there is no hierarchy which does not possess first, middle, and last powers, the holy order of the archangels is received into the communicative middle of the hierarchy’s extremes.” Since, he says, there is no hierarchy that does not have first, middle, and last powers, [Col. 1088D] therefore “the holy order of archangels is received into the communicative middle of the hierarchy’s extremes”: that is, it is received so as to be in the middle, sharing in the hierarchy of the extremes—that is, in their sacred authority; or it is received into the hierarchical middle, that is, to possess a hierarchical middle which communicates the properties of the extremes. This is what follows: “For it shares both in the most sacred principalities and in the holy angels.” He subsequently shows in what respect it shares in each, saying: “With the former, because it is turned primarily toward the superessential Principle and, as far as possible, is re-formed unto it; and because it unifies the angels according to its well-adorned, ordered, and invisible leadings.”

In this respect, he says, the order of archangels shares with [Col. 1089A] the principalities in the same power: because “it is turned toward its superessential Principle and re-formed unto it,” as far as it is possible for it; and because it also unifies—that is, gathers into the unity of the same Principle—the angels following it, leading them according to the invisible and ordered guidances under which it must lead those subject to it and following it. Thus the order of archangels shares in the power of the principalities in that, after their likeness or imitation, it turns both itself and those following it toward its first Principle and gathers them together. Nor does the order of archangels share only with the principalities placed above it, but also with the angels placed below it. This is what he adds: “With the latter, because it receives divine illuminations hierarchically through the first [Col. 1089B] powers, belongs to the prophetic order, announces them to the angels in a godlike manner, and through the angels makes them manifest to us according to the sacred analogy of each of those divinely illuminated.”

With the former, that is, with the principalities, the order of archangels shares, as we have said above. With the latter, that is, with the angels, it shares in this: that it also belongs to the prophetic order—that is, it is a prophetic order, ordained for prophecy, declaring divine mysteries to the angels as inferiors. It receives divine illuminations through the first powers, that is, through the principalities, which are prior and higher. It receives them, I say, “hierarchically,” that is, as hierarchical order and disposition require: namely, that inferiors should receive their illuminations from superiors. “Receiving,” [Col. 1089C] I say, “and announcing them”—namely, the illuminations which it receives from its superiors—to the inferior angels. It announces them, however, in a godlike manner, so that in receiving from its superiors it preserves the hierarchical ordering, while in imparting to inferiors it does not depart from conformity to God, who, supreme over all, bestows his gifts for participation upon all who are subject to him. For to receive illumination from a superior is hierarchical; to give it to an inferior is divine.

Accordingly, the archangelic order, set in the middle according to the disposition of hierarchy, shares with both superiors and inferiors: receiving divine illuminations from the superior principalities, announcing them to the inferior angels, and through the angels [Col. 1089D] announcing these same divine illuminations to us, who are, as it were, last and lowest, according to the sacred analogy of each of those divinely illuminated—that is, according to the manner and measure of each one of us in receiving that same divine illumination. Or: it announces them to us through the angels according to the sacred analogy of each of those angels divinely illuminated; that is, they announce the divine illumination through each angel only insofar as each is fitted both to receive it within himself and to announce it through himself to others.

It follows: “For the angels themselves, as we have already said, completely bring to completion all the dispositions of the heavenly minds, according to what is to be completed.” As though he said: The archangelic order fittingly announces divine illuminations to us through the angels, because the angels themselves are last in the heavenly disposition and nearest to human beings; and in them all dispositions or orders of heavenly minds—that is, of angels—are completed, terminated, and brought to perfection. Thus the angels complete all the heavenly orders according to what is to be completed—understand, in their case; or, more explicitly, according to the manner in which the orders of angels themselves are to be completed. How the angels perfect or complete the heavenly orders he adds, saying: “For among the heavenly essences they possess the angelic property, and are more fittingly called angels among us than are the prior [Col. 1090A] orders, insofar as their hierarchy and their adornment are more concerned with what is manifest to us.”

It is not surprising, he says, that the heavenly orders terminate in them, because among all the heavenly essences it is their distinctive office to announce divine mysteries to us. They possess the angelic property in that it is their characteristic to be messengers to us. Therefore, among us they are more fittingly called angels than the prior or higher orders, insofar as their hierarchy—that is, their authority or office—is concerned with what is more manifest to us; and insofar as their adornment, disposition, or order is more “around,” that is, more circumscribable and intelligible to us, since by their ministry they draw near to visible things. Therefore their order is more “around,” that is, more knowable or comprehensible, [Col. 1090B] because it is nearer to us.

It follows: “For the most excellent disposition, as has been said, must be thought to order the second, as one first approaching the hidden One himself, secretly forming [form] it. And the second, which is completed by the holy dominations, powers, and authorities, must be thought to preside over the hierarchy which consists of principalities, archangels, and angels. The first hierarchy does so more manifestly; that which follows it, more hiddenly. And the manifesting disposition of principalities, archangels, and angels must, consequently, preside over human hierarchies, so that there may be ascent, conversion, participation, and unity toward God in due order.”

The most excellent disposition, that is, the highest hierarchy, must be thought, he says, to order the second, as first—that is, principally—approaching the hidden One himself, that is, God, secretly, or incomprehensibly, forming it. The second hierarchy, completed by the holy dominations, powers, and authorities, must be thought to preside over the hierarchy composed of principalities, archangels, and angels. The first hierarchy, that is, the highest, must be thought to receive divine illuminations more manifestly, or to preside more manifestly over the third; while that which follows it, that is, the second, presides more hiddenly. The disposition—that is, hierarchy—of principalities, archangels, and angels, [Col. 1090C] which manifests, that is, makes known and gives knowledge, must be thought to preside over human hierarchies consequently, that is, after it has been commanded by those above it. Thus there is, in due order, ascent, conversion, participation, and unity toward God: namely, so that human minds, converted through the lower hierarchy to the middle, and from the middle to the highest, may ascend to that one thing to be participated in, which is God.

It follows: “And there is also a procession from God, most excellently implanted in all hierarchical beings, coming upon them communicatively and with most sacred adornment.” In such an order, he says, the one Good is shared by all, proceeding from God into all hierarchical orders, so as to adorn them by coming upon them and being implanted in them through participation. This is what he says: “And there is also,” that is, likewise, a procession from God of that highest Good, implanted most excellently in all hierarchical orders, coming upon them “communicatively,” that is, for communication, and with most sacred adornment. For herein lies the greatness of the adornment of the divine disposition: though all participate in the one Good, it does not come to be communicated in one manner; rather, some receive it through others and in turn offer it for communication to those after them. Thus among those spirits the first hierarchy offers divine illuminations for communication to the second, the second to the third, and the third to ours—that is, the human hierarchy.

This is what he next adds, saying: “Therefore theology assigns our hierarchy to angels, naming Michael prince of the Jewish people, and others as rulers of the different nations.” Therefore, he says—that is, because inferiors are ruled by superiors—theology, that is, divine Scripture, assigns our hierarchy to angels for governance, naming Michael prince of the Jewish people and naming other angels as the different princes of the nations; as we read in Daniel that the prince of the Persians and the prince of the Greeks are named. Nor is it only in those testimonies that angels are proved to rule human beings: Scripture elsewhere also testifies, saying: “The Most High established the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God” (Dan. X). The boundaries—that is, the divisions or distributions—of the nations the Most High established according to the number [Col. 1091A] of the angels of God, because he adapted the number of nations to the number of angels, so that individual angels should preside over individual nations; although, because in another translation not angels but “sons of God” are named there, something else may seem to be signified.

It follows: “But if anyone should say: How was the people of the Hebrews alone brought back to divine illuminations? It must be answered that the righteous dominations of angels are not to be accused because the other nations erred into non-existent gods; rather, those nations themselves, by their own turnings away, fell from the straight leading-back toward the divine through self-love and pride, to the worship of things divinely and rationally shown to them.” [Col. 1092A] As though he said: It indeed appears surprising. If anyone, he says, wonders why the good angels allowed those nations over which they presided to fall away from knowledge of the true God, the answer is that this did not occur through the angels’ fault. The righteous dominations of angels ought not to be accused on account of the error of the other nations, those not from Israel, into non-existent gods—that is, because in their error they worshipped those who were not gods. Rather, those people themselves must be blamed: by their own turnings, that is, by their own will, falling away from the straight leading-back—that is, the knowledge through which a human being is led back to the divine—they believed gods to be gods who were not gods. They themselves, I say, are to be accused, because by their own will, insofar as they possessed free choice, they fell from truth into error, believing those to be gods who were not gods; and this through self-love, because they loved themselves more than God and sought their own glory, [Col. 1092B] and were therefore proud; and through pride concerning the things divinely shown to them—that is, things divinely revealed to them and also rationally shown to them for divine worship: matters from which they could reasonably or plausibly have understood how they ought to worship God. For, as the Apostle says: “Although they knew God, they did not glorify him as God; but they became vain in their reasonings. For, claiming to be wise [behold pride], they became fools, and their senseless heart was darkened [behold the error into non-existent gods], because they served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever” (Rom. I).

[Col. 1092C] Or “with God repaying them divinely and rationally”—understand, to them—“for worship”; that is, wisely and fittingly, as was proper for worshippers of false gods, namely the things shown to them, that is, those which appeared to them to be gods but were not. For in this God wisely and rationally repaid them: as the Apostle says, because they did not approve having God in knowledge, God gave them up to a reprobate mind, to do what they ought not in themselves. For they had to be punished in themselves, who had sinned in themselves.

[Col. 1092D] It follows: “This is also reported to have been suffered by the Hebrew people itself”: namely, that it departed from the worship of God, just as the other nations had departed into the worship of idols; or “this,” that is, a like divine vengeance, because it likewise departed from the worship of God and rejected the knowledge of God. For the divine voice says to Israel itself: “You rejected the knowledge of God, and went after your own heart.” Leaving God, namely, who is worshipped inwardly with a pure mind, you went outward through love of visible things, by which your heart—that is, perverse desire and will—was drawing you away. In all these matters the power of free choice appears, since, without compulsion, a human being, whether helped toward good or permitted toward evil, inclines by his own will. This is what follows: “For we do not have a compelled life.” A will can be given free to a rational creature, but it can in no way be compelled. And just as it is not within our power that the gift of divine illumination be offered to us, so it is only within our power that what is offered be received. For it is sometimes offered even when we do not will it, [Col. 1093A] but it is never received except when we will it. And when we will, we indeed will from God, because good will is God’s gift. But when we do not will, we do not will from ourselves, because not to will is nothing other than not to will: this is the abandonment of the good unto non-being and nothing—nothing that was made without him.

Therefore “the divine lights of provident illumination,” because through them God illuminates providently, are not “revealed through the proper power of providence”: that is, through the power of those who become provident by receiving them; or of those provided for, that is, those foreseen or predestined by God to receive them. It should be noted that where our text has “are revealed,” another text has “are darkened”; and though these differ, they nevertheless concern the establishment of the same truth: namely, that whether the divine lights are revealed—that is, made manifest—or darkened—that is, hidden and concealed—does not rest in the power of those receiving them, but in the will of the giver. [Col. 1093B] Yet although that manifestation or concealment is not in their power, reception never occurs except with their will, because it is a rational good that can be received only by one who knows and wills. Therefore it happens either through a perverse will that they are rejected entirely, or through a difference in good will that they are participated in differently. This is what he says: “But the dissimilarity of intellectual visions,” that is, of the spiritual eyes of rational minds, “causes the gift of light,” coming “from the superabundant,” that is, from the exceedingly full and excellently full paternal [Col. 1093C] goodness; this dissimilarity, I say, makes that gift either wholly unshared and undistributed for the reformation of those visions, or produces different participations—that is, small or great, dim or bright—of the one, fountain-like, simple, ever-unchanging, and super-diffused ray. [Col. 1093D] For the ray of divine illumination, descending from the fountain of goodness, is one and simple in itself and ever the same; it is super-diffused over all rational minds, and is shared by them differently, not according to its own simplicity but according to their diversity. Either they are perverse and entirely reject it, causing it not to be shared or distributed in any way for their reformation; or they are good in different ways and receive it differently.

It follows: “Further, for the other nations also, from whom we too have looked back toward it, there was prepared for all, open for imparting, the great and abundant sea of divine light; nor did foreign gods rule them, but the one Principle of all; and angels, exercising priesthood according to each nation, led those following them back to it.” As though he said: That good angels were set over the nations may be proved not only from the statement that the Most High established the boundaries of peoples according to the number of the angels of God, but also from the fact that foreign gods did not rule those nations from the beginning, but one God. For it is altogether probable [Col. 1094A] that the good Lord should have appointed good ministers under himself in his commonwealth. Through their ministry it also later came about that we, who believed from among the nations, looked through faith toward God and toward the fullness of his illumination, being led back through them; and they certainly would not have done this had they not been good.

This is what he says. Further, this too can prove that good angels were set over the nations: namely, that for those other nations, which were not from Israel, from whom nations we also, who later believe, have looked back—being converted through faith toward that great and abundant sea of divine light—this sea was prepared and open to all for imparting or bestowal, because it bestows and gives itself to all who will and desire to receive it. [Col. 1094B] Foreign gods did not rule those nations, although this might seem to be so because they worshipped idols and adored false gods. Rather, the one God ruled and governed them, because, just as there is one Principle of all from whom all things exist, so there is one Lord and ruler under whose authority all things are established. As he is good in himself, so he appointed good ministers under himself, angelic governors and guides; and those angels led us, who followed in faith, back to that Principle of ours. They led us back, I say, inasmuch as they exercised priesthood—that is, sacred pre-eminence—among each nation: that is, each angel, among the nation in which he exercised priesthood, that is sacred authority, brought to faith those who believed and looked back toward their Principle.

[Col. 1094C] It follows: “Melchizedek, it must be understood, was a high priest most dear to the Lord of beings—not of beings, but of the truly existing Most High God.” While treating of the ministry and office of angels, he suddenly introduces an account of Melchizedek; not because, as some have thought, he was himself an angel, or because he judges that Melchizedek’s priesthood should on that account be recalled among angelic ministries, but in order to show that the conversion of unbelievers from among the nations to faith and the worship of the true God was accomplished not only by the work and ministry of angels, but also by that of holy and God-pleasing human beings set over other human beings in divine matters.

[Col. 1094D] Accordingly, in the manner in which angels, by the office of their pre-eminence, exercised priesthood among the nations, converting them to faith in the true God, Melchizedek must be understood to have been a high priest most dear to the Lord of all beings—indeed, rather, of non-beings—but of the truly existing Most High God. The wording is perplexed, but this is its sense. Since he had said that Melchizedek was most dear to the Lord of all beings, he corrects his expression, because he had called “beings” those who truly are not, and adds “of non-beings,” according to what is written: “All nations are before him as though they were not” (Isa. XL). [Col. 1095A] And, as though it were asked who then exists, he adds: “The Most High God alone, who possesses true existence.” The reason he did not say “the truly existing Most High God,” but “of the truly existing Most High God,” is resemblance to the preceding expression, so that “of non-beings” might be answered by the same case: “of the truly existing Most High God.” Or it may be read thus: Melchizedek, most dear to the Lord of all beings, must be understood to have been priest not of merely any beings but of the truly existing Most High God, as it is written: “For he was priest of God Most High” (Gen. XIV).

[Col. 1095B] And it follows: “For thus the theologians simply called Melchizedek not only a friend of God but also a priest.” I rightly said, he says, that Melchizedek must be understood to be a priest, because the theologians—that is, those who write divine things—did not merely call him a friend of God, but also a priest. And why they called him a priest he adds, saying: “Was it not in order openly to signify to the wise that not only those from among them are converted to the God who truly is, but that he, as high priest, will also lead others by the leading-back which is toward the true and sole divinity?” That Melchizedek, who was not from the Jews, was called not only a friend of God but also priest of God—did they do this for that reason? Certainly they did so in order openly to signify to the wise that not only those from among them, that is, from Israel, who alone then seemed to have been led back and converted to divine knowledge, are converted to God himself, that is, to faith in and knowledge of God, who truly is; but that he will also lead many others from among the nations out of the darkness of ignorance by that leading-back which is toward the true and sole divinity, that is, toward knowledge of God.

[Col. 1095C] Not that Melchizedek himself is read to have converted any from Israel, which was not yet a people, unless perhaps Israel is understood in the earlier fathers, some of whom may perhaps in Melchizedek’s time have been led through him to knowledge of God. Or it may be read thus: he was called not only friend of God but priest also because he converted—understand, those who were ignorant and uninstructed—to God himself, in whom one must truly believe. And if someone should object that Melchizedek, who was not from Israel but was a foreigner, converted no one to faith in God because Israel alone knew God, the answer is that not only persons from Israel were converted to faith in God, but also many from the other nations; and the conversion of these others took place through Melchizedek. At that time, namely when he blessed Abraham, he was called priest of God Most High, though he was not from Israel, to show that he would lead many out to God and that God would have both priest and people not only in Israel but also among the nations. Therefore he did not say “he led out,” but “he will lead out.” With reference to the time when these words were spoken, he signifies the future: either the time when Melchizedek himself later converted persons from the nations to God, or when Christ, of whom he was a type, led many not only from Israel but also from all nations through faith into his Church, out of the darkness of unbelief.

It follows: “And this also we shall recall to your most priestly [Col. 1096A] understanding: that, when an angel ruled Pharaoh among the Egyptians and a proper governor presided over the prince of the Babylonians, all providence and the provident and authoritative power of dominion was distributed according to the divisions; and ministers of the true God were appointed as guides for those nations through the manifestation of vision-forms made by angels—visions continually revealed from God through angels to the holy men Joseph and Daniel.”

He adds yet another authority by which he wishes to prove that good angels were set by God over the nations: namely, that among the Egyptians an angel shows Pharaoh a vision and thereby warns him concerning the coming famine; that same vision being afterward manifested through Joseph. [Col. 1096B] Likewise, to the prince of the Babylonians, namely Nebuchadnezzar, his proper governor—that is, his own appointed superior, his own angel—forms a vision and afterward discloses it by explaining it through Daniel. In all these things it appears that God possesses both providence, dominion, and power over all things, according as this was set forth, distinguished, or distributed through those visions. The visions were first revealed to angels by God and then immediately, through angels, to the holy men Joseph and Daniel.

[Col. 1096C] This is what he says: O Timothy, we shall remind your most priestly understanding—that is, your understanding, you who are high priest—not only of the foregoing matters but also of this: that, when an angel ruled Pharaoh among the Egyptians and a proper governor, that is an angel set over him, ruled the prince of the Babylonians, the provident and authoritative power of divine providence and dominion was distributed according to those visions. That is, it was shown that God distributes his providence and power for governing individual nations; and it was also shown that ministers of the true God were appointed as guides for those nations. How this was shown he adds: through the manifestation of vision-forms made by angels—that is, of a vision in which forms or figures made by angels in the minds of the prophets were displayed to signify future events, such as the cows and ears of grain which Pharaoh saw (Gen. XLI), and the tree and statue which Nebuchadnezzar saw (Dan. II). By the manifestation of such a vision, therefore, divine providence and power, disposing the nations through angels, was shown: a vision, I say, first revealed to angels by God and then immediately revealed through angels from God to the holy men Joseph and Daniel.

[Col. 1097A] It follows: “For there is one Principle and providence of all; and it must in no way be thought that the Jews alone were led fully by the Divinity, while angels ruled the other nations either in a special manner, or with equal honour, or with opposing powers, or that certain other gods ruled them.” The repetition proves what he said above: that there is one Principle and providence of all—that is, one God from whom all things exist and by whom all things are ruled. Therefore one must in no way suppose that the Divinity led the Jews—that is, gave guidance to the Jews—fully or absolutely, that is, through itself without the mediating ministry of angels, while angels ruled the other nations specially, that is, in a particular manner or with less excellent authority; or with equal honour, that is, with authority equal to and like divine dominion; or with opposing powers—understand, dominions—such as the apostate angel is read to have claimed when he said he would set his seat in the north and would be like the Most High in power (Isa. XIV). Nor should one suppose that certain other gods ruled the other nations, as though all things were not subject to the power and dominion of the one true God.

[Col. 1097B] It must not, he says, be so understood as though the true God possesses authority only over the Jews, while either angels or other supposed gods rule the other nations by a power equal or unequal, yet contrary and foreign to divine dominion. Or it may be read thus: The Divinity must in no way be thought to have given leadership to the Jews through itself, without the interposition of the subject angelic power, while angels ruled the other nations in a special manner—that is, particularly, namely nations lower in authority and rank than the Jews; or with equal honour, namely nations equal in power and honour; or even in opposing nations, which were opposed and hostile to the Jews, attacking and oppressing them. It is not, he says, to be supposed that God led the Jews through himself because they were more honourable than all the other nations, while he left the other nations, as lower and more contemptible, to angelic dominion. For in other nations there were undoubtedly many not only equally honourable but also stronger and more powerful, who oppressed the Jews themselves by their power and strength.

[Col. 1097C] For the saying, “When the Most High divided the nations, he established the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the angels of God; but the Lord’s portion was his people, Jacob the cord of his inheritance,” must not be understood as though he gave the other nations to angels for governance while reserving Israel alone for himself—that is, for his own providence and government—so that either Israel should be ordered without angels by God himself or angels should order the remaining nations without him. For Michael is read to have been set over Israel, and God is recalled in sacred Scripture as possessing and governing all nations.

[Col. 1097D] Thus it must be understood that “that saying,” in which this is said to be taken, “is according to sacred understanding,” that is, according to an understanding which does not depart from what is sacred, namely from truth. This, however, is the sacred understanding: that we understand the saying not as if God, in dividing our guidance—that is, that of the human race—with certain other gods or angels, divided it into the sovereignty of Israel and the guidance of the nations, content himself with Israel—that is, with sovereignty in Israel—or retaining Israel to himself so that he alone might be its ruler and guide. It must not, I say, be understood thus. [Col. 1098A] Rather, it is to be understood as though the providence of the Most High—one and at the same time over all, because it provides for all—salvifically distributed all human beings among the restorative guidances of their respective angels: guidances by which, as blind persons in the darkness of ignorance, they might be led by the hand and restored to the light of truth; while Israel alone was converted to illumination and knowledge of the true God almost beyond all nations. For this reason Israel alone is read to have been received and led by God as his portion: [Col. 1098B] because it alone, at that time, of all nations was recalled to the knowledge of God and established in divine worship. “Therefore,” he says, “theology, signifying that he,” that is, God, “possessed Israel for service of the true God,” says: “The Lord’s portion came to be,” namely Israel itself. Thus Israel was his portion, being so possessed by him that it possessed and had him.

[Col. 1098C] It follows: “And, showing that he also distributed each of the other nations individually to a holy angel, it said that Michael led the Jewish people into knowledge through him of the one Principle of all.” In saying that Michael led the Jewish people, sacred Scripture plainly shows that God also distributed leadership among the other nations individually—that is, severally—to a holy angel; or, more explicitly, one leadership to one angel, or each to each, or individual charges to individuals. He distributed them, I say, so that each nation might know, through its angel, the one Principle of all, from whom all things exist and under whom all things are ruled. To show this, he says, sacred Scripture called Michael the leader of the Jewish people, whom God had specially undertaken to guard under his own providence and government.

[Col. 1098D] For in saying this, Scripture openly teaches us that there is one providence presiding over all things, under which the angels ruling the individual nations extend or advance those nations which follow them by essential will—that is, by naturally implanted free choice—toward their own Principle, namely by exhorting and helping them. Scripture, he says, called Michael the leader of the Jewish people, whose leader it had elsewhere recalled to be God himself. In this it “openly teaches us that there is one providence of all, superessentially set above all,” that is, presiding not only by power but also by nature over all invisible and visible powers, namely angels and human beings. For this is the good found in both. [Col. 1099A] It also shows that “all angels, ruling among the individual nations under that providence, extend each” nation—or the individual powers of those nations—toward God, understood, “as toward their own Principle”: powers, I say, “following by essential will,” that is, by natural free choice. For angels rouse human minds [Col. 1100A] to love God by suggesting virtues, not by the necessity of compulsion, but as “following by will.”

## CHAPTER X TITLE. Repetition of the Ordering of the Angelic Assembly.

[Col. 1099]

## TEXT.

[Col. 1099A]

Thus the most honorable ordering of souls about God, itself united in this way and ordered by perfecting illumination, ascends immediately into that illumination; being more hidden and more manifest, it is purified, illumined, and perfected by the illumination of the Godhead. More hidden indeed, [Col. 1099B] as more invisible, more simplified, and more unified; more manifest, however, because it shines from illumination given beforehand, and shines first, is more universal, and is more fully diffused into that form as is fitting. From it, again, the second hierarchy is proportionally led back; from the second, the third; and from the third, the hierarchy among us is led back, according to the law of the ordering that fittingly adorns, in divine harmony and proportion, to the preeminent principle and consummation of every good order, namely of hierarchy as a whole. All are manifesters and angels—that is, messengers—of those before them: the most honorable beings are messengers of God who moves them, while the rest are proportionally messengers of those moved by God. For the superessential harmony of all things has foreseen for each rational and intellectual being, through sacred adornment [Col. 1099C] and ordered guidance, only so much as each order of hierarchies has been sacredly and fittingly placed. And we see every hierarchy divided into first, middle, and last powers. Moreover, that same arrangement, to speak particularly of each, has been distinguished by the divine harmonies themselves. Therefore theologians say that even the most divine seraphim cry one to another (Isa. IV), plainly declaring, as I think, that those who are first transmit theological utterances to those who are second.

Perhaps I may also add, not incongruously, that every celestial and human soul, considered in itself, possesses its own first, middle, and last orders and powers, proportionally disclosed through the proper upward leadings of hierarchical illuminations in each case; [Col. 1099D] through these each becomes a participant, as is lawful and possible for it, in the utterly unknowable purification, the fullness of light, and the perfection that is perfect before all else. For nothing is perfect through itself and in need of universal perfection, except that which is truly most perfect and perfect-before-all.

## EXPOSITION

The title of the tenth chapter is: “A recapitulation of the angelic ordering of the Synagogue.” For here is briefly repeated what was said above: namely, that the Synagogue—that is, the assembly or multitude—of angels is ordered in all its first, second, and third ranks. The chapter begins thus:

“Thus the most honorable ordering of souls about God, itself united in this way and ordered by perfecting illumination, ascends immediately into that illumination; [Col. 1100A] being more hidden and more manifest, it is purified, illumined, and perfected by the illumination of the Godhead.”

He speaks of the first hierarchy, which consists of three orders: seraphim, cherubim, and thrones. This ordering or arrangement of souls—that is, of spirits—is the most honorable or excellent of all. [Col. 1100B] It is united about God: that is, both harmoniously joined among itself and immediately associated with God. It is so ordered by perfecting illumination—that is, divine illumination—which alone shines and illumines perfectly. For whoever are illumined by it are assimilated to it by shining, and imitate it by illumining others. Yet neither in their shining are they made equal to it, nor in their illumining are they comparable with it. Therefore this hierarchy, which alone is immediately illumined by that illumination, is uniquely ordered by perfecting illumination. Others, who receive lesser illuminations mediately, are fittingly disposed and ordered at a lower level.

But this hierarchy is ordered—or, to state it more expressly, is made pontifical, that is, elevated into a pontifical order or dignity—by perfecting, or *teletarchic*, divine illumination, which is the chief [Col. 1100C] of sanctification: that is, the first, greatest, and unique cause of sanctification. It is therefore fittingly set above all in dignity, ascending immediately into that illumination; being more hidden and more manifest, it is purified, illumined, and perfected by that same illumination of the Godhead.

How the first hierarchy, because it receives divine illumination immediately, is both more hidden and more manifest, he explains in the words following:

“More hidden indeed, as more invisible, more simplified and unified; more manifest, however, as that which shines from light previously given, shines first, is more universal, and is more fully diffused into that form as is fitting.”

It is more hidden, he says, because it is more invisible, more simplified, and more unified. It is more hidden insofar as it is more invisible and nearer to the simplicity and unity of the Godhead.
