It is more manifest, however, because it shines from light given to it beforehand—that is, before it was given to others—and therefore shines first and more excellently. It is also more manifest because it is more universal: in it one likeness exists in many, because what is more common and applies to more beings is more knowable.

He next shows why it is more universal and more like the divine form: because the form—that is, the divine illumination by which it is formed so as to shine—is more fully, that is, more expressly or abundantly, diffused into it than into the subordinate hierarchies. The sense is this: because divine illumination is first poured into this hierarchy, [Col. 1101A] it is thereby illumined more perfectly. And the more perfectly the spirits within it receive the one illumination, the more perfectly and clearly they shine, becoming one in the one form of the one light. What in them is variously distinguished by nature appears no longer dissimilar when one form of brightness comes upon all. Thus this hierarchy shines more perfectly because it shines earlier; and because it shines more perfectly, it shines more universally, more similarly, or more expressly. Because it shines more expressly, it shines more manifestly. Therefore what is essentially more hidden is formally more manifest; and what is subtler by nature is clearer by grace.

He continues:

“From it, again, the second hierarchy is proportionally led back; from the second, the third; and from the third, [Col. 1101B] the hierarchy among us is led back, according to the law of the ordering that fittingly adorns, in divine harmony and proportion, to the preeminent principle and consummation of every good order.”

From the first hierarchy, he says, the second is led back or converted; from the second, the third is converted; and from the third is converted the hierarchy that is among us. For the first angelic hierarchy converts the second, the second the third, and the third angelic hierarchy converts the human hierarchy.

He explains how it converts, saying: it leads back hierarchically to the preeminent principle and consummation of every good order—that is, to God, who is the principle and perfection of every good and beautiful arrangement. It leads back hierarchically, that is, according to the office, [Col. 1101C] ordering, or law of the hierarchies: in them it has been ordered that superiors, according to their measure and power, should convert inferiors to their principle by illumining and instructing them. They convert according to the law of the ordering that fittingly adorns: that is, the divine ordering that adorns all things. Its law and institution is that some are illumined by others and converted in divine harmony and proportion, that is, in the concord and proportion bestowed by God upon the universe. For when participation in the good is proportionally transmitted from some to others, concord in the universe is completed and perfected.

When he says that it is “again led back,” this should be understood as a second leading-back. The first leading-back occurs when the first beings, illumined by God himself, are converted to God himself. The second occurs when the second are led back by the first, or the third by the second. [Col. 1101D]

“All are manifesters and angels of those before them.” All celestial spirits, he says, are manifesters and angels, that is, messengers, of those before them. What they receive from those preceding them, they announce and make manifest to those who follow them.

He continues:

“The most honorable beings are messengers of God who moves them; the rest are proportionally messengers of those moved by God.”

He had said that all are messengers from those preceding them to those following. Now he distinguishes: the most honorable—that is, the most excellent—spirits, who have only God before them, are messengers of God himself, who moves them by inspiration so that through them he may reveal his secrets [Col. 1102A] to those who follow. The rest are messengers, to those who follow after them, of those moved by God.

They are messengers proportionally: that is, the second are messengers of the first, and of God through the first; the third, of the second and of the first through the second, and of God through the second and first; and the others who follow in this manner thereafter. How each reveals divine secrets proportionally he explains in what follows, showing that to each is given only as much power as accords with the order and position in which it is placed. This is what he says:

“For the superessential harmony of all things has foreseen for each rational and intellectual being, through sacred adornment and ordered guidance, only so much as each order of hierarchies has been sacredly and fittingly placed.” [Col. 1102B]

The superessential harmony, he says—that is, divine providence, which has disposed all things harmoniously—has foreseen for each rational or intellectual being only so much power or capacity, with sacred adornment and ordered guidance, namely adorning sacredly and leading in an ordered way, as each order of hierarchies has been sacredly and fittingly placed: that is, as befits the holiness and propriety of each order.

He then adds distinctions concerning the order in each hierarchy:

“And we see every hierarchy divided into first, middle, and last powers or orders.”

And this applies not only to each hierarchy, but also to each order throughout the several hierarchies. Thus he continues:

“Moreover, that same arrangement, to speak particularly of each, has been distinguished by the divine harmonies themselves.” [Col. 1102C]

Divine providence itself, he says, has distinguished or differentiated each arrangement—that is, each order—by divine harmonies, so that there might be distinction without discord. This must be said particularly of every hierarchy: individual orders possess particular distinctions.

He continues:

“Therefore theologians say that even the most divine seraphim cry one to another, plainly declaring, as I think, that those who are first transmit theological utterances to those who are second.”

Because individual orders are distinct within themselves, theologians therefore say that the seraphim—[Col. 1102D] who are most divine, that is, nearest to the Godhead—cry one to another, as is read in Isaiah (Isa. VI). In saying that they cry one to another, they plainly declare that those who are first in that order transmit theological—that is, divine—utterances to those who are second in the same order. It is thus clear that one and the same order has first and second members. If this is truly understood of the first and highest order, it cannot in any way be doubted concerning those that follow.

He continues:

“Perhaps I may also add, not incongruously, that every celestial and human soul, considered in itself, possesses its own first, middle, and last orders and powers, assigned through the proper upward leadings of hierarchical [Col. 1103A] illuminations proportionally manifested in each case; through these each becomes a participant, as is lawful and possible for it, in the utterly unknowable purification, the fullness of light, and the perfection that is perfect before all else.”

The meaning is this: not only is the universal hierarchy divided into first, middle, and last hierarchies; each hierarchy into first, middle, and last orders; and each order into first, middle, and last spirits; but individual angelic and human spirits themselves are virtually distinguished within themselves, containing first, middle, and last powers. Through these, by their own upward leadings—that is, liftings or ascents—they ascend proportionally through hierarchical illuminations, from the lowest to the middle and from the middle to the highest. [Col. 1103B] They thus become participants, as far as possible for them, in divine purification, which is utterly unknowable or hidden because it purifies inwardly; in divine light, which is fullest because it drives away all darkness; and in divine perfection, which is perfect before all else because it is prior to all in eternity, superior in dignity, and fuller in truth.

He calls hierarchical illuminations proportional because, in the sacred powers where some are constituted higher and others lower, not all receive divine illuminations in one manner. To the higher and more capacious, more is granted in gifts of grace; to the lower, a lesser participation is offered according to the measure of their capacity. Accordingly, as divine illuminations are bestowed differently upon different orders and souls in individual [Col. 1103C] hierarchies, each soul also advances within itself through those same illuminations, growing by a rational distinction from lesser things to greater.

This is what he means in saying, “Perhaps I may also add, not incongruously,” as though he said: I can fittingly state not only of individual hierarchies or orders that they have first, middle, and last orders or spirits; perhaps I may also fittingly add to what has been said that every celestial and human soul, according to itself or within itself, has particular—that is, proper—first, middle, and last orders and powers: namely, powers ordered in its first, middle, and last place.

He then states for what purpose it has differing powers: [Col. 1103D] namely, for its own upward leadings, [Col. 1104A] so that each may possess its own ascents and advances toward better things, as it is written: “He has set ascents in his heart” (Ps. LXXXIII); and again: “They go up from strength to strength; and the God of gods shall be seen in Zion.” For these upward leadings—that is, ascents—some powers are arranged as lower and others as higher, so that by ascending from lower things to higher, they may at last become participants in the highest good, which is the God of gods in Zion.

Every spirit, he says, has its own first, middle, and last powers for making its own upward leadings—that is, ascents. I mean the upward leadings already mentioned: those, namely, through each order of hierarchical illuminations. [Col. 1104B] For when we showed how distinct orders receive differing illuminations in the distribution of hierarchies, we also showed how inferiors rise proportionally—that is, by a rational difference of advancement—through superiors to the highest things.

Therefore he said: “upward leadings of hierarchical illuminations proportionally manifested,” that is, manifested in proportions; or manifested through the preceding discussion, in which it was shown that these ascents occur proportionally. Or the phrase may mean proportionally manifested because the more ascent increases, the more knowledge increases. For these ascents, therefore, grades of powers have been arranged, through which ascents each thing—that is, each soul ascending through them—becomes a participant [Col. 1104C] in the utterly unknowable purification, the fullness of light, and the perfection that is perfect before all else. It becomes a participant, I say, insofar as it is lawful and possible for it to become a participant: lawful with respect to the dignity of participating in the good, possible with respect to its own capacity.

He continues:

“For nothing is perfect through itself and in need of universal perfection, except that which is truly most perfect and perfect-before-all.”

Rightly, he says, did I call divine perfection “perfect-before-all,” because all things that are perfect are perfected from it. For nothing is perfect through itself; nothing is not through itself imperfect and in need through itself of invisible, or every, perfection, except that highest good, [Col. 1104D] which is truly most perfect because nothing is lacking to it, and perfect-before-all because its fullness is eternal.

## TITLE OF CHAPTER XI. Why all celestial essences are commonly called celestial powers.

[Col. 1103]

## TEXT

[Col. 1103D]

After these points have been defined, it is fitting to understand why we are accustomed alike to call all angelic essences celestial powers. For it must not be said, as in the case of angels, that the order of the holy powers is itself the last of all. The arrangements of the higher essences participate in the holy and beautiful illumination of the lowest; [Col. 1104D] but the lowest do not in any way participate in that of the first. Why, then, are all divine intellects called celestial powers, whereas seraphim, thrones, and dominions are by no means so called? For the lowest are participated in by the highest through their universal properties. Angels themselves, and archangels before angels, and principalities and powers after the virtues, are arranged by theology; yet they are often commonly called by us, together with the other [Col. 1105A] holy essences, celestial powers. But when we use the designation “celestial powers” commonly of all, we do not introduce some confusion of the properties of individual orders. Rather, since all divine intellects are divided in themselves, by a supramundane account, into essence, power, and operation, whenever we indiscriminately call all together, or some of them, celestial essences or celestial powers, we must understand that we signify those of whom we speak periphrastically, from the essence or power that belongs to each of them. For it is not easy for us to attach to lower essences the higher property of the holy powers, already distinguished by us, without overturning the unconfused ordering of angelic adornments. For, according to the explanation often rightly given by us, the more firmly established [Col. 1105B] orders abundantly possess even the sacred properties of the lower; but the last do not possess the higher universals of the greater, since the illuminations first appearing in them are distributed to them particularly through the first, proportionally.

## EXPOSITION

The title of the eleventh chapter is: “Why all celestial essences are commonly called powers.” The question is this: since only one order among the celestial spirits is called “powers,” why is this term bestowed commonly upon all? He says:

“After these points have been defined, it is fitting to understand why we are accustomed alike to call all angelic essences celestial powers.” [Col. 1105C]

This indeed is worthy of inquiry, because the reason here is not the same as that which we gave when we call all celestial essences angels. That is: the order of angels is the last; therefore its name is extended to the higher orders because they participate in its property. Since all higher orders participate in all the properties of the lower, they also fittingly sometimes assume their name. But we cannot say the same when we call all celestial spirits powers. Since some orders are lower than the powers themselves, they do not participate in the property of the higher orders and therefore seem not to participate in the name either.

This is what he says: “For it must not be said, as in the case of angels, that the order of the holy powers is itself the last of all.” [Col. 1105D] If this were true, it would not be surprising if all the other orders shared their name, because, as higher, they would share their property. Thus he continues: “The arrangements of the higher essences participate in the holy and beautiful illumination of the lowest essences,” that is, of the last spirits; “but the lowest arrangements do not in any way participate in the illumination of the first essences.”

He continues:

“Why, then, are all divine intellects called celestial powers, whereas seraphim, thrones, and dominions are by no means so called?” [Col. 1106A]

It is fitting, he says, to understand why all divine intellects are called celestial powers, though seraphim, thrones, and dominions are not called such in any way. That angels are so called is no wonder, because angels are last and their property is universally shared by the higher orders. This is what he says: “For the lowest essences,” such as angels, “are participated in by the highest powers” in all their properties. But the properties of higher beings do not come universally to be shared by lower beings. Therefore it is remarkable how angels, and those before angels—archangels, principalities, and powers—assume the name of powers when they do not participate in their property, since they are “arranged after the powers [Col. 1106B] by theology,” that is, are reported by divine Scripture as arranged after the powers. Yet “they are called by us celestial powers, alike with the other holy essences.”

He continues:

“But when we use the designation ‘celestial powers’ commonly of all, we do not introduce some confusion of the properties of individual orders.”

He now resolves why the name “powers” is assigned to lower orders. “We say,” he states, “that in using the designation ‘celestial powers’ commonly of all, we introduce no confusion in the properties of each arrangement.” That is, in making the name common, we do not confuse the distinctive property. Rather, when we call lower orders powers, we signify not the property of that particular order, but the power common to all.

For all divine intellects are divided into three, not one from another, but each according to itself or within itself, “by a supramundane account,” that is, spiritually. Their division does not arise from an analysis into parts, for there is no divisibility of essence there; rather it is a spiritual distinction, in which not a whole is divided into parts but a nature is distinguished by properties. He then adds the three things into which every spirit is divided in itself: “into essence, power, and operation.” In every spirit these three exist: first, essence, in which it subsists; next, power, by which it has capacity; then operation, [Col. 1106D] through which it acts.

“Therefore, when we call all together,” namely spirits, “or some of them, indiscriminately,” that is, without distinction or commonly, “either celestial essences or celestial powers, we must understand that we signify those of whom we speak periphrastically,” that is, by circumlocution, “from the essence or power that belongs to each of them”: namely from that which is common to all, not from what is properly peculiar and distinguishes the dignity of a particular order.

Why he refuses to attribute the particular property of one order to other subordinate orders he explains:

“For it is not easy for us to attach to lower essences the higher property of the holy powers, already distinguished by us,” that is, properly and particularly attributed to them, “without overturning [Col. 1107A] the ordering of the unconfused angelic adornments.” If I did so, I would overturn or pervert the ordering of angelic adornments, which is unconfused.

He shows how the ordering of angelic adornments—that is, of angelic orders beautifully or ornately arranged—is unconfused: they retain their own distinction and do not mingle with higher beings, whose properties they are not to share.

“The more firmly established arrangements,” that is, the higher orders, “abundantly,” or fully, “possess even the sacred properties of the lower; but the last do not possess the higher universals of the greater.”

A little earlier we said how, in that realm where God is all in all, something can be proper to one being without not also being common to all. Here too the author has not wholly passed over how this should be understood in what he says: “They possess abundantly.” Thus the property that belongs to higher beings and not to lower is understood in this: the higher possess abundantly whatever the lower possess, [Col. 1108A] whereas the lower do not abundantly possess whatever the higher possess.

For what can be so great there that it does not pass into the communion of all, where charity is common and greater than all? Therefore all things belong to all. Yet this alone is proper there: that something belongs abundantly to one which does not belong abundantly to all. The higher powers universally and abundantly possess the powers of the lower; but the lower do not equally possess the powers of the higher universally, that is, according to the whole fullness of divine illuminations “which first appear in them only particularly.” Not “first appearing in them,” but “first appearing particularly in them.” For in the others—that is, the higher—they appear first universally; then afterwards they are distributed through those first beings proportionally, that is, according to proportion and not according to their whole fullness. [Col. 1108B]

## TITLE OF CHAPTER XII. Why the hierarchs among human beings are called angels.

[Col. 1107]

## TEXT

[Col. 1107B]

This too is asked by those who study the intelligible utterances attentively. For if the last beings do not participate in the universalities of the higher powers, why is the high priest among us called by the utterances an angel of God Almighty? (Mal. II; Apoc. II.) Yet the explanation is not contrary, I think, to what has previously been defined. For we say that the last are excluded from the universal and higher power of the greater adornments. Yet they participate in a middle and proportional power, according to the one, all-joining fellowship of all. For example, the order of the holy cherubim participates in wisdom and higher knowledge. The arrangements of essences beneath them also participate in wisdom and knowledge, but in a particular and subordinate manner relative to them. To be in any way a participant in wisdom and knowledge is common to all godlike intellects; but to participate attentively, first, second, or lower, is by no means common, but belongs to each according to the analogy previously proper to it. No one, unless mistaken, would perhaps define this otherwise of all divine minds. For just as the first possess more abundantly the holy and beautiful [Col. 1107D] properties of the lower, so the last possess those of the prior beings, though not similarly but at a lower degree. Therefore, I think, there is nothing disordered if theology calls the high priest among us an angel, since he participates in the proper power of angels by a prophetic property and is extended, as far as is possible for human beings, toward their manifesting likeness.

You will also find that theology calls gods both the celestial essences above us and, among us, men most beloved by God and wondrous. The divine mystery itself is, in a manner beyond essence, at once removed from all and set above all; and none of those things that proceed from it can properly or in every respect be called like to it. Nevertheless, whatever intellectual or rational being is universally converted, by whatever capacity it has, toward unity with it and stretches unceasingly, as far as possible, toward its divine illuminations, has become worthy—if it is right to say so—of divine imitation and divine naming. [Col. 1108B]

## EXPOSITION

The title of the twelfth chapter is: “Why the hierarchs among human beings are called angels.” Its sense is this: why those who are hierarchs—that is, sacred rulers among or according to human beings—such as high pontiffs, priests of any rank, and other ministers of the word of God, are called angels, when it has been said above that lower beings, since they do not participate in the properties of higher beings, ought not to assume their names either.

For if the order of angels, because it is lower than the powers, cannot share their name according to the powers’ proper characteristic, then human beings—who are unquestionably lower than angels—cannot assume the angels’ name according to their proper characteristic. But this question is resolved by what we said above: spiritual gifts of grace, which pass into the communion of all, [Col. 1108D] also bring their appellation into the participation of all. Although they produce a distinct appellation insofar as certain beings possess them singularly and excellently, yet insofar as they are common in some manner, their names too are sometimes extended to common use as the circumstances require.

“This too is asked by those who study the intelligible utterances attentively.” By those who study attentively—that is, learned investigators—of intelligible utterances, namely divine utterances, which are intelligible, that is, spiritual and profound utterances concerning intelligible things, the following question is asked: why human beings set over others are called angels. [Col. 1109A]

He then supplies the reason why this is asked: “For if the last,” that is, lower orders, “do not participate in the universalities of the higher powers,” that is, in the properties that are universally—or, more expressly, wholly, fully, and perfectly—in the higher beings, “why is the priest who is highest among us,” that is, among human beings, “called by the utterances an angel of God Almighty?” If he does not have the singularity of that property, why does he assume the expression of its name? It seems contrary that a name denoting distinction should be extended to what is common.

Yet, he says, “this explanation,” or assertion, “is not contrary, I think, to what has previously been defined,” namely concerning the distinctions of individuals. For in granting such a common use of the designation to many, we do not remove the distinctions of individuals. [Col. 1109B]

“For we truly say that the last,” that is, the lowest orders, “are excluded from the universal and higher power of the greater adornments,” that is, of the more excellent orders: namely, they do not participate in the powers of higher beings according to the universality, totality, or fullness in which those higher beings participate. Yet they may sometimes fittingly share their name, because although they do not participate in that power according to an equal fullness, they nevertheless participate according to a similar imitation.

“For they participate,” he says, “in a middle and proportionate [degree],” with “power” understood; that is, they participate in the power of those [above them]. Though not with the highest participation, in which they would be equal, they nevertheless participate with a middle—or moderate and somewhat lower—participation, in which they can be similar. This participation, however, occurs not according to the individual perfection of each, but “according to one common and unifying fellowship of all together”; that is, not according to what is individual to each, but according to what is common to all. Since this is one thing—that is, common to all—in it all are united and joined together. Accordingly, insofar as something is common to all, individual names are drawn into a common signification; for, as we have said, even what belongs to some by excellence is common to all by participation.

“For example, the order of the holy cherubim participates in wisdom and higher knowledge,” etc. By the example that follows he proves what he has said: namely, that what certain persons possess excellently comes, according to a lower communion, into the participation of all. Thus the order of the holy cherubim participates in wisdom and higher knowledge. “But the dispositions of the essences,” that is, the orders of spirits beneath the cherubim themselves, “also participate in wisdom and knowledge indeed, but in a partial manner and subject to them”; that is, not as perfectly or as excellently as they do. And truly wisdom and knowledge are not participated in by the cherubim alone, but also by other, lower beings; [Col. 1110A] for “to be altogether in the participation of wisdom and knowledge,” that is, universally, “is common to all deiform intellects,” that is, to all spirits conformed and made like to God through implanted reason. To participate in wisdom in some way is common to all. But “to participate in it attentively and first,” that is, explicitly and principally, “or second, or even below it, is by no means common to all.” For those who do not participate first participate second, or below—that is, more lowly and imperfectly; but they do not participate first. For whoever has perfection also has a beginning; but not whoever has a beginning can immediately have perfection.

“But” each has only [Col. 1110B] one thing “as is determined for each,” or dispensed, or as one definite thing is assigned “according to its own analogy”; that is, according to the rule, mode, or measure proper to it, which was predestined and foreseen for it before all things in God’s eternal providence. “And this”—namely, that lower beings perhaps participate in the powers of higher beings, not according to fullness, but in some manner—“someone will define,” or affirm, “concerning all divine minds,” that is, rational spirits, “without error” in this, because it is true. “For just as the first and higher orders possess more abundantly the holy and beautiful properties of the lesser, so the last and lesser themselves possess those properties which belong to the former—not, however, in the same way, but below,” that is, more imperfectly than the former.

Therefore, he says, [Col. 1110C] “as I think, nothing is out of order” — with “was” or “is done” understood — “if theology calls the high priest among us an angel”: that is, him who among us human beings exercises the highest priesthood; or it calls him an angel in relation to us because he announces God’s word to us. He is therefore an angel because he is “participating according to his own power,” that is, according to the grace granted to him in his own office: “participating,” I say, “in the prophetic property” of angels, because it belongs to him to prophesy and announce God’s word, as angels announce it. And he is also, I say, “extended,” or advanced, or raised up, to a manifesting likeness of those angels, because in this he resembles angels: he manifests [Col. 1110D] or reveals God’s secrets for the instruction of those subject to him. Nor is it surprising that human beings are called angels, since angels and human beings alike have been called gods.

This is what he says: “You will find, moreover, that theology calls the heavenly and higher essences themselves gods,” that is, angels; and not them alone, but also “certain” men among us—that is, men of our race—namely, “wonderful and most beloved of God.” He then adds the reason why human beings are called angels or gods: namely, because the divinity, though secret and removed from every creature by the excellence of its nature, is nevertheless in some manner conceived and participated in by rational minds which, through virtue, turn themselves toward its unity and illumination. Therefore, insofar as they are participants in divinity, they may not inappropriately be called gods in some respect.

This is what he says: “And indeed the divine secret,” that is, the secret of divinity, “is both remote and superessentially set above all things together; and none of those things which are from it,” with “created” understood, “can altogether and properly be called like to it,” because Creator and creature cannot explicitly be alike. “Yet whatever power of intellectual and rational beings,” that is, of angels, “and,” to speak universally, “whatever [Col. 1112A] power,” whether of angels or humans, “is turned toward its unity,” namely that of divinity, and whatever power is continually stretched forth to receive the divine illuminations of Deity itself: that power has been made worthy of divine imitation through likeness and of divine univocal naming through appellation. That power, I say, has been made worthy according to power—that is, worthy insofar as it is power. Yet this is so only if it is right to say that any power, however great, can be worthy “of divine imitation and divine univocal naming.”

## Title of Chapter XIII. Why the prophet Isaiah is said to have been purified by a seraph.

[Col. 1111]

## Text

[Col. 1111B]

“Come, then, let us examine this also according to our capacity: why the theologians say that a seraph was sent” (Isa. VI). For someone may answer that it was not one of the subordinate angels, but one of the greatest and most inward essences, who purified the priest. Some therefore say that, according to the definition already given of the fellowship of all intellects, Scripture does not say that one of the first minds around God came for the theologian’s purification; but that a certain angel presiding over us performed the prophet’s purifying rite and was called a seraph by equivocation, because of the fiery and heavenly cleansing of the sins mentioned and the restoration of the purified person to divine obedience. And they say that Scripture simply called one “from among the seraphim,” [Col. 1111C] not one of those stationed around God, but one of the purifying powers presiding over us.

But another gave me a defense, not altogether unsuitable, concerning this matter. For he says that the great angel who at that time formed the vision in order to teach the theologian divine things referred his own purifying sacrificial action to God, and, after God, to the hierarchy that acts first. Is not this reasoning true, then? For the man who said this explains how the divine power, coming into all things, fills them and passes through all things immeasurably, and again is invisible to all—not only as superessentially removed from all things, but also as secretly allowing its providential operations to enter into all things. Yet it shines forth proportionately in all intellectual beings; and, imparting its own illumination to the most precious [Col. 1111D] essences, it distributes itself in good order through them, as though through first beings, into the others established beneath them, according to the contemplative measure of each disposition.

To state this more plainly, by examples proper to the matter—although deficient in relation to God, who is removed from all things, yet clearer to us—the distributions of the sun’s rays, well distributed into the first matter, fill that which is brightest of all, and through it more clearly disclose their own splendors. But when they reach denser materials, their distributive manifestation is more obscure, owing to the unfitness of the materials to be illuminated for receiving the distributive condition of illumination; and shortly thereafter, from this cause, it is contracted almost into complete non-distribution. Again, the heat of fire distributes itself more fully into things more receptive [Col. 1112B] and well suited and readily adaptable to its likeness. But in essences opposed to its reforming action it manifests no hidden trace of its primary operation. And this is further so because it is admitted into things not akin to it through things which have suitable conditions: first making readily movable things fiery through fiery things, and through these proportionately warming either water or something else not readily ignited.

Accordingly, after the analogy of this natural ordering, the supernatural ordering itself of every good visible and invisible adornment fittingly manifests, first to the highest essences, the brightness of illumination appearing as in most abundant outpourings; and through them the essences that come after participate in the divine ray. For these, being first in knowing God and supremely desiring the divine power, [Col. 1112C] have been made worthy to become first agents, insofar as possible, by power and action like to God. They themselves extend the essences after them, in a deiform manner, to similar power, abundantly communicating to them from the brightness which comes upon them; and these, in turn, communicate it to their subjects. Thus through every order the first transmits to that which follows it.

Does not water itself reach all proportionately? Therefore, for all who are illuminated together, God is indeed by nature the principle of illumination, truly and properly, as the essence of light and the cause both of their being and of their seeing. Then the being which remains above in a deiform and God-like manner conveys after itself the divine lights to each one, through itself, into that being. Therefore they regard the most excellent disposition of heavenly minds as, after God, the principle for all the other [Col. 1112D] essences, as is fitting, of all sacred and divine knowledge and divine imitation, since divine illumination is distributed through them to all, including ourselves. For this reason they refer every sacred and God-like operation, first to God as its cause, and then to the first deiform intellects as the first agents and teachers of divine things.

Does not the first disposition of the holy angels possess, more than all others together, the fiery property, the abundant communication of divine wisdom, the mystical knowledge of the highest divine illuminations, and the seated property signifying divine receptivity? But the dispositions of subordinate essences participate in the fiery, wise, and knowing power receptive of God in a lower degree; and, looking toward the first, and through them having been made worthy as first agents by imitation of God, they are led back, so far as possible, into deiformity. Therefore they place the aforesaid holy properties, participation in which comes to those existing after them through the first, in those very beings after God, as in hierarchies.

He therefore says this, saying (ibid.) that the vision descending from that [hierarchy] was received by the theologian through one of the holy and blessed angels ruling over us; and that, before he led him by illumination into that holy contemplation, [Col. 1113A] the angel placed it within that holy contemplation. The theologian saw the highest essences—so far as one may speak in symbols—stationed after God and around God and with God; and he saw the super-principal summit, surpassing all even those supernaturally exalted powers, set above in the midst of the established powers.

Thus the theologian learned from the visions that the divine is, in accordance with every superessential excellence, incomparably set above every invisible and visible power; that it is universally remote from all and is not like even the first essences among beings. He further learned that it is the principle of all and the substantial cause, and the immutable foundation in the secret singularity of the things that are; from it even the most firmly established powers have being and well-being. Then he was taught the deiform powers of the most holy seraphim: through their sacred name, which is “fiery,” concerning which we shall say shortly as much as is possible for us, he was introduced into deiform ascents of fiery power. Through the sacred formation of their outspread wings he was introduced into absolute and highest extension toward the divine in the first, [Col. 1113B] middle, and last intellects.

Further, when the intellectual theologian saw their manifold and multiform vision, their distinction of wings beneath their feet and wings beneath their faces, and their perpetual motion by means of the wings in the middle, he was led back to an invisible understanding of what had been seen: namely, to the many-wayed and many-sighted power of the highest intellects; to their sacred awe in their supermundane avoidance of proud, bold, and impossible investigation of higher and lower things; and to the unceasing, lofty flight of movement in actions imitating God according to measure.

He was also taught that divine and most precious hymnody, as the angel forming the vision instructed the theologian according to his capacity and communicated his own sacred knowledge to him. The angel also taught him this: purification, for those who are purified, is participation, insofar as possible, in the unknown brightness of God. This purification, from the causes remote in divinity itself—by which it perfects all sacred intellects in superessential hiddenness—is in some manner more manifest to the highest powers around it, and more fully manifests and distributes itself to them. Then it brings its manifest illumination to second, last, or our intellectual powers in proportion as each has become deiform in relation to it, so that they may praise the unknown character of its own hiddenness. It shines through each order, to the second through the first. And, to say it briefly, it is first led from the hidden into the manifest through the first powers.

Therefore the theologian learned from the angel leading him into light that purification and all divine operations shine forth through the first essences and are distributed to all the rest, according to each one’s analogy for deifying participations. [Col. 1114A] For this reason he consequently assigned the fiery purifying property to the seraphim after God. Nothing, therefore, is disordered if the seraph is said to purify the theologian. For God thus purifies all, being the cause of every purification.

But let us use a closer example. Just as the high priest among us, purifying or illuminating through his ministers or priests, is himself said to purify and illuminate, because the orders purified through him refer their own sacred operations through themselves to him; so too the angel who effected the theologian’s purification referred his own purifying knowledge and power, first to God as cause, then to the seraph itself as the high priest who acts first. It is as if someone, teaching the purified person with angelic reverence, should say: “For the purification to be effected in you, the first principle before me is the exalted Essence, Creator, and Cause, which brings the first essences into being and keeps them stationed around itself; preserves them unturned and free from falling; and moves itself into the first participations of its own providential operations. For this is what the seraph’s mission teaches me to declare. But the high priest and leader after God is the disposition of the essences above us, from whom I have learned to purify in a deiform manner. He, therefore, purifies you through me; through him the Cause and Maker of all purification brought its own providential actions from hiddenness even to us.”

This, indeed, he taught me. But I transmit it to you, and I leave it to your intellectual and discriminating knowledge either to free the other of the stated explanations from doubt and honor it before the other as having what is consequent, reasonable, and equally true; or to discover for yourself what is closer to the truly true; or to learn it from another—God granting it, revealing it first to the angels who receive it and to us, the friends of angels, through his more lovable contemplation.

## Exposition

“Come, let us examine this also according to our capacity.” “Come,” he says, “O Timothy: after the matters already discussed, let us also consider this according to our power and possibility—namely, why the theologians say that one of the seraphim was sent” in Isaiah, when, with tongs, he took a coal from the altar and purified the prophet’s lips (Isa. VII [apparently VI]). It is necessary to consider and discuss this question because one may doubt whether by “seraph” here one of the higher order is to be understood, owing to the propriety of the name; or one of the lower orders, owing to the propriety of the ministry, because it belongs to the weak and lowest beings to administer our hierarchy. The question must therefore be examined in order that ambiguity of opinion may be removed.

For perhaps “someone may answer that it was not one of the subordinate [angels],” that is, one of the angels, “who purified the priest,” namely Isaiah, [Col. 1115A] “but one of the inward and greatest essences,” that is, the highest spirits. Yet this too may seem doubtful to someone because the highest orders are not sent to dispense or administer external affairs.

Therefore “some say that, according to the definition of the fellowship of all intellects already given” by us—that is, according to what we defined above, that all spirits have a certain fellowship among themselves in properties and names—Scripture “does not name,” that is, does not say, “one of the first minds,” that is, of the first spirits stationed around God, as having come for the theologian’s purification. But they say that “one rather of those presiding over us,” who preside only over us human beings, “performed the prophet’s purifying sacrifice,” that is, performed a holy action and offered to God, as it were, an acceptable sacrifice, and “was called seraph by equivocation,” that is, by similarity of name, not by excellence of property.

He then adds in what likeness an angel of the lowest order was called a seraph: “because of the fiery and heavenly cleansing,” or purification, “of the sins” of the prophet already mentioned above, and because of the “raising,” or quickening, of the “purified person unto divine obedience.” For just as fire cleanses rust by burning it and brings what is dead and extinguished to life by warming it, so by this divine fire he was both cleansed from sins and inflamed with love for God. Since this was done through the ministry of an angel, some say that sacred “Scripture simply called one from among the seraphim,” not one of the powers “stationed around God,” but rather one “of the purifying powers presiding over us,” that is, one of the angels appointed over us—that is, human beings—yet called seraph because of similarity of action.

It follows: “But another offered me a defense not altogether unsuitable concerning such a position.” Some, he says, maintain that the angel who purified the prophet belonged to the highest spirits, because he is called seraph. Others say that he belonged to the lower spirits and was called seraph only because of similarity of action. Thus each plausibly defines the matter in accordance with his own opinion. But “another,” agreeing wholly neither with the former nor with the latter, “offered me a certain apology,” that is, excuse, satisfaction, or defense, “not altogether unsuitable,” regarding such a position—that is, a definition by which the state of the matter is described; or concerning such an objection, that is, a question which presses in a certain way and is troublesome until it is resolved.

He then adds what satisfaction or defense this man gave concerning the question: “For he says”—with the person offering the defense understood—“that the great angel, who at that time was forming the vision in order to teach the theologian divine things,” that is, in the theologian’s mind, whom that angel was to teach divine things through the vision, “referred his own purifying sacrificial action,” that is, the operation by which he himself then properly and individually purified and sanctified the prophet’s lips, “to God,” that is, attributed it to God; “and after God he referred it to the hierarchy that acts first,” that is, to the hierarchy in which and through which God acts first, before all others.

He attributed his own action to that hierarchy because from it, after God, he principally received the power to act thus. And this is the reason why the seraph is called supreme: namely, because the angel who did this, just as he received it principally after God from the seraphim, so also attributed it after God to the seraphim themselves. Such, therefore, was the explanation that man gave concerning this question.

“And is not this reasoning true?” These are the words of the author, who seems to accommodate his own opinion to this view. This reasoning appears true because the man “who said this” explains how “the divine power, coming into all things, fills all things”; and it not only comes, but also reaches and penetrates all things, immeasurably passing through them, “and is invisible to all.” Again, it is invisible in this way, transcending all things without limit, just as it is invisible to all things subsisting before all things without beginning. Or again, “it is invisible” through immensity, as it is invisible through eternity: for just as temporal intelligence cannot grasp eternity, so circumscribed nature cannot comprehend immensity. Or again, “it is invisible,” that is, not only in itself, insofar as it is essentially and ineffably removed from all things, but also to us, insofar as it is incomprehensibly hidden from all.

Therefore it is invisible in itself and invisible to us, and in both ways remains incomprehensible. This is what he says: “It is not only invisible in itself, as superessentially removed from all things, but it is also invisible in us, as secretly allowing,” or causing to penetrate, “its providential operations into all things.” Thus the divine power is invisible in itself as remote, and invisible in us as hidden in operation, because according to its providence it works in us.

“Yet,” though it is thus invisible, it shines forth, pouring itself out for manifestation “upon all intellectual beings,” that is, rational minds. It shines forth, I say, “proportionately,” that is, more to some and less to others, according to each one’s measure and capacity. And although it shines forth commonly upon all, it nevertheless excels in “imparting its own illumination to the most precious essences,” that is, the most subtle and excellent spirits; “through these essences,” namely, “as though through first beings,” it afterward distributes itself in good order “to other essences,” namely those “established beneath” these first beings—that is, made firm, stationed, or disposed beneath them.

It distributes itself, I say, “according to the contemplative commensuration of each disposition,” that is, according to the degree in which each disposition or order is capable, by its own measure, of that contemplation. This distribution of divine illumination, reaching recipients differently according to their measure, I shall explain “more plainly by examples proper to the matter”—proper, that is, though “deficient in relation to God, who is removed from all things.” They are deficient in comparison with God, who is removed from all things and cannot properly be shown by any likeness. Thus they are deficient and not proper; yet they are proper because “clearer to us.” They are not proper to divine majesty, but proper to human capacity; not proper as the matter exists in God, but proper as it can be shown to us.

To show by examples not proper to God but proper to us the distribution of divine illumination, I offer this comparison. “The distributions of the sun’s rays, well distributed into the first matter, fill that which is brightest of all, and through it more clearly disclose their own splendors.” The distributions, or outpourings, of the sun’s ray, he says, well distributed into the first matter—that is, entering that matter which is first, namely best, purest, and most apt for illumination—fill such matter, finding no obstacle to light in any part of it. By filling it they make it brighter, the most radiant of all; and thus through it the ray itself more clearly displays its own splendors. For the more perfectly it shines, the more perfectly it is illuminated; and the more perfectly it is infused into that matter, the more clearly it is reflected from it.

“But when it reaches denser materials,” that is, materials more dense and less apt for illumination, “it has there a more obscure distributive manifestation.” For as it is imperfectly received when poured into them, so when it shines through them and appears outwardly, it appears obscurely. This comes from “the unfitness of the materials to be illuminated”; their unfitness harms and hinders “the distributive condition of illumination,” that is, the distribution or reception of illumination itself. Thus it shines more perfectly in pure and polished bodies, but is diminished in denser and coarser ones; and then, descending to others still less fit, it is, through this deficiency—that is, after this deficiency—contracted almost into complete non-distribution. For, descending from the most subtle materials, by which it is perfectly received, to less apt materials, by which it is imperfectly received, it finally reaches substances so foul, gross, and dull that they almost entirely repel light and can receive no illumination.

In this manner spiritual light, coming to rational minds, perfectly enlightens those it finds pure and cleansed, but illuminates with lesser brightness—and, so to speak, with a dimmer light—those it finds less fit. Those which it finds altogether opposed and foul it leaves wholly free from its participation and communion. Thus through the likeness of visible things the truth of invisible things is shown.

[Col. 1118A] Not only in light, but also in material heat, there is an image of invisible truth. For heat itself kindles more intensely those bodies which it finds more suited to receive it; it affects others less, until at last, encountering things wholly contrary and dissimilar, it displays in them no effect of its operation.

This is what he says: “Again, the heat of fire,” as though he said: Not only in the brilliance of light but also in the heat of fire can the aforesaid likeness be seen. “For the heat of fire distributes itself more fully into more receptive” bodies, understood, and into those well suited to its likeness, so that they may be warmed by heat; for there is likeness between what is hot and heat, just as between what is white and whiteness, good and goodness, and in general between every property and its affection.

But when heat itself comes “to essences opposed to its reforming operations,” because they resist by a contrary quality the warming by which they ought to be reformed into the likeness of heat, that heat “shows no trace,” or at least no “hidden,” that is, obscure, “trace of its primary operation” in them. That is, it shows no effect there from which it may be recognized, even faintly, that it has at least some beginning of operation in them.

In this way rational substances either receive the fire of heavenly love, if they are fit and prepared habitations suitable for its reception, or wholly repel it if they differ by a contrary quality and cannot be kindled. I pray that no foulness of earthly stains may repel from my soul the light of inward brightness, and that no coldness of malice may exclude the warmth of holy devotion; but that it may shine and be warmed from heaven, reformed into divine likeness. O what an essence joined to superessential good; what a blessed nature full of supernatural good! Happy is that being which has been made worthy to be restored in this way. If this is granted me, I have no further complaint about all those things which have gone before.

The creature shows its maker, and the form of marvelous works commends the beauty of the author. There is one goodness and one beauty, and goodness itself is beauty itself. The highest good and the highest beauty: in the highest good is every good, one good; and in the highest beauty is every beauty, [Col. 1118D] one beauty. Visible nature could not contain all things in that one. Therefore many good things were made by God, that they might display the one highest good; likewise many beautiful things, that they might show the image of the one highest beauty.

Many lives also were established in those whose condition deserved to possess something more, namely in those things made good and beautiful, yet unable to receive the good which is life. And all these lives emulate the one highest life: each in its own kind, in what it is, in the degree in which it is from that life, and according to that life which alone is true.

But there are two principles of bodily life: heat and moisture. One, namely moisture, supplies life’s nourishment; the other, namely heat, gives life sensation. Without heat that which subsists does not live; without moisture that which lives does not subsist. Therefore these are infused in due proportion into everything to be vivified, so that each life may receive from them, as it ought, the measure of its capacity, and so that lower lives may progress through the grades of their increase toward the image of the highest life.

For the first grade of bodily life is sensation; the second, entering through sensation, imagination; the third, memory of things conceived by imagination; the fourth, in accordance with a passive application of sensation, a certain providence without the discernment of intelligence. In this there is, as it were, an image of reason, but no reason. Accordingly, some brute animals seem more cunning than others of their kind, imitating the providence of a rational mind with a certain facility resembling sensation. Yet this is shown to be more an affection of sensation than an operation of intelligence.

In all these things bodily life imitates spiritual life: first, in that it senses; second, in that it conceives sensation; third, in that it retains what it has conceived; fourth, in that, whether among imagined things or sensible things, through the affection of sensation, according to a certain likeness of reason, it inclines itself either to desire or to flee. Thus in all these things bodily lives bear the image of spiritual lives, and through their intermediate forms emulate the highest life so far as they can.

For spiritual lives themselves receive from the highest life the fact that they are lives, participating in the spiritual heat and moisture descending from it, by which they are nourished and vivified in order to live. [Col. 1119C] These two, understood spiritually, perfect spiritual life: spiritual moisture nourishes through joy; and no life can endure unless it has its heat and moisture to nourish and give sensation, so that it may subsist in being life. The more it has these, the more rightly it is called life. As there are many lives because there are many participations, and every participation is from one source and every life is from one source, so the highest good, diffusing itself into all things, establishes every life and, by forming every life, leads it back to the highest life.

It follows: “And this is further so.” As though he said: It is not only an argument for invisible truth that some bodies receive bodily light and material heat while others [Col. 1119D] wholly repel them; it is also an argument that less hot things are kindled through things more hot. This, he says, is a further argument—not greater than the preceding arguments, but additional to them—of invisible truth.

For the material heat of fire itself is admitted and infused into bodies “which are not akin” to it, that is, are not themselves fit to receive it; it is infused into them, I say, “through others having suitable conditions,” that is, through things suitably disposed toward it. These first receive it, “making readily movable things fiery, as though by fiery things.” Heat itself makes fiery, through fiery things which burn more intensely, other things that are secondarily and less heated. Yet they too are made fiery through fiery things because they are readily moved and suited for receiving heat.

Thus, through things fiery and first and principally heated, it first makes other things fiery; and through these fiery things it then warms things still colder and more remote: either water or something else, that is, “something else not easily ignited,” namely among things which do not readily become fiery. It warms them, I say, “proportionately,” that is, each according to its own mode, measure, and capacity for receiving heat.

It follows: “Accordingly, in conformity with this,” etc. He adapts the comparison. “According to this,” he says, “principle,” that is, comparison, “of natural ordering,” that is, the ordering of natural and visible things, “the supernatural ordering” also—that is, the distribution of divine grace [Col. 1120B], which is “the ordering of every good adornment,” that is, of every order well and beautifully disposed, whether “visible,” as among human beings, or “invisible,” as among angels—this supernatural ordering, I say, fittingly manifests first “the brightness of illumination,” that is, manifestation or revelation, to “the highest essences,” that is, the supreme spirits: that brightness, I say, “first appearing” in them, as being “in most abundant effusions,” that is, as it is fitting for it to appear when it pours itself out copiously, or in those upon whom it has poured itself out most abundantly. “And through them,” namely the highest essences, those essences “which are after” them participate in the divine ray, that is, divine brightness. “For these” [Col. 1120C], namely the highest essences, “are the first to know God and to desire the divine power preeminently.” And because they know and love principally, they have been made worthy “to become foremost agents, as far as possible, in power and action like God”; that is, that before all others, immediately after God, they may act upon all things subject to them, bestowing divine power, and may thereby become like God, because they impart to those below them the power which they receive from above. For they extend the essences which are after them, or subject to them, “to a like power,” namely one like their own power—as befits a power disposed in a godlike manner—because, in doing this, they imitate God by their power, “abundantly transmitting to them,” namely to the subject essences, “from the brightness coming upon them.” And those [Col. 1120D], namely the subject essences, in turn transmit to those subject to themselves; and thus, while the outpouring of the divine gift runs through each one, “the first transmits to that which is after it,” and so onward to the end.

It follows: “Water itself,” etc. After proposing a comparison from fire with respect to brightness and heat, he again proposes another comparison from water. “Does not water itself,” he says, “reach all things proportionately?” The moisture of water, which diffuses itself through all parts of earthly bodies, fills all things proportionately, moistening some more and others less, according as each is more or less capable of being moistened. Thus in this example likewise the distribution of divine grace, which does not come to all in an equal [Col. 1121A] manner, is fittingly shown.

It follows: “Therefore,” etc. Since, he says, just as one visible light illuminates many things and many shining things shine from that light, so invisible light illuminates all things that shine invisibly. “Therefore God is the principle of illumination,” or of “illuminating, together with all who are illuminated.” Nor is this surprising, since he himself is light—not light in just any way, but by nature, that is, naturally, truly, and properly. Naturally, because from himself; truly, because in himself; and properly, because through himself. Naturally, because he is light from the fact that he is light; truly, because he is the very thing which is light; and properly, because he is light through that very thing which is light. For natural is that which is not assumed from elsewhere; true is that which is possessed essentially; proper is that which is not conferred through another. Thus God is light; and I say too little when I say that he is light, since he is the very essence of light. Others that shine are not the essence of light, but effects. Therefore they are lights from light; but he is light from what he is. “And he is also causal of the being and seeing,” that is, of the essence and vision of light itself. It is as though he said: God is the essence of light, and also the cause of that essence itself, because what is light is light essentially, and what is essentially so is from itself. Thus he is the cause of the essence of light, and not only of the essence of light, but also of the very vision or manifestation of light, because he not only has from himself that he is essentially light [Col. 1121C], shining by nature, but also that he shines temporally, illuminating by grace.

It follows: “Then, remaining set above in a godlike manner and like God,” etc. In God, he says, light itself is not other than the essence itself of him for whom being and being light are the same, who is from himself the principle of illuminating, because he illuminates from himself those who shine first. Then, that is, next after him—namely, God—whatever remains “set above in a godlike manner and like God,” that is, according to conformity and likeness to God, becomes, implicitly, a principle of illuminating what is after it, “by itself conveying divine lights into that” which is placed after it. The sense is this: God, who is set above all things, illuminates by himself those nearest to him; and thus, illuminating those who first shine, he becomes the principle of illumination. Then each of those first shining beings, set above all those subject to it according to conformity and likeness to God, becomes the principle of illumination for each subject being, conveying divine lights by itself into that subject being. That he used the neuter “set above,” where he ought to have said “set above” [masculine], whether referring to an order or an angel, is done after the manner of Scripture, especially when unknown and wonderful things are discussed: “that thing” is said, as though one said, “whatever that may be.” But when he adds “to each one after it,” it seems as though that superior being, whatever it is, being one, is the principle of illumination for the individual beings [Col. 1122A] subject to it, so that it supplies light not as many to many, but as one to many. Yet when afterward he adds, “conveying divine lights into that,” he seems to make one administer illumination not to many but to one. Hence it is clear that, according to the manner of Scripture, number is put interchangeably for number, or genus for genus, without changing the truth of the same meaning.

It follows: “Therefore the highest disposition of the heavenly minds.” He infers from the foregoing, as though saying: Since the first disposition has received the divine gift and provides illumination to all who are subject to it, “therefore the essences of all the remaining dispositions marvel,” that is, the spirits of all the remaining orders [Col. 1122B] contemplate with admiration and astonishment “the highest disposition of heavenly minds, the principle after God, as is fitting.” For it is fitting that they should recognize God as the first principle, and then revere, in their own manner, those who are first after God as a principle for those following, through whom divine grace descends to those subject to them. This is what follows: “They marvel that they are the principle of all sacred and divine knowledge and divine imitation,” which flow to those below through them, as divine illumination distributed through them to all the other heavenly powers—and not only to them, but also to us, namely human beings, who receive divine illuminations through their mediation. And because all the remaining heavenly essences are illuminated through the first ones, whatever sacred or God-like work they can perform they attribute first to God, who is the cause of all things, and then to those first spirits, through whose action and mediation they receive divine grace. This is what he says: “For this reason,” namely because the rest are illuminated through those whom God has illuminated, the remaining beings “refer every sacred and God-like operation of their own to God indeed as causal,” because he is the first cause of all things; “then they refer it to the first intellects,” that is, the highest spirits, who are godlike or conformed to God in that they bestow spiritual gifts—not, however, as God does, who is the first cause from whom they come, but [Col. 1122D] as first effects through whom they come. Therefore they refer their good to those through whom it comes, “as through the first agents and teachers of divine” gifts. They are agents insofar as they move by effecting; teachers insofar as they preside by directing.

It follows: “Do then the first,” etc. *Num* here means “is it not?” “Do not, therefore,” he says, “the first disposition of the holy angels,” which is so much more sublime than all the rest, “possess more than all the others” the supreme and “fiery property,” that is, charity, as in the seraphim; and the “abundant,” that is, overflowing, “transmission of divine wisdom, and the mystical knowledge of the highest divine illuminations,” that is, the mystical, hidden, or profound highest knowledge which it receives from divine illuminations, as in the cherubim; and the seated property, as in the thrones, bearing God and “signifying divine reception,” because in their being called thrones it is plainly signified that they receive God seated and resting in themselves. The sense is: Does not the first hierarchy possess, more excellently and abundantly than all others, the fire of charity, the light of knowledge, and the judgment of discernment? Certainly it possesses all these things more than all the others. But the “dispositions of the subordinate essences,” that is, the subject orders, also participate in “fiery power,” that is, charity, as do the seraphim; in wise and knowing [Col. 1123B] power, that is, knowledge, as do the cherubim; and in the power of receiving God, as do the thrones. They participate, I say, but “below,” that is, more imperfectly than the first; and “looking to the first,” that is, imitating the first, and “through them,” namely the first, being led back to that measure of godlikeness possible to them—that is, led back to as much godlikeness as is possible to them—they are made worthy, through those first beings, “to become foremost agents in divine imitation,” that is, to act before and more excellently than all others, from God and according to God.

It follows: “Therefore the holy properties spoken of,” etc. Since, he says, those following receive gifts of grace through the first beings, the holy properties already mentioned—such as burning the prophet’s lips with a coal, which seems proper to the seraphim, and teaching knowledge, which seems proper to the cherubim—such properties, “participation in which comes through the first essences,” the other essences “subsisting after them” attribute, I say, “to them,” namely to those first beings through whom they participate in them, “as to hierarchs,” that is, rulers and superiors, in order that they may refer them to those from whom they received them. They “attribute” them, I say, “to them after God,” because they first attribute them to God, then to those nearest after God. When he says that the subsequent essences “become participation” in the properties of the first, his manner of speaking is as if he said: They become participants in the properties of the first, because what the first possess by property the second share by participation.

It follows: “Thus he says these things, saying,” etc. That man, he says, whom I mentioned above, who offered me a not unsuitable explanation, says that the vision mentioned above—the question having arisen concerning the purification of the prophet’s lips—was “received by the theologian,” namely Isaiah, “through one of the holy and blessed” angels “ruling over us,” human beings, “descending from that,” namely the first hierarchy. For he says that the vision which Isaiah saw descended from the first hierarchy and was brought to the prophet [Col. 1124A] through an angel of the lowest order, those who are last among angels and rule only over us. Therefore he says that this angel, “before his illuminating guidance” of Isaiah—that is, before that revelation by which he guided and instructed the prophet, and by which he himself had previously been illuminated by the first hierarchy—“referred back to” that holy contemplation, that is, to the first hierarchy itself, from which he understood that he had received what he had and done what he did. Isaiah himself also “sees seated above,” that is, seated high and sublimely, “the highest essences, placed after God and around God and with God, as far as may be said in symbols,” that is, figures and likenesses. For it is altogether symbolic and figurative that God is said, under a bodily likeness, to sit upon a high throne and that the seraphim are reported to stand around and beside him. Isaiah also sees a summit more sublime “than all those,” namely the highest essences of the blessed spirits, “even in a most hidden manner”: a summit, I say, “set above the principal summit,” that is, God, who is highest and principal over all, “in the midst of the firmly established powers.” For in the midst of the powers—that is, holy spirits, established and made stable by their eternal placing around God above all things—God himself, highest and principal, is seen sitting upon a high and exalted throne. “Therefore, in these visions the theologian,” Isaiah, learned this: “that the divine,” that is, divinity [Col. 1124C], “is incomparably set above every superessential preeminence of every invisible and visible power”; that is, divinity incomparably transcends, in every mode of surpassing, every visible and invisible power. Nor is it surprising that the divine itself transcends all things, “since indeed,” that is, certainly, “it is removed from all things,” namely by excellence, as being universal in contrast with all things which are partial, and so remote and excellent that it “is not like even the first essences of the things which are,” but stands far apart and transcends them. When he says “the first essences of the things which are,” it is as though he said, the essences of those who are first, or the essences which are first: that is, the supreme spirits among the angels. Nor did he merely learn that the divine is removed from all things and like none. “But further,” or moreover, he learned that it “is the principle of all things,” because all things are from it; and the sanctifying cause, because through it all things subsist; and the immutable foundation of things which are, by a hidden singularity, because all things subsisting persevere in it. By its hidden and secret divinity, unity, containing all things, gathers the totality together, and singularity binds multiplicity. From it come both being and well-being even to the most firmly established powers, that is, those spirits established and made stable in the highest power and blessedness, who have from it not only that they are, but also that they are blessed. Thus he learned all this [Col. 1125A] in that vision concerning the excellence of divinity. “Then” he also learned and “was taught that the godlike powers of the same most holy seraphim”—or, more expressly, of those same most holy seraphim—were in the seraphim through conformity to God, even as he had learned that these powers were in God; for what God has by nature, they have by grace, being conformed to God. He next states what and what kind of powers he learned were in the seraphim, and from what he learned them, saying: “From their sacred name, namely that which is fiery.” For *seraphim* is interpreted “burning” or “following,” and signifies what is fiery. “Concerning this fiery quality,” he says, we shall “a little later set forth, as far as we can, anagogical explanations,” that is, upward leadings, “of fiery power,” namely the charity of the seraphim, “into what is godlike”: that is, into a reality so worthy and similar to God. Or thus: from that sacred name, he says, the prophet learned anagogies, that is, upward leadings, ascents, or advances of fiery power, namely the charity of the seraphim. “But from the extended sacred formation of the wings,” that is, the sacred arrangement of wings spread out, the prophet learned “the unrestricted and most lofty extension toward the divine” which belongs “to the first, middle, and last intellects.” Therefore, through the name which suggests fiery quality, he learned fiery power—that is, charity ascending to lofty things in desire; but through the spreading of the wings, he learned knowledge reaching out into distant things by subtlety and extending itself as far as apprehending divine things, in the first, middle, and last intellects—that is, in the spirits first, middle, and last in that order; or in the first intellects, which apprehend divine things above themselves; the middle, which apprehend them in themselves; and the last, which apprehend them beneath themselves. This extension or reaching-out of knowledge is unrestricted because, diffusing itself toward immensity, it is not enveloped by any mist of ignorance; and it is most lofty because, advancing toward the highest things, it is not weighed down by any weakness. And he knew not only from the things mentioned the power of their love and knowledge, “but the intellectual theologian [Col. 1125D] Isaiah also saw their manifold and multiform character, and saw the vision divided by wings beneath the feet and divided by wings beneath the faces; and he also saw the perpetual motion,” namely that which is always present, in the middle wings. Through all this he “was led back” and instructed to an invisible knowledge of the things seen. For by seeing the distinction of the wings stretched downward beneath the feet, the wings extended upward beneath the face of the seated one, and the wings in the middle always moving, he saw their manifold power: multiplied in operation, as signified by motion, and multiform in knowledge and love, as signified by extension. In all these things he was led back and admonished so as invisibly to know what he had seen under the appearance of visible things [Col. 1126A], “the many-wayed and many-seeing power of these highest intellects being manifested to him through all these things.” This power is many-wayed insofar as it is moved in many ways by desire, and many-seeing insofar as it is blessed in many ways by possession. It is many-wayed in what it pursues by searching; many-seeing in what it finds by penetrating. There are many ways by which one goes toward the one good; therefore it is rightly many-wayed. But why many-seeing, when that which is seen is one, unless it is because all things are seen in the one? Thus the prophet was led back to knowledge of the truth, the many-wayed and many-seeing power of the highest intellects having been shown to him through sacred images. He was also shown “their sacred fear,” or reverence, which they have “in a supermundane manner,” that is, impassibly and purely, “toward proud, audacious, and impossible investigation of higher and lower things”: that is, lest they proudly, audaciously, and impossibly investigate beyond the measure of their capacity the secrets of God, which are higher than they by majesty and lower by depth. For this reason they veil their heads, confessing that higher things are hidden from them; for this reason they veil their feet, declaring that lower and deeper things are impenetrable. Because of these things they fear to be proud and audacious in investigating what is impossible. They are proud toward heights, audacious toward depths: proud lest they be exalted too much, audacious lest they be hurled down. Therefore they have sacred fear in this, because it is holy to fear what, if presumptuously undertaken, would harm them; and they possess it supermundanely, because they fear without passion or affliction. For they fear [Col. 1126C] yet are not affected; they tremble yet are not shaken. Securely they stand in awe, and without any disturbance or corruption of their repose they fear to pass beyond the measure of their capacity toward incomprehensible majesty. The prophet was led to knowledge of all these things by seeing the matters mentioned above in the spreading of the wings.
