And he also saw the unceasing and ever lofty flight, namely the enduring motion in the movement of the wings. This movement consists in the proportioning of God-imitating actions: that is, in their actions by which they imitate God, proportioning themselves to their capacity so that they presume to do nothing beyond reason and measure.

It follows: “But he was also instructed in that divine and very [Col. 1126D] precious hymnody.” It is as though he said: He knew not only the seraphim’s power from their appearance, but also learned from their voice their hymnody, that is, divine praise, “the angel forming the vision for the theologian according to the capacity” of the latter and “transmitting his own sacred knowledge”; for through this sacred vision the angel caused the theologian to know what he himself knew. Therefore the angel “taught him,” namely the theologian, by purifying with a coal taken from the altar the lips of one who already seemed righteous, “that the participation of the unknown divine brightness itself, received as far as possible, is purification even for those who are however perfect.” For however purified a person may be, on receiving it he becomes still more purified.

[Col. 1127A] It follows: “But this,” etc. He has said that reception of divine brightness is purification. He now consequently shows that this brightness, proceeding from the hiddenness of the highest divinity, manifests itself first to the highest powers placed more openly near it, in order to perfect and illuminate all sacred intellects; and he shows how it is in its own and true being. Then, after the first, it shows itself to the second; afterward to the last; and finally even to our human intellects. Thus, descending, it brings its illumination to every power according as each has been made godlike by it. This is what he says: “This brightness, proceeding from the remote causes of divinity,” issuing from that divinity, “perfects all sacred intellects,” that is [Col. 1127B], rational minds, illuminating them “by superessential concealment,” that is, by a profoundly hidden and secret inspiration. Proceeding from those remote causes toward manifestation, it becomes first more manifest as it is—that is, according to its true being—to the highest powers placed near it; and it manifests and distributes itself to them “more” than to others. “Then,” after them, it manifests itself to the second, “then to the last,” and finally “to our intellectual powers,” that is, rational minds. And thus, descending from the first to the last, it brings its illumination through each power, making it manifest in each to the extent that each power exists from that brightness itself in a godlike way, that is, according to [Col. 1127C] conformity to God. For it illuminates each power more insofar as it adapts it more to godlikeness. He adds why this brightness proceeds toward manifestation: “For the praise of the unknown character of its own hiddenness.” We perceive something of it for this reason: so that in it, and through that which in it is hidden, unknown, and altogether incomprehensible, we may give praise.

It follows: “It shines through the first upon each of the second.” For it shines everywhere upon the second through the first, or through the first beings. “And, if it is necessary to say briefly,” this may be stated in sum: “what is first is led from hiddenness into manifestation through the first powers.” For what it is in itself is altogether hidden, and then it first begins to be seen when it first begins to be possessed. For it is never seen by anyone except by one who possesses it. “Therefore the theologian learned this from the angel who leads to light.” He learned this from the angel who guides into brightness. This is a new compound, *lucem ducente*, as though one said *luciductore*, “light-guide.” Therefore the theologian learned this from him. What did he learn? Namely this: “That purification and all divine operations, shining forth through the first essences, are distributed through them to all the rest according to the analogy,” that is, the mode and measure, “of each of the others for deifying participations.” “Therefore he assigned the fiery purifying property,” that angel, that is, attributed it “to the seraphim immediately after God”; and thus “it is not disorderly” to say that a seraph purifies [Col. 1128A] the theologian. For God also purifies all, “of whose whole purification,” or of whose purification all things, “he is the cause.” And not only God: in this example it may more clearly be seen how someone is said to do something not merely through whom it is done, but also from whom it is done. For “we shall use a closer example.” Thus a seraph is said to purify one whom an inferior angel purifies, having received the power and command from the seraph, “just as, among us, the high priest purifying or illuminating through his ministers or priests is himself said to purify and illuminate, the orders purified through him attributing their own sacred operations to him.” What he works through them is attributed to him through them. “Thus the angel himself, accomplishing the purification of the theologian, attributes his own purifying knowledge and power first to God as causal, then to the seraph himself as the first acting high priest.” Thus the angel attributes first to God and then to the seraph what he has done, through whom he did it. “As perhaps someone might say,” that is, by way of example: “If someone, with angelic reverence,” that is, under the person of an angel, which is to be revered, “while teaching” the prophet “that he had been purified by him, should say” to him: “O Isaiah, I am not the principle of the purification to be accomplished in you,” namely through me, “but before me there is a sublime principle,” namely God, who is the “essence, Creator, and cause” of all things, and who brings the first essences into being; “who holds them about himself by their placement,” that is [Col. 1128C], by stable firmness; “and preserves them unturned and free from falling,” that is, lest they turn away from him and fall together; “and moves himself into the first participation of his own providential operations,” that is, operations which he performs according to providence, because everything which he does temporally he has ordered in eternal providence. God’s proper operation is when he acts through himself without an intervening creature; from this, surely, comes the first participation, because those who become the first effects of his operation receive him without a mediator. For God’s first operation is when he moves himself from himself; first participation is when he gives himself through himself. And that creature is the highest to which the first operation comes [Col. 1128D] and in which the first participation is through it, descending afterward to those which follow. In this way the subject angel attributes to the higher seraph what he does, since he received from it the ability to do so. “For this,” namely that he had received from another the ability to do it, he says, “is taught to me by the mission of the seraph, to make these things manifest,” or signify. He says that the one who, providing the explanation of all the foregoing, taught him, also said that the mission of the seraph signifies this: namely, that it had received from the one from whom it came the ability to perform what it did. Therefore the angel can fittingly say to the prophet: “I am not the principle of the purification which I perform in you. But before me is the exalted and first principle,” God, who is Creator and cause of all things. Then there is “the order [Col. 1129A] of the excellent essences,” that is, the order of the highest spirits, which is “priest and guide after God,” bestowing divine things and leading back to God, “from which order I too have been taught to purify in a godlike manner,” as I now do in you. “It” namely that order “purifies you through me,” because it taught me to purify; “through which” order the cause and maker of all purification, namely divinity, “brings forth its providential actions from hiddenness even to us,” the lowest angels. If an angel performing purification were to say these and similar words to the prophet, it would not be unfitting. Hence it is clear that when a seraph is said to fly to the prophet and to purify the prophet, it may fittingly be understood that this operation was administered through a subject angel but attributed to the superior from whom it came.

It follows: “This man indeed taught me these things.” These are the author’s words as he returns to his subject. The man, he says, who offered me an explanation, taught me all the foregoing matters. “But I, O Timothy, hand over to you” all things either said or approved by me, but which admit of both sides. “To your intellectual and discriminating knowledge,” that is, discernment, “I concede that one side of the stated explanations may be freed,” namely by you, “from doubt,” that is, considered established and indubitable, “and that it may be honored before the other as possessing coherence, reasonableness, and equal truth.” I grant this both to your will and your discernment and knowledge: choose, removing doubt, one side of these opinions [Col. 1130A] and esteem it above the other as true and reasonable. “Or,” if this does not please you, I grant you “to discover by yourself what is nearer to the truly true. Or,” if this too does not please you, I grant you “to learn it from another, God of course granting this,” whether you recognize it in this or any other way—yet with angels first receiving that knowledge of truth from God and afterward revealing it through angels to holy men who are friends of angels, namely to us, so that they may reveal it to us. Or thus: I also grant you to reveal it to us “through contemplation more beloved to him,” angels and friends of angels first receiving the knowledge of truth. A marvelous statement. Angels receive from God and human beings from angels; and human beings again, taught by angels, teach other human beings. Thus instruction in truth comes through some to others, and many seem to be masters and teachers of truth. Yet no one is taught unless illumined by contemplation of him. Other teachers render a ministry; one teacher alone gives understanding. He can teach without others; others cannot without him. You give me a word—but what is a word without understanding? Understanding indeed comes through a word. But he who inwardly illumines places understanding in the heart, not he who merely sounds outwardly. His anointing teaches us concerning all things. You speak outwardly, but you do not anoint inwardly. Therefore your instruction is indeed dear to me; but his contemplation is more dear, because even what is dear in your instruction comes only from his contemplation.

## TITLE OF CHAPTER XIV. What the transmitted number of angels signifies.

[Col. 1129]

## TEXT.

[Col. 1129C]

What the transmitted number of angels signifies. This too, I think, deserves intellectual consideration: namely, that the tradition of the divine utterances concerning angels says that there are “thousands of thousands” and “ten thousand times ten thousand” (Dan. 7), folding back into itself and multiplying the highest numbers known to us, and thereby plainly signifying the innumerable orders of the heavenly essences. For the blessed hosts of supermundane intellects are many; they surpass the weak and constricted proportional measurement of the material numbers known to us, and are defined only by the supermundane and heavenly understanding and knowledge, according to the capacity of the divine, manifold, wisdom-making knowledge most richly bestowed upon them, of the principle which subsists superessentially above all things [Col. 1129D], and of the substantializing cause, containing power, and all-encompassing perfection.

“**What is meant by the given angelic number**,” that is, the number given or defined by Holy Scripture? Not only, he says, are the foregoing matters so; but this too “is worthy of intellectual knowledge”: namely, why a certain and definite number is assigned to angelic spirits:

[Col. 1130C]

“because the tradition” of the divine “utterances says that there are thousand thousands and ten thousand times ten thousand” angels, “folding back into itself the highest numbers according to us,” that is, the numbers which are highest according to us. I say “folding back into itself,” that is, in the utterance of the words which it contains: folding the words back into words and multiplying some by others, just as thousands are folded into “thousand times,” and ten thousands into “ten thousand times,” by multiplication. It might more plainly have said, “folding the numbers back into themselves,” although it is expressed more precisely thus, because not the numbers but the names of the numbers, placed within themselves by multiplication, are folded back.

Therefore, if the tradition of the utterances, signifying the multitude of heavenly spirits, says that there are thousand thousands and ten thousand times ten thousand angels,

[Col. 1130D]

folding the highest numbers according to us into themselves, or comparing them with one another, and multiplying some by others, it thereby “openly signifies that the orders of heavenly essences are innumerable.” For in setting down the greatest numbers, it plainly intimates what it would still have said had it been able to say more.

It should certainly be known that what it says, “thousand thousands and ten thousand times ten thousand,” is not contained in our translation in this form; rather, it has “thousands of thousands” and “ten thousand times one hundred thousand.” Yet this pertains to the same truth. Therefore, wishing to signify infinitude, it set down the greatest finite numbers, because “the blessed armies are many,” that is, the blessed multitudes serving God, “of supermundane intellects, surpassing the weak and restricted measure of material numbers according to us, and defined by the gnostic,” that is, cognitive, “knowledge”; or rather, by the divine knowledge which knows all things, alone knows the number of those heavenly powers, alone distinguishes them, and knows them fully according to the soundness—that is, the purity or integrity—of their simple and incorruptible nature, bestowed upon them most richly and abundantly by the supermundane and

[Col. 1131A]

heavenly, wisdom-making intelligence and knowledge of the divine and manifold knowledge of the Principle of all things that are, which subsists superessentially, and of the substantializing Cause of all things, and of the Power containing all things, and of the Consummation encompassing all things.”

The sense is this: only the wisdom of God, which is gnostic—that is, knowing all things—knows definitely and perfectly the number of those heavenly essences in that purity and integrity in which it created and formed them. This knowledge is heavenly, divine, and manifold: heavenly by its purity, divine by its truth, manifold by its incomprehensibility. And since it is such in itself, it is also wisdom-making in its work, wisely making all things and establishing nothing worthy of reproof.

And this such wisdom, through which all things were created and all things are known, is itself the wisdom of him who is the Principle of all things that are—for all things are from him—subsisting through himself superessentially, that is, perfect and needing nothing; and who is the substantializing Cause of all things, because he causes all things to subsist, so that they may be; and is the Power containing all things, so that they remain what they are; and is the Consummation

[Col. 1132A]

encompassing all things, lest they dissolve or fall away from being what they are. It is therefore no wonder if those spirits, whose number is incomprehensible to us, can be distinguished by such great and such mighty knowledge: by that knowledge through which all things, when they were not, were created; and in which they now subsist, lest things made should return to nothing.

## Book Ten

## Title of Chapter XV. What are the figurative images of the angelic powers, and what follows—that is, the rest?

[Col. 1131]

## Text

[Col. 1131C]

Come then, let us speak of what remains, relaxing, if it seems good, our intellectual eye, which has been intent with angelic strength upon sublime contemplations, and descending to the divided and manifold breadth of the multiform variety of angelic specifications; yet again analytically reflecting these very things, as though incongruous, into the simplicity of heavenly minds.

But let this one thing be known beforehand to you: namely, how the sacred distinctions of formed images signify the same dispositions of heavenly essences—at one time as ordering, and again as ordered; as ordering the last, and as ordered first; and as having, as was said, first, middle, and last powers—without any disordered account being introduced, according to the manner of such unfoldings.

[Col. 1131D]

For if we were to say that certain ones are ordered by prior ones, and then that those same prior ones order them, and again that those who order the last are ordered by those very ones whom they order, the matter set forth would truly be mixed with much disorder and confusion. But if we say that the same beings both order and are ordered, not, however, that they order the same beings by whom they are ordered, or are ordered by the same beings whom they order; but that each is ordered by those prior to it and orders those that are last, then perhaps someone may not inconsequentially say that the forms made sacred in the divine utterances may at times fittingly and truly be applied to the first, middle, and last powers alike.

Thus, that they are reversibly extended upward, and firmly enfolded upon themselves as guardians of their own powers,

[Col. 1132C]

and that they are providently present, by a sociable procession, in the participation of power toward those who come to them—these things he will truly ascribe to all heavenly essences, although to some in a superordinate and universal way, as has often been said, and to others in a particular and subordinate way.

But we must begin reasonably, and inquire, in the first distinction of the forms, why theology is found to honor almost above all others the sacred depiction made of fire. For you will find it not only fashioning fiery wheels, but also fiery living creatures and men flashing like fire; placing heaps of fiery coals around the heavenly essences; and describing rivers blazing with fire with immeasurable sound (Ezek. 1; Dan. 7; 4 Kings 2). It also says that thrones are fiery; and it signifies by their very name that the highest seraphim burn from heaven; and it assigns to them the property and operation of fire; and, in every way above and below, it especially honors the fiery fashioning of forms.

Therefore I judge the fiery image to signify what is most God-like in heavenly minds. For the holy theologians themselves (Heb. 10) often describe the superessential and formless Essence in fire, as possessing many images of the divine property, if it is permitted to say so, insofar as images of it exist among visible things. For sensible fire, it must be said, comes clearly into all things and through all things, and yet is removed from all things; it is at once luminous and as though hidden; unknown in itself when no material is laid beneath it, in which it manifests its own operation; immeasurable and invisible; by itself powerful over all things and able to move to its own operation whatever is done in them; giving itself to all that approach it in whatever manner; renewing; a guardian of nature; illuminating with veiled splendors; incomprehensible; clear; discriminating; springing upward; bearing upward; keenly penetrating; lofty; not admitting the indignity of diminution; always in motion; moved by itself; moving another; comprehending;

[Col. 1133A]

incomprehensible; needing no other; secretly increasing from itself; manifesting its own magnitude in the materials it receives; active; powerful; invisibly present to all things at once; when neglected, not thought to be; yet it is consumed, and, as by a certain vindication, naturally and properly flashes forth suddenly; and again it is incomprehensibly intangible, undiminished in all the richest communications of itself.

Perhaps someone will find many other beautiful properties of fire, as images of divine operation in insensible things. Knowing this, the God-wise depict the heavenly essences in the form of fire, signifying their God-likeness and, so far as possible, their imitation of God.

They also describe them in human form because of their intellectual nature, their upward-looking powers of vision, the upright and shining character of the form, and the natural primacy and royalty of humanity, as well as the lesser degree of sense in comparison with the remaining powers of irrational animals. Humanity is powerful in all things by the strength of intellect, by the constancy of rational knowledge, and by the freedom and great power natural to the soul.

Moreover, I think that heavenly powers may be found signified through every part of our manifold bodily division. The visual powers signify the supremely clear regard toward divine lights; and again, a tender, fluid, unrefracted, swiftly moving, pure, and impassibly full reception of divine illuminations. The powers of smell signify a reception, insofar as possible, of the distribution of the sweet fragrance beyond intellect, a discerning knowledge of what is not so, and an utter rejection of it. The powers of hearing signify the receptive and knowing participation in divine inspiration. The powers of taste signify the fullness receptive of invisible foods, divine foods, and nourishing advances. The powers of touch signify the discerning knowledge of what is suitable or harmful. The eyelids and

[Col. 1133C]

eyebrows signify the guarding of divine visions and intelligence. Youth and mature age signify the ever-renewing power of life. The teeth signify the division of the nourishment that perfects; for every intellectual essence, by a provident power, divides and multiplies the uniform intelligence bestowed upon it by what is more divine, according to an analogy suited to the guidance of what is lower.

The shoulders, arms, and hands signify the productive, operative, and active power. The heart is the symbol of the life that is God-like, sowing in a God-like manner its own vital power into the things first conceived intellectually. The breast again signifies firmness and guardianship, protecting the life-giving distribution proceeding from the heart beneath it. The back signifies the simultaneous continuity of all fruitful powers. The feet signify the mobile, swift, and running motion that always proceeds toward divine things; and for this reason theology depicted the feet of holy intellects as winged (Ezek. 1). For what is winged signifies anagogic swiftness, the heavenly activity of the journey upward, and a removal from every low thing by upward movement.

Likewise, being naked and unshod (Gen. 18, 19) signifies freedom from bonds, lowliness, immeasurability, purity in relation to the things outside, and assimilation, as far as possible, to divine simplicity. But because the Wisdom that is both simple and exceedingly manifold again clothes the naked and gives them certain vessels to carry, come, let us unfold, so far as we can, the sacred garments and implements of heavenly minds.

[Col. 1134A]

A bright and fiery garment (Apoc. 1), I think, signifies what is God-like and luminous after the image of fire, because of the repose in heaven, where the light must be called wholly invisible, or intellectually illuminating, or intellectually illuminated. Priestly clothing signifies a leading toward divine and mystical contemplations and the whole vocation of life. Belts signify the guarding of their fruitful powers and the habit that gathers them into unity in themselves and easily carries them circularly about themselves, without fall, by similarity of nature.

Rods signify royal and princely authority, defining all things aright. Spears and axes signify the separating power of dissimilarities, and the sharp, effective, and active power of discerning. Geometrical and architectural instruments signify the foundational, constructive, and perfecting power, and whatever belongs to the providence that leads and turns back secondary things.

[Col. 1134B]

At times the instruments employed by holy angels are symbols for us of divine judgments: some declaring corrective discipline or punishing justice; others freedom from distress, the end of discipline, the restoration of earlier beneficence, or the addition of other goods, small or great, sensible or invisible (Ezek. 10; Judg. 6; 2 Macc. 5; Ezek. 31; Apoc. 3; Zech. 8). In general, the discerning mind would perhaps not hesitate fittingly to unite visible things with invisible realities.

That they too are called winds signifies their swiftness, their effect reaching almost everywhere without delay, and their movement carrying what is below upward from above, and what is below toward above: raising secondary things to a higher height and moving primary things toward a communicative and provident procession toward lesser things (Gen. 28; John 1).

Perhaps someone will say that the windy designation of aerial spirits signifies the God-likeness of heavenly beings; for this too bears an image and form of divine operation, as symbolic theology shows in many respects through its fourfold division: through its mobile, generative, swift, and powerful capacity of nature, and through the unknown and invisible hiding-place of moving principles and ends. “For you do not know,” he says, “whence it comes or whither it goes” (John 3;

[Col. 1134D]

Isa. 5).

Theology also clothes them in the appearance of a cloud, thereby signifying that the sacred intellects are supermundanely filled with hidden light, receiving magnificently its first manifestation and distributing it richly, luminously, and proportionately to secondary things. It signifies also that they possess a generative, life-giving, active, and perfecting power, according to the intellectual conception of rains: receiving in their bosom moist showers and calling them forth into living births.

Theology likewise gives heavenly essences the appearance of bronze, electrum, and many-colored stones (Isa. 35; Apoc. 1; Dan. 2). Electrum, as being both golden and silver-like, signifies incorruptible radiance, as in gold; abundant, undiminished, and undefiled radiance; and, as in silver, open, light-bearing, and heavenly brightness. In bronze, according to the explanations given, either a fiery or a golden quality is to be understood. The many-colored appearances of stones are to be understood as signifying: those like white stones, light-bearing brightness; those like red stones, golden brightness; and those like pale stones, youthfulness and newness. In each kind you will find an anagogic interpretation of the symbolic images.

But since I judge that these matters have been sufficiently stated by us according to our ability, we must proceed to the sacred exposition of the animal-shaped sacred formation of heavenly minds. The lion must be understood to signify the princely, robust, untamed, and hidden power of the ineffable divinity; and the likeness of intellectual traces, veiled and perhaps mystically clad in splendid apparel, restored into itself according to divine illumination.

[Col. 1135B]

The form of the ox signifies what is firm and new, renewing intellectual furrows for the reception of heavenly and generative rains, and what is guarding and exceedingly strong. The form of the eagle signifies what is royal, lofty-flying, swift, sharp for powerful nourishment, temperate, agile, well-contrived, and immediately, rightly, and unswervingly contemplative—through the healthy gaze of contemplative powers—toward the abundant and much-luminous ray of the divine sun, in longing.

The form of horses signifies obedience and willingness to accept the bridle. A white horse signifies what is truly luminous and, as it were, most akin to divine light; black horses, what is hidden; a red horse, what is fiery and active; and horses mixed of white and black, the power which unites extremes in perfection, connecting first things to second and second things to first, reversibly and providently.

But if we did not limit the measure of our discourse, and if we were to unite, part by part, the properties of the animals mentioned and all their bodily forms with the heavenly powers through dissimilar likenesses, this might perhaps not be unfitting. Their fury would correspond to intellectual strength, of which fury is the final image; their desire, again, to divine love. And, to speak summarily, by referring at once all the senses and manifold parts of irrational animals to the immaterial intelligences and uniform powers of heavenly essences.

[Col. 1135D]

For the wise, not only these things themselves suffice: the interpretation of one significant image is sufficient for a similar explanation of related images. It should also be considered that rivers, wheels, and chariots have been said to be joined to heavenly essences (Dan. 7; Ezek. 1, 10). Fiery rivers signify the divine processions, granting them a copious and unfailing influx and nourishing them with life-giving fruitfulness. Chariots signify the union of likenesses in fellowship (4 Kings 1; Ezek. 1). Winged wheels, moving without turning in the things before them, signify the power of their operation proceeding along a straight and just path, their intellectual revolution being supermundanely directed, all together, into the same path, straight and without deviation.

There is also another anagogic interpretation of the symbolic description of the intellectual wheels. For, as the theologian says, they were called “gel, gel, gel” (Ezek. 10). According to the Hebrew word, this signifies “revolutions” and “revelations.” The fiery and God-like wheels have revolutions in their ever-moving motion around the one Good itself; and revelations in the manifestation of secrets, the circular leading of subordinate things, and the perfecting descent of higher illuminations into those things that are subject.

[Col. 1136B]

There remains for us an explanation concerning the joy of the heavenly orders. They are not at all receptive of the passible pleasure that belongs to us. Yet they are said to rejoice together with God (Luke 16) at the finding of the lost, according to a God-like feast; at the God-like character of their providence and of the salvation of those returning to God; at incorruptible joy; and at that ineffable beneficence in whose participation even holy men have often been made sharers through the deifying descents from above of divine illuminations.

Thus much have I said concerning the sacred formations—deficient indeed in careful exposition of them, yet sufficient, I think, to prevent us from remaining basely among figurative imaginations. And if you ask why we have not subsequently mentioned all the angelic powers, operations, or images in the sacred utterances, we reply truthfully that, concerning those whose supermundane knowledge we do not know, we seek another guide to teach us concerning them (Job 12). Some things, however, we have omitted as equally powerful with those mentioned, providing for the measure of the discourse and honoring in silence the mystery that is above us.

## Exposition

[Col. 1136D]

The title of the fifteenth and final chapter is: “What are the figurative images of the angelic powers, and what follows—that is, the rest?” For up to this point he has treated the invisible properties of angels: namely, those gifts of powers, the invisible operations in them. He now begins, in due sequence, to treat visible forms, which sacred Scripture attributes to them with mystical meaning through the images and likenesses of bodily things.

“Come, then”—*fer, age, dic, eia*—is an exhortatory expression, whether addressed to himself or to Timothy, to whom he speaks: “Come, let us say what remains.” What remains? Namely, that we, “if it seems good,” may relax our intellectual eye, hitherto “intent upon sublime contemplations” by considering “angelic strength”; and, with the eye turned back, may descend “to the divided and manifold breadth of the multiform variety of angelic specifications.” That is, to the multiform variety, or the variety of many forms, which is found in angelic specifications or formations. In this variety, because there is a broad multitude or much breadth, division is found in place of simplicity and multiplicity in place of unity.

Thus let us say what remains, relaxing our eye from invisible things and descending to visible ones. “Again into these things,” namely descending and fixing our consideration upon them, yet again “reflecting” them—or reflecting the images themselves—“analytically,” that is, resolutively, “into the simplicity of heavenly minds,” as though they were “incongruous,” that is, unsuitable, in themselves.

[Col. 1137A]

And this is the sense: descending in contemplation from invisibles to visibles, and fixing our consideration upon those visible things, we again reflect those things into the simplicity of invisible realities, resolving and expounding them, or showing how that which is visible signifies that which cannot be seen. Otherwise the visible formation would be inconsequential and unsuitable if, in that simple nature, it were believed to exist in the truth of essence what is attributed to it in manifold signification according to the various species of bodily things.

Therefore, just as we descend by representing simple natures through visible things, so we ascend and, as it were, turn ourselves back resolutively to divine consideration when, by spiritually expounding those same forms, we declare them to be understood mystically. We descend when we adapt, by signification, the multiplicity of bodily formations to the simplicity of heavenly natures; we ascend when we resolve that same multiplicity of visible figures, by expounding it, into the understanding of simple truth.

It follows: “But let one thing,” etc. O Timothy, before we treat the visible formations of angels, let one thing be known beforehand to you, so that you may first know it. What is it? Namely, that you may know “how the sacred distinctions of formed images,” that is, how the sacred Scriptures, distinct in the images which they form concerning the angels themselves, “signify and represent the same dispositions,” that is, the orders, “of heavenly essences.”

[Col. 1137C]

At times they signify lower ones as “ordering,” and again the same ones as “ordered” by higher ones. In this they signify in some way that they are middle beings: they have lower beings whom they order, and higher beings by whom they are ordered. “And again, at times, they signify even the last dispositions as ordering and the first as ordered.” This seems surprising, since neither the lower have those whom they may order nor the higher those by whom they may be ordered.

Yet it is thereby understood that, although the highest have no angels above them by whom they are ordered, they nevertheless have God, by whom they are ordered and sanctified. And the lowest, although they have no angels beneath them whom they may order, nevertheless have human beings, who are ordered, disposed, and sanctified by them. Or perhaps, in the fact that the highest are presented as ordered and the lowest as ordering, it is signified that some differ from others among them: among the higher there are certain lower ones who are ordered in something by others established in the same order; and among the lower there are certain higher ones who order in something others placed in the same order.

This is what follows: the utterances signify the same dispositions as having first, middle, and last powers. As was said above, each disposition possesses, in its persons, and each person possesses, in its properties, first, middle, and last powers. Thus, he says, the distinctions of sacred formations represent first, middle, and last spirits within the same order, and first, middle, and last powers within the same person, “without any disordered account being introduced,” according to the manner of these unfoldings—that is, expositions.

[Col. 1138B]

For if it is understood in the way we have explained above, there is nothing unsuitable in this representation. And I rightly say that there is no unsuitability in this representation, in which the same beings are introduced as both ordering and ordered, because there is no confusion or transposition of correct disposition when they are introduced as ordered by some and ordering others.

But if they were said to order and be ordered with respect to the same persons, it would be unsuitable. This is what he says: “If indeed we were to say that certain”—supply, dispositions, for instance the middle—“are ordered by prior ones,” and then that these “prior ones order,” or are orderers of, “the same” middle dispositions; and again that through these middle ones they are “orderers” or orderresses of the last: if, he says, we were to say in reversed order that these prior orderers of the middle and last are ordered by those very beings whom they order, “the matter set forth would truly be mixed with much disorder and confusion,” because it would not be ordered for some to be ordered by those whom they order.

“But if we say that the same beings,” under different respects, “both order and are ordered, yet are not orderers of those by whom they are ordered, nor ordered by those whom they order; but each,” that is, each remaining distinct without confused reciprocity, “is ordered by prior ones and orders the last,” there is no unsuitability. Accordingly, perhaps “someone may not inconsequentially,” that is, not unsuitably, “say that sacredly made forms found in the utterances may at times fittingly and truly,” that is, suitably and truthfully, “be applied” to the same first, middle, and last powers.

[Col. 1138D]

It follows: “And thus upward,” etc. As if he said: Since someone can truly say that the same forms are suitably applied to the first, middle, and last powers, therefore the person who says this will not falsely unite—that is, will commonly attribute—to all heavenly essences: being extended upward through love of God, being established within themselves through self-guardianship, and proceeding below them through love of neighbor.

This is what he says: “being reversibly extended upward,” namely through love of God, “and firmly enfolded upon themselves,” that is, constrained and surrounded: constrained lest good flow out, surrounded lest evil flow in. Because they are enfolded upon themselves, they are “guardians of their own powers,” that is, they guard their own powers. Therefore, this being extended upward and enfolded within themselves, “and their being in the participation of power”—supply, ready—“providently,” that is, attentively or devoutly, “toward those who come to them by a sociable procession”: these three things someone will truly attribute commonly to all heavenly essences.

[Col. 1139A]

That is, they are extended upward through love of God; they are enfolded upon themselves through self-guardianship; and they are ready providently, attentively, and devoutly to share their power with those who come to them, proceeding through social love and offering themselves freely to social love. All these things may therefore be ascribed commonly to all, “although” they belong to some “superordinately and universally,” that is, excellently and fully, as “has often already been said,” and to others particularly and subordinately.

It follows: “But we must begin reasonably,” etc. As if he said: Since we must treat angelic formations, we must first begin reasonably—that is, rationally—and inquire, in the first distinction of the forms, why “theology is found to honor the sacred fiery description,” that is, the formation in which the appearance of fire is proposed as a sign, “almost above all other descriptions.” For one rarely finds any visible species—if indeed one finds one—having greater excellence for demonstrating invisible things.

“Therefore you will find it,” namely theology, “not only fashioning fiery wheels” for signifying the invisible beings themselves, “but also fiery living creatures and men flashing as fire.” You will also find theology “placing heaps of fiery coals around the heavenly essences” and describing “rivers blazing with fire with immeasurable sound.”

[Col. 1139C]

And not only this: theology also says that fiery thrones are in heaven; it says that the highest seraphim themselves are signified by their name as burning from heaven; and it assigns to the seraphim the property and operation of fire. And, briefly, in every way above and below, everywhere it especially honors the fiery fashioning of forms.

It follows: “Therefore, fiery,” etc. As if he said: Since theology so highly venerates fiery formation, “therefore” I judge the fiery image to signify what is most God-like in heavenly minds—that is, the power in them which is most God-like. And rightly so, because “the theologians themselves often describe in fire,” that is, in the appearance and figure of fire, even the “superessential and formless essence” of divinity, which is superessential by majesty and formless by incomprehensibility.

They describe it in fire “as possessing many images of divine property,” insofar as an image of divine property can exist among “visible” things. Yet I say this only “if it is permitted to say so,” namely that divine property, which is exceedingly incomprehensible and invisible, possesses any likeness.

It follows: “For fire,” etc. He now begins to describe the properties of fire, in which he displays its marvelous nature, quality, and power and demonstrates its excellent signification. “For sensible fire,” he says, “is.” “It must indeed be said thus,” namely that it is sensible. He adds this because perhaps some might think, since the nature of fire is perceived by sense only in underlying material, that fire is not a body at all.

[Col. 1140A]

He therefore says that fire is truly sensible and is a body, although much more excellent and subtle than all other bodily things, close to spiritual nature, and therefore displaying its effect in a manner much unlike all other things. “For fire clearly comes into all things and through all things, and yet is removed from all things.” It is near by presence and far by excellence. It is in all things because it makes itself visible through illumination; and it is far from all things because it does not make itself perceptible through a distinct perception of its substance.

This is what follows: it is at once “luminous and as though hidden.” It is luminous because it is perceived in underlying material; hidden because in its own essence it is not bodily seen. It is “unknown in itself when no material is laid beneath it,” because without underlying material, as was said, it cannot be perceived; and it is in that material that it manifests its own operation.

Hence it seems in a certain way more incorporeal, because it does not come to sense apart from underlying material. Thus fire seems in some way to stand midway between invisible and visible things: incorporeal insofar as it approaches the former, bodily insofar as it approaches the latter.

It is also immeasurable because it grows without limit and, so long as underlying material is sufficient, does not fail. It is invisible because in its pure substance, outside underlying material, it is not seen. It is also “by itself powerful over all things,” namely things, and powerful “over all things which occur in them,” namely in those things, “toward its own operation.”

[Col. 1140C]

For in fire there is the first bodily motion, which moves all other things and is itself moved by no other. Therefore, whatever happens in all things belongs not properly to the things in which it occurs but rather to fire itself, through which it occurs.

It follows: “Mobile, giving itself to all who approach in whatever manner.” Because it moves by its own motion, it diffuses itself into all things, moving each thing according as it approaches it more or less—that is, according as it is found more or less movable. It is also “renewing” of all things, because it renews things that are growing old, lest they wholly fail and pass into nothing. For we see each year how fire renews nature: things that had grown old in winter cold revive when warmed by spring heat. Therefore fire is “the guardianship” of “nature,” because it preserves nature lest it entirely cease to be, if it were always subject to decline and never restored.

It is also “illuminating,” because it illuminates all things “with veiled splendors.” Its splendors shine outward for illumination, but are veiled when, drawn back again, they hide themselves within the secret of their nature. Therefore it is “incomprehensible,” because, poured forth outwardly, it is perceived by sense, but, withdrawn inwardly, it is not comprehended. It is also “clear,” appearing manifestly, and “discriminating,” distinguishing diverse things. And it is “springing upward,” because it is fed below and moves upward: grasping lower things with its heat, but springing to higher things through its own lightness.

Therefore it follows: “Bearing upward,” because, lacking weight, it seeks the heights; “and keenly moving,” because by the motion of its own power it penetrates all things; “and lofty,” because it rises above all things: for whatever is bodily besides it is by nature beneath it. “Not liable to the outrage of diminution”: for, just as when it is poured out it is not increased, so, when it is received, it is not diminished; neither, in that in which it seems to receive increase, does it receive glory, nor, in that in which it is thought to be diminished, does it suffer insult; because what it is in itself, it is always wholly. It is also “ever-moving,” that is, possessing motion; and it is “self-moving,” because the motion it possesses is not from another; and in moving itself, it moves all other things that have motion. Therefore it is “moving another,” and is itself “comprehending” while “incomprehended.” For, changing all matter by its own power through use and consumption, it draws it into itself; and it is held by no body, since, when that which it burns has been consumed, it returns into itself.

It is therefore “not in need of another,” because by the matter placed beneath it, in which it burns, it is not so much sustained in being as confined to being there; and, if it seems to grow from that matter [Col. 1141D], it does not receive from it the substance of growth, although from it it takes the occasion of growing in it. For it does not become greater in itself, but rather in that matter. Hence he says that it is “secretly growing from itself”: for, visibly, it seems to grow from the material placed beneath it; but in truth it grows from itself—not so as to become greater in itself, but so as to be more extensively present in that matter. Accordingly, when it seems to grow in things placed beneath it, it receives its increase from itself, “merely manifesting its own magnitude to those materials” in which it is; that is, it grows in the matter which it receives—that is, grasps—so that it appears greater in it, yet is not greater in itself. For there [Col. 1142A] it does not acquire magnitude, but displays it, at times manifesting there what it always possesses in itself.

It is also “active” and “powerful,” because it acts and moves powerfully, destroying all obstacles; and it is “simultaneously and invisibly present to all.” In certain things it is visible only, but it is invisibly present to all. This appears from the fact that it is sometimes shaken out, by the impact and collision of bodies, even from a place where it did not appear to be. When “neglected” and unmoved, or remaining at rest, it is thought not to exist; but, when aroused and stirred by rubbing or friction, “as though by a certain vengeance it suddenly flashes forth,” leaping out and raging against those things which it has seized. Yet it does this “naturally and properly,” that is, from its own power and capacity. [Col. 1142B] “And again, incomprehensibly impalpable”: when it slips back, it remains beyond sensory apprehension; “not diminished” by extinction, just as it is not increased by kindling. It does all this “in all” things, “by its most abundant communications of itself”; for whatever it imparts from itself to things placed beneath it for some operation, it does not possess less in itself, but remains always full.

I have enumerated these properties of fire; and perhaps someone may discover “many other properties of fire,” namely, beautiful likenesses “of the divine operation,” so that, that is, it may be a likeness “in sensible images.” And therefore “the theosophers, knowing this,” that is, knowing such great excellence in fire, “conform,” or portray, “the heavenly essences from fire,” signifying thereby “their God-like character [Col. 1142C] and their capacity for imitation of God,” insofar as this can be present in them. Nor do they conform them from fire alone, “but also describe them in human form,” that is, in the form of a human being, on account of their intellectual or rational character—that is, their rationality—just as the human being alone among all visible things is found to be rational.

Likewise, they describe them in human form because of their “contemplative,” that is, contemplative powers, which they possess by holding themselves upward, just as the human being alone among all living creatures has an upright face directed toward things above; and they also describe them in human form because of the “straightness,” that is, uprightness, of the human figure, because the human stature is erect, not bent downward like that of other [Col. 1142D] animals; and because of the “splendid,” that is, clear and manifest, distinction of the human figure, because by this very uprightness it presents a more conspicuous and more graceful appearance; and because of the “princely and royal” character given to humankind “according to nature,” so that it may rule and have dominion over the other creatures; and because it is “least in sense in comparison with the other powers of irrational animals,” that is, because the human being is less vigorous in bodily sensation than other living creatures, which have received a greater power of sensation than he.

This is so because of the lesser power in sensation, and because of its being omnipotent in power—or because it is “powerful” in every power—“according to the greatness of understanding and the enduring continuity of rational knowledge,” [Col. 1143A] “and because of the freedom and supreme power” that are in it “according to the nature of the soul.” For this reason the angel is described in human form: because, insofar as the human being is less strong in sense, where he is surpassed by beasts, so much the more powerful is he in reason, intelligence, and the freedom of natural choice, wherein he is likened to angels.

“It is,” however, etc. As if he said: Not only for the reasons I have stated is human form suitably applied to angels by way of signification; rather, “it is,” that is, it is possible, “to find the heavenly powers through each part of our manifold bodily division.” For spiritual powers can be found, by mystical signification, in each part of the human body, because all visible things have some [Col. 1143B] signification in relation to invisible things. Thus those who rightly consider may infer invisible things from visible ones.

Hence it is possible to find this, by “saying,” that is, by those who say that “the very bright faculty of sight” given to humanity “for the divine luminaries”—such as the sun, moon, and stars—“signifies the contemplative powers,” that is, those present in rational beings. Likewise, they say that the faculty of outward sight signifies a certain “reception” of divine illuminations—“tender,” that is, readily perceptive; “clear,” that is, seeing distinctly; “not rebuffed,” that is, effectually apprehending; “keenly mobile,” because it is not rebuffed; “pure,” because it is clear; “impassibly full,” because it is tender. [Col. 1143C]

Thus they speak of bodily sight. “The sense of smell,” however, they say signifies the discriminative powers in bodily matters: that receptive faculty of the distribution, gift, or outpouring of spiritual grace which is “sweet-smelling beyond intellect.” Receptive, I say, insofar as it can be receptive; and discriminative by knowledge, and wholly rejecting, of things which are not so—that is, of things which do not smell sweetly. That is, they say that smell especially signifies that power or faculty of the soul which spiritually distinguishes between things that spiritually smell good and those which do not, desires what smells good, and rejects what smells bad.

“The powers of hearing,” they say, signify that which in the soul is “participatory [Col. 1143D] and gnostic,” that is, cognizant and receptive of divine inspiration. “The powers of taste,” etc.: he says the same thing, namely that the powers of taste signify “the fullness of invisible and divine foods,” by which heavenly essences are refreshed; and also the receptive capacity for nourishing advances—that is, that which receives for them nourishing increases. “The powers of touch,” they say, signify that which in the soul discerns by knowledge what is fitting or harmful.

They say that “the eyelids and eyebrows” signify the guardianship of the intelligence of divine visions; that youthful and mature age signify that which in the soul is the “vital power ever renewing” it. “The teeth,” [Col. 1144A] by which food is divided, ground, and conveyed into the body for nourishment, they say signify the “divisive power of the implanted nourishing perfection” within the rational spirit itself. For every intellectual essence, by provident power, divides and multiplies the uniform understanding given to it by a more divine essence, as though it were a whole food: grinding it down and adapting it “to the guiding proportion of the inferior,” that is, to the measure by which it can be conveyed into the participation of inferior knowledge. For unless it ground down what it receives in its greatness to a measure, it could by no means pass into the participation of inferior understanding.

“The shoulders, arms, and likewise the hands,” they say, signify the productive, operative, and active power. “The heart,” [Col. 1144B] they say, “is a symbol,” that is, a figure, “of God-like life,” sowing, scattering, or diffusing “its own vital power into those things which have been foreknown”; just as the heart, in motion, diffuses life into the other members. Therefore they say that the heart in God, or in the rational spirit, is that power from which vital grace is diffused into others whom God has foreseen as to receive it. For it is given only to those who have been foreseen as receiving it and predestined to life.

“The breast,” again, they say, signifies that which is hard, firm, and protective of that life-giving distribution proceeding “from the heart,” as from that which lies beneath the breast; for the heart is placed beneath the breast, so that it may be fortified and protected by it. “The back,” they say, signifies the continuity [Col. 1144C] of all fruitful powers; for, as vertebra is joined to vertebra in the back, so one virtue adheres to another among the virtues.

“The feet,” they say, signify the mobile, swift, and running character of motion always proceeding toward divine things. “For this reason,” because they have swift motion, “theology has portrayed the feet of holy intellects as winged.” And rightly so, because “the winged signifies anagogic,” that is, upward-leading, “swiftness”; it also signifies heavenly activity, that is, heavenly action, impulse, or the advancement of a journey upward; and it signifies separation from every low thing—that is, from humility, abasement, or depression. [Col. 1144D] This separation is in them through that which bears upward, because, insofar as they are borne upward, they are removed from all things that are below.

The very lightness of the wings signifies that there is nothing earthly or weighty in them, “but everything rises to the height purely and without heaviness.” Their being “naked and barefoot” likewise signifies their detachment, freedom, immeasurability, and purity from every addition of things that are outside. That is, the fact that angels are described as naked and barefoot signifies that they are detached, free, and pure from every addition or conjunction of external things, namely visible things, and are thereby immeasurable. For the less they are confined by bodily mixture or addition, [Col. 1145A] the more immeasurably they are expanded through the purity of understanding. “Naked and barefoot” also signifies their likeness, insofar as possible, to the divine simplicity: pure from bodily admixture, they do not subsist from a double substance. This statement refutes those who say that angels have bodies. For the author testifies that they are pure from every addition of external things and, through their naked and pure essence in which they subsist, imitate divine simplicity.

It follows: “But since again,” etc. As if he said: I have said that holy Scripture, in describing angels as naked, signifies their purity and simplicity. But since that same wisdom, simple through truth and greatly varied [Col. 1145B] through the diversity of its forms, “since,” I say, such wisdom “again both clothes the naked and gives them certain vessels,” that is, instruments, “to carry about—come, let us unfold,” insofar as we can, “the sacred garments and instruments of the heavenly minds.” For, as has been said, they are described as clothed, and certain vessels or instruments are assigned to them to carry in that mystical description. And rightly do I say, Let us unfold what these signify, because all are significant.

First, I think that the “bright and fiery garment” assigned to them signifies the God-like quality in them “according to the image of fire,” which likeness is an image of God-likeness. And I think that the “splendid,” that is, the bright, is attributed to them because of the repose [Col. 1145C] “in heaven, where there is light”—not just any light, but light “wholly invisible.” (For this is how it must be said: the light which is there is altogether invisible.) Or it is intellectually illuminating, as in God, or intellectually illuminated, as in angels.

The “priestly garment,” I think, signifies guidance, leadership, or direction toward divine and mystical contemplations, and signifies “the vow of the whole life.” For the priestly garment signifies that they are guides toward divine and mystical contemplations—that is, divine and mystical visions—teaching those subject to them toward knowledge, and exhorting them to dedicate their lives to God and confirming their devotion to good works.

“The girdles,” they say, signify the guarding of the fruitful virtues; [Col. 1145D] and they signify the habit which gathers these virtues together, causing them to turn unitedly into themselves and to be carried circularly around themselves, with a capacity free from falling away from likeness of nature. The sense is this: the girdle, which surrounds and constricts the loins and navel, where the generative power of propagation lies, signifies the custody of fruitful virtues. This custody surrounds, guards, and constricts the virtues lest, in their multiplication, they loosen or overflow beyond the bounds of justice.

The girdle also signifies, in that by encircling the body it turns back into and is united with itself in a circle, the habit of virtues gathering the virtues into one, lest they overflow or depart from the unity of concord. [Col. 1146A] That habit, I say, bends itself circularly about itself through the coherence of all things and through the mutual consideration of the virtues themselves. It bends about itself with ease, because, through likeness and concord, progress from virtue to virtue is easy; and this ease is free from falling away from the likeness of nature. For the progress of virtues is not a corruption but a restoration of nature.

“They say that rods,” or sceptres, signify “the royal and princely, and that which determines all things rightly”; for the rod is straight and is a royal implement. “Weapons and axes,” by which whole things are usually cut, divided, or cleft, they say signify the power which separates dissimilarities, that is, the faculty which separates dissimilarities and discerns between good and evil; [Col. 1146B] and they signify the sharpness of the discerning powers, that is, subtlety in examining, and efficacy and activity in carrying things through to completion. “Geometrical and architectural vessels,” that is, instruments for measuring and building, signify “the founding, building, perfecting power, and whatever other works belong to the providence which leads back and converts secondary things.” For the providence of the first and higher beings, which converts and leads back the second and lower beings toward the better, founds, builds, and perfects a spiritual edifice in them. The signs of this work are geometrical and architectural instruments, formed in the vision according to bodily appearance.

It follows: “It is,” etc. As if he said: The things attributed to angels according to visible forms [Col. 1146C] are not only signs of their invisible power, but at times also signify what takes place in us and around us. This is what he says: “It is,” that is, it happens, that “those instruments,” that is, implements, “which are displayed,” that is, presented or present, “by the holy angels, are symbols,” that is, signs and manifestations, “of divine judgments” exercised upon us or concerning us. Some instruments signify corrective discipline, namely God’s, such as the rod which appears to strike; others signify punitive justice, such as axes and swords. Other instruments signify freedom, or release from distress; the end of discipline—that is, [Col. 1146D] correction and punishment; the restoration of former beneficence; or the addition of further gifts after those previously given, whether small or great, sensible, as in bodily goods, or invisible, as in spiritual goods.

And, to speak universally, perhaps the discerning mind would not hesitate entirely—that is, in every respect—to fittingly unite, that is, to adapt by signification, visible things to invisible, leaving nothing among all visible things that could not be shown to have some signification in relation to invisible things. And rightly so: for even the fact that angels “are called winds” signifies their [Col. 1147A] swiftness and the effect of their action, reaching nearly all things without delay. It also signifies their transit-like movement “from above to things below, and” again from things below “to things above.”

He next adds what that movement bears from one direction to the other. I mean the movement “raising secondary things,” that is, lower things, to higher eminence, and “moving first things,” that is, higher things, “toward a communicative and provident procession to lesser things,” so that they may proceed to the lesser—that is, lower—beings, providing for them and communicating their power to them.

It follows: “But perhaps someone will say,” etc. He had said above that angels are called winds because of their swiftness. He now adds that perhaps [Col. 1147B] someone may say that they are called winds because of their divine likeness, because wind too possesses, in some respect, a form and image of divine operation. He says that he has demonstrated this by many examples or arguments elsewhere in his theology concerning the fourfold discernment—that is, concerning the signification of the four elements—a work which we do not possess.

“He says, perhaps someone,” that is, some person, “will say that the windy designation of the aerial spirits signifies” not only swiftness but also the God-like character—that is, the God-likeness—of heavenly spirits. “For this [element] too has within itself an image and form of divine operation,” as is shown by many examples in “symbolic theology,” that is, theology demonstrated through symbols—that is, through visible figures and likenesses—“by the fourfold discernment,” where, through each of the four elements, it is shown how visible things are both likenesses and signs of invisible things.

According to that discernment, then, it has been demonstrated how this element, namely wind, possesses an image and form of divine operation. He next adds in what respect it possesses this image and form: “according to the motive, generative, swift, and powerful capacity of its nature,” because moving air imparts motion and growth to things, and, running swiftly, powerfully or violently drives from without; “and according to the hidden [Col. 1147D] and invisible recess of moving principles and consummations.” For the movement of wind comes outwardly to the senses, but sense does not grasp the beginning or end of its motion. Hence it is written: “He brings forth winds from his treasuries” (Ps. 134 [Vulgate numbering]). To bring winds forth from treasuries is to bring the breathings of winds out, from hidden and concealed causes, to sensory perception through manifest agitation.

According to this likeness, the Creator Spirit also, secretly presiding over all things and remaining invisible, moves and advances all things by his power. The things moved are seen, but he who moves is not seen; powerful in acting and swift in accomplishing. His works are indeed perceived outwardly, but the hidden and invisible recess of the first causes and principles moving those works to their effect [Col. 1148A] is not penetrated. Likewise, the hidden recess of their consummations is not penetrated: for when something is moved toward its effect, we see what comes to be, but do not see why it comes to be in this way or toward what end it comes to be.

This is what is signified in the vision of the seraphim, who cover the head and feet of the One seated on the throne: we see the middle operations of divine activity, which take place in time; but we cannot investigate the first things which were before time and the final things which will be after time, because the recess of the moving principles and consummations is invisible and unknown to us. Likewise, when the Spirit comes to the heart, it is indeed sensed in the fact that it is perceived. But “whence it comes or whither it goes” is not investigated. Whence it comes is its beginning; whither it goes is its consummation and end. Therefore [Col. 1148B] he says: “But you do not know whence it comes or whither it goes,” because the recess alike of its beginning and its end is unknown and invisible.

Therefore you do not know whence it comes, because you do not discover in yourself the merit for which you might say that grace has been given to you. You do not know whither it goes, because you do not understand to whom you may come in faith from the gift received. According to these considerations, then, every wind possesses an image and form of divine operation.

It follows: “But also [the form] of a cloud,” etc. Not only, he says, does theology call angels winds, “but it also surrounds, or adapts to them, the form of a cloud,” calling them clouds and thereby signifying that the holy intellects are supermundanely—that is, spiritually—filled full of hidden light, that is, invisible charity. I mean those [Col. 1148C] “receiving magnificently,” that is, excellently, the first manifestation of that light at its first appearing, because it is first shown to them and is excellently received by them. Thus they “receive its first manifestation magnificently” and gloriously; and they also distribute that manifestation to the things which are second after them, distributing it brightly, that is, clearly, and proportionately, that is, according to the measure of each. So too clouds first receive the light of the sun and then diffuse into things beneath the light which shines from them.

Thus angels are also called clouds because “in them there subsists the universal, life-giving, active, and perfecting power, according to the intellectual conception [Col. 1148D] of spiritual rains.” Just as clouds, by pouring out rains that make the earth fruitful, give things growing from it the power of generation, life, growth, and perfection, so they are called clouds because of such a conception of rains—namely one that calls forth, provokes, or draws into vital births the receiving bosom, that is, the earth, which receives the rains in its bosom. It calls forth, I say, by “moist rains,” that is, through moist showers. For by rains it provokes the earth, nourishing it so that it may produce vital offspring.

It follows: “It also,” etc. As though he were saying: Theology itself describes the angels not only under the figure of a cloud, “but also assigns to the heavenly essences the appearance of air, of electrum, and of many-coloured stones” by signification [Col. 1149A]. And rightly so. For “electrum,” being “at once gold-like and silver-like, signifies,” inasmuch as it possesses in gold, “an incorruptible splendour, at once abundant, undiminished, and undefiled”; just as gold is never tarnished by verdigris, but has a pure and enduring brilliance. “And,” inasmuch as it possesses in silver, it signifies “a clear, luminous, heavenly radiance,” just as silver is bright and shining. Thus electrum, in each of its aspects—gold and silver—signifies what is gleaming and resplendent, that is, bright and fiery: for the heavenly wisdom shining in those spirits is bright through knowledge and fiery through love. This, then, is signified in the higher spirits by the appearance of electrum.

But to them “in air” must be attributed [Col. 1149B] either something fiery or something gold-like, according to the explanations already given—namely, in the exposition of electrum, where a similar appearance is found in some respect. “The many-coloured appearances of stones, however, must be understood to signify either something luminous, as white ones do; or something gold-like, as red ones do; or something youthful and new, as pale ones do.” And, briefly, “in each particular appearance you will find an anagogical—that is, spiritual—interpretation of the typical,” that is, figurative, images.

“But since I think that these matters have been sufficiently stated by us according to our capacity, we must now pass on” to “the holy unfolding,” that is, exposition, “of the sacredly figured animal forms of the heavenly minds” [Col. 1149C], so that we may explain the animal forms sacredly assigned to the heavenly minds in order to signify them.

For the lion must be understood to signify what is princely, strong, and untamed, which subsists spiritually in them; and also “the assimilative character of intellectual tracks” proceeding “toward the hiddenness,” that is, the secret, “of the ineffable divinity.” These tracks, insofar as spiritual power is able, imitate the tracks of a lion. For just as a lion effaces its tracks with its tail and in a sense levels and restores what it had imprinted with its foot, so that its path may remain hidden, so the invisible progress of heavenly spirits is in some fashion formed, “with its way restored into itself,” that is, brought back [Col. 1149D] to its former condition and made level again, when the traces of its tracks have been effaced “by a surrounding veil”; or, perhaps more mystically stated, it is restored in its course by a splendid garment—that is, a distinguished, excellent, bright, and glorious apparel—which comes to them “according to divine illumination.”

For as they proceed inwardly to contemplate the light of the secret divinity, their tracks are effaced by the supervening splendour; because everything that formerly adhered through knowledge is wiped from memory when the desired brightness is manifested to desiring minds. Hence Paul says: “One thing: forgetting those things which are behind, I stretch myself out toward those which are before.” To proceed, therefore, as though one’s tracks had been effaced is for the mind, all thought of images being removed, to advance toward the contemplation of the unbounded light [Col. 1150A]. There indeed the intellect, surrounded by the splendour of supervening brightness and covered as it were by a garment, cannot itself see anything within itself except that light. All these things, then, must be understood as signifying the form of the lion.

“The form of the ox” must be understood to signify firmness and newness, and a recalling—or renewing—and restoring of the intellectual furrows for receiving the heavenly and generative rains; and it also signifies “what is guarding and exceedingly strong.” Since the ox plants its foot firmly, it signifies the firmness and stability of immutability. In that it furrows the earth and renews it for the reception of heavenly rains, by which it is made fruitful for generation, it signifies the inward newness by which the mind is tempered and fitted to receive heavenly grace; fertilized by this grace, it brings forth the shoots of virtues. Thus, in that the ox excels in the strength of its neck and guards while bearing the yoke, is signified the guarding of the mind by which it perseveres without failure, in every act, in watchfulness over itself.

“The form of the eagle” must be understood to signify what is royal, because it surpasses other birds; “high-soaring,” because by flight it carries itself aloft; swift-flying, because it flies quickly; and, in regard to its powerful sustenance, “keen and temperate,” because, flying on high, it sharply surveys its food, moderately desires it, and powerfully seizes it [Col. 1150C]. The eagle’s form also signifies agility, because it is ready in moving itself; it signifies what is well-contrived, because in its movement it adapts itself fittingly; and it signifies contemplation “of the abundant and intensely shining ray of the divine sun”—that is, “intensely shining” is one expression.

I say “contemplation” through the desire “of inwardly contemplative virtues,” that is, virtues contemplating within or inward things; and I mean contemplation “with sound, immediate, direct, and unbending gazes,” just as the eagle beholds the sun’s ray with eyes not repelled by it. All these things, therefore, must be understood as signifying the form of the eagle in contemplative spirits.

“The form of horses” must be understood to signify obedience and submission to the bridle. The white form signifies what is “truly luminous and, as it were, most akin to the divine light.” The form of those horses “which are black” signifies the hiddenness, that is, the concealed incomprehensibility, of the divine, just as black colour is dark and repels sight [Col. 1150D]. The red colour signifies what is fiery and active, because it suggests the fervour of good will exercised in action. The form of horses “mingled from white and black” signifies “the joining of extremes by perfecting power”: this power joins through charity [Col. 1151A] “first things to second things, and second things to first things, reciprocally,” and thereby connects them, so that they may be joined to one another by mutual love and providence.

This, then, can be understood in the forms mentioned above. And perhaps, “if we were not limiting the measure of our discourse”—that is, if we did not intend to bring the discourse to an end at this point and not proceed further by expounding each individual matter—and if we did not limit all the properties and all the bodily configurations of the animals mentioned above “through the parts” already described—that is, if we did not mean, by what we have already said in part about them, to signify under one likeness everything that may universally be said concerning them, whether in their inward properties or outward configurations—if this were not so, I say, because we do not wish to proceed through every point, “we might perhaps not unsuitably have joined to the heavenly powers,” even rage, “according to dissimilar likenesses.” As was said above, some dissimilarities are like, and others unlike.

Accordingly, in this manner we might fittingly have assigned “rage” to the heavenly powers in order to signify their intellectual strength [Col. 1151B], “of which rage is the most remote image,” because it signifies by opposition and from afar. Likewise, we might fittingly have assigned the concupiscence of irrational creatures to signify divine love. “And, to speak universally,” as must be said summarily, we might fittingly have assigned at once “all the senses and all the manifold parts of irrational animals” to those spiritual beings through signification—senses and parts, I say, leading us by their signification “back to the immaterial,” that is, spiritual, “intelligences and the uniform powers of the essence of heavenly beings.” For by those things which are described corporeally and materially in the senses and members of irrational animals, we are stirred up to the immaterial—that is, spiritual—understanding of those powers which exist uniformly and purely in the essence of spiritual beings.

Many other things could be said; “but not only these things themselves which have been said are sufficient for the wise, but also the interpretation of one significant image” is sufficient for explaining related, that is, similar, images “in a similar way.” Therefore [Col. 1151D] “we must also consider this”: that the angels themselves have been called rivers, wheels, and connected chariots—that is, these are assigned by signification to the heavenly essences; or rather, we must consider that in the heavenly essences rivers, wheels, and connected chariots—that is, mutually coupled and joined—have been so named.

For “fiery rivers signify divine outpourings,” that is, the advances or effusions of divine grace, “bestowing” upon the heavenly essences “an abundant,” that is, “unfailing, influx,” and nourishing them with life-giving fruitfulness. Chariots, in which many things joined together are borne onward at once, signify “the uniting fellowship of likenesses” found in them, through which they move harmoniously and with one consent toward all things [Col. 1152A]. “Wheels,” being winged—that is, agile—and proceeding without turning back, that is, without retreat, and unbendingly, that is, without deviation, “toward the things before them,” that is, what lies ahead, signify “the power of operation” of those essences: an operation proceeding “by a straight and just way,” through the intellectual revolution of all those essences together, directed supermundanely—that is, spiritually—along that same straight way, so that they may advance together and harmoniously on the intended course, without bending—that is, without deviation—and directly, that is, without retreat. This, then, is what the wheels signify.
