And not only this: it is also possible, or appropriate, “by another anagogy,” that is, spiritual interpretation, “to interpret the figurative description of the intellectual wheels.” For they, namely the angels, “were called,” as the theologian—that is, the prophet—says: “Gel, gel, gel.” Ezekiel says that, when the wheels appeared and ran, an angel called them rolling things in his hearing. Thus *gel* was called out and cried, whether to them or by them. “This,” namely *gel*, “according to the Hebrew word, signifies revolutions and revelations” [Col. 1152B].

He adds the reason for each interpretation: “For fiery and God-formed wheels have revolutions around the selfsame Good, with ever-moving motion.” Just as a circle turns back into itself because it is always moving around one and the same thing, namely its centre, so spiritual wheels turn back into themselves as it were while, through contemplation, they continually move around that selfsame Good—that is, God—as around their centre. Thus they move in an ever-moving motion, because their desire is unquenchable and that which they desire is incomprehensible. For all these reasons spiritual wheels have revolutions.

They have “revelations,” however, in the manifestation “of mysteries and in the circling return of those subject to them,” because they descend to those below in order to illuminate them, but return again in order to lead them upward through contemplation. Thus they have revelations in “the conducting down of the perfection of lofty illuminations to those beneath”; for the illuminations [Col. 1152D] which they receive from above they convey downward for the perfection of those below, and through these they again lead those same subjects up to higher things.

It follows: “There remains for us,” etc. After explaining the material figures and descriptions, he turns again to inward realities, intending finally to contemplate the joys of the angels. And fittingly the discourse concerning heavenly things ends in joy, because joy is the end of all heavenly things. “There remains for us a discourse for the explanation of the joy of heavenly orders,” because this alone now remains: to offer some discourse, for explanatory purposes, concerning the joy of heavenly beings.

And he rightly said that a discourse remains, not simply concerning joy, but concerning the joy of heavenly beings [Col. 1153A], because heavenly orders “are not at all recipients of that passible delight which belongs to us,” but are said “to rejoice with God” in the finding of the lost, as when, on the return of the lost sheep and the finding of the drachma, they are invited to rejoice. They rejoice according to that God-like exultation which is represented and perfected in the fatted calf when the prodigal son returns.

Or the passage may be read thus: They are said to rejoice with God at the finding of the lost, not because they are affected by any temporal and suddenly arising passible gladness, but “according to the God-like feast,” that is, the delight and pleasantness which they enjoy impassibly, imitating God’s eternal joy. And [Col. 1153B] they are said to rejoice with God in a God-like manner “in the providence and salvation of those returning to God,” because, in likeness to God, they provide for the salvation of those who return to God.

They are also said to rejoice with God according to “the joy of incorruption,” that is, an incorrupt joy, or one wholly and perfectly sweet, into which no bitterness is mingled; and according to that “ineffable beneficence” of divine grace by which it refreshes holy hearts with an outpoured inward sweetness. They have been made participants in this sweetness or beneficence; and so also have holy men, through the deifying arrivals of divine illuminations coming down from above.

“So much has been said by me,” etc. He forms a conclusion in which he brings the narrative to an end by a brief recapitulation. “So much,” he says, “has been said by me concerning the holy forms”: said, I mean, in a manner deficient for their diligent manifestation—that is, deficient in relation to a careful and perfect explanation of the forms themselves. For he confesses that what has been said by him is less than sufficient for a diligent and complete manifestation of the holy forms. Yet, though they are not perfect for that purpose, they are nevertheless, “as I think,” perfect for another purpose: namely, that we may not remain humbly [Col. 1154A] in figurative imaginings—that is, so that we may learn at least not to remain “humbly,” that is, basely, in figurative imaginings, believing that there is nothing other than what we find written according to the outward forms of visible things. Rather, instructed by figurative things, we should rise to the knowledge of what is true.

“But if you should also say,” whether you are some other person or Timothy, “how have we not made remembrance,” or mention, “of all the angelic powers,” operations, and images which are found “in the Scriptures?” Then, after what we have said, “we answer what is true”: namely, that concerning those powers, operations, or images “whose supermundane,” that is, exceedingly lofty, “knowledge we have not known, we desire another guide of light to teach us,” that is, to teach us and lead us into the light of knowledge [Col. 1154B].

“But we have passed over certain things as equal in power to those which have been said,” that is, equal to and not greater than them. Yet we did so “providing for the measure of our discourse,” that is, taking care lest our discourse exceed its proper bounds and say too much, if we were to say even all that we could say. Likewise, we honoured with silence “the mystery that is above us.” Silence honours mystery, because greater reverence is sometimes rendered to that which is left unspoken. And some things which could be said must sometimes be concealed, so that there may always remain something inward to seek, and lest it become cheapened if everything is expounded [Col. 1154C].

These things, indeed, I have ventured to offer on the hierarchy of blessed Dionysius, according to the possibility of my understanding. But I fear that, by adding my own material to his, I may be convicted of having plastered a marble wall with mud. Therefore let presumption turn into devotion and implore. Yet it gives me comfort that, in him whom he undertook to expound, wisdom transcends while holiness condescends.

B
